name: .sav file structure and metadata
origin: SPSS Inc. system file format; open readers such as ReadStat (Evan Miller) and pyreadstat
summary: Understanding and using the metadata stored in SPSS .sav files, such as variable labels, value labels, missing-value codes and measurement levels, so survey data move between tools without losing meaning.
description: A .sav file holds more than a data matrix: it stores variable names, variable labels (the question text), value labels (e.g. 1 = 'Strongly disagree'), user-defined missing values (e.g. 98 = 'Don't know', 99 = 'Refused'), measurement levels, formats and weights. Survey platforms export to .sav precisely because this metadata functions as a codebook. Losing it, for example by exporting to CSV, causes classic errors: 'Don't know' codes averaged as scale points, reversed value orders, and unlabelled variables. Rigour comes from inspecting the dictionary before analysis, using tools such as pyreadstat that read metadata into Python, converting user-missing codes explicitly, and producing a codebook from the file itself.
steps: Import the .sav with metadata (in SPSS, DISPLAY DICTIONARY; in Python, pyreadstat.read_sav returning data and meta).
Review variable labels, value labels and declared missing codes for every analysis variable.
Convert user-defined missing codes (e.g. 98, 99, -1) to system missing before computing statistics.
Verify value label direction for each scale, especially items that will be reverse-coded.
Generate a codebook from the metadata and store it with the project.
When writing back to .sav, preserve or add labels so the processed file is self-documenting.
outputs: A verified data dictionary, a generated codebook and analysis-ready data with missing codes handled.
useWhen: Any project receiving survey data from Qualtrics, Alchemer, panel providers or partners as .sav, or moving data between SPSS and Python or R.
avoidWhen: Not relevant for purely qualitative or log data; for CSV-only sources, build a separate codebook.
whyLost: Metadata handling is taught in social science data management, but UX teams often export CSV and lose labels without noticing.
whereToUse: Survey-heavy UX programmes, market research handovers and longitudinal tracking.
example: A SaaS team's satisfaction average looks implausibly high. Inspecting the .sav metadata shows 'Not applicable' was coded 9 on a 1-7 scale; once declared missing, the mean falls from 5.9 to 5.2.
sources: SPSS Syntax Editor
Python integration (SPSS Python plugin)
pyreadstat for Python ↔ SPSS bridge
Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
Miller, E. ReadStat library documentation
The Inquiry Series, C6 — SPSS for UX Researchers — The Right Way
reference: IBM SPSS Statistics Command Syntax Reference

name: 5-Second Test
origin: Christine Perfetti, User Interface Engineering, around 2005
summary: Participants see a design for five seconds and then recall what they noticed, measuring first impressions, visual hierarchy and clarity of the value proposition.
description: The five-second test shows a participant a screen, often a landing page or key view, for about five seconds, then hides it and asks what they remember, what the page was about, who it was for or what they could do there. The short exposure approximates the first glance many users give before deciding whether to stay. It assesses whether the core message, primary call to action and visual hierarchy communicate immediately. Rigour comes from a single clear question focus per test, consistent exposure times, recruiting people unfamiliar with the design, enough participants (around 20 to 50) to quantify recall, coding open-ended answers against intended messages, and comparing variants rather than interpreting one result in isolation.
steps: Define what the design should communicate at a glance, such as purpose, audience and main action.
Prepare a static screenshot at the size it will be seen.
Write 3 to 5 recall questions, starting with an open question about what the page was about.
Show the design for 5 seconds to each participant who has not seen it before.
Collect responses from 20 to 50 participants, usually remotely.
Code answers against the intended messages and compute the proportion who recalled each.
Compare variants and iterate on hierarchy or copy.
outputs: Recall rates for key messages, coded first impressions, and comparisons of variants on clarity.
useWhen: For landing pages, home screens, onboarding screens and ads where the first impression and value proposition must land immediately.
avoidWhen: Avoid for assessing task flows or interaction; use usability testing. Not suited to dense screens meant for study, such as dashboards.
whyLost: Still in use: Quick first-impression test; useful remotely; low friction for participants.
whereToUse: Landing pages; onboarding screens; any design where first impression is critical.
example: An AI writing tool tests two landing pages with 40 participants each. Only 30 percent recall the product's purpose from version A versus 70 percent from version B, which leads with a concrete example.
sources: Usability Engineering
reference: Perfetti, C. (2005). 5-second tests: Measuring your site's content pages. User Interface Engineering.

name: A/B Test Design Beyond Conversion Rates
origin: Kohavi et al. on overall evaluation criteria and guardrails (2007 onwards); King, Churchill and Tan (2017)
summary: Designs online experiments around a pre-specified hierarchy of primary, secondary and guardrail metrics, with power analysis, so decisions reflect user experience and long-term value, not conversion alone.
description: Many A/B tests optimise a single short-term conversion metric, which can reward dark patterns and miss harm to retention, trust or support load. Rigorous experiment design pre-registers a metric hierarchy: a primary decision metric (or overall evaluation criterion) that predicts long-term value, secondary metrics that explain the mechanism, and guardrail metrics that must not degrade, such as latency, error rates, unsubscribes, complaints or retention. A power analysis sets sample size and duration for the primary metric's minimum detectable effect, and the analysis plan specifies decision rules before data arrive. King, Churchill and Tan add the UX perspective: grounding hypotheses in qualitative insight and treating experiments as part of a learning agenda. Holdout groups and longer-term follow-ups detect novelty effects and delayed harm.
steps: Before any A/B test:
Primary metric — what single metric determines ship/no-ship?
(2) Secondary metrics — what additional signals support the decision?
(3) Guardrails — what metrics must not worsen (latency, error rate, NPS)?
(4) Power calculation for primary metric. Run the test. Report: did primary metric move? Did guardrails hold? Did secondary metrics tell a consistent story?
outputs: Pre-registered experiment plan with metric hierarchy, power calculation, guardrail results, decision record and a learning log linked to hypotheses.
useWhen: Any product experiment, especially changes that could trade short-term conversion against retention, trust or wellbeing (pricing, notifications, onboarding nudges).
avoidWhen: When traffic is too low to power the primary metric (use qualitative testing or Bayesian or sequential designs), or when randomisation is impossible (use quasi-experimental methods).
whyLost: Experimentation platforms made it trivial to launch tests on a single conversion metric, and teams under growth pressure skipped pre-registration and guardrails.
whereToUse: All A/B testing. Particularly important for any test where short-term conversion and long-term retention may trade off (dark pattern detection).
example: A subscription news app tests a more aggressive paywall prompt. Conversion rises 9%, but the pre-registered guardrail of 28-day reader retention drops 4%, so the variant is rejected and a softer metered version is tested next.
sources: Designing with Data — O'Reilly
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang & Ya Xu)
reference: King R, Churchill EF & Tan C (2017) Designing with Data: Improving the User Experience with A/B Testing. O'Reilly Media

name: A/B Testing
origin: R. A. Fisher's experimental design, 1920s to 1930s; online controlled experiments popularised by Kohavi and colleagues, 2000s
summary: Randomly assigns users to design variants and compares behavioural outcomes, giving causal evidence of a change's effect at scale.
description: A/B testing is a randomised controlled experiment in a live product. Users are randomly assigned to a control and one or more variants, and a predefined outcome metric, such as conversion, retention or task completion, is compared between groups. Randomisation balances known and unknown confounders, so differences can be attributed to the change. Rigour comes from a pre-registered primary metric and minimum detectable effect, a sample size calculated from power analysis, a fixed duration covering full weekly cycles, checks for sample ratio mismatch, guardrail metrics to catch harm, and avoiding repeated peeking without sequential correction. A/B tests show what changed behaviour, not why, so they pair well with qualitative research.
steps: Write a hypothesis and choose one primary metric, plus guardrail metrics.
Set the minimum detectable effect and compute the required sample size with a power analysis (typically 80 percent power, alpha 0.05).
Implement random assignment at the appropriate unit (user, account or session) and validate with an A/A test if new to the platform.
Run for the precomputed duration, at least one full weekly cycle, without stopping early unless using sequential methods.
Check sample ratio mismatch and data quality before analysis.
Analyse the primary metric with confidence intervals and review guardrails and pre-planned segments.
Decide, document and share results, including null results.
outputs: Effect estimates with confidence intervals for primary and guardrail metrics, and a documented ship or no-ship decision.
useWhen: When you have enough traffic to detect meaningful effects and need causal evidence about whether a design change improves behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid with low traffic, when outcomes take months to observe, for exploring why users behave as they do, or for ethically sensitive manipulations; use usability testing, interviews or quasi-experiments.
whyLost: Still in use: Gold standard for validating design changes at scale; widely supported by product analytics tools.
whereToUse: High-traffic digital products where behavioral metrics are trackable; conversion optimization.
example: A food-delivery app tests showing total delivery fees earlier in checkout. With 400,000 users per arm, conversion falls 0.3 percent but refund requests fall 12 percent, and the team ships the change on net value.
sources: Designing with Data
Quantifying the User Experience
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi, Tang & Xu)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. & Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press.

name: Abductive Reasoning in Research Synthesis
origin: Charles Sanders Peirce, 1870s-1900s; abductive analysis by Timmermans and Tavory, 2012
summary: Makes the leap from surprising observations to the most plausible explanation explicit, generating and testing competing hypotheses during synthesis.
description: Peirce identified abduction as the form of inference that generates hypotheses: a surprising fact C is observed; if A were true, C would follow; so there is reason to suspect A. Research synthesis is largely abductive, yet it usually happens implicitly. Timmermans and Tavory's abductive analysis turns it into a method: researchers deliberately look for surprising findings relative to existing theory and assumptions, generate several candidate explanations, and revisit the data to test which best explains the evidence, using variation across cases and over time. Rigour comes from documenting surprises, writing rival hypotheses explicitly, specifying what evidence would distinguish them, and seeking disconfirming cases. This guards against the common failure of jumping to a single convenient insight.
steps: List the team's prior assumptions and expectations before analysis begins.
During analysis, log surprising observations that contradict those expectations.
For each surprise, write at least three rival explanations.
Specify what evidence in the existing data or new research would distinguish between them.
Revisit the data and, if needed, run targeted follow-up research to test the rivals, actively seeking disconfirming cases.
Report the best-supported explanation with its rivals and the evidence that ruled them out.
outputs: Surprise log, rival hypothesis tables, evidence matrix, explained findings with confidence levels.
useWhen: Discovery synthesis, interpreting unexpected analytics results, and any study where findings may be shaped by team assumptions.
avoidWhen: Purely confirmatory evaluation with predefined measures; use hypothesis-driven experimental designs.
whyLost: Latent: Epistemological foundation for design research; rarely made explicit; valuable for teaching research reasoning.
whereToUse: Research synthesis; design thinking; hypothesis generation in discovery research.
example: A fintech team was surprised that users with high balances ignored a savings feature. Rival explanations were distrust, existing savings elsewhere and confusion; targeted interviews showed most already held savings at another bank, redirecting the feature toward account consolidation.
sources: How to Make Sense of Any Mess
Abductive Analysis (Timmermans & Tavory)
Collected Papers of Charles Sanders Peirce
Timmermans & Tavory, Theory construction in qualitative research: From grounded theory to abductive analysis (2012), Sociological Theory
Tavory & Timmermans, Abductive Analysis: Theorizing Qualitative Research (2014)
reference: Timmermans, S., & Tavory, I. (2012). Theory construction in qualitative research: From grounded theory to abductive analysis. Sociological Theory, 30(3), 167-186.

name: Accessibility Evaluation
summary: Systematic assessment of conformance with accessibility standards and real usability for disabled people, combining automated scans, expert audit and testing with disabled users.
description: Accessibility evaluation assesses whether a product can be perceived, operated, understood and used robustly by people with disabilities, including those using assistive technologies such as screen readers, switch devices, magnifiers and voice control. It combines automated scanning, which detects only a minority of issues, manual expert audit against WCAG success criteria, assistive-technology testing, and usability testing with disabled participants. Conformance is necessary but not sufficient: a product can pass criteria and still be hard to use. Rigour comes from defining scope and target conformance level, sampling representative pages and flows, testing with multiple assistive technologies, documenting each failure against its criterion with evidence, and including disabled people in evaluation rather than relying solely on simulations.
steps: Define scope, target standard and level (for example WCAG 2.2 AA) and sample representative pages and flows.
Run automated scanning tools to catch detectable issues.
Conduct a manual audit against each applicable success criterion, including keyboard-only navigation and colour contrast.
Test key flows with screen readers and other assistive technologies on target platforms.
Run usability sessions with 5 or more disabled participants across disability types.
Document issues with criterion, location, severity and remediation advice.
Retest fixes and track conformance over time.
outputs: A conformance report with failures mapped to criteria, severity and remediation guidance, plus usability findings from disabled users.
useWhen: For all digital products, especially government, healthcare, education and finance, and before procurement or legal conformance claims.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying only on automated tools or simulations; they miss most real barriers. Use expert audit plus testing with disabled users.
whyLost: Still in use: Legal and ethical imperative; growing regulatory pressure worldwide.
whereToUse: All digital products; particularly critical for government, healthcare, and education.
example: A university learning platform audits its exam submission flow. Screen-reader testing reveals that a countdown timer steals focus every minute, making submission nearly impossible, and it is fixed before exams.
sources: ISO Standard on Ergonomics
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (W3C)
reference: W3C (2023). Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2. World Wide Web Consortium.

name: ACSI (American Customer Satisfaction Index)
origin: Claes Fornell, Ross School of Business, University of Michigan (1994)
summary: A national satisfaction index model linking expectations, perceived quality and value to satisfaction, loyalty and complaints, with a website survey version.
description: The ACSI publishes 0 to 100 satisfaction indexes for hundreds of companies, industries and government services. Its model treats customer expectations, perceived quality and perceived value as drivers of satisfaction, which in turn drives loyalty and complaints, estimated with structural modelling. For websites, a core survey of 14 to 20 ten-point questions covers quality and freshness of information, clarity of organisation, overall satisfaction and loyalty. Sauro and Lewis note there is little published psychometric data, but it is widely used for tracking, especially by US government sites, which makes it a common external benchmark.
steps: Use the ACSI website or e-government question set, usually through a licensed provider.
Survey site visitors with the core 10-point items plus custom questions.
Compute the satisfaction index and driver scores.
Compare with published ACSI scores for the sector.
Use driver impacts to prioritise improvements.
outputs: A satisfaction index comparable with published sector scores, plus driver estimates.
useWhen: Public-sector or large consumer sites that need comparison with published national benchmarks.
avoidWhen: Task-level diagnosis is needed, or the cost of a licensed provider is not justified.
whyLost: It lives in marketing and government reporting rather than UX research.
whereToUse: Government websites, utilities, retail and financial services.
example: A federal benefits site scores 68 against a 74 e-government average; the driver model points to search as the largest gap.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Measuring the User Experience (Tullis & Albert)
reference: Fornell, C. et al. (1996). The American Customer Satisfaction Index: Nature, purpose, and findings. Journal of Marketing 60(4).

name: ACT-R Cognitive Modelling
origin: John R. Anderson, Carnegie Mellon, 1993 onward; perceptual-motor extension by Michael Byrne (2001); CogTool by Bonnie John et al. (2004)
summary: Builds executable simulations of users from a validated cognitive architecture to predict task time, errors and learning on interface designs.
description: ACT-R is a cognitive architecture with modules for declarative memory, procedural rules, vision, motor and goals, each with parameters fitted across decades of experiments. Modelling a user means writing production rules for a task and running the model against a simulated interface; the architecture constrains timing, memory retrieval (with activation and decay), visual attention and motor movement. Predictions include task time distributions, memory errors and learning curves. CogTool made the approach accessible by generating ACT-R KLM-style models from storyboards. ACT-R is the most rigorous way to answer 'how will a skilled user perform on this design?' without testing, and to explain why.
steps: Specify the task, user expertise and interface precisely, including screen layouts and timings.
Use CogTool for keystroke-level prediction from storyboards, or write ACT-R productions for more complex cognition.
Set architecture parameters to defaults and avoid fitting free parameters to the data you will predict.
Run the model many times (e.g. 100+) to get time and error distributions.
Validate against a small sample of human data; aim for predictions within about 10-20% of observed means.
Use the model to compare design variants and inspect which modules (visual search, retrieval, motor) drive differences.
outputs: Predicted task time distributions, error and learning predictions, and module-level explanations of performance differences.
useWhen: Skilled, repetitive tasks where small time differences matter at scale, or where testing is expensive (safety-critical, specialised users).
avoidWhen: Novel creative tasks or attitudes and preferences; the architecture does not model motivation well.
whyLost: Modelling expertise is rare and slow to acquire; CogTool stopped being maintained, and product cycles favour A/B tests.
whereToUse: Call centre and back-office tools, in-vehicle interfaces, medical order entry, high-frequency trading screens.
example: An airline's check-in kiosk redesign is modelled in CogTool. The model predicts a 4-second saving per passenger from reordering fields; validation with 10 users confirms 3.5 seconds, worth thousands of agent hours annually.
sources: Anderson et al., An integrated theory of the mind (2004), Psychological Review
Byrne, ACT-R/PM and menu selection (2001), IJHCS
John et al., Predictive human performance modeling made easy (2004), CHI
Cognitive Modeling: Nine Paradigms (slide deck)
reference: Anderson, J. R., et al. (2004). An integrated theory of the mind. Psychological Review, 111(4), 1036-1060.

name: Active Inference (Free Energy) Models
origin: Karl Friston, 2005-2010 onward; Active Inference textbook by Parr, Pezzulo and Friston (2022)
summary: Models users as agents minimising expected free energy, balancing goal-seeking (pragmatic value) with uncertainty-reducing exploration (epistemic value).
description: Active inference frames perception and action as minimising variational free energy, a bound on surprise under an internal generative model. Agents act to fulfil preferred observations and to reduce uncertainty, which naturally explains curiosity, information-seeking and exploration-exploitation trade-offs. Formally, models are partially observable Markov decision processes in which policies are scored by expected free energy, decomposed into epistemic and pragmatic value. For UX, it offers a single principled account of why users explore new interfaces, check status, seek confirmation and abandon when predictions fail. Applications remain experimental, but simulation studies can test whether a design reduces users' uncertainty where it matters.
steps: Specify the user's generative model: hidden states, observations the interface provides, and actions available.
Define preferences as prior beliefs about desired observations (e.g. task completed, no error message).
Implement the model with a discrete-state active inference toolkit (e.g. SPM DEM routines or pymdp).
Simulate behaviour under design variants, separating epistemic actions (checking, exploring) from pragmatic ones.
Compare simulated with observed behaviour, for example frequency of status-checking actions.
Use the model to identify where interfaces leave users uncertain and add observations that resolve it.
outputs: A generative model of the user, simulated policies, epistemic versus pragmatic action predictions and design implications.
useWhen: Research teams exploring theory-driven explanations of exploration, checking behaviour and uncertainty in interfaces.
avoidWhen: Applied product decisions on tight timelines; simpler usability or analytics methods answer most questions.
whyLost: The mathematics is demanding and the framework is young and contested; it has hardly been applied to HCI beyond a few papers.
whereToUse: Status and progress design, onboarding exploration, AI agents that communicate uncertainty, health self-monitoring apps.
example: A delivery app's users repeatedly refresh order status. An active inference simulation predicts this checking as epistemic action driven by uncertainty about arrival time; adding a confidence band to the ETA reduces refreshes in a field test.
sources: Friston, The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory? (2010), Nature Reviews Neuroscience
Parr, Pezzulo & Friston, Active Inference: The Free Energy Principle in Mind, Brain, and Behavior (2022)
reference: Parr, T., Pezzulo, G., & Friston, K. J. (2022). Active Inference. MIT Press.

name: Active UX Surveillance
origin: Active surveillance and population health surveys; adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Periodically assesses representative user populations with standard task batteries, exposure measures and harm reports to estimate UX harm missed by logs.
description: Active surveillance collects data specifically for monitoring, through surveys, structured observations and periodic studies of representative samples, and captures conditions passive systems miss: behavioural risk factors and diffuse harms not tied to clinical records. The treatise proposes active UX surveillance: periodic structured assessment of representative populations, measuring failure rates on standard task batteries, exposure to specific patterns and reported harms. It argues this is expensive but no more so than routine national health surveys. Representative sampling, standardised instruments and repeated waves allow prevalence estimates, trends and demographic distributions comparable across products and over time.
steps: Define the population and draw a representative sample (probability panel or weighted quota).
Develop a standard task battery and validated harm and exposure questionnaires.
Administer in waves (for example annually) with consistent protocols.
Weight data to the population and estimate prevalence with CIs.
Analyse distribution by demographics and trends over time.
Publish findings and feed into interventions and regulation.
outputs: Population prevalence estimates, trend series, demographic distributions, benchmark task performance.
useWhen: Measuring harms spanning many products, cross-industry benchmarking, regulatory monitoring.
avoidWhen: Single-product questions answerable with that product's logs.
whyLost: No institution owns cross-product UX health; UX research is funded per product.
whereToUse: Regulators, consumer groups, national digital service agencies, industry consortia.
example: An annual panel of 5,000 adults attempts standard tasks (cancel a subscription, change consent) on top apps; cancellation failure prevalence falls from 22% to 11% after new rules.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) methodology
Groves RM et al. (2009) Survey Methodology. 2nd ed
reference: Groves RM et al. (2009) Survey Methodology. 2nd ed. Wiley.

name: Activity Theory Analysis
origin: Lev Vygotsky (1930s), Alexei Leont'ev (1978); Yrjö Engeström's activity system model, 1987; brought to HCI by Bødker, Kuutti and Nardi in the 1990s
summary: Analysing work as a mediated activity system and its activity-action-operation levels, using contradictions between elements as drivers of breakdown and design opportunity.
description: Activity theory analyses human activity as purposeful and mediated by tools within a social context. Leont'ev's hierarchy distinguishes activity (motive-driven, such as patient care), action (conscious goal-directed steps, such as entering a medication record) and operation (automated routines like typing that break when conditions change). Engeström's activity system extends the unit of analysis to subject, object, tools, rules, community and division of labour. Contradictions between these elements, for example a tool designed for billing used within a care activity, show up as frustration, workarounds and non-standard behaviour, and are treated as sources of change. The framework helps explain why technically usable systems fail in practice.
steps: Define the activity under study and its object (the motive the activity serves), drawing on fieldwork data.
Map the activity system: subject, object, mediating tools, rules, community, division of labour and outcome.
Classify observed behaviour into activity, action and operation levels, noting where operations break down into conscious actions.
Identify contradictions within and between system elements, evidenced by frustration, workarounds or rule-breaking.
Trace each contradiction historically: how did the tool, rule or role come to conflict with the object?
Translate priority contradictions into design opportunities and test them with participants.
outputs: Activity system diagrams, level analyses, a catalogue of evidenced contradictions, and design opportunities linked to them.
useWhen: Organisational or professional settings where tools are embedded in complex social practice and adoption fails despite adequate usability.
avoidWhen: Narrow interface optimisation questions; use usability testing or task analysis.
whyLost: Its vocabulary is dense and was eclipsed in HCI by more lightweight frameworks, leaving it in Scandinavian HCI, education and CSCW research.
whereToUse: Clinical information systems, education technology, public sector digital transformation, and enterprise tool rollouts.
example: Teachers resist a grading platform that is fast to use. Activity analysis shows a contradiction between the tool's numeric rubrics and the school's object of formative feedback, leading to narrative feedback fields.
sources: Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (Hollnagel)
HCI Encyclopedia
Unified Theories of Cognition (Newell)
Learning by Expanding (Engeström)
Activity, Consciousness, and Personality (Leont'ev)
Acting with Technology (Kaptelinin & Nardi)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 15 — Activity Theory, Contradictions & the Zone of Proximal Development
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Engeström Y (1987) Learning by Expanding
Nardi BA (Ed) (1996) Context and Consciousness: Activity Theory and Human-Computer Interaction
Kaptelinin V & Nardi BA (2006) Acting with Technology: Activity Theory and Interaction Design
reference: Engeström, Y. (1987). Learning by Expanding: An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Developmental Research. Orienta-Konsultit.

extra.The Three Levels: Activity: The motive-level of behaviour — why is this person doing anything at all? What is the broader social and personal objective? (A nurse enters patient data because her activity is patient care, not data entry.) Action: Goal-directed behaviour — what specific goal is the person pursuing right now? Actions are conscious and deliberate. (Entering a specific patient's medication record.) Operation: Automatised behavior that was once an action but has become unconscious through practice. (Touch-typing, mouse movement.) Operations fail when conditions change unexpectedly.
extra.Contradiction Analysis: Contradictions are the engine of change in activity systems. They arise when one component of the system (tool, subject, rules, community, division of labor, object, outcome) conflicts with another. The most common UX contradiction: a tool designed for one activity is used in the context of a different activity. Identify contradictions by: observing where participants express frustration, develop workarounds, or engage in non-standard behavior. Each contradiction is a design opportunity.

name: Actor-Network Theory Tracing
origin: Michel Callon, Bruno Latour and John Law, 1980s (Callon's scallops study, 1986; Latour, Reassembling the Social, 2005)
summary: Follows how human and non-human actors (people, devices, documents, algorithms) are enrolled into networks that make a technology work or fail, without assuming a priori who acts.
description: ANT treats humans and non-humans symmetrically as actants that mediate action. Researchers 'follow the actors', tracing associations and the work of translation by which actors are enrolled: problematisation, interessement, enrolment and mobilisation (Callon). Stable networks become black boxes; controversies reveal how they are assembled. For UX, ANT is useful when products only work because many elements align (regulations, data standards, partner apps, informal intermediaries, devices) and when failures arise because a non-human actor (a PDF form, an API, a fax machine) quietly holds a network together. It shifts analysis from user-interface to socio-material assemblage.
steps: Choose a controversy, failure or innovation where the network is visible.
Follow actors through observation, documents and interviews, recording all human and non-human participants.
Map associations and translations: who or what enrols whom, through what devices and inscriptions.
Identify obligatory passage points and black boxes that hold the network together.
Analyse where translations fail or betrayals occur, causing the network to destabilise.
Derive design and strategy implications for enrolling or re-arranging actors.
outputs: Actor-network maps, accounts of translation and failure points, and strategic implications.
useWhen: Adoption or failure of products embedded in complex socio-technical ecosystems, platform strategies and infrastructures.
avoidWhen: Narrow usability questions where interface-level analysis suffices.
whyLost: ANT is known in STS and some CSCW work, but its theoretical vocabulary and lack of a step-by-step protocol limit practitioner use.
whereToUse: Health information exchange, open banking, smart city deployments, AI in professional workflows, B2B platforms.
example: An e-prescribing rollout stalls. ANT tracing reveals the paper prescription pad was an obligatory passage point for pharmacy reimbursement; the network re-stabilises only after the insurer accepts digital records.
sources: Latour, Reassembling the Social: An Introduction to Actor-Network-Theory (2005)
Callon, Some elements of a sociology of translation (1986), in Law (ed.), Power, Action and Belief
Law, After Method: Mess in Social Science Research (2004)
reference: Latour, B. (2005). Reassembling the Social. Oxford University Press.

name: Adaptive Choice-Based Conjoint (ACBC)
origin: Developed by Sawtooth Software (Johnson and Orme, 2007; released 2009)
summary: A conjoint survey that adapts to each respondent: they configure their ideal product, rule out unacceptable options, then make choices among tailored alternatives.
description: Standard choice-based conjoint shows everyone the same kind of randomised product profiles, many of which a given person would never consider. ACBC runs in three stages. In a build-your-own section the respondent picks their preferred level of each attribute. A screening section then shows near-variations of that product and asks whether each is a possibility, which reveals must-have and unacceptable levels. Finally a choice tournament asks them to pick between the products that survived screening. Because every task is close to what the respondent actually wants, the data is more engaging and gives better predictions with fewer respondents, and it captures non-compensatory rules ('anything without offline mode is out') that ordinary conjoint models struggle with. The cost is a longer survey and specialist software for design and estimation.
steps: Define attributes and levels from qualitative research, keeping them concrete and mutually exclusive.
Set up the build-your-own, screening and choice tournament sections in ACBC-capable software.
Pilot with a few respondents to check length (often 15 to 20 minutes) and comprehension.
Field to the target sample, typically 150 to 300 per segment.
Estimate part-worth utilities, usually with hierarchical Bayes, and identify must-haves and unacceptables.
Run market or tier simulations to compare candidate products, bundles or prices.
outputs: Part-worth utilities per respondent, lists of must-have and unacceptable features, and a simulator for product and pricing scenarios.
useWhen: High-stakes product, tier or pricing decisions with many attributes, especially where some features are deal-breakers.
avoidWhen: Flat lists of features with no attribute structure (use MaxDiff), early discovery, or teams without access to conjoint software.
whyLost: ACBC lives in commercial market research tools. UX teams that use conjoint usually stop at standard CBC, and many do not know the adaptive version exists.
whereToUse: Subscription tier design, hardware configuration, SaaS packaging and pricing, B2B feature bundles.
example: For a project-management tool, ACBC shows that single sign-on is a must-have for 70% of enterprise respondents, so it moves from the top tier to every business plan.
sources: Feature Prioritization Methods (slide deck)
Orme, B., Getting Started with Conjoint Analysis (2014)
reference: Johnson, R. M., & Orme, B. K. (2007). A new approach to adaptive CBC. Sawtooth Software Conference Proceedings. Orme, B. (2014). Getting Started with Conjoint Analysis (3rd ed.). Research Publishers.

name: Adjusted-Wald Confidence Interval for Completion Rates
origin: Agresti & Coull (1998); recommended for small-sample usability data by Sauro & Lewis (2005)
summary: A confidence interval for a task success rate that stays accurate with the tiny samples typical of usability tests.
description: Completion rates from usability tests are binomial proportions measured on 5 to 20 people. The textbook Wald interval (p plus or minus z times the standard error) collapses at these sizes: it can run below 0% or above 100% and covers the true rate far less often than its nominal 95%. The adjusted-Wald interval fixes this by adding z²/2 successes and z² trials (about two successes and four attempts at 95%) before computing the interval. Sauro and Lewis showed it has the best average coverage of the common options for usability data, beating the exact Clopper-Pearson interval, which is too conservative. It turns "4 of 5 users succeeded" into an honest statement such as "between 36% and 98% of all users would likely succeed".
steps: Count successes x and attempts n for the task, using a pre-agreed success rule.
Choose the confidence level (90% is common for formative work, 95% for summative claims) and look up z.
Compute the adjusted proportion p_adj = (x + z²/2) / (n + z²).
Compute the margin z × sqrt(p_adj(1 − p_adj) / (n + z²)) and form p_adj ± margin, truncating at 0 and 100%.
Report the observed rate, the interval and n together, and plot intervals as error bars when comparing tasks.
outputs: A completion rate with a defensible lower and upper bound for the whole user population.
useWhen: Reporting any success, conversion or agreement proportion from a sample under about 100, especially formative tests with 5 to 15 users.
avoidWhen: Very large analytics samples, where any interval method gives the same answer, or when you need a one-sided test against a goal (use a binomial test against the benchmark).
whyLost: UX inherited the habit of reporting raw percentages from small tests and either skipped intervals entirely or used the Wald interval from introductory statistics, which fails at small n. The fix is a two-line formula, but it lives mainly in quantitative UX books.
whereToUse: Any usability test report, unmoderated task studies, tree tests and first-click tests where success rates drive decisions.
example: Seven of eight participants complete a new checkout. The adjusted-Wald 95% interval is roughly 52% to 99%, so the team can say most users will succeed but cannot yet claim the 95% target was met.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
reference: Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2005). Estimating completion rates from small samples using binomial confidence intervals. Proceedings of HFES 49.

name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect Measurement
origin: Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura (1995); replicated by Noam Tractinsky (1997, 2000)
summary: Measures how much visual appeal inflates perceived usability by separating aesthetic ratings from objective performance, controlling for aesthetics as a confound in evaluations.
description: The aesthetic-usability effect is the finding that people rate attractive interfaces as easier to use, even when objective performance is equal or worse. Kurosu and Kashimura found apparent usability correlated more with aesthetics than with inherent usability, and Tractinsky replicated the effect across cultures and found it persisted after use. For research this is a confound: polished prototypes can mask usability problems in satisfaction scores, and comparisons between a polished and a rough variant are biased. Measurement involves collecting aesthetic ratings, subjective usability (for example SUS) and objective performance (success, time, errors) for the same interface, then estimating how much aesthetics predicts perceived usability after controlling for performance. Controlled studies vary visual polish while holding interaction constant.
steps: Two-condition study: same functional design with aesthetic enhancement (improved visual design) vs. baseline.
Before usability testing, collect aesthetic rating.
After testing, collect perceived usability.
Compare: does aesthetic rating predict perceived usability beyond actual performance?
Measure: aesthetic rating × task performance correlation.
Large positive correlation = halo effect present.
Partial out aesthetics from perceived usability measures.
outputs: Correlations or regression estimates of aesthetics on perceived usability controlling for performance, gap between perceived and objective usability, and fidelity-matching guidance.
useWhen: Comparing designs of differing visual fidelity, interpreting satisfaction scores, testing visual redesigns, and studies of emotional design.
avoidWhen: When you only measure objective performance and do not rely on subjective ratings; then the confound does not affect conclusions.
whyLost: The effect is widely cited as a design principle but seldom measured; most teams treat subjective ratings at face value and do not control for visual fidelity.
whereToUse: UX evaluation design (control for aesthetics), A/B testing interpretation (aesthetic changes confound usability changes), design ROI research.
example: A SaaS team finds its redesigned dashboard scores 12 points higher on SUS but task completion is unchanged. Regressing SUS on aesthetic ratings and performance shows the gain is almost entirely visual appeal, so usability work continues.
sources: Universal Principles of Design — William Lidwell
Designing for Emotion (Walter)
Well Designed (Kolko)
100 Things Every Designer Should Know (Weinschenk)
Tractinsky, Katz & Ikar, What is beautiful is usable (Interacting with Computers, 2000)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 36 — Emotional Design Hierarchies & the Aesthetic-Usability Effect
reference: Kurosu M & Kashimura K (1995) Apparent usability vs. inherent usability: Experimental analysis on the determinants of the apparent usability. CHI 1995 Conference Companion

name: Affective State Measurement
origin: Rosalind Picard, 1997; James Russell, 1980
summary: Measures users' emotional states during interaction by combining self-report on valence and arousal with physiological and behavioural signals such as skin conductance and facial expression.
description: Grounded in Picard's affective computing and Russell's circumplex model, which locates emotions on dimensions of valence (pleasant to unpleasant) and arousal (calm to activated), this method measures emotional responses during interaction. It triangulates three channels: self-report (e.g. Self-Assessment Manikin or moment-by-moment ratings), physiological signals (electrodermal activity, heart rate variability) and expressive behaviour (facial expression, voice). Signals are time-aligned with interaction logs so peaks can be attributed to specific events. Rigour requires baselines per participant, artefact handling, awareness that physiological arousal does not indicate valence alone, validation of automated classifiers against human coding, and careful ethics given the intimacy of emotional data.
steps: Multi-channel affect measurement protocol:
Physiological: EDA (electrodermal activity) = arousal level. HRV = cognitive load and stress.
(2) Facial: FACs (facial action coding system) or automated tools (Affectiva, Microsoft FER).
(3) Voice: pitch, rate, and energy features from audio.

(4) Self-report: SAM (Self-Assessment Manikin — valence and arousal). Triangulate: agreement across channels = high confidence. Disagreement = the most interesting data (which channel is wrong, and why?).
outputs: Time-aligned valence and arousal traces, emotional peaks linked to interface events, triangulated self-report and sensor data.
useWhen: Experiences where emotion is central or risky: games, health, finance stress, onboarding anxiety, error recovery and AI interactions.
avoidWhen: Avoid when inferences from sensors cannot be validated, when consent and privacy cannot be assured, or when simple post-task ratings will do; use SAM or interviews instead.
whyLost: Sensors, signal processing and validity problems kept affective computing in labs; UX settled for satisfaction ratings.
whereToUse: Emotion-informed UX design, accessibility for emotional expression, health and wellbeing product research, affective gaming UX.
example: A loan application flow is tested with 20 participants wearing skin-conductance sensors; arousal spikes cluster at the credit check consent step, and adding a plain-language explanation reduces spikes and abandonment.
sources: Affective Computing — Rosalind Picard
reference: Picard RW (1997) Affective Computing. MIT Press

name: Affective state taxonomy
origin: Rosalind Picard, Affective Computing (1997); dimensional models from Russell's circumplex (1980) and Mehrabian and Russell's PAD model (1974); learning-centred states from D'Mello and Graesser (2012)
summary: Defines the set of affective states that matter in a product context, with dimensional coordinates and observable indicators, so emotion can be measured consistently across channels.
description: Emotion measurement fails when teams do not define what they are measuring. Basic emotion categories such as anger, fear and joy rarely occur during product use; states such as confusion, frustration, boredom, engagement, anxiety and relief are far more frequent, as D'Mello and Graesser showed in learning technologies. An affective state taxonomy specifies the states relevant to the domain, locates each on dimensions such as valence and arousal (and sometimes dominance), and defines the indicators expected in each channel: self-report wording, facial action units, physiological markers and behavioural signals. It also defines which states are desirable, which are acceptable and which are failure signals. Rigour comes from grounding the taxonomy in observation of the domain, operational definitions, and checking inter-rater agreement when coding states.
steps: Collect candidate states from domain observation, interviews and literature, aiming for 6 to 12 states relevant to the product (for example confusion, frustration, anxiety, relief, confidence, boredom).
Define each state operationally, and place it on valence and arousal dimensions (and dominance if control matters, as in financial decisions).

For each state, specify expected indicators per channel: self-report items, facial cues, physiological signals such as heart rate variability or electrodermal activity, and behaviours such as hesitation or rage clicks.
Classify states as target, acceptable or failure states for each journey stage, for example anxiety acceptable at loan submission but a failure state after approval.
Pilot the taxonomy by having 2 coders label 30 to 50 video segments, aiming for Cohen's kappa of 0.60 or above, and refine definitions.
Use the taxonomy to structure multi-channel affective studies and to report results consistently over time.
outputs: A defined set of affective states with dimensional coordinates, channel-specific indicators, journey-stage targets, and coder agreement statistics.
useWhen: Planning emotion measurement, comparing affective data across studies, or designing emotionally sensitive flows such as finance, health or education.
avoidWhen: You only need a single satisfaction rating, or affect is not relevant to the decision; avoid inventing taxonomies without domain observation.
whyLost: It is standard in affective computing and learning sciences research, but UX emotion work often jumps to tools such as facial coding without defining the states that matter.
whereToUse: Loan and insurance applications, health diagnostics, learning platforms, customer support, AI assistant interactions, games.
example: Before a study of a high-stakes loan application, the team defined 8 states, including anxiety, confusion, relief and distrust, with indicators across facial, heart rate variability and verbal channels. Coders reached kappa 0.71, and relief at approval became a target state to design for.
sources: Affective Computing (Picard)
Methods Atlas — affective measurement (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 37 — Picard's Affective Framework — Multi-Channel Emotion Measurement
reference: Picard, R. W. (1997). Affective Computing. MIT Press; Russell, J. A. (1980). A circumplex model of affect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 39(6), 1161–1178; D'Mello, S., & Graesser, A. (2012). Dynamics of affective states during complex learning. Learning and Instruction, 22(2), 145–157.

name: Affinity Diagramming
origin: Jiro Kawakita, 1960s (KJ method); adapted for UX in Contextual Design by Beyer & Holtzblatt
summary: A bottom-up synthesis method in which individual observations are clustered by affinity into labelled groups, revealing themes from raw qualitative data.
description: Affinity diagramming organises large numbers of individual observations, quotes or interpretation notes into groups based on their natural affinity, building a hierarchy from the bottom up. It derives from Jiro Kawakita's KJ method, developed to make sense of anthropological field data, and was adapted in Contextual Design to synthesise contextual inquiry notes. Notes are grouped without predefined categories, and each group receives a label written as a first-person statement of the insight it contains, then groups are clustered into higher-level themes. Rigour comes from writing atomic notes that each carry one idea with a source code, resisting pre-set categories, writing insight labels rather than topic labels, and keeping a traceable link from every theme back to participants.
steps: Write each observation, quote or interpretation as an atomic note tagged with a participant code.
Clear a large wall or digital board and place notes one at a time, grouping those that share an underlying meaning.
Keep groups small (about 4 to 6 notes) and split larger ones.
Label each group with an insight statement written in the user's voice, not a topic heading.
Cluster groups into higher-level themes and label those.
Walk the wall to check coverage and identify gaps or contradictions.
Derive design implications and questions from each top-level theme.
outputs: A hierarchical affinity diagram with labelled insight groups, top-level themes and traceable links to source data.
useWhen: After interviews, contextual inquiries or workshops, when a team needs to synthesise many observations and build shared understanding.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a substitute for systematic coding when findings must be defended rigorously; use thematic analysis or grounded theory. Not suitable for quantitative data.
whyLost: Still in use: Collaborative synthesis staple; surfaces team consensus; democratizes analysis across disciplines.
whereToUse: After any qualitative fieldwork; workshop synthesis; cross-functional alignment sessions.
example: After 12 contextual inquiries with warehouse supervisors, a logistics SaaS team builds an affinity diagram of 400 notes. A top-level theme, 'I trust my own whiteboard more than the system', drives a new shift-planning view.
sources: Rapid Contextual Design
Lost Methods in UX
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Beyer H & Holtzblatt K (1998) Contextual Design
Kawakita J (1967) Hassoho (Abduction)
Scupin R (1997) The KJ method: a technique for analyzing data derived from Japanese ethnology. Human Organization
reference: Kawakita, J. (1975). The KJ Method: A Scientific Approach to Problem Solving. Kawakita Research Institute; Beyer, H. & Holtzblatt, K. (1998). Contextual Design.

name: Affordance Analysis
origin: James J. Gibson, 1977/1979; adapted for design by Donald Norman, 1988
summary: Maps the action possibilities an interface offers against those users actually perceive, separating real affordances from signifiers to find hidden and false affordances.
description: Gibson defined affordances as action possibilities that exist in the relation between an actor and an environment. Norman brought the idea into design and later clarified that what designers control are signifiers: perceivable cues that communicate an affordance. Affordance analysis operationalises this distinction. For each element the analyst records what actions are actually possible, what actions are signalled, and what actions users perceive. Gaver's taxonomy then classifies the result as a perceptible affordance, a hidden affordance (possible but not signalled, such as an undiscovered swipe) or a false affordance (signalled but not possible, such as decorative text styled like a link). Rigour comes from checking perception empirically, through first-click tests, prediction prompts or observation, rather than relying on designer intuition, and from considering the actor's capabilities, including motor and sensory impairments.
steps: Inventory interactive and non-interactive elements on the screens or physical product under review.
For each element record actual possible actions and the signifiers that communicate them.
Ask 5-8 users to predict what each element does or where they would act to achieve a goal, without instruction.
Classify each element as perceptible, hidden or false affordance using Gaver's taxonomy.
Prioritise hidden affordances on critical paths and false affordances that cause wasted actions.
Redesign signifiers and re-test predictions, including users with different motor and sensory capabilities.
outputs: Affordance inventory, classification of perceptible, hidden and false affordances, signifier redesign recommendations.
useWhen: Gesture, touch, AR/VR and novel interaction designs where discoverability is uncertain, or flat visual styles that may have removed cues.
avoidWhen: When the issue is content comprehension or navigation structure; use tree testing or content testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Foundational HCI concept; but widely misunderstood — real vs. perceived affordances conflated.
whereToUse: Interaction design; product design; AR/VR interaction.
example: A banking app hid account actions behind a left swipe. Affordance analysis showed only 2 of 8 participants predicted the gesture; adding a visible overflow menu as a signifier removed the hidden affordance on the critical path.
sources: The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
Design for How People Think
The Design of Everyday Things (Don Norman)
Goldstein, E. B., Sensation and Perception
Gibson, J. J., The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979)
Whalen, J., Design for How People Think (2019)
Sensation and Perception (Goldstein)
Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (Gibson)
Design for How People Think (Whalen)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 11 — Perception — Before Cognition
reference: Gaver, W. W. (1991). Technology affordances. Proceedings of CHI '91, 79-84.

name: After-Action Review
origin: US Army, mid-1970s at the National Training Center; TC 25-20 (1993)
summary: A short, structured debrief asking what was planned, what actually happened, why there was a difference, and what to sustain or improve.
description: The AAR was developed by the US Army to learn from training exercises. Its four questions (What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we sustain or improve?) are answered by participants themselves, facilitated rather than judged, immediately after the event. Ground truth from instrumentation is used to correct memory. Its rigour comes from comparing intent with observed outcome, from rank-free participation, and from repetition across many events, which allows patterns to be aggregated. In UX it suits research operations (after each study), design sprints and launches, and also field studies with users who perform team activities.
steps: Schedule the AAR immediately after the event, within hours, with all participants present.
Restate the objectives and plan (what was supposed to happen) using written records.
Reconstruct what actually happened using data, recordings and logs, letting participants add their perspectives.
Discuss causes of differences, focusing on the system and decisions rather than individuals.
Agree 2-3 items to sustain and 2-3 to improve, with owners.
Store AARs in a searchable log and review trends quarterly.
outputs: Brief AAR records with plan-versus-actual comparisons and sustain/improve actions; a longitudinal lessons log.
useWhen: After research studies, launches, sprints or team exercises, and in field research on teams performing coordinated tasks.
avoidWhen: Major incidents with harm, where a formal blameless postmortem is more appropriate.
whyLost: Retrospectives in agile replaced AARs with looser 'what went well' formats that lack the plan-versus-actual comparison and ground truth.
whereToUse: Research operations, launch reviews, incident drills, game days, customer onboarding programmes.
example: After each usability study, a research team runs a 20-minute AAR. Over six months the log shows recurring recruitment mismatches, prompting a screener redesign that cuts no-shows by half.
sources: US Army, TC 25-20: A Leader's Guide to After-Action Reviews (1993)
Darling, Parry & Moore, Learning in the thick of it (2005), Harvard Business Review
reference: US Army (1993). TC 25-20: A Leader's Guide to After-Action Reviews.

name: After-Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ)
origin: James R. Lewis, IBM (1991)
summary: A three-item post-task questionnaire covering ease, time taken and quality of support information.
description: The ASQ is asked straight after each task scenario. Its three seven-point items cover satisfaction with ease of completion, with the time it took, and with the support information (help, messages, documentation). It predates the Single Ease Question and covers slightly more ground, at the cost of two extra items per task. Sauro and Lewis's comparisons of post-task questionnaires found the ASQ, SEQ and SMEQ all correlate well with task performance, so the choice comes down to whether separate time and support ratings are useful.
steps: Ask the three items immediately after each task.
Average the items into a task score (lower is better on the original scale).
Compare tasks and designs using means and confidence intervals.
Inspect the support item separately when help or messages are part of the design.
outputs: A post-task satisfaction score per task with a separate read on support materials.
useWhen: Tasks where help content or system messages are under evaluation.
avoidWhen: Long studies with many tasks, where the single-item SEQ reduces fatigue.
whyLost: Superseded in practice by the one-item SEQ.
whereToUse: Enterprise software tests, documentation and help-centre evaluations.
example: A tax tool's "claim a deduction" task scores fine on ease but poorly on the support item, pointing to inline help.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
reference: Lewis, J. R. (1991). Psychometric evaluation of an after-scenario questionnaire for computer usability studies: the ASQ. SIGCHI Bulletin 23.

name: Age-Period-Cohort Analysis
origin: Lexis diagrams (Wilhelm Lexis, 1875); Mason, Mason, Winsborough and Poole (1973); Yang and Land (2013)
summary: Separates whether changes in a metric come from user tenure (age), calendar events (period) or sign-up cohort, despite their linear dependence.
description: In products, a user's tenure (age), the calendar date (period) and sign-up cohort are linked (period = cohort + age), so ordinary regression cannot separate them. Yet the distinction matters: falling engagement could be because users tire with tenure, because of a seasonal or competitive period effect, or because recent cohorts are lower quality. APC methods use Lexis diagrams for visual decomposition, constrained models, intrinsic estimators, or hierarchical APC models (cross-classified random effects) with explicit, stated identifying assumptions. Done carefully, APC prevents misattributing acquisition-mix effects to product changes.
steps: Build a dataset of outcomes by tenure interval and calendar period (e.g. weeks), with cohort implied.
Visualise with Lexis surfaces or heat maps of rates by age and period.
Choose an APC approach and state its identifying assumption (e.g. hierarchical APC with random period and cohort effects).
Estimate age, period and cohort effects with uncertainty.
Check robustness across alternative specifications.
Interpret effects in light of known events (launches, seasonality, acquisition campaigns).
outputs: Lexis visualisations, estimated age, period and cohort effects with uncertainty and robustness checks.
useWhen: Long-running products with changing acquisition and many calendar events, where retention or engagement trends are debated.
avoidWhen: Short histories or when one of the three effects can be ruled out by design.
whyLost: Cohort tables in analytics tools show the data but no method to decompose it; demographic methods are rarely known.
whereToUse: Subscription retention, gaming engagement, marketplace activity, learning platforms.
example: A meditation app's engagement decline is decomposed: tenure effects are stable, but cohorts acquired via a 2025 influencer campaign have much lower engagement, a cohort effect, not product decay.
sources: Yang & Land, Age-Period-Cohort Analysis: New Models, Methods, and Empirical Applications (2013)
Mason et al., Some methodological issues in cohort analysis of archival data (1973), American Sociological Review
reference: Yang, Y., & Land, K. C. (2013). Age-Period-Cohort Analysis. CRC Press.

name: Agent Decomposition (Society of Mind)
origin: Marvin Minsky, 1986
summary: Decomposes complex user behaviour into many simple interacting 'agents' (sub-processes with goals), revealing conflicts and coordination failures that explain behaviour.
description: Minsky's Society of Mind proposed that intelligence arises from the interaction of many simple, mindless agents, each performing a narrow function, organised into agencies with conflicting and cooperating goals. As an analytic method, agent decomposition models a user's behaviour in a complex situation as a set of such agents (for example, a goal to save, a habit to browse, a need for social approval) and maps how they compete, which wins in which context, and what arbitrates between them. This makes inconsistent behaviour explicable and suggests interventions that strengthen, weaken or coordinate specific agents. Rigour comes from grounding each agent in observed evidence, specifying activation conditions, and testing predictions against behaviour.
steps: Agent-level error analysis: for any UX error, decompose into agent-level failures:
Attention agent: was the relevant information in the attentional field?
(2) Recognition agent: was the stimulus correctly identified?
(3) Memory agent: was the correct action retrieved?
(4) Execution agent: was the action performed correctly?
(5) Goal agent: was the current action aligned with the active goal? Each agent failure type maps to a specific design intervention.
outputs: An agent map of competing sub-goals and processes, identified conflicts and arbitration points, and design interventions targeting specific agents.
useWhen: Analysing apparently irrational or inconsistent behaviour, such as self-control conflicts and multitasking, and designing multi-agent AI systems and their interfaces.
avoidWhen: Avoid when standard task analysis suffices; the framework is metaphorical and should not be presented as a validated cognitive model.
whyLost: Minsky's theory was influential in AI but never operationalised as an HCI method; behavioural economics now explains similar conflicts with dual-process models.
whereToUse: Complex error analysis, multi-step task design, expert system interface design.
example: A budgeting app models users as a 'saver' agent and an 'impulse' agent plus a 'social' agent responding to friends' spending; designing a commitment device for the saver at payday reduces overspending.
sources: The Society of Mind — Marvin Minsky
reference: Minsky M (1986) The Society of Mind. Simon & Schuster

name: Agent-Based Modelling
donor: Complexity science, ecology and computational social science
origin: Thomas Schelling's segregation model (1971); Joshua Epstein and Robert Axtell (Growing Artificial Societies, 1996); ODD protocol by Volker Grimm et al. (2006, 2020)
summary: Simulates many heterogeneous agents following behavioural rules to see how collective patterns such as adoption, congestion or polarisation emerge.
description: Agent-based models represent individual users (or sellers, bots, moderators) with their own attributes and decision rules, interacting with each other and an environment. Macro patterns emerge from micro rules, often in surprising ways, as Schelling showed with mild preferences producing strong segregation. ABMs suit questions where heterogeneity, networks and local interaction matter. Rigour comes from grounding rules in empirical research (including qualitative), documenting with the ODD protocol, validating against multiple observed patterns (pattern-oriented modelling) and exploring parameter space systematically rather than presenting single runs.
steps: Define the question and the emergent pattern to explain or predict.
Specify agent types, attributes, decision rules and interactions, grounded in research data.
Document the model using the ODD protocol and implement it (NetLogo, Mesa, AnyLogic).
Calibrate and validate against several observed patterns at different levels.
Run parameter sweeps and sensitivity analysis with many replications.
Test interventions in simulation and design field experiments to confirm key predictions.
outputs: A documented ABM, validation evidence, emergent pattern explanations and intervention scenarios.
useWhen: Two-sided markets, social features, communities, multiplayer systems and policies where interactions drive outcomes.
avoidWhen: Individual usability problems or when behaviour rules cannot be grounded in evidence.
whyLost: ABM requires programming and sits in complexity science; UX research rarely builds simulations.
whereToUse: Marketplace pricing and matching, social network feeds, moderation policies, crowd and venue experiences, game economies.
example: A dating app models how changes to swipe limits affect match distribution. The ABM shows limits reduce inequality of matches without lowering total matches, a prediction later confirmed in an experiment.
sources: Epstein & Axtell, Growing Artificial Societies (1996)
Grimm et al., The ODD protocol for describing agent-based and other simulation models: A second update (2020), JASSS
Wilensky & Rand, An Introduction to Agent-Based Modeling (2015)
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: Wilensky, U., & Rand, W. (2015). An Introduction to Agent-Based Modeling. MIT Press.

name: Agent-Host-Environment Analysis of UX Harm
origin: Classical epidemiological triad (19th-20th c.); adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Decomposes a UX harm into agent (pattern), host (user susceptibility), environment (platform, context) and mechanism to target interventions at each.
description: The epidemiological triad holds that disease results from interaction of an agent, a susceptible host and an environment that brings them together. The treatise uses this structure throughout: a dark pattern is the agent, the user the host, the platform and situation the environment, with cognitive bias exploitation as the mechanism of action and modifying factors altering susceptibility. Structuring a harm this way prevents single-cause thinking ('users should read more carefully') and maps interventions to each vertex: remove or weaken the agent (redesign), protect the host (literacy, defaults, accessibility) and change the environment (platform rules, regulation, timing). The roach motel case study in the treatise is an exemplar of this analysis.
steps: Define the harm outcome precisely with a case definition.
Characterise the agent: pattern features and the cognitive or structural mechanism it exploits.
Characterise hosts: which users are susceptible and why (literacy, stress, age, disability).
Characterise the environment: platform, context, incentives, time pressure.
Gather evidence for each element from research, logs and literature.
List interventions per vertex and estimate feasibility and impact.
outputs: Triad map of the harm, evidence summary, intervention matrix by vertex.
useWhen: Analysing dark patterns, persistent harms, or failures whose causes span design, users and context.
avoidWhen: Simple defects with a single obvious cause.
whyLost: Epidemiological reasoning never migrated into UX analysis.
whereToUse: Trust and safety, dark pattern audits, financial harm reviews, accessibility harm analysis.
example: Triad analysis of 'accidental international roaming charges' identifies the agent (buried toggle default on), hosts (infrequent travellers) and environment (arrival stress), leading to arrival-time prompts plus default-off.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rothman KJ, Greenland S & Lash TL (2008) Modern Epidemiology
Gordis L (2014) Epidemiology. 5th ed
reference: Gordis L (2014) Epidemiology. 5th ed. Elsevier Saunders.

name: AI as instrument, not analyst
aka: Instrumental stance on AI in research
origin: Epistemological position developed in qualitative methods debates from 2023; draws on the idea of the researcher as instrument in qualitative inquiry (Lincoln and Guba, 1985)
summary: An epistemological stance that treats AI as a measurement and processing instrument to be calibrated and validated, while interpretation, judgement and accountability for findings remain with researchers.
description: In qualitative research the researcher is traditionally the primary instrument, bringing reflexivity and accountability to interpretation. Framing AI as an analyst blurs responsibility and invites unexamined authority for fluent outputs. Framing it as an instrument means it is specified (model, version, prompts), calibrated (validated against human judgement on samples), scoped (used for tasks like transcription, segmentation and deductive tagging), and reported like any instrument, with its error characteristics. Interpretive moves such as abstraction, theorising, judging significance and recommending action stay with people who can be accountable. The stance is a governance principle that shapes pipeline design, checkpoints and reporting.
steps: Write a short statement of AI's role for the project, listing tasks delegated and tasks reserved for researchers.
Specify the AI instrument fully: tool, model version, prompts, parameters.
Calibrate against human judgement on samples and report its error characteristics.
Reserve interpretive decisions (themes, theory, significance, recommendations) for researchers and record who made them.
Maintain reflexive memos on how AI outputs may have shaped researchers' thinking.
Report AI's role as an instrument in methods sections and stakeholder briefings.
outputs: A role statement, instrument specification, calibration results and documented human interpretive decisions.
useWhen: Setting governance for any AI-assisted research practice, and when stakeholders treat AI summaries as findings.
avoidWhen: Not a rejection of AI assistance; avoid using the stance to justify unvalidated automation by calling it an 'instrument' without calibration.
whyLost: A new framing; tool marketing presents AI as an analyst or 'insight generator', so the instrumental stance must be argued for actively.
whereToUse: Research operations policies, academic UX, regulated research and leadership education about AI insight tools.
example: A product leadership team asks for 'AI insights' from a vendor tool. The research lead reframes it as an instrument, calibrates its tagging against researcher coding (kappa 0.62, below threshold) and limits its use to search and retrieval until it improves.
sources: Local Whisper (privacy)
data anonymisation pipeline
IRR reporting standards
publication disclosure norms
Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985) Naturalistic Inquiry
Braun, V. & Clarke, V. (2022) Thematic Analysis: A Practical Guide
The Inquiry Series, C14 — Ethical Constraints & Epistemological Limits of AI-Assisted Qualitative Research
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985) Naturalistic Inquiry

name: AI Explainability Auditing for UX
donor: Machine learning interpretability and human-AI interaction
origin: Explainable AI techniques such as LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016) and SHAP (Lundberg and Lee, 2017); human-centred XAI by Liao et al. (2020)
summary: Audits whether AI explanations help users understand, calibrate trust in and correct AI outputs, testing explanation types against users' actual questions and decisions.
description: Machine learning teams generate explanations such as feature importance, SHAP values, LIME local explanations, saliency maps and counterfactuals mainly for developers. An explainability audit asks whether these serve users. It starts by eliciting users' explanation needs, for example why this output, why not another, what would change it, and how confident the system is, using Liao's XAI question bank. It then evaluates candidate explanations on comprehension, decision accuracy, trust calibration (do users rely on the AI when it is right and override it when wrong), time and perceived usefulness, ideally in controlled studies with known correct and incorrect AI outputs. Explanations that increase trust without improving calibration are flagged as harmful. Regulatory requirements, such as the right to explanation under GDPR and the EU AI Act, add urgency.
steps: Explainability UX audit:
Identify every AI decision point visible to users.
(2) For each, apply: a SHAP or LIME explanation (which features drove this decision?).
(3) Translate the technical explanation into user-facing language.
(4) Test: do users understand the explanation? Can they predict how to change the outcome? User explainability score = % who can accurately predict what change would change the AI's output.
outputs: Inventory of user explanation needs, evaluation of explanation types on comprehension and calibration, flagged misleading explanations, and recommended explanation designs.
useWhen: AI products making consequential recommendations: credit, hiring, healthcare, insurance, content moderation and enterprise decision support.
avoidWhen: When the AI's outputs are low-stakes and easily verified by users, or when no model access exists to generate faithful explanations; then focus on error recovery design.
whyLost: Explainability is studied by ML researchers and a small human-AI interaction community; product UX teams rarely have model access or methods to evaluate explanations with users.
whereToUse: AI product UX research, recommendation system design, automated decision UX (credit, content moderation, medical AI), LLM interface design.
example: A lender's credit-limit model shows SHAP-based reasons to applicants. An audit with 60 participants finds the explanations raise trust but not understanding, while a counterfactual explanation ('a limit of £2,000 would be possible with 6 more months of history') improves both.
sources: AI for Humans — Jeff Heaton
Ribeiro, Singh & Guestrin, 'Why should I trust you?' Explaining the predictions of any classifier (KDD 2016)
Liao, Gruen & Miller, Questioning the AI: Informing design practices for explainable AI user experiences (CHI 2020)
Lundberg & Lee, A unified approach to interpreting model predictions (NeurIPS 2017)
reference: Liao QV, Gruen D & Miller S (2020) Questioning the AI: Informing design practices for explainable AI user experiences. CHI 2020

name: AI objective function audit
origin: Goodhart's law (Charles Goodhart, 1975); Raji et al.'s internal algorithmic auditing framework, 2020; alignment literature (Christian, 2020)
summary: Examines what an AI system is actually optimised for, compares it with user and business values, and identifies where optimising the proxy harms the intended outcome.
description: Every recommender, ranking or personalisation system optimises an objective: clicks, engagement time, trades or conversions. These are proxies for what users and the business actually value, and Goodhart's law predicts divergence when they are optimised hard. An objective function audit documents the objective, training labels, reward signals and constraints; maps them against stated values (user wellbeing, financial health, informed decisions); and tests for divergence using behavioural and attitudinal data. It draws on algorithmic auditing frameworks and alignment research. Rigour comes from tracing objectives in code and documentation, interviewing model owners, gathering user evidence on outcomes, and proposing measurable alternative objectives or constraints.
steps: Document the system's objective, loss function, reward signals, training labels and constraints by interviewing model owners and reviewing documentation.
Articulate intended user and business values explicitly, drawing on research and policy.
Map each objective component to the values it is assumed to proxy and note where links are weak.
Gather evidence of divergence: compare optimised metrics with wellbeing, satisfaction or long-term outcomes for affected users.
Identify failure modes, such as engagement driven by anxiety or churn hidden behind short-term clicks.
Recommend revised objectives, constraints or guardrail metrics and a monitoring plan.
outputs: An audit report mapping objectives to values, evidence of divergence, failure modes and recommended objective changes and guardrails.
useWhen: Before launching or scaling AI-driven ranking, recommendation or nudging, and when metrics improve but user outcomes or sentiment worsen.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple rule-based features with no optimisation, or where model owners cannot share objective details; use external behavioural audits instead.
whyLost: Responsible AI work is often siloed in policy or ML teams, and UX researchers are rarely asked what systems optimise.
