whereToUse: Investment and trading recommendations, social and content feeds, health engagement nudges, AI assistants with engagement metrics.
example: An investment AI optimised for engagement increases logins by 20%, but interviews and surveys show rising anxiety and impulsive trades. The audit recommends a confidence-weighted objective and a wellbeing guardrail.
sources: The Alignment Problem (Brian Christian)
Artificial Intelligence for Humans (Jeff Heaton)
Methods Atlas (Vivek Gopinath)
Raji et al. (2020) Closing the AI accountability gap: defining an end-to-end framework for internal algorithmic auditing
The Alignment Problem (Christian)
AI for Humans (Heaton)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 58 — AI Explainability & Value Alignment Audit
reference: Raji, I. D. et al. (2020) Closing the AI accountability gap: defining an end-to-end framework for internal algorithmic auditing. FAT* '20, 33-44.

name: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
origin: Emerging practice with large language models, 2023 onward; builds on computer-assisted qualitative data analysis and content analysis reliability norms
summary: Applying a human-built codebook to large transcript corpora with an LLM, validated against human coding with kappa thresholds and human review of low-confidence output.
description: Large language models can apply qualitative codes at a scale no team can match, but they also produce plausible yet wrong labels. This method keeps theory and interpretation human. Researchers first build a codebook with definitions, inclusion and exclusion rules and examples, then human-code 20 to 25 percent of the corpus as a test set. The model is prompted to return structured output (code, supporting quote, confidence, rationale) for each segment, and human-AI agreement is computed; deployment proceeds only above a threshold such as kappa 0.70, with low agreement treated as evidence of codebook ambiguity. The model codes the rest, with periodic human spot checks and review of low-confidence segments. Humans produce the themes and conclusions.
steps: Develop the coding manual first: Code definitions, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and worked examples — exactly as for human coding.
Structured JSON output schema: {'{'}code_name, supporting_quote, confidence_score, rationale{'}'}. Enables systematic comparison with human codes.
Human baseline coding first: Human coders code 20–25% of the corpus. This becomes the IRR test set.
Calculate IRR human vs. AI: κ > 0.70 before deploying the AI on the remaining corpus. If κ < 0.70, revise coding instructions — the failure reveals ambiguity in your scheme.
AI codes remaining corpus with human spot-checking every 10th transcript. Flag segments with confidence < 0.7 for human review.
Human interpretation: The AI produces labelled segments. Humans produce themes, propositions, and the final analysis.
outputs: A validated codebook, human-AI agreement statistics, coded corpus with quotes and confidence scores, review logs, and human-authored themes.
useWhen: Large corpora (hundreds of interviews, thousands of tickets or open-ended responses) where a stable codebook exists or can be built.
avoidWhen: Small studies where human coding is quick, interpretive approaches such as IPA, or sensitive data that cannot be processed by external models without consent and safeguards.
whyLost: It is rapidly being adopted because LLMs make scale cheap; the risk is skipping human baselines and reliability checks.
whereToUse: Support ticket and review analysis, open-ended survey coding, research repositories, and large multi-market interview programmes.
example: A telecom codes 5,000 complaint transcripts. After human-AI kappa reaches 0.74 on 1,000 double-coded segments, the model codes the remainder and humans review the 8% flagged low-confidence before synthesis.
sources: AI for Humans (Heaton)
Anthropic Claude API (claude-sonnet-4-20250514)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology (Krippendorff)
reference: Krippendorff, K. (2018). Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology (4th ed.). Sage.

name: Alarm Flood Analysis (EEMUA 191 / ISA-18.2)
origin: EEMUA Publication 191 (1999) after the 1994 Texaco Milford Haven explosion; ANSI/ISA-18.2 (2009)
summary: Measures alarm and notification rates against benchmarks, identifies floods, chattering and stale alarms, and rationalises each alarm against a required operator response.
description: Process industries learned that operators drown when alarms exceed what a human can process. EEMUA 191 set benchmarks: an average of about one alarm per 10 minutes per operator is acceptable, more than 10 alarms in 10 minutes constitutes a flood, and every alarm must require a defined operator action. Analysis uses alarm logs to compute rates, top-ten 'bad actors', chattering alarms (repeated within seconds), standing alarms and priority distributions (recommended roughly 80% low, 15% medium, 5% high). Rationalisation then reviews each alarm's cause, consequence, required response and time available. Notifications, badges and AI alerts in digital products suffer exactly the same pathologies, and this is a ready-made quantitative method.
steps: Export notification or alert logs per user or operator with timestamps, type and priority.
Compute average rates per 10 minutes and per hour, peak 10-minute counts and the percentage of time in flood (>10 per 10 minutes).
Identify bad actors: the top 10 sources by volume, chattering alerts (repeats within 60 seconds) and standing alerts never cleared.
Check priority distribution against roughly 80/15/5 low/medium/high and look for priority inflation.
Rationalise each alert in a workshop: what action is required, how quickly, what happens if ignored; delete or demote alerts with no required action.
Re-measure rates and user response times after changes, and set ongoing monitoring targets.
outputs: Alarm/notification performance metrics, a bad-actor list, a rationalised alert catalogue with required actions and priorities.
useWhen: Users ignore or disable notifications, operators miss critical alerts, or a product sends many automated alerts.
avoidWhen: Products with very few notifications; standard usability testing suffices.
whyLost: Alarm management is an industrial discipline with standards UX designers never read. Product teams measure notification engagement rather than overload.
whereToUse: Observability and incident tools, security operations, clinical monitoring, fintech fraud queues, mobile push strategy.
example: An observability platform finds on-call engineers average 34 alerts per hour during incidents, with 60% from five chattering sources. Rationalisation removes alerts with no required action and adds hysteresis, reducing incident alert load by 70%.
sources: EEMUA Publication 191, Alarm Systems: A Guide to Design, Management and Procurement (3rd ed., 2013)
ANSI/ISA-18.2, Management of Alarm Systems for the Process Industries (2009/2016)
reference: EEMUA (2013). Publication 191: Alarm Systems. Engineering Equipment and Materials Users Association.

name: Algorithmic Experience Research
donor: Science and technology studies and social computing
origin: Algorithm awareness studies by Eslami et al. (2015); 'algorithmic experience' framing by Alvarado and Waern (2018)
summary: Longitudinal study of how people perceive, theorise about and are affected by recommendation feeds and automated decisions, combining log data with interviews.
description: Algorithmic experience research investigates the user side of algorithmic systems: whether people know an algorithm is shaping what they see, the folk theories they hold about it, how they try to steer it, and how its outputs affect behaviour, mood and wellbeing over time. Because effects accumulate slowly and are personalised, single-session usability tests miss them. Rigorous designs combine longitudinal diaries or experience sampling with logged exposure data, folk-theory elicitation interviews, and, where possible, controlled variation of the algorithm (for example a chronological feed holdout). Analysis links what people believe about the system to what it actually does, revealing misattribution, learned helplessness or gaming. The approach is well developed in social computing research but rarely operationalised in product UX teams.
steps: Define the algorithmic surface (feed ranking, recommendations, pricing, moderation) and the experience outcomes of interest (control, trust, wellbeing, diversity).
Recruit 15-30 participants and obtain consent to pair their exposure logs with self-reports.
Run baseline interviews eliciting folk theories: what the participant thinks drives what they see, and how they try to influence it.
Collect 2-6 weeks of diary or experience-sampling entries tied to specific algorithmic moments, alongside logged exposure.
Where feasible, introduce a controlled variation (for example a holdout with reduced personalisation) and compare experience measures.
Analyse gaps between folk theories and actual system behaviour, and link exposure patterns to experience outcomes.
Translate findings into transparency, control and ranking-objective recommendations.
outputs: Folk-theory taxonomy, longitudinal experience trajectories, exposure-outcome associations, and design recommendations for control and transparency.
useWhen: Products driven by feeds, recommendations or automated decisions where long-term wellbeing, trust or perceived control matter: social media, streaming, gig-work platforms, news.
avoidWhen: When you only need to tune ranking metrics (use online experiments) or when you cannot access logs, in which case limit claims to perceptions.
whyLost: Latent: Critical and growing area; limited standardized methods; primarily academic.
whereToUse: Social platforms; content recommendation; AI-driven personalization.
example: A food-delivery platform studies 20 couriers over four weeks pairing their dispatch logs with diaries. Couriers believe acceptance rate drives job allocation, which it does not, leading to unsafe acceptance of distant jobs; the team publishes allocation factors in-app.
sources: AI for Humans
The Alignment Problem
Eslami et al., 'I always assumed that I wasn't really that close to [her]' (CHI 2015)
Alvarado & Waern, Towards Algorithmic Experience (CHI 2018)
reference: Eslami M et al. (2015) 'I always assumed that I wasn't really that close to [her]': Reasoning about invisible algorithms in news feeds. CHI 2015

name: Analogical Reasoning Analysis for Onboarding
origin: Dedre Gentner's structure-mapping theory (1983); developmental work by Usha Goswami
summary: Analyses interface metaphors as structure mappings from a known source domain, identifying correct, missing and misleading relational correspondences to design onboarding that transfers knowledge.
description: Gentner's structure-mapping theory explains analogy as mapping relational structure, not surface features, from a familiar source to a new target. Goswami showed that even young children reason analogically when they know the source domain's relations. Interface metaphors (desktop, folders, wallet, cart, inbox) work the same way: users import the source's relations, and the analogy succeeds when relations hold and misleads when they do not. The method lists the source's key relations, maps each to the target system, and classifies them as valid, absent or misleading. Onboarding and design then reinforce valid mappings, explicitly flag misleading ones, and use worked comparisons that make relational similarity salient, which research shows improves transfer. Testing checks whether users predict system behaviour from the metaphor correctly.
steps: Test analogical transfer for any new interface concept: teach users the concept in one interface context (source).
Present an unfamiliar but structurally analogous interface (target).
Measure: how much does source learning transfer to target performance?
High transfer (> 70% performance improvement vs. control) = the analogy is structurally sound.
Low transfer = the analogy's structure doesn't match the target domain.
outputs: Source-to-target relation mapping table with valid, absent and misleading correspondences; prediction-test results; onboarding content built on comparisons.
useWhen: Introducing new product categories, naming features with metaphors, onboarding novices, and diagnosing errors caused by inappropriate metaphors.
avoidWhen: When users are already experts in the target domain, or the interface uses no metaphor; use task analysis or usability testing.
whyLost: Analogy research flourished in cognitive and developmental psychology, but UX treats metaphors as copywriting or visual choices rather than testable structure mappings.
whereToUse: Onboarding design, tutorial design, cross-product migration, help documentation, AI interface explanation design.
example: A crypto wallet app uses a 'wallet' metaphor, but mapping shows the misleading relation that losing the wallet means losing only its contents, not access to funds held elsewhere. Onboarding adds a comparison to a house key to correct recovery-phrase expectations.
sources: Wiley-Blackwell Handbook of Childhood Cognitive Development — Usha Goswami
Gentner, Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy (Cognitive Science, 1983)
Goswami, Analogical Reasoning in Children (1992)
reference: Gentner D (1983) Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science 7(2):155-170

name: Analogical transfer test
origin: Dedre Gentner's structure-mapping theory (1983) and Gick and Holyoak's analogical problem solving studies (1980, 1983)
summary: Tests which relational inferences users carry from a source domain metaphor into a product, revealing correct transfer, missing transfer and harmful over-transfer.
description: When a product borrows a metaphor (wallet, folder, cart, inbox, assistant), users infer how it behaves by mapping relations from the familiar source domain onto the new target. Structure-mapping theory predicts that people transfer relational structure, not surface features, and that they may also transfer relations the designer never intended. An analogical transfer test presents the metaphor and asks users to predict system behaviour in scenarios that probe specific relations: is money in the wallet insured, can someone take it, does it disappear if the phone is lost? Answers are scored against the system's actual behaviour. Rigour comes from deriving probes systematically from the source-domain relational structure, including probes for intended, unintended and absent mappings, and from comparing alternative metaphors on the same probe set.
steps: Map the source domain's key relations (for a wallet: carried on the person, can be lost or stolen, holds cash, no interest, no institution behind it) and the target system's actual relations.
Classify each relation as intended transfer, harmful transfer (true in source, false in system) or missing transfer (true in system, absent in source).
Write 8 to 15 scenario probes, each targeting one relation, phrased as predictions: 'Your phone is stolen. What happens to the money?'
Present the metaphor in context to 15 to 30 participants per segment and collect predictions and confidence ratings (1 to 5) for each probe.
Score each prediction as correct or incorrect against system behaviour and compute per-relation transfer rates, flagging harmful transfers held by more than 20% of participants with high confidence.

Repeat with one or two alternative metaphors on the same probes and choose the metaphor with the highest correct transfer and lowest confident harmful transfer, or plan explicit explanation for the remaining gaps.
outputs: A relational mapping table, per-probe transfer and confidence rates for each candidate metaphor, and a list of harmful over-transfers requiring design or onboarding fixes.
useWhen: Choosing or defending a core product metaphor; users hold wrong expectations about security, reversibility or ownership; introducing novel concepts such as AI agents or digital assets.
avoidWhen: The concept is already well understood without metaphor, or you only need label findability; use tree testing or comprehension testing instead.
whyLost: Analogical reasoning research stayed in cognitive science and education, while UX metaphor critique (for example of the desktop) remained rhetorical rather than experimental.
whereToUse: Digital money and crypto products, cloud storage, AI agent and assistant design, health records, smart-home automations.
example: Users of a 'digital wallet' predicted that a lost phone meant lost money (67%) and that balances earned no protection. The system was account-based and recoverable; the team kept the term but added a recovery explanation at onboarding, and the harmful transfer fell to 18%.
sources: Pocket Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
Embodied Mind (Varela)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 20 — Semiotics, Icons & Cross-Cultural Sign Failure
reference: Gentner, D. (1983). Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science, 7(2), 155–170.

name: Analysis of Competing Hypotheses
origin: Richards Heuer, CIA, 1970s; Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (1999)
summary: Evaluates evidence against all plausible hypotheses in a matrix, focusing on disconfirmation, to counter confirmation bias in explaining what is happening.
description: Analysts, like researchers, tend to pick a favoured explanation and collect supporting evidence. ACH lists all reasonable hypotheses, lists significant evidence and arguments, and marks in a matrix whether each item is consistent, inconsistent or not applicable to each hypothesis. The key insight is that evidence consistent with all hypotheses has no diagnostic value; hypotheses are ranked by how much evidence is inconsistent with them, not consistent. Analysts then assess sensitivity to critical evidence, identify missing evidence that would discriminate, and report conclusions with milestones for re-evaluation. It is a rigorous structure for UX synthesis questions like 'why did activation drop?'.
steps: Brainstorm all plausible hypotheses with a diverse group, including unpopular ones.
List evidence and assumptions: data, findings, logs, absence of expected evidence.
Build the matrix and rate each item's consistency with each hypothesis; note diagnosticity.
Refine the matrix: delete non-diagnostic evidence, add hypotheses if needed.
Rank hypotheses by inconsistent evidence; test sensitivity to a few critical items and their reliability.
Report conclusions with relative likelihoods and define indicators that would change the judgement.
outputs: An ACH matrix, ranked hypotheses, diagnostic evidence, evidence gaps and monitoring indicators.
useWhen: Explaining ambiguous phenomena (metric drops, puzzling behaviour, mixed research results) where several explanations compete.
avoidWhen: Questions with a single obvious explanation, or purely generative exploration.
whyLost: Structured analytic techniques remained in intelligence agencies; UX synthesis relies on affinity mapping and narrative.
whereToUse: Root cause investigations, competitive analysis, research synthesis disputes, AI behaviour investigations.
example: Activation fell 9%. ACH across five hypotheses shows most evidence is consistent with all of them, but the timing of the decline in one acquisition channel is inconsistent with a UX cause, pointing to traffic mix change.
sources: Heuer, Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (1999), CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence
Heuer & Pherson, Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis (2nd ed., 2014)
reference: Heuer, R. J. (1999). Psychology of Intelligence Analysis. CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence.

name: Analytic Generalisation
donor: Case study and qualitative social science methodology
origin: Robert K. Yin, developed in his case study writing and restated in Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2011; 2nd ed. 2016); contrasted with statistical generalisation by Bromley, Burawoy, Mitchell, Small and others
summary: A two-step argument that generalises findings from a small qualitative study to concepts and theory, and then from those concepts to other similar situations, instead of to a population.
description: Yin argues that every study, including a laboratory experiment, is a single study, and that the way findings travel beyond it is usually not statistical. Analytic generalisation is a two-step process. First, the researcher makes a conceptual claim: the findings are shown to inform a particular set of concepts, theoretical constructs or a hypothesised sequence of events, ideally ones already present in the literature. Second, the same concepts are applied to argue that other similar situations are implicated. The claim is an argument, not a proof, so it has to be built carefully and be resistant to logical challenge, and it is much stronger when plausible rival explanations have been actively tested and rejected. Yin distinguishes it from transferability, which makes a more modest claim that depends on how similar the sending and receiving contexts are. For UX teams this addresses the recurring objection that eight interviews cannot generalise: the answer is to state which mechanism or concept the study supports or challenges, show the evidence, and say which other products, segments or flows share that mechanism, rather than implying population percentages.
steps: Before fieldwork, name the concepts, theories or hypothesised sequence of events the study could inform
Identify plausible rival explanations and plan to collect evidence that could support them
After analysis, state whether and how the findings supported or challenged each concept, citing the evidence
Test and document the rivals; reject them only where diligent search found no supporting evidence
Raise the claim to the conceptual level and write it as a mechanism, not a frequency
Name the other situations (products, segments, flows) that share the mechanism and argue why the concept applies there
Treat the generalised claim as a working hypothesis to be checked by later studies
outputs: A written generalisation argument linking findings to named concepts, the rivals tested, and a list of other situations to which the concepts are claimed to apply.
useWhen: Small-sample qualitative or single-case studies whose findings need to inform decisions beyond the specific participants, product or site studied.
avoidWhen: The decision needs a population estimate such as prevalence or market size; use a sample survey or analytics instead.
whyLost: UX reporting tends to borrow survey language (most users, 6 of 8) and so either overclaims or apologises for sample size; the theoretical framing analytic generalisation needs is seldom taught in practitioner training.
whereToUse: Discovery research reports, single-customer or single-market case studies, research that must justify reuse across product lines.
example: Interviews with ten clinic administrators show that a scheduling tool is abandoned when it shifts accountability for double bookings onto front-desk staff. The team frames this as a blame-shifting mechanism, rules out the rival that the interface was simply hard to learn, and argues the same mechanism will apply to the company's rota and shift-swap products.
sources: Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2016). Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.

name: Analytic Hierarchy Process
origin: Thomas Saaty, 1970s (The Analytic Hierarchy Process, 1980)
summary: Structures a decision into a hierarchy of criteria, derives weights from pairwise comparisons and checks the consistency of judgements.
description: AHP decomposes a complex decision (choosing among design directions, vendors or roadmap items) into goal, criteria, sub-criteria and alternatives. Stakeholders compare elements pairwise on Saaty's 1-9 scale; the principal eigenvector of each comparison matrix gives weights, and the consistency ratio (target below 0.10) flags incoherent judgements. Weights combine to rank alternatives. Group judgements can be aggregated by geometric mean. AHP has known criticisms (rank reversal) but makes stakeholder priorities explicit, auditable and testable, a strong upgrade on informal prioritisation meetings.
steps: Define the decision goal, criteria (e.g. user value, effort, risk, strategic fit) and alternatives.
Build the hierarchy and confirm criteria are independent and complete.
Collect pairwise comparisons from stakeholders using the 1-9 scale.
Compute weights (eigenvector) and the consistency ratio; revisit judgements above 0.10.
Score alternatives on each criterion (pairwise or rated), synthesise and rank.
Run sensitivity analysis on weights and share the rationale transparently.
outputs: Criteria weights, consistency ratios, ranked alternatives and sensitivity analyses.
useWhen: Multi-stakeholder prioritisation or design direction decisions with several competing criteria.
avoidWhen: Many alternatives (pairwise burden grows quickly) or decisions dominated by a single criterion.
whyLost: Product teams use simple scoring frameworks (RICE, effort-impact) without weighting rigour or consistency checks.
whereToUse: Roadmap prioritisation, vendor and tool selection, design concept selection, research portfolio planning.
example: A health platform's leadership weights patient safety, clinician time and revenue via AHP. Consistency checks expose contradictory judgements from one executive, and the final ranking moves a safety feature to the top.
sources: Saaty, The Analytic Hierarchy Process (1980)
Saaty, Decision making with the analytic hierarchy process (2008), International Journal of Services Sciences
Feature Prioritization Methods (slide deck)
reference: Saaty, T. L. (1980). The Analytic Hierarchy Process. McGraw-Hill.

name: Analytic Induction
origin: Florian Znaniecki, 1934; developed by Alfred Lindesmith (1947) and Donald Cressey (1953)
summary: Iteratively revising a hypothesis or redefining the phenomenon case by case until a proposition holds for every examined case without exception.
description: Analytic induction is a case-by-case logic for testing explanations with qualitative data. The researcher defines the phenomenon, states a working hypothesis about its causes, and examines cases one at a time. Each case that does not fit forces either reformulation of the hypothesis or a justified redefinition of the phenomenon to exclude it; negative cases are never discarded silently. The process continues until a universal statement holds for all cases examined, and the final report documents the trajectory of reformulations and the scope conditions. Classic studies (Lindesmith on opiate addiction, Cressey on embezzlement) showed that small samples can support strong causal propositions when every exception is confronted.
steps: Formulate a provisional definition of the phenomenon to be explained and a working hypothesis about its causes or conditions.
Examine a case. Does the case fit the hypothesis? If yes: proceed to next case.

If the case does not fit: either (a) reformulate the hypothesis to accommodate the case, or (b) redefine the phenomenon to exclude the case (and justify this exclusion). Do not discard the negative case.
Continue until a universal proposition is reached: a statement that holds for all examined cases without exception.
Report: state the final hypothesis, document the trajectory of reformulation, and specify the scope conditions (for what kinds of cases does the hypothesis hold?).
outputs: A final hypothesis that holds for all cases, a documented reformulation history, and explicit scope conditions.
useWhen: When you have a sharply defined outcome (adopted, abandoned, made a critical error) and want a necessary-condition explanation from a modest number of rich cases.
avoidWhen: When outcomes are probabilistic or multi-causal at scale; use regression, qualitative comparative analysis or cross-case analysis instead.
whyLost: Criticised in sociology for seeking universal laws and largely displaced by grounded theory, it never entered UX curricula.
whereToUse: Root-cause investigation of critical failures, safety incidents, and conversion or adoption outcomes in B2B products with small numbers of high-value accounts.
example: A SaaS team studies 14 enterprise accounts that churned. The first hypothesis (no executive sponsor) fails on two cases; reformulating to 'no sponsor and no admin who completed onboarding' holds across all 14, giving a clear intervention target.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Rocking Qualitative Social Science
The Polish Peasant / The Method of Sociology (Znaniecki)
Other People's Money (Cressey)
reference: Znaniecki, F. (1934). The Method of Sociology. Farrar & Rinehart.

name: Analytic Memo Writing
origin: Glaser & Strauss, 1967; Strauss, 1987 (Qualitative Analysis for Social Scientists)
summary: Writing dated, code-linked memos throughout analysis as the primary act of theorising, also creating an audit trail of interpretive decisions.
description: Memoing treats writing as thinking. Instead of documenting conclusions reached elsewhere, the analyst writes continuously: a code memo for every new code (scope, properties, illustrative incidents), category memos during axial coding, free-form theoretical memos about surprises and contradictions, and methodological memos recording sampling and procedural decisions. Memos are dated and tagged to the codes they discuss, so they can be sorted later into the skeleton of a report or theory. The practice slows premature closure, captures fleeting insights before they are lost, and makes interpretation traceable. Methodological memos also satisfy Lincoln and Guba's dependability criterion by forming part of the audit trail.
steps: Write a memo every time a new code is created. Every time.
Write a memo every time you notice a connection between two codes.
Write a memo every time you encounter data that surprises you or challenges your expectation.
Date every memo and tag it with the codes it relates to.
Treat memo-writing as primary analysis, not documentation of analysis done elsewhere.
outputs: A searchable corpus of code, category, theoretical and methodological memos that can be sorted into report structure and serve as an audit trail.
useWhen: Any qualitative analysis beyond a quick debrief, especially multi-week studies, team analysis, or work that must be audited or reused later.
avoidWhen: Very rapid evaluative tests where findings are logged directly as issues; even then, a short methodological memo is advisable.
whyLost: Analysis moved into collaborative whiteboards where only clusters survive, and the reflective writing that produced them is rarely kept or valued.
whereToUse: Research repositories, long-running discovery programmes, AI-assisted analysis workflows (to record human interpretive decisions), and regulated research needing audit trails.
example: While coding interviews about an insurance claims app, a researcher writes a memo noting that 'waiting' is described as active monitoring, not passivity. Sorting memos later shows this idea anchors the final model of claim anxiety.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Qualitative Analysis for Social Scientists (Strauss)
Constructing Grounded Theory (Charmaz)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 26 — Grounded Theory — Generating Theory from Data
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Charmaz, K. (2014). Constructing Grounded Theory (2nd ed.). Sage.

extra.Types of Memo: Code memo: Written for a specific code. Describes: what the code covers, its properties and dimensions, incidents that illustrate it, and how it relates to other codes. Written every time a new code is created. Category memo: Written for an emerging category during axial coding. Explores the category's properties (what makes something an instance of this category?) and its relationship to causal conditions, contexts, and consequences. Theoretical memo: Free-form thinking about theoretical connections, surprises, contradictions, and emerging propositions. The most analytically valuable memos. No format requirements — the goal is to think in writing. Methodological memo: Documents decisions about sampling, analysis procedures, and deviations from plan. Creates the audit trail that Lincoln & Guba's dependability criterion requires.

name: Anchoring Vignettes
donor: Political science and health survey research
origin: Gary King, Christopher Murray, Joshua Salomon and Ajay Tandon, 2004
summary: Respondents rate short fixed scenarios on the same scale as themselves, allowing correction for groups using the response scale differently.
description: When users in different countries or segments rate 'ease of use' on a 1-5 scale, differences may reflect different interpretations of the scale (differential item functioning), not experiences. Anchoring vignettes describe hypothetical people or situations at fixed levels of the construct. Because the vignettes are identical for everyone, differences in how they are rated reveal each group's response scale. Nonparametric methods recode self-ratings relative to vignette ratings; parametric models (CHOPIT) estimate thresholds. This is the leading solution for cross-cultural and cross-segment comparability of self-report scales.
steps: Write 3-5 vignettes describing fixed levels of the construct (e.g. users with varying difficulty completing a task).
Ask respondents to rate themselves and each vignette on the same scale, randomising vignette order.
Check vignette equivalence and response consistency (vignettes rated in expected order).
Recode self-ratings relative to vignettes (nonparametric C-scores) or fit a CHOPIT model.
Compare groups on corrected scores and report how conclusions change.
Retain vignettes for future waves to monitor scale-use drift.
outputs: DIF-corrected comparisons across groups, threshold estimates and vignette diagnostics.
useWhen: Comparing self-reported experience across countries, cultures, age groups or professions.
avoidWhen: Within-group comparisons over time with stable populations, or when objective measures exist.
whyLost: It is published in political science and health metrics, and global UX programmes rarely address scale-use differences.
whereToUse: Global satisfaction programmes, cross-market benchmarks, international health app outcomes, B2B surveys across roles.
example: A global CSAT programme shows Japan lowest. Anchoring vignettes reveal Japanese respondents rate identical vignettes lower; after correction Japan ranks mid-table, redirecting investment.
sources: King, Murray, Salomon & Tandon, Enhancing the validity and cross-cultural comparability of measurement in survey research (2004), American Political Science Review
King & Wand, Comparing incomparable survey responses (2007), Political Analysis
reference: King, G., et al. (2004). American Political Science Review, 98(1), 191-207.

name: ANOVA for Multi-Design Comparisons (One-Way and Two-Way)
summary: Tests whether three or more designs differ on a continuous measure, and whether two factors interact.
description: When comparing more than two designs, running every pairwise t-test inflates false positives. ANOVA tests all groups at once by comparing variation between groups to variation within them (the F-statistic). Two-way ANOVA adds a second factor, such as device or experience level, and tests their interaction: does the new design help novices more than experts? Significant results are followed by planned contrasts or corrected post-hoc comparisons. Bruce and Bruce also show a resampling (permutation) version that avoids distributional assumptions.
steps: Define factors and levels (for example, design A/B/C by device desktop/mobile).
Log-transform task times; check group variances are not wildly different.
Run one-way or two-way ANOVA and read the F tests for main effects and interactions.
Follow significant effects with corrected pairwise comparisons (Tukey, Holm, Bonferroni).
Report effect sizes (partial eta squared) and plots of group means with intervals.
outputs: Tests of differences among several designs and of interactions between factors.
useWhen: Three or more design variants, or two crossed factors.
avoidWhen: Binary outcomes (use logistic regression or chi-square) or only two groups (a t-test is simpler).
whyLost: Not lost, but UX teams often avoid multi-arm studies or analyse them with multiple t-tests.
whereToUse: Design explorations with several prototypes, multi-variant tests, device-by-design studies.
example: Three navigation prototypes on two devices: the two-way ANOVA shows no overall design effect but a strong interaction, as the mega-menu fails only on mobile.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Sauro & Lewis (2016), chapter 10; Bruce & Bruce (2017), Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, chapter 3.

name: Anthropometric Analysis
origin: Military human engineering, 1940s-1970s; Pheasant (1986)
summary: Uses population body-dimension data and percentile limits to size reach, grip, touch targets and viewing geometry for the intended user range.
description: Anthropometric analysis designs for the range of human bodies using population databases of dimensions such as finger breadth, hand length, reach envelope and eye height. Designers set design limits (often 5th to 95th percentile of the target population) and check that clearances, reaches and target sizes accommodate them. The treatise lists anthropometric databases among the rigorous human factors methods UX abandoned. In digital products it governs touch target sizing, thumb reach zones on large phones, wearable fit, kiosk height and XR interaction volumes. Rigour comes from using data for the actual target population (age, sex, nationality, disability) rather than designing for an imaginary average user.
steps: Define the user population, including age range, regions and disability groups.
Identify the body dimensions that constrain the design (for example fingertip width, thumb reach, standing eye height).
Obtain percentile data from a relevant anthropometric database or measure a sample.
Set accommodation targets, commonly 5th-95th percentile, or wider for safety-critical products.
Check designs with digital human models or physical mock-ups at the boundary percentiles.
Document accommodation achieved and residual exclusion.
outputs: Design limits table, reach and target-size specifications, accommodation percentage.
useWhen: Touch, wearable, kiosk, automotive and XR products where body dimensions constrain use.
avoidWhen: Purely cognitive or content problems; screen-only desktop software rarely needs it.
whyLost: UX grew from graphic design and software, not ergonomics engineering, and assumed screens removed the body from the problem.
whereToUse: Large-phone thumb zones, smartwatches, ticket kiosks, in-car touchscreens, VR controllers, accessible public terminals.
example: A transit agency's kiosk places the payment slot at a height that only 60% of wheelchair users can reach; percentile analysis sets a new range accommodating 95%.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Pheasant S & Haslegrave CM (2006) Bodyspace: Anthropometry, Ergonomics and the Design of Work
Parkinson MB et al. on design for human variability
reference: Pheasant S & Haslegrave CM (2006) Bodyspace: Anthropometry, Ergonomics and the Design of Work. 3rd ed. CRC Press.

name: Anthropometric Percentile Accommodation Analysis
origin: Military anthropometric surveys (1940s-1960s); codified by Stephen Pheasant (Bodyspace, 1986)
summary: Uses population body-dimension data to design for a target percentage of users, typically the 5th to 95th percentile, and checks combined accommodation.
description: Anthropometry provides distributions of body dimensions such as hand length, finger breadth, reach and eye height for defined populations. Designers choose the limiting user for each dimension (smallest for reach, largest for clearance) and design for a target range. A key subtlety is that accommodating 90% on each of several dimensions accommodates far fewer people on all of them simultaneously, so multivariate methods or digital human models are needed. For digital products, the method applies to touch target size, thumb reach zones, wearable fit, kiosk heights and VR headset adjustment, and it forces explicit decisions about who is excluded, an inclusive design question with numbers.
steps: Identify the target population and source matching anthropometric data (age, sex, nationality, disability).
List the design-relevant dimensions and the limiting user for each (e.g. 5th percentile thumb reach, 95th percentile finger pad width).
Calculate percentile values with appropriate clothing or posture corrections.
Assess multivariate accommodation by simulation or boundary manikins, as univariate 5-95 limits exclude more than 10% combined.
Prototype at the limiting dimensions and test with participants recruited at the extremes.
Document the percentage accommodated and who remains excluded, with adjustable or alternative options for them.
outputs: Design dimension specifications, accommodation percentages, a list of excluded groups and mitigation options.
useWhen: Physical products, wearables, kiosks, automotive HMIs, touch-target sizing and one-handed reach zones.
avoidWhen: Purely software decisions without physical dimensions.
whyLost: Digital UX treats bodies as interchangeable cursor operators and adopts platform guidelines without knowing their anthropometric basis.
whereToUse: Mobile thumb zones for large phones, smartwatch UIs, ATMs and kiosks, VR and AR devices, accessible hardware.
example: A bank sizes its new ATM screen and keypad height using wheelchair-user reach data, accommodating 95% of seated users instead of the previous design that excluded most of them.
sources: Pheasant & Haslegrave, Bodyspace: Anthropometry, Ergonomics and the Design of Work (3rd ed., 2006)
ISO 7250-1:2017 Basic human body measurements for technological design
reference: Pheasant, S., & Haslegrave, C. M. (2006). Bodyspace (3rd ed.). CRC Press.

name: Anticipatory Failure Determination (AFD)
donor: Systems engineering / TRIZ inventive problem solving
origin: Boris Zlotin, Alla Zusman and colleagues (Ideation International), 1990s, based on Altshuller's TRIZ
summary: Inverts failure analysis by asking how one could deliberately make the system fail, then uses resource analysis to find and block those routes.
description: Listed in the treatise's borrowing matrix for systems engineering, AFD applies TRIZ to failure. Instead of asking 'what might go wrong?', which is limited by imagination and optimism, analysts take a subversion stance: 'how could we make this fail?' They then search for the resources (substances, fields, time, user behaviours, system states) in the system that would enable that failure, and design out the routes. For UX, the subversive question becomes 'how would we design this flow to make users lose money, leak data or give up?', a stance that surfaces dark-pattern-like risks and abuse cases that conventional reviews miss.
steps: Define the undesired outcome (for example user unknowingly shares location).
Reformulate as an invention problem: how could we deliberately cause it?
Brainstorm subversion scenarios using existing system resources and user behaviours.
Check which scenarios are already possible in the current design.
Design countermeasures that remove the enabling resources.
Re-run subversion on the revised design.
outputs: Subversion scenarios, resource inventory, countermeasures.
useWhen: Anticipating misuse, abuse, privacy and safety failures; red-teaming designs and AI features.
avoidWhen: Mature, well-characterised failures already covered by FMEA data.
whyLost: TRIZ is niche even in engineering; UX never adopted structured inventive methods.
whereToUse: Trust and safety, privacy-by-design, AI red-teaming, child safety features, fraud prevention.
example: Asked 'how could we make users accidentally publish private notes?', a team finds a share link inherited by duplicated notes, and fixes it before launch.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kaplan S, Visnepolschi S, Zlotin B & Zusman A (1999) New Tools for Failure and Risk Analysis: Anticipatory Failure Determination and the Theory of Scenario Structuring. Ideation International
Altshuller G (1984) Creativity as an Exact Science
Kaplan, Visnepolschi, Zlotin & Zusman, New Tools for Failure and Risk Analysis: Anticipatory Failure Determination and the Theory of Scenario Structuring (1999), Ideation International
Savransky, Engineering of Creativity (2000)
reference: Kaplan S et al. (1999) New Tools for Failure and Risk Analysis: Anticipatory Failure Determination (AFD). Ideation International.

name: App Usage Analytics as Qualitative Trace Data
origin: Trace ethnography (Geiger and Ribes, 2011) and qualitative web analytics practice
summary: Reads behavioural logs, session paths, errors and abandonment points as qualitative evidence of intent and struggle, reconstructing session narratives rather than only counting events.
description: Digital trace data — logs, clicks, navigation paths, search queries, error patterns, abandonment points — is usually treated as quantitative. But trace data can also be analysed qualitatively: as evidence of users' intentions, confusions, mental models, and strategies. The key shift is from counting events to interpreting patterns of events as evidence of underlying experience. This is 'qualitative in spirit even when the data is structured' — the analyst is asking 'what does this pattern mean?' rather than 'how often does this occur?'
steps: Session narrative reading: For a sample of individual sessions, reconstruct a narrative of what the user was trying to do: what problem were they solving? Where did they encounter difficulty? How did they respond to difficulty?

Path analysis as intention mapping: What navigation paths do users take? Which paths suggest clear intention? Which suggest confusion, search, or guessing? The shape of a path is evidence of a mental model.
Error pattern analysis: Which errors recur across users? What do they reveal about shared misunderstandings or failed affordances? Errors are qualitative data about the user-interface mismatch.

Abandonment context analysis: For sessions that end in abandonment: what was the user trying to do? At what point did they give up? What preceded the abandonment? This sequence is the qualitative story of a failed experience.

Triangulate with interview data: Use the patterns identified in trace data as prompts for qualitative interviews: 'I can see that lots of users do X at this point — does that match your experience? What were you thinking when you did that?'
outputs: Reconstructed session narratives, path-based intention hypotheses, recurring error and abandonment contexts, and interview probes grounded in observed behaviour.
useWhen: You have rich event or session data and need to understand what users were trying to do when metrics change, or to generate grounded hypotheses before interviews.
avoidWhen: You need to quantify prevalence or test causal impact; use product analytics or A/B testing. Logs cannot reveal motivations alone, so do not substitute this for talking to users.
whyLost: Analytics and qualitative research sit in different teams and tools, so logs are aggregated into funnels while the individual session stories they contain are rarely read.
whereToUse: SaaS onboarding, e-commerce checkout, search and navigation, AI assistant conversation logs, and churn investigations.
example: A SaaS team reads 40 session replays and event sequences from users who abandoned setup. Narratives show users repeatedly toggling between pricing and integrations, suggesting doubt about whether their tool is supported, which interviews confirm.
sources: Behavioral Drift Playbook (Gopinath)
Practical Web Analytics for User Experience (Beasley)
Social Media Research Methods
reference: Geiger, R. S. & Ribes, D. (2011). Trace ethnography: Following coordination through documentary practices. Proceedings of HICSS-44.

name: Appraisal Theory Analysis (Martin and White)
origin: James Martin and Peter White, 2005 (The Language of Evaluation), building on Michael Halliday's systemic functional linguistics
summary: Codes evaluative language into attitude (affect, judgement, appreciation), engagement and graduation to analyse how users express feelings and stance far more precisely than sentiment scores.
description: Sentiment analysis reduces evaluation to positive or negative. Appraisal theory distinguishes Attitude: Affect (emotions: 'I was furious'), Judgement (evaluating people's behaviour: 'they were dishonest') and Appreciation (evaluating things: 'the app is clunky'); Engagement (how voices are positioned: acknowledging, denying, conceding); and Graduation (force and focus: 'really', 'kind of'). This reveals, for example, whether complaints target the product (appreciation) or the company's integrity (judgement), which have different implications. Systematic coding with defined categories and reliability checks provides rigorous evaluative analysis of interviews, reviews and support conversations.
steps: Select texts and define the evaluative targets of interest (product, company, self, others).
Code instances of Affect, Judgement and Appreciation with polarity and target.
Code Engagement (monoglossic vs heteroglossic resources) and Graduation (force, focus).
Check inter-coder reliability on a subset and refine coding guidelines.
Aggregate patterns by target, segment and context; read examples in context.
Translate findings into design or communication actions (e.g. integrity concerns need trust repair, not UI polish).
outputs: Appraisal-coded corpus, distributions of attitude types by target, engagement patterns and interpretations.
useWhen: Analysing complaints, reviews, interviews or social media where the type of evaluation matters.
avoidWhen: When only broad positive or negative polarity is needed at large scale with no time for coding.
whyLost: Systemic functional linguistics is specialised and largely confined to linguistics and education research.
whereToUse: Complaint analysis, brand trust research, AI response tone evaluation, employee feedback.
example: Appraisal coding of 500 app reviews after a pricing change shows a shift from Appreciation of the app to negative Judgement of the company ('greedy', 'sneaky'), signalling a trust issue rather than a usability one.
sources: Martin & White, The Language of Evaluation: Appraisal in English (2005)
Halliday & Matthiessen, Halliday's Introduction to Functional Grammar (4th ed., 2014)
reference: Martin, J. R., & White, P. R. R. (2005). The Language of Evaluation. Palgrave Macmillan.

name: Appropriateness assessment for AI-assisted coding
aka: When AI coding is appropriate vs. inappropriate
origin: Emerging methodological debate from 2023 (e.g. Braun and Clarke's position on reflexive TA; Morgan, 2023)
summary: A structured judgement of whether AI coding fits a given study, based on epistemology, data sensitivity, task type and validation capacity, before any automation is used.
description: Not all qualitative work suits AI assistance. Deductive coding against a clear codebook, large corpora, and descriptive content analysis are better fits; reflexive thematic analysis, interpretative phenomenological analysis and work where researcher positionality is central are poor fits, because coding there is the researcher's own interpretive engagement. Data sensitivity, consent terms, participant vulnerability and language also matter, as does whether the team can validate outputs. A structured assessment makes the decision explicit and defensible, rather than defaulting to automation because tools are available. Rigour comes from documenting criteria, the decision and its rationale, and revisiting it if validation results are poor.
steps: Identify the analytic approach and its epistemology (e.g. deductive content analysis, codebook TA, reflexive TA, IPA).
Classify the task: deductive application of codes, inductive suggestion, summarisation or interpretation.
Assess data sensitivity, consent terms and participant vulnerability, and whether local processing is required.
Assess validation capacity: can humans code a 10-20% sample to measure agreement?
Decide: AI not used, AI as suggester only, or AI as primary coder with validation; document the rationale.
Revisit the decision if agreement falls below the pre-set threshold (e.g. kappa below 0.70) or new risks emerge.
outputs: A documented appropriateness decision with criteria, rationale and conditions for revisiting.
useWhen: Before any AI-assisted qualitative study, especially those to be published or involving sensitive data.
avoidWhen: Not needed for non-research uses such as meeting notes, but any output presented as research findings should go through it.
whyLost: Methodological guidance has lagged behind tool adoption, so most teams adopt AI coding without explicit fitness judgements.
whereToUse: Academic UX research, health and public-sector research, and research operations policies.
example: A team planning an IPA study of people living with chronic pain decides AI will only transcribe, not code, because interpretation is the method and data are sensitive. A parallel deductive analysis of 5,000 app reviews uses AI coding with validation.
sources: Local Whisper (privacy)
data anonymisation pipeline
IRR reporting standards
publication disclosure norms
Braun, V. & Clarke, V. (2022) Thematic Analysis: A Practical Guide
Morgan, D. L. (2023) Exploring the use of artificial intelligence for qualitative data analysis: The case of ChatGPT. International Journal of Qualitative Methods
The Inquiry Series, C14 — Ethical Constraints & Epistemological Limits of AI-Assisted Qualitative Research
reference: Morgan, D. L. (2023) Exploring the use of artificial intelligence for qualitative data analysis: The case of ChatGPT. International Journal of Qualitative Methods 22

name: Arts-Based Research
origin: Elliot Eisner, 1990s; Patricia Leavy, 2009
summary: Uses art-making (drawing, collage, poetry, performance) as a means of eliciting and representing experience that participants struggle to put into words.
description: Arts-based research treats artistic practice as a legitimate mode of inquiry: participants (and sometimes researchers) create drawings, collages, poems, photographs or performances that express experiences, and these artefacts are analysed together with the participant's account of them. The premise is that some knowledge is tacit, emotional or embodied and is distorted when forced into propositional speech. ABR is rigorous when the art-making prompt is carefully framed, the participant's own interpretation is captured rather than the researcher reading meaning into images, analysis is systematic across artefacts, and the study is explicit about what claims it can make. It also offers evocative ways to represent findings to stakeholders, strengthening empathy without sacrificing traceability to the data.
steps: Choose ABR form appropriate to the research question and population:
Visual narrative — participants draw or collage their experience of using a product.
(2) Photovoice — participants photograph their usage context and caption the photos.
(3) Drama/role-play — participants enact future use scenarios.

(4) Musical mapping — participants select music that represents their emotional experience of the product. Analyze: what does the form of the artifact (not just its content) reveal about the experience?
outputs: Participant-made artefacts with their own interpretations, thematic analysis of artefacts and talk, evocative representations for stakeholder communication.
useWhen: Exploring emotional, embodied, or tacit experiences (illness, grief, money anxiety, identity), with participants for whom verbal interviews are limiting, or when findings must move stakeholders emotionally.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need measurable or generalisable answers, when participants would find art-making patronising or exposing, or when time is very short; use interviews or surveys instead.
whyLost: ABR lives in education and health social science; UX borrowed fragments (collage in generative sessions) without the analytic framework that treats art as data.
whereToUse: Designing for non-verbal populations, emotional experience research, health and wellbeing product research, cross-cultural UX research.
example: A mental health app team asks young adults to make collages of 'a bad week with my phone'; the artefacts reveal notification shame that never surfaced in interviews, reshaping the notification strategy.
sources: Research Design — Patricia Leavy
Research Design (Leavy)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection
Autoethnography
Diary Methods
Method Meets Art (Leavy)
The Inquiry Series, Vol II, Ch 33
The Inquiry Series, Ch 33 — Participatory & Arts-Based Methods
