name: Bayesian Cognitive Models
origin: John Anderson's rational analysis (1990); Thomas Griffiths and Joshua Tenenbaum, 2000s
summary: Models how users infer hidden states, categories or intentions as Bayesian inference over priors and evidence, predicting judgements and where they will go wrong.
description: Bayesian cognitive models treat perception and judgement as inference: people combine prior beliefs with the likelihood of observed evidence to form posterior beliefs. An ideal observer model computes what a perfectly rational user would infer given the information an interface provides, setting a benchmark for human performance. Deviations reveal either faulty priors (for example, from other apps' conventions) or information loss in the interface. Applied to UX, such models can predict how users will interpret ambiguous icons, how many examples they need to learn a category, how they update trust after an AI error, or how they estimate quantities from charts.
steps: Define the inference problem the user faces, the hypothesis space and the evidence the interface provides.
Elicit or estimate users' priors through questions or pilot judgements.
Specify the likelihood of evidence under each hypothesis, given the interface's cues and noise.
Compute posterior predictions, or an ideal observer benchmark, for each design condition.
Collect human judgements and compare to model predictions, fitting a small number of parameters if justified.
Use discrepancies to redesign cues or set expectations that shift priors.
outputs: A probabilistic model of user inference, predictions per design, benchmarks of ideal performance and diagnosed sources of bias.
useWhen: Users must interpret uncertain information: forecasts, AI confidence, ambiguous signals, data visualisations, risk communication.
avoidWhen: Problems without a clear inferential structure, or with no capacity for quantitative modelling.
whyLost: It requires probabilistic modelling skills and remains in cognitive science journals; UX uses heuristics-and-biases lists instead.
whereToUse: Weather and health risk apps, AI confidence displays, fraud warnings, chart design, search result interpretation.
example: A weather app wants users to interpret '30% chance of rain'. A Bayesian model shows users' priors depend on their region; displaying a comparison to typical days for their location brings judgements closer to the ideal observer.

Tenenbaum, Kemp, Griffiths & Goodman, How to grow a mind (2011), Science
Anderson, The Adaptive Character of Thought (1990)
Cognitive Modeling: Nine Paradigms (slide deck)

name: Bayesian Design of Experiments for UX
origin: Bayesian experimental design (Lindley, 1956; Chaloner and Verdinelli, 1995); engineering application by Swiler (2001)
summary: Uses prior knowledge from earlier studies to plan experiments that maximise expected information per participant, often with sequential stopping, so fewer participants answer the question.
description: Bayesian design of experiments chooses sample sizes, conditions and stopping rules by their expected information gain or decision value given a prior distribution, rather than by fixed-power calculations alone. In UX, priors come from past studies, benchmarks or qualitative research. For a task success rate a Beta prior can be updated after each participant, with the study stopping once the posterior is precise enough or the decision is clear. For A/B tests, informed priors and expected-loss stopping rules can shorten experiments. Rigour requires stating and justifying priors, running prior sensitivity analyses, simulating the design's operating characteristics before running it, and reporting posteriors and decision thresholds transparently. McElreath's Statistical Rethinking provides an accessible modelling foundation.
steps: Step 1: Quantify prior from previous studies (what distribution of effect sizes is plausible?).
Step 2: Set stopping criterion: posterior 90% CI width < 0.10 (for proportions) or < 0.5 SDs (for continuous).
Step 3: After each batch of N participants, update posterior.
Stop when criterion is met.
Compare: Bayesian sequential design typically reduces required N by 20–40% vs. fixed N design.
outputs: Documented priors with sensitivity analysis, simulated design properties, sequential stopping rule, posterior estimates and decision outcome.
useWhen: Expensive or hard-to-recruit participants (clinicians, executives), repeated benchmark studies with good prior data, and experiments where early stopping saves cost.
avoidWhen: When there is no defensible prior and stakeholders require classical frequentist reporting, or when the team cannot simulate and justify the design; use standard power analysis.
whyLost: UX statistics training rarely goes beyond frequentist tests, and Bayesian design developed in engineering and clinical trials where specialist statisticians are available.
whereToUse: Iterative UX research programs, longitudinal studies, any research area with substantial prior knowledge from previous waves.
example: A medical-device team needs to show nurses can complete a dose-programming task. Using a Beta prior from a previous model, a sequential design stops at 14 participants when the posterior probability of success above 90% exceeds 0.95.

Statistical Rethinking (Richard McElreath)
Bayesian Methods for Interaction & Design
Behavioral Drift Playbook (Gopinath)

Statistical Rethinking (McElreath)

name: Bayesian Estimation for Small-Sample UX Studies
origin: Gelman et al., 1995; van de Schoot & Miočević, 2020
summary: Estimates UX metrics from small samples as posterior distributions, using informative or weakly informative priors to give stable, interpretable probability statements.
description: Bayesian estimation treats unknown quantities, such as a completion rate or the difference in task time between designs, as distributions updated by data. With small samples, frequentist tests are underpowered and produce binary significant or not-significant verdicts; Bayesian models instead yield full posterior distributions, from which teams can read the probability that a metric exceeds a threshold or that one design outperforms another. Weakly informative or evidence-based priors stabilise estimates, and hierarchical models borrow strength across tasks or participants. Modern tools such as PyMC, Stan and brms make this practical. Rigour comes from justifying priors, running prior predictive and sensitivity checks, verifying MCMC convergence, and reporting posteriors rather than only point estimates.
steps: Small-sample UX study protocol:
N < 10 per group → do not use any frequentist significance tests. Report: effect size, bootstrapped 95% CI (10,000 resamples), and Bayes Factor (how much evidence for the effect vs. the null).
(2) N 10–20 → use permutation tests for significance; Bayesian credible intervals for estimation.
(3) N > 20 → standard methods apply with distributional checks. R packages: bayestestR (Bayesian estimation), coin (permutation tests), boot (bootstrap).
outputs: Posterior distributions and credible intervals for metrics, probabilities of exceeding thresholds or of one design beating another, and prior sensitivity analyses.
useWhen: Small-sample usability tests, early-stage comparisons, rare-segment analysis, and any decision best framed as 'how likely is it that...'.
avoidWhen: Avoid when priors cannot be justified and samples are large enough for standard methods to agree; avoid if stakeholders will misread priors as bias without explanation.
whyLost: Frequentist tests dominate UX training and tools; Bayesian methods need probabilistic programming skills and are seen as advanced.
whereToUse: Expert evaluation studies, prototype testing, any UX study where large samples are impractical.
example: A health app compares two medication reminder designs with 12 participants each; a Bayesian model gives an 87% probability that design B reduces missed doses by at least one per week, informing a decision to pilot B.

name: Bayesian Sequential Design
origin: Sequential analysis from Abraham Wald, 1947; Bayesian sequential designs in clinical trials (Berry, 1980s onwards); Schönbrodt et al., 2017
summary: Collects data in batches and stops when a pre-specified posterior or Bayes factor criterion is met, using fewer participants than fixed-N designs while controlling decision error.
description: Fixed-sample studies commit to a sample size in advance, often wasting participants when effects are clear or stopping too early when they are not. Bayesian sequential designs update the posterior after each batch and stop when a pre-registered criterion is met: for example, the probability that variant B beats A exceeds 95 percent, a Bayes factor exceeds 10 for either hypothesis, or the credible interval is narrower than a target precision. Because Bayesian inference conditions on observed data, monitoring does not invalidate it in the way repeated significance testing inflates frequentist error, though operating characteristics should still be checked by simulation. Priors can be informed by earlier qualitative or quantitative work. Rigour comes from pre-specifying priors, stopping rules and maximum sample size.
steps: Define the decision, the outcome metric and the model (for example Beta-Binomial for task success or conversion).
Specify priors, using weakly informative priors or ones informed by previous studies, and document them.
Pre-register the stopping rule (for example posterior probability above 0.95, Bayes factor above 10 or below 1/10, or a target interval width) and a maximum sample size.
Simulate the design to check expected sample size and error rates under plausible effect sizes.
Collect data in batches, updating the posterior after each batch and stopping as soon as the criterion or the maximum is reached.
Report the posterior, the stopping point, prior sensitivity and the full sequence of interim results.
outputs: A pre-registered design, priors and stopping rules, simulation-based operating characteristics, posterior distributions, and decision outcomes with the sample used.
useWhen: Participants or traffic are expensive, effects may be large, decisions need to be made as soon as evidence suffices, or you are running usability benchmarks and A/B tests with a Bayesian approach.
avoidWhen: Stakeholders or regulators require fixed-N frequentist analysis, or you cannot pre-specify stopping rules; use a fixed-sample design or group-sequential frequentist methods.
whyLost: Researchers use fixed-N designs even when sequential designs are valid, because UX statistics teaching centres on t-tests and many experiment platforms only recently added Bayesian options.
whereToUse: A/B testing in low-traffic products, usability benchmark studies, unmoderated testing with costly panels, and clinical or fintech research with limited participants.
example: A fintech team tests two onboarding variants with a Beta-Binomial model and a 0.95 posterior stopping rule, checking every 50 users. Variant B reaches 0.97 probability of higher completion after 300 users, half the fixed-N plan.
sources: Statistical Rethinking (McElreath)
Bayesian Methods for Interaction & Design
Behavioral Drift Playbook (Gopinath)
Bayesian Data Analysis (Gelman et al.)

The Inquiry Series, Ch 40 — Bayesian Thinking & Sequential Study Design

name: Bayesian Structural Time Series (CausalImpact)
origin: Kay Brodersen, Fabian Gallusser, Jim Koehler, Nicolas Remy and Steven Scott, Google, 2015
summary: Forecasts what a metric would have done without an intervention using a state-space model with control series, giving posterior intervals for the effect.
description: BSTS models a time series with components for local trend, seasonality and a regression on control series not affected by the intervention, with spike-and-slab priors selecting relevant controls. Trained on the pre-period, it produces a counterfactual forecast for the post-period; the difference from observed data, with full posterior intervals, estimates the effect cumulatively and pointwise. Key assumptions are that control series are unaffected by the intervention and that the relationship between treated and control series is stable. It is accessible through the CausalImpact package, but rigorous use requires checking pre-period fit and assumption validity rather than running defaults.
steps: Choose the target series and candidate control series that are predictive but unaffected by the change.
Fit the model on a long pre-period and inspect one-step-ahead prediction accuracy.
Run the post-period counterfactual and inspect pointwise and cumulative effects with credible intervals.
Test robustness with placebo interventions in the pre-period and alternative control sets.
Check that control series did not shift at the intervention date.
Report effect estimates with intervals and model diagnostics.
outputs: Counterfactual forecast, pointwise and cumulative effect estimates with credible intervals, and diagnostics.
useWhen: Single-series launches or campaigns with good control series and enough history.
avoidWhen: When controls may be contaminated by the change, or when randomised holdouts are possible.
whyLost: Used by marketing analysts, but rarely by UX researchers, who see time series as an analytics team concern.
whereToUse: Feature launches, SEO and content changes, campaign effects, outage impact on engagement.
example: A publisher rewrites article templates site-wide. Using traffic to unchanged partner sites and search trend data as controls, CausalImpact estimates a 5% (95% interval 2-8%) lift in pages per session.
sources: Brodersen et al., Inferring causal impact using Bayesian structural time-series models (2015), Annals of Applied Statistics
Scott & Varian, Predicting the present with Bayesian structural time series (2014), International Journal of Mathematical Modelling and Numerical Optimisation
reference: Brodersen, K. H., et al. (2015). Annals of Applied Statistics, 9(1), 247-274.

name: Bayesian Updating of Drift Risk
origin: Thomas Bayes, 1763; Pierre-Simon Laplace
summary: Treats each user's drift as a probability updated as new behavioural signals arrive, P(drift | signals) ∝ P(signals | drift) · P(drift), to flag risk before churn.
description: Bayes' rule combines a prior belief with the likelihood of new evidence to form a posterior. In Vivek Gopinath's drift playbook, drift risk is treated as a probability updated over time: with a prior drift risk of 20%, observing three sessions with entropy below 1.5 and promo CTR below 25% yields a posterior of about 65%. The update provides an intuitive, continuously revised early warning that complements the DriftScore and machine-learning baselines (logistic regression as interpretable baseline, random forests or GBMs for nonlinear interactions, ARIMA or Prophet for forecasting decay). Rigour depends on calibrating likelihoods from historical data on users who did and did not later disengage.
steps: Set a prior drift probability from historical base rates (example: 20%).
Define the evidence signals and thresholds (e.g. entropy < 1.5 and CTR < 25% in a session).
Estimate likelihoods of these signals among users who later drifted versus those who did not.
Update the posterior per user as each session's signals arrive.
Trigger interventions when the posterior crosses a threshold and log outcomes.
Recalibrate priors and likelihoods periodically against observed churn or disengagement.
outputs: Per-user posterior drift probabilities and alert triggers.
useWhen: When you need a continuously updated, explainable risk estimate from sparse longitudinal signals.
avoidWhen: When there is no historical data to calibrate likelihoods; priors and likelihoods would be guesses.
whyLost: Bayesian reasoning is standard in statistics but rarely used directly by UX researchers.
whereToUse: Retention programmes, personalisation triggers, subscription health monitoring.
example: An e-commerce user starts at 20% drift risk; after three sessions of low entropy and ignored promos the posterior reaches about 65%, triggering a short re-onboarding tour.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study
reference: Gelman, A., Carlin, J. B., Stern, H. S., Dunson, D. B., Vehtari, A., & Rubin, D. B. (2013). Bayesian Data Analysis (3rd ed.). CRC Press.

name: Becker-DeGroot-Marschak Willingness-to-Pay Auction
origin: Gordon Becker, Morris DeGroot and Jacob Marschak, 1964
summary: Participants state a maximum price; a random price is drawn and they buy only if it is below their bid, making truthful reporting the best strategy.
description: Stated willingness to pay is inflated by hypothetical bias. In BDM, the participant states a bid; a price is drawn at random from a distribution; if the price is at or below the bid, the participant must buy at the drawn price (not the bid), otherwise not. Because the bid does not affect the price paid, the dominant strategy is to bid one's true valuation. With real money and real products, BDM yields incentive-compatible, individual-level WTP. Careful instructions and practice rounds matter because participants often misunderstand the mechanism. It gives UX and pricing research behavioural valuation data rather than survey hypotheticals.
steps: Define the product or feature and ensure it can actually be sold or delivered at the drawn price.
Explain the mechanism clearly, with practice rounds using low-stakes items and comprehension checks.
Collect bids, then draw the random price from a pre-announced distribution.
Execute the transaction for winning bids so incentives are real.
Analyse the distribution of WTP, build a demand curve and compare segments or product variants.
Compare with stated WTP to estimate hypothetical bias for future surveys.
outputs: Incentive-compatible WTP distribution, demand curve and hypothetical bias estimates.
useWhen: You need trustworthy valuations for a product, feature, data access or premium tier, and can execute real transactions.
avoidWhen: Products that cannot be sold in the session, or participants unable to grasp the mechanism.
whyLost: It requires real money and an experimental economics mindset, absent from UX research operations.
whereToUse: Premium features, in-app purchases, hardware accessories, privacy-for-payment trade-offs, health products in developing markets.
example: A photo app runs BDM for a lifetime filter pack with 300 users paying real money. Median WTP is $3.40, versus $7.10 in a parallel hypothetical survey, revealing a hypothetical bias factor of about 2.
sources: Becker, DeGroot & Marschak, Measuring utility by a single-response sequential method (1964), Behavioral Science
Wertenbroch & Skiera, Measuring consumers' willingness to pay at the point of purchase (2002), Journal of Marketing Research
reference: Becker, G. M., DeGroot, M. H., & Marschak, J. (1964). Behavioral Science, 9(3), 226-232.

name: Behavioral feature matrix construction from session logs
origin: Web usage mining (Srivastava, Cooley, Deshpande & Tan, 2000); feature engineering practice in applied ML
summary: Transforms raw event logs into a user-by-feature matrix of meaningful behavioural measures that can feed clustering, modelling and dimensionality reduction.
description: Every computational behavioural analysis depends on how raw events are turned into features. This method defines the unit (user, session, week), the observation window, and families of features: frequency, recency, intensity, breadth of feature use, sequence patterns, timing and outcome-related measures. Good features are grounded in qualitative understanding of what behaviours mean, robust to logging changes, and normalised appropriately. Rigour lies in documenting a data dictionary, handling sparsity and skew (log transforms, ratios), avoiding leakage of outcomes into features, checking correlations and redundancy, and testing whether results are stable across alternative feature sets. Poor featurisation is the most common reason segmentation and prediction projects fail.
steps: Define the analysis unit, observation window (e.g. 90 days) and population with clear eligibility rules.
Draft feature families from qualitative insight: frequency, recency, depth, breadth, sequence and timing measures.
Compute features with documented SQL or code and a data dictionary specifying event definitions and transformations.
Transform skewed counts (log1p), convert totals to rates where exposure differs, and standardise.
Remove near-zero-variance features and check pairwise correlations (consider dropping one of pairs above 0.9).
Check for leakage of outcome information and test downstream results with an alternative feature set for robustness.
outputs: A documented, reproducible user-by-feature matrix with data dictionary, transformations and quality checks.
useWhen: Before behavioural segmentation, drift scoring, dimensionality reduction or predictive modelling from product logs.
avoidWhen: Avoid when logging is unreliable or inconsistent across platforms (fix instrumentation first) or when sample sizes are too small for computational analysis.
whyLost: It is treated as engineering plumbing rather than research design, so the researcher's judgement about what behaviour means is rarely embedded.
whereToUse: Investment and trading platforms, SaaS product analytics, health app engagement modelling, content platforms.
example: From 18 months of trading logs, the team builds 200 features including trades per active week, share of trades placed within 10 minutes of a news view, and asset class entropy, which feed a UMAP map of investor archetypes.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Space and Time (Marc Leordeanu)
Srivastava et al. (2000) Web usage mining
Feature Engineering and Selection (Max Kuhn & Kjell Johnson)
Pattern Recognition & ML (Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Time & Space
The Inquiry Series, Ch 52 — Dimensionality Reduction — The Geometry of Behavioral Space
reference: Kuhn, M. & Johnson, K. (2019) Feature Engineering and Selection: A Practical Approach for Predictive Models. CRC Press.

name: Behavioral prediction gap test
origin: Research on the intention-behaviour gap (Sheeran, 2002) and stated versus revealed preference (Samuelson, 1948); applied to product adoption in The Inquiry Series
summary: Compares what users predict they will do with what they actually do in the same situation, quantifying the say-do gap and its drivers.
description: People are poor predictors of their own behaviour: Sheeran's meta-analysis found intentions explain only about 28% of variance in behaviour. In UX, interviews and surveys capture predictions such as 'I would use this weekly', which are then treated as evidence of demand. The behavioural prediction gap test pairs a prediction with a later measured behaviour for the same individuals and computes the gap per behaviour and segment. It distinguishes inclined abstainers (said yes, did not) from disinclined actors, which point to different interventions: the former need ability or prompts, the latter suggest habitual or social drivers. Rigour comes from individual-level pairing, precise behavioural definitions and pre-specifying the observation window.
steps: Define 3 to 8 target behaviours with observable criteria and an observation window, for example 'submits at least one digital form in the next 14 days'.
Recruit 30 to 200 participants whose subsequent behaviour you can observe through logs or diaries, with consent to link predictions to behaviour.
Collect predictions using probability scales (0% to 100%) rather than yes or no, plus the reasons and anticipated barriers.
Observe actual behaviour over the window via analytics, diary or field observation, blind to individual predictions where feasible.
Compute per-person and per-behaviour gaps, the share of inclined abstainers and disinclined actors, and the correlation between prediction and behaviour.
Interview 6 to 12 inclined abstainers to identify which barrier (motivation, ability, prompt, habit, social context) prevented the predicted behaviour.
outputs: Prediction-behaviour gap metrics per behaviour, a 2x2 of intenders and actors, a ranked list of barriers explaining the gap, and corrected demand estimates.
useWhen: Decisions rest on stated intent (concept tests, surveys); adoption is lower than research predicted; you need to separate motivation problems from execution problems.
avoidWhen: Behaviour cannot be observed at individual level, or the decision is reversible and cheap to test directly with a live experiment or fake-door test.
whyLost: UX knows 'watch what users do, not what they say' as a slogan, but rarely pairs predictions with behaviour at the individual level, so the gap is asserted rather than measured.
whereToUse: Digital health adoption, savings and pension features, subscription intent, enterprise tool rollouts, behaviour-change products.
example: Health workers predicted an average 85% probability of entering visits digitally the same day; logs showed 31%. Interviews with inclined abstainers found they completed paper first out of habit and audit fear, shifting the roadmap from motivation messaging to removing the paper step.
sources: Heuristics & Biases (Kahneman ed.)
Judgment Under Uncertainty
Choices Values & Frames (Kahneman/Tversky)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 21 — Heuristics, Biases & the Architecture of Judgment
reference: Sheeran, P. (2002). Intention–behavior relations: A conceptual and empirical review. European Review of Social Psychology, 12(1), 1–36.

name: Behavioral Spectral Framework
donor: Astrophysics signal processing (Matteo Paz's NEOWISE Fourier-wavelet pipeline) translated into behavioural science
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A five-stage mixed-methods workflow treating behavioural telemetry as light-curves: decompose into frequency features, annotate them qualitatively, model and visualise rhythm, then validate meaning.
description: Inspired by Matteo Paz's 2024 Fourier and wavelet pipeline for detecting variable objects in the NEOWISE survey, the framework treats engagement, sentiment and physiological traces as 'light-curves of cognition' with periodic behaviour (habit cycles), transient events (frustration bursts) and drift (learning, fatigue). The five stages are Signal Framing, Spectral Decomposition, Contextual Annotation, Modeling and Visualization, and Validation and Iteration. It explicitly names where translation fails (stationarity, irregular sampling, semantic noise, label scarcity, non-equivalence of energy and meaning, intentionality, ethics) and redesigns around them: recurrence over strict periodicity, Lomb-Scargle for uneven events, noise retained as emotion, wavelets as a behavioural microscope, metadata context anchors and a human-in-the-loop quant → qual → quant loop. The integration equation states: meaningful behavioural insight = spectral precision × contextual anchoring × interpretive dialogue. It is presented as a conceptual playbook; the case is hypothetical.
steps: Signal Framing: choose the behavioural signal (e.g. interaction density per minute), align time resolution to the hypothesised rhythm, capture context variables and secure informed consent.
Pre-process: normalise timestamps, interpolate small gaps (< 30 seconds) and retain longer gaps as disengagement indicators.

Spectral Decomposition: apply Fourier for global periodicity, CWT or STFT for temporal localisation and Lomb-Scargle for irregular events; extract dominant frequencies, power distribution, spectral entropy and phase coherence.
Contextual Annotation: align spectral peaks and bursts with transcripts, logs or video, open-code each event (frustration, curiosity, learning, boredom) and build a Spectral Annotation Matrix.
Modeling and Visualization: train interpretable models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM) on spectral features and produce spectrograms, entropy drift plots and coherence maps.
Validation and Iteration: correlate spectral metrics with SUS, NPS or TLX, verify interpretations in post-analysis participant interviews, and re-analyse with updated codes.
Run an ethical check: use insights to improve design, not to infer private cognition without consent or to manipulate behaviour.
outputs: Per-user or per-session rhythm signatures, a Spectral Annotation Matrix, spectrograms, entropy drift and coherence maps, a behavioural resonance map and validated interpretations.
useWhen: When dense, time-stamped behavioural or physiological data exist and you suspect rhythm, bursts or drift carry meaning (onboarding overload, habit formation, human-AI turn-taking).
avoidWhen: When data are sparse, labels absent and no qualitative follow-up is possible; spectral output without narrative validation risks false precision. Use standard funnel analytics instead.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath; signal-processing methods remain siloed in physics, engineering and neuroscience.
whereToUse: Fintech onboarding, emotional journey mapping, agentic AI interaction, longitudinal habit formation, multimodal biometric studies.
example: In a hypothetical fintech onboarding study, high-frequency bursts (0.8–1.2 Hz) cluster at KYC and form-filling, spectral entropy falls from 0.89 to 0.62 by session three, and a Random Forest separates stable from volatile sessions with 82% accuracy.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
Matteo Paz (2024), A Sub-Millisecond Fourier and Wavelet Based Model to Extract Variable Candidates from the NEOWISE Single-Exposure Database

uxguy.in
