name: Bradley-Terry Paired Comparison Scaling
origin: Ralph Bradley and Milton Terry, 1952 (anticipated by Zermelo, 1929)
summary: Estimates a latent strength for each item from many pairwise choices, handling incomplete designs, ties and covariates with uncertainty.
description: The Bradley-Terry model sets the probability that item i beats item j as pi_i / (pi_i + pi_j), equivalent to a logistic model on strength differences. It accommodates incomplete comparison designs (not every pair compared), allows home-advantage or position effects, and extends to ties, covariates and random effects. It underpins comparative judgement in educational assessment and human preference modelling for language models (RLHF reward models). For UX, it lets you scale many design variants, AI outputs or content items from simple pairwise preferences collected adaptively, with confidence intervals rather than raw win rates.
steps: Define items and the comparison question (e.g. 'Which response is more helpful?').
Design comparisons: random or adaptive pairing so the comparison graph is connected; randomise left/right.
Collect judgements from raters, recording rater and position.
Fit a Bradley-Terry model (BradleyTerry2, choix) with position effects and optional rater random effects.
Report strengths with confidence intervals and check model fit and intransitivities.
Use adaptive pairing to refine estimates among close competitors.
outputs: Latent strength scores with intervals, position-bias estimates and rankings.
useWhen: Comparing many alternatives where absolute ratings are unreliable: AI outputs, designs, copy, images.
avoidWhen: When attribute-level trade-offs are needed (use conjoint) or with very few items.
whyLost: UX uses rating scales and simple preference counts; paired comparison models are known mainly in sports, education and ML.
whereToUse: LLM response evaluation, design variant preference, icon sets, voice selection, content headline testing.
example: An AI writing tool evaluates 12 prompt strategies with 3,000 pairwise human judgements. Bradley-Terry estimates show two strategies statistically tied at the top and reveal a strong left-position bias of 6 points.
sources: Bradley & Terry, Rank analysis of incomplete block designs: I. The method of paired comparisons (1952), Biometrika
Agresti, Categorical Data Analysis (3rd ed., 2013)
Turner & Firth, Bradley-Terry models in R: the BradleyTerry2 package (2012), Journal of Statistical Software
Feature Prioritization Methods (slide deck)
reference: Bradley, R. A., & Terry, M. E. (1952). Biometrika, 39(3/4), 324-345.

name: Brand Lift and Drag Measurement
origin: Advertising effectiveness research; applied to UX benchmarks by Sauro (2018)
summary: Measures how using a product changes how people feel about the brand, by asking before and after the experience.
description: A good experience should improve brand perception and a bad one should damage it. Brand lift measurement asks participants to rate the brand (favourability, trust or likelihood to use) before they attempt tasks and again afterwards. The change, analysed as paired data, is the experience's effect on the brand: lift if positive, drag if negative. Breaking results down by task success and prior experience shows which failures hurt the brand most, connecting UX metrics to outcomes marketing and leadership care about.
steps: Ask a brand attitude question before any task (for example, a 7-point favourability rating).
Run the tasks and standard metrics as usual.
Ask the identical brand question at the end.
Compute the paired change per participant and test it with a paired t-test or sign test.
Cross-tabulate lift against task success, product and prior experience.
outputs: A measured brand effect of the experience, linked to the tasks that caused it.
useWhen: Benchmarks and competitive studies where you need to connect UX to brand value.
avoidWhen: Unbranded prototypes, or short studies where asking twice will feel repetitive.
whyLost: Brand belongs to marketing and UX rarely borrows its measures, so experience effects on brand go unreported.
whereToUse: Consumer brands, retail, travel and financial services websites.
example: Participants who failed the "find opening hours" task showed a 0.8-point brand drag, double that of any other task failure.
sources: Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience, chapter 11.

name: Brier Score and Calibration Analysis
origin: Glenn Brier, 1950 (weather forecast verification); Murphy decomposition (1973); Tetlock's Good Judgment Project (2011-2015)
summary: Scores probabilistic predictions against outcomes and decomposes accuracy into calibration and resolution, applicable to researchers, users and AI systems.
description: The Brier score is the mean squared difference between forecast probabilities and outcomes (0 or 1); lower is better. Murphy's decomposition separates reliability (calibration: do 70% forecasts happen 70% of the time?), resolution (do forecasts discriminate?) and uncertainty. Calibration curves plot predicted against observed frequency. Weather forecasters became well calibrated through feedback. In UX this applies three ways: calibrating researchers' and teams' predictions about tests and launches; evaluating AI confidence displays shown to users; and measuring whether users' own confidence judgements are calibrated.
steps: Collect probabilistic forecasts (e.g. teams predict the probability each A/B test wins, or an AI model gives confidence scores).
Record outcomes once known.
Compute Brier scores and Murphy decomposition; plot calibration curves with binned or smoothed estimates.
Compare forecasters or models, and against base-rate forecasts (Brier skill score).
Feed results back to forecasters regularly to improve calibration.
For AI products, recalibrate model confidence (e.g. temperature scaling) before displaying it to users.
outputs: Brier scores, skill scores, calibration curves and recalibration recommendations.
useWhen: Evaluating predictions by people or models, especially confidence shown to users or used in decisions.
avoidWhen: When forecasts are not probabilistic and cannot be made so.
whyLost: Forecast verification lives in meteorology and intelligence; UX teams rarely track the accuracy of their own predictions.
whereToUse: AI confidence displays, research team prediction markets, risk scores, health predictions, recommendation confidence.
example: A product team logs probabilities for 80 A/B tests. Their Brier score is worse than always predicting the 30% base win rate, revealing overconfidence; quarterly calibration feedback improves it.
sources: Brier, Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability (1950), Monthly Weather Review
Murphy, A new vector partition of the probability score (1973), Journal of Applied Meteorology
Tetlock & Gardner, Superforecasting (2015)
reference: Brier, G. W. (1950). Monthly Weather Review, 78(1), 1-3.

name: Brunswik Lens Model Analysis
origin: Egon Brunswik, 1952-1956; operationalised by Kenneth Hammond (1955) and the lens model equation of Tucker (1964)
summary: Compares how cues relate to a true criterion with how people actually weight those cues, quantifying judgement accuracy, consistency and cue misuse.
description: The lens model places a distal criterion (e.g. actual trustworthiness of a seller) on one side and a person's judgement on the other, connected through a set of proximal cues (ratings, photos, response time). Regressing the criterion on cues gives ecological validities; regressing judgements on cues gives cue utilisation. The lens model equation decomposes achievement (the correlation between judgement and criterion) into environmental predictability, judge consistency and matching of cue weights. For UX, this precisely diagnoses whether users misjudge because the interface presents weak cues, because they weight cues wrongly, or because they are inconsistent, and so tells you whether to change the cues or help users use them.
steps: Define the criterion users are judging and obtain ground-truth values for a set of cases (e.g. 50-100 profiles, products or messages).
Identify the cues available in the interface and code their values for each case.
Have participants judge each case; include repeated cases to estimate consistency.
Regress criterion on cues (environment side) and each participant's judgements on cues (judge side).
Compute the lens model equation components: achievement, environmental predictability, judge consistency (Rs) and knowledge (G).
Redesign: add or strengthen valid cues, de-emphasise invalid but salient ones, and retest achievement.
outputs: Cue validity and utilisation weights, lens model statistics, and a diagnosis of judgement failure sources.
useWhen: Users judge quality, risk, authenticity or relevance from interface cues: reviews, phishing, listings, AI answers, medical images.
avoidWhen: Tasks without a measurable criterion, or with very few cases.
whyLost: The method lives in judgement and decision-making research and requires regression across many cases per judge, which UX studies rarely design for.
whereToUse: Marketplaces (seller trust), security warnings, misinformation labels, recruiting platforms, AI answer credibility.
example: A rental marketplace studies how renters judge listing quality. Renters heavily weight photo count, which has near-zero validity, and ignore host response rate, which predicts satisfaction; the listing page is redesigned to make response rate prominent.
sources: Brunswik, Perception and the Representative Design of Psychological Experiments (1956)
Hammond & Stewart (eds.), The Essential Brunswik (2001)
Cooksey, Judgment Analysis: Theory, Methods, and Applications (1996)
reference: Cooksey, R. W. (1996). Judgment Analysis. Academic Press.

name: BSF Stage 1 — Wavelet Decomposition
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025 (uxguy.in)
summary: Decomposes user behaviour time series into components at multiple temporal scales, separating session-level activity from weekly routines and lifecycle trends.
description: Wavelet decomposition is the first stage of the Behavioral Spectral Framework playbook. User activity is represented as a time series, for example events per hour or per day for each user, and decomposed into components at several temporal resolutions, analogous to a discrete wavelet transform. Unlike a single Fourier transform, wavelets localise patterns in time, so a weekly routine that begins in month two or a burst of activity around a billing event can be detected where it occurs. The stage turns undifferentiated activity counts into separate layers that later stages map, filter and model. Its rigour depends on consistent time binning, sufficient series length relative to the slowest scale studied, handling of missing periods, and checking that the components sum back to the original signal.
steps: Choose the unit of analysis (user, account or cohort) and a consistent time bin such as hourly or daily event counts.
Ensure each series spans at least three to four cycles of the slowest rhythm to be studied.
Handle gaps explicitly, distinguishing true inactivity from missing data.
Apply a multi-level wavelet decomposition (for example a discrete wavelet transform with a Haar or Daubechies basis).
Verify that reconstructed components sum to the original series within tolerance.
Store components per scale for each unit for use in frequency mapping.
outputs: Multi-scale behavioural components per user or cohort, with energy per scale and time localisation of patterns.
useWhen: When analysing long behavioural logs where micro and macro rhythms are mixed and averages hide when patterns start or stop.
avoidWhen: Avoid with short or sparse series, or when the team lacks signal-processing skills; use simpler cohort retention curves instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Novel analytical approach within BSF; enables pattern detection across micro and macro behavioral timescales.
whereToUse: Longitudinal behavioral data analysis; session-level vs. lifecycle-level behavior separation.
example: A language-learning app decomposes 120 days of daily practice counts per learner and finds a strong 7-day component emerging only after week three, which pinpoints when habit forms.
sources: wavelet.pdf
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Behavioral Spectral Framework playbook (uxguy.in).

name: BSF Stage 2 — Frequency Mapping
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025 (uxguy.in)
summary: Assigns decomposed behavioural components to high, mid and low frequency bands and labels each band with concrete behaviours to inform prioritisation.
description: Frequency mapping is the second stage of the Behavioral Spectral Framework. Components produced by wavelet decomposition are placed on a frequency axis: high-frequency bands represent repeated micro-habits such as checking or scrolling, mid-frequency bands represent routines such as weekly planning, and low-frequency bands represent milestone events such as renewals or annual reporting. Each band is then labelled with the specific features and behaviours that contribute most energy to it. The result is a spectrum showing which rhythms dominate a product and which features serve each rhythm. Its rigour comes from defining band boundaries before analysis, attributing energy to features using event-level data, and comparing spectra across segments rather than relying on a single global picture.
steps: Define band boundaries in advance, for example under 1 day, 1 to 14 days and over 14 days.
Aggregate the energy of decomposed components into each band per user and segment.
Attribute band energy to features by recomputing spectra on feature-specific event streams.
Label each band with its dominant behaviours and features.
Compare spectra between retained and churned users or between segments.
Translate dominant and missing rhythms into feature prioritisation hypotheses.
outputs: A behavioural spectrum per segment, feature-to-band attribution and prioritisation hypotheses tied to rhythms.
useWhen: When deciding which features to invest in for habit-forming or engagement-loop products; when segments differ in how they use a product over time.
avoidWhen: Avoid if wavelet decomposition has not been done or event data cannot be attributed to features; use feature adoption funnels instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Part of BSF playbook; provides quantifiable metaphor for behavior regularity.
whereToUse: Feature usage analytics; habit-formation product design; engagement loop design.
example: A project-management SaaS maps its spectrum and finds retained teams concentrate energy in a weekly band driven by sprint review features, while trial teams show only high-frequency task edits. The team prioritises weekly review onboarding.
sources: wavelet.pdf
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Behavioral Spectral Framework playbook (uxguy.in).

name: BSF Stage 3 — Noise Filtering
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025 (uxguy.in)
summary: Removes accidental, exploratory and outlier interactions from the behavioural spectrum with explicit thresholds so design decisions rest on genuine usage patterns.
description: Noise filtering is the third stage of the Behavioral Spectral Framework. Not every logged interaction represents a meaningful behaviour: accidental taps, one-off exploration, bot or test traffic, and extreme outlier users all add energy to the spectrum without reflecting stable patterns. This stage applies threshold-based filtering analogous to wavelet denoising, removing components whose energy falls below a defined level and excluding units that meet explicit outlier rules. Its purpose is to prevent teams from over-engineering for edge-case behaviour. Rigour comes from writing filtering rules before seeing results, reporting how much data each rule removes, running sensitivity checks with alternative thresholds, and keeping excluded data available so that genuinely important minority behaviours are not silently discarded.
steps: Write filtering rules in advance, covering bots and internal accounts, accidental interactions (for example sessions under 3 seconds) and outlier users.
Apply energy thresholds to each band to suppress low-energy components.
Report the proportion of events and users removed by each rule.
Run a sensitivity analysis with stricter and looser thresholds and check that conclusions hold.
Review excluded data for meaningful minority patterns, such as accessibility-related usage, before discarding.
Pass the filtered spectrum to pattern reconstruction.
outputs: A filtered behavioural spectrum, an exclusion log with removal rates and a sensitivity report.
useWhen: When usage analytics or A/B test results are distorted by accidental or outlier behaviour; before building personas or models from logs.
avoidWhen: Avoid when edge cases are the research focus, as in accessibility or error research; analyse those directly with critical incident or error studies.
whyLost: Still in use: Critical BSF stage; prevents over-engineering for edge-case behaviors.
whereToUse: Usage analytics cleanup; A/B test interpretation; longitudinal study data processing.
example: An e-commerce team finds that a feature's apparent daily usage is driven by accidental taps on a sticky banner. Filtering sessions under 2 seconds removes 40 percent of its events and changes the prioritisation decision.
sources: wavelet.pdf
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Behavioral Spectral Framework playbook (uxguy.in).

name: BSF Stage 4 — Pattern Reconstruction
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025 (uxguy.in)
summary: Rebuilds clean, representative behavioural trajectories from filtered signals, producing data-grounded archetypes for each frequency band.
description: Pattern reconstruction is the synthesis stage of the Behavioral Spectral Framework. Having decomposed, mapped and filtered behavioural signals, the analyst recombines the retained components to reconstruct a clean picture of typical user trajectories at each frequency level. Similar reconstructed trajectories are grouped into behavioural archetypes, such as daily checkers, weekly planners or event-driven visitors, each described by its dominant rhythms and features. These archetypes can ground personas and journey maps in behavioural evidence rather than in anecdote. Rigour comes from checking reconstruction fidelity against raw data, testing archetype stability across time windows and samples, and triangulating archetypes with qualitative research to explain the reasons behind each pattern.
steps: Recombine filtered components to reconstruct a clean trajectory per user.
Group reconstructed trajectories by similarity of band energy profiles.
Describe each group as an archetype with its dominant rhythms, features and size.
Test stability by repeating the grouping on a different time window or random half of the data.
Triangulate each archetype with 3 to 5 interviews to explain motivations behind the pattern.
Feed archetypes into personas, journey maps and the prediction layer.
outputs: Behavioural archetypes with rhythm profiles and sizes, reconstruction fidelity checks and inputs for personas and journey maps.
useWhen: When building or validating personas and journey maps from behavioural data; when stakeholders need representative patterns rather than raw dashboards.
avoidWhen: Avoid if earlier BSF stages have not been completed or data is thin; use qualitative persona development or cluster analysis on simpler features.
whyLost: Still in use: BSF synthesis stage; produces actionable behavioral archetypes grounded in signal analysis.
whereToUse: Persona construction grounded in behavioral data; journey map validation.
example: A streaming service reconstructs three archetypes: nightly bingers, weekend family viewers and event-driven sports viewers. Interviews explain the third group's churn after seasons end, informing an off-season content strategy.
sources: wavelet.pdf
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Behavioral Spectral Framework playbook (uxguy.in).

name: BSF Stage 5 — ML Prediction Layer
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025 (uxguy.in)
summary: Applies clustering and sequence-prediction models to reconstructed behavioural patterns to forecast future behaviour and flag users at risk of churn.
description: The ML Prediction Layer is the quantitative capstone of the Behavioral Spectral Framework. Features derived from the earlier stages, such as band energies, rhythm stability and archetype membership, are fed into machine-learning models. Clustering refines segments, while sequence or classification models predict future behaviour such as churn, downgrade or adoption of a feature. Because inputs are interpretable behavioural rhythms rather than opaque raw events, predictions can be explained in design terms, for example 'loss of the weekly rhythm precedes churn by three weeks'. Rigour comes from time-based train and test splits, comparison against simple baselines, calibration checks, and treating predictions as triggers for research and intervention design rather than as final truths.
steps: Assemble features from previous BSF stages for a defined prediction window, such as the next 30 days.
Split data by time so models are trained on earlier periods and tested on later ones.
Train baseline models (for example logistic regression) and more complex models, and compare them on held-out data.
Check calibration and fairness across key segments.
Interpret the most predictive rhythm features and translate them into intervention hypotheses.
Test interventions with an experiment rather than assuming the prediction implies causation.
outputs: Validated risk scores, interpretable predictors of churn or adoption, and intervention hypotheses ready for experimentation.
useWhen: For churn prediction, proactive intervention design and personalisation when rich, long behavioural logs exist.
avoidWhen: Avoid when data is small or the aim is to understand reasons; use interviews or survival analysis. Do not use predictions as causal evidence; run A/B tests.
whyLost: Still in use: BSF's quantitative capstone; bridges behavioral science and predictive analytics.
whereToUse: Churn prediction; proactive intervention design; personalization system inputs.
example: A subscription fitness app finds that a drop in the weekly workout-band energy predicts cancellation four weeks ahead. Flagged users receive a tested re-engagement plan, and an A/B test confirms a reduction in churn.
sources: wavelet.pdf
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Behavioral Spectral Framework playbook (uxguy.in).

name: Building a qualitative coding agent (LLM API)
origin: Emerging practice from 2023 onwards (e.g. Xiao et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2024), using large language model APIs such as Anthropic's Claude
summary: Programming a large language model, via its API, to apply a defined codebook or propose first-order codes for transcript segments, with structured outputs that analysts verify.
description: A qualitative coding agent wraps an LLM in a controlled procedure: a system prompt with the research question and codebook, segment-by-segment input with participant metadata, and outputs constrained to a JSON schema (code, rationale, verbatim evidence span, confidence). Run through the API rather than a chat window, it is repeatable, logged and scalable to hundreds of transcripts. It is most defensible for deductive coding against a well-defined codebook, and as a first-pass suggester in inductive work. Rigour comes from pinning the model version and temperature, requiring verbatim evidence for every code, measuring agreement with human coders (e.g. Cohen's kappa) on a held-out sample before scaling, logging all prompts and outputs, and keeping humans responsible for interpretation.
steps: Write the research question and a codebook with definitions, inclusion and exclusion criteria and examples for each code.
Segment transcripts (e.g. by speaker turn) and remove or anonymise personal data before any API call; check the data-processing terms.
Define a JSON output schema requiring code IDs, a rationale and a verbatim quote span, and validate every response against it.
Pin the model version and set temperature to 0 or low; log prompts, model ID and outputs per segment.
Have two humans code a held-out sample of 10-20% of segments and compute agreement with the agent; proceed only if kappa is about 0.70 or higher for key codes.
Run at scale, auto-check that quoted spans exist verbatim in the source, and route low-confidence or disputed segments to human review.
outputs: Coded segments with evidence spans and rationales, agreement statistics against human coders, and full prompt and output logs.
useWhen: Large qualitative corpora (dozens to hundreds of interviews, thousands of open-ended responses) with a stable codebook, or as a first-pass suggester to speed human coding.
avoidWhen: Avoid for small studies where reading everything is feasible, for sensitive data that cannot leave controlled infrastructure, and for deeply interpretive or reflexive approaches where coding is the researcher's own sense-making.
whyLost: It spread quickly from 2023 because LLM APIs made scalable coding cheap, but rigorous, validated use remains uncommon.
whereToUse: Research operations at scale, voice-of-customer programmes, multi-country interview studies and open-ended survey analysis.
example: A fintech research team codes 240 interviews against a 28-code trust codebook. On a 15% human-coded sample the agent reaches kappa 0.78, rising to 0.84 after refining two ambiguous code definitions, and all quotes are verified as verbatim before reporting.
sources: Anthropic Claude API (claude-sonnet-4-20250514)
structured outputs (JSON schema)
asyncio
Xiao, Z. et al. (2023) Supporting qualitative analysis with large language models: Combining codebook with GPT-3 for deductive coding. IUI Companion
Gao, J. et al. (2024) CollabCoder: A lower-barrier, rigorous workflow for inductive collaborative qualitative analysis with large language models. CHI
Saldaña, J. (2021) The Coding Manual for Qualitative Researchers, 4th ed.
The Inquiry Series, C12 — AI Agents for Structured Qualitative Analysis at Scale
reference: Xiao, Z. et al. (2023) Supporting qualitative analysis with large language models. IUI 2023 Companion

name: Bunching Estimation at Thresholds
origin: Emmanuel Saez (2010); Raj Chetty et al. (2011); Henrik Kleven and Mazhar Waseem (2013); review by Kleven (2016)
summary: Measures how many people cluster just at a threshold (free shipping minimum, plan limit, deadline) relative to a smooth counterfactual, revealing behavioural responses.
description: When a price schedule has a kink or notch, such as a tax bracket or a free shipping minimum, people bunch just at or above it. Bunching estimators fit a smooth polynomial to the distribution away from the threshold, estimate the counterfactual density in the excluded region, and compute excess mass. This quantifies responsiveness (an elasticity), and gaps above notches reveal dominated choices people avoid. Product pricing and limits are full of thresholds: free tier caps, minimum order values, character limits, streak deadlines. Bunching reveals how strongly users react and whether thresholds distort behaviour in desired ways.
steps: Identify a threshold in a product rule (e.g. free shipping at $50) and obtain the distribution of the running variable (basket value).
Plot a fine histogram and look for excess mass at the threshold and missing mass nearby.
Fit a flexible polynomial to bins outside an excluded window around the threshold.
Estimate excess mass and its standard error via bootstrap of residuals.
Translate into a behavioural elasticity or count of users changing behaviour, and check sensitivity to window and polynomial choices.
Use findings to set or redesign thresholds and test changes experimentally.
outputs: Excess mass estimates, counterfactual distributions, implied elasticities and robustness checks.
useWhen: Products with pricing thresholds, quotas, limits or deadlines where users can adjust behaviour.
avoidWhen: Discrete or sparse running variables with too few observations near the threshold.
whyLost: It comes from tax economics; product analytics rarely examines distributions at thresholds formally.
whereToUse: Free shipping minimums, freemium limits, storage caps, loyalty tiers, gig-worker earnings thresholds.
example: An e-commerce site finds substantial bunching of baskets at $50-52 above the free-shipping threshold. Excess mass implies 8% of shoppers add items to qualify; testing $45 and $55 thresholds follows.
sources: Kleven, Bunching (2016), Annual Review of Economics
Saez, Do taxpayers bunch at kink points? (2010), American Economic Journal: Economic Policy
Kleven & Waseem, Using notches to uncover optimization frictions (2013), Quarterly Journal of Economics
reference: Kleven, H. J. (2016). Bunching. Annual Review of Economics, 8, 435-464.

name: Capture-Recapture Estimation of Usability Problems
origin: Lincoln-Petersen estimator (Petersen 1896, Lincoln 1930); Chao estimators (1987); applied to software inspections by Eick et al. (1992)
summary: Estimates the total number of problems (including undetected ones) from the overlap between problems found by independent evaluators or sessions.
description: Ecologists estimate population size by capturing and marking animals, then recapturing: if few recaptured animals are marked, the population is large. The same logic applies to usability problems found by independent evaluators: if two evaluators find many of the same problems, few remain undiscovered. The Lincoln-Petersen estimator N = n1 x n2 / m, and more robust models (Chao's estimators, models allowing heterogeneous detectability), estimate total problems and hence the proportion found. Software engineering adopted this for code inspections. It provides an evidence-based answer to 'have we found enough?', better than rules of thumb about five users.
steps: Have two or more evaluators or independent session sets identify problems separately.
Consolidate problems carefully into a master list, with clear matching rules agreed beforehand.
Build a capture history matrix of which evaluator found which problem.
Estimate total problems using Lincoln-Petersen (two captures) or Chao and heterogeneity models (multiple captures).
Compute the proportion discovered and its confidence interval.
Decide whether to continue evaluation based on estimated undiscovered problems, especially severe ones.
outputs: Estimated total problem count, proportion discovered and confidence intervals.
useWhen: Planning or stopping evaluations such as heuristic reviews, usability tests and accessibility audits.
avoidWhen: When problem matching is unreliable or evaluators are not independent.
whyLost: Usability sample-size debates used binomial discovery models instead, and ecological methods never entered HCI teaching.
whereToUse: Heuristic evaluations, accessibility audits, content audits, bug bashes, AI red teaming.
example: Three evaluators audit an app for accessibility issues; capture histories estimate 112 total issues with 78 found (70%), so a fourth audit focused on screen readers is scheduled.
sources: Chao, Estimating the population size for capture-recapture data with unequal catchability (1987), Biometrics
Eick et al., Estimating software fault content before coding (1992), ICSE
Seber, The Estimation of Animal Abundance and Related Parameters (2nd ed., 1982)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)

name: Card Sorting
donor: Psychology (sorting and categorisation tasks); library science
origin: Psychological sorting tasks (e.g. Kelly, Miller); adopted for IA in the 1990s, codified by Spencer (2009)
summary: Participants group content items into categories that make sense to them, revealing mental models to inform navigation, labels and taxonomy.
description: Card sorting asks participants to organise a set of content items, written on cards, into groups. In an open sort they create and name their own groups, revealing how they conceptualise the domain. In a closed sort they place items into predefined categories, testing a proposed structure. Hybrid sorts allow both. Aggregated results show which items are consistently grouped together and what labels users apply. The rigour lies in selecting a representative set of 30 to 60 items with clear, non-leading labels, recruiting enough participants for stable patterns (around 15 to 30 for open sorts), and analysing with similarity matrices and hierarchical clustering rather than eyeballing, while reading participants' comments for the reasons behind their groupings.
steps: Define the scope and select 30 to 60 representative content items, writing labels that avoid shared keywords that cue grouping.
Choose open, closed or hybrid format based on whether you are exploring or testing a structure.
Pilot with 2 participants to catch ambiguous cards.
Run the sort with 15 to 30 participants per user group, moderated or online.
Build a similarity matrix and dendrogram from the groupings.
Analyse group labels and participant comments to understand reasoning.
Draft a candidate structure and validate it with tree testing.
outputs: Similarity matrices, dendrograms, frequently used category labels and a candidate information architecture.
useWhen: When designing or reorganising navigation, menus, taxonomies or feature groupings and you need users' mental models.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the problem is findability in an existing structure; use tree testing. Avoid with very large or highly heterogeneous item sets without first scoping them.
whyLost: Still in use: Foundational IA method with strong evidence base; increasingly done digitally with tools like Optimal Workshop.
whereToUse: Website/app navigation design; content taxonomy; feature categorization.
example: A pharmacy e-commerce site runs an open sort with 25 customers on 50 products. Shoppers group by symptom ('cold and flu') rather than by product type, prompting a symptom-led navigation that is then tree tested.
sources: Information Architecture
Lost Methods in UX
Card Sorting: Designing Usable Categories (Spencer)
Information Architecture (O'Reilly)
Everyday Information Architecture (Martin)
How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Spencer D (2009) Card Sorting: Designing Usable Categories
Rugg G & McGeorge P (2005) The sorting techniques: a tutorial paper. Expert Systems 22(3)
reference: Spencer, D. (2009). Card Sorting: Designing Usable Categories. Rosenfeld Media.

extra.Three Variants: Open card sort: Participants group cards AND create their own category labels. Reveals participants' mental model of the domain — the categories they naturally form and the labels that feel right to them. Best for: early-stage IA research when you don't know what categories should exist. Closed card sort: Participants sort cards into pre-defined categories. Tests whether your proposed categories match users' mental models. Best for: validating an existing IA or evaluating a proposed redesign. Hybrid: Participants sort into pre-defined categories but can create new categories when items don't fit. Tests current IA while allowing participants to surface missing categories.

name: Card-Based Value Elicitation
donor: Value sensitive design and values psychology
origin: Shalom Schwartz's theory of basic values (1992); Envisioning Cards by Batya Friedman and David Hendry (2012)
summary: Uses structured card sets representing values or value-related prompts to help users and stakeholders articulate, prioritise and trade off values relevant to a technology.
description: Values are hard to elicit directly; people struggle to articulate them and give socially desirable answers. Card-based methods give tangible prompts: Schwartz value cards (e.g. security, autonomy, benevolence) can be sorted and ranked; Envisioning Cards prompt consideration of stakeholders, time, values and pervasiveness. Combined with laddering or think-aloud during sorting, they surface value priorities, conflicts and trade-offs. Rigorous use draws cards from validated value theories, records sorting data for quantitative analysis (rank orders, Q-sort-like distributions) and couples sorting with qualitative explanation. It is especially relevant for AI, privacy and wellbeing design.
steps: Select a card set grounded in theory (Schwartz values, VSD values, Envisioning Cards) and adapt wording to context.
Introduce the technology or scenario to participants.
Ask participants to sort cards by importance, or into piles (most to least relevant), thinking aloud.
Probe trade-offs: present pairs of values in tension within the scenario.
Record rankings and explanations; analyse rank orders quantitatively and explanations qualitatively.
Translate value priorities and conflicts into design requirements and evaluation criteria.
outputs: Value rankings, identified conflicts and trade-offs, explanations and value-based design requirements.
useWhen: Designing technologies with ethical, social or personal value implications, or with diverse stakeholders.
avoidWhen: Purely functional tasks where values are not at stake.
whyLost: Value sensitive design is respected academically but its methods remain under-used in industry practice.
whereToUse: AI assistants, health data sharing, children's technology, workplace monitoring, civic tech.
example: Parents sort value cards about a child-location app: 'safety' ranks high but 'child autonomy' ranks close; trade-off probes lead to a design where children see when they are located.
sources: Schwartz, Universals in the content and structure of values (1992), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology
Friedman & Hendry, The Envisioning Cards: A toolkit for catalyzing humanistic and technical imaginations (2012), CHI
Friedman & Hendry, Value Sensitive Design: Shaping Technology with Moral Imagination (2019)
reference: Friedman, B., & Hendry, D. G. (2019). Value Sensitive Design. MIT Press.

name: Case Study Method
origin: Robert K. Yin, 1984 (Case Study Research: Design and Methods)
summary: An empirical design for investigating a contemporary phenomenon in its real-world context, using multiple evidence sources, replication logic and a chain of evidence to support analytic generalisation.
description: Yin's case study method is a research design, not a story format. It suits 'how' and 'why' questions about contemporary phenomena where the researcher has little control and the boundary between phenomenon and context is blurred. The design defines the case and unit of analysis precisely, states propositions, and for multiple cases uses replication logic: literal replication (cases expected to show similar results) and theoretical replication (cases expected to differ for predictable reasons). Evidence comes from several sources, such as documents, archives, interviews, observation and artefacts, converging on findings. A case study protocol and database maintain a chain of evidence from question to conclusion. Findings generalise analytically to theory rather than statistically to populations.
steps: Case definition: Define the unit of analysis precisely: a person, a product launch, a team, a feature adoption cycle. Must be defensible — why is this a meaningful unit?

Replication logic (for multiple cases): Literal replication (similar cases should produce similar results) and theoretical replication (different cases should produce different results for predictable reasons).
Multiple evidence sources: Documents, interviews, observations, artifacts, archival records. Each source has different strengths; convergence across sources builds confidence.
Chain of evidence: Research question → case study protocol → data collection → case study database → report. An external auditor should be able to follow this chain.

Analytic generalisation: Case study findings generalise to theory (theoretical propositions), not to populations. State explicitly which theoretical propositions your case confirms, disconfirms, or refines.
outputs: A case study protocol, a case database, within-case and cross-case analyses, pattern-matching results against propositions, and theory-level conclusions.
useWhen: Explaining how and why something happened in context, such as a product adoption in an organisation, a failed launch or a workflow change, especially across 1 to 10 deliberately selected cases.
avoidWhen: You need to estimate prevalence or effect sizes; use surveys or experiments. If you want to describe a culture over time, Organisational Ethnography is more suitable.
whyLost: In UX, 'case study' came to mean a portfolio narrative, so the research design with replication logic and a chain of evidence was largely forgotten.
whereToUse: B2B and enterprise adoption, post-mortems of launches, digital transformation programmes, multi-site rollouts, and evaluating service changes in health or government.
example: An enterprise software company studies 4 customer deployments, 2 successful and 2 stalled, selected for theoretical replication. Converging interviews, usage logs and project documents show that stalls stem from absent internal champions, not product gaps.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Robert Yin)
Case Study Research Design and Methods (Yin)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2018). Case Study Research and Applications: Design and Methods (6th ed.). Sage.

name: Catastrophe Flags Analysis
origin: Proposed by Gilmore (1993); developed as an empirical programme for psychology by van der Maas and colleagues (van der Maas and Molenaar 1992 onwards).
summary: A checklist of eight observable signatures (sudden jump, multimodality, inaccessibility, divergence, hysteresis, anomalous variance, divergence of linear response, critical slowing down) used together to decide whether a behaviour changes through a genuine tipping point rather than a smooth acceleration.
description: Many behaviour changes look sudden in a time series: a user abandons a product, a habit forms, an attitude flips. The book points out that a fast but continuous acceleration and a true phase transition can produce identical curves. What separates them is whether the in-between states are stable. Gilmore's catastrophe flags are a set of phenomena that a cusp (two stable states with an unstable region between) predicts and a smooth process does not. No single flag is decisive, but combinations are: the book singles out inaccessibility plus hysteresis as convincing. Some flags need only cross-sectional data (multimodality, divergence of the distribution as a splitting variable such as involvement increases), others need repeated measures (sudden jumps, critical slowing down) or experimental control of a variable (hysteresis, inaccessibility). For UX research the flags give a disciplined way to test claims such as 'adoption tips once a team reaches a critical mass' or 'trust collapses suddenly after errors', instead of reading tipping points into any steep curve. The choice of which flags to test depends on what you can measure and manipulate.
steps: Define the behavioural variable and state the two hypothesised stable modes, the unstable middle and the candidate control variables (one shifting the balance, one splitting the modes, such as involvement).
Start with cross-sectional data: test the distribution of the behavioural variable for multimodality with a mixture model; if it is unimodal, reconsider the hypothesis.
Test divergence: check whether the distribution becomes bimodal only at high values of the proposed splitting variable.
Where you have dense repeated measures, test for sudden jumps with change-point methods and look for rising variance, autocorrelation or slower recovery before transitions.
Where you can manipulate the normal variable, run an ascending and descending sweep to test hysteresis, and try to hold participants in the middle state to test inaccessibility.
Tabulate which flags were found and judge the combined evidence; then consider fitting the cusp model directly.
outputs: A flag-by-flag evidence table stating which signatures of a tipping point are present, absent or untested, with a judgement on whether the change is discontinuous.
useWhen: You suspect a behaviour, attitude or adoption state flips between two states and want evidence stronger than a steep curve, especially before designing interventions that assume a tipping point.
avoidWhen: The behaviour is naturally continuous with no plausible stable alternative states, or you have neither dense time series, large cross-sectional samples nor any experimental control.
whyLost: Catastrophe theory suffered a backlash in the late 1970s and its testing programme stayed inside developmental and mathematical psychology; UX tipping-point talk usually relies on curve shape alone.
whereToUse: Habit formation, churn and reactivation, trust collapse after failures, team adoption of collaboration tools, opinion shifts about features or brands.
example: A team-chat product believes teams 'tip' into daily use. Researchers check whether the distribution of weekly active-days per team is bimodal, whether bimodality appears only in teams with high manager involvement, and whether churned-and-returned teams show hysteresis (they need more colleagues active to re-adopt than they had when they dropped off).
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: Category-Theoretic Design System Modelling
origin: Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane, 1945
summary: Uses category theory's objects, morphisms and composition to model how design-system components and transformations compose, exposing inconsistencies in component APIs.
description: Category theory describes mathematical structures in terms of objects and the arrows (morphisms) between them, with an emphasis on composition: if arrows compose associatively and have identities, the system behaves predictably when assembled. Applied to design systems, components, tokens and states can be modelled as objects, and transformations such as theming, responsive resizing or state transitions as morphisms. The question becomes whether these transformations compose consistently: does applying dark mode then compact density give the same result as the reverse? Do component variants form well-defined structures? The method is formal and largely analytical, drawing on functional programming practice where these ideas are already embedded. Its rigour comes from specifying composition laws explicitly and testing them, often by property-based testing in code, so that design systems scale without combinatorial surprises.
steps: Identify the objects to model: components, tokens, themes, states and layouts.
Specify transformations between them (theming, density, responsive breakpoints, state changes) as morphisms.
State the composition laws the system should obey, such as order independence of theme and density.
Check laws against the design system, using property-based tests in code or systematic visual comparison.
Log violations where composition produces inconsistent or undefined results.
Refactor component APIs and token structures so transformations compose predictably.
outputs: Formal model of design-system objects and transformations, stated composition laws, violation log, API refactoring recommendations.
useWhen: Large, multi-brand or multi-platform design systems with many interacting variants, especially in functional UI codebases.
avoidWhen: Small component libraries or teams without mathematical or functional programming expertise; use a design-system audit instead.
whyLost: Latent: Theoretical; growing interest in functional programming UI (e.g. Elm, Haskell ecosystems).
whereToUse: Design system architecture; component API design; functional UI frameworks.
example: A multi-brand banking design system had 4 brands, 2 modes and 3 densities. Modelling transformations as composable maps exposed 37 components where brand-then-dark differed from dark-then-brand, which the team fixed by restructuring token layers.
sources: Where Mathematics Comes From
Category Theory for the Sciences (David Spivak)
reference: Spivak, D. I. (2014). Category Theory for the Sciences. MIT Press.

name: Causal effect estimation from observational data
origin: Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983; Robins's g-methods, 1986 onward
summary: Estimates the effect of a feature or intervention from logs or surveys by adjusting for confounding with methods such as weighting, matching, g-computation or doubly robust estimation.
description: When experiments are impossible, causal effects can still be estimated under the assumptions of exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding given covariates), positivity (every user could have received each treatment) and consistency (a well-defined treatment). Estimators include outcome regression (g-computation), inverse probability of treatment weighting, matching, and doubly robust methods such as augmented IPW or targeted maximum likelihood, which remain consistent if either the treatment or outcome model is correct. For time-varying treatments, marginal structural models handle confounders affected by earlier treatment. Rigour requires a DAG-justified adjustment set, balance and overlap diagnostics, bootstrapped intervals and sensitivity analysis such as E-values for unmeasured confounding.
steps: Specify the causal question and target trial, then select covariates from a DAG.
Estimate propensity scores and an outcome model; inspect overlap and trim extreme weights (e.g. truncate at the 1st and 99th percentiles).
Estimate the effect with a doubly robust estimator (AIPW or TMLE) and compare with IPW and g-computation estimates.
Verify covariate balance after weighting with standardised mean differences below 0.1.
Compute bootstrap confidence intervals with at least 1,000 resamples.
Report an E-value or similar sensitivity analysis showing how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be to explain away the effect.
outputs: Adjusted causal effect estimates with intervals, diagnostics, comparisons across estimators and a sensitivity analysis.
useWhen: Questions about feature or policy effects where randomisation was not done, especially with rich logs of pre-treatment behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid when assignment is driven by unmeasured factors, when positivity fails (some segments never get treatment), or when an experiment is feasible.
whyLost: These methods are routine in epidemiology and economics, but product analytics typically reports raw differences between users and non-users.
whereToUse: Retrospective feature evaluation, health app engagement effects, fintech product impact where regulation limits experiments.
example: An investment platform estimates the effect of price alerts on panic selling during volatility. AIPW adjusting for portfolio size, experience and prior trading shows alerts reduce panic sells by 18%, robust to an E-value of 1.9.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
DAGs+SEM Playbook (Vivek Gopinath)
VanderWeele & Ding (2017) Sensitivity analysis in observational research: introducing the E-value
Causal Inference (Hernán & Robins)

The Inquiry Series, Ch 48 — Target Trial Emulation — Causal Evidence from Log Data

name: Causal Forests for Heterogeneous Effects
origin: Stefan Wager and Susan Athey (2018); Athey, Tibshirani and Wager, generalised random forests (2019)
summary: Uses honest random forests to estimate how treatment effects vary across users, with valid confidence intervals and tests for heterogeneity.
description: Causal forests adapt random forests to estimate conditional average treatment effects. Splits are chosen to maximise treatment effect heterogeneity, and 'honesty' uses separate subsamples for choosing splits and estimating effects, yielding asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Built-in diagnostics include calibration tests for heterogeneity and best linear projections of effects onto covariates. Compared with ad hoc segment slicing of A/B results, which inflates false discoveries, causal forests provide disciplined discovery of who benefits and who is harmed, and can work with observational data under unconfoundedness with orthogonalisation.
steps: Start with randomised experiment data (preferred) or observational data with plausible unconfoundedness.
Select pre-treatment covariates that might moderate effects, e.g. tenure, device, prior usage.
Fit a causal forest (grf package) with honest splitting and sufficient trees (e.g. 2,000+).
Run the calibration test for heterogeneity and compute the average treatment effect with confidence interval.
Summarise heterogeneity with best linear projection and by ranking users into quantiles of predicted effect (RATE or TOC curves).
Validate key subgroups in a follow-up experiment before acting.
outputs: Conditional effect estimates, heterogeneity tests, variable importance for moderation, and targeting evidence.
useWhen: Large experiments where you suspect effects differ across users and want principled subgroup discovery.
avoidWhen: Small experiments (under a few thousand users) or when averages suffice for the decision.
whyLost: It is recent and computational, sitting in econometrics and data science rather than UX research.
whereToUse: Feature launches across diverse user bases, personalisation, health and finance interventions, accessibility features.
example: A language-learning app's new review schedule has a small average effect. A causal forest shows strong benefit for learners with irregular study habits and slight harm for daily learners, leading to adaptive scheduling.
sources: Wager & Athey, Estimation and inference of heterogeneous treatment effects using random forests (2018), JASA
Athey, Tibshirani & Wager, Generalized random forests (2019), Annals of Statistics

name: Causal Inference Methods
origin: Donald Rubin, 1974 (potential outcomes); Judea Pearl, 2000; Hernán and Robins, 2020
summary: Estimates causal effects from observational data using designs such as difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables and matching when randomised tests are impossible.
description: The fundamental problem of causal inference is that we never observe the same user both with and without a treatment. Randomised experiments solve this by design; when they are not possible, quasi-experimental methods approximate them. Difference-in-differences compares changes over time between affected and unaffected groups, assuming parallel trends. Regression discontinuity exploits thresholds that assign treatment. Instrumental variables use a factor that affects treatment but not outcome directly. Propensity score matching balances observed confounders. Synthetic control builds a weighted comparison from untreated units. Rigour comes from stating the causal question and assumptions explicitly (ideally with a DAG), choosing a design whose assumptions are plausible, testing them where possible (pre-trend checks, balance diagnostics), and running sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding.
steps: State the causal question precisely, including treatment, outcome, population and time frame.
Draw a DAG of plausible causes to identify confounders and choose an identification strategy.
Select a design (difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables, matching or synthetic control) whose assumptions fit the situation.
Prepare data and test assumptions, such as parallel pre-trends or covariate balance after matching.
Estimate the effect with confidence intervals.
Run sensitivity and placebo analyses and report limitations alongside the estimate.
outputs: Causal effect estimates with intervals, assumption diagnostics, sensitivity analyses, documented identification strategy.
useWhen: Evaluating features launched without experiments, policy or pricing changes, regional rollouts and situations where randomisation is unethical or impossible.
avoidWhen: When an A/B test is feasible, since randomisation is more reliable; or when data lack a credible comparison group.
whyLost: Latent: Growing in data science; rarely used in UX research; powerful for evaluating natural experiments.
whereToUse: Feature impact evaluation; policy evaluation; retrospective study design.
example: A retention lift after a feature launch coincided with a competitor's outage. Difference-in-differences using markets without the outage showed the feature's true effect was near zero, preventing a misguided expansion.

name: Causal Layered Analysis
origin: Sohail Inayatullah, 1998
summary: Analyses an issue at four layers (litany, systemic causes, worldview/discourse, myth/metaphor) to uncover deep assumptions and reframe problems and futures.
description: CLA examines issues at increasing depth. The litany is the public, quantitative view (headlines, metrics). The systemic layer covers social, economic and technical causes. The worldview layer examines discourses and paradigms that make those systems seem natural. The myth/metaphor layer captures deep, often emotional stories. Alternative futures are created by changing the metaphor and rebuilding upward. It is a rigorous way to move beyond surface metrics in UX strategy: for example, the litany 'low engagement' may rest on a worldview that 'more use equals value' and a metaphor of 'capturing attention'.
steps: Choose the issue and collect material: data, documents, interviews, media.
Describe the litany: common statements, metrics and visible problems.
Identify systemic causes: structures, incentives, technical and economic factors.
Surface worldviews and discourses that legitimise the system, including stakeholder differences.
Identify myths and metaphors underlying the worldviews, from interviews and language.
Construct alternative metaphors and rebuild new worldviews, systems and litanies; derive strategic options.
outputs: A four-layer analysis, alternative metaphors and reconstructed futures with strategic implications.
useWhen: Stuck strategic problems, reframing product purpose, or exploring cultural assumptions.
avoidWhen: Operational problems with clear technical causes.
whyLost: It belongs to critical futures studies and its poststructuralist framing feels abstract to product teams.
whereToUse: Digital wellbeing, social platforms, AI product purpose, healthcare and education reform.
example: A fitness app's CLA moves from the litany 'users quit after 3 weeks' to the metaphor 'body as machine to optimise'. A new metaphor, 'body as companion', leads to features centred on enjoyment and recovery.
sources: Inayatullah, Causal layered analysis: Poststructuralism as method (1998), Futures
Inayatullah (ed.), The Causal Layered Analysis Reader (2004)
reference: Inayatullah, S. (1998). Causal layered analysis. Futures, 30(8), 815-829.

name: Causal Loop Diagram from Qualitative Data
origin: Jay Forrester's system dynamics (1960s); causal loop diagrams popularised by Peter Senge, 1990; qualitative-data methods by Kim & Andersen, 2012
summary: Translating causal claims from qualitative data into variables and signed links, exposing reinforcing and balancing loops and evidence-backed leverage points.
description: Causal loop diagrams come from system dynamics, where problems are explained by feedback structure rather than single causes. Building them from qualitative data starts by extracting causal claims from transcripts or codes ('when X rises, Y falls'), turning them into variables, and drawing signed arrows. Tracing closed paths reveals reinforcing loops (vicious or virtuous cycles) and balancing loops (self-correction). An evidence audit marks every arrow with its supporting data, and unsupported links are labelled as hypotheses. Leverage points are variables central to several loops. Kim and Andersen's method for purposive text data emphasises traceability from text to diagram, guarding against analysts imposing their own model.
steps: List all causal claims emerging from your analysis: 'when X increases/decreases, Y increases/decreases.'
Draw nodes for each variable. Draw arrows for causal relationships with direction and sign (+/−).
Identify feedback loops: Trace paths returning to their starting node. Label reinforcing loops (R) and balancing loops (B).
Evidence audit: Every arrow must correspond to evidence in your data. Arrows without evidence are hypotheses — label [HYPOTHESIS].
Leverage points: Where would a design intervention have the largest systemic effect? Variables in multiple loops with high centrality.
outputs: A causal loop diagram with signed links and labelled loops, an evidence table per arrow, hypothesised links, and candidate leverage points.
useWhen: Problems with circular causality and unintended consequences, such as marketplace dynamics, trust spirals, support load or habit loops.
avoidWhen: Linear task problems or simple usability issues; use task analysis or usability testing. For quantified dynamics, move to stock-and-flow simulation.
whyLost: System dynamics is taught in management and policy schools, and UX synthesis rarely represents feedback loops explicitly.
whereToUse: Two-sided marketplaces, social platforms and content moderation, healthcare service systems, and organisational adoption of tools.
example: Interviews with ride-hail drivers yield claims linking surge pricing, driver positioning and rider wait times. The diagram reveals a reinforcing loop where drivers chase surges and leave suburbs underserved, pointing to a leverage point in positioning incentives.
sources: Qualitative Data Analysis (Miles & Huberman)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
The Fifth Discipline (Senge)
Business Dynamics (Sterman)
Creating System Dynamics Models from Qualitative Data (Kim & Andersen)
reference: Kim, H. & Andersen, D. F. (2012). Building confidence in causal maps generated from purposive text data. System Dynamics Review, 28(4), 311-328.

name: Causal Loop Diagrams (System Dynamics)
origin: Jay Forrester (1961); John Sterman (2000); Donella Meadows (2008)
summary: Maps reinforcing and balancing feedback loops, stocks and flows in a product ecosystem to anticipate second-order effects of design changes.
description: Causal loop diagrams represent variables linked by arrows marked with polarity; loops are reinforcing (amplifying) or balancing (stabilising), and delays are marked. Stock-and-flow models allow simulation. The treatise's transfer: model product feedback loops (engagement increases network effects, which increase retention, which increases engagement). A locally optimal change can set off a reinforcing loop that degrades experience over time, and CLDs make second-order effects visible before they occur. Dark pattern analysis particularly benefits: a dark pattern's short-term gain may initiate a trust-erosion loop that produces long-term harm. Rigour comes from grounding links in evidence and testing dynamic hypotheses with simulation.
steps: Define the problem behaviour over time (for example declining trust despite rising engagement).
Identify key variables and draw causal links with polarities, from data and stakeholder workshops.
Identify loops, mark delays and label them reinforcing or balancing.
Locate leverage points and likely unintended consequences of planned changes.
Optionally build a stock-and-flow simulation and calibrate with historical data.
Use the model in decision reviews and monitor indicators for each loop.
outputs: Causal loop diagrams, identified loops and leverage points, optional simulation results.
useWhen: Platform, marketplace and social features; engagement strategies; ethics reviews.
avoidWhen: Isolated interface details with no feedback effects.
whyLost: System dynamics stayed in management science and policy; UX focused on single interactions.
whereToUse: Marketplaces, social networks, recommendation systems, subscription businesses, dark pattern assessment.
example: A CLD of a dating app shows that boosting notifications increases short-term activity but feeds a 'match fatigue' loop that reduces reply rates after 3 weeks; the team caps notifications.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Forrester JW (1961) Industrial Dynamics
Sterman JD (2000) Business Dynamics: Systems Thinking and Modeling for a Complex World
Meadows DH (2008) Thinking in Systems
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: Sterman JD (2000) Business Dynamics: Systems Thinking and Modeling for a Complex World. McGraw-Hill.

name: Causal networks
origin: Miles and Huberman, Qualitative Data Analysis (1984; 2nd ed. 1994)
summary: Builds evidence-backed diagrams of the variables and causal links that explain an outcome within each case, then compares networks across cases to find recurring causal streams.
description: Miles and Huberman argued that qualitative data can support causal explanation because field research observes local mechanisms directly: who did what, under which conditions, with what result. A causal network is a display of the most important variables in a case, drawn as boxes, with arrows showing directional influence, accompanied by a narrative that explains each link with evidence. Variables are rated (for example high, moderate or low) and links are justified from coded data. Cross-case analysis then compares networks to identify causal streams, chains of variables that recur across cases leading to the same outcome. Rigour comes from explicit evidence for every arrow, inclusion of antecedent and intervening variables, informant review of the network, and predictions that can be checked later.
steps: Choose the outcome to explain (for example sustained digital record use at 6 months) and list candidate antecedent and intervening variables from coded data and memos, typically 10 to 25 per case.
Rate each variable for the case on a simple scale (high, moderate, low) using documented decision rules and evidence.
Draw directional links between variables only where field evidence supports them, and annotate each link with its evidence source and strength.
Write an accompanying narrative that walks through the network causally, citing excerpts for each link.
Have one or two key informants review the network and narrative, and revise links they convincingly dispute.
Compare networks across cases to identify causal streams that recur, and mark streams specific to subsets of cases.
Derive predictions from the cross-case streams and check them against new cases or later outcomes.
outputs: Per-case causal network diagrams with evidence-annotated links and narratives, cross-case causal streams, and testable predictions.
useWhen: Explaining why outcomes differ across sites, accounts or users; building theory of change for interventions; designing quantitative studies to test mechanisms.
avoidWhen: You need to estimate effect sizes or prove causation statistically (use experiments or causal inference on logs); or data are too thin to evidence links.
whyLost: Causal claims from qualitative data are often discouraged in UX ('qual is for why, not cause'), so the causal network technique never crossed from evaluation research into practice.
whereToUse: Multi-site rollouts, enterprise adoption, health system digitisation, service design evaluation, churn explanation in B2B accounts.
example: Causal networks for 12 clinics showed a recurring stream: power outages led to data loss, which led to supervisor distrust, then paper audit requirements, then duplicate entry, then non-adoption. Fixing offline sync alone was predicted insufficient unless audit policy changed, which later data confirmed.
sources: Qualitative Data Analysis (Miles & Huberman) via Sage Handbook
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods
The Inquiry Series, Ch 29 — Miles & Huberman — Systematic Qualitative Data Analysis
reference: Miles, M. B., & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Sage.

name: Causal thinking audit for research reports
donor: Epidemiology / research methodology, adapted for UX
origin: Adapted from reporting standards (e.g. Hernán's causal language guidance, 2018) in Vivek Gopinath's DAGs+SEM Playbook
summary: A structured review of a research report that checks every causal claim against its design, flags confounds and rewrites overclaims before decisions are made.
description: The causal thinking audit treats a research report as data to be tested. Each sentence implying cause (drives, leads to, because of, improves) is extracted, matched to the evidence and design behind it, and checked for the threats that could produce the same pattern: confounding (such as a market rally lifting retention), selection, reverse causation, regression to the mean and collider bias. The audit then asks what counterfactual the claim implies and whether the data could distinguish it. It draws on Hernán's argument that hiding causal intent behind associational language is worse than stating it with explicit assumptions. Rigour comes from a fixed checklist, independent auditors and a documented verdict per claim.
steps: Extract every explicit or implied causal claim from the report into a table.
For each claim record the design behind it (experiment, quasi-experiment, observational log, survey, qualitative) and its rung on Pearl's ladder.
Check each claim against a fixed threat list: confounding, selection bias, reverse causation, regression to the mean, collider bias, seasonality or market events.
Sketch a minimal DAG for contested claims and identify any open backdoor paths.
Assign a verdict per claim (supported, supported with stated assumptions, overclaimed, unsupported) and propose reworded language or a follow-up design.
Have a second auditor review independently and reconcile disagreements before the report is circulated.
outputs: An annotated claims table with verdicts, threat analysis, revised wording and a list of follow-up studies needed for key decisions.
useWhen: Before research findings feed strategy, roadmaps or board decks; when a metric moved and the team is ready to credit a feature.
avoidWhen: Avoid for purely exploratory reports with no causal intent, or when time-critical decisions are low-stakes and easily reversed.
whyLost: UX critique traditions focus on method execution, not causal logic, and few teams have the epidemiological vocabulary to run such a review.
whereToUse: Research ops quality gates, growth team post-mortems, fintech and health products under regulatory scrutiny, and executive readouts.
example: An investment app attributes a 15% retention lift to a new dashboard. The audit notes the launch coincided with a market rally; comparing against a non-exposed cohort shows the lift is almost entirely market-driven, and the claim is withdrawn.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
DAGs+SEM Playbook (Vivek Gopinath)
Nash Equilibrium Playbook (Vivek Gopinath)
Causal Inference (Hernán & Robins)
DAGs+SEM Playbook (Gopinath)
Nash Equilibrium Playbook (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 45 — The Causal Revolution — Pearl's Ladder & the Fundamental Problem

name: Centrality analysis
donor: Social network analysis and graph theory
origin: Linton Freeman's centrality measures, 1977-1978; PageRank, Brin and Page, 1998
summary: Ranks nodes in an information architecture by structural importance, identifying hubs, bottlenecks and peripheral content, and compares structural with intended importance.
description: Centrality metrics quantify how important a node is in a network. Degree centrality counts links; closeness centrality measures average distance to all other nodes; betweenness centrality counts how often a node lies on shortest paths between others, identifying bottlenecks; eigenvector centrality and PageRank weight links from important nodes more heavily. In an IA, these show which pages carry structural load and which important content is marginal. High-betweenness nodes are single points of failure: if they are confusing or broken, many journeys fail. Comparing the centrality ranking with business or user priority reveals misalignment. Rigour comes from a complete graph, using directed versions where links are one-way, and weighting by transition data where available.
steps: Extract the IA graph with directed edges and, optionally, transition weights from analytics.
Compute degree, closeness, betweenness and PageRank for all nodes in a tool such as NetworkX or Gephi.
Rank nodes and list the top 5% by betweenness as potential bottlenecks.
Compare centrality ranks with a priority ranking of content or tasks (from stakeholder input or top-tasks surveys) using Spearman's rank correlation.
Inspect high-betweenness nodes for usability quality and resilience; inspect high-priority, low-centrality nodes for missing links.
Propose link changes and recompute centrality to check alignment improves.
outputs: Centrality rankings, bottleneck list, priority-centrality alignment score, and recommended structural changes.
useWhen: For large IAs, knowledge graphs, intranets and documentation; when priority content is hard to reach; for resilience planning.
avoidWhen: For small or linear structures; use a simple sitemap review. For user mental models, use card sorting.
whyLost: Centrality is central in network science and SEO but has not entered UX research methods practice, where IA work is mostly qualitative.
whereToUse: Documentation portals, enterprise knowledge bases, medical device menus, e-commerce category structures, and AI retrieval corpora.
example: Centrality analysis of a 3,000-page help centre shows 'Account settings' has the highest betweenness while 'Cancel subscription', a top task, ranks in the bottom 20%. Adding links from billing and profile pages raises its closeness and halves related support contacts.
sources: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J., Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (O'Reilly, 4th ed., 2015)
Martin, L. M., Everyday Information Architecture (2019)
Covert, A., How to Make Sense of Any Mess (2014)

How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert)

name: CFA (Confirmatory Factor Analysis)
origin: Karl Jöreskog, 1969
summary: Tests whether survey items measure a pre-specified set of latent constructs as theorised, giving fit indices, loadings and evidence of construct validity.
description: Confirmatory factor analysis specifies in advance which items load on which latent factors (e.g. five trust items on Interface Trust, four on Institutional Trust) and tests how well this structure reproduces the observed covariance matrix. Unlike EFA, items are not allowed to load freely on all factors. CFA provides standardised loadings, factor correlations and global fit, and it is the measurement model underlying any SEM. Rigour comes from theory-led specification, adequate sample size (commonly 200 or more), appropriate estimators for ordinal Likert data (WLSMV), reporting multiple fit indices, examining convergent and discriminant validity, and testing measurement invariance before comparing groups.
steps: Specify the measurement model from theory or a prior EFA on a separate sample: which items load on which factors.
Collect data from at least 200 respondents (more for complex models) and inspect item distributions.
Fit the model with an estimator suited to the data (WLSMV for ordinal items, MLR for continuous-like items).
Evaluate fit with CFI and TLI at or above 0.95, RMSEA at or below 0.06, and SRMR at or below 0.08.
Check standardised loadings (ideally above 0.5, preferably 0.7), average variance extracted above 0.5 and discriminant validity (HTMT below 0.85).
Test measurement invariance (configural, metric, scalar) before comparing groups, and avoid purely data-driven modification indices.
outputs: A validated measurement model with loadings, fit indices, reliability, convergent and discriminant validity evidence and invariance results.
useWhen: Validating a UX questionnaire's structure, confirming a scale works in a new population or language, and as the measurement step before SEM.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you have no prior structure (use EFA), with samples under about 150, or for single-item measures.
whyLost: CFA is routine in psychology and marketing research, but UX teams usually adopt or invent questionnaires without testing their structure.
whereToUse: Trust, perceived usefulness and AI-reliance scales, localisation of standard questionnaires, enterprise satisfaction instruments.
example: A fintech team confirms that its 12-item digital trust scale has three factors in a new sample of 420 users, with CFI 0.97 and RMSEA 0.045, before using the scale to compare markets.
