name: Change Blindness Testing
origin: Rensink, O'Regan and Clark, 1997; Simons and Levin, 1997
summary: Tests whether users notice changes to a screen that occur during transitions, reloads or interruptions, revealing state changes that go unseen.
description: Change blindness is the striking failure to notice large changes in a visual scene when the change coincides with a disruption such as a blink, saccade, screen flash, page reload or interruption. Because visual memory retains little detail, people rely on attention to detect change, and without a transient motion signal changes are often missed. In UX this explains why updated totals, validation messages, reordered lists or silently refreshed data go unnoticed. As a method, researchers present the before and after states with realistic transitions and measure whether and how quickly participants detect the change, adapting the flicker paradigm. Rigour comes from controlling the transition type, measuring detection rates and latency, and comparing techniques such as animation, highlighting or persistent change markers that restore the missing transient signal.
steps: Identify state changes in the product that users must notice (totals, errors, reordering, live data updates).
Build prototypes that reproduce the real transition (full reload, fade, instant swap) and variants with change cues such as motion or highlighting.
Give 10-20 participants a primary task, then trigger the change without warning.
Record whether each participant reports the change and the latency to detection.
Compare detection rates across transition variants; treat detection under 80% for safety or money-critical changes as a defect.
Adopt the cue design that maximises detection and verify it does not create excessive distraction.
outputs: Detection rates and latencies by transition type, list of unseen state changes, recommended change-signalling patterns.
useWhen: Single-page apps, live dashboards, checkout totals, form validation and any interface where content updates without a full navigation.
avoidWhen: When the problem is comprehension of a change users did notice; use think-aloud usability testing.
whyLost: Siloed: Well-documented in perception psychology; rarely applied deliberately in UX practice.
whereToUse: Animation and transition design; onboarding change communication; screen reader design.
example: An e-commerce checkout recalculated shipping silently after an address change. Only 6 of 15 participants noticed the new total; animating the price change and briefly highlighting it raised detection to 14 of 15.
sources: Sensation and Perception
Design for How People Think
reference: Simons, D. J., & Levin, D. T. (1997). Change blindness. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 1(7), 261-267.

name: Change-Point Detection
donor: Statistical quality control and signal processing
origin: E. S. Page (1954, CUSUM); PELT by Killick, Fearnhead and Eckley (2012); Bayesian online change-point detection by Adams and MacKay (2007)
summary: Statistically locates the points in a time series where its mean, variance or trend changes, distinguishing real shifts from noise.
description: Metric dashboards invite people to see changes in noise. Change-point methods formalise detection: CUSUM accumulates deviations from a target and signals when they exceed a threshold; offline methods such as PELT or binary segmentation find the optimal set of change locations with a penalty for complexity; Bayesian online methods give a running probability that a change has just occurred. Applied to UX metrics (task success, satisfaction, error rates, support contacts), they identify when behaviour shifted, which can then be linked to releases or external events, and they support alerting on real regressions.
steps: Choose the metric series and its time resolution; consider seasonality and remove it if needed.
Specify the type of change to detect (mean, variance, slope) and an appropriate cost function.
Run offline detection (e.g. PELT with a BIC-like penalty) on historical data to find past changes.
Check sensitivity of detected points to the penalty and validate against known events.
For monitoring, configure CUSUM or Bayesian online detection with an acceptable false alarm rate.
Investigate each detected change with release notes, segment breakdowns and qualitative data.
outputs: Detected change points with magnitudes and confidence, and a monitoring configuration.
useWhen: Monitoring UX metrics over time, investigating when a problem started, or annotating long-term trends.
avoidWhen: Very short or highly irregular series; or when the change date is known (use ITS).
whyLost: Product dashboards rely on eyeballing and simple thresholds; change-point methods remain in statistics and engineering.
whereToUse: Experience metrics programmes, app performance, support volumes, review ratings, AI quality monitoring.
example: PELT on daily app rating data finds a mean shift on 14 March, two days after an SDK upgrade, rather than at the redesign date the team suspected.
sources: Page, Continuous inspection schemes (1954), Biometrika
Killick, Fearnhead & Eckley, Optimal detection of changepoints with a linear computational cost (2012), JASA
Adams & MacKay, Bayesian online changepoint detection (2007), arXiv
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: Killick, R., Fearnhead, P., & Eckley, I. A. (2012). JASA, 107(500), 1590-1598.

name: Channel Capacity Analysis
donor: Information theory and early human factors
origin: Shannon and Weaver, 1949; George Miller, 1956
summary: Treats human perception and response as limited-bandwidth channels, estimating transmitted information in bits to compare display codes and modalities.
description: Early human factors researchers applied Shannon's communication model to people, measuring how many bits per second or how many distinguishable levels a perceptual channel could carry. Miller's 'magical number seven' paper summarised findings that absolute judgement of a single dimension saturates at about 2.5 bits, roughly seven categories, while multidimensional stimuli carry more. The method computes transmitted information from stimulus-response confusion matrices, revealing how many levels of colour, size, pitch or vibration users can reliably distinguish. This gives a rigorous basis for coding decisions: how many alert tones, colour categories or haptic patterns can be used before confusion rises. It faded as cognitive models and usability testing took over, but remains valuable for designing multimodal codes.
steps: Define the coding dimension(s) to evaluate (e.g. tones, colours, vibration patterns) and candidate levels.
Run an absolute identification task in which 10-20 participants identify randomly presented levels, with many trials per level.
Build stimulus-response confusion matrices.
Compute transmitted information in bits and the effective number of distinguishable levels (2^bits).
Compare codes and modalities, and test combinations of dimensions for added capacity.
Set the number of levels to stay within capacity with a safety margin for real-world conditions.
outputs: Confusion matrices, transmitted information per code, maximum reliable number of levels per channel, coding recommendations.
useWhen: Designing alert tones, haptic vocabularies, colour coding in dense displays and multimodal signals in vehicles, medical devices or wearables.
avoidWhen: General screen usability questions; use usability testing or cognitive load assessment.
whyLost: Extinct: Grounded early HCI but supplanted by cognitive load frameworks and more applied usability methods.
whereToUse: Multimodal design; information display; notification channel design.
example: A smartwatch team planned eight distinct vibration patterns for notification types. Identification testing showed transmitted information of 1.9 bits, about four reliable levels, so they reduced to four patterns plus a visual glance.
sources: Human-Computer Interaction
The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two (George Miller)
The Mathematical Theory of Communication (Shannon & Weaver)
reference: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information. Psychological Review, 63(2), 81-97.

name: CHECk Ethical Checklists
origin: Read, Horton and colleagues in the ChiCI group, University of Central Lancashire (2013); applied in Chapter 1
summary: Two short checklists that make researchers question their own values before a study with children, and plan how children can give genuinely informed consent.
description: CHECk is an ethics tool for design and evaluation work with children. Its premise is that ethics is more than a signed consent form: in a school, teachers consent on behalf of a class, and a child may find it hard to refuse. CHECk1 asks six questions before any activity, pushing the team to be honest about why they are building the technology, why children are involved, and what values drive the work. CHECk2 looks before and beyond the activity from the child's side: what the children will be told about the activity, how their contributions will be used and disseminated, and who will get credit for their ideas. The aim is 'ethical symmetry', where children consent in their own right rather than adults consenting for them. Completing the checklists also surfaces weaknesses in study design and forces the team to work out how to explain the study in words children understand. The chapter also varied how much ethical information children received, showing that the briefing itself can be studied. For UX teams working with minors or other groups with unequal power, CHECk is a practical way to move beyond compliance.
steps: Before planning sessions, have the team answer the six CHECk1 questions in writing about the purpose of the technology and of involving children.
Revisit the study design in light of the answers, dropping or changing activities that cannot be justified.
Work through CHECk2: decide what children will be told, how their data and ideas will be used and credited, and how this will be explained.
Write a child-friendly script for the briefing and for asking assent, and make it easy for a child to decline.
Run the study, giving every child the same briefing, and debrief afterwards on how their contribution will be used.
Keep the completed checklists with the study records and review them after the study.
outputs: Completed CHECk1 and CHECk2 forms, a revised study plan and a child-appropriate briefing and assent script.
useWhen: Planning research or co-design with children, especially in schools where institutional consent can mask a child's reluctance.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for formal ethics review or legal safeguarding requirements, which still apply.
whyLost: It is known mainly within child-computer interaction; mainstream UX ethics practice focuses on consent forms and data protection rather than values reflection.
whereToUse: Children's products, edtech, school-based studies, research with other dependent groups.
example: Before testing a reading game in a primary school, the team completes CHECk1 and realises the main reason for involving children is to publish a paper; they add a feedback session in which children see how their comments changed the game and learn who will be credited.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Sim, G., Read, J. C. and Horton, M. (2016). Practical and ethical concerns in usability testing with children. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 1. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Chi-Square and Fisher's Exact Tests
origin: Karl Pearson (1900); R. A. Fisher (1922, 1935)
summary: Tests whether categorical outcomes differ across groups, such as preference by device or success by design.
description: The chi-square test compares observed counts in a contingency table with the counts expected if the variables were unrelated. Fisher's exact test computes the exact probability for small tables. Bruce and Bruce present a resampling approach that shuffles labels to build the null distribution directly, which makes the logic intuitive. For 2×2 tables Sauro and Lewis recommend the N-1 chi-square over both the classic test and Fisher's test; for larger tables the standard chi-square applies when expected counts are adequate.
steps: Build the contingency table of counts.
Check expected counts; for small 2×2 tables use the N-1 variant, for tiny tables use Fisher's exact test.
Compute the statistic and p-value (or simulate by permutation).
Inspect standardised residuals to see which cells drive the result.
Report counts, percentages and an effect size such as Cramér's V.
outputs: A test of association between categorical variables.
useWhen: Comparing preferences, choices or success across several groups.
avoidWhen: Paired data (use McNemar) or ordinal outcomes where order matters (use ordinal regression).
whyLost: Not lost; frequently misapplied to small samples or paired data.
whereToUse: Preference tests, card-sort agreement, survey categorical items.
example: Preference for three icon sets differs by age band (χ² = 14.2, p = 0.007); residuals show older users strongly favour labelled icons.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 3; Sauro & Lewis (2016), chapter 5.

name: Choice Architecture Optimisation for Option Sets
origin: Iyengar & Lepper, 2000; Schwartz, 2004; Thaler & Sunstein, 2008
summary: Designs the number, structure, ordering and defaults of options shown to users, testing how choice overload and decision stakes affect choice quality and satisfaction.
description: Schwartz documents the choice overload effect (Iyengar & Lepper 2000) and provides practical guidance: more options reliably reduce decision quality, increase regret, and reduce satisfaction — especially for maximizers (who always want the best) vs. satisficers (who accept 'good enough'). Applied to UX: the optimal number of options is not a universal constant but depends on user type and decision stakes.
steps: Measure choice-induced regret: after task completion with N options, ask 'How confident are you that you made the best choice?' (1–7).
Run across 3, 6, 12, and 24 options.
Plot confidence as a function of N.
The option count at which confidence peaks = the optimal set size for this user and decision type.
Also measure: did users check back or reconsider?
High reconsideration rate = choice overload signal.
outputs: Recommended option counts and groupings per context, default and ordering decisions, experimental evidence on choice quality, regret and conversion.
useWhen: Plan pickers, product catalogues, configuration screens, investment or insurance choices, and clinical option sets where too many or poorly structured options harm decisions.
avoidWhen: Avoid when options are few and familiar, or when ethical risk of steering is high without transparency; use neutral presentation and decision aids instead.
whyLost: Choice overload became a slogan ('fewer options') rather than a tested design variable, and replication debates made teams wary of applying it rigorously.
whereToUse: Pricing tier design, settings page organization, filter and facet design, onboarding option sets, feature comparison tables.
example: An insurer tests showing 3, 6 or 12 health plans with a recommended default; 6 grouped plans with a comparison table produce the highest satisfaction and lowest switching in the following year.
sources: The Paradox of Choice — Barry Schwartz
Paradox of Choice (Schwartz)
Think Bigger (Iyengar)
Happiness by Design (Dolan)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 22 — Choice Architecture, Default Effects & Option Set Design
reference: Schwartz B (2004) The Paradox of Choice: Why More Is Less. Ecco

name: Choice paralysis detection
origin: Iyengar and Lepper's jam study (2000) and Schwartz's The Paradox of Choice (2004); moderated by Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd's meta-analysis (2010)
summary: Detects whether the number or complexity of options is causing users to defer, abandon or regret decisions, using behavioural deferral signals and controlled set-size variation.
description: Iyengar and Lepper found shoppers were about ten times more likely to buy jam from a display of 6 than of 24 flavours, but Scheibehenne and colleagues' 2010 meta-analysis of 63 conditions found a mean effect near zero with large variance. Choice overload is real only under certain moderators: no clear prior preference, options hard to compare, high complexity, time pressure and a goal of choosing quickly. Choice paralysis detection therefore does not assume overload; it tests for it. It combines log signals (deferral, dwell without selection, back-and-forth comparison, abandonment) with controlled variation of set size or structure, and checks moderators. Rigour lies in treating overload as a conditional hypothesis and measuring deferral and post-choice satisfaction, not just conversion.
steps: Define deferral behaviours in logs: leaving a choice screen without selecting, repeated toggling between options, dwell times above the 90th percentile without action, and returns to the same screen.
Plot deferral and abandonment rates against the number of options shown and option similarity across existing sessions to spot dose-response patterns.
Assess known moderators for your context: preference uncertainty, comparability of options, decision complexity and time pressure, using 5 to 8 interviews or a short survey.
Run a controlled test that varies set size (for example 4 versus 12 options) or structure (categorised versus flat, with versus without a recommendation) with random assignment.
Compare selection rate, time to decision, post-choice satisfaction and regret (a short 3 to 5 item scale) across arms.
Conclude overload only if the larger or flatter set reliably increases deferral or regret; otherwise look for other causes such as missing information or trust.
outputs: Deferral metrics by set size and structure, experimental effect sizes, moderator assessment, and recommendations on set size, categorisation and recommended defaults.
useWhen: Users stall on plan pickers, catalogues, configuration screens or clinical option lists; teams debate cutting options without evidence.
avoidWhen: Users are experts with strong preferences who benefit from breadth, or traffic is too low for controlled variation; use moderated observation and interviews instead.
whyLost: The jam study became a design platitude ('fewer options are better') while the failed replications and moderator findings never reached practice, so overload is asserted rather than detected.
whereToUse: E-commerce category pages, pension and investment fund menus, insurance plan selection, triage and clinical decision support, AI model or template pickers.
example: A pension app offered 38 funds and saw 62% of new members defer the investment choice. A test of a 5-option tiered menu with a recommended default reduced deferral to 21% without lowering satisfaction, confirming overload under high preference uncertainty.
sources: Paradox of Choice (Schwartz)
Think Bigger (Iyengar)
Happiness by Design (Dolan)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 22 — Choice Architecture, Default Effects & Option Set Design
reference: Scheibehenne, B., Greifeneder, R., & Todd, P. M. (2010). Can there ever be too many options? A meta-analytic review of choice overload. Journal of Consumer Research, 37(3), 409–425; Iyengar, S. S., & Lepper, M. R. (2000). When choice is demotivating. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 995–1006.

name: Chunking and Progressive Disclosure (Empirical Application)
origin: George Miller (1956) and Nelson Cowan (2001) on memory capacity; codified for design in Lidwell, Holden and Butler (2003)
summary: Designs and tests information grouping and staged disclosure based on working-memory evidence, adjusting chunk size and disclosure depth to users' expertise.
description: Chunking is the grouping of information into meaningful units so that more can be held and processed; progressive disclosure staggers information so only what is needed now is shown. In UX both survive as slogans, notably the misapplied '7 plus or minus 2' rule for menus. The empirical application restores what the evidence says: working memory holds about four chunks (Cowan) rather than seven, chunk size depends on expertise because experts recognise larger meaningful units, and chunking matters for material that must be remembered, not for visible items users can scan. The method analyses which information users must hold in mind, groups it into meaningful units, defines disclosure levels by task frequency, and tests recall, error rate and time across variants for novices and experts separately.
steps: Audit every multi-item display: how many items are in each visual group?
Measure chunking effectiveness: test recall of chunked vs. non-chunked versions (target: chunked version produces ≥30% better recall at 5 minutes).
For expert users: increase chunk size — experts' larger schemas allow larger chunks.
For novices: reduce chunk size and increase visual separation.
outputs: Memory-load analysis of tasks, chunking scheme and disclosure levels, comparative recall, error and time data by expertise group.
useWhen: Complex forms, configuration screens, onboarding, data-dense dashboards and any interface where users must retain information across steps.
avoidWhen: When applied to scannable menus and lists where everything stays visible (memory limits do not apply), or as a reason to arbitrarily cap items at seven.
whyLost: Miller's 7 plus or minus 2 became a design myth, applied to visible menus rather than memory, while the newer evidence on four-chunk capacity and expertise effects never replaced it in practice.
whereToUse: Navigation design, settings page organization, dashboard layout, onboarding flow segmentation.
example: A broker's account-opening flow asks users to remember a 16-digit reference across screens. Chunking it as 4-4-4-4 and carrying it forward visibly cuts transcription errors from 9% to 2% among novice investors.
sources: Universal Principles of Design — William Lidwell
Miller, The magical number seven, plus or minus two (Psychological Review, 1956)
Cowan, The magical number 4 in short-term memory (Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2001)
reference: Lidwell W, Holden K & Butler J (2010) Universal Principles of Design. Revised ed. Rockport Publishers

name: Chunking effectiveness measurement
origin: Miller, 1956; Chase and Simon's chess chunking studies, 1973
summary: Measures whether the way information is grouped in an interface, such as codes, numbers or steps, actually improves recall and transcription accuracy.
description: Chunking is the recoding of several elements into a single meaningful unit, which effectively expands working memory. Interfaces chunk information through formatting (spacing card numbers into groups of four), structure (grouping steps into phases) and meaning (familiar patterns). Whether a chunking scheme helps is an empirical question: chunks only work if users perceive them as units. The measurement compares recall or transcription accuracy and time for alternative groupings, using span tasks or realistic transcription tasks. It can also reveal 'chunk boundary' errors, where users split or merge groups unexpectedly. Rigour comes from counterbalancing conditions, using realistic materials, and measuring both accuracy and time, as well as delayed recall where retention matters.
steps: Identify information users must read, remember or transcribe (codes, IDs, phone numbers, step sequences).
Create alternative groupings (for example 3-3-4 versus 4-3-3 versus unchunked) based on hypotheses about meaningful units.
Run a within-subjects test with 15-30 participants, counterbalancing order, using realistic materials and a short distraction interval before recall or transcription.
Measure accuracy, time and error position, coding errors at chunk boundaries separately.
Analyse with repeated-measures tests or mixed models and identify the grouping that maximises accuracy.
Adopt the best grouping across the product consistently and verify in live data where possible.
outputs: Accuracy and time per chunking scheme, boundary error analysis, and a recommended grouping standard.
useWhen: When users must transcribe or remember codes, IDs or sequences; designing OTP codes, reference numbers or step-by-step procedures.
avoidWhen: When information can be auto-filled or kept visible, making memory unnecessary; remove the memory demand instead.
whyLost: Chunking is cited constantly, but almost nobody tests whether a grouping works; formatting conventions are chosen by habit.
whereToUse: Banking (IBANs, sort codes), healthcare identifiers, two-factor codes, booking references and device serial numbers.
example: A hospital tests 10-digit patient IDs in 3-3-4 versus 5-5 groupings. With 24 nurses, the 3-3-4 format reduces transcription errors by 41%, with most errors in the 5-5 format occurring at the fifth digit.
sources: Sternberg, R. J., Cognitive Psychology
Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
MIT Psychology course materials
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Cognitive Psychology (Sternberg, Goldstein)
MIT Psychology
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 10 — Memory — The Architecture of Knowledge
reference: Chase, W. G. & Simon, H. A. (1973). Perception in chess. Cognitive Psychology, 4(1), 55-81.

name: Claims Analysis
donor: HCI design rationale and cognitive psychology
origin: John M. Carroll & Mary Beth Rosson, 1992
summary: Identifies the psychological claims, the upsides and downsides, that a design feature makes about users, and traces them to outcomes in usage scenarios.
description: Claims analysis is a design rationale technique from scenario-based design. For each key feature of a design, the analyst writes a claim describing the feature together with its hypothesised positive and negative psychological consequences for users, for example 'animated tutorial: + shows the task in context, - may be hard to follow at the user's own pace'. Claims are derived by walking through usage scenarios and asking questions grounded in Norman's stages of action. They make design trade-offs explicit, connect design decisions to psychological theory, and can be reused across projects as a body of design knowledge. Rigour comes from grounding claims in specific scenarios, stating both upsides and downsides, linking claims to evidence or theory, and testing important claims with users.
steps: Write usage scenarios that describe realistic user goals and activities with the design.
Walk through each scenario, identifying the features that most affect user experience.
For each feature, write a claim stating its hypothesised upsides and downsides for users.
Ground each claim in theory or evidence, such as Norman's stages of action or prior studies.
Review claims as a team to identify trade-offs and design alternatives.
Test the most consequential claims in usability sessions and update the claims library.
outputs: A set of claims with upsides and downsides per feature, documented design trade-offs and a reusable claims library.
useWhen: For scenario-based design, making trade-offs explicit in early design, documenting design rationale and teaching design reasoning.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need empirical evidence of user behaviour; claims are hypotheses. Use usability testing or experiments to confirm them.
whyLost: Extinct: Academic origin; complex to apply; practitioner knowledge base has largely dissolved.
whereToUse: Scenario-based design research; evaluating design tradeoffs with psychological grounding.
example: An AI assistant team writes a claim for 'auto-applied suggestions': it saves effort but may reduce user awareness of changes. Testing confirms users miss edits, so suggestions become reviewable diffs.
sources: Human-Computer Interaction
Lost Methods in UX
Usability Engineering: Scenario-Based Development (Rosson & Carroll)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Carroll JM & Rosson MB (1992) Getting around the task-artifact cycle. ACM TOIS 10(2)
Carroll JM (Ed) (1995) Scenario-Based Design
Rosson MB & Carroll JM (2002) Usability Engineering: Scenario-Based Development of HCI
reference: Carroll, J. M. & Rosson, M. B. (1992). Getting around the task-artifact cycle: How to make claims and design by scenario. ACM Transactions on Information Systems, 10(2), 181-212.

name: Classifier Evaluation (Confusion Matrix, Precision, Recall, ROC, Lift)
origin: Signal detection theory (1950s) and information retrieval (1960s); standard in machine learning
summary: Measures how well a classifier, human coder or AI feature sorts things correctly, and what kinds of mistakes it makes.
description: Accuracy alone hides the errors that matter. A confusion matrix counts true and false positives and negatives. Precision says how many flagged items were right; recall says how many of the real items were caught; specificity covers the negatives. The ROC curve shows the trade-off across thresholds and AUC summarises it. Lift shows how much better than random the top-ranked cases are. For UX researchers these are essential when evaluating AI features (does the spam filter or recommendation help users?), auto-coding tools, and screening questions in recruitment.
steps: Collect ground-truth labels for a test set.
Build the confusion matrix at the chosen threshold.
Compute precision, recall, specificity and F1.
Plot ROC and precision-recall curves and compute AUC.
Choose thresholds based on the user cost of each error type, not on accuracy.
outputs: A profile of a classifier's errors and a justified operating threshold.
useWhen: Evaluating AI features, automated coding, fraud and spam filters, or screener questions.
avoidWhen: There is no reliable ground truth.
whyLost: UX evaluates AI features by satisfaction and task success but rarely by error profile, even though error types drive trust.
whereToUse: AI product evaluation, research ops tooling, content moderation UX.
example: An AI meeting-notes feature has 92% precision but 61% recall for action items; users trust what it shows but miss many tasks, so the UI adds a "check for missed items" prompt.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 5.

name: Clinical Decision Analysis (Decision Trees)
origin: Howard Raiffa (Decision Analysis, 1968); Milton Weinstein and Harvey Fineberg (Clinical Decision Analysis, 1980)
summary: Models a decision as a tree of choices, chance events with probabilities and outcomes with values, and computes expected values with sensitivity analysis.
description: Decision trees make uncertainty explicit: decision nodes, chance nodes with probabilities (from data or calibrated judgement) and terminal outcomes with values or utilities. Folding back the tree computes expected values; one- and two-way sensitivity analyses and threshold analysis show which parameters could change the decision; probabilistic sensitivity analysis via Monte Carlo propagates uncertainty. Clinical medicine uses this for test-or-treat decisions, which map neatly onto UX questions like whether to add a confirmation step (test) versus allow and offer undo (treat), or whether to show an AI warning given false-positive rates.
steps: Frame the decision, alternatives, time horizon and outcome metric.
Draw the tree with decision and chance nodes, using realistic event sequences.
Estimate probabilities from logs, research or calibrated experts, and values for outcomes.
Fold back to compute expected values for each alternative.
Run one-way, threshold and probabilistic sensitivity analyses.
Present the decision, its robustness and the parameters worth researching further.
outputs: Decision tree, expected values, sensitivity and threshold analyses and recommended choice.
useWhen: Design decisions under uncertainty with identifiable probabilities and consequences, such as safeguards, warnings and verification steps.
avoidWhen: Decisions with poorly defined alternatives or outcomes; start with VFT or qualitative research.
whyLost: UX debates such choices qualitatively; decision modelling is taught in medicine and business schools.
whereToUse: Fraud and security friction, AI warning thresholds, confirmation dialogs, health app triage.
example: A bank models whether to add a step-up verification for new payees. With fraud probability 0.3%, loss $2,000 and abandonment cost of $1.20 per prompted user, the threshold analysis shows verification pays only for transfers above $400.
sources: Weinstein & Fineberg, Clinical Decision Analysis (1980)
Hunink et al., Decision Making in Health and Medicine (2nd ed., 2014)
Raiffa, Decision Analysis: Introductory Lectures on Choices under Uncertainty (1968)
reference: Hunink, M. G. M., et al. (2014). Decision Making in Health and Medicine (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

name: Cluster Analysis
origin: Robert Tryon, 1939; k-means by MacQueen, 1967; Ward's method, 1963
summary: Groups users or observations into homogeneous segments based on similarity across variables, used for behavioural segmentation and data-driven personas.
description: Cluster analysis is a family of unsupervised techniques that partition observations into groups whose members are more similar to each other than to members of other groups. Common methods include k-means, hierarchical clustering, Gaussian mixture models and density-based approaches. In UX it supports segmentation from behavioural logs or survey responses and provides quantitative grounding for personas. Results depend heavily on choices: which variables, how they are scaled, the distance measure, the algorithm and the number of clusters. Rigour comes from theory-driven variable selection, standardisation, comparing solutions with internal validity indices such as silhouette scores, testing stability with resampling or split halves, and checking that clusters differ meaningfully on external variables not used in clustering.
steps: Define the purpose of segmentation and select variables that relate to it.
Clean data, handle missing values and standardise variables.
Reduce dimensionality or remove highly correlated variables if needed.
Run one or more algorithms and compare solutions with different numbers of clusters using silhouette, elbow or information criteria.
Test stability by re-running on random subsamples or split halves.
Profile clusters on clustering and external variables and name them.
Validate usefulness with stakeholders and qualitative research before building personas or targeting.
outputs: Cluster assignments, cluster profiles, validity and stability metrics, and segment descriptions for personas or targeting.
useWhen: For user segmentation from behavioural or survey data, data-driven persona development and identifying distinct usage patterns.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you have predefined groups to compare (use group comparisons) or very few observations; avoid treating clusters as real types without stability checks.
whyLost: Still in use: Core data science technique; widely used in product analytics for segmentation.
whereToUse: User segmentation; behavioral clustering; persona generation from data.
example: A music streaming service clusters 200,000 users on listening behaviour and finds five stable segments, including 'background workers' who stream long sessions with skips disabled. Interviews confirm the segment and inspire a focus mode.
sources: Cluster Analysis for Researchers
scikit-learn
Cluster Analysis (Everitt et al.)
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Everitt, B. S., Landau, S., Leese, M. & Stahl, D. (2011). Cluster Analysis (5th ed.). Wiley.

name: Cluster Validation
origin: Rousseeuw, 1987; Everitt et al., 2011
summary: Evaluates whether user segments from cluster analysis are real, stable and useful using internal indices, resampling stability and external validation, not just visual inspection.
description: Cluster algorithms always return clusters, whether or not the data contain meaningful groups. Cluster validation tests whether a segmentation reflects real structure. Internal validity uses indices such as the silhouette coefficient, Calinski-Harabasz and Davies-Bouldin to compare solutions; the gap statistic compares clustering against a null reference. Stability is assessed by bootstrapping or subsampling and measuring agreement between solutions (e.g. Jaccard coefficients or adjusted Rand index). External validity checks whether clusters differ on variables not used to create them, such as retention or revenue, and whether they make sense qualitatively. Rigour comes from pre-specifying the candidate range of clusters, standardising variables appropriately, and reporting weak structure honestly.
steps: Cluster validation protocol:
Run clustering for k = 2..10.
(2) For each k, compute: silhouette score (higher is better, range -1 to 1; good clusters > 0.5), Calinski-Harabasz index (higher is better), Davies-Bouldin index (lower is better).
(3) Plot all three indices vs. k. Identify the k where the silhouette score peaks or the 'elbow' in CH/DB indices.
(4) Also compute gap statistic (compares within-cluster dispersion to random data).
(5) Report: which k did you choose, and why? Include all validation metrics.
outputs: Silhouette and other validity indices across solutions, stability estimates under resampling, external validation against outcomes, and a justified number of clusters.
useWhen: Any behavioural or attitudinal segmentation that will inform personas, targeting or strategy.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting clusters from data with no cluster structure; if validity indices are uniformly weak, use continuous dimensions or latent class models instead.
whyLost: Segmentation is commonly run with k-means and a scatterplot; validation methods remain in statistics and data mining texts.
whereToUse: Persona research validation, card sort analysis, behavioral segmentation, any UX analysis using clustering.
example: A fitness app's six-cluster segmentation shows an average silhouette of 0.18 and clusters that reshuffle under bootstrap; a three-cluster solution is stable (Jaccard above 0.85) and predicts retention, so it is adopted.
sources: Cluster Analysis for Researchers — (various)
reference: Rousseeuw PJ (1987) Silhouettes: A graphical aid to the interpretation and validation of cluster analysis. Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 20:53-65

name: Cluster validation with qualitative investigation
origin: Mixed-methods sequential explanatory design (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2007); applied to segmentation in Vivek Gopinath's Methods Atlas
summary: Tests whether statistically derived clusters correspond to genuinely different people, goals and contexts by investigating exemplar members through interviews, replays or diaries.
description: Statistical validity does not make a segment meaningful. This method samples high-membership and boundary users from each cluster and investigates them qualitatively, through session replays, interviews or short diaries, to check whether the cluster reflects a coherent motivation or context, or an artefact of features and scaling. A blind sorting step, where researchers group exemplar profiles without knowing labels, tests whether clusters are recognisable. Findings feed back into feature engineering and naming. Rigour comes from purposive sampling (core and boundary cases), blinding where possible, explicit criteria for confirming, splitting or merging clusters, and documenting disconfirming evidence.
steps: Select 4-6 high-membership users and 2-3 boundary users per cluster for investigation.
Review session replays or event timelines for each, then conduct 30-45 minute interviews or 1-week diaries with a subset.
Ask researchers blind to cluster labels to sort anonymised profiles into groups and compare with algorithmic clusters (e.g. agreement above 70%).
Code interviews for goals, triggers and contexts, and compare themes within versus across clusters.
Decide for each cluster whether to confirm, rename, split, merge or discard it, and record the evidence.
Feed findings into revised features or segmentation and repeat if major changes occur.
outputs: Validated, renamed or restructured segments with qualitative evidence, a blind sorting agreement score and archetype narratives.
useWhen: After behavioural clustering when segments will drive personas, roadmaps or personalisation.
avoidWhen: Avoid when clusters fail basic statistical validation (fix them first) or when users cannot be recontacted for privacy reasons; use replay-only review then.
whyLost: Quantitative and qualitative teams work separately, so clusters are named from centroid tables and never met as people.
whereToUse: Behavioural persona programmes in fintech, health, SaaS and media; validating AI-driven segmentation.
example: Interviewing exemplar users from a 'dormant' cluster reveals two different groups: deliberate long-term holders and confused abandoners. The team splits the cluster and designs different re-engagement messages.

Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Methods Atlas (Vivek Gopinath)
Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (John Creswell & Vicki Plano Clark)
Cluster Analysis for Researchers
Pattern Recognition & ML (Bishop)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 51 — Behavioral Clustering & Probabilistic Segmentation
