name: Co-design Workshops
origin: Scandinavian participatory design, 1970s; generative toolkits by Liz Sanders, 2000s
summary: Brings users and stakeholders into structured sessions to make artefacts and concepts together, surfacing tacit needs and building shared ownership of solutions.
description: Co-design descends from the Scandinavian participatory design movement, which held that people affected by technology should shape it. Sanders and Stappers developed generative toolkits (collage, mapping, prototyping kits) that help participants express tacit and latent needs through making rather than only telling. A co-design workshop sequences activities from sensitising (often a pre-session diary) through making and presenting to collective refinement. Rigour comes from careful recruitment so that the people affected are represented, well-designed toolkits matched to the question, facilitation that balances power between users and professionals, and systematic analysis of produced artefacts and discussions rather than treating outputs as finished designs. Co-design can be generative, exploring futures, or evaluative, reshaping existing concepts.
steps: Define the question and the level of participation (consultation, collaboration, or user-led decision-making).
Recruit 6-12 participants per session representing affected groups, including those often excluded.
Send a sensitising activity such as a short diary or workbook a few days before.
Run the workshop with structured making activities using toolkits matched to the question.
Have participants present their artefacts and explain meanings; record and photograph everything.
Analyse artefacts and transcripts thematically and feed back outcomes to participants.
outputs: Participant-made artefacts, concept sketches, thematic analysis, shared design principles, stakeholder buy-in.
useWhen: New services, community and public-sector projects, products for marginalised groups, and early-stage concepts where tacit needs matter.
avoidWhen: When you need evaluative performance data or decisions are already fixed; use usability testing, and do not use co-design as consultation theatre.
whyLost: Still in use: Enables rapid generation; builds stakeholder ownership; useful at any project stage.
whereToUse: New product development; service design; community-centered design.
example: A diabetes management app ran co-design workshops with teenagers and parents. Teens' collages emphasised privacy from parents, leading to a shared-but-filtered data view that neither group had requested in interviews.
sources: Modular Design Frameworks
Convivial Toolbox (Sanders & Stappers)
Routledge International Handbook of Participatory Design (Simonsen & Robertson)
reference: Sanders, E. B.-N., & Stappers, P. J. (2008). Co-creation and the new landscapes of design. CoDesign, 4(1), 5-18.

name: Coefficient H (Maximal Reliability)
origin: Hancock & Mueller, 2001
summary: Estimates construct reliability from optimally weighted CFA loadings, giving a better reliability index than Cronbach's alpha for UX scales with unequal item quality.
description: Cronbach's alpha is commonly misused as a measure of reliability, but it is actually a lower bound on reliability and is sensitive to the number of items. Coefficient H (Hancock & Mueller 2001) — also called maximal reliability — is theoretically superior: it represents the reliability of the construct estimated from a set of items using their optimal (CFA-derived) weights.
steps: Compute Coefficient H for any UX scale:
Run CFA on the scale items.
(2) Extract standardized factor loadings λ_i.
(3) Compute H = 1 / (1 + 1/Σ(λ_i²/(1-λ_i²))).
(4) Compare H to alpha: if H substantially exceeds alpha, the scale has poor items that alpha is masking (some items are carrying all the reliability).
(5) Target H > 0.80 for research purposes, > 0.90 for individual assessment. R: in semTools package: maximalRelia().
outputs: Coefficient H per construct alongside omega and alpha, item loadings, and decisions on item retention for UX scales.
useWhen: Developing or validating UX questionnaires (trust, satisfaction, usability) with factor analysis, especially when items differ in quality.
avoidWhen: Avoid when scales are scored as unweighted sums and you need the reliability of that sum (report omega); avoid with very small samples where CFA is unstable.
whyLost: Alpha is the default in software and reviews, and reliability theory beyond alpha is rarely taught outside psychometrics.
whereToUse: UX scale development, SUS validity assessment, any UX measurement instrument development.
example: A team validating a 6-item AI-trust scale finds alpha=0.74 but coefficient H=0.88, driven by two strong items; combined with omega, this guides which items to keep in a shorter version.
sources: Survey Scales — (various)
reference: Hancock GR & Mueller RO (2001) Rethinking construct reliability within latent variable systems. In Cudeck R, du Toit S & Sörbom D (Eds.) Structural Equation Modeling: Present and Future. Scientific Software International

name: Cognitive Bias Audit
origin: Grounded in Tversky and Kahneman, 1974; audit format developed in applied behavioural design
summary: Systematically reviews a product's flows and the team's own decisions for heuristics and biases, distinguishing biases exploited in users from biases embedded by designers.
description: A cognitive bias audit applies the heuristics-and-biases programme as a structured inspection. It has two faces. Facing outward, it walks each user decision point and asks which judgement heuristics (representativeness, availability, anchoring, conjunction errors, framing) are likely operating, and whether the design mitigates, exploits or ignores them. Facing inward, it examines the team's own assumptions, for example through a prediction gap test in which stakeholders predict user behaviour before data is revealed, exposing overconfidence and availability effects in product decisions. Rigour comes from using an explicit bias checklist with definitions, recording evidence for each finding, rating severity, and validating predictions against behavioural data. Without this structure, 'bias' becomes rhetorical; with it, the audit becomes repeatable and comparable across releases.
steps: Assemble a bias checklist with operational definitions (e.g. anchoring, availability, representativeness, conjunction fallacy, framing, default effect).
Walk each decision point in the user journey and record which biases plausibly operate and whether the design mitigates or exploits them.
Run a prediction gap test: have 5-10 stakeholders predict key user metrics before revealing actual data.
Quantify prediction errors and identify systematic team biases such as overestimating advanced feature use.
Rate each finding by severity and evidence strength, separating ethical risks from optimisation opportunities.
Recommend mitigations and validate the highest-priority ones with behavioural data or experiments.
outputs: Bias inventory per decision point, prediction gap scores for the team, severity-rated recommendations.
useWhen: Ethics reviews, high-stakes decision flows (credit, health, insurance), and when product strategy rests on untested team assumptions.
avoidWhen: When you lack behavioural data to check claims and stakeholders expect quick wins; start with analytics or a usability study.
whyLost: Latent: Concept exists but systematic audit methodology rarely formalized in practice.
whereToUse: Product ethics review; conversion optimization; deceptive pattern identification.
example: A community health app team predicted 60% of health workers used the advanced referral feature; logs showed 9%. The prediction gap test reframed the roadmap toward the basic flow and the audit flagged anchoring in default dosage fields.
sources: Heuristics and Biases
Thinking Fast and Slow
Heuristics & Biases (Kahneman ed.)
Judgment Under Uncertainty
Choices Values & Frames (Kahneman/Tversky)
Thinking, Fast and Slow (Daniel Kahneman)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 21 — Heuristics, Biases & the Architecture of Judgment
reference: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131.

name: Cognitive Dimensions of Notations
origin: Thomas Green, 1989; Green and Marian Petre, 1996; questionnaire by Blackwell and Green, 2000
summary: A vocabulary of about 14 dimensions, such as viscosity, hidden dependencies and premature commitment, for evaluating how well a notation or information artefact supports an activity.
description: The framework evaluates notations (programming languages, diagram editors, spreadsheets, design tools) not by surface usability but by how their structure supports different activities: incrementation, transcription, modification, exploratory design and searching. Dimensions include viscosity (resistance to change), visibility, premature commitment, hidden dependencies, role-expressiveness, error-proneness, abstraction gradient, secondary notation, progressive evaluation, provisionality, closeness of mapping, consistency, diffuseness and hard mental operations. Dimensions trade off against each other, and the profile needed depends on the activity. It gives designers and users a shared 'discussion tool' and is excellent for evaluating complex creation tools, including no-code builders and prompt interfaces.
steps: Identify the notation and the main user activities (e.g. exploratory design versus modification).
Define the desired profile: which dimensions matter most for those activities.
Evaluate the notation against each dimension with concrete examples, or administer the Blackwell-Green CD questionnaire to experienced users.
Record trade-offs, such as reducing viscosity at the cost of increased abstraction.
Compare against the desired profile and prioritise design changes.
Optionally run targeted tasks (e.g. modification tasks) to measure the most problematic dimensions.
outputs: A cognitive dimensions profile, trade-off notes and prioritised design changes for the notation.
useWhen: Evaluating creation and authoring tools: IDEs, design tools, spreadsheets, workflow builders, prompt editors, data modelling tools.
avoidWhen: Simple consumer flows without a notation or structure being built.
whyLost: It stayed in the psychology-of-programming community (PPIG) and was not packaged as a commercial UX method.
whereToUse: No-code platforms, AI prompt and agent builders, BI tools, CAD, design systems tooling.
example: A workflow automation builder scores high on hidden dependencies: changing one step silently breaks others. The team adds dependency highlighting and a dry-run mode, improving modification task success.
sources: Green & Petre, Usability analysis of visual programming environments: a 'cognitive dimensions' framework (1996), Journal of Visual Languages and Computing
Blackwell & Green, A Cognitive Dimensions questionnaire optimised for users (2000), PPIG
reference: Green, T. R. G., & Petre, M. (1996). Journal of Visual Languages & Computing, 7(2), 131-174.

name: Cognitive ecosystem mapping
origin: Edwin Hutchins, Cognition in the Wild, 1995; DiCoT framework by Blandford and Furniss, 2006
summary: Maps how cognition is distributed across people, artefacts, space and time in a work system, showing where information is stored, transformed and propagated.
description: Distributed cognition treats the unit of analysis as the whole functional system, not the individual mind. Hutchins showed how navigating a ship is accomplished by crew, instruments and charts together, with representations transformed as they move between media. Cognitive ecosystem mapping applies this to UX by observing work in context and modelling information flows, representational states, physical layout, artefacts and social structures. Clark's extended mind thesis adds that tools can be constitutive parts of cognition. The DiCoT framework structures the analysis into information flow, physical layout and artefact models. Rigour comes from extended observation, tracing specific representations across media, and validating models with participants. The output shows where knowledge lives and where it is fragile.
steps: Define the functional system and its goal (for example 'completing a robotic procedure safely').
Observe the work in context for multiple sessions (at least 3-5 full cycles), recording artefacts, communications and movements.
Build DiCoT models: information flow (who and what passes information to whom), physical layout (where things are and who can see them) and artefacts (what each representation encodes).
Trace key pieces of information through all transformations, noting media changes and delays.
Identify fragile points: single points of storage, lossy transformations, unshared representations and visibility gaps.
Validate models with participants and derive design opportunities for shared representations or redundancy.
outputs: DiCoT information flow, layout and artefact models, traced information journeys, fragility points and design opportunities.
useWhen: For collaborative, artefact-rich work such as clinical teams, control rooms, logistics and multi-device workflows.
avoidWhen: For individual, single-device tasks; use contextual inquiry or task analysis.
whyLost: Influential in CSCW and academic HCI, but its demanding fieldwork and abstract framing kept it out of mainstream product research.
whereToUse: Operating theatres, emergency departments, air traffic control, trading floors, logistics hubs, and human-AI teams.
example: Mapping a robotic procedure shows the instrument count lives in three places: the console, a nurse's tablet and a whiteboard, updated at different times. The map leads to a shared count display visible to the whole team.
sources: Hutchins, E., Cognition in the Wild (1995)
Clark, A., Supersizing the Mind (2008)
Clark, A., Being There: Putting Brain, Body, and World Together Again (1997)
Cognition in the Wild (Hutchins)
Supersizing the Mind (Clark)
Being There (Clark)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 14 — Distributed Cognition & Cognitive Ecosystems
reference: Hutchins, E. (1995). Cognition in the Wild. MIT Press.

name: Cognitive Interviewing for Questionnaire Design
origin: CASM movement, 1980s; Roger Tourangeau's four-stage response model, 1984; Gordon Willis, 2005
summary: Think-aloud and verbal probing with a few respondents to reveal how they comprehend, recall, judge and map answers to survey items before fielding.
description: Cognitive interviewing tests survey questions against how people actually answer them. Following Tourangeau's model, answering involves comprehension, retrieval from memory, judgement or estimation, and mapping the answer onto the response format; each stage can fail. In a cognitive interview, a small sample of target respondents answers draft items while thinking aloud or responding to scripted and spontaneous probes such as 'what does this question ask?' or 'how did you arrive at that?'. Problems are coded by stage and items failing for several participants are revised and retested. It is routine in national statistics offices and catches ambiguous terms, vague quantifiers, inaccessible memories and ill-fitting scales that no statistical analysis can fix after fielding.
steps: Recruit 5–10 participants from your target population. Think-aloud or verbal probing — choose one consistently.
For each question: ask the participant to answer it while thinking aloud, then probe on comprehension, retrieval strategy, and response mapping.
Code problems by type. Revise items that show comprehension, retrieval, or response problems in 3+ participants.
Re-test revised items with a new subsample before final deployment.
outputs: An item-by-item problem log coded by response stage, revised items, and a pretest report documenting changes.
useWhen: Before any survey that will inform decisions, especially new scales, translated instruments, satisfaction or NPS-like items, and items about frequency or recall.
avoidWhen: When re-using a fully validated instrument unchanged in the same population; then a light pilot for flow suffices.
whyLost: UX surveys are often written quickly in survey tools and launched without pretesting, so the survey-methodology practice never became standard.
whereToUse: In-product surveys, satisfaction trackers, onboarding questionnaires, clinical outcome questionnaires in health apps, and localised surveys.
example: Testing a fintech satisfaction survey, five of eight participants interpret 'transactions' as only card payments. The item is rewritten to list transfer types, avoiding a systematically biased metric.
sources: Analysis of the Cognitive Interview in Questionnaire Design
Survey Methodology (Groves et al.)
International Handbook of Survey Methodology
Statistics for Behavioral Sciences
Discovering Statistics via SPSS (Field)
Survey Methodology (Groves)
Cognitive Interviewing: A Tool for Improving Questionnaire Design (Willis)
The Psychology of Survey Response (Tourangeau, Rips & Rasinski)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 42 — Ordinal Logic — Treating Likert & Survey Data Correctly
reference: Willis, G. B. (2005). Cognitive Interviewing: A Tool for Improving Questionnaire Design. Sage.

extra.The Four-Stage Response Model: Comprehension: Does the respondent interpret the question as intended? Probe: "What do you think this question is asking?" Common comprehension failures: technical terms with multiple meanings, ambiguous timeframes ("recently"), vague quantifiers ("often"). Retrieval: Can the respondent retrieve the information from memory to answer? Probe: "How did you come up with that answer?" Many questions assume accessible memories that do not exist — respondents fabricate responses rather than admit non-recall. Estimation / Judgment: When exact recall is impossible, how do the respondent estimate? What strategy do they use? Different strategies produce systematically different answers — the question should constrain the strategy. Response mapping: Does the response scale capture the respondent's answer? Probe: "Where on this scale does your answer fall, and does any option capture it exactly?" Response option overlap, order effects, and missing options all produce measurement error.

name: Cognitive Load Assessment (Cognitive Load Theory)
origin: John Sweller, 1988
summary: Applies Sweller's distinction between intrinsic, extraneous and germane load to diagnose and measure where an interface wastes users' limited working memory.
description: Cognitive Load Theory holds that working memory is severely limited, so any task imposes intrinsic load (the inherent complexity of the material), extraneous load (demands created by poor presentation) and germane load (effort that builds lasting schemas). In UX the method is to decompose a task, attribute each demand to one of these sources and then measure load directly. Rigour comes from pairing a structured element-interactivity analysis with validated measures: subjective scales such as the Paas mental-effort rating or NASA-TLX, secondary-task reaction times, and physiological proxies such as pupil dilation or heart-rate variability. The aim is not to minimise all load but to strip extraneous load so that capacity is available for the intrinsic work and for learning. Comparing load profiles across design variants, with expertise level controlled, turns an often-cited theory into a measurable design criterion.
steps: Decompose the target task into steps and list the information elements a user must hold simultaneously at each step (element interactivity).
Classify each demand as intrinsic, extraneous or germane, flagging split attention, redundancy and unnecessary recall as extraneous sources.
Select load measures: a 9-point Paas mental-effort rating after each task, NASA-TLX for multidimensional workload, and optionally a secondary-task reaction time or pupillometry.
Run 8-20 participants per variant, stratified by domain expertise because the expertise-reversal effect changes which designs help.
Compare load scores alongside task success and time; a design that lowers effort ratings by about one scale point with equal accuracy is a meaningful gain.
Redesign to remove extraneous load (integrate split sources, chunk, use worked examples or progressive disclosure) and re-measure.
outputs: Element-interactivity map, load attribution by step, effort and workload scores per variant, prioritised list of extraneous-load fixes.
useWhen: Data-dense, instructional or high-stakes task interfaces where users report feeling overwhelmed, or when comparing designs that differ mainly in presentation complexity.
avoidWhen: Simple, low-frequency tasks where completion rates and observation already explain the problem; use standard usability testing instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Core theoretical foundation for UX design; explains why complexity fails users.
whereToUse: Any interface; particularly instructional, data-heavy, or task-intensive products.
example: A lending platform's loan-officer console showed borrower data across three tabs. Load analysis attributed most effort to split attention; consolidating key fields onto one panel cut Paas ratings from 6.8 to 5.1 with no loss of decision accuracy.
sources: Cognitive Psychology
100 Things Every Designer Should Know
Unmasking the Face (Ekman & Friesen)
Designing Across Senses (Noessel)
Affective Computing (Picard)
Cognitive Load Theory (Sweller, Ayres & Kalyuga)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 38 — FACS, Micro-Expression Analysis & Psychophysiology
reference: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

name: Cognitive Mapping and Concept Mapping
origin: Joseph Novak, 1972 (concept maps); cognitive mapping from Edward Tolman (1948) and Robert Axelrod (1976)
summary: Participants generate and link concepts into a network, externalising how they understand a domain; maps are analysed and aggregated to reveal shared and divergent mental models.
description: Concept mapping asks people to externalise their understanding of a domain as nodes (concepts) and labelled links (relationships). In Novak's hierarchical form, a focus concept sits at the top with progressively specific concepts below and cross-links connecting branches; in cognitive mapping, arrows often represent causal beliefs. Participants generate 10 to 15 concepts, arrange them, and label the relationships while thinking aloud. Analysis counts nodes, links and cross-links, compares structures between groups such as novices and experts, and aggregates individual maps into a group map of frequently shared links. The method is rigorous when the elicitation prompt is standardised, structure is scored consistently, and individual maps are kept separate from the analyst's interpretation.
steps: Concept elicitation: Ask participants to generate 10–15 concepts associated with a domain. Write each on a card.
Relationship mapping: Participants arrange cards spatially and draw arrows between related concepts. For each arrow: label the relationship ('causes', 'is part of', 'prevents', 'requires').
Hierarchical variant (Novak concept maps): Root concept at the top; subordinate concepts below; cross-links between branches.
Analysis: Count nodes, links, and cross-links across participants. High cross-link density = rich, well-integrated understanding. Low = fragmented understanding.
Group concept map: Aggregate individual maps into a group map showing the most frequently appearing concepts and relationships — your population-level mental model.
outputs: Individual concept maps, structural metrics (nodes, links, cross-links, hierarchy depth), an aggregated group map, and a comparison of mental models across segments.
useWhen: You need to understand how users mentally organise a complex domain (insurance, investing, data permissions, ML systems) to inform IA, onboarding or explanations, or to compare novice and expert understanding.
avoidWhen: You only need labels and groupings for navigation; card sorting is faster. If you need to find usability problems, use usability testing.
whyLost: Mental model research in UX shifted to Indi Young's task-based mental model diagrams and card sorting, while scored concept mapping remained in education research.
whereToUse: Financial literacy and investing products, AI explainability, enterprise domain modelling, healthcare self-management, and onboarding design.
example: An investing app asks 12 new investors to map 'how my money grows'. Most maps omit fees and link 'risk' only to 'loss', never to 'return'. Onboarding is redesigned to make the risk-return link and fee drag explicit.
sources: Personal Construct Psychology (Kelly)
Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (Hollnagel)
reference: Novak, J. D. & Gowin, D. B. (1984). Learning How to Learn. Cambridge University Press.

name: Cognitive Task Analysis
donor: Cognitive psychology; naturalistic decision making; military and aviation human factors
origin: Developed from the late 1970s and 1980s; Klein, Calderwood & MacGregor (Critical Decision Method, 1989)
summary: Elicits the knowledge, cues, judgements and decision strategies behind expert performance, capturing the cognitive demands that behavioural task analysis misses.
description: Cognitive task analysis extends traditional task analysis to the mental side of work: the knowledge, cues, judgements, decisions and strategies experts use, particularly under uncertainty and time pressure. Methods include the Critical Decision Method, which probes a specific challenging incident through repeated sweeps, knowledge audits, simulation interviews and think-aloud with protocol analysis. Outputs capture what experts notice that novices miss, how they assess situations and what makes decisions difficult. Rigour comes from anchoring elicitation in real incidents, structured probes for cues, goals, options and expectancies, multiple experts to separate idiosyncratic from shared knowledge, and representing findings in decision requirements tables that link to design and training implications.
steps: Identify the critical decisions and expert population, and recruit 6 to 10 experts of varied experience.
Run Critical Decision Method interviews: elicit a challenging incident, build a timeline, then probe decision points for cues, goals, options and expectations.
Supplement with knowledge audits or simulation interviews using realistic scenarios.
Transcribe and code the data for cues, strategies, difficulties and errors.
Build decision requirements tables describing each critical decision, why it is difficult, cues used and common errors.
Validate with additional experts and translate findings into design and training requirements.
outputs: Decision requirements tables, cue inventories, expert strategies, sources of difficulty, and design and training requirements.
useWhen: For high-stakes, time-pressured or uncertain decision environments such as healthcare, aviation, emergency response, security operations and finance.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple procedural tasks; use hierarchical task analysis. Avoid when experts cannot be accessed; cognitive walkthrough is a weaker alternative.
whyLost: UX generalised CTA into 'interviews' and lost the specific multi-sweep probes. Klein's work is known in defence and healthcare rather than product design.
whereToUse: Healthcare; aviation; emergency response; any high-stakes decision environment.
example: A security operations centre runs Critical Decision Method interviews with eight analysts about recent incidents. Analysts rely on rare correlations between login location and data volume, which the new alert design surfaces explicitly.
sources: Handbook of Cognitive Task Design
Lost Methods in UX
Working Minds (Crandall, Klein & Hoffman)
Klein, Calderwood & MacGregor, Critical decision method for eliciting knowledge (1989), IEEE Transactions on SMC
Crandall, Klein & Hoffman, Working Minds: A Practitioner's Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis (2006)
Hoffman, Crandall & Shadbolt, Use of the critical decision method to elicit expert knowledge (1998), Human Factors
reference: Crandall, B., Klein, G. & Hoffman, R. R. (2006). Working Minds: A Practitioner's Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis. MIT Press.

name: Cognitive Task Design
origin: Erik Hollnagel, 2003; Hollnagel & Woods, 2005
summary: Designs work and tools as joint cognitive systems, focusing on how people and technology together maintain control, rather than on screens or tasks in isolation.
description: Cognitive task design, as framed by Erik Hollnagel, treats people and technology as a joint cognitive system whose purpose is to maintain control over a process in a changing environment. Rather than decomposing tasks into steps, it analyses goals, the means of control, the demands of anticipation and feedback, and how control can be lost under time pressure or surprise. Design then aims to support control: making system state and intentions visible, supporting anticipation, balancing automation and human authority, and preserving the ability to recover. The approach draws on cognitive systems engineering and resilience engineering. Rigour comes from field-based analysis of real work, models such as the contextual control model, and evaluating designs in realistic scenarios.
steps: Cognitive task design audit: for each task in a user flow, evaluate:
Complexity match — does the cognitive demand of this step exceed the expected user's capacity?
(2) Feedback adequacy — is the feedback at this step sufficient to confirm correct action?
(3) Error detectability — can users detect if they've made an error at this step?
(4) Attention allocation — does this step require divided attention?
(5) Mental model support — for multi-user tasks, what shared representation is provided?
outputs: Models of the joint cognitive system, control and goal analyses, identified brittleness and coordination demands, and design requirements for supporting control.
useWhen: Complex sociotechnical work: control rooms, healthcare, aviation, emergency response, and AI-assisted decision tools where human and automation share control.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple consumer tasks where standard task analysis and usability testing are enough.
whyLost: Cognitive systems engineering stayed in safety-critical industries and academia; mainstream UX adopted lighter task-analysis tools.
whereToUse: Complex professional tool design, safety-critical system evaluation, collaborative software design.
example: A hospital introducing an AI sepsis alert applies cognitive task design and finds nurses lose control when alerts arrive without rationale; the redesign shows contributing signals and supports escalation.
sources: Handbook of Cognitive Task Design — Hollnagel (ed.)
reference: Hollnagel E (Ed.) (2003) Handbook of Cognitive Task Design. Lawrence Erlbaum

name: Cognitive Task Design Audit
origin: Adapted from Erik Hollnagel (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design, 2003
summary: Auditing qualitative findings against three task design dimensions (complexity match, feedback adequacy, error detectability) to turn observations into design-relevant diagnoses.
description: Cognitive task design, as framed by Hollnagel and colleagues, treats a task as joint work between people and systems, designed to fit the actual cognitive demands of the work. This audit applies three lenses to qualitative evidence. Complexity match asks whether the designed task reflects the real cognitive complexity, signalled by elaborate workarounds or decisions users cannot articulate. Feedback adequacy asks whether users can tell their actions had the intended effect, signalled by re-checking and repeated actions. Error detectability asks whether users can notice errors before consequences become severe, signalled by errors found only at submission or by others. Mapping observations onto these dimensions converts scattered findings into structured design problems.
steps: Assemble qualitative evidence from interviews, observation or diary data for the task under study.
Code each relevant observation against the three dimensions: complexity match, feedback adequacy and error detectability.
For each dimension, rate the task (for example adequate, partial, failing) and cite the supporting incidents.
Identify the task steps where failures cluster and estimate the severity of consequences at each.
Translate each failing dimension into a design requirement, such as an explicit state indicator or pre-commit review step.
Review the audit with designers and engineers and track requirements into the backlog.
outputs: A task-by-dimension audit grid, severity-rated failure points, and a set of design requirements tied to evidence.
useWhen: Complex, high-consequence workflows (clinical, financial, operational) where qualitative data show confusion, rechecking or late error discovery.
avoidWhen: Simple consumer flows with low error cost, or when you lack observational data; use heuristic evaluation or usability testing first.
whyLost: Cognitive systems engineering stayed in safety-critical industries and its vocabulary never became part of mainstream UX synthesis.
whereToUse: Electronic health records, trading and payments operations, industrial control dashboards, and AI-assisted decision tools where users must detect model errors.
example: Observation of pharmacists using an e-prescribing system shows repeated re-opening of orders after submission. The audit rates feedback adequacy as failing and error detectability as partial, leading to a confirmation summary with dose highlighting.
sources: Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (Hollnagel)
Human-Computer Interaction (Alan Dix)
Shneiderman & Plaisant
Movie Booking Playbook (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 16 — Cognitive Task Modeling — GOMS, KLM & CPM-GOMS
reference: Hollnagel, E. (Ed.) (2003). Handbook of Cognitive Task Design. Lawrence Erlbaum.

extra.The Three Dimensions: Complexity match: Does the task design match the actual cognitive complexity of the work? Signs of complexity mismatch from qualitative data: users developing elaborate workarounds, users unable to articulate a decision they are clearly making, users describing a task as simultaneously easy and confusing. Feedback adequacy: Does the system provide adequate, timely, and interpretable feedback for users to know whether their actions are having the intended effect? Signs of feedback failure from qualitative data: users pausing and re-checking, users expressing uncertainty about system state, users re-doing actions because they could not confirm the first action worked. Error detectability: Can users detect when they have made an error before the consequences become severe? Signs of error detectability failure from qualitative data: users discovering errors only at submission, users describing errors discovered by other people, users reporting that the system "never tells you when something goes wrong."

name: Cognitive Walkthrough
origin: Lewis, Polson, Wharton & Rieman, 1990; streamlined by Spencer, 2000
summary: An expert method that steps through a task action by action, asking whether a new user would know what to do and recognise progress, to assess learnability.
description: The cognitive walkthrough evaluates how easily a new or infrequent user can learn to complete a task by exploration. It rests on the CE+ theory of exploratory learning: users pick actions whose labels match their goal and judge progress from feedback. Evaluators define a user profile and the correct action sequence for a task, then at each step ask four questions: will the user try to achieve the right effect, will they notice the correct action is available, will they associate the action with the effect they want, and will they see that progress is being made? Each 'no' is recorded as a failure story with its cause. Rigour comes from a precise action sequence, an explicit user profile and disciplined answers to the questions, rather than general opinions about the design.
steps: Define the target user profile, including prior knowledge and goals.
Select key tasks and write the correct action sequence for each.
Assemble 2 to 4 evaluators and a recorder.
For each action, answer the four walkthrough questions (or Spencer's two streamlined questions) and record a credible success or failure story.
Log each failure with the step, the question failed and the likely cause.
Rate severity and propose design fixes, then verify priority problems with a small usability test.
outputs: Step-by-step failure stories, a list of learnability problems linked to specific actions, and design recommendations.
useWhen: For early wireframes, walk-up-and-use systems such as kiosks, infrequently used but critical flows, and when users are hard to reach.
avoidWhen: Avoid for assessing efficiency for expert users or overall satisfaction; use KLM for expert time and usability testing or questionnaires for experience.
whyLost: Vestigial: Largely replaced by heuristic evaluation and usability testing; but still uniquely suited to evaluating learnability without users.
whereToUse: Early-stage wireframe evaluation; systems with infrequent but critical use; accessibility review.
example: A government benefits portal team walks through the 'report a change of circumstances' flow. At step four they conclude a first-time user would not associate 'Amend claim' with reporting a new job, and relabel the entry point.
sources: Human-Computer Interaction
Lost Methods in UX
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Wharton C, Rieman J, Lewis C & Polson P (1994) The cognitive walkthrough method: a practitioner's guide. In Nielsen & Mack (Eds) Usability Inspection Methods
Polson PG, Lewis C, Rieman J & Wharton C (1992) Cognitive walkthroughs. IJMMS 36
Spencer R (2000) The streamlined cognitive walkthrough method, working around social constraints encountered in a software development company. CHI 2000
reference: Wharton, C., Rieman, J., Lewis, C. & Polson, P. (1994). The cognitive walkthrough method: A practitioner's guide. In Nielsen & Mack (Eds.), Usability Inspection Methods. Wiley.

name: Cognitive Work Analysis (CWA)
origin: Jens Rasmussen (1986); Kim Vicente (1999)
summary: Five-phase formative analysis of work constraints (domain, control tasks, strategies, social organisation, competencies) that maps the space of viable actions instead of one procedure.
description: CWA analyses complex sociotechnical work through five phases: Work Domain Analysis (purposes, functions and physical resources, often as an abstraction hierarchy), Control Task Analysis (what must be controlled, via decision ladders), Strategies Analysis (different ways control can be achieved), Social Organisation and Cooperation Analysis (who does what) and Worker Competencies Analysis (skill, rule and knowledge requirements). The treatise calls it the most comprehensive UX analysis framework ever developed. Its distinctive stance is formative: rather than specifying the one correct procedure, it maps constraints and the space of viable strategies, so interfaces support adaptation to unanticipated events. Rated MEDIUM priority (evidence 5, feasibility 2, impact 5).
steps: Define system boundaries and purposes; gather documents, observations and expert interviews.
Build the work domain abstraction hierarchy from purposes down to physical objects.
Analyse control tasks with decision ladders for key situations.
Identify alternative strategies and the conditions favouring each.
Allocate functions across actors and automation; analyse competencies with the skills-rules-knowledge taxonomy.
Derive display and interaction requirements, often via ecological interface design.
outputs: Abstraction hierarchy, decision ladders, strategy maps, allocation and competency analyses, design requirements.
useWhen: Complex, dynamic, safety-critical systems where unanticipated events must be handled.
avoidWhen: Simple, well-defined consumer tasks; use HTA or usability testing.
whyLost: CWA is heavy, academic and taught in human factors engineering rather than design programmes. UX favours quick descriptive methods.
whereToUse: Healthcare, manufacturing, air traffic, financial infrastructure operations, emergency response, industrial IoT, AI oversight consoles.
example: A grid operator's CWA reveals operators lack displays of the 'balance supply and demand' functional level; adding a functional overview helps them handle novel renewable fluctuations.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)

name: Cohen's Kappa and Krippendorff's Alpha (Inter-Rater Reliability)
origin: Jacob Cohen, 1960; Klaus Krippendorff, 1970s
summary: Chance-corrected agreement statistics showing qualitative coding is systematic rather than one researcher's opinion: κ for two coders, α for more coders, missing data or ordinal scales.
description: When coding qualitative data such as error types, coders may disagree; percent agreement overstates reliability because some agreement occurs by chance. Cohen's κ = (Po − Pe)/(1 − Pe), where Po is observed agreement and Pe chance-expected agreement computed from row and column proportions. Landis and Koch bands: < 0.20 poor, 0.21–0.40 fair, 0.41–0.60 moderate, 0.61–0.80 substantial, 0.81–1.00 almost perfect. Krippendorff's α = 1 − Do/De generalises to any number of coders, missing data and nominal, ordinal or interval data; α ≥ 0.80 is reliable, 0.67–0.80 tentatively acceptable. Vivek Gopinath's playbooks require double-coding 30–40% of sessions and κ ≥ 0.70, with codebook refinement and re-coding (including a 20% re-code sample) if lower. In his worked example, two coders classify 60 breakdowns: Po = 0.833, Pe = 0.366, κ = 0.737, substantial agreement.
steps: Finalise a codebook with definitions and examples before coding.
Have two or more coders independently code 30–40% of sessions.
Build a coder A × coder B contingency table.
Compute Po as diagonal agreements / total and Pe as the sum over categories of row proportion × column proportion.
Compute κ = (Po − Pe)/(1 − Pe), or Krippendorff's α for more than two coders, missing data or ordinal data.
If κ < 0.70, refine the codebook, retrain and re-code; report the statistic alongside findings.
outputs: A reliability statistic with interpretation band and an improved codebook.
useWhen: Whenever qualitative codes are counted, compared or used as variables (error taxonomies, thematic counts, drift signals).
avoidWhen: For interpretive, reflexive analyses where agreement is not the goal; percent agreement alone is too naive.
whyLost: Standard in content analysis and clinical research, but UX coding is often done solo on sticky notes, so reliability is rarely reported.
whereToUse: Error taxonomy coding, usability issue classification, support-ticket coding, AI output evaluation rubrics.
example: Two researchers code 60 usability breakdowns into Slip, Lapse and Mistake and reach κ = 0.74, allowing the team to state that the Mistake classification is not a single opinion.

name: Coherence score optimisation
aka: Choosing number of topics by coherence
origin: Mimno et al., 2011 (UMass coherence); Newman et al., 2010 (PMI); Röder, Both and Hinneburg, 2015 (C_v)
summary: Using topic coherence metrics to compare topic models and choose the number of topics, combined with human judgement of interpretability.
description: Topic coherence measures how often a topic's top words co-occur in the corpus or a reference corpus, approximating whether humans would find the topic meaningful. Common measures include UMass, NPMI and C_v (which Röder et al. found correlated best with human ratings). Practitioners fit models across a range of k and plot coherence to find a peak or plateau. Rigour comes from treating coherence as one input: perplexity correlates poorly with interpretability (Chang et al., 2009), coherence can reward generic topics, and it should be paired with stability across seeds, topic diversity and analyst reading of representative documents.
steps: Define the candidate range of topic numbers (e.g. k from 5 to 50 in steps of 5, then finer around promising values).
Fit models for each k with at least 3 random seeds.
Compute C_v and NPMI coherence (gensim CoherenceModel) and topic diversity (proportion of unique top words).
Plot mean coherence with variability against k and identify peaks or plateaus.
Have two analysts rate interpretability of topics for the 2-3 best candidates, including a word-intrusion test if feasible.
Choose k based on coherence, stability, diversity and human ratings, and document the decision.
outputs: Coherence and diversity plots across k, human interpretability ratings and a justified choice of topic number.
useWhen: Any topic modelling of UX text where the number of topics must be chosen and defended.
avoidWhen: Do not rely on coherence alone or on perplexity; for embedding-based clustering, evaluate cluster stability and outlier rates instead.
whyLost: A technical step from NLP research that UX teams rarely perform because they use vendor tools that pick topics automatically.
whereToUse: Large-scale feedback analysis, research repositories and longitudinal topic tracking.
example: A telecom app team compares LDA models from 10 to 40 topics on 30,000 complaints. C_v peaks at 18 and 22; analyst ratings favour 18, which avoids splitting billing complaints into near-duplicate topics.

name: Cohort Analysis
origin: Wade Hampton Frost, 1939 (cohort analysis in epidemiology); adopted in product analytics, 2000s
summary: Groups users by a shared starting event or characteristic and tracks their behaviour over time, separating lifecycle effects from changes across cohorts.
description: Cohort analysis originated in epidemiology and demography, where Frost showed that tracking groups born in the same period revealed patterns hidden in cross-sectional data. In product analytics, cohorts are usually defined by sign-up week or month, or by an acquisition source or first action, and retention or other behaviour is measured at fixed intervals afterwards. Cohort tables and retention curves reveal whether newer cohorts retain better than older ones, where curves flatten, and whether a product change affected users who joined after it. Rigour comes from consistent cohort definitions, fixed time intervals relative to each cohort's start, distinguishing age, period and cohort effects, ensuring adequate cohort sizes, and avoiding survivorship bias when comparing later behaviour. Behavioural cohorts (users who did X in week one) suggest, but do not prove, causal drivers.
steps: Define the cohort grouping (e.g. sign-up week) and the outcome metric (e.g. weekly active, purchase).
Build a cohort table with outcome rates at fixed intervals from each cohort's start.
Plot retention curves and check where they flatten and whether newer cohorts differ.
Segment cohorts by acquisition channel, plan or first-week behaviour.
Interpret differences carefully, separating age, period and cohort effects.
Test hypothesised drivers experimentally rather than relying on behavioural cohort correlations.
outputs: Cohort tables, retention curves, cohort comparisons, hypotheses about retention drivers.
useWhen: Retention research, evaluating the long-term effect of product changes, subscription and engagement analysis.
avoidWhen: Products with too few users for stable cohorts, or when you need causal proof; use experiments or causal inference methods.
whyLost: Still in use: Core retention analysis method; available in product analytics tools.
whereToUse: Retention research; feature impact analysis; subscription product analytics.
example: A meditation app's monthly cohorts showed week-4 retention rising from 22% to 31% for users who joined after a new onboarding launched, with no change in acquisition mix, supporting the onboarding's effect.
sources: Advancing into Analytics
The age selection of mortality from tuberculosis in successive decades (Wade Hampton Frost)

name: COM-B and Behaviour Change Wheel Analysis
origin: Susan Michie, Maartje van Stralen and Robert West, 2011; BCT Taxonomy v1 (Michie et al., 2013)
summary: Diagnoses a target behaviour by capability, opportunity and motivation, then systematically selects intervention functions and specified behaviour change techniques.
description: COM-B states that behaviour occurs when people have the capability (physical, psychological), opportunity (physical, social) and motivation (reflective, automatic). The Behaviour Change Wheel links COM-B deficits to nine intervention functions (education, persuasion, incentivisation, coercion, training, restriction, environmental restructuring, modelling, enablement) and policy categories. The BCT Taxonomy v1 provides 93 defined, reliably codable techniques. The approach replaces ad hoc 'nudge' brainstorming with a traceable chain from diagnosis to intervention, and gives a shared vocabulary for specifying and evaluating features intended to change behaviour.
steps: Specify the target behaviour precisely: who, what, when, where, how often, with whom.
Diagnose barriers and enablers with interviews, observation or the COM-B questionnaire, mapping each to the six COM-B components.
Select intervention functions linked to the diagnosed deficits using BCW matrices and APEASE criteria (affordability, practicability, effectiveness, acceptability, side-effects, equity).
Choose specific BCTs from the taxonomy and translate them into product features.
Specify features with BCT labels so they can be evaluated and replicated.
Evaluate with experiments and process evaluation measuring changes in the COM-B mechanism.
outputs: Behavioural diagnosis, intervention function selection, BCT-coded feature specifications and evaluation plan.
useWhen: Products whose purpose is behaviour change: health, finance, sustainability, learning, safety.
avoidWhen: Usability problems with no behavioural target, where standard usability methods are better.
whyLost: UX imported behavioural design via popular nudge books and the Fogg model, while the more systematic implementation-science framework stayed in health research.
whereToUse: Digital health and therapeutics, savings apps, sustainability features, workplace safety tools.
example: A medication adherence app diagnoses that missed doses stem from automatic motivation and physical opportunity (pills not visible), not knowledge. It drops educational content and adds habit-stacking prompts (BCT 8.3) and refill logistics.

name: Communalities interpretation
origin: Thurstone's multiple factor analysis, 1930s-1947
summary: Reading how much of each survey item's variance is explained by the retained factors, to identify weak items and judge whether the factor solution is adequate.
description: An item's communality (h squared) is the proportion of its variance accounted for by the common factors; the remainder is unique variance (specific variance plus error). Initial communalities in principal axis factoring are squared multiple correlations; extraction communalities reflect the final solution. Low communalities (commonly below about 0.40, and certainly below 0.20) suggest the item is unrelated to the other items, poorly worded or measuring something else. Communalities above 1 (Heywood cases) signal a misspecified solution. MacCallum et al. (1999) showed that high communalities reduce the sample size needed for stable solutions, so they also inform design. Rigour comes from reading communalities alongside loadings and content, not mechanically deleting items.
steps: Request initial and extraction communalities in the EFA output.
Flag items with extraction communalities below about 0.40 and treat those below 0.20 as strong candidates for removal.
Investigate any communality at or above 1.0 as a Heywood case and revisit the number of factors or extraction method.
Review flagged items' wording and content coverage before deleting; a low communality can mean a unique but important facet.
Remove items one at a time and re-run, monitoring changes in other communalities and loadings.
Report mean communality; with averages above about 0.60, smaller samples (around 100-200) can give stable solutions.
outputs: Item communality table, a list of weak items with decisions and an assessment of solution adequacy.
useWhen: During EFA of UX attitude scales and when trimming long questionnaires.
avoidWhen: Not used for formative indices (where items are not expected to correlate) or for single-item measures.
whyLost: A technical step of factor analysis that is invisible to those who never run EFA, which describes most UX practice.
whereToUse: Scale development and adaptation for AI trust, financial confidence and satisfaction instruments.
example: In a 20-item AI assistant trust scale, the item 'The assistant is fun to use' has a communality of 0.14. On review it measures enjoyment rather than trust, so it moves to a separate engagement scale.

name: Competitive UX Benchmarking
origin: Sauro, Benchmarking the User Experience (2018); MeasuringU practice
summary: Measures your product and competitors on the same tasks and metrics so you know where you stand.
description: A competitive benchmark runs identical tasks and questionnaires on two or more products. Key design choices are within-subjects (each person uses every product, which is efficient and allows direct preference questions but introduces carryover) versus between-subjects (cleaner but needing more people), and the mixed design where each participant uses their current product plus one competitor. Sauro's ten best practices include counterbalancing order, controlling for prior experience (prior users always rate a product higher), choosing tasks every product supports, and adjusting for brand attitudes. Results are reported as task and study metrics with confidence intervals and significance markers.
steps: Pick competitors and tasks that every product supports equivalently.
Choose within, between or mixed design based on sample, carryover and task length.
Counterbalance product order and record prior experience with each brand.
Collect task metrics, SUPR-Q or SUS, preference and brand attitude before and after.
Analyse with appropriate within or between tests, control for prior experience (for example weighted t-tests), and report gaps with intervals.
outputs: A scorecard showing where you lead and lag competitors, task by task.
useWhen: Setting strategy, making a business case for redesign, or after a competitor launch.
avoidWhen: Products are not truly comparable, or you cannot get legitimate access to competitor flows.
whyLost: Not lost, but frequently run informally by expert review rather than with users and statistics.
whereToUse: Travel, banking, insurance, retail, SaaS categories with a few strong rivals.
example: Four hotel booking sites are tested with 200 people each; one competitor completes "change dates" 30 points better, and its flow becomes the redesign reference.
sources: Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience, chapters 2 and 13.

name: Complete UX Practitioner Curriculum
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: A proposed core curriculum restoring human factors, cognitive science, causal inference, field methods, rigorous qualitative and quantitative analysis, cross-domain methods and UX Epidemiology.
description: The treatise argues UX education has narrowed to design thinking, interviews, usability testing, IA, interaction and visual design and prototyping tools, a small fraction of the field's heritage, partly because educators teach what they know. Its proposed curriculum covers: human factors foundations (task analysis, GOMS, KLM, CPM-GOMS, anthropometrics, environmental ergonomics, UFMEA); cognitive science (full verbal protocol analysis, predictive models, repertory grid, concept mapping, SDT, NDM); causal inference (Bradford Hill, Rubin, DAGs, DiD, RDD, PSM); ethnographic and field methods (full contextual inquiry, thick description, ethnomethodology, participatory design); rigorous qualitative analysis (grounded theory, Braun and Clarke, Miles and Huberman, phenomenography, micro-phenomenology, discourse analysis); quantitative methods (multilevel modelling, Bayesian inference, IRT/Rasch, scale construction, lag sequential analysis, experimental design beyond A/B); history and theory of HCI; cross-domain methods; and UX Epidemiology.
steps: Audit the current curriculum against the proposed areas.
Prioritise areas using the Method Recovery Priority Index and programme goals.
Design modules pairing primary readings with applied exercises.
Recruit instructors from donor disciplines where needed.
Assess students on applying methods to real questions.
Review content periodically against the canon.
outputs: Curriculum map, module designs, assessment plan.
useWhen: Designing UX degrees, bootcamps, in-house academies and researcher career frameworks.
avoidWhen: Single-method training needs.
whyLost: Original proposal of the treatise.
whereToUse: Universities, corporate research academies, professional certification bodies.
example: An in-house academy adds a causal inference module and a qualitative rigour module; within a year research reports cite estimands and audit trails routinely.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Lost Methods in UX treatise, Chapter 33
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 33 (A Curriculum for the Complete UX Practitioner).

name: Compositionality audit for UI copy
donor: Philosophy of language and formal semantics
origin: Principle of compositionality attributed to Frege; Fodor's language of thought, 1975; Fodor and Pylyshyn, 1988
summary: Checks whether UI labels and messages combine predictably, so that the meaning of a compound phrase follows from its parts and users can generalise across the interface.
description: Compositionality holds that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by its parts and how they are combined. Fodor argued thought itself is compositional, and systematic: anyone who understands 'save draft' and 'delete file' should understand 'delete draft'. Interface language can violate this when the same verb means different things in different contexts ('Save' commits to a record for one role but stores locally for another), when compound labels have idiosyncratic meanings, or when combinations are missing. A compositionality audit inventories verbs, objects and modifiers, builds a grid of their combinations, and checks each for consistent meaning and behaviour. Rigour comes from mapping each label to its actual system effect, not its dictionary meaning.
steps: Extract all action labels, menu items and messages and decompose them into verbs, objects and modifiers.
For each verb, list every system effect it triggers across contexts and roles.
Build a verb-by-object grid and mark combinations as consistent, inconsistent or missing.
Flag verbs with more than one distinct effect and compounds whose meaning does not follow from parts.
Test predictions with 6-10 users: show novel combinations and ask what will happen; target at least 80% correct predictions.
Define a compositional vocabulary with one effect per verb and apply it across the product.
outputs: A verb-object grid, an inconsistency list, prediction accuracy data, and a compositional UI vocabulary.
useWhen: For large products with many actions, multi-role systems, design system content guidelines, and command languages.
avoidWhen: For small, single-purpose interfaces; standard content review suffices.
whyLost: Compositionality is foundational in semantics and cognitive science but has not been framed as a UX content method.
whereToUse: Enterprise software, clinical systems, developer tools, voice commands, and AI agent instructions.
example: In a surgical system 'Save' stores a preset for surgeons, commits the record for nurses and exports logs for admins. The audit splits it into 'Save preset', 'Sign record' and 'Export logs', and novel-combination predictions rise from 55% to 90%.

name: Computational Cognitive Modelling for UX Prediction
origin: Newell, 1990 (unified theories); O'Reilly & Munakata, 2000
summary: Builds runnable simulations of the cognitive processes users employ, predicting performance, errors and learning on a design before testing with people.
description: Computational cognitive modelling expresses hypotheses about perception, memory, attention and decision-making as runnable programs (symbolic architectures such as ACT-R and EPIC, or connectionist networks) and simulates users interacting with a design. Because the model is explicit, it yields quantitative predictions of task times, error likelihoods and learning trajectories, and it explains why a design performs as it does. In UX the method allows many variants to be screened before recruiting participants and supports decisions in domains where testing is expensive or risky. Rigour depends on grounding the model in established architecture parameters, validating predictions against at least some human data, and reporting where the model's assumptions are likely to break down, such as novel strategies or emotional states.
steps: Select a cognitive phenomenon relevant to the interface:
For navigation: use a spreading activation model to predict which labels users will associate.
(2) For decision-making: use a drift-diffusion model to predict decision time and error rates for different option set sizes.

(3) For learning: use a reinforcement learning model to predict which feature interaction sequences users will learn. Run the model with parameters fitted from prior research. Use model predictions to design the study's hypotheses.
outputs: An executable model, predicted task times, error rates and learning curves per design variant, and a mechanistic explanation of why one design outperforms another.
useWhen: Safety-critical or high-volume interfaces where small performance differences matter, comparing many design variants cheaply, or explaining a puzzling performance pattern mechanistically.
avoidWhen: Avoid for exploratory or attitudinal questions, novel domains where cognitive processes are unknown, or teams without modelling expertise; use KLM/GOMS for simple predictions or empirical testing.
whyLost: HCI's cognitive modelling tradition (GOMS, ACT-R, EPIC) peaked in the 1990s; modelling expertise was scarce and rapid empirical testing became cheaper than building models.
whereToUse: Theoretically grounded UX research, pre-study prediction (Forward-Thinking Playbook Stage 1), cognitive modeling for safety-critical interface design.
example: An air-traffic tool team uses an ACT-R model to compare two alert-handling layouts, predicting a 400 ms advantage and fewer missed alerts for one variant before a costly simulator study confirms it.
sources: Computational Experiments in Cognitive Neuroscience — Yuko Munakata
Cognitive Modeling: Nine Paradigms (slide deck)
reference: Munakata Y (2004) Computational cognitive neuroscience: Modelling the brain. Trends in Cognitive Sciences 8(3)

name: Computational Thing Analysis
origin: Janlert & Stolterman, 2017
summary: Analyses interactive artefacts in terms of their 'thingness' and interactivity (states, faces, expressions) to understand how they demand attention and shape engagement.
description: Janlert and Stolterman analyse what it means for a thing to be interactive. They distinguish an artefact's internal states from its outward faces and expressions, and examine how interactivity introduces demands: interactive things invite, require and sometimes compete for attention, keeping people busy. Computational thing analysis applies this vocabulary to a product, inventorying its states and how they are expressed, the modes of interaction it supports (from operating to conversing to coexisting) and the cumulative attention load it places on users within an ecology of devices. The analysis informs choices about how much interaction a thing should demand. Rigour comes from systematic inventory and comparison of alternatives, ideally grounded with field observation of use.
steps: Character analysis of interface elements: for each significant interface element, measure:
Interactional richness — how many distinct ways can this be interacted with?
(2) Behavioral consistency — does it behave consistently across all interaction modes?
(3) Character coherence — does it have a consistent 'personality' across states?
(4) Addressability — can users directly address it, or only access it indirectly? High interactional complexity + consistent character = 'thing-ness' that feels solid and reliable.
outputs: An analysis of an artefact's states, faces and interaction modes, its demands on attention, and design alternatives with different interaction characters.
useWhen: Designing ambient, IoT, wearable and AI devices where the character of interaction and attention demands matter more than screen usability.
avoidWhen: Avoid for routine screen-based usability questions; it is an analytical framework, not an evaluative method, so pair it with field studies.
whyLost: It is recent interaction design theory read mainly in academic HCI; practice lacks time for theoretical analysis of interaction character.
whereToUse: Interface element design, design system component character design, interactive data visualization design.
example: A smart thermostat team analyses how often the device 'calls' for attention and in what states; reducing its expressive states and moving adjustments to a quiet mode lowers user irritation in a field trial.
sources: Things That Keep Us Busy — Janlert & Stolterman
reference: Janlert L-E & Stolterman E (2017) Things That Keep Us Busy: The Elements of Interaction. MIT Press

name: Concept Mapping
origin: Joseph Novak, 1972-1984
summary: Elicits a user's knowledge as a network of concepts joined by labelled propositions, exposing misconceptions and the structure of their mental model.
description: The treatise's curriculum lists concept mapping alongside the repertory grid as a mental model research method. Developed by Novak to track how students' understanding of science changed, a concept map is a node-link diagram where links carry verbs that form propositions ('interest - compounds into - debt'). Elicited individually, often with a focus question and a parking lot of seed concepts, maps reveal which concepts users hold, how they connect them and where misconceptions sit. Maps can be scored for structural complexity and accuracy against an expert map. This yields evidence of mental models rather than inferences from verbal reports.
steps: Write a focus question and a list of 10-20 seed concepts from domain analysis.
Have each participant build a map, adding concepts and labelled links, thinking aloud.
Probe unclear links and missing concepts at the end.
Code maps for propositions, hierarchy, cross-links and misconceptions.
Compare user maps to an expert reference map or across segments.
Translate misconceptions into content, onboarding or model-design changes.
outputs: Individual concept maps, proposition inventories, misconception list, comparison with expert models.
useWhen: Understanding mental models of complex domains such as privacy, credit, insurance, AI capability.
avoidWhen: Simple tasks with little conceptual content; when categorisation alone is needed (use card sorting).
whyLost: Remained in education research; UX settled on interviews and card sorting for mental models.
whereToUse: Financial literacy features, privacy settings, AI explanations, medical condition education.
example: Users' maps of 'how my credit score works' show 60% link 'checking my score' to 'lowers score', a misconception the app addresses with a reassurance message on the check screen.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Novak JD & Gowin DB (1984) Learning How to Learn
Novak JD & Cañas AJ (2008) The theory underlying concept maps and how to construct and use them. IHMC
