name: Conceptually ordered display
origin: Miles and Huberman, Qualitative Data Analysis (1984; 2nd ed. 1994)
summary: Arranges qualitative data by concepts or variables rather than by case or time, revealing how themes cluster, relate and vary across participants.
description: Among Miles and Huberman's display families, conceptually ordered displays organise data around concepts. A conceptually clustered matrix places research questions or themes that belong together as columns, with participants or cases as rows, so the analyst can see how answers to related questions co-vary. Other forms include thematic conceptual matrices, folk taxonomies (hierarchies of how participants classify things) and cognitive maps. The approach helps move from codes to an understanding of how concepts hang together and which participants share configurations. Rigour comes from grouping columns on conceptual grounds stated in advance or derived explicitly from the data, from consistent cell entries (short quotes or ratings with sources), and from verification tactics such as clustering, counting and checking outliers.
steps: Identify a set of related concepts or research questions that should be examined together, for example motives, barriers and workarounds for digital entry.
Group concepts into clusters with stated rationale, and set them as matrix columns; set participants or cases as rows.
Fill each cell with a short summary, rating or quote with identifier, using a written entry rule to ensure consistency.
Sort rows to bring similar profiles together, and look for clusters of participants with similar configurations across columns.
Where participants use their own classifications, build a folk taxonomy showing their categories and subcategories.
Write analytic text describing clusters, relationships among concepts and outliers, and test conclusions by re-sorting the matrix on different columns.
outputs: Conceptually clustered matrices or taxonomies, participant clusters with shared configurations, and analytic text on concept relationships.
useWhen: Understanding how several related themes co-occur; finding participant types from qualitative data; examining users' own classification systems.
avoidWhen: The question is about sequence or process (use time-ordered displays or journey maps), or the dataset is too small for patterns to emerge.
whyLost: UX segmentation from qualitative data moved to persona workshops and behavioural variable scales, rarely using systematic concept-by-case matrices.
whereToUse: Qualitative segmentation and persona grounding, mental model research, information architecture based on user taxonomies, adoption barrier studies.
example: A 20-participant cross-cultural matrix clustered columns on trust, effort and social visibility. Sorting revealed three configurations of adoption barrier that recurred across all three regions, showing the barriers were universal rather than culture-specific.
sources: Qualitative Data Analysis (Miles & Huberman) via Sage Handbook
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods
The Inquiry Series, Ch 29 — Miles & Huberman — Systematic Qualitative Data Analysis
reference: Miles, M. B., & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Sage.

name: Confidence Intervals for Task Time (Log-Transformed and Median)
origin: Log-normal modelling of response times; small-sample recommendations in Sauro & Lewis (2010)
summary: Puts honest bounds around how long a task takes, using log times for small samples and the median for large ones.
description: Task times are positively skewed: most people finish quickly and a few take much longer. The arithmetic mean is pulled upward by the slow tail and a normal-theory interval around it is misleading. For samples under about 25, Sauro and Lewis recommend transforming times to natural logs, computing a t-based interval on the log scale, and exponentiating back, which gives the geometric mean and an asymmetric interval that respects the skew. For larger samples the median is the better centre and its interval comes from binomial order statistics. Both answer the stakeholder question "how long will this take most people?" without one slow participant distorting the picture.
steps: Decide when the clock starts and stops, and whether failed attempts are excluded (they usually are for time-on-task).
For n under 25: take ln of each time, compute mean and SD of the logs, form the t interval, then exponentiate the mean and both bounds.
For n of 25 or more: sort the times and find the ranks np ± z√(np(1−p)) with p = 0.5; the times at those ranks bound the median.
Report the geometric mean or median with its interval, not the arithmetic mean.
When comparing to a target time, check whether the target lies above the upper bound.
outputs: A typical task time with an interval that reflects the skew of real timing data.
useWhen: Benchmarking efficiency, setting time targets, or reporting time-on-task from moderated or unmoderated studies.
avoidWhen: Tasks where time is not meaningful (exploratory browsing, learning tasks) or when most attempts failed.
whyLost: Reports still default to the arithmetic mean and standard deviation from spreadsheet functions. The log and order-statistic approaches sit in specialist texts.
whereToUse: Enterprise workflows, call-centre and back-office tools, onboarding flows and any product where speed is a selling point.
example: Ten participants file an expense claim. The arithmetic mean is 142 s, but the geometric mean is 118 s with a 95% interval of 96 to 145 s, so the 3-minute target is comfortably met.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
reference: Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2010). Average task times in usability tests: what to report? CHI 2010.

name: Confirmability Audit
origin: Lincoln & Guba, 1985
summary: Showing that each qualitative finding can be traced to specific data and documented decisions rather than to researcher preference.
description: Confirmability is the qualitative parallel to objectivity: findings should be shaped by participants and data, not by researcher motivations or interests. Lincoln and Guba recommended a reflexive journal alongside the audit trail. Reflexive memos record expectations before each session, surprises and emotional reactions afterwards, and moments where interpretations were influenced by prior beliefs or stakeholder pressure. During analysis, each major interpretation is checked against the memos: did the researcher expect this before seeing the data? Was disconfirming evidence noticed and recorded? Rigour comes from writing memos at the time rather than retrospectively, structuring them with consistent prompts, and having a second analyst review the link between memos and findings.
steps: Build a findings-to-evidence table listing each finding with the specific data extracts and participants that support it.
Link every major analytic decision (code merges, weighting of participants, exclusions) to a dated rationale in the memo or decision log.
Keep a reflexivity journal and summarise in the report how the researcher's assumptions may have shaped interpretation.
Ask a second researcher to trace a sample of findings back to raw data and to flag any inference that goes beyond the evidence.
Revise or qualify findings that cannot be grounded, and report the audit outcome.
outputs: A findings-to-evidence traceability table, reflexivity statement and an audit note identifying any findings revised or qualified.
useWhen: Before high-stakes readouts, when the researcher has a strong prior or stake in the outcome, and when findings will be challenged.
avoidWhen: When outputs are raw observations with no interpretation; a simple evidence log is enough.
whyLost: Industry reports compress evidence into a few illustrative quotes, so systematic traceability is rarely built or audited.
whereToUse: Strategy and investment decisions, AI ethics and fairness research, regulated health research, and contested internal debates.
example: Before presenting that SMB customers distrust automated bookkeeping, the researcher builds a traceability table. A peer finds two claims rest on a single participant, and they are reframed as hypotheses for further study.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba) via Sage Handbook
Qualitative Research Ethics (Sage)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 27 — Lincoln & Guba — Trustworthiness in Qualitative Research
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

extra.Confirmability Audit: Can you trace every finding back to specific data extracts? If a finding cannot be grounded in specific data, it is an inference too far. Can you trace every analytical decision (why this code rather than that one, why these codes were merged, why this participant was given more weight) back to a documented rationale? Could another researcher, given the same raw data and your methodological documentation, reach similar conclusions? (Not identical — similar, within a defensible range of interpretation.)

name: Confirmatory factor analysis fit indices (CFI/RMSEA)
origin: Jöreskog, 1969 (CFA); Bentler, 1990 (CFI); Steiger and Lind, 1980 (RMSEA); Hu and Bentler, 1999 (cut-offs)
summary: Testing whether a hypothesised factor structure fits survey data using indices such as CFI, TLI, RMSEA and SRMR before trusting scale scores or SEM paths.
description: Confirmatory factor analysis specifies in advance which items load on which factors and tests how well that model reproduces observed covariances. Because the chi-square test rejects almost any model at large N, approximate fit indices are used: the Comparative Fit Index (CFI) and Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) compare the model with a null model; RMSEA estimates misfit per degree of freedom with a confidence interval; SRMR summarises residual correlations. Common guidelines (Hu and Bentler, 1999) are CFI and TLI of 0.95 or above, RMSEA of 0.06 or below and SRMR of 0.08 or below, but these are heuristics, not laws. Rigour comes from reporting all indices with the estimator used, inspecting local misfit through modification indices and residuals, and resisting atheoretical re-specification.
steps: Specify the measurement model from theory or a prior EFA, with at least 3 items per factor.
Fit with an estimator suited to the data: ML or MLR for approximately continuous items, WLSMV for ordinal items with 5 or fewer categories.
Report chi-square (df, p), CFI, TLI, RMSEA with 90% CI and SRMR.
Judge fit against conventional guides (CFI/TLI 0.95 or above, RMSEA 0.06 or below, SRMR 0.08 or below) and treat values near the boundaries cautiously.
Inspect standardised residuals and modification indices, and only free parameters with a substantive justification.
Test measurement invariance across key segments (configural, metric, scalar) before comparing segment means, accepting a change in CFI of 0.01 or less.
outputs: A fit table, standardised loadings, factor correlations, invariance results and a judgement on whether the measurement model is acceptable.
useWhen: Validating a scale structure from an EFA in a new sample, checking that a standard instrument works in a new population, or as the measurement step before SEM.
avoidWhen: Avoid with samples below about 200, with poorly theorised structures (use EFA), or when the goal is simply a total score from a long-validated instrument.
whyLost: CFA requires SEM software and training typical of psychology or marketing doctoral programmes, so it stayed in academic and market research.
whereToUse: Cross-market UX measurement, scale validation for AI and trust instruments, and measurement models preceding SEM in strategic research.
example: A fintech team validates a three-factor trust scale in a holdout sample of 510. The model gives CFI 0.96, RMSEA 0.052 (90% CI 0.044-0.061) and SRMR 0.041, and scalar invariance holds across novice and expert investors, so segment means can be compared.

name: Confounder/mediator/collider identification
origin: Formalised by Pearl (1995), Greenland, Pearl & Robins (1999); collider bias by Cole et al. (2010)
summary: Classifies each variable relative to a cause and outcome as a confounder, mediator or collider, which decides whether to adjust for it.
description: Whether to control for a variable depends on its causal role, not its correlation. A confounder causes both the treatment and the outcome and must be adjusted for. A mediator lies on the causal path and adjusting for it removes part of the effect you want to measure. A collider is caused by both treatment and outcome (or their causes); adjusting for or selecting on it creates spurious associations. In UX, selection on colliders is common: analysing only users who completed onboarding, or only survey respondents, can manufacture effects such as a trust badge appearing to harm conversion. Rigour comes from reading roles off an explicit DAG rather than intuition.
steps: Draw the DAG for the treatment and outcome of interest, including key unmeasured variables.

For each other variable, trace its paths: if it causes both treatment and outcome it is a confounder; if it sits between them it is a mediator; if two arrows point into it it is a collider on that path.
Check sample filters and inclusion rules as potential collider selection (e.g. analysing only active users).
Decide adjustment: include confounders, exclude mediators for total effects, and never condition on colliders or their descendants.
Document the role of every variable in a table alongside the evidence for its placement.
outputs: A variable-role table, an annotated DAG and an adjustment decision for each candidate covariate, including warnings on biased filters.
useWhen: Before any observational analysis, driver model or segment comparison that will be read causally.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on it when the DAG is pure speculation with no domain input; gather qualitative evidence or run an experiment first.
whyLost: UX analytics habitually controls for everything available, and the collider concept is counter-intuitive and absent from most UX training.
whereToUse: Analysis of logs, survey driver models, selection into beta programmes, and survivorship issues in retention studies.
example: Analysis shows users who saw a trust badge are less likely to buy. The DAG reveals the analysis was restricted to users who reached checkout, a collider of badge exposure and purchase intent; removing the filter reverses the sign.
sources: DAGs+SEM Playbook (Vivek Gopinath)

Statistical Rethinking (Richard McElreath)
Cole et al. (2010) Illustrating bias due to conditioning on a collider

name: Conjoint Analysis
origin: Luce & Tukey, 1964; Green & Srinivasan, 1978; Louviere et al., 2000
summary: Estimates how much users value each feature and level by having them choose between systematically varied product bundles, yielding part-worth utilities and trade-offs.
description: Conjoint analysis infers how people value the attributes of a product from the choices they make between profiles that vary those attributes systematically. In choice-based conjoint, respondents see sets of two to four hypothetical products defined by attribute levels (features, price, service terms) and choose one, repeated over about 10 to 15 tasks. An experimental design ensures attributes are balanced and uncorrelated; hierarchical Bayesian or multinomial logit models then estimate part-worth utilities for each level. Because respondents must trade off, the method avoids the 'everything is important' problem of rating scales. Rigour lies in attribute definition grounded in qualitative research, efficient designs, holdout tasks to validate predictions, and adequate sample sizes (often 300+).
steps: DCE design:
Select 4–8 design attributes and 2–4 levels each.
(2) Generate an efficient choice design (D-optimal or orthogonal array).
(3) Present participants with 8–12 choice sets, each comparing 2–3 design alternatives.
(4) Fit conditional logit or mixed logit model.
(5) Extract part-worth utilities for each attribute level.
(6) Calculate willingness-to-trade-off: how much of attribute A is the user willing to sacrifice to gain attribute B? Software: R (mlogit, logitr) or NLOGIT.
outputs: Part-worth utilities, attribute importance, willingness-to-pay estimates, preference segments, and a market simulator for configuration scenarios.
useWhen: Pricing and packaging, feature prioritisation under trade-offs, plan design, and any case where users would say they want everything if asked directly.
avoidWhen: Avoid for novel features users cannot imagine, very many attributes (more than about 6-8), or behavioural rather than stated preference questions; use prototypes or experiments.
whyLost: Conjoint is standard in market research but rarely in UX; it requires experimental design software, larger samples and statistical modelling.
whereToUse: Feature prioritization with real trade-off data, pricing research, design option comparison, accessibility feature investment decisions.
example: A project management SaaS runs choice-based conjoint with 400 users on tiers varying storage, integrations, guest access and price; integrations drive most utility, reshaping the mid tier.

name: Conjugate Prior Updating
origin: Raiffa & Schlaifer, 1961 (conjugate families); DeGroot, 1970
summary: Carries evidence forward across iterative studies by updating a conjugate prior (e.g. Beta for completion rates) with each round's data, yielding a running posterior.
description: Conjugate prior updating exploits the algebraic property that, for certain likelihood and prior pairs, the posterior belongs to the same family as the prior. For binary UX outcomes such as task success, a Beta(a,b) prior combined with s successes and f failures yields a Beta(a+s, b+f) posterior; Gamma-Poisson and Normal-Normal pairs handle counts and continuous measures. The posterior from one study becomes the prior for the next, so evidence accumulates transparently across iterative rounds instead of being thrown away. Its rigour lies in explicit prior specification, sensitivity checks against weakly informative priors, and decision rules stated in probability terms (e.g. P(success rate > 0.8) > 0.9) before data are collected. It also forces teams to decide when a redesign is substantial enough to warrant discounting or resetting prior evidence.
steps: For binary UX outcomes (completion rate, error rate): use Beta-Binomial conjugate model.
Prior: Beta(α₀, β₀) where α₀ = prior successes + 1, β₀ = prior failures + 1.
After new data (s successes, f failures): Posterior = Beta(α₀ + s, β₀ + f).
Posterior mean = (α₀ + s) / (α₀ + β₀ + s + f). 95% credible interval: qbeta(0.025, α, β) to qbeta(0.975, α, β) in R.
Each new study updates the prior rather than starting from scratch.
outputs: A posterior distribution per metric (e.g. Beta(a,b) for task success), credible intervals after each round, probability-of-threshold statements and an audit trail of how evidence accumulated.
useWhen: Iterative rounds of small-sample testing on the same metric (completion, error rate, conversion) where you want each round to build on the last rather than start from zero; when stakeholders ask 'how confident are we now?'.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the design changed so much between rounds that earlier data no longer describes the same system (reset the prior or use a hierarchical model), or when the metric is not well described by a conjugate family; use full MCMC Bayesian estimation instead.
whyLost: Bayesian updating never entered UX curricula, which teach frequentist tests on single studies; each usability round is treated as a fresh, isolated sample, so accumulated evidence is discarded.
whereToUse: Iterative usability research programs, longitudinal benchmark tracking, any research program with multiple waves of data collection.
example: A fintech team runs five-person rounds on a card-activation flow. Starting from Beta(1,1), round one (4/5 success) gives Beta(5,2); after three rounds the posterior Beta(17,4) shows an 89% probability that the true completion rate exceeds 70%, which is enough to ship.
sources: Probability and Statistics — Morris H. DeGroot
reference: DeGroot MH & Schervish MJ (2012) Probability and Statistics. 4th ed. Addison-Wesley

name: Conjunction Fallacy Check in UX Survey Design
origin: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, 1983
summary: Audits survey items and research artefacts for compound, stereotype-matching scenarios that respondents rate as more probable than their simpler components, inflating confidence in specific user stories.
description: The conjunction fallacy occurs when people judge a specific conjunction of events (A and B) as more probable than one of its constituents (A alone), because the detailed scenario matches a stereotype; the classic example is the Linda problem. In UX research it appears in two places. Survey items that bundle several conditions into a vivid scenario, such as 'a busy parent who shops on mobile at night and abandons at payment', attract higher agreement than their components, overstating how common such users are. Teams commit the same error when detailed personas or journey stories feel more plausible than broader evidence supports. The check decomposes compound items into components, compares ratings, and flags inversions where the conjunction outscores a constituent. It enforces a basic probability constraint on attitudinal and planning data.
steps: Audit scenario-based survey questions for conjunction fallacy.
Compare rates for specific vs. general versions.
Use probability inflation ratio as distortion measure.
outputs: List of compound survey items and research claims, component-versus-conjunction comparisons, flagged inversions and rewritten single-concept items.
useWhen: Reviewing survey instruments, persona and scenario validation surveys, and stakeholder estimates of segment prevalence.
avoidWhen: When items already measure single concepts, or when you have behavioural data for prevalence (use logs rather than judgements).
whyLost: It is taught as a famous bias experiment but was never turned into a routine instrument-review step in UX, where questionnaire design is often informal.
whereToUse: UX survey instrument design, persona validation, user journey likelihood estimation.
example: A health app's persona validation survey asks how likely a user is to be 'a shift worker who forgets medication and wants reminders'. Respondents rate it 68% likely, versus 52% for 'a shift worker who forgets medication', so the team splits items and stops treating the persona as dominant.
sources: Heuristics and Biases — Kahneman (ed.)
Tversky & Kahneman, Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: The conjunction fallacy in probability judgment (Psychological Review, 1983)
reference: Tversky A & Kahneman D (1983) Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: The conjunction fallacy in probability judgment. Psychological Review 90(4):293-315

name: Connectionist Distributed Representation for Mental Model Theory
donor: Cognitive science and philosophy of mind
origin: Rumelhart and McClelland (PDP, 1986); Paul Churchland (1988)
summary: Treats user mental models as graded similarity spaces and prototypes rather than explicit rule sets, eliciting them with similarity judgements and typicality ratings.
description: Classic mental-model research in HCI assumed users hold explicit, rule-like representations of how systems work. Connectionist theory, championed by Rumelhart, McClelland and the Churchlands, proposes that knowledge is distributed across weighted connections, so concepts behave like prototypes in a similarity space: membership is graded, typical examples are processed faster, and generalisation follows similarity rather than rules. Applied to UX, this suggests eliciting mental models through similarity judgements, typicality ratings and sorting tasks, then analysing them with multidimensional scaling or clustering, rather than asking users to state rules. Predictions follow: novel features are understood by their nearest prototype, and errors arise where a feature sits between prototypes. The approach faded as HCI moved away from cognitive theory.
steps: Instead of eliciting mental model rules ('users think the system works like X'), elicit mental model similarity spaces: present users with N interface elements, collect all pairwise similarity ratings, build a multidimensional scaling (MDS) solution.
The MDS space IS the mental model — a geometric representation of how elements cluster and relate.
Compare MDS spaces across user segments to reveal mental model differences.
outputs: Similarity matrices, MDS or cluster maps of users' conceptual space, typicality ratings, identified prototypes and boundary cases likely to cause confusion.
useWhen: Understanding how users conceptualise categories of features, content or products, planning new features that must fit existing conceptions, and diagnosing category confusion.
avoidWhen: When users do hold explicit procedural knowledge that can simply be asked about or observed; use interviews or task analysis.
whyLost: Interest in cognitive theory waned in practical HCI after the 1990s, and connectionist ideas moved into machine learning rather than user research.
whereToUse: Mental model research, IA design, navigation label design, expert-novice interface comparison.
example: A streaming service collects similarity ratings for 30 content types; MDS shows 'documentary series' sits between documentaries and drama, explaining why users cannot find them. The service adds the category to both browse rows.
sources: Matter and Consciousness — Paul M. Churchland
Rumelhart & McClelland, Parallel Distributed Processing (1986)
Rosch, Principles of categorization (1978)
Cognitive Modeling: Nine Paradigms (slide deck)
reference: Churchland PM (1988) Matter and Consciousness. Revised ed. MIT Press

name: Connectionist Priming for Interface Habituation Research
origin: McClelland and Rumelhart's interactive activation model (1981); PDP (1986)
summary: Uses priming paradigms to measure how learned interface conventions pre-activate expectations, predicting errors when a new design partially matches a familiar pattern.
description: Connectionist models explain priming as residual or spreading activation in a network of associated units: exposure to part of a learned pattern pre-activates the rest. For interfaces, years of exposure to conventions (a red button meaning danger, a gear meaning settings, bottom-right meaning proceed) create strong patterns. When a new design partially matches one, the remaining expectations are activated automatically, which can speed use when consistent or cause capture errors when not. Priming paradigms quantify this: participants are briefly exposed to conventional or modified elements, then respond to a target, and facilitation or interference in response time and error rate measures the strength of the habit. The method predicts where deviating from a convention will be costly and where a new convention can be learned.
steps: Design stimuli varying the degree of prototype match (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of features matching a learned interface pattern). Measure:
response time as a function of match level,

error type when match is partial (do errors reflect the prototype or a novel response?). Errors that match the prototype even at 50% match = strong connectionist priming. Use to predict error patterns after design changes.
outputs: Priming effect sizes for key conventions, identified partial-match conflicts with predicted capture errors, and guidance on which conventions to keep or break.
useWhen: Redesigns that change familiar conventions, migrations between platforms, safety-critical controls, and design system changes affecting habitual users.
avoidWhen: When teams need quick qualitative insight; priming experiments require controlled reaction-time setups. Use first-click or usability testing instead.
whyLost: Connectionist theory moved into machine learning while HCI dropped reaction-time paradigms, so the bridge between priming research and interface conventions disappeared.
whereToUse: Interface redesign error prediction, design system consistency analysis, expert user migration planning.
example: A trading platform plans to swap buy and sell button colours to match a new brand. A priming study with 40 traders shows 11% more errors on colour-incongruent trials, and the swap is abandoned.
sources: Parallel Distributed Processing — David E. Rumelhart
McClelland & Rumelhart, An interactive activation model of context effects in letter perception (Psychological Review, 1981)
reference: Rumelhart DE, McClelland JL & PDP Research Group (1986) Parallel Distributed Processing: Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition, Vol. 1. MIT Press

name: Constant Comparison Across a Programme of Research
origin: Extension of Glaser & Strauss's constant comparative method (1967) to multi-study research programmes
summary: Maintaining a persistent code library and running theoretical memo across studies so each new study refines a cumulative theory rather than starting from scratch.
description: Most organisations run studies as isolated projects, each re-discovering similar themes in new vocabulary. This approach extends constant comparison from incidents within one study to codes and categories across a programme. A persistent, versioned code library acts as a sensitising framework for each new study, without dictating codes. After every study, new codes are compared with the library: recurring codes gain strength, context-specific ones reveal scope conditions, and contradictions trigger revision. A running theoretical memo records how understanding evolves ('Study 1 established X; Study 3 showed X fails when Y'). The result is cumulative theory with documented boundaries, and a research repository organised by concepts rather than by project.
steps: Maintain a persistent code library across all studies in the research programme. Begin new studies with the existing library as a sensitising framework.
After each study: compare new codes to those from previous studies. Which appear consistently? Which only in specific contexts?
Build a running theoretical memo tracking how understanding of the phenomenon has evolved: 'Study 1 established X. Study 2 refined to Y under conditions Z. Study 3 revealed X does not hold when…'
Cross-study negative cases: A finding that holds in one context and not another is a scope condition — and scope conditions are theoretical contributions.
outputs: A versioned cross-study code library, a running theoretical memo, scope conditions from cross-study contrasts, and a concept-organised repository.
useWhen: Organisations running repeated research in one domain over months or years, research repositories, and long-lived product areas.
avoidWhen: One-off studies in unrelated domains, or when an existing library would bias genuinely new exploration; then start fresh and compare afterwards.
whyLost: Research repositories store atomised findings by project, and few teams maintain a shared, theory-oriented code library.
whereToUse: Research ops and insight repositories, platform teams in large SaaS companies, and health or fintech organisations with ongoing programmes.
example: A fintech's fifth study on fraud anxiety uses the shared code library. A new code, 'delegated vigilance' (relying on family to spot scams), contradicts an earlier finding and is logged as a scope condition for older users.
sources: Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
The Discovery of Grounded Theory (Glaser & Strauss)
reference: Glaser, B. G. & Strauss, A. L. (1967). The Discovery of Grounded Theory. Aldine.

name: Construct definition before data collection
origin: Construct validity tradition from Cronbach and Meehl, 1955; scale development guidance by DeVellis (1991) and MacKenzie, Podsakoff and Podsakoff (2011)
summary: Requires a written, bounded definition of each construct, its dimensions and its boundaries before any instrument is chosen or data collected.
description: Many measurement failures begin with an unspecified construct: teams collect 'engagement' or 'delight' data and then decide afterwards what it meant. Construct definition before data collection inverts this. The researcher writes a conceptual definition that states the construct's domain, its dimensions, whether it is reflective or formative, what it is distinct from, and the conditions under which it applies. MacKenzie and colleagues recommend checking definitions for ambiguity, clarifying the entity it applies to (user, session, product), and separating the construct from its causes and consequences. This prevents circularity, where a construct is defined by whatever the available metric happens to capture, and makes later validity testing possible.
steps: Name the construct and collect existing definitions from literature and from stakeholders.
Write a conceptual definition specifying its property, the entity it describes, and its domain.
List dimensions and decide whether the construct is reflective (indicators caused by it) or formative (indicators define it).
State what the construct is not, naming at least two neighbouring constructs it must be distinguished from.
Have 3-5 experts rate whether the definition is clear and complete, and revise until agreement is reached.
Lock the definition in the research plan and choose or build instruments only after this.
outputs: A signed-off construct definition document with dimensions, boundaries, model type and neighbouring constructs.
useWhen: At the start of metric programmes, surveys, benchmarks and experiments; when stakeholders disagree what a key outcome means.
avoidWhen: When the goal is to discover what matters to users without prior constructs; use grounded or exploratory qualitative research first.
whyLost: Construct definition is standard in psychology and management science, but UX moves fast and assumes shared meanings, so it is almost never formalised.
whereToUse: Defining trust, workload, engagement, wellbeing, AI reliance and accessibility outcomes in product strategy.
example: Before measuring 'trust in the surgical robot', the team defines it as surgeons' willingness to rely on robot output under uncertainty, distinguishing it from satisfaction and from perceived reliability, and identifies it as reflective with three dimensions.
sources: Dix, A., Statistics for HCI: Making Sense of Quantitative Data (2020)
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
Leavy, P., Research Design: Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed Methods, Arts-Based, and Community-Based Participatory Research Approaches (2017)
Statistics for HCI (Alan Dix)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Research Design (Leavy)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 8 — Measurement Theory — Before You Measure Anything
reference: MacKenzie, S. B., Podsakoff, P. M. & Podsakoff, N. P. (2011). Construct measurement and validation procedures in MIS and behavioral research. MIS Quarterly, 35(2), 293-334.

name: Content Analysis
origin: Harold Lasswell and Bernard Berelson, 1940s to 1952; qualitative content analysis by Philipp Mayring, 1980s; Krippendorff, 1980
summary: Systematic coding of text, images or video into categories to describe patterns and frequencies, with explicit codebooks and reliability checks.
description: Content analysis systematically categorises the content of communication, such as reviews, support tickets, social media posts, interview transcripts or interface copy, to make replicable and valid inferences. Quantitative content analysis counts the occurrence of predefined categories; qualitative content analysis develops categories from the data and attends to meaning in context. Both depend on a clear codebook with definitions, examples and boundary rules. Its strength in UX lies in turning large volumes of unstructured feedback into measurable patterns that can be tracked over time. Rigour comes from defining units of analysis, sampling systematically, piloting the codebook, measuring inter-coder reliability (for example Krippendorff's alpha of 0.8 or higher), and reporting frequencies with appropriate caveats.
steps: Define research questions, the corpus and the unit of analysis, such as a review, sentence or ticket.
Sample the corpus systematically, for example stratified by time or product area.
Develop a codebook deductively from theory or inductively from a subsample, with definitions and examples.
Pilot the codebook with two coders and refine until reliability is acceptable (alpha at least 0.8 or kappa at least 0.7).
Code the full sample, manually or with supervised machine assistance checked against human coding.
Analyse frequencies, co-occurrence and trends, and interpret them with illustrative examples.
outputs: A codebook, coded corpus, category frequencies and trends, reliability statistics and illustrative examples.
useWhen: For analysing large volumes of reviews, support tickets, social posts or open-ended survey responses, and tracking feedback categories over time.
avoidWhen: Avoid when deep interpretation of meaning is the aim; use thematic or discourse analysis. Avoid counting categories in small interview samples as if they were representative.
whyLost: Still in use: content analysis is versatile and maps well onto the large volumes of reviews, support tickets, social posts and open-ended responses that product teams accumulate, and it is now often accelerated with machine-assisted coding.
whereToUse: Analysing app store reviews, support tickets and chat logs; open-ended survey responses at scale; competitive content audits; monitoring feedback categories after releases; auditing interface copy and AI outputs.
example: A smart-home company codes 3,000 app store reviews with a 14-category codebook. Pairing failures account for 31 percent of one-star reviews in the quarter after a firmware release, prioritising a pairing fix.

name: Content Audit
origin: Jeffrey Veen and Jesse James Garrett era IA practice (late 1990s); codified by Kristina Halvorson (2009)
summary: A systematic inventory and evaluation of existing content for accuracy, usefulness, duplication and fit with user needs, producing keep, revise, merge or delete decisions.
description: A content audit catalogues every content item in scope (pages, articles, help docs, emails, in-product strings) and evaluates each against defined criteria. The quantitative inventory captures URL, title, type, owner, date, traffic and links; the qualitative audit scores items for accuracy, relevance to user tasks, readability, findability, brand fit and ROT status (redundant, outdated, trivial). Rigour comes from explicit criteria with scoring rubrics, a sampling strategy when the estate is too large to audit fully, inter-rater calibration among auditors, and linking scores to behavioural evidence such as traffic, search exits and support contacts. The output is not a spreadsheet for its own sake but a decision for each item and an evidence base for information architecture, migration and governance.
steps: Define the audit's purpose (migration, IA redesign, governance) and scope, and decide between a full inventory or a stratified sample.
Crawl or export the inventory with metadata: URL, title, content type, owner, last updated, traffic, inbound links and search exits.
Agree a scoring rubric (for example 1-3 for accuracy, relevance, readability, findability, currency) and calibrate auditors on 20 shared items.
Audit each item against the rubric and tag ROT status, flagging duplicates and gaps against known user tasks.
Combine scores with analytics to assign actions: keep, revise, merge, archive or delete, with an owner for each.
Summarise patterns (gaps, duplication clusters, ownerless content) and feed them into IA and governance decisions.
outputs: Content inventory spreadsheet, scored audit, ROT rate, gap analysis against user tasks, and an action plan with owners.
useWhen: Before a site migration, IA redesign or content strategy, or when users report they cannot find or trust information.
avoidWhen: When the problem is a single flow rather than a content estate, or when there is no owner to act on the results; then start with governance.
whyLost: Still in use: Essential before any content redesign; often reveals significant waste and gaps.
whereToUse: Website redesign; content strategy projects; knowledge base maintenance.
example: A university with 18,000 web pages audits a 10% stratified sample before a CMS migration. A 46% ROT rate and 140 near-duplicate admissions pages justify cutting the migration scope by a third.
sources: Strategic Content Design
Content Strategy for the Web (Kristina Halvorson)
Content Strategy at Work (Margot Bloomstein)
reference: Halvorson K & Rach M (2012) Content Strategy for the Web. 2nd ed. New Riders

name: Content model validation
origin: Structured content practice from content strategy (Rockley, 2002; Wachter-Boettcher, 2012) and conceptual data modelling (Chen, 1976)
summary: Tests whether a structured content model's types, attributes and relationships actually fit real content, user needs and publishing contexts before it is built.
description: A content model defines content types (article, product, procedure), their attributes and the relationships between them. Validation checks it in three ways: against real content (can a representative sample be decomposed into the model without forcing or loss?), against user tasks (do the types and relationships support the queries and journeys users need?), and against channels (can the content render appropriately in each output, from web to voice to device screens?). Rigorous validation borrows from data modelling: test with real instances, look for overloaded fields and free-text dumping grounds, and measure fit. In practice validation is often a stakeholder walkthrough of a diagram, which is why the method is vestigial.
steps: Gather a stratified sample of real content, at least 30-50 items across all candidate types and sources.
Attempt to decompose each item into the model, recording forced fits, missing attributes, overloaded fields and unused attributes.
Compute fit metrics: percentage of items modelled without loss (target at least 90%) and percentage of attributes used in at least 20% of items.
Test task support by writing the queries and journeys users need and checking the model can answer them through its relationships.
Prototype rendering for each target channel and check required fields exist for each.
Revise the model and repeat with a fresh sample before implementation in the CMS.
outputs: A validated content model, fit metrics, a list of revisions, and channel rendering checks.
useWhen: Before building or migrating a CMS, designing structured or headless content, or preparing content for AI retrieval.
avoidWhen: When content is small and stable; a simple content inventory will do. For user mental models, use card sorting first.
whyLost: Content modelling became a CMS configuration task done by developers, and validation shrank to diagram sign-off.
whereToUse: Headless CMS projects, medical device instructions, product information management, documentation, and retrieval-augmented AI systems.
example: A medical device firm models procedures with steps, warnings and instrument references. Testing 60 real procedures shows 30% of warnings are tied to multiple steps, which the model cannot express; adding a many-to-many relationship prevents warnings being duplicated or lost.
sources: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J., Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (O'Reilly, 4th ed., 2015)
Martin, L. M., Everyday Information Architecture (2019)
Covert, A., How to Make Sense of Any Mess (2014)
Information Architecture (O'Reilly)

How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 7 — Graph Theory & the Architecture of Information

name: Content Modeling for Information Architecture
donor: Information architecture, data modelling and library science
origin: Domain modelling in software engineering and the BBC's domain-driven design work (Mike Atherton, 2000s); practical method by Lisa Maria Martin (2019)
summary: Maps the content types, attributes and relationships a system manages, creating a semantic model of the domain that underpins navigation, CMS structure and reuse.
description: A content model describes what kinds of things exist in a domain (for example recipes, ingredients, chefs, techniques), what attributes each has, and how they relate. Unlike a sitemap, which shows navigation, a content model shows the underlying semantic structure from which navigation, templates, search and APIs can be derived. The research side of content modelling grounds the model in user mental models and domain language, using interviews, card sorts and content audits, rather than in organisational silos. Rigour comes from defining each type and attribute precisely, testing the model against real content and user tasks, and validating that the relationships support the journeys users need. The BBC's work on programmes and food showed how a domain model enables pages, links and reuse at scale.
steps: Step 1: Inventory all content types (pages, components, objects) in the system.
Step 2: For each type, list attributes (what properties does each instance have?).
Step 3: Map relationships between types (one-to-many, many-to-many).
Step 4: Validate with users: do the content types match users' mental models? (Card sort or open labeling task).
Mismatches between the content model and users' mental models = IA problems.
outputs: Content types with attribute definitions, relationship diagram, mapping to user tasks and vocabulary, and CMS and template specifications.
useWhen: Content-heavy products, headless CMS projects, knowledge bases, e-commerce catalogues, and multi-channel content reuse.
avoidWhen: For small, mostly static sites with few content types, or when navigation labels rather than structure are the problem; use tree testing or card sorting.
whyLost: IA in practice became sitemaps and navigation design, while content modelling was left to developers configuring CMS schemas without user research.
whereToUse: Large site/app IA redesign, content management system design, search and filter UX, API design with user-facing implications.
example: A recipe platform models recipes, ingredients, techniques and equipment as linked types. Users can now navigate from a technique to all recipes using it, and search for 'recipes I can make with a cast-iron pan', features impossible with the old page-based structure.
sources: Everyday Information Architecture — Lisa Maria Martin
Designing Connected Content (Carrie Hane & Mike Atherton)
reference: Martin LM (2019) Everyday Information Architecture. A Book Apart

name: Content Strategy
donor: Publishing, editorial practice and information science
origin: Ann Rockley (2002) and Kristina Halvorson (2009, Content Strategy for the Web)
summary: Plans the creation, delivery, governance and lifecycle of useful content, aligning content with user needs and business goals through audits, models and standards.
description: Content strategy plans for the creation, publication, governance and maintenance of useful, usable content. It addresses what content is needed and why, for whom, in what formats and structures, with what voice and tone, and who owns and maintains it over time. Core practices include content audits and inventories, gap analysis against user needs, content models and structured content types, style and voice guidelines, editorial workflows and governance. Its research side draws on user needs analysis, search data and content testing. Rigour comes from basing decisions on quantitative and qualitative audits rather than opinion, defining user needs explicitly, measuring content performance (findability, comprehension and task completion), and maintaining governance so quality does not decay after launch.
steps: Conduct a quantitative inventory and qualitative audit of existing content.
Research user needs and tasks, using search logs, support data and interviews.
Perform a gap analysis between user needs and existing content.
Define content types, structured content models and metadata.
Set voice, tone and style guidelines and test key content for comprehension.
Establish governance: ownership, workflows, review cycles and retirement rules.
Measure content performance and iterate.
outputs: Content inventory and audit, gap analysis, content models, style guides, governance plan and content performance metrics.
useWhen: For content-heavy products such as publishing, e-commerce, documentation, public services and product UI copy systems, especially when content quality has decayed.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating it as a one-off copywriting task; without governance it fails. For specific comprehension questions, run content usability testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Essential for content-heavy products; growing recognition of content as core UX concern.
whereToUse: Publishing platforms; e-commerce; enterprise documentation; product content systems.
example: A tax authority audits 9,000 web pages and finds 40 percent are outdated or duplicated. User needs research drives a consolidation to 2,500 pages with structured content types and owners, cutting related support calls.
sources: Strategic Content Design
Content Strategy for the Web (Halvorson & Rach)
reference: Halvorson, K. & Rach, M. (2012). Content Strategy for the Web (2nd ed.). New Riders.

name: Content tone matrix
origin: Editorial style practice; popularised for product UI by Mailchimp's 'Voice and Tone' guide (Kate Kiefer Lee, 2011) and NN/g's four tone dimensions (Moran, 2016); pragmatic grounding in Grice (1975)
summary: A grid mapping user situations and emotional states to the tone a product should take, audited against Gricean maxims so wording implies only what it should.
description: A content tone matrix crosses the situations a product speaks in (onboarding, success, error, payment failure, account lock, bereavement) with the emotional state the user is likely in and specifies the tone for each cell along defined dimensions, typically formal to casual, serious to playful, respectful to irreverent, enthusiastic to matter-of-fact. Its rigour comes from two sources. First, the cells are derived from evidence about user state (support tickets, interviews, diary entries) rather than brand aspiration. Second, each sample string is audited pragmatically: does it say as much as needed and no more (Quantity), is it true (Quality), relevant (Relation) and clear (Manner)? Because users read implicatures, not just literal meaning, an error message that is jaunty or vague can imply blame or triviality. The matrix turns tone from a stylistic preference into a testable specification.
steps: Inventory every message context in the product (aim for full coverage, typically 30 to 120 message types) and group them into 8 to 15 situation types such as success, recoverable error, blocking error, money movement and irreversible action.

For each situation, estimate the user's likely affective state and stakes using evidence: support tickets, session recordings and at least 5 to 8 interviews with users who recently experienced that situation.

Define 3 to 5 tone dimensions with anchored endpoints (for example NN/g's funny-serious, formal-casual, respectful-irreverent, enthusiastic-matter-of-fact) and set a target position on each for every situation row.

Write 2 to 3 exemplar strings per cell and run a Gricean maxim audit on each, flagging any string that over- or under-informs, asserts something not guaranteed, is irrelevant to the user's goal, or is ambiguous.

Test the highest-stakes cells (errors, money, health, security) with 5 to 10 users using a comprehension and implicature probe: 'What is this message telling you? Whose fault is it? What will you do next?'

Revise cells where more than 1 in 5 participants draw an unintended implicature (for example self-blame or false reassurance), then publish the matrix in the design system with do and do-not examples.
Re-audit quarterly or whenever new message types ship, sampling live strings against the matrix.
outputs: A situation-by-tone matrix with target positions per dimension, exemplar and counter-example strings per cell, a maxim-audit log of violations, and implicature test results for high-stakes messages.
useWhen: A product speaks in many contexts with varying stakes; error, payment or health messages are generating confusion, blame or distrust; multiple writers or LLM-generated strings need a shared, checkable tone standard.
avoidWhen: The product has only a handful of messages (just write and test them directly), or the problem is information architecture or task flow rather than wording; use a usability test or cognitive walkthrough instead.
whyLost: It survived because content design became a profession and design systems needed shareable tone rules. What was largely lost is the pragmatic grounding: many matrices encode brand personality without testing what users infer.
whereToUse: Fintech error and decline messaging, health and insurance notifications, conversational and LLM-driven interfaces needing tone guardrails, localisation into cultures with different politeness norms.
example: A lending app's playful 'Oops! Something went wrong' appeared on declined applications. A tone matrix placed 'application declined' at serious, respectful, matter-of-fact, and the maxim audit flagged the Quantity violation of giving no reason; the rewritten message stated the reason category and next step, and complaint volume on that screen fell.
sources: Development of Language (Gleason)
Conversational Design (Hall)
Methods Atlas — Gricean audit (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 18 — Pragmatics — What Language Actually Does
reference: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and Conversation. In Cole & Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts; Moran, K. (2016). The Four Dimensions of Tone of Voice. Nielsen Norman Group.

name: Contextual Inquiry
donor: Anthropology and ethnography, adapted for systems design
origin: Karen Holtzblatt & Hugh Beyer, late 1980s (Contextual Design, 1998)
summary: An in-situ interview where the researcher observes and questions users as they do real work, revealing practices, workarounds and context invisible in the lab.
description: Contextual inquiry combines observation and interviewing in the user's own environment while they carry out their actual work. The researcher adopts the stance of an apprentice learning from a master, guided by four principles: context (go where the work happens), partnership (interpret jointly with the user), interpretation (share and check meanings as you go) and focus (a clear research scope that steers attention). Because users demonstrate rather than describe, contextual inquiry exposes tacit knowledge, workarounds, artefacts and interruptions that people omit in conventional interviews. Rigour comes from observing ongoing work rather than demos, interpreting with the participant in the moment, holding interpretation sessions within 48 hours, and capturing findings in structured work models and affinity diagrams.
steps: Define a project focus that states which work practices you need to understand.
Recruit 6 to 12 participants across key roles and sites, and arrange to visit during real work.
Open with a brief conventional interview to understand role and context (about 15 minutes).
Transition to observing ongoing work, asking about actions as they happen and sharing interpretations for the user to confirm or correct.
Collect or photograph artefacts such as notes, printouts and spreadsheets.
Wrap up by summarising your understanding and checking it with the participant.
Hold a team interpretation session within 48 hours and capture notes, work models and affinity notes.
outputs: Interpretation notes, work models (flow, sequence, artefact, cultural, physical), artefact collections and an affinity diagram of insights.
useWhen: When designing tools embedded in complex real-world work, when users cannot articulate tacit practices, or when workarounds and environment matter.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need statistical generalisation or when work cannot be observed for privacy or safety reasons; use surveys, diaries or retrospective critical incident interviews instead.
whyLost: Vestigial: the label is widely used, but most teams now run a remote interview with screen-share and call it contextual inquiry, losing the in-situ observation, joint interpretation and work modelling that gave the method its power.
whereToUse: Workplace tools; healthcare systems; any product embedded in complex real-world workflows.
example: A clinical informatics team shadows ward nurses during medication rounds. They observe nurses writing doses on gloves because the EHR session times out, a workaround never mentioned in interviews, which reshapes the barcode scanning design.

Rapid Contextual Design (Holtzblatt)
Universal Methods of Design (Martin)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
