extra.Four Principles (Holtzblatt & Beyer): Context: Conduct the interview where the work happens. Not in a conference room. Not remotely. At the desk, on the floor, in the vehicle, in the field. The environment contains information that the participant cannot verbalise because they no longer notice it. Partnership: The researcher takes the role of apprentice — genuinely curious, asking the participant (master) to explain their work. Not expert evaluator; not passive observer. Engaged learner. Interpretation: Share your interpretations with the participant in real time. "I notice you always copy that data to a spreadsheet before you enter it — is that a workaround for something?" This surfaces tacit knowledge that pure observation misses. Focus: Stay focused on the work that matters to your research question. When the participant goes off-topic, return gently: "I'm curious to understand more about how you handle [the specific task] — can we go back to that?"
extra.Work Artifact Analysis: During CI, collect all artifacts the participant has created or modified: post-it notes, custom spreadsheets, printed manuals with annotations, physical workarounds. Photograph and catalog. Analyse for: (1) information the interface failed to surface (filled gaps); (2) actions the interface failed to afford (physical workarounds); (3) mental models embedded in artifact structure (how they organised their workaround reveals how they think about the underlying task).

name: Contextual Inquiry with Work Artefact Analysis
origin: Contextual inquiry by Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt (1990s), artefact models in Contextual Design (1998); catalogued by Martin and Hanington (2012)
summary: Contextual inquiry that systematically collects and analyses the notes, printouts, spreadsheets and workarounds people create, revealing tacit needs and shadow systems interviews miss.
description: Contextual inquiry pairs observation and interview in the user's own setting under a master-apprentice model. Artefact analysis extends it by treating the physical and digital things people create or use as data in their own right: sticky notes on monitors, annotated printouts, personal spreadsheets, cheat sheets, renamed folders and custom tools. Each artefact is photographed or collected, and analysed for its structure, the information it carries, who creates and uses it, and the breakdowns it compensates for. Workarounds often form a shadow information system that reveals what the official product fails to support. Holtzblatt and Beyer's artefact model formalises this analysis. In contemporary practice contextual inquiry survives in shortened forms, and the systematic artefact component is usually dropped.
steps: During field observation, collect all artifacts users have created or modified: post-it notes, custom spreadsheets, printed manuals with annotations, physical workarounds. Photograph and catalog. Analyze artifact content for:
information the interface failed to surface (filled gaps),
actions the interface failed to afford (physical workarounds),
mental models embedded in artifact structure.
outputs: Artefact inventory with photographs, artefact models (structure, content, usage, breakdowns), workaround catalogue and design requirements derived from shadow systems.
useWhen: Workplace and professional tools, healthcare, logistics, finance operations, and any setting where people supplement official systems with their own records.
avoidWhen: When access to the work setting is impossible or artefacts are confidential and cannot be recorded; use diary studies or remote contextual interviews with screen sharing instead.
whyLost: Time-boxed research cut field visits short and remote research removed the opportunity to see artefacts, so the artefact model from Contextual Design became the first part dropped.
whereToUse: Enterprise software redesign, complex professional tool research, any context where workarounds and adaptations are common. Connects to niche construction theory — workarounds are niche construction.
example: At a primary-care clinic, researchers photograph post-it notes stuck to a shared tablet listing patients awaiting callbacks. The notes form a shadow triage queue, leading the EHR vendor to add a visible callback list.
sources: Universal Methods of Design — Bella Martin
Ethnographic Thinking (Hasbrouck)
Handbook of Ethnography
Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Contextual Design (Hugh Beyer & Karen Holtzblatt)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 31 — Ethnographic Fieldwork — Thick Description & Niche Construction
reference: Martin B & Hanington B (2012) Universal Methods of Design: 100 Ways to Research Complex Problems. Rockport Publishers

name: Continuous Discovery Infrastructure
origin: Teresa Torres, 2021 (Continuous Discovery Habits)
summary: A standing weekly interview cadence run by product trios and fed into a living opportunity solution tree linking evidence to decisions.
description: Continuous discovery reframes research from episodic projects into an ongoing team habit. Torres recommends that the product trio (product manager, designer, engineer) talk to customers at least weekly, supported by automated recruitment such as in-product intercepts and customer success referrals. Short interviews collect specific recent stories rather than opinions. Insights are mapped onto an opportunity solution tree: a desired outcome at the top, opportunities (needs, pain points) beneath, then candidate solutions and the assumption tests that evaluate them. The tree is updated after each session and replaces static reports. Its strength is sustained exposure and traceability from evidence to decisions; its risk is shallow, unsystematic synthesis when no trained researcher supports it.
steps: Standing recruitment pipeline: In-product banners, email lists, customer success referrals. Maintain a pool of willing participants contactable for a 20-minute conversation with 24-hour notice.

Interview structure (20 min): 5 min — how has the product been part of your life since we last spoke? 10 min — follow the story of one specific recent moment. 5 min — what's coming up that will involve the product?
Living Opportunity Solution Tree: Outcome → opportunities (unmet needs from interviews) → solutions → experiments. Update after every session. Replaces the traditional research report.
Team involvement: Engineers and PMs attend at least every 4th session. Direct exposure changes how teams interpret research.
Cadence: Weekly, not only when there's a 'big question.' Consistency is the point.
outputs: A standing recruitment pipeline, weekly interview snapshots, a living opportunity solution tree, and assumption test results.
useWhen: Product teams making frequent decisions who need steady contact with customers and a traceable link between evidence and roadmap.
avoidWhen: Deep foundational questions, sensitive populations, or rigorous measurement; use dedicated studies by trained researchers.
whyLost: It spread rapidly through product management, because it fits agile cadences and gives teams direct ownership of discovery.
whereToUse: B2B SaaS, consumer subscription apps, marketplaces and fintech product teams with direct customer access.
example: A payroll SaaS trio runs three 20-minute calls each week from an in-app intercept. After six weeks, the tree shows 'year-end filing anxiety' as the largest opportunity, reshaping the next quarter's roadmap.
sources: Continuous Discovery Habits (Teresa Torres)
Practical Empathy (Indi Young)
reference: Torres, T. (2021). Continuous Discovery Habits. Product Talk LLC.

name: Continuous Wavelet Transform (Scalograms)
origin: Jean Morlet & Alex Grossmann, 1984
summary: Localises frequency content in time by sliding scaled wavelets across a signal, revealing when bursts, transitions and slow drifts occur in behaviour.
description: Where Fourier reveals global rhythm, wavelets reveal local story. The continuous wavelet transform correlates the signal with a wavelet at many scales and positions, producing a time-frequency scalogram. In the Behavioral Spectral Framework, short-scale bursts are read as spikes of cognitive load, surprise or momentary confusion, long-scale drifts as slow learning, sustained focus, fatigue or attention decay, and coexisting scales as multitasking or conflicting goals. Recommended adaptations include adaptive scales, wavelet energy envelopes to estimate task load and recovery time after failures, and scalograms aligned with qualitative annotations. The synthesis method extracts dominant bands with FFT, then localises them in time with CWT or STFT and aligns them with coded moments. In the fintech case, Frustration-coded moments consistently coincided with transient high-frequency spikes in the wavelet energy map.
steps: Choose a mother wavelet and a range of scales matched to the behaviours of interest.
Compute the CWT of the behavioural signal and plot the scalogram.
Compute wavelet energy envelopes to estimate load and recovery time after failure events.
Detect bursts and drifts and export their timestamps.
Align bursts with qualitative annotations (video, transcript, sentiment) in a Spectral Annotation Matrix.
Report scalograms with annotation overlays.
outputs: Scalograms, burst timestamps, energy envelopes and annotated overlays.
useWhen: When you need to know when within a session or journey rhythm changes, not just which rhythms exist.
avoidWhen: When signals are too short or sparse to resolve scales, or no qualitative alignment is possible.
whyLost: Standard in geophysics, EEG and engineering, absent from UX training.
whereToUse: Micro-frustration detection, recovery-time measurement, emotional journey mapping, biometric UX.
example: A scalogram of a checkout session shows a short-scale burst at the OTP step followed by a slow rebound, quantifying recovery time after the failure.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
Matteo Paz (2024), A Sub-Millisecond Fourier and Wavelet Based Model to Extract Variable Candidates from the NEOWISE Single-Exposure Database
reference: Torrence, C., & Compo, G. P. (1998). A practical guide to wavelet analysis. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 79(1), 61–78.

name: Contradiction identification
origin: Yrjö Engeström, Learning by Expanding, 1987, building on Vygotsky and Leont'ev
summary: Identifies systemic tensions within and between elements of an activity system, such as tools, rules and division of labour, that explain recurring breakdowns and workarounds.
description: Engeström's activity system model includes subject, object, tools, rules, community and division of labour. Contradictions are historically accumulating structural tensions: primary (within an element, such as a tool being both a commodity and an instrument), secondary (between elements, such as a new tool clashing with existing rules), tertiary (between old and new forms of the activity) and quaternary (between neighbouring activity systems). Contradictions surface as disturbances, breakdowns, workarounds and complaints. Identifying them shifts analysis from individual usability problems to systemic causes, and Engeström argues they are the engine of change. Rigour comes from tracing disturbances in data to specific element pairs, distinguishing contradictions from one-off problems, and validating with participants.
steps: Model the activity system: subject, object, tools, rules, community, division of labour and outcome.
Collect disturbance data from observation, interviews and incident logs: breakdowns, workarounds, conflicts and complaints.
Code each disturbance against the element pairs involved, recording evidence.
Classify recurring tensions as primary, secondary, tertiary or quaternary contradictions.
Validate with participants in a workshop (for example a Change Laboratory session) to confirm and prioritise contradictions.
Generate design and organisational interventions that address the contradiction, not just the disturbance.
outputs: An activity system model, a coded disturbance set, a contradiction map by type, and intervention ideas.
useWhen: When products are adopted in complex workplaces with persistent workarounds, and when design goals clash with actual use.
avoidWhen: For simple consumer tasks where social and organisational structures are not relevant; use usability testing.
whyLost: Activity theory was prominent in 1990s HCI (Kuutti, Nardi, Bødker) but its vocabulary proved heavy for practitioners, and it retreated to academic and workplace studies.
whereToUse: Hospital technology adoption, enterprise software rollouts, education technology, and AI tools in professional work.
example: Surgeons use a robot's camera auto-follow feature far less than designed. Contradiction analysis traces this to a secondary contradiction between the tool and hospital rules requiring the assistant to control the camera for training.
sources: Newell, A., Unified Theories of Cognition (1990)
Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
Unified Theories of Cognition (Newell)
Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (Hollnagel)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 15 — Activity Theory, Contradictions & the Zone of Proximal Development
reference: Engeström, Y. (1987). Learning by Expanding: An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Developmental Research. Orienta-Konsultit.

name: Control Theory and Feedback Loop Analysis
origin: Norbert Wiener (Cybernetics, 1948); Duane McRuer and Henry Jex (1967, crossover model); William Powers (Behavior: The Control of Perception, 1973)
summary: Models users and systems as closed feedback loops with gain, delay and noise, predicting oscillation, overshoot and instability in interaction.
description: Control theory analyses closed loops: a controller compares a reference with feedback and acts to reduce error. Delays and high gain cause oscillation and instability. In manual control, McRuer's crossover model showed humans adapt their dynamics so the combined human-machine system behaves like an integrator near crossover frequency, with effective time delay of roughly 0.1-0.3 seconds. Perceptual control theory frames behaviour as controlling perception. For UX, loops are everywhere: scrolling with inertia, sliders with lag, thermostats, recommendation feedback, algorithmic pricing. Analysing gain, latency and feedback quality predicts overshoot (users scrolling past), hunting (repeatedly adjusting) and runaway loops (filter bubbles).
steps: Draw the loop: user goal (reference), action, system dynamics, feedback display, perception.
Measure system parameters: latency, gain (output per input), noise and feedback resolution.
Collect interaction traces (e.g. cursor, scroll, setting adjustments) and identify overshoot and oscillation.
Fit simple models (e.g. first-order plus delay) or apply crossover model reasoning.
Adjust gain, damping, latency or feedback (e.g. preview, rate-aided control) and predict effects.
Test changes with tracking or adjustment tasks, measuring settling time and overshoot.
outputs: Loop diagrams, measured gain and delay, overshoot and settling metrics, and tuned interaction parameters.
useWhen: Continuous control interactions, adjustable settings with lag, and algorithmic feedback loops affecting users.
avoidWhen: Discrete form-filling or content questions without dynamic feedback.
whyLost: Manual control research declined with the shift from vehicles to GUIs, and design rarely uses engineering dynamics.
whereToUse: Scrolling and zoom physics, smart thermostats, drone and robot control, audio mixing, recommender feedback loops.
example: A smart thermostat app shows users repeatedly overshooting set points because heating response is delayed 20 minutes; adding a predicted temperature curve (feedback of future state) reduces adjustment cycles by 60%.
sources: McRuer & Jex, A review of quasi-linear pilot models (1967), IEEE Transactions on Human Factors in Electronics
Jagacinski & Flach, Control Theory for Humans (2003)
Powers, Behavior: The Control of Perception (1973)
reference: Jagacinski, R. J., & Flach, J. M. (2003). Control Theory for Humans. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Controlling for Prior Experience (Weighted t-Test)
origin: Post-stratification weighting from survey statistics; applied to UX benchmarks by Sauro (2018)
summary: Adjusts competitive comparisons so a product is not rewarded just because more of its testers already used it.
description: People who already use a product rate it higher and perform better on it. If one product's sample contains more existing users than another's, comparisons are biased. Sauro's approach weights each group so that the proportion of experienced and new users matches across products (or a target mix), then runs a weighted t-test. This is a simple form of post-stratification. It is especially important in competitive benchmarks recruited from general panels, where a market leader will naturally have more prior users.
steps: Record prior experience with each product (for example: never, under a year, over a year).
Choose a target mix of experience levels, such as the overall sample proportions.
Compute weights for each participant so each product's sample matches the target mix.
Run a weighted t-test or weighted regression on the metric of interest.
Report unweighted and weighted results side by side.
outputs: Comparisons fair to products with different user bases.
useWhen: Competitive and retrospective benchmarks where samples differ in familiarity.
avoidWhen: Experience groups are tiny, which makes weights unstable.
whyLost: Weighting is routine in survey research but almost unheard of in usability reports.
whereToUse: Competitive benchmarks, multi-brand customer surveys.
example: A market leader's SUS lead of 9 points shrinks to 3 after weighting for its much larger share of existing customers.
sources: Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience, chapter 11.

name: Convergent and Discriminant Validity (CR, AVE, Fornell-Larcker, HTMT)
origin: Claes Fornell & David Larcker, 1981; HTMT by Henseler, Ringle & Sarstedt, 2015
summary: Checks from CFA loadings that each construct's items converge (CR, AVE ≥ 0.50) and that constructs are distinct (Fornell-Larcker criterion or HTMT < 0.85).
description: Before interpreting structural paths, the measurement model must show that indicators measure their construct well and that constructs are not redundant. With standardised loadings λi and error variances θi = 1 − λi², composite reliability CR = (Σλi)² / ((Σλi)² + Σθi) and average variance extracted AVE = Σλi² / (Σλi² + Σθi). Convergent validity requires AVE ≥ 0.50; discriminant validity requires each construct's √AVE to exceed its correlations with other constructs (Fornell-Larcker) or the heterotrait-monotrait ratio to be below 0.85. Vivek Gopinath's payments case reports Trust CR 0.87/AVE 0.69, Fraud Risk 0.82/0.61, Slowness 0.81/0.57 and Support 0.83/0.62, with Cronbach's α of 0.86 (TR) and 0.79 (SL), and drops indicators loading below 0.60 unless theory demands.
steps: Run CFA and obtain standardised loadings for each construct.
Compute θi = 1 − λi² for each indicator.
Compute CR and AVE per construct; require AVE ≥ 0.50.
Compute √AVE and compare with inter-construct correlations (Fornell-Larcker), or compute HTMT and require < 0.85.
Drop or revise indicators with loadings < 0.60 unless theory demands them, and re-run.
Report CR, AVE, α and the discriminant test in the measurement table.
outputs: A measurement validity table with CR, AVE, α and discriminant tests.
useWhen: Whenever latent constructs measured by multi-item scales feed an SEM or regression.
avoidWhen: With single-item measures or purely observed variables.
whyLost: Routine in marketing and IS research, but UX surveys rarely report construct validity beyond α.
whereToUse: Trust, security, ease and satisfaction scales in fintech and SaaS research.
example: Before modelling tap-to-pay adoption, the researcher confirms that Trust (AVE 0.69) and Fraud Risk (AVE 0.61) are distinct constructs with HTMT below 0.85.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments
Campbell & Fiske, Convergent and discriminant validation by the multitrait-multimethod matrix (1959), Psychological Bulletin
Eid & Diener (eds.), Handbook of Multimethod Measurement in Psychology (2006)
reference: Fornell, C., & Larcker, D. F. (1981). Evaluating structural equation models with unobservable variables and measurement error. Journal of Marketing Research, 18(1), 39–50.

name: Conversation Analysis
origin: Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff and Gail Jefferson, 1974 (turn-taking paper, Language)
summary: Micro-analyses naturally occurring talk, including talk with machines, for turn-taking, sequence structure and repair, revealing the implicit rules users bring to interaction.
description: Conversation Analysis studies the sequential organisation of real talk: how turns are allocated, how adjacency pairs (question and answer, offer and acceptance) structure exchanges, how trouble is repaired, and how dispreferred responses are delayed and mitigated. It works from recordings transcribed in Jefferson notation, capturing pauses to a tenth of a second, overlaps and intonation. Because CA treats interaction as orderly at the finest level, it is unusually powerful for conversational interfaces: it shows exactly where a voice assistant or chatbot breaks users' expectations of how the next turn should go. Rigour comes from using naturally occurring rather than elicited data, detailed transcription, and grounding every claim in participants' own displayed orientations in the next turn.
steps: Collect naturally occurring interaction data: CA requires authentic data — actual user-chatbot logs, voice assistant recordings, or customer service chat transcripts.
Jefferson transcription notation: Capture overlapping speech ([ ]), latency ((0.5)), elongated sounds (::), cut-off words (-). The transcript is an analytic document.
Identify sequential structure: What adjacency pairs exist (question-answer, greeting-greeting)? Where do sequences complete normally and where do they break? Breakdowns are your design data.
Repair sequences: When non-understanding is signalled (explicit question, repetition, silence), how is repair initiated? Failure to achieve repair is the UX problem.
Preferred vs. dispreferred responses: Dispreferred responses (disagreement, rejection) are typically delayed, prefaced, or mitigated. CA reveals the social logic of how users phrase requests.
outputs: Jefferson-notated transcripts, a collection of sequence types and repair patterns, documented breakdown points in human-machine dialogue, and design rules for turn design.
useWhen: Designing or evaluating chatbots, voice assistants, LLM agents, call-centre scripts or any product where interaction is turn-based talk, and you have real conversation logs or recordings.
avoidWhen: You only have interview data about conversations rather than the conversations themselves, or you need fast directional feedback; use usability testing of the conversational flow instead.
whyLost: Transcription is slow and the notation intimidating, and CA's refusal to speculate about intentions frustrates teams wanting quick insight, so it stayed in sociology and academic HCI.
whereToUse: Conversational AI and LLM assistants, voice interfaces, customer support chat, telehealth consultations, and multi-party collaboration tools.
example: Analysing 200 logged exchanges with a banking chatbot, a researcher finds users repeat their question with added detail when the bot answers after a long latency, treating the delay as non-understanding. Adding a brief acknowledgement turn cuts repetition.
sources: Handbook of Discourse Analysis
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Moore, R. J. & Arar, R. (2019) Conversational UX Design
reference: Sacks, H., Schegloff, E. A. & Jefferson, G. (1974). A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language, 50(4), 696-735.

name: Conversation Analysis Applied to UI
origin: Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff and Gail Jefferson (1974); Suchman (1987); Moore and Arar (2019)
summary: Micro-analyses turn-taking, adjacency pairs, repair and preference organisation in human-system dialogue to pinpoint where conversational interfaces break down.
description: Conversation analysis studies the sequential organisation of talk: turn-taking, adjacency pairs (question-answer), repair sequences and preference organisation. Suchman applied it to HCI, showing that plan-based models miss the situated, moment-by-moment character of interaction. The treatise's transfer: analyse chatbot and voice transcripts for repair sequences (retries, corrections, clarifications), system misattributions (treating the wrong prior turn as relevant) and failed adjacency pairs (responding to the wrong question). CA offers a principled vocabulary for diagnosing exactly where breakdowns occur, and Moore and Arar's Natural Conversation Framework operationalises CA patterns for conversational design.
steps: Collect real interaction transcripts or recordings, with consent.
Transcribe in CA detail where needed (timing, overlaps, pauses for voice).
Identify sequences: adjacency pairs, insertion sequences, repairs and closings.
Locate breakdowns: failed pairs, misattributions, repair loops and abandonment.
Build a collection of instances for each breakdown type.
Design conversational patterns (clarification, confirmation, repair) and re-analyse after release.
outputs: Annotated transcripts, breakdown collections, conversational pattern library.
useWhen: Chatbots, voice assistants, IVR, LLM chat interfaces, multi-turn agents.
avoidWhen: Non-conversational GUIs; use other evaluation methods.
whyLost: Requires specialist transcription and analysis skills; conversational UX revived but mostly with intent-accuracy metrics.
whereToUse: Customer service bots, LLM assistants, voice in cars, healthcare triage bots.
example: CA of 300 bank chatbot transcripts finds 22% of breakdowns occur when users answer the bot's question with a question; adding insertion-sequence handling halves escalations at that point.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Sacks H, Schegloff EA & Jefferson G (1974) A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language 50:696-735
Suchman L (1987) Plans and Situated Actions
Moore RJ & Arar R (2019) Conversational UX Design
reference: Sacks H, Schegloff EA & Jefferson G (1974) A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language 50(4):696-735.

name: Conversation Analysis for Chatbot Evaluation
origin: Sacks, Schegloff & Jefferson, 1974; applied by Erika Hall, 2018
summary: Analyses chatbot or voice assistant transcripts turn by turn using conversation analysis concepts such as adjacency pairs, repair and preference organisation.
description: Conversation analysis (CA) studies how people organise talk-in-interaction: turn-taking, adjacency pairs such as question and answer, repair of misunderstandings, and preference for certain responses over others. Applied to chatbots and voice assistants, CA examines real transcripts turn by turn to see where the system violates conversational expectations, for example by failing to recognise repair initiations, answering a question that was not asked, or producing dispreferred responses without mitigation. Because breakdowns are located precisely in the sequence, the findings map directly onto dialogue design changes. Rigour comes from systematic transcription, analysing sequences rather than isolated utterances, building collections of comparable cases, and checking interpretations against what the next turn reveals about how the user understood the system.
steps: Collect 50+ chatbot conversation transcripts. Code each turn for:
adjacency pair completion (does the bot's response constitute an appropriate second pair part?),
repair (does the bot handle user corrections?),

topic closure (does the conversation reach a coherent ending?). Compute violation rates per category. Target: adjacency pair completion > 85%, repair success > 70%. Violations are redesign priorities.
outputs: Annotated transcripts, a catalogue of breakdown types (failed repair, misaligned turns, dispreferred responses), frequency counts and design recommendations for dialogue flows.
useWhen: Evaluating chatbots, voice assistants and LLM-based agents where conversational breakdowns, not screen layouts, drive the experience.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need large-scale quantitative evaluation alone (use automated metrics and log analytics), or when transcripts are unavailable or cannot be ethically used.
whyLost: Conversation analysis is a demanding academic discipline; conversational UX grew fast from engineering, evaluated with intent accuracy and CSAT rather than interaction structure.
whereToUse: Chatbot and voice assistant UX, LLM interface evaluation, IVR system design, customer service bot testing.
example: A bank reviews 200 transcripts of its AI assistant and finds users repeatedly attempt self-repair ('no, I meant...') that the bot treats as new intents; adding repair handling cuts escalations by a fifth.
sources: Conversational Design — Erika Hall
reference: Sacks H, Schegloff EA & Jefferson G (1974) A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language 50(4):696-735

name: Conversational implicature audit
origin: H. P. Grice, 1975; Levinson's theory of generalised conversational implicature, 2000
summary: Identifies what users are likely to infer beyond the literal content of interface messages, checking for unintended implications that mislead decisions.
description: Implicature is meaning communicated beyond what is literally said, inferred from the assumption that the speaker is cooperative. 'Some of your files were backed up' implies not all; 'Your password was changed recently' may imply a security problem. Levinson identified generalised implicatures that arise by default, such as scalar inferences. Interfaces generate implicatures constantly, often unintended: an error message that blames a component implies the user did nothing wrong; a confirmation without a warning implies there are no consequences. An implicature audit lists each message's literal content and probable inferences, checks them against truth and intent, and tests with users. Rigour comes from eliciting inferences from users, not only expert judgement, and focusing on decision-relevant implications.
steps: Select messages that inform decisions: errors, warnings, status, confirmations, recommendations and AI answers.
For each, write the literal content and expert-predicted implicatures (scalar, relevance, manner-based).
Elicit actual inferences from 10-20 users with questions such as 'What does this tell you?' and 'What would you do next?'
Code inferences as intended, unintended but harmless, or unintended and harmful; flag any harmful inference held by more than 20% of users.
Rewrite to cancel harmful implicatures explicitly or change what is said.
Re-test rewritten messages with new participants.
outputs: A message inventory with literal content, intended and actual inferences, harmful implicature list, and rewrites.
useWhen: When messages influence safety, financial or health decisions; for AI outputs; when users act on misread messages.
avoidWhen: For simple, low-stakes messages where inference cannot cause harm; a style guide review is enough.
whyLost: Implicature is core pragmatics but UX writing focuses on clarity and tone, not on systematically checking what is implied.
whereToUse: Clinical alerts, banking notifications, security messages, AI assistants, and legal consent.
example: After a surgical robot error, the message 'Arm 2 recovered successfully' leads 60% of surgeons to infer the procedure can continue as normal, although calibration was lost. The message is revised to state recalibration is required.
sources: Gleason, J. B., The Development of Language
Hall, E., Conversational Design (2018)
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas (Gricean audit)
Development of Language (Gleason)
Conversational Design (Hall)
Methods Atlas — Gricean audit (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 18 — Pragmatics — What Language Actually Does
reference: Levinson, S. C. (2000). Presumptive Meanings: The Theory of Generalized Conversational Implicature. MIT Press.

name: Cooper-Harper Rating Scale
origin: George Cooper and Robert Harper, NASA, 1969 (NASA TN D-5153); modified for workload by Wierwille and Casali, 1983
summary: A decision-tree rating scale in which evaluators answer sequential yes/no questions about controllability and adequacy before assigning a 1-10 rating.
description: Cooper-Harper was designed for test pilots to rate aircraft handling qualities. Instead of asking for a number directly, the scale leads raters through a decision tree: Is it controllable? Is adequate performance attainable with tolerable workload? Is it satisfactory without improvement? Only then do they choose among three descriptors in the relevant branch. This anchoring produces highly consistent ratings and clear thresholds, with ratings of 4 and above indicating deficiencies that warrant improvement and 7 and above major deficiencies. The Modified Cooper-Harper version adapts it to cognitive workload for non-control tasks. The decision-tree structure is a valuable model for any UX rating that needs reliable, actionable categories.
steps: Define the task, performance standards (desired and adequate) and the conditions under which it is rated.
Have expert or trained raters perform the task under each design condition.
Administer the decision tree immediately after each trial, following the yes/no questions in order.
Record the final 1-10 rating and the rater's comments explaining deficiencies.
Compare designs by median rating and by the proportion of ratings falling in 'deficiency warrants improvement' (4-6) or 'major deficiencies' (7-9).
Use comments to diagnose the specific causes of poor ratings.
outputs: Anchored ratings per condition, proportions in each deficiency band, and qualitative diagnostic comments.
useWhen: Expert evaluation of control-intensive interactions (gestures, game controllers, drones, vehicle HMIs) where consistent go/no-go thresholds matter.
avoidWhen: General satisfaction or attitudinal research; use SUS or UEQ.
whyLost: It belongs to flight test culture and requires trained raters. UX favours numeric Likert scales without decision-tree anchoring.
whereToUse: Drone and robotics control apps, game controllers, in-car touch controls, accessibility switch control.
example: Evaluating a remote drone inspection app, trained pilots rate precision hover with on-screen sticks at 6 (moderate compensation required) and with physical controller at 3, justifying controller support.
sources: Cooper & Harper, The use of pilot rating in the evaluation of aircraft handling qualities (1969), NASA TN D-5153
Wierwille & Casali, A validated rating scale for global mental workload measurement applications (1983), Human Factors Society
reference: Cooper, G. E., & Harper, R. P. (1969). NASA Technical Note D-5153.

name: Corpus Keyness Analysis
origin: Mike Scott (WordSmith Tools, 1996-1997); Paul Rayson and Roger Garside (log-likelihood comparison, 2000); Paul Baker (Using Corpora in Discourse Analysis, 2006)
summary: Statistically compares word frequencies between a target corpus and a reference corpus to find words and collocations that are unusually frequent, revealing distinctive concerns.
description: Corpus linguistics provides robust statistics for comparing language across groups. Keyness compares each word's frequency in a target corpus (e.g. churned users' feedback) with a reference corpus (e.g. retained users' feedback) using log-likelihood or chi-square, with effect sizes such as log ratio. Collocation analysis (MI, t-score, log-Dice) shows which words co-occur, and concordance lines show words in context so interpretation stays grounded. Unlike word clouds or sentiment scores, keyness gives significance and effect size for differences and links back to actual utterances. It sits between qualitative reading and topic modelling, and works well with small to mid-size corpora.
steps: Assemble a target corpus and an appropriate reference corpus, with comparable text types.
Tokenise and lemmatise consistently; decide on handling of case and stop words.
Compute keyness (log-likelihood) and effect size (log ratio) for each word, applying minimum frequency and dispersion thresholds.
Examine collocates of key words and read concordance lines to interpret usage.
Group key words into semantic fields and relate them to user concerns.
Report keyness tables with statistics and illustrative concordances.
outputs: Ranked keyword lists with significance and effect sizes, collocation networks, concordances and interpreted semantic fields.
useWhen: Comparing feedback, reviews, tickets or interview transcripts across groups, versions or time.
avoidWhen: Very small text samples (a few interviews) where close reading suffices.
whyLost: UX text analysis jumped from manual coding to sentiment tools and topic models, skipping corpus linguistics' statistical comparison methods.
whereToUse: Churn feedback, app store reviews before and after releases, support chat logs, community forums.
example: Comparing reviews of the old and new app versions, keyness shows 'buried', 'hunt' and 'used to' as top keywords in the new corpus; concordances reveal frustration about relocated features.
sources: Baker, Using Corpora in Discourse Analysis (2006)
Rayson & Garside, Comparing corpora using frequency profiling (2000), Workshop on Comparing Corpora
Scott & Tribble, Textual Patterns: Key Words and Corpus Analysis in Language Education (2006)
reference: Baker, P. (2006). Using Corpora in Discourse Analysis. Continuum.

name: Correlation Analysis with Confidence Intervals
origin: Galton and Pearson (1890s); Fisher z transformation for intervals (1915)
summary: Measures how strongly two UX measures move together, with an interval showing how sure you can be.
description: Correlation quantifies association: does SUS track completion, does NPS rise with ease ratings, do two tasks share difficulty. Pearson r suits continuous measures, Spearman ranks suit skewed or ordinal data, and phi suits two binary variables. Sauro and Lewis emphasise reporting confidence intervals (via the Fisher z transformation) because small-sample correlations are very unstable: r = 0.5 from 20 people could plausibly be anywhere from about 0.07 to 0.77. They also give sample size formulas for detecting a correlation of a given size and benchmarks for magnitude in UX data.
steps: Plot the two variables in a scatterplot first to check for non-linearity and outliers.
Choose Pearson, Spearman or phi to fit the data types.
Compute r and its p-value.
Transform to Fisher z, form the interval and transform back.
Interpret magnitude in context and avoid causal language.
outputs: A correlation coefficient with its interval and significance.
useWhen: Checking whether metrics agree, validating questionnaires, exploring drivers before regression.
avoidWhen: You need to know cause or the effect of one variable holding others fixed (use experiments or regression).
whyLost: Commonly reported without intervals or scatterplots, so weak relationships from small samples get over-read.
whereToUse: Questionnaire validation, metrics programmes, survey analysis.
example: Across 30 tasks, SEQ and completion rate correlate at r = 0.62 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.80), supporting SEQ as a quick proxy.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Sauro & Lewis (2016), Quantifying the User Experience, chapter 10.

name: Counterfactual Probing
origin: Operationalised for UX in Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Interview probes asking participants to contrast before and after a change, or an alternative design, to explain the mechanism behind a measured effect.
description: Quantitative evidence can show that risk fell but not why. Counterfactual probing asks participants to reason about the alternative world: 'If we labelled it Price Alerts at top level, would you choose differently? Why?', or, after a change, how the old and new experiences differ. In the playbook, quotes such as 'Before, I always checked Notifications first' and 'Now Alerts is right where I expect it under Markets' explain the mechanism behind a hazard ratio of 0.68: fewer mistakes and better mental-model alignment. Responses are written into mechanism memos linking minimised QCA paths, quotes and HRs. Rigour comes from pairing probes with measured effects rather than relying on stated preference alone, since participants' counterfactual predictions are fallible.
steps: Identify the measured effect or design change whose mechanism needs explaining.
After the task, ask participants what they expected and whether an alternative label or structure would change their choice.
For post-change sessions, ask participants to contrast the old and new experience in their own words.
Code answers for mechanism (e.g. mental-model alignment, reduced time pressure, increased confidence).
Write mechanism memos linking codes to the quantitative effect.
Treat stated counterfactuals as supporting evidence, not proof, and confirm with behavioural data.
outputs: Mechanism quotes and memos explaining why a measured effect occurred.
useWhen: Alongside A/B or survival results, or in moderated sessions testing label or structure alternatives.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for behavioural evidence; people are poor predictors of their own future behaviour.
whyLost: Counterfactual reasoning is central to causal inference but rarely structured as an interview technique in UX.
whereToUse: IA and labelling changes, onboarding redesigns, pricing page changes, AI feature explanations.
example: After a relabelling lowers abandonment, participants say 'Now Alerts is right where I expect it', confirming the mental-model mechanism behind the hazard ratio.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Causal Inference
Counterfactuals (David Lewis)
The Book of Why (Pearl & Mackenzie)
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Section 4.4.

name: Cox Proportional Hazards Survival Analysis
origin: David R. Cox, 1972
summary: Models when users abandon or complete a task, estimating hazard ratios for design variants and covariates such as SNR and mistake rate rather than only whether they finish.
description: Survival analysis models time to an event while handling censoring. The Cox model, h(t|X) = h0(t)·exp(βX), leaves the baseline hazard unspecified and estimates hazard ratios (HR): the relative risk of the event per unit time. In Vivek Gopinath's playbook the event is abandonment of a task, and the model includes design variant, SNR and mistake rate: in a 600-participant prototype A/B, the new IA had HR 0.68 [0.59, 0.77] (32% lower abandonment risk), each +0.10 SNR HR 0.92, and each extra mistake per minute HR 1.28. The playbook stresses that reporting only completion rates ignores when users abandon, and that the proportional hazards assumption must be tested with Schoenfeld residuals. HRs become decision bars (HR ≤ 0.80) and are re-checked in production during validation (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.63–0.82).
steps: Define the event (abandonment) and time origin (task start), and log time to completion or abandonment per participant with censoring.
Choose covariates from earlier stages (variant, SNR, mistake rate, segment).
Fit h(t|X) = h0(t)·exp(β1·Variant + β2·SNR + β3·Mistake rate).
Report HRs with 95% CIs and p-values, interpreting HR < 1 as reduced risk.
Test the proportional hazards assumption with Schoenfeld residuals.
Compare HRs with the decision bar (e.g. HR ≤ 0.80) and re-estimate in production.
outputs: A hazard ratio table with intervals, survival curves per variant, and a verdict against the bar.
useWhen: When timing matters: when users drop off in a multi-step flow, onboarding or trial, not only whether.
avoidWhen: When there is no time-to-event structure or very few events; use logistic regression or descriptive funnels.
whyLost: Latent: survival analysis is standard in medicine and widely used in data science for churn, but it is almost absent from UX research literature and training, where retention is still reported as simple percentages that ignore censoring.
whereToUse: Onboarding, KYC, checkout, free-trial conversion, feature adoption timing.
example: A trading app's new IA cuts abandonment hazard by 32% (HR 0.68), and every extra mistake per minute raises it by 28%, supporting a bundled labelling and error-proofing fix.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation

name: CPM-GOMS
donor: Cognitive psychology and operations research (critical path method)
origin: Bonnie E. John, 1990; validated in Project Ernestine by Gray, John & Atwood, 1993
summary: A GOMS variant modelling skilled performance as parallel cognitive, perceptual and motor operators in a schedule chart, whose critical path predicts total task time for design alternatives.
description: GOMS analyses skilled performance in terms of Goals, Operators, Methods and Selection rules. Traditional GOMS treats perceptual, cognitive and motor activities as sequential; CPM-GOMS expresses tasks with parallel activities (listening to a customer while visually searching while typing) as a schedule chart. Each activity is a box with a duration, dependencies are lines between boxes, and the critical path, the longest dependent sequence, determines total task time. Large models are built from small building-block schedule charts for system response time, perception of sounds and visual information, conversation and hand movements, then used for what-if evaluation of alternative designs. In Project Ernestine it predicted that a new telephone operator workstation would be slower, saving an organisation millions of dollars. Vivek Gopinath's forward-thinking playbook uses it in Stage 1 with operator estimates of about 1.2s cognitive, 0.4s perceptual and 0.2–0.3s motor to set predicted-time benchmarks and decision bars.
steps: Decompose the task into goals and methods with a detailed understanding of the work.
Represent each perceptual, cognitive and motor operator as a box with an estimated duration (the playbook uses cognitive ≈ 1.2s, perceptual ≈ 0.4s, motor ≈ 0.2–0.3s).
Draw dependency lines between boxes using goal decomposition and operator-placement heuristics (e.g. the 'collect' key cannot be pressed until the word 'collect' is perceived and verified).
Assemble the full task model from building-block schedule charts for system response, perception, conversation and hand movements, using project management software.
Identify the critical path, the longest dependent sequence, which predicts total task time.
Run what-if evaluations by swapping building blocks for alternative designs and compare predicted times.
Set decision bars from the prediction (e.g. predicted ideal 6s; observed median > 15s indicates breakdown) and compare with observed data.
outputs: A schedule chart, critical path, predicted task time per design alternative, and benchmarks for later testing.
useWhen: Routine, skilled, high-frequency tasks with parallel activity where seconds matter (call centres, trading, data entry, operator consoles).
avoidWhen: Creative, exploratory or novice tasks where performance is not skilled and routine; use usability testing or cognitive walkthrough.
whyLost: Building models is laborious and requires cognitive psychology expertise; agile UX shifted to observe-first testing, leaving predictive modelling in academic niches.
whereToUse: Contact centre tooling, trading terminals, clinical order entry, logistics scanners, any flow where seconds translate to cost.
example: Before redesigning a trading app's alert creation, a researcher models scan, decide, move and type operators and predicts a 5.5–6.0s ideal, with two wrong tabs adding 6–10s, giving a benchmark for the tree test.

name: Crab Canon Walkthrough
origin: Adapted for UX from the 'Crab Canon' dialogue in Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), modelled on the crab canon in Bach's Musical Offering, which reads the same forwards and backwards
summary: Walk a flow backwards from its end state, checking at each step that the user can undo it, can tell where they are, and would make sense of the screen arriving from the other direction.
description: A crab canon is a piece of music that works played forwards or backwards. Hofstadter uses it, and a dialogue written the same way, to show structures that hold up when reversed. Most walkthroughs only go forwards, along the path designers intended, so they miss what happens when people change their mind, press back, cancel half-way or arrive at a middle step from a link or notification. The crab canon walkthrough starts at the end of a flow and moves backwards one step at a time. At each step the reviewer asks four questions: can this step be undone, and does undoing it restore what was there before; can the user tell what the previous step was; does the screen make sense if you arrive here from the step after it; and what happens to data entered on later steps. The result is a list of one-way doors and broken return paths that forward testing seldom finds.
steps: Choose a flow and write down its steps in forward order, including the end state.
Start at the end state and move back one step at a time, using the product's own back, cancel and undo controls where they exist.
At each step answer: can it be undone; does undo restore the previous state exactly; can the user tell where they came from; does the screen make sense when reached from the following step.
Record what happens to data entered later in the flow when the user goes back.
Mark one-way doors (steps that cannot be undone) and check each is intentional and clearly signalled before the user takes it.
Repeat with entry points in the middle of the flow, such as deep links and notifications.
outputs: A reversed step list with undo, orientation and data-loss findings for each step, and a register of one-way doors with whether each is signalled.
useWhen: Checkout, onboarding, booking and configuration flows; anything with irreversible actions; flows that users often abandon and return to.
avoidWhen: Single-screen tasks, or flows already covered by thorough exploratory testing of back and cancel paths.
whyLost: Cognitive walkthroughs and heuristic reviews follow the intended path forwards. 'User control and freedom' is a heuristic, but there is no standard procedure that systematically walks the reverse path.
whereToUse: E-commerce checkout, insurance and loan applications, account deletion, device setup, admin configuration.
example: Walking back from a booking confirmation shows that 'Back' from the payment step clears the passenger names, and that the seat map makes no sense when reached from a reminder email. Neither appeared in forward testing.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. Dialogue 'Crab Canon'.

name: CREAM (Cognitive Reliability and Error Analysis Method)
origin: Erik Hollnagel, 1998
summary: Assesses how working conditions set a person's control mode (scrambled, opportunistic, tactical, strategic) and uses this to predict or retrospectively explain cognitive failures.
description: CREAM is a second-generation HRA method that rejects context-free error probabilities. It uses nine Common Performance Conditions, including adequacy of the human-machine interface, available time, time of day, training and crew collaboration, rated as improving, not significant or reducing performance. The count of improving versus reducing conditions places the operator in one of four contextual control modes, each with an error probability interval. CREAM also offers a retrospective analysis with classification groups linking observed error modes (phenotypes) to causes (genotypes) through cause-consequence tables. For UX, it formalises the idea that the same interface yields very different reliability under different contexts, and it gives a structured way to analyse failures in terms of observation, interpretation, planning and execution.
steps: Describe the task and its context; perform a task analysis down to cognitive activities (observe, interpret, plan, execute).
Rate the nine Common Performance Conditions using field observation, interviews and log evidence.
Count improving and reducing conditions and determine the expected control mode from the CREAM diagram.
For predictive use, identify likely cognitive function failures per step and adjust estimates by control mode.
For retrospective use, trace observed error modes back through antecedent-consequent tables to plausible root causes.
Recommend design changes that shift conditions from reducing to improving, especially interface adequacy and time available.
outputs: Common Performance Condition profile, predicted control mode, error probability interval, and causal chains for observed errors.
useWhen: Tasks performed under highly variable conditions (night shifts, emergencies, mobile use on the move) where context dominates reliability.
avoidWhen: Lightweight consumer usability questions; use usability testing or heuristic evaluation.
whyLost: Developed for nuclear and process control, with a dense vocabulary of phenotypes and genotypes. UX rarely separates context-driven reliability from interface quality.
whereToUse: On-call incident tooling, emergency services dispatch, field service apps, clinical night-shift software.
example: An on-call alerting app is evaluated with CREAM for 3 a.m. pages. Most conditions are reducing, predicting an opportunistic control mode; the team simplifies the first-response screen to a single recommended action with a runbook link.
sources: Hollnagel, Cognitive Reliability and Error Analysis Method: CREAM (1998)
reference: Hollnagel, E. (1998). Cognitive Reliability and Error Analysis Method (CREAM). Elsevier.

name: Credibility audit
aka: Prolonged engagement, triangulation and member checking
origin: Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba, Naturalistic Inquiry (1985)
summary: Checks whether qualitative findings credibly represent participants' realities using prolonged engagement, persistent observation, triangulation, peer debriefing, negative case analysis and member checking.
description: Lincoln and Guba proposed credibility as the qualitative parallel to internal validity: confidence that findings are a plausible representation of participants' realities. They specified techniques: prolonged engagement (enough time to understand the culture and build trust), persistent observation (depth on the most relevant elements), triangulation across sources, methods, investigators and theories, peer debriefing, negative case analysis, referential adequacy and member checking with participants. A credibility audit applies these as a checklist with evidence, so that each finding's support is visible. Later critiques note that member checking can be problematic when participants disagree with analytical interpretations, so the audit treats participant feedback as data rather than a veto. Rigour lies in planning these techniques into the study design, not adding them after analysis.
steps: At design stage, plan which credibility techniques apply and their scale, for example at least 2 site visits per location, 3 data sources and 2 analysts.
Ensure prolonged engagement: spend enough time in context to see routine and exceptional days, and log time in the field.
Triangulate each key finding across at least two of: data sources (interviews, observation, logs, documents), methods, investigators and theoretical lenses, and record convergence or divergence.
Conduct negative case analysis: search for cases that contradict each finding and revise the finding until it accounts for them or explicitly bounds its scope.
Run peer debriefing with a researcher outside the project who challenges interpretations, logging questions and responses.
Member check by sharing synthesised findings (not transcripts) with 3 to 6 participants or community representatives, and record agreement, corrections and disagreements as additional data.
Produce a finding-by-technique matrix showing the credibility evidence for each major finding.
outputs: A credibility matrix linking each finding to triangulation, negative cases, peer debriefing and member-check evidence, plus field-time logs and revised findings.
useWhen: Qualitative findings will drive costly or high-stakes decisions, face sceptical stakeholders, or describe groups the team is distant from.
avoidWhen: Quick tactical studies where findings are low stakes and easily reversible; a lighter peer review is proportionate. Avoid member checking as validation of complex theoretical interpretations participants were never asked to hold.
whyLost: The trustworthiness criteria are standard in academic qualitative research but rarely enter industry UX, where speed is prioritised and credibility is asserted through quotes and video clips.
whereToUse: Healthcare and public-sector research, strategic discovery, research informing regulation or policy, multi-country studies.
example: A study claimed rural health workers distrusted sync. The audit triangulated interviews with sync logs and observations, found two negative cases at a clinic with reliable power, and narrowed the finding to 'distrust where outages had previously caused data loss', which member checks confirmed.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba) via Sage Handbook
Qualitative Research Ethics (Sage)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 27 — Lincoln & Guba — Trustworthiness in Qualitative Research
reference: Lincoln, Y. S., & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

name: Credibility Techniques (Lincoln and Guba)
origin: Yvonna Lincoln & Egon Guba, 1985 (Naturalistic Inquiry)
summary: A set of six techniques establishing that qualitative findings faithfully represent participants' realities: engagement, observation, triangulation, peer debriefing, negative cases and member checks.
description: Credibility is Lincoln and Guba's naturalistic counterpart to internal validity. Rather than claiming objectivity, it asks whether the researcher's reconstruction of participants' realities is plausible to them and defensible to others. Six techniques support it: prolonged engagement (enough time in context to learn culture and spot misinformation), persistent observation (depth on the most relevant elements), triangulation across methods, sources, investigators or theories, peer debriefing with an outsider who challenges interpretations, negative case analysis, and member checking. Each is planned in advance and documented so a reader can judge how far the findings can be trusted. Together they make qualitative trust an evidenced property rather than an assertion.
steps: Plan which credibility techniques the study will use and how they will be documented, before fieldwork begins.
Build prolonged engagement and persistent observation into the schedule, for example repeat visits or multi-day immersion rather than single sessions.
Triangulate at least two methods or sources for each major finding and record convergence and divergence.
Hold regular peer debriefs with a researcher outside the study and minute the challenges raised and how they were resolved.
Conduct negative case analysis on each emerging finding and member-check key interpretations with a diverse subsample.
Report the techniques used, their outcomes and their limits in the methods section.
outputs: A credibility plan and log: engagement time, triangulation matrix, peer debrief notes, negative case record and member-check outcomes.
useWhen: When qualitative findings will drive major decisions or be challenged, in regulated or public-sector contexts, and in academic-industry work.
avoidWhen: Rapid tactical usability rounds where findings are low-stakes and quickly retested; a light peer review suffices.
whyLost: Industry research reports rarely include methods sections, so trustworthiness criteria were reduced to the occasional mention of triangulation.
whereToUse: Health, government and financial services research; foundational studies feeding strategy; research quality frameworks in research operations.
example: A public-benefits portal team spends two weeks embedded in welfare offices, triangulates interviews with case-file review, and runs weekly peer debriefs. The credibility log lets policy leads accept a counterintuitive finding about form abandonment.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Research Ethics
Practice of Qualitative Research
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

extra.Six Credibility Techniques: Prolonged engagement: Spending sufficient time in the field to learn the culture, test for misinformation, and build trust. No prescribed duration — sufficient time is when you stop being surprised by what you see. Document your engagement time in methods reporting. Persistent observation: Identifying the characteristics and elements most relevant to the problem and focusing on them in depth. Breadth of observation is produced by prolonged engagement; depth by persistent observation of key elements. Triangulation: Using multiple methods, multiple sources, multiple investigators, or multiple theories to check the consistency of findings. Method triangulation (interview + observation + document analysis) is the most common. Note: triangulation does not require convergence — divergence is equally informative. Peer debriefing: Regular sessions with a peer who is outside the study. The peer's role: ask hard questions, probe for bias, challenge interpretations that seem too convenient. Document these sessions. Negative case analysis: Actively seeking and accounting for cases that disconfirm emerging findings. A study that reports no negative cases has not looked hard enough. Member checking: Systematically soliciting participants' feedback on the researcher's interpretation of their data. This is the most important credibility technique and the most commonly done poorly. See Method 25.

name: Crisp-Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (csQCA)
origin: Charles C. Ragin, 1987
summary: Set-theoretic analysis of small-N cases that identifies which combinations of binary conditions are sufficient or necessary for an outcome such as abandonment.
description: QCA treats cases as configurations of conditions and uses Boolean minimisation to find combinations sufficient for an outcome, reasoning with necessity and sufficiency rather than correlation. It suits small moderated samples where statistics are weak. In Vivek Gopinath's playbook, conditions are calibrated to binary membership (Low SNR = 1 if element SNR < 0.50; High Mistakes = 1 if ≥ 1/min; High TLX = 1 if frustration > 60; Timed OTP), a truth table is built from interview and usability cases, and minimisation (Quine-McCluskey, e.g. the QCA package in R) yields solutions such as Low SNR * High Mistakes ⇒ Abandon. A light necessity check asks whether Low SNR appears in nearly all abandonment cases; if so it becomes a hard guardrail (element SNR ≥ 0.60). Sufficient paths are used to bundle prescriptions and the truth table is rebuilt on a fresh sample during validation.
steps: Choose the outcome (e.g. Abandon) and 3–5 candidate conditions from earlier evidence.
Calibrate each condition to crisp membership with explicit thresholds (Low SNR if element SNR < 0.50; High Mistakes if ≥ 1/min; High TLX if frustration > 60).
Build a truth table with one row per case from interviews and usability sessions.
Minimise configurations with Quine-McCluskey or QCA software to derive sufficient paths.
Run a necessity check on key conditions.
Link solutions to quotes and hazard ratios in mechanism memos, bundle fixes accordingly, and re-run on a fresh sample after the fix.
outputs: Minimised sufficient paths, necessity results and mechanism memos.
useWhen: Small-N studies (10–40 cases) where you suspect conjunctural causation: failure needs several conditions together.
avoidWhen: Large samples where regression is feasible, or when conditions cannot be calibrated meaningfully.
whyLost: Established in comparative social science but almost unknown in UX, where small-N work is treated as purely descriptive.
whereToUse: Moderated usability studies, enterprise deployments with few accounts, B2B churn case reviews, service design pilots.
example: Across usability cases, QCA shows Low SNR combined with High Mistakes is sufficient for abandonment, so the team ships labelling and clutter reduction together rather than one alone.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Ragin, C. C. (1987). The Comparative Method: Moving Beyond Qualitative and Quantitative Strategies. University of California Press.

name: Critical Incident Technique
origin: John C. Flanagan, 1954
summary: Collects detailed accounts of specific events that were exceptionally good or bad, then classifies them to reveal what determines success or failure in an experience.
description: The Critical Incident Technique, developed by John Flanagan from aviation psychology work during the Second World War, collects detailed accounts of specific incidents in which behaviour or experience was notably effective or ineffective. Asking about concrete events rather than general opinions reduces vague answers and gives behaviourally specific data. Each incident is captured with its situation, actions, outcome and feelings, and incidents are then content-analysed and classified into categories that reveal the critical factors driving good and bad experiences. In UX, CIT works in interviews, surveys and diaries, and in reviews of support data. Rigour comes from a clear definition of what counts as critical, structured probes for each incident, collecting enough incidents for categories to stabilise (often 50 to 100 or more), and checking classification reliability.
steps: Define "critical": Incidents that were either significantly more positive or more negative than the participant's baseline expectation. Not typical experiences — threshold-crossing events.

Collection: "Think about the last [time period]. Tell me about a time when using [product] was particularly [difficult / helpful / frustrating / satisfying]." The temporal framing matters — recent incidents are more accessible and more accurately recalled.
Structured probe: For each incident: (a) What was the situation? (b) What did you do? (c) What was the outcome? (d) How did you feel? (e) What would you have done differently?

Diary integration: Deploy CIT as a diary trigger: "Tonight, if you had an experience with [product] that you would call particularly [good/bad], write it down using this template." This captures incidents in near-real-time rather than in retrospective interviews.

Analysis: Code incidents for: type of event, trigger, participant action, outcome, and emotional response. Frequency analysis: which types of critical incidents are most common? Impact analysis: which types have the largest effect on overall satisfaction?
outputs: A categorised set of positive and negative incidents with frequencies, critical factors driving experience, and impact estimates on satisfaction.
useWhen: When you need concrete, behaviourally specific evidence of what makes experiences succeed or fail, for error analysis, service quality or rare but important events.
avoidWhen: Avoid for routine, unremarkable behaviour, which participants do not remember as incidents; use observation, diaries or analytics.
whyLost: Renamed: the term itself has faded in UX, but the method lives on as 'tell me about the last time...' interviewing, incident-triggered diaries and structured story collection, usually without Flanagan's classification and reliability steps.
whereToUse: Error analysis; training design; understanding exceptional and problematic use cases.
example: A health insurer collects 120 critical incidents about claims from interviews and diaries. Negative incidents cluster around 'no status update after submission', which becomes the top fix ahead of form redesign.

name: Cronbach's α and McDonald's ω
origin: Lee Cronbach, 1951; Roderick McDonald, 1970/1999
summary: Coefficients estimating how consistently a set of items measures one construct; omega is the modern, less restrictive alternative to alpha.
description: Cronbach's alpha estimates reliability from item inter-correlations, but assumes all items contribute equally to the construct (tau-equivalence) and a single factor, which rarely holds; when violated it typically underestimates reliability, and it rises simply with more items. McDonald's omega uses factor loadings from a fitted model, allowing items to differ in strength, and omega hierarchical indicates how much variance is due to a general factor in multidimensional scales. Rigour means checking unidimensionality before computing either, reporting omega (with alpha for comparability), reporting confidence intervals, and not treating high values as proof of validity. Values above 0.95 often signal redundant items.
steps: Confirm the scale or subscale is unidimensional with a factor analysis before computing reliability.
Compute omega total from a one-factor model and alpha for comparison, each with 95% confidence intervals (e.g. via pingouin or psych).
Interpret values: 0.70 is a minimum for group research, 0.80 or above is good, and above 0.90 is needed for individual-level decisions.
Inspect item-total correlations (flag below 0.3) and alpha-if-item-deleted to find weak items.
For multidimensional scales, compute omega hierarchical and subscale omegas rather than a single overall alpha.
outputs: Reliability coefficients with intervals for each scale and subscale, item diagnostics and recommendations on item removal.
useWhen: Whenever a multi-item scale score is used, including adopting an existing questionnaire in a new context.
avoidWhen: Avoid for single-item measures, formative indices (where items need not correlate), or as a substitute for validity evidence.
whyLost: Alpha is reported routinely and uncritically as a stamp of quality; omega and the assumptions behind alpha are seldom understood in UX.
whereToUse: Survey programmes, benchmark questionnaires, trust and satisfaction indices, academic-industry studies.
example: A team's 6-item trust subscale has alpha 0.71 but omega 0.79 because one item loads weakly; removing the item raises omega to 0.83 and sharpens the scale's correlation with retention.

name: Cross-Case Analysis
origin: Robert Yin, 1984 (Case Study Research); Miles & Huberman, 1984
summary: Comparing fully analysed cases on theoretically motivated dimensions to find patterns, explanations and scope conditions that transcend individual cases.
description: Cross-case analysis compares multiple participants, sites or accounts after each has been analysed in its own right. Premature comparison flattens within-case detail, so within-case analysis comes first. The analyst then defines comparison dimensions grounded in theory or the research question, rather than comparing everything with everything, and looks for informative contrasts: similar cases with different outcomes, and different cases with the same outcome. Yin's pattern matching and replication logic treat each case like an experiment that should confirm or contradict a proposition. The result is an explanation of the pattern plus scope conditions stating where it holds. Displays such as case-ordered matrices make the comparison transparent.
steps: Within-case analysis first: Fully analyse each case before cross-case comparison. Premature cross-case comparison collapses important within-case variation.
Define comparison dimensions: Theoretically motivated dimensions — not everything versus everything.
Pattern matching: Similar cases producing different outcomes, or different cases producing the same outcome — these are the analytically richest comparisons.
Build the explanation: What explains the pattern of similarities and differences? This is your theoretical contribution.
Specify scope conditions: For what types of cases does this pattern hold? This is the boundary of your theory.
outputs: Within-case summaries, cross-case comparison matrices, explanatory propositions, and scope conditions.
useWhen: Multi-site, multi-account or multi-segment studies where you need to explain why outcomes differ across cases.
avoidWhen: Single-case deep dives or when cases are too few and too similar to compare; use within-case analysis or IPA.
whyLost: Synthesis in UX often pools all data into one affinity wall, losing case boundaries and the comparative logic.
whereToUse: Enterprise customer studies, multi-country research, service evaluations across locations, and B2B churn or success analyses.
example: Comparing eight hospitals adopting an e-prescribing system, two similar hospitals show opposite outcomes. Cross-case analysis attributes the difference to whether pharmacists were involved in configuration.
sources: Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
