name: Cross-Cultural Survey Equivalence Testing
origin: Harkness, 2003 (TRAPD); Vandenberg & Lance, 2000 (invariance)
summary: Ensures a UX survey measures the same constructs in the same way across languages and cultures, through team translation and measurement invariance testing.
description: Cross-cultural survey equivalence testing addresses whether scores from different language or cultural groups can be compared. It has two parts. First, translation and adaptation follow a team approach such as TRAPD (translation, review, adjudication, pretesting, documentation), with cognitive interviews in each locale to check that items are understood as intended. Second, multi-group confirmatory factor analysis tests measurement invariance in steps: configural (same factor structure), metric (equal loadings, allowing comparison of relationships) and scalar (equal intercepts, allowing comparison of means). Partial invariance can sometimes be accepted with justification. Rigour comes from documenting adaptation decisions, adequate samples per group, and limiting claims to the level of invariance achieved.
steps: International UX survey protocol:
Translation: forward translation, back-translation, cognitive interview in each language.
(2) Functional equivalence: focus groups in each culture to confirm the construct is relevant.
(3) Metric equivalence: run measurement invariance testing (configural → metric → scalar CFA) before computing cross-cultural means.
(4) If scalar invariance fails: report country-specific results separately, do not aggregate.
(5) Use MACS (mean and covariance structures) analysis to identify which items lack equivalence.
outputs: Translated instruments with documented adaptation decisions, invariance test results (configural, metric, scalar), and a judgement on which cross-country comparisons are valid.
useWhen: Global products comparing satisfaction, trust or usability scores across markets; multilingual benchmarking; and instruments launched in new regions.
avoidWhen: Avoid comparing scores across countries without it; when invariance fails, compare within-country patterns or use qualitative research instead.
whyLost: Global UX teams machine-translate surveys and compare means directly; equivalence testing lives in cross-cultural psychology and international survey programmes.
whereToUse: International UX benchmark programs, global product research, multi-country satisfaction surveys.
example: A ride-hailing app compares trust scores across Japan, Brazil and Germany; scalar invariance fails for one item because 'reliable' translates differently, so comparisons use a reduced set of invariant items.
sources: International Handbook of Survey Methodology — (various)
reference: Harkness JA, van de Vijver FJR & Mohler PPh (Eds.) (2003) Cross-Cultural Survey Methods. Wiley

name: Cross-Cultural UX Research
origin: Cross-cultural usability work by Nielsen, del Galdo and Fernandes in the 1990s; methods consolidated by Quesenbery and Szuc (Global UX, 2011)
summary: Planning, running and interpreting research across cultures so that instruments, moderation and analysis are equivalent, and culture-specific behaviours and signs are correctly read.
description: Cross-cultural UX research adapts the whole research process for multiple cultural contexts. Instruments must achieve conceptual and linguistic equivalence through translation and back-translation, not literal word swaps. Moderation styles must account for differences in politeness norms, criticism avoidance and the effect of the moderator's status, which can mask problems in think-aloud sessions. Local researchers or cultural brokers help recruit, moderate and interpret. A related technique is the cross-cultural sign audit, which tests whether icons, colours, metaphors and gestures carry the intended meaning in each locale. Rigour comes from piloting instruments in every locale, using same-culture moderators where possible, checking response-style biases (such as acquiescence or extreme responding) before comparing scores, and analysing findings jointly with local team members.
steps: Define which comparisons matter and whether you need cross-locale comparability or deep local understanding.
Partner with local researchers or cultural brokers in each market for recruitment, moderation and interpretation.
Translate instruments with forward and back-translation, cognitively pretest them with 3-5 participants per locale, and adapt examples.
Adjust moderation: use same-culture moderators, indirect probing where direct criticism is unusual, and suitable session settings.
Run a sign and icon audit testing whether key symbols, colours and metaphors are interpreted as intended in each locale.
Check survey data for response-style differences before comparing means, and analyse qualitative data jointly with local partners.
outputs: Locale-validated instruments, culture-specific findings and shared patterns, sign-failure inventory and market-specific design recommendations.
useWhen: Launching or adapting products in new markets, global products with diverse user bases, and comparative studies across regions.
avoidWhen: When you only need to check translation and formatting (use localization testing) or when comparisons across cultures are not needed for the decision.
whyLost: Still in use: Critical for global products; growing body of methodology.
whereToUse: Global product teams; market entry research; localisation validation.
example: A payments app expanding to India and Indonesia finds rural users interpret the trash-can icon as 'save for later' and that participants in moderated sessions praise designs they later abandon. Switching to local moderators and a text label surfaces the real issues.

Usability and Internationalization
Pocket Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
Embodied Mind (Varela)
Global UX: Design and Research in a Connected World (Whitney Quesenbery & Daniel Szuc)
Usability and Internationalization of Information Technology (Nuray Aykin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 20 — Semiotics, Icons & Cross-Cultural Sign Failure

name: Cross-Domain Borrowing Matrix
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Maps each donor discipline to the UX problem it addresses, its key methods, the transfer mechanism and the main training barrier to adoption.
description: Appendix C of the extended treatise maps 13 donor disciplines (epidemiology, econometrics, cognitive science, linguistics, social science, machine learning, statistics, psychophysics, systems engineering, clinical research, anthropology, philosophy, network science) against the UX problem addressed, key methods, transfer mechanism and training barrier. Transfer mechanisms are classified as direct transplant, direct structural transplant, conceptual reframe, measurement upgrade or level-of-analysis shift. For example, econometrics addresses quasi-experimental causal inference via DiD, RDD, IV and PSM by direct transplant, with econometrics training as the barrier; network science addresses system-level dynamics by a level-of-analysis shift. The matrix turns 'borrow from other fields' into a structured adoption plan.
steps: Identify the UX problem class you cannot address well with current methods.
Locate donor disciplines that solve structurally equivalent problems.
List candidate methods and classify the transfer mechanism.
Identify the training barrier and the collaborators or courses that would remove it.
Pilot one method on a real question with a donor-discipline expert.
Document adaptations and add the method to the team's library.
outputs: Borrowing matrix tailored to the organisation, pilot plans, adaptation notes.
useWhen: Expanding a research team's methodological range; curriculum and hiring plans.
avoidWhen: When existing UX methods already answer the question well.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: Research strategy, cross-functional collaboration with data science, academic partnerships.
example: A research lead uses the matrix to pair UX researchers with economists on DiD analyses of regional launches, with a short training to cross the barrier.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Lost Methods in UX treatise, Appendix C
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Appendix C (The Cross-Domain Borrowing Matrix).

name: Cross-Impact Analysis
donor: Futures research (RAND and Institute for the Future)
origin: Theodore Gordon and Olaf Helmer, 1966 (Kaiser Aluminum 'Future' game); cross-impact balances by Wolfgang Weimer-Jehle (2006)
summary: Systematically assesses how the occurrence of one future event or trend changes the likelihood of others, producing consistent scenarios from interacting factors.
description: Delphi gives independent estimates for future events, but events interact. Cross-impact analysis builds a matrix in which experts judge how each event's occurrence would change the probability of each other event. Monte Carlo simulation then generates consistent scenario sets and adjusted probabilities. Cross-impact balance analysis (CIB) uses qualitative influence judgements between descriptor states to find internally consistent scenarios. For product strategy, it structures how trends such as regulation, AI capability, user trust and competitor moves interact, producing scenarios that are consistent rather than arbitrary combinations.
steps: Select key events or descriptors (e.g. regulation passes, AI cost falls, trust scandal occurs) with defined states.
Estimate initial probabilities or state plausibilities with experts (e.g. via Delphi).
Fill the cross-impact matrix: how each event or state influences each other one.
Run Monte Carlo simulation (probabilistic CIA) or consistency analysis (CIB) to derive scenarios.
Review resulting scenarios for plausibility and robustness.
Use scenarios to stress-test product strategy and research priorities.
outputs: Cross-impact matrix, adjusted probabilities, consistent scenario sets and strategy stress tests.
useWhen: Strategic planning with multiple interacting uncertainties.
avoidWhen: Few uncertainties or short horizons; simple scenario 2x2s may suffice.
whyLost: It is a specialist futures method; product strategy uses informal scenario discussions.
whereToUse: AI product strategy, fintech regulation, healthcare policy, platform ecosystems.
example: A health AI firm uses CIB with 8 descriptors; consistent scenarios show that strict liability regulation combined with clinician shortages favours assistive over autonomous products, reshaping roadmap bets.
sources: Gordon & Hayward, Initial experiments with the cross impact matrix method of forecasting (1968), Futures
Weimer-Jehle, Cross-impact balances: A system-theoretical approach to cross-impact analysis (2006), Technological Forecasting and Social Change
Gordon, Cross-impact method (2009), Futures Research Methodology 3.0
reference: Weimer-Jehle, W. (2006). Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 73(4), 334-361.

name: Cross-modal interference measurement
origin: Multisensory interference paradigms (for example McGurk and MacDonald, 1976; crossmodal Stroop tasks); applied in human factors by Wickens and Spence
summary: Measures performance costs when information arrives through two senses at once, revealing when audio, visual and haptic channels help or hinder each other.
description: Multiple resource theory predicts less interference across modalities, but cross-modal interference still occurs, especially when signals conflict in meaning or spatial location, compete for central processing, or capture attention involuntarily (auditory onsets are particularly hard to ignore). Spence and colleagues showed spatial co-location of cues across modalities improves performance while mismatched locations impair it. Measurement uses controlled paradigms in which participants perform a primary task in one modality while signals arrive in another under congruent, incongruent and neutral conditions, recording response time and error costs. In UX this answers practical questions such as whether spoken alerts disrupt reading or whether haptic feedback conflicts with visual cues.
steps: Define the primary task and modality and the secondary signals in other modalities.
Construct congruent, incongruent and neutral conditions (for example spoken 'left' with a left versus right visual cue; co-located versus separated sound sources).
Run a within-subjects study with 16-24 participants, counterbalanced, with at least 30 trials per condition.
Compute interference cost as performance in incongruent minus congruent or neutral conditions for response time and accuracy.
Test whether costs exceed acceptable limits (for example more than 100 ms or a 5% error increase on safety-critical responses).
Adjust timing, spatial location or content of cross-modal signals and re-test.
outputs: Interference costs per condition, response time and accuracy comparisons, and design rules for combining modalities.
useWhen: When adding sound, voice or haptic channels to visual interfaces, designing alerts in multitasking contexts, or building AR/VR.
avoidWhen: When tasks are not concurrent; use a single-modality usability test.
whyLost: Cross-modal research is extensive in psychology but UX designers add sound and haptics by intuition and do not measure interference.
whereToUse: Automotive HMIs, surgical consoles, wearables, AR glasses, and voice assistants combined with screens.
example: A surgical robot plays spoken instrument names while showing icons. When the spoken and displayed instruments differ, response time increases by 240 ms and errors double, so the voice channel is restricted to alerts that confirm the visual cue.
sources: Salvendy, G. (ed.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Handbook of Human Factors & Ergonomics (Salvendy)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 12 — Multiple Resource Theory — The Bandwidth of the Human
reference: Spence, C. & Driver, J. (Eds.) (2004). Crossmodal Space and Crossmodal Attention. Oxford University Press.

name: Cross-Tabulation of UX Metrics
origin: Pearson (1904) contingency tables; staple of market research tabulation
summary: Breaks metrics down by participant groups in a table to see where experiences differ.
description: Cross-tabulation lays one variable against another, for example task success by device, or NPS category by customer tenure, to show how outcomes vary across segments. It is the first step in "why" analysis for benchmarks. Sauro advises collapsing sparse categories (such as merging 7-point responses into top-box and the rest) so cells have enough data, then testing differences with chi-square or N-1 tests. Done carelessly, slicing by many variables generates false positives, so pre-planned comparisons and multiple-comparison corrections matter.
steps: Choose the outcome and the grouping variables you planned to examine.
Collapse sparse categories so each cell has adequate counts.
Build tables with row or column percentages as appropriate.
Test differences with chi-square, N-1 or Fisher tests, correcting for multiple comparisons.
Present only meaningful splits, with counts shown.
outputs: Tables showing which groups differ on key metrics.
useWhen: Exploring differences across devices, segments, tenure or regions in survey and benchmark data.
avoidWhen: Small samples sliced many ways, which manufactures spurious findings.
whyLost: Not lost, but rarely done with significance testing and multiplicity control in UX reporting.
whereToUse: Benchmark reports, survey analysis, analytics segment reviews.
example: Task success on a tablet is 22 points lower than on desktop, significant after correction, prompting a tablet-specific review.

name: Cross-volume method chaining (DSRP to ethnography to DAG to SEM to GMM)
donor: Mixed-methods research design; systems thinking; causal inference; psychometrics; machine learning
origin: Vivek Gopinath, The Inquiry Series, building on Cabrera's DSRP, Pearl's DAGs and latent-variable modelling
summary: A deliberate sequence in which each method's output becomes the next method's input, moving from systems framing to ethnographic mechanism to causal graph, measurement model and segmentation.
description: Method chaining makes the hand-offs between methods explicit and testable. DSRP (Distinctions, Systems, Relationships, Perspectives) frames the problem space and surfaces candidate constructs. Ethnography grounds those constructs in observed practice and mechanisms. The mechanisms are formalised as a directed acyclic graph that states which variables cause which, and which are confounders. The DAG's latent constructs are then measured with a validated survey and estimated in a structural equation model, and the resulting factor scores or behavioural features feed a Gaussian mixture model that segments users probabilistically. The rigour lies in traceability: every SEM path should trace back to an ethnographic observation, every segment should be interpretable through the SEM constructs, and each link carries its own validity check rather than inheriting confidence from the previous stage.
steps: Map the problem with DSRP, listing distinctions, part-whole systems, relationships and stakeholder perspectives, and extract 5-12 candidate constructs.
Run ethnographic fieldwork (typically 10-20 participants) to confirm, discard or refine each construct and to describe causal mechanisms in participants' terms.
Translate mechanisms into a DAG, mark confounders, mediators and colliders, and check it with domain experts before measurement.
Develop or adopt multi-item scales (at least 3 items per construct) and collect survey data large enough for SEM (commonly N of 200 or more).
Fit a CFA then SEM, accepting the measurement model only at acceptable fit (e.g. CFI of 0.95 or above, RMSEA of 0.06 or below, SRMR of 0.08 or below).
Fit GMMs on factor scores or behavioural features, choose the number of components by BIC and interpretability, and require each segment to be at least about 5% of the sample.
Write a traceability matrix linking each segment and path back to field evidence, and flag links supported by only one stage.
outputs: A construct inventory, field-grounded mechanism descriptions, a validated DAG, a fitted measurement and structural model, probabilistic user segments and a traceability matrix.
useWhen: When a programme must move from an ill-defined problem to quantified, segment-level decisions while keeping qualitative grounding, and when the team has the skills and sample to support SEM and mixture modelling.
avoidWhen: Avoid when samples are small (under about 200), when constructs are already well established, or when a simple experiment can answer the question directly; then use a focused A/B test or a single validated survey.
whyLost: An original integrative framework; in most organisations these methods sit in different teams (qual researchers, data scientists, survey specialists), so the hand-offs are never designed.
whereToUse: Fintech segmentation, health behaviour programmes, B2B SaaS adoption strategy, and any product where personas need to be both statistically defensible and ethnographically grounded.
example: An investment app maps the trust problem with DSRP, observes 16 investors at home, and finds that perceived control mediates trust. A DAG and SEM on 600 survey responses confirm the path, and GMM on factor scores yields four trust segments that drive differentiated onboarding.
sources: Forward-Thinking Playbook (Gopinath)

name: Cultural Consensus Analysis
origin: A. Kimball Romney, Susan Weller and William Batchelder, 1986
summary: Estimates whether a group shares a single body of knowledge, each person's competence in it, and the culturally correct answers, without knowing the answers in advance.
description: The cultural consensus model treats agreement among informants as evidence of shared knowledge. Factor analysis of the respondent-by-respondent agreement matrix tests whether a single dominant factor exists (first-to-second eigenvalue ratio above about 3), estimates each informant's cultural competence, and weights their answers to derive the 'culturally correct' answer key. Residual agreement analysis reveals subcultures. In UX, consensus analysis tells you whether a user group shares a mental model or vocabulary (e.g. what counts as 'urgent'), who the most knowledgeable informants are, and whether different groups hold different models, all with modest samples of 20-30.
steps: Develop items about the domain (true/false, multiple choice, or rankings), often derived from free lists or interviews.
Administer to informants from the target group(s).
Compute the agreement matrix corrected for guessing and factor it (e.g. with UCINET or the CCTpack/AnthroTools packages).
Check the eigenvalue ratio for a single culture and that competences are positive.
Estimate the culturally correct answers and informant competences; examine residuals for subgroups.
Use results to define shared models for design and to select expert informants for deeper interviews.
outputs: Evidence for or against shared knowledge, competence scores, consensus answer key and subgroup patterns.
useWhen: Checking whether users share a mental model, vocabulary or norms before designing for 'the user'.
avoidWhen: Preference or attitude questions where there is no 'correct' cultural answer to estimate.
whyLost: It is known only in anthropology and some public health research; UX assumes or asserts shared models.
whereToUse: Clinical terminology, enterprise workflows across sites, community norms on platforms, financial literacy.
example: Consensus analysis of nurses' triage priority judgements finds two subcultures (ICU and ward nurses) with different answer keys, so the alerting tool supports configurable priorities per unit.
sources: Romney, Weller & Batchelder, Culture as consensus: A theory of culture and informant accuracy (1986), American Anthropologist
Weller, Cultural consensus theory: Applications and frequently asked questions (2007), Field Methods
reference: Romney, A. K., Weller, S. C., & Batchelder, W. H. (1986). American Anthropologist, 88(2), 313-338.

name: Cultural Dimension Analysis for Global UX
origin: Geert Hofstede, 1980/2001; Quesenbery & Szuc, 2011
summary: Uses cultural dimension frameworks (e.g. power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance) to form hypotheses about how design should differ across markets, then tests them.
description: Cultural dimension analysis draws on frameworks such as Hofstede's (power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity, long-term orientation, indulgence), and alternatives by Hall, Trompenaars or the GLOBE project, to anticipate how expectations about authority, information density, social proof, trust and risk might differ across markets. As championed in Global UX by Quesenbery and Szuc, the rigorous use is as a hypothesis generator: dimension scores suggest where design assumptions may not travel, and local research then tests those hypotheses with real users. The method guards against ecological fallacy by never applying national averages to individuals and by attending to within-country diversity, generational change and domain-specific behaviour.
steps: Cultural dimension audit for international product design:
For each target market, look up Hofstede scores (hofstede-insights.com).
(2) High power distance → users expect explicit hierarchical authority signals; formal language; deferential interface tone.
(3) High uncertainty avoidance → users prefer explicit instructions, fewer choices, more confirmation steps, warnings about irreversible actions.
(4) Individualism → 'you' framing; Collectivism → 'we' framing and social proof. Test: do survey ratings or A/B test results differ by Hofstede score?
outputs: Market profiles on cultural dimensions, design hypotheses per market, and research plans to validate or refute them locally.
useWhen: Planning research and localisation for global products, entering new markets, and explaining market differences in metrics.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating national scores as descriptions of individuals or as conclusions; they are coarse hypotheses. Use local field research for actual design decisions.
whyLost: Hofstede's framework was popular in early-2000s HCI but criticised for stereotyping; teams abandoned it rather than using it carefully as a hypothesis generator.
whereToUse: International product design, localization research, cross-cultural UX research design.
example: A health insurer entering Japan hypothesises that high uncertainty avoidance favours detailed policy explanations; local testing confirms it for claims, but not for onboarding, where brevity wins.
sources: Global UX — Quesenbery & Szuc
reference: Hofstede G (2001) Culture's Consequences: Comparing Values, Behaviors, Institutions and Organizations Across Nations. 2nd ed. Sage

name: Cultural Dimensions Analysis
origin: Geert Hofstede (Culture's Consequences, 1980); Fons Trompenaars (1993); applied to web design by Aaron Marcus and Emilie Gould (2000)
summary: Using national cultural dimensions such as power distance, individualism and uncertainty avoidance to generate hypotheses about how design should differ between markets.
description: Cultural dimensions analysis applies frameworks such as Hofstede's six dimensions (power distance, individualism, masculinity, uncertainty avoidance, long-term orientation, indulgence) or Trompenaars' seven to anticipate how users in different markets may respond to design choices. For instance, high uncertainty-avoidance cultures may want more explicit guidance and reassurance, and high power-distance cultures may respond to authority cues. Used rigorously, dimension scores are hypothesis generators, not conclusions: they describe national averages, are partly dated, and can stereotype individuals. Good practice uses the dimensions to design specific comparative studies, measures individual-level cultural values within the actual user sample, and checks whether predicted differences appear in behaviour. Marcus and Gould showed how website conventions vary along these dimensions, but few teams follow through with empirical validation.
steps: Select the markets to compare and retrieve dimension scores for each from published sources.
Identify design decisions plausibly sensitive to the dimensions with the largest gaps (for example onboarding guidance and uncertainty avoidance).
Write explicit, testable hypotheses linking each dimension gap to an expected difference in preference or behaviour.
Measure individual-level values in your own sample with a validated short scale rather than assuming national scores apply.
Test the hypotheses with comparative studies such as A/B tests per market or matched usability sessions.
Report which predicted differences held, which did not, and avoid generalising to individuals.
outputs: Dimension gap profile across markets, testable design hypotheses, individual-level value measures and validated or refuted localisation decisions.
useWhen: Early planning for multi-market products to decide where localisation beyond language may matter and what to test.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for research with actual users in each market; never use national scores to stereotype individuals or justify untested design changes.
whyLost: Popular in international business, it was criticised for essentialism and remains rarely used rigorously in UX beyond localisation checklists.
whereToUse: Global product design; localization strategy; international IA.
example: An e-commerce platform entering Japan and Germany hypothesises that high uncertainty avoidance calls for more detailed return policies at checkout. A market-level A/B test confirms a 6% conversion lift in Japan but none in Germany.

Culture's Consequences (Geert Hofstede)
Marcus & Gould, Crosscurrents: cultural dimensions and global web user-interface design (Interactions, 2000)
Global UX (Quesenbery & Szuc)
Handbook of Ethnography

extra.The Six Dimensions Applied to UX: Power Distance: High PD cultures expect authority and hierarchy to be visible. Low PD cultures prefer egalitarian interfaces. Research implication: in high PD contexts, interfaces that position the system as an expert or authority may be trusted more; peer-recommendation features work better in low PD contexts. Individualism vs. Collectivism: Individualist cultures: personal benefit, privacy, individual control. Collectivist cultures: group benefit, shared visibility, social approval. Research implication: sharing features, privacy controls, and default settings should differ by cultural context. Uncertainty Avoidance: High UA cultures: prefer explicit rules, formal processes, complete information before action. Low UA cultures: comfortable with ambiguity and experimentation. Research implication: onboarding, help systems, and error messages should be more comprehensive in high UA contexts. Long-term vs. Short-term Orientation: Long-term: patience, persistence, investment in the future. Short-term: tradition, social obligation, quick results. Research implication: progress indication, savings features, and reward systems should calibrate to temporal orientation.

name: Cultural Probes
donor: Interaction design and critical design (Royal College of Art)
origin: William Gaver, Anthony Dunne and Elena Pacenti, 1999
summary: Deliberately ambiguous kits of cameras, postcards, maps and diaries that provoke participants' self-documentation, yielding inspiration for design rather than comparable data.
description: Cultural probes (Gaver, Dunne & Pacenti, 1999) are deliberately incomplete research instruments — packages of materials given to participants that are designed to be provocative and ambiguous rather than systematic. Unlike diary studies, probes are not designed to collect comparable data across participants. They are designed to evoke unexpected, personal, and creative responses that inspire designers rather than generate findings. Probes are a research inspiration tool, not an analysis tool.
steps: Define the inspirational territory you want to open up (not hypotheses to test) and the population, often one hard to observe directly.
Design a probe kit of 5-8 open-ended items, such as a disposable camera with 10-15 printed prompts, a map to annotate, postcards with provocative questions and a small diary.
Make the materials crafted and personal so participants feel invited to play rather than report, and pilot the kit with one or two people.
Hand over kits in person with a brief explanation and leave them with participants for 1-4 weeks, with a light-touch reminder midway.
Collect the returns and review them as a team, treating ambiguous responses as prompts for design thinking rather than coding them for frequency.
Follow up with interviews or design responses that reflect the returns back to participants, and keep the probes' fragments visible during ideation.
outputs: Returned artefacts (photos, annotated maps, postcards, diaries), team reflections, design provocations and follow-up interview prompts.
useWhen: Early, open-ended exploration of intimate, domestic or remote contexts where direct observation is intrusive or impossible, and when the goal is design inspiration.
avoidWhen: When you need systematic, comparable or quantifiable data (use a diary study or experience sampling) or when stakeholders will treat probe returns as evidence of prevalence.
whyLost: Vestigial: Creative and valuable for hard-to-reach populations; time-intensive; rarely applied rigorously.
whereToUse: Cross-cultural design; marginalized populations; distant communities.
example: A smart-home start-up mails probe kits to 12 multi-generational households asking them to photograph 'something in your home that only one person knows how to work'. The returns reveal informal gatekeepers of household technology, reframing the product around shared control.

extra.Probe Package Design: Disposable camera: With 10–15 printed prompts attached — questions like "photograph something that represents your relationship with this software," "photograph the moment you feel most frustrated today," "photograph something that doesn't belong." Diary: Open sentence completions rather than closed questions. "Today I felt… when I tried to…" "The most unexpected thing that happened with my [product] today was…" "If this product could speak, it would say…" Map: A large-format map of the participant's environment with instructions: "Mark where you use this product most. Mark where you never use it. Mark where you wish you could." Postcards: Addressed back to the research team. Prompts on the back: "The one thing I wish the product understood is…" "If I could change one thing tomorrow, it would be…"

name: CUPED Variance Reduction
origin: Alex Deng, Ya Xu, Ron Kohavi and Toby Walker, Microsoft, 2013
summary: Uses each user's pre-experiment metric as a covariate to remove predictable variance from A/B test outcomes, shrinking confidence intervals substantially.
description: CUPED adjusts each user's outcome Y by subtracting theta times (X minus mean X), where X is a pre-period covariate (often the same metric before the experiment) and theta is cov(X,Y)/var(X). Because X is measured before assignment, it is independent of treatment, so the estimate remains unbiased while variance falls by a factor of 1 - rho squared. With typical correlations of 0.5-0.7 this cuts required sample sizes by 25-50%. It is a control-variate technique well known in Monte Carlo and survey sampling. UX-led experiments, which are often underpowered, benefit greatly, yet many teams compare raw means.
steps: Choose a pre-period covariate strongly correlated with the outcome (e.g. same metric over the prior 2-4 weeks).
Ensure the covariate is measured strictly before randomisation; handle new users without history (impute or use other covariates).
Compute theta from pooled data across both arms.
Compute adjusted outcomes and estimate the treatment effect and its standard error.
Report variance reduction achieved and compare with the unadjusted estimate as a sanity check.
Use the expected variance reduction in power calculations for future tests.
outputs: Variance-reduced effect estimates with tighter confidence intervals, and realised variance reduction.
useWhen: A/B tests on metrics with stable per-user history, especially when traffic is limited.
avoidWhen: Tests mostly on new users without history, or with covariates possibly affected by treatment.
whyLost: It is known inside large experimentation platforms but not in UX training, and smaller teams use naive calculators.
whereToUse: B2B SaaS with modest traffic, engagement metrics, revenue per user, task time in repeated-use tools.
example: A B2B app with 6,000 weekly users tests a new editor. Adjusting by pre-period edit counts (rho = 0.7) halves variance, detecting a 4% improvement in two weeks instead of four.
sources: Deng, Xu, Kohavi & Walker, Improving the sensitivity of online controlled experiments by utilizing pre-experiment data (2013), WSDM
Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020)
reference: Deng, A., Xu, Y., Kohavi, R., & Walker, T. (2013). WSDM '13, 123-132.

name: Cusp Catastrophe Model Fitting
origin: Maximum likelihood approach by Loren Cobb and colleagues (Cobb 1978; Cobb and Zacks 1985), implemented in the cusp R package by Grasman, van der Maas and Wagenmakers (2009).
summary: A maximum likelihood model, fitted like a regression, that tests whether a behavioural outcome is better described by a cusp with two stable states controlled by a 'normal' and a 'splitting' variable than by a linear model.
description: The cusp catastrophe describes a behaviour that changes smoothly when a splitting variable is low but jumps between two stable states, with hysteresis, when it is high. Cobb made this deterministic model statistical by adding stochastic noise to the dynamics, which yields a probability distribution that can be unimodal or bimodal depending on the control variables. As in regression, the behavioural state is a weighted sum of measured outcome items, and the normal (alpha) and splitting (beta) controls are each linear functions of measured predictors. Estimation gives coefficients, standard errors and fit indices, and the cusp is compared with linear and logistic alternatives using AIC and BIC. A classic example in the book is attitude data where intensity of feeling loads only on the splitting axis: low-involvement respondents are spread around the middle, high-involvement respondents polarise. The book's rules are to simulate data from the model first to understand power, to use independent cross-sectional observations (the method is not valid for time series), and to remember that a better cusp fit is evidence, not proof. For UX this turns claims about polarised attitudes or all-or-nothing adoption into testable models.
steps: Specify the behavioural outcome and candidate predictors for the normal axis (pushes the outcome up or down) and the splitting axis (amplifies polarisation, such as involvement).
Simulate data from a cusp with plausible parameters and fit it, to check that your sample size can recover the effects.
Inspect the data descriptively: histograms overall and at high levels of the splitting predictor, and pairwise plots.
Fit the full cusp model with each predictor allowed on both axes, then reduced models that drop non-significant paths.
Compare the cusp with linear and logistic models using AIC and BIC, and check how many observations lie inside the bifurcation set.
Interpret which predictors act on which axis and report the result alongside other catastrophe flags.
outputs: Estimated normal and splitting coefficients, model comparison indices against linear alternatives, and a plot of cases located in the cusp's control plane.
useWhen: You have a large cross-sectional sample with a continuous outcome and theory that some factor (involvement, experience, stakes) makes responses polarise rather than shift.
avoidWhen: Data are repeated measures from the same people (observations must be independent), the sample is small, or there is no theoretical candidate for a splitting variable.
whyLost: It requires comfort with nonlinear likelihood models and catastrophe theory, which carried a poor reputation after early overclaiming; UX surveys are usually analysed with linear models.
whereToUse: Attitude and trust surveys, adoption intent studies, satisfaction data where involvement may polarise responses, privacy concern research.
example: A survey of 3,000 users rates a controversial AI feature. Researchers fit a cusp with perceived usefulness on the normal axis and personal involvement with the topic on the splitting axis, and find that highly involved users split into enthusiasts and rejecters while low-involvement users sit near neutral, a pattern a linear model misses.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: Custom component creation (spaCy)
origin: spaCy v3 component API (Explosion, 2021)
summary: Writing bespoke processing steps for an NLP pipeline, such as speaker filters, codebook taggers or anonymisers, so research-specific logic runs consistently over every transcript.
description: spaCy lets researchers register custom components that run inside the pipeline and add extension attributes to documents, sentences and tokens (e.g. doc._.participant_id, sent._.speaker, sent._.code_candidates). This turns study-specific rules into reusable, testable code: removing moderator turns, tagging sentences that match codebook definitions, redacting personal data, or attaching interview metadata. Rigour comes from unit tests for each component, clear documentation of rules, versioning components with the pipeline, and evaluating outputs on annotated samples just as for statistical components. Keeping such logic inside the pipeline, rather than in scattered post-processing scripts, also ensures every transcript receives identical treatment.
steps: Specify the component's job, inputs and outputs (e.g. add sent._.speaker from diarisation data).
Register extension attributes and implement the component with @Language.component or a factory.
Insert it at the correct pipeline position (e.g. after the parser and before downstream taggers).
Write unit tests on small example texts covering normal and edge cases.
Evaluate on a sample of real transcripts and record precision and recall where applicable.
Package and version components with the pipeline configuration so others can reproduce runs.
outputs: Tested, versioned custom components and enriched documents with research-specific attributes.
useWhen: When research-specific logic must be applied consistently across large corpora, such as speaker filtering, codebook tagging or anonymisation.
avoidWhen: Avoid for one-off analyses where a short script suffices; avoid encoding interpretive judgements as rigid rules.
whyLost: Building components needs software engineering skills uncommon among qualitative researchers.
whereToUse: Research operations pipelines, anonymisation of transcripts, codebook pre-tagging and multi-study repositories.
example: A health research team writes an anonymiser component that replaces names, dates of birth and clinic names with tags. Tested on 50 annotated transcripts it achieves 0.98 recall, and it is reused across five studies.

name: Custom NLP pipeline construction (spaCy)
origin: spaCy library, Matthew Honnibal and Ines Montani (Explosion), 2015; transformer pipelines from spaCy v3 (2021)
summary: Assembling a sequence of language processing components that turns interview transcripts into structured, analysable data such as entities, sentences, phrases and quotes.
description: spaCy processes text through an ordered pipeline: tokenisation, part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, named entity recognition and any custom components. For qualitative UX research a pipeline might segment transcripts into sentences, remove moderator turns, tag product features and emotions, extract candidate quotes and attach metadata (participant, segment, timestamp). The rigour comes from designing the pipeline around research questions rather than generic NLP, evaluating each component against a hand-annotated sample (precision, recall, F1), pinning model versions, and keeping the pipeline as a pre-processing instrument that supports, rather than replaces, interpretive analysis.
steps: Define the research questions and the structured outputs the pipeline must produce (e.g. feature mentions, pain-point sentences, quotes).
Start from a pinned pre-trained model (e.g. en_core_web_trf for accuracy, en_core_web_sm for speed).
Add components in order: sentence segmentation, speaker filtering, entity ruler for domain terms, custom attribute extractors.
Hand-annotate 100-200 sentences as a gold standard and measure precision, recall and F1 per component.
Iterate until key components reach agreed thresholds (e.g. F1 of 0.80 or above), then freeze and version the pipeline.
Export results to a table linked back to transcript IDs and timestamps for analysts to verify.
outputs: A versioned pipeline, per-component evaluation scores and a structured dataset of sentences, entities and quotes linked to transcripts.
useWhen: Large qualitative corpora (dozens to hundreds of transcripts, open-ended survey responses, support tickets) needing consistent structure before analysis.
avoidWhen: Avoid for small studies (under about 15 interviews) where manual coding is faster and richer, and never as a replacement for interpretive analysis.
whyLost: NLP pipelines are standard in computational linguistics and industry text analytics, but qualitative UX researchers rarely have programming support.
whereToUse: Interview repositories, voice-of-customer programmes, support ticket analysis and AI-assisted coding pipelines.
example: A SaaS company processes 300 customer interviews through a spaCy pipeline that removes moderator speech, tags 40 product feature names and extracts complaint sentences, producing a feature-by-complaint table that analysts then read and code.

name: CxPi (Forrester Customer Experience Index)
origin: Forrester Research, annual report since 2007
summary: Three questions on how well a company meets needs, how easy it is to deal with and how enjoyable it is, each scored as top-two minus bottom-two.
description: Forrester's CxPi asks consumers about their interactions with a firm over the past 90 days: how well it met their needs (usefulness), how easy it was to do business with (usability) and how enjoyable it was (enjoyability). Each uses a five-point scale from very negative to very positive and is scored like NPS as a net percentage: top two boxes minus bottom two. The index is the average of the three. Sauro and Lewis note it has no published psychometric data but is a common industry tracking metric. For UX teams it is a quick way to place the usability of an experience alongside usefulness and emotion in terms executives already recognise.
steps: Ask the three questions about recent interactions on five-point scales.
For each, compute the percentage in the top two boxes minus the bottom two.
Average the three net scores for the index.
Track over time and compare with Forrester's published industry results where relevant.
outputs: Net scores for usefulness, ease and enjoyment, and an overall index.
useWhen: Executive-level tracking that needs to sit alongside industry reports.
avoidWhen: Diagnostic research or small samples; net scores need large samples to be stable.
whyLost: Market research ownership and proprietary benchmarks.
whereToUse: Banks, airlines, insurers, telecoms and retailers.
example: A telecom scores well on usefulness but its ease score is net negative, building the case for a self-service redesign.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Forrester Research (2011). The Customer Experience Index, 2011.

name: Cynefin Sense-Making Framework
origin: Dave Snowden, IBM Institute for Knowledge Management, 1999-2003; Kurtz and Snowden (2003); Snowden and Boone (2007)
summary: Classifies situations as clear, complicated, complex, chaotic or confused, each calling for different research and decision approaches.
description: Cynefin distinguishes ordered domains, where cause and effect are knowable (clear: sense-categorise-respond; complicated: sense-analyse-respond, needing expertise), from unordered domains (complex: probe-sense-respond via safe-to-fail experiments; chaotic: act-sense-respond). A central zone of confusion (aporetic) covers not knowing which applies. Properly used, Cynefin is constructed by groups through contextualisation exercises, placing their own situations onto the framework from narrative data, rather than assigning domains top-down. For UX, it guides methodological choice: complicated problems call for expert analysis and rigorous evaluation, complex ones for portfolios of small probes and narrative sensing (e.g. SenseMaker).
steps: Collect situations or decisions as short narratives from teams or users.
Run a contextualisation workshop: place items relative to each other, then draw domain boundaries emergently.
For each domain, agree appropriate approaches: best practice, expert analysis, safe-to-fail probes or rapid action.
For complex items, design a portfolio of parallel probes with amplification and dampening criteria.
Monitor through narrative sensing and indicators, and re-assess domain placement over time.
Watch for complacency moving clear items toward chaos.
outputs: Domain classification of situations, matched research and decision approaches and probe portfolios.
useWhen: Choosing research strategy under uncertainty, especially for new markets, AI products and organisational change.
avoidWhen: Well-defined evaluation questions where the method choice is already clear.
whyLost: Widely shown as a 2x2-like slide, with domains assigned top-down and the contextualisation and narrative practices dropped.
whereToUse: Product strategy for emerging technologies, research portfolio planning, incident response, organisational change.
example: A team building an AI tutor contextualises its open questions: model accuracy is complicated (expert evaluation), but how students integrate the tutor into study habits is complex, so it runs five small classroom probes instead of one large study.
sources: Kurtz & Snowden, The new dynamics of strategy: Sense-making in a complex and complicated world (2003), IBM Systems Journal
Snowden & Boone, A leader's framework for decision making (2007), Harvard Business Review
Snowden et al., Cynefin: Weaving Sense-Making into the Fabric of Our World (2020)

name: D-prime calculation
origin: Tanner and Swets, 1954; Green and Swets, Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics, 1966
summary: Separates a user's true ability to detect a signal (d') from their willingness to respond (criterion), using hit and false-alarm rates.
description: Signal detection theory models any yes/no detection, such as noticing an alert or spotting a fraudulent transaction, as a decision between overlapping noise and signal-plus-noise distributions. Sensitivity d' = z(hit rate) - z(false alarm rate) measures how far apart those distributions are, independent of response bias; criterion c = -0.5[z(H) + z(F)] captures how liberal or conservative the observer is. This matters because raw accuracy confounds the two: an operator who responds to everything has a perfect hit rate and poor discrimination. In UX, d' tells you whether a design change made signals genuinely more discriminable or merely shifted users' thresholds. Rigour requires a design with both signal and noise trials, enough trials per cell, and corrections for perfect rates.
steps: Define the detection task with explicit signal-present and signal-absent trials, for example true alerts versus benign events, in a realistic ratio.
Run each participant through at least 50 signal and 50 noise trials per condition (more if rates are near ceiling) and record hits, misses, false alarms and correct rejections.
Correct rates of 0 or 1 with the log-linear correction (add 0.5 to each cell count and 1 to each trial total).
Compute d' = z(H) - z(F) and criterion c for each participant and condition.
Compare conditions with a within-subjects test on d' (for example paired t-test across 12-20 participants); interpret d' near 1 as weak, 2 as good, and above 3 as excellent discrimination.
Report d' and c separately and recommend design changes for sensitivity (signal salience) versus bias (cost of misses, instructions, alarm credibility).
outputs: d' and criterion per participant and condition, statistical comparison across designs, and a diagnosis of whether failures are perceptual or decisional.
useWhen: When users must detect rare events (alerts, anomalies, fraud flags, AI hallucinations) and you need to know whether a design improves discrimination or just shifts bias.
avoidWhen: When there is no meaningful 'noise' condition or the task is not a binary judgement; use task success or ROC analysis with confidence ratings for graded responses.
whyLost: d' is standard in psychophysics, radiology and aviation but UX reports accuracy and conversion, which hide bias; few UX researchers are trained in SDT.
whereToUse: Alarm and alert design, content moderation tools, security warnings, fraud review queues, and human review of AI outputs.
example: A clinical decision-support vendor tests two alert designs. Hit rate rises from 80% to 92% with the red banner, but false alarms rise too; d' is unchanged at 1.9, showing the banner only made clinicians more trigger-happy. A redesign that adds patient-specific context raises d' to 2.6.
sources: Van Drongelen, W., Signal Processing for Neuroscientists
MacKay, D. J. C., Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003)
Gopinath, V., Forward-Thinking Playbook

name: D-separation
origin: Judea Pearl, 1988
summary: A graphical rule that reads off a DAG which variables should be statistically independent given others, enabling tests of causal assumptions against data.
description: D-separation determines whether a set of variables blocks every path between two other variables in a DAG. A path is blocked if it contains a non-collider that is conditioned on, or a collider that is not conditioned on (nor any of its descendants). If all paths are blocked, the two variables are d-separated and must be conditionally independent in any data generated by that graph. This gives two uses for UX research: checking a proposed causal model by testing its implied independencies against survey or log data, and understanding why controlling for a variable opens or closes bias. Rigour comes from computing implications mechanically with software and testing them with appropriate conditional independence tests.
steps: Encode the DAG in a tool such as DAGitty or the Python package pgmpy.
List all implied conditional independencies the graph makes, which the tool generates automatically.
Test each implication in data with partial correlations or conditional independence tests, correcting for multiple tests.
Treat strong violations (e.g. partial correlation above 0.1 with a tight interval) as evidence the graph is missing an edge or variable.
Revise the DAG and repeat, documenting every change and its evidential basis.
outputs: A list of testable implications, test results, a revised and better-supported causal graph, and clear explanations of adjustment choices.
useWhen: Validating a causal model built from qualitative work or expert judgement before using it for adjustment or SEM.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the graph has few implied independencies (dense graphs) or when data is too small for reliable conditional independence tests.
whyLost: It is a technical result in graphical models, rarely taught outside CS and epidemiology, and UX teams seldom formalise causal models to the point of needing it.
whereToUse: Mixed-methods trust and adoption research, survey-based SEM in fintech, model checking for causal analysis of product logs.
example: A DAG implies that app-store rating is independent of feature usage once satisfaction is conditioned on. Survey data shows a strong residual association, revealing a missing path from usage to rating via in-app prompts.
sources: DAGs+SEM Playbook (Vivek Gopinath)

Statistical Rethinking (Richard McElreath)

name: DAG + SEM Mixed-Methods Protocol
aka: DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX
donor: Causal inference (DAGs) and psychometrics (SEM) joined with qualitative research
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Turns qualitative themes into a causal DAG, tests it with CFA and SEM, and binds each estimated path to a quote and a design prescription.
description: Reports usually end with themes or dashboards; what is missing is a mechanism showing how a perception change propagates through behaviour to outcomes. In this protocol the DAG expresses the mechanism and SEM estimates its strength. Qualitative discovery yields a codebook of constructs; the DAG makes causal assumptions and confounders explicit and identifies mediators and colliders; a CFA measurement model validates latent constructs; the structural model estimates DAG paths with direct, indirect and total effects; and a joint display maps qual mechanism → quant evidence → prescribed change. In the tap-to-pay case (n = 520, MLR), FR → TR −0.45, SR → TR +0.31, TR → DC −0.50, DC → SL +0.42, SL → AD −0.28 and TR → AD +0.26, with indirect effect ≈ +0.059 and total TR → AD ≈ +0.32. Robustness checks include multi-group invariance, common method bias, sensitivity to confounders and out-of-sample validation. Qual arrays and the DAG are kept under version control.
steps: Run qualitative discovery (interviews, think-aloud) and build a codebook of constructs, marking each as latent or observed (e.g. Trust, Fraud Risk, Double-Checking, Slowness, Support, Adoption).
Draw the DAG from qual: write causal assumptions, confounders to adjust (past fraud, device type, tenure) and colliders not to control.
Design 3-item Likert batteries per latent construct; screen missingness < 10% (FIML), check Cronbach's α ≥ 0.70 and run CFA, dropping loadings < 0.60 unless theory demands.
Check convergent validity (AVE ≥ 0.50, CR) and discriminant validity (Fornell-Larcker or HTMT < 0.85).
Estimate the structural model per the DAG with robust ML (MLR) and report CFI, TLI (≥ 0.95), RMSEA (≤ 0.06) and SRMR (≤ 0.08).
Decompose direct, indirect and total effects (|β| ≈ 0.10 small, 0.30 medium, 0.50 large) and never interpret paths without quotes beside them.
Run robustness checks: multi-group invariance (iOS/Android, new/veteran), common method bias via behavioural covariates, confounder sensitivity and split-sample or time-based validation.
Bind paths to prescriptions in a joint display and validate with A/B tests, guardrails and brief qual follow-ups (e.g. decision bar +5–8 points adoption in 4 weeks; 5 post-launch sessions).
outputs: A versioned DAG, CFA table with loadings, CR and AVE, SEM path diagram with fit indices and effect decomposition, a joint display and a reporting template.
useWhen: When latent constructs (trust, perceived security, ease) matter, when multiple mediators exist and indirect effects matter, and when qual narratives must be aligned with quantitative tests.
avoidWhen: When samples are small (SEM typically needs several hundred cases), constructs are not yet understood, or the question is purely descriptive; use interviews or simple regression instead.
whyLost: Original protocol by Vivek Gopinath; DAGs and SEM are standard in epidemiology and psychology but rarely joined to UX qualitative work.
whereToUse: Banking and payments adoption, trust and security features, AI feature adoption, healthcare apps.
example: A bank's tap-to-pay adoption lags despite a bug-free flow; interviews reveal double-checking from low trust; SEM confirms trust reduces double-checking (−0.50), which raises perceived slowness (+0.42), which suppresses adoption (−0.28), so the team ships a trust explainer, one-tap verification and adaptive 2FA together.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments.

name: DAG construction from qual themes
donor: Epidemiology / causal inference with qualitative research
origin: Vivek Gopinath, DAGs+SEM Playbook; building on Pearl (1995) and participatory causal mapping
summary: Translates themes and mechanisms from qualitative research into an explicit directed acyclic graph that can guide measurement and causal analysis.
description: Qualitative research produces rich mechanism stories but rarely commits them to a testable structure. This method converts coded themes into nodes and stated mechanisms into directed edges, producing a DAG that encodes assumptions about what causes what. Each edge must be traceable to evidence (quotes, observations) or labelled as an assumption. The resulting graph identifies which variables must be measured, which are confounders, mediators or colliders, and what quantitative design could test the story. Rigour comes from evidence tracing per edge, deliberately adding plausible unmeasured common causes, checking acyclicity, and testing the graph's implied conditional independencies against data where available.
steps: List candidate variables from the theme codebook, phrasing each as a measurable quantity (e.g. perceived interface trust, frequency of double-checking).
For each causal statement in the data, add a directed edge and log the supporting excerpts; mark edges without direct evidence as assumptions.
Add plausible unmeasured common causes (e.g. financial literacy, market conditions) as latent nodes, even if not mentioned by participants.
Check acyclicity; represent feedback loops by time-indexing variables (trust at t1 to behaviour at t2).
Review the DAG with researchers and domain experts in a workshop, recording disagreements as alternative graphs.
Derive testable implications (conditional independencies) with DAGitty and plan the measures and design needed to test key paths.
outputs: An evidence-linked causal DAG, alternative graphs, a list of variables to measure and testable implications for quantitative follow-up.
useWhen: After qualitative discovery when the team wants to test a mechanism quantitatively, design a survey or SEM, or analyse logs causally.
avoidWhen: Avoid when qualitative data is thin or purely descriptive, or when the question is exploratory and premature formalisation would close down inquiry.
whyLost: Qualitative and quantitative UX work are usually run by different people, and DAGs are taught in epidemiology rather than design research, so the bridge is rarely built.
whereToUse: Mixed-methods programmes in fintech, health and AI products; designing surveys for SEM; framing log analyses and experiments.
example: Field interviews with traders reveal that distrust of the payment interface leads to double-checking, which delays Tap to Pay adoption. The team encodes this as a DAG with financial literacy as a confounder, then measures each node in a survey for path analysis.
sources: DAGs+SEM Playbook (Vivek Gopinath)

name: DAG-informed covariate selection
origin: Greenland, Pearl & Robins, 1999; VanderWeele's disjunctive cause criterion, 2019
summary: Chooses which variables to include as controls in a model by reading them off a causal diagram, rather than by significance tests or data availability.
description: Covariate selection by stepwise regression or 'include everything' can introduce bias by adjusting for mediators or colliders, or leave confounding by omitting unmeasured causes. DAG-informed selection uses the backdoor criterion to pick a minimal sufficient set, adds precision variables that predict the outcome only, and excludes instruments, mediators and colliders. When the full DAG is uncertain, VanderWeele's disjunctive cause criterion offers a practical rule: adjust for any pre-treatment variable that causes the treatment, the outcome or both, excluding known instruments. Rigour comes from deciding covariates before seeing outcome data and showing robustness across plausible adjustment sets.
steps: List all available pre-treatment variables and place them in the DAG.
Derive minimal sufficient adjustment sets for the effect of interest using DAGitty.
Add outcome-only predictors for precision, and remove variables affected by treatment, colliders and pure instruments.
Where the DAG is uncertain, apply the disjunctive cause criterion and record which variables were included on that basis.
Pre-register or time-stamp the covariate list before running outcome models.
Run the analysis with two or three plausible adjustment sets and report how much the estimate changes.
outputs: A justified covariate list, the DAG used, estimates under alternative adjustment sets and a robustness statement.
useWhen: Any observational analysis, quasi-experiment or covariate-adjusted A/B test where the choice of controls affects conclusions.
avoidWhen: Avoid for purely predictive models, where covariates should be chosen by out-of-sample performance rather than causal role.
whyLost: UX statistics training focuses on model fitting, and covariate choice is treated as a technical detail rather than a causal decision.
whereToUse: Feature impact analysis, adjusted retention comparisons, CUPED-style variance reduction choices and survey driver models.
example: Evaluating a goal-setting feature, the team avoids controlling for post-launch engagement (a mediator) and instead adjusts for pre-launch activity and account age. The estimated retention effect is 4 points, versus near zero in the 'control for everything' model.
sources: DAGs+SEM Playbook (Vivek Gopinath)

name: Data display (matrices, networks, flowcharts)
origin: Miles and Huberman, Qualitative Data Analysis (1984; 2nd ed. 1994)
summary: Organises reduced qualitative data into structured matrices and networks so patterns, comparisons and explanations can be seen and verified, rather than inferred from narrative text.
description: Miles and Huberman argued that extended narrative text is a weak display for analysis: it is sequential, bulky and lets analysts jump to vivid but unrepresentative conclusions. Displays, defined as organised, compressed assemblies of information, allow conclusion drawing. Matrices cross two dimensions (for example cases by variables, time periods by roles), and networks show nodes and links (flows, causes, relationships). Their sourcebook catalogues dozens of display types, including checklist matrices, time-ordered matrices, role-ordered matrices, conceptually ordered displays, effects matrices and causal networks. Rigour comes from explicit decision rules for what enters each cell, and from verification tactics such as counting, noting patterns, checking extreme cases and following up surprises applied to the display.
steps: Choose a display type to suit the analytic question: time-ordered for process, role-ordered for perspectives, case-by-variable for comparison, network for causation or flow.
Define rows, columns or node types precisely, and write decision rules for cell entries, such as what counts as evidence, how to rate strength and how to cite sources.
Populate the display from reduced data, citing case and excerpt identifiers for each entry and marking missing data explicitly.
Read the display using verification tactics: count, note patterns and clusters, make contrasts, check outliers and extreme cases, and look for negative evidence.
Write a short analytic text for each display summarising patterns and the conclusions drawn, and keep the display and text together.
Revise or build follow-up displays when conclusions raise new questions, iterating between reduction, display and conclusions.
outputs: A set of matrices or networks with documented entry rules, analytic text for each, and verified conclusions with traceable evidence.
useWhen: Comparing across multiple cases, roles or time periods; testing explanations against all the data; presenting rigorous qualitative analysis to decision-makers.
avoidWhen: Very small samples where displays add overhead without insight, or highly interpretive phenomenological work where categorising into cells distorts meaning.
whyLost: UX inherited the affinity wall and journey map but not the broader display catalogue, so systematic comparison across cases is replaced by memorable anecdotes.
whereToUse: Multi-segment research, multi-market studies, account-based B2B research, service blueprint evidence, longitudinal studies.
example: A role-ordered matrix with health workers, supervisors and district managers as rows and adoption barriers as columns showed that supervisors alone cited audit requirements, revealing the real blocker sat in the supervisory role.

name: Data Mining Project Process (Define, Prepare, Implement, Deploy)
origin: Glenn Myatt (2007), in the tradition of data mining process models such as CRISP-DM
summary: A four-stage plan for analytics projects: define the problem and deliverables, prepare the data, select and optimise analyses, then deploy and measure the results.
description: Myatt frames every exploratory analysis or data mining project as four linked steps, with iteration between them. Problem definition breaks a headline goal into questions the data can answer, sets specific measurable success criteria tied to a business objective, states deliverables (report, rules, embedded model, new workflow), the accuracy needed and the relative cost of the two kinds of wrong prediction, checks the data represent the target population, and assigns roles: project leader, subject matter expert, analyst, IT expert and consumer of the results. A plan adds timetable, constraints, privacy issues, risks and a cost-benefit case. Data preparation characterises, cleans, transforms and segments the data. Implementation selects among summary tables, graphs, statistics, grouping and prediction methods according to whether the task is summarising, finding hidden relationships or predicting, and optimises them. Deployment delivers a report or integrated model, plans change management and training, measures business impact, ideally with a randomised field comparison of users with and without the model, monitors models as data age, and ends with a project review. For UX analytics it gives a scoping discipline that ties exploratory work to decisions.
steps: Write the headline objective and break it into answerable data questions with measurable success criteria.
Define deliverables, required accuracy, speed constraints and the consequences of each type of error.
Assemble a cross-disciplinary team, agree roles and share a glossary of terms.
Plan: data sources, privacy and legal issues, timetable with review points, risks and cost-benefit.
Prepare the data, then select, run and optimise the analysis methods that fit the questions.
Deploy results as a report, rules or integrated model, with training and change management.
Measure impact against the success criteria (ideally with a randomised comparison), monitor over time and run a project review.
outputs: A project plan with success criteria, a prepared data set, analysis results and a deployment and evaluation plan.
useWhen: Starting an analytics or data mining project on product data that must lead to a decision or a deployed model.
avoidWhen: A quick one-off query or a small qualitative study where the overhead of formal planning outweighs the benefit.
whyLost: UX teams borrow agile research plans and rarely adopt data mining process models, which stay in data science and BI groups.
whereToUse: Churn analysis, personalisation, segmentation projects, survey analytics, analytics programmes run jointly by UX and data teams.
example: Asked to 'improve web sales', a team defines three data questions (which visitor groups buy, how usage patterns group, how usage relates to buying), sets a target of a 10% lift in conversion for a targeted segment, agrees that missing a likely buyer costs more than a wasted prompt, and plans an A/B rollout to measure the model's impact.
sources: Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
reference: Myatt, G. J. (2007). Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley-Interscience.

name: Data Preparation and Transformation for Analysis
aka: Normalisation, value mapping, discretisation and aggregation
origin: Standard data mining practice, codified as a six-step preparation table by Glenn Myatt (2007)
summary: A structured sequence for turning raw, multi-source data into a clean analysis table: characterise, clean, remove, transform and segment, while recording every change.
description: Analyses of product data usually start with data collected for another purpose, and Myatt argues this step is often the most time-consuming and decides the quality of everything after it. The procedure first builds a single data table and characterises each variable (continuous or discrete, scale of measurement, role, frequency distribution). Cleaning then consolidates inconsistent category labels, inspects outliers with histograms, box plots and z-scores, converts or removes non-numeric entries in numeric fields, puts measurements on a single unit, handles missing values and removes duplicate records. Variables that are constant, mostly missing or redundant with others are dropped. Transformations follow: normalisation (min-max, z-score, decimal scaling) so variables with large ranges do not dominate distance-based methods; log, exponential or Box-Cox transforms towards normality; value mapping of ordinal text to numbers and nominal values to dummy variables; discretisation (binning) of continuous values or generalising many categories into fewer; and aggregation into derived variables. Finally the table may be segmented into subsets. Each transformation is recorded so results can be translated back to original units before presentation.
steps: Assemble data from all sources into one table with one row per observation (user, session, account).
Characterise every variable: type, scale of measurement, role (descriptor or response) and frequency distribution.
Clean: merge inconsistent labels, review outliers with subject experts, fix or remove non-numeric values, unify units, deal with missing values and remove duplicates.
Remove constants, mostly-missing variables and variables that add no information beyond highly correlated ones.
Transform as needed: normalise, apply log or Box-Cox transforms, map ordinal and nominal values to numbers or dummy variables, bin continuous values, and derive aggregate variables.
Segment the table into random or problem-driven subsets, noting the criteria used.
Document every step and keep the inverse of each transformation for reporting results.
outputs: A prepared, documented analysis table plus a log of cleaning rules and transformations.
useWhen: Before clustering, prediction, association rules or any analysis of logs, CRM exports, survey exports or joined data sets.
avoidWhen: The data are already a curated, documented analysis table, or a tiny study where each record can be checked by hand.
whyLost: UX researchers often receive analytics dashboards rather than raw tables, so preparation is left to data teams and rarely taught as a research method.
whereToUse: Product analytics, survey analysis, CRM and support data, joined behavioural and attitudinal data sets.
example: Before clustering trial users, a researcher merges event logs with signup survey answers, consolidates 14 spellings of job titles into six roles, converts sessions-per-week and minutes-per-session to a 0 to 1 range, dummy-codes acquisition channel and drops a constant 'region' column.
sources: Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
reference: Myatt, G. J. (2007). Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley-Interscience.

name: Data privacy in AI processing (local vs. cloud)
donor: Information privacy law; research ethics; security engineering
origin: Data protection principles (GDPR, 2016/2018; data minimisation and privacy by design, Cavoukian, 2009)
summary: Deciding where participant data are processed, on local hardware or with cloud AI providers, based on consent, sensitivity, legal obligations and provider terms, and minimising what leaves controlled systems.
description: Interview audio and transcripts contain personal and often special-category data (health, finances, ethnicity). Sending them to cloud transcription or LLM APIs creates processing by third parties, possibly across borders, with retention and training implications. Local processing (whisper.cpp, local NLP and open-weight models) keeps data in controlled systems at the cost of setup and sometimes accuracy; cloud processing offers capability under contractual safeguards such as zero-retention terms and data processing agreements. Rigour comes from a data protection impact assessment, consent wording that matches actual processing, anonymisation or pseudonymisation before any external processing, data minimisation, and documentation of the decision.
steps: Classify data sensitivity (e.g. special-category, financial, children's data) and check consent terms for AI and third-party processing.
Conduct or update a data protection impact assessment for the pipeline.
Default to local processing for raw audio and identifiable transcripts where feasible.
Before any cloud call, pseudonymise names, places, organisations and identifiers, and verify redaction recall on a sample (aim for 0.95 or above).
Use providers with data processing agreements, no-training and limited-retention terms, and approved data residency.
Document the decision, data flows and retention, and delete intermediate data according to schedule.
outputs: A data flow map, DPIA, processing decision record, redaction validation and retention schedule.
useWhen: Every AI-assisted research pipeline, especially in health, finance, children's services, the public sector or the EU and UK.
avoidWhen: Not a reason to avoid AI entirely; with proper safeguards cloud processing is often acceptable. Purely public data (e.g. app store reviews) needs lighter treatment, though terms of service still apply.
whyLost: Privacy review traditionally focused on recruitment and storage; AI processing pathways are new and researchers often assume tool terms cover them.
whereToUse: Health research, fintech, public services, enterprise customer research and research operations policies.
example: A mental health app team transcribes locally with whisper.cpp, runs a spaCy anonymiser validated at 0.97 recall, and only then sends pseudonymised segments to a cloud LLM under a zero-retention agreement, as described in the participant consent form.
