name: Documentary Method of Interpretation
origin: Karl Mannheim, 1920s; developed as an empirical method by Ralf Bohnsack, 1980s to 1990s
summary: Distinguishes what participants explicitly say from the implicit, taken-for-granted orientations their way of talking reveals, using formulating and reflecting interpretation plus systematic comparison.
description: The Documentary Method of Interpretation (Ralf Bohnsack, developed from Karl Mannheim's sociology of knowledge) distinguishes between two levels of meaning: the communicative meaning (what is explicitly said or shown) and the documentary meaning (the implicit orientations, habitual practices, and taken-for-granted frameworks that are enacted in communication without being directly said). The method has been applied to interview data, group discussions, and visual data. It is particularly valuable for UX research where the explicit content of what users say differs systematically from what their behaviour and interaction reveals about their underlying orientations.
steps: Formulaic interpretation: Identify the topic — what is explicitly communicated? Paraphrase without interpretation.

Reflective interpretation: How is the topic addressed? What is the mode of discussion — narrative, argumentation, description, evaluation? What does the form of expression reveal about the speaker's implicit orientation?

Comparative analysis: Compare how different participants, groups, or interviews address the same topic. Where the topic is the same but the mode of addressing it differs, the difference reveals different orientations.

Sinusoid of experience: Identify the arc of a topic discussion — when does it become animated? When does it go flat? Heightened engagement reveals what matters to participants at the level of orientation, not just stated preference.

Validation through contrast: Validate your interpretation of a group's orientation by identifying contrast cases — groups or individuals who do not share that orientation. The contrast makes the orientation visible.
outputs: Formulating and reflecting interpretations, comparative case analyses, reconstructed orientation frameworks, and typologies of implicit orientations across groups.
useWhen: Explicit statements and actual practice diverge, or you need to understand implicit orientations shared within groups, such as teams, households or professions, especially from group discussions.
avoidWhen: You need quick thematic summaries or explicit opinions; use thematic analysis. It requires training and time, so avoid on tight timelines.
whyLost: It is taught mainly in German-language sociology and education research, with limited English-language guidance until recently.
whereToUse: Team and workplace tool adoption, household technology use, professional cultures (clinicians, engineers), and group discussions in strategy research.
example: In group discussions with finance teams, everyone explicitly endorses automation, but the way they recount month-end close emphasises personal checking. The reconstructed orientation of 'accountability through touch' explains low trust in auto-reconciliation.
sources: Bohnsack — Documentary Method
Handbook of Qualitative Methods (Flick)
How to Analyse Interviews: A Documentary Method of Interpretation (arxiv)
reference: Bohnsack, R., Pfaff, N. & Weller, W. (eds.) (2010). Qualitative Analysis and Documentary Method in International Educational Research. Barbara Budrich.

name: Double Diamond
origin: UK Design Council, 2005
summary: A process model that alternates divergent and convergent phases, first on the problem (discover, define) then on the solution (develop, deliver), to plan and communicate research.
description: The Double Diamond, published by the UK Design Council in 2005 after studying design processes in leading companies, describes design as two diamonds. In the first, teams diverge to discover the problem space through research, then converge to define a clear problem. In the second, they diverge to develop multiple solutions, then converge to deliver a tested solution. The 2019 update framed it within a wider 'framework for innovation' with principles and methods. As a research planning tool, its value lies in making explicit which phase a project is in and which methods suit it: generative research in Discover, synthesis in Define, ideation and prototyping in Develop, evaluation in Deliver. Rigour comes from defined exit criteria for each phase, so teams do not skip problem definition.
steps: Map the project onto the four phases and agree what evidence is needed to leave each one.
In Discover, run generative research (interviews, observation, data review) to widen understanding.
In Define, synthesise findings into a clear problem statement and success criteria.
In Develop, generate and prototype multiple solution concepts.
In Deliver, test, refine and launch the chosen solution, measuring against the success criteria.
Loop back to earlier phases when evidence shows the problem was mis-defined.
outputs: Phased research plan, problem definition, concept portfolio, tested solution, shared process vocabulary for stakeholders.
useWhen: Scoping projects, planning research across a programme, and aligning stakeholders on when to explore versus decide.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for actual methods; it structures work but does not tell you how to do research.
whyLost: Still in use: Intuitive visualization of design process; useful for stakeholder communication.
whereToUse: Design process communication; project scoping; team alignment.
example: A fintech research lead used the Double Diamond to show executives that a requested feature build had skipped Define. Two weeks of discovery reframed the problem from 'add budgeting' to 'reduce overdraft surprises', changing the roadmap.
sources: Universal Methods of Design
Framework for Innovation (UK Design Council)
reference: Design Council (2005). The 'double diamond' design process model. Design Council, London.

name: Double Machine Learning
origin: Victor Chernozhukov, Denis Chetverikov, Mert Demirer, Esther Duflo, Christian Hansen, Whitney Newey and James Robins (2018)
summary: Estimates a causal effect from observational data with many confounders by using flexible ML to partial out confounding, with valid inference via cross-fitting.
description: With rich observational data, analysts often regress outcomes on treatment plus many controls, or use ML predictions naively, both of which bias estimates. DML fits ML models for the outcome given covariates and for the treatment given covariates, then regresses the residualised outcome on the residualised treatment. Neyman orthogonality makes the estimate insensitive to small errors in the ML models, and cross-fitting avoids overfitting bias, so standard errors are valid. It still relies on no unmeasured confounding, so it pairs with DAG reasoning and sensitivity analysis. For UX analytics with hundreds of behavioural features, it is a principled upgrade on 'controlled for everything' regressions.
steps: Draw a DAG and choose covariates that block backdoor paths; exclude mediators and colliders.
Split data into K folds (typically 5) for cross-fitting.
In each fold, fit flexible models (e.g. gradient boosting) for outcome and treatment on covariates using the other folds.
Compute residuals and regress outcome residuals on treatment residuals to estimate the effect.
Aggregate across folds and compute robust standard errors.
Run sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding and compare with simpler estimators.
outputs: A debiased causal effect estimate with confidence interval and sensitivity analysis.
useWhen: Observational analysis with many potential confounders and enough data, such as feature usage effects on retention.
avoidWhen: Small samples, unmeasured key confounders, or when an experiment can be run.
whyLost: It is new and technically demanding, and UX analytics often stops at correlation.
whereToUse: Product analytics, marketplace analytics, health app engagement effects, support channel effects.
example: A marketplace estimates the effect of seller response time on sales. DML with 300 behavioural covariates reduces the naive estimate by half, informing a realistic target for seller tools.
sources: Chernozhukov et al., Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters (2018), Econometrics Journal
reference: Chernozhukov, V., et al. (2018). The Econometrics Journal, 21(1), C1-C68.

name: Doubly robust estimation
origin: James Robins, Andrea Rotnitzky and Lue Ping Zhao, 1994; Bang and Robins, 2005
summary: Combining an outcome model with a propensity model so the causal effect estimate is consistent if either model is correctly specified.
description: Doubly robust estimators such as AIPW combine regression adjustment (modelling the outcome) with inverse probability weighting (modelling treatment assignment). If either the outcome model or the propensity model is correct, the estimate is consistent, giving two chances to get it right. Modern versions use machine learning for both nuisance models with cross-fitting (double/debiased machine learning, Chernozhukov et al., 2018) to avoid overfitting bias, and allow heterogeneous effect estimation by segment. Rigour comes from a DAG-based covariate set, overlap checks and weight trimming, cross-fitting, and reporting the estimate alongside simpler estimators and a sensitivity analysis. It cannot fix unmeasured confounding.
steps: Specify the causal question, time zero and DAG-based confounder set.
Fit a propensity model and an outcome model, using flexible learners (e.g. gradient boosting) where appropriate.
Use 5-fold cross-fitting so each unit's nuisance predictions come from models not trained on it (econml or causalml).
Check overlap and trim or truncate propensity scores outside about 0.01 to 0.99.
Compute the AIPW or DML estimate with robust or bootstrap confidence intervals.
Compare with regression-only and weighting-only estimates, examine heterogeneity by segment, and add an E-value sensitivity analysis.
outputs: An average treatment effect with CI, comparisons with single-model estimators, optional segment-level effects and sensitivity results.
useWhen: High-stakes observational effect estimation with many covariates and large logs, where modelling mistakes are likely and an experiment was not run.
avoidWhen: Avoid with small samples (under a few hundred per arm), poor overlap or unmeasured key confounders; use experiments or simpler, transparent methods.
whyLost: Used by causal data scientists in large tech and health organisations but not by UX researchers, who lack the statistical training and data access.
whereToUse: Large-scale SaaS and marketplace feature evaluation, fintech risk features, health programme impact and personalisation effect heterogeneity.
example: A marketplace estimates the effect of a seller analytics dashboard on sales. With 60 covariates and 25,000 sellers, a cross-fitted AIPW estimate shows a 6% lift (CI 3-9%), consistent with matching but with tighter intervals, and larger for new sellers.

dowhy
causalml
econml
statsmodels

name: Drift Diffusion Modelling of Decisions
origin: Roger Ratcliff, 1978
summary: Fits choice and full response-time distributions to separate the quality of evidence, caution, bias and non-decision time behind users' decisions.
description: The drift diffusion model treats a two-choice decision as noisy evidence accumulating toward one of two boundaries. Its parameters have psychological meaning: drift rate (how clear the evidence is), boundary separation (how cautious the user is), starting point (prior bias toward one option) and non-decision time (perception and motor). Fitting the model to accuracy and the full RT distributions, rather than mean RT, disentangles explanations that look identical in averages. For UX, it answers whether a design makes information clearer (higher drift), makes users more careful (wider boundary), or biases them (starting point), which is directly relevant to defaults, warnings and dark-pattern assessment.
steps: Design a two-choice task representing the real decision (e.g. accept/reject a suggestion, safe/phishing).
Collect many trials per participant (ideally 100+ per condition) with precise RT logging.
Clean data by removing implausibly fast responses (e.g. < 200 ms) and extreme slow outliers.
Fit the DDM with established tools (e.g. HDDM, fast-dm, or EZ-diffusion for quick estimates).
Compare parameters across design conditions using hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
Interpret: drift changes imply clearer information, boundary changes imply caution, starting-point shifts imply bias or nudging.
outputs: Estimated drift, boundary, bias and non-decision parameters per condition, with posterior comparisons.
useWhen: Evaluating how warnings, defaults, layouts or AI suggestions change rapid binary decisions, and distinguishing clarity from bias.
avoidWhen: Slow deliberative decisions or multi-option choices without adaptations; too few trials per person.
whyLost: It requires many trials and mathematical psychology expertise. UX reports mean task time or conversion, which conflates mechanisms.
whereToUse: Security warnings, content moderation tools, AI suggestion acceptance, cookie consent and default design.
example: A phishing warning redesign speeds decisions. DDM shows the speedup comes from higher drift (clearer evidence) rather than lower boundary (carelessness), supporting the redesign as genuinely better.
sources: Ratcliff, A theory of memory retrieval (1978), Psychological Review
Ratcliff & McKoon, The diffusion decision model: theory and data for two-choice decision tasks (2008), Neural Computation
Wiecki, Sofer & Frank, HDDM (2013), Frontiers in Neuroinformatics
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: Ratcliff, R., & McKoon, G. (2008). The diffusion decision model. Neural Computation, 20(4), 873-922.

name: DriftScore (Behavioral Drift Score)
donor: Product analytics and composite index construction
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A 0–1 composite of normalised entropy, CTR, diversity and attention-decay signals, weighted by regression, where higher values mean greater risk that a user is drifting.
description: The DriftScore combines normalised telemetry signals into a single risk index: DriftScore = w1(1 − entropy_norm) + w2(1 − ctr_norm) + w3(1 − diversity_norm) + w4(attention_decay). Signals are normalised to [0,1] with higher meaning more engagement, then inverted where needed so higher scores mean more drift risk. Weights are set by regression or optimisation. In the e-commerce case with weights [0.4, 0.3, 0.3], P1 (entropy 1.0, CTR 0.18, 2 categories) scores 0.72 and P3 (0.9, 0.12, 1 category) 0.81, both drifting, while P2 (2.2, 0.44, 5 categories) scores 0.38. An action threshold is suggested, such as Score ≥ 0.50 for 2 consecutive weeks. The score's rigour comes from transparent components that map back to Honeycomb dimensions, and it is the objective that adaptive interventions and Thompson Sampling try to reduce.
steps: Select drift signals from telemetry: interaction entropy, recommendation or promo CTR, category or feature diversity, and attention decay (scroll depth, dwell).
Normalise each signal to [0,1] with higher meaning more engagement, then convert to risk (1 − entropy_norm, 1 − ctr_norm, 1 − diversity_norm, attention_decay).
Estimate weights via regression or optimisation against a later outcome such as churn or disengagement (examples use [0.3, 0.25, 0.2, 0.25] or [0.4, 0.3, 0.3]).
Compute the weighted sum per user per period.
Apply an action threshold, e.g. intervene if Score ≥ 0.50 for 2 consecutive weeks.
Use the score as the objective for adaptive interventions and A/B validation, and pair high scorers with interviews or diaries to confirm the mechanism.
outputs: Per-user drift risk scores, a ranked list of drifting users, and a trackable objective for interventions.
useWhen: When you need an operational early-warning metric for engagement erosion that product teams can monitor and act on.
avoidWhen: When signals are sparse or weights cannot be estimated; a hand-tuned score without validation can mislabel engaged but focused users.
whyLost: Original metric by Vivek Gopinath; most engagement scores reward frequency and miss narrowing behaviour.
whereToUse: E-commerce and OTT personalisation, CRM triggers, subscription retention, in-app re-onboarding.
example: An e-commerce team flags users whose DriftScore exceeds 0.50 for two weeks and routes them to a short tour of neglected categories, then tracks score reduction in an A/B test.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study

name: Dual-task performance testing
origin: Dual-task methods from Kahneman, Attention and Effort, 1973; secondary-task workload measurement in aviation human factors (Ogden et al., 1979)
summary: Measures the mental workload of a primary task by how much performance on a concurrent secondary task drops, giving an objective index of spare capacity.
description: If a primary task consumes most available capacity, performance on a secondary task, such as responding to a tone or a peripheral light, will degrade. Dual-task testing exploits this: it measures secondary task response time or accuracy while users perform the primary task under different designs, and compares against a single-task baseline. The difference indexes workload; designs that leave more spare capacity are less demanding. A detection response task (DRT, ISO 17488) standardises this for driving. The method can also test whether two real tasks can be performed together. Rigour requires choosing a secondary task that draws on the relevant resources, checking that primary task performance is maintained, and counterbalancing.
steps: Define the primary task and design variants to compare.
Choose a secondary task matched to the resources in question, such as a detection response task (respond to a vibration or light every 3-5 s).
Measure single-task baselines for both tasks for each participant.
Run dual-task conditions with 12-24 participants, counterbalanced, instructing them to prioritise the primary task.
Compute dual-task costs (secondary response time increase and miss rate) and check primary task performance did not drop.
Compare designs and set workload thresholds; for example, ISO 17488 DRT results are interpreted relative to reference tasks.
outputs: Single and dual-task performance data, dual-task cost per design, and a workload comparison between designs.
useWhen: When comparing designs for workload in demanding contexts like driving, surgery or control rooms, or when subjective workload scales seem insensitive.
avoidWhen: When tasks are low workload or a secondary task would be unsafe; use NASA-TLX or physiological measures instead.
whyLost: Well established in automotive and aviation human factors but largely absent in mainstream UX, which relies on self-report.
whereToUse: In-vehicle infotainment, surgical consoles, AR headsets, voice interfaces, and cockpits.
example: During simulated suturing, surgeons respond to a vibrotactile detection task with a 380 ms baseline. Using the current alert panel raises it to 720 ms; a simplified panel brings it to 480 ms, indicating substantially more spare capacity.
sources: Salvendy, G. (ed.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Handbook of Human Factors & Ergonomics (Salvendy)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 12 — Multiple Resource Theory — The Bandwidth of the Human
reference: International Organization for Standardization (2016). ISO 17488: Road vehicles, transport information and control systems, detection-response task (DRT) for assessing attentional effects of cognitive load in driving.

name: Early-Warning Signals of Critical Transitions
origin: Marten Scheffer, Stephen Carpenter and colleagues (2009, Nature); Vasilis Dakos et al. (2012)
summary: Detects rising autocorrelation, variance and slower recovery in a time series as signs that a system is approaching a tipping point, such as collapse of engagement.
description: Ecologists found that systems near a bifurcation recover more slowly from small perturbations, a phenomenon called critical slowing down. This appears in time series as rising lag-1 autocorrelation, rising variance and sometimes skewness or flickering, before a regime shift such as a lake turning turbid or a fishery collapsing. Rolling-window analysis with trend tests (Kendall's tau) and surrogate data provides statistical evidence. Applied at the level of individual users or communities, these indicators may warn that engagement, community health or a habit is losing resilience before it collapses, giving a theory-grounded alternative to opaque churn prediction.
steps: Select time series that represent system state (e.g. daily activity of a community, a user's weekly usage).
Detrend or filter the series (e.g. Gaussian kernel) to remove long-term trends.
Compute rolling-window indicators: lag-1 autocorrelation, variance, skewness.
Test for rising trends with Kendall's tau and compare with surrogate series to assess significance.
Validate on historical cases: do indicators rise before known collapses (churn, community death)?
Use validated indicators for monitoring and target resilience-building interventions.
outputs: Rolling indicator trends, statistical tests of early warnings, validation results and monitoring rules.
useWhen: Monitoring systems that can tip, such as online communities, habits, marketplaces, or individual engagement.
avoidWhen: Short, noisy series or systems driven by abrupt external shocks without approach to a tipping point.
whyLost: The method is recent and confined to ecology, climate and psychiatry research.
whereToUse: Community platforms, multiplayer games, habit-based apps, mental health apps, marketplaces.
example: A forum platform finds that in subreddits which later died, lag-1 autocorrelation of daily posts rose for 8 weeks before decline. A moderator alert based on this indicator enables early intervention.
sources: Scheffer et al., Early-warning signals for critical transitions (2009), Nature
Dakos et al., Methods for detecting early warnings of critical transitions in time series (2012), PLoS ONE
Scheffer, Critical Transitions in Nature and Society (2009)
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: Scheffer, M., et al. (2009). Nature, 461(7260), 53-59.

name: Ecological Interface Analysis
donor: Ecological psychology and cognitive systems engineering
origin: James J. Gibson, 1979; Vicente and Rasmussen, 1992 (EID)
summary: Applies Gibson's direct perception to make a domain's constraints and invariants directly visible, so users perceive system state instead of computing it.
description: Gibson argued that perception directly picks up information specified in the environment, such as invariants in the optic array, without elaborate inference. Ecological Interface Design (Vicente and Rasmussen) carried this into complex systems: rather than displaying raw variables, the interface should make the work domain's functional relationships and constraints perceptually obvious, so that operators can see when the system is heading out of bounds. The analytical method starts with an abstraction hierarchy of the work domain, from purpose to physical form, then designs displays whose geometry maps those relationships, such as configural graphics where a shape distorts when a constraint is violated. Rigour comes from deriving display elements from a formal domain analysis and testing fault detection, particularly for unanticipated events, against conventional displays.
steps: Build an abstraction hierarchy of the work domain from functional purpose down to physical form.
Identify key constraints and invariants operators must monitor, especially those violated in faults.
Design configural or emergent-feature displays where constraint violations produce visible changes in shape or pattern.
Prepare scenarios including routine, anticipated-fault and unanticipated-fault conditions.
Test with 8-16 domain users comparing detection time and diagnosis accuracy against the existing display.
Iterate on mappings that fail to support perception of the relevant constraint.
outputs: Abstraction hierarchy, constraint inventory, ecological display concepts, fault detection performance comparison.
useWhen: Process control, medical monitoring, energy, aviation and complex dashboards where operators must detect abnormal states quickly.
avoidWhen: Simple consumer interfaces without rich domain constraints; standard visual design and usability testing are enough.
whyLost: Latent: Theoretical basis for affordance concepts; ecological interface design; increasingly relevant for AR/VR.
whereToUse: Ecological interface design; AR/VR; ambient computing.
example: A grid-battery operator dashboard listed 40 numeric readings. An ecological redesign mapped charge balance to a polygon that skewed visibly when cells diverged; operators detected an injected imbalance fault in 8 seconds rather than 47.
sources: The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
Cognitive Work Analysis (Kim Vicente)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Vicente KJ & Rasmussen J (1992) Ecological interface design: theoretical foundations. IEEE SMC 22(4):589-606
Burns CM & Hajdukiewicz J (2004) Ecological Interface Design

name: Economic Games (Prisoner's Dilemma, Public Goods, Trust and Ultimatum)
donor: Experimental economics and behavioural game theory
origin: Prisoner's dilemma (Flood and Dresher, RAND, 1950); ultimatum game (Güth, Schmittberger and Schwarze, 1982); trust game (Berg, Dickhaut and McCabe, 1995); public goods with punishment (Fehr and Gächter, 2000)
summary: Incentivised interactive games that measure cooperation, trust, reciprocity and fairness, used to test how design features change social behaviour.
description: Economic games put participants in standardised strategic situations with real money. The prisoner's dilemma and public goods game measure cooperation when individual and group interests conflict; the trust game measures how much one sends to another who may return it; the ultimatum game measures fairness norms and rejection of unfair offers. Repeated versions, communication and punishment options test institutions. Because they have known equilibria and large comparative literatures, deviations are interpretable. For UX of social, collaborative and marketplace products, games embedded in prototypes test how reputation systems, anonymity, visibility or AI mediators change cooperative behaviour, beyond what users say.
steps: Choose the game that matches the social dilemma in the product (e.g. trust game for marketplace transactions).
Implement the game with real, meaningful incentives (e.g. oTree), and design conditions varying product features (reputation display, anonymity).
Recruit participants and run sessions with clear instructions, comprehension checks and random matching.
Record decisions over multiple rounds and post-game beliefs.
Analyse contributions, trust and reciprocity with mixed models accounting for groups and rounds.
Translate behavioural differences into design implications and validate in field data.
outputs: Cooperation, trust and fairness measures by design condition, with dynamics over rounds.
useWhen: Designing reputation, review, collaboration, sharing-economy or community features where social behaviour determines outcomes.
avoidWhen: Individual tasks without strategic interdependence.
whyLost: Experimental economics labs and UX research teams rarely overlap; games feel artificial to practitioners.
whereToUse: Marketplaces, peer-to-peer lending, open-source and community platforms, team tools, multiplayer games.
example: A P2P rental platform tests reputation badges in a trust game; showing transaction history raises amounts sent by 28% and reciprocation by 15%, while star ratings alone do not differ from control.
sources: Camerer, Behavioral Game Theory (2003)
Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe, Trust, reciprocity, and social history (1995), Games and Economic Behavior
Fehr & Gächter, Cooperation and punishment in public goods experiments (2000), American Economic Review
reference: Camerer, C. F. (2003). Behavioral Game Theory. Princeton University Press.

name: EEG in UX Research
origin: Hans Berger, 1924 (EEG); applied in HCI and neuroergonomics from the 1990s-2000s
summary: Records electrical brain activity during interaction to estimate workload, attention and engagement continuously, without interrupting the task.
description: Electroencephalography measures voltage fluctuations from neural activity via electrodes on the scalp, with millisecond temporal resolution but poor spatial resolution. In HCI, frequency-band measures (for example frontal theta increases and parietal alpha decreases with workload) and event-related potentials (such as the P300 to unexpected or task-relevant events) provide continuous indices of cognitive state. Modern dry-electrode and mobile headsets make field studies possible but reduce signal quality. Rigour is demanding: controlling artefacts from movement, blinks and muscle tension; using baselines and within-subject designs; time-locking events precisely; using sufficient trials; and validating indices against behavioural and subjective measures. Claims about specific emotions or 'engagement' from consumer headsets should be treated cautiously, since many proprietary metrics lack peer-reviewed validation.
steps: Define the cognitive state of interest (e.g. workload) and the EEG index that has evidence for it.
Choose equipment suited to the setting (research-grade lab system or validated mobile headset).
Design within-subject tasks with baselines and precisely time-stamped events, with enough repetitions per condition.
Record from 15-30 participants, monitoring signal quality during sessions.
Pre-process: filter, remove artefacts (e.g. with ICA) and extract band power or ERP components.
Analyse condition differences and validate against NASA-TLX, performance or other measures.
outputs: Workload, attention or ERP indices by condition and over time, validated against behavioural and subjective measures.
useWhen: High-stakes or high-workload interfaces (aviation, driving, clinical), adaptive interfaces, gaming and VR studies needing continuous measures.
avoidWhen: Routine product questions answerable by usability testing or questionnaires; most teams lack the expertise and the effect on design decisions is small.
whyLost: Siloed: Specialist equipment; interpretation expertise required; mostly academic and specialized neuromarketing.
whereToUse: High-stakes interface evaluation; gaming; immersive/VR experience research.
example: An automotive HMI team compared two touchscreen menu designs while participants drove in a simulator. Frontal theta indicated higher workload for the deeper menu, consistent with more lane deviations, supporting the flatter design.
sources: Neuroscience Exploring the Brain
Signal Processing for Neuroscientists
Neuroergonomics: The Brain at Work (Parasuraman & Rizzo)
reference: Parasuraman, R., & Rizzo, M. (Eds.) (2007). Neuroergonomics: The Brain at Work. Oxford University Press.

name: Effect size (Cohen's d, η², ω²)
origin: Jacob Cohen (1962; 1988); eta squared from Pearson (1905); omega squared from Hays (1963)
summary: Quantifies how large a difference or relationship is, independent of sample size, so UX decisions rest on magnitude rather than on statistical significance alone.
description: Statistical significance depends heavily on sample size; effect size measures magnitude. Cohen's d expresses a mean difference in standard deviation units, with conventional benchmarks of 0.2 small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large, which Cohen himself cautioned were a last resort. Eta squared (η²) is the proportion of variance explained in ANOVA but is positively biased in samples; omega squared (ω²) corrects this bias and is preferred for population inference. For proportions, absolute differences, relative risk and odds ratios are often more meaningful to stakeholders. In UX, raw unstandardised effects such as seconds saved or percentage points of conversion are frequently the most interpretable. Rigour comes from reporting effect sizes with confidence intervals, choosing the measure that fits the design, and interpreting magnitude against practical criteria.
steps: Choose the effect size suited to the design: Cohen's d or Hedges' g for two means, ω² or partial ω² for ANOVA, r for correlations, and risk differences or odds ratios for proportions.
Compute the effect size and its 95% confidence interval, using Hedges' g correction for small samples (below about 20 per group).
Also report the unstandardised effect in natural units, such as seconds, percentage points or scale points.
Interpret magnitude against practical benchmarks agreed with stakeholders, such as a minimum of 10 seconds saved or 1 point on SUS, not only Cohen's conventions.
Use the effect size and interval from completed studies to inform power analyses and priors for future studies.
Report effect sizes for non-significant results too, to support meta-analysis and avoid file-drawer bias.
outputs: Standardised and raw effect sizes with confidence intervals, interpreted against practical significance thresholds.
useWhen: Reporting any comparison or relationship, planning studies, comparing results across studies, and judging whether a significant difference matters.
avoidWhen: Purely descriptive qualitative work; for highly skewed or ordinal data, use rank-based effect sizes such as Cliff's delta or rank-biserial correlation instead of d.
whyLost: Effect sizes are routinely required in academic psychology but UX reports and A/B dashboards often show only p-values or 'significant' flags.
whereToUse: A/B test readouts, usability benchmark comparisons, survey segment differences, research meta-analysis across studies.
example: Two onboarding designs differed in SEQ ratings with p = 0.003 across 1,200 users, but Cohen's d was 0.17 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.28), equivalent to 0.2 scale points. The team judged the difference too small to justify the costlier design.
sources: Statistics for Dummies series (Rumsey)
Designing Experiments & Analyzing Data (Maxwell & Delaney)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 41 — Frequentist Inference Done Right
reference: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum; Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science. Frontiers in Psychology, 4, 863.

name: Effect size calculation
origin: Jacob Cohen, 1962 and 1988; advocated by the APA Task Force on Statistical Inference (Wilkinson, 1999)
summary: Quantifying how large a difference or relationship is, with a confidence interval, so UX findings convey practical importance rather than just statistical significance.
description: An effect size expresses magnitude on an interpretable scale: raw differences (seconds saved, percentage-point completion gains), standardised differences (Cohen's d, Hedges' g), variance explained (eta squared, R squared), odds ratios, or rank-based measures (rank-biserial r, Cliff's delta). A p-value conflates effect size with sample size, so large analytics samples make trivial differences 'significant' and small usability samples hide large ones. Rigour comes from choosing the effect size that matches the design (Hedges' g for small samples, d_z for paired designs), always reporting a confidence interval, preferring unstandardised units when they are meaningful to stakeholders, and judging importance against a pre-stated smallest effect of interest rather than Cohen's generic benchmarks.
steps: Before analysis, state the smallest effect size of interest in product terms (e.g. 5 percentage points in completion, 10 seconds in task time).
Choose the effect size matching the design: Hedges' g for independent small samples, d_z or d_av for paired data, odds ratio for binary outcomes, rank-biserial for ordinal tests.
Compute it with a confidence interval (pingouin.compute_effsize with bootstrap CIs, or analytical intervals).
Report the unstandardised difference alongside the standardised value whenever units are meaningful.
Interpret against the pre-stated threshold and prior benchmarks, using Cohen's 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 only as a last resort.
Use the observed effect and its interval to plan the sample size for follow-up studies.
outputs: Effect estimates with confidence intervals, a comparison against the smallest effect of interest and inputs for future power analysis.
useWhen: Every comparative or correlational quantitative UX analysis, especially A/B tests with huge samples and small usability studies where significance is unreliable.
avoidWhen: Not a substitute for causal design; an effect size from confounded observational data is still biased. For purely descriptive single-group studies, report confidence intervals around the estimate instead.
whyLost: UX reporting borrowed significance testing from marketing and analytics dashboards, which emphasise p-values and lift; effect sizes with intervals are taught but rarely reported.
whereToUse: A/B testing programmes, usability benchmarking, survey segment comparisons and research-informed prioritisation.
example: A fintech A/B test on 400,000 users reports p below 0.001 for a new transfer flow. The effect size shows a 0.3 percentage-point completion gain with CI 0.1 to 0.5, below the 1-point threshold the team had set, so the change is not prioritised.

name: Effort × impact grid
origin: Popularised in consulting and lean practice; related to Eisenhower matrix and value-versus-complexity grids
summary: Plots candidate actions on estimated impact versus effort to prioritise quick wins and major bets, ideally using evidence-based impact estimates rather than guesses.
description: The effort-impact grid sorts possible design changes or research recommendations into quadrants: quick wins (high impact, low effort), major projects, fill-ins and money pits. Its weakness in common use is that both axes are guessed in a workshop, so the grid launders opinion into apparent rigour. A rigorous version grounds impact in research evidence (affected users times severity times outcome effect, or model-based forecasts), estimates effort with engineering input, attaches uncertainty to each estimate, and revisits placements after delivery. It is a communication and decision tool, not an analysis in itself.
steps: List candidate actions derived from research findings.
Estimate impact from evidence, e.g. affected users times severity times expected outcome change, with low and high bounds.
Obtain effort estimates from engineering and design (e.g. person-weeks or t-shirt sizes with ranges).
Plot items on the grid, showing uncertainty as bars or ellipses rather than points.
Discuss borderline items, agree priorities and record the rationale.
After delivery, compare realised impact and effort with estimates to calibrate future grids.
outputs: A prioritised action list with evidence-based placements, uncertainty and a recorded rationale.
useWhen: Turning a set of research findings into a prioritised roadmap with stakeholders.
avoidWhen: Avoid when impact cannot be estimated at all (do more research), or for decisions with strong dependencies and strategic factors better handled by RICE scoring or roadmapping.
whyLost: The 2x2 is ubiquitous but usually populated with gut-feel estimates, so its rigour has been hollowed out.
whereToUse: Research readouts, usability findings prioritisation, product roadmap workshops, design sprints.
example: A fintech team plots 14 usability issues using impact estimates from funnel analysis and severity ratings. Fixing the ID upload error is a clear quick win with an estimated 3-point completion gain for one week of effort.
sources: Storytelling with Data (Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic)
Articulating Design Decisions (Tom Greever)
Envisioning Information (Edward Tufte)
Rubin & Chisnell, Handbook of Usability Testing (severity rating)
Storytelling with Data (Knaflic)
Articulating Design Decisions (Greever)
Envisioning Information (Tufte)

name: Effort × Impact Prioritisation Grid
donor: Management consulting and lean product practice
origin: Practitioner tool, widely used in product management
summary: A 2×2 grid placing evidence-based fixes by effort and impact so low-effort, high-impact changes ship first and high-effort, low-impact ones are deferred.
description: The grid sorts prescriptions into four quadrants: low effort/high impact (prioritise immediately, e.g. relabel Notifications), high effort/high impact (schedule for roadmap, e.g. redesign the OTP flow), low effort/low impact (opportunistic, e.g. tweak copy) and high effort/low impact (avoid or defer). In Vivek Gopinath's Prescribe stage the impact rating is grounded in quantitative drivers (hazard ratios, SHAP importance, Monte Carlo lifts) rather than opinion, and each fix also carries a decision bar. The playbook warns that not quantifying effort leads teams to miss low-effort, high-impact fixes that should leapfrog others.
steps: List candidate fixes from the evidence ⇒ prescription table.
Rate impact from quantitative drivers (HR, SHAP rank, forecast lift).
Rate effort with design and engineering partners.
Place each fix in one of the four quadrants.
Sequence: low effort/high impact now, high effort/high impact on roadmap, defer high effort/low impact.
Attach decision bars to each fix and revisit after validation.
outputs: A prioritised quadrant chart and sequenced fix list.
useWhen: When a study produces several recommendations and the team must sequence them.
avoidWhen: When impact cannot be estimated from evidence; the grid then becomes guesswork. Use an experiment or forecast first.
whyLost: Survives because it is simple and fits product planning rituals; rigour depends on evidence-based impact ratings.
whereToUse: Research readouts, sprint planning, roadmap reviews.
example: Relabelling Notifications lands in low effort/high impact and ships this sprint, while redesigning the OTP flow is high effort/high impact and goes on the quarterly roadmap.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers

name: Eidetic variation
origin: Edmund Husserl (Ideas, 1913; Experience and Judgment, 1939); adapted for empirical psychology by Amedeo Giorgi and for qualitative research by Moustakas (1994)
summary: Identifies the essential structure of an experience by imaginatively varying its features and noting which changes would make it no longer the same kind of experience.
description: Husserl proposed that the essence of a phenomenon can be found by freely varying its features in imagination: if a feature can be removed or changed and the experience remains the same kind of experience, it is contingent; if changing it destroys the experience, it is essential. In empirical phenomenology, the researcher applies this to participants' descriptions. For example, in the experience of 'submitting a claim and waiting', is uncertainty about receipt essential, or would a confirmed receipt leave the experience intact? This distinguishes invariant structures from incidental details of particular cases. For UX it offers a disciplined way to decide what a design must address and what can vary. Rigour comes from systematic variation of each constituent, documented reasoning, and checking variations against actual participant accounts.
steps: Start from a set of rich first-person descriptions of the experience, typically 5 to 15 participants, already broken into meaning units.
List candidate constituents of the experience, such as waiting, uncertainty, being judged, effort, and dependence on others.
For each constituent, imagine it removed or radically altered and ask whether the experience would still be the same kind of experience, recording the reasoning.
Check imagined variations against actual cases: do any participants' accounts lack the constituent while remaining the same experience?
Classify constituents as essential (invariant) or contingent (variable), and describe how essential constituents relate to one another.
Translate the essential structure into design requirements and the contingent features into acceptable design variation.
outputs: A documented set of variation analyses, a list of essential and contingent constituents, and an essential structure statement with design implications.
useWhen: Understanding the core of an experience across varied contexts; deciding which aspects of a service must be preserved when redesigning or digitising it.
avoidWhen: Questions are about frequency, preference or usability defects; use surveys or usability testing. Not appropriate without rich first-person descriptions.
whyLost: Phenomenological philosophy is rarely taught in UX, and 'phenomenology' in practice often means only open-ended interviews, without the analytic operations such as variation.
whereToUse: Health and insurance claims, bereavement and life-event services, financial stress experiences, AI-mediated service experiences, high-anxiety moments.
example: Analysing accounts of submitting digital health insurance claims, researchers varied 'confirmation of receipt'. Imagining it removed turned the experience into anxious limbo, and two participants who lacked it described exactly that, so confirmation was classified as essential and prioritised over speed.
sources: Fundamentals of Qualitative Research
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 30 — Phenomenological Methods — The Structure of Lived Experience
reference: Giorgi, A. (2009). The Descriptive Phenomenological Method in Psychology: A Modified Husserlian Approach. Duquesne University Press; Husserl, E. (1913/1983). Ideas Pertaining to a Pure Phenomenology. Nijhoff.

name: Eligibility criteria definition
origin: Clinical trial methodology, mid-20th century; target trial framing by Hernán & Robins, 2016
summary: Defines precisely which users enter an analysis or study, using criteria measurable at time zero, so the population matches the decision and avoids selection bias.
description: In clinical trials, eligibility criteria define who could be randomised; in target trial emulation they must be applied using only information available at time zero. UX analyses frequently violate this, for example by restricting to users who remained active for 30 days, which conditions on the future and builds survivorship bias into the comparison. Good criteria are explicit, measurable, tied to the population a decision will affect, and documented with a participant flow diagram showing how many were excluded at each step. The same discipline improves recruitment screeners for qualitative studies, where vague criteria produce unrepresentative samples.
steps: State the decision and the population it will affect (e.g. new retail investors in their first 90 days).
Write inclusion and exclusion criteria using only variables known at or before time zero.
Check every criterion for dependence on post-baseline information (activity after time zero, survival, later purchases) and remove such criteria.
Apply criteria sequentially to the data and record counts excluded at each step in a CONSORT-style flow diagram.
Compare included and excluded users on key characteristics to describe generalisability.
outputs: Explicit criteria, a participant flow diagram with counts, and a statement of the population the results apply to.
useWhen: Every observational log analysis, target trial emulation, experiment population definition and recruitment screener.
avoidWhen: Rarely wrong to apply; it is lighter-weight in early exploratory qualitative work where breadth matters more than a precise population.
whyLost: Clinical research mandates it, but UX analyses define populations ad hoc in queries, and filters conditioning on the future go unnoticed.
whereToUse: Retention and feature-effect analyses, experiment targeting, regulated fintech and health studies, research recruitment.
example: An analysis of a savings nudge restricts to users with at least 3 deposits in month one. Rewriting criteria to use only information at sign-up removes a survivorship bias that had doubled the apparent effect.
sources: Causal Inference: What If (Miguel Hernán & James Robins)
DAGs+SEM Playbook (Vivek Gopinath)
CONSORT 2010 Statement (Schulz, Altman & Moher)
Causal Inference (Hernán & Robins)
DAGs+SEM Playbook (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 48 — Target Trial Emulation — Causal Evidence from Log Data
reference: Schulz, K. F., Altman, D. G. & Moher, D. (2010) CONSORT 2010 Statement: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials. BMJ, 340, c332.

name: Elim-First attribute identification
donor: Mathematical psychology and consumer decision research
origin: Amos Tversky's elimination by aspects model (1972); non-compensatory choice research by Payne, Bettman and Johnson (1993)
summary: Identifies the attributes users apply first to eliminate options before any trade-off, so designs surface and satisfy these screening criteria.
description: Tversky's elimination by aspects model describes choice as sequential: people pick an important attribute, discard all options that fail it, and repeat until one option remains. It is non-compensatory, so excellence on other attributes cannot rescue an option eliminated early. Elim-First attribute identification finds which attributes users eliminate on first and the cut-offs they use. In UX this explains why a technically superior option is never considered: it failed a screening aspect such as 'works offline', 'in my language' or 'no upfront fee' before comparison began. Rigour comes from process-tracing methods (information display boards, think-aloud, eye tracking or click-stream order) rather than stated importance ratings, which systematically confuse screening and trade-off attributes.
steps: List 8 to 20 candidate attributes for the decision from interviews and competitor analysis, defining each with clear levels.
Build an information display board or mock comparison interface where attribute values are hidden until clicked, so search order and stopping can be logged.
Run 15 to 40 participants through 3 to 6 realistic choice tasks while thinking aloud, logging which attribute they open first, which options they discard and why.
Classify each attribute by whether it was used to eliminate options, the order of use, and the stated cut-off (for example 'more than 2% fee, gone').

Rank attributes by elimination frequency and median position in the search sequence; attributes used for elimination by more than about 40% of participants in the first two steps are screening attributes.
Validate with a larger survey using a screening question format (for example 'Would you consider an option that...?') and check the design surfaces screening attributes early and visibly.
outputs: A ranked list of screening attributes with typical cut-offs, search-order patterns by segment, and design recommendations for what must appear first in listings, comparison tables and onboarding.
useWhen: Users face many alternatives (plans, providers, products, clinical options) and conversion is low even though your option is strong on paper; you need to design filters, comparison tables or recommendation logic.
avoidWhen: Decisions are genuinely compensatory and low in number of options; conjoint analysis or MaxDiff better quantifies trade-offs.
whyLost: Choice process tracing stayed in decision science and marketing academia; UX and product research adopted stated-importance surveys and conjoint, which assume compensatory trade-offs.
whereToUse: Fintech and insurance comparison, marketplace search and filters, health plan selection, B2B vendor evaluation, AI recommendation explanations.
example: A savings product with the best rate saw few sign-ups. Process tracing showed 55% of rural participants first eliminated any option without withdrawal at local agents; once agent withdrawal was surfaced as the first filter and badge, consideration rose sharply.
sources: Heuristics & Biases (Kahneman ed.)
Judgment Under Uncertainty
Choices Values & Frames (Kahneman/Tversky)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 21 — Heuristics, Biases & the Architecture of Judgment
reference: Tversky, A. (1972). Elimination by aspects: A theory of choice. Psychological Review, 79(4), 281–299.

name: Elimination by Aspects in Interface Choice Design
donor: Mathematical psychology and consumer decision research
origin: Amos Tversky, 1972
summary: Models how users choose by eliminating options that fail on the most important attribute in turn, guiding design of comparison, filtering and plan-selection interfaces.
description: Elimination by aspects is a non-compensatory choice model: rather than weighing all attributes, decision makers select an attribute (with probability proportional to its importance), eliminate options lacking it, and repeat until one option remains. Strengths on other attributes cannot compensate for failing an early cut. Consumer research uses it to explain filtering behaviour and choice overload. For interface design, the model predicts that users facing many options will screen on a few key aspects, so comparison tables, filters and pricing pages should expose the aspects people eliminate on first and in the right order. The method elicits elimination sequences through process tracing (think-aloud, information boards, filter logs) and fits attribute weights, distinguishing compensatory from lexicographic strategies.
steps: Identify first-elimination attributes through interview: 'What would make you immediately reject this option?' Surface that attribute first and most prominently.
outputs: Ranked elimination aspects, observed screening sequences, proportion of users using non-compensatory strategies, and recommendations for filter order and comparison design.
useWhen: Designing plan pickers, product listings, filters, comparison tables and any interface where users choose among many options with multiple attributes.
avoidWhen: When choices involve few options or genuine trade-offs that users weigh carefully (use conjoint analysis), or when you lack process data on how people screen.
whyLost: It is standard in consumer behaviour and choice modelling but did not migrate to UX, where choice interfaces are usually tested only for conversion rather than decision strategy.
whereToUse: Pricing pages, feature comparison tables, filter UI design.
example: A mobile carrier's plan page lists 14 plans with 9 attributes. Filter logs and think-aloud sessions show users eliminate first on data allowance, then contract length, so the page leads with those two filters and conversion rises with fewer plan-comparison exits.
sources: Preference, Belief, and Similarity — Amos Tversky
Tversky, Elimination by aspects: A theory of choice (Psychological Review, 1972)
Payne, Bettman & Johnson, The Adaptive Decision Maker (1993)
reference: Tversky A (1972) Elimination by aspects: A theory of choice. Psychological Review 79(4):281-299

name: Eliminative Materialism Critique of Mental Model Constructs
aka: Construct validity audit of mental-model terms
origin: Paul and Patricia Churchland (1981, 1986)
summary: Interrogates whether folk-psychological constructs such as user intention, goal and mental model are valid units of analysis, prompting operational definitions and behavioural evidence.
description: Eliminative materialism argues that folk psychology, the everyday vocabulary of beliefs, desires and intentions, is a theory that may be false and could be replaced by a mature neuroscience. Whatever its philosophical merits, it raises a practical question for UX research: constructs such as 'user intention', 'goal' and 'mental model' are folk concepts that researchers often treat as directly observable. The method is a construct audit. For each such construct in a study, the researcher states its operational definition, what evidence would indicate it (verbal reports, choices, eye movements, errors), and whether different measures converge. Where they do not, findings are reframed in terms of observed behaviour and predictions. This improves construct validity and guards against reifying participants' after-the-fact explanations as causes.
steps: Apply eliminative skepticism to UX research constructs: for each construct used in research ('the user intended to...', 'the user's mental model is...'), ask:
is this construct operationalized in behavior, or inferred?

(2) would different explanatory constructs (neural, computational, behavioral) better predict the phenomenon? Use behavioral measures (response time, error pattern, eye movement) alongside inferential mental-model constructs.
outputs: Construct inventory with operational definitions, convergent evidence assessment, and reframed findings that distinguish observed behaviour from inferred mental states.
useWhen: Research that leans on inferred mental states: mental-model studies, intent modelling, AI 'understanding' claims and theory-building in research programmes.
avoidWhen: Routine evaluative studies where folk terms are used loosely without affecting decisions; the audit adds little there.
whyLost: It is a philosophical position confined to philosophy of mind and cognitive science; UX research has little tradition of auditing the validity of its own constructs.
whereToUse: Research construct validity analysis, theory-driven UX research, neuroscience-informed user modeling, AI behavior explanation research.
example: A team claims users 'intend' to save articles for later because they say so in interviews. A construct audit shows save actions are rarely followed by returns, so the team reframes the feature as bookmarking-as-closure and measures it accordingly.
sources: Neurophilosophy — Patricia Smith Churchland
Churchland PM, Eliminative materialism and the propositional attitudes (Journal of Philosophy, 1981)
reference: Churchland PS (1986) Neurophilosophy: Toward a Unified Science of the Mind-Brain. MIT Press

name: EM algorithm for missing session data
origin: Arthur Dempster, Nan Laird & Donald Rubin, 1977
summary: Estimates model parameters and plausible values for incomplete session data by alternating between expected values of missing parts and maximum likelihood updates.
description: Session logs are routinely incomplete: dropped events, SDK failures, consent opt-outs, cross-device gaps. Deleting incomplete records biases analyses unless data are missing completely at random. The EM algorithm treats missing values as latent: the E-step computes their expected sufficient statistics given current parameters and observed data, and the M-step updates parameters to maximise likelihood. Iterating converges to maximum likelihood estimates under a missing-at-random assumption. EM also underlies Gaussian mixtures and many latent variable models. For inference, multiple imputation (e.g. MICE) often complements EM, so uncertainty from missingness is carried into standard errors. Rigour requires describing missingness patterns, reasoning about the mechanism and running sensitivity analysis for missing-not-at-random scenarios.
steps: Quantify missingness per variable and per session and visualise patterns (e.g. missing by platform or app version).
Assess the plausible mechanism (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) with domain knowledge and tests such as Little's MCAR test.
Specify a model for the data (e.g. multivariate normal or mixture) and run EM from several starting values until log-likelihood changes fall below a tolerance (e.g. 1e-6).
Use EM estimates for parameters, or create 5-20 multiple imputations to propagate uncertainty into analyses.
Compare results with complete-case analysis and run a sensitivity analysis under plausible MNAR departures.
Fix the instrumentation causes of missingness where possible.
outputs: Parameter estimates and imputed datasets that account for missingness, with documented assumptions and sensitivity results.
useWhen: When behavioural or survey datasets have substantial missingness (e.g. above 5%) that complete-case analysis would bias.
avoidWhen: Avoid when data are missing not at random with no plausible model, or when missingness is trivial; fix logging if it is systematic.
whyLost: UX analysts usually drop incomplete records; missing data theory is taught in statistics programmes rather than research practice.
whereToUse: Cross-device behavioural analysis, consent-limited analytics, longitudinal panels, survey programmes with item non-response.
example: Twelve percent of investment sessions lack portfolio-view events because of an SDK bug on older Android devices. EM-based estimation under a missing-at-random model corrects an apparent under-engagement of Android users that complete-case analysis had shown.

Deep Learning (Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio & Aaron Courville)
Methods Atlas (Vivek Gopinath)

Deep Learning (Goodfellow)

The Inquiry Series, Ch 53 — Generative Models & Synthetic User Testing

name: Embodied Cognition Research
origin: Varela, Thompson and Rosch, 1991; Dourish, 2001 (embodied interaction)
summary: Studies how bodily action, posture, gesture and physical setting shape users' thinking, to design and evaluate spatial, gestural and tangible interactions.
description: Embodied cognition rejects the view that thinking is purely symbolic manipulation in the head. Perception, action and environment are treated as constitutive of cognition: people think with gestures, use spatial arrangement to reason and offload memory onto objects. Paul Dourish brought this into HCI as embodied interaction, arguing that meaning arises through engaged action. As a research approach it combines observation of bodily behaviour (gesture coding, posture, movement traces), manipulation of physical conditions (sitting vs standing, hands free vs encumbered) and measures of task performance and comprehension. Rigour comes from treating the body and setting as variables rather than noise, coding movement systematically, and testing whether interaction designs that align with natural action, such as spatial mappings or physical metaphors, improve learning and accuracy compared with abstract alternatives.
steps: Specify which bodily dimensions matter for the product: gesture, posture, reach, locomotion, tool use or spatial layout.
Observe 6-12 users performing tasks in realistic physical settings, recording video from at least two angles.
Code gestures, body movements and environmental offloading using a predefined scheme, double-coding at least 20% of footage.
Introduce controlled manipulations (e.g. encumbered hands, different spatial mappings) to test embodied hypotheses.
Compare performance, errors and comprehension across conditions and relate them to coded behaviour.
Translate findings into interaction mappings, gesture vocabularies and spatial layouts aligned with natural action.
outputs: Gesture and movement codebook, behaviour-performance analysis, embodied interaction design principles for the product.
useWhen: AR/VR, gesture and voice-plus-gesture interfaces, wearables, tangible and in-vehicle interfaces where the body is part of the interaction.
avoidWhen: Standard desktop or mobile screen flows with conventional input; conventional usability testing is more efficient.
whyLost: Latent: Strong in academic cognitive science; slowly entering UX for embodied/spatial computing design.
whereToUse: AR/VR design; gesture interfaces; physical-digital interaction; tangible computing.
example: A VR training product for warehouse pickers tested abstract menu selection against reaching to virtual shelves. Coding showed users mimed real reaching anyway; the spatial mapping cut training errors by a third.
sources: The Embodied Mind
Supersizing the Mind
Designing Across Senses
Where the Action Is (Paul Dourish)
reference: Dourish, P. (2001). Where the Action Is: The Foundations of Embodied Interaction. MIT Press.

name: Embodied Experience Research
origin: Draws on Varela, Thompson & Rosch (1991) and Christopher Noessel's work on multi-sensory interaction design
summary: Investigates how bodily and multi-sensory experience (sound, touch, haptics, motion) shapes product perception, through a sensory channel audit and embodied-metaphor interviews.
description: Most UX research assumes experience is visual and verbal. Embodied cognition argues that understanding is grounded in bodily experience, so people describe and judge products through physical metaphors: something feels 'heavy', 'sticky' or 'smooth'. This approach first audits every sensory channel a product engages (visual, auditory, haptic, motion, even temperature or smell for physical products) and checks for cross-sensory incoherence, such as a playful sound on a serious error. It then uses embodied interview prompts that ask participants to describe the feel of using the product in physical terms, and maps those metaphors to specific interaction moments. Rigour comes from systematic channel coverage and from analysing metaphors across participants rather than collecting colourful quotes.
steps: Sensory channel audit: List all sensory channels your product engages: visual, auditory, haptic, proprioceptive. Most UX research studies only visual.

Cross-sensory coherence check: Conflicting sensory signals? Visual communicates 'calm/trustworthy' while audio communicates 'urgent'? Incoherence produces users reporting something 'feels wrong' without specifying why.

Embodied interview technique: 'If you had to describe the feeling of using this in physical terms — texture, weight, temperature — what would you say?' Embodied metaphors reveal non-verbal experience.
Analysis: Map embodied metaphors to product moments. Clusters at specific interaction points reveal tacit reactions participants cannot articulate functionally.
outputs: A sensory channel inventory, a cross-sensory coherence report, coded embodied metaphors mapped to product moments, and recommendations for sound, haptic and motion design.
useWhen: Products with significant non-visual channels: wearables, voice and in-car interfaces, haptic mobile interactions, connected devices, or brands where 'feel' is a differentiator.
avoidWhen: The product is a primarily textual or data-entry interface where sensory design is not a lever; standard usability testing is more efficient. For measuring arousal use Multi-Channel Affective Measurement.
whyLost: UX research developed in screen-based, visual-first contexts and lacks vocabulary and tools for non-visual channels, so embodiment stayed in academic HCI and industrial design.
whereToUse: Wearables and health devices, automotive HMI, voice assistants, haptics on mobile, smart home products, and premium consumer brands.
example: A smartwatch team audits notification feedback and finds the same strong vibration for a calendar nudge and a heart-rate alert. Embodied interviews show users describe the watch as 'nagging'; distinct haptic patterns by urgency follow.
sources: Designing Across Senses (Chris Noessel)
Affective Computing (Picard)
Embodied Mind (Varela)
reference: Varela, F. J., Thompson, E. & Rosch, E. (1991). The Embodied Mind. MIT Press.

name: Embodied Simulation and Interface Metaphor Grounding
origin: Lawrence Barsalou (1999); Glenberg and Kaschak's action-sentence compatibility effect (2002); Benjamin Bergen (2012)
summary: Tests whether interface labels, gestures and metaphors evoke mental simulations compatible with the required action, using response-time compatibility effects and comprehension measures.
description: Embodied simulation theory holds that understanding language involves partially re-enacting the perceptual and motor experiences it describes. Glenberg and Kaschak's action-sentence compatibility effect showed that people respond faster when the response direction matches the motion implied by a sentence. Bergen summarises evidence that people simulate orientation, direction, shape and effort. For interfaces, labels and metaphors such as 'swipe up to archive' or 'pull to refresh' are understood partly by simulation, so mismatches between the implied and the required action slow responses and cause errors. The method identifies the action or spatial content each label implies, measures response times and errors when required actions match or conflict with it, and favours wording and gesture mappings that evoke compatible simulations.
steps: Test simulation ease of interface labels: present labels in isolation, ask users to describe the action the label refers to and mime the motion (if applicable). Measure:
response latency (faster = easier simulation),
action consistency across participants (% agreement on the described action),
simulation accuracy (does the simulated action match the actual afforded action?). Labels with latency > 1.5s or accuracy < 70% are redesign candidates.
outputs: Inventory of implied actions in labels and gestures, compatibility test results (response time and error differences), and revised mappings.
useWhen: Gesture-based interfaces, spatial and direction labels, AR and VR controls, automotive controls and any label tied to a physical action.
avoidWhen: For abstract labels with no spatial or motor content, or when you lack the ability to measure response times precisely; use comprehension testing.
whyLost: Embodied cognition remained in psycholinguistics labs, and its reaction-time paradigms were never translated into practical UX test protocols.
whereToUse: Feature naming, CTA design, gesture interface label design, voice assistant command design. Bergen's book provides the most accessible empirical grounding for embodied interface metaphor research.
example: A photo app labels a gesture 'push back to dismiss' while requiring an upward swipe. A compatibility test shows 120 ms slower responses and 8% more errors than with the label 'swipe up to dismiss', so the copy is changed.
sources: Louder Than Words — Benjamin K. Bergen
Glenberg & Kaschak, Grounding language in action (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2002)
Barsalou, Perceptual symbol systems (Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 1999)
reference: Bergen BK (2012) Louder Than Words: The New Science of How the Mind Makes Meaning. Basic Books

name: Emotional Design Audit (Walter Hierarchy)
donor: Interaction design, adapted from Maslow's hierarchy of needs
origin: Aarron Walter, 2011 (Designing for Emotion)
summary: Scores a product against Walter's functional, reliable, usable and pleasurable tiers to show where design investment will pay off before pursuing delight.
description: Aarron Walter adapted Maslow's hierarchy to products: a design must first be functional, then reliable, then usable, and only then can it be pleasurable. The audit scores each tier from 1 to 5 using evidence (defect and outage data for reliability, usability findings for usability, affective measures for pleasure) rather than opinion. The hierarchy is treated as strict: investment in personality, micro-interactions or brand moments is wasted while a lower tier sits below 4. The audit then identifies a small number of peak emotional moments in the journey (first use, success, recovery from error) where pleasure work should concentrate. Its value is as a prioritisation discipline that stops teams polishing delight on top of unreliable foundations.
steps: Score each level (1–5): Functional (does it work?), Reliable (consistently?), Usable (without frustration?), Pleasurable (genuine positive emotion?).
The hierarchy is strict: A product cannot be experienced as pleasurable if it is not usable. Do not invest in pleasurability before usability is solid.
Focus investment where the lowest level falls below 4.
Peak moment design: Three peak emotional moments in the user journey (first use, first success, error recovery). Design each for a specific positive emotional response at the appropriate tier.
Validate tier placement with multi-channel affective measurement.
outputs: A tier scorecard with evidence for each score, the lowest failing tier flagged as the investment priority, and a shortlist of peak moments for emotional design work.
useWhen: Teams are debating whether to invest in delight, brand or personality versus fixing reliability and usability, or you need a simple frame to communicate design priorities to stakeholders.
avoidWhen: You need a validated measurement of emotional experience; this is a heuristic prioritisation tool. Use Multi-Channel Affective Measurement or a validated scale such as AttrakDiff or UEQ instead.
whyLost: It is remembered as a pyramid diagram on slides rather than run as an evidence-based scoring exercise, so the strict ordering and the evidence requirement are usually dropped.
whereToUse: Product roadmap reviews, design-system and brand refreshes, mature SaaS products considering 'delight' initiatives, and consumer apps with high churn.
example: A budgeting app team wants animated celebrations for savings goals. The audit scores reliability at 2 because bank syncs fail weekly, so the celebrations are deferred and sync failures fixed first; pleasure work then focuses on the first successful sync.
sources: Designing for Emotion (Aarron Walter)

name: Emotional Design Hierarchy Scoring
donor: Design practice drawing on motivational psychology
origin: Aarron Walter (2011), adapting Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs (1943)
summary: Scores an experience at each level of a hierarchy, functional, reliable, usable and pleasurable, ensuring lower levels are secure before investing in delight.
description: Walter's emotional design hierarchy adapts Maslow's needs hierarchy to products: an experience must first be functional (it works), then reliable (it works consistently), then usable (people can use it easily), and only then pleasurable (people enjoy it and form an emotional connection). Most teams stop at usable, while others add delight to flows that are not yet reliable, which backfires. As a scoring method, each key flow is rated at each level using evidence: defect and error logs for functional and reliability, usability metrics for usable, and affect measures (for example semantic differentials, emotional response cards or sentiment in feedback) for pleasurable. The result is a profile showing where investment should go. It pairs with aesthetic-usability effect measurement to prevent pleasure masking usability problems.
steps: Audit the current design against the hierarchy: score each level (1–5).
Calculate: what is the minimum score at each level?
Focus improvement where the lowest level falls below 3.
Once lower levels score ≥ 4, invest in the next level.
For emotional design: identify three peak moments in the user journey (first use, achievement, recovery from error) and design each to produce a specific positive emotion.
outputs: Per-flow scores at each hierarchy level with supporting evidence, identification of the lowest unmet level, and prioritised investments.
useWhen: Prioritising design investment across flows, planning delight or brand work, and diagnosing why emotional design efforts are not landing.
avoidWhen: When basic functionality and reliability are clearly unmet (fix those first without a scoring exercise), or when you need validated psychometric measures of emotion.
whyLost: Delight became a buzzword, and the hierarchy is quoted on slides but rarely scored with evidence at each level.
whereToUse: Consumer product emotional design, brand-aligned interaction design, onboarding experience design, long-term engagement design.
example: A savings app plans celebratory animations on goal completion, but scoring shows the deposit flow fails reliability with 3% failed transfers. The team fixes reliability first, then the success screen's pleasurable tier lifts goal-setting retention.
sources: Designing for Emotion — Aarron Walter
Well Designed (Kolko)
100 Things Every Designer Should Know (Weinschenk)

The Inquiry Series, Ch 36 — Emotional Design Hierarchies & the Aesthetic-Usability Effect

name: Empirical touch target derivation
origin: Parhi, Karlson and Bederson, 2006; Holz and Baudisch, 2010; Henze et al., 2011 large-scale touch studies
summary: Derives minimum touch target sizes from measured touch-offset distributions for a specific device, posture and population, rather than relying on generic guidelines.
description: Platform guidelines (44 pt on iOS, 48 dp on Android, 9-10 mm physical) are averages from particular populations and conditions. Empirical derivation measures where real users actually touch when aiming at targets, under the real conditions of use: gloves, motion, one-handed grip, tremor or screen angle. Touch points form a roughly bivariate normal distribution around the intended centre, often systematically offset. The target size needed for a given hit rate follows from the distribution's spread: covering about plus or minus 2 standard deviations gives roughly 95% accuracy in each dimension. Rigour comes from realistic conditions, enough taps per location to estimate offsets across the screen, and reporting sizes for the accuracy required by the task's risk level.
steps: Define the conditions of use (device, mount angle, gloves, posture, motion, user population) and the required accuracy (for example 99% for irreversible actions, 95% for routine).
Build a calibration task presenting crosshair targets at a grid of at least 9-25 screen locations.
Collect at least 20 taps per location per participant from 12-20 participants under realistic conditions.
Compute mean offset vectors and standard deviations in x and y for each location.
Derive target size as the width covering the required proportion of the distribution (about 4 SD for 95%, 5.2 SD for 99%) and apply location-specific offset correction where offsets exceed 1 mm.
Validate derived sizes in a task-level test with fresh participants and compare error rates against guideline sizes.
outputs: Touch offset maps, spread statistics, derived minimum target sizes per accuracy level and screen region, and offset-correction parameters.
useWhen: When users operate under unusual constraints (gloves, vibration, tremor, kiosks at odd angles, children, older adults) or when touch errors are costly.
avoidWhen: For standard consumer apps used in ordinary conditions where platform guidelines are adequate; use guideline audits instead.
whyLost: Platform guidelines made calibration feel unnecessary, so teams cite them uncritically; calibration studies survive mainly in academic HCI and specialist device makers.
whereToUse: Surgical and industrial touchscreens, automotive displays, field service tablets, accessibility for motor impairments, and public kiosks.
example: Theatre nurses wearing double sterile gloves showed touch spreads of 3.1 mm SD and a 2 mm downward offset on a tilted console. Derived 99% targets were 16 mm, far above the 9 mm guideline, and the redesign cut mis-taps from 7% to under 1%.
