name: End-to-end research pipeline orchestration
origin: Workflow management tools such as Make (1976), Apache Airflow (Airbnb, 2014) and Prefect (2018)
summary: Defining the whole research data flow, from audio to transcripts, NLP, AI coding and synthesis, as orchestrated, logged tasks so it runs reliably, resumes after failure and can be reproduced.
description: An orchestrator (Prefect, Airflow, or a Makefile for small projects) represents each stage as a task with inputs, outputs and dependencies: convert audio, transcribe, diarise, run the NLP pipeline, run AI coding passes, aggregate and produce reports. It handles retries, caching of completed steps, parallelism and logging. For research this gives reproducibility (one command reruns everything), auditability (logs show what ran on which data with which versions) and robustness for hundreds of files. Rigour comes from idempotent tasks, versioned configuration, explicit quality gates between stages, and storing intermediate outputs so any result can be traced back.
steps: Map the pipeline as a dependency graph of stages with defined inputs and outputs.
Implement each stage as an idempotent task that can be rerun safely and skips already-processed files.
Configure retries (e.g. 3 with backoff) for API and transcription failures, and log errors per file.
Place quality gates between stages that halt or flag runs failing thresholds.
Store configuration (model versions, prompts, thresholds) in version-controlled files and record them with each run.
Run end to end on a pilot batch of 5-10 files before full scale, then schedule or trigger runs as new data arrive.
outputs: An orchestrated pipeline, run logs, cached intermediate outputs and reproducible final datasets and reports.
useWhen: Programmes processing many recordings or documents repeatedly, such as continuous interviewing, multi-country studies or ongoing feedback analysis.
avoidWhen: Avoid for one-off small studies; a script or notebook is enough. Orchestration overhead only pays off with repetition or scale.
whyLost: Orchestration is a data engineering discipline; research teams rarely run pipelines large or repeated enough to need it, until AI-assisted analysis.
whereToUse: Research operations, continuous discovery, voice-of-customer programmes and research repositories.
example: A research operations team processes 40 new interviews weekly. A Prefect flow converts, transcribes, diarises, codes and aggregates them overnight, with failed files retried and a summary report waiting each morning.

name: Endowment effect test
origin: Richard Thaler (1980) and Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler's mug experiments (1990)
summary: Measures how much more users value something once they own it, by comparing willingness to accept giving it up with willingness to pay to acquire it.
description: In Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler's experiments, owners of a coffee mug demanded roughly twice what non-owners would pay for it. The endowment effect explains why users resist giving up configured settings, saved data, legacy plans or familiar workflows, and why trials, customisation and early ownership cues raise retention. The test randomly endows some participants with an item (a plan, a feature, a data asset, a design they built) and compares the price or effort they require to give it up with what non-endowed participants would pay or do to get it. A ratio of willingness to accept to willingness to pay well above 1 indicates endowment. Rigour comes from random assignment of ownership, incentive-compatible elicitation such as the Becker-DeGroot-Marschak mechanism, and controls for information differences.
steps: Choose the good to test: a feature, plan, saved configuration, content library or self-made artefact, and define how ownership is created (granted, trialled or self-built).
Randomly assign 40 to 100 participants per condition to owner and non-owner conditions, ensuring both groups receive identical information about the good.

Elicit willingness to accept from owners and willingness to pay from non-owners using an incentive-compatible method such as Becker-DeGroot-Marschak, or a realistic equivalent like choosing between keeping the good and a credit amount.
Compute the median WTA/WTP ratio with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval and test the difference with a Mann-Whitney U test.
Add a variant that varies ownership duration or effort invested (for example 1 day versus 14 days of trial, or a template versus a self-built item) to estimate how endowment grows.
Apply results to design decisions about trials, migration paths, downgrades and customisation, and check them against observed retention.
outputs: WTA/WTP ratios with confidence intervals, the effect of ownership duration or effort, and implications for trials, migrations and pricing.
useWhen: Designing free trials, onboarding personalisation, plan downgrades, data migrations or feature sunsets, where ownership may shape value.
avoidWhen: You cannot create genuine ownership in the study, or the decision is simple enough to test directly with a retention A/B test of trial length.
whyLost: UX speaks loosely of 'investment' and the IKEA effect in growth design, but the experimental WTA/WTP protocol remained in economics labs.
whereToUse: SaaS trials and freemium, data portability and migration, legacy plan grandfathering, creator tools, subscription cancellation flows (ethically).
example: A note-taking app tested whether users who had built their own templates for 14 days valued premium templates more. Owners demanded a credit 2.4 times higher than non-owners would pay, and the team moved the template builder into the trial's first session.
sources: Prospect Theory works (Kahneman/Tversky)
Nash Equilibrium in UX (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 23 — Reference Points, Prospect Theory & the Mechanics of Satisfaction
reference: Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J. L., & Thaler, R. H. (1990). Experimental tests of the endowment effect and the Coase theorem. Journal of Political Economy, 98(6), 1325–1348.

name: Enhanced Cognitive Interview (Forensic)
origin: Ronald Fisher and Edward Geiselman, 1984-1992 (Memory-Enhancing Techniques for Investigative Interviewing, 1992)
summary: A memory-retrieval interview protocol that uses context reinstatement, report-everything instructions, varied retrieval orders and perspectives to elicit more accurate recall of past events.
description: Developed to improve eyewitness interviews, the cognitive interview applies memory research: mentally reinstating the physical and emotional context of the event, asking witnesses to report everything without editing, recalling events in different orders (e.g. reverse), and from different perspectives. The enhanced version adds rapport building, transferring control to the witness, open-ended questioning, witness-compatible questioning and avoidance of interruption. Meta-analyses show substantial increases in correct details with little increase in errors. Not to be confused with cognitive interviewing for questionnaire pretesting, it is ideal for UX interviews about past incidents, purchases or experiences where memory quality matters.
steps: Build rapport and explain that the participant is the expert and should report everything, even trivial details.
Guide context reinstatement: ask them to picture the place, time, device, mood and what they were trying to do.
Elicit a free narrative without interruption; take notes for later probes.
Probe with open, participant-compatible questions about images and details they mentioned.
Use varied retrieval: reverse order, different perspectives, focusing on specific senses or screens.
Summarise back, invite corrections and close with neutral, non-leading questions.
outputs: Richer, more accurate accounts of past experiences with fewer leading-question distortions.
useWhen: Interviewing about specific past events: incidents, fraud experiences, purchase decisions, errors, switching moments.
avoidWhen: Questions about general attitudes or hypothetical futures, where episodic recall is not the goal.
whyLost: Forensic psychology is far from UX training, and the name collides with survey 'cognitive interviewing'.
whereToUse: Fraud and scam victim research, incident investigations, JTBD switch interviews, healthcare adverse events.
example: Interviewing scam victims, researchers use context reinstatement and reverse-order recall; participants recall the exact screen where a fake banking notification appeared, details absent from standard interviews, informing a warning redesign.
sources: Fisher & Geiselman, Memory-Enhancing Techniques for Investigative Interviewing: The Cognitive Interview (1992)
Memon, Meissner & Fraser, The cognitive interview: A meta-analytic review and study space analysis of the past 25 years (2010), Psychology, Public Policy, and Law
reference: Fisher, R. P., & Geiselman, R. E. (1992). Memory-Enhancing Techniques for Investigative Interviewing. Charles C. Thomas.

name: Entity-level aggregation
origin: Aspect-based opinion mining, Hu and Liu, 2004
summary: Rolling up extracted entities and their associated sentiment, context and speakers across a corpus to see which features, competitors or workflows matter to whom.
description: After entities are extracted, aggregation turns mentions into analysable summaries: how many participants (not mentions) referred to each feature, with what sentiment or evaluation, in which segments, and alongside which other entities. The participant-level count matters because one talkative participant can dominate mention counts. Aspect-based analysis (Hu and Liu, 2004) links opinions to the entity they target rather than to the whole document. Rigour comes from normalising entity variants (lemmatisation, alias tables), counting at the participant level, reporting co-occurrence carefully, and treating counts as pointers back to transcripts rather than as prevalence estimates for the user population.
steps: Normalise entity mentions to canonical names using an alias table (e.g. 'auto-pay', 'autopay', 'recurring payments').
Attach to each mention its speaker, participant attributes, sentence-level sentiment or evaluation and context.
Aggregate at participant level: number and percentage of participants mentioning each entity, by segment.
Compute entity co-occurrence within participants or passages and visualise as a matrix or network.
Link every aggregate cell back to its underlying quotes so analysts can read the evidence.
State clearly that counts describe the sample, not population prevalence, unless sampling supports inference.
outputs: Entity-by-segment tables, sentiment summaries, co-occurrence matrices and drill-down links to quotes.
useWhen: Summarising large interview, feedback or ticket corpora by feature or topic, and comparing segments.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting mention counts as importance in small qualitative samples; importance should come from analysis of meaning and consequence.
whyLost: Aspect-based analysis lives in commercial text analytics and NLP research; UX researchers rarely have entity-extracted data to aggregate.
whereToUse: Voice-of-customer dashboards, support ticket analysis, competitive research and research repositories.
example: Across 150 interviews, aggregation shows 62% of enterprise participants but only 18% of SMB participants mention 'permissions', mostly negatively, and it co-occurs with 'admin onboarding'. Analysts read the linked quotes before prioritising.

name: Environmental Ergonomics Assessment
origin: Human factors engineering, post-WWII; ISO 11064 and related standards
summary: Measures the physical conditions of use (lighting, glare, noise, temperature, vibration, posture) and their effect on interaction performance.
description: Environmental ergonomics studies how ambient conditions affect human performance. The treatise names environmental analysis as one of the rigorous human factors methods UX left behind. An assessment measures luminance and glare, ambient noise, vibration, temperature, gloves or protective equipment, and posture at the actual point of use, then tests whether display legibility, audio cues, touch accuracy and attention hold up. Its rigour lies in instrumented measurement (lux meter, sound level meter) and in testing interfaces under representative conditions rather than in a quiet lab. For mobile, field and industrial software, environmental conditions often explain failures that lab testing cannot reproduce.
steps: List the environments where the product is used and select representative sites.
Measure illumination, glare, noise, vibration, temperature and equipment constraints at each site.
Observe posture, grip, gloves and interruptions during real use.
Test legibility, audio cue detection and touch accuracy under the measured conditions or a lab simulation.
Identify mismatches between interface specifications and environmental limits.
Set environmental design requirements such as contrast ratios, cue loudness and target size for gloved use.
outputs: Environmental measurement log, failure list under conditions, environment-adjusted design requirements.
useWhen: Field, industrial, outdoor, vehicle and clinical products; any case where lab results do not match field complaints.
avoidWhen: Products used only in controlled office settings; standard usability testing suffices.
whyLost: UX matured around desktop office software where environment seemed constant, and lost contact with the ergonomics community.
whereToUse: Outdoor mobile apps, factory HMIs, delivery-driver apps, ambulance and ICU software, in-car UX.
example: Delivery drivers miss order notifications; site measurements show 85 dB cab noise and direct sunlight on the screen. The team adds haptic alerts and a high-contrast outdoor mode.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Parsons KC (2000) Environmental ergonomics: a review of principles, methods and models. Applied Ergonomics
Salvendy G (Ed) Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
reference: Parsons KC (2000) Environmental ergonomics: a review of principles, methods and models. Applied Ergonomics 31(6):581-594.

name: Environmental Legibility Analysis (Lynch)
origin: Kevin Lynch, 1960
summary: Uses sketch maps and Lynch's five elements (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks) to assess how easily users form a cognitive map of a space or information architecture.
description: Lynch's The Image of the City asked residents to draw maps and describe journeys, revealing that legible cities are structured by paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks. The treatise notes that environmental legibility, how easily a user builds a cognitive map of a space, translates directly to information architecture. Applied to digital products, participants sketch the structure of a site or app from memory, describe how they would get somewhere, and the analyst codes the sketches for Lynch elements, distortions and omissions. The result shows which sections function as districts, which pages act as landmarks and where users lack a coherent map, complementing tree tests that measure findability without revealing the mental map.
steps: Recruit users with varying exposure to the product (new, regular, expert).
Ask each to sketch the product's structure from memory and describe routes to key destinations.
Code sketches for paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks, plus omissions and distortions.
Aggregate into a composite image showing commonly recalled elements.
Compare with the actual IA to locate illegible regions.
Strengthen landmarks, districts and edges in the design and re-test.
outputs: Coded sketch maps, composite cognitive map, legibility gaps, IA recommendations.
useWhen: Large sites, apps with deep navigation, VR worlds, multi-product suites.
avoidWhen: Single-screen tools or when only findability metrics are needed (use tree testing).
whyLost: Spatial metaphors for information faded after the 1990s; IA adopted card sorting and tree testing instead.
whereToUse: Enterprise suites, documentation sites, e-commerce category structures, VR and game worlds.
example: Sketch maps of a cloud console show users recall only three 'districts' out of nine; services not near a remembered landmark are rarely found, so the team introduces persistent service-group landmarks.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Lynch K (1960) The Image of the City
Kitchin R (1994) Cognitive maps: what are they and why study them? J Environmental Psychology
Dillon A & Vaughan M (1997) 'It's the journey and the destination': shape and the emergent property of genre. Interacting with Computers

name: Environmental Psychology Assessment
origin: Roger Ulrich (1984), Rachel and Stephen Kaplan (1989), Kevin Lynch (1960)
summary: Applies environmental psychology instruments (legibility, restorativeness, preference, wayfinding) to digital and spatial environments to assess their psychological effects.
description: Environmental psychology studies how designed environments affect behaviour, emotion and cognition. The treatise cites Ulrich's restorative environments research, the Kaplans' attention restoration theory and Lynch's environmental legibility as sources of methods for assessing the psychological effects of spaces that apply directly to digital environments. In the 1990s these informed work on information spaces and virtual environments; with VR and AR, the treatise argues, they are more relevant than ever. Typical instruments include preference ratings, perceived restorativeness scales, sketch maps, wayfinding tasks and physiological stress measures. The priority index rates the area HIGH (evidence 5, impact 5).
steps: Specify the environment (virtual, physical-digital or information space) and outcomes (stress, legibility, wayfinding, preference).
Select validated instruments such as perceived restorativeness scales, sketch maps or wayfinding tasks.
Expose participants to the environment or controlled variants, in situ or in VR.
Measure behavioural, self-report and where feasible physiological responses.
Compare variants and relate spatial features to outcomes.
Derive design guidance for spatial structure, landmarks and restorative qualities.
outputs: Environment ratings, wayfinding performance, legibility maps, design guidance.
useWhen: VR/AR environments, large information spaces, physical-digital services such as hospitals and stations.
avoidWhen: Small, task-bound interfaces with no spatial or environmental character.
whyLost: 1990s information-space work faded with the web's page paradigm; few UX researchers train in environmental psychology.
whereToUse: Metaverse and XR apps, wellbeing apps, hospital wayfinding apps, smart buildings, games.
example: A VR meditation app compares three environments on the Perceived Restorativeness Scale and a post-session attention task; the forest scene improves attention scores while the abstract scene does not.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Ulrich RS (1984) View through a window may influence recovery from surgery. Science 224

Lynch K (1960) The Image of the City

name: Epidemic Models (SIR/SEIR) for Adoption and Virality
origin: William Kermack and Anderson McKendrick, 1927
summary: Models users moving between compartments (susceptible, exposed, infected/active, recovered/churned) to estimate spread rates, reproduction numbers and saturation.
description: Compartmental models describe populations moving between states via rates: in SIR, susceptible people become infected through contact (rate beta) and recover (rate gamma). The basic reproduction number R0 = beta/gamma determines whether spread grows. SEIR adds an exposed (latent) stage; SIRS allows reinfection. Fitted to adoption or referral data, these models describe viral growth, word-of-mouth, feature adoption within organisations and even spread of misinformation or abusive behaviour on platforms. They distinguish contact rate from 'stickiness' (recovery) and quantify interventions, much more precisely than a 'viral coefficient' computed from a single cohort.
steps: Define compartments relevant to the product (e.g. unaware, aware, active, lapsed) and transitions.
Collect time series of counts in each compartment, or referral chains if available.
Fit model parameters by maximum likelihood or Bayesian methods, with uncertainty.
Estimate effective reproduction number over time and check fit to observed curves.
Simulate interventions: increasing contact (sharing), reducing churn (recovery), seeding.
Validate predictions on new cohorts or markets.
outputs: Fitted transmission and churn rates, reproduction numbers, projected adoption curves and intervention scenarios.
useWhen: Products growing by word-of-mouth or referrals, internal spread within organisations, or harmful content spreading on platforms.
avoidWhen: Growth driven mainly by paid acquisition or one-off external events.
whyLost: Growth teams use simple viral coefficients; epidemiological modelling skills are rare in product teams.
whereToUse: Referral programmes, collaboration tool spread within enterprises, social features, misinformation dynamics.
example: A note-taking app fits an SEIR model to team-level adoption and finds R below 1 in teams under 10 people because of a long latent period; a shared template launch shortens latency and lifts R above 1.
sources: Kermack & McKendrick, A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics (1927), Proceedings of the Royal Society A
Anderson & May, Infectious Diseases of Humans (1991)
Keeling & Rohani, Modeling Infectious Diseases in Humans and Animals (2008)
reference: Kermack, W. O., & McKendrick, A. G. (1927). Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 115(772), 700-721.

name: Equivalence testing (TOST)
origin: Donald Schuirmann (1987), developed for bioequivalence trials; popularised in psychology by Daniël Lakens (2017)
summary: Tests whether an effect is small enough to be considered practically equivalent to zero, allowing teams to conclude 'no meaningful difference' rather than merely 'not significant'.
description: A non-significant result does not show that two designs are equivalent; it may reflect low power. Equivalence testing reverses the logic: you set equivalence bounds, the smallest effect that matters (for example ±2 percentage points of conversion or ±0.3 SEQ points), and run two one-sided tests to check whether the effect is significantly above the lower bound and significantly below the upper bound. If both are significant, you conclude equivalence. Equivalently, the 90% confidence interval lies entirely within the bounds. Non-inferiority tests use only one bound, asking whether a new design is not meaningfully worse. In UX this supports decisions like simplifying a flow, migrating platforms or adding a guardrail without harming a metric. Rigour comes from pre-specifying bounds based on practical relevance and powering the test for equivalence.
steps: Set equivalence bounds based on the smallest effect of interest, justified by business or user impact, for example ±0.25 standard deviations or ±1.5 percentage points.
Plan the sample for equivalence power (often larger than for a difference test), using tools such as the TOSTER package or G*Power-like calculators.
Collect data and run two one-sided tests at alpha 0.05: H01 effect ≤ lower bound and H02 effect ≥ upper bound.
Conclude equivalence if both nulls are rejected, which corresponds to the 90% confidence interval lying within the bounds.
Report the TOST p-values, the 90% and 95% intervals, and the ordinary difference test so readers see both perspectives.
For one-sided questions such as 'the new flow is not worse', run a non-inferiority test with a single margin.
outputs: Equivalence or non-inferiority conclusions with TOST p-values, confidence intervals relative to pre-set bounds, and documented bound justifications.
useWhen: Showing that a redesign, migration, cost-saving simplification, accessibility change or guardrail metric did not meaningfully harm outcomes.
avoidWhen: No defensible smallest effect of interest can be agreed, or samples are too small to achieve narrow intervals; report estimates with intervals and acknowledge uncertainty.
whyLost: Equivalence testing is routine in pharmaceutical regulation but almost absent from UX, where non-significant results are routinely misread as proof of no effect.
whereToUse: Platform migrations, design system rollouts, accessibility improvements, removing steps from flows, guardrail metrics in A/B tests, AI model replacements.
example: After replacing a three-step checkout with a two-step one, the team needed to show conversion did not fall. With bounds of ±1 percentage point, the 90% CI for the difference was -0.4 to +0.7, so TOST supported equivalence (p = 0.008), allowing rollout.

name: Error Taxonomy (Slips, Lapses, Mistakes)
aka: Error Taxonomy (Reason's Slips, Lapses and Mistakes)
origin: Donald Norman, 1981 (action slips); James Reason, 1990 (Human Error)
summary: A coding scheme classifying each breakdown as a Slip (right intention, wrong execution), Lapse (attention or memory failure) or Mistake (wrong mental model), each implying a distinct fix.
description: Derived from Norman's analysis of action slips and Reason's Generic Error Modelling System, the taxonomy explains why users fail. In Vivek Gopinath's operationalisation: Slip, correct goal but wrong execution (mis-tap adjacent row); Lapse, attention or memory failure (forgot OTP digits after switching apps, timed out); Mistake, wrong mental model or decision (looked under Notifications for price alerts). Each maps to a design lever: slips to motor and affordance fixes (hit areas, spacing, error prevention), lapses to memory and attention support (progress save, copy/paste, timer messaging), mistakes to IA, labelling or conceptual change. Sessions are moderated think-alouds (n = 10–15, 30–40 minutes) on the same tasks as the tree test, with a short example-rich codebook and two coders on 30–40% of sessions (κ ≥ 0.70). Results are tabulated by step per 100 sessions.
steps: Write a one-page codebook defining Slip, Lapse and Mistake with product-specific examples.
Run 10–15 moderated think-aloud sessions of 30–40 minutes on the target tasks, recording screen and audio.
Code every breakdown with step, error code, coder ID and quote.
Double-code 30–40% of sessions and compute Cohen's κ; if below 0.70, refine definitions and examples, retrain and re-code.
Tabulate codes by step per 100 sessions (e.g. Find Alerts: 12 slips, 18 lapses, 39 mistakes; OTP: 6, 22, 5).
Map each dominant error type to its fix family and enter it in a joint display.
outputs: A coded error table by step with κ, representative quotes and fix families.
useWhen: When you need to explain why errors occur and turn findings into specific design levers.
avoidWhen: When there are too few observable breakdowns to code, or for attitudinal questions; use interviews or surveys.
whyLost: Rigorous in aviation, medicine and nuclear safety, but UX usually reports generic 'errors' without mechanism or reliability.
whereToUse: Fintech flows, OTP and verification steps, medical devices, enterprise forms, AI-assisted workflows.
example: Coding trading-app sessions shows Mistakes dominate navigation and rule definition while Lapses dominate the timed OTP step, leading to relabelling for the former and an extended OTP window with reassurance copy for the latter.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Reason J (1990) Human Error. Cambridge University Press
Rasmussen J (1983) Skills, rules, and knowledge. IEEE SMC
Norman DA (1981) Categorization of action slips. Psychological Review
Design for How People Think
Human-Computer Interaction
The Design of Everyday Things (Don Norman)
Human Error (James Reason)

name: Ethical Reporting
origin: Social science research ethics; codified in professional codes such as the British Sociological Association and AAA ethics guidelines
summary: Protects participants in published findings through anonymisation, composite cases, renewed consent and harm assessment, guarding against identification, stigma and misrepresentation.
description: Harm to participants often happens after the interview, when findings circulate. Ethical reporting treats the report itself as a risk. Names are replaced with consistent pseudonyms and indirect identifiers (role, location, rare conditions, distinctive phrases) are removed or generalised, since in small organisations or niche user groups a job title plus a quote can identify someone. Where identifiable detail is analytically necessary, researchers may construct composite cases and must say so. Consent is revisited when findings will be published more widely than originally agreed. Before release, a harm assessment asks how participants would be affected if their manager, community or insurer read the report, and whether the framing stigmatises a group. Rigour lies in anticipating secondary audiences and documenting each protective decision.
steps: Anonymisation protocol: Replace all names with pseudonyms consistently. Remove identifying details: job titles, locations, specific dates. Check: could someone reading this identify this participant?
Composite cases: When direct quotes could identify a participant, construct composite cases preserving the analytical insight. Disclose compositing in the methods section.
Consent for publication: Original consent may not cover all subsequent publication contexts. Confirm with participants before each new publication context.
Harm assessment: Could any participant be harmed by this report being read by their employer, family, or government? If yes: what further steps are required?
outputs: An anonymisation log, de-identified quotes and cases, composite case disclosures, consent records for publication, and a documented harm assessment.
useWhen: Reporting research with employees, patients, vulnerable or small populations, B2B customers who could be recognised, or when findings will be shared externally, published or stored in a widely accessible repository.
avoidWhen: It always applies when data comes from people; only its intensity varies. For data governance before analysis, see Ethics of AI-Assisted Qualitative Analysis and consent procedures.
whyLost: UX teams focus ethics on recruitment and consent forms and treat internal reports as safe, while repositories and screenshots spread identifiable data far beyond the original audience.
whereToUse: Internal enterprise research, healthcare and fintech studies, research repositories and highlight reels, conference talks and case studies, and employee experience research.
example: Research with 9 nurses on a ward system includes quotes criticising a named manager. The researcher removes ward identifiers, generalises roles, merges two accounts into a disclosed composite, and confirms consent before the findings go to hospital leadership.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Research Ethics
User Research (Marsh)
Research Design (Leavy)
reference: Wiles, R. (2013). What Are Qualitative Research Ethics? Bloomsbury.

name: Ethics of AI-Assisted Qualitative Analysis
origin: Emerging practice, 2023 onwards, following LLM adoption in qualitative data analysis software
summary: A governance protocol for using AI in qualitative analysis, covering disclosure, data privacy, reliability checks against human coders, and human authority over interpretation.
description: Generative AI can now segment, code and summarise interview transcripts in minutes, but it does not interpret. This protocol treats AI as a junior coder whose work must be disclosed, validated and overruled where necessary. It specifies what to report (model, version, prompts, tasks delegated), how to protect participant data (local or contractually bounded models, de-identification before upload, consent wording that covers machine processing), and how to establish reliability: AI-applied codes are compared with an independent human coder using Cohen's kappa before the AI output is trusted at scale. Interpretation, theme construction and claims about meaning remain human work. Its rigour lies in treating AI output as a measurement instrument with error that must be quantified, rather than as an oracle, and in an audit trail that lets reviewers see exactly where machine judgement entered the analysis.
steps: Disclosure in reporting: Report which AI system, for which coding tasks, with what IRR validation. Non-disclosure is an ethical violation.
Data privacy: Cloud-based AI processes data on external servers. Use local models for sensitive participant data where consent does not cover external processing.
IRR requirement: AI-assisted coding without IRR validation is not rigorous. κ must be calculated and reported.
Human final authority: AI produces coded segments. Humans produce analysis, themes, and theoretical propositions.
outputs: An AI-use disclosure statement, a data-handling plan, human-AI agreement statistics (kappa per code), a log of overruled AI codes, and an audit trail separating machine coding from human interpretation.
useWhen: Your team is using LLMs or AI features in qualitative tools to code, cluster or summarise research data, especially with sensitive participants or findings that will inform consequential decisions.
avoidWhen: No AI is involved in the analysis, or the AI is used only for transcription with human verification. If you need to analyse data rigorously by hand, use Reflexive Thematic Analysis or Template Analysis directly.
whyLost: It is too new to be lost: the practice is known in principle but rarely operationalised, because AI coding features shipped faster than the governance norms around them and speed is the selling point.
whereToUse: Research repositories with AI tagging, synthesis of large interview sets, regulated domains (health, finance, government) where participant data cannot leave controlled infrastructure, and any research ops function setting policy for AI tooling.
example: A health-tech team uses an LLM to code 60 patient interviews. They run it on a locally hosted model, have a researcher independently code 15% of transcripts, find kappa of 0.58 on the 'medication anxiety' code, rewrite the code definition, retest to 0.76, and disclose the whole process in the report.
sources: AI for Humans (Heaton)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Research Ethics
reference: Braun, V. & Clarke, V. (2022). Thematic Analysis: A Practical Guide. Sage.

name: Ethnographic Decision Models (Gladwin)
origin: Christina Gladwin, 1970s-1989 (Ethnographic Decision Tree Modeling, 1989)
summary: Elicits the decision criteria people actually use from interviews, builds them into explicit decision trees, and tests their predictive accuracy on a new sample.
description: Gladwin studied why farmers chose particular crops or practices. She elicited decision criteria from informants, structured them as hierarchical decision trees with elimination by aspects and constraints, and then tested the trees on a separate sample of decision-makers, typically achieving 85-95% prediction accuracy. Errors were examined to refine the model. The method combines qualitative elicitation with quantitative validation, producing an explicit, testable model of real decision processes rather than assumed rational choice. For UX, it suits choices like which plan to buy, whether to switch providers, or whether to use a feature, producing models that can guide design and messaging.
steps: Choose a specific, recurrent decision (e.g. choosing a mobile money provider) and a sample of decision-makers.
Interview 20-30 informants about recent decisions, eliciting criteria, constraints and alternatives in their own terms.
Build a composite decision tree with ordered criteria, aspects and constraints.
Test the model on a new sample of 20-60 decision-makers by predicting their actual choices.
Analyse errors, revise the model and re-test where feasible.
Translate the model into design: support key criteria, remove constraints, and match messaging to decision order.
outputs: A validated decision tree model, prediction accuracy and an error analysis.
useWhen: Understanding and predicting real-world choices with a handful of key criteria, particularly in unfamiliar contexts.
avoidWhen: Highly impulsive or habitual choices without deliberation, or very complex trade-offs better modelled with conjoint.
whyLost: It belongs to economic anthropology and lost visibility as discrete choice models dominated decision research.
whereToUse: Financial inclusion products, B2B purchasing, health service choices, agritech, energy tariff switching.
example: A study of 30 street vendors in Nairobi yields a decision tree for accepting digital payments: the first criterion is whether customers expect it, then settlement speed. Tested on 50 vendors, it predicts 88% of choices.
sources: Gladwin, Ethnographic Decision Tree Modeling (1989), Sage Qualitative Research Methods Series 19
Bernard, Research Methods in Anthropology (6th ed., 2017)
reference: Gladwin, C. H. (1989). Ethnographic Decision Tree Modeling. Sage.

name: Ethnographic Research
origin: Bronisław Malinowski, 1922 (participant observation); brought into HCI by Lucy Suchman and colleagues at Xerox PARC, 1980s
summary: Extended immersion in people's settings to understand the culture, practices, values and meanings that shape behaviour and technology use.
description: Ethnographic research is a long-form, immersive approach from anthropology in which the researcher spends extended time in a community or setting, participating in and observing everyday life. The aim is a 'thick description' of practices, beliefs, social relations and meanings from the participants' perspective, including the tacit and taken-for-granted. In HCI, ethnography has shown how work and technology use are socially organised and situated. Rigour comes from prolonged engagement, detailed field notes written promptly, reflexivity about the researcher's influence, triangulation across observation, conversation and artefacts, and an iterative movement between fieldwork and analysis. Rapid or focused ethnography compresses the timeline but must still preserve immersion and reflexivity.
steps: Define a broad research question and negotiate access to the setting with gatekeepers and consent.
Spend extended time in the field, from several days for focused ethnography to weeks or months for full studies.
Combine participant observation, informal conversations and artefact collection.
Write detailed field notes the same day, separating observation from interpretation.
Keep a reflexive journal on your own position and influence.
Analyse iteratively, returning to the field to test emerging interpretations.
Produce thick descriptions and translate them into design implications.
outputs: Field notes, thick descriptions, cultural models of practice, artefacts and design implications grounded in context.
useWhen: For new market entry, unfamiliar cultures, underserved populations, or when social and cultural context strongly shapes behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid when questions are narrow, time is short or results must be statistically generalised; use contextual inquiry, interviews or surveys.
whyLost: Siloed: Lives mainly in academic HCI and specialized agency work; rarely done in product teams due to time and cost.
whereToUse: New market entry; complex cultural contexts; designing for underserved populations.
example: A mobile money provider sends researchers to spend three weeks in market towns in East Africa. They find that phones are often shared within households and that agents act as trusted advisers, reshaping PIN and account-recovery design.
sources: Handbook of Ethnography
Ethnographic Thinking
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Hammersley, M. & Atkinson, P. (2007). Ethnography: Principles in Practice (3rd ed.). Routledge.

name: Ethnographic Thick Description
origin: Clifford Geertz (1973); in technology research Xerox PARC (Suchman, Nardi, O'Day) and Intel (Bell, Salvador), 1980s-2000s
summary: Sustained fieldwork producing interpretive accounts that give full weight to context, meaning and participants' own categories rather than lists of needs.
description: Thick description is Geertz's term for accounts that interpret behaviour within its web of meaning, distinguishing a wink from a twitch. The ethnographic tradition in technology research brought trained anthropologists into product companies, spending extended time in the field, building sustained relationships and producing accounts both specific and theoretically rich. The treatise stresses that the difference from brief interview research is not only depth but epistemological orientation: what kinds of claims can be made, on what basis and with what confidence. Ethnographers did not arrive with questions and leave with needs; they let the participants' categories reorganise the research question. Thick description ethnography is in the treatise's curriculum.
steps: Negotiate access and define a field site and an open research question.
Spend extended time in the field (weeks to months), using participant observation and informal interviews.
Write detailed fieldnotes daily, separating description from interpretation.
Collect artefacts, photos and documents, and follow emerging threads.
Analyse iteratively, building interpretations grounded in members' categories.
Write a narrative account with implications for design and strategy, including reflexive notes.
outputs: Fieldnotes, interpretive ethnographic account, cultural models, strategic implications.
useWhen: Entering unfamiliar cultures, markets or practices; strategic questions about meaning and adoption.
avoidWhen: Narrow evaluation questions or tight timelines; use usability testing or rapid contextual interviews.
whyLost: Expensive, slow and hard to justify against sprint timelines; corporate ethnography teams were cut after the 2000s.
whereToUse: Emerging markets, financial inclusion, healthcare at home, family technology use, AI adoption in professions.
example: A remittance company embeds researchers with migrant families in two countries for six weeks; thick description reveals money transfers function as obligations negotiated in group chats, leading to a shared-request feature.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Geertz C (1973) The Interpretation of Cultures
Blomberg J et al. (1993) Ethnographic field methods and their relation to design. In Participatory Design
Nardi BA & O'Day VL (1999) Information Ecologies
Ethnographic Thinking (Hasbrouck)
Handbook of Ethnography
Rocking Qualitative Social Science
The Inquiry Series, Ch 31 — Ethnographic Fieldwork — Thick Description & Niche Construction
reference: Geertz C (1973) Thick description: toward an interpretive theory of culture. In The Interpretation of Cultures. Basic Books.

name: Ethnomethodology
origin: Harold Garfinkel, 1967 (Studies in Ethnomethodology); brought to HCI by Lucy Suchman (1987) and workplace studies
summary: Studies the practical methods people use to produce and recognise orderly social activity, showing how interaction with technology is accomplished moment by moment.
description: Ethnomethodology, founded by Harold Garfinkel, studies the methods members of a society use to make sense of and produce everyday social order. It treats rules, plans and categories not as causes of action but as resources people use and account for in situated activity. Lucy Suchman's Plans and Situated Actions applied it to show that users of a photocopier help system improvised in ways the system's plan-based model could not follow, a foundational insight for HCI. Ethnomethodological studies of work examine how coordination is achieved in settings like control rooms. Rigour comes from detailed analysis of recorded naturally occurring activity, focus on members' own categories and practices rather than analysts' theories, and close attention to sequence and embodied action.
steps: Select a setting where practical activity with technology can be recorded naturally, such as a control room or shared workspace.
Obtain consent and record video and audio of ongoing activity.
Transcribe selected episodes in detail, including talk, gesture and screen activity.
Analyse how participants make actions recognisable and accountable to each other, using their own categories.
Identify the practical methods that produce order, coordination and repair.
Translate findings into design implications for supporting situated action.
outputs: Detailed analyses of situated practices, descriptions of how coordination and sense-making are accomplished, and design implications.
useWhen: For collaborative and coordination-intensive tools, voice and conversational interfaces, and understanding how users make sense of system behaviour in practice.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need fast, broad answers or quantified results; use contextual inquiry or analytics. Requires specialist sociological training.
whyLost: Extinct in UX: Deep sociological foundations make practical application rare outside academic HCI.
whereToUse: Voice UI; social platforms; collaborative tool design.
example: A voice assistant team records families using a smart speaker at dinner. Analysis shows children treat the device's silence as a turn for someone else, so families talk over its responses, informing turn-taking cues.
sources: Handbook of Ethnography
Studies in Ethnomethodology (Garfinkel)
Plans and Situated Actions (Suchman)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Garfinkel H (1967) Studies in Ethnomethodology
Suchman L (1987) Plans and Situated Actions
Dourish P & Button G (1998) On 'technomethodology'. Human-Computer Interaction 13(4)
reference: Garfinkel, H. (1967). Studies in Ethnomethodology. Prentice-Hall; Suchman, L. A. (1987). Plans and Situated Actions. Cambridge University Press.

name: Ethnomethodology and Breaching Experiments
origin: Harold Garfinkel, 1967 (Studies in Ethnomethodology)
summary: Reveals the taken-for-granted methods people use to produce order by observing sense-making and, ethically, introducing small breaches that make tacit expectations visible.
description: Ethnomethodology (Garfinkel, 1967) studies how people practically produce and sustain the sense of orderly social life in everyday interaction. Its central insight: the rules and methods people use to make sense of their social world are so taken-for-granted that they are invisible — until they are broken. Garfinkel's 'breaching experiments' deliberately violated ordinary conversational and social rules to expose the tacit normative structure that ordinarily makes interaction seamless. Applied to UX: breaching reveals the implicit interaction contracts users bring to interfaces — contracts that, when violated, produce confusion, frustration, or the specific error type known as 'violation of expectation.'
steps: Naturalistic observation of sense-making: Observe how people handle moments of ambiguity, confusion, or breakdown in digital interactions. Focus on the repair work they do to restore sense — what assumptions do they invoke?

Indexicality analysis: Identify all the things that are left unsaid, pointed to, or taken for granted in a user's verbal account of their experience. These are the tacit background expectations that must be in place for interaction to work.

Breaching experiment design (applied): Deliberately introduce a small, controlled violation of a design convention — a non-standard icon placement, an unexpected response, a missing affordance. Observe the recovery work users do. What assumptions are they repairing from?

Documentary method: Analyse how users interpret ambiguous interface elements by treating their interpretation as 'documents of a pattern.' What underlying pattern are they reading the element against?
Analysis: Code repair sequences for: (a) what rule was assumed, (b) how the violation was detected, (c) what repair strategy was used, (d) whether repair succeeded or failed.
outputs: Documented sense-making practices, indexical expressions and assumed rules, breach-response records, repair sequence codes, and design implications about users' tacit expectations.
useWhen: You need to surface tacit conventions users rely on but cannot articulate, such as expectations of conversational agents, collaborative tools or interface conventions, or to understand why small changes cause disproportionate disruption.
avoidWhen: Breaches could cause distress, financial loss or deception without debriefing; use naturalistic observation of existing breakdowns instead. For broad attitude data, use interviews or surveys.
whyLost: Ethnomethodology influenced early HCI through Lucy Suchman and CSCW but its dense theory and the ethical difficulty of breaching meant it stayed in academic sociology.
whereToUse: Conversational AI, collaborative and real-time tools, interface conventions in redesigns, automation hand-offs, and multi-party workflows.
example: Testing an AI meeting assistant, researchers deliberately have it respond slightly out of turn in a lab session. Participants' repairs ('sorry, were you talking to me?') reveal the tacit turn-taking rules the assistant must respect.
sources: Studies in Ethnomethodology (Garfinkel)
Sage Research Methods — Understanding Qualitative Research and Ethnomethodology (ten Have)
Handbook of Ethnography
Plans and Situated Actions (Suchman)
reference: Garfinkel, H. (1967). Studies in Ethnomethodology. Prentice-Hall.

name: Ethogram and Focal Sampling (Altmann)
origin: Ethograms from classical ethology (Tinbergen, Lorenz); sampling methods formalised by Jeanne Altmann (1974)
summary: Uses a defined catalogue of behaviours and explicit sampling rules (focal, scan, ad libitum, continuous or instantaneous) to observe behaviour systematically and quantifiably.
description: Ethologists build an ethogram: a complete, mutually exclusive catalogue of behaviours with operational definitions. Altmann's landmark paper showed how sampling choices bias results: ad libitum notes over-represent conspicuous behaviour; focal sampling follows one individual for a set period; scan sampling records all individuals' behaviour at intervals; continuous recording captures true frequencies and durations, while instantaneous (point) sampling estimates time budgets. Inter-observer reliability is tested. UX field observation is usually ad libitum, biased toward the memorable. Applying ethological rules yields defensible quantitative observation in stores, clinics, homes and offices.
steps: Conduct preliminary observation to draft an ethogram of relevant behaviours with operational definitions.
Choose sampling rules (focal or scan) and recording rules (continuous or instantaneous at set intervals, e.g. 30 s).
Train observers and test inter-observer agreement (kappa above 0.7) before data collection.
Collect observations according to a schedule that samples times, places and individuals representatively.
Compute frequencies, durations, time budgets and transitions, with appropriate statistics.
Combine with interviews to interpret patterns.
outputs: An ethogram, time budgets, behaviour frequencies and durations, transition data and reliability statistics.
useWhen: Observing behaviour in physical or social settings where quantitative description matters, such as retail, clinics, classrooms or homes.
avoidWhen: When the research question is about meaning and experience rather than behaviour frequency.
whyLost: UX inherited ethnography from anthropology rather than ethology, so systematic behaviour sampling never arrived.
whereToUse: Retail self-service, hospital wards, smart home use, classroom technology, warehouse work, public kiosks.
example: Observing self-checkout with 10-minute scan sampling across 40 hours, researchers find staff intervention occupies 38% of attendant time, mostly for age verification, informing a digital ID feature.
sources: Altmann, Observational study of behavior: sampling methods (1974), Behaviour
Martin & Bateson, Measuring Behaviour: An Introductory Guide (4th ed., 2021)
reference: Altmann, J. (1974). Observational study of behavior: sampling methods. Behaviour, 49(3-4), 227-267.

name: EXAMINE for distributional assumptions
origin: SPSS EXAMINE (Explore) procedure; exploratory data analysis, John Tukey, 1977
summary: Using SPSS EXAMINE to inspect distributions, normality, outliers and homogeneity of variance by group before choosing parametric or non-parametric tests.
description: EXAMINE produces box plots, stem-and-leaf plots, Q-Q plots, normality tests (Kolmogorov-Smirnov with Lilliefors correction, Shapiro-Wilk), extreme values and Levene's test for homogeneity of variance, overall or split by group. Its purpose is to decide whether assumptions of t-tests, ANOVA or regression are plausible. Rigour comes from interpreting plots rather than relying on significance tests of normality, which are underpowered in small samples and over-sensitive in large ones, checking assumptions within groups rather than overall, and choosing robust alternatives (Welch's test, rank tests, bootstrapping, log transforms) when assumptions fail.
steps: Run EXAMINE with the outcome as the dependent list and the grouping variable as the factor, requesting plots, normality tests and Levene's test.
Inspect Q-Q plots and box plots within each group, giving more weight to plots than to normality p-values.
Note extreme values flagged by box plots (beyond 1.5 or 3 interquartile ranges) and trace them back to raw data.
Check homogeneity of variance; if the largest group variance is more than about 4 times the smallest or Levene's test is significant, use Welch-type tests.
For skewed task times, log-transform and re-examine, or switch to non-parametric or bootstrap methods.
Document the assumption decisions in the analysis log.
outputs: Distribution plots, normality and variance diagnostics, a list of extreme values and a justified test choice.
useWhen: Before comparing groups or fitting linear models, especially with small UX samples, task times and satisfaction scores.
avoidWhen: Do not use normality test p-values as a gate for large samples; with N in the thousands, focus on effect sizes and robust methods.
whyLost: Assumption checking is taught but often skipped in UX because dashboards and A/B tools hide the statistical machinery.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarking, survey group comparisons and pre-post evaluations.
example: Before comparing onboarding completion times across three app versions, EXAMINE shows heavy right skew and a variance ratio of 6 between groups, so the team uses Welch's ANOVA on log times.
sources: SPSS Syntax Editor
Python integration (SPSS Python plugin)
pyreadstat for Python ↔ SPSS bridge
Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
Tukey, J. W. (1977) Exploratory Data Analysis
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2016) Quantifying the User Experience, 2nd ed.
The Inquiry Series, C6 — SPSS for UX Researchers — The Right Way
reference: Tukey, J. W. (1977) Exploratory Data Analysis

name: Expectation Ratings (Expected vs Experienced Difficulty)
origin: Albert & Dixon (2003); quadrant analysis in Tullis & Albert (2008)
summary: Compares how hard users expect each task to be with how hard it turns out, mapping tasks into fix-it-fast, promote-it, big-opportunity and leave-alone quadrants.
description: Before doing any tasks, participants rate how difficult they expect each one to be. After each task, they rate how difficult it actually was, using the same 7-point scale. Plotting expectation against experience separates four groups: tasks expected to be easy that turned out hard ("fix it fast", the main source of dissatisfaction); tasks expected to be hard that were easy ("promote it"); tasks hard before and after ("big opportunity"); and tasks easy before and after ("don't touch it"). The method adds context a single post-task rating lacks, because the same difficulty score means something different if users expected it. Sauro reports that users predict task-level usability fairly well, which makes the gaps meaningful.
steps: List the study tasks and show them all to participants before testing.
Collect an expectation rating for each task on a 7-point difficulty scale.
Run the tasks, collecting the experience rating after each one on the same scale.
Average both ratings per task and plot expectation on one axis and experience on the other.
Prioritise the quadrant where tasks were expected to be easy but were hard.
outputs: A quadrant chart prioritising tasks by the gap between expectation and experience.
useWhen: Prioritising fixes across many tasks, or finding features worth marketing.
avoidWhen: Participants cannot understand tasks before attempting them, or there are only one or two tasks.
whyLost: Most teams collect only a post-task rating; the extra pre-task step seems like overhead.
whereToUse: Benchmark studies, onboarding evaluations, feature prioritisation.
example: Users expect "change delivery address" to be trivial but rate it 2.8 after trying, placing it in fix-it-fast ahead of harder-looking tasks.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Measuring the User Experience (Tullis & Albert)
reference: Albert, W. & Dixon, E. (2003). Is this what you expected? The use of expectation measures in usability testing. UPA 2003.

name: Expectation-Maximisation for Incomplete Behavioural Data
origin: Arthur Dempster, Nan Laird and Donald Rubin, 1977
summary: Estimates models from behavioural or survey data with missing values by iterating expectation and maximisation steps, avoiding the bias of deleting incomplete users.
description: Behavioural and survey data in UX are routinely incomplete: users drop out of diary studies, abandon multi-step surveys or sessions end early. Deleting incomplete cases (listwise deletion) or filling gaps with means biases results whenever missingness relates to the outcome, such as frustrated users quitting. The expectation-maximisation algorithm estimates parameters by alternating an E-step, computing expected values of the missing or latent quantities given current parameters, and an M-step, updating parameters to maximise likelihood given those expectations, until convergence. It provides maximum-likelihood estimates under the missing-at-random assumption and underpins mixture models and latent variable models. Good practice diagnoses missingness patterns, states the assumption, compares results with complete-case analysis and, where uncertainty must be propagated, uses multiple imputation alongside.
steps: Frame incomplete session data as a latent variable problem: complete session outcome is the latent variable; observed partial session data is the observation.
Apply EM: E-step estimates the probability of each possible complete session given the partial data; M-step updates model parameters.
Compare: EM-estimated completion rates vs. naïve complete-case analysis.
Large differences indicate non-random missingness (MNAR — missing not at random).
outputs: Missingness diagnostics, maximum-likelihood parameter estimates, comparison with complete-case results, and documented assumptions about the missing-data mechanism.
useWhen: Longitudinal and diary studies with dropout, partial survey responses, sessions with incomplete event logs, and fitting mixture or latent variable models.
avoidWhen: When missingness is clearly not at random (data missing because of the unobserved value itself) without a model for it; use sensitivity analysis or pattern-mixture models, and avoid it when only a trivial fraction is missing.
whyLost: UX analysis tools default to deleting incomplete records, and EM sits inside statistical software rather than in UX training, so it vanished from practitioner awareness.
whereToUse: Onboarding completion rate estimation, task completion analysis with partial sessions, churn modeling with incomplete histories.
example: A 12-week wellbeing app diary study loses 35% of participants by week 8, mostly those reporting low mood. EM estimates of the mood trajectory show a smaller improvement than the complete-case analysis, preventing an overstated efficacy claim.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning — Bishop
Little & Rubin, Statistical Analysis with Missing Data
Dempster, Laird & Rubin, Maximum likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm (JRSS B, 1977)
reference: Dempster AP, Laird NM & Rubin DB (1977) Maximum likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 39(1):1-38

name: Expected Value of Information Analysis
donor: Bayesian decision theory and health economics
origin: Howard Raiffa and Robert Schlaifer (1961); Ronald Howard (1966, information value theory); widely used in health economics
summary: Calculates how much a piece of research is worth by estimating how likely it is to change a decision and how much that change would gain.
description: Research has value only if it might change a decision. The expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the expected gain from knowing the true state before deciding, an upper bound on what any study is worth. The expected value of sample information (EVSI) estimates the gain from a specific study design with its sample size and noise. Health technology assessment uses VOI to prioritise trials. For UX research operations, VOI provides a principled way to prioritise studies, size them and decide when to stop researching and ship, using rough distributions of uncertainty and decision payoffs, as Hubbard advocates.
steps: Define the decision, alternatives and the outcome metric in value terms (revenue, retention, harm).
Quantify current uncertainty about key parameters with calibrated estimates (e.g. 90% intervals).
Model payoffs of each alternative as a function of uncertain parameters.
Compute EVPI by simulation: expected payoff with perfect information minus expected payoff of the best current choice.
For candidate studies, compute EVSI given sample size and measurement error, and compare with research cost.
Prioritise studies with highest net value and identify parameters worth measuring (partial EVPI).
outputs: EVPI and EVSI estimates, ranked research options by net value, and parameters that matter most.
useWhen: Prioritising research, deciding study size, or justifying research investment to leadership.
avoidWhen: Exploratory generative research whose value is in reframing the decision itself.
whyLost: UX research rarely quantifies decisions or uncertainty, and decision theory was never part of its training.
whereToUse: Research roadmaps, pricing decisions, large redesigns, regulated launches, AI investment decisions.
example: A team debates a $40,000 study on a checkout redesign. VOI shows EVPI of $25,000 because the redesign wins in nearly all plausible scenarios; the study is replaced by a cheap monitoring plan.
sources: Raiffa & Schlaifer, Applied Statistical Decision Theory (1961)
Howard, Information value theory (1966), IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics
Hubbard, How to Measure Anything (3rd ed., 2014)
reference: Howard, R. A. (1966). Information value theory. IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics, 2(1), 22-26.

name: Experience Curve and Learning Study
origin: Power law of practice (Newell & Rosenbloom, 1981); learning curves from T. P. Wright, 1936
summary: Multi-session study tracking task time, errors, strategies and mental models as users progress from novice to expert, fitted to learning curves.
description: Most usability tests capture first-use performance only. A learning study brings participants back over six to ten sessions across weeks, using a standard task battery plus novel transfer tasks. Task time is fitted to the power law of practice (T = a n^-b), giving estimates of initial difficulty and learning rate; errors, verbalisation (which falls as skills automate) and strategy shifts are tracked alongside. Mental models are probed at intervals by asking participants to explain how the system works. The result distinguishes products that are hard at first but efficient for experts from those that plateau, identifies early struggles that predict abandonment, and reveals expert strategies novices never discover.
steps: Multi-session design: 6–10 sessions per participant over 2–4 weeks. Standardised task battery + novel transfer tasks per session.
Track across sessions: Task time (model as power function T=a·n^−b), error rate, strategy shifts, verbalisation rate (automatisation decreases verbalisation).
Mental model probing: After sessions 1, 3, 6, and 10: 'How would you explain how this works to someone new?' Track model evolution.
Strategy transition documentation: Note when participants shift from novice strategies (exploratory, high-verification) to expert strategies (direct, minimal checking).
Analysis: Fit learning curves. Identify early struggles predicting abandonment; habituation speed for key workflows; expert strategies novices never develop without explicit support.
outputs: Fitted learning curves per task, error and verbalisation trends, strategy transition records, mental model evolution notes, and plateau diagnoses.
useWhen: Professional and high-frequency tools where expert efficiency matters, comparing designs on learnability, or deciding on onboarding and training investments.
avoidWhen: Walk-up-and-use products used once or rarely; use first-use usability testing.
whyLost: Repeated sessions are expensive and slow, so industry relies on single-session tests and rarely fits learning curves.
whereToUse: Creative and developer tools, clinical systems, trading platforms, keyboard-driven productivity software, and enterprise migrations.
example: Comparing two layouts for a call-centre CRM over eight sessions, one is 20% slower at session one but reaches a 30% faster plateau by session six, reversing the decision a first-use test would have produced.

name: Experience Prototyping
origin: Marion Buchenau and Jane Fulton Suri, IDEO, 2000 (DIS conference paper)
summary: Simulates the intended experience, not the artefact, using role play, repurposed objects, staged environments or video, to test experience qualities before any functional prototype exists.
description: Experience prototyping (Buchenau & Suri, IDEO) simulates the designed experience — not the designed artefact — using any available means: role play, existing products repurposed, environments physically modified, videos showing the experience as it would unfold. The goal is to enable stakeholders (researchers, designers, users) to experience and evaluate the quality of a designed experience before investing in its technical realisation. Unlike paper prototyping (which tests interface logic) and concept testing (which collects opinions), experience prototyping tests whether a designed experience feels right when embodied.
steps: Experience specification: Define the experience qualities you are testing — not the features or functions, but the experiential qualities: 'trust at first use,' 'feeling of control,' 'sense of being understood.' These are your evaluation criteria.

Prototype the experience: Assemble any combination of available materials that can simulate the experience. This might include: a role-play scenario, a video of the experience unfolding, physical materials representing key moments, or a wizard-of-oz simulation.

Participant enactment: Have participants experience the prototype, ideally in a realistic context. Their experience of the prototype — their emotional, embodied, and cognitive responses — is the research data.
Debrief: Immediately after the experience: 'What did you feel during that?' 'What moments felt right?' 'What moments felt off?' 'What did you find yourself wanting that wasn't there?'
Iteration: Revise the experience specification or the design based on the debrief. Re-prototype. Experience prototyping is intrinsically iterative.
outputs: Experience specifications, enacted prototypes, debrief findings about felt experience, and iterated experience qualities guiding design.
useWhen: The quality of an experience over time and in context matters more than interface details, such as services, physical-digital products, AI interactions or emotionally significant moments.
avoidWhen: You need to test interface usability or detailed interactions; use prototype usability testing. Avoid if the context cannot be credibly simulated.
whyLost: It survives under names such as bodystorming, service walkthroughs and Wizard of Oz, but its focus on specifying and testing experience qualities is often lost.
whereToUse: Service design, connected and in-car devices, AI assistants, healthcare encounters, retail and hospitality experiences.
example: Before building a voice assistant for hospital porters, designers role-play the assistant in a ward corridor with a researcher speaking responses. Porters find unprompted announcements intrusive near patients, so a proximity-aware quiet mode is designed.
sources: Buchenau & Suri (IDEO 2000) — Experience Prototyping

name: Experience Sampling Diary Design
origin: Csikszentmihalyi & Larson, 1987; Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli, 2003
summary: Designs diary and experience-sampling studies by choosing signal schedules, prompt structure and response formats that capture experience close to when it happens.
description: Experience sampling and diary designs capture experience in situ, reducing recall bias. The key design choice is the sampling scheme: interval-contingent (fixed times), signal-contingent (random prompts within windows) or event-contingent (participants report whenever a defined event occurs). Each suits different phenomena and introduces different biases. Researchers must also decide between structured responses, which enable quantitative within-person analysis, and free-form entries, which capture richer meaning, and they must balance prompt frequency and length against burden and attrition. Data are analysed with multilevel models for within-person variation and thematic coding for open text. Rigour comes from piloting burden, monitoring compliance, defining events precisely, and accounting for reactivity.
steps: Selection protocol:

If the research question is about temporal patterns (how does experience change over a day/week?): interval-contingent with appropriate interval (hourly for micro-patterns, daily for behavioral patterns).
(2) If about specific events (how do users experience errors, completions, first uses?): event-contingent, triggered by the specific event.
(3) If about representative experience (what is using this product actually like?): signal-contingent, 3–7 random prompts per day. Avoid mixing types in a single study.
outputs: Time-stamped in-the-moment responses, within-person patterns over days, contextual data, and qualitative entries tied to specific moments.
useWhen: Understanding experiences that are frequent, fleeting or context-dependent (mood, interruptions, usage contexts, habits) that retrospective interviews distort.
avoidWhen: Avoid when burden would be too high for the population, when the phenomenon is rare (use event-contingent diaries or interviews), or when a single snapshot answers the question.
whyLost: Diary studies are common but designed informally; the sampling design choices from psychology (interval, signal, event-contingent schedules, burden trade-offs) are rarely made explicitly.
whereToUse: Longitudinal UX research, habit and behavior change research, mobile product experience research.
example: A note-taking app sends 40 participants five random prompts daily for ten days asking what they are doing and whether they captured a thought; data show most lost ideas occur while commuting, prompting a voice-capture feature.
sources: Diary Methods — (various)
reference: Bolger N, Davis A & Rafaeli E (2003) Diary methods: Capturing life as it is lived. Annual Review of Psychology 54:579-616

name: Experience Sampling Method
origin: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi & Reed Larson, 1970s to 1987; EMA by Stone & Shiffman, 1994
summary: Participants report momentary experience in real time when prompted at random or event-based moments, minimising recall bias and capturing experience in context.
description: The Experience Sampling Method, developed by Csikszentmihalyi and Larson, and the closely related Ecological Momentary Assessment from behavioural medicine, prompt participants several times a day to report what they are doing, feeling and experiencing at that moment. Prompts may be random within time windows, at fixed intervals or triggered by events, such as app use or location. Because reports are immediate and in situ, ESM reduces recall bias and captures variation within people across contexts. Data form many short, repeated measures per person and require multilevel analysis. Rigour comes from a sampling schedule matched to the phenomenon, very short questionnaires (under about two minutes), compliance monitoring (aiming for at least 70 to 80 percent), and analysis that separates within-person from between-person variation.
steps: Define the momentary experiences and contexts of interest.
Choose signal-, interval- or event-contingent sampling and set the schedule, for example 5 to 8 random prompts per day for 7 to 14 days.
Design a short questionnaire of validated momentary items that takes under two minutes.
Pilot on the target platform and adjust burden.
Recruit 20 to 50 or more participants, brief them and monitor compliance daily.
Clean data, applying compliance and response time rules.
Analyse with multilevel models to separate within-person and between-person effects.
outputs: Repeated momentary reports, within-person patterns across contexts and time, compliance statistics and multilevel model estimates.
useWhen: For emotional and mood-related UX, mental health and wellbeing apps, momentary context of use and experiences that fluctuate through the day.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the phenomenon is rare or not tied to moments; use event-based diaries or critical incident interviews. Avoid when burden would be unacceptable for participants.
whyLost: It survived because remote tools made it cheap and it fills a clear gap between interviews and analytics; the risk is weak design, with long entry forms, no trigger logic and poor compliance.
whereToUse: Emotional UX; mental health apps; in-situ product experience capture.
example: A mindfulness app runs a 10-day EMA with 40 users, prompting six times daily about stress and app use. Multilevel models show stress drops after use only when sessions occur before 6 pm, informing reminder timing.
