name: Fogg Behavior Model
origin: B.J. Fogg, 2009
summary: Diagnoses why a target behaviour does not occur by checking whether motivation, ability and a prompt converge at the same moment.
description: The Fogg Behavior Model states that a behaviour occurs when motivation, ability and a prompt converge at the same moment (B=MAP). Motivation and ability trade off along an action line: hard behaviours require high motivation, while easy behaviours can occur with modest motivation. Without a prompt, nothing happens regardless of the other two. Used diagnostically, the model asks of each failed step which element is missing: is the user unmotivated, is the action too hard (in time, money, physical or mental effort, social deviance or non-routine), or is there no well-timed prompt? It favours increasing ability by simplification over raising motivation. Rigour comes from defining a specific target behaviour, using data to locate failure points, and testing interventions.
steps: For any target behavior that users fail to perform: FBM diagnosis.
(1) Is motivation present? (would the user do it if it were trivial?) YES → ability or prompt failure. NO → motivation problem.
(2) Is ability present? (does the user know how and have the resources?) NO → redesign for simplicity.

(3) Is a prompt present at the right moment? NO → add timely, relevant trigger. This diagnostic protocol prevents designing expensive motivation interventions for what are actually friction or timing problems.
outputs: A behaviour diagnosis per step (motivation, ability or prompt deficit), simplification and prompt designs, and hypotheses for experiments.
useWhen: Diagnosing drop-off at a specific behaviour (activation, habit, form completion) and designing prompts and simplifications in health, finance and productivity products.
avoidWhen: Avoid for complex, deliberative decisions or when ethical risk of manipulation is high; use decision analysis or COM-B for richer behaviour change diagnosis.
whyLost: Widely cited, but usually applied as a slogan; the diagnostic discipline of identifying which factor is missing at each step is rarely done.
whereToUse: Behavior change apps, onboarding design, feature adoption, call-to-action design, notification strategy.
example: A savings app sees users not setting up round-ups; diagnosis shows motivation is high but ability is low (bank linking takes nine steps), so the team cuts linking to three steps and adds a payday prompt.
sources: Persuasive Technology — B.J. Fogg
reference: Fogg BJ (2009) A behavior model for persuasive design. Persuasive '09 Proceedings, ACM

name: Fogg Behavior Model diagnostic
origin: B. J. Fogg, 'A behavior model for persuasive design' (2009); Persuasive Technology (2003); later Tiny Habits (2019) with 'prompt' replacing 'trigger'
summary: Diagnoses why a target behaviour does not occur by checking whether motivation, ability and a prompt are all present at the same moment.
description: The Fogg Behavior Model states that a behaviour occurs when motivation, ability and a prompt converge at the same moment. Motivation and ability trade off along an action line: hard behaviours need high motivation, easy behaviours need little. Fogg breaks ability into six simplicity factors (time, money, physical effort, mental effort, social deviance and non-routine) and motivation into three pairs (pleasure and pain, hope and fear, social acceptance and rejection). As a diagnostic it locates non-occurrence: a user above the action line with no prompt needs a prompt; a prompted user below the line needs ability raised before motivation. Rigour comes from measuring each component at the moment of the target behaviour rather than in general, and from using the simplicity factors to find the weakest link.
steps: Specify one target behaviour precisely: who, what action, in what context and how often, for example 'health worker enters the visit record before leaving the household'.
Observe or reconstruct 10 to 20 moments where the behaviour should have occurred, using field observation, diaries or session data.
For each moment, rate motivation (high, medium, low) with evidence, then rate ability using the six simplicity factors and identify the scarcest factor.
Check whether a prompt was present, noticed and timed when motivation and ability were both adequate, and classify prompts as spark, facilitator or signal.
Plot each moment against the action line and classify failures as no prompt, low ability, low motivation or mistimed prompt.
Design interventions for the dominant failure type, prioritising ability and prompts before motivation, and test with a before-after or A/B comparison of the behaviour rate.
outputs: A behaviour specification, a moment-by-moment M-A-P classification, the dominant failure mode and scarce simplicity factor, and targeted interventions with measured effects.
useWhen: A specific behaviour is not happening as intended (adoption, logging, adherence) and you need to locate the cause quickly.
avoidWhen: The behaviour is embedded in social or organisational systems where individual M-A-P framing misses structural causes; use the ∆U model or contextual inquiry. Avoid using it to engineer compulsive engagement.
whyLost: It survived because it is simple, memorable and taught widely in product courses; the risk is vestigial use as a slogan without measuring components at the moment of behaviour.
whereToUse: Health adherence and data entry, savings behaviours, onboarding activation, learning habits, enterprise tool adoption.
example: Health workers delayed digital entry until evening. The diagnostic found motivation was high but ability was low because entry took 7 minutes in a household with no seating; reducing the form to 3 essential fields at the point of care, with the rest later, doubled same-visit entry.
sources: Persuasive Technology (Fogg)

The Inquiry Series, Ch 24 — Behavior Models, Habits & the Anatomy of Non-Adoption

name: Forecast Stage (Forward-Thinking Loop)
aka: Stage 4: Forecast with Simulation and Explainability
donor: Simulation, machine learning explainability and diary research
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Stage 4 of the forward-thinking loop: estimate rollout impact with Monte Carlo journey simulation, rank drivers with SHAP, and check emotional sustainability with diary trajectories.
description: Forecasting bridges small-sample evidence and large-scale rollout by producing a distribution of outcomes rather than a single number. Monte Carlo samples step-level success probabilities across 10,000 virtual users to yield a completion distribution with a 95% interval, and supports what-if scenarios. A gradient boosting model trained on a 70/30 split with task time, error counts, SNR, retries and TLX features is decomposed with SHAP to rank drivers. Qualitative forecasting via diary studies arrays sentiment trajectories (clarity, trust, frustration per session) into patterns such as 'fast trust gain', 'fragile success' and 'churn risk', since negative sentiment drift predicts future drop-off even when completion rises. Rigour comes from stated assumptions (stationarity, approximate independence, like-for-like traffic, no leakage), sensitivity checks (best/mid/worst ±10–20%, segment splits, volume scaling) and calibration plots.
steps: Collect empirical step probabilities from the variant (e.g. Find 81%, Set Rule 75%, OTP 85%, Confirm 95%).
Simulate 10,000 virtual journeys, sampling success or failure at each step, and report mean completion with a 95% CI (example: 49% [46%, 52%]).
Run what-if scenarios on the weakest step (OTP improved to 92% gives 54% [51%, 57%]) and sensitivity checks of ±10–20%, segment splits and volume scaling.
Train a gradient boosting model on a 70/30 split using pre-outcome task features, validate on holdout data and check calibration with reliability plots.
Compute SHAP values to rank drivers (e.g. mistake rate 0.33, SNR 0.27, OTP time 0.18, frustration 0.13, retries 0.09).
Array diary entries into trajectories (session index, clarity −2..+2, trust 1..5, frustration 0..100, success, quote) and cluster them into patterns.
Link top SHAP drivers to trajectory clusters and present Monte Carlo curves alongside two or three curated trajectories.
outputs: Monte Carlo completion distributions with intervals, what-if scenarios, a SHAP driver ranking, trajectory clusters and a reporting checklist.
useWhen: When stakeholders ask what impact to expect at rollout and which lever to pull first.
avoidWhen: When step probabilities are unstable or traffic mix will change radically; avoid one-number forecasts and post-outcome features.
whyLost: Original stage design by Vivek Gopinath; forecasting with uncertainty is common in data science but rarely owned by UX research.
whereToUse: Funnel rollouts, onboarding redesigns, OTP and verification changes, roadmap prioritisation.
example: For a trading app's alert flow, Monte Carlo predicts 49% end-to-end completion; improving OTP to 92% shifts it to 54%, while diary trajectories warn of a 'fragile success' cluster linked to high mistake rates.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Stage 4.

name: Forward-Thinking UX Research Loop
aka: Predict → Diagnose → Prove → Forecast → Prescribe → Validate
donor: UX research practice integrating human factors, causal inference and forecasting
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A six-stage mixed-methods loop (Predict, Diagnose, Prove, Forecast, Prescribe, Validate) that turns backward-looking findings into predictions, prescriptions and validated outcomes tied to decision bars.
description: The loop answers a common failure of UX reporting: statements such as 'users struggled with navigation' that do not tell teams what to change or what impact to expect. Each stage has paired quant and qual methods: Predict (CPM-GOMS, mental models), Diagnose (tree testing, error taxonomy, signal-to-noise ratio), Prove (A/B, Cox survival, quasi-experiments, QCA), Forecast (Monte Carlo, SHAP), Prescribe (joint display, effort × impact) and Validate (confirmatory A/B, guardrails, field drift checks). The loop is a menu rather than a checklist: researchers pick the strongest feasible method per stage, document assumptions, and tie results to decision bars set in advance. Its rigour comes from evidence building across stages, so a hypothesis from Predict is tested in Diagnose and Prove, its impact forecast, its fix prescribed and the forecast compared with actuals. A Miles & Huberman qualitative cycle runs alongside to keep qual auditable.
steps: Predict: model the task with CPM-GOMS and capture 4–8 mental-model interviews to produce a falsifiable hypothesis and decision bar (e.g. predicted ideal 6s, breakdown if observed median exceeds 15s).
Diagnose: run an unmoderated tree test (N = 80–150), 10–15 moderated think-alouds coded as Slip/Lapse/Mistake (κ ≥ 0.70), and an element and behavioural SNR audit; synthesise in a joint display.

Prove: test the fix causally with a randomised or prototype A/B and a Cox proportional hazards model of time to abandonment; use QCA, Rubin matching or Bradford Hill criteria when randomisation is not possible.
Forecast: simulate 10,000 virtual journeys with Monte Carlo from step probabilities and rank drivers with SHAP on a held-out gradient boosting model; pair with diary-based sentiment trajectories.
Prescribe: map each driver to a mechanism and a fix using a 'because → therefore' structure, place fixes on an effort × impact grid, and attach a decision bar to each.

Validate: run a confirmatory A/B with pre-registered bars, monitor guardrails (latency, crashes, tickets), re-run the evidence array to confirm the recursive loop is broken, and check drift at 1, 3 and 6 months.
Report forecast versus actual (e.g. 'predicted +11% lift, observed +14%, sustained at +12% after 3 months') and iterate the loop.
outputs: A chained evidence trail: hypotheses and benchmarks, misroute heatmaps and coded errors, hazard ratios, forecast distributions with intervals, an effort × impact prescription set, and a validation verdict against pre-set bars.
useWhen: When stakeholders need decisions and expected impact rather than descriptive findings, especially for high-traffic flows where traffic allows experiments and forecasts.
avoidWhen: When the question is open-ended discovery with no defined task or outcome; use ethnographic or generative methods first. Do not force every stage when budget or traffic is lacking.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath; it recombines rigorous but siloed methods (GOMS, survival analysis, QCA, Monte Carlo) that rarely appear together in UX practice.
whereToUse: Fintech and trading apps, onboarding and KYC flows, checkout, enterprise SaaS workflows, AI product features with measurable completion outcomes.
example: A trading app's price-alert task shows 62% completion. The team predicts misroutes to 'Notifications', diagnoses Mistakes via tree test and taxonomy, proves a new IA with HR 0.68, forecasts completion with Monte Carlo, prescribes relabelling, and validates OTP success rising from 65% to 82%.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation

name: Fourier Spectral Analysis of Behavioural Telemetry
origin: Joseph Fourier, 1822; FFT by Cooley & Tukey, 1965
summary: Decomposes a behavioural time series into frequency components to reveal which tempos dominate activity, from daily habits to rapid micro-fluctuations.
description: Fourier analysis represents a signal as a sum of sinusoids; the power spectrum shows how much energy sits at each frequency. Vivek Gopinath's Behavioral Spectral Framework treats it as an 'X-ray of habit': dominant low frequencies indicate stable long-term habits, strong high-frequency energy indicates micro-fluctuation, distraction or reactivity, and multiple harmonics suggest layered goals. Because human behaviour is non-stationary, the playbook recommends windowed transforms (STFT) or treating frequency change itself as a dependent variable, recurrence strength over strict periodicity, and broad-band power ratios rather than single peaks. In the fintech case, STFT showed a dominant band of 0.15–0.25 Hz and high-frequency bursts of 0.8–1.2 Hz at KYC and form-filling. Interpretability is a strength: frequency maps to pace, amplitude to intensity and phase to timing, but amplitude is not the same as engagement and must be read with context.
steps: Frame the signal (e.g. interaction density per minute) with time resolution matched to the hypothesised rhythm.
Resample or interpolate small gaps, keeping long gaps as meaningful silence, or switch to Lomb-Scargle for irregular events.
Compute the FFT for global periodicity, or STFT windows to see change over time.
Extract dominant frequencies, broad-band power ratios (slow versus fast) and relative energy drift ΔP/P.
Compare spectra across cohorts (novice versus expert, calm versus stressed).
Interpret peaks with context metadata and qualitative evidence before reporting.
outputs: Power spectra, dominant bands, band power ratios and spectrograms per user or cohort.
useWhen: When dense, time-stamped behaviour may contain rhythms (daily, weekly or within-session cycles).
avoidWhen: With sparse or event-driven data (use Lomb-Scargle) or when signals are strongly non-stationary (use wavelets).
whyLost: Spectral methods are routine in physics, engineering and neuroscience but almost never taught to UX researchers.
whereToUse: Habit formation, engagement rhythm, onboarding overload, biometric and EEG UX studies.
example: A spectral analysis of onboarding telemetry shows a 0.15–0.25 Hz interaction rhythm interrupted by 0.8–1.2 Hz bursts at KYC, pointing to cognitive overload at verification.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
Matteo Paz (2024), A Sub-Millisecond Fourier and Wavelet Based Model to Extract Variable Candidates from the NEOWISE Single-Exposure Database
reference: Cooley, J. W., & Tukey, J. W. (1965). An algorithm for the machine calculation of complex Fourier series. Mathematics of Computation, 19(90), 297–301.

name: Fractal Analysis of Interface Structure
origin: Benoît Mandelbrot, 1975
summary: Measures the fractal dimension and self-similarity of layouts and information hierarchies, characterising complexity consistently across scales.
description: Fractal geometry describes structures that show similar patterns at different scales, quantified by a fractal dimension. Box-counting estimates this by covering an image or structure with grids of decreasing size and measuring how the number of occupied boxes grows. In UX the method has been applied in two ways. Visually, the fractal dimension of screen layouts and images correlates with perceived complexity and aesthetic preference, with mid-range values often preferred. Structurally, information hierarchies can be examined for self-similarity: whether each level follows the same organising pattern, which supports learnability. The approach is rigorous when measurement is standardised (consistent resolution, thresholding and scale range), when dimension estimates are reported with fit quality, and when results are related to user judgements or performance rather than treated as aesthetic verdicts.
steps: Select artefacts to analyse: screen captures at fixed resolution or hierarchy trees of the IA.
Pre-process consistently, for example converting screens to edge maps with a fixed threshold.
Apply box-counting across at least 5 scales and fit log(N) against log(1/size) to estimate fractal dimension.
For hierarchies, compare branching patterns across levels to assess self-similarity.
Collect complexity or preference ratings from 20-50 users for a subset to calibrate interpretation.
Use calibrated dimension values to compare designs and flag screens outside the preferred range.
outputs: Fractal dimension estimates per screen or structure, self-similarity assessment, calibration against user ratings.
useWhen: Comparing visual complexity across large sets of screens, aesthetic research, and multi-scale navigation systems such as maps or zoomable interfaces.
avoidWhen: Routine product decisions; heuristic evaluation and usability testing give more actionable findings for most teams.
whyLost: Latent: Research novelty; not yet practical in standard UX work.
whereToUse: Complex information architecture analysis; multi-scale navigation systems.
example: A mapping app compared fractal dimension of its map tiles at each zoom level. Levels with dimension above 1.7 drew the most 'too busy' ratings, guiding which label layers to suppress at those zooms.
sources: Unsupervised Learning in Time and Space
The Fractal Geometry of Nature (Benoît Mandelbrot)
reference: Mandelbrot, B. B. (1982). The Fractal Geometry of Nature. W. H. Freeman.

name: Fractional Factorial Experiments
origin: Ronald Fisher (1926, 1935); fractional factorials by David Finney (1945); Box, Hunter and Hunter (1978)
summary: Tests several design factors simultaneously in a carefully chosen subset of combinations, estimating main effects and key interactions with far fewer runs.
description: A full factorial with k two-level factors needs 2^k combinations. Fractional factorials run a fraction (e.g. 2^(k-p)) chosen so that main effects and important interactions remain estimable, with known aliasing patterns described by resolution (Resolution IV: main effects clear of two-way interactions). This is vastly more efficient than one-factor-at-a-time testing, and it reveals interactions, such as a headline that only works with a particular image. Web 'multivariate testing' often runs full factorials without design, or runs many separate A/B tests and misses interactions. Proper DoE plans the fraction, randomises, analyses with ANOVA or regression and confirms surprising interactions.
steps: Select factors (e.g. 5 design elements) and levels (usually 2 each) based on hypotheses.
Choose a fractional design with adequate resolution (e.g. 2^(5-1) Resolution V, 16 cells) and document the alias structure.
Randomise users to cells and compute sample size per cell for target effect sizes.
Analyse with regression including main effects and estimable interactions; use half-normal plots to spot active effects.
Interpret aliasing carefully and run a confirmatory follow-up if a key effect is aliased.
Combine the best levels and validate the combined design against control.
outputs: Main effect and interaction estimates, alias structure, and an optimised combination validated in a confirmatory test.
useWhen: Several design changes are candidates at once and interactions are plausible, with enough traffic or participants.
avoidWhen: Single changes, or very low traffic where even fractional designs are underpowered.
whyLost: A/B testing culture privileges one change at a time, and 'multivariate testing' tools hid design theory behind full factorial grids.
whereToUse: Landing pages, onboarding sequences, email templates, pricing page elements, conversational AI prompt variants.
example: An onboarding team tests 6 factors in a 2^(6-2) design with 16 cells. Two main effects and one interaction (progress bar only helps with fewer steps) are found, informing the final flow.
sources: Box, Hunter & Hunter, Statistics for Experimenters (2nd ed., 2005)
Fisher, The Design of Experiments (1935)
Montgomery, Design and Analysis of Experiments (9th ed., 2017)
reference: Box, G. E. P., Hunter, J. S., & Hunter, W. G. (2005). Statistics for Experimenters. Wiley.

name: Frame Analysis (Goffman)
origin: Erving Goffman, 1974
summary: Explains misunderstandings as frame misalignments: users interpret interfaces through organising schemas that define what is happening and what actions are appropriate.
description: Goffman argued people interpret experience through frames, organising schemas that define what is going on, who participates and what actions are appropriate; frames can be keyed or transformed, and misalignment produces confusion and offence. The treatise applies this to UX: users misunderstand features because they apply the wrong frame. A 'Save as Draft' button means different things to someone in an email frame versus a word-processor frame. Frame analysis explains why failures obvious to designers are invisible to users, and implies making the intended frame legible rather than assuming users import the right one. Analysis examines cues users rely on, frames they invoke in talk and behaviour, and breaks where the frame shifts.
steps: Collect data where users interpret new or ambiguous features (interviews, think-aloud, support logs).
Identify the frames users invoke ('this is like a bank transfer', 'this is a game').
Identify the frame designers intended and cues that signal it.
Locate misalignments and the cues that trigger the wrong frame.
Redesign framing cues: naming, metaphors, onboarding, visual conventions.
Verify that users now invoke the intended frame.
outputs: Frame inventory, misalignment map, framing design recommendations.
useWhen: Onboarding, new paradigms (AI, crypto, new categories), naming, migration between products.
avoidWhen: Mechanical usability issues with no interpretive component.
whyLost: Goffman is widely cited for 'presentation of self', but Frame Analysis is long and dense, and UX uses 'framing' mostly in the copywriting sense.
whereToUse: AI assistants (tool vs agent vs person frame), payments, privacy settings, product migrations.
example: Users treat a 'Pay later' option as a store discount (retail frame) not credit (lending frame); adding credit-framed cues and an APR line reduces later disputes.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Goffman E (1974) Frame Analysis: An Essay on the Organization of Experience
Tannen D (Ed) (1993) Framing in Discourse
Goffman, Frame Analysis: An Essay on the Organization of Experience (1974)
Goffman, Forms of Talk (1981)
reference: Goffman E (1974) Frame Analysis: An Essay on the Organization of Experience. Harvard University Press.

name: Frame Analysis for UX Copy and Product Narrative
origin: Erving Goffman (Frame Analysis, 1974); George Lakoff's cognitive framing (1996, 2004); framing effects by Tversky and Kahneman (1981)
summary: Identifies the conceptual frames that product language activates and tests alternative framings, since frames shape how users interpret features, prices, risks and their own role.
description: Words activate frames, structured knowledge that organises interpretation. Lakoff showed in political communication that once a frame is activated, facts are understood through it and negating a frame reinforces it. Tversky and Kahneman showed that logically equivalent descriptions (90% survival versus 10% mortality) change decisions. For product UX, terms such as 'subscription' versus 'membership', 'fees' versus 'contributions', 'monitoring' versus 'insights', or 'AI assistant' versus 'autopilot' bring frames that determine expectations, trust and blame. Frame analysis inventories the key terms and metaphors in product copy and narrative, identifies the frames and roles they imply for user and product, checks for frame conflicts, and tests alternatives with comprehension, association and choice tasks or A/B experiments.
steps: Frame audit for any product:
What neural frame does the product name activate?
(2) What frame does each major feature name activate?
(3) Are these frames consistent with the product's value proposition?

(4) Do any frame activations conflict (e.g., a 'security product' using 'surveillance' framing)? Test: show users the product name and ask for free associations (as in semantic memory mapping). Frames inconsistent with the value proposition need renaming.
outputs: Frame inventory of key product terms and narratives, implied roles and expectations, frame conflicts, and tested alternative framings with effects on understanding and behaviour.
useWhen: Naming features and products, pricing and consent language, AI capability descriptions, sensitive domains such as health, money and data, and repositioning.
avoidWhen: For routine microcopy with no conceptual weight, or when the issue is plain comprehension; use readability testing or UX writing research.
whyLost: Framing theory lives in linguistics, politics and behavioural economics; UX adopted it only as 'positive wording' tips without systematic analysis or testing.
whereToUse: Product naming, feature naming, marketing copy, onboarding narrative, error message design.
example: A driving-assistance feature called 'Autopilot' implies the car is in charge. Association tests show users expect hands-off capability, so a rename to 'Assisted Steering' with the driver framed as supervisor is tested and reduces overreliance in simulator studies.
sources: Don't Think of an Elephant — George Lakoff
Goffman, Frame Analysis (1974)
Tversky & Kahneman, The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (Science, 1981)
Dont Think of an Elephant
Metaphors We Live By
Frame Analysis (Erving Goffman)
The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (Tversky & Kahneman)
reference: Lakoff G (2004) Don't Think of an Elephant! Know Your Values and Frame the Debate. Chelsea Green Publishing

name: Frame conflict analysis
origin: Donald Schön and Martin Rein, Frame Reflection (1994); grounded in Lakoff's frame semantics (1987)
summary: Identifies where the frames a product's language and design activate collide with users' existing frames, predicting resistance, misinterpretation and distrust.
description: Users approach a new product already inhabiting frames: money is 'kept safe in a bank', a clinic visit is 'seeing the doctor', a loan from a relative is 'help', not 'credit'. Products import their own frames through language, flows and metaphors. Frame conflict analysis maps both sets explicitly, then locates conflicts: points where the product's frame assigns roles, obligations or values that contradict the user's frame. Schön and Rein showed that intractable policy disputes arise from such conflicts rather than from disagreement about facts, and the same applies to adoption disputes. Rigour comes from deriving the user frame from fieldwork rather than assumption, specifying each frame's roles and entailments, and tracing each conflict to observed behaviour such as abandonment, workarounds or complaints.
steps: Extract the product's frames from its copy, flows, icons and onboarding: list each frame with its roles (who acts, who is responsible), entailments and values.
Elicit users' existing frames for the same domain through 8 to 15 contextual interviews or a frame audit, capturing the language users use for the activity unprompted.
Build a side-by-side frame table with matched roles (for example product 'account holder' versus user 'member of savings group') and mark each pairing as aligned, neutral or conflicting.

For every conflict, state the predicted behaviour (refusal, workaround, misattribution of fault) and check it against behavioural evidence such as drop-off points, support tickets or observed workarounds.
Rank conflicts by severity multiplied by frequency of the affected moment, focusing on moments of commitment such as payment, consent and data sharing.
Design reframing options (change the term, change the role, bridge with a familiar frame) and test each with 5 to 8 users using comprehension and expectation probes.
outputs: A frame comparison table, a ranked list of frame conflicts with linked behavioural evidence, and reframing options with test results.
useWhen: Adoption is stalling despite good usability scores; a product is moving into a community with established informal practices; stakeholders argue over terminology without resolution.
avoidWhen: Users already share the product's frame (mature professional tools), or the problem is task-level friction; a usability test will resolve it faster.
whyLost: It belongs to policy studies and cognitive linguistics, and UX absorbed only the shallow word 'framing' from behavioural economics (gain versus loss wording) rather than the structured comparison of frame roles and entailments.
whereToUse: Financial inclusion and informal-economy fintech, digital health in community settings, government service digitisation, AI assistants entering professional workflows.
example: A savings app framed deposits as 'locking' money for interest, while women's savings group members framed savings as money available to help neighbours in emergencies. The conflict explained why users withdrew within days; reframing to 'set aside with emergency access' lowered early withdrawals.
sources: Women Fire & Dangerous Things (Lakoff)
Metaphors We Live By (Lakoff)
Methods Atlas — frame audit (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 19 — Neural Framing & the Architecture of Meaning
reference: Schön, D. A., & Rein, M. (1994). Frame Reflection: Toward the Resolution of Intractable Policy Controversies. Basic Books.

name: Free Listing and Cultural Salience Analysis
origin: Systematic data collection in anthropology (Weller and Romney, 1988); Smith's salience index (J. Jerome Smith, 1993); Sutrop (2001)
summary: Asks people to list all items in a domain, then uses frequency and order of mention to identify the domain's boundaries and most salient items.
description: Free listing is a simple, powerful elicitation: 'list all the ways you pay bills' or 'all the things you worry about when travelling with children'. Items mentioned often and early are culturally salient. Smith's S combines frequency and rank; Sutrop's index is a related measure. Saturation in free lists can be checked as new respondents add few new items. Free lists define the domain for later card sorts, pile sorts and surveys, ensuring the item set reflects users' categories rather than designers'. With 20-30 respondents per group, cross-group comparisons reveal different mental landscapes.
steps: Choose a clear domain prompt and pilot it for interpretability.
Ask each respondent to list as many items as they can, with neutral prompts for more (e.g. 'what else?').
Clean and standardise items carefully, preserving respondents' language where possible.
Compute frequency, mean rank and Smith's salience index for each item.
Plot salience distributions and identify the domain core and periphery; check saturation.
Use salient items to build card sorts, survey options, navigation labels or intents.
outputs: Ranked item lists with salience indices, domain definitions and group comparisons.
useWhen: Defining the content of a domain from users' perspective before IA work, surveys or conjoint designs.
avoidWhen: When the domain is fixed by system constraints and users' categories do not matter.
whyLost: Anthropological systematic data collection never entered UX training; designers generate item lists themselves.
whereToUse: Navigation and taxonomy design, survey option design, chatbot intent discovery, JTBD needs elicitation.
example: A travel insurer asks 40 travellers to list worries before a trip. 'Losing passport' and 'medical costs abroad' are most salient; 'trip cancellation', the product's lead feature, is peripheral, prompting a messaging change.
sources: Weller & Romney, Systematic Data Collection (1988)
Smith, Using ANTHOPAC 3.5 and a spreadsheet to compute a free-list salience index (1993), Cultural Anthropology Methods
Bernard, Research Methods in Anthropology (6th ed., 2017)
reference: Weller, S. C., & Romney, A. K. (1988). Systematic Data Collection. Sage.

name: Free Recall and Recognition Testing
donor: Experimental psychology of memory; advertising research
origin: Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885); serial position curve by Bennet Murdock (1962); day-after recall testing in advertising (Burke, 1940s-50s)
summary: Measures what users remember from an interface or content using free recall, cued recall and recognition tests, with signal-detection scoring and serial position analysis.
description: Memory tests reveal what information actually survives an interaction. Free recall (write down everything you remember) indexes accessibility; cued recall tests specific items; recognition (old/new judgements among foils) indexes availability and is scored with hit and false-alarm rates (d'). Serial position curves show primacy and recency effects, informing order of information. Delayed tests (e.g. 24 hours) measure retention. In UX, these tests evaluate onboarding, safety information, terms, privacy notices and content design: if users cannot recall the key point, comprehension testing alone overstated success.
steps: Define the key information units users should retain and create recognition foils of similar plausibility.
Expose participants to the interface or content under realistic conditions without warning of a memory test (incidental learning) where appropriate.
Administer free recall immediately and score against the information units; then administer cued recall and recognition.
Optionally retest after 24 hours or one week to measure retention.
Score recognition with hit and false-alarm rates and compute d'; plot serial position of recalled items.
Compare designs or orderings and redesign to place critical information where recall is highest.
outputs: Recall percentages per information unit, recognition d', serial position curves, retention over time.
useWhen: Evaluating onboarding, safety warnings, privacy notices, financial disclosures, learning products and content strategies.
avoidWhen: Tasks where information is always available on screen and need not be remembered.
whyLost: UX focuses on task completion and satisfaction rather than retention; memory testing is seen as academic or advertising-specific.
whereToUse: Medication guides, insurance disclosures, onboarding tours, AI capability explanations, security training.
example: A bank tests two fee disclosure designs. Immediate recall of the overdraft fee is 34% vs 71%, and one-week recognition d' differs by 0.8, guiding the regulator-facing redesign.
sources: Ebbinghaus, Über das Gedächtnis (1885)
Murdock, The serial position effect of free recall (1962), Journal of Experimental Psychology
Baddeley, Eysenck & Anderson, Memory (3rd ed., 2020)
reference: Murdock, B. B. (1962). The serial position effect of free recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(5), 482-488.

name: FREQUENCIES and DESCRIPTIVES (descriptive screening)
origin: SPSS FREQUENCIES and DESCRIPTIVES procedures; exploratory screening tradition following Tukey (1977)
summary: Systematically producing frequency tables and descriptive statistics for every variable before analysis, to catch coding errors, impossible values and distribution problems.
description: FREQUENCIES produces counts, percentages, valid and missing counts and optional percentiles and charts for each variable; DESCRIPTIVES gives means, standard deviations, ranges, skewness and kurtosis for scale variables and can save z-scores. Used as a deliberate screening pass, they reveal out-of-range codes, unexpected missingness, ceiling and floor effects, and highly skewed variables before they contaminate models. Rigour lies in running them on every variable, comparing results against the questionnaire's response options and expected sample sizes, and recording the problems found. In UX the step is usually skipped in favour of jumping to charts of headline means.
steps: Run FREQUENCIES on every categorical and rating variable and DESCRIPTIVES on every continuous variable, from syntax.
Compare observed values with permitted response options and flag any out-of-range or unlabelled codes.
Check valid N against expected N and investigate variables with more than about 5% missing.
Inspect skewness and kurtosis (values beyond about plus or minus 2 warrant attention) and look for ceiling or floor effects (more than about 15% at the extreme).
Save z-scores and flag absolute values above 3.29 as potential univariate outliers.
Record issues and fixes in the cleaning log before running inferential analyses.
outputs: Frequency tables, descriptive statistics, a list of anomalies and a cleaning log.
useWhen: The first analytic step for every survey or quantitative UX dataset, and after each new data wave.
avoidWhen: Not a substitute for multivariate screening (Mahalanobis distance) or for distributional checks with EXAMINE when assumptions matter.
whyLost: Dashboards and survey tools show headline charts instantly, so systematic univariate screening seems redundant to many UX teams.
whereToUse: Survey programmes, benchmarking studies and any SPSS-based analysis.
example: An e-commerce satisfaction survey's FREQUENCIES output shows a value of 11 on a 0-10 NPS item for 37 respondents. The cause is a platform export bug, fixed before the quarterly NPS is reported.
sources: SPSS Syntax Editor
Python integration (SPSS Python plugin)
pyreadstat for Python ↔ SPSS bridge
Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
Tukey, J. W. (1977) Exploratory Data Analysis
Tabachnick, B. G. & Fidell, L. S. (2019) Using Multivariate Statistics, 7th ed.
The Inquiry Series, C6 — SPSS for UX Researchers — The Right Way
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Tabachnick, B. G. & Fidell, L. S. (2019) Using Multivariate Statistics, 7th ed.

name: Full Four-Level Affinity Diagram
donor: Contextual Design (HCI), drawing on Japanese KJ method
origin: Jiro Kawakita's KJ method, 1960s; adapted by Karen Holtzblatt & Hugh Beyer in Contextual Design, 1998
summary: Building a complete bottom-up affinity hierarchy from hundreds of contextual inquiry notes, labelled at four levels and walked top-down to drive design.
description: The Contextual Design affinity diagram organises hundreds of interpretation notes from contextual inquiry into a four-level hierarchy built bottom-up. Individual notes, each one observation or interpretation from one participant, are grouped in small clusters; each cluster is labelled with a first-person statement of the shared need or practice; these are grouped under broader work themes, and finally under three to five global concerns. Labels are written in the user's voice and must say something new, not just name a topic. The team then walks the wall from top to bottom, generating design ideas at each level. Rigour comes from volume (often 100 or more notes per participant group), grounding in interpretation sessions, and bottom-up grouping without predefined categories.
steps: Data collection: Each researcher: 8–15 contextual inquiry sessions, 100–150 data notes per researcher. One observation, quote, or interpretation per note.
Level 1 — Individual findings (yellow): Each note = one finding from one participant. Clusters of 3–8 related notes.
Level 2 — Work groups (pink labels): Name each cluster with the shared work practice or user need.
Level 3 — Work themes (blue labels): Broader work themes or design concerns grouping yellow clusters.
Level 4 — Global concerns (green labels): 3–5 global themes pervading the entire affinity.
Walking the wall: Read level 4 → 3 → 2 → 1. Design decisions emerge from this inversion.
outputs: A four-level affinity wall with user-voice labels, global concerns, and design ideas generated during the wall walk.
useWhen: Synthesising substantial contextual or field data (eight or more sessions) with a team, to build shared understanding and design direction.
avoidWhen: Small evaluative studies (use an issue log) or when categories are predefined by the question (use framework analysis).
whyLost: It was compressed into quick sticky-note clustering with topic labels, losing the bottom-up rule, user-voice labels and wall walk.
whereToUse: Enterprise and workplace software discovery, service design programmes, cross-functional team synthesis, and remote whiteboard workshops.
example: After 12 contextual inquiries with warehouse supervisors, a team builds a 600-note affinity. A global concern, 'I am always firefighting yesterday's exceptions', reorients the dashboard design toward exception queues.
sources: Rapid Contextual Design (Holtzblatt)
Universal Methods of Design (Martin)
Contextual Design (Beyer & Holtzblatt)
reference: Holtzblatt, K. & Beyer, H. (2016). Contextual Design: Design for Life (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Fun Toolkit
origin: Janet Read and Stuart MacFarlane (2006), refined by Read (2008); applied by Sim, Read and Horton in Chapter 1
summary: A set of three pictorial, writing-free survey tools (Smileyometer, Again Again table and Fun Sorter) for getting children to rate how much fun a product is.
description: The Fun Toolkit is a survey kit designed for children who cannot yet handle conventional questionnaires. The Smileyometer is a visual analogue scale of five faces from 'Awful' to 'Brilliant', coded 1 to 5. It is given before use, showing only a first screen, to capture expectations, and again after use to capture experienced fun; the difference between the two is itself informative. The Again Again table asks the child to tick yes, maybe or no to 'Would you like to do this again?' for each activity, which is coded 2, 1 and 0 and works as a behavioural-intention proxy for enjoyment. The Fun Sorter asks children to rank several products against criteria, so it is only meaningful in comparative studies. Because none of the tools need writing, they are quick to complete in a classroom. The chapter shows their main weakness: children tend to rate highly to please the adult (satisficing), so scores cluster near the top and are best read as relative rather than absolute. Pairing the toolkit with observation and retrospective problem reporting gives a fuller picture of usability and experience for children's products.
steps: Decide which tools fit: Smileyometer and Again Again table for a single product, add the Fun Sorter only when comparing products.
Show the child the opening screen and collect a 'before' Smileyometer rating of expectations.
Let the child use or play the product for a set but flexible period, observing as they go.
Collect the 'after' Smileyometer and the Again Again table (yes, maybe, no).
Code Smileyometer responses 1 to 5 and Again Again responses 2, 1, 0; compute averages and before-after differences.
Interpret scores alongside observation, watching for ceiling effects and satisficing, and note session factors such as time of day.
outputs: Before and after fun ratings, change scores, a would-play-again score and, in comparative studies, rankings of products.
useWhen: Evaluating games, apps or learning tools with children of roughly primary-school age, especially in schools or labs where writing or long questionnaires are impractical.
avoidWhen: Participants are teenagers or adults who can complete standard scales, or when you need fine-grained diagnostic data rather than overall appeal.
whyLost: It is well established in child-computer interaction research but rarely used outside it, since most commercial UX work involves adult users.
whereToUse: Children's games, educational software, toys with digital components, kids' apps.
example: A team testing a language-learning platform game with 7 to 8 year olds collects a Smileyometer rating from the start screen, lets each child play for about ten minutes, then collects a second Smileyometer and an Again Again response; most children say they would play again, but a third rate it lower after play than before, pointing to an experience that missed expectations.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Sim, G., Read, J. C. and Horton, M. (2016). Practical and ethical concerns in usability testing with children. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 1. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Function Allocation (Fitts List / MABA-MABA)
aka: Men are better at, machines are better at
origin: Paul Fitts et al., 1951 (Human engineering for an effective air-navigation and traffic-control system)
summary: Systematically decides which functions should be performed by people and which by machines, based on comparative strengths and the needs of the joint system.
description: The original Fitts list compared human and machine capabilities (humans better at improvisation and judgement; machines at speed, precision and repetition) to allocate functions. Later work criticised static allocation and proposed dynamic or adaptive allocation and the joint cognitive system perspective, in which the question is how people and automation coordinate rather than who does what. A rigorous allocation analysis lists system functions, evaluates candidate allocations against criteria (performance, workload, situation awareness, skill retention, accountability), and checks for leftover-task problems where people are given only what automation cannot do. With AI assistants this extinct method is suddenly central: every agentic feature is an allocation decision usually made by engineering convenience.
steps: List the system's functions independently of who or what performs them, from a goal-means or task analysis.
For each function, identify candidate allocations: human, machine, shared, or adaptive.
Evaluate candidates against explicit criteria: accuracy, speed, workload, situation awareness, skill decay, accountability, user values.
Check the residual human role for coherence, avoiding 'leftover' allocations that leave people monitoring without context.
Define handover and takeover protocols, including how humans are brought back into the loop.
Test the allocation with simulation or Wizard of Oz under normal and degraded automation conditions.
outputs: A function allocation matrix with rationale, handover protocols, and evaluation results for candidate allocations.
useWhen: Designing AI copilots, agents, automation features or any product that changes who does what.
avoidWhen: Purely manual tools with no automation decisions.
whyLost: The static Fitts list was rightly criticised and the topic faded from HCI as consumer software rarely automated whole functions. Generative AI has made it relevant again without the method being remembered.
whereToUse: AI writing and coding assistants, autonomous agents, smart home automation, clinical decision support.
example: A legal AI tool allocates clause extraction to the machine but leaves lawyers verifying hundreds of extractions with no context. Reallocation makes the AI flag only low-confidence clauses with reasoning, preserving lawyer situation awareness.
sources: Fitts (ed.), Human Engineering for an Effective Air-Navigation and Traffic-Control System (1951)
Dekker & Woods, MABA-MABA or Abracadabra? Progress on human-automation co-ordination (2002), Cognition, Technology & Work
Hollnagel & Woods, Joint Cognitive Systems (2005)
reference: Fitts, P. M. (Ed.) (1951). Human Engineering for an Effective Air-Navigation and Traffic-Control System. National Research Council.

name: Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM)
origin: Erik Hollnagel, 2004-2012
summary: Models everyday work as coupled functions whose normal performance variability can resonate into unexpected outcomes, rather than as failure chains.
description: Listed in the treatise's borrowing matrix for systems engineering, FRAM describes a system as functions, each characterised by six aspects: input, output, precondition, resource, control and time. Analysts describe how functions are coupled and how the variability of each function's output (timing, precision) can combine and resonate to produce unexpected outcomes, good or bad. It is grounded in Safety-II: success and failure have the same sources, so understanding everyday performance matters more than counting errors. For UX, FRAM models service journeys or workflows across people, interfaces and automation to find where small, normal variations (a late update, an imprecise entry) amplify, guiding where to dampen variability or add monitoring.
steps: Define the purpose and scope of analysis (an event or typical work).
Identify functions and describe their six aspects from work-as-done data.
Characterise potential output variability for each function.
Map couplings and identify where variability can aggregate (functional resonance).
Propose ways to monitor and dampen unwanted variability or amplify useful variability.
Validate the model with practitioners.
outputs: FRAM model of coupled functions, variability analysis, resonance points, design and monitoring proposals.
useWhen: Complex sociotechnical services where outcomes emerge from normal variability rather than discrete failures.
avoidWhen: Simple linear tasks; HTA or UFMEA are more efficient.
whyLost: FRAM lives in resilience engineering and patient-safety circles, and its abstract hexagon diagrams are unfamiliar to designers. UX tends to study individual tasks rather than coupled organisational functions.
whereToUse: Hospital discharge, airline disruption handling, delivery networks, human-AI workflows.
example: A FRAM model of hospital discharge shows that slight delays in pharmacy sign-off couple with transport booking to cause evening discharges; the discharge app adds a predicted sign-off time.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Hollnagel E (2012) FRAM: The Functional Resonance Analysis Method
Hollnagel E (2004) Barriers and Accident Prevention
Hollnagel, FRAM: The Functional Resonance Analysis Method (2012)
Hollnagel, Safety-I and Safety-II (2014)
reference: Hollnagel E (2012) FRAM: The Functional Resonance Analysis Method: Modelling Complex Socio-technical Systems. Ashgate.

name: Functionalism and Multiple Realisability in UI Design
origin: Hilary Putnam (1967); Jerry Fodor; collected in Haugeland (ed.), Mind Design II (1997)
summary: Defines interface elements by their functional role, the inputs, outputs and relations they support, so equivalent functions can be realised differently across platforms and modalities.
description: Functionalist philosophy of mind: mental states are defined by their functional role (causal relations to inputs, outputs, and other mental states), not by their physical substrate. Multiple realizability: the same functional state can be realized by different physical implementations. Applied to UX: the same user cognitive state (confusion, engagement, flow) can be produced by many different interface implementations — and any interface producing the right functional role produces the right experience.
steps: Identify the target cognitive/emotional state (e.g., flow, trust, engagement). Apply functional role analysis: what must be true of a design to produce this state?
(1) What inputs (interface properties) must be present?
(2) What other states must it connect to (preconditions, consequences)?
(3) What outputs (user behaviors) should it produce? Any design satisfying all three criteria should work — test multiple realizations.
outputs: Functional role specifications for key components, platform-specific realisations that preserve role, and equivalence tests across devices and modalities.
useWhen: Multi-platform and multimodal products, design systems spanning web, mobile, voice and wearables, and accessibility alternatives that must be functionally equivalent.
avoidWhen: For single-platform visual design questions, or when the team needs empirical user data rather than conceptual specification.
whyLost: It remained a philosophical thesis; design systems grew around visual components rather than functional roles, so the framing never migrated into practice.
whereToUse: Design principle formulation, cross-platform design consistency, AI system behavior design, emotional design research.
example: A bank's design system defines a 'confirm irreversible transfer' role by its required inputs, feedback and reversibility. The web modal, the watch double-tap and the voice assistant's spoken confirmation are tested to ensure all three realise the same role.
sources: Mind Design II — MIT Press (Haugeland, ed.)
Putnam, Psychological predicates (1967)
Fodor, The Language of Thought (1975)
reference: Haugeland J (Ed.) (1997) Mind Design II: Philosophy, Psychology, Artificial Intelligence. MIT Press

name: Funnel Analysis
origin: AIDA sales funnel (E. St. Elmo Lewis, 1898); digital conversion funnels from web analytics, late 1990s
summary: Measures the proportion of users completing each step of a defined sequence to locate where and for whom drop-off occurs.
description: Funnel analysis defines an ordered sequence of events, such as landing, sign-up, verification and first action, and calculates the share of users progressing from each step to the next within a time window. The biggest relative drops point to where to look. Rigour depends on careful event definitions, choosing whether steps must occur in strict order, setting a sensible conversion window, and segmenting by acquisition channel, device and user type, since aggregate funnels hide very different behaviours. Comparing funnels before and after changes requires controlling for seasonality and traffic mix, ideally through experiments. Funnels show where users leave but not why, so the method is strongest when paired with session replay, usability tests or intercept surveys at the leaking step.
steps: Define the target sequence and the exact events representing each step, verifying instrumentation.
Choose ordering rules and a conversion window appropriate to the flow (e.g. same session or 7 days).
Compute step-to-step and overall conversion rates over a stable period.
Segment by channel, device, platform, new versus returning and other relevant attributes.
Identify the largest relative drops and investigate them with qualitative methods.
Test fixes with A/B experiments and monitor funnel metrics post-launch.
outputs: Funnel chart, step conversion rates, segment comparisons, prioritised drop-off points.
useWhen: Onboarding, checkout, sign-up, multi-step forms and any conversion-critical flow with event tracking.
avoidWhen: Non-linear exploratory products where users do not follow fixed sequences; use path analysis instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Core product analytics technique; supported by all major analytics platforms.
whereToUse: Onboarding; checkout; multi-step forms; any conversion-critical flow.
example: A fintech onboarding funnel showed 71% of users dropping at ID verification on Android only. Session replays showed the camera permission prompt failing on certain devices, and a fix lifted completion by 18 points on Android.
sources: Practical Web Analytics for User Experience
Lean Analytics (Croll & Yoskovitz)
reference: Beasley, M. (2013). Practical Web Analytics for User Experience. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Future Workshop
origin: Robert Jungk and Norbert Müllert, 1970s-1987; adopted in Scandinavian PD (Kensing and Madsen, 1991)
summary: A three-phase workshop of critique, fantasy and implementation that lets affected people articulate problems and envision alternatives on their own terms.
description: The future workshop, named in the treatise among the Scandinavian participatory methods, structures participation in three phases. In the critique phase, participants list problems with the current situation without solution-talk. In the fantasy phase, they invert critiques into utopian visions, suspending constraints. In the implementation phase, they assess what can be realised and plan actions. The structure protects participants' framing of problems, separates divergent and convergent thinking, and is designed for people without design training. Kensing and Madsen paired it with metaphorical design to generate system visions with workers.
steps: Prepare: recruit affected participants, a facilitator and a neutral venue; agree the theme.
Critique phase: brainstorm and cluster problems with the current situation, using short statements.
Fantasy phase: invert the key critiques into ideal futures, banning feasibility objections.
Implementation phase: evaluate fantasies against constraints and identify realisable steps.
Agree action plans with owners and follow-up dates.
Feed outputs into design and report back to participants.
outputs: Critique clusters, utopian visions, prioritised implementation plans.
useWhen: Early-stage visioning with stakeholders, especially where power or trust issues exist.
avoidWhen: Detailed design or evaluation questions; use prototyping or testing instead.
whyLost: Overtaken by design-thinking ideation formats that drop the critique phase and the activist framing.
whereToUse: Civic services, union or worker-facing tools, NHS service redesign, community technology.
example: Library staff run a future workshop on a new self-service system; the critique phase surfaces fear of losing patron contact, and the fantasy phase produces a 'roaming librarian' concept that becomes the service model.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Jungk R & Müllert N (1987) Future Workshops: How to Create Desirable Futures
Kensing F & Madsen KH (1991) Generating visions: future workshops and metaphorical design. In Design at Work
Jungk & Müllert, Future Workshops: How to Create Desirable Futures (1987)
Kensing & Madsen, Generating visions: Future workshops and metaphorical design (1991), in Greenbaum & Kyng (eds.), Design at Work
reference: Kensing F & Madsen KH (1991) Generating visions: future workshops and metaphorical design. In Greenbaum & Kyng (Eds) Design at Work. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Future-Oriented Diary and Pre-Mortem Protocol
origin: Pre-mortem from Gary Klein, 2007; expectation-experience comparison from expectancy research
summary: Participants predict an experience before it happens and record the reality afterwards; the gap measures mental model accuracy, with a pre-mortem variant for risks.
description: This protocol pairs a prediction entry before a task with an experience entry immediately after. Participants say what they expect will happen, what will be easy or hard, and how long it will take; afterwards they report what actually happened. The gap between prediction and experience is the data: it locates inaccurate mental models, system behaviour users find systematically surprising, and miscalibrated confidence. The pre-mortem variant, adapted from Gary Klein's project risk technique, asks experienced users to imagine that a new feature has failed after six months and explain why, generating a risk inventory before launch. Both make expectations explicit rather than inferred after the fact.
steps: Prediction diary entry (before use): Before the participant begins a task or interaction, ask them to predict: "What do you think will happen? What will be easy? What will be difficult? How long do you think it will take?"
Experience diary entry (after use): Immediately after: "What actually happened? What was easier or harder than expected? How long did it actually take?"

Gap analysis: The gap between prediction and experience is your data. A prediction gap reveals: (a) where mental models are inaccurate, (b) where the system's behaviour is systematically unexpected, (c) where user confidence is miscalibrated.

Pre-mortem variant: Before a new feature or redesign launches, ask experienced users to imagine that the feature has failed completely after 6 months of use. "What went wrong? Why did users stop using it?" The resulting list is your risk inventory for user research.
outputs: Prediction-experience gap tables, mental model inaccuracies, calibration measures, and a user-generated risk inventory.
useWhen: Testing mental models of new or complex features, onboarding expectation-setting, or anticipating failure modes before a launch.
avoidWhen: When participants have no basis to predict (wholly novel concepts), or for routine tasks where predictions add nothing; use concept testing or usability tests.
whyLost: Pre-mortems are known as team rituals, but structured prediction-versus-experience recording with users is rarely run.
whereToUse: Onboarding, AI features where expectations are often wrong, financial products with delays (transfers, claims, loans), and feature launches.
example: Before a first international transfer, users predict arrival time and fees; afterwards they record reality. A consistent one-day overestimate of speed leads to clearer arrival estimates on the confirmation screen.
sources: User Research (Marsh)
Validating Product Ideas (Tomer Sharon)
Just Enough Research (Hall)
Performing a Project Premortem (Klein)
reference: Klein, G. (2007). Performing a project premortem. Harvard Business Review, 85(9), 18-19.

name: Futures Wheel
origin: Jerome Glenn, 1971
summary: Places a change at the centre and maps its direct, second-order and third-order consequences in rings, revealing knock-on effects and risks.
description: The futures wheel is a structured brainstorming method for exploring consequences. A trend or decision sits in the centre; first-order consequences are drawn around it; each generates second-order consequences, and so on. Participants label consequences as positive or negative, likely or speculative, and link interactions. Done rigorously, it uses diverse participants, evidence for first-order effects, and follow-up assessment of likelihood and impact, turning results into risk registers or research questions. For UX, it is a quick way to examine second-order effects of features, such as how a 'read receipts' feature changes social obligations, before launch.
steps: Write the change (feature, policy, trend) precisely in the centre.
With a diverse group, generate first-order consequences for different stakeholders.
For each, generate second- and third-order consequences, drawing links between rings.
Mark consequences as desirable or undesirable and estimate likelihood and impact.
Identify consequences needing evidence and convert them into research questions or metrics.
Feed high-impact negative consequences into design mitigations and monitoring.
outputs: A futures wheel diagram, prioritised second-order effects, research questions and mitigations.
useWhen: Assessing the downstream effects of a feature, policy or technology trend before committing.
avoidWhen: Well-understood changes with established evidence of effects.
whyLost: Futures tools are seen as speculative; UX evaluates features at first order through testing.
whereToUse: Social features, AI automation, policy changes, pricing changes, platform rules.
example: A futures wheel for 'AI auto-replies in messaging' surfaces third-order effects: recipients start distrusting quick replies, prompting a disclosure indicator and further research on norms.
sources: Glenn, The futures wheel (2009), in Glenn & Gordon (eds.), Futures Research Methodology Version 3.0, Millennium Project
Glenn, Futurizing teaching vs futures course (1972), Social Science Record
reference: Glenn, J. C. (2009). The Futures Wheel. In Futures Research Methodology 3.0. The Millennium Project.

name: Gabor-Granger Pricing
origin: André Gabor and Clive Granger, 1960s (Price as an indicator of quality, 1966)
summary: Asks purchase intention at a sequence of prices to build a demand curve and identify the revenue-maximising price.
description: Respondents are shown a product and asked if they would buy at a given price; depending on the answer, the price moves up or down a ladder, typically 5-7 price points. Aggregating gives the proportion willing to buy at each price, a demand curve, and multiplying by price gives a revenue curve with a maximum. The method is simple and suits single products with known value. Its weaknesses are hypothetical bias and anchoring from the starting price, so rigour comes from randomising start points, calibrating stated intent (e.g. 'definitely' responses weighted) and validating against behavioural tests.
steps: Define the product, context and 5-7 realistic price points.
Randomise the starting price across respondents to manage anchoring.
Ask purchase likelihood at each price, moving up after yes and down after no.
Calibrate stated likelihood (e.g. count only top-box, or apply calibration factors from past launches).
Construct demand and revenue curves with confidence intervals and identify revenue-maximising price by segment.
Validate with a live price test or fake-door experiment where possible.
outputs: Demand curve, revenue curve, price elasticity estimates and segment differences.
useWhen: Pricing a single, well-understood product or plan with a plausible price range.
avoidWhen: Products where features vary with price (use conjoint) or new categories with no reference (start with Van Westendorp).
whyLost: Pricing research sits outside UX, and the method's simplicity hides its biases.
whereToUse: Subscription plans, in-app purchases, B2B seat pricing, add-ons.
example: A meditation app's Gabor-Granger study with 1,200 users finds revenue peaks at $59 per year, but a live A/B price test shows actual conversion 40% lower than stated, so stated figures are recalibrated for future studies.
sources: Gabor & Granger, Price as an indicator of quality: report on an enquiry (1966), Economica
Nagle & Müller, The Strategy and Tactics of Pricing (6th ed., 2018)
reference: Gabor, A., & Granger, C. W. J. (1966). Price as an indicator of quality. Economica, 33(129), 43-70.

name: Galvanic Skin Response
origin: Charles Féré, 1888; Ivan Tarchanoff, 1890
summary: Measures changes in skin conductance driven by sweat gland activity as an index of physiological arousal, detecting stress or frustration moments during interaction.
description: Electrodermal activity reflects sympathetic nervous system activation: as arousal rises, eccrine sweat glands, particularly on palms and fingers, increase skin conductance. The signal has a slow tonic level and phasic responses (skin conductance responses) occurring one to three seconds after a stimulus. It indicates arousal intensity, not valence, so it cannot distinguish excitement from frustration without other data. In UX it is used to identify moments of stress, surprise or frustration in tasks, games and immersive experiences. Rigour comes from controlling temperature and movement, recording baselines, separating tonic and phasic components, time-locking responses to events, using within-subject comparisons because individual differences are large, and combining EDA with video, self-report or facial coding to interpret valence.
steps: Define events or segments of interest and how arousal relates to the research question.
Attach sensors to fingers or palm (or validated wrist devices) and control room temperature.
Record a resting baseline of several minutes before tasks.
Run tasks with precisely time-stamped events and record video for context, with 15-30 participants.
Decompose the signal into tonic and phasic components and count or measure responses in windows 1-4 seconds after events.
Interpret peaks alongside video, self-report or facial coding to determine valence.
outputs: Arousal timelines, event-locked response counts and amplitudes, annotated stress or frustration moments.
useWhen: Detecting frustration or stress in usability studies, games, VR, automotive and high-stakes tasks where self-report may be unreliable.
avoidWhen: When valence matters more than arousal, when participants move a lot, or when observation and think-aloud already reveal the issues.
whyLost: It persists in psychophysiology, neuromarketing and games research but UX rarely invests in lab equipment and signal-processing expertise, and earlier wrist wearables produced unreliable data.
whereToUse: Emotional response research; frustration detection; high-stakes usability testing.
example: A telehealth app recorded EDA from 20 older adults during first video consultations. Phasic peaks clustered at the camera permission prompt, consistent with think-aloud remarks of anxiety, leading to a pre-call camera check.
sources: Sensation and Perception
Electrodermal Activity (Wolfram Boucsein)
Unmasking the Face (Ekman & Friesen)
Designing Across Senses (Noessel)
Affective Computing (Picard)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 38 — FACS, Micro-Expression Analysis & Psychophysiology
reference: Boucsein, W. (2012). Electrodermal Activity (2nd ed.). Springer.

name: Game Experience Questionnaire (GEQ)
origin: IJsselsteijn, de Kort and Poels, Game Experience Lab, Eindhoven (2008); used in Chapters 6 and 11
summary: A modular self-report questionnaire measuring player experience during and after play, including competence, immersion, flow, challenge, affect and tiredness.
description: The GEQ has four modules: a core module for the experience of play, an in-game module for brief measurement during play, a social presence module for play with others, and a post-game module for how players feel afterwards. Items are rated on a scale from 0 (not agree) to 4 (completely agree) and averaged into components. In the core module these are competence, sensory and imaginative immersion, flow, tension, challenge, negative affect and positive affect; the post-game module covers positive experience, negative experience and tiredness. Researchers choose modules to suit the study; Chapter 6 dropped the social presence and in-game modules because the game had no other players and short play time. The chapter also shows good practice: recode reversed items, check each component's Cronbach's alpha, drop items with low item-scale correlation and discard unreliable components before comparing conditions. In that study a tangible interface produced higher competence, immersion and positive affect than an equivalent tablet interface. Chapter 11 uses a home-made questionnaire under the same name, so check which instrument a report means.
steps: Choose the modules relevant to the study (core, in-game, social presence, post-game).
Administer the core and post-game modules immediately after a defined play session; use in-game items at breaks if needed.
Recode reversed items and compute component scores as item means.
Check reliability per component, removing weak items and setting aside unreliable components.
Compare components between conditions or versions with suitable tests.
Interpret results with interviews or observation to explain differences.
outputs: Component scores for player experience (competence, immersion, flow, challenge, affect, tiredness and so on) for each condition.
useWhen: Comparing game versions, controllers or interfaces on player experience, or tracking experience across iterations.
avoidWhen: Products are not games, or you need a short instrument with strong published validation; some GEQ components have shown weak reliability.
whyLost: Widely used in games research, but general UX teams tend to use broader instruments such as UEQ or AttrakDiff.
whereToUse: Video games, tangible and mixed-reality games, serious games, gamified interfaces.
example: A study compares a tangible block controller with a tablet version of the same puzzle game using the GEQ core and post-game modules; the tangible group scores higher on competence and positive affect, while flow and challenge do not differ.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Menestrina, Z., Conci, A., Siesser, A., Masu, R., Bianchi, M. and De Angeli, A. (2016). Tangible and graphical game interfaces: an experimental comparison. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 6. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Game Thinking Progression Design
origin: Amy Jo Kim, 2018
summary: Applies game design's player journey (onboarding, habit building, mastery) to product design, co-developed with early superfans through rapid prototyping.
description: Game thinking, as articulated by Amy Jo Kim, transfers how successful games structure experience to non-game products. It defines a player journey in three stages: onboarding (learning the ropes), habit building (a compelling core loop that brings people back) and mastery (deeper challenges and status for experienced users). Rather than designing for everyone, the team identifies early superfans, people who already have the problem intensely, and co-creates with them through fast, cheap prototypes and short test cycles. Progression milestones and the core learning loop are designed explicitly and validated against behaviour. Rigour comes from grounding loops in real user motivation, measuring retention at each journey stage, and iterating rather than adding mechanics.
steps: Map the mastery journey:
Onboarding — what is the 'beginner's mind' moment?
(2) Habit building — what's the core loop that keeps users returning?
(3) Mastery — what does expert use look like and feel like?
(4) For each stage: what is the intrinsic reward?
(5) Select mechanics that amplify each stage's intrinsic reward: leveling (mastery), streaks (habit), discovery (onboarding). Avoid mechanics that don't map to a stage.
outputs: A player journey map, a core learning loop, superfan research insights, progression milestones and prototype test findings.
useWhen: New products seeking product-market fit, engagement-driven products, learning and community platforms where progression and mastery sustain use.
avoidWhen: Avoid for utilitarian tools where users want to finish and leave; avoid when engagement is not in users' interest.
whyLost: Gamification hype focused on surface mechanics; Kim's systems-level game thinking stayed within the startup coaching world.
whereToUse: Community platform design, enterprise software engagement, health behavior apps, learning products.
example: A language-learning startup identifies twelve superfans, maps their journey from first lesson to daily habit to conversational mastery, and prototypes a weekly challenge loop tested with them before scaling.
sources: Game Thinking — Amy Jo Kim
reference: Kim AJ (2018) Game Thinking: Innovate Smarter and Drive Deep Engagement with Design Techniques from Hit Games. Gamethinking.io

name: Game-Theoretic Analysis of Multi-User Systems
origin: John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern, 1944; John Nash, 1950
summary: Models how users' choices interact strategically in multi-user products, predicting equilibria such as free-riding or gaming and testing design changes to incentives.
description: Game theory models situations where each actor's best choice depends on what others do. In multi-user products, such as marketplaces, reviews, referrals, social feeds and collaborative tools, individual behaviour that is sensible for one user can produce collective outcomes no one wants: review inflation, free-riding on shared content, race-to-the-bottom pricing. The method formalises the actors, their available strategies and payoffs, then identifies Nash equilibria and checks whether they match observed behaviour. Rigour comes from making payoffs explicit and grounding them in data, testing robustness to assumptions, and validating predictions with behavioural logs or controlled experiments. It moves teams beyond individual-level UX thinking to see how design rules create incentives across the whole population.
steps: Identify the actors (e.g. buyers, sellers, creators, moderators) and the strategic decisions each makes.
Specify strategies and estimate payoffs for each actor, using data where possible.
Build a payoff matrix or extensive-form model and identify equilibria.
Compare predicted equilibria with observed behaviour from logs or research.
Model proposed design changes as altered payoffs and predict the new equilibrium.
Validate with experiments or staged rollouts and monitor for unintended strategic responses.
outputs: Strategic model of actors and payoffs, equilibrium predictions, design changes ranked by predicted incentive effect.
useWhen: Marketplaces, social platforms, ratings and review systems, referral schemes and any feature where users' outcomes depend on each other.
avoidWhen: Single-user tools without strategic interdependence; standard usability and behavioural research suffice.
whyLost: Latent: Academically interesting; rarely applied in UX practice outside platform/marketplace design.
whereToUse: Social platforms; marketplace design; multiplayer features; incentive system design.
example: A freelance marketplace saw average ratings drift to 4.9. Modelling revealed mutual reciprocity as the equilibrium of a simultaneous reveal-later system; switching to blind double reviews was predicted and then shown to widen rating variance.
sources: Preference Belief and Similarity
Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (von Neumann & Morgenstern)
reference: Osborne, M. J. (2004). An Introduction to Game Theory. Oxford University Press.

name: GameFlow Evaluation
donor: Games research, building on flow theory
origin: Sweetser and Wyeth (2005), based on Csikszentmihalyi's flow elements; applied by Hernandez Luna and Golightly in Chapter 8
summary: Evaluating enjoyment by checking a game against eight flow-based elements: concentration, challenge, player skills, control, clear goals, feedback, immersion and social interaction.
description: GameFlow translates Csikszentmihalyi's elements of flow into eight criteria for enjoyable games. Concentration: the game provides stimuli worth attending to. Challenge: difficulty matches skill and offers levels. Player skills: players can start without a manual and learning is part of the fun.
