name: GOMS and KLM with Expert User Timing Studies
origin: Stuart Card, Thomas Moran and Allen Newell (1980, 1983)
summary: Predicts expert task times by decomposing tasks into GOMS methods and keystroke-level operators, calibrated with timing studies of real expert users and devices.
description: GOMS (Goals, Operators, Methods, Selection rules) models skilled, error-free performance; its simplest variant, the Keystroke-Level Model, predicts execution time by summing standard operator times: keystroke (about 0.2 s for a skilled typist), pointing (about 1.1 s), homing hands between devices (0.4 s) and mental preparation (1.35 s), using placement rules for M operators. Predictions typically fall within about 20% of observed expert times. Its rigour, and its decline, lie in calibration: standard operator times are population averages from 1980s hardware. Running short timing studies with actual expert users on current devices to re-estimate operator times, especially for touch, and validating model predictions against observed times, makes KLM a cheap way to compare designs for high-frequency tasks without large experiments.
steps: Empirically derive KLM parameters for your specific user group and device: time 20+ participants performing each operator type in isolation.
Compute trimmed means.
For touch interfaces: separate tapping (0.3–0.5s) from swipe (0.2–0.4s).
For elderly users: K≈0.35s, P≈1.5s.
For expert keyboard users: K≈0.12s.
Apply updated parameters to KLM predictions for the target interface.
outputs: Task method decompositions, calibrated operator times for the target population and device, predicted versus observed task times, and design comparisons in seconds saved per task.
useWhen: High-frequency expert workflows such as call centres, data entry, trading, clinical documentation, and choosing between design alternatives before building.
avoidWhen: For novice use, learning, error-prone tasks or open-ended creative work, which GOMS does not model; use usability testing or cognitive walkthrough.
whyLost: GOMS was associated with desktop-era research and seen as laborious, and teams stopped calibrating operator times, so predictions on modern touch devices drifted and lost credibility.
whereToUse: Mobile UX performance prediction, accessibility-aware time estimates, expert vs. novice interface benchmarking, call-center UI optimization.
example: A contact-centre CRM compares two layouts for logging a call outcome. Calibrated KLM predicts 4.1 s saved per call, which at 60,000 calls a day justifies the redesign; a timing study with 8 agents confirms a 3.7 s saving.
sources: Human-Computer Interaction (Dix, Finlay, Abowd & Beale)
The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (Card, Moran & Newell)
Human-Computer Interaction — Alan Dix
reference: Card SK, Moran TP & Newell A (1983) The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction. Lawrence Erlbaum

name: Gower's Distance for Mixed-Data Clustering
origin: J. C. Gower (1971), Biometrics
summary: Measures similarity between users described by a mix of numbers and categories, so they can be clustered properly.
description: Persona and segment data mixes types: age and session counts are numeric, role and plan are categorical, some answers are yes or no. Standard k-means needs numeric data, and one-hot encoding distorts distances. Gower's distance scales each variable to 0 to 1 by its own type (range-normalised difference for numbers, match or mismatch for categories) and averages them. It pairs with hierarchical clustering or PAM (k-medoids). Bruce and Bruce also warn about dominant variables and scaling issues that silently shape clusters.
steps: Assemble mixed variables per user and decide which to include.
Compute the Gower distance matrix, optionally weighting variables.
Cluster with hierarchical clustering or PAM.
Choose the number of clusters with silhouette widths and interpretability.
Profile and name clusters, then validate with qualitative follow-up.
outputs: Segments based on all the data types you collected.
useWhen: Clustering survey or CRM data with categorical and numeric variables.
avoidWhen: Very large datasets (the distance matrix grows quadratically) or purely numeric data.
whyLost: UX segmentation commonly runs k-means on whatever is numeric and drops the rest.
whereToUse: Data-driven personas, B2B account segmentation, research panel stratification.
example: Clustering 900 B2B users on role, company size, plan and usage with Gower distance gives five segments; k-means on usage alone had missed the admin segment.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
reference: Gower, J. C. (1971). A general coefficient of similarity and some of its properties. Biometrics 27; Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 7.

name: GRADE Evidence Grading
donor: Evidence-based medicine and clinical guideline development
origin: GRADE Working Group, Gordon Guyatt and colleagues, 2000-2008
summary: Rates the certainty of a body of evidence as high, moderate, low or very low by assessing risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias.
description: GRADE separates the quality of evidence from the strength of a recommendation. Evidence from randomised trials starts high and observational evidence low; ratings are downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency across studies, indirectness (different population or outcome), imprecision (wide intervals) and publication bias, and upgraded for large effects, dose-response or when confounding would reduce the effect. The Evidence-to-Decision framework then weighs benefits, harms, values, resources and feasibility. Research repositories in UX store 'insights' without any certainty grading, so a single five-person study and a replicated experiment look equally authoritative. GRADE offers a rigorous, transparent grading scheme.
steps: Define the question and the critical outcomes for the decision.
Gather the body of evidence for each outcome (studies, experiments, analytics).
Assign a starting certainty by design (experiments high, observational and qualitative lower).
Assess and document downgrades for bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias, and possible upgrades.
Assign a final certainty rating per outcome and present a summary-of-findings table.
Use an Evidence-to-Decision table to make and explain recommendations, stating strength (strong or conditional).
outputs: Certainty ratings per outcome, summary-of-findings tables and transparent recommendations.
useWhen: Building research repositories, writing design guidelines, or making recommendations from mixed-quality evidence.
avoidWhen: Single exploratory studies where grading adds little; or for qualitative evidence alone, consider GRADE-CERQual.
whyLost: Medical evidence frameworks were not part of UX's culture, which favours storytelling over graded certainty.
whereToUse: Insight repositories, design system guidelines, accessibility standards, AI product policy decisions.
example: A research repository tags each insight with GRADE certainty. A popular insight that 'users want dark mode' is rated low (indirect, self-report), while 'inline validation reduces errors' is rated high from replicated experiments.
sources: Guyatt et al., GRADE: an emerging consensus on rating quality of evidence and strength of recommendations (2008), BMJ
Lewin et al., Applying GRADE-CERQual to qualitative evidence synthesis findings (2018), Implementation Science

name: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) for UX Outcomes
origin: Friedman (2001) gradient boosting; Chen & Guestrin (2016) XGBoost
summary: A high-accuracy model that builds many small trees in sequence, each correcting the last, for predicting churn, satisfaction or conversion.
description: Boosting fits a series of shallow trees where each new tree focuses on the errors of the ensemble so far. XGBoost adds regularisation and efficient computation, and it wins many prediction competitions on tabular data. Bruce and Bruce explain the key hyperparameters (learning rate, depth, subsampling, regularisation) and how to tune them with cross-validation to avoid overfitting. Paired with SHAP values, boosting becomes an explainable driver model for large behavioural datasets.
steps: Prepare a tabular dataset of user features and an outcome.
Split into training and test sets (or use cross-validation).
Tune learning rate, tree depth, subsampling and regularisation.
Evaluate on held-out data with AUC, precision and recall.
Explain predictions with SHAP values and validate surprising drivers qualitatively.
outputs: An accurate predictive model with explainable drivers.
useWhen: Large behavioural or survey datasets where prediction accuracy matters.
avoidWhen: Small samples or when a simple, transparent model is enough.
whyLost: Considered a data science tool; UX rarely builds predictive models.
whereToUse: Churn prediction, satisfaction prediction from telemetry, support contact prediction.
example: A model predicting which new customers will contact support within 30 days reaches AUC 0.84, and SHAP shows address validation errors are the top driver.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 6.

name: Granger Causality Testing
origin: Clive Granger, 1969
summary: Tests whether past values of one time series improve prediction of another beyond its own past, a disciplined but limited form of temporal causal evidence.
description: X Granger-causes Y if lagged values of X significantly improve a model predicting Y from its own lags. Estimated within vector autoregression (VAR) models with stationarity checks and lag selection by information criteria, the test provides evidence about temporal precedence and predictive information. It is not proof of causation: common causes and unmeasured variables can produce Granger causality, and instantaneous effects are missed. Used carefully, it helps untangle feedback between metrics, such as whether support contacts predict churn or churn predicts support contacts, and whether engagement drives content creation or vice versa.
steps: Choose the time series pairs or sets and an appropriate aggregation interval.
Test for stationarity (ADF, KPSS) and difference or detrend as needed.
Fit a VAR model selecting lag length by AIC or BIC.
Run Granger tests in both directions and check residual diagnostics.
Report results as predictive precedence, and check robustness to lag choices and added control series.
Corroborate with experiments or other causal designs before acting.
outputs: VAR models, directional Granger test results and impulse response functions.
useWhen: Exploring temporal relationships and feedback between aggregated metrics with long series.
avoidWhen: Making strong causal claims, or with short series; use experiments or quasi-experiments.
whyLost: It is standard in econometrics but rarely considered in product metric analysis, where correlation charts dominate.
whereToUse: Marketplace supply and demand dynamics, content creation and consumption, support load and churn.
example: A marketplace tests whether seller listings Granger-cause buyer visits or vice versa. Buyer visits predict new listings two weeks later but not the reverse, shifting growth investment to demand.
sources: Granger, Investigating causal relations by econometric models and cross-spectral methods (1969), Econometrica
Lütkepohl, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis (2005)
reference: Granger, C. W. J. (1969). Econometrica, 37(3), 424-438.

name: Graph-Theoretic Navigation Analysis
origin: Leonhard Euler, 1736; hypertext metrics by Botafogo, Rivlin and Shneiderman, 1992
summary: Models a site or app as a directed graph and computes path length, centrality and connectivity to find unreachable, overburdened or poorly linked content.
description: Any navigation structure can be represented as a directed graph: screens or pages are nodes, links are edges. Graph theory then provides precise metrics. Shortest path lengths show how many steps separate users from key content; centrality measures show which pages carry most navigational load; compactness and stratum metrics, proposed by Botafogo and colleagues for hypertext, characterise how interconnected and how linear a structure is. Strongly connected components reveal sections users cannot leave without the back button. The method is rigorous when the graph is extracted automatically from a crawl or app state model, metrics are weighted by actual traffic or task importance, and changes are simulated before implementation. It complements tree testing by covering the full link structure, not just the hierarchy.
steps: Crawl the site or export the app's screen map to build a directed graph of nodes and links.
Compute shortest path lengths from entry points to key task destinations.
Calculate centrality (degree, betweenness, PageRank) and identify overloaded hubs and orphaned nodes.
Weight metrics by traffic or task priority using analytics data.
Simulate structural changes (new links, merged sections) and recompute metrics.
Validate the preferred structure with tree testing or first-click testing before implementation.
outputs: Navigation graph, path length and centrality tables, orphan and bottleneck lists, simulated metric changes for redesign options.
useWhen: Large websites, intranets, documentation and multi-screen apps undergoing IA redesign.
avoidWhen: Small sites where a sitemap review is enough, or when the problem is labelling rather than structure; use card sorting or tree testing.
whyLost: Latent: Used in IA research; rarely applied in standard practice outside web analytics.
whereToUse: IA optimization; site redesign; search architecture.
example: A university website crawl of 9,000 pages found admissions deadlines were six clicks from the home page and that 1,200 pages were orphaned. Adding three cross-links cut the median path to key admissions pages from 5.2 to 2.8 clicks.
sources: Where Mathematics Comes From
Structural analysis of hypertexts (Botafogo, Rivlin & Shneiderman)
reference: Botafogo, R. A., Rivlin, E., & Shneiderman, B. (1992). Structural analysis of hypertexts: Identifying hierarchies and useful metrics. ACM Transactions on Information Systems, 10(2), 142-180.

name: Graphical Vector Autoregression for Experience Sampling Data
origin: Part of the network psychometrics toolkit described in Isvoranu et al. (2022), with R packages graphicalVAR, mlVAR, psychonetrics and mgm; discussed in the book with reference to Epskamp et al. (2018).
summary: Fitting a vector autoregressive model to repeated self-reports or behaviour logs to obtain a directed temporal network (what predicts what at the next moment) and an undirected contemporaneous network (what co-occurs within the same moment).
description: When people answer the same short questionnaire many times a day, or when behaviour is logged at regular intervals, the data can show how states influence each other over time. Graphical vector autoregression regresses each variable at one time point on all variables at the previous time point, with regularisation, and models the remaining same-moment associations as a partial correlation network. The result is a temporal network with arrows, read as predictive (Granger-type) relations, and a contemporaneous network. Versions exist for a single person, for many people with multilevel estimation, and for panel data. The book lists practical threats: these models need many reliable, stationary measurements; the sampling rate must be fast enough for the process studied; equal spacing between measurements is assumed unless continuous-time models are used; and predictive arrows are not proof of causation, which ultimately requires intervention. For UX, the method can show whether frustration tends to precede abandonment, whether stress predicts later use of a wellbeing feature, or how motivation, effort and use feed each other during habit formation.
steps: Choose a small set of states or behaviours to track and an interval that matches how fast they change.
Collect intensive repeated measures (experience sampling prompts or regular log aggregates) over days or weeks.
Check and handle trends, missing prompts and unequal spacing; detrend or model time as needed.
Fit a single-person graphical VAR or a multilevel VAR across participants.
Inspect the temporal, contemporaneous and, for multilevel models, between-person networks.
Interpret arrows as predictive relations, then test promising links with an intervention study.
outputs: Temporal (directed), contemporaneous and between-person networks of the tracked variables, per person or across the sample.
useWhen: You run diary or experience sampling studies, or have regular behavioural logs, and want to understand sequences and feedback among states rather than averages.
avoidWhen: There are fewer than several dozen measurements per person, measurement intervals are irregular and long, or stakeholders will read arrows as proven causes.
whyLost: UX diary studies are usually analysed qualitatively or with averages; intensive longitudinal modelling sits in clinical and personality psychology and needs statistical expertise.
whereToUse: Habit-formation studies, wellbeing and health apps, workplace tools where stress and productivity interact, learning products tracking motivation and practice.
example: Sixty users of a language-learning app answer five questions about motivation, boredom, perceived progress and stress four times a day for three weeks, alongside logged practice. A multilevel VAR shows that perceived progress predicts motivation at the next prompt and boredom predicts skipped practice, while stress links to boredom only within the same moment.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: Greimas Actantial Model Analysis
origin: Algirdas Julien Greimas, 1966 (Sémantique structurale)
summary: Maps any narrative onto six roles (subject, object, sender, receiver, helper, opponent) to reveal how users and brands cast the product in their stories.
description: Greimas generalised Propp's folktale functions into six actants on three axes: desire (subject seeks object), communication (sender initiates the quest for a receiver) and power (helpers and opponents). Any story, including a user's account of adopting a product or a company's marketing narrative, can be mapped this way. The analysis reveals whether users cast the product as helper, opponent, object or sender, who the real subject is, and what the object of desire truly is. Comparing user narratives with the company's intended narrative exposes mismatches; mapping complaints shows when the product becomes an opponent. The semiotic square can extend analysis of underlying value oppositions.
steps: Collect narratives: interview stories, reviews, social posts, and the company's own marketing narrative.
For each narrative, identify the subject and object of desire.
Identify sender (what motivates the quest) and receiver (who benefits).
Identify helpers and opponents, noting where the product, competitors, institutions or people appear.
Compare actantial structures across user segments and against the intended brand narrative.
Derive implications for positioning, onboarding narrative and features that shift the product into the helper role.
outputs: Actantial maps per narrative, segment comparisons and narrative mismatch analysis.
useWhen: Understanding the role a product plays in users' lives and stories, and aligning brand narrative with lived experience.
avoidWhen: Task-level usability questions.
whyLost: Structural semiotics is taught in literature and some marketing schools, but rarely applied in UX research.
whereToUse: Brand and positioning research, health and fitness apps, financial planning tools, AI assistants' perceived role.
example: Analysing 60 reviews of a budgeting app, researchers find users cast the app as an opponent (a nagging parent) to the subject's desire for freedom. Repositioning it as a helper toward 'freedom from money worry' improves retention messaging.
sources: Greimas, Structural Semantics: An Attempt at a Method (1983 English translation of 1966)
Chandler, Semiotics: The Basics (3rd ed., 2017)
Floch, Semiotics, Marketing and Communication (2001)
reference: Greimas, A. J. (1983). Structural Semantics. University of Nebraska Press.

name: Greimasian Actantial Model for Task Narratives
origin: Algirdas Julien Greimas, 1966
summary: Maps a user task as a narrative of six actants (subject, object, sender, receiver, helper, opponent) to locate where motivation, goal or support breaks down.
description: Greimas reduced narrative structure to six actants present in any goal-directed action: Subject (who pursues), Object (the goal), Sender (the motivation or commissioning force), Receiver (the beneficiary), Helper (forces aiding) and Opponent (forces obstructing). The treatise proposes mapping any user task this way: the user seeks a goal, sent by their motivation, received by a beneficiary, aided by interface affordances that work and blocked by friction, confusion or error. The framework identifies where the narrative breaks: no clear Object, a Sender misaligned with what the design assumes, or Opponents invisible to the designer. It is especially useful when the beneficiary differs from the user (for example a carer acting for a parent).
steps: Select a task or journey and gather research data about it.
Identify the Subject and Object of the task from the user's perspective.
Identify the Sender (motivation) and Receiver (beneficiary), noting when they are third parties.
List Helpers and Opponents, including non-interface forces (family, policy, time).
Locate narrative breakdowns: unclear Object, misaligned Sender, unrecognised Opponents.
Redesign to clarify the Object, align with the true Sender and neutralise Opponents.
outputs: Actantial maps per task, breakdown diagnosis, design implications.
useWhen: Motivation and friction analysis, onboarding narratives, user story structuring, proxy-use scenarios.
avoidWhen: Low-level interaction problems; use usability testing or KLM.
whyLost: Almost unknown outside literary semiotics; never introduced into UX.
whereToUse: Onboarding, caregiver and proxy access flows, behaviour change apps, B2B buying journeys.
example: Mapping a pension consolidation task shows the Sender is a partner's insistence, not the user's goal; the Receiver is the household, so the redesign adds shared progress for partners.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Greimas AJ (1966) Sémantique structurale (Structural Semantics: An Attempt at a Method)
Barthes R (1977) Introduction to the structural analysis of narratives

name: Gricean maxim audit (Quantity/Quality/Relation/Manner)
origin: H. P. Grice, 'Logic and Conversation', 1975
summary: Evaluates interface and conversational messages against Grice's four maxims to find where text says too much or too little, misleads, is irrelevant or is unclear.
description: Grice's cooperative principle holds that conversational partners expect contributions to be as informative as required and no more (Quantity), truthful and evidenced (Quality), relevant (Relation), and clear, brief and orderly (Manner). Users read interface text as cooperative communication, so violations produce misunderstanding or unintended inferences. A Gricean maxim audit reviews each message, especially errors, confirmations, warnings and chatbot responses, against each maxim, records violations, and rates severity by consequence. It is particularly valuable for conversational interfaces and AI outputs, which can be fluent yet violate Quality (unsupported claims) or Quantity (padding). Rigour comes from using two independent reviewers, explicit criteria per maxim and validation with users on high-severity items.
steps: Collect all messages in scope: errors, warnings, confirmations, empty states, tooltips and conversational responses.
Define operational criteria for each maxim (for example Quantity: includes cause and next step, no unrequested detail).
Have two reviewers independently rate each message on each maxim as met, minor violation or major violation; reconcile disagreements.
Rate severity by consequence of misunderstanding (for example 1-4 scale) and prioritise major violations with high severity.
Rewrite flagged messages and test with 5-10 users using interpretation questions.
Encode maxim criteria into content guidelines and review checklists.
outputs: A message-by-maxim violation matrix with severity, rewritten messages, user interpretation results, and guideline updates.
useWhen: For error messages, warnings, chatbots, AI assistants, and any product where text drives decisions.
avoidWhen: When the issue is visual or interaction design rather than language; use heuristic evaluation.
whyLost: Grice is foundational in linguistics and taught in conversation design, but rarely applied as a systematic audit in UX writing.
whereToUse: Conversational AI, clinical alerts, financial messages, legal and consent text, and developer error messages.
example: A surgical console error says 'Instrument fault. Contact support.' The audit flags Quantity (no cause or safe action) and Relation (support is irrelevant mid-procedure). The rewrite names the faulty arm and the immediate safe action.

Hall, E., Conversational Design (2018)

name: Gricean Pragmatics Analysis
origin: H. Paul Grice, 1975
summary: Audits system messages and conversational turns against Grice's maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner to find where the system breaks conversational expectations.
description: Grice proposed that conversation rests on a cooperative principle, expressed as four maxims: say as much as needed and no more (quantity), say what you believe true and have evidence for (quality), be relevant (relation), and be clear, brief and orderly (manner). Listeners infer meaning, called implicature, when a speaker appears to flout a maxim. Users apply the same expectations to interfaces and especially to chatbots and AI assistants. A pragmatics audit codes each system utterance against the maxims and also looks for unintended implicatures, such as a vague error implying user fault. Rigour comes from coding transcripts with two coders, rating severity, and validating with users by asking what they inferred from messages. It is particularly useful for diagnosing why technically correct responses feel unhelpful or evasive.
steps: Collect system utterances: error messages, microcopy and samples of chatbot or assistant transcripts (e.g. 100-300 turns).
Code each utterance for violations of quantity, quality, relation and manner, noting the likely implicature.
Have a second coder code at least 20% and reconcile disagreements.
Test a sample of flagged utterances with 6-10 users, asking what they understood and inferred.
Rewrite violating utterances and prompt or response policies to satisfy the maxims.
Re-evaluate with users or by measuring downstream outcomes such as resolution rates and repeat queries.
outputs: Maxim violation log with implicatures, severity ratings, rewritten messages and conversational guidelines.
useWhen: Chatbots, AI assistants, voice interfaces, error messages and microcopy where tone and helpfulness matter.
avoidWhen: Visual or navigation problems; use usability testing or heuristic evaluation.
whyLost: Siloed: Linguistics literature; content designers occasionally apply it implicitly.
whereToUse: Conversational design; microcopy; error messages; chatbot dialogue.
example: A bank's chatbot answered 'I can help with many things!' to specific dispute questions. The audit flagged relation and quantity violations in 38% of turns; rewritten responses with direct answers and next steps cut repeat queries by a quarter.
sources: Conversational Design
The Development of Language
Logic and Conversation (H. Paul Grice)
reference: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts (pp. 41-58). Academic Press.

name: Ground-truth labelling from qualitative review
donor: Content analysis / machine learning annotation practice
origin: Content analysis reliability (Krippendorff, 1980; Cohen's kappa, 1960) applied to ML annotation
summary: Researchers code a sample of sessions, tickets or transcripts against an explicit codebook to create reliable labels for training and validating classifiers.
description: Classifiers inherit the quality of their labels. This method treats labelling as qualitative research: build a codebook with operational definitions and examples of each state (e.g. frustrated, confused, exploring), train coders, double-code a substantial sample, measure inter-rater reliability and resolve disagreements before labels are used. Labelling from session replays or think-aloud data captures meaning that event logs miss, and the disagreements themselves often reveal ambiguous states worth studying. Rigour comes from a stratified sample covering edge cases, blind double coding, reliability thresholds, documented adjudication and auditing label drift over time.
steps: Draft a codebook with definitions, inclusion and exclusion rules, and anchor examples for each label.
Draw a stratified sample of sessions, oversampling suspected rare states, typically 200-500 for initial modelling.
Train 2-3 coders on 20-30 practice sessions and refine the codebook.
Double-code at least 20% of the sample blind and compute Cohen's kappa or Krippendorff's alpha, targeting 0.70 or above (0.80 for high-stakes uses).
Adjudicate disagreements, update the codebook, and record label confidence for ambiguous cases.
Re-audit a fresh sample periodically to detect drift in user behaviour or coder interpretation.
outputs: A labelled dataset with codebook, reliability statistics, adjudication log and confidence ratings, ready for model training and evaluation.
useWhen: Before training or validating any classifier of user states, intents or feedback categories, or evaluating LLM-based coding.
avoidWhen: Avoid when labels can be derived objectively from outcomes (e.g. purchase), or when states are too ambiguous for agreement; explore them qualitatively first.
whyLost: Labelling is often outsourced as low-skill work, separating it from the qualitative expertise that makes labels meaningful.
whereToUse: Frustration detection, support ticket classification, AI conversation quality evaluation, content moderation research.
example: Three researchers code 300 trading session replays for frustration with a codebook, reaching Krippendorff's alpha of 0.78. Disagreements cluster around 'deliberate hesitation' during large orders, which becomes a separate label.

Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Peter Bruce, Andrew Bruce & Peter Gedeck)

name: Grounded Theory
origin: Barney Glaser & Anselm Strauss, 1967; later Strauss & Corbin (1990) and Charmaz (2006)
summary: A methodology for generating explanatory theory from data through iterative coding, constant comparison and theoretical sampling until categories are saturated.
description: Grounded theory builds theory inductively from data rather than testing prior hypotheses. Data collection and analysis proceed together: early interviews or observations are coded line by line (open coding), codes are related to one another around core categories (axial coding) and integrated into a central explanatory model (selective or theoretical coding). Constant comparison checks each new incident against existing codes and categories, while theoretical sampling chooses the next participants specifically to develop or challenge emerging categories. Memo writing captures analytic thinking throughout. Collection stops at theoretical saturation, when new data no longer adds properties to categories. The output is a theory of a process, not a list of themes, which is what distinguishes it from basic thematic analysis.
steps: Start with a broad research question and an initial sample of participants likely to experience the phenomenon.
Collect and transcribe data from the first few interviews, then code line by line using gerunds to capture actions and processes.
Write memos continuously, comparing incidents with codes and codes with categories.
Use theoretical sampling to select further participants who can develop or challenge emerging categories.
Relate categories through axial coding and identify a core category.
Continue until theoretical saturation, typically after 20 to 30 interviews, then integrate categories into an explanatory model.
Write up the theory with its categories, properties and conditions, supported by data excerpts.
outputs: An explanatory theory of the process under study, with core category, related categories and properties, memos and a coded dataset.
useWhen: When studying a poorly understood process or phenomenon where existing theory is inadequate, such as how trust in an AI tool develops over time.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you only need a descriptive summary of themes or have a fixed timeline of a few days; use thematic analysis or affinity diagramming.
whyLost: Vestigial: the name is widely invoked but practice is usually reduced to one round of coding into themes, losing theoretical sampling, constant comparison and theory building. It is often confused with thematic analysis and dismissed as too academic for product timelines.
whereToUse: Long-term research programs; generating theory from novel phenomena; design research publishing.
example: A health-tech researcher interviews 24 clinicians about adopting an AI triage assistant, sampling sceptics once an early 'earned trust' category emerges. The resulting theory shows trust is built through visible failure handling, informing the product's explanation design.

name: Grounded Visual Analysis
origin: Applications of grounded theory to visual data, 2000s (e.g. Konecki, 2011)
summary: Applies grounded theory's open coding, constant comparison and theoretical sampling to visual data such as photos, videos, screenshots and user-generated images.
description: Grounded Visual Analysis applies the constant comparative method and theoretical sampling principles of Grounded Theory to visual data — photographs, video clips, screenshots, diagrams, or any visual material. Just as textual Grounded Theory generates conceptual codes from textual data, Grounded Visual Analysis generates conceptual codes from visual elements and their patterns. It treats visual data not as illustration of findings but as the primary evidential material from which theory is generated.
steps: Open visual coding: View/examine visual data without pre-defined categories. For each image or clip, ask: what is happening here? What visual elements are most salient? What patterns or tensions are present? Apply codes to visual properties (composition, colour, focus, scale, relationship between elements) as well as content.
Constant comparison across visual data: Compare each new image to all previously coded images. What is the same? What is different? Does this image challenge existing codes or confirm them?

Theoretical sampling of visual data: After initial coding, collect additional visual data based on what the emerging theory requires — images from different contexts, different users, different time points.
Axial visual coding: Build categories around central visual themes. What causal conditions, contexts, and consequences surround each major visual pattern?

Triangulate with verbal data: Compare visual analysis findings to verbal data from the same participants or context. Convergence confirms; divergence reveals aspects of experience that one mode expresses but the other does not.
outputs: Open and axial visual codes, comparison memos, theoretically sampled image sets, visual categories, and triangulated findings with verbal data.
useWhen: Visual material is central, such as participant photos, screenshots of user set-ups, social media imagery, or interface screenshot collections, and you want inductive categories.
avoidWhen: Images are only illustrative of verbal findings, or you have predefined categories; use Qualitative Content Analysis. For meaning-making in designed visuals, use Multimodal Discourse Analysis.
whyLost: Visual data in UX is usually treated as illustration for decks rather than coded systematically, and visual grounded theory sits at a niche intersection of methods.
whereToUse: Photo diary studies, home-screen and workspace screenshot studies, social media imagery around products, and competitor interface audits.
example: Researchers collect 300 home-screen screenshots from banking app users. Open coding and comparison reveal a category of 'financial hiding', apps deliberately buried in folders, which interviews connect to money anxiety.
sources: Grounded Theory (Charmaz)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Research Design (Leavy)
reference: Konecki, K. T. (2011). Visual grounded theory: A methodological outline and examples from empirical work. Revija za sociologiju, 41(2), 131-160.

name: Guardrail metric monitoring
donor: Online experimentation / clinical trial safety monitoring
origin: Online experimentation practice (Kohavi et al.); data safety monitoring boards in clinical trials
summary: Tracks metrics that must not deteriorate while a primary metric is optimised, with thresholds that trigger investigation or rollback.
description: Guardrail metrics protect against shipping changes that win on the target metric but harm something important: latency, error rates, support contacts, unsubscribes, accessibility, user wellbeing or revenue. In experimentation, they are pre-specified with non-inferiority margins; after launch, they are monitored continuously with alerting thresholds. They echo safety monitoring in clinical trials, where efficacy is never judged without harm data. Rigour requires choosing guardrails that capture plausible harms identified through research, setting margins before data arrives, powering tests to detect meaningful degradation, and making escalation paths explicit. UX research contributes by identifying user-experience harms that standard engineering guardrails miss.
steps: Identify plausible harms of the change from research, risk review and past incidents.
Select 3-6 guardrail metrics covering system health, user experience and trust or wellbeing.
Set non-inferiority margins or alert thresholds before launch (e.g. support contacts may not rise by more than 5% relative).
Power experiments so a breach of the margin can be detected, using one-sided tests for degradation.
Monitor guardrails in dashboards with automated alerts and a named owner.
On a breach, pause or roll back and investigate with qualitative follow-up before resuming.
outputs: A guardrail set with thresholds, monitoring dashboards and alerts, and documented breach responses.
useWhen: Any experiment or launch optimising a primary metric, especially where gains could come at users' expense.
avoidWhen: Avoid using too many guardrails (false alarms multiply) or guardrails without pre-set thresholds.
whyLost: Guardrails are well established in mature experimentation cultures and spreading, though UX-specific harms are often missing from them.
whereToUse: A/B testing programmes, AI feature launches, fintech and health products, growth experiments.
example: A trading app's new one-tap order raises trade volume but its guardrail on order cancellations within 60 seconds rises 30% above threshold. Investigation shows accidental orders, and the team adds a confirmation for large trades.
sources: Storytelling with Data (Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic)
Articulating Design Decisions (Tom Greever)
Envisioning Information (Edward Tufte)

Storytelling with Data (Knaflic)
Articulating Design Decisions (Greever)
Envisioning Information (Tufte)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 59 — Research Communication — From Evidence to Strategic Brief

name: Guerrilla Research (Intercept and Rapid Testing)
origin: Popularised 2000s (Nielsen's discount argument; Krug 2000; lean UX)
summary: Rapid, low-cost intercept interviews, five-participant tests and remote sessions run inside agile cycles; useful for quick checks, weak for complex work systems.
description: The treatise describes the 'guerrilla substitution': brief intercept interviews, five-participant usability tests and remote moderated sessions became the standard toolkit as contextual inquiry declined. Practised well, guerrilla research catches obvious usability problems fast and keeps teams in contact with users. The treatise's critique is that it is often used beyond its range. It cannot surface deep understanding of work systems, organisational culture, artefact ecologies, informal workarounds or the social dimensions of tool use, and organisations that rely on it have degraded their capacity to understand complex systems. Recruiting convenience samples, no severity rating and no analysis protocol amplify its weaknesses. This entry captures the method with that perspective: legitimate as a quick evaluative check, risky as a substitute for field research.
steps: State a narrow evaluative question that a 10-20 minute session can answer.
Recruit participants who match the target user, not just whoever is nearby; screen with 2-3 questions.
Run 5-8 short sessions with a fixed task script and consistent prompts.
Log observed problems against tasks and rate severity.
Synthesise within 24 hours and state explicitly what the method cannot tell you.
Escalate to field research when findings point to workflow or context issues.
outputs: Quick problem list with severities, quotes, go/no-go signal for a design iteration.
useWhen: Early checks of comprehension, labels and flows on consumer-facing designs within a sprint.
avoidWhen: Complex professional work, organisational dynamics or high-stakes decisions; use contextual inquiry or ethnography.
whyLost: Survived and dominated because it is fast, cheap and legible to stakeholders: competitive displacement by faster methods.
whereToUse: Consumer apps, marketing pages, retail, early prototype comprehension checks.
example: A coffee chain's app team runs six intercept tests in-store on a new pre-order button and finds two label problems in an afternoon, but defers a staff workflow question to field observation.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Nielsen J (1994) Guerrilla HCI: using discount usability engineering to penetrate the intimidation barrier
Krug S (2010) Rocket Surgery Made Easy

name: Guttman Scaling
origin: Louis Guttman, 1944; probabilistic extension by Robert Mokken (1971)
summary: Tests whether items form a cumulative hierarchy, so that endorsing a harder item implies endorsing all easier ones, revealing ordered stages of adoption or capability.
description: A Guttman scale is cumulative: if a respondent agrees with item 4, they also agree with items 1-3. The coefficient of reproducibility (target above 0.9) measures how well responses fit this pattern. Mokken scale analysis provides a probabilistic, nonparametric version with Loevinger's H coefficients (H above 0.3 weak, above 0.5 strong scale). Cumulative scales are natural for capability or adoption ladders: digital skills, feature maturity, privacy protective behaviours, automation trust. They reveal the order in which people acquire behaviours, which directly informs progressive onboarding.
steps: Draft items expected to form a cumulative hierarchy (e.g. increasingly advanced feature uses).
Collect binary or polytomous responses from a sample of users.
Order items by popularity and respondents by total score; inspect the response matrix for errors.
Compute the coefficient of reproducibility, or run Mokken scale analysis (H and Hi coefficients, monotonicity checks).
Remove or revise items that break the hierarchy, and test invariant item ordering across groups.
Use the scale to place users on stages and design progression accordingly.
outputs: A validated cumulative scale, item ordering and user stage distribution.
useWhen: Measuring progressive capability, adoption or maturity, where items naturally build on one another.
avoidWhen: Constructs without a natural order, or multidimensional behaviours.
whyLost: Classical test theory and factor analysis became the default for scale building, and deterministic Guttman scales rarely fit perfectly.
whereToUse: Feature maturity models, digital literacy, security hygiene, B2B platform adoption, onboarding progression.
example: A Mokken analysis of 10 spreadsheet features shows a strong scale (H = 0.56) from formatting through formulas, pivot tables and scripts, guiding the order of in-product tips.
sources: Guttman, A basis for scaling qualitative data (1944), American Sociological Review
Mokken, A Theory and Procedure of Scale Analysis (1971)
van der Ark, Mokken scale analysis in R (2007), Journal of Statistical Software
reference: Guttman, L. (1944). American Sociological Review, 9(2), 139-150.

name: Habit loop analysis
origin: Habit research by Wendy Wood and colleagues (2002 onwards), Graybiel's basal ganglia work, popularised as the cue-routine-reward loop by Charles Duhigg (2012); automaticity measures by Verplanken and Orbell (2003) and Gardner et al. (2012)
summary: Maps the cues, routines and rewards sustaining existing behaviours and measures their automaticity, explaining why old practices persist and how new ones could become habitual.
description: Habits are context-response associations learned through repetition and maintained with little intention; Wood and colleagues found around 43% of daily actions are performed habitually in the same context. A habit loop analysis identifies the stable context cues (time, place, preceding action, people) that trigger a routine, the routine itself, and the reward that reinforced it, for both the old behaviour you are replacing and the new behaviour you want. Rigour requires measuring automaticity with a validated scale, such as the 4-item Self-Report Behavioural Automaticity Index (SRBAI), and measuring context stability, rather than inferring habits from frequency. Lally and colleagues (2010) found habit formation took a median of 66 days, ranging from 18 to 254, which sets realistic expectations.
steps: Choose the old behaviour to displace and the new behaviour to establish, and define the performance context for each.
Through 8 to 15 contextual interviews or a 1 to 2 week diary study, record for each occurrence the time, place, preceding action, people present and immediate outcome.
Identify stable cues (present in at least about 70% of occurrences), the routine sequence and the immediate rewards, including social and emotional rewards.
Measure automaticity with the 4-item SRBAI (1 to 7 scale) for old and new behaviours; scores above about 5 indicate strong habits that will resist intention-based interventions.
Design the new behaviour to attach to existing stable cues, reduce friction in the routine and deliver an immediate reward, or disrupt the old behaviour's cues where possible.
Track repetition in a stable context and re-measure automaticity at about 4, 8 and 12 weeks, expecting formation over roughly 2 to 3 months.
outputs: Cue-routine-reward maps for old and new behaviours, automaticity scores, context stability evidence, and a habit-formation design with a measurement plan.
useWhen: A legacy behaviour persists despite a better alternative; designing for daily or repeated use; adoption decays after initial launch novelty.
avoidWhen: The behaviour is infrequent or highly deliberative (annual tax filing, major purchases), where habit is not the mechanism; use decision-focused methods instead. Avoid designing compulsive loops that harm users.
whyLost: Popularised habit models such as Duhigg's loop and Eyal's Hooked became workshop canvases, while validated automaticity measurement and context-stability analysis from habit science were dropped.
whereToUse: Health worker data entry, medication adherence, financial routines, learning apps, enterprise system adoption replacing paper or spreadsheets.
example: Health workers filled a paper register after digital entry because the end-of-day register ritual at the clinic desk was a strong habit (SRBAI 6.1). Attaching a 'close the day' digital tally to the same desk moment, and removing the blank register from the desk, lowered paper duplication over 10 weeks.
sources: Persuasive Technology (Fogg)
Behavioral Drift Playbook (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 24 — Behavior Models, Habits & the Anatomy of Non-Adoption
reference: Wood, W., & Rünger, D. (2016). Psychology of habit. Annual Review of Psychology, 67, 289–314; Gardner, B., Abraham, C., Lally, P., & de Bruijn, G.-J. (2012). Towards parsimony in habit measurement. IJBNPA, 9, 102.

name: Hallway Usability Testing (Krug Method)
aka: Discount Usability Testing Protocol (Nielsen's Original Method)
origin: Jakob Nielsen, 1989 (discount usability); Steve Krug, 2010
summary: Low-cost monthly usability tests with three participants, observed live by the team and followed by a debrief that commits to fixing the worst problems.
description: Steve Krug's method makes usability testing a lightweight organisational habit. Once a month, the team tests with three participants in a morning, using think-aloud on realistic tasks. Stakeholders observe live from another room, each noting the three most serious problems they saw. Over lunch, a debrief combines the lists, agrees the top problems and commits to the smallest fixes that will solve them, since 'tweaking' beats redesigning. The rigour lies not in sample size but in discipline: a fixed cadence, recruiting people who are reasonably representative, a written script, mandatory observation by decision-makers, and a deliberate focus on fixing the worst problems first rather than producing long reports.
steps: Monthly rhythm:
Recruit 3 participants per session.
(2) Test with 3–4 realistic scenarios (15–20 min each).
(3) Same-day team debrief: show 2–3 critical clips to the team.
(4) Team votes: each person gets 3 votes for 'most important problems'.
(5) Fix the top 3 voted problems before next month's session.
(6) Repeat. The iterative rhythm, not the individual session, is the method.
outputs: A short list of the most serious usability problems, team-agreed fixes, and a regular testing rhythm that builds shared understanding.
useWhen: Teams without dedicated researchers, early and iterative design stages, and organisations needing to build a habit of watching users.
avoidWhen: Avoid for measurement, benchmarking, specialist or vulnerable user groups, or when the problem is not usability; use summative testing or properly recruited studies.
whyLost: 'Hallway testing' survived as a phrase, but the rigour of Krug's method (a monthly cadence, whole-team observation, a debrief limited to the top problems) was dropped in favour of ad hoc tests with colleagues.
whereToUse: Any product team without a dedicated UX researcher. The most actionable usability testing protocol for resource-constrained teams.
example: A small charity web team tests its donation flow with three supporters on the first Friday of every month; observers each list their top three problems, and the team fixes the shared top one before the next session.
sources: Don't Make Me Think / Rocket Surgery Made Easy — Steve Krug
UX for Lean Startups
Usability Engineering (Nielsen)
Usability Engineering — Jakob Nielsen
Nielsen & Landauer, A mathematical model of the finding of usability problems (INTERCHI 1993)
Nielsen, Usability engineering at a discount (1989)
