name: Hawkes Point Processes
origin: Alan G. Hawkes, 1971
summary: Models behavioural events as a point process where each event temporarily raises (or suppresses) the chance of further events, capturing bursts and cascades in interaction data.
description: A Hawkes process has a conditional intensity equal to a baseline rate plus decaying contributions from past events, so events cluster in self-exciting bursts, as in earthquake aftershocks or trading activity. The Behavioral Spectral Framework proposes representing behavioural events as point processes such as Hawkes models to capture self-excitation and suppression, as part of handling irregular sampling intelligently, alongside Lomb-Scargle periodograms and survival models of inactivity. The appeal for UX is that clicks, retries and messages are event-driven: a failed attempt may trigger a rapid cascade of retries (excitation), while a confusing screen may suppress further action. The playbook mentions the technique as a direction rather than a worked protocol, so the steps below follow standard practice.
steps: Collect event timestamps per user, with event types if relevant.
Specify a baseline rate and an excitation kernel (e.g. exponential decay).
Fit the model by maximum likelihood.
Interpret the branching ratio (how many follow-on events each event triggers) and decay time.
Compare parameters across cohorts or design variants.
Validate with goodness-of-fit checks and qualitative review of bursts.
outputs: Estimated baseline rates, excitation strengths and decay times per cohort.
useWhen: When interaction events cluster in bursts and you want to model contagion or retry cascades.
avoidWhen: When events are regular or few, or a simple rate comparison answers the question.
whyLost: Established in seismology, finance and social media research, but not in UX methods.
whereToUse: Retry storms in payments, notification cascades, social feed engagement, support contact bursts.
example: Modelling OTP retries as a Hawkes process shows each failure triggers about 0.6 further attempts within seconds, quantifying retry cascades before a UI change.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
reference: Hawkes, A. G. (1971). Spectra of some self-exciting and mutually exciting point processes. Biometrika, 58(1), 83–90.

name: HAZOP (Hazard and Operability Study)
origin: ICI, UK, mid-1960s; codified by Trevor Kletz; IEC 61882
summary: A facilitated team review that applies guidewords such as NO, MORE, LESS, REVERSE and OTHER THAN to each design parameter to find deviations, causes and consequences.
description: HAZOP breaks a system into nodes and, for each parameter at each node, applies standard guidewords to generate deviations: NO flow, MORE pressure, LATE action, REVERSE sequence. A multidisciplinary team, led by an independent chair and a scribe, discusses each deviation's credible causes, consequences and existing safeguards, and records actions. Its power is that guidewords force systematic imagination: the team cannot skip combinations, and the independent chair prevents groupthink. Applied to UX, nodes become screens or system states, parameters become data, timing, user intent and notifications, and guidewords surface edge cases such as duplicate submissions, stale data and out-of-order events that ordinary design reviews miss.
steps: Define scope and split the user journey or system into nodes (screens, services, states).
For each node, list parameters: data values, timing, sequence, user intent, permissions, notifications.
Assemble a team of 4-8 (design, engineering, support, domain expert) with an independent chair and a scribe.
Systematically apply guidewords (NO, MORE, LESS, AS WELL AS, PART OF, REVERSE, OTHER THAN, EARLY, LATE, BEFORE, AFTER) to every parameter.
For each meaningful deviation, record causes, consequences, existing safeguards and recommended actions with owners.
Track actions to closure and repeat the HAZOP when the design changes materially.
outputs: HAZOP log of deviations, causes, consequences, safeguards and actions; a prioritised edge-case backlog.
useWhen: Designs with many states, integrations and concurrent events (payments, bookings, IoT, sync), particularly before build.
avoidWhen: Early concept work where parameters are undefined; use pre-mortem or scenario analysis instead.
whyLost: It is seen as an engineering safety ritual tied to process plants, and its sessions are long and disciplined. Design reviews in UX favour taste-based critique over systematic deviation analysis.
whereToUse: Payments and refunds, booking systems, connected devices, offline sync, AI agents executing multi-step actions.
example: A ride-hailing team HAZOPs the 'driver arrived' node. 'EARLY' plus 'location' reveals arrivals flagged at the wrong entrance of large venues; the team adds pickup-point confirmation and a grace period.
sources: Kletz, HAZOP and HAZAN (4th ed., 1999)
IEC 61882:2016 Hazard and operability studies (HAZOP studies): Application guide
reference: IEC 61882:2016. Hazard and operability studies (HAZOP studies) - Application guide.

name: HEART Framework
aka: HEART (Human Error Assessment and Reduction Technique)
origin: Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson and Xin Fu, Google, 2010
summary: Structures UX metric selection across Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention and Task success, using a Goals-Signals-Metrics process to link user goals to measurable data.
description: HEART was developed at Google to give large-scale web products user-centred metrics beyond page views. The five categories are Happiness (attitudes, often via surveys), Engagement (depth and frequency of use), Adoption (new users of a product or feature), Retention (users returning) and Task success (efficiency, effectiveness, error rate). The companion Goals-Signals-Metrics process is the method's core: for each relevant category, the team states the goal, identifies behavioural or attitudinal signals that indicate progress, and defines specific metrics, usually as rates or averages that can be compared over time or between experiment arms. Rigour comes from selecting only categories relevant to the product's goals, ensuring signals are actually instrumented and sensitive to change, and reviewing metrics with qualitative research so they do not drift from user value.
steps: Agree the product or feature goals with stakeholders.
Select the HEART categories relevant to those goals; not all five need to be used.
For each category, write goals, then candidate signals (behavioural or attitudinal) that would indicate progress.
Turn signals into specific metrics with definitions, data sources and time windows.
Check instrumentation, baselines and sensitivity, and set targets.
Review metrics regularly and in experiments, revisiting them as the product evolves.
outputs: Goals-Signals-Metrics table, metric definitions and baselines, UX dashboard and targets.
useWhen: Defining UX success metrics for a product or feature, aligning with OKRs, and instrumenting new launches.
avoidWhen: Small products without analytics infrastructure or when the question is exploratory; start with qualitative research.
whyLost: Quantitative HRA belongs to nuclear and rail safety cases. UX lacks the habit of estimating error probabilities and the name collision with Google HEART obscures it further.
whereToUse: Metric framework design; OKR alignment; product analytics instrumentation.
example: A health booking app used GSM to define task success as the percentage of booking attempts completed within three minutes and retention as patients rebooking within 90 days, replacing a vague 'engagement' target.
sources: Measuring the User Experience
Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale (Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu)
Williams, A data-based method for assessing and reducing human error to improve operational performance (1988), IEEE Conference on Human Factors and Power Plants
Kirwan, A Guide to Practical Human Reliability Assessment (1994)
reference: Rodden, K., Hutchinson, H., & Fu, X. (2010). Measuring the user experience on a large scale: User-centered metrics for web applications. Proceedings of CHI 2010, 2395-2398.

name: Heatmap and Scrollmap Interpretation Protocol
origin: Click and scroll heatmap tools from the mid-2000s (Crazy Egg 2005, later Hotjar); interpretation protocol by Dushyant Kanungo (2016)
summary: A structured protocol for reading click, move, attention and scroll maps, segmenting data and setting thresholds, so heatmaps produce defensible findings rather than impressions.
description: Heatmaps are popular because they look self-explanatory, which is exactly why they are misread. A rigorous interpretation protocol distinguishes map types: click maps show where people acted, move maps loosely approximate attention, attention or eye-tracking maps show fixations, and scroll maps show the proportion of visitors reaching each depth. It requires sufficient sample sizes (often a few thousand page views per segment), segmentation by device, traffic source and new versus returning users, since aggregate maps blend different behaviours, and comparison with a baseline or variant. Analysts look for specific signals: clicks on non-interactive elements, rage or dead clicks, steep scroll drop-offs above key content, and false floors. Findings are stated as hypotheses and confirmed with session recordings, usability tests or experiments.
steps: Heatmap interpretation protocol:

Compare attention heatmap to click heatmap — elements with high attention but low clicks = visible but not compelling; elements with low attention but high clicks = users are clicking without reading.
(2) Overlay scroll map to identify scroll depth at which each CTA becomes visible — first ensure users reach the element before worrying about its design.
(3) Code rage clicks as a frustration signal requiring qualitative investigation.
outputs: Segmented heatmap and scrollmap readings, list of signals (dead clicks, false floors, ignored calls to action) with sample sizes, and hypotheses for testing.
useWhen: Landing pages, long-form content, product pages and onboarding screens with enough traffic, and as triage before usability testing or A/B tests.
avoidWhen: With low traffic, highly dynamic or personalised pages where maps cannot align elements, or when you need to know why users behave as they do; use usability testing.
whyLost: Heatmap tools made the outputs easy to produce, so interpretation became impressionistic, and segmentation and sample-size discipline were rarely practised.
whereToUse: Landing page optimization, onboarding funnel analysis, e-commerce UX, content page design.
example: An e-commerce product page scroll map shows a sharp drop at 40% depth on mobile only, just above shipping information. Segmenting reveals a full-width image creating a false floor; replacing it raises views of shipping details from 38% to 61%.
sources: UX Decoded — Dushyant Kanungo
Web Analytics 2.0 (Avinash Kaushik)
Practical Web Analytics for User Experience
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Kanungo D (2016) UX Decoded: A Practical Guide to User Experience. BPB Publications

name: Hedonic Quality (HQ) Questionnaire
origin: Hassenzahl, Platz, Burmester & Lehner (2000); later expanded into AttrakDiff
summary: Seven bipolar items measuring a product's non-task appeal (interesting, exciting, original, innovative), separate from its ergonomic usability.
description: Hassenzahl's HQ questionnaire was one of the first instruments to measure user experience beyond usability. Its seven 7-point bipolar items are interesting–boring, costly–cheap, exciting–dull, exclusive–standard, impressive–nondescript, original–ordinary and innovative–conservative. In studies with industrial software prototypes and display types, factor analysis separated hedonic quality from ergonomic quality (simple, clear), and both contributed about equally to overall appeal. Hedonic quality did not correlate with mental effort while ergonomic quality did, evidence the two are distinct. The work grew into AttrakDiff with pragmatic quality and the stimulation, identification and evocation facets of hedonic quality.
steps: Administer the seven HQ items, alongside ergonomic or pragmatic quality items.
Average items for hedonic and ergonomic scores.
Plot the two dimensions to see whether a design is usable but dull, or exciting but awkward.
Relate both to overall appeal or preference with regression.
outputs: Separate hedonic and ergonomic quality scores and their contribution to appeal.
useWhen: Designs where delight, novelty or brand expression matter alongside usability.
avoidWhen: Purely functional tools where appeal is irrelevant.
whyLost: Superseded under a new name by AttrakDiff and later the UEQ.
whereToUse: Consumer products, automotive interiors, games, branded experiences.
example: Two music app concepts score equally on ergonomic quality, but one scores far higher on hedonic quality and wins on appeal.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Hassenzahl, M., Platz, A., Burmester, M. & Lehner, K. (2000). Hedonic and ergonomic quality aspects determine a software's appeal. CHI 2000.

name: Hermeneutic Circle
origin: Friedrich Schleiermacher and Wilhelm Dilthey, 19th century; Martin Heidegger and Hans-Georg Gadamer, 20th century
summary: An iterative interpretive method moving between parts and the whole of a text or dataset, revising each in light of the other until a coherent, deep interpretation emerges.
description: The hermeneutic circle is the methodological principle that understanding proceeds through an iterative movement between the parts of a text (or interaction, or cultural product) and the whole — understanding the parts in light of the whole, and revising understanding of the whole in light of the parts. No final 'correct' interpretation is reached — understanding deepens with each turn of the circle. Applied to UX qualitative data: the hermeneutic circle formalises the iterative nature of good qualitative analysis and guards against both premature closure (settling on an interpretation too quickly) and infinite regress (perpetual revision without ever reaching understanding).
steps: Initial reading — the whole: Read the full dataset (or a complete interview, observation, or case) to develop a preliminary understanding of the whole.
Attention to parts: Re-read specific segments that seem significant, puzzling, or contradictory. How do they relate to your preliminary understanding of the whole?
Revision of the whole: How does closer attention to these parts change your understanding of the whole? Revise your interpretation accordingly.
Iteration: Return to the parts, now read in light of the revised understanding of the whole. Each iteration deepens rather than replaces the previous understanding.

Productive friction: The hermeneutic circle is most productive when parts and whole are in tension — when a specific segment resists your understanding of the whole, or when your understanding of the whole cannot account for a specific segment. These points of resistance are where understanding is most deepened.
outputs: Iterative interpretive memos, revised whole-case interpretations, documentation of how puzzling parts changed the reading, and a coherent interpretive account.
useWhen: You need deep understanding of a small number of rich cases, transcripts or artefacts, especially where meaning is ambiguous or contradictions appear.
avoidWhen: You need fast, broad coverage or reproducible coding; use Qualitative Content Analysis or Template Analysis.
whyLost: It is a philosophical principle rather than a packaged procedure, so UX analysts rarely make it explicit, even though skilled synthesis implicitly relies on it.
whereToUse: In-depth interview synthesis, analysing contradictory feedback, persona refinement, IPA-style studies, and interpreting long-form user writing.
example: A researcher puzzled by a participant who praises a budgeting app yet stopped using it rereads the transcript as a whole, then the praise, then the whole again, recognising the praise as about who she wanted to be, not how she lived.
sources: Fundamentals of Qualitative Research
Phenomenological Method in Qualitative Psychology (PMC 2016)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Gadamer, H.-G. (1975). Truth and Method. Sheed & Ward.

name: Heuristic Evaluation
origin: Jakob Nielsen & Rolf Molich, 1990
summary: Several evaluators independently inspect an interface against recognised usability principles, producing a severity-rated list of problems without involving users.
description: Heuristic evaluation is an inspection method in which a small group of evaluators independently examine an interface and judge its compliance with a set of usability principles, most commonly Nielsen's ten heuristics. Each evaluator works alone, typically making two passes: one to understand the flow and another to inspect elements in detail. Findings are then aggregated, de-duplicated and rated for severity. The method rests on the observation that individual evaluators find only a fraction of problems, while three to five independent evaluators together find most of them. Rigour comes from independence before aggregation, citing the specific heuristic and location for each problem, using a shared severity scale and recognising that heuristics predict, but do not prove, user difficulty.
steps: Choose the heuristic set (for example Nielsen's ten, or domain-specific heuristics) and define scope and key tasks.
Brief 3 to 5 evaluators, ideally with usability and domain knowledge.
Have each evaluator inspect the interface independently in at least two passes, recording each problem, its location and the heuristic violated.
Merge findings into a single list and remove duplicates.
Have evaluators independently rate severity on a 0 to 4 scale and average the ratings.
Report prioritised problems with recommendations and validate the most severe with users where possible.
outputs: A consolidated, severity-rated list of usability problems mapped to heuristics and screens, with recommendations.
useWhen: Early in design or when time and budget prevent user testing; as a quick audit before testing to remove obvious problems.
avoidWhen: Avoid as the only evidence for high-stakes decisions or for novel interaction paradigms the heuristics do not cover; use usability testing with representative users.
whyLost: Still in use: Efficient expert method; widely taught and understood; useful when budget or time precludes user testing.
whereToUse: Any UI at any stage; particularly useful early in design before investing in user testing.
example: A SaaS analytics vendor runs a heuristic evaluation with four evaluators before a beta. They find no undo for deleting dashboards and inconsistent filter terminology, both fixed before user sessions begin.
sources: Usability Engineering
Don't Make Me Think
Usability Inspection Methods (Nielsen & Mack)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Nielsen J & Molich R (1990) Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces. CHI
Nielsen J (1994) Heuristic evaluation. In Nielsen & Mack (Eds) Usability Inspection Methods
Handbook of Usability Testing
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Nielsen, J. & Molich, R. (1990). Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces. Proceedings of CHI '90, 249-256.

name: Heuristic Evaluation with Inter-Evaluator Reliability
origin: Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich, 1990
summary: Heuristic evaluation as originally specified: several independent evaluators, aggregation of all unique problems, and measured overlap between evaluators to judge coverage and reliability.
description: Heuristic evaluation has evaluators inspect an interface against a set of usability heuristics. Nielsen and Molich found that single evaluators detect only about 20-50% of problems, so the method's validity depends on several evaluators (typically three to five) working independently and on aggregating every unique problem found by anyone, not averaging or voting. Evaluator independence must be preserved until individual reports are complete. Reliability is assessed by computing the overlap between evaluators (for example, any-two agreement) and how many problems were found by only one person, which indicates how far from saturation the evaluation is. Severity is rated afterwards, ideally independently. In current practice heuristic evaluation is often a single designer's review, which keeps the name but loses the statistical basis of the method.
steps: 3–5 evaluators: each independently evaluates the interface against all 10 heuristics.
No discussion during individual phases.
After all have finished: aggregate lists.
Count unique problems.
Measure evaluator reliability: Fleiss' κ on binary problem detection (did evaluator i find problem j?).
Low κ (< 0.40) means evaluators are finding different problems — discuss and align on heuristic interpretation before proceeding.
outputs: Individual evaluator reports, an aggregated list of unique problems with heuristics violated, evaluator overlap and any-two agreement statistics, and independent severity ratings.
useWhen: Early and cheap inspection of prototypes or live products, before user testing, and in audits where evaluator coverage must be justified.
avoidWhen: As a replacement for testing with users, for domain-specific tools where evaluators lack domain knowledge (use double experts or user testing), or with a single evaluator.
whyLost: Time pressure reduced it to one person's expert review, and the multi-evaluator aggregation and reliability analysis that underpin its effectiveness were forgotten.
whereToUse: Expert evaluation, design system auditing, pre-testing validation. The inter-evaluator reliability component is the most commonly skipped step.
example: Four evaluators independently review an insurance claims portal and find 47 unique problems, but only 9 are found by more than one evaluator. The low overlap prompts adding a fifth evaluator with claims expertise, who finds 8 more.
sources: Usability Engineering — Jakob Nielsen
Hertzum & Jacobsen, The evaluator effect (International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction, 2001)
reference: Nielsen J & Molich R (1990) Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces. Proceedings of CHI 1990:249-256

name: Hick's Law Analysis
origin: William Hick, 1952; Ray Hyman, 1953
summary: Models decision time as a logarithmic function of the number and probability of choices, to estimate how option sets affect selection speed.
description: The Hick-Hyman law states that choice reaction time increases with the information content of the choice: RT = a + b·log2(n + 1) for n equally likely options, or more generally with the entropy of the choice set when probabilities differ. It applies to decisions where users already know the options and must select one, not to visual search through unfamiliar lists, where time grows roughly linearly. Its rigorous use in UX means checking whether that precondition holds, estimating choice probabilities from usage data, and fitting parameters for the specific context. This avoids the common misapplication of citing Hick's law to justify removing options. Properly applied, it shows that ordering by frequency, grouping and reducing entropy can speed selection, and that splitting choices across many levels can cost more than it saves.
steps: Confirm the task is a choice among known options rather than search through unfamiliar items.
Estimate option probabilities from usage logs and compute the entropy of the choice set.
Run a timed selection task with 10-20 participants across set sizes or layouts.
Fit RT against log2(n + 1) or entropy and check the fit.
Use the model to compare flat, grouped and frequency-ordered designs, including the added cost of extra navigation levels.
Choose the structure minimising total predicted time, then validate with usability testing.
outputs: Choice entropy estimates, fitted reaction-time model, predicted decision times for alternative option structures.
useWhen: Menu design, quick actions, keyboard shortcuts, settings and options panels used repeatedly by experienced users.
avoidWhen: Novice users scanning unfamiliar lists, where search time dominates; use eye tracking or tree testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Simple, memorable, and defensible with stakeholders; though often over-applied.
whereToUse: Navigation design; option set design; cognitive load reduction.
example: A point-of-sale app had 24 equally weighted product buttons. Usage logs showed 6 items accounted for 70% of sales; entropy-based modelling supported a frequency-weighted layout that cut median selection time by 0.4 seconds.
sources: Human-Computer Interaction
reference: Hick, W. E. (1952). On the rate of gain of information. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 4(1), 11-26.

name: Hidden Markov Models for Navigation Analysis
origin: Leonard Baum et al. (1966); Lawrence Rabiner (1989)
summary: Infers latent user states (exploring, task-focused, confused, recovering) from clickstream sequences and estimates transitions between them.
description: An HMM models observed sequences as emissions from hidden states with transition probabilities. Given clicks, page visits or actions, inference recovers the most likely state sequence (Viterbi) and transition matrix. The treatise poses a classic question: is a long session engagement or confusion? An HMM trained on labelled sessions can separate these as different hidden states with different observable signatures, then label new sessions. This turns ambiguous metrics such as session length into state-based measures (time in 'confused' state). Model selection uses information criteria and interpretability, and states should be validated against qualitative evidence such as recordings or think-aloud.
steps: Define the observation alphabet (event types, page categories, dwell bins).
Optionally label a sample of sessions with states via observation or recordings.
Fit HMMs with different numbers of states using Baum-Welch or supervised estimation.
Select the model by BIC, held-out likelihood and interpretability.
Decode sessions with Viterbi and compute time-in-state metrics.
Validate states qualitatively and track state metrics across releases.
outputs: State definitions, transition matrix, per-session state sequences, state-based metrics.
useWhen: Interpreting long or ambiguous sessions, detecting confusion at scale, onboarding state inference.
avoidWhen: Short sessions with few events, or when simple funnels answer the question.
whyLost: Requires ML skills rarely present in UX teams; analytics tools offer funnels instead.
whereToUse: Onboarding flows, search behaviour, e-learning, complex SaaS configuration, support portals.
example: An HMM on tax software logs finds a 'looping' state where users alternate between two forms; 12% of sessions spend over five minutes there, pinpointing a confusing deduction section.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rabiner LR (1989) A tutorial on hidden Markov models and selected applications in speech recognition. Proc IEEE 77(2):257-286
Baum LE & Petrie T (1966) Statistical inference for probabilistic functions of finite state Markov chains. Ann Math Stat 37
reference: Rabiner LR (1989) A tutorial on hidden Markov models and selected applications in speech recognition. Proceedings of the IEEE 77(2):257-286.

name: Hidden Markov Models of User Behaviour
origin: Leonard Baum and colleagues, late 1960s; popularised by Lawrence Rabiner's tutorial (1989)
summary: Infers unobserved user states (e.g. exploring, struggling, committed) from sequences of observable actions, with transition probabilities between states.
description: An HMM assumes a sequence of hidden states, each emitting observable events with characteristic probabilities, and Markov transitions between states. Fitted with the Baum-Welch (EM) algorithm and decoded with the Viterbi algorithm, it labels each moment of a session with the most likely latent state and estimates how users move between states. For UX this turns clickstreams into interpretable phases such as browsing, comparing, confused and ready-to-buy, and allows analysis of what triggers transitions into struggle or out of it. Model selection (number of states via BIC and interpretability) and validation against qualitative ground truth make it rigorous rather than a black box.
steps: Define observable event types and encode sessions as sequences, possibly with dwell times.
Fit HMMs with different numbers of states (e.g. 2-8) using Baum-Welch with multiple random starts.
Select the number of states using BIC, stability across runs and interpretability.
Inspect emission and transition matrices; name states with help from session replays or think-aloud data.
Decode sessions with Viterbi and analyse state durations and transitions associated with outcomes.
Validate by checking decoded states against independently coded sessions (e.g. replay-coded 'struggling').
outputs: Latent state definitions, transition matrices, decoded session timelines and state-outcome relationships.
useWhen: You have large sequential logs and want to discover latent phases or detect struggle in real time.
avoidWhen: Small samples, or when states are directly observable; simpler funnel or sequence analysis may suffice.
whyLost: HMMs belong to speech and bioinformatics; UX analytics focuses on funnels and aggregate metrics.
whereToUse: E-commerce browsing, learning platforms, SaaS onboarding, support chatbots, games.
example: An HMM on a tax-filing app finds a 'looping' state where users bounce between two forms. Users entering it have 3x abandonment; a contextual help trigger reduces time spent in that state.
sources: Rabiner, A tutorial on hidden Markov models and selected applications in speech recognition (1989), Proceedings of the IEEE
Zucchini, MacDonald & Langrock, Hidden Markov Models for Time Series (2nd ed., 2016)
reference: Rabiner, L. R. (1989). Proceedings of the IEEE, 77(2), 257-286.

name: Hierarchical structure analysis
donor: Information architecture and cognitive psychology of menus
origin: Menu depth/breadth research by Miller (1981), Kiger (1984) and Larson and Czerwinski (1998); Simon's 'Architecture of Complexity', 1962
summary: Analyses the depth, breadth, balance and consistency of an interface hierarchy, checking it against evidence on navigation performance and against how users group content.
description: Hierarchies trade depth against breadth. Research from the 1980s and 1990s found broad, shallow menus (for example 8x8 rather than 2x2x2x2x2x2) generally faster and less error-prone, provided items are well grouped and labelled, because each extra level adds a decision and a chance to go astray. Hierarchical structure analysis measures depth to each leaf, breadth at each node, balance (variation of depth), and consistency of classification principle at each level, then compares against user mental models from card sorting or tree testing. Simon's insight that near-decomposable hierarchies are easier to understand provides the theoretical basis. Today the term survives but usually means drawing a sitemap rather than analysing it.
steps: Export the full hierarchy (sitemap, menu tree, settings tree) with every node and leaf.
Compute depth to each leaf, breadth per node, mean and maximum depth, and depth variance; flag leaves deeper than 4 levels and nodes with fewer than 3 or more than about 12 unclustered children.
Check each level for a single, consistent classification principle (by task, object, audience or time).
Run a tree test with 50+ participants on 8-10 key tasks to measure success and directness.
Correlate failures with depth, breadth and classification inconsistencies.
Propose a restructured hierarchy and re-test with a new tree test.
outputs: Depth and breadth metrics, a structure diagnostics report, tree test results correlated with structural features, and a revised hierarchy.
useWhen: When menus, settings or sites have grown organically; when users cannot find features; before migrations or redesigns of navigation.
avoidWhen: When users mainly search or follow links rather than browse; analyse search logs and IA graph centrality instead.
whyLost: Menu depth-breadth research faded from practice after the 1990s; IA kept the vocabulary but dropped quantitative structure analysis.
whereToUse: Enterprise settings, e-commerce category trees, government sites, intranets, and device menus.
example: A surgical robot's settings tree reaches 7 levels with one branch holding 31 items. Restructuring to a maximum depth of 3 with consistent task-based grouping raises tree test success from 58% to 84%.
sources: Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 6 — Strange Loops, Recursive Failures & Navigation Traps
Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
Gödel Escher Bach (Hofstadter)
reference: Larson, K. & Czerwinski, M. (1998). Web page design: implications of memory, structure and scent for information retrieval. Proceedings of CHI '98.

name: Hierarchical Task Analysis
origin: John Annett and Keith Duncan, 1967
summary: Decomposes a goal into sub-goals, operations and plans, using a P x C stopping rule to locate the steps where interface support matters most.
description: Hierarchical Task Analysis (Annett and Duncan) represents work as a hierarchy of goals and sub-goals, down to operations, with a plan at each level specifying the order and conditions under which sub-goals are carried out. Its distinctive rigour lies in the stopping rule: decomposition continues only while the product of the probability of inadequate performance (P) and the cost of that failure (C) is unacceptable. This focuses analytical effort on steps that are both error-prone and consequential, rather than exhaustively documenting everything. Data comes from observation, interviews, documents and walkthroughs with experienced performers. HTA is the foundation for many human-factors techniques, including SHERLOCK-style error prediction, workload analysis and training design.
steps: Define the top-level goal: What does the user ultimately want to achieve? State as an active goal.
Decompose to sub-goals: Continue decomposing until you reach operations — individual actions that cannot be further decomposed.
Specify plans: For each goal with multiple sub-goals: what plan governs how they are ordered? Sequential (1,2,3), conditional (if X then 1, else 2), or cyclic (repeat until condition).
Apply stopping rule: Stop decomposing when the cost of inadequate performance exceeds the cost of further analysis.
Apply P × C criterion: For each sub-goal: P = probability of failure without support; C = cost of failure. High P × C = design priority.
outputs: A hierarchical task diagram and tabular HTA with plans, P x C ratings for sub-goals, and a list of high-priority steps requiring interface, training or automation support.
useWhen: Designing or redesigning complex, procedural or safety-relevant work, such as clinical workflows, financial operations, industrial control or enterprise configuration, and you need to know where support matters.
avoidWhen: Tasks are exploratory, creative or poorly structured, where hierarchical goals do not exist in advance; use contextual inquiry or Cognitive Task Analysis instead.
whyLost: UX replaced it with user flows and journey maps that show sequence but not plans, conditions or P x C prioritisation, so the name survives without its analytic engine.
whereToUse: Clinical systems, payments operations, aviation and automotive interfaces, enterprise admin tools, and automation decisions for AI agents taking over task steps.
example: Analysing payroll correction in an HR platform, a team builds an HTA of 34 operations. P x C ratings flag 'confirm tax period' as rare but costly when wrong, so the interface adds a forced confirmation only at that step.
sources: Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (Hollnagel)
Human-Computer Interaction (Alan Dix)
Stanton, N. A. (2006) Hierarchical task analysis: developments, applications and extensions, Applied Ergonomics
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Annett J & Duncan KD (1967) Task analysis and training design
Stanton NA (2006) Hierarchical task analysis: developments, applications and extensions. Applied Ergonomics
Kirwan B & Ainsworth LK (1992) A Guide to Task Analysis
Handbook of Cognitive Task Design
A Guide to Task Analysis (Kirwan & Ainsworth)
Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C., Designing the User Interface
Gopinath, V., Movie Booking Playbook
Shneiderman & Plaisant
Movie Booking Playbook (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 16 — Cognitive Task Modeling — GOMS, KLM & CPM-GOMS
reference: Annett, J. & Duncan, K. D. (1967). Task analysis and training design. Occupational Psychology, 41, 211-221.

name: Hierarchical topic modelling
origin: hLDA (nested Chinese restaurant process), Blei, Griffiths and Jordan, 2004/2010; hierarchical reduction in BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2022)
summary: Organising topics into a tree of broad themes and narrower sub-topics, so large text corpora can be explored at the right level of detail for each decision.
description: Flat topic models force a single granularity. Hierarchical approaches produce a tree: either generatively (hLDA) or, more commonly today, by agglomerating fine-grained BERTopic clusters using the similarity of their c-TF-IDF or embedding representations. Executives can see a handful of broad themes while product teams drill into specific sub-topics. Rigour comes from choosing a linkage method, validating that merges are semantically sensible by reading documents, keeping the tree shallow enough to interpret (typically 2-3 levels), and labelling each level with consistent conventions. The hierarchy is an analytic aid, analogous to arranging codes into categories in qualitative analysis.
steps: Fit a fine-grained topic model (e.g. BERTopic with a small min_cluster_size giving 50-200 topics).
Compute the topic hierarchy (BERTopic hierarchical_topics with a chosen linkage, e.g. Ward or average).
Visualise the dendrogram and choose 2-3 cut levels that give interpretable groupings.
Read representative documents at each merge to confirm semantic coherence, and override merges that are wrong.
Label parent and child topics consistently and record definitions.
Report prevalence at each level and map leaf topics to owning teams or journeys.
outputs: A labelled topic tree, dendrogram, prevalence by level and a mapping of sub-topics to owners.
useWhen: Very large or diverse corpora where stakeholders need different levels of granularity, such as company-wide feedback or support data.
avoidWhen: Avoid for small or homogeneous corpora where a flat model with 10-20 topics suffices.
whyLost: Hierarchical topic models were academic for years; embedding-based tools made them practical only recently.
whereToUse: Enterprise voice-of-customer programmes, support taxonomy design, app store review analysis and research repository navigation.
example: A SaaS company's 200,000 support tickets yield 140 fine topics, merged into 12 parent themes such as 'billing' and 'integrations'. Product teams drill into child topics like 'Salesforce sync duplicates'.

hdbscan

name: Honeycomb × SNR × PBUH Scorecard
donor: UX evaluation; information theory; behavioural science
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Studio Aghora (uxguy.in)
summary: A weighted composite scorecard combining Morville's UX Honeycomb, SNR interface scores and PBUH adoption stages into one instrument for holistic product audits.
description: The Honeycomb × SNR × PBUH Scorecard fuses three lenses into a single audit instrument. Morville's UX Honeycomb contributes seven quality facets: useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, credible and valuable. The SNR Interface Evaluation Framework contributes a measure of information clarity on key screens. The PBUH model contributes a view of where users stall between perception, behaviour, utility and habit. Each lens is scored with explicit rubrics, then combined using weights agreed with stakeholders in advance, giving a product health score with traceable components. Its rigour comes from rubric definitions, multiple raters, fixed weights set before scoring and the ability to decompose the composite back into its parts, which prevents the single number from hiding where problems are.
steps: Agree the product scope, key tasks and weighting of the three lenses with stakeholders before scoring.
Score each Honeycomb facet on a defined 1 to 5 rubric using expert review and available research evidence.
Compute SNR scores for the screens supporting key tasks.
Rate each PBUH stage using analytics and research evidence.
Have at least two raters score independently and reconcile differences above one rubric point.
Combine scores using the agreed weights and present both the composite and the component breakdown.
Repeat on the same rubric for competitors or future releases to benchmark.
outputs: A composite product health score, component scores per lens, a heat map of weak facets and prioritised recommendations.
useWhen: For UX audits, product health reviews and competitive benchmarking where a multi-dimensional but comparable assessment is needed.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need causal evidence or user-reported attitudes; use experiments or standardised questionnaires such as SUS instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Vivek synthesis framework; enables multi-dimensional UX audit in one instrument.
whereToUse: UX audits; competitive benchmarking; product health reviews.
example: An e-commerce marketplace audits itself and two competitors. The scorecard shows strong desirability but low findability and poor SNR on search results, and the PBUH lens shows weak habit formation, focusing the next roadmap on search.
sources: Studio Aghora
uxguy.in
reference: Gopinath, V. Honeycomb × SNR × PBUH Scorecard (uxguy.in); Morville, P. (2004). User Experience Design (UX Honeycomb).

name: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints
donor: Human-computer interaction; machine learning; qualitative methods
origin: Interactive machine learning (Fails and Olsen, 2003); human oversight principles in AI governance (e.g. EU AI Act, 2024)
summary: Scheduling deliberate points where researchers review, correct and approve AI outputs, so interpretive decisions stay with humans and errors are caught early.
description: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints place researcher judgement where it matters most: approving the codebook, reviewing code merges, validating second-order categories and signing off synthesis claims, plus reviewing flagged low-confidence items. They are distinct from quality gates: gates are automated thresholds, checkpoints are human decisions. Rigour comes from specifying what is reviewed, by whom, how much (e.g. 100% of theme statements, a sample of codes), recording decisions and corrections, and feeding corrections back into prompts or codebooks. Guarding against automation bias, where reviewers rubber-stamp plausible AI output, requires reviewers to examine evidence, not just summaries, and periodic blind checks.
steps: Identify decisions that must remain human: research questions, codebook approval, abstraction to themes, claims in reports.
Define each checkpoint's scope, reviewer, sample size and acceptance criteria.
Present evidence (quotes in context) alongside AI suggestions, not summaries alone.
Record every accept, edit or reject decision with a reason.
Feed corrections back into codebooks or prompts and re-run affected items.
Run periodic blind checks where reviewers code items without seeing AI suggestions, to monitor automation bias.
outputs: Checkpoint plan, decision logs, corrected outputs and measures of AI-human disagreement over time.
useWhen: Any AI-assisted research where findings will inform decisions, and particularly in sensitive or regulated domains.
avoidWhen: Do not use checkpoints as a fig leaf for large-scale unread automation; if reviewers cannot meaningfully examine evidence, reduce scale or automation.
whyLost: Popular AI analysis tools emphasise speed and automation, so deliberate human checkpoints are rarely designed.
whereToUse: AI-assisted research operations, health and finance research and policy-relevant UX studies.
example: In a 300-interview programme, researchers review every proposed theme with linked quotes. They reject 4 of 22 AI-proposed themes as artefacts of interview guide wording, and edits are fed into the next run.
sources: Whisper.cpp
spaCy

name: Hysteresis Testing with Ascending and Descending Sweeps
origin: Used in the van der Maas lab for proportional reasoning (Jansen and van der Maas 2001), the speed-accuracy trade-off (Dutilh et al. 2011) and apparent motion perception (Ploeger, van der Maas and Hartelman 2002), where the method of modified limits was applied.
summary: An experimental design that slowly increases and then decreases a control variable and checks whether the switch between two behaviours happens at different points on the way up and the way down.
description: Hysteresis means a system's state depends on its history: when a control variable is raised, the switch to a new state happens late, and when it is lowered again the switch back happens even later. It is one of the strongest signs of two co-existing stable states. The book describes demonstrating it by gradually varying a stimulus dimension (for example the aspect ratio of a motion display) in both directions and recording where percepts switch. Because a lagging switch could simply reflect slow responding, the method of modified limits is used: participants respond only after a whole trial, and trials of different lengths reveal at which parameter value the switch was perceived. A related test, inaccessibility, asks participants to hold an intermediate state (for example 75 percent accuracy) and checks whether they instead alternate between the two modes. In UX, hysteresis explains why restoring a feature, a price or a performance level may not win back users lost when it degraded, and why defaults that crossed a threshold stay sticky. Testing it directly gives evidence for designing asymmetric interventions.
steps: Choose a manipulable control variable that you think pushes behaviour between two states (for example latency, price, notification frequency, cognitive load).
Define an objective record of which state the participant is in at each level.
Present the variable in a slow ascending series and a slow descending series, counterbalancing order across participants.
Guard against response lag, for example by asking for a judgement only at the end of trials of varying length (method of modified limits).
Estimate the switch point in each direction and test whether the two differ; optionally test inaccessibility by asking participants to maintain an intermediate state.
Report the width of the hysteresis loop and its implications for recovery strategies.
outputs: Switch points for the upward and downward direction, the size of the hysteresis gap, and evidence on whether an intermediate state is stable.
useWhen: You need to know whether undoing a change will reverse its effect, or whether a behaviour switch reflects two stable states.
avoidWhen: You cannot vary the control variable gradually in both directions, or carry-over effects such as learning or fatigue would swamp any hysteresis.
whyLost: UX experiments usually compare fixed conditions between groups; within-person sweeps in both directions come from psychophysics and are rarely taught to product researchers.
whereToUse: Performance and latency tolerance, pricing and paywall thresholds, notification load, automation trust, game difficulty tuning.
example: In a lab study, response latency of a search box is raised from 100 ms to 2 s in small steps and then lowered again. Participants switch from typing full queries to waiting for suggestions at 900 ms on the way up but only switch back at 300 ms on the way down, showing that recovering speed alone will not restore the earlier behaviour quickly.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: IA graph analysis
origin: Hypertext structural metrics by Botafogo, Rivlin and Shneiderman, 1992; network science metrics (Freeman, 1978)
summary: Treats an information architecture as a network of nodes and links and computes structural metrics that predict findability, bottlenecks and isolation.
description: Any site, app or knowledge base can be represented as a directed graph: nodes are pages, screens or content objects; edges are navigational links, relations or transitions. Graph analysis computes properties that matter for findability: path lengths between nodes, diameter, connectivity, centrality, clustering, and structural metrics such as Botafogo's compactness and stratum. These reveal whether important content is many hops from entry points, whether parts of the structure are poorly connected, and which nodes are bottlenecks. Weighting edges with real transition frequencies turns the structural graph into a behavioural one. Rigour comes from complete graph extraction, consistent node definitions, and validating structural predictions with tree tests or log-based task success.
steps: Extract the graph: crawl the site or export app routes and links, defining nodes and edges consistently (for example one node per template instance).
Load into a graph tool (NetworkX, Gephi) and compute node count, edge count, diameter, average shortest path, connected components and compactness.
Compute shortest path length from main entry points to each key task destination and flag destinations more than 3 clicks from entry in time-critical contexts.
Compute centrality measures to find hubs and bottlenecks, and community detection to compare clusters with the intended taxonomy.
Overlay behavioural transition weights from analytics to compare designed versus used structure.
Propose structural changes and simulate their effect on path lengths before validating with a tree test.
outputs: A network model of the IA, structural metrics, path-length maps to key tasks, centrality rankings, and recommended link changes.
useWhen: For large or legacy sites and apps, knowledge bases and settings structures; when planning IA changes; when findability problems are diffuse.
avoidWhen: For small sites where structure is obvious; use a card sort or tree test directly.
whyLost: 1990s hypertext research produced these metrics, but web IA moved to card sorting and sitemaps, leaving network analysis to SEO tools.
whereToUse: Enterprise intranets, documentation sites, government services, e-commerce, and surgical or industrial device menus.
example: Graph analysis of a surgical robot's 210-screen IA shows the instrument calibration screen is 6 hops from the home state and reachable only through settings. Adding a contextual link from the instrument status bar cuts it to 2 hops.
sources: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J., Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (O'Reilly, 4th ed., 2015)
Martin, L. M., Everyday Information Architecture (2019)
Covert, A., How to Make Sense of Any Mess (2014)

name: Iatrogenic UX Harm Analysis
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Examines harm caused by interventions meant to protect users (regulations, safeguards, policies), as with cookie consent banners producing near-universal uninformed consent.
description: In medicine, iatrogenic harm is caused by treatment. The treatise defines iatrogenic UX harm as design harm caused by an intervention (regulatory, organisational or technical) intended to protect users. Its canonical case is the cookie consent epidemic: GDPR's informed-consent requirement was implemented almost universally through banners that undermined informed consent via choice overload, asymmetric defaults and dark-pattern accept buttons. The regulation acted as a vector transmitting a new pathogen across the European-facing web at once, which then spread globally. Research finds 80-95% click 'Accept All' without reading; virtually no one makes a genuinely informed decision. Iatrogenic analysis evaluates protective interventions for their actual user outcomes, including second-order harms such as habituation and consent fatigue.
steps: Identify the protective intervention and its intended user outcome.
Define measures of the intended outcome (for example informed consent) and possible harms (time, fatigue, habituation).
Measure real-world implementation and behaviour across products.
Compare outcomes with the intervention's goals and with alternatives.
Identify design features driving harm (defaults, asymmetry, frequency).
Recommend redesigned implementations or policy changes and evaluate them.
outputs: Evaluation of intended versus actual outcomes, iatrogenic harm estimates, redesign and policy recommendations.
useWhen: Evaluating consent flows, warnings, security friction, compliance-driven UI and safety features.
avoidWhen: When no protective intent is involved; use standard harm analysis.
whyLost: Original framing of the treatise; compliance UI is rarely evaluated for its effect on users.
whereToUse: Privacy and consent, security warnings, age verification, AI safety disclaimers, accessibility overlays.
example: An analysis of AI disclaimers shows users stop reading them after the third exposure while over-trusting outputs; replacing static disclaimers with contextual uncertainty cues improves verification.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Utz C et al. (2019) (Un)informed consent: studying GDPR consent notices in the field. CCS
Nouwens M et al. (2020) Dark patterns after the GDPR. CHI
Illich I (1976) Limits to Medicine: Medical Nemesis
reference: Nouwens M et al. (2020) Dark patterns after the GDPR: scraping consent pop-ups and demonstrating their influence. Proceedings of CHI 2020.

name: Icon simulation test
donor: Safety ergonomics and standards for public information symbols
origin: Graphical symbol comprehension testing developed through ISO 9186 (first edition 1989) and ANSI Z535.3 (1991) for public and safety signage
summary: Measures whether users correctly interpret icons by showing them in a simulated context and scoring open-ended interpretations against standardised comprehension thresholds.
description: Standards bodies test public and safety symbols rigorously before adoption: participants see a symbol in a realistic context, describe its meaning in their own words, and judges score the answers against the intended referent. ISO 9186 sets an acceptance criterion of 66.7% correct comprehension for public information symbols, while ANSI Z535.3 requires 85% correct with no more than 5% critical confusions for safety symbols. An icon simulation test brings this protocol to UI: the icon is placed in a mocked-up context screen that simulates the real moment of use, and responses are categorised as correct, partly correct, wrong, opposite or critical confusion. Rigour comes from open-ended rather than multiple-choice responses, independent judging and pre-set thresholds.
steps: Define the referent for each icon in one sentence and decide the acceptance threshold: 66.7% correct for general function icons, 85% correct with at most 5% critical confusions for destructive, financial or safety actions.
Build a context screen for each icon that simulates the moment of use without textual labels that give away the meaning.
Recruit at least 50 participants for a standards-grade test, or 20 to 30 per segment for a diagnostic test, representative of the target users' language, age and digital experience.
Show each icon in context in randomised order and ask 'What does this symbol mean?' and 'What would you expect to happen if you selected it?', recording verbatim responses.
Have at least two judges independently categorise each response as correct, partly correct, wrong, opposite or critical confusion, resolving disagreements by discussion and reporting agreement.
Compute per-icon comprehension rates with 95% confidence intervals (adjusted Wald) and compare the lower bound against the threshold for high-stakes icons.
Redesign icons that fail, consider adding text labels, and retest with new participants.
outputs: Per-icon comprehension percentages with confidence intervals, critical confusion rates, categorised verbatims, and a pass or fail decision per icon against the threshold.
useWhen: Icons appear without labels, carry safety or financial consequences, or serve users across languages and literacy levels.
avoidWhen: Icons always have visible text labels, or you need to test navigation success rather than sign meaning; use first-click or task-based usability testing instead.
whyLost: The protocol stayed in standards and safety ergonomics, while UX teams adopted quick preference polls or multiple-choice recognition tests that inflate comprehension.
whereToUse: Medical devices, automotive HMIs, kiosks and ATMs, low-literacy fintech, global consumer apps, AI status icons.
example: A ride-hailing app tested an unlabelled shield icon intended as 'safety tools'. Only 38% interpreted it correctly and 12% read it as 'insurance purchase', a critical confusion; the team added a label and a distinct help symbol.
sources: Pocket Universal Principles of Design (Lidwell)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
Embodied Mind (Varela)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 20 — Semiotics, Icons & Cross-Cultural Sign Failure
reference: ISO 9186-1:2014 Graphical symbols: Test methods, Part 1: Method for testing comprehensibility; ANSI Z535.3 Criteria for Safety Symbols.

name: IHCLab Usability Test for Serious Games
aka: Group usability test for serious games
origin: Santana-Mancilla, Gaytan-Lugo and Rodriguez-Ortiz, IHCLab, University of Colima (Chapter 11)
summary: A summative lab method for serious games in which a group of 5 to 20 learners is introduced, shown a live demo, given a task list and then answers selectable questionnaires on heuristics, game experience and use for learning.
description: The IHCLab method evaluates finished serious games with all participants at once in a lab configured with a computer per user, cameras on faces, observers and a moderator with a projector. Sessions last an hour to an hour and a half in four phases. First, a ten-minute introduction and a short profile questionnaire. Second, a projected live demo that puts the game's controls in context. Third, participants work through a task list in the game while observers watch. Fourth, the team chooses one or more of three questionnaires: a game heuristics questionnaire of ten player-answered questions generalised from Desurvire's playability heuristics (consistency, customisation, predictable controls, skippable non-playable content, status information, help and training); a game experience questionnaire with four 1 to 10 ratings (fun, difficulty adapting to controls, excitement, ease of meeting the objective) and seven 5-point indicators such as efficiency, immersion and learning curve; and a two-question use for learning survey on comfort and motivation to use such a game for education. The method is practical for schools and universities, though its questionnaires are home-grown rather than validated.
steps: Set up a lab with one machine per participant, face cameras, observer positions and a projector.
Recruit 5 to 20 representative learners and open with an introduction and profile questionnaire.
Give a live projected demo of the game and its controls.
Hand out a task list and let participants complete it while observers note difficulties.
Administer the chosen questionnaires: heuristics, game experience, use for learning, or a combination.
Chart results per item and highlight heuristics or indicators with poor ratings for redesign.
outputs: Observer notes and per-item questionnaire results on usability heuristics, experience and perceived educational value.
useWhen: Evaluating finished educational or serious games with classes of learners when time and lab slots are limited.
avoidWhen: You need validated, comparable measures or detailed individual problem discovery.
whyLost: It is a lab-specific methodology published in one book chapter and not widely adopted.
whereToUse: Serious games, edtech, training simulations, university and school settings.
example: Twenty third-graders test a reading comprehension game together; the heuristics questionnaire shows poor results for customisation and for skipping text, the latter being intentional because reading is the learning goal.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Santana-Mancilla, P. C., Gaytan-Lugo, L. S. and Rodriguez-Ortiz, M. A. (2016). Usability testing of serious games: the experience of the IHCLab. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 11. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Imbalanced Data Strategies (Undersampling, Oversampling, SMOTE)
origin: Chawla et al. (2002) SMOTE; cost-sensitive learning literature
summary: Techniques for modelling rare but important events, such as errors, cancellations or accessibility failures, without the model ignoring them.
description: When only 2% of sessions end in a critical error, a model that predicts "no error" is 98% accurate and useless. Imbalanced data strategies rebalance the training data by undersampling the common class, oversampling or up-weighting the rare class, or generating synthetic rare cases (SMOTE). Cost-based classification sets thresholds by the real cost of each mistake. Bruce and Bruce stress evaluating with precision, recall and lift rather than accuracy.
steps: Quantify the class imbalance and the cost of missing a rare case.
Try undersampling, oversampling, weighting or SMOTE on the training set only.
Fit the model and evaluate on an untouched test set with recall, precision and AUC.
Set the decision threshold using the cost of errors.
Review predicted rare cases qualitatively.
outputs: Models that actually detect rare but important user events.
useWhen: Predicting rare outcomes: critical errors, fraud, cancellations, complaints.
avoidWhen: Classes are balanced, or rare events are too few to learn from (under a few dozen).
whyLost: A modelling concern that UX analytics rarely encounters because it seldom models at all.
whereToUse: Error monitoring, support escalation prediction, safety-critical telemetry.
example: Oversampling failed-payment sessions lifts recall from 12% to 68%, surfacing a pattern of address-format errors in one region.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 5.

name: Impedance Matching Analysis
origin: Maximum power transfer theorem (Moritz von Jacobi, c. 1840); impedance matching in transmission line and acoustic engineering
summary: Treats an interface as a coupling between a source (system) and load (user) and asks where mismatches in rate, granularity or format reflect energy back as friction.
description: In electrical systems, maximum power transfers when source and load impedances match; mismatches reflect energy, causing loss and distortion. Acoustic and mechanical engineering use matching layers and transformers to couple dissimilar media. As an analytical lens for UX, impedance matching asks whether the information rate, chunk size, vocabulary and pacing of a system match the user's capacity and goals at each interface. Mismatches produce 'reflections': repeated questions, backtracking, ignored outputs. The rigorous version quantifies both sides (system output rate and granularity versus measured user processing rate and needs) and designs 'transformers' (summaries, progressive disclosure, adaptive pacing). It remains an analogy-driven framework, so it should be paired with empirical measures.
steps: Identify the interfaces where information or control passes between system and user (or between teams).
Characterise the source: output rate, granularity, format, vocabulary, timing.
Characterise the load: user processing rate (e.g. reading speed, decision time), needed granularity, vocabulary.
Measure reflections: re-reads, follow-up questions, undo, abandonment at each interface.
Design matching elements (summaries, chunking, adjustable verbosity, pacing controls) to reduce mismatch.
Re-measure reflections and throughput after changes.
outputs: An interface mismatch map, reflection metrics and designed matching components.
useWhen: Systems that emit large or fast outputs to people (AI assistants, alerts, dashboards, reports), or handoffs between experts and novices.
avoidWhen: When the analogy adds nothing beyond standard usability analysis; prefer direct empirical methods.
whyLost: Physical analogies were never systematically translated into HCI, apart from loose references to 'bandwidth'.
whereToUse: LLM response length and structure, notification streams, executive dashboards, clinician-patient information handoffs.
example: An AI coding assistant emits 60-line answers; logs show users re-prompt for summaries 40% of the time. Adding an adjustable verbosity 'transformer' with a summary first matches load and halves re-prompts.
sources: Pozar, Microwave Engineering (4th ed., 2011)
Card, Moran & Newell, The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (1983)

name: Implicit Association Test (IAT)
origin: Anthony Greenwald, Debbie McGhee and Jordan Schwartz, 1998
summary: Measures the relative strength of automatic associations between concepts (e.g. a brand and 'trustworthy') from response-time differences in a categorisation task.
description: In the IAT, participants rapidly sort words or images into categories using two keys. When concepts that are strongly associated share a key, responses are faster. The D-score, computed from latency differences between compatible and incompatible blocks, indexes relative association strength. Brief IAT and single-category IAT variants shorten the procedure. The IAT has real limitations: test-retest reliability around 0.5 and modest prediction of individual behaviour, so it is best used for group-level comparisons. For UX and brand research it offers a measure less susceptible to self-presentation than stated attitudes, useful where users may not admit or know their associations.
steps: Define two target concepts (e.g. our app vs competitor) and two attribute categories (e.g. safe vs risky), with 4-6 stimuli each.
Implement the standard 7-block procedure or a Brief IAT using validated software.
Counterbalance block order across participants.
Compute D-scores using the Greenwald, Nosek and Banaji (2003) improved algorithm, excluding trials over 10 s and participants with excessive fast responses.
Compare group-level D-scores across conditions or segments, and correlate with explicit measures.
Interpret cautiously: report reliability and avoid individual-level claims.
outputs: Group D-scores, explicit-implicit comparison and reliability estimates.
useWhen: Measuring brand or feature associations where social desirability distorts self-report, at group level.
avoidWhen: Diagnosing individuals or predicting individual behaviour; use behavioural data. Avoid ethically sensitive labelling of participants.
whyLost: Contested validity debates and lab requirements kept it in social psychology and market research niches.
whereToUse: Brand perception of AI products, privacy trust, health app stigma, rebrand evaluation.
example: A mental health app tests whether its new name is implicitly associated with 'clinical' versus 'everyday'. The IAT shows a strong clinical association despite neutral explicit ratings, prompting a naming rethink.
sources: Greenwald, McGhee & Schwartz, Measuring individual differences in implicit cognition: The implicit association test (1998), JPSP
Greenwald, Nosek & Banaji, Understanding and using the IAT: I. An improved scoring algorithm (2003), JPSP
reference: Greenwald, A. G., McGhee, D. E., & Schwartz, J. L. K. (1998). JPSP, 74(6), 1464-1480.

name: Implicit Processing Assessment in UX Evaluation
origin: Greenwald et al., 1998 (IAT); Goldstein, 2015 (synthesis)
summary: Measures responses users cannot or will not report, using implicit techniques such as reaction-time association tests, priming and behavioural traces alongside self-report.
description: Much of what shapes user experience happens outside awareness: rapid evaluative judgments, primed associations and attentional capture that users cannot accurately report. Implicit processing assessment combines self-report with measures designed to tap these processes, such as reaction-time association tasks, affective priming, first-impression tests with very short exposures, and behavioural traces. The value lies in the dissociation: where implicit and explicit measures disagree, self-report is likely shaped by social desirability, rationalisation or limited introspective access. Rigour requires adequate trials and samples to overcome reaction-time noise, established paradigms rather than ad hoc tasks, and caution in interpretation given ongoing debates about the reliability and predictive validity of implicit measures.
steps: Research design implication: never rely solely on self-report for any UX variable that may be processed unconsciously.
For each research question, identify: is the phenomenon likely conscious (reportable) or unconscious (implicit)?
Conscious → survey, interview, think-aloud.
Unconscious → reaction time, eye-tracking, physiological measures, implicit association test, behavioral observation.
Mismatch between explicit attitude and implicit measure = valuable research finding.
outputs: Implicit association scores, priming effects, dissociations between implicit and explicit measures, and interpretation of where self-report misleads.
useWhen: Brand perception, trust, stigma-related products, and any case where social desirability or limited introspective access makes self-report unreliable.
avoidWhen: Avoid when explicit attitudes are what matter for the decision, when sample sizes are too small for reaction-time noise, or when the team cannot interpret implicit measures cautiously; use standard surveys and interviews.
whyLost: Implicit methods remain contested in psychology and require experimental software and statistical skill; UX practice centres on self-report and observed behaviour.
whereToUse: Trust research (explicit trust ratings often diverge from behavioral trust), aesthetic evaluation, emotional response measurement.
example: A telehealth service runs an online implicit association task with 200 users and finds that 'video consultation' is implicitly associated with 'less thorough' even among users who rate it highly, prompting design cues that signal clinical rigour.
sources: The Mind — E. Bruce Goldstein
reference: Greenwald AG, McGhee DE & Schwartz JLK (1998) Measuring individual differences in implicit cognition: The Implicit Association Test. JPSP 74(6)

name: Implicit vs. explicit measure mismatch analysis
origin: Dual-attitude and implicit measurement research (Greenwald and Banaji, 1995; Wilson, Lindsey and Schooler, 2000); multi-channel affect sensing (Picard, 1997)
summary: Treats systematic disagreement between what users report and what implicit, physiological or behavioural measures show as a finding to explain, not as noise to discard.
description: Explicit self-reports and implicit measures often diverge: a participant reports feeling calm while electrodermal activity and hesitation spike, or rates a flow 'easy' after visibly struggling. The usual response is to pick the measure judged more valid. The mismatch approach instead treats divergence as information. Social desirability, politeness to the researcher, lack of interoceptive awareness, reconstructive memory and dual attitudes each predict different mismatch patterns. Analysing where, when and for whom measures diverge reveals hidden anxiety, face-saving or adaptation. Rigour requires time-aligned data across channels, pre-defined thresholds for what counts as divergence relative to each person's baseline, and follow-up probes such as cued retrospective interviews to interpret mismatches rather than speculating.
steps: Choose paired measures for the constructs of interest, for example self-reported anxiety (a 1 to 7 rating) with electrodermal responses, or perceived ease (Single Ease Question) with task time and errors.
Record baselines for each participant (for example 2 to 5 minutes of rest for physiology) and time-align all channels to task events.
Standardise each measure within participant (z-scores against baseline) and define divergence, for example a self-report at or below the participant's median while the implicit measure exceeds +1 SD.
Map mismatches by task moment and participant, and classify patterns: under-reporting, over-reporting, delayed response or segment-specific divergence.
Run cued retrospective interviews, replaying the moments of mismatch to participants and asking what they were experiencing and why they rated as they did.
Interpret patterns against candidate mechanisms (social desirability, low awareness, adaptation) and report mismatches as findings with design implications.
outputs: Time-aligned multi-channel data, a mismatch map by moment and participant, mechanism interpretations from cued retrospection, and design implications.
useWhen: Stakes or social pressure may bias self-report (finance, health, employer-provided tools); satisfaction scores conflict with behaviour; studying anxiety or trust.
avoidWhen: Sample sizes are too small for within-person baselines, or you lack the equipment and expertise to collect reliable physiological data; use behavioural versus self-report comparison only.
whyLost: UX tends to report self-report and behavioural or biometric data side by side, choosing one when they conflict, so the mismatch itself is rarely analysed.
whereToUse: Loan and credit applications, medical decision interfaces, workplace tools, AI trust research, accessibility and older-adult research.
example: During a loan application, participants rated anxiety low (2 of 7) while heart rate variability dropped sharply at the income disclosure screen. Cued retrospection revealed fear of rejection hidden out of politeness, leading the team to explain how income data is used.
sources: Affective Computing (Picard)
Methods Atlas — affective measurement (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 37 — Picard's Affective Framework — Multi-Channel Emotion Measurement
reference: Picard, R. W. (1997). Affective Computing. MIT Press; Wilson, T. D., Lindsey, S., & Schooler, T. Y. (2000). A model of dual attitudes. Psychological Review, 107(1), 101–126.

name: Importance-Performance Analysis
origin: Martilla and James (1977) in the Journal of Marketing; cited by Veal and Darcy as a standard evaluation and service-quality technique in sport and leisure management
summary: Asks customers to rate how important each attribute of a service is and how well it performs, then plots the two scores on a grid to show where effort should go.
description: Importance-performance analysis is a survey-based evaluation technique. A list of service attributes is drawn up, and each respondent rates every attribute twice: once for how important it is to them and once for how well the provider currently performs on it. Mean scores are plotted on a two-dimensional grid with importance on one axis and performance on the other, and the grid is divided into four quadrants, usually at the overall means. Attributes that are important but performing poorly are the priority for action; important and well-performing ones should be maintained; unimportant but well-performing ones may be absorbing effort that could go elsewhere; and unimportant, poorly performing ones are low priority. Veal and Darcy list it alongside cost-benefit analysis and conjoint analysis as a formal technique for evaluating options, and note its closeness to the SERVQUAL approach, which compares expectations with performance. For UX teams it is a quick way to turn a satisfaction survey into a prioritised list of product attributes. Unlike regression-based key driver analysis, it uses stated importance rather than derived importance, so it is simple to explain but prone to everything being rated important.
steps: Identify the attributes of the product or service to assess, from earlier interviews, focus groups, support data or the literature.
Write paired items for each attribute: an importance rating and a performance (satisfaction) rating on the same scale.
Survey a representative sample of current users and compute the mean importance and mean performance for each attribute.
Plot each attribute on a grid with importance on one axis and performance on the other, and draw cross-hairs at the grand means or the scale midpoints.
Read off the four quadrants: concentrate here, keep up the good work, low priority and possible overkill.
Check the stability of the result by segment and, where possible, compare stated importance with importance derived from regression.
Turn the 'concentrate here' quadrant into a ranked backlog and repeat the survey after changes to track movement.
outputs: An importance-performance grid, a table of mean scores and gaps per attribute, and a short prioritised list of attributes needing attention.
useWhen: You need a simple, explainable way to prioritise many service or product attributes from user ratings, for example after a release or for an annual satisfaction programme.
avoidWhen: Respondents cannot judge importance meaningfully, the attribute list is unfinished, or you need causal evidence of what drives satisfaction or retention.
whyLost: UX adopted regression-based key driver analysis and NPS-style dashboards, and stated-importance ratings are criticised for ceiling effects, so the simpler grid stayed mainly in tourism, leisure and service marketing.
whereToUse: Customer satisfaction surveys, service design programmes, SaaS feature satisfaction tracking, venue and event apps, public service digital channels.
example: A sports club booking app surveys 600 members on twelve attributes such as finding a free court, paying, cancelling and notifications. The grid shows cancelling a booking as highly important but rated poorly, while social sharing performs well but matters little, so the team moves effort from sharing features to a clearer cancellation flow.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
Feature Prioritization Methods (slide deck)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge. Martilla, J. A. and James, J. C. (1977) Importance-performance analysis. Journal of Marketing, 41(1), 77-79.

name: Inattentional blindness detection
origin: Mack and Rock, 1998; Simons and Chabris's 'gorillas in our midst' study, 1999
