summary: Tests whether users engaged in a demanding primary task fail to notice salient but unexpected events, such as alerts, that they would easily see if looking for them.
description: Inattentional blindness is the failure to notice a fully visible but unexpected object when attention is engaged elsewhere. Simons and Chabris showed around half of viewers counting basketball passes missed a person in a gorilla suit. Detection depends on the load of the primary task and the similarity of the unexpected item to attended items, not just on its salience. Testing it requires surprise: participants must not expect the event, so each participant can usually contribute only one 'critical trial', which drives sample size. The method complements salience audits, showing whether prominent design actually captures attention under realistic workload. Rigour comes from realistic task load, single critical trials, and careful post-trial questioning that avoids leading questions.
steps: Define the primary task at realistic load and the unexpected event (for example a new alert appearing mid-task).
Recruit enough participants for proportion estimates; since each gives one critical trial, aim for at least 20-30 per condition.
Run the task, introduce the event once without warning, and afterwards ask open then progressively specific questions ('Did you notice anything unusual?').
Compute detection rates per condition with confidence intervals and compare designs with a chi-square or Fisher's exact test.
Optionally include eye tracking to distinguish 'looked but did not see' from never fixated.
Redesign events to resemble attended features or interrupt the primary task channel, and re-test with new participants.
outputs: Detection rates per design and load condition, eye-tracking evidence where used, and design changes that improve capture of unexpected events.
useWhen: When critical alerts or changes must be noticed during demanding work, such as surgery, driving, monitoring or trading.
avoidWhen: When events are expected or users actively search for them; use visual search or d' testing instead.
whyLost: Widely known as a psychology curiosity, but rarely operationalised in UX because the one-trial design needs many participants.
whereToUse: Surgical and clinical displays, driver assistance HMIs, cockpit and control room design, and security monitoring.
example: In a simulation, 11 of 24 surgeons focused on suturing fail to notice a prominent yellow pressure warning. Moving the warning into the endoscopic field and pairing it with a tone raises detection to 22 of 24.
sources: Bear, M., Connors, B. & Paradiso, M., Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain
Garrett, B., Brain & Behavior: An Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Neuroscience (Bear et al.)
Brain & Behaviour (Garrett)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 9 — Attention — The Gatekeeper
reference: Simons, D. J. & Chabris, C. F. (1999). Gorillas in our midst: sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events. Perception, 28(9), 1059-1074.

name: Inclusive Design Research
origin: Roger Coleman (inclusive design, UK, 1994); popularised by Kat Holmes and Microsoft's Inclusive Design toolkit (2016)
summary: Research with people across disability, age, culture and cognition, recruiting from the margins to reveal exclusions that average-user research hides.
description: Inclusive design research treats exclusion as a mismatch between a person and a designed environment rather than a property of the person. Instead of recruiting a representative middle, the researcher deliberately recruits people at the edges: blind and low-vision users, people with motor, cognitive or hearing impairments, older adults, people with low literacy or limited bandwidth, and people experiencing temporary or situational limitations. Their workarounds expose design constraints that also affect everyone else. Rigour comes from a documented recruitment frame across a persona spectrum (permanent, temporary, situational), accessible study logistics (formats, consent, assistive technology, paid access support), and analysis that traces each finding to a specific exclusion mechanism rather than a generic 'accessibility issue'. It goes beyond WCAG compliance, which checks conformance, by asking whether people can actually accomplish meaningful goals.
steps: Define the exclusion spectrum for the product: list permanent, temporary and situational limitations across vision, hearing, motor, cognition, speech, language and context.
Recruit at least 5-8 participants from the edges of that spectrum, through disability organisations or specialist panels, budgeting for access support and fair compensation.
Adapt study logistics in advance: accessible consent forms, the participant's own devices and assistive technology, flexible session lengths and breaks.
Run sessions on real goals in the participant's own setup, observing workarounds, abandonment points and the effort each step costs.
Code every barrier against the mismatch it reveals (sensory, motor, cognitive, linguistic, situational) and note who else the same barrier affects.
Co-create or test solutions with the same participants and verify the fix extends to mainstream users.
Report findings as exclusion mechanisms with severity and reach, alongside any WCAG success criteria they map to.
outputs: Exclusion map across the persona spectrum, prioritised barrier list with affected populations, workaround catalogue, and design principles for inclusion.
useWhen: When a product serves the general public, regulated sectors, or ageing and diverse populations; when you need to know whether people can actually complete goals rather than whether the code conforms.
avoidWhen: When you only need a conformance check (use an accessibility audit against WCAG) or when you cannot fund access support and fair compensation, in which case partner with a disability organisation first.
whyLost: Still in use: Growing legal, ethical, and business case; Microsoft, BBC, and Apple frameworks widely adopted.
whereToUse: All digital products; especially public services, health, and education.
example: A UK bank tests its mobile cheque-deposit flow with a screen-reader user, a person with tremor and a user with dyslexia. The camera auto-capture timeout fails all three, and extending it plus adding a manual capture button also cuts abandonment among sighted users in low light.
sources: ISO Standard on Ergonomics
Designing Across Senses
Mismatch: How Inclusion Shapes Design (Kat Holmes)
Microsoft Inclusive Design Toolkit
reference: Holmes K (2018) Mismatch: How Inclusion Shapes Design. MIT Press

name: Indicators and Signposts Monitoring
origin: Military indications and warning (I&W) practice from the Cold War; structured technique in Heuer and Pherson (2010)
summary: Defines in advance observable indicators that would signal which of several scenarios or hypotheses is unfolding, and monitors them systematically.
description: Rather than waiting for certainty, analysts define for each scenario or hypothesis a set of indicators: observable events or trends that would be more likely if it were true. Good indicators are observable, valid (diagnostic between scenarios), reliable, stable and unique. A monitoring matrix tracks indicator status over time (e.g. green, amber, red), and changes trigger reassessment. For UX and product strategy, this turns research conclusions and scenario plans into living monitoring systems: which signals would tell us our assumptions about AI adoption, competitor behaviour or user needs are wrong?
steps: List the scenarios or hypotheses to discriminate between.
For each, brainstorm indicators that would be observable if it were unfolding.
Screen indicators for observability, diagnosticity, reliability and timeliness.
Define thresholds and data sources (analytics, research, market data) for each indicator.
Monitor on a fixed cadence and record status in an indicator matrix.
Trigger reassessment and decision reviews when indicators cross thresholds.
outputs: Indicator lists per scenario, a monitoring matrix and trigger-based decision reviews.
useWhen: Strategic uncertainty with competing futures or hypotheses, and when research conclusions need ongoing validation.
avoidWhen: Stable, well-understood domains where standard KPI monitoring suffices.
whyLost: It is an intelligence and military practice; product teams track KPIs but rarely define diagnostic indicators for hypotheses.
whereToUse: AI product strategy, market entry, regulatory change, platform shifts, long-term research programmes.
example: A fintech defines indicators distinguishing 'users want AI financial advice' from 'users want only automation'. Rising rates of follow-up questions on AI summaries trigger an earlier investment in advisory features.
sources: Heuer & Pherson, Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis (2nd ed., 2014)
Grabo, Anticipating Surprise: Analysis for Strategic Warning (2002)
reference: Grabo, C. M. (2002). Anticipating Surprise: Analysis for Strategic Warning. Joint Military Intelligence College.

name: Information Architecture
donor: Library and information science; cognitive psychology
origin: Richard Saul Wurman, 1976 (term); Louis Rosenfeld & Peter Morville, 1998 (Information Architecture for the World Wide Web)
summary: The practice of designing organisation, labelling, navigation and search systems so people can find, understand and manage information, informed by research on users, content and context.
description: Information architecture is the structural design of shared information environments. Rosenfeld, Morville and Arango describe four interlocking systems: organisation (how content is grouped), labelling (how it is named), navigation (how people move through it) and search (how people query it). IA practice balances users (their tasks and mental models), content (its volume, types and metadata) and context (business goals, constraints and culture). As a research-driven practice it draws on card sorting, tree testing, content inventories, search log analysis and usability testing. Rigour comes from basing structures on evidence of user mental models and tasks rather than organisational charts, designing controlled vocabularies and metadata, testing structures before visual design, and measuring findability after launch.
steps: Audit existing content with a content inventory, noting types, volume, owners and metadata.
Research users' tasks and mental models with interviews, search log analysis and card sorting.
Define organisation schemes, controlled vocabularies and metadata.
Draft the hierarchy, labels and navigation and test them with tree testing.
Design search, including synonyms and facets, using search log evidence.
Validate the integrated design with usability testing and measure findability after launch.
outputs: Content inventory, site maps and hierarchies, labelling systems, controlled vocabularies, metadata schema and findability metrics.
useWhen: For information-dense products such as websites, intranets, documentation, e-commerce catalogues and enterprise tools, and for redesigns of navigation and search.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating IA as just a site map exercise without research; run card sorting, tree testing and search analysis. For simple single-task apps, a lighter flow design suffices.
whyLost: Still in use: Foundational practice; increasingly integrated with content strategy and SEO.
whereToUse: Any information-dense product; websites; enterprise tools; documentation systems.
example: A medical knowledge base reorganises 4,000 articles. Search logs show clinicians search by symptom while content is organised by specialty, so a faceted symptom-and-specialty structure is designed and tree tested, raising findability from 52 to 81 percent.
sources: Information Architecture
Everyday Information Architecture
Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (Rosenfeld, Morville & Arango)
reference: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J. (2015). Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (4th ed.). O'Reilly.

name: Information Foraging Analysis
origin: Peter Pirolli and Stuart Card, Xerox PARC, 1995-1999
summary: Models information seeking as foraging that maximises information gain per unit cost, quantifying information scent, patch residence and diet choice.
description: Borrowing from optimal foraging theory in ecology, Pirolli and Card modelled users as foragers who move between information patches (pages, search results, documents) and decide when to leave a patch using Charnov's marginal value theorem: leave when the rate of gain in the current patch drops below the average rate in the environment. Information scent, the perceived value of a link from its proximal cues, determines navigation, and was computationally modelled with spreading activation (SNIF-ACT). Rigorous application measures scent quantitatively, predicts navigation choices and patch-leaving, and compares predicted and observed paths. UX retains 'information scent' as a slogan while dropping the models and measurements.
steps: Define the user's information goal precisely and the information environment (patches, links, cues).
Measure information scent: have participants or a semantic model rate how likely each link leads to the goal.
Predict navigation by choosing the highest-scent link at each step, and predict patch-leaving via the marginal value theorem.
Collect navigation and dwell data with logs or a tree-test-like task.
Compare predicted and observed paths and patch residence times; identify scent misleads and dead patches.
Rewrite labels and summaries to strengthen accurate scent and re-measure.
outputs: Scent ratings per link, predicted versus observed path match, patch residence analysis and label improvements.
useWhen: Diagnosing navigation, search results, documentation sites and content-heavy products where users hunt for information.
avoidWhen: Transactional flows with no information seeking.
whyLost: The slogan 'follow the scent' entered practitioner vocabulary without the quantitative modelling, which requires cognitive modelling skills.
whereToUse: Documentation portals, intranets, e-commerce category pages, search results and AI answer citations.
example: A developer docs site measures scent ratings for 40 nav labels against 12 tasks. Labels like 'Concepts' have low scent; renaming to task-oriented labels raises first-click success from 48% to 71%.
sources: Pirolli & Card, Information foraging (1999), Psychological Review
Pirolli, Information Foraging Theory: Adaptive Interaction with Information (2007)
reference: Pirolli, P., & Card, S. (1999). Information foraging. Psychological Review, 106(4), 643-675.

name: Innovation Diffusion Analysis
origin: Everett Rogers, Diffusion of Innovations (1962); Frank Bass diffusion model (1969)
summary: Analysis of how a product or feature spreads through a population using Rogers' adopter categories and innovation attributes, optionally modelled with Bass or S-curve forecasts.
description: Innovation diffusion analysis explains and forecasts adoption over time. Rogers identified five attributes that predict adoption rate (relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability) and adopter categories along a normal distribution: innovators (2.5%), early adopters (13.5%), early majority (34%), late majority (34%) and laggards (16%). Bass's model formalises the cumulative S-curve with coefficients for innovation (external influence) and imitation (word of mouth). In UX and product work, the method combines attribute assessment through interviews or surveys with fitting adoption curves to feature-usage logs, and can simulate adoption under different design scenarios with Monte Carlo methods. Its rigour lies in separating attribute-driven barriers from network effects and in forecasting with explicit uncertainty rather than assuming adoption will follow launch.
steps: Define the innovation (product, feature or behaviour) and the population that could adopt it.
Assess the five innovation attributes through interviews or a survey, identifying which attribute most limits adoption.
Extract adoption timestamps from logs and plot cumulative adoption, classifying adopters into Rogers' categories by time of adoption.
Fit a Bass diffusion model to estimate innovation (p) and imitation (q) coefficients, with confidence intervals.
Simulate adoption under alternative design or launch scenarios (for example improved trialability), using Monte Carlo runs to express uncertainty.
Interview representatives of the late majority and non-adopters to explain barriers, and recommend interventions targeted to each category.
outputs: Attribute assessment, adopter segmentation, fitted S-curve and Bass coefficients, scenario forecasts and targeted adoption interventions.
useWhen: Planning launches and rollouts, diagnosing stalled feature adoption, forecasting uptake of new behaviours, and choosing between trialability, observability or simplicity interventions.
avoidWhen: When adoption data is too sparse to fit curves or the product is not a discretionary choice (mandated enterprise tools follow organisational decisions, not diffusion dynamics); use change-management or task analysis instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Framework for adoption strategy; technology adoption lifecycle widely referenced.
whereToUse: New product launch; feature adoption strategy; cross-chasm product design.
example: A banking app's new budgeting feature plateaus at 11% adoption. A Bass fit shows a low imitation coefficient, and interviews reveal the feature is invisible to others, so the team adds shareable monthly summaries and simulates a lift in q before rollout.
sources: Diffusion of Innovation
Monte Carlo Methods with R (Robert & Casella)
Diffusion of Innovations (Rogers)
Forward-Thinking Playbook (Gopinath)
Bass, A new product growth for model consumer durables (Management Science, 1969)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 56 — Monte Carlo Simulation & Predictive Forecasting
reference: Rogers EM (2003) Diffusion of Innovations. 5th ed. Free Press

name: Inside-Out and Backwards Composing
origin: Robert K. Yin, Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2011; 2nd ed. 2016), Chapter 11
summary: A drafting sequence for research reports that starts with the evidence displays (the inside) and the back-end material such as the methods appendix, and writes the surrounding narrative last.
description: Yin offers two ways to start composing a qualitative report without stalling. Composing inside out means drafting the 'inside' first: the quotations, word tables, vignettes, data arrays, pictures and numeric tables that will carry the evidence. Doing this forces a decision about exactly which evidence will be used, exposes gaps in the analysis that send the researcher back to the data, and lets the researcher test different sequences of the pieces; trying these sequences tends to reveal the beginning, middle and end of the 'outside' narrative. Yin argues this suits the inductive character of qualitative work, since insights come from concrete field events. Composing backwards means writing back-end material first, especially an extended methods statement covering the research lens, along with appendices such as an illustrative case and the reference list, so that a real part of the report exists before the main text. For UX researchers, who often get stuck on the executive summary, the approach yields an evidence-led deck or report in which every claim has its display already built, and keeps the narrative from drifting away from the data.
steps: List the candidate evidence pieces: quotes, word tables, vignettes, matrices, images and numeric tables
Edit and finalise each piece for presentation, starting anywhere, even with the easiest
Return to the data where a piece reveals an incomplete analysis
Arrange the pieces in alternative sequences and test which order tells the clearest story
Draft back-end material: methods and research-lens statement, appendices and references
Write the surrounding narrative, introduction and conclusions around the chosen sequence
outputs: A set of finished evidence displays in a tested sequence, a methods appendix, and a report narrative built around them.
useWhen: Writing up qualitative or mixed findings, especially when the author is stuck or the material is large.
avoidWhen: The output is a short decision memo whose conclusion is fixed in advance and needs only one or two supporting points.
whyLost: UX reporting habits come from consulting and product writing, which start from the headline recommendation; writing advice from qualitative methodology texts rarely reaches practitioners.
whereToUse: Research reports, readout decks, case studies and research repository entries.
example: After a diary study, a researcher builds twelve slides of quotes, a journey matrix and three participant vignettes before writing any headline. Shuffling them shows the strongest story starts with the vignettes, and the methods slide is written while the narrative is still unclear.
sources: Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2016). Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.

name: Insight sentence pattern
origin: Design research and IDEO-style insight practice; structured insight formats in research communication
summary: A structured sentence format that states who, what they do or feel, why, and the implication, turning a finding into an actionable, evidence-bound insight.
description: Many reports present observations ('users find the dashboard confusing') rather than insights. The insight sentence pattern enforces a structure such as: [user group] [behaviour or belief] because [underlying reason or mechanism], which means [implication for the product], supported by [evidence and strength]. This forces researchers to name the mechanism, scope the claim to a population, and link it to a decision. Its rigour lies in the evidence clause: each insight cites the number and type of sources, notes counter-evidence and states confidence, preventing the format from becoming a slogan generator. Well-formed insights travel better across organisations and support traceability to design decisions.
steps: Draft the insight in the pattern: who, does or believes what, because why, so what, with evidence.
Check that the 'because' clause names a mechanism supported by data, not a restatement of the behaviour.
Scope the population precisely and avoid universal claims unsupported by the sample.
Attach evidence: number of participants or data sources, key quotes or metrics, and counter-evidence.
Assign a confidence level and test the sentence with a stakeholder for clarity and actionability.
Link each insight to decisions or prescriptions it informs.
outputs: A set of structured, evidence-tagged insight statements linked to decisions.
useWhen: Synthesising research into communicable findings for cross-functional teams and leadership.
avoidWhen: Avoid forcing early exploratory observations into insight form before mechanisms are understood; keep them as open questions.
whyLost: Insight formats are widely used but often reduced to catchy statements with no evidence clause or mechanism, leaving the form without the rigour.
whereToUse: Research readouts, research repositories, strategy decks, design briefs.
example: Instead of 'users don't trust Tap to Pay', the insight reads: 'Experienced card users double-check every Tap to Pay transaction because the interface gives no settlement confirmation, so adoption stalls after first use (14 of 18 interviews; 62% double-check rate in logs).'
sources: Storytelling with Data (Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic)
Articulating Design Decisions (Tom Greever)
Envisioning Information (Edward Tufte)
Insight-driven research communication guidance (e.g. Sharon, It's Our Research)
Storytelling with Data (Knaflic)
Articulating Design Decisions (Greever)
Envisioning Information (Tufte)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 59 — Research Communication — From Evidence to Strategic Brief
reference: Sharon, T. (2012) It's Our Research: Getting Stakeholder Buy-in for User Experience Research Projects. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Instrumental Variables (IV)
origin: Philip Wright (1928); Angrist, Imbens and Rubin (1996)
summary: Uses a variable that shifts exposure but affects outcomes only through exposure to estimate causal effects when users self-select into treatment.
description: An instrument must be relevant (it strongly predicts treatment) and valid (it affects the outcome only through treatment, the exclusion restriction). Two-stage least squares estimates the effect for compliers, the local average treatment effect. The treatise's transfer: when you cannot randomise who uses a new UI, find a plausible instrument, such as a server-side flag randomly assigned for technical reasons, a geographic boundary creating differential access, or a temporal event creating quasi-random exposure. Encouragement designs, where users are randomly nudged toward a feature, are the most practical UX instrument. Weak instruments (first-stage F below about 10) give biased estimates, and exclusion must be argued, not tested.
steps: Define the treatment (actual exposure) and the outcome; identify a candidate instrument.
Argue relevance and exclusion explicitly, ideally with a DAG.
Estimate the first stage and check instrument strength (F above 10).
Estimate the effect with 2SLS and robust standard errors.
Characterise compliers and state that the estimate is a LATE.
Test sensitivity to plausible exclusion violations.
outputs: LATE estimate, first-stage diagnostics, complier description, assumption statement.
useWhen: Opt-in features with self-selection, encouragement designs, natural experiments from technical randomness.
avoidWhen: When no credible instrument exists; a weak or invalid instrument is worse than an honest observational estimate.
whyLost: Rarely taught outside economics; exclusion arguments are unfamiliar to UX and analytics teams.
whereToUse: Feature adoption effects on retention, AI assistant usage effects, opt-in privacy controls, education nudges.
example: A random 50% of users receive an email encouraging use of a new budgeting feature; IV estimates that actually using it lowers overdraft incidents by 12% among compliers, while naive comparison suggested 35%.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Angrist JD, Imbens GW & Rubin DB (1996) Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables. JASA 91:444-455
Angrist JD & Pischke J-S (2008) Mostly Harmless Econometrics
Angrist, Imbens & Rubin, Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables (1996), JASA
Angrist & Pischke, Mostly Harmless Econometrics (2009)
Cinelli, C., Forney, A. & Pearl, J., A Crash Course in Good and Bad Controls (2022)
reference: Angrist JD, Imbens GW & Rubin DB (1996) Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables. Journal of the American Statistical Association 91(434):444-455.

name: Intent Taxonomy Development for Conversational AI
origin: Dialogue act research (Austin, Searle; Traum & Larsson, 2003)
summary: Builds a hierarchical, mutually exclusive taxonomy of what users want from a conversational system, grounded in real utterances and validated for coder agreement.
description: Intent taxonomy development treats the set of user goals a conversational system must handle as a qualitative coding problem. Researchers sample real utterances from transcripts, search logs or support tickets, code them inductively, and organise codes into a hierarchy of intent families and specific intents with written definitions, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and example utterances. The taxonomy is tested by independent coders for agreement (e.g. Cohen's kappa above 0.7), with confusable pairs refined or merged. Frequency counts show coverage and the long tail, guiding which intents to support. Grounding in dialogue act theory helps distinguish what users want from how they phrase it. Rigour comes from real data, reliability testing and periodic re-coding as usage evolves.
steps: Step 1: Collect 500+ real user utterances from existing channels (support transcripts, search logs, app store reviews).
Step 2: Open card sort of utterances — what does this user want to do?
Step 3: Cluster into intent categories.
Step 4: Test taxonomy completeness: for a new set of 100 utterances, can every one be classified into an existing intent?
Coverage < 80% = taxonomy is incomplete.
Step 5: Validate with users: show them the intent labels — do they recognize them as their goals?
outputs: An intent hierarchy with definitions and example utterances, coverage statistics, inter-rater agreement, confusion pairs and gaps for design.
useWhen: Designing or auditing chatbots, voice assistants and LLM agents; analysing support transcripts; prioritising which intents to support or route.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on a fixed taxonomy for open-ended LLM interactions without regular re-coding; avoid building from invented utterances rather than real data.
whyLost: Intent design is done by NLU engineers as a training-data task; the qualitative coding rigour that would make it a research method is absent.
whereToUse: Chatbot design, voice assistant development, LLM intent routing, search UX, customer service automation.
example: An insurer codes 3,000 chat logs, producing 42 intents in 8 families with kappa 0.81; 'is my claim stuck?' accounts for 19% of traffic but had no dedicated intent, so a status flow is built first.
sources: Chatbot Research and Design — (various)
reference: Traum DR & Larsson S (2003) The information state approach to dialogue management. In van Kuppevelt & Smith (Eds.) Current and New Directions in Discourse and Dialogue. Kluwer

name: Intention-to-Treat Analysis
origin: Austin Bradford Hill (1961) and Richard Peto et al. (1976); codified in CONSORT (1996 onward)
summary: Analyses all users in the arm they were randomised to, regardless of whether they actually experienced the treatment, preserving the benefits of randomisation.
description: In product experiments, not everyone assigned to a feature sees it: they never reach the page, the client fails to load, or they opt out. Analysing only those exposed (per-protocol or triggered analysis without care) breaks randomisation if exposure depends on user characteristics affected by treatment. ITT compares groups as randomised, estimating the effect of offering the treatment, which is unbiased though diluted. Triggered analysis is valid only when the trigger condition is identical and computed counterfactually in both arms. Complier average causal effects can then be recovered with IV methods. CONSORT-style flow diagrams make attrition visible.
steps: Record assignment for every randomised user and the point of assignment.
Define exposure precisely and log counterfactual triggers in control (would have seen the feature).
Analyse the primary outcome by assigned arm for all randomised users (ITT).
Run a triggered analysis only on counterfactually defined triggered users in both arms.
Estimate complier effects with IV (assignment as instrument) if needed.
Report a CONSORT-style flow diagram of assignment, exposure and attrition per arm.
outputs: ITT effect estimates, valid triggered or complier estimates, and a participant flow diagram.
useWhen: Any experiment where exposure or compliance is incomplete, including opt-in features and multi-step flows.
avoidWhen: Never wholly; but report triggered effects for interpretability when correctly constructed.
whyLost: Experimentation dashboards often filter to exposed users silently, and UX teams are unaware of the bias this introduces.
whereToUse: Feature experiments below the fold, onboarding variants, email-driven experiments, clinical and wellness apps.
example: A meditation app tests a new session player. Analysing only users who opened a session shows +12% completion, but ITT shows +2%, since the new player caused fewer weakly engaged users to open sessions at all.
sources: Hollis & Campbell, What is meant by intention to treat analysis? (1999), BMJ
Schulz, Altman & Moher, CONSORT 2010 Statement (2010), BMJ
Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020)

name: Intentional analysis
origin: Franz Brentano (1874) and Edmund Husserl's noesis and noema (Ideas, 1913); used in phenomenological psychology by Giorgi and others
summary: Analyses experiences as directed acts of consciousness, distinguishing how something is experienced (noesis) from what is experienced as meaningful (noema).
description: Phenomenology holds that consciousness is always consciousness of something: experiences are intentional, directed at objects. Husserl distinguished the noesis, the act of experiencing (perceiving, remembering, doubting, hoping), from the noema, the object as it is meant or experienced. Intentional analysis applies this to participants' accounts: for each experienced object, such as a claim form, a status screen or an approval message, it asks how the participant was relating to it (anticipating, fearing, checking, trusting) and what the object meant to them in that act. Two people looking at the same 'pending' screen may experience different noemata: a promise or a threat. For UX this exposes why identical interfaces produce different experiences. Rigour comes from systematically pairing acts and objects across meaning units and checking them against participants' language.
steps: Collect detailed first-person descriptions of a specific episode of use, using prompts that elicit what the participant was attending to and how, from 6 to 15 participants.
Divide each description into meaning units at shifts in meaning, and for each identify the object of attention.

For each object, characterise the noetic act (seeing, anticipating, doubting, remembering, evaluating) and the noematic sense (what the object meant as experienced, for example 'a verdict', 'a receipt').
Compare noetic-noematic pairs across participants for the same interface objects, noting where the same object is experienced in different modes.
Relate patterns to participants' situations and histories that shape their intentional stance.
Derive design implications for how objects should present themselves to support the intended mode of experience, and test with comprehension probes.
outputs: A table of meaning units with objects, noetic acts and noematic senses, cross-participant comparisons, and design implications for how interface objects are experienced.
useWhen: Identical designs produce divergent emotional responses; designing status, waiting and decision communications in high-stakes services.
avoidWhen: You need behavioural metrics or usability defects; use task-based testing. Not suitable without rich descriptive accounts.
whyLost: Its technical philosophical vocabulary keeps it in phenomenological psychology and nursing research, and UX has no equivalent vocabulary for the mode in which an interface object is experienced.
whereToUse: Insurance and benefits claims, medical results portals, loan decisions, job application tracking, AI explanations of decisions.
example: Participants experienced the 'Claim under review' status in two modes: some anticipated it as a receipt confirming progress, others doubted it as a verdict deferred. Adding an expected decision date and a list of checks completed shifted most accounts toward the receipt mode.
sources: Fundamentals of Qualitative Research
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 30 — Phenomenological Methods — The Structure of Lived Experience
reference: Husserl, E. (1913/1983). Ideas Pertaining to a Pure Phenomenology and to a Phenomenological Philosophy, First Book. Nijhoff; Giorgi, A. (2009). The Descriptive Phenomenological Method in Psychology. Duquesne University Press.

name: Interaction Entropy (Shannon)
origin: Claude Shannon, 1948
summary: Shannon entropy of each user's distribution of actions or categories, used as a measure of behavioural variety whose decline signals drift even when visit frequency holds steady.
description: Shannon entropy H = −Σ p log p measures the spread of a distribution; for a user's actions it is high when they use many features evenly and low when they repeat a few. Vivek Gopinath's drift playbook uses interaction entropy over the action distribution per user as the lead drift indicator, alongside category diversity per session, recommendation CTR and attention decay, because drift reduces variety even when frequency is constant. Illustrative values: entropy falling from 2.4 to 1.1 (generic) or 2.6 to 1.2 (e-commerce, 10,000 users over 3 months). Thresholds feed Bayesian updating (entropy < 1.5 for three sessions) and decision bars (entropy > 2.0 for 70% of active users within 4 weeks). The forward-thinking playbook also uses action entropy rising from 1.1 to 1.9 as a long-term validation signal.
steps: Define the action or category vocabulary from telemetry (user_id, session_id, ts, action, category).
Compute each user's action distribution per period.
Calculate H = −Σ p log p per user per period, normalising if comparing vocabularies of different size.
Track entropy longitudinally alongside frequency to separate narrowing from disengagement.
Set thresholds for intervention and decision bars (e.g. entropy < 1.5 triggers nudges; target > 2.0).
Pair low-entropy users with interviews or diaries to understand why.
outputs: Per-user entropy trajectories, drift thresholds and cohort comparisons.
useWhen: When frequency metrics look healthy but you suspect users are narrowing to shallow routines.
avoidWhen: When products are intentionally single-purpose; low entropy may mean efficient use rather than drift.
whyLost: Information-theoretic measures are rare in product analytics, which favour counts and rates.
whereToUse: E-commerce, OTT, super-apps, SaaS feature adoption, post-launch validation.
example: An e-commerce team sees entropy fall from 2.6 to 1.2 while logins hold; after re-onboarding with cross-category bundles, entropy rises from 1.2 to 2.4.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Shannon, C. E. (1948). A mathematical theory of communication. Bell System Technical Journal, 27(3), 379–423.

name: Interaction Ritual Theory Design Lens
aka: IR theory lens for social games
origin: Collins (2004); turned into design guidelines for colocated games by Xu and MacIntyre in Chapter 9
summary: Analysing existing social experiences through the ingredients of successful face-to-face interaction to derive design guidelines for colocated, social products.
description: Collins' interaction ritual theory holds that successful social interactions share four ingredients: bodily copresence, a barrier to outsiders (a sense of who is taking part), a mutual focus of attention, and a shared mood. When these are present, emotions are observed and amplified in a feedback loop, producing group solidarity and 'emotional energy' that makes people want to repeat the interaction. Chapter 9 uses the theory as a lens to analyse many genres of social games, from card and board games to rhythm and motion games, and derives guidelines for each ingredient. Examples include natural mapping of body movement to game state, rewarding players for reading each other's expressions, signalling who is in the circle of play, common objects that every player attends to, turn structures that make players the focus of attention, and game-generated moments everyone can laugh at together. A subset of the guidelines is then built into a prototype and tested with groups. The lens helps teams avoid the pitfall of assuming colocation makes an experience social, when people may simply play 'alone together'.
steps: Identify the social experience you want to support and gather examples of existing products and activities in that space.
Analyse each example against the four ingredients: copresence, boundary, mutual focus and shared mood.
Derive design guidelines for each ingredient from what works in the examples.
Select the guidelines most relevant to your context and turn them into concrete design choices.
Build a prototype and observe groups using it, coding behaviours against the ingredients.
Refine the guidelines based on which behaviours appeared.
outputs: A set of theory-grounded design guidelines and evidence on which ones produced the intended social behaviours.
useWhen: Designing products for groups who share a physical space, such as party games, tabletop and AR experiences, museum or classroom technology.
avoidWhen: Interaction is solitary or purely remote, or the team needs immediate evaluative data rather than design direction.
whyLost: Sociological theories are rarely taught in UX, and turning them into actionable guidelines takes time.
whereToUse: Colocated multiplayer games, AR and tabletop systems, shared displays, social features in physical venues.
example: Designing a phone-based AR party game, a team adds a shared virtual object in the middle of the table that everyone must watch, and audio cues that make all players react at the same moment, and then observes more cross-player talk and laughter.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Xu, Y. and MacIntyre, B. (2016). NerdHerder: designing colocated physical-digital games with sociological theories. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 9. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Intercept Survey
donor: Recreation, tourism and facility management research
origin: Long-standing visitor and user survey practice; Veal and Darcy describe it as the most common type of survey used by sport managers and set out sampling rules for it
summary: Questionnaire survey of people while they are using a site or service, with strict selection rules so the sample represents users rather than whoever is easiest to approach.
description: A site, user or visitor survey questions people at the place where they use a facility or service; when respondents are stopped as they enter or leave, or on their way, it is often called an intercept survey, and a cordon survey if all approaches are covered. Veal and Darcy describe it as managers' most common survey and give four uses: defining the catchment area, profiling users, collecting opinions, and, by comparing the user profile with census data, estimating who the non-users are. Interviewer completion is preferred to handing out forms, which gives low and self-selected response. Sampling must follow strict rules: when the interviewer is stationary and users move (ISUM), stop the next person through the gate as soon as the previous interview is finished; when users are stationary and the interviewer moves (USIM), follow a set route and approach every nth group. Because interview rates vary between quiet and busy periods, observed counts are used to weight the results. In UX the same discipline applies to in-product intercept surveys and in-store or event intercepts, where 'whoever answered' is not a sample of users.
steps: Define the population (all users of the site or service in a period) and what you need to learn about them.
Write a short questionnaire, about five minutes, covering origin, visit details, user profile and opinions.
Choose the selection mode: ISUM (stationary interviewer at entrances or exits, next person after each interview) or USIM (mobile interviewer on a fixed route, every nth group).
Schedule interviewing across days and times, and run parallel counts of users per period.
Train and supervise interviewers so they never choose respondents on any other basis.
Weight the results by the counts so busy and quiet periods are represented in proportion.
Analyse catchment, profile and opinion data, and compare the profile with population data to describe non-users.
outputs: A weighted user profile, catchment information, satisfaction and opinion data, and an estimate of under-represented groups.
useWhen: You need representative data about the people actually using a place, event or service, at the point of use.
avoidWhen: You need to reach non-users or lapsed users, or the interruption would harm the experience or safety at the site.
whyLost: It survives in UX as in-app and website intercept surveys, but the sampling rules and count-based weighting that make it representative are rarely applied.
whereToUse: Venues, events, stores, transport, museums and attractions, and in-product or website intercepts triggered during use.
example: At a marathon expo, interviewers at the two exits stop the next visitor after each completed interview, collecting 300 short interviews about the event app. Hourly gate counts show that the afternoon crowd was under-sampled, so afternoon responses are weighted up before satisfaction is reported.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge.

name: Interface Complexity Metrics
origin: Thomas McCabe, 1976 (cyclomatic complexity); adapted in HCI research from the 1990s
summary: Quantifies interface complexity with formal metrics, such as cyclomatic complexity of navigation, feature interaction counts and entropy, to compare and track complexity over time.
description: Software engineering measures code complexity with metrics such as McCabe's cyclomatic complexity, the number of independent paths through a program. Analogous metrics for interfaces count independent paths through a task flow, decision points per screen, states per component, feature interactions or information entropy. Visual complexity measures based on element counts, alignment and grouping have also been validated against perceived complexity. The method selects metrics appropriate to the question, computes them consistently across designs or releases, and validates them against user outcomes. Rigour comes from clear operational definitions, automated computation where possible so measurements are reproducible, and checking that metrics correlate with task time, errors or perceived complexity in your context, since complexity metrics without behavioural validation can mislead.
steps: Choose metrics suited to the question: path complexity of flows, decision points, component states, visual complexity or entropy.
Write operational definitions and, where possible, automate computation from design files, code or state models.
Compute metrics for the current design and for alternatives or past releases.
Validate selected metrics against user outcomes such as task time, errors or perceived complexity ratings.
Set thresholds or budgets for metrics that correlate with outcomes.
Track metrics over releases and flag increases for review.
outputs: Complexity metric definitions, scores per design and release, validation correlations, complexity budgets.
useWhen: Governing complexity in growing enterprise products and design systems, reviewing architecture, and evaluating AI-generated interfaces.
avoidWhen: One-off evaluations where usability testing will reveal problems more directly, or when metrics cannot be validated.
whyLost: Latent: Research-stage metrics; no standard tools or benchmarks in UX.
whereToUse: Design system complexity management; architecture review; AI-generated UI evaluation.
example: An ERP vendor computed decision points and independent paths for 120 workflows. Workflows above 15 independent paths had twice the error rate in support data, so the team set a path budget for new features.
sources: Handbook of the Philosophy of Science
A Complexity Measure (Thomas McCabe)
reference: McCabe, T. J. (1976). A complexity measure. IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, SE-2(4), 308-320.

name: Interface language predictability testing
origin: Draws on embodied simulation research (Bergen, 2012) and label testing practice in usability engineering
summary: Measures whether users can correctly predict what will happen when they act on a label or read a message, as a direct quantitative test of interface language.
description: Bergen's embodied simulation account suggests understanding language involves mentally simulating what it describes. If interface language is clear, users' simulations of an action's outcome should match what the system does. Predictability testing measures this directly: participants see a label, button or message in context and predict the outcome before acting, choosing from options or describing it freely. Prediction accuracy and confidence quantify clarity, and calibration (confidence versus accuracy) reveals dangerous confident errors. Unlike preference tests or comprehension questions, this targets the action-outcome link that matters for safety. Rigour comes from realistic context, randomised presentation, enough participants per label, and analysing errors by type.
steps: Select labels and messages linked to consequential or ambiguous outcomes.
Present each in realistic context to 15-30 participants (remote unmoderated is suitable) and ask for a predicted outcome and confidence (0-100%).
Code predictions as correct, partially correct or wrong, ideally with two coders.
Compute accuracy per label (target at least 80% for routine and 95% for irreversible actions) and identify confident errors (wrong with confidence above 70%).
Revise low-scoring labels and test alternatives side by side.
Add the test to content governance for new labels.
outputs: Prediction accuracy and confidence per label, a list of confident errors, and tested label alternatives.
useWhen: When naming actions with consequences, writing error and confirmation messages, or comparing label options.
avoidWhen: For exploratory vocabulary discovery; use interviews or card sorting first.
whyLost: Label testing exists in content design, but most teams test preference or comprehension rather than outcome prediction and calibration.
whereToUse: Fintech confirmations, healthcare actions, privacy settings, AI agent actions, and destructive operations.
example: For a surgical console's 'Release' button, only 46% of nurses correctly predict it disengages instruments; 30% confidently expect it to unlock the arm. Renaming to 'Disengage instruments' raises accuracy to 94%.
sources: Fodor, J., The Language of Thought (1975)
Coulson, S., Semantic Leaps (2001)
Bergen, B., Louder Than Words (2012)
Lakoff, G., Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things (1987)
Language of Thought (Fodor)
Semantic Leaps (Coulson)
Louder Than Words (Bergen)
Women Fire & Dangerous Things (Lakoff)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 17 — Mentalese, Compositionality & the Language of Thought
reference: Bergen, B. K. (2012). Louder Than Words: The New Science of How the Mind Makes Meaning. Basic Books.

name: Interpretive Description
origin: Sally Thorne, 1997 (with Kirkham and MacDonald-Emes); book 2008
summary: An applied qualitative approach that combines methodological flexibility with interpretive rigour, judging quality by whether findings are credible and useful for practice.
description: Interpretive Description (Sally Thorne) is a qualitative approach developed specifically for applied practice disciplines where research must be both epistemologically sound and practically useful. It occupies a middle ground: more structured than phenomenology, less theory-generating than Grounded Theory, less policy-oriented than Framework Analysis. It is appropriate when you want systematic interpretation of qualitative data in service of understanding that can be directly applied to practice — which describes most applied UX research.
steps: Establish the applied logic: Interpretive description begins with the recognition that the researcher has a substantive purpose. What will this research be used for? Who needs to understand what? Let this purpose guide analytic choices.
Data collection: Multiple data collection approaches are encouraged — different methods access different aspects of the phenomenon. Do not rely on a single method.

Analytic strategy: Read for patterns, themes, and exceptions. Build interpretations that are responsive to the data and useful to practitioners. Seek logic beyond frequency — what matters is not what most people said but what understanding is revealed.

Thematic development as applied insight: Each theme should represent a genuine insight — something that practitioners would not have known without the research, and that can change how they understand and act.

Credibility through pragmatic utility: The quality criterion for interpretive description is not theoretical elegance but practical usefulness. Does the interpretation help practitioners understand something they need to understand?
outputs: Interpretive themes framed as applied insights, explicit links to practice implications, an audit trail, and credibility evidence including practitioner review.
useWhen: Research must be practically actionable for a practice discipline such as clinicians, designers or product teams, and you want rigour without committing to a single philosophical tradition.
avoidWhen: You aim to build formal theory (use grounded theory) or describe the essence of experience (use phenomenology). For simple descriptive summaries, a lighter thematic approach suffices.
whyLost: It is well established in nursing but unknown in UX, even though its pragmatic, practice-oriented logic closely matches what applied UX research needs.
whereToUse: Health and care products, clinical decision support, applied product discovery, service design, and any research done for a practitioner audience.
example: Studying how community nurses use a scheduling tool, researchers combine interviews and shadowing, build themes around practical dilemmas such as 'protecting visit time', and check credibility with nurse managers before translating them into design guidance.
sources: Interpretive Description (Sally Thorne)
Developing Qualitative Methods — or Same Old Wine (PMC)
reference: Thorne, S. (2016). Interpretive Description: Qualitative Research for Applied Practice (2nd ed.). Routledge.

name: Interpretive Repertoires and Ideological Dilemmas
origin: Margaret Wetherell and Jonathan Potter, 1987 to 1992; Michael Billig et al., 1988
summary: Identifies the culturally shared repertoires of terms and metaphors people draw on, and the contradictions (ideological dilemmas) they navigate when talking about a topic.
description: Interpretive repertoires (Wetherell & Potter) are culturally shared building blocks of conversation — recurrently used systems of terms, metaphors, and figures of speech that construct a particular version of an object, person, or action. Ideological dilemmas (Billig) are the contradictions within common-sense ideology that force people to navigate between competing cultural commitments. Together, these concepts reveal how people draw on available cultural resources (repertoires) to manage social life, and how they navigate the contradictions between them. Applied to UX: they reveal the competing cultural frameworks available to users for making sense of technology — and the tensions between them.
steps: Identify interpretive repertoires: In your data, what recurrent systems of terms, metaphors, and phrases are used to construct versions of the phenomenon? Each repertoire is a coherent way of talking about something — and different repertoires construct it differently.
Map repertoire distribution: Who uses which repertoires? In what contexts? Repertoire use is not random — it is strategically deployed to accomplish interactional purposes.

Identify ideological dilemmas: Where do participants show inconsistency or tension between competing cultural commitments? ('I believe in privacy but I want personalisation.' 'I want simplicity but I need features.') These are ideological dilemmas.

Dilemma navigation analysis: How do participants navigate the tension? What rhetorical moves do they use to manage the contradiction? What does the navigation reveal about their priorities and values?

Application to design: Understanding the repertoires available to users for making sense of your product reveals what framings are available and which are absent — and which repertoire framings your product currently invokes.
outputs: A catalogue of interpretive repertoires, their distribution across speakers and contexts, documented ideological dilemmas, and design implications for framing and messaging.
useWhen: Users talk about a topic in contradictory ways, such as privacy versus convenience, AI as helper versus threat, or saving versus enjoying life, and you need to understand the cultural resources behind their talk.
avoidWhen: You need quick attitude measurement or task insight; use surveys or usability testing. For structured viewpoint segmentation, consider Q Methodology.
whyLost: It belongs to discursive psychology, which UX rarely meets, and its findings concern cultural framings rather than features.
whereToUse: Privacy and data products, AI adoption, sustainability and ethical consumption, personal finance messaging, and brand positioning.
example: Interviews on data sharing show users switch between a 'nothing to hide' repertoire and a 'they sell everything' repertoire. Consent copy that acknowledges both, offering benefit and control together, outperforms purely reassuring copy.
sources: Mapping the Language of Racism (Wetherell & Potter)
Ideological Dilemmas (Billig et al.)
Handbook of Discourse Analysis
reference: Billig, M., Condor, S., Edwards, D., Gane, M., Middleton, D. & Radley, A. (1988). Ideological Dilemmas. Sage.

name: Interrupted Time Series (ITS)
origin: Campbell and Stanley (1963); Wagner et al. (2002) segmented regression
summary: Models a long series of measurements before and after a change to estimate immediate level shifts and slope changes beyond the pre-existing trend.
description: Named in the treatise's borrowing matrix among epidemiology's key methods, ITS uses many time points before and after an intervention to estimate whether it changed the level and trend of an outcome, controlling for the pre-existing trend, seasonality and autocorrelation. It is one of the strongest quasi-experimental designs when no control group exists, and adding a comparison series makes it stronger. For UX, it evaluates releases, policy changes and outages with daily or weekly metrics such as support contacts, error rates or task completion. Typical requirements are at least 8-12 points per segment and attention to concurrent events that could explain changes.
steps: Define the intervention date and outcome series at consistent intervals.
Collect sufficient pre- and post-intervention points (ideally 12 or more each).
Fit segmented regression with terms for baseline trend, level change and slope change.
Model seasonality and autocorrelation (for example ARIMA errors).
Add a control series or outcome if available and check for co-interventions.
Report level and slope changes with CIs and visualise the counterfactual trend.
outputs: Level and slope change estimates, counterfactual plot, diagnostics.
useWhen: Evaluating whole-population changes (releases, regulations, pricing) with routinely collected metrics.
avoidWhen: Few data points or many simultaneous changes; consider DiD with a control group.
whyLost: Product analytics relies on simple before-after charts; time-series modelling sits with data science.
whereToUse: Support contact volumes, error rates, accessibility complaint trends, regulatory impact (consent, cancellation rules).
example: After a simplified cancellation flow, ITS on weekly complaints shows an immediate 30% level drop with no change in pre-existing slope, isolating the effect from a long-term decline.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Wagner AK et al. (2002) Segmented regression analysis of interrupted time series studies. J Clin Pharm Ther 27
Bernal JL, Cummins S & Gasparrini A (2017) Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions. Int J Epidemiol
Wagner et al., Segmented regression analysis of interrupted time series studies in medication use research (2002), Journal of Clinical Pharmacy and Therapeutics
Bernal, Cummins & Gasparrini, Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions: a tutorial (2017), International Journal of Epidemiology
Shadish, Cook & Campbell, Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs (2002)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
reference: Bernal JL, Cummins S & Gasparrini A (2017) Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions: a tutorial. International Journal of Epidemiology 46(1):348-355.

name: Interviews
origin: Qualitative research interviewing tradition, early 20th century onward
summary: One-to-one conversations that explore people's experiences, needs, behaviours and reasoning in depth, the core qualitative data collection method in UX.
description: Research interviews are guided conversations in which a researcher explores a participant's experiences, practices, needs, motivations and mental models. They can be structured, semi-structured or unstructured, with semi-structured interviews most common in UX: a guide sets topics while allowing the researcher to follow interesting threads. Interviews are most reliable when they ask about specific past behaviour rather than hypothetical futures or general opinions. Rigour comes from clear research questions, a guide built around concrete recent episodes, open and non-leading questions, active listening and follow-up probes, careful recruitment for variation, recording and transcription, and systematic analysis such as thematic analysis rather than memory-based summaries.
steps: Define research questions and the decisions the interviews will inform.
Recruit 6 to 15 participants per segment, aiming for variation in relevant characteristics.
Write a semi-structured guide focused on specific past episodes ('tell me about the last time...').
Pilot the guide and refine questions that lead or confuse.
Conduct 45 to 60 minute sessions, using open questions and probes such as 'what happened next?'.
Record and transcribe with consent, and write a summary note after each session.
Analyse systematically, for example with thematic analysis, and report themes with evidence.
outputs: Transcripts, session notes, themes with supporting quotes, and insights about needs, behaviours and motivations.
useWhen: For discovery and need-finding, understanding motivations and context, eliciting mental models, and follow-up after quantitative findings.
avoidWhen: Avoid for measuring prevalence or predicting behaviour from stated intentions; use surveys or analytics. For observing actual use, use contextual inquiry or usability testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Versatile and accessible; central to virtually every discovery phase.
whereToUse: Discovery research; need-finding; mental model elicitation; post-task debrief.
example: A neobank interviews 12 freelancers about the last time they set aside money for tax. Most use a separate account with ad hoc transfers, leading to an automated tax pot feature.
sources: The Science and Art of Interviewing
Qualitative Interviewing
Interviewing Users (Portigal)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Kvale, S. & Brinkmann, S. (2015). InterViews: Learning the Craft of Qualitative Research Interviewing (3rd ed.). Sage; Portigal, S. (2013). Interviewing Users. Rosenfeld Media.

name: Ishikawa (Fishbone) Diagram
origin: Kaoru Ishikawa, 1940s-1968 (Guide to Quality Control)
summary: Structures candidate causes of an effect under fixed category spines, ensuring a team considers people, process, tools, materials, environment and measurement.
description: The fishbone places the effect at the head and draws major cause categories as bones, traditionally the 6Ms: Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement and Mother Nature (environment). Teams brainstorm causes under each category, then sub-causes. The value is breadth: the fixed categories counter the tendency to blame the most salient cause, typically the user. In proper quality practice the diagram is only a hypothesis generator, followed by data collection (check sheets, Pareto analysis) to confirm which causes actually matter. UX versions often stop at the brainstorm. Adapted categories for digital products might be Users, Interface, Content, Data, Platform, Policy and Context.
steps: Write a specific, measurable effect statement at the head of the fish.
Choose 5-7 category bones suited to the product (e.g. users, interface, content, data, platform, policy, environment).
Brainstorm causes under each category with a cross-functional group, then add sub-causes by asking why.
Mark the causes for which evidence already exists and those that are hypotheses.
Collect data to test the top hypotheses using check sheets, log queries or targeted sessions, and draw a Pareto chart of confirmed causes.
Act on the vital few causes that account for most occurrences.
outputs: A categorised cause map, a hypothesis list, and a Pareto chart of verified causes.
useWhen: A team needs to broaden its thinking about causes of a known problem before investigating.
avoidWhen: When the causal structure involves interactions and feedback; use causal loop diagrams or fault trees. Never as a substitute for verification.
whyLost: Adopted as a whiteboard template without the Pareto and data-verification steps that made it a quality tool.
whereToUse: Churn spikes, support volume increases, quality defects in content or data, accessibility regressions.
example: An e-commerce team uses a fishbone for rising returns of apparel. Check sheets on 400 returns show that two causes under 'Content' (inconsistent size charts, misleading colour photography) explain 62% of returns.
sources: Ishikawa, Guide to Quality Control (1968; English 1976)
Tague, The Quality Toolbox (2nd ed., 2005)
reference: Ishikawa, K. (1976). Guide to Quality Control. Asian Productivity Organization.

name: Ising Attitude Network Model
origin: Causal attitude network model by Dalege et al. (2016), formalised as a random field Ising model with attention as inverse temperature (Dalege et al. 2018); fitted with IsingFit (Dalege et al. 2017).
summary: A model and analysis that treats an attitude as a network of binary feelings, beliefs and behaviours whose alignment depends on attention to the topic, fitted to survey data to reveal attitude structure and estimate its consistency.
description: In this model each node is an evaluative reaction toward an object (a belief such as 'is honest', a feeling such as 'angry', a behaviour such as 'eats meat'). Nodes influence each other through weighted links and have their own thresholds, and an external field such as a campaign can push all nodes. Attention or involvement works like inverse temperature: when people attend to the object, the network 'freezes' into a consistent positive or negative configuration and becomes hard to move (hysteresis); when attention is low, reactions are loosely connected and responsive to outside pressure but do not stick. Empirically, binary or dichotomised items are fitted with IsingFit, communities of items are detected (for example warmth and competence beliefs), and Gibbs entropy can quantify how consistent an attitude network is. A learning variant shows how repeated high attention strengthens links so that later consistency needs less attention. For UX and product research, the model gives a structured way to analyse attitudes to brands, features or technologies, to judge how settled they are, and to reason about why persuasion fails with highly involved users while low-involvement users are easily swayed but quickly revert.
steps: Write items for distinct beliefs, feelings and behaviours toward one attitude object, scored as binary or dichotomised.
Collect a large sample, ideally with a measure of involvement or attention to the topic.
Fit an Ising network with IsingFit and plot it, adding community detection to group related reactions.
Compare networks or connectivity between high- and low-involvement groups.
Estimate attitude consistency, for example with Gibbs entropy on small networks.
Use simulation of the model to reason about how involvement and messaging would change the attitude, and test those predictions.
outputs: An estimated attitude network with thresholds and item communities, connectivity and entropy comparisons between groups, and simulation-based predictions about persuadability.
useWhen: You are studying attitudes toward a product, brand or technology and need to understand their structure and stability, not only their average valence.
avoidWhen: Items are few or redundant, the sample is small, or the attitude object is not something people hold several distinct reactions toward.
whyLost: It comes from recent social psychology and statistical physics and has not been translated into product research practice, which relies on single attitude scores.
whereToUse: Attitudes to AI features, privacy and data sharing, sustainability behaviours, brand perception, health-behaviour apps.
example: Researchers survey 4,000 people about an electric-vehicle charging app using binary items on reliability, cost, environmental feelings and frustration. The network of highly involved drivers is dense and polarised while that of casual drivers is sparse, so the team targets casual drivers with simple reliability messaging and expects little movement among committed critics.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: ISO 9241-9 Device Assessment Questionnaire
origin: ISO (2000); used with Fitts' throughput testing by Young, Kehoe and Murphy in Chapter 7
summary: A standard post-task rating questionnaire for pointing and input devices, covering items such as smoothness, force, mental effort, accuracy, speed and overall evaluation.
description: ISO 9241-9 sets out how to evaluate non-keyboard input devices. Alongside performance testing with Fitts' throughput, it includes a comfort and usability questionnaire answered after each device is used. Items cover aspects such as the force required, smoothness of operation, mental effort, accuracy, speed of cursor movement and an overall evaluation, each on a bipolar rating scale. In Chapter 7 the questionnaire was given after a standard pointing task and again after 15 minutes of in-game play for each of four controllers (mouse, touchpad, Steam controller and DualShock 4), presented in counterbalanced order. Responses were treated as ordinal, compared with Kruskal-Wallis tests and shown as diverging stacked bar charts, and open-ended questions were added because earlier work suggested the standard items alone were not enough. The authors frame the battery as covering three linked concerns, functionality, usability and user experience (McNamara and Kirakowski), so that objective performance, ratings and comments are read together. The questionnaire is a ready-made, comparable way to capture how hardware feels to use.
steps: Select devices to compare and a counterbalanced order of use.
Have participants complete a standard task (for example multidirectional pointing) and, separately, a realistic in-context task with each device.
Administer the device assessment items after each device.
Add open-ended questions about what was good or bad about each device.
Analyse ratings as ordinal data with non-parametric tests and diverging stacked bar charts.
Read ratings alongside throughput, error data and comments to explain differences.
outputs: Per-device ratings of effort, smoothness, accuracy, speed, comfort and overall quality, with statistical comparisons and qualitative comments.
useWhen: Comparing controllers, mice, touchpads, styluses or other input hardware, or new input mappings in software.
avoidWhen: The interface does not involve a physical input device, or only overall satisfaction matters.
whyLost: Mostly used in input-device research; UX teams rarely evaluate hardware and often skip standardised device questionnaires.
whereToUse: Game controllers, peripherals, VR and AR controllers, automotive and medical input devices.
example: A group of players use four controllers in a shooter game; ratings show the Steam controller needs too little force for moving and aiming, while the mouse is rated smoothest and most accurate.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Young, G. W., Kehoe, A. and Murphy, D. (2016). Usability testing of video game controllers: a case study. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 7. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Isomorphism Check
aka: Mental model to system isomorphism mapping
origin: Adapted for UX from Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), chapters II and IV, where meaning arises when one structure maps onto another
summary: Lay the user's mental model and the system's real structure side by side and find exactly where the mapping between them breaks.
description: Hofstadter argues that symbols carry meaning only when there is an isomorphism, a part-for-part and rule-for-rule correspondence, between a formal system and something in the world. An interface works the same way: people act on a model of the system they carry in their heads, and things go wrong where that model and the real structure stop corresponding. An isomorphism check makes both structures explicit. You elicit the user's model (entities, relationships, the rules they believe apply) and draw the system's actual model (objects, states, rules) in the same notation, then pair the parts one by one. Elements with no partner, partners with the wrong relationship and rules that hold on one side but not the other are the places where users will form false beliefs, and they explain errors that look random in testing.
steps: Draw the system's model: the objects users deal with, how they relate, and the rules that change them, in plain words.
Elicit users' models through think-aloud, teach-back (ask them to explain the product to a new colleague) or a drawing task, with 5 to 8 people.
Redraw each user's model in the same notation as the system model.
Pair elements across the two models and mark each pair as matched, missing on one side, or mismatched in relationship or rule.
Check whether each mismatch predicts an error or confusion you have seen in testing, support tickets or analytics.
Decide per mismatch whether to change the system to fit the model, or change what the interface shows so the model can be corrected.
outputs: A side-by-side map of the user and system models with every broken correspondence marked and linked to the errors it causes.
useWhen: Users make errors that seem irrational, a product's underlying model is unusual (permissions, sync, versioning, billing), or before redesigning navigation built around internal structures.
avoidWhen: Simple linear flows with little hidden state, or when you only need to know whether a task succeeds rather than why.
whyLost: Mental model work in UX usually stops at describing what users believe. The stricter idea, that understanding depends on a structural correspondence you can check part by part, stayed in logic and cognitive science and was never turned into a routine audit.
whereToUse: Sharing and permissions models, sync and offline states, file and version systems, financial products with hidden rules.
example: Users believe a shared folder is a copy that belongs to them; the system treats it as a link to the owner's folder. The check shows 'delete' has no matching rule in the users' model, which explains why people delete shared work believing only their copy goes.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. Chapters II (Meaning and Form in Mathematics) and IV (Consistency, Completeness, and Geometry).

name: Item Response Theory
origin: Georg Rasch, 1960; Frederic Lord, 1950s to 1980
summary: Models the probability of item responses as a function of a latent trait and item properties, enabling precise scale calibration, item selection and adaptive questionnaires.
description: Item response theory models how a person's level on a latent trait, such as perceived usability, digital literacy or trust, and the properties of each item jointly determine response probabilities. Item parameters include difficulty (location) and discrimination, and polytomous models such as the graded response model handle Likert items. Unlike classical test theory, IRT gives item-level information, shows where on the trait each item measures precisely, supports equating across versions, and makes computerised adaptive testing possible. For UX scales, IRT can identify redundant items, create short forms that preserve precision and check that items function equally across groups through differential item functioning analysis. Rigour comes from adequate samples (often 300 or more), checking unidimensionality and local independence, model fit assessment and DIF testing.
steps: Define the latent trait and assemble a pool of candidate items.
Collect responses from a large, diverse sample, typically 300 or more.
Check unidimensionality (for example with factor analysis) and local independence.
Fit an appropriate model, such as Rasch, 2PL or graded response, and assess item and model fit.
Inspect item parameters and information curves to find redundant or poorly discriminating items.
Test for differential item functioning across key groups such as language or age.
Build short forms or adaptive versions and validate them against the full scale.
outputs: Item difficulty and discrimination parameters, test and item information curves, DIF results, short forms and adaptive questionnaires.
useWhen: For developing and refining UX questionnaires, short-form creation, cross-cultural or cross-group fairness checks and adaptive surveys.
avoidWhen: Avoid with small samples or when using established scales unchanged; classical reliability checks may suffice. Not needed for one-off descriptive surveys.
whyLost: Latent: Used in assessment; rarely applied in UX scale design despite offering advantages over classical test theory.
whereToUse: UX scale development; adaptive survey design; usability scale validation.
example: A government digital service develops a digital confidence scale for 2,000 citizens. IRT shows four items cluster at low difficulty and one item functions differently for older adults, producing a fair 8-item adaptive version.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience
Item Response Theory for Psychologists (Embretson & Reise)
reference: Embretson, S. E. & Reise, S. P. (2000). Item Response Theory for Psychologists. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Item Response Theory (IRT) / Rasch Model
origin: Georg Rasch (1960); Frederic Lord and Melvin Novick (1968)
