name: Latin Square and Williams Counterbalancing
origin: Ronald Fisher (1925-1935); Evan Williams (1949) for carryover-balanced designs
summary: Orders conditions in within-subjects studies so each appears equally often in each position, and with Williams designs, follows each other equally often.
description: In within-subject usability studies, order and carryover effects (practice, fatigue, learning) confound condition comparisons. A Latin square assigns condition orders so each condition appears once in each position across a set of participants. A Williams (balanced Latin square) design additionally ensures each condition immediately follows every other equally often, balancing first-order carryover; for an odd number of conditions, two squares are needed. Analysis should include order and participant as factors. Many UX studies 'randomise' with a handful of participants, which leaves imbalance; or they simply fix order. Proper counterbalancing is cheap rigour.
steps: List the conditions (designs, tasks) to be compared within subjects.
Generate a Williams design for the number of conditions (one square for even n, two for odd n).
Recruit participants in multiples of the number of sequences so the design is complete.
Assign participants to sequences at random.
Analyse with mixed models including condition, period and (optionally) carryover terms, with participant as random effect.
Report order effects and check whether any condition shows asymmetric transfer.
outputs: A balanced condition order plan, estimates free of first-order order effects, and period/carryover diagnostics.
useWhen: Within-subjects comparisons of designs or tasks in lab or remote studies.
avoidWhen: Strong asymmetric transfer (e.g. learning a concept that cannot be unlearned); use between-subjects designs.
whyLost: Small UX studies often fix order or use loose randomisation, and the statistical rationale was dropped from practitioner training.
whereToUse: Prototype comparisons, benchmark studies, accessibility comparisons, voice versus touch studies.
example: A study compares four checkout prototypes with 16 participants. Using a Williams design, analysis reveals a strong period effect (later checkouts faster) that would otherwise have favoured the last-presented design.
sources: Williams, Experimental designs balanced for the estimation of residual effects of treatments (1949), Australian Journal of Scientific Research
MacKenzie, Human-Computer Interaction: An Empirical Research Perspective (2013)

name: Layered Elaboration
origin: Walsh and colleagues (2010); adapted by Moffatt et al. for TableTalk Poker in Chapter 10
summary: A paper prototyping technique in which participants build and change an interface on stacked transparencies, each layer holding one element, so ideas can be added without destroying earlier ones.
description: Layered elaboration uses sheets of transparency laid over each other so that designs can be built and revised in layers. In the TableTalk Poker project, each layer held one salient interface element: the table, players, cards, prompts or chat. Water-soluble markers and sticky notes let participants move, add and remove buttons, text and screens on the fly. The team made three rough variants, briefed participants on the basics of the game, and then simulated play with sticky notes while participants carried out tasks such as joining a game, raising a bet, checking, calling, folding and chatting, thinking aloud as they went. Researchers watched for gaps in the interaction and noted desired layout changes. Because paper reduced attachment to any one design, participants mixed and matched elements across variants and reached a consensus design heavily shaped by their ideas. The team used younger adults without online gaming experience as proxies, because prototyping with older adults had proved difficult in earlier work, and then moved to iterative usability testing with older adults.
steps: Prepare a few rough design variants split into layers, one element per transparency.
Brief participants on the domain so they understand the tasks.
Ask participants to perform tasks on the layered prototype, simulating system responses with sticky notes, while thinking aloud.
Invite participants to move, redraw, add or remove elements on any layer.
Repeat across variants and discuss as a group to converge on a preferred design.
Photograph each state and carry the consensus design into higher-fidelity prototyping and testing.
outputs: A participant-shaped consensus design, photographed intermediate versions and notes on interaction gaps.
useWhen: Early co-design of screen layouts with non-designers, especially when you want them to build on each other's ideas.
avoidWhen: The design depends on motion, timing or rich interaction that paper cannot represent.
whyLost: Digital prototyping tools have displaced physical paper and transparency methods in most teams.
whereToUse: Game interfaces, apps for novice or older users, children's products, early concept work.
example: Three women new to online gaming rework a poker table interface on transparencies, moving the chat layer and simplifying prompts, and agree a design that combines the table layout of one variant with the prompts of another.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Moffatt, K., Shim, N., Birnholtz, J. and Baecker, R. M. (2016). Testing the usability, usefulness, and user experience of TableTalk Poker, a social game for seniors. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 10. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Layering and Separation
origin: Edward Tufte, 1990
summary: Organises dense information into visually distinct layers through colour, weight and value, so primary content stands forward and supporting context recedes.
description: Layering and separation is Tufte's principle that complex information becomes readable when it is organised into visually distinct strata. Using differences in colour, value, weight and saturation, primary data is placed on the top visual layer while grids, labels and contextual data recede into lighter, quieter layers. Tufte also warns of the '1+1=3' effect: two adjacent strong elements create a third, unintended visual element (the space between them) that adds noise. As a method, the analyst inventories what information a display contains, ranks it by task importance, assigns layers, and checks whether visual weight matches importance. Rigour comes from basing the ranking on task analysis and verifying the result with search or comprehension tasks.
steps: For any complex UX research visualization or interface design: identify information layers (primary data, secondary context, annotation, background structure).
Assign distinct visual properties to each layer: primary data = darkest/most saturated, secondary = lighter, annotation = smallest/most restrained, background = barely visible.
Test: can a viewer correctly identify the layer of any element in < 1 second?
outputs: A layered visual hierarchy specification, reduced visual noise, interface or chart redesigns with distinct primary, secondary and background layers.
useWhen: Dense interfaces and displays: dashboards, maps, clinical and trading screens, data-heavy reports, where everything currently competes for attention.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a purely aesthetic exercise without checking with users which information is primary; for task priority questions, do task analysis first.
whyLost: Visual hierarchy is taught as a design rule of thumb; Tufte's analytic method of designing and evaluating layers, including '1+1=3' effects, is rarely applied.
whereToUse: Dashboard design, complex data visualization, research report design, information architecture visual hierarchy.
example: A trading platform redesigns its order book by pushing gridlines and historical data into light grey and keeping live bids in high-contrast type; traders locate the best bid 30% faster in testing.
sources: Envisioning Information — Edward Tufte
reference: Tufte ER (1990) Envisioning Information. Graphics Press

name: Leave-one-out cross-validation
origin: Peter Lachenbruch & M. Ray Mickey, 1968; Mervyn Stone, 1974
summary: Estimates how well a model generalises by training on all but one case and testing on the excluded case, repeated for every case.
description: Evaluating a classifier or model on the data used to fit it overstates performance. LOO-CV fits the model n times, each time leaving one observation out and predicting it, then aggregates prediction errors. It uses nearly all data for training each time, which suits small UX datasets such as 50-300 labelled sessions or participants. Its estimates have low bias but can have high variance, and for large datasets 5- or 10-fold cross-validation is more efficient. Rigour requires that all preprocessing and feature selection occur inside each fold to avoid leakage, and that when participants contribute multiple observations, all of a participant's data are left out together (leave-one-subject-out).
steps: Define the performance metric (accuracy, AUC, RMSE) and decide the unit to leave out (observation or participant).
For each unit, fit the full pipeline (scaling, feature selection, model) on the remaining data.
Predict the held-out unit and record the prediction.
Aggregate predictions to compute performance metrics and a confusion matrix.
Compare against a baseline (e.g. majority class or mean prediction) and against k-fold results for stability.
outputs: An approximately unbiased estimate of out-of-sample performance with per-case predictions for error analysis.
useWhen: Small samples where holding out a separate test set would waste data, such as classifier validation on a few hundred labelled sessions.
avoidWhen: Avoid for large datasets (use k-fold), for time-ordered data (use forward-chaining validation) or when observations from the same user would leak across folds.
whyLost: It is standard in statistics and ML but rarely used in UX, where models are seldom built or validated by researchers.
whereToUse: Validating small-sample classifiers of user states, predictive models from usability studies, and PLS or LDA models.
example: With 240 labelled sessions from 60 participants, the team uses leave-one-subject-out validation, which reveals that accuracy falls from 91% (observation-level LOO) to 84% once participant-level leakage is removed.

name: Levels of Automation Analysis
origin: Thomas Sheridan and William Verplank, 1978; Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens, 2000
summary: Rates automation at each information-processing stage (acquisition, analysis, decision, action) on a 10-point scale to evaluate workload, trust and out-of-the-loop risk.
description: Sheridan and Verplank's ten-level scale runs from the computer offering no assistance to the computer acting entirely autonomously and ignoring the human. Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens added four stages: information acquisition, information analysis, decision selection and action implementation, each of which can be automated to a different level. The analysis profiles a system as a vector of levels and evaluates primary consequences (workload, situation awareness, complacency, skill degradation) and secondary ones (reliability, cost of errors). It gives designers a precise vocabulary instead of 'AI-powered', and predicts known pathologies: high automation at decision stages with imperfect reliability produces automation bias.
steps: Decompose the feature into the four stages: acquisition, analysis, decision, action.
Assign the current and proposed level of automation (1-10) for each stage.
Estimate automation reliability at each stage from model evaluations or logs.
Evaluate human performance consequences: workload, situation awareness, complacency and skill loss; flag high decision automation with reliability below roughly 0.9.
Prototype alternative profiles and test with users using detection of automation errors as a key measure.
Choose the profile that balances efficiency with error detection, and document override and transparency mechanisms.
outputs: An automation profile per feature, predicted risks, and empirical comparison of profiles.
useWhen: Deciding how much an AI feature should suggest, decide or act, and how to expose it.
avoidWhen: Features without automated decision or action components.
whyLost: Known from human factors textbooks, but product teams discuss automation as a binary capability. It is rarely operationalised in AI product reviews.
whereToUse: AI agents, autocomplete and autocorrect, fraud decisions, clinical alerts, autonomous driving interfaces.
example: An expense tool's AI categoriser is set at level 7 for action (executes then informs). Testing shows users catch only 30% of miscategorisations, so it moves to level 5 (executes if the user approves) for amounts above a threshold.
sources: Sheridan & Verplank, Human and computer control of undersea teleoperators (1978), MIT
Parasuraman, Sheridan & Wickens, A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation (2000), IEEE Transactions on SMC-A
reference: Parasuraman, R., Sheridan, T. B., & Wickens, C. D. (2000). A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation. IEEE Trans. SMC Part A, 30(3), 286-297.

name: Levels-of-Description Analysis
origin: Adapted for UX from Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), the 'Ant Fugue' dialogue and chapter X (Levels of Description, and Computer Systems)
summary: Describe the same behaviour at several levels, from clicks to tasks to goals to the organisation, and look for patterns that only appear at one level.
description: In the Ant Fugue, Aunt Hillary is an ant colony that holds conversations although no single ant knows anything; the meaning exists only at the level of the whole colony. Hofstadter's point is that a system can be described at several levels, each with its own regularities, and that explanations often fail because they look at the wrong level. UX data is usually analysed at one level: click paths, or tasks, or goals. This method writes up the same set of observations at four or five levels in parallel and compares them. Problems that look like noise at the click level can be obvious at the goal level, such as people repeating a task because their real goal spans several sessions, and organisational patterns can explain individual behaviour that interviews treat as personal preference.
steps: Pick a behaviour to explain and gather the data you have on it: logs, observation, interviews.
Define the levels you will use, for example action (clicks and keystrokes), task, goal, role or team, and organisation or market.
Describe the behaviour at each level separately, using only evidence that belongs to that level.
Note the regularities that appear at each level and check whether they are visible from the levels above and below.
Mark patterns that appear at one level only; these are usually where explanations have been going wrong.
Write the explanation at the level where the pattern lives, and design the intervention for that level.
outputs: A level-by-level description of one behaviour, with the patterns each level reveals and a statement of which level an intervention should target.
useWhen: Quantitative and qualitative findings seem to contradict each other, fixes at the interface level have not changed outcomes, or behaviour emerges from groups rather than individuals.
avoidWhen: Simple usability defects with an obvious local cause, or when you have data at only one level.
whyLost: Levels of description are standard in cognitive science and systems thinking but UX teams split work by data type instead: analysts own clicks, researchers own goals. Nobody owns the comparison across levels.
whereToUse: Collaboration tools, enterprise software, marketplaces, any product where team or market behaviour shapes individual use.
example: Click data shows people abandoning an expense form; at the goal level they are collecting receipts across a week; at the team level, managers approve on Fridays. The fix is a saved-draft weekly report, not a shorter form.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. Dialogue ...Ant Fugue, and Chapter X (Levels of Description, and Computer Systems).

name: Leverage Points Analysis (Meadows)
aka: Places to intervene in a system
origin: Donella Meadows, 1997-1999 (Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System)
summary: Ranks possible interventions in a system from weak (parameters, numbers) to strong (feedback structure, rules, goals, paradigms) to find where change is most effective.
description: Meadows listed twelve places to intervene, in increasing order of effectiveness: constants and parameters; buffer sizes; stock-and-flow structure; delays; balancing feedback loops; reinforcing feedback loops; information flows; rules; power to self-organise; goals; paradigms; and the power to transcend paradigms. Most organisational effort goes to the weakest points (tweaking numbers), while the strongest are hardest and most resisted. Applied after mapping a system (e.g. with causal loop diagrams), the list classifies candidate interventions and challenges teams to consider structural ones such as changing information flows (who sees what) or goals (what metric the product optimises).
steps: Map the system with causal loops or stocks and flows, based on research.
List candidate interventions from the team and stakeholders.
Classify each intervention by Meadows' leverage level.
Generate additional interventions at higher leverage levels (information flows, rules, goals).
Assess feasibility, risks and resistance for each.
Prioritise a portfolio including at least one higher-leverage intervention, with monitoring.
outputs: A leverage-classified intervention list, new structural options and a prioritised portfolio.
useWhen: Systemic problems (wellbeing, misinformation, marketplace fairness) where parameter tweaks have failed.
avoidWhen: Contained usability problems with clear local fixes.
whyLost: It is cited in sustainability and systems thinking circles; UX treats it as an inspirational essay rather than an analytic step.
whereToUse: Digital wellbeing, platform governance, sustainability features, healthcare services, AI alignment of product goals.
example: A social app tried to reduce compulsive use with time limits (a parameter). Leverage analysis leads to changing information flows (showing users their weekly regret ratings) and the goal metric (from time spent to satisfied sessions).
sources: Meadows, Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999), Sustainability Institute
Meadows, Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008)
Abson et al., Leverage points for sustainability transformation (2017), Ambio
reference: Meadows, D. H. (1999). Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System. The Sustainability Institute.

name: Life-History Interviewing
origin: Chicago School, 1920s; Schütze, 1977; Blee & Taylor, 2002
summary: Invites participants to narrate their life or a long-term domain history in their own order, revealing how past experiences shape current behaviour and meaning.
description: Life-history or biographical narrative interviewing asks participants to tell the story of their life, or of their relationship with a domain such as money, illness, or work tools, in their own order and words. The interviewer begins with a single open narrative prompt and avoids interrupting, then follows up on the narrative's own themes and turning points before asking any external questions. Because people organise experience as narrative, this reveals how past events, identities and relationships explain present choices and resistance, which topic-driven interviews miss. Analysis reconstructs timelines, turning points and biographical patterns across participants. Rigour comes from minimal steering during the main narrative, careful transcription and ethical attention to sensitive disclosures.
steps: Life-history interview protocol for technology use:
Start: 'Tell me about the first time you remember using [product or product category].'
Follow the timeline: 'And then what happened with your use of it?'
Probe critical moments: 'When did your relationship with it change significantly?'
Present: 'How does your past experience affect how you use it now?'
Analyze: map critical moments on a timeline; identify what events shifted the relationship; connect to current behavior patterns.
outputs: Narrative transcripts, timelines of turning points, identified biographical patterns and their links to current product use and needs.
useWhen: Understanding long-term relationships with money, health, work or technology, and why people persist with or resist certain tools.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need specific feedback on a design or when time is short; avoid for topics participants find traumatic without proper safeguards.
whyLost: Life-history work lives in sociology and oral history; UX interviews are short and topic-driven, leaving no room for biographical narrative.
whereToUse: Longitudinal product research, migration UX research, professional tool adoption research, any product with a history.
example: A health worker refuses to abandon a paper form; a life-history interview reveals it was a lifeline during a past system outage, explaining her distrust and leading to an offline-first design.

name: Likert Scale Design
origin: Rensis Likert, 1932
summary: Constructs multi-item summated attitude scales from agreement statements, with item analysis and reliability checks, to measure an attitude more validly than single questions.
description: Likert's original method was not a single agree-disagree question but a procedure for building a scale: write many statements about an attitude object, administer them, keep items that correlate well with the total, and sum responses into a score. Most UX surveys keep the response format and discard the procedure, using single Likert-type items and treating them as interval data. The rigorous approach defines the construct, writes balanced items, pilots them, runs item analysis (item-total correlations, Cronbach's alpha above about 0.7, ideally factor analysis), and analyses summed scales rather than individual items. Response format decisions, such as 5 versus 7 points, labelled anchors and a midpoint, should be deliberate. Single items should be analysed as ordinal, using medians and non-parametric tests or top-box proportions.
steps: Define the construct to measure and write 10-20 candidate statements covering it, mixing positive and negative wording carefully.
Choose a response format (typically 5 or 7 points with fully labelled anchors).
Pilot with 50-100 respondents representative of the target population.
Run item analysis: drop items with item-total correlations below about 0.3 and check Cronbach's alpha of 0.7 or above.
Check dimensionality with exploratory factor analysis if the construct may have facets.
Field the final scale and analyse summed scores; analyse single items as ordinal data.
outputs: Validated multi-item attitude scale, reliability statistics, scoring instructions, scale scores for respondents.
useWhen: Measuring attitudes and perceptions such as trust, satisfaction or perceived value where no validated scale exists.
avoidWhen: When a validated instrument already exists (SUS, UEQ, UMUX-Lite), or when you need behaviour rather than attitudes; use analytics or observation.
whyLost: The response format survived and became ubiquitous, but the scale-construction procedure (item analysis, summation, reliability) was largely dropped, leaving single items analysed as if they were interval measures.
whereToUse: Any attitudinal survey; satisfaction measurement; scale construction.
example: An AI writing assistant team needed to measure trust. They drafted 16 items, piloted with 120 users, removed 6 weak items and achieved alpha of 0.88 on a two-factor scale that then tracked trust across model releases.

name: LIME for local explanation
origin: Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Sameer Singh & Carlos Guestrin, 2016
summary: Explains an individual AI prediction by fitting a simple interpretable model to the black-box model's behaviour around that specific case.
description: LIME perturbs the input around a case of interest, records how the model's predictions change, and fits a sparse linear model weighted by proximity, yielding the features that most influenced that prediction locally. It is model-agnostic and works for tabular data, text (which words drove a classification) and images. For UX research, LIME helps audit specific decisions users complain about and prototype explanation content. Its limits are well documented: explanations can be unstable across runs, depend on perturbation and kernel width choices, and can be manipulated. Rigour requires repeated runs to check stability, comparison with SHAP, and validation that explanations help real users.
steps: Select cases to explain, prioritising complaints, edge cases and high-stakes decisions.
Configure LIME with an appropriate perturbation strategy and kernel width for the data type.
Generate explanations limited to 5-10 features for readability.
Rerun each explanation 10 or more times with different seeds and check that the top features are stable.
Compare with SHAP attributions and flag disagreements.
Use stable explanations to audit decisions and draft user-facing explanation prototypes for testing.
outputs: Local explanations for selected predictions, stability assessments and candidate explanation content for users.
useWhen: Investigating specific AI decisions, especially for text classifiers or opaque models, and prototyping case-level explanations.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on single LIME runs, using it for global model understanding (use SHAP or global surrogates), or presenting it as ground truth to regulators.
whyLost: LIME is well known in ML research and responsible AI, but stays with data scientists rather than UX researchers.
whereToUse: Content moderation decisions, loan or investment recommendations, support ticket routing, AI-driven health triage.
example: Users complain that an investment app labelled their portfolio 'aggressive'. LIME on 20 such cases repeatedly highlights a single crypto holding as the driver, prompting both a model review and clearer explanation copy.

name: Lincoln and Guba Trustworthiness Criteria
origin: Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba, 1985 (Naturalistic Inquiry)
summary: Replaces positivist validity and reliability with credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability, each secured by specific techniques such as member checking and audit trails.
description: Lincoln and Guba argued that qualitative research should not be judged by quantitative criteria but has its own parallel standards. Credibility (parallel to internal validity) is supported by prolonged engagement, triangulation, peer debriefing, negative case analysis and member checking. Transferability (external validity) is supported by thick description that lets readers judge applicability to their context. Dependability (reliability) and confirmability (objectivity) are supported by an audit trail documenting raw data, analytic decisions and reflexive notes, which an external auditor could follow. The framework turns 'qualitative is subjective' into a set of checkable practices. Its rigour comes from planning these techniques into the design rather than asserting trustworthiness afterwards.
steps: Plan trustworthiness techniques at the design stage, mapping each of the four criteria to at least one concrete technique and recording the plan in the research protocol.
Secure credibility through triangulation of sources or methods, peer debriefing with a researcher outside the project, and member checking of key interpretations with a subset of participants.
Search actively for negative cases and revise interpretations until they account for disconfirming evidence or the exceptions are explicitly explained.
Write thick description of participants, setting and context so readers can judge transferability to their own product or population.
Maintain an audit trail of raw data, codebooks, memos, decision logs and reflexive notes throughout the study, not reconstructed afterwards.
Report which techniques were used for each criterion, what they changed, and remaining limitations, in a dedicated methods or trustworthiness section.
outputs: A trustworthiness plan, triangulation and member-checking records, negative case notes, thick description, an audit trail, and a trustworthiness section in the report.
useWhen: Qualitative findings will drive significant decisions, will be challenged by quantitative stakeholders, or must be defensible in regulated, academic or high-stakes contexts.
avoidWhen: Never ignore the principles, but for small tactical studies apply a lightweight version (triangulation, negative cases, decision log). For quantitative measurement validity, use psychometric validation instead.
whyLost: Not taught in UX bootcamps; qual seen as inherently subjective
whereToUse: Healthcare and public sector research, foundational discovery studies, research repositories, research operations quality standards, and any study presented to sceptical executives.
example: A team studying rural health workers' distrust of a reporting app triangulates interviews with usage logs, member-checks the 'surveillance' interpretation with 5 workers, and keeps an audit trail. When challenged by leadership, the documented process makes the findings defensible.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba)
The Inquiry Series, Vol II, Ch 27
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

name: Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classification
aka: LDA for supervised classification of session data
Linear Discriminant Analysis for Behavioural Classification
origin: R.A. Fisher, 1936
summary: Finds the linear combinations of behavioural metrics that best separate known user groups, classifying new users and showing which variables discriminate most.
description: Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) finds the linear combinations of predictor variables that maximise the ratio of between-group to within-group variance for a set of known groups. Applied to UX, the predictors are behavioural metrics (feature use, session frequency, error counts, time on task) and the groups are meaningful labels such as retained versus churned or novice versus expert. LDA both classifies new users and, through its standardised coefficients, explains which behaviours most strongly separate groups, which makes it more interpretable than black-box classifiers. Rigour comes from checking assumptions (approximate multivariate normality, homogeneity of covariance via Box's M), using cross-validated rather than resubstitution accuracy, and reporting chance-corrected performance against base rates.
steps: Label a subset of sessions with behavioral categories (ground truth from qualitative analysis or screen recording review).
Extract behavioral features for all sessions.
Fit LDA: find the discriminant function that maximally separates labeled classes.
Validate: leave-one-out cross-validation accuracy.
Extract discriminant loadings: which features most separate the classes?
High-loading features = the behavioral markers most diagnostic of the classification.
outputs: Discriminant functions with standardised coefficients, classification accuracy and confusion matrix, group centroids plotted in discriminant space.
useWhen: You have labelled groups (churned vs retained, expert vs novice, converters vs not) and want to know which behaviours distinguish them and to classify new users interpretably.
avoidWhen: Avoid when groups are unknown (use clustering), when assumptions of multivariate normality and equal covariance are badly violated (use logistic regression or random forests), or with very few cases per group.
whyLost: UX quantitative training stops at t-tests and regression; classical multivariate methods were superseded in data science by ML classifiers, leaving no one to bring LDA to UX.
whereToUse: Behavioral session classification at scale, identifying frustrated users in real time, expert-novice classification from interaction logs.
example: A SaaS analytics team labels 3,000 accounts as power users or strugglers; LDA shows that use of saved filters and keyboard shortcuts carries the largest discriminant weights, guiding onboarding priorities.

name: Linguistic Relativity Analysis
origin: Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, 1920s-1940s; modern experimental work by Boroditsky and others
summary: Investigates how the vocabulary and grammatical categories of a product or a user's language shape how users conceptualise and perform tasks.
description: The linguistic relativity hypothesis, in its modern weak form, holds that language influences habitual thought: the categories a language marks make some distinctions more salient. Experimental work on colour, spatial frames of reference and time supports measurable, if modest, effects. For products, two forms matter. First, product vocabulary itself is a small language: terms like 'archive', 'workspace' or 'project' impose categories that shape users' mental models. Second, users' native languages may carry distinctions that localisation flattens or invents. The method combines vocabulary analysis with elicitation (free listing, sorting) and comparative tasks across language groups. Rigour comes from comparing groups that differ in language but match on other factors, and from testing whether vocabulary choices change task performance, not just preference.
steps: Inventory the product's core vocabulary and the conceptual categories each term implies.
Run free-listing and sorting exercises with users to elicit their own terms and categories.
For localised products, compare categories across language groups with matched participants (e.g. 10-15 per language).
Design term variants that imply different conceptual models.
Test variants with task-based measures (success, errors, predictions of system behaviour), not just preference.
Adopt vocabulary that aligns with users' categories and document locale-specific choices.
outputs: Product vocabulary map, user category elicitations, cross-language comparison, vocabulary recommendations with performance evidence.
useWhen: Naming core product concepts, localisation for markets with different linguistic categories, and conversational interfaces.
avoidWhen: Minor copy changes; standard content testing is lighter.
whyLost: Latent: Research basis for content design and localization; rarely invoked explicitly.
whereToUse: International product design; vocabulary design; conversational UI.
example: A project management tool localised 'board' and 'backlog' into Japanese with literal terms. Sorting tasks showed users grouped work differently, so the team adopted locally used terms and saw onboarding task success rise.
sources: The Development of Language

name: Link Analysis
origin: Chapanis and colleagues, 1940s-1959
summary: Maps frequency and importance of transitions between interface elements to arrange them so that common sequences need minimal movement and switching.
description: Link analysis records the links between elements of a system (eye movements between displays, hand movements between controls, navigation between screens or menu items) and weights them by frequency and importance. A link diagram or matrix is then used to rearrange elements so that strongly linked pairs are adjacent, sequences flow in a consistent direction and important links are short. The treatise notes its obvious application to navigation design, dashboard layout and the organisation of frequently accessed controls, yet it has been replaced by intuitive information architecture without empirical grounding. Modern analytics make it easier than ever: clickstream transition matrices provide link frequencies automatically. The priority index rates its recovery feasibility at five stars.
steps: Define the elements (screens, panels, controls, menu items) and the users and tasks of interest.
Collect link data from observation, eye tracking or clickstream logs across representative sessions.
Build a link matrix of frequencies, weighted by importance or criticality where relevant.
Draw the link diagram and identify long, crossing or high-weight links.
Rearrange layout or navigation to shorten high-weight links and reduce crossings.
Re-measure link lengths or transition costs on the revised design.
outputs: Link frequency/importance matrix, link diagram, optimised layout with quantified distance reduction.
useWhen: Dashboard and control-panel layout, navigation restructuring, toolbars and command placement.
avoidWhen: Early discovery where tasks are unknown; use contextual inquiry first. Not suitable for content comprehension problems.
whyLost: Developed for physical cockpits and panels and never translated into digital IA practice, which favoured card sorting and intuition.
whereToUse: Analytics dashboards, IDEs, clinical systems, game HUDs, mobile tab bar design, warehouse layouts in AR.
example: A logistics dashboard's clickstream shows 62% of transitions run between the map and the exceptions list, which sit on opposite sides of two tabs. Placing them side by side cuts mean task time by 19%.

name: List Experiment (Item Count Technique)
origin: Judith Droitcour Miller (1984); statistical methods by Graeme Blair and Kosuke Imai (2012)
summary: Control respondents count how many of several neutral items apply to them; treatment respondents get the same list plus a sensitive item; the difference estimates prevalence.
description: In a list experiment, respondents report only how many items on a list apply, never which. The treatment list includes the sensitive item; the difference in mean counts between groups estimates its prevalence. Because individual answers are hidden, social desirability bias is reduced. Design rules include choosing control items to avoid floor and ceiling effects (including negatively correlated items), and testing the 'no design effect' assumption. Multivariate methods (list package) allow regression on covariates. Unlike randomised response, there is no device to explain, which helps online.
steps: Choose 3-4 control items, mixing high and low prevalence and negatively correlated items to avoid ceiling effects.
Randomly assign respondents to control or treatment (control list plus sensitive item).
Ask only for the count of items that apply.
Estimate prevalence as the difference in mean counts with standard errors.
Test design effects and floor or ceiling issues; use multivariate list models for covariates.
Compare with direct questions in a separate group to estimate social desirability bias.
outputs: Prevalence estimates for the sensitive item, covariate associations and bias estimates.
useWhen: Sensitive attitudes or behaviours online where randomised response is hard to explain.
avoidWhen: Small samples, since list experiments are statistically inefficient.
whyLost: It is known in political science but rarely in product or UX survey design.
whereToUse: Shadow AI use at work, discriminatory attitudes in hiring platforms, workarounds that break policy, dishonest reviews.
example: An enterprise AI vendor estimates how many employees paste confidential data into public chatbots. Direct questions give 9%; a list experiment gives 27%, supporting investment in a sanctioned tool.
sources: Blair & Imai, Statistical analysis of list experiments (2012), Political Analysis

name: Listening to Think vs. Listening to React
origin: Indi Young, 2015
summary: A listening discipline in which interviewers suspend their own reactions, solutions and judgements to follow and understand the participant's reasoning.
description: Indi Young distinguishes listening to react, where the listener is formulating a reply, solution, judgement or relevant anecdote, from listening to understand the other person's thinking. In research interviews, reacting introduces bias: interviewers lead, fill silences, or steer towards the product, and participants adapt their answers. Listening to think means noticing one's reactions, setting them aside, and responding with reflections and requests for depth ('what went through your mind then?'). It is practised by reviewing recordings to find moments of reacting and by deliberate practice. Rigour comes from making these behaviours observable: transcripts can be audited for leading turns, interviewer talk ratio and missed opportunities to probe the participant's reasoning.
steps: Listening practice protocol:
Before sessions: write down 3 things you expect to hear. Set these aside.
(2) During session: 0-second rule — do not speak for the first 0 seconds after a participant finishes (wait for them to continue).
(3) When you do speak: reflect, don't evaluate ('So you felt frustrated when...', never 'That must have been frustrating').
(4) After session: compare what you heard against your pre-session expectations. Surprises are the most valuable data.
outputs: Interviews with richer reasoning and fewer leading questions, self-review notes on reacting moments, and improved interviewer practice over time.
useWhen: Training interviewers, discovery interviews about how people think, and any research where the interviewer's reactions could distort what participants say.
avoidWhen: Not a standalone method; avoid treating it as a substitute for interview design. In evaluative testing, structured protocols matter more.
whyLost: Interview skill is taught as question lists; the internal discipline of listening is rarely articulated or practised deliberately.
whereToUse: Qualitative interview training, empathy research, any interview situation where researcher bias affects data quality.
example: Reviewing a recording, a researcher spots that she jumped to suggest a feature when a farmer mentioned late payments; in later sessions she reflects back instead, uncovering how payment delays affect credit with seed suppliers.
sources: Practical Empathy — Indi Young
reference: Young I (2015) Practical Empathy: For Collaboration and Creativity in Your Work. Rosenfeld Media

name: LLMs as qualitative analysis tools and their limits
origin: Emerging practice from 2022 onward following large language models (e.g. GPT-3, Brown et al., 2020)
summary: Uses large language models to assist coding, summarising and theme development in qualitative data, with explicit validation against human coding and safeguards against fabrication.
description: LLMs can apply codebooks to thousands of excerpts, propose candidate themes, summarise transcripts and retrieve quotes, making scale analysis possible. Their limits are equally important: hallucinated or misattributed quotes, flattening of minority and contradictory views, sensitivity to prompt wording, bias toward plausible-sounding generic themes, and opaque reasoning. Rigorous use treats the LLM as a coder whose reliability must be measured against humans, keeps humans responsible for interpretation, verifies every quote against the source, logs prompts and model versions, and handles data under privacy and consent constraints. Deductive coding with a clear codebook is the most reliable use; inductive theme generation needs the most scrutiny.
steps: Confirm consent and data governance permit processing transcripts with the chosen model, and redact personal data.
Develop a codebook through human analysis of a subset of the data first.
Prompt the LLM to apply the codebook with justifications and verbatim excerpts, fixing model version and temperature (e.g. 0).
Compare LLM codes with human codes on at least 100-200 excerpts and compute Cohen's kappa; require 0.7 or above per code before relying on it.
Verify every quoted excerpt programmatically against source text to catch fabrication.
Use LLM-proposed themes as prompts for human interpretation, explicitly searching for disconfirming and minority cases.
Document prompts, versions, agreement statistics and human decisions in the analysis audit trail.
outputs: LLM-assisted codes or themes with measured agreement against humans, verified quotes, an audit trail and a stated scope of trustworthy use.
useWhen: Large qualitative datasets, deductive coding with a stable codebook, quote retrieval and first-pass summarisation where humans review the results.
avoidWhen: Avoid when data cannot leave secure environments, for small studies where full human analysis is feasible, or for interpretive work on sensitive or marginal experiences without deep human engagement.
whyLost: It is spreading rapidly because of cost and speed pressure; the risk is the vestigial version, where unvalidated summaries replace analysis.
whereToUse: Research repositories, large interview programmes, support ticket coding, open-ended survey analysis, AI product research.
example: A team uses an LLM to apply a 14-code trust codebook to 3,000 interview excerpts. Agreement with human coders reaches kappa 0.82 on most codes but 0.45 on 'ambivalence', which remains human-coded.

name: Local Batch Transcription Pipeline (Whisper)
origin: OpenAI Whisper, 2022; whisper.cpp (Georgi Gerganov), 2022; pyannote.audio diarisation (Hervé Bredin)
summary: Transcribing large interview sets locally with Whisper, adding speaker diarisation and auditing word error rate, keeping audio within your environment.
description: Transcription is a bottleneck and a privacy risk when audio is uploaded to third-party services. A local pipeline runs speech recognition on the researcher's own machine or controlled server. Audio is normalised (for example 16 kHz WAV via ffmpeg), transcribed in batch with whisper.cpp or Whisper with explicit language settings and word-level timestamps, and segmented by speaker using pyannote.audio diarisation aligned to the timestamps. Quality is audited by sampling transcripts, computing word error rate against human correction, and retranscribing or correcting where WER exceeds a threshold such as 10 percent. Documenting that audio never left the environment supports ethics approvals and data protection commitments.
steps: Local setup: Install whisper.cpp locally (does not send audio to external servers). Convert audio to WAV at 16kHz: ffmpeg -i input.mp3 -ar 16000 output.wav
Batch transcription: Run whisper.cpp on all files. Set language explicitly. Request word-level timestamps.
Speaker diarisation: Run pyannote.audio to identify speaker turns. Align with Whisper timestamps to produce speaker-labelled transcripts.
Quality audit: Sample 3 transcripts per 20 for human review. Calculate Word Error Rate (WER). If WER > 10%: retranscribe manually.
Privacy documentation: Running entirely locally = no audio leaves your environment. Document this in ethics reporting.
outputs: Speaker-labelled, timestamped transcripts, WER audit results, and privacy documentation for ethics records.
useWhen: Programmes with dozens to hundreds of recordings, sensitive data that should not leave your infrastructure, or multilingual studies.
avoidWhen: A handful of sessions where a research tool's built-in transcription is permitted, or where no one can maintain the pipeline; heavily accented or noisy audio may still need human transcription.
whyLost: It spread quickly because open models made accurate local transcription cheap and solved privacy constraints on cloud tools.
whereToUse: Health and finance research with strict data policies, academic studies, multilingual field research, and research repositories.
example: A hospital research team transcribes 140 patient interviews on an offline workstation. A WER audit on 21 transcripts averages 6%, and two noisy ward recordings are corrected manually.

name: Local Whisper deployment (whisper.cpp)
origin: OpenAI Whisper model, Radford et al., 2022; whisper.cpp C/C++ port by Georgi Gerganov, 2022
summary: Running the Whisper speech recognition model on a researcher's own machine so interview recordings are transcribed accurately without sending participant audio to a cloud service.
description: Whisper is a transformer speech recognition model trained on about 680,000 hours of multilingual audio, robust to accents and background noise. whisper.cpp is an efficient C/C++ implementation that runs on laptops and workstations (CPU, Apple Silicon or GPU) using quantised model weights. Local deployment keeps raw participant audio on controlled hardware, which simplifies consent, GDPR and data processing agreements and is often required in health, finance and public-sector research. Rigour comes from pinning the model size and version (e.g. large-v3 for accuracy, medium or small for speed), setting language and decoding parameters explicitly, recording them for provenance, and auditing a sample of transcripts against human references, since Whisper can hallucinate fluent text during silence or noise.
steps: Check consent and data protection terms, and confirm that local processing satisfies them.
Build whisper.cpp and download a pinned model (e.g. ggml-large-v3, or a quantised q5 variant for constrained hardware), recording its checksum.
Convert audio to 16 kHz mono WAV, which whisper.cpp expects.
Run transcription with explicit language, timestamps and output formats (txt, srt or json), and enable voice activity detection where available to reduce hallucination in silences.
Batch-process recordings with a script that logs model, parameters, runtime and any errors per file.
Audit a stratified sample of transcripts (e.g. 10% or at least 5 files) for word error rate before analysis.
outputs: Time-stamped transcripts, a processing log with model and parameters, and an audit of transcription quality.
useWhen: Transcribing interviews, usability sessions and diary audio where privacy, cost or volume make cloud services unsuitable.
avoidWhen: Avoid when certified human transcription is required (legal, some clinical contexts), for very poor audio with heavy overlap, or when no one can audit the output; use professional transcription then.
whyLost: Local, high-quality speech recognition only became practical in 2022-23; it spread rapidly because it removes a major cost and privacy bottleneck in qualitative research.
whereToUse: Health and fintech research under strict data protection, public-sector UX, multilingual research and large interview programmes.
example: A health research team transcribes 120 patient interviews on an encrypted workstation with whisper.cpp large-v3. No audio leaves the device, and an audit of 12 files shows a 6% word error rate, mainly on drug names, which are corrected by a glossary pass.

name: Localization Testing
origin: Software localisation industry practice from the 1980s (LISA standards); usability framing by del Galdo and Nielsen (1996)
summary: Evaluating whether a localised product works linguistically, culturally and functionally in a target locale, from translation quality to layout expansion and format conventions.
description: Localization testing checks that a product adapted for a locale actually works for people there. It spans linguistic quality (accuracy, terminology, register, consistency with platform conventions), functional and layout issues (text expansion of 30% or more in languages such as German, truncation, right-to-left mirroring, font rendering, input methods) and cultural fit (imagery, colours, examples, legal and payment norms, date, number, address and currency formats). Rigour combines pseudo-localisation to catch internationalisation defects before translation, structured linguistic review by native-speaker reviewers with an error typology and severity scoring, and task-based usability sessions with local users. Issues are logged against locale and string identifiers so they can be fixed at source.
steps: Run pseudo-localisation builds (expanded, accented strings) to expose hard-coded text, truncation and encoding defects before translation.
Prepare a locale checklist covering formats, right-to-left support, input methods, legal text, payments and imagery.
Have native-speaker reviewers assess strings in context using an error typology (accuracy, terminology, style, locale convention) with severity scores.
Run task-based usability sessions with 5-8 local users per priority locale on key journeys.
Log each issue with locale, string ID, screenshot, category and severity, and route it to engineering, translation or content.
Retest fixes and track linguistic quality scores per release.
outputs: Pseudo-localisation defect list, linguistic quality scores, locale checklist results, usability findings per locale and a prioritised fix log.
useWhen: Before launching in a new market or language, after major UI changes in localised products, and when locale-specific support issues rise.
avoidWhen: When the question is whether the product concept fits the culture at all (use cross-cultural UX research), or before internationalisation is in place.
whyLost: Still in use: Essential for international product teams.
whereToUse: Any product expanding to new language markets.
example: A travel booking app launching in Arabic uses pseudo-localisation to find 140 truncated strings, then sessions with users in Riyadh show the mirrored calendar confuses date-range selection. A redesigned range picker cuts booking errors in the locale.

name: Log File Analysis
origin: Web server log analysis, early 1990s; transaction log analysis in library science, 1970s-1980s
summary: Reconstructs user behaviour, errors and usage patterns directly from raw server, application or search logs, independent of analytics tool sampling and schemas.
description: Before packaged analytics, researchers studied behaviour from raw logs: web server requests, application events and search queries. Transaction log analysis in library catalogues and information retrieval pioneered rigorous techniques such as session reconstruction, query reformulation analysis and failure rate measurement. Today logs remain the richest source where analytics tools are absent or inadequate: APIs, developer tools, back-end errors, search systems and legacy software. The method involves parsing logs, reconstructing sessions with sensible timeout rules, classifying events and computing behavioural measures. Rigour comes from documenting cleaning decisions (bot filtering, deduplication, session timeout, typically 30 minutes), validating reconstructed sessions against known cases, protecting privacy, and acknowledging that logs show actions but not intentions.
steps: Identify available logs and their fields, and agree privacy and access controls.
Parse and clean logs: remove bots and health checks, normalise identifiers and timestamps.
Reconstruct sessions using a documented timeout rule (often 30 minutes of inactivity).
Classify events and compute measures such as error rates, query reformulations, task completion proxies and usage frequency.
Validate reconstructions against a sample of known sessions or test accounts.
Report patterns and follow up with qualitative research to explain them.
outputs: Cleaned session dataset, behavioural metrics, error and failure patterns, documented cleaning rules.
useWhen: APIs and developer platforms, search systems, enterprise and legacy software without analytics tools, and error investigations.
avoidWhen: Products with well-instrumented analytics where questions are standard; use the analytics platform. Avoid where logs contain sensitive data without proper governance.
whyLost: Siloed: Increasingly replaced by purpose-built analytics tools; survives in developer/security contexts.
whereToUse: Error pattern analysis; API usage research; legacy system analysis.
example: A developer API team parsed 30 days of gateway logs and found 22% of new integrators repeated the same 401 error more than five times. The fix was clearer authentication error messages and a docs example, which halved repeat errors.
sources: Practical Web Analytics for User Experience

name: Log parsing
origin: Web server log analysis from the early 1990s (Common Log Format); web usage mining literature (Srivastava et al., 2000)
summary: Converting raw event or server logs into a clean, typed, ordered event table with consistent user identifiers, timestamps and event names.
description: Product logs arrive as JSON event streams, server logs or analytics exports with inconsistent schemas, time zones, duplicate events and renamed events across releases. Log parsing builds a reliable event table: parse each record, normalise timestamps to UTC, resolve user identity across devices where consented, map event names through a versioned taxonomy, deduplicate and order events. Rigour lies in validating the output against known totals (for example daily active users from the analytics platform), quantifying dropped or malformed records, and documenting schema changes, because an unnoticed instrumentation change can masquerade as a behaviour change.
steps: Obtain the event schema and instrumentation change history from engineering before parsing.
Parse records into a typed table (user_id, session_id, timestamp, event, properties) using pandas or a streaming parser for large files.
Normalise all timestamps to UTC and order events within user by timestamp and sequence number.
Map raw event names to a versioned taxonomy so renamed events are unified across releases.
Remove exact duplicates and report the percentage of malformed or dropped records (investigate if above about 1%).
Reconcile daily totals with the source analytics platform within an agreed tolerance before analysis.
outputs: A clean event table, a versioned event taxonomy, a parsing quality report and reconciliation against platform totals.
useWhen: Any behavioural analysis built on raw events: funnels, sessionisation, survival analysis, sequence mining or behavioural segmentation.
avoidWhen: Unnecessary if a well-governed analytics warehouse already provides modelled event tables; use those, but still check the taxonomy history.
whyLost: Parsing is seen as engineering work and is delegated, so UX researchers rarely see the decisions that shape their behavioural data.
whereToUse: SaaS and e-commerce analytics, mobile apps with offline event batching, AI products logging prompts and responses.
example: A mobile banking app's funnel shows a sudden drop at the 'confirm payee' step. Parsing the raw logs reveals the event had been renamed in a release; after mapping both names, the funnel is stable.

name: Log-Transformation of Task Completion Times
origin: Cordes, 1993; Sauro & Lewis, 2010
summary: Analyses task times on a log scale because they are positively skewed, reporting geometric means and back-transformed confidence intervals rather than arithmetic means.
description: Task completion times are bounded at zero and strongly right-skewed: most users finish near a typical time while a few take much longer. Arithmetic means and normal-theory confidence intervals are therefore biased upward and unstable, particularly in the small samples typical of usability studies. The protocol log-transforms each time, computes means and confidence intervals on the log scale, and back-transforms them, yielding the geometric mean and asymmetric intervals. Research by Sauro and Lewis shows the geometric mean is the better estimate of the median for samples under about 25. Plotting the log-scale distribution also exposes structure, such as bimodality, that indicates distinct user strategies hidden by an average.
steps: For any task time data:
Plot histogram and QQ plot.
(2) Apply Shapiro-Wilk test (n<50) or Kolmogorov-Smirnov (n≥50).
(3) If right-skewed: compute ln(time) for each observation.
(4) Run t-test on log-transformed data.
(5) Back-transform: geometric mean = exp(mean_log), CI bounds = exp(mean_log ± 1.96×se_log).
(6) Report: 'Geometric mean task time: 45s [95% CI: 38–53s]'.
outputs: Geometric mean task times, back-transformed confidence intervals, valid comparisons between designs, and distribution diagnostics revealing bimodal populations.
useWhen: Any quantitative usability study comparing or benchmarking task times, especially with small samples where a few slow participants distort arithmetic means.
avoidWhen: Avoid when times are not skewed or when you need the arithmetic mean for cost calculations (total time cost); for heavily bimodal data, model the subgroups instead.
whyLost: Practitioners report arithmetic means because tools default to them and stakeholders expect them; the statistical rationale is taught in specialist texts only.
whereToUse: All task-time UX analyses. The most common statistical error in UX benchmarking studies.
example: An investment platform's task times average 94 s, but the geometric mean is 61 s; the log-scale histogram is bimodal, revealing a subgroup that re-verifies every trade, which becomes a separate design problem.

name: Logistic regression for binary outcomes
origin: David Cox, 1958; Joseph Berkson's logit, 1944
summary: Modelling the probability of a binary UX outcome, such as task success, conversion or churn, from several predictors, with results expressed as odds ratios.
description: Logistic regression models the log-odds of a binary outcome as a linear function of predictors, keeping predicted probabilities between 0 and 1. Coefficients exponentiate to odds ratios: the multiplicative change in the odds of success per unit increase in a predictor. It is the right tool for task completion, conversion, churn and error occurrence, where linear regression would give impossible predictions and invalid inference. Rigour comes from enough events per variable (traditionally at least 10), checking linearity of continuous predictors in the logit, multicollinearity and influential cases, assessing discrimination (AUC) and calibration (calibration plots or Hosmer-Lemeshow), and translating odds ratios into predicted probabilities or marginal effects that stakeholders understand.
steps: Define the binary outcome precisely and ensure at least about 10 events per predictor in the smaller outcome class.
Fit the model (SPSS LOGISTIC REGRESSION or statsmodels Logit) with predictors chosen from theory.
Check linearity of continuous predictors in the logit (Box-Tidwell or spline terms), VIFs and influential cases.
Report odds ratios with 95% CIs and compute average marginal effects or predicted probabilities for key scenarios.
Assess discrimination (AUC; around 0.7 acceptable, 0.8 good) and calibration, preferably with cross-validation.
For ordinal outcomes switch to PLUM (ordinal logistic) and for clustered users use mixed-effects logistic models.
outputs: Odds ratios with CIs, predicted probabilities or marginal effects, discrimination and calibration statistics.
useWhen: Modelling task success in usability benchmarks, conversion or churn drivers, error occurrence and adoption.
avoidWhen: Avoid for rare events with few cases (use penalised Firth regression), ordered categories (use ordinal regression), repeated measures (use mixed models) or causal claims without a causal design.
whyLost: It survived because binary outcomes are everywhere in product analytics and it is well supported in every statistics package.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarks, e-commerce conversion, SaaS churn, fintech application completion and AI feature adoption.
example: In a 60-participant benchmark, logistic regression shows that prior experience with comparable banking apps increases the odds of completing a transfer (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.4-6.8), translating to predicted success of 58% for novices versus 81% for experienced users.

name: Lomb-Scargle Periodogram
origin: Nicholas R. Lomb, 1976; Jeffrey D. Scargle, 1982
summary: Estimates periodicity in unevenly sampled data without interpolation, avoiding the false cycles that standard FFTs create from irregular, event-driven behavioural timestamps.
description: Astronomical observations are irregularly spaced, so Lomb and Scargle developed a least-squares fit of sinusoids at candidate frequencies that works directly on uneven timestamps. Behavioural data are even more event-driven: users act when motivated, not on a schedule. Applying a standard FFT produces aliasing (false periodicities from uneven intervals) and leakage (energy spread across frequencies), and treats meaningful silences such as disengagement as noise. The Behavioral Spectral Framework therefore prescribes Lomb-Scargle for irregular event sampling, alongside Gaussian-process interpolation with uncertainty bounds, survival or hazard models for inactivity intervals and point-process models, and insists that gaps be treated as behaviour (rest, hesitation, reflection) rather than void.
steps: Collect raw event timestamps without forcing a uniform grid.
Choose a frequency grid spanning the rhythms of interest (e.g. daily, weekly, within-session).
Compute the Lomb-Scargle periodogram and assess peak significance (e.g. false-alarm probability).
Separately model long inactivity gaps with survival or hazard functions.
Compare periodograms across users or cohorts.
Interpret peaks with qualitative and contextual evidence.
outputs: Periodograms with significant periods for irregular behavioural data.
useWhen: When behavioural events arrive irregularly (app opens, purchases, messages) and you want genuine periodicity.
avoidWhen: When data are evenly sampled and dense (a standard FFT suffices) or very few events exist.
whyLost: Born and kept in astronomy; product analytics rarely considers the sampling assumptions behind spectral tools.
whereToUse: App-open rhythms, purchase cycles, medication adherence apps, messaging behaviour.
example: Purchase timestamps from a grocery app, analysed with Lomb-Scargle, reveal a robust 7-day cycle that an FFT on daily bins had smeared with spurious peaks.

name: Longitudinal Mixed-Method Integration
origin: Mixed-methods design tradition (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2007); longitudinal mixed methods literature
summary: Combining continuous quantitative tracking with qualitative waves sampled by trajectory type to explain why user trajectories diverge.
description: This design runs a quantitative backbone (behavioural analytics or validated repeated surveys) across a whole panel and uses its trajectories to drive qualitative sampling. Analysts first identify trajectory patterns: fast improvers, plateauers, abandoners. Participants are then purposively selected from each pattern rather than by convenience, and interviewed with explanation-focused prompts that reference their own data. Integration happens in a longitudinal joint display: trajectory lines per group alongside a timeline of qualitative events, showing which events coincide with inflection points. The design avoids both purely descriptive analytics and qualitative findings that cannot be connected to measured outcomes.
steps: Quantitative backbone: Behavioural analytics or validated survey measures tracking the full panel continuously. Identify trajectory patterns: who improves fastest? Who plateaus? Who abandons?
Qualitative sampling from quantitative patterns: Select participants for qualitative interviews based on trajectory, not convenience. Purposively sample fast improvers, plateau-ers, and abandoners.
Explanation-focused interviews: 'I can see your engagement with [feature] has changed significantly over 6 weeks — what has been happening?'
Longitudinal joint display: Quantitative trajectory (line chart per group) alongside qualitative event timeline. Show how qualitative events correspond to quantitative inflection points.
outputs: Trajectory clusters, purposively sampled interview findings per cluster, and a longitudinal joint display linking events to inflection points.
useWhen: Explaining divergent adoption, retention or performance trajectories over weeks or months when both logs and participant access exist.
avoidWhen: When no reliable longitudinal metric exists or the team cannot recontact users; use cross-sectional mixed methods or a diary study.
whyLost: Analytics and research teams often work separately, so trajectory-driven sampling and formal integration are rarely planned.
whereToUse: Subscription and SaaS onboarding, health behaviour apps, education platforms, and fintech savings products.
example: A language app clusters six-week streak trajectories into three groups. Interviews with plateauers reveal that difficulty jumps at unit 4 coincide with their flatline, which the joint display makes visible to the team.

name: Longitudinal Panel Study
origin: Lazarsfeld, 1940s panel studies; Menard, 2002
summary: Measures the same participants repeatedly over months to observe how attitudes, behaviour and experience change, separating within-person change from between-person differences.
description: A longitudinal panel study follows a fixed sample of participants across multiple measurement waves, using the same instruments at each point so that change can be attributed to time, experience or intervention rather than to differences between samples. In UX it captures what single-session studies miss: the learning curve, the decay of novelty, the formation or collapse of habits, and how attitudes shift as products become embedded in routines. Rigour depends on a planned wave schedule, measurement invariance across waves, active retention strategies (incentives tied to completion, consistent contact) and explicit analysis of attrition bias. Analysis typically uses within-person models such as growth curves or mixed-effects regression, complemented by repeat interviews that explain inflection points in the trajectories.
steps: Panel design: recruit N ≥ 30 participants representing your target population. Establish baseline measures (task performance, satisfaction, usage patterns). Contact at pre-specified intervals (1, 4, 12, 26 weeks). At each wave: same task battery + usage log review + short interview. Analyze:
attrition pattern — who drops out and why?
(2) individual change trajectories — who improves, plateaus, regresses?
(3) cohort effects — do users who started in different months show different trajectories?
outputs: Wave-by-wave datasets on a fixed panel, within-person trajectories, attrition analysis, change estimates (e.g. growth curves) and qualitative accounts of adoption over time.
useWhen: Questions about adoption, habit formation, learning, novelty wear-off, churn and long-term satisfaction, where a single snapshot cannot distinguish change from cohort differences.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need an answer in weeks, or when attrition will be severe and unmanageable; use a diary study or cross-sectional survey with retrospective items, and accept their limits.
whyLost: Product cycles are shorter than panel timelines and research budgets are allocated per sprint; analytics cohorts are used as a cheap substitute, though they capture behaviour without attitudes.
whereToUse: Product launch tracking, long-term onboarding research, habit formation studies, product lifecycle research.
example: A health app recruits 120 newly diagnosed diabetes patients and surveys and interviews them at onboarding, 1, 3 and 6 months, revealing that perceived usefulness drops at month three exactly when glucose logging becomes routine.

extra.Three Design Variants: Pure panel: Same participants, same measures, at multiple time points. Reveals individual change trajectories. Attrition is rarely random — document and test for non-random dropout. Rotating panel: A proportion is replaced at each wave. Balances longitudinal tracking with sample refresh. Cohort design: Follow groups sharing a common starting event (new users signing up in the same month). Reveals how start conditions shape subsequent trajectories.

name: Longitudinal Qualitative Interviewing
origin: Qualitative longitudinal research tradition (Saldaña, 2003; Timescapes programme, UK, 2007-2012)
summary: Interviewing the same participants repeatedly over months so that change in experience, language and meaning between waves becomes the unit of analysis.
description: Longitudinal qualitative interviewing returns to the same people over months or years, treating change itself as the object of study. Each wave revisits what changed, what stayed the same and what was unexpected, with the interviewer referencing the participant's earlier words to prompt reflection. Analysis compares waves within each person, looking at shifts in vocabulary, metaphor, emphasis and self-description, before comparing trajectories across participants. Saldaña's guidance frames analytic questions about what increases, decreases, emerges, ceases and remains constant. Trust and clear relationship boundaries are critical, since repeated contact builds rapport but also risks dependence and participant fatigue.
steps: Establish the relationship: Longitudinal interviewing depends on trust. Begin each interview reconnecting to the previous conversation: 'When we last spoke you mentioned X — has that changed?'

Interview continuity: Each wave covers (a) what has changed, (b) what stayed the same, (c) what was unexpected. Use the previous transcript as a resource — reference what participants said previously.
Change as unit of analysis: Analyse what changes between waves. Shifts in language, vocabulary, metaphor, and emphasis between waves are the core data.
Relationship boundary management: Establish from the start that this is a research relationship with defined roles and a known end point.
outputs: Within-person change narratives, wave-by-wave comparison tables, cross-case trajectory types, and longitudinal quotes.
useWhen: Adoption, habit formation, life transitions or long service journeys where meaning and behaviour evolve, such as illness, parenthood, new jobs or retirement.
avoidWhen: When change can be measured adequately through logs or surveys, or budgets cannot support retention; use a diary study or panel survey.
whyLost: UX studies are typically single-wave, and repeated interviewing with change-focused analysis remains a sociological speciality.
whereToUse: Health condition management, onboarding to complex B2B platforms, financial wellbeing products, and education technology.
example: A diabetes app team interviews 10 newly diagnosed users at months 1, 3 and 6. Language shifts from 'the app tells me' to 'I know my numbers', showing when to reduce guidance and hand control back.
