name: Longitudinal Research Design
origin: Panel and cohort designs from the 1930s to 1950s (e.g. Lazarsfeld's panel studies, 1940s)
summary: Measures the same variables in the same participants at multiple time points to describe change, separate within-person from between-person effects and strengthen causal inference.
description: Longitudinal research designs repeatedly measure the same participants over time, rather than comparing different people at one moment. Panel studies follow a fixed sample, cohort studies follow groups defined by a shared starting event, and intensive longitudinal designs collect many measurements over shorter periods. Because they observe change within people, longitudinal designs can separate genuine development from cohort differences, establish temporal order and support stronger causal inference than cross-sectional surveys. In UX they reveal how perceptions shift from onboarding to maturity and whether early experiences predict later behaviour. Rigour comes from planned measurement intervals that match the pace of change, consistent instruments, retention strategies and attrition analysis, and analysis methods such as mixed-effects or growth curve models that handle missing data.
steps: Define the changes of interest and the timescale over which they occur.
Choose a design (panel, cohort or intensive longitudinal) and set measurement waves, for example at weeks 1, 4, 12 and 26.
Use consistent, validated instruments across waves and link with behavioural logs where possible.
Recruit a sample large enough to absorb expected attrition, often 20 to 40 percent.
Run retention strategies such as incentives per wave and reminders.
Analyse attrition patterns and use mixed-effects or growth curve models to estimate change.
Report trajectories, predictors of change and limitations.
outputs: Trajectories of change over time, within-person and between-person effects, predictors of later outcomes and attrition analyses.
useWhen: For habit formation, long-term adoption, perception change after onboarding and understanding whether early experience predicts later behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid when decisions are needed within weeks or when change can be captured in logs alone; use cross-sectional surveys, diary studies or survival analysis.
whyLost: Vestigial: Expensive and slow; rarely done in product UX at rigor; diary studies are informal substitute.
whereToUse: Habit formation research; long-term product adoption; health behavior tracking.
example: A digital therapeutics company surveys 500 new users at weeks 1, 4, 12 and 26 and links responses to usage. Growth models show early perceived personalisation predicts adherence at week 26 better than week-one engagement does.
sources: Handbook of Longitudinal Research
Applied Longitudinal Data Analysis (Singer & Willett)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rothman KJ, Greenland S & Lash TL (2008) Modern Epidemiology
Doll R & Hill AB (1954) The mortality of doctors in relation to their smoking habits. BMJ
von Elm et al., The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement (2007), The Lancet
Rothman, Greenland & Lash, Modern Epidemiology (3rd ed., 2008)
reference: Singer, J. D. & Willett, J. B. (2003). Applied Longitudinal Data Analysis: Modeling Change and Event Occurrence. Oxford University Press.

name: Longitudinal Scalogram Analysis
origin: Louis Guttman, 1944 (scalogram analysis); longitudinal extensions in developmental research
summary: Tests whether behaviours or abilities are acquired in a consistent cumulative order over time, revealing natural adoption sequences.
description: Scalogram analysis, introduced by Louis Guttman, tests whether a set of items forms a cumulative scale: if a person endorses or achieves a harder item, they also endorse or achieve all easier ones. Longitudinal scalogram analysis applies this logic over time to test whether people acquire behaviours or capabilities in a consistent order, such as developmental stages in children. In UX this suits feature adoption: do users typically adopt basic features before advanced ones, and in what order? A consistent sequence suggests a natural learning path that onboarding and progressive disclosure can follow. Rigour comes from clear item definitions, adequate observation windows, coefficients of reproducibility (traditionally 0.90 or more) and scalability, probabilistic extensions such as Mokken scaling to handle error, and checking whether sequences differ across segments.
steps: Define the set of behaviours or features whose acquisition order is of interest.
Define criteria for 'acquired' (for example used at least three times within 30 days).
Extract per-user acquisition status at regular time points from logs or repeated surveys.
Order items by difficulty (proportion acquired) and test cumulative patterns with coefficients of reproducibility and scalability.
Apply probabilistic extensions such as Mokken scaling to tolerate error.
Examine transitions over time and compare sequences across segments.
Translate the sequence into onboarding and progressive disclosure design.
outputs: Cumulative adoption sequences, scalability and reproducibility coefficients, segment differences and recommended learning paths.
useWhen: For feature adoption sequencing, onboarding optimisation and engagement progression where a natural learning order is hypothesised.
avoidWhen: Avoid when behaviours are independent or adoption is driven by unrelated needs; use survival analysis or cluster analysis.
whyLost: Latent: Rarely used in UX; powerful for studying feature adoption order and behavior progression.
whereToUse: Feature adoption sequencing; onboarding optimization; engagement progression modeling.
example: A design tool analyses adoption of eight features among 50,000 new users over 90 days. Components are adopted before auto-layout and before variables in 94 percent of cases, so onboarding teaches components first.
sources: Longitudinal Scalogram Analysis
Measurement and Prediction (Stouffer et al.)
reference: Guttman, L. (1944). A basis for scaling qualitative data. American Sociological Review, 9(2), 139-150.

name: Lorenz Curve and Gini Coefficient for Engagement Concentration
origin: Max Lorenz (1905); Corrado Gini (1912); Herfindahl-Hirschman index (1945/1950)
summary: Plots and quantifies how unequally activity, value or exposure is distributed across users, creators or items.
description: The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of a quantity (sessions, revenue, views) against the cumulative share of units ranked from smallest to largest; the Gini coefficient is twice the area between the curve and the line of equality, from 0 (perfect equality) to 1. Concentration measures such as the Herfindahl index complement it. For products, these measures reveal dependence on a few power users, inequality of exposure among creators or sellers, and fairness of recommendation systems. Tracking Gini over time shows whether changes broaden or concentrate engagement, which raw averages hide.
steps: Choose the quantity and units (e.g. views per creator, sessions per user, revenue per account).
Sort units by the quantity and compute cumulative shares.
Plot the Lorenz curve and compute the Gini coefficient with bootstrap confidence intervals.
Compute complementary measures (top 1% share, Herfindahl index, Palma ratio).
Compare across segments, time or experiment arms.
Interpret implications for risk (dependence on few users), fairness and design.
outputs: Lorenz curves, Gini coefficients and concentration metrics with trends and comparisons.
useWhen: Assessing concentration of engagement, revenue or exposure, and the fairness effects of algorithms or features.
avoidWhen: When the distribution shape is irrelevant to the decision.
whyLost: Product dashboards focus on totals and averages; inequality measures are seen as economics, not UX.
whereToUse: Creator platforms, marketplaces, recommendation systems, community participation, B2B account usage.
example: A marketplace's new ranking algorithm raises total sales 3% but increases the Gini of seller sales from 0.71 to 0.79, prompting a fairness review and an exposure floor for new sellers.
sources: Lorenz, Methods of measuring the concentration of wealth (1905), Publications of the American Statistical Association
Cowell, Measuring Inequality (3rd ed., 2011)
reference: Cowell, F. A. (2011). Measuring Inequality (3rd ed.). Oxford University Press.

name: LOSA and Threat and Error Management (TEM)
origin: Robert Helmreich and the University of Texas Human Factors Research Project with Continental Airlines, 1990s; ICAO Doc 9803 (2002)
summary: Trained observers record threats, errors and undesired states during normal operations under strict non-jeopardy conditions, then analyse how they were managed.
description: LOSA observes routine work, not incidents. Peer observers ride along on normal flights and code, with a standard form, the threats (external complications such as weather or ATC), errors made by the crew, whether each was detected and managed, and any undesired aircraft states that followed. Data are confidential and de-identified, which is what makes honest observation possible. The TEM framework then reveals which threats are most frequent, which errors go unmanaged and which countermeasures work. For UX this is an exceptional model for observing expert users of complex tools in their real work: it counts errors that never become incidents, measures recovery, and reveals the gap between procedures and practice.
steps: Agree with the organisation the ten LOSA operating characteristics, especially anonymity, voluntary participation and non-jeopardy.
Train observers who know the domain to use a TEM coding form for threats, errors, undesired states and their management.
Observe a representative sample of normal work sessions (aviation LOSAs typically use 50-100+ observations).
Code each threat and error with type, who detected it, response (managed, mismanaged, unmanaged) and outcome.
Aggregate to find prevalence and mismanagement rates, and identify the threats and interface features most associated with unmanaged errors.
Feed back findings to frontline users and designers, and repeat the audit after changes to measure improvement.
outputs: TEM database, prevalence and management rates for threats and errors, priority targets for design and training.
useWhen: Expert professional users operate complex software in high-stakes settings and you need to see everyday errors and recoveries, not just incidents.
avoidWhen: Consumer products with short sessions, or settings where anonymity cannot be guaranteed; use session replay analysis or diary studies.
whyLost: It requires organisational trust and trained domain observers, and its output is safety data rather than product features. UX field research rarely codes errors systematically.
whereToUse: Air traffic tools, clinical teams using EHRs, security operations centres, financial trading desks, network operations.
example: A security operations team allows 60 anonymised shift observations of analysts using a SIEM. TEM coding shows alert-triage errors are usually caught but alert-suppression errors go unmanaged 40% of the time, prompting a redesign of suppression rules UI.
sources: ICAO, Line Operations Safety Audit (LOSA), Doc 9803 (2002)
Helmreich, Klinect & Wilhelm, Models of threat, error and CRM in flight operations (1999)
reference: ICAO (2002). Line Operations Safety Audit (LOSA), Doc 9803.

name: Loss aversion measurement
origin: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory (1979) and cumulative prospect theory (Tversky and Kahneman, 1992), which estimated a median loss aversion coefficient of about 2.25
summary: Estimates how much more heavily users weigh losses than equivalent gains in a product context, yielding a loss aversion coefficient to guide framing and change design.
description: Prospect theory proposes that outcomes are evaluated as gains or losses from a reference point, with losses weighted more heavily; Tversky and Kahneman estimated the coefficient lambda at about 2.25. Later work shows lambda varies by domain, stakes and person, and some studies find much smaller effects for routine amounts. Loss aversion measurement estimates lambda for your users and domain, typically through mixed gambles (accept or reject a 50/50 chance to win X or lose Y) or through paired gain and loss framings of product changes (losing a feature versus gaining it). The coefficient tells you how much benefit a change must deliver to offset what users lose, which is central to migrations, price changes and feature removals. Rigour requires incentive-compatible or realistic stakes and enough trials per person for stable estimates.
steps: Choose the domain of interest (money, time, features, status) and define the reference point users hold, for example their current plan or their current workflow.

Build a mixed-gamble task with 20 to 50 trials varying gain and loss amounts (for example gains of 10 to 40 against losses of 5 to 20 units), or a set of paired product scenarios framed as equivalent gains and losses.
Run the task with at least 50 to 100 participants from the target population, using real or realistic stakes where ethically feasible.
Estimate lambda per participant by fitting the acceptance threshold (the gain-to-loss ratio at which acceptance reaches 50%) or with a logistic choice model, and summarise the median and spread.
Translate lambda into design thresholds: a change that removes value worth L must provide perceived gains of roughly lambda times L to be accepted.
Validate predictions against real behaviour, such as uptake of a migration or churn after a feature change, and update estimates.
outputs: Distribution of loss aversion coefficients for your users and domain, segment differences, and quantitative thresholds for framing and compensating changes.
useWhen: Planning migrations, feature removals, price or plan changes, or framing decisions where users must give something up to gain something.
avoidWhen: You only need to choose between two framings of a message; an A/B test of the framings is quicker. Avoid when stakes cannot be made realistic, since hypothetical gambles may overstate or understate lambda.
whyLost: Loss aversion is cited constantly in UX but almost never measured: designers apply the textbook 2 to 1 ratio as a slogan rather than estimating it for their users and stakes.
whereToUse: Product migrations and redesigns, subscription pricing changes, savings and investment framing, health insurance plan changes, deprecating legacy features.
example: Before retiring a paper-like batch entry mode, a team measured lambda for time saved versus time lost among clinic staff and found a median of 2.8. The new mode saved 40 seconds per record but cost 20 seconds in a rare case, so they removed that loss rather than relying on net benefit.
sources: Prospect Theory works (Kahneman/Tversky)
Nash Equilibrium in UX (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 23 — Reference Points, Prospect Theory & the Mechanics of Satisfaction
reference: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1992). Advances in prospect theory: Cumulative representation of uncertainty. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 5(4), 297–323; Gächter, S., Johnson, E. J., & Herrmann, A. (2022). Individual-level loss aversion in riskless and risky choices. Theory and Decision, 92, 599–624.

name: M-Mode / I-Mode Observation
origin: Adapted for UX from the MU-puzzle in Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979), chapter I
summary: Code each moment of a session by whether the person is applying rules mechanically or stepping back to reason about the system, and study what makes them switch.
description: In the MU-puzzle Hofstadter separates working inside a system, applying its rules step by step (the Mechanical mode), from thinking about the system, noticing patterns and asking whether the goal is reachable at all (the Intelligent mode). People using software move between the same two modes. Most of the time they follow learned steps without thought; when something unexpected happens they shift to reasoning about how the product works. Those shifts are expensive and revealing: they mark where the interface stopped carrying people and where their understanding gets tested. This method adds a mode code to ordinary usability or field observation. Every segment is coded M (following steps, little hesitation, no talk about the system) or I (pausing, theorising aloud, trying something to see what happens), and the analysis focuses on the triggers for each switch into I-mode and on whether people come back to M-mode with a correct theory or a wrong one.
steps: Run normal think-aloud sessions or field observation, recorded so moments can be timestamped.
Agree on markers for each mode before coding, such as hesitation over 3 seconds, statements about how the system works, or exploratory clicks for I-mode.
Code the timeline of each session into M and I segments; have two people code a sample and resolve differences.
List every switch from M to I with what happened just before it.
Group the triggers (unexpected state, missing feedback, broken pattern, error message) and note the theory each person formed.
Prioritise triggers that are frequent, long-lasting or lead to wrong theories.
outputs: A timeline of mechanical and reasoning modes per participant, a ranked list of triggers that knock people out of routine use, and the theories they form at each.
useWhen: Studying routine or expert use where people rarely voice problems, comparing learnability between versions, or finding where automation surprises users.
avoidWhen: First-time exploratory use, where nearly everything is reasoning, or very short tasks with too few segments to code.
whyLost: Usability coding counts errors and task time but rarely codes the kind of thinking people are doing. Hofstadter's distinction was framed as a lesson about formal systems, so it never reached evaluation practice.
whereToUse: Expert tools, operations consoles, form-heavy workflows, automation and AI features that sometimes act on their own.
example: In an invoicing tool, accountants stay in M-mode until the tax total changes after they edit a date. Every participant switches to I-mode there, and half leave with the wrong theory that the date sets the tax rate, which explains a run of support tickets.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. Chapter I (The MU-puzzle).

name: Magnitude Estimation and Stevens' Power Law
origin: S. S. Stevens, 1950s (On the psychophysical law, 1957; Psychophysics, 1975)
summary: Participants assign numbers proportional to perceived magnitude, yielding ratio-scale data and power-law exponents that describe how perception scales with the stimulus.
description: In magnitude estimation, participants see a reference stimulus (modulus) and assign numbers to others in proportion: twice as intense gets twice the number. Geometric means across participants, plotted against stimulus intensity on log-log axes, typically give a straight line whose slope is the power-law exponent (psi = k x phi^n). Exponents differ by dimension: perceived brightness is compressive (about 0.33), electric shock expansive (about 3.5). Magnitude estimation was used in early HCI and usability research (McGee, 2003, applied it to usability judgements), offering ratio-level measurement of subjective experience that Likert scales cannot provide.
steps: Select stimuli spanning the range of interest (e.g. 6-10 levels of load time or visual clutter).
Present a modulus stimulus with an assigned or free number, then present test stimuli in random order with repeats.
Instruct participants to assign numbers proportional to perceived magnitude, allowing any positive number.
Normalise each participant's responses and compute geometric means per stimulus.
Fit a power function by linear regression on log-log values and report the exponent with confidence intervals.
Use the exponent to predict perceived improvement from physical changes, or compare designs on ratio-scale judgements.
outputs: Ratio-scale perception data and power-law exponents per dimension or design.
useWhen: You need ratio-level comparisons of perceived quantities, such as 'how much slower does it feel?' or 'how much more cluttered?'.
avoidWhen: Participants who struggle with numerical judgement, or when only rank order matters; use paired comparisons.
whyLost: Likert scales became the default, and ratio scaling was seen as cumbersome. McGee's usability magnitude estimation never caught on.
whereToUse: Perceived performance budgets, visual density, sound loudness in notifications, perceived price fairness.
example: A web team measures perceived slowness for load times from 0.5 to 8 seconds. The exponent of 0.6 shows halving a 4-second load feels like a 34% improvement, not 50%, setting realistic expectations.
sources: Stevens, Psychophysics: Introduction to Its Perceptual, Neural, and Social Prospects (1975)
Stevens, On the psychophysical law (1957), Psychological Review
McGee, Usability magnitude estimation (2003), Proceedings of HFES
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Stevens, S. S. (1957). On the psychophysical law. Psychological Review, 64(3), 153-181.

name: Manifold learning
origin: Isomap by Tenenbaum, de Silva & Langford, 2000; LLE by Roweis & Saul, 2000
summary: A family of methods that assume high-dimensional user data lies on a lower-dimensional curved surface and recover its intrinsic coordinates.
description: Manifold learning starts from the idea that although users are described by hundreds of variables, real behaviour varies along a few underlying degrees of freedom, such as engagement and sophistication, arranged on a curved manifold. Methods such as Isomap (geodesic distances), locally linear embedding, Laplacian eigenmaps, diffusion maps, t-SNE and UMAP attempt to unfold it. For UX, the payoff is identifying the intrinsic dimensionality of behaviour and continuous trajectories, such as how users progress from novice to expert, rather than forcing discrete segments. Rigour involves estimating intrinsic dimension, comparing methods, checking neighbourhood preservation (trustworthiness and continuity scores) and validating interpretations with external data.
steps: Construct and standardise the behavioural feature matrix, removing noise with PCA if dimensions are very high.
Estimate intrinsic dimensionality (e.g. maximum likelihood estimator or PCA residual variance) to decide target dimensions.
Apply two or more manifold methods (e.g. Isomap, diffusion maps, UMAP) with a range of neighbourhood sizes.
Evaluate embeddings with trustworthiness and continuity metrics (values above 0.9 indicate good neighbourhood preservation).
Interpret embedding coordinates by correlating them with original features and outcomes.
Track user trajectories over time in the embedding to study progression or drift.
outputs: Low-dimensional coordinates of the user space, intrinsic dimension estimates, quality metrics and interpretations of behavioural continua and trajectories.
useWhen: When behaviour appears to vary continuously and you want to understand progression, continua or the true number of behavioural dimensions.
avoidWhen: Avoid when linear PCA suffices, with small samples (manifold estimates are unstable), or when stakeholders need simple explainable segments.
whyLost: It is an academic ML topic; UX has absorbed only its most popular tools (t-SNE, UMAP) without the underlying framing.
whereToUse: Expertise progression in complex tools, behavioural drift analysis, learning curves in education technology and investment platforms.
example: Diffusion maps on 18 months of trading behaviour reveal a one-dimensional progression from cautious single-asset holders to diversified active traders. Plotting user trajectories shows most stall at a specific point linked to options education.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Space and Time (Marc Leordeanu)
Tenenbaum, de Silva & Langford (2000) A global geometric framework for nonlinear dimensionality reduction
Pattern Recognition & ML (Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Time & Space
The Inquiry Series, Ch 52 — Dimensionality Reduction — The Geometry of Behavioral Space
reference: Tenenbaum, J. B., de Silva, V. & Langford, J. C. (2000) A global geometric framework for nonlinear dimensionality reduction. Science, 290(5500), 2319-2323.

name: Mann-Whitney U test
origin: Frank Wilcoxon, 1945; Henry Mann and Donald Whitney, 1947
summary: A non-parametric test comparing two independent groups on ordinal or skewed outcomes, such as task times or rating scores, without assuming normality.
description: The Mann-Whitney U test ranks all observations from both groups together and tests whether values from one group tend to be larger than those from the other. It is the default alternative to the independent t-test when outcomes are ordinal (single Likert items, SEQ scores) or heavily skewed (task times, error counts) and samples are small. Its null hypothesis is stochastic equality, P(X greater than Y) = 0.5; it only tests medians if both distributions have the same shape. Rigour comes from reporting the U statistic, exact or normal-approximation p-value, tie handling and an effect size such as the rank-biserial correlation or common-language effect size, rather than a p-value alone. For paired designs the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is used instead.
steps: Confirm the design has two independent groups and the outcome is ordinal or a skewed continuous measure.
Plot both distributions (histograms or box plots) and check whether shapes are similar before interpreting the result as a median difference.
Run the test (scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu or pingouin.mwu) with a two-sided alternative unless a direction was pre-registered.
Use the exact test for small samples (roughly n below 20 per group without ties) and the normal approximation with tie correction otherwise.
Report U, p, group medians with interquartile ranges, and the rank-biserial correlation (about 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large).
For task times, consider also comparing geometric means on log-transformed data as Sauro and Lewis recommend.
outputs: U statistic, p-value, group medians and IQRs, and a rank-based effect size with confidence interval.
useWhen: Comparing two designs or user groups on single-item ratings, task times, error counts or other skewed outcomes, particularly with small to moderate samples.
avoidWhen: Avoid for paired or repeated-measures data (use Wilcoxon signed-rank), for more than two groups (use Kruskal-Wallis), or for multi-item scale scores that are approximately normal (a Welch t-test is more powerful). For ordinal outcomes with covariates use ordinal regression.
whyLost: It survived because it is taught in every introductory statistics course and is robust for the small, skewed samples typical of usability testing.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarking, comparative evaluation of prototypes, accessibility studies with small samples and satisfaction comparisons between segments.
example: An e-commerce team compares checkout task times for two designs with 14 and 15 participants. Times are right-skewed, so a Mann-Whitney test shows design B faster (rank-biserial r = 0.42), reported with medians of 74 s and 112 s.

bambi
statsmodels

name: Markov Chain Funnel Modelling
origin: Andrey Markov (1906); absorbing chain theory by John Kemeny and J. Laurie Snell (Finite Markov Chains, 1960); attribution use by Anderl et al. (2016)
summary: Models user journeys as states with transition probabilities, including absorbing states like conversion and exit, to compute completion probabilities and step importance.
description: Linear funnels assume users move forward step by step, but real journeys loop, skip and backtrack. A Markov chain estimates the probability of moving from each state (page, screen, step) to every other. With absorbing states for success and abandonment, the fundamental matrix N = (I - Q)^-1 gives expected visits to each state and absorption probabilities from any starting point. Removal effects, setting a state's transitions to exit, quantify each state's contribution to conversion. Higher-order chains capture memory. This gives a principled, whole-journey model for diagnosing where loops waste effort and which steps matter most.
steps: Define states at an appropriate granularity and absorbing states (conversion, exit, timeout).
Estimate the transition matrix from session logs, checking sample size per row.
Compute the fundamental matrix, expected steps to absorption and absorption probabilities.
Calculate removal effects for each state to gauge its contribution to success.
Test whether a first-order model is adequate versus higher-order (e.g. likelihood ratio or BIC).
Simulate design changes by modifying transition probabilities and predict their effect on conversion.
outputs: Transition matrices, absorption probabilities, expected path lengths, state removal effects and what-if simulations.
useWhen: Non-linear journeys with loops and multiple entry points, or for attribution across touchpoints.
avoidWhen: Simple linear flows where a standard funnel suffices, or sparse data with many states.
whyLost: Funnel visualisations in analytics tools assume linear steps; Markov modelling requires matrix algebra few UX teams practise.
whereToUse: E-commerce browsing, SaaS onboarding, help centre navigation, multi-channel marketing journeys.
example: A travel site models 18 states. Removal effects show the 'compare' page contributes 22% of bookings despite low traffic, while a 'deals' page creates loops that add 1.8 expected steps without raising conversion.
sources: Kemeny & Snell, Finite Markov Chains (1960)
Anderl, Becker, von Wangenheim & Schumann, Mapping the customer journey: Lessons learned from graph-based online attribution modeling (2016), International Journal of Research in Marketing
reference: Kemeny, J. G., & Snell, J. L. (1960). Finite Markov Chains. Van Nostrand.

name: Markov Decision Process Models of Interaction
donor: Operations research; reinforcement learning; computational cognitive science
origin: Bellman (1957) for MDPs; computational rationality in HCI by Howes, Lewis, Oulasvirta and colleagues, 2009-2018
summary: Models users as agents choosing actions to maximise expected reward under cognitive and perceptual bounds, and derives predicted optimal behaviour for a given interface.
description: An MDP specifies states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards; a POMDP adds partial observability, which suits users who cannot see everything. Computational rationality assumes users adapt their strategies optimally to the interface, given bounds such as limited visual acuity and memory. Solving the model (often by reinforcement learning) yields predicted behaviour: where users look, when they give up, which menu strategies they adopt. Comparing interfaces then means comparing the optimal policies and their expected costs. This gives UX a principled theory of why users behave as they do, and a way to explore design spaces in simulation before testing.
steps: Define the task as states, actions, observations and rewards, including time costs and task success value.
Specify bounded cognitive and perceptual constraints (foveal vision, memory decay, motor noise) based on literature.
Solve for the optimal or near-optimal policy using dynamic programming or reinforcement learning.
Generate predicted behaviour (fixations, clicks, abandonment, strategy choice) for each design variant.
Validate against empirical data from a small study or logs, checking qualitative patterns and quantitative fit.
Use the model to explore further design variants and to explain observed behaviour.
outputs: A formal user model, predicted policies and behaviours for designs, and validation statistics.
useWhen: You need to explain adaptive strategies or optimise layouts and menus in a large design space.
avoidWhen: Exploratory problems with unclear goals or rewards; qualitative research is needed first.
whyLost: It requires machine learning and cognitive modelling expertise uncommon in UX teams, and is published in CHI and cognitive science rather than practitioner venues.
whereToUse: Menu and layout optimisation, notification timing, adaptive interfaces, recommender interaction design.
example: A POMDP model of visual search through a product grid predicts that users adopt a left-column strategy when thumbnail quality is low. Testing confirms it, and the design team improves thumbnails rather than reordering items.
sources: Oulasvirta, Kristensson, Bi & Howes (eds.), Computational Interaction (2018)
Lewis, Howes & Singh, Computational rationality: Linking mechanism and behavior through bounded utility maximization (2014), Topics in Cognitive Science
Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed., 2018)
reference: Lewis, R. L., Howes, A., & Singh, S. (2014). Computational rationality. Topics in Cognitive Science, 6(2), 279-311.

name: Mathematical Metaphor Analysis for Data Visualisation
origin: George Lakoff and Rafael Núñez (2000); conceptual metaphor theory by Lakoff and Johnson (1980)
summary: Audits visualisations for the conceptual metaphors they rely on, such as more is up or time is a path, predicting misreadings when encodings violate those metaphors.
description: Lakoff and Núñez argue that mathematical understanding rests on conceptual metaphors grounded in bodily experience: numbers as collections, arithmetic as object manipulation, functions as motion along a path, and more as up. Visualisations inherit these metaphors. Viewers expect higher to mean more, left-to-right to mean later in time, bigger area to mean larger quantity, and closeness to mean similarity. When an encoding violates the metaphor, for example an inverted y-axis, a ranking where 1 is at the bottom, or a radial chart where time runs counter-clockwise, readers make predictable errors even when legends are correct. The method lists the metaphors each chart relies on, flags violations and conflicts between metaphors, and tests comprehension of flagged charts with quick judgement tasks.
steps: For any data visualization: identify the conceptual metaphors it employs.
A bar chart uses: MORE IS UP (quantity mapped to vertical height), CATEGORIES ARE CONTAINERS (bars as separate spatial regions).
Test: do users' intuitions align with the mathematical properties of the metaphor?
For each metaphor, find the breaking point — where the intuitive metaphor diverges from the mathematical reality.
Design to minimize metaphor violations.
outputs: Metaphor inventory per visualisation, flagged violations and conflicts, comprehension test results, and recommended encodings.
useWhen: Dashboards, financial and health data displays, data journalism, analytics products and any chart where misreading has consequences.
avoidWhen: When the problem is data quality or statistical literacy rather than encoding; use comprehension testing or data literacy research.
whyLost: Conceptual metaphor theory stayed in cognitive linguistics, while visualisation research adopted perceptual effectiveness rankings (Cleveland and McGill) instead.
whereToUse: Data visualization design, dashboard design, financial data UX, scientific data communication, AI output visualization.
example: A cloud cost dashboard shows savings as downward bars. Metaphor analysis flags a 'more is up' conflict, and a comprehension test shows 30% of finance users read the largest saving as the smallest; the chart is redrawn with upward bars.
sources: Where Mathematics Comes From — George Lakoff
Lakoff & Johnson, Metaphors We Live By (1980)
Cleveland & McGill, Graphical perception (JASA, 1984)
reference: Lakoff G & Núñez RE (2000) Where Mathematics Comes From: How the Embodied Mind Brings Mathematics into Being. Basic Books

name: Matrix Analysis (Miles & Huberman)
origin: Jane Ritchie and Liz Spencer, National Centre for Social Research, late 1980s (Framework); Miles and Huberman matrix displays
summary: Summarises qualitative data into purpose-built case-by-dimension matrices, reading across rows for cases and down columns for patterns, to answer several research questions systematically.
description: Matrix analysis (Spencer et al.) involves constructing bespoke matrices in which the rows represent cases (participants) or time points, and the columns represent dimensions defined by the research questions. Unlike Framework Analysis (which uses a pre-existing thematic framework), matrix analysis builds matrices specifically tailored to the current research question. It is particularly useful in evaluation research and applied policy research where multiple specific questions must be answered from the same dataset.
steps: Define the matrix dimensions: Each column of the matrix should correspond directly to a research question or a key dimension of the analysis.
Unit of analysis: Each row should represent a coherent unit — a participant, a site, a time point, a case.
Population of cells: For each cell, summarise the relevant data in 2–4 sentences. The summary is interpretive, not descriptive — it makes the analytical meaning of the data visible.
Read across rows: What is the full picture for this participant/case? What pattern of responses does this person show?
Read down columns: What is the pattern across all participants on this dimension? Where is there convergence? Where is there divergence?
Cross-matrix synthesis: Build a higher-order analysis that integrates patterns from multiple columns. What do the patterns across dimensions tell you that no single dimension reveals alone?
outputs: Populated analysis matrices with cell summaries and source references, within-case and cross-case patterns, typologies, and an audit trail linking claims to data.
useWhen: You have multiple defined research questions, a moderate dataset (about 10 to 50 cases), several analysts, and need transparent comparison across participants or segments.
avoidWhen: The analysis is highly exploratory with no defined dimensions; start with Reflexive Thematic Analysis or grounded theory. For very small studies, matrices may add overhead.
whyLost: Spreadsheets of notes are common in UX, but the disciplined framework procedure, with defined dimensions, summarised cells, source references and two-direction reading, stayed in health and policy research.
whereToUse: Multi-segment interview studies, evaluation research, longitudinal studies across time points, team synthesis, and research repositories.
example: A fintech team interviews 24 small-business owners across three segments. A matrix with columns for each research question shows retailers depend on cash-flow forecasts while service firms care about invoicing, guiding segment-specific roadmaps.
sources: Framework Analysis and Matrix Methods (Ritchie & Spencer)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Miles MB & Huberman AM (1994) Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook. 2nd ed
Miles MB, Huberman AM & Saldaña J (2014) Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook. 3rd ed
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Gale, N. K. et al. (2013). Using the framework method for the analysis of qualitative data in multi-disciplinary health research. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 13, 117.

name: MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling)
origin: Jordan Louviere and George Woodworth (1987-1990); Finn and Louviere (1992); Louviere, Flynn and Marley (2015)
summary: Respondents repeatedly choose the most and least important items from small subsets, producing ratio-quality importance scores without scale-use bias.
description: Rating scales suffer from everyone rating everything as important, and from cultural differences in scale use. MaxDiff shows respondents subsets of items (typically 4-5 per screen) from a list of 10-30, asking for the best and worst. Balanced incomplete block designs ensure each item appears equally and with each other item. Hierarchical Bayes multinomial logit estimates individual-level utilities, which can be rescaled to probability shares. The method discriminates strongly and works across cultures. Vestigial use runs MaxDiff in survey tools with poor designs and only counts-based scores, and uses it for things that are not comparable, such as features with very different scopes.
steps: Define a list of comparable items (features, needs, messages), worded at similar levels of specificity.
Generate a balanced design: each respondent sees each item about 3 times, 4-5 items per set.
Field to an adequate sample (e.g. 200+ per segment of interest).
Estimate utilities with hierarchical Bayes MNL; check fit (RLH) and remove speeders.
Rescale to probability shares and compare segments with credible intervals.
Optionally add an anchored question to identify absolute importance thresholds.
outputs: Individual and aggregate importance scores, segment comparisons and anchored thresholds.
useWhen: Prioritising features, needs, value propositions or messages across many items.
avoidWhen: Items of very different scope, or when you need absolute willingness to pay (use conjoint or BDM).
whyLost: Survey platforms made it a menu option, removing design and estimation rigour; results are often treated as precise rankings without uncertainty.
whereToUse: Roadmap prioritisation, onboarding message testing, needs research for JTBD, international product research.
example: A project management tool tests 20 candidate features with 600 users via MaxDiff. Three features take 40% of preference share among team leads but barely register among individual contributors, shaping a tiered roadmap.
sources: Louviere, Flynn & Marley, Best-Worst Scaling: Theory, Methods and Applications (2015)
Finn & Louviere, Determining the appropriate response to evidence of public concern (1992), Journal of Public Policy & Marketing
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Feature Prioritization Methods (slide deck)
reference: Louviere, J. J., Flynn, T. N., & Marley, A. A. J. (2015). Best-Worst Scaling. Cambridge University Press.

name: McNemar Exact Test for Paired Proportions
origin: Quinn McNemar (1947)
summary: Compares success rates when the same participants tried both designs.
description: In within-subjects studies each person attempts the task on both designs, so the two completion rates are not independent and the two-proportion test is wrong. McNemar's test looks only at the discordant pairs: people who succeeded on A but failed on B, and the reverse. If the designs were equally good these should be roughly equal. The exact version uses a binomial test on the discordant counts and works with small samples. Sauro and Lewis pair it with an adjusted-Wald interval for the difference in matched proportions, so the size of the improvement can be reported too.
steps: Build the 2×2 table of outcomes per participant: both succeed, A only, B only, both fail.
Take the discordant counts b (A only) and c (B only).
Run an exact binomial test of b against b + c with p = 0.5 (or the mid-p variant for less conservatism).
Compute an adjusted interval for the difference in matched proportions.
Report the discordant counts, p-value and interval.
outputs: A test of whether one design succeeds more often for the same people.
useWhen: Within-subjects comparisons of binary outcomes: success, preference, error presence.
avoidWhen: Different people saw each design (use the N-1 two-proportion test).
whyLost: Within-subjects designs are common in UX but analysts reach for the independent-groups tests they know.
whereToUse: Counterbalanced prototype comparisons, before/after studies with the same panel, competitive head-to-heads.
example: Fifteen people try both search layouts. Six succeed only on the new one, one only on the old. The exact McNemar p is 0.125, so a larger sample is needed before claiming the win.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
reference: McNemar, Q. (1947). Note on the sampling error of the difference between correlated proportions. Psychometrika 12.

name: Measurable UX Honeycomb
aka: Morville's UX Honeycomb with behavioural proxies
origin: Peter Morville, 2004; behavioural proxies by Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Morville's seven UX qualities turned into measurable behavioural proxies and survey constructs, used as the anchor dimensions for detecting where engagement erodes.
description: Peter Morville's 2004 honeycomb lists seven qualities of good UX: useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, credible and valuable. It is widely reproduced as a poster but rarely measured. Vivek Gopinath's drift playbook operationalises each facet as a behavioural proxy: Useful → unprompted return to feature; Desirable → exploration beyond minimal path; Findable → short path to target content across sessions; Accessible → completion parity across devices or modalities; Usable → error rate, success rate, time-on-task stability; Credible → adoption of recommendations without double-checking; Valuable → long-term retention, upgrade, advocacy. A 30-item Likert survey aligned to the facets is factor-analysed; in the worked example the seven collapse into Trust (credible + valuable), Ease (usable + accessible) and Engagement (useful + desirable + findable). The playbook justifies Honeycomb over HTA (bounded tasks) and Information Foraging Theory (drift is absence of foraging).
steps: List the seven Honeycomb facets and decide which are plausible drift dimensions for the product.
Map each facet to a behavioural proxy available in telemetry (e.g. Credible → recommendation adoption without double-checking).
Write a 30-item Likert survey aligned to the facets.
Run EFA on the survey (example n = 300) and report Cronbach's α per factor (Trust 0.84, Ease 0.81, Engagement 0.86).
Read the signature: Engagement weakening while Ease stays strong indicates drift rather than a usability break.
Track proxies longitudinally and tie qualitative quotes to facets (e.g. 'Recommendations feel off' → Credible erosion).
outputs: A facet-to-proxy measurement map, factor structure with reliabilities, and a diagnosis of which facets are eroding.
useWhen: When you need a simple, teachable framework to locate perception-level erosion across a whole product.
avoidWhen: For bounded task diagnostics such as checkout (use HTA or usability testing); the honeycomb is too coarse for step-level errors.
whyLost: The honeycomb survived as a slide but not as a measurement model; rigour was lost when it became a checklist.
whereToUse: E-commerce, content and OTT, SaaS health scoring, drift and retention research.
example: An e-commerce app's survey shows Ease strong but Engagement weak, and interviews cite 'I only open for daily deals now', pointing to Desirable and Credible erosion rather than a usability defect.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study
reference: Morville, P. (2004). User Experience Design (the UX Honeycomb), Semantic Studios.
keywords: useful usable desirable findable accessible credible valuable

name: Mechanism Design
origin: Leonid Hurwicz, 1960s-1970s; Hurwicz, Maskin and Myerson (Nobel 2007)
summary: Works backwards from a desired outcome to design the rules, information and incentives of a system so that self-interested users produce that outcome.
description: Mechanism design inverts game theory: instead of predicting behaviour from fixed rules, it asks which rules will make strategic participants produce a desired outcome. Key properties are incentive compatibility (truthful behaviour is each participant's best strategy), individual rationality (participation is worthwhile) and efficiency or fairness of the outcome. In product terms, the 'mechanism' includes matching rules, pricing, reputation systems, what information is revealed when, and how rewards are allocated. A rigorous application specifies the objective formally, enumerates the information each party holds privately, proposes rules, proves or simulates their incentive properties, and then tests them with real users, since bounded rationality means people do not always follow the theoretically optimal strategy. Market designers such as Roth applied it successfully to kidney exchange and school choice.
steps: State the platform's objective formally (e.g. maximise successful matches subject to fairness constraints).
Identify participants, their private information and their likely strategic incentives.
Propose candidate rules: matching algorithm, pricing, information disclosure and reputation rules.
Analyse or simulate incentive compatibility and individual rationality under each candidate.
Pilot the preferred mechanism with real users and check for deviations from predicted behaviour.
Refine the interface so the incentive-compatible strategy is also easy to understand and act on.
outputs: Formal objective, mechanism specification, incentive analysis or simulations, pilot behavioural results.
useWhen: Designing marketplaces, allocation systems, bidding, reputation and reward schemes where participants can game the rules.
avoidWhen: Products without strategic participants or scarce resources; and where you lack data to estimate preferences.
whyLost: Rigorous in economics and computer science, it requires formal modelling skills UX teams rarely have, so platform rules are usually set by product and growth teams without explicit incentive analysis.
whereToUse: Marketplace platforms; auction UI; incentive and reward system design.
example: A volunteer shift app let volunteers grab shifts first-come-first-served, leaving unpopular slots empty. A redesigned mechanism using ranked preferences and a deferred-acceptance match filled 96% of shifts and reduced last-minute dropouts.
sources: Preference Belief and Similarity
Who Gets What and Why (Alvin Roth)
reference: Hurwicz, L., & Reiter, S. (2006). Designing Economic Mechanisms. Cambridge University Press.

name: Mediation analysis
origin: Baron & Kenny, 1986; bootstrap indirect effects by Preacher & Hayes, 2004/2008; causal mediation by Robins, Greenland and Pearl, 1992-2001
summary: Decomposes the effect of a cause on an outcome into a direct path and an indirect path through a mechanism, quantifying how a design change works.
description: Mediation analysis estimates whether X affects Y through an intermediate variable M, for example a redesign increases adoption because it raises perceived trust. The indirect effect (the product of the X-to-M and M-to-Y paths) is tested with bootstrap confidence intervals rather than the outdated Baron and Kenny causal-steps logic. Modern causal mediation makes the assumptions explicit: no unmeasured confounding of X-M, M-Y and X-Y, and no M-Y confounder affected by X. Rigour requires temporal ordering (M measured after X and before Y), ideally a randomised X, and sensitivity analysis for unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding. It is the quantitative bridge between a qualitative mechanism story and a measurable causal claim.
steps: Specify the mechanism from qualitative evidence and draw it as a causal diagram including likely confounders of M and Y.
Design measurement so X precedes M and M precedes Y; randomise X where possible.
Fit the mediator model (M on X plus covariates) and the outcome model (Y on X and M plus covariates).
Estimate the indirect effect with 5,000 or more bootstrap resamples and report the 95% percentile or bias-corrected interval.
Report the proportion mediated with caution and run a sensitivity analysis (e.g. the rho parameter of Imai et al.) for unmeasured M-Y confounding.
Interpret the mechanism in design terms and state the assumptions that would overturn it.
outputs: Direct, indirect and total effect estimates with bootstrap intervals, proportion mediated, a sensitivity analysis and a defensible mechanism statement.
useWhen: When you know or have tested that a change works and need to show why, or when choosing which intermediate experience metric to optimise.
avoidWhen: Avoid with cross-sectional single-survey data where ordering is unknown, when X is not randomised and confounders are unmeasured, or with tiny samples; use qualitative process tracing or a randomised mediator manipulation instead.
whyLost: Baron and Kenny's steps were widely misused and discredited, and the modern causal version needs assumptions most UX teams never articulate. It stayed in psychology and epidemiology.
whereToUse: Trust and adoption research in fintech, AI product explainability effects, onboarding mechanism studies, and justifying north-star intermediate metrics.
example: An experiment shows a new portfolio summary raises weekly retention. Mediation analysis finds 60% of the effect runs through reduced anxiety scores measured on day 3, so the team prioritises anxiety-reducing features over more data density.
sources: Applied Predictive Modeling (Max Kuhn & Kjell Johnson)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chris Chapman & Elea McDonnell Feit)
Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis (Andrew Hayes)
Explanation in Causal Inference (Tyler VanderWeele)
Applied Predictive Modeling (Kuhn & Johnson)
R for Marketing Research (Chapman & Feit)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 43 — Regression, Moderation & Mediation for UX Researchers
reference: Hayes, A. F. (2022) Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis, 3rd ed. Guilford Press.

name: Mediation analysis across activity hierarchy
origin: Aleksei Leont'ev's activity-action-operation hierarchy, 1978; applied to HCI by Kuutti (1996) and Kaptelinin and Nardi (2006)
summary: Analyses how tools mediate work at three levels, activity (motive), action (goal) and operation (conditions), and how use shifts between levels as skills automate or break down.
description: Leont'ev described human activity as a hierarchy: activities driven by motives, actions directed at conscious goals, and operations performed automatically under conditions. Tools mediate each level differently. As skill develops, actions become operations (automated); when breakdowns occur, operations become conscious actions again. Mediation analysis maps how a tool supports each level and examines transitions. A well-designed tool supports the motive, makes goals achievable and lets operations automate; poor tools force operations back into conscious attention. In UX this connects interface details to deeper motives, and explains why small interaction friction disrupts expert work. Rigour comes from observing breakdowns where levels shift, and from interviews that connect actions to motives.
steps: Identify the activity and its motive through interviews (for example 'restoring patient health safely').
Decompose into actions with goals and operations with conditions, through observation and task analysis.
For each level, describe how the tool mediates it: what it supports, constrains or ignores.
Observe breakdowns where operations become conscious actions and record the trigger (at least 3-5 work sessions).
Identify misalignments, such as tools optimised for actions that do not serve the motive.
Propose design changes that support automation of operations and alignment with motives.
outputs: A three-level activity hierarchy model, mediation analysis per level, breakdown records, and design recommendations.
useWhen: When studying tools in professional practice, explaining why technically usable tools disrupt work, or connecting UI decisions to motives.
avoidWhen: When you need quick usability findings on discrete tasks; use usability testing or HTA.
whyLost: Activity theory's hierarchy was influential in 1990s HCI but was displaced by simpler task analysis and jobs-to-be-done framing.
whereToUse: Clinical tools, professional creative software, enterprise workflows, and AI assistants for experts.
example: Surgeons' instrument swaps are automated operations on their old system, but on the new robot a confirmation dialog forces them into conscious action mid-procedure. Analysis shows this undermines the motive of uninterrupted focus, and the dialog is replaced by a reversible action.
sources: Newell, A., Unified Theories of Cognition (1990)
Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
Unified Theories of Cognition (Newell)
Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (Hollnagel)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 15 — Activity Theory, Contradictions & the Zone of Proximal Development
reference: Kaptelinin, V. & Nardi, B. A. (2006). Acting with Technology: Activity Theory and Interaction Design. MIT Press.

name: Member Checking
origin: Lincoln & Guba, 1985
summary: Sharing specific interpretations with a diverse subsample of participants to check resonance, treating disagreement as data rather than as correction.
description: Member checking is the process of sharing your analytical interpretations with participants to check whether they recognise their experience in your analysis. It is NOT: showing participants a draft report, asking if they agree with your conclusions, or using participant approval as proof of validity. Participants are not co-authors of the analysis — they are informants about whether the interpretation resonates with their experience.
steps: What to share: Share your interpretation of specific themes — not the full report. "I noticed that several participants described a moment where they stopped trusting the system. I'm interpreting this as a trust collapse triggered by perceived unpredictability. Does this match your experience?"
How to ask: Open-ended, not leading. "Does this capture your experience?" not "Is this correct?" The former invites elaboration and correction; the latter invites agreement.
Who to check with: A purposive subsample of participants — those who represent diversity in your sample (not just the most articulate or most agreeable).

What to do with disagreement: Participant disagreement is data, not error correction. If a participant disagrees with your interpretation, ask: why do they see it differently? Is this a data-based correction or a politically motivated one? Document the disagreement and your reasoning.
outputs: Participant responses to specific interpretations, a record of agreements, elaborations and disagreements, and revised or qualified interpretations.
useWhen: When interpretations concern participants' own experience and meaning, especially across cultures, with marginalised groups, or where misinterpretation carries ethical risk.
avoidWhen: When findings concern behaviour participants cannot introspect on (use observation or analytics), or when sharing interpretations could cause harm or bias later waves of a longitudinal study.
whyLost: It decayed into sending participants a summary or asking 'did we get it right', which yields polite agreement and little validation.
whereToUse: Health and social care research, participatory design, global and cross-cultural studies, and co-design programmes with ongoing participant panels.
example: After interviews with gig workers about algorithmic pay, the team shares its interpretation of 'pay as gamble' with six varied participants. Two reject the gambling frame and describe it as 'being managed', refining the model.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

name: Membership Categorisation Analysis
origin: Harvey Sacks, 1972; developed by Stephen Hester and Peter Eglin, 1997
summary: Analyses how people invoke social categories, such as novice, admin or patient, and their bound activities to accomplish actions in talk and text, including interface language.
description: Membership Categorisation Analysis, founded by Harvey Sacks, examines how people use categories in practice. Categories belong to collections (membership categorisation devices, such as 'family' or 'stage of life') and carry category-bound activities and predicates: we expect certain things of a 'beginner' or an 'admin'. By invoking a category, speakers justify, excuse or account for actions ('I'm not a tech person, so...'). MCA collects these invocations from transcripts and user-generated text and analyses what they accomplish, what inferences they license and what they exclude. Applied to interfaces, it audits the categories a product imposes on users and checks them against those users apply to themselves. Rigour comes from grounding claims in actual category use rather than analyst-imposed labels.
steps: Identify category invocations: In interview transcripts or user-generated content, mark every moment where a category is explicitly or implicitly invoked: 'as a user,' 'for someone like me,' 'unlike professionals,' 'that's for tech people.'

Category-bound activities analysis: What activities does the invoked category make relevant? Categories come pre-loaded with expected activities — invoking 'novice' makes asking for help relevant; invoking 'expert' makes independent action relevant.
Category-based inference analysis: What do users assume follows from a category? 'This is a children's product' triggers a set of assumptions about safety, simplicity, and appropriate content.

Interface category audit: What categories does the interface's language and design invoke? 'Advanced Settings' invokes a category of user who is not the default — what does that categorisation do to users who find themselves on that page?
outputs: A catalogue of category invocations, category-bound activities and predicates, inference patterns, and an interface category audit comparing system labels with users' self-categorisations.
useWhen: Personas, roles, permissions or labelling are contested, users describe themselves in ways the product does not anticipate, or self-categorisation ('not a numbers person') affects engagement.
avoidWhen: You need behavioural measures or task performance; categories in talk are not demographics. For broader discourse and power questions, use Critical Discourse Analysis.
whyLost: It is a specialist offshoot of conversation analysis taught almost exclusively in sociology departments, and UX treats categories as segmentation variables rather than as things people do in talk.
whereToUse: Role and permission design, persona critique, onboarding self-selection ('I am a...'), community and marketplace labels, and health or finance products where identity affects engagement.
example: In interviews about an investing app, users repeatedly say 'I'm not an investor, I'm just saving'. MCA shows 'investor' is bound to risk-taking and expertise, so onboarding language is reframed around 'growing savings', lifting completion.
sources: Harvey Sacks: Lectures on Conversation
Handbook of Discourse Analysis
Conversation Analysis and Ethnomethodology (saylordotorg)
reference: Hester, S. & Eglin, P. (eds.) (1997). Culture in Action: Studies in Membership Categorization Analysis. University Press of America.

name: Memory Work
donor: Feminist sociology and qualitative sport and leisure research
origin: Collective memory-work, usually traced to Frigga Haug's group in Germany; cited by Veal and Darcy via Onyx and Small (2001) and Markula and Friend (2005)
summary: Participants each write a short account of a remembered experience on the topic, then read the accounts aloud and analyse them together as a group.
description: Memory work is a structured way of eliciting people's memories of events, which Veal and Darcy describe as a focus group aided by individual writing. Each participant writes a short account of a specific experience related to the research topic, for example power relationships in a sport organisation. The written accounts are read aloud in a group session and discussed, and the discussion may be followed by further writing or interviews. Writing first gives each person time to recall an episode in detail and in their own words before group dynamics take hold, while the group discussion brings out common patterns, differences and the taken-for-granted assumptions inside each story. In its original collective form participants act as co-researchers, analysing their own stories rather than handing them to a researcher. For UX it offers a route into experiences that are emotional, social or embarrassing, such as first encounters with a technology, moments of exclusion, or breakdowns of trust, and it fits co-design work where participants should own the interpretation. It needs a group with enough trust to share personal writing.
steps: Choose a focused trigger, such as 'a time when an app made you feel left out', and recruit a small group with shared relevant experience.
Ask each person to write a short, concrete account of one specific episode, in the third person if that eases disclosure.
Bring the group together and have each account read aloud.
Discuss each account: what happened, what was assumed, what is missing, and how it compares with the others.
Identify common themes and contradictions across the accounts with the participants.
Optionally ask for rewritten or further accounts, or follow up with individual interviews.
Combine the texts and discussion notes into an analysis that participants can check.
outputs: A set of written memory accounts, recorded group discussion, and jointly identified themes about the experience.
useWhen: You want rich, reflective accounts of sensitive or formative experiences and want participants to take part in interpretation.
avoidWhen: Participants lack trust or time, writing would exclude some people, or you need behavioural detail best gathered by observation.
whyLost: It is little known outside feminist and educational research, and UX interviews and focus groups rarely include a structured individual writing stage.
whereToUse: Inclusive design research, onboarding and first-use experiences, trust and safety, workplace tools, community and co-design programmes.
example: To understand why older members stop using a club's app, six members each write about a time they felt shut out by club technology, read the stories aloud and find a shared theme of being told 'it is all on the app' at the moment they needed a person.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge. Onyx, J. and Small, J. (2001) Memory-work: the method. Qualitative Inquiry, 7(6), 773-786.

name: Mental Chronometry
origin: F. C. Donders (1868); Saul Sternberg (1969)
summary: Infers the duration and structure of mental processing stages from response times under systematically manipulated conditions.
description: Named in the treatise's borrowing matrix for cognitive science, mental chronometry measures response times to infer cognitive processes. Donders' subtraction method compares tasks differing by one stage; Sternberg's additive factors method shows that factors affecting the same stage interact while those affecting different stages add. Related laws (Hick-Hyman for choice, Fitts for pointing) give predictive models. In UX it lets researchers attribute slowness to specific stages, such as visual search, decision or response selection, and test whether a design change shortens the stage it targets. Rigour requires many trials, control of speed-accuracy trade-offs and appropriate RT distributions (often log-transformed or ex-Gaussian).
steps: Hypothesise processing stages involved in the interaction.
Design conditions that selectively manipulate each stage (for example number of options, visual clutter).
Collect many trials per participant and condition, recording RT and accuracy.
Clean and transform RTs; analyse with mixed models.
Test additivity or interactions to locate stage effects.
Translate findings into design choices that target the slow stage.
outputs: RT estimates per condition, stage attribution, design implications.
useWhen: Optimising high-frequency micro-interactions, menus, icons, alerts and decision screens.
avoidWhen: Long, multi-step tasks where RT is confounded by many stages; use KLM or task analysis.
whyLost: Considered lab psychology; UX measures overall task time instead of stage-level processing.
whereToUse: Icon recognition, menu design, notification triage, AR overlays, gaming UI.
example: Menu RT grows with item count far less with alphabetic ordering than with categorical ordering for known-item search, an interaction revealing the search stage dominates.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Donders FC (1868/1969) On the speed of mental processes. Acta Psychologica 30
Sternberg S (1969) The discovery of processing stages. Acta Psychologica 30
Posner MI (1978) Chronometric Explorations of Mind
reference: Sternberg S (1969) The discovery of processing stages: extensions of Donders' method. Acta Psychologica 30:276-315.

name: Mental Model Diagram
origin: Indi Young, 2008
summary: Builds a large diagram of users' tasks, thoughts and motivations grouped into towers and mental spaces, aligned beneath with the features that support them.
description: Indi Young's mental model diagram represents what people think, feel and do while pursuing a purpose, independent of any product. Non-directed interviews are transcribed and decomposed into atomic task-like behaviours, which are grouped bottom-up into towers and then into mental spaces arranged left to right across the diagram. Beneath a horizontal line, the team maps the features, services and content that currently support each tower. Gaps and weak support become opportunity areas, while the upper half remains stable over years because it describes people rather than technology. Rigour comes from deep, non-directed interviewing, faithful extraction of participants' own reasoning, and disciplined bottom-up grouping that resists imposing product categories.
steps: Step 1: Conduct 8–15 behavioral interviews.
Step 2: Extract behaviors and motivations as individual 'task' statements.
Step 3: Group related tasks into 'mental space' towers.
Step 4: Align existing product features to towers.
Step 5: Identify alignment gaps.
Build: a visual diagram with user behaviors above a horizontal line and product features below.
Width of alignment = product-market fit visualization.
outputs: A mental model diagram with towers and mental spaces, a support layer of current features, gap analysis and opportunity areas.
useWhen: Strategy and discovery work on broad problem spaces where you need a durable map of user reasoning independent of the current product, to find gaps and align teams.
avoidWhen: Avoid for narrow usability questions or when time is short; the full method needs many non-directed interviews and substantial synthesis. Use journey mapping or a jobs-to-be-done analysis for lighter needs.
whyLost: The full method is labour-intensive; 'mental model' became a loose phrase in UX, and the diagram was replaced by quicker journey maps.
whereToUse: Product gap analysis, roadmap prioritization, feature discovery research, product strategy validation.
example: A bank interviews 24 people about managing household money and builds a diagram with towers like 'decide whether we can afford it'; the support layer shows no feature addresses joint decision-making between partners.
sources: Mental Models — Indi Young
Mental Models
reference: Young I (2008) Mental Models: Aligning Design Strategy with Human Behavior. Rosenfeld Media

name: Mental Model Elicitation (Expected IA)
origin: Kenneth Craik, 1943 (mental models); expected-IA protocol in Gopinath, 2025
summary: Short contextual interviews asking where users expect to find a function and why, sketched as an 'expected IA' and compared with the real IA to predict misroutes.
description: Mental models are users' internal guesses of where something should be; when they do not match the information architecture, users wander, backtrack or give up. In the forward-thinking playbook the method is deliberately light: 4–8 quick contextual interviews with a prompt such as 'If you wanted to set a price alert, where would you look first? Why?', simple diagrams of each participant's expected IA, and a comparison with the actual IA. In the worked example 5 of 8 participants said alerts should be under Markets while the app placed them under Notifications, a mismatch that predicts confusion before any tree test. Verbatims and sketches are compiled in one worksheet and coded with short low-granularity labels such as 'Alerts under Markets' or 'Notifications = OS updates'. Combined with CPM-GOMS, it yields a falsifiable hypothesis about why and where time will spike.
steps: Choose the target functions whose location is in question.
Run 4–8 quick contextual interviews asking where participants would look first and why.
Sketch each participant's expected IA as a simple diagram.
Compile verbatims and sketches into one worksheet (participant, exact quote, expected IA, initial hunch).
Code utterances with short labels and count agreement (e.g. 5/8 expect Alerts under Markets).
Compare expected and actual IA and write a falsifiable misroute hypothesis for tree testing.
outputs: Expected-IA sketches, label codes, agreement counts and a misroute hypothesis.
useWhen: Early in IA work or before a tree test, to predict where and why users will misroute.
avoidWhen: When you need quantitative findability evidence; follow up with a tree test or first-click test.
whyLost: Mental-model research survives in UX, though often as an unstructured conversation rather than a coded comparison with the actual IA.
whereToUse: Navigation redesigns, fintech feature placement, enterprise settings, IA migrations.
example: Five of eight trading-app users say price alerts belong under Markets while the app buries them in Notifications, predicting misroutes later confirmed at 31% in a tree test.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Mental Models
Cognitive Psychology

name: Mentalese consistency check
donor: Philosophy of mind and cognitive science
origin: Jerry Fodor's language of thought hypothesis, 1975
summary: Tests whether users across roles hold the same underlying concepts for interface terms, by eliciting their conceptual representations rather than their vocabulary.
description: Fodor's language of thought hypothesis proposes that thinking occurs in an internal representational system, 'Mentalese', distinct from natural language. Whatever its status as a theory, it suggests a useful distinction for UX: users can share a word but not a concept, or share a concept expressed with different words. A Mentalese consistency check elicits the concepts users attach to key terms using non-verbal or structured methods, such as sorting scenarios, predicting outcomes, or drawing what the term refers to, and compares these across roles and with the system's model. Where concepts diverge under the same word, the interface is ambiguous even if every label passes a copy review. Rigour comes from scenario-based elicitation and systematic comparison across groups.
steps: Select critical terms used across roles (for example 'case', 'save', 'complete', 'session').
Write 8-12 scenarios illustrating different possible referents or effects of each term.
Ask participants from each role (5-8 per role) to judge which scenarios the term applies to and predict system effects.
Compare judgement patterns across roles and with the system's actual model; compute agreement (for example Fleiss' kappa within and between roles).
Flag terms with between-role agreement below about 0.6 or mismatches with system behaviour.
Resolve by splitting terms, adding qualifiers, or adjusting system behaviour, then re-check.
outputs: Concept maps per term and role, agreement statistics, divergences from the system model, and terminology changes.
useWhen: For multi-role systems, cross-disciplinary products, and terms carried across organisations or languages.
avoidWhen: When users are homogeneous and terminology is standard; a simple vocabulary review is enough.
whyLost: The language of thought is a philosophical hypothesis with no tradition of applied use; the practical idea of eliciting concepts rather than words has not been named in UX.
whereToUse: Healthcare systems shared by clinicians and administrators, legal tech, enterprise platforms, and AI assistants interpreting user intent.
example: Surgeons, nurses and administrators all endorse 'Complete' as a clear label, but scenario judgements show surgeons mean 'procedure finished', nurses 'counts reconciled' and admins 'billed'. Agreement between roles is 0.31, so the state is split into three explicit statuses.
