name: Meta-Analysis of UX Studies
origin: Gene Glass (1976) coined the term; DerSimonian and Laird (1986) random-effects model; Cochrane Collaboration (1993)
summary: Statistically combines effect sizes from multiple studies or experiments, estimating an overall effect, its heterogeneity and moderators.
description: Organisations run hundreds of studies and experiments but rarely combine them. Meta-analysis converts each study's result into a common effect size with its variance, pools them (fixed or random effects, the latter allowing true effects to vary), and quantifies heterogeneity (tau squared, I squared, prediction intervals). Meta-regression explores moderators like platform or market. Publication bias checks (funnel plots, Egger's test) are directly relevant to internal research too, as unreported null tests bias institutional memory. Within a company, meta-analysis of past A/B tests yields realistic priors and shows whether design patterns generalise.
steps: Define the question and inclusion criteria for studies or experiments.
Extract effect sizes and their standard errors consistently (e.g. log odds ratios, standardised mean differences).
Fit a random-effects model and report the pooled effect, confidence interval and prediction interval.
Quantify heterogeneity (I squared, tau) and run meta-regression on planned moderators.
Assess small-study or publication bias with funnel plots and sensitivity analyses.
Summarise implications, including when the pattern should not be expected to replicate.
outputs: Pooled effect sizes, heterogeneity estimates, moderator analyses, forest plots and bias assessment.
useWhen: Synthesising multiple experiments or studies on a recurring design question, or building priors.
avoidWhen: Studies too heterogeneous in question or measures to combine meaningfully; use narrative or qualitative synthesis.
whyLost: UX research operations focus on new studies and repositories of insights, not quantitative synthesis.
whereToUse: A/B test programmes, design pattern libraries, benchmark programmes, academic HCI syntheses.
example: A retailer meta-analyses 47 past tests of urgency messages. The pooled effect on conversion is small (+0.8%) with wide prediction interval and evidence of small-study effects, so urgency is no longer a default recommendation.
sources: Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins & Rothstein, Introduction to Meta-Analysis (2009)
DerSimonian & Laird, Meta-analysis in clinical trials (1986), Controlled Clinical Trials
Higgins et al. (eds.), Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (2019)

name: Metaphor Identification Procedure (MIP/MIPVU)
origin: George Lakoff and Mark Johnson (Metaphors We Live By, 1980); Pragglejaz Group (2007); Gerard Steen et al. (MIPVU, 2010)
summary: Reliably identifies metaphorically used words in user language and groups them into conceptual metaphors that reveal how users think about a product or domain.
description: Conceptual metaphor theory holds that we understand abstract domains through concrete ones (ARGUMENT IS WAR; TIME IS MONEY). Identifying metaphors in discourse used to be intuitive and unreliable. The Pragglejaz Group's MIP gives a step-by-step procedure: read the text, determine lexical units, establish each unit's contextual meaning, check whether it has a more basic meaning in other contexts, and mark it metaphorical if the contextual meaning contrasts with but can be understood by comparison with the basic one. MIPVU refines this and reports high inter-coder reliability. Applied to interviews and reviews, it reveals users' conceptual models (the cloud as a place, AI as a person, money as water) that shape expectations and errors.
steps: Select texts: interview transcripts, reviews, support chats about the domain.
Apply MIP/MIPVU word by word: determine lexical units, contextual and basic meanings, and mark metaphor-related words, using a dictionary such as Macmillan for basic senses.
Check reliability with two coders on a sample (kappa typically above 0.8 is attainable).
Group metaphor-related words into source-target mappings (e.g. DATA IS A LIQUID: leaks, flows, streams).
Compare dominant metaphors across segments and contexts, and relate them to expectations and errors.
Use productive metaphors in interface language and avoid misleading ones.
outputs: Reliably coded metaphors, conceptual metaphor inventory, segment comparisons and language recommendations.
useWhen: Understanding how users conceptualise abstract products (cloud, AI, privacy, money) and designing interface metaphors and copy.
avoidWhen: Concrete, task-focused language where metaphor is minimal.
whyLost: Cognitive linguistics methods stayed in linguistics; UX discusses interface metaphors without analysing users' metaphors systematically.
whereToUse: AI assistants, privacy settings, cloud storage, personal finance, health conditions.
example: MIPVU analysis of 40 interviews about an AI assistant finds users predominantly use AI IS AN EMPLOYEE metaphors, expecting accountability; the product adds visible 'work history' and correction features.
sources: Pragglejaz Group, MIP: A method for identifying metaphorically used words in discourse (2007), Metaphor and Symbol
Steen et al., A Method for Linguistic Metaphor Identification: From MIP to MIPVU (2010)
Lakoff & Johnson, Metaphors We Live By (1980)

name: Metaphor-based icon simulation test
donor: Cognitive linguistics (conceptual metaphor theory) and icon comprehension testing
origin: Combines Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual metaphor theory (1980) with icon comprehension testing traditions (ISO 9186) and embodied simulation accounts of meaning (Barsalou, 1999)
summary: Tests whether users possess the source-domain experience a metaphorical icon depends on, by asking them to simulate and predict what tapping it will do.
description: Most interface icons are metaphors: a trash can for deletion, a floppy disk for saving, a wallet for stored value. Embodied cognition holds that understanding a metaphor involves mentally simulating the source experience. If a user has never handled the source object, or handles it differently, the simulation fails or produces the wrong prediction. This test separates two layers that ordinary icon tests conflate: recognising the depicted object, and simulating the right action from it. Participants first name the object, then describe what they would expect to happen if they used it, and finally predict the system consequence. Rigour comes from scoring each layer separately, sampling users with different source-domain experience, and using pre-set pass thresholds rather than impressionistic judgement.
steps: Select the metaphorical icons that carry critical or irreversible actions, and for each write down the intended source object, the intended simulated action and the intended system consequence.

Recruit at least 15 to 20 participants per segment, deliberately including users whose material environment differs from the designers' (for example no desktop computers, no paper filing, cash-only economies).
Present each icon in isolation, then in context, and ask in sequence: 'What object is this?', 'What would you do with this object in daily life?', 'If you tap it here, what will happen?'
Score each response on three layers (object recognised, source action correct, system consequence correct) using a pre-agreed rubric, with a second scorer on at least 25% of responses.

Apply a pass criterion per icon, for example at least 85% correct system-consequence predictions and no more than 5% critical confusions for destructive actions, following ANSI Z535.3 practice for safety symbols, or 66.7% under ISO 9186 for general symbols.
Diagnose failures by layer: object not recognised means a depiction problem; object recognised but wrong action means a metaphor transfer failure requiring a different source domain or a text label.
Redesign and retest failing icons with fresh participants until they meet the threshold.
outputs: Per-icon, per-segment scores on recognition, source-action simulation and consequence prediction, a list of critical confusions, and design recommendations by failure layer.
useWhen: Shipping icon-heavy interfaces to users with different material cultures, literacy levels or ages; icons trigger irreversible or financial actions.
avoidWhen: Icons are always paired with clear text labels and users read them, or the icon set is a mature platform convention for an expert audience; use a standard first-click test.
whyLost: UX icon testing collapsed into simple recognition or preference tests, and the embodied simulation layer from cognitive science was never operationalised, so failures caused by missing source experience go undiagnosed.
whereToUse: Low-literacy and first-time smartphone users, healthcare devices, kiosks, cross-cultural apps, children's products.
example: In a clinic tablet app, rural health workers recognised the trash-can icon as a bin but simulated 'storing for later', because at their clinic waste paper was kept and reused. Destructive-action predictions were only 40% correct; adding the label 'Delete forever' and a confirmation raised correct predictions above 90%.
sources: Women Fire & Dangerous Things (Lakoff)
Metaphors We Live By (Lakoff)
Methods Atlas — frame audit (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 19 — Neural Framing & the Architecture of Meaning

name: Method Lifecycle Analysis
donor: Diffusion of innovations / history of science
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Places a method on a lifecycle of lab development, early adoption, mainstream simplification, decline and obsolescence, to anticipate degradation.
description: The treatise argues methods have lifecycles. A method begins in an academic or research lab, refined against theory and validated in controlled studies. Early adoption follows among practitioners close to the research context through training, associations or conferences. If it reaches critical mass it enters mainstream practice, typically becoming simplified, standardised and stripped of theoretical nuance. Decline then follows from some combination of the seven causes. Lifecycle analysis shows that the mainstream phase itself is where vestigialisation happens, so organisations can protect a method's rigour while scaling it, for example by maintaining a canonical protocol, training and quality checks.
steps: Gather the method's publication history, adoption evidence and current practice descriptions.
Date its phases: development, early adoption, mainstream, decline.
Compare current practice with the original protocol to measure simplification.
Identify at-risk elements (theory, analysis steps, quality checks).
Plan protections: canonical protocols, training, quality review.
Revisit periodically.
outputs: Lifecycle timeline, fidelity gap analysis, protection plan.
useWhen: Scaling a method across a large team, or auditing whether a popular method has degraded.
avoidWhen: Brand-new methods with no adoption history.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: ResearchOps, method playbooks, UX education.
example: A team scaling 'jobs-to-be-done' interviews to 30 PMs documents the original protocol and adds review checklists to avoid it becoming a vestigial survey.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rogers EM (2003) Diffusion of Innovations. 5th ed
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 19/31 (Lifecycle of a UX Method).

name: Method Recovery Priority Index
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Rates lost and cross-domain methods on evidence base, recovery feasibility and expected impact (1-5 stars) to assign HIGH or MEDIUM revival priority.
description: The treatise's appendix rates candidate methods on three dimensions: Current Evidence Base (how much validated research supports the method), Recovery Feasibility (how practical it is to revive in contemporary contexts) and Expected Impact (the improvement in UX outcomes widespread recovery would bring), each scored one to five stars, with an overall priority of HIGH or MEDIUM. For example, Wizard of Oz scores 4/5/5 (HIGH), Braun and Clarke thematic analysis 5/5/5 (HIGH), and CWA and STAMP/STPA 5/2/5 (MEDIUM because feasibility is low). The index makes recovery investment explicit and comparable, and can be applied by any team to its own candidate methods with local feasibility judgements.
steps: List candidate methods for recovery or adoption.
Rate evidence base from the literature (1-5).
Rate recovery feasibility given skills, tools, time and organisational context (1-5).
Rate expected impact on decisions and user outcomes (1-5).
Assign priority (for example HIGH when impact and evidence are high and feasibility is at least 3).
Plan recovery for HIGH methods and revisit ratings annually.
outputs: Scored priority table, recovery roadmap.
useWhen: Planning training, method adoption and ResearchOps investment.
avoidWhen: Single-study method choice.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: Research leadership planning, curricula, professional association agendas.
example: A research org scores 15 methods; DiD and multilevel modelling score HIGH with feasibility 4 given its data team, so both become quarterly training priorities.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Drummond MF et al. (2015) Methods for the Economic Evaluation of Health Care Programmes (priority-setting analogue)
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Appendix B (Method Recovery Priority Index).

name: Methodological Diversity as Risk Management
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Treats a research organisation's method range as a portfolio, maintaining dormant competence in diverse methods as insurance against changing conditions.
description: The treatise draws on agricultural monoculture: identical crops are maximally efficient in good conditions and maximally vulnerable to pathogens and stress. A research organisation relying on one methodological approach is efficient when it fits and maximally vulnerable when conditions change (new technologies, new questions, regulation). Methodological diversity is therefore organisational risk management, and maintaining dormant capacity is like insurance: costly when unused, valuable when needed. The practice audits the method portfolio against anticipated questions, identifies concentration risk (for example only interviews and A/B tests) and invests in training, partnerships and protocols to keep a broader range available.
steps: Inventory methods the team can execute competently today.
Map them against the question types the organisation faces or may face.
Identify concentration risk and uncovered question types.
Decide which dormant capacities to maintain (training, partners, templates).
Exercise dormant methods periodically through small projects.
Review the portfolio annually alongside strategy changes.
outputs: Method portfolio map, coverage gaps, capacity maintenance plan.
useWhen: Research org planning, after strategy shifts (for example AI products, regulation).
avoidWhen: Very small teams where focus is necessary; partner externally instead.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: Research leadership, ResearchOps, agencies, in-house labs.
example: A fintech research team relying on interviews and A/B tests adds causal inference and UFMEA capacity before entering regulated lending, which pays off in the regulator's first review.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Markowitz H (1952) Portfolio selection. J Finance (portfolio analogy)
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 34 (Methodological Diversity as Risk Management).

name: Metric-wellbeing gap measurement
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Methods Atlas; informed by subjective wellbeing measurement (Diener, 1984) and digital wellbeing research
summary: Quantifies the divergence between the metric a product optimises and users' measured wellbeing or long-term outcomes, showing when success on the metric masks harm.
description: Products often succeed on engagement metrics while users feel worse or make poorer decisions. This method pairs behavioural metrics with validated wellbeing or outcome measures for the same users (such as anxiety, decision confidence, financial health or regret) collected through surveys or experience sampling, and models the relationship. A gap exists when high metric values coincide with flat or worse wellbeing, or when increments in the metric yield diminishing or negative wellbeing returns. Rigour requires validated wellbeing instruments, linking at the user level with consent, longitudinal measurement to separate cause from selection, and segment-level analysis because harms often concentrate in vulnerable groups.
steps: Select the optimised metric (e.g. weekly sessions) and validated wellbeing or outcome measures relevant to the domain (e.g. a financial anxiety scale).
Recruit a consented panel of at least 300-500 users and link survey responses to behavioural data.
Measure wellbeing at baseline and again after 4-12 weeks, or use experience sampling around product use.
Model wellbeing as a function of the metric, plotting the relationship and testing for non-linearity.
Compute a gap index, such as the proportion of high-metric users in the bottom wellbeing quartile, by segment.
Report the gap with guardrail recommendations and, where possible, test alternative designs experimentally.
outputs: A quantified metric-wellbeing relationship, gap indices by segment and recommendations for guardrails or objective changes.
useWhen: When engagement or conversion is optimised in domains where user wellbeing or outcomes matter, such as finance, health, social and gaming.
avoidWhen: Avoid when no validated wellbeing measure fits the domain, without user consent for linking data, or for low-stakes utilities.
whyLost: Product teams track what is easy to log; wellbeing measurement requires surveys, consent and longitudinal design that rarely fit sprint cycles.
whereToUse: Investment and trading apps, social media, mobile games, health and fitness apps, AI companions.
example: An investment platform links engagement data with a financial anxiety scale for 800 users. The top engagement decile has anxiety scores 0.6 SD higher than median users, prompting a calmer notification strategy and an anxiety guardrail.

Artificial Intelligence for Humans (Jeff Heaton)

Diener (1984) Subjective well-being
Peters, Calvo & Ryan (2018) Designing for motivation, engagement and wellbeing in digital experience

name: Micro-Phenomenological Interviewing
origin: Pierre Vermersch (1994, explicitation interview); Claire Petitmengin (2006)
summary: Guides participants to re-live a specific moment and describe its pre-reflective, moment-by-moment texture, bypassing narrative rationalisation.
description: Micro-phenomenological interviewing accesses the pre-reflective structure of lived experience: what was happening before the participant conceptualised and narrativised it. The interviewer helps the participant select a singular, specific moment, re-evoke it sensorially and describe its unfolding with content-free questions ('At that precise moment, what were you paying attention to? What did you notice first? How did you know?'), avoiding 'why' questions that trigger justification. Responses are analysed for diachronic (temporal unfolding) and synchronic (configuration at a moment) structures. The treatise contrasts it with standard interviews that elicit narrative reconstructions: the data are more granular and less shaped by post-hoc rationalisation. Rated MEDIUM priority.
steps: Have the participant choose one specific, recent instance of the experience.
Guide evocation of the moment through sensory and contextual cues until they speak in present tense.
Ask content-free 'how' and 'what' questions to unfold the experience step by step; avoid 'why'.
Reformulate the participant's words back and probe gaps in the sequence.
Transcribe and analyse diachronic and synchronic structure across participants.
Derive generic structures and design implications for the micro-moments.
outputs: Fine-grained experiential descriptions, diachronic and synchronic structures, micro-moment insights.
useWhen: First-use moments, emotional or intuitive decisions, flow states, moments of trust or hesitation.
avoidWhen: Broad attitudes or prevalence questions; large samples.
whyLost: Never migrated from consciousness studies; requires substantial interviewer training.
whereToUse: Onboarding first impressions, purchase hesitation, AI trust judgements, creative tool flow, health symptom checking.
example: Interviews about the moment users hesitated before confirming a crypto transfer reveal a pre-reflective 'double check the first and last characters' gesture; the design highlights those characters.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Petitmengin C (2006) Describing one's subjective experience in the second person. Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences 5:229-269
Vermersch P (1994) L'entretien d'explicitation
Petitmengin C et al. (2019) Discovering the structures of lived experience. Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences
reference: Petitmengin C (2006) Describing one's subjective experience in the second person: an interview method for the science of consciousness. Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences 5(3-4):229-269.

name: Micro-Phenomenology and Explicitation Interview
origin: Pierre Vermersch, 1994 (explicitation interview); Claire Petitmengin, 2006 (micro-phenomenology)
summary: A guided interview that helps participants re-evoke a specific singular moment and describe its fine-grained, pre-reflective experiential structure, which ordinary recall misses.
description: Micro-phenomenology (Claire Petitmengin) and the Explicitation Interview (Pierre Vermersch) are techniques for accessing the detailed lived experience of specific moments — including the pre-reflective, bodily, and implicitly enacted aspects of experience that ordinary retrospective description cannot reach. Where standard phenomenological interviews produce generalised accounts ('usually when I do X...'), micro-phenomenology aims at one specific singular moment: 'right at that moment, what was happening in your experience?' Applied to UX: it accesses the moment-by-moment phenomenological texture of a specific interaction — the exact sequence of awarenesses, doubts, decisions, and embodied responses that constitute the interaction as it is lived.
steps: Select a specific singular moment: 'I'd like to understand what happened for you at one very specific moment — the moment when you realised something wasn't working as expected. Can you go back to that particular moment?'

Evocation posture: Help the participant return experientially to the moment — not report about it. Use: 'As you return to that moment — what do you notice first?' 'As you are there, what is happening in your body?' The present-tense phrasing is deliberate.

Sequential micro-structure: Once the participant is in evocation, explore the temporal micro-structure: 'Just before that, what happened?' 'At that precise moment, what was the first thing you were aware of?' 'And then?'

Pre-reflective access: Guide the participant toward what was happening before they started thinking about it: 'Before you had time to think — what was already happening?' 'Was there a bodily sense of anything?'
Analysis: Build a detailed temporal map of the experiential sequence for this singular moment. Compare across participants to identify shared experiential structures.
outputs: Detailed descriptions of singular moments, temporal and diachronic maps of experience, synchronic structure of each phase, and generic structures across participants.
useWhen: You need to understand fast, implicit moments such as the instant of distrust, a decision to abandon, an insight or an error, where users give generalised or rationalised accounts.
avoidWhen: You need breadth across many users or general opinions; use semi-structured interviews or surveys. Avoid if interviewers are untrained, as leading questions destroy the method.
whyLost: It is rooted in French phenomenology and requires extensive training in non-inductive questioning, so it has stayed in cognitive science and education research.
whereToUse: Trust and security decisions, error and recovery moments, expert decision-making, meditation and wellbeing products, and responses to AI outputs.
example: Investigating why users ignore a phishing warning, a researcher asks each participant to re-evoke one specific instance. Descriptions reveal a felt sense of 'this is routine' forming before the warning was read, informing warning timing.
sources: Petitmengin (Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences 2006)
Vermersch Explicitation Interview
Editorial: Working with Others' Experience (Springer, 2023)
reference: Petitmengin, C. (2006). Describing one's subjective experience in the second person. Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences, 5, 229-269.

name: Miles & Huberman Qualitative Analysis Cycle
origin: Matthew B. Miles & A. Michael Huberman, 1984/1994 (data displays); five-phase compiling-to-concluding cycle associated with Robert K. Yin, 2011
summary: A staged qualitative analysis cycle (compile, disassemble, reassemble and array, interpret, conclude) run alongside a project so qual evidence stays auditable from first interviews to final validation.
description: Vivek Gopinath's forward-thinking playbook attributes this cycle to Miles & Huberman and maps each phase to a loop stage: Compiling (Stage 1: raw mental-model quotes and sketches in one sheet), Disassembling (Stages 1–2: short codes for expectations and breakdowns, taxonomy coding with reliability), Reassembling/Arraying (Stages 2 and 4: participant × episode arrays and trajectory patterns), Interpreting (Stages 3 and 5: mechanism memos mapped to prescriptions) and Concluding (Stage 6: forecast versus actual, mechanism repair, residual risks). Miles and Huberman's lasting contribution is the systematic use of data displays such as matrices and arrays; the five-phase compiling-to-concluding sequence is most closely associated with Robert K. Yin. Its rigour lies in an audit trail where every claim can be traced back through arrays and codes to raw data.
steps: Compiling: gather verbatims, sketches and notes into one structured worksheet.
Disassembling: code utterances into short, low-granularity labels or taxonomy codes, with reliability checks where codes are counted.
Reassembling/Arraying: build participant × episode or trajectory arrays and sort them to reveal patterns.
Interpreting: write mechanism memos connecting patterns to quantitative results and prescriptions.
Concluding: compare forecast with actual, judge whether the mechanism was repaired, and document residual risks for the next loop.
outputs: An auditable chain of worksheets, codes, arrays, memos and conclusions.
useWhen: Any mixed-methods programme where qualitative evidence must remain traceable across stages.
avoidWhen: Quick one-off interviews where a lightweight synthesis suffices.
whyLost: Displays and staged analysis are standard in qualitative methodology, but UX synthesis has collapsed into sticky-note clustering without an audit trail.
whereToUse: Longitudinal UX programmes, mixed-methods studies, regulated domains needing traceability.
example: In a trading app programme, the team compiles mental-model quotes, codes them, arrays error episodes, writes mechanism memos and finally documents forecast versus actual, all in one traceable workbook.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M., & Saldaña, J. (2014). Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook (3rd ed.). SAGE.

name: Miles and Huberman Analytic Displays
aka: Miles and Huberman Data Display Analysis
origin: Matthew Miles & A. Michael Huberman, 1984 (Qualitative Data Analysis); 3rd ed. with Johnny Saldaña, 2014
summary: A three-part analytic system of data reduction, structured data displays (matrices, networks) and explicit conclusion verification for systematic applied qualitative analysis.
description: Miles and Huberman argued that qualitative analysis fails mostly because researchers keep data as unbroken text that cannot be overviewed. Their framework has three concurrent components: data reduction (memoing, coding, pattern noting), data display (case-ordered meta-matrices, conceptually ordered displays, time-ordered matrices, causal networks) and conclusion drawing with verification (negative cases, rival explanations, member checks, comparing cases where a finding should and should not appear). Displays are the analytic engine: rows of cases against columns of themes reveal within-case and cross-case patterns simultaneously. Their sourcebook catalogues dozens of display types with tactics for generating and testing meaning, making qualitative inference explicit, replicable and auditable.
steps: Write analytic memos and develop a start list of codes from your research questions, then code the data and note emerging patterns.
Choose a display suited to the question: a case-ordered meta-matrix for cross-participant comparison, a time-ordered matrix for change, or a causal network for explanation.
Populate cells with condensed summaries and short quotes, keeping a decision rule for what goes into each cell so displays are reproducible.
Read across rows and down columns to note patterns, contrasts, clusters and outliers; record each tentative conclusion as a memo.
Verify each conclusion using negative cases, rival explanations, checks with participants and comparison of cases where the finding should and should not hold.
Report the displays alongside conclusions so readers can see the evidence behind every claim.
outputs: Case-by-theme meta-matrices, time-ordered and conceptually ordered displays, causal network diagrams, and a list of verified conclusions with evidence.
useWhen: Multi-site or multi-segment studies, evaluation research, or any study with more than about ten cases where cross-case patterns and explanations must be defended.
avoidWhen: For a handful of usability sessions or purely exploratory immersion where premature structure would constrain discovery; use rapid debriefs or open coding instead.
whyLost: Spreadsheets of quotes and sticky-note walls replaced deliberate display design, and the sourcebook's density kept it within academic evaluation research.
whereToUse: Multi-market studies, enterprise rollouts across sites, service evaluations in health and public sector, and longitudinal programmes needing traceable synthesis.
example: A payments company studies merchant onboarding across five countries. A case-ordered meta-matrix (merchants by onboarding barriers) shows that document verification delays explain churn only where local IDs are not machine-readable, a pattern invisible in the per-market reports.
sources: Qualitative Data Analysis (Miles & Huberman) via Sage Handbook
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods
Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (Miles & Huberman)
The Inquiry Series, Vol II, Ch 29
reference: Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M. & Saldaña, J. (2014). Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook (3rd ed.). Sage.

extra.The Three Components: Data Reduction: Selecting, focusing, simplifying, abstracting, and transforming raw data. This includes: writing memos (analytic notes on what you are finding), coding (applying conceptual labels), and pattern noting (identifying recurring patterns before formal coding). Data reduction is not about removing data — it is about making it manageable and conceptually ordered. Data Display: Organised assemblies of information that allow conclusion drawing. Displays include: matrices (cases × themes), networks (showing relationships between concepts), causal flow charts, and taxonomies. The critical insight from Miles & Huberman: you cannot analyse what you cannot see. Most qual analysis fails because researchers keep their data as text, which is impossible to overview. Display tools make patterns visible. Conclusion Drawing & Verification: From the beginning of data collection, the researcher is noting regularities, patterns, explanations, causal flows, and propositions. These tentative conclusions are then verified against the data. Verification strategies: looking for negative cases, checking rival explanations, getting feedback from participants (member checking), comparing cases where the finding should be present and where it should be absent.
extra.Key Display Tools: Case-ordered descriptive meta-matrix: Rows = participants, columns = themes. Cells contain summary data for each participant on each theme. Shows both within-case patterns and cross-case comparisons simultaneously. Conceptually ordered display: Organises data around a conceptual framework (theoretical, causal, or experiential). Not organised by participant or time — organised by concept. Best for building toward theoretical explanation. Causal network: A network diagram showing the causal relationships between variables as found in the data. Not imposed before analysis — built from the data. Arrows indicate direction of causal influence; node sizes indicate centrality. Event-listing matrix: Chronicles events chronologically for each case. Used for process-oriented research where temporal sequence matters.

name: Minimum description length estimation
origin: Jorma Rissanen, 1978, building on Kolmogorov (1965) and Solomonoff (1964)
summary: Estimates interface complexity as the length of the shortest description needed to specify it, approximated by compression, to compare designs' structural regularity objectively.
description: Kolmogorov complexity defines the complexity of an object as the length of the shortest program that produces it; it is uncomputable, but the minimum description length principle approximates it by the shortest two-part code (model plus data given model). In UX the object is a layout, a navigation structure or an interaction grammar. A design built from a few consistent rules has a short description; a design full of exceptions has a long one. Practically, analysts encode screens or task flows in a structured representation and use a general compressor (gzip, LZMA) or a hand-built grammar to estimate description length, then compare variants. The rigour lies in fixing the encoding scheme before comparing, using normalised compression distance for pairs, and treating results as relative rankings, not absolute truths.
steps: Choose the object to measure (screen layouts, navigation graph, command grammar) and define a fixed, documented serialisation format for it.
Serialise each design variant identically, removing incidental noise such as IDs and timestamps.
Compress each serialisation with at least two compressors (for example gzip and LZMA) and record compressed size; use the ratio compressed/raw as the description-length estimate.
For pairs of designs or screens, compute normalised compression distance NCD = (C(xy) - min(C(x),C(y))) / max(C(x),C(y)) to quantify consistency across screens.
Alternatively write a two-part MDL code: count the rules needed to generate the design plus the exceptions not covered by rules.
Rank variants by estimated description length and test whether the ranking predicts learnability, for example via trials-to-criterion with 8-12 novice participants.
outputs: Description-length estimates per variant, a consistency (NCD) matrix across screens, a list of exceptions inflating complexity, and optionally validation against learnability data.
useWhen: When comparing design systems or interaction grammars for internal consistency; when arguing that a redesign is structurally simpler; when auditing sprawl in large enterprise products.
avoidWhen: When perceived visual complexity or aesthetics is the question (use rated complexity scales or eye tracking), or when designs cannot be serialised comparably. It is a structural proxy, not a usability measure.
whyLost: Kolmogorov complexity and MDL live in theoretical computer science and statistics; their uncomputability and abstract framing meant they never crossed into UX despite obvious relevance to consistency and learnability.
whereToUse: Design system governance, enterprise suites with many modules, command-line and gesture grammars, and AI agent tool schemas.
example: A SaaS team compares two settings architectures. Serialised as JSON and compressed, variant B is 31% shorter because its sections follow one pattern; a learnability study with 10 new admins confirms B reaches criterion in fewer trials.
sources: MacKay, D. J. C., Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003)

name: Missing data handling with MICE imputation
origin: Donald Rubin, 1987 (multiple imputation); van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011 (MICE)
summary: Replacing missing survey or behavioural values with multiple plausible imputations, then pooling results, so estimates are not biased by who skipped questions.
description: Missing data are rarely random: busy, dissatisfied or less literate users skip more items. Listwise deletion discards cases and biases estimates unless data are missing completely at random (MCAR); single mean imputation shrinks variance. Multiple imputation by chained equations models each incomplete variable from the others in turn, generates m complete datasets with appropriate random variation, analyses each, and pools estimates with Rubin's rules so uncertainty from missingness is reflected in standard errors. It is valid under missing at random (MAR) assumptions given the variables included. Rigour comes from diagnosing the missingness pattern, including auxiliary variables that predict missingness, imputing enough datasets, checking imputed distributions and running sensitivity analyses for missing-not-at-random scenarios.
steps: Describe the missingness pattern: percentage missing per variable and per respondent, and which variables predict missingness.
Decide the assumption (MCAR, MAR or MNAR) and include auxiliary variables related to missingness in the imputation model.
Impute with MICE (e.g. scikit-learn IterativeImputer with sample_posterior=True, or statsmodels MICE), using m of at least 20 or roughly the percentage of incomplete cases.
Check convergence across iterations and compare imputed with observed distributions.
Fit the analysis model on each imputed dataset and pool estimates and standard errors with Rubin's rules.
Compare against complete-case results and a delta-adjusted MNAR sensitivity scenario, and report all three.
outputs: Pooled estimates with correct standard errors, missingness diagnostics and a sensitivity comparison.
useWhen: Surveys with more than about 5% missing on key variables, longitudinal or diary studies with drop-out, and SEM or regression on incomplete data.
avoidWhen: Avoid for trivial missingness (under about 5% and plausibly MCAR), for data structurally not applicable (skip logic), or where full-information maximum likelihood in SEM handles missingness directly.
whyLost: Multiple imputation is standard in epidemiology and clinical trials but UX tools default to deleting incomplete responses, and the statistical machinery was never taught in UX curricula.
whereToUse: Satisfaction tracking, diary and longitudinal studies, health app outcome research and survey-to-SEM pipelines.
example: A diary study of a budgeting app loses 30% of entries by week three, mostly among users who stopped budgeting. MICE with engagement data as auxiliaries shows that the complete-case analysis overstated satisfaction by 0.6 points on a 7-point scale.

name: Mixed Methods Research
origin: Formalised by John Creswell, Abbas Tashakkori and Charles Teddlie, 1990s-2000s
summary: Deliberately integrates qualitative and quantitative methods in one study design so each compensates for the other's limits, with explicit points of integration.
description: Mixed methods research combines qualitative and quantitative data within a single study or programme, with a planned rationale for doing so. Creswell's core designs are convergent (collect both in parallel and compare), explanatory sequential (quantitative then qualitative to explain results) and exploratory sequential (qualitative then quantitative to test or measure what was found). What distinguishes mixed methods from simply running two studies is integration: deciding in advance where and how the strands connect, through sampling, instrument design, joint displays or meta-inferences. Rigour comes from stating the purpose of mixing (triangulation, complementarity, development, expansion), choosing a design accordingly, maintaining quality standards for each strand, and explicitly handling convergence and divergence between results rather than presenting them side by side.
steps: State the research questions and the purpose of mixing (e.g. explanation, development, triangulation).
Choose a design: convergent, explanatory sequential or exploratory sequential, and plan the timing and priority of strands.
Plan integration points: how sampling, instruments or analysis will connect the strands.
Collect and analyse each strand to its own quality standards.
Integrate results using joint displays that place quantitative and qualitative findings side by side by theme.
Draw meta-inferences, explicitly addressing convergence, complementarity and contradiction.
outputs: Mixed methods design diagram, strand findings, joint displays, integrated meta-inferences.
useWhen: Substantial research programmes, complex questions needing both breadth and depth, and decisions requiring both scale and explanation.
avoidWhen: Narrow questions answerable by one method, or when time does not allow both strands to meet quality standards.
whyLost: Still in use: Recognized as gold standard for complex UX questions combining breadth and depth.
whereToUse: Any substantial UX research program; product-market fit assessment; feature evaluation.
example: A telehealth provider ran an exploratory sequential study: 14 interviews identified five barriers to video consultations, which became survey items fielded to 2,000 patients, sizing each barrier by age group.

name: Mixed-Methods Behavioral Drift Detection Framework
donor: UX research, telemetry analytics and Bayesian modelling
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A five-step mixed-methods pipeline detecting when users stay active but engagement erodes qualitatively, from Honeycomb anchoring through surveys, telemetry, DriftScore modelling and bandit-optimised interventions.
description: Behavioral drift is defined as users remaining active while their engagement changes qualitatively: repeating shallow actions, ignoring micro-feedback such as toasts and nudges, and reducing variety even when frequency is constant. Drift is not churn; it is the erosion of desirability and trust while activity persists, and is detectable earlier. The pipeline: (1) anchor in Morville's UX Honeycomb with behavioural proxies; (2) a 30-item Honeycomb Likert survey with EFA plus semi-structured interviews and affinity mapping; (3) longitudinal telemetry tracking interaction entropy, category diversity, recommendation CTR and attention decay, with diary and interview signals; (4) Bayesian updating of drift risk and a 0–1 DriftScore; (5) adaptive interventions (re-onboarding, dynamic UI scaling, context-aware nudging) optimised with Thompson Sampling and validated by A/B and longitudinal interviews. Honeycomb is chosen over HTA (bounded tasks) and IFT (drift is the absence of foraging).
steps: Anchor drift dimensions in Morville's Honeycomb and map each to a behavioural proxy (e.g. Desirable → exploration beyond minimal path; Credible → adopting recommendations without double-checking).
Field a 30-item Likert survey aligned to the Honeycomb (worked example n = 300) and run EFA; the example yields Trust, Ease and Engagement factors (α = 0.84, 0.81, 0.86).

Run semi-structured interviews ('Tell me about the last time you discovered something new here') and affinity-map themes such as repetitive content, off-target recommendations and notification fatigue; double-code 30–40% with κ ≥ 0.70.
Track telemetry longitudinally: Shannon interaction entropy, categories per session, promo/recommendation CTR, scroll depth and dwell, and frequency versus variety.
Update drift probability with Bayes (prior 20%; after three sessions with entropy < 1.5 and CTR < 25%, posterior ≈ 65%) and compute a weighted 0–1 DriftScore.
Deploy adaptive interventions (personalised re-onboarding, dynamic UI scaling, context-aware nudging) and allocate them per user with Thompson Sampling.
Validate with A/B tests on DriftScore reduction and entropy lift plus longitudinal interviews, against a decision bar (e.g. entropy > 2.0 for 70% of active users within 4 weeks).
outputs: Honeycomb proxy map, factor structure with reliabilities, longitudinal drift indicators, per-user DriftScores and posterior drift risk, intervention policy and validation results.
useWhen: When a product works and is bug-free but engagement depth fades: users log in yet stop exploring or ignore nudges.
avoidWhen: For bounded task failures such as checkout errors (use HTA or usability testing) or when telemetry is unavailable.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath; engagement metrics usually track frequency, which hides qualitative erosion until churn.
whereToUse: E-commerce, OTT and content apps, calendars and productivity tools, fintech dashboards, recommendation-driven products.
example: In an e-commerce app with 10,000 users over 3 months, entropy fell from 2.6 to 1.2 and promo CTR from 47% to 19% while cart completion dipped only 62% to 58%; re-onboarding and adaptive nudges lifted entropy from 1.2 to 2.4 and promo CTR by 23 points.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study

name: Mixed-Methods Integration Typology
origin: Creswell & Plano Clark, 2007/2017
summary: Specifies how qualitative and quantitative strands connect (explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential, convergent, embedded) and integrates them deliberately, for example through joint displays.
description: Mixed-methods integration typology, formalised by Creswell and Plano Clark, distinguishes core designs by how qualitative and quantitative strands relate. In an explanatory sequential design, quantitative results are explained by subsequent qualitative work; in an exploratory sequential design, qualitative findings build an instrument or hypotheses tested quantitatively; in a convergent design, both strands are collected in parallel and compared; in embedded designs, one strand supports the other within a larger study. The defining requirement is integration: connecting samples, building instruments, merging results in joint displays, and drawing meta-inferences. Rigour comes from choosing the design for the question, specifying the point of integration in advance, and reporting where strands converge, complement or conflict.
steps: Declare your integration type before data collection. It determines sequence, priority, and purpose of each strand.
At the integration point: build a joint display showing both strands simultaneously.
For convergent designs: compare findings from each strand explicitly. Document both convergence and divergence. Divergence requires explanation.
outputs: A chosen integration design, an integration plan, joint displays linking qual and quant findings, and meta-inferences with explicit agreement or discordance.
useWhen: Studies combining analytics or surveys with interviews or observation, explaining quantitative patterns, building instruments from qualitative work, or triangulating findings.
avoidWhen: Avoid labelling a study 'mixed methods' when strands are merely run side by side; if integration is not planned, report them as separate studies.
whyLost: UX does mixed methods constantly but informally; formal designs and integration techniques from methodology literature are rarely used, so strands are not truly integrated.
whereToUse: Research program design, product development research, any study where multiple data types are needed.
example: Clustering of investment app users finds five archetypes; an explanatory sequential follow-up interviews six users per cluster, and a joint display links each cluster to the motives explaining its behaviour.
sources: Mixed Methods — short guide to applied mixed methods research
Oxford Handbook of Multimethod & Mixed Methods Research

name: Mock-up and Trial Sessions (Cooperative Prototyping)
origin: UTOPIA project (Ehn, Kyng, Bødker et al.), 1981-1985; Bødker and Grønbæk (1991)
summary: Users try out tangible mock-ups and early prototypes in simulated work situations, modifying them with designers on the spot.
description: In the UTOPIA project with Nordic graphic workers, designers built mock-ups of page-layout systems from cardboard, paper and slides so typographers could experience and evaluate future technology in realistic work situations. The treatise lists mock-up and trial sessions among the core Scandinavian methods. Cooperative prototyping (Bødker and Grønbæk) extended this with computer prototypes modified during sessions. The rigour lies in grounding evaluation in simulated real work, letting users' tacit skills surface through use rather than description, and treating the mock-up as a shared language rather than a test object. Unlike usability testing, users co-author changes.
steps: Build a mock-up or modifiable prototype representing the future system in its work setting.
Prepare realistic work scenarios drawn from current practice.
Have users enact the scenarios with the mock-up, thinking aloud and improvising.
Pause to discuss breakdowns and modify the mock-up together on the spot.
Record changes and the reasons users gave for them.
Iterate across sessions, gradually increasing fidelity.
outputs: Evolved mock-ups, documented breakdowns and user-authored changes, requirements grounded in tacit skill.
useWhen: Designing tools for skilled work where tacit knowledge matters and users should co-author design.
avoidWhen: When summative performance data is needed; use controlled usability testing.
whyLost: Collapsed into prototype testing where users evaluate but do not co-author; the political framing was lost.
whereToUse: Professional creative tools, clinical devices, factory HMIs, assistive technology.
example: Radiographers enact a scan-booking scenario with a foam-board console mock-up and rearrange controls to match their two-handed positioning routine; the arrangement is carried into the hardware design.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)

name: Mode Effects Analysis in Survey Administration
origin: de Leeuw, 2005; Dillman et al., 2014
summary: Checks and designs for how administering a survey by web, app, phone, in person or SMS changes who responds and how they answer.
description: Mode effects are differences in survey results caused by how a survey is administered. Modes differ in who they reach (selection effects) and in how respondents answer (measurement effects): interviewer-administered modes increase social desirability and acquiescence, aural modes produce recency effects while visual modes produce primacy effects, and small screens increase satisficing and item nonresponse. Mode effects analysis plans for these differences through unified mode design (constructing questions that function equivalently across modes), randomised split-mode experiments to estimate measurement effects, and statistical adjustment when modes are mixed. In UX it is essential when moving surveys between channels, combining in-app and email samples, or reaching low-literacy or offline users by phone, so that trend breaks are not misinterpreted.
steps: When a UX survey must be administered in multiple modes (e.g., mobile and desktop): test for mode effects before reporting aggregate results.
Run the same survey on a random split of participants across modes.
For each item, test: Mann-Whitney U test for significant differences between modes.
If significant: report mode-specific results, not aggregates.
Key rule: never compare results collected in different modes without testing for mode effects.
outputs: Mode comparison estimates, a mode-appropriate unified questionnaire, adjusted results, and guidance on which modes can be pooled.
useWhen: Surveys administered across channels (in-app plus email, phone for low-literacy users), trend comparisons where the mode changed, and sensitive topics.
avoidWhen: Avoid when a single mode is used consistently and comparisons over time keep that mode; then focus on other error sources.
whyLost: UX surveys switch channels for convenience (in-app, email, intercepts) without recognising that mode alters responses, so trend breaks are misread as experience changes.
whereToUse: Multi-channel UX research programs, CSAT surveys administered across devices, international UX research where mode varies by region.
example: A telecom moves its satisfaction survey from phone to SMS and scores drop by 8 points; a split-sample test shows most of the drop is a mode effect (less social desirability), not worse service.
sources: Survey Methodology — Groves et al.
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: de Leeuw ED (2005) To mix or not to mix data collection modes in surveys. Journal of Official Statistics 21(2):233-255

name: Moderated Usability Testing
origin: Usability labs, 1980s (e.g. IBM, Digital Equipment Corporation)
summary: A usability test in which a facilitator guides each session live, probing behaviour and adapting follow-up questions to understand problems in depth.
description: In moderated usability testing a researcher conducts each session in real time, in person or remotely, introducing tasks, observing behaviour and asking follow-up questions. The facilitator can clarify task misunderstandings, probe unexpected behaviour and explore the reasoning behind actions, which makes it well suited to complex flows, early concepts and specialist users. The trade-off is that the facilitator can also bias participants. Rigour comes from a written discussion guide with consistent task wording, neutral probes, deliberate decisions about when to intervene, separating observation from interpretation through note-takers or observers, and debriefing with observers after each session. Small samples of five to eight participants per segment are typical for formative work.
steps: Write a discussion guide with introduction, warm-up questions, task scenarios and debrief questions.
Recruit 5 to 8 participants per segment and schedule 45 to 60 minute sessions.
Pilot the guide and adjust timing and wording.
Facilitate sessions using neutral language, asking open follow-ups such as 'what did you expect to happen?' after tasks.
Have a separate note-taker log observations and quotes with timestamps.
Debrief with observers after each session and capture emerging issues.
Analyse across sessions, rate severity and report recommendations.
outputs: Detailed observations and quotes, explanations of why problems occur, severity-rated findings and recommendations.
useWhen: For complex task flows, early concepts and prototypes that need explanation, specialist or vulnerable users, and when qualitative depth matters.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need large samples or rapid turnaround across many variants; use unmoderated remote testing. Avoid probing during timed tasks used for benchmarks.
whyLost: Still in use: Richer than unmoderated; enables real-time hypothesis adjustment; essential for nuanced insight.
whereToUse: Complex task flows; early-stage concepts; when qualitative depth is needed.
example: A clinical trial platform runs moderated remote sessions with six research coordinators. Probing reveals that they export data to spreadsheets because they distrust the in-app audit trail, an insight unmoderated tests would have missed.

Handbook of Usability Testing (Rubin & Chisnell)

Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)

name: Moderation (interaction effects)
origin: Reuben Baron & David Kenny, 1986; probing methods by Leona Aiken & Stephen West, 1991
summary: Tests whether the effect of one variable on an outcome depends on the level of a third variable, revealing for whom and when a design works.
description: Moderation asks whether a relationship changes across conditions: does a redesign reduce errors for novices but not experts, or does a trust badge raise conversion only on mobile? It is modelled by adding a product term (X times W) to a regression; a reliable interaction coefficient means the slope of X differs by W. Rigour lies in centring continuous predictors, powering the study for the interaction (which typically needs around four times the sample of a main effect of similar size), probing with simple slopes at meaningful values and Johnson-Neyman regions, and pre-registering moderators rather than hunting through segments. Epidemiology calls the same idea effect modification, and it underpins heterogeneous treatment effect analysis in experimentation.
steps: Pre-specify the focal predictor, the moderator and the theoretical reason the effect should differ.
Power the study for the interaction specifically; plan roughly four times the sample needed to detect the main effect.
Mean-centre continuous predictors and fit the model with both main effects and the product term.
Probe a significant interaction with simple slopes at the moderator's mean and plus or minus one SD, or at real segment values.
Compute the Johnson-Neyman interval to show the moderator range where the effect is non-zero.
Plot predicted outcomes by moderator level and report the interaction effect size with a confidence interval.
outputs: Interaction coefficients, simple-slope estimates, Johnson-Neyman regions and interaction plots showing which users or contexts the effect holds for.
useWhen: When you suspect a design effect varies by expertise, device, segment, market or context, and need to state for whom a change works.
avoidWhen: Avoid post-hoc segment fishing across dozens of moderators, underpowered samples, or when you need the mechanism rather than the condition (use mediation analysis).
whyLost: UX teams usually split results by segment informally instead of testing interactions, so differences in subgroup p-values get misread as moderation. The formal method stayed in psychology and epidemiology.
whereToUse: Personalisation decisions, accessibility and expertise effects, mobile versus desktop A/B results, heterogeneous treatment effects in experiments, and market-specific launches.
example: A fintech A/B test shows a simplified onboarding has no average effect on completion. An interaction with prior investing experience reveals a 9-point gain for first-time investors and a 4-point loss for experienced ones, leading to an adaptive flow.
sources: Applied Predictive Modeling (Max Kuhn & Kjell Johnson)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chris Chapman & Elea McDonnell Feit)
Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis (Andrew Hayes)
Multiple Regression: Testing and Interpreting Interactions (Leona Aiken & Stephen West)
Applied Predictive Modeling (Kuhn & Johnson)
R for Marketing Research (Chapman & Feit)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 43 — Regression, Moderation & Mediation for UX Researchers

name: Modular Interface Evaluation (Fodor's Criteria)
origin: Jerry Fodor, 1983
summary: Evaluates which interface responses rely on fast, automatic, encapsulated perceptual processes versus slow central reasoning, designing critical signals for the former.
description: Fodor argued that input systems such as vision and language parsing are modular: domain-specific, mandatory, fast, informationally encapsulated (unaffected by beliefs) and shallow in output, in contrast to slow, flexible central reasoning. Modular interface evaluation applies these criteria to interface signals, asking which information users must process quickly and reliably and whether it is presented in forms that engage modular perception (distinct colour, motion, sound, spatial position) or forms that require central interpretation (codes, text, calculation). Signals critical under time pressure should exploit modular processing; information requiring judgement can rely on central processes. Rigour comes from a systematic signal inventory, grounding in perception research, and confirming classifications with reaction-time or detection measures.
steps: Module quality audit for design systems: for each interface component, evaluate:
Domain-specificity (does it do exactly one thing?),
Mandatory operation (does it always behave consistently?),
Informational encapsulation (does it work without depending on external state?),
Graceful failure modes (when it fails, does it fail predictably?). Score each criterion 0–2. Components scoring < 6/8 are architectural debt.
outputs: A classification of interface signals by processing type, identified signals that wrongly rely on central reasoning, and redesigns using perceptually modular cues.
useWhen: Safety-critical warnings, time-pressured interfaces, automotive and medical displays where responses must be fast and resistant to distraction.
avoidWhen: Avoid when tasks are deliberative by nature; the modularity framework is contested, so prefer empirical reaction-time testing for final decisions.
whyLost: Fodor's modularity thesis shaped 1980s cognitive science; HCI absorbed preattentive processing findings but dropped the framework itself.
whereToUse: Design system architecture, component library design, microfrontend UX architecture, API design.
example: An infusion pump's critical alarm relies on reading a text code; reclassifying it to use a distinct sound and colour, processed automatically, cuts response times in simulation.
sources: The Modularity of the Mind — Jerry Fodor
reference: Fodor JA (1983) The Modularity of Mind. MIT Press

name: Monte Carlo Journey Simulation
origin: Stanisław Ulam & Nicholas Metropolis, 1940s; funnel application in Gopinath, 2025
summary: Simulates thousands of synthetic user journeys from observed step success probabilities to forecast end-to-end completion as a distribution with intervals and to test what-if improvements.
description: Monte Carlo simulation estimates outcomes by repeated random sampling. Applied to UX funnels, each virtual user passes or fails each step according to empirical step probabilities, and the share completing across many runs gives a completion distribution rather than a single number. In Vivek Gopinath's playbook, step probabilities of 81%, 75%, 85% and 95% across 10,000 virtual users give a mean completion of 49% [46%, 52%]; improving OTP to 92% gives 54% [51%, 57%], showing small step tweaks compound into larger overall lifts. Assumptions are stated explicitly: stationarity, approximate independence of steps, like-for-like traffic and no leakage. Sensitivity checks vary the improved step by ±10–20%, split by segment, and scale by expected weekly starts. CIs can be converted to SD with SD ≈ (upper − lower)/(2 × 1.96). The same technique forecasts ΔU under redesign scenarios in the Nash protocol.
steps: Collect empirical step-level success probabilities from experiments or analytics.
For each of 10,000 virtual users, sample success or failure at each step using those probabilities.
Aggregate the share of virtual users finishing and repeat to obtain a completion distribution.
Report the mean and 95% interval.
Run what-if scenarios by changing the probability of a target step.
Run sensitivity checks (best/mid/worst ±10–20%, segment splits, volume scaling) and state assumptions.
Compare the forecast with the observed lift after launch.
outputs: Completion distributions per scenario with intervals, what-if lifts and stated assumptions.
useWhen: When stakeholders ask what impact to expect at rollout and which step improvement matters most.
avoidWhen: When step outcomes are strongly correlated or traffic mix will change; model dependencies explicitly or use observed cohort data.
whyLost: Common in finance and engineering, but UX researchers rarely forecast impact with uncertainty.
whereToUse: Onboarding and KYC funnels, checkout, roadmap business cases, design adoption scenarios.
example: A trading app forecasts that raising OTP success to 92% lifts end-to-end completion from about 49% to 54%, and later observes a larger lift than predicted.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
reference: Metropolis, N., & Ulam, S. (1949). The Monte Carlo method. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 44(247), 335–341.

name: Monte Carlo simulation for completion rate forecasting
origin: Stanislaw Ulam & John von Neumann, 1946-1949 (Los Alamos)
summary: Forecasts the range of likely completion or adoption rates for a flow by repeatedly simulating users through uncertain step-level probabilities.
description: Instead of a single forecast, Monte Carlo simulation represents each uncertain input (step pass-through rates, traffic, effect of a redesign) as a probability distribution, typically drawn from study data, and simulates thousands of possible outcomes. The result is a distribution of completion rates from which you can read medians, intervals and the probability of hitting a target. For a five-step onboarding with each step's pass rate estimated from a usability study or analytics, simulation propagates uncertainty that point estimates hide. Rigour lies in grounding input distributions in data (e.g. Beta distributions from observed successes and failures), modelling correlations between steps, running enough iterations (10,000 or more) and checking sensitivity to assumptions.
steps: Map the flow into steps and identify uncertain inputs: per-step completion probabilities, traffic, expected redesign effects.
Specify a distribution for each input from data, e.g. Beta(successes + 1, failures + 1) for step pass rates from a study.
Model dependencies between steps where evidence suggests correlation (e.g. users who struggle early also struggle later).
Simulate at least 10,000 iterations, computing end-to-end completion for each.
Summarise the outcome distribution with median, 80% and 95% intervals and the probability of exceeding targets.
Run sensitivity analysis (e.g. tornado chart) to show which steps most influence the forecast.
outputs: A probabilistic forecast of completion or adoption, probabilities of meeting targets and a sensitivity ranking of steps.
useWhen: Forecasting the impact of redesigns before launch, setting realistic targets, or communicating uncertainty from small-sample usability data.
avoidWhen: Avoid when inputs are pure guesses with no data or expert calibration, or when a simple analytic calculation conveys the uncertainty adequately.
whyLost: Monte Carlo is standard in finance, engineering and operations research, but UX forecasts are usually single numbers or not made at all.
whereToUse: Onboarding and checkout redesigns, KYC flows in fintech, feature adoption forecasts, research-backed business cases.
example: Usability testing of a new KYC flow gives per-step success counts from 12 participants. Simulation with Beta distributions forecasts a median completion of 71% (80% interval 58-81%), with only a 22% chance of reaching the 80% target, prompting a fix to the ID upload step.

name: Morville's User Experience Honeycomb
origin: Peter Morville, Semantic Studios, 2004
summary: A seven-facet framework (useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, credible, valuable) used to diagnose and prioritise where an experience falls short.
description: Morville drew the honeycomb to move IA and UX beyond usability alone. Its facets are useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, credible and valuable (the centre). The intended use is diagnostic and strategic: teams choose which facets matter most for a product and context, assess each with appropriate evidence, and re-weight priorities. Many teams now treat it as a poster. Made rigorous, each facet is operationalised with a measure (e.g. findability with tree testing success, credibility with Stanford web credibility guidelines or a validated scale, accessibility with WCAG audit), scored, and tracked, turning a diagram into a balanced scorecard.
steps: With stakeholders, rank the seven facets by importance for this product, user segment and context, and record the rationale.
Operationalise each facet with a measure: e.g. task success (usable), tree testing (findable), WCAG audit (accessible), credibility scale (credible), willingness to pay or retention (valuable).
Collect data for each facet using the appropriate method and sample.
Score facets on a common normalised scale and plot against importance to reveal gaps.
Prioritise improvements where important facets score lowest.
Re-measure each release to track the profile over time.
outputs: A weighted facet profile with evidence-based scores, gap analysis and prioritised improvements.
useWhen: Product strategy reviews, setting a balanced UX scorecard, or diagnosing why a usable product still fails.
avoidWhen: When you need causal explanations of a specific problem; use targeted research methods.
whyLost: The honeycomb became a slide illustration and lost its role as a diagnostic, prioritisation tool with measures.
whereToUse: Content-rich sites, health information, government services, marketplaces, AI products where credibility matters.
example: A health information site scores well on usable and findable but poorly on credible. Credibility interviews and a validated scale lead to visible author credentials and review dates, raising trust and return visits.
sources: Morville, User Experience Design (2004), Semantic Studios
Morville & Rosenfeld, Information Architecture for the World Wide Web (3rd ed., 2006)

name: Motivational Interviewing Applied to UX
origin: William Miller, 1983; Miller & Rollnick, 1991 (Motivational Interviewing)
summary: Adapting motivational interviewing's open questions, affirmations, reflections and change talk to surface ambivalence and hidden barriers behind non-adoption.
description: Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick, originally developed for addiction counselling) is a directive, client-centred counselling style that elicits behaviour change by helping clients explore and resolve ambivalence. In UX research, it is invaluable for understanding non-adoption, under-adoption, and the gap between stated intentions ("I want to use it") and actual behaviour ("I never do"). Standard interviews fail here because ambivalence is socially uncomfortable to express — participants perform coherence they do not feel.
steps: Frame the session around the participant's own goals in the domain rather than around the product.
Use open questions to explore current behaviour and its fit with their goals, avoiding yes/no and leading phrasing.
Offer genuine affirmations of effort and reasoning to build the safety needed for honest disclosure.
Use reflective listening, slightly amplifying what is said, to surface implicit meaning and test interpretations.
Explore both sides of the ambivalence explicitly: what they like, the downsides, and what happens if nothing changes.
Analyse transcripts for sustain talk versus change talk and map the barriers that sit between stated intention and behaviour.
outputs: Maps of ambivalence (benefits, costs, status quo pull), a catalogue of unstated barriers to adoption, and quotes illustrating change and sustain talk.
useWhen: Researching non-adoption, under-use, or the intention-behaviour gap, such as health apps, savings tools, security features or new workflows people say they want but do not use.
avoidWhen: Usability evaluation or factual task research; also avoid steering participants toward behaviour change, which turns research into persuasion. Use standard semi-structured interviews.
whyLost: It belongs to clinical training and carries a therapeutic aim, so UX has not adopted its techniques despite their fit for adoption research.
whereToUse: Digital health and wellbeing apps, personal finance and savings products, security and privacy feature adoption, and enterprise tool rollouts.
example: Users of a diabetes app say they 'mean to' log meals. MI-style reflections reveal that logging makes them feel judged by an imagined clinician, a barrier never stated in earlier surveys, leading to a non-judgemental logging mode.
sources: Listening to People
Qualitative Interviewing
Practical Empathy (Young)
Motivational Interviewing: Helping People Change (Miller & Rollnick)
reference: Miller, W. R. & Rollnick, S. (2013). Motivational Interviewing: Helping People Change (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

extra.Four Core MI Techniques: Open questions: Questions that cannot be answered yes/no. "What would need to be different for you to use it more?" "What concerns do you have about making that change?" Affirmations: Genuine recognition of the participant's efforts and strengths — not compliments. "It sounds like you've put real thought into how to make this work for you." This builds the relationship that makes honest disclosure possible. Reflective listening: Reflecting the participant's meaning back to them, slightly amplified. If the participant says "It's just a bit slow," you might reflect: "So the slowness is affecting your willingness to use it at all." This surfaces implicit meaning. Eliciting change talk: Ask about both sides of the ambivalence directly. "What do you like about it?" then "What are the downsides for you?" then "If things stayed exactly as they are, what would happen?" The gap between the ideal and the actual is where the real research data lives.

name: Motivational Interviewing for Behaviour Change Research
origin: Miller & Rollnick, 1991
summary: Adapts motivational interviewing techniques (open questions, reflections, eliciting ambivalence and change talk) to research how users think about changing behaviour.
description: Motivational interviewing, developed by Miller and Rollnick, is a collaborative conversational style for exploring a person's own reasons for change. Its core skills, known as OARS (open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries), together with the elicitation of 'change talk' and 'sustain talk', make it well suited to research about behaviours users are ambivalent about: saving, exercising, medication adherence, reducing screen time. Adapted for research, the interviewer does not steer towards change but maps the participant's ambivalence, values and perceived barriers, which are typically hidden behind socially desirable answers. Rigour comes from training in reflective listening, separating research from intervention through ethics review, and coding transcripts for change and sustain talk.
steps: MI techniques for UX research:
Open questions: 'What's your relationship with [behavior]?' rather than 'Why don't you use this feature?'
Reflective listening: reflect back what users say without evaluation.
(3) Elicit change talk: 'If you did start [behavior], what would be different?'
Explore ambivalence: 'What makes it hard? What would make it easier?' MI surfaces the real barriers that users are reluctant to articulate to a researcher associated with the product.
outputs: Maps of ambivalence (reasons for and against change), change and sustain talk excerpts, readiness profiles and design implications for behaviour change products.
useWhen: Research for health, finance, sustainability and habit products, where users are ambivalent about a change and direct questions produce socially desirable answers.
avoidWhen: Avoid using it to persuade research participants; the aim is understanding. Avoid when topics are not about behaviour change, and do not substitute for clinical care.
whyLost: MI is a clinical intervention with certification and fidelity coding; UX has not adapted it as a research protocol, and the line between research and intervention needs care.
whereToUse: Health behavior change app research, sustainability UX research, financial behavior research, any product addressing behavior change.
example: A smoking-cessation app team uses MI-style reflections in interviews and uncovers that users value cigarettes as their only private break, so the product adds 'replacement break' features rather than more warnings.

name: Mouse-Tracking of Decision Conflict
origin: Michael Spivey, Marc Grosjean and Günther Knoblich, 2005; Jonathan Freeman and Nalini Ambady, MouseTracker (2010)
summary: Analyses the curvature and timing of cursor movements toward choices to reveal hidden attraction to the unchosen option during a decision.
description: In mouse-tracking studies, participants start at the bottom centre and move to one of two response options at the top corners. Because the hand moves continuously while the decision unfolds, trajectories curve toward the competing option when it exerts pull. Measures include maximum deviation, area under the curve, x-flips (direction changes) and initiation time. These indices reveal conflict, ambivalence and the time course of competing considerations, which final choices hide. Unlike session replay heatmaps, mouse-tracking uses controlled, normalised trajectories and statistical comparison. In UX it measures hesitation at consent dialogues, pricing choices and trust decisions.
steps: Design a two-option choice screen with a start button at bottom centre and options in the top corners.
Require movement to begin within a time limit (e.g. 400 ms) to ensure online decision tracking.
Record cursor coordinates at high sampling rate; time-normalise trajectories into 101 steps.
Compute maximum deviation, area under the curve, x-flips and initiation time.
Compare conditions with mixed-effects models, and inspect bimodality to distinguish graded pull from discrete changes of mind.
Relate conflict measures to later behaviour (e.g. regret, cancellations).
outputs: Trajectory plots and conflict indices per condition, with statistical comparisons.
useWhen: Measuring ambivalence or temptation in binary choices: consent, upsell, risky actions, AI suggestions.
avoidWhen: Touch-only interfaces (use touch trajectory analogues carefully) or complex multi-step tasks.
whyLost: It is a cognitive science paradigm; UX uses session replays without controlled designs.
whereToUse: Cookie consent, subscription upsells, privacy permissions, misinformation labelling, recommendation acceptance.
example: An insurer tests add-on cover offers. Mouse trajectories show strong pull toward 'decline' even when users accept, indicating pressured acceptance; the team reframes the offer and cancellations fall.
sources: Spivey, Grosjean & Knoblich, Continuous attraction toward phonological competitors (2005), PNAS
