name: Multi-Armed Bandit Testing for Adaptive UX
donor: Statistics, operations research and reinforcement learning
origin: William Thompson (1933); Robbins (1952); upper confidence bound algorithms by Auer et al. (2002)
summary: Adaptive experiments that shift traffic toward better-performing variants during the test, using Thompson sampling or UCB to balance learning against serving users the best option.
description: A fixed A/B test splits traffic evenly until the end, accepting the cost of showing an inferior variant to half of users. Multi-armed bandits treat each variant as an arm with unknown reward and allocate traffic adaptively: Thompson sampling draws from each arm's posterior distribution (for example a Beta distribution for conversion) and serves the arm with the highest draw, while UCB serves the arm with the highest optimistic estimate. Over time traffic concentrates on the best arm, reducing regret. Bandits suit short-lived decisions (headlines, promotions), many variants and personalisation via contextual bandits. The trade-offs are real: adaptive allocation complicates unbiased effect estimation, is vulnerable to time-varying effects and delayed rewards, and is poor for learning why something works. Rigour means choosing bandits for optimisation, not inference, and logging allocation probabilities.
steps: Implement Thompson sampling or UCB (Upper Confidence Bound) algorithm.
Initialize: equal traffic to all variants.
After each observation: update posterior (Thompson) or confidence bound (UCB).
Shift traffic toward higher-performing variant.
Stop when posterior probability that the best variant is best exceeds 0.95.
Compare total cost (regret) to equivalent fixed A/B test.
outputs: Allocation trajectories, posterior estimates per variant, cumulative regret, chosen winning variant, and logged propensities for later analysis.
useWhen: Optimising many variants quickly, time-limited content such as campaigns or headlines, personalisation with contextual bandits, and cases where serving losing variants is costly.
avoidWhen: When you need an unbiased effect estimate or a causal explanation, when rewards are delayed (retention), or when guardrails must be assessed; use a fixed A/B test.
whyLost: Bandits matured in machine learning and ad tech; UX research culture is built on hypothesis testing and explanation, so adaptive allocation is seen as an engineering optimisation rather than a research method.
whereToUse: Feature rollouts where delayed testing is costly, personalization testing, any experiment where learning speed matters.
example: An e-commerce site tests six hero banners for a 10-day sale using Thompson sampling. By day three, 70% of traffic goes to two banners, recovering most of the conversion that an even split would have lost.

name: Multi-Attribute Utility Analysis (MAUT/SMART)
origin: Ralph Keeney and Howard Raiffa (1976); Ward Edwards' SMART (1977) and Edwards and Barron's SMARTER (1994)
summary: Evaluates alternatives on multiple attributes with explicit single-attribute utility functions and trade-off weights derived by swing weighting.
description: MAUT formalises trade-offs: each attribute gets a value or utility function mapping its range to 0-1, and weights reflect how much the decision-maker values swinging each attribute from worst to best. Swing weighting avoids the common error of weighting by abstract importance without regard to ranges. SMART and SMARTER simplify elicitation (rank-order centroid weights). The additive model ranks alternatives, and sensitivity analysis shows how robust the choice is. For UX, MAUT supports decisions where user outcomes compete with cost, risk and accessibility, and can model users' own multi-attribute choices.
steps: Define objectives and measurable attributes with ranges for each alternative.
Elicit single-attribute value functions (linear or curved) with stakeholders or users.
Elicit weights with swing weighting: rank swings from worst to best, then assign relative points.
Score alternatives and compute weighted totals.
Run sensitivity analysis on weights and value functions; identify dominated alternatives.
Document trade-offs and the rationale for the final decision.
outputs: Value functions, swing weights, alternative scores, sensitivity analysis and decision rationale.
useWhen: Complex design or product decisions with several measurable, competing objectives.
avoidWhen: Decisions with few attributes or where one constraint dominates.
whyLost: Decision analysis lives in operations research and policy; product teams use informal scoring.
whereToUse: Platform choices, design system adoption, accessibility trade-offs, AI model selection balancing quality, latency and cost.
example: Choosing among three LLMs for a support bot, swing weighting shows the team values a jump in resolution rate more than a 50% cost cut; the mid-cost model wins and the result is robust to weight changes of plus or minus 20%.
sources: Keeney & Raiffa, Decisions with Multiple Objectives (1976)

name: Multi-Channel Affective Measurement
origin: Rosalind Picard, MIT Media Lab, 1997 (Affective Computing)
summary: Measures emotional response by triangulating self-report, physiological signals and behaviour in the same session, exposing mismatches between what users say and what they feel.
description: Emotion is not a single signal. Self-report captures what people are willing and able to articulate; physiology (electrodermal activity, heart rate variability, pupil dilation) captures arousal without valence; behaviour (facial expression, hesitation, posture, interaction patterns) captures expression shaped by social context. Picard's affective computing framework treats each channel as a partial, noisy measurement of an underlying affective state. The rigour comes from declaring channels and hypotheses before collection, synchronising all channels to interface events, and treating disagreement between channels as data rather than error: a participant who says a flow was 'fine' while skin conductance spikes at a fee disclosure is telling you something no single channel could. Post-hoc selection of whichever channel supports a story is the characteristic failure the protocol is designed to prevent.
steps: Declare all channels before data collection. Post-hoc triangulation is selection bias.
Collect all channels simultaneously or within the same session.
Implicit vs. explicit mismatch analysis: Participant says 'it was fine' but shows elevated GSR and long hesitation times. The mismatch IS the finding — report it, do not average it away.
outputs: A time-synchronised affective record per participant, event-locked arousal and expression profiles, a list of self-report versus physiology mismatches, and emotion hotspots mapped to specific interface moments.
useWhen: Emotion is central to the outcome (trust, anxiety, delight) in high-stakes flows such as loan applications, medical results or payments, and you suspect users under-report or cannot articulate their reactions.
avoidWhen: You need only task success or attitudes; the cost of sensors and analysis is not justified. Avoid treating physiology as valence. For lighter evidence use Think-Aloud with Emotional Annotation or a validated self-report scale such as SAM or PANAS.
whyLost: It requires sensors, signal-processing skills and synchronisation tooling that few UX teams have, and commercial biometrics vendors sold single-channel dashboards that blurred the triangulation logic.
whereToUse: Fintech onboarding and credit decisions, health result delivery, automotive and in-car interfaces, games, and evaluating AI agents whose behaviour may provoke unease users will not voice.
example: A bank tests its loan-application flow with 16 participants wearing EDA wristbands and webcam expression capture. Most rate the flow as easy, yet arousal peaks and brow-lowering cluster at the credit-check consent screen; reframing that screen reduces both the peak and drop-off.
sources: Affective Computing (Rosalind Picard)

name: Multi-modal signal separation
donor: Signal processing and multisensory human factors
origin: Source separation from signal processing (blind source separation, 1980s-90s) applied to display modality allocation in human factors, building on Wickens (1984)
summary: Analyses whether concurrent signals in different sensory channels remain distinguishable, and reallocates them so critical messages are not masked by competing signals.
description: In signal processing, source separation recovers independent signals from a mixture. The UX analogue asks whether users can separate concurrent alerts, sounds, haptics and visuals that arrive together, or whether they blur into a single undifferentiated stream. The method inventories every signal source, maps its modality, frequency band, timing and spatial location, and identifies overlaps where two signals share a channel and are likely to mask each other (for example two tones within the same critical band, or two flashing elements in peripheral vision). It then reallocates signals across modalities or dimensions so that each critical message occupies a distinct channel. Rigour comes from measuring physical properties (frequency, loudness, onset timing) and testing identification accuracy under realistic concurrency.
steps: Inventory all signal sources in the environment, including other devices, with modality, frequency or colour, onset pattern, duration and location.
Plot signals on a channel map (modality by dimension by time) and mark overlaps occurring within 500 ms of each other or in the same auditory critical band.
Measure the ambient noise floor and check each auditory alert sits at least 10-15 dB above masked threshold, per common alarm standards.
Run an identification test where participants (8-15) must name which of several concurrent signals occurred; target at least 90% correct identification for critical alarms.
Reallocate confused signals to different modalities, rhythms or spatial locations, and prioritise or suppress lower-priority signals during critical events.
Re-test identification accuracy and response time under the worst-case concurrency scenario.
outputs: A channel allocation map, a list of masking conflicts, identification accuracy per signal, and a revised multimodal signal scheme.
useWhen: When many devices or features emit alerts in the same environment; when users report not knowing which alarm is sounding; when adding haptic or audio feedback to an existing product.
avoidWhen: When signals are rare and isolated; a simple notification review suffices. For attention allocation without concurrency problems, use a saliency or pre-attentive audit.
whyLost: The concept is mature in signal processing and auditory alarm research, but UX teams design per product, not per environment, so cross-device masking is rarely analysed.
whereToUse: Operating theatres and ICUs, vehicle cockpits, smart homes, wearables, and multi-app mobile notification ecosystems.
example: In an ICU, infusion pumps and ventilators use similar 960 Hz tones. A separation analysis shows nurses identify the source correctly only 54% of the time; giving the pump a distinct rhythmic pattern and a bedside light raises identification to 93%.

name: Multi-pass analysis pipeline
origin: Draws on multi-cycle coding (Saldaña) and grounded theory's open, axial and selective coding (Strauss and Corbin, 1990); implemented with LLM APIs from 2023
summary: Splitting AI-assisted qualitative analysis into separate, checkable passes, such as segmenting, first-order coding, consolidation, second-order categorisation and synthesis, rather than one prompt.
description: Asking a model to 'find themes' in a corpus in one step produces unverifiable, often generic output. A multi-pass pipeline mirrors established qualitative cycles: pass one segments and cleans; pass two applies first-order codes segment by segment with evidence; pass three consolidates near-duplicate codes into a codebook; pass four groups codes into second-order categories; pass five drafts synthesis with links to evidence. Each pass has a narrow task, a schema, logged outputs and a human review point. Rigour comes from the separation (errors are traceable to a pass), from never letting later passes see only summaries without evidence, and from human decisions at the abstraction steps.
steps: Define the passes and each pass's input, output schema and review owner.
Pass 1: segment transcripts by speaker turn and remove moderator text and personal data.
Pass 2: generate first-order codes per segment with verbatim evidence, validated against the schema.
Pass 3: cluster and merge similar codes into a draft codebook; a researcher reviews merges.
Pass 4: propose second-order categories with linked codes; researchers revise and approve.
Pass 5: draft synthesis statements, each linked to supporting codes and quotes, and check counts of participants per theme.
Log every pass's outputs and keep them so any theme can be traced back to segments.
outputs: Pass-by-pass outputs, a reviewed codebook, second-order categories and evidence-linked synthesis.
useWhen: Large-scale AI-assisted qualitative analysis where traceability from themes to quotes matters.
avoidWhen: Overkill for small studies; avoid single-prompt 'summarise the themes' approaches altogether for anything reported as research.
whyLost: The idea mirrors classic qualitative cycles, but popular AI tools offer one-click summarisation that hides the passes.
whereToUse: Research operations, continuous discovery programmes, large interview studies and multilingual synthesis.
example: A SaaS team analysing 180 churn interviews runs five passes. At pass 3 a researcher splits a merged code 'pricing' into 'price level' and 'pricing model confusion', which become distinct themes with different owners.

name: Multilayer Perceptron Neural Network Prediction
origin: Backpropagation networks from machine learning; presented as a practical prediction method with a tuning experiment by Glenn Myatt (2007)
summary: Trains a layered network of weighted nodes on example records to predict a numeric or categorical outcome, tuning layers, cycles and learning rate against cross-validated accuracy.
description: A multilayer perceptron has an input layer with one node per normalised descriptor variable, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer with one node per response. Every connection carries a weight, initially random, and each node combines its weighted inputs through an activation function. During learning, training examples are presented one at a time and backpropagation adjusts the weights to reduce the error between predicted and actual outputs; one presentation is a cycle (epoch). The analyst sets the number of hidden layers and nodes, the number of cycles and the learning rate. Myatt treats model building as a designed experiment: try combinations of inputs, hidden layers and cycle counts, score each with cross-validated r squared or error, watch for the point where accuracy stops rising or falls (overtraining), and pick the simplest model that performs well. Networks capture non-linear relationships and tolerate noise, but they are a black box, so for UX work they suit prediction tasks where accuracy matters more than explanation, and should be paired with an explanation method or a simpler comparison model.
steps: Define the outcome to predict (for example 30-day retention or task time) and the accuracy the decision needs.
Prepare and normalise descriptor variables; dummy-code categories.
Hold out a test set or set up k-fold cross-validation.
Design a tuning grid over input sets, number of hidden layers and nodes, number of cycles and learning rate.
Train each configuration and record cross-validated accuracy, plotting accuracy against cycles to spot overtraining.
Choose the simplest configuration with near-best accuracy and compare it with a transparent model such as a regression or decision tree.
Inspect mispredicted cases and translate outputs back to original units before reporting.
outputs: A trained prediction model, a table of tuning results and cross-validated accuracy figures.
useWhen: You have hundreds or more labelled records, relationships are likely non-linear, and prediction accuracy matters more than an explanation.
avoidWhen: Samples are small, stakeholders need to understand why a prediction was made, or a regression or tree performs as well.
whyLost: Within UX, simpler interpretable models and, more recently, gradient boosting dominate tabular prediction; neural networks are left to data science teams.
whereToUse: Churn and retention scoring, predicting task time or satisfaction from telemetry, lead and upgrade propensity, personalisation.
example: A team predicts which trial users will convert from 12 behavioural features. A one-hidden-layer network at 10,000 cycles reaches a cross-validated accuracy similar to a two-layer version, so the simpler model is kept and benchmarked against logistic regression before being used to time an upgrade prompt.
sources: Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
reference: Myatt, G. J. (2007). Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley-Interscience.

name: Multilevel (Hierarchical) Models
origin: Stephen Raudenbush and Anthony Bryk (HLM, 1980s-2002); Harvey Goldstein (1987); Laird and Ware (1982)
summary: Models data nested in groups (tasks within participants, users within companies, sessions within users) with random effects, giving correct uncertainty and partial pooling.
description: UX data are almost always nested: multiple tasks per participant, many sessions per user, users within accounts, ratings by several raters. Treating these as independent observations understates uncertainty and inflates false positives; averaging per participant throws away information. Multilevel models include random intercepts and slopes for grouping factors, estimate variance at each level (and the intraclass correlation), and partially pool estimates so small groups borrow strength from the whole. Crossed random effects for participants and items (tasks, stimuli) allow generalisation beyond the specific tasks tested, a point emphasised in psycholinguistics. Bayesian versions (brms, Stan) handle small samples well.
steps: Identify the nesting and crossing structure: participants, tasks, sessions, accounts, raters.
Specify the model with fixed effects for design conditions and random effects for grouping factors, including random slopes where justified.
Choose an appropriate likelihood (e.g. log-normal for task times, binomial for success, ordinal for ratings).
Fit with lme4, glmmTMB or brms; check convergence and simplify random structure if needed.
Report fixed effects with intervals, variance components and ICCs.
Use posterior or model-based predictions for new participants and tasks to show generalisable effects.
outputs: Effect estimates with correct uncertainty, variance components, ICCs and shrunken group estimates.
useWhen: Any repeated-measures usability study, benchmark, diary, multi-rater or multi-account data.
avoidWhen: Truly independent single observations per unit; simple models suffice.
whyLost: UX statistics training stops at t-tests and ANOVA, and tools like SUS calculators assume independence.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarks with many tasks, diary studies, B2B analytics by account, multi-site research.
example: A benchmark compares two designs across 8 tasks and 24 participants. A crossed random-effects model shows the design effect holds generally, though one task drives much of the variance, unlike the inflated paired t-test.
sources: Raudenbush & Bryk, Hierarchical Linear Models (2nd ed., 2002)
Gelman & Hill, Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models (2007)
Baayen, Davidson & Bates, Mixed-effects modeling with crossed random effects for subjects and items (2008), Journal of Memory and Language
reference: Gelman, A., & Hill, J. (2007). Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models. Cambridge University Press.

name: Multilevel Modelling (HLM / Mixed-Effects Models)
origin: Harvey Goldstein (1986); Stephen Raudenbush and Anthony Bryk (1992, 2002)
summary: Models nested data (events within sessions within users within products) to partition variance and produce correct standard errors for repeated measures.
description: Multilevel models include random effects for each level of a hierarchy, partitioning variance and accounting for non-independence of observations within units. Without them, repeated observations from one user are treated as independent, inflating effective sample size and producing anti-conservative inference. The treatise calls this essential for any UX study with repeated measures, multiple sessions per user or multi-site data, and notes most UX statistical analysis ignores clustering entirely, treating 100 clicks from one user as 100 observations, which systematically produces false confidence. Mixed models also handle unbalanced designs, crossed random effects (participants and tasks) and growth curves for longitudinal data. Rated HIGH priority.
steps: Identify the nesting or crossing structure (events, sessions, users, tasks, sites).
Specify fixed effects for predictors of interest and random intercepts (and slopes) for grouping levels.
Fit with appropriate likelihood (for example glmer for binary outcomes) and check convergence.
Compute intraclass correlations to see variance at each level.
Compare models with likelihood ratio tests or information criteria.
Report fixed effects with correct CIs and variance components.
outputs: Effect estimates with valid uncertainty, variance components, ICCs, growth curves.
useWhen: Repeated-measures usability studies, diary and ESM data, clickstreams, multi-product benchmarks.
avoidWhen: Truly independent single observations per participant; ordinary regression suffices.
whyLost: UX statistics training stops at t-tests and chi-square; analytics tools aggregate away the nesting.
whereToUse: Benchmark programmes, longitudinal studies, A/B tests with repeated sessions, multi-site research.
example: A within-subjects test of two dashboards with 12 users and 10 tasks each shows p = 0.01 with a naive t-test on 120 trials, but p = 0.21 with crossed random effects for users and tasks.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Raudenbush SW & Bryk AS (2002) Hierarchical Linear Models. 2nd ed
Gelman A & Hill J (2006) Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models
Goldstein H (1986) Multilevel mixed linear model analysis using iterative generalized least squares. Biometrika
reference: Raudenbush SW & Bryk AS (2002) Hierarchical Linear Models: Applications and Data Analysis Methods. 2nd ed. Sage.

name: Multimodal Discourse Analysis
aka: Kress and van Leeuwen visual grammar
origin: Gunther Kress and Theo van Leeuwen, 1996 (Reading Images: The Grammar of Visual Design)
summary: Analyses how text, image, layout, colour, sound and motion combine or conflict to make meaning in interfaces, using representational, interactional and compositional metafunctions.
description: Multimodal discourse analysis treats every semiotic mode in an interface as meaningful and analyses how they work together. Following Kress and van Leeuwen, each mode is examined for three functions: representational (what it depicts and which actions or participants it shows), interactional (the relationship it constructs with the viewer, through gaze, distance, angle and modality), and compositional (how elements are arranged, with given-new and ideal-real positioning, salience and framing). The analysis then asks whether modes reinforce one another or contradict, since contradictions such as cheerful illustration on a serious financial warning create confusion and mistrust. Rigour comes from applying the framework consistently across a defined set of screens rather than offering aesthetic critique.
steps: Mode inventory: For each key screen, list all active semiotic modes: linguistic (text), visual (images, icons), spatial (layout), aural (sound), gestural (animation).
Representational analysis: What does each mode represent? What processes, participants, and circumstances does it show?
Interactional analysis: What relationships between interface and user does each mode enact? (Demand vs. offer; close vs. distant; high vs. low modality.)
Compositional analysis: How are modes combined? What is given vs. new? What is ideal vs. real? What has visual salience?
Coherence vs. conflict: Do modes reinforce each other or contradict? Conflicts are the source of users reporting something 'feels wrong' without knowing why.
outputs: A mode inventory per screen, a metafunction analysis, a list of cross-modal conflicts with severity, and design recommendations for coherence.
useWhen: Visual and verbal elements carry the message: marketing and onboarding screens, illustration systems, data visualisation, warnings, video and motion-heavy products, or brand redesigns.
avoidWhen: The interface is mostly functional forms with little visual rhetoric, or you need behavioural outcome data; pair with usability or comprehension testing instead.
whyLost: Its academic vocabulary is dense, design teams rely on visual intuition and brand guidelines, and the method was taught in linguistics and media studies rather than design or HCI programmes.
whereToUse: Design-system illustration guidelines, health and finance warning screens, onboarding carousels, dashboards, AI-generated imagery in products, and accessibility reviews of meaning carried only visually.
example: A mental-health app pairs crisis-line information with bright, playful illustrations. Analysis shows the interactional meaning (casual, distant) contradicts the linguistic urgency; a calmer visual treatment and direct-gaze photography test better for trust.
sources: Reading Images: Grammar of Visual Design (Kress & van Leeuwen)
Handbook of Discourse Analysis
reference: Kress, G. & van Leeuwen, T. (2006). Reading Images: The Grammar of Visual Design (2nd ed.). Routledge.

name: Multiple comparisons correction
origin: Bonferroni inequality (Carlo Bonferroni, 1936; applied by Dunn, 1961); Holm's step-down procedure (1979); Benjamini and Hochberg's false discovery rate (1995)
summary: Controls the inflated chance of false positives when many metrics, segments or variants are tested, using family-wise or false discovery rate procedures.
description: With an alpha of 0.05, testing 20 independent null comparisons gives about a 64% chance of at least one false positive. UX analyses routinely test many metrics, segments, variants and survey items, then report the significant ones. Corrections control this inflation. Family-wise error rate (FWER) methods, Bonferroni (alpha divided by number of tests) and the more powerful Holm step-down procedure, limit the probability of any false positive and suit confirmatory decisions. False discovery rate (FDR) methods, notably Benjamini-Hochberg, limit the expected proportion of false positives among discoveries and suit exploratory screening of many metrics. Rigour also includes reducing the number of tests through a pre-registered primary metric and treating secondary findings as exploratory.
steps: List all planned comparisons: metrics, segments, variants and time windows; designate one or a few primary outcomes in advance.
Decide the error rate to control: FWER for confirmatory decisions (use Holm), or FDR for exploratory screening (use Benjamini-Hochberg at q = 0.05 or 0.10).
For Holm, sort p-values ascending and compare the k-th smallest with alpha/(m − k + 1), stopping at the first non-significant result.
For Benjamini-Hochberg, sort p-values and find the largest k where p(k) ≤ (k/m)q; reject hypotheses 1 to k.
Report both raw and adjusted p-values, along with effect sizes and intervals.
Label unplanned or segment-level findings as exploratory and confirm important ones in a follow-up test.
outputs: Adjusted p-values or decisions under FWER or FDR, a clear separation of confirmatory and exploratory findings, and follow-up test recommendations.
useWhen: Testing multiple metrics, segments, variants or survey items; reviewing dashboards with many significance flags; post-hoc comparisons after ANOVA.
avoidWhen: Only one pre-registered primary comparison is being tested; or Bayesian hierarchical models are used, which handle multiplicity through partial pooling.
whyLost: Corrections are taught in statistics courses but experimentation dashboards often flag dozens of metrics as significant without adjustment, and segment fishing is common.
whereToUse: A/B tests with many metrics, survey crosstabs, multi-variant tests, analytics segment exploration.
example: A Trust Badge test reported significant gains in 3 of 24 metric-segment combinations. After Benjamini-Hochberg at q = 0.05, none remained significant, and the team ran a follow-up test focused on the one pre-registered metric.
sources: Statistics for Dummies series (Rumsey)
Designing Experiments & Analyzing Data (Maxwell & Delaney)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 41 — Frequentist Inference Done Right
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate: A practical and powerful approach to multiple testing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 57(1), 289–300; Holm, S. (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, 6(2), 65–70.

name: Multiple regression
origin: Francis Galton and Karl Pearson (1880s-1900s); least squares from Legendre and Gauss (1805-1809)
summary: Models a continuous outcome as a weighted sum of several predictors, estimating each predictor's unique contribution while holding the others constant.
description: Multiple regression fits an outcome such as task time, error count or a SUS score as a linear combination of predictors, for example interface complexity, user expertise and device type. Each coefficient estimates the expected change in the outcome per unit change in that predictor, conditional on the others, which is what separates it from a pile of bivariate correlations. Rigour comes from pre-specifying the model, checking assumptions (linearity, independent errors, homoscedasticity, normal residuals, low collinearity), reporting effect sizes with confidence intervals rather than p-values alone, and validating predictive accuracy on held-out data. In UX it is the workhorse behind driver analysis, benchmarking and predicting error rates from design attributes, but it is descriptive unless the causal structure justifies the covariates chosen.
steps: Write the outcome, the candidate predictors and the reason each is included before looking at the data, ideally with a causal diagram.
Plan sample size: a common rule is at least 10-20 observations per predictor, or run a power analysis (e.g. G*Power, f2 = 0.15 for a medium effect).
Clean and code predictors: centre continuous variables, dummy-code categories with a clear reference level, and inspect distributions.
Fit the model and inspect diagnostics: residual plots, Q-Q plot, VIF (investigate above 5, act above 10) and Cook's distance (flag above 4/n).
Report standardised and unstandardised coefficients with 95% confidence intervals, plus R-squared and adjusted R-squared.
Validate with k-fold cross-validation (k = 5 or 10) and report out-of-sample RMSE or R-squared, not only in-sample fit.
Translate coefficients into design language, e.g. each additional form field adds 4.2 s (95% CI 3.1-5.3) to completion time.
outputs: A fitted model with coefficients, confidence intervals, explained variance, diagnostic plots, cross-validated prediction error and a plain-language driver ranking.
useWhen: Predicting a continuous UX outcome from several design or user attributes; key-driver analysis of satisfaction; estimating how much of a metric each factor explains while controlling for the others.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the outcome is binary or a count (use logistic or Poisson regression), when predictors vastly outnumber cases (use PLS or regularised regression), or when you need causal claims without a defensible adjustment set (use an experiment or DAG-guided analysis).
whyLost: It survives in survey driver analysis but is often run as a click-through in a tool, with no diagnostics, no validation and coefficients read causally. The rigour lives in quantitative UX teams rather than general practice.
whereToUse: Satisfaction driver analysis, benchmarking studies, predicting task time or error rate from interface metrics, pricing and plan research, and model-based design trade-offs in SaaS and fintech.
example: A trading app team regresses order-entry error rate on screen complexity score, user tenure and device. Complexity carries a coefficient of 0.8 errors per 100 orders per point after adjusting for tenure, which justifies simplifying the order ticket before onboarding work.
sources: Applied Predictive Modeling (Max Kuhn & Kjell Johnson)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chris Chapman & Elea McDonnell Feit)
Applied Linear Statistical Models (Kutner, Nachtsheim, Neter & Li)
Applied Predictive Modeling (Kuhn & Johnson)
R for Marketing Research (Chapman & Feit)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 43 — Regression, Moderation & Mediation for UX Researchers
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Kutner, M., Nachtsheim, C., Neter, J. & Li, W. (2005) Applied Linear Statistical Models, 5th ed. McGraw-Hill.

name: Multiple Resource Theory for Multimodal UX Design
donor: Engineering psychology and aviation human factors
origin: Christopher Wickens (1980, 1984, 2002)
summary: Predicts interference between concurrent tasks from their demands on separate resources (modality, code, stage and visual channel) and assigns interface information to reduce conflict.
description: Wickens' multiple resource theory proposes that attention draws on partly separate pools defined by four dimensions: processing stage (perception and cognition versus response), perceptual modality (visual versus auditory), processing code (spatial versus verbal), and visual channel (focal versus ambient). Tasks that share resources interfere more than tasks using different ones; for example, reading a text notification while navigating a map competes visually and verbally, whereas a spoken direction while watching the road shares less. The computational model sums demand scores and resource-conflict penalties to predict interference. In UX this supports designing in-car, wearable, AR, cockpit-like and multitasking interfaces: allocate information to modalities and codes that do not conflict with the primary task, then validate with dual-task performance and workload measures such as NASA-TLX.
steps: Map each interface element to its primary resource pool: text/labels (visual-verbal), icons (visual-spatial), audio feedback (auditory-verbal), spatial navigation (visual-spatial).
For complex tasks with dual demands: route elements to different pools.
Example: visual task with audio secondary feedback = minimal interference.
Visual task with text instructions = high interference (same pool).
Measure dual-task interference: performance on primary task with vs. without secondary task.
outputs: Task demand profiles across the four dimensions, predicted interference scores, modality assignments for interface information, and dual-task validation results.
useWhen: Driving, aviation, medical monitoring, AR and wearables, voice-plus-screen experiences, and any product used while doing something else.
avoidWhen: For single-task desktop interfaces with no concurrent activity; standard usability testing is enough.
whyLost: It is foundational in aviation and automotive human factors but rarely taught in UX, where multimodal design is decided by intuition.
whereToUse: Multi-modal interface design, dashboard design for demanding contexts, vehicle HMI, surgical robot interface, industrial IoT.
example: An in-car navigation team plans to show text messages on the central screen. Multiple resource analysis predicts high visual-verbal conflict with driving, and a simulator dual-task study confirms lane deviation increases, so messages are read aloud with a steering-wheel reply.
sources: Handbook of Perception and Cognition — Benjamin Martin Bly
Wickens, Multiple resources and performance prediction (Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science, 2002)
Engineering Psychology and Human Performance (Wickens et al.)
reference: Wickens CD (2002) Multiple resources and performance prediction. Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science 3(2):159-177

name: Multiverse and Specification Curve Analysis
origin: Sara Steegen, Francis Tuerlinckx, Andrew Gelman and Wolf Vanpaemel (2016); Uri Simonsohn, Joseph Simmons and Leif Nelson (2020)
summary: Runs an analysis under every reasonable combination of analytic choices and reports the distribution of results, exposing how fragile a finding is.
description: Any analysis involves many defensible choices: exclusion rules, metric definitions, time windows, covariates, model types. Each path through this 'garden of forking paths' could give a different answer. Multiverse analysis enumerates the reasonable choices and runs all combinations; specification curve analysis plots the sorted estimates and indicates which choices drive variation, with a permutation-based joint test. If a finding holds across most specifications, it is robust; if it appears only under a few, it was probably a by-product of choice. Product analytics and UX metrics are especially vulnerable because metric definitions are flexible.
steps: List every analytic decision point and the reasonable options at each (e.g. 3 exclusion rules x 4 windows x 2 models).
Justify inclusion of options in advance, ideally pre-registered.
Run the analysis for every combination and store estimates and uncertainty.
Plot the specification curve: estimates sorted by size with indicators of which choices were used.
Conduct inference across specifications (e.g. permutation test of the share of significant same-sign results).
Report the full distribution and identify choices that change conclusions.
outputs: A specification curve plot, the distribution of estimates and identification of influential choices.
useWhen: Findings rest on analytic choices with no single correct option, especially high-stakes metric claims.
avoidWhen: Simple pre-registered analyses with clearly correct choices.
whyLost: It arose from the psychology replication crisis, which UX largely did not engage with.
whereToUse: Retention and engagement claims, survey index construction, A/B metrics with flexible definitions, research repository meta-claims.
example: A claim that dark mode increases session length holds in only 14 of 96 specifications, mostly those excluding sessions under 10 seconds. The team reports the effect as not robust.
sources: Steegen et al., Increasing transparency through a multiverse analysis (2016), Perspectives on Psychological Science
Simonsohn, Simmons & Nelson, Specification curve analysis (2020), Nature Human Behaviour
reference: Simonsohn, U., Simmons, J. P., & Nelson, L. D. (2020). Nature Human Behaviour, 4, 1208-1214.

name: MUSHRA Listening Test (ITU-R BS.1534)
aka: Multiple Stimuli with Hidden Reference and Anchor
origin: ITU-R Recommendation BS.1534, 2001 (revised 2015)
summary: A standardised listening test in which trained listeners rate several audio versions against a known reference, with a hidden reference and low-quality anchors to validate ratings.
description: MUSHRA asks listeners to rate multiple stimuli on a 0-100 continuous quality scale, simultaneously, with free switching between them and an open reference. Among the stimuli are a hidden copy of the reference and one or more anchors (e.g. a 3.5 kHz low-pass filtered version). Listeners who fail to rate the hidden reference near 100 are excluded under post-screening rules. The design yields sensitive, reliable comparisons for intermediate audio quality. For UX, it is a model of rigour for any perceptual comparison: voice assistant TTS, notification sounds, call quality, audio in video products. Its anchors and hidden reference make rater reliability measurable.
steps: Prepare stimuli: the reference, the systems under test, a hidden reference and the standard anchors, loudness-normalised.
Recruit and train listeners (typically 15-20 experienced listeners) with a familiarisation phase.
Run trials with all stimuli for an item presented together in random order, rated on 0-100.
Apply post-screening: exclude listeners rating the hidden reference below 90 for more than 15% of items.
Analyse with mixed models or ANOVA, reporting means and 95% confidence intervals per system.
Relate quality differences to perceptual attributes through follow-up descriptive analysis if needed.
outputs: Mean quality scores with confidence intervals per system, listener reliability data.
useWhen: Comparing voice synthesis, codecs, noise suppression, audio branding or alert sounds at intermediate quality differences.
avoidWhen: Very small impairments (use ITU-R BS.1116 ABX-style tests) or general preference questions in context.
whyLost: Audio quality testing lives in audio engineering, and UX teams rarely evaluate sound with standardised methods.
whereToUse: Voice assistants and TTS, video conferencing, hearing-aid apps, games, in-car audio cues.
example: A voice AI team compares four TTS voices in MUSHRA with 20 listeners; the hidden reference screens out three unreliable raters, and one voice is shown to be significantly more natural on long passages.
sources: ITU-R BS.1534-3 (2015) Method for the subjective assessment of intermediate quality level of audio systems
Bech & Zacharov, Perceptual Audio Evaluation: Theory, Method and Application (2006)
reference: ITU-R (2015). Recommendation BS.1534-3.

name: Mystery Shopping
origin: Long-standing market research practice; described by Veal and Darcy as a potentially fruitful but underexploited form of observation in sport facilities
summary: A trained researcher uses a service incognito, as an ordinary customer would, and reports against a checklist of quality features.
description: Mystery shopping is a form of observational research in which the researcher plays the role of a user, visitor or customer to find out what the experience of using a facility, product or service is really like. The mystery shopper uses the facilities or services on an incognito basis, carrying a checklist of features to observe, such as cleanliness, the availability and clarity of information, and staff performance, and writes a report after the visit. Veal and Darcy point out that it draws on the observer's expertise to judge service quality and to notice details, for example safety problems, that routine users might miss. They also warn that ethical and industrial relations issues can arise because of the deception involved, since the researcher is typically acting for management and staff are being assessed without knowing it. In UX and service design the method is useful for evaluating end-to-end journeys that cross digital and human touchpoints, such as sign-up, delivery, returns or support, where lab testing cannot reproduce the real service and staff behaviour.
steps: Define the journey or service episodes to be evaluated and the standards they should meet.
Build a checklist of observable features, with clear rating criteria, covering every touchpoint in the journey.
Agree the ethical position with management and, where appropriate, staff representatives, including how findings about individuals will be used.
Brief and train shoppers to behave like typical customers and to record observations soon after each episode.
Carry out the visits or online journeys across a planned spread of locations, channels, days and times.
Compile checklist scores and narrative reports, and look for patterns rather than blaming individual staff.
Feed the findings into journey maps and service blueprints and recheck after changes.
outputs: Completed checklists and narrative reports for each episode, aggregated scores by touchpoint, and a list of service and experience failures.
useWhen: You need an honest picture of a live, multi-channel service experience as customers actually receive it, including staff behaviour and offline steps.
avoidWhen: Covert assessment of staff would breach trust or agreements, the service cannot be used without real personal or financial commitments, or the issue is purely interface usability.
whyLost: UX grew around lab and remote testing of interfaces, while mystery shopping stayed in retail operations and quality assurance; its deception and staff-monitoring connotations also make researchers wary.
whereToUse: Omnichannel retail, banking and insurance onboarding, customer support, delivery and returns, hospitality and venue booking, public services.
example: A ticketing company asks researchers to buy, transfer and refund tickets as ordinary fans across the app, phone line and stadium box office. Checklists show that the refund promise in the app is not honoured at the box office, a failure no usability test of the app alone would have found.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge.

name: N-1 Two-Proportion Test
origin: Pearson; N-1 adjustment recommended by Campbell (2007) and adopted for UX by Sauro & Lewis
summary: Compares two independent success or conversion rates accurately, even when samples are small.
description: Comparing completion or conversion rates between two designs, tested on different people, is the most common quantitative UX comparison. The classic chi-square test is inaccurate when expected cell counts are small, and Fisher's exact test is overly conservative, so real differences get missed. Campbell's simulation work showed that multiplying the chi-square statistic by (N−1)/N gives accurate Type I error rates across almost all sample sizes, as long as every expected count is at least one. The equivalent z-test version also yields a confidence interval around the difference, which tells stakeholders how big the improvement might be, not only whether it is real.
steps: Record successes and totals for each independent group.
Check that every expected cell count is at least 1; if not, use Fisher's exact test.
Compute the pooled proportion and z = (p1 − p2) / sqrt(P(1−P)(1/n1 + 1/n2)), then multiply by sqrt((N−1)/N).
Convert to a two-tailed p-value.
Compute an adjusted-Wald interval around the difference and report both.
outputs: A p-value and an interval for the difference between two rates.
useWhen: Between-subjects comparisons of success, conversion, click-through or preference rates.
avoidWhen: The same people saw both designs (use McNemar), or there are more than two groups (use chi-square with follow-ups).
whyLost: Analytics tools default to large-sample z-tests, and most UX practitioners never meet the small-sample correction.
whereToUse: Small A/B tests, competitive benchmarks, prototype comparisons with 20 to 50 people per arm.
example: Design A: 11 of 20 complete; design B: 18 of 21. The N-1 test gives p = 0.02 and the 90% interval for the difference runs from about 12 to 50 points.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
reference: Campbell, I. (2007). Chi-squared and Fisher-Irwin tests of two-by-two tables with small sample recommendations. Statistics in Medicine 26.

name: Naive Bayes Classification
origin: Bayes' theorem with independence assumption; widely used in text classification since the 1990s
summary: A fast, simple classifier that predicts categories (such as ticket topic or churn risk) from features assumed independent.
description: Naive Bayes estimates, for each class, the probability of each feature value, then multiplies them to score a new case. The "naive" assumption that features are independent is usually wrong, but the ranking of classes is often still good. It trains in seconds, needs little data and is easy to explain. In UX research it is useful for auto-tagging open-ended survey responses or support tickets into known codes after a human has coded a training set, and as a quick baseline before more complex models.
steps: Code a training set by hand (for example 500 verbatims into themes).
Convert text or categorical predictors into features (words, answers).
Estimate class priors and conditional probabilities, with smoothing for unseen values.
Predict classes for new cases and evaluate with a confusion matrix on held-out data.
Review misclassified examples and refine codes or features.
outputs: A classifier that tags new records into known categories.
useWhen: Scaling up manual coding of text or categorical data with a simple, transparent model.
avoidWhen: Features are strongly dependent and calibrated probabilities matter.
whyLost: UX qualitative coding stayed manual while text classification grew up in data science.
whereToUse: Support ticket triage, open-ended survey coding, app review analysis.
example: After coding 600 app reviews, a Naive Bayes model tags 20,000 more into eight themes at 81% accuracy, enough to track theme trends weekly.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), Practical Statistics for Data Scientists, chapter 5.

name: Named entity recognition for UX research domains
origin: NER defined at MUC-6, 1995; spaCy EntityRuler and trainable NER
summary: Training or configuring entity recognition to detect UX-relevant entities, such as product features, competitors, devices, workflows and emotions, in transcripts and feedback.
description: Generic NER detects people, organisations and places, which is useful mainly for anonymisation. UX research needs domain entities: feature names, screens, competitor products, job roles, workarounds, devices and emotions. spaCy supports rule-based patterns (EntityRuler) and trainable statistical NER on annotated examples. A hybrid approach typically works best: rules for known vocabulary, trained models for variants and new mentions. Rigour comes from a clear annotation guideline, double annotation with agreement measurement, held-out evaluation with precision, recall and F1, and error analysis. Generic NER is also used to detect personal names and places for anonymisation, with high recall prioritised.
steps: Define an entity schema of 5-12 types with written definitions and examples.
Build an EntityRuler with known terms (feature names from the product, competitor list).
Annotate 300-1,000 sentences with two annotators, measuring agreement (e.g. F1 between annotators of 0.80 or above) and refining guidelines.
Train or fine-tune the NER component on the annotated data, holding out 20% for evaluation.
Evaluate per entity type and inspect errors, especially missed variants and false positives.
Deploy with the rules first and model second, and re-evaluate when the product vocabulary changes.
outputs: An entity schema and guideline, an annotated corpus, a trained NER component with per-type scores, and entity mentions across the corpus.
useWhen: Large corpora of interviews, feedback or tickets where systematic counts of feature, competitor or emotion mentions are needed, and for anonymisation.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the corpus is small or the questions are about meaning and context rather than mentions; manual coding is better there.
whyLost: Domain NER requires annotation effort and NLP skills that UX teams rarely have, so it stayed in text analytics and computational linguistics.
whereToUse: Voice-of-customer analytics, competitive intelligence from interviews, feedback triage and transcript anonymisation.
example: A fintech research team trains NER for 'feature', 'competitor' and 'workaround' across 220 transcripts. It reveals 140 mentions of spreadsheet workarounds, concentrated among small-business users, which prompts a dedicated study.
sources: spaCy (en_core_web_trf transformer model)
spacy-transformers
textacy
displacy visualisation
Grishman, R. & Sundheim, B. (1996) Message Understanding Conference-6: A brief history. COLING
Jurafsky, D. & Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing, 3rd ed. draft
The Inquiry Series, C10 — spaCy — Building NLP Pipelines for Qualitative Research
reference: Grishman, R. & Sundheim, B. (1996) Message Understanding Conference-6: A brief history. COLING 1996

name: Narrative Inquiry
origin: D. Jean Clandinin and F. Michael Connelly, 1990 to 2000 (Narrative Inquiry)
summary: Studies experience through the stories people live and tell, working within a three-dimensional space of temporality, sociality and place, and keeping stories whole rather than fragmenting them.
description: Narrative inquiry treats story as both the phenomenon and the method: people understand their lives narratively, so research should attend to stories in context. Clandinin and Connelly define a three-dimensional inquiry space: temporality (past, present and future), sociality (personal and social conditions, including the researcher's relationship to participants) and place. Researchers collect field texts such as conversations, journals, artefacts and field notes over extended relationships, write tentative interim texts shared with participants, and only then compose research texts. Unlike thematic coding, narrative inquiry resists breaking stories into fragments, keeping sequence and context intact. Its rigour lies in relational responsibility, sustained engagement and 'wakefulness' to simplification.
steps: Field texts (data collection): Collect field texts — stories told through interviews, journal entries, letters, photographs, documents, oral histories.
Maintain narrative stance: Resist the analytical impulse to fragment stories into codes before the full narrative is preserved.
Interim texts: Write early interpretations that are tentative and open to revision as more field texts are gathered.
Research texts (final accounts): Transform field texts into research texts that tell a story about the experience while honouring the narrative complexity of participants' own stories.
Wakefulness: Continuously guard against reducing rich life complexity to a simple analytical category.
outputs: Field texts, interim narrative accounts negotiated with participants, final narrative research texts, and cross-narrative resonances that inform design.
useWhen: Experience unfolds over time and context, such as illness, education, caregiving or career, and you need to understand the meaning of a journey rather than discrete tasks.
avoidWhen: You need structured, comparable data across many participants or answers to tactical questions; use semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis or a diary study.
whyLost: It requires long relationships and produces narrative texts rather than actionable lists, which clashes with sprint-based research, so it stayed in education and health research.
whereToUse: Long-term health conditions, education and learning products, caregiving and family services, career platforms, and longitudinal research programmes.
example: A diabetes app team follows 6 newly diagnosed people over 4 months, co-writing their narratives. The stories show the app is experienced as a reminder of failure after setbacks, leading to a 'fresh start' mode after missed weeks.
sources: Narrative Inquiry (Clandinin & Connelly)
Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Qualitative Interviewing
Fundamentals of Qualitative Research
Narrative Methods for the Human Sciences (Riessman)
reference: Clandinin, D. J. & Connelly, F. M. (2000). Narrative Inquiry: Experience and Story in Qualitative Research. Jossey-Bass.

name: NASA-TLX
origin: Sandra Hart and Lowell Staveland, NASA Ames, 1988
summary: A six-dimension subjective workload measure (mental, physical and temporal demand, performance, effort, frustration) producing an overall workload score per task.
description: NASA-TLX was developed at NASA Ames to measure perceived workload in complex tasks such as piloting. Participants rate six subscales on 0-100 scales: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance (reverse-anchored from good to poor), effort and frustration. The original version weights subscales through 15 pairwise comparisons; the Raw TLX simply averages them and performs comparably in most studies. The method's strength is sensitivity to design differences and its diagnostic subscales, which show whether workload stems from time pressure, mental demand or frustration. Rigour comes from administering it immediately after each task, comparing within subjects where possible, reporting subscale profiles not just the total, and keeping interpretation relative, since absolute TLX values vary widely across task types.
steps: Define tasks to compare and administer TLX immediately after each one.
Explain each subscale definition to participants before the first rating, noting the reversed performance anchor.
Collect ratings on 0-100 scales in 5-point increments for all six subscales.
Optionally run the 15 pairwise comparisons for weighting, or use the Raw TLX average.
Analyse totals and subscale profiles, using within-subject comparisons with 12-24 participants.
Relate high subscales to design causes and pair with performance data.
outputs: Overall workload score per task and condition, subscale profiles, statistical comparisons between designs.
useWhen: Comparing interface alternatives for demanding tasks, safety-critical systems, clinical tools, automotive and enterprise workflows.
avoidWhen: Simple, low-demand consumer tasks where differences will be small; SUS or task metrics are more informative.
whyLost: Still in use: Validated; widely used in human factors and increasingly in UX.
whereToUse: Task workload assessment; comparing interface alternatives; safety-critical design.
example: An EHR vendor compared two medication reconciliation designs with 16 nurses. The new design reduced Raw TLX from 58 to 41, mainly through lower temporal demand and frustration, with no change in accuracy.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
Development of NASA-TLX (Hart & Staveland)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Hart, S. G., & Staveland, L. E. (1988). Development of NASA-TLX (Task Load Index): Results of empirical and theoretical research. Advances in Psychology, 52, 139-183.

name: Nash Equilibrium Analysis
origin: John F. Nash, 1950
summary: Identifies strategy profiles where no player can improve their payoff by deviating alone, explaining why inferior designs persist and what would have to change for a new form to win.
description: A strategy profile (s1*, ..., sn*) is a Nash equilibrium if, for every player i, playing si* yields at least as much as any alternative given all others play their equilibrium strategies. Three properties matter for design research: equilibrium is stable but not necessarily optimal (as in the Prisoner's Dilemma), systems can have multiple equilibria, and disruption requires a change in the environment rather than a better individual choice. Vivek Gopinath's paper uses it as a diagnostic and generative lens rather than a precise predictor, because design actors are partially rational with incomplete information. Players include makers, suppliers, retailers, users, critics, regulators and craft communities; payoffs include cultural legitimacy, perceived quality, adoption and recognition. Mixed-strategy equilibria explain hybrids such as Indian homes keeping both dining chairs and floor seating, each activated by context. The lens is operationalised through the Deviation Utility model.
steps: List the players in the design ecosystem.
List each player's available strategies.
Describe the payoffs each strategy combination yields, including cultural, social and material payoffs.
Check whether any single player gains by deviating unilaterally from the current form.
Distinguish stability, stagnation (collectively suboptimal equilibrium) and multiple or mixed-strategy equilibria.
Identify environmental changes (technology, regulation, cultural movement, new channels) that would shift payoffs for several players at once.
outputs: A player-strategy-payoff map, equilibrium diagnosis and candidate levers for change.
useWhen: When designs, standards or conventions persist despite better alternatives, or when adoption depends on several actors moving together.
avoidWhen: When a single user's choice is independent of others' choices; standard usability and preference research suffices.
whyLost: Central to economics, rarely translated into design research instruments.
whereToUse: Platform standards, payment methods, marketplaces, craft and cultural products, media formats.
example: Analysing three-act film structure, studios, distributors, audiences, critics and filmmakers all face penalties for deviating, explaining why a demonstrably engaging non-linear form fails in mainstream cinema but thrives on the festival circuit.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
reference: Nash, J. F. (1950). Equilibrium points in n-person games. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 36(1), 48–49.

name: Nash Equilibrium Design Research Protocol
donor: Game theory, behavioural economics and design theory
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A six-stage protocol (Predict, Diagnose, Prove, Forecast, Prescribe, Validate) that maps a design ecosystem's players and payoffs, measures ΔU and targets interventions at what keeps a form in equilibrium.
description: The protocol treats a stable design form as a Nash equilibrium: a state where no single actor (maker, user, retailer, critic, cultural norm) gains by deviating unilaterally, regardless of whether a superior alternative exists. It distinguishes design stability (the form still satisfies all players' payoffs) from design stagnation (a collectively suboptimal equilibrium), and introduces the design plateau: a form that no longer serves needs, whose stakeholders know better options exist, yet persists because individual switching costs exceed individually capturable gains. Plateaus dissolve through ecosystem change that shifts payoffs for several players at once, not through a better object alone. The six stages run from ecosystem mapping and baseline ΔU, through qualitative coding against ΔU components, statistical confirmation (surveys, factor analysis, SEM), Monte Carlo scenario forecasting and targeted prescriptions, to validation by trials and re-estimated ΔU. Cases include the Indian pressure cooker, Khurja ceramics, floor seating and the three-act film structure.
steps: Predict: map the ecosystem's players, their strategies and the payoff structures maintaining the current form, and compute a baseline ΔU for the proposed alternative.
Diagnose: gather think-alouds, in-depth interviews and contextual observation, and code evidence against ΔU components to find the drivers of Uh, E and P.
Classify the situation as stability, stagnation or plateau, and note mixed-strategy or multiple co-existing equilibria.
Prove: test with surveys, factor analysis and SEM whether the identified components statistically predict preference for the existing form.
Forecast: simulate adoption under redesign scenarios (e.g. SNR raised from 0.35 to 0.75 and E halved) with Monte Carlo to express uncertainty.

Prescribe: design interventions at the most negative components (raise SNR, reduce E, build T, restructure the ecosystem around P), including channel or institutional changes, not only object changes.
Validate: confirm with controlled trials, A/B tests where possible, longitudinal observation and qualitative follow-up; re-estimate ΔU against baseline and synthesise in a joint display.
Check ethics: work with communities on which components they wish to preserve, especially in craft contexts.
outputs: Ecosystem player-payoff map, ΔU baseline and component profile, equilibrium classification, scenario forecasts, targeted interventions and a validation comparison.
useWhen: When a design form persists despite better alternatives, when planning disruptive redesigns, or when working with craft, cultural or platform ecosystems with many interdependent actors.
avoidWhen: For single-user usability problems with no ecosystem dynamics; use usability testing. Avoid using the power analysis against the communities studied.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath; game theory has rarely been operationalised as a design research instrument.
whereToUse: Platform and payment migrations, enterprise software replacement, craft and cultural product design, media formats, marketplace design.
example: Analysing why the whistle-valve pressure cooker persists, a researcher maps manufacturers, retailers, users, repair shops and sensory norms, finds high Uh, low T and high P, and recommends building repair-ecosystem trust before launching a silent digital model.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Equilibrium and the Design Object, Section 9.1.

name: Naturalistic Decision Making / Recognition-Primed Decision Model
origin: Gary Klein, 1989-1999
summary: Describes how experts recognise situations and mentally simulate a single workable option, implying interfaces should support recognition rather than option comparison.
description: Klein's research with firefighters, commanders and nurses found that experts in real conditions rarely compare options analytically. They recognise a situation as an instance of a known pattern, which brings cues, goals, expectancies and a typical action, then mentally simulate that action; if it works they act, otherwise they modify or try the next. Decision quality comes from the richness of the pattern library. The treatise's transfer: expert users of complex tools pattern-match and act, so UX for experts should support recognition through consistent visual language, strong affordances and predictable behaviour, reducing the need for deliberation. Methodologically, NDM uses cognitive task analysis such as the Critical Decision Method to elicit cues and expectancies. Rated HIGH priority.
steps: Identify critical, time-pressured decisions made by expert users.
Conduct Critical Decision Method interviews on specific challenging incidents, probing cues, expectancies and options considered.
Extract the cues experts use to recognise situation types and their typical actions.
Build decision requirements tables linking decisions, cues, difficulties and errors.
Design displays that make recognition cues salient and support mental simulation.
Evaluate with scenario-based simulations under time pressure.
outputs: Decision requirements tables, cue inventories, recognition-supporting design requirements.
useWhen: Expert, time-pressured, high-stakes tools: clinical, security, emergency, trading, operations.
avoidWhen: Novice consumer choices where deliberate comparison is appropriate (for example insurance plan comparison).
whyLost: Lives in defence and human factors; consumer UX focused on novices and choice architecture.
whereToUse: SOC analyst consoles, ICU dashboards, dispatch, incident response tooling, air traffic control.
example: Critical Decision Method interviews with SOC analysts show they triage alerts by three recognisable cue patterns; the console redesign surfaces those cues in alert cards and cuts triage time by 30%.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Klein G (1998) Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions
Klein GA, Calderwood R & MacGregor D (1989) Critical decision method for eliciting knowledge. IEEE SMC
Lipshitz R et al. (2001) Taking stock of naturalistic decision making. J Behav Decis Making 14(5)
reference: Klein G (1998) Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions. MIT Press.

name: Navigation Design Patterns
origin: Christopher Alexander's pattern language (1977) applied to interfaces; Jenifer Tidwell, Designing Interfaces (2005)
summary: A repertoire of proven navigation structures, such as mega-menus, faceted navigation, breadcrumbs and progressive disclosure, chosen and evaluated against content and task needs.
description: Navigation design patterns are reusable solutions to recurring navigation problems, documented in pattern libraries such as Tidwell's Designing Interfaces. They include global and local navigation, mega-menus, faceted navigation and filters, breadcrumbs, tabs, hub-and-spoke, progressive disclosure and bottom navigation on mobile. Following Alexander's pattern language, each pattern describes a context, a problem, forces in tension and a solution. Using patterns well is a research question as much as a design one: the right choice depends on content volume and structure, users' tasks and mental models, and device constraints. Rigour comes from matching patterns to evidence about tasks and structure, testing them with tree tests, first-click tests and usability sessions, and measuring navigation success after launch.
steps: Clarify the content structure, scale and primary user tasks from IA research.
Identify candidate patterns that fit the structure and device constraints.
Document the forces each pattern balances, such as discoverability versus screen space.
Prototype the most promising patterns with realistic content.
Test with first-click tests, tree tests or usability sessions on key tasks.
Select the pattern, document it in the design system, and monitor navigation metrics after launch.
outputs: Selected navigation patterns with rationale, prototypes, test results and design system documentation.
useWhen: For complex websites, e-commerce catalogues and enterprise applications choosing or revising navigation structures.
avoidWhen: Avoid copying patterns without evidence that they fit your content and tasks; start with card sorting and tree testing. Not a research method on its own.
whyLost: Still in use: Pattern libraries enable consistent application; documented in Designing Interfaces.
whereToUse: Complex websites; e-commerce; enterprise applications.
example: An electronics retailer compares a mega-menu with faceted category landing pages for 3,000 products. First-click tests with 100 users show faceted landing pages lead to 23 percent more correct first clicks for comparison tasks.
sources: Designing Interfaces
A Pattern Language (Alexander)
reference: Tidwell, J., Brewer, C. & Valencia, A. (2020). Designing Interfaces (3rd ed.). O'Reilly.

name: Negative Case Analysis
origin: Analytic induction (Florian Znaniecki, 1934; Alfred Lindesmith, 1947); formalised as a credibility technique by Lincoln and Guba, 1985
summary: Actively searches for cases that contradict emerging patterns and revises interpretations until they account for them, guarding qualitative analysis against confirmation bias.
description: Once a pattern appears in qualitative data, analysts tend to stop looking for evidence against it. Negative case analysis reverses this: every emerging claim is treated as a hypothesis, and the analyst deliberately searches for participants, episodes or data points that do not fit. Each negative case is then examined. It may require revising the claim, narrowing its scope, adding a condition, or identifying a separate pattern. Rooted in analytic induction, the technique aims for interpretations that account for all cases or explain exceptions explicitly. It is a core credibility strategy in Lincoln and Guba's framework. Its rigour comes from documenting the search, the cases found and the revisions made, rather than mentioning exceptions in passing.
steps: State each emerging finding as an explicit, testable claim with its intended scope.
Systematically search the full dataset for disconfirming evidence, including participants who behaved differently, contradictory statements and unexpected outcomes.
If needed, recruit additional participants likely to contradict the claim, such as power users, churned users or a different segment.
Examine each negative case to determine whether it reflects data error, a different condition, or a genuine limit to the claim.
Revise the claim by narrowing scope, adding conditions or creating a separate finding, and recheck against all data.
Report negative cases and the resulting revisions alongside each finding.
outputs: Explicit claims, a log of negative cases found and examined, revised findings with conditions and scope, and reported exceptions.
useWhen: Any qualitative synthesis where findings will drive decisions, especially when a pattern emerged quickly, the team has a preferred hypothesis, or stakeholders will challenge the findings.
avoidWhen: It should rarely be skipped. For quantitative data, use outlier analysis and robustness checks instead.
whyLost: Confirmation bias; researchers stop when the pattern appears
whereToUse: Interview synthesis, usability findings, persona development, research repositories, and validating AI-generated summaries that tend to over-generalise.
example: A team concludes users abandon a savings app because of fees. A search finds 4 of 14 churned users never encountered fees; their accounts reveal goal completion as a second churn path, leading to a 'next goal' feature.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba) via Sage Handbook
Qualitative Research Ethics (Sage)
The Inquiry Series, Vol II, Ch 27
The Inquiry Series, Ch 27 — Lincoln & Guba — Trustworthiness in Qualitative Research
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

name: Negative Case Analysis and Rival Explanations
origin: Lincoln & Guba, 1985 (Naturalistic Inquiry); rival explanations from Robert Yin's case study method
summary: Actively searching for data that contradict an emerging explanation and testing it against rival explanations, the main safeguard against confirmation bias in qualitative work.
description: Qualitative analysts naturally notice what fits their developing story. Negative case analysis reverses this: after each analytic pass the researcher states the working explanation, then searches for incidents that contradict it, and decides whether to refine the explanation with specified conditions, revise it fundamentally, or collect more data. Rival explanation testing generates at least two alternative accounts for each major finding and compares how well each accounts for all the data, including the anomalies. Both are reported openly; a study claiming no negative cases signals that the search was not conducted. The technique converts qualitative interpretation into something closer to falsification and is one of Lincoln and Guba's credibility techniques.
steps: After every axial coding session: List your current working theory. Now actively search your data for incidents that contradict it. These are negative cases — data points that do not fit your emerging explanation.

For each negative case: Ask — does this require me to (a) refine my theory to account for this as an exception with specifiable conditions, (b) revise my theory fundamentally, or (c) collect more data in this domain (theoretical sampling)?

Rival explanations: For each major finding, generate at least 2 alternative explanations that would also fit the data. Systematically compare your preferred explanation against each rival. Which one better accounts for all the data, including negative cases?
Document in findings: Report your negative cases and how you handled them. A study that reports zero negative cases is not rigorous — it means you stopped looking when you found confirmation.
outputs: A documented list of negative cases and how each was handled, a rival-explanations table per finding, and a refined explanation with scope conditions.
useWhen: Before presenting any qualitative finding that will drive a significant decision, when the team has a favoured hypothesis, or when findings look suspiciously clean.
avoidWhen: Purely descriptive inventories (feature request lists) where no explanatory claim is made; there, focus on coverage instead.
whyLost: Stakeholder pressure for confident, tidy narratives and the absence of review culture in industry mean disconfirming evidence is rarely sought or reported.
whereToUse: Strategy research, pricing and adoption studies, AI product evaluations where teams are invested in a hypothesis, and research review or critique sessions.
example: A team believes users abandon a meal-kit subscription because of price. Searching for negative cases reveals high-income churners who cite menu fatigue; testing rivals shows that variety, not price, explains most cancellations.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Case Study Research (Yin)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Lincoln, Y. S. & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. Sage.

name: Negative Control Analysis
origin: Marc Lipsitch, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen and Ted Cohen (2010); placebo tests in econometrics
summary: Tests an analysis on an outcome or exposure that should show no effect; any 'effect' found reveals confounding or bias in the method.
description: A negative control outcome is one that cannot plausibly be affected by the treatment but shares the same confounders; a negative control exposure is one that cannot affect the outcome but shares confounding with the real exposure. If the analysis finds an effect on a negative control, the method is biased. Examples in UX: a new search feature should not change the rate of password resets; users exposed to a campaign last month should not show effects before it started. Negative controls are cheap, powerful falsification checks for observational analyses and also for A/B tests with suspected sample ratio mismatch or instrumentation issues.
steps: Identify the main causal analysis and its likely sources of bias (self-selection, seasonality, instrumentation).
Choose negative control outcomes affected by the same biases but not by the treatment.
Choose negative control exposures or placebo times (e.g. a fake launch date) where appropriate.
Run the identical analysis pipeline on the negative controls.
Interpret non-null results as evidence of bias and adjust or abandon the method.
Report negative control results alongside main estimates.
outputs: Negative control estimates that validate or challenge the causal analysis.
useWhen: Any observational or quasi-experimental claim, and as a check on experiment instrumentation.
avoidWhen: When no plausible negative control exists; use sensitivity analysis instead.
whyLost: It is standard practice in pharmacoepidemiology but almost unknown in product analytics.
whereToUse: Feature adoption studies, campaign evaluations, health app outcome claims, before-after analyses.
