example: Users who enabled AI summaries appear to churn 30% less. A negative control outcome, churn in the month before enabling, shows a similar 'effect', revealing selection bias.
sources: Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen & Cohen, Negative controls: a tool for detecting confounding and bias in observational studies (2010), Epidemiology
Arnold et al., Negative control outcomes: a tool to detect bias (2016), International Journal of Epidemiology
reference: Lipsitch, M., Tchetgen Tchetgen, E., & Cohen, T. (2010). Epidemiology, 21(3), 383-388.

name: Nested and Multilevel Sampling
origin: Multilevel theory in organisational research (Klein & Kozlowski, 2000); nested sampling designs in mixed methods (Onwuegbuzie & Collins, 2007)
summary: Sampling individuals within teams, departments and organisations, and collecting data at each level, so organisational context is analysed rather than ignored.
description: In organisational settings, individuals' experiences are shaped by the team, department and company they belong to. Sampling only individuals, often one or two per company, confounds personal and contextual effects. Nested sampling maps the hierarchy (organisation, unit, team, individual), selects units at each level, and samples several individuals within each so that within-unit and between-unit variation can be compared. Organisation-level data such as policies, tools, size and structure are collected alongside interviews. Analysis treats cross-level relationships as findings: where organisational logics conflict with individual practice, or how team norms change the same tool's use. Quantitative variants support multilevel models.
steps: Map the levels: Organisation → department → team → individual. Each level is a potential unit of analysis and source of variation.
Sample at each level: Do not sample only individuals and ignore the organisational context. The team and organisation within which individuals are nested shape their experience.
Interlevel data collection: When selecting an individual, also collect organisational-level data providing context.
Interlevel analysis: Treat interlevel relationships as data. How does organisational context shape individual experience? Where do individual and organisational logics conflict?
outputs: A multilevel sampling frame, paired individual and unit-level data, cross-level analysis, and explanations separating individual from contextual effects.
useWhen: B2B and enterprise research where adoption and experience depend on team or organisational context, such as rollouts or admin-user dynamics.
avoidWhen: Consumer products with independent individual users; use purposive or maximum variation sampling.
whyLost: Recruiting several people per customer account is hard and slow, so B2B studies sample individuals across many accounts and lose context.
whereToUse: Enterprise SaaS adoption, healthcare systems across hospitals, education platforms across schools, and internal tool research.
example: Studying a CRM rollout, researchers sample three companies, two sales teams in each and four reps per team. Differences in use are explained by team-level quota policies rather than individual skill.
sources: Sampling and Choosing Cases in Qualitative Research
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods
Multilevel Theory, Research, and Methods in Organizations (Klein & Kozlowski)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Klein, K. J. & Kozlowski, S. W. J. (Eds.) (2000). Multilevel Theory, Research, and Methods in Organizations. Jossey-Bass.

name: Net Promoter Score
origin: Fred Reichheld, Bain & Company and Satmetrix, 2003
summary: A single 0-10 likelihood-to-recommend question; promoters (9-10) minus detractors (0-6) gives a loyalty score from -100 to +100.
description: NPS asks 'How likely are you to recommend [product] to a friend or colleague?' on an 11-point scale. Respondents scoring 9-10 are promoters, 7-8 passives and 0-6 detractors; NPS equals the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors. Reichheld claimed it predicted growth better than other measures, a claim later research has disputed. Its strengths are simplicity, executive familiarity and benchmarking. Its weaknesses are statistical: collapsing an 11-point scale into three categories discards information and increases variance, so margins of error are wide unless samples are large. Rigour comes from consistent timing and sampling, reporting confidence intervals, always asking a follow-up open question for reasons, analysing the full distribution or mean, and not treating NPS as a measure of usability.
steps: Define the population and trigger (relationship survey at a fixed interval, or transactional after an event).
Ask the standard question with the 0-10 scale and an open follow-up asking for the main reason.
Sample randomly and collect enough responses; a margin of error of ±5 points typically needs several hundred responses.
Calculate NPS with confidence intervals and also report the mean and distribution.
Code open-ended reasons thematically or with text analytics, split by promoters and detractors.
Track over time and segment, and connect drivers to product changes.
outputs: NPS with confidence intervals, response distribution, coded reasons by group, trend and segment reports.
useWhen: Relationship loyalty tracking, executive reporting and benchmarking against industry figures.
avoidWhen: Measuring usability or task experience (use SUS, UMUX-Lite or task metrics), products users cannot recommend (e.g. internal tools), or small samples.
whyLost: Still in use: Executive-friendly simplicity; enables benchmarking; but over-relied upon as sole UX metric.
whereToUse: Customer satisfaction tracking; executive reporting; loyalty measurement.
example: A B2B payroll provider tracked NPS quarterly with 900 responses. Coding detractor comments showed most cited payment run errors, not the interface, redirecting investment to reliability engineering.
sources: Measuring the User Experience
The One Number You Need to Grow (Fred Reichheld)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Reichheld, F. F. (2003). The one number you need to grow. Harvard Business Review, 81(12), 46-54.

name: Netnography
origin: Robert V. Kozinets, late 1990s; books 2010 and 2020
summary: Adapts ethnography to online communities, combining archived data, real-time observation and interaction to understand digital cultures, norms and identities.
description: Netnography (Robert Kozinets, 2010/2020) is an adaptation of ethnographic methods for studying online communities and digital culture. It treats online communities as real social communities deserving the same ethnographic attention as physical communities — with specific adaptations for the textual, asynchronous, and often pseudonymous nature of online interaction. In UX research, netnography is appropriate for understanding how user communities form around products, how users collectively develop workarounds, how opinions about product changes form and spread, and what social norms govern discussion in product communities.
steps: Site identification and access: Identify the online communities relevant to your research question. Determine access type: full member (active participant), lurker (observer only), or archival (using public historical data). Declare which you will use.
Cultural entrée: Observe the community before posting or engaging. Understand the community's norms, vocabulary, hierarchies, and conventions. What counts as appropriate behaviour here?
Data collection: Collect: archived posts and discussions, real-time observation notes, interviews with community members (with consent), your own participation reflections.

Ethical netnography: Public ≠ consented. Just because content is publicly accessible does not mean its creators expected or consented to it being used in research. Apply the Public Benefit / No Harm test rigorously. Pseudonymise all identifiers.
Analysis: Apply ethnographic analysis — cultural themes, social norms, identity performance, meaning-making — to the digital data.
outputs: A documented site and data set, immersion journal, cultural themes, community norms and identities, and implications for community-centred products.
useWhen: Users form communities online around your product or domain (gaming, crypto, health conditions, creators, open source) and you need cultural understanding rather than complaint counts.
avoidWhen: You need representative population data, or the community is private or vulnerable and consent is impractical; use interviews with consent. For simple review mining, use Social Media and Digital Trace Data Analysis.
whyLost: Marketing adopted 'social listening' dashboards, which reduce communities to sentiment counts and drop the ethnographic immersion and ethics that netnography requires.
whereToUse: Gaming and creator platforms, patient communities, crypto and fintech communities, open-source products, and community-led growth.
example: A team researching a fitness platform spends 8 weeks in its subreddit and Discord. Netnography reveals 'streak shame' rituals, users publicly confessing breaks, which inspires a forgiving streak feature and community celebrations of returns.
sources: Netnography (Robert Kozinets)
Social Media Research Methods
Research Methods for Everyday Life
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Kozinets, R. V. (2020). Netnography: The Essential Guide to Qualitative Social Media Research (3rd ed.). Sage.

name: Network Analysis
origin: Jacob Moreno, 1934 (sociometry); formalised by Wasserman and Faust, 1994
summary: Maps and measures relationships among users, content or features as a network, revealing communities, influencers, bridges and structural dependencies.
description: Network analysis represents entities as nodes and relationships as edges, then computes structural properties. Social network analysis, from Moreno's sociograms onward, measures centrality (who is most connected or most between), clustering, communities and structural holes. In UX contexts networks can be built from user interactions (follows, messages, collaboration), content links or co-usage of features. The analysis shows how communities form, who brokers information, which features are used together, and how changes might ripple through. Rigour comes from defining nodes and edges precisely, choosing appropriate thresholds and time windows, using validated community detection algorithms, checking robustness to parameter choices, and combining structure with qualitative understanding of what relationships mean. Ethical handling of relational data is essential because it reveals information about people who did not consent individually.
steps: Define nodes and edges precisely (e.g. users as nodes, collaboration on a document as edges) and the time window.
Extract relational data from logs or surveys, applying privacy safeguards.
Compute network metrics: degree, betweenness, clustering and density.
Detect communities with a validated algorithm (e.g. Louvain) and test robustness to parameters.
Interpret structures with qualitative research into what relationships mean.
Use findings to design features (e.g. supporting bridges) and simulate effects of changes.
outputs: Network maps, centrality and community metrics, identified brokers and isolated groups, design implications.
useWhen: Social and collaborative products, community platforms, enterprise adoption analysis and feature co-usage studies.
avoidWhen: Products without meaningful relationships between users or items, or where relational data cannot be ethically obtained.
whyLost: Latent: Used in social media research; growing in UX for community and platform design.
whereToUse: Social feature design; content recommendation; community product research.
example: An enterprise collaboration tool mapped co-editing networks across a client's departments. Finance was isolated with one bridging user; designing cross-team templates and onboarding that bridge increased cross-department collaboration.
sources: Social Media Research Methods
Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications (Wasserman & Faust)
van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Wasserman, S., & Faust, K. (1994). Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications. Cambridge University Press.

name: Network Super-Spreader Analysis of Design Patterns
origin: Network epidemic modelling (Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani 2001); adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Models pattern spread over the network of platforms, design systems and publications to identify super-spreader nodes where intervention has outsized effect.
description: Network epidemiology recognises that transmission follows contact networks and that highly connected nodes, super-spreaders, drive epidemics disproportionately. The treatise identifies UX super-spreaders: large platforms, design system providers and influential design thought-leaders and publications. When a major design system adopts a flawed pattern, it transmits it to all products built on it simultaneously; when a widely read publication promotes a pattern as best practice, adoption accelerates. Network models identify these nodes and prioritise them as intervention targets: regulatory pressure on platforms, engagement with design system maintainers and attention to influential publications have greater population impact than equivalent effort on individual products.
steps: Construct the network of influence: products, design systems, platforms, publications and links (dependencies, citations, copying).
Compute centrality measures (degree, betweenness, eigenvector) and identify hubs.
Overlay pattern adoption timing to see spread paths.
Simulate spread and targeted interventions on high-centrality nodes.
Prioritise engagement with super-spreader nodes.
Monitor downstream adoption after intervention.
outputs: Influence network, super-spreader list, simulated intervention impact.
useWhen: Planning ecosystem-level interventions against harmful patterns or to spread good ones.
avoidWhen: When network data cannot be assembled credibly.
whyLost: Network epidemiology never applied to design ecosystems.
whereToUse: Regulators, design-system governance, standards bodies, accessibility advocacy.
example: Mapping npm dependencies shows three UI kits underlie 60% of a sector's checkout pages; fixing a pre-ticked consent component in those kits removes the pattern from most of the sector.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Pastor-Satorras R & Vespignani A (2001) Epidemic spreading in scale-free networks. Phys Rev Lett 86
Newman MEJ (2010) Networks: An Introduction
reference: Pastor-Satorras R & Vespignani A (2001) Epidemic spreading in scale-free networks. Physical Review Letters 86(14):3200-3203.

name: Neural frame audit
donor: Cognitive linguistics (frame semantics, conceptual metaphor theory)
origin: Charles Fillmore (frame semantics, 1976–1982) and George Lakoff (Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things, 1987; Don't Think of an Elephant, 2004); operationalised as a UX protocol in Gopinath's Methods Atlas
summary: Elicits free associations to a product name or key term, codes them into the conceptual frames they activate, and checks whether those frames support or undermine the intended meaning.
description: Frame semantics holds that every word evokes a structured scene, with roles, expectations and values, and that people reason within the frame a word activates rather than from its dictionary definition. A neural frame audit applies this to product language. Participants give rapid free associations to a product name, feature label or category term; associations are coded into frames (for example 'wallet' evoking loss, theft, pickpocketing, cash or carrying) and the roles and inferences each frame licenses are made explicit. The audit compares the frame users actually activate with the frame the product team intended. Rigour comes from timed elicitation that limits deliberate rationalisation, structured coding with a second coder, and sampling across the segments whose frames are likely to differ, such as rural and urban or first-time and experienced users.
steps: List the 3 to 10 load-bearing terms to audit: product name, category noun, primary actions and key metaphors (for example 'wallet', 'top up', 'credit').

Recruit 12 to 30 participants per segment whose frames may differ, and run a timed free-association task: show each term and collect the first 3 to 5 words or images within about 20 seconds, in the participant's own language.
Follow with a short laddering probe on the first association: 'What happens in that situation? Who is involved? What could go wrong?' to surface the frame's roles and expected events.
Code associations into candidate frames using a codebook developed on the first 20% of data; have a second coder code at least 25% and aim for Cohen's kappa of 0.70 or above before proceeding.
For each term, tabulate frame frequencies by segment and record the inferences each dominant frame licenses (for example 'wallet' implies money can be stolen or lost).

Compare dominant frames against the intended frame and flag terms where the intended frame is activated by fewer than about half of participants in any priority segment, or where a threat frame dominates.
Generate alternative terms, re-run the elicitation on them with fresh participants, and select terms whose dominant frame matches intent.
outputs: A frame inventory per term and segment, frequency tables of activated frames, a list of licensed inferences and risks, and recommended term replacements with comparative evidence.
useWhen: Naming a product or feature, entering a new culture or literacy context, or when adoption data suggests a label is creating distrust or the wrong mental model.
avoidWhen: The question is whether users can find or operate a labelled control (use tree testing or first-click testing), or the vocabulary is technical and fixed by regulation.
whyLost: Frame analysis lived in cognitive linguistics and political communication (for example the FrameWorks Institute), where it is rigorous, but UX naming work drifted to preference polls and brand workshops that ask which name users like rather than what scene it evokes.
whereToUse: Naming in financial inclusion and health products, AI feature naming, public-sector service labels, market entry localisation.
example: A payments team tested 'Digital Wallet' with first-time rural users in India. Dominant associations were theft, loss and 'phone gets stolen, money gone', a threat frame; 'Bank on phone' activated a safety and institution frame and was adopted for onboarding copy.
sources: Women Fire & Dangerous Things (Lakoff)
Metaphors We Live By (Lakoff)
Methods Atlas — frame audit (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 19 — Neural Framing & the Architecture of Meaning
reference: Lakoff, G. (1987). Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things: What Categories Reveal about the Mind. University of Chicago Press; Fillmore, C. J. (1982). Frame Semantics. In Linguistics in the Morning Calm.

name: NGOMSL
origin: David Kieras, 1988-1997
summary: Structured natural-language GOMS notation that predicts both execution time and learning time from the number and complexity of methods.
description: NGOMSL, listed in the treatise's glossary as the natural-language member of the GOMS family, writes methods as program-like statements ('Method for goal: delete file. Step 1. Accomplish goal: select file...'). Because each statement corresponds to a production rule in cognitive complexity theory, counting statements yields estimates of learning time, and counting executed statements plus operators yields execution time. This makes NGOMSL distinctive: it predicts how much there is to learn and how much transfer exists between consistent methods, quantifying the benefit of consistency. Its rigour comes from explicit, inspectable method descriptions that any analyst can audit, and from its grounding in Kieras and Polson's cognitive complexity theory.
steps: List the user goals and top-level tasks to be modelled.
Write NGOMSL methods for each goal, step by step, down to primitive operators.
Identify shared submethods across tasks to quantify consistency and transfer.
Count new statements to estimate learning time (around 30 s per statement in classic estimates).
Estimate execution time from statement counts and operator times.
Compare alternative designs on learning and execution predictions.
outputs: Method listings, learning-time and execution-time predictions, consistency and transfer analysis.
useWhen: Evaluating consistency of a command set or design system, estimating training cost for enterprise software.
avoidWhen: Highly visual, exploratory or parallel tasks; use CPM-GOMS for parallelism or usability testing for exploration.
whyLost: GOMS family modelling faded as iterative testing became cheap and as interfaces became less procedural. NGOMSL's learning predictions were never taught widely.
whereToUse: Enterprise suites with training costs, design-system consistency audits, migration between product versions.
example: An ERP vendor writes NGOMSL methods for approving, rejecting and escalating purchase orders in two designs. The unified design shares 70% of statements and is predicted to cut training time by about a third.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kieras DE (1997) A guide to GOMS model usability evaluation using NGOMSL. In Handbook of HCI
John BE & Kieras DE (1996) The GOMS family of user interface analysis techniques
Kieras, A Guide to GOMS Model Usability Evaluation using NGOMSL (1997), in Helander et al. (eds.), Handbook of Human-Computer Interaction
John & Kieras, The GOMS family of user interface analysis techniques: comparison and contrast (1996), ACM TOCHI
reference: Kieras DE (1997) A guide to GOMS model usability evaluation using NGOMSL. In Helander M et al. (Eds) Handbook of Human-Computer Interaction. Elsevier.

name: Niche Construction and Work Artifact Analysis
donor: Evolutionary biology (niche construction) and cognitive anthropology
origin: Niche construction theory (Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman, 2003); cognitive niche ideas from Andy Clark; artefact models from Contextual Design
summary: Cataloguing and analysing the notes, spreadsheets and physical workarounds users create to repair systems, as precise evidence of unmet needs.
description: Niche construction refers to the way organisms modify their environment to make it more habitable. In UX research, users engage in cognitive niche construction when they modify their digital or physical environment to compensate for interface failures — creating post-it notes, custom spreadsheets, printed cheat sheets, physical labels, workaround procedures. These artifacts are not noise — they are the most precise data you can collect about unmet needs. Every workaround specifies exactly what the system fails to do.
steps: During CI or observation: Actively look for artifacts. Scan the physical environment: post-it notes on screens, stickers on hardware, printed documents with annotations, personal notebooks, custom labels. Scan the digital environment: desktop files, browser bookmarks, copy-paste documents, personal databases.

Photograph and catalog every artifact: With participant permission, photograph all artifacts. Note: location (where is it?), proximity (is it always within reach?), frequency of use (evidence of wear and handling).

Analyse each artifact for three things: (1) What information does it contain that the system fails to surface? (Gap in information provision.) (2) What action does it support that the system fails to afford? (Gap in affordance.) (3) What mental model does its structure reveal? (Gap in conceptual alignment.)

Ask about each artifact: "Tell me about this — what is it for?" "When do you use it?" "How long have you had it?" "What would happen if you didn't have it?" These questions reveal the system failure the artifact compensates for.
outputs: A photographed artefact catalogue, analysis of information, affordance and mental model gaps per artefact, and derived requirements.
useWhen: Field studies of established workflows where users have adapted their environment, especially legacy systems and complex professional work.
avoidWhen: New-to-world products with no existing practice, or fully digital consumer flows with little room for user-created artefacts; use diaries or generative sessions.
whyLost: Artefact collection is mentioned in contextual inquiry, but systematic coding of artefacts is usually skipped in favour of interview quotes.
whereToUse: Healthcare, logistics, manufacturing, finance operations, small business tools and any legacy system replacement project.
example: Visiting hospital wards, researchers photograph handwritten bed-status boards beside the electronic system. Analysing the boards reveals that nurses track 'expected discharge time', a field the system lacks.
sources: Universal Methods of Design (Martin)
Ethnographic Thinking (Hasbrouck)
Rapid Contextual Design (Holtzblatt)
Handbook of Ethnography
Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Niche Construction: The Neglected Process in Evolution (Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman)
Supersizing the Mind (Clark)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 31 — Ethnographic Fieldwork — Thick Description & Niche Construction
reference: Odling-Smee, F. J., Laland, K. N. & Feldman, M. W. (2003). Niche Construction. Princeton University Press.

name: Nominal Group Technique
origin: Andre Delbecq and Andrew Van de Ven, 1968 to 1971
summary: A structured group process of silent generation, round-robin sharing, clarification and independent voting that prevents dominant voices from shaping collective judgement.
description: Unstructured group discussions are distorted by status, confidence and talkativeness. The Nominal Group Technique (Delbecq and Van de Ven) structures a meeting so that individuals generate ideas silently and independently first, typically for 10 to 15 minutes. Ideas are then shared one at a time in round-robin order and recorded verbatim without debate, discussed only to clarify meaning, and ranked or rated privately by each participant. Votes are aggregated mathematically, and an optional second discussion and re-vote addresses items with divergent scores. The group is 'nominal' because members work individually within a group setting. Its rigour lies in separating generation from evaluation and replacing negotiation with independent, aggregated judgement.
steps: Silent idea generation: Participants work individually in silence for 10–15 minutes, writing responses on paper. No discussion.
Round-robin recording: Each participant shares one idea in turn. All ideas recorded visibly. No evaluation during this phase. Continue until all ideas are recorded.
Clarification discussion: The group discusses each idea for clarification only — questions of understanding are answered; advocacy is not permitted.
Individual ranking/rating: Each participant independently ranks or rates each idea. Votes are tallied.
Discussion and re-vote (optional): Discuss ideas with significantly divergent vote patterns. Allow final re-vote after discussion.
outputs: A complete idea list, aggregated rankings or ratings, a prioritised shortlist, and a record of where opinion diverged.
useWhen: You need to generate and prioritise requirements, risks, problems or research questions with a team or stakeholder group of about 5 to 12 people, especially where hierarchy could bias the outcome.
avoidWhen: You want free-flowing exploration, relationship building or co-design; use a facilitated workshop. For dispersed experts or anonymous judgement over time, use the Delphi Method.
whyLost: Design-thinking workshops popularised dot-voting and brainstorming, which kept the sticky notes but lost NGT's silent generation, round-robin recording and private ranking.
whereToUse: Stakeholder prioritisation, research planning, clinical and service design with mixed-status teams, retrospectives, and patient or user advisory panels.
example: A hospital digital team runs NGT with nurses, doctors and administrators to prioritise pain points in shift handover software. Silent generation surfaces 41 issues; private ranking puts a nurse-raised medication-reconciliation issue first, which open discussion had previously overlooked.
sources: Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods
Research Methods for Everyday Life
reference: Delbecq, A. L., Van de Ven, A. H. & Gustafson, D. H. (1975). Group Techniques for Program Planning. Scott, Foresman.

name: Non-Evaluative Listening and the Pause Rule
origin: Indi Young, 2015 (Practical Empathy)
summary: An interviewing discipline of listening to understand rather than react, using deliberate silence and non-evaluative reflection to surface participants' deeper reasoning.
description: Indi Young identifies two modes of listening: listening to react (preparing your response while the other person speaks) and listening to think (fully receiving what is said before forming any response). Most researchers — even experienced ones — listen to react, which means they process only the part of the participant's response that fits their existing mental model. The 0-second rule: when a participant stops speaking, you impose a minimum 0-second wait (in practice, 2–3 seconds of silence) before saying anything. This silence creates space for the participant to elaborate, correct themselves, or reveal the deeper thought they were managing.
steps: Before the session: Write your research questions on a card. Once the session begins, the card stays face down. Your questions are not the script — they are the territory. Follow the participant into their own territory.

During the session: When the participant finishes speaking, count two seconds before responding. Notice the impulse to fill silence — resist it. The participant will often fill it themselves with the most important thing they have to say.

After each response: Before asking the next question, reflect back what you heard: "It sounds like…" without evaluation or interpretation. This is not paraphrasing — it is demonstrating that you received what was said.
After the session: Review the recording. Mark every moment where you spoke within 1 second of the participant. These are your interruptions. Count them. Target: fewer than 5 per hour-long session.
outputs: Richer, less led transcripts; an interruption count per session as a quality metric; reflected summaries of participants' reasoning.
useWhen: Generative interviews about reasoning, motivation and inner thinking, and when coaching interviewers who talk too much or lead participants.
avoidWhen: Structured task-based sessions where tight time control matters (usability testing with fixed tasks); use a systematic probe schedule instead.
whyLost: Interview training in UX focuses on question lists and scripts, and the listening skill itself is rarely taught, practised or measured.
whereToUse: Generative discovery, mental model research, interviewer training programmes, and sensitive topics in health or personal finance.
example: An interviewer studying how freelancers set prices stops filling silences. After a three-second pause, a participant adds that she under-prices out of fear of losing her only client, which becomes the central insight.
sources: Practical Empathy (Indi Young)
Mental Models (Indi Young)
Listening to People
Listening (Blee)
Practical Empathy (Young)
Mental Models (Young)
Qualitative Interviewing
The Inquiry Series, Ch 32 — Advanced Elicitation — The Archaeology of the Interview
reference: Young, I. (2015). Practical Empathy: For Collaboration and Creativity in Your Work. Rosenfeld Media.

name: Non-Inferiority and Equivalence Trials for Design Changes
origin: Clinical trial methodology from the 1980s-1990s; ICH E9 and E10 guidelines (1998, 2000); CONSORT extension (Piaggio et al., 2006/2012)
summary: Tests whether a new design is not worse than the current one by more than a pre-specified margin, the right question for simplifications, migrations and cost-saving changes.
description: Many design changes aim not to improve a metric but to avoid harming it: a cheaper infrastructure, a simpler UI, an accessibility fix, removing a feature. Failing to find a significant difference in a standard A/B test does not prove no harm. Non-inferiority trials define a margin (the largest acceptable loss) in advance and test whether the confidence interval's lower bound lies above minus the margin. The margin must be justified clinically, or here, by business and user impact. Sample sizes are planned for this hypothesis. This brings honest inference to the many 'no significant difference, ship it' decisions in product teams.
steps: Specify the primary metric and justify the non-inferiority margin (e.g. no more than 0.5 percentage point loss in conversion).
Compute sample size for the non-inferiority hypothesis at the desired power.
Run the randomised test, using intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses.
Compute the one-sided confidence interval (e.g. 97.5%) for the difference.
Conclude non-inferiority only if the lower bound exceeds minus the margin in both analyses.
Report the margin rationale and the CI, not just a p-value.
outputs: A justified margin, CI-based non-inferiority conclusion and transparent reporting.
useWhen: Shipping simplifications, migrations, accessibility changes, cost reductions or removals where harm must be ruled out.
avoidWhen: When you expect and need improvement; use a superiority test.
whyLost: Product experimentation platforms default to superiority tests, and teams misread non-significance as equivalence.
whereToUse: Platform migrations, design system rollouts, feature deprecations, AI model swaps to cheaper models.
example: Moving to a cheaper LLM for support replies, the team pre-specifies a margin of 1 point on resolution rate. The lower bound of the CI is -0.6, so non-inferiority is concluded and the change ships.
sources: Piaggio et al., Reporting of noninferiority and equivalence randomized trials: extension of the CONSORT 2010 statement (2012), JAMA
FDA, Non-Inferiority Clinical Trials to Establish Effectiveness: Guidance for Industry (2016)

name: Non-Negative Matrix Factorisation for Behavioural Analysis
aka: Non-negative Matrix Factorisation (NMF) for Usage Archetypes
origin: Daniel Lee and Sebastian Seung, 1999 (Paatero and Tapper 1994 as positive matrix factorisation)
summary: Decomposes a users-by-features usage matrix into additive, non-negative archetypes so each user is described as a weighted mix of interpretable usage styles.
description: NMF factorises a non-negative data matrix into two non-negative matrices, producing parts-based, additive representations. Unlike PCA, factors have no negative loadings, so each is interpretable as a coherent pattern that adds to others. The treatise's transfer: apply to clickstream matrices where rows are users or sessions and columns are features, actions or screens. NMF yields K archetypes, each a distinct usage style, and users are described as weighted combinations rather than forced into exclusive clusters, which matches reality where one person is part 'reporter', part 'collaborator'. Choosing K uses reconstruction error, stability across runs and interpretability. Archetypes ground personas in behavioural data. Rated MEDIUM priority.
steps: Build a users-by-features matrix of counts or durations over a defined window.
Normalise (for example TF-IDF style or per-user scaling) to reduce dominance of heavy users.
Fit NMF for a range of K (for example 3-12) with multiple initialisations.
Choose K using reconstruction error, stability and interpretability.
Label archetypes from top-loading features and validate with qualitative interviews of high-weight users.
Track archetype weights over time and use them for segmentation and personas.
outputs: Archetype definitions, per-user archetype weights, archetype trends.
useWhen: Large behavioural logs where overlapping usage styles need discovery, persona grounding.
avoidWhen: Small samples, or when exclusive segments are operationally required.
whyLost: Lives in data science; UX segmentation relies on surveys or k-means clusters that force exclusive membership.
whereToUse: SaaS feature adoption, creative tools, streaming, banking app usage, developer platforms.
example: NMF on a project-management tool's logs finds five archetypes; 'planner' weight predicts seat expansion, so the onboarding emphasises planning features for new admins.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Lee DD & Seung HS (1999) Learning the parts of objects by non-negative matrix factorization. Nature 401:788-791
Paatero P & Tapper U (1994) Positive matrix factorization. Environmetrics
Lee & Seung, Learning the parts of objects by non-negative matrix factorization (1999), Nature
Brunet et al., Metagenes and molecular pattern discovery using matrix factorization (2004), PNAS
reference: Lee DD & Seung HS (1999) Learning the parts of objects by non-negative matrix factorization. Nature 401:788-791.

name: Non-Response Bias Assessment
origin: Long-standing survey practice; described by Gratton and Jones (2010) as profiling the achieved sample, comparing it with population figures and comparing follow-up respondents with original respondents.
summary: Checking whether the people who answered a survey differ from those who did not, before generalising the results.
description: Almost no survey gets answers from everyone it samples. People lack time, motivation or the right knowledge, fill it in wrongly or cannot be reached, so the achieved sample can differ from the population in ways that skew results. Gratton and Jones describe three checks. First, profile the achieved sample on age, gender and other relevant variables, often graphically, to spot unusual patterns. Second, where population figures exist, compare the respondents against them; if one group is under-represented the sample is biased in that respect. Third, send a follow-up (letter or email with another copy of the questionnaire and a fresh cut-off date, worded as a reminder rather than a repeat of the original appeal, and without coercion) and compare those who respond late with the original respondents, treating late responders as a proxy for non-responders. In UX, product data makes this unusually powerful: the user database records plan, tenure, activity level and platform for every sampled person, so respondents can be compared with non-respondents directly, and survey results can be weighted or caveated when the heaviest users are over-represented.
steps: Before fielding, record the characteristics of everyone in the issued sample (from the sampling frame or product data).
After the main cut-off, compare respondents with the issued sample or population on those characteristics, using tables or charts.
Send a follow-up reminder to non-respondents with a new copy or link and a fresh deadline, framed as a reminder and without pressure.
Compare late (follow-up) respondents with early respondents on key answers and characteristics.
Decide whether differences matter for the conclusions; weight the data, restrict claims to the groups that responded, or caveat the findings.
Report response rate and the results of the bias checks alongside the survey findings.
outputs: Response-rate figures, a respondent versus non-respondent (or population) comparison table, early versus late comparisons, and a judgement on how far results can be generalised.
useWhen: Survey findings will inform decisions or be quoted as representing the user base, especially with low response rates or one-off email and in-app surveys.
avoidWhen: The study makes no claim of representativeness, such as a recruitment screener or an exploratory qualitative survey.
whyLost: UX surveys are often treated as directional, and response rates of a few per cent are accepted without asking who did not answer; the check belongs to survey methodology training that many UX researchers have not had.
whereToUse: In-app satisfaction surveys, relationship NPS, churn and cancellation surveys, annual user surveys, B2B customer studies.
example: An annual user survey shows 70% satisfaction. Joining responses to account data reveals that respondents log in four times as often as non-respondents. A reminder wave brings in lighter users, whose satisfaction is notably lower, so the team reports results by activity band rather than a single headline figure.
sources: Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
reference: Gratton, C. and Jones, I. (2010) Research Methods for Sports Studies, 2nd edn. London and New York: Routledge.

name: Nudge Design
origin: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, 2008
summary: Structures choice architecture (defaults, ordering, framing, social norms, timing) to steer behaviour while preserving freedom of choice, then tests the effect.
description: A nudge is any aspect of choice architecture that alters behaviour predictably without forbidding options or significantly changing economic incentives. Typical tools are defaults, option ordering, salience, social norms, feedback, reminders and simplification. In UX, nudge design means auditing an existing choice environment, identifying the choice architecture levers already in play (every interface has defaults, whether chosen deliberately or not), and redesigning them toward outcomes users would endorse on reflection. Rigour rests on three practices: tying each nudge to a mechanism, testing it experimentally against a control because effects are often smaller than headline studies suggest, and applying transparency and reversibility tests so nudges do not drift into sludge or dark patterns. Meta-analyses show defaults are typically the strongest lever.
steps: Identify the decision and the outcome users would endorse on reflection.
Audit current choice architecture: existing defaults, option order, framing, salience and timing.
Select candidate nudges, prioritising defaults and simplification, and state the expected mechanism.
Apply ethics checks: is it transparent, easy to opt out of, and aligned with user welfare?
Run a randomised experiment against the current design with pre-registered primary metrics.
Monitor longer-term outcomes and opt-out rates to detect backfire or reactance.
outputs: Choice architecture audit, nudge specification with mechanism and ethics rationale, experimental effect estimates.
useWhen: Onboarding settings, privacy and security choices, health and financial decisions where a better default or framing benefits users.
avoidWhen: When users need deliberate, informed choice (e.g. medical consent) or when the nudge benefits only the business; use transparent decision aids instead.
whyLost: Still in use: Widely adopted in product, public policy, and health design; though ethical concerns are growing.
whereToUse: Onboarding; default settings; health behavior; financial decision-making products.
example: A password manager changed the default for two-factor authentication from off to on during setup with a single-tap opt-out. In a four-week test, activation rose from 18% to 71% with an opt-out rate of 9%.
sources: Behavioral Science
Designing for Behavior Change
Nudge (Thaler & Sunstein)
reference: Thaler, R. H., & Sunstein, C. R. (2008). Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness. Yale University Press.

name: Number Needed to Treat and Harm
origin: Andreas Laupacis, David Sackett and Robin Roberts, 1988
summary: Expresses an intervention's effect as how many users must be exposed for one to benefit (NNT) or be harmed (NNH), making trade-offs concrete.
description: Relative effects (a 20% lift) are easily misunderstood. NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction: if a design reduces abandonment from 10% to 8%, 50 users must see it to prevent one abandonment. NNH, similarly, is the reciprocal of absolute risk increase for an adverse outcome, such as accidental purchases or complaints. Reporting both side by side shows whether benefits outweigh harms, and confidence intervals around them highlight uncertainty. This brings ethical clarity to experiments with dark-pattern risks and helps stakeholders reason about impact in human terms.
steps: Identify the benefit outcome and any harm outcomes for an intervention.
Compute absolute risk differences between treatment and control for each, with confidence intervals.
Convert to NNT and NNH (1 / absolute difference) and their intervals, handling intervals that cross zero carefully.
Express results as 'for every X users exposed, one gains benefit; for every Y, one is harmed'.
Weigh benefits against harms, considering severity.
Include NNT/NNH in experiment reports and decision memos.
outputs: NNT and NNH with confidence intervals and a benefit-harm summary.
useWhen: Communicating experiment results, especially where interventions carry potential harms.
avoidWhen: Continuous outcomes without meaningful thresholds, unless dichotomised thoughtfully.
whyLost: Product teams report relative lifts that look impressive; harm outcomes are rarely tracked alongside.
whereToUse: Persuasive design experiments, upsells, notifications, health app nudges, AI safety features.
example: A pre-checked insurance add-on increases attach rate (NNT 12 for one extra sale) but also refund requests (NNH 30). Leadership sees that every 2.5 extra sales brings one dissatisfied customer and removes the default.
sources: Laupacis, Sackett & Roberts, An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment (1988), New England Journal of Medicine
Altman, Confidence intervals for the number needed to treat (1998), BMJ
reference: Laupacis, A., Sackett, D. L., & Roberts, R. S. (1988). NEJM, 318(26), 1728-1733.

name: Object Elicitation Interview
donor: Material culture studies and qualitative psychology
origin: Material culture and qualitative interviewing traditions; formalised in qualitative psychology (Willig, 2016)
summary: Participants bring meaningful objects to the interview, which anchor discussion and help bridge from concrete, sensory detail to broader experience and meaning.
description: Object elicitation (Willig, 2016; objects used in clinical and qualitative interviewing) involves participants bringing physical objects that are meaningful to their experience, which are then used as interview stimuli. Objects anchor abstract or emotionally complex experiences in the concrete, multi-sensory world — they allow participants to show rather than only tell, and they access sensory and tactile dimensions of experience that purely verbal methods miss.
steps: Brief participants in advance: 'Before our interview, I'd like you to choose one or two objects that feel meaningful to your experience of [phenomenon]. Bring them to the interview. They can be anything.'
Opening with the object: Begin the interview by asking about the object: 'Tell me about this object and why you brought it.' Let the object-story be the entry point.

Sensory engagement with the object: Encourage participants to handle the object during the interview. 'What does it feel like to hold this?' 'When you look at it, what comes to mind?' Sensory engagement with the object mediates richer recall.
Moving from object to experience: Use the object as a bridge: 'This object seems connected to [theme] — can you tell me more about that?'

Analysis: Analyse both the object chosen (what the participant chose to represent their experience) and the narrative around the object (how it is talked about). The choice of object is itself a form of data.
outputs: Photographs or records of chosen objects, interview narratives anchored in them, analysis of object choice and discussion, and insights into meaning and practice.
useWhen: Experience is tied to material things, such as money tools, medication, devices, workspaces or sentimental items, or abstract topics need a concrete starting point.
avoidWhen: Topics have no material dimension, or object choice could be burdensome or exposing; use Photo Elicitation or standard interviews.
whyLost: UX artefact analysis focuses on workplace documents and screens, while object-based interviewing stayed in material culture, psychology and museum studies.
whereToUse: Personal finance (wallets, notebooks), medication management, home technology, legacy and digital inheritance, and physical-digital product ecosystems.
example: Older adults are asked to bring 'something you use to keep track of your money'. Notebooks, envelopes and a printed bank statement anchor interviews revealing that physical records are trusted as proof, shaping a printable statement feature.
sources: When Words Fail Us — Elicitation Techniques (PMC 2024)
Elicitation in Qualitative Interviewing (QualPage)
reference: Willig, C. (2016). Reflections on the use of object elicitation. Qualitative Psychology, 4(3), 211-222.

name: Objective-Question-Method Chain
origin: Popularised for UX by David Travis (Think Like a UX Researcher, 2019); rooted in classic research-design teaching
summary: A planning discipline that derives research methods from decision-linked objectives and research questions, producing a documented chain stakeholders agree to before fieldwork.
description: The chain inverts the common habit of choosing a method first ('let's run a survey') and back-filling a rationale. It starts from the decision the team must make, states objectives as information needs, decomposes each into two to five answerable research questions, and only then selects the method that yields valid evidence for each question with the available population, time and budget. The full chain (objective, question, method, participants, analysis plan, intended use of findings) is written down and shared before fieldwork, acting as a contract with stakeholders. Its rigour lies in traceability: every session, item and analysis step can be justified by a question, and every question by a decision. Gaps and redundant methods become visible, and post-hoc reframing of results becomes harder.
steps: Define objectives: What does the team need to know to make a good decision? State objectives as information needs, not methods ("understand why users abandon the checkout flow" not "run a usability test").
Derive research questions: What specific questions, if answered, would satisfy each objective? Each objective typically generates 2–5 research questions. Write them as questions, not hypotheses.

Select methods: For each question: which method provides valid evidence for this specific question, with this population, in this timeframe? Map methods to questions. If multiple methods answer the same question, choose the lowest cost.
Document the chain: Objective → Research Question → Method → Participant → Analysis Plan → How findings will be used. Share this before fieldwork. This is your contract with stakeholders.
outputs: A one-page research plan table linking objectives, research questions, methods, sample, analysis plan and decision use; an explicit list of questions out of scope.
useWhen: At the start of any study or research roadmap, when stakeholders arrive with a method request, when several teams compete for research capacity, or when you need to defend why a method was chosen.
avoidWhen: For tiny tactical checks where the question and method are obvious (a five-user usability retest); for open-ended exploratory immersion where questions should emerge from fieldwork, use ethnographic or grounded approaches with a lighter charter.
whyLost: Agile cadences and tool-led research ops encourage method-first requests ('book five interviews'), so the written chain is skipped and its logic survives only as a slogan.
whereToUse: Research intake processes, quarterly research roadmaps, research ops templates, and stakeholder kick-offs for high-stakes decisions in fintech, health and enterprise SaaS.
example: A banking team asks for a survey on why customers abandon loan applications. Mapping the chain shows the objective is to locate where and why abandonment happens, which funnel analytics plus session-replay review and ten follow-up interviews answer better than a survey. The plan is signed off before recruitment begins.
sources: Think Like a UX Researcher (David Travis)
Understanding Your Users (Kathy Baxter)
reference: Travis, D. & Hodgson, P. (2019). Think Like a UX Researcher. CRC Press.

name: Old Brain / New Brain Design Audit
origin: Susan Weinschenk, 2009; drawing on MacLean's triune brain model
summary: Audits a design for how it engages fast, automatic responses (danger, faces, food, novelty) versus deliberative reasoning, ensuring key elements work at both levels.
description: Susan Weinschenk's 'old brain / new brain' framing, derived from the triune brain model, divides processing into fast, automatic responses to danger, faces, food, novelty and movement, emotional responses, and slow deliberative reasoning. Although the anatomical model is outdated, the practical idea maps onto well-supported dual-process accounts. The audit examines each key screen for what will capture automatic attention, what emotional tone it sets, and whether deliberative content supports the decision once attention is captured. Mismatches, such as decorative imagery outcompeting a critical warning, are flagged. Rigour comes from framing findings in contemporary attention and dual-process terms, avoiding manipulative uses, and validating predictions with eye tracking, first-click or five-second tests.
steps: Old-brain filter test for landing pages and critical interfaces:
Show the interface for 50ms (single frame).
(2) Ask: 'What caught your attention?'
Code responses: contrast elements, faces, movement indicators, large text.
(4) Compare to intended attention hierarchy.
(5) Elements that pass the 50ms filter = old-brain salient. Elements that don't = invisible to first-pass attention. Redesign: ensure the most critical element passes the old-brain filter first.
outputs: An audit of automatic attention triggers and deliberative content per screen, mismatches between what grabs attention and what matters, and redesign suggestions.
useWhen: Landing pages, alerts, onboarding, and persuasion-sensitive screens where first impressions and automatic attention shape outcomes.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting the triune brain as anatomy (it is outdated); avoid manipulative exploitation of automatic responses. Prefer dual-process framing and empirical testing.
whyLost: The underlying triune-brain neuroscience was discredited, so the method was dismissed with it, although its practical dual-process audit remains useful.
whereToUse: Landing page design, notification design, mobile first-screen design, critical alert design.
example: A surgical alert system relies on a small text banner; the audit shows nothing triggers automatic attention, so the redesign adds motion onset and a distinct sound for critical alerts only.
sources: Neuro Web Design — Susan Weinschenk
Neuroscience (Bear et al.)
Brain & Behaviour (Garrett)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 9 — Attention — The Gatekeeper

name: Online and Remote Qualitative Research Adaptations
donor: Qualitative social research and internet research
origin: Online interviewing literature from the 2000s (Salmons; James and Busher); widespread adoption from 2020
summary: Adapts interviews, think-aloud and observation for video, chat and asynchronous channels, addressing rapport, environment, consent, data loss and the strengths of each digital mode.
description: Remote research is not simply in-person research over video. Each channel changes what data you get. Video calls lose body language below the shoulders, shared physical context and some rapport cues, but gain access to participants in their own environment and screen sharing for remote think-aloud. Asynchronous text interviews give participants time to reflect and suit sensitive topics, but lose spontaneity. Rigorous adaptation means planning rapport building explicitly, briefing participants on technology, recording and privacy, piloting the setup, choosing synchronous or asynchronous modes deliberately, and documenting observational limits in the report. Digital think-aloud needs careful handling of latency, screen-sharing fatigue and participants' unfamiliarity with tools. The rigour lies in treating mode as a methodological decision with known effects.
steps: Rapport in digital environments: Building the research relationship without physical co-presence requires: longer warm-up conversations, careful attention to what participants can see in the researcher's video frame, explicit discussion of how the technology will be used.

Managing the digital environment: Briefing participants on: screen sharing, recording consent, muting background noise. Technical problems are not interruptions to research — participants' responses to technical failure are data.

Asynchronous qualitative data: Text-based asynchronous interviews (via email, messaging apps, or online platforms) allow participants to respond in their own time, to choose their words carefully, and to share images and documents easily. The absence of real-time dynamics changes the data character.

Observational limitations: Video interviews lose: body language below the torso, spontaneous environmental observations, and the researcher's co-presence in the participant's physical context. Compensate with explicit questions about the environment.

Digital think-aloud: Screen-sharing enables remote think-aloud protocols. Participants can share their screen while narrating their interaction with a digital product in their natural environment — ecological validity advantage over lab-based think-aloud.
outputs: A remote study protocol with mode rationale, technology and consent briefing materials, recordings and transcripts, and documented observational limits.
useWhen: Participants are geographically dispersed, hard to reach, or more comfortable at home; budgets are tight; or the product is itself used remotely on personal devices.
avoidWhen: Physical context, environment or embodied interaction matter (use field methods such as Walking Interview or contextual inquiry), or participants lack reliable connectivity or devices.
whyLost: It is active and dominant since 2020, though many teams adopted remote tools without adapting rapport, consent and observational practices to the medium.
whereToUse: Global SaaS and consumer apps, remote usability testing, sensitive topics via asynchronous text, accessibility research with participants using their own assistive technology, and rapid discovery.
example: A mental-health startup offers participants a choice between video and asynchronous chat interviews. Chat participants disclose more about medication side-effects, so the team uses chat for sensitive topics and video for app walkthroughs.
sources: A Pilot Study Conducting Online Think Aloud Qualitative Method (PMC 2022)
Sage Research Methods Community — Elicitation Interviews Online
reference: Salmons, J. (2015). Qualitative Online Interviews: Strategies, Design, and Skills (2nd ed.). Sage.

name: Ontological Structure Mapping for IA
origin: Abby Covert (How to Make Sense of Any Mess, 2014)
summary: Maps an information space at three layers, ontology (what things are), taxonomy (how they are classified) and choreography (how people move through them), to diagnose where IA breaks.
description: Covert distinguishes three layers of information architecture. Ontology is the set of things that exist in the space and what is meant by each term; taxonomy is how those things are arranged and classified; choreography is the rules for interaction and movement through the structure. Many IA redesigns only reshuffle the taxonomy, while the real problem is ontological, for example teams and users meaning different things by 'account', 'project' or 'member', or choreographic, such as an order of steps that contradicts users' expectations. The method elicits terms and definitions from stakeholders and users (controlled vocabulary workshops, interviews, card sorts), identifies conflicts in meaning, maps classification schemes, and traces key journeys through the structure. Findings are recorded as a shared vocabulary and diagrams for each layer.
steps: Before any IA redesign:
Ontology audit — what are the fundamental entities in this domain? Are they correctly identified?
(2) Taxonomy audit — how are entities classified? Do the classification criteria match users' classification criteria?
(3) Choreography audit — what paths through the taxonomy do users take for each goal? Sequence the redesign: fix ontology first, taxonomy second, choreography third.
outputs: Controlled vocabulary with definitions, ontology conflicts, taxonomy diagrams, choreography maps of key journeys, and diagnosis of which layer drives each problem.
useWhen: IA redesigns, products with confusing terminology, mergers of systems or organisations, and SaaS products whose core objects are misunderstood.
avoidWhen: When the vocabulary is already shared and the problem is only labelling or navigation depth; use tree testing.
whyLost: Covert's book is popular, but the three-layer diagnosis is usually reduced to card sorting and sitemap work, leaving ontology unexamined.
whereToUse: IA redesign, search and navigation redesign, content strategy, any product where users can't find things.
example: A project-management SaaS finds 'workspace', 'team' and 'organisation' are used interchangeably by staff and users. Ontology mapping resolves definitions before navigation is redesigned, and support tickets about permissions drop.
sources: How to Make Sense of Any Mess — Abby Covert
Information Architecture for the Web and Beyond (Rosenfeld, Morville & Arango)
reference: Covert A (2014) How to Make Sense of Any Mess: Information Architecture for Everybody. CreateSpace

name: Ontology/taxonomy/choreography audit
origin: Dan Klyn's ontology/taxonomy/choreography model of IA, around 2010; Abby Covert, How to Make Sense of Any Mess, 2014
summary: Audits an information system on three layers: what things mean (ontology), how they are arranged (taxonomy), and how they move and sequence in use (choreography).
description: The ontology/taxonomy/choreography model separates three layers of information architecture. Ontology concerns meaning: what the core concepts are, what they are called, and how they relate, including whether teams and users share definitions. Taxonomy concerns arrangement: the categories, hierarchies and facets used to organise those concepts. Choreography concerns movement: how concepts appear, sequence and interact across time, channels and flows. Many IA problems are misdiagnosed at the wrong layer, for example reorganising menus (taxonomy) when the underlying term means different things to different users (ontology). The audit checks each layer with appropriate evidence: controlled vocabulary review and interviews for ontology, structure analysis and card sorting for taxonomy, and journey and flow analysis for choreography.
steps: Inventory the core concepts and terms used in the product, documentation and internal systems.
Ontology: interview 5-8 stakeholders and 5-8 users about what key terms mean; record conflicting definitions and build a controlled vocabulary with relationships.
Taxonomy: analyse category structures for consistency of classification principle and run an open or closed card sort (15-30 participants) where meaning is stable.
Choreography: map how concepts appear across journeys and channels, noting where order, timing or context changes their meaning.
Diagnose each problem at the correct layer and prioritise ontology fixes first, since they propagate.
Document the vocabulary, taxonomy and choreography rules as a shared reference for design and content.
outputs: A controlled vocabulary with definitions and relationships, a taxonomy review, choreography maps, and a layered problem diagnosis.
useWhen: When terms are used inconsistently, when reorganisation has not fixed findability, when merging products or teams, or when building content models.
avoidWhen: When the problem is purely visual or interaction-level; use usability testing or heuristic evaluation.
whyLost: It survived because practitioner IA books and community teaching kept it simple and memorable, though often applied only to taxonomy.
whereToUse: Enterprise SaaS, healthcare systems, multi-brand e-commerce, design systems, and knowledge graphs for AI retrieval.
example: In a surgical system, 'case' means a patient procedure to surgeons, a support ticket to service engineers and a storage container to nurses. An ontology fix with distinct terms resolves a navigation problem the team had tried to solve by moving menu items.
sources: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J., Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (O'Reilly, 4th ed., 2015)
Martin, L. M., Everyday Information Architecture (2019)
Covert, A., How to Make Sense of Any Mess (2014)

Everyday Information Architecture (Martin)
How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 7 — Graph Theory & the Architecture of Information

name: Open Coding (Constant Comparative Method)
origin: Barney Glaser & Anselm Strauss, 1967 (The Discovery of Grounded Theory); elaborated by Strauss & Corbin, 1990
summary: Line-by-line coding of raw qualitative data, constantly comparing each new incident and code with all existing ones to build grounded, saturated concepts.
description: Open coding is the first stage of Grounded Theory analysis. You break the data apart, line by line or sentence by sentence, and apply descriptive codes that stay as close to the data as possible. The constant comparative method means that every new code is immediately compared to all existing codes — if two codes represent the same phenomenon, they are merged into a single code. If a code covers two distinct phenomena, it is split. This process continues until you can no longer find incidents that require new codes (theoretical saturation).
steps: Read the entire transcript once without coding. Write a one-paragraph summary of what the session was about. This is your orienting memo.

Begin line-by-line coding from the top of the transcript. For each meaningful unit (clause, sentence, or short paragraph), ask: "What is happening here? What is this person doing, thinking, or feeling? What category does this belong to?"
Write codes in the margin. Keep codes short (3–5 words) and active (use gerunds: "avoiding the feature" not "avoidance").
After every 5–10 codes: compare each new code to all existing codes. Merge identical codes. Split codes that cover more than one phenomenon.
Write a memo for every code that surprises you or challenges your expectation. These memos are your analytic raw material.
After completing one transcript: compile a full code list. Repeat with the next transcript, constantly comparing new codes to existing ones.
Stop when new transcripts add no new codes. This is saturation — but only if you have used theoretical sampling (see Method 14) to ensure the absence of codes is meaningful, not accidental.
outputs: A code list with definitions, in-vivo and descriptive codes, code memos, and a record of merges, splits and saturation status.
useWhen: When you need concepts that genuinely emerge from data rather than from a prior framework, especially in new domains, novel behaviours, or when explaining a process no existing model covers.
avoidWhen: When the questions are tightly defined and a coding frame already exists (use framework analysis or Mayring content analysis), or when time permits only rapid synthesis (use a rapid affinity or debrief matrix).
whyLost: UX practice compressed it into sticky-note clustering without line-by-line coding, memoing or theoretical sampling, so the name survives while the comparative discipline does not.
whereToUse: Foundational discovery for new product categories, trust and adoption studies in health and fintech, AI product behaviour research, and any study meant to produce a reusable conceptual model.
example: Analysing 20 interviews with rural health workers about a digital records app, a researcher codes line by line and repeatedly compares incidents of 'double-entering on paper'. Merging and splitting codes surfaces a concept of 'insurance against system loss' that reframes the design problem.
sources: Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick ed.)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
The Discovery of Grounded Theory (Glaser & Strauss)
Basics of Qualitative Research (Strauss & Corbin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 26 — Grounded Theory — Generating Theory from Data
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)

extra.Two Types of Code: In-vivo codes: Codes taken directly from the participant's own words. They preserve the participant's framing and are often the most analytically powerful. Example: a participant says "I just stopped trusting it" → code: "stopped trusting it." Descriptive codes: Researcher-generated descriptions of what is happening in the data. Less tied to specific language but more comparable across participants. Example: "trust collapse following system error."

name: Open, axial and selective coding pipeline
origin: Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss, The Discovery of Grounded Theory (1967); the three-stage pipeline formalised by Strauss and Corbin, Basics of Qualitative Research (1990)
summary: A staged coding procedure that fractures data into concepts, relates them around axes of conditions, actions and consequences, then integrates them into one core theory.
description: Grounded theory generates theory from data rather than testing prior hypotheses. Strauss and Corbin's pipeline has three stages. Open coding breaks data into line-by-line or incident-level concepts and groups them into categories with properties and dimensions. Axial coding reassembles categories by relating each to subcategories through a coding paradigm of conditions, actions and interactions, and consequences. Selective coding chooses a core category that explains most variation and integrates the others around it into a storyline. The process runs alongside constant comparison, memo writing and theoretical sampling, so later interviews target gaps in emerging categories. Rigour comes from this iteration, from extensive memoing, and from testing the theory against negative cases, not from coding volume. UX often borrows the label while doing a single round of theme clustering.
steps: Collect an initial set of 6 to 10 interviews or observations around a broad research question, transcribed verbatim.

Open code line by line or incident by incident, naming concepts with gerunds where possible (for example 'hedging against audit'), and write memos on each emerging category's properties and dimensions.
Use constant comparison: compare each new incident with prior incidents in the same category and refine category definitions in memos.
Axial code by relating categories using the paradigm of causal conditions, context, intervening conditions, action and interaction strategies, and consequences, diagramming the relations.
Theoretically sample: select the next participants or sites to fill gaps and test variation in the emerging categories, typically reaching 20 to 30 interviews.
Selective code by identifying the core category that relates to most others, writing the storyline, and validating it against all cases, including negative cases.
Stop when theoretical saturation is reached, when new data add no new properties to core categories, and document the theory as propositions with a diagram.
outputs: A codebook with category properties and dimensions, analytic memos, axial diagrams, a core category and storyline, and a substantive theory expressed as propositions.
useWhen: Explaining a process or phenomenon with no adequate existing theory, such as why users distrust a system, how adoption unfolds, or how teams negotiate tool use.
avoidWhen: You have a predefined question needing quick descriptive answers (use framework or thematic analysis), or no ability to sample iteratively; grounded theory without theoretical sampling becomes ordinary coding.
whyLost: UX adopted the vocabulary of 'coding' and 'grounded' but fixed samples, compressed timelines and sticky-note affinity work removed theoretical sampling, constant comparison and memoing, which are the method's core.
whereToUse: Trust and adoption studies, new-domain discovery, B2B workflow research, AI use in professional settings, health worker behaviour.
example: From 20 rural health worker interviews, open coding produced 140 codes; axial coding related 'audit exposure', 'paper as proof' and 'device dependency' around a core category, 'protecting the self from blame'. The resulting theory of digital distrust explained why workers kept paper duplicates even when the app worked.
sources: Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 26 — Grounded Theory — Generating Theory from Data
reference: Strauss, A., & Corbin, J. (1990). Basics of Qualitative Research: Grounded Theory Procedures and Techniques. Sage; Glaser, B. G., & Strauss, A. L. (1967). The Discovery of Grounded Theory. Aldine.

name: Operationalization protocol
donor: Philosophy of science and social science methodology
origin: Percy Bridgman's operationalism, 1927; developed in social science methodology by Lazarsfeld (1958) and others
summary: Translates an abstract construct into specific, observable indicators and procedures, documenting how each indicator maps to the construct and what it leaves out.
description: Operationalisation is the bridge between a concept such as 'ease of use' and data. A rigorous protocol specifies the construct's dimensions, chooses indicators for each, defines the exact measurement procedure (instrument, wording, timing, scoring, units), and states the expected relationships between indicators. Lazarsfeld's sequence of imagery, specification of dimensions, selection of indicators, and formation of indices remains a sound template. Good protocols also record what each indicator misses (construct under-representation) and what irrelevant variance it may capture. In UX the step is commonly skipped: teams pick a familiar metric because it is available, leading to measures that do not represent what stakeholders mean.
steps: Write a one-paragraph conceptual definition of the construct, citing literature or stakeholder interviews.
Break it into dimensions (for example ease of use as efficiency, learnability, error tolerance and perceived effort).
Select at least two indicators per dimension, mixing behavioural and attitudinal where possible.
Specify the exact procedure for each indicator: instrument, wording, scale, timing, scoring rule and unit.
State expected correlations between indicators (convergent) and with unrelated measures (discriminant), and pilot with 5-10 participants.
Record known gaps and threats, and freeze the protocol before main data collection.
outputs: An operationalisation table (construct, dimensions, indicators, procedures, expected relations), pilot results and a frozen measurement plan.
useWhen: Before any metric programme, benchmark, survey, or experiment, especially when stakeholders use vague terms like engagement, trust or ease.
avoidWhen: For purely exploratory qualitative research aimed at discovering what constructs exist; do interviews or ethnography first.
whyLost: UX inherited ready-made metrics (SUS, NPS, conversion) and skipped the step of deciding what they should measure.
whereToUse: Product metrics frameworks, OKRs, AI trust measurement, regulated medical usability (IEC 62366), and benchmarking programmes.
example: A surgical robotics team asked for 'ease of use' data. The protocol splits it into setup efficiency (time to dock), error tolerance (recoverable errors per case), learnability (cases to proficiency) and perceived workload (NASA-TLX), each with a specified procedure.
sources: Dix, A., Statistics for HCI: Making Sense of Quantitative Data (2020)
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
Leavy, P., Research Design: Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed Methods, Arts-Based, and Community-Based Participatory Research Approaches (2017)
Statistics for HCI (Alan Dix)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Research Design (Leavy)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 8 — Measurement Theory — Before You Measure Anything
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
