name: Positionality Audit for Global Products
origin: Inspired by Nicholas Dirks, 2001 (Castes of Mind), on how classification systems encode the classifier's worldview
summary: Auditing a product's categories, mandatory fields and flows to identify where they encode designers' cultural assumptions rather than users' realities.
description: Dirks showed how colonial census categories did not simply describe Indian society but reshaped it in the administrators' image. A positionality audit applies this insight to digital products: every classification system (user types, content categories, form fields, relationship options) originates in someone's social reality and can impose it on others. The audit asks who designed each category, which elements are mandatory, and what identities, relationships or practices cannot be expressed. Names and gender fields are typical flashpoints: single given and family name fields, fixed title lists and binary gender options fail many users. Findings are tested with users from non-dominant contexts, producing evidence-based changes to data models.
steps: Who designed the categories? For every classification system in your product (user types, content categories, task flows, form fields): what cultural context did it come from? Whose social reality does it represent?

What is mandatory vs. optional? Mandatory fields, categories, and flows impose the designer's framework on users who may not share it. Document every mandatory element and question its cultural assumptions.

What is missing? What social realities, identity categories, relationship types, or cultural practices cannot be expressed in the current category system? Conduct research with users from the non-dominant cultural context to identify category impositions.

Name vs. gender fields: The most culturally imposed fields in most global products. Research: how do target users name themselves? What gender categories exist and are meaningful in their cultural context? How do naming conventions, honorifics, and title systems differ?
outputs: An inventory of categories and mandatory fields with their cultural assumptions, a list of inexpressible realities, and data-model change recommendations.
useWhen: Before launching in new regions, when redesigning sign-up and profile data models, or when complaints suggest users cannot represent themselves.
avoidWhen: Products with no user-facing classification or personal data; or when used as a desk exercise without validating with affected users.
whyLost: It draws on postcolonial scholarship rarely read in design; mainstream practice reduces it to inclusive-language guidelines.
whereToUse: Identity and KYC flows, healthcare records, government services, social and dating platforms, and HR systems.
example: A global HR platform audits its employee profile and finds that 'emergency contact relationship' offers only nuclear family options. Interviews in Ghana and the Philippines lead to free-text and extended family options.
sources: Castes of Mind (Nicholas Dirks)
Global UX (Quesenbery & Szuc)
Handbook of Ethnography
Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names (McKenzie)
reference: Dirks, N. B. (2001). Castes of Mind: Colonialism and the Making of Modern India. Princeton University Press.

name: Positive Design Contagion Strategy
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Deliberately increases the transmissibility and persistence of good design patterns through awards, open pattern libraries, business-value case studies and regulatory floors.
description: The treatise argues good design can spread like disease, and that understanding positive contagion matters as much as understanding pathogen transmission. Mechanisms include awards and recognition (reputational incentives diffusing as competitors match recognised excellence), open design systems and pattern libraries (making good patterns as easy to copy as bad ones), case studies demonstrating business value (economic incentives) and regulatory requirements for accessibility and transparency (raising the floor). Intervention programmes should increase the basic reproduction number of good design: more transmissible, more persistent when adopted and more resistant to displacement by inferior patterns under competitive pressure. The strategy pairs with vector analysis, using the same channels for good patterns.
steps: Select beneficial patterns with evidence of user benefit.
Package them for easy transmission: open components, documentation and code.
Seed adoption through super-spreader nodes (major design systems, platforms).
Publish business-value case studies and recognise adopters.
Advocate for standards or regulation that make the pattern the floor.
Measure adoption R and persistence over time.
outputs: Packaged good patterns, adoption metrics, contagion plan.
useWhen: Spreading accessible, honest or safety patterns across an organisation or industry.
avoidWhen: Patterns without clear evidence of benefit.
whyLost: Original framing of the treatise.
whereToUse: Design-system teams, government design standards, accessibility advocacy, industry consortia.
example: A government publishes an open 'clear cancellation' component and case study showing reduced complaints; adoption spreads to 40% of regulated firms within a year.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rogers EM (2003) Diffusion of Innovations. 5th ed
Centola D (2018) How Behavior Spreads: The Science of Complex Contagions
reference: Centola D (2018) How Behavior Spreads: The Science of Complex Contagions. Princeton University Press.

name: Posterior credible intervals
origin: Bayesian inference tradition (Laplace; Jeffreys, Theory of Probability, 1939); modern practice in Gelman et al. (Bayesian Data Analysis) and Kruschke (2015)
summary: Reports the range within which a parameter lies with a stated probability given the data and prior, providing intuitive uncertainty statements for UX metrics.
description: A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with 95% probability given the model and data, which is how most stakeholders already misinterpret frequentist confidence intervals. Credible intervals can be equal-tailed (2.5th to 97.5th percentiles) or highest density intervals, the narrowest range containing 95% of the posterior. Kruschke recommends combining HDIs with a region of practical equivalence (ROPE) to decide whether an effect is meaningfully different from zero. Credible intervals work for any posterior quantity: rates, differences, ratios and predictions. Rigour comes from reporting the prior, checking model fit, using enough posterior samples for stable intervals, and stating the decision rule that links intervals to actions.
steps: Fit a Bayesian model appropriate to the metric, such as Beta-Binomial for rates, log-normal for times or ordinal regression for ratings, with a stated prior.
Draw sufficient posterior samples (for example at least 4,000 effective samples) and check convergence diagnostics such as R-hat below 1.01 where MCMC is used.
Compute the 95% (or 89%, following McElreath) equal-tailed or highest density interval for each quantity of interest.
Define a region of practical equivalence based on the smallest meaningful effect, for example ±1 percentage point in conversion.
Apply the decision rule: effect credible if the HDI lies outside the ROPE, practically equivalent if inside, undecided otherwise.
Report intervals with plain-language statements, such as 'there is a 95% probability the completion rate is between 72% and 89%'.
outputs: Credible intervals for key parameters, ROPE-based decisions, posterior plots and plain-language uncertainty statements.
useWhen: Communicating uncertainty to stakeholders, making decisions on small or sequential samples, or reporting any parameter estimated with a Bayesian model.
avoidWhen: The organisation's governance requires frequentist error-rate guarantees (for example regulated trials), or no defensible prior or model is available; report confidence intervals and explain them properly.
whyLost: UX statistics training and tooling is frequentist, and credible intervals require modelling skills and software that most teams have not adopted.
whereToUse: Small-sample usability benchmarks, low-traffic A/B tests, satisfaction metrics, fintech and health experiments.
example: A fintech A/B test reported a posterior uplift of 2.8% with a 95% HDI of 0.6% to 5.1% against a ROPE of ±0.5%, so the team concluded the effect was practically meaningful and could state a 97% probability that the uplift exceeded 0.5%.
sources: Statistical Rethinking (McElreath)
Bayesian Methods for Interaction & Design
Behavioral Drift Playbook (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 40 — Bayesian Thinking & Sequential Study Design
reference: Kruschke, J. K. (2015). Doing Bayesian Data Analysis (2nd ed.). Academic Press; McElreath, R. (2020). Statistical Rethinking (2nd ed.). CRC Press.

name: Power-Law Distribution Analysis
origin: Vilfredo Pareto (1896); George Zipf (1949); rigorous fitting by Aaron Clauset, Cosma Shalizi and Mark Newman (2009)
summary: Tests whether usage, content popularity or query frequency follows a power law, with proper estimation and comparison against alternative heavy-tailed distributions.
description: Many product phenomena are heavy-tailed: a few users generate most activity, a few queries dominate search, a few items get most views. Claims of 'power laws' are often made from straight-ish lines on log-log plots, which is unreliable. Clauset, Shalizi and Newman's method estimates the exponent by maximum likelihood, selects the lower cutoff x_min via Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, tests goodness of fit with bootstrapping, and compares the power law against log-normal, exponential and stretched exponential alternatives with likelihood ratio tests. Getting the distribution right matters: it determines whether averages are meaningful, how to sample users for research and how to design for the head versus the long tail.
steps: Collect the quantity (e.g. sessions per user, views per item, queries per term).
Plot the complementary cumulative distribution on log-log axes for exploration only.
Estimate x_min and the exponent alpha by maximum likelihood (e.g. powerlaw Python package).
Run bootstrap goodness-of-fit tests (p above 0.1 supports plausibility).
Compare against log-normal and other alternatives with likelihood ratio tests.
Interpret implications: concentration, sampling strategies, and design for head and tail.
outputs: Fitted distribution parameters, goodness-of-fit and model comparison results, and design implications.
useWhen: Analysing concentration of usage, content, queries, errors or revenue, and planning research sampling.
avoidWhen: Small datasets (under a few hundred observations in the tail) where distinctions are untestable.
whyLost: The 'long tail' entered product vocabulary as a slogan without the statistical methods to test it.
whereToUse: Search query analysis, content libraries, creator platforms, power user research, error frequency analysis.
example: A music app finds track plays fit a log-normal better than a power law; this implies the 'long tail' is thinner than assumed, and discovery features should target the mid-tail instead.
sources: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman, Power-law distributions in empirical data (2009), SIAM Review
Newman, Power laws, Pareto distributions and Zipf's law (2005), Contemporary Physics
reference: Clauset, A., Shalizi, C. R., & Newman, M. E. J. (2009). SIAM Review, 51(4), 661-703.

name: Pragmatic Competence Analysis for Interface Language
origin: H. P. Grice (1975) conversational maxims; developmental pragmatics in Gleason (ed.), The Development of Language
summary: Audits interface and conversational language against pragmatic expectations, Grice's maxims, implicature and politeness, and tests what users infer beyond the literal words.
description: Pragmatics studies how people infer meaning beyond literal content using context and shared conventions. Grice proposed that speakers follow a cooperative principle with maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner; when an utterance seems to violate one, listeners infer an implicature. Users apply the same expectations to interfaces, especially conversational ones: an error message that says less than needed implies there is nothing more to know, an overly polite refusal implies optional compliance, and an irrelevant suggestion implies the system misunderstood. Developmental research shows pragmatic competence varies with age, culture and neurodiversity, so implied meanings are not universal. The method audits strings and dialogue turns against the maxims, predicts likely implicatures, and tests users' inferences with comprehension probes.
steps: Apply Gricean maxim analysis to all interface text:
Quantity — does the message say exactly as much as needed?
(2) Quality — is the message truthful and not misleading?
(3) Relation — is the message relevant to the user's current context?
(4) Manner — is the message clear, brief, and orderly? For each text element, score violations on 1–4 and prioritize the highest-violation elements for rewrite.
outputs: Maxim-by-maxim audit of strings and dialogue flows, predicted implicatures, observed user inferences, and rewritten language for clarity across user groups.
useWhen: Chatbots and voice assistants, error messages, notifications, AI refusals and products for children, older adults or neurodivergent users.
avoidWhen: For purely visual or structural problems, or when standard comprehension testing already explains the issue.
whyLost: Pragmatics is well developed in linguistics and child-language research but UX writing adopted style guides rather than pragmatic theory.
whereToUse: Error message design, onboarding copy, chatbot dialogue design, microcopy auditing.
example: A banking chatbot replies 'I can help with many things!' when asked to dispute a charge. Users infer disputes are impossible (relation maxim) and leave; a reply naming the dispute path and handoff fixes completion.
sources: The Development of Language — Jean Berko Gleason
Grice, Logic and conversation (in Syntax and Semantics 3, 1975)
Levinson, Pragmatics (1983)
reference: Grice HP (1975) Logic and conversation. In Cole P & Morgan JL (Eds.) Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts. Academic Press

name: Pre-attentive feature audit
origin: Anne Treisman's feature integration theory, 1980; applied to visualisation by Healey and Enns (2012) and Ware
summary: Checks whether critical elements differ from their surroundings in a single pre-attentive feature strongly enough to pop out, rather than requiring serial search.
description: Some visual features, including colour hue, orientation, size, motion, flicker and enclosure, are processed in parallel across the visual field, so a unique target 'pops out' in under about 200-250 ms regardless of the number of distractors. Conjunctions of features (for example red and vertical among red horizontals and green verticals) usually require serial search, with time increasing per item. A pre-attentive feature audit lists each critical element, identifies the feature it relies on to stand out, and checks whether that feature is unique among distractors and differs strongly enough. Overuse of the same feature (everything red) destroys pop-out. Rigour comes from measuring search slopes in a quick visual search test, where flat slopes (below about 10 ms per item) indicate pre-attentive pop-out.
steps: List the elements that must be found immediately (alerts, status changes, primary actions).
For each, identify the distinguishing feature and list all other elements on screen sharing that feature.

Flag targets that rely on feature conjunctions, share their feature with 3 or more distractors, or use weak differences (for example small hue shifts, or colour alone for colour-vision-deficient users).
Run a visual search test: 10-15 participants, set sizes such as 8, 16 and 32 elements, measuring response time slopes per item.
Treat slopes under about 10 ms per item as pop-out and above about 20-30 ms per item as serial search; redesign serial-search targets.
Reserve pre-attentive features for critical signals in the design system and re-test.
outputs: A feature audit table, search slope results per target, and a reservation scheme for pre-attentive features.
useWhen: For dashboards, monitoring displays, alert design and data visualisation where critical items must be noticed instantly.
avoidWhen: When the problem is meaning or decision-making rather than detection; use comprehension testing.
whyLost: Visualisation researchers use it, but UX visual design relies on intuition and brand styling, often spending pre-attentive features on decoration.
whereToUse: Clinical monitors, control rooms, financial dashboards, maps, and status indicators in design systems.
example: On a surgical console red is used for alerts, the brand logo, three buttons and a progress bar. The audit shows alerts have a 38 ms-per-item search slope; reserving red and adding motion for alerts brings the slope to 4 ms.
sources: Bear, M., Connors, B. & Paradiso, M., Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain
Garrett, B., Brain & Behavior: An Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Neuroscience (Bear et al.)
Brain & Behaviour (Garrett)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 9 — Attention — The Gatekeeper
reference: Treisman, A. M. & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.

name: Pre-attentive processing analysis
origin: Treisman's feature integration theory, 1980; scene gist research by Potter (1975) and Oliva (2005)
summary: Analyses what users perceive within the first fraction of a second of seeing a screen, before focused attention, to check whether its gist communicates the right state.
description: Within about 50-100 ms people extract the gist of a scene: its category, layout and dominant features. Lindgaard and colleagues found web page aesthetic judgements form within 50 ms. Pre-attentive processing analysis examines what a screen communicates at this level, as distinct from what users eventually find by searching. It combines expert analysis of global features (layout, colour distribution, contrast, grouping) with brief-exposure tests in which participants see the screen for 50-500 ms and report what state it is in or what they noticed. For safety displays, the question is whether a normal versus abnormal state is distinguishable at a glance. Rigour comes from controlled exposure times, masking to prevent afterimages, and comparing several screen states.
steps: Define the gist each screen state must communicate (for example normal, warning, critical; or ready versus not ready).
Analyse global features per state: overall colour distribution, contrast, layout changes, motion; flag states that differ only in small local details.
Run brief-exposure trials with 12-20 participants: present screenshots for 50, 100 and 250 ms followed by a mask, and ask them to classify the state.
Compute classification accuracy per exposure duration and state; target above 90% at 250 ms for safety-critical distinctions.
Redesign states that fail by changing global features rather than adding local detail.
Re-test with fresh participants.
outputs: Gist requirements per state, global feature analysis, classification accuracy by exposure time, and redesigned state encodings.
useWhen: For monitoring and status displays, landing pages, product first impressions, and any glanceable interface such as watches or car dashboards.
avoidWhen: For detailed reading or complex decision tasks; use comprehension tests or think-aloud.
whyLost: Gist research is well established in vision science but practitioners use only the commercial five-second test, which measures recall rather than glance-level perception.
whereToUse: Surgical console status, vehicle displays, smartwatch complications, operations dashboards and first-impression testing.
example: A surgical console's normal and fault states differ only in a small status icon; at 100 ms participants classify them at chance. Changing the header bar colour in fault states raises classification to 96% at 100 ms.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Sensation and Perception
Gibson, J. J., The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979)
Whalen, J., Design for How People Think (2019)
Sensation and Perception (Goldstein)
Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (Gibson)
Design for How People Think (Whalen)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 11 — Perception — Before Cognition
reference: Oliva, A. (2005). Gist of the scene. In L. Itti, G. Rees & J. Tsotsos (Eds.), Neurobiology of Attention. Elsevier.

name: Pre-registration
origin: Clinical trial registration (ICMJE 2005); open-science pre-registration (Nosek et al. 2018)
summary: Records hypotheses, primary outcomes, sample size and analysis plan before data collection to prevent outcome switching and p-hacking.
description: The treatise repeatedly cites pre-registration: research protocol pre-registration as a DAG revival context, and pre-registration of hypotheses as missing from industry A/B testing. Pre-registration time-stamps a plan specifying hypotheses, primary and secondary outcomes, sample size with power justification, exclusion rules and analysis, separating confirmatory from exploratory findings. It counters the garden of forking paths, where flexible analysis turns noise into apparent effects. In product organisations it can be lightweight: an internal registry where experiment and study plans are frozen before launch and results are reported against them, including null results.
steps: Write hypotheses and designate one or a few primary outcomes.
Justify sample size with a power or precision analysis.
Specify exclusion rules, analysis models, multiplicity corrections and stopping rules.
Register the plan in an internal or public registry with a timestamp.
Run the study and analyse as planned; label deviations and exploratory analyses.
Report all registered outcomes, including nulls.
outputs: Time-stamped protocol, confirmatory results, transparent deviation log.
useWhen: Experiments and quantitative studies informing significant decisions; claims shared externally.
avoidWhen: Purely exploratory qualitative discovery, though a brief intent note still helps.
whyLost: Pre-registration is standard in clinical trials and growing in psychology, but product teams see it as bureaucratic, and experimentation platforms rarely enforce it.
whereToUse: Experimentation platforms, UX benchmarks, research claims in sales or regulatory contexts.
example: An e-commerce team registers 'checkout completion' as primary outcome; when a secondary metric moves but the primary does not, the result is reported as null rather than reframed as a win.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Nosek BA et al. (2018) The preregistration revolution. PNAS 115(11)
Simmons JP, Nelson LD & Simonsohn U (2011) False-positive psychology. Psychological Science
Statistics for Dummies series (Rumsey)
Designing Experiments & Analyzing Data (Maxwell & Delaney)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 41 — Frequentist Inference Done Right
reference: Nosek BA et al. (2018) The preregistration revolution. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115(11):2600-2606.

name: Predicate logic for invariants
origin: Floyd (1967) and Hoare (1969) on program assertions; interaction properties formalised by Dix and Harrison (PIE model, 1980s)
summary: Writes the properties an interface must always satisfy as logical statements, so that designs and implementations can be checked against them systematically.
description: An invariant is a condition that must hold in every reachable state. Expressed in predicate logic, interface invariants make design intentions testable: 'for all states s, displayed_mode(s) = actual_mode(s)'; 'for all states s, if armed(s) then stop_enabled(s)'; 'for all actions a, if destructive(a) then reversible(a) or confirmed(a)'. Dix and Harrison's work defined classes of interaction properties such as predictability, observability and reachability in this way. Invariants can then be checked by model checkers, property-based tests or runtime assertions. Rigour comes from precise variable definitions, quantifiers that cover all states and actions, and linking each invariant to a hazard or usability principle.
steps: Identify hazards and usability principles that must never be violated (mode visibility, reversibility, stop availability, consent).
Define the state variables and predicates needed to express them unambiguously.
Write each invariant in predicate logic with explicit quantifiers, and a plain-language paraphrase for stakeholders.
Check invariants against a state model with a model checker (for example NuSMV, UPPAAL or TLA+) or encode them as property-based tests running thousands of generated action sequences.
Investigate every counter-example trace, deciding whether to change the design or refine the invariant.
Keep invariants as living requirements, re-checking at each release.
outputs: A catalogue of formal invariants with plain-language versions, verification results, counter-example traces, and regression tests.
useWhen: When certain design properties must hold universally, such as safety, privacy consent, reversibility or mode visibility, and you need evidence.
avoidWhen: When requirements are exploratory or still changing weekly; use heuristic evaluation and scenario walkthroughs until the design stabilises.
whyLost: The logic is standard in verification research but UX expresses principles as guidelines, not checkable statements, so invariants live in engineering if anywhere.
whereToUse: Medical devices, autonomous vehicles, financial controls, privacy and consent flows, and AI agent guardrails.
example: An AI agent platform formalises 'for all actions a, if a sends external email then user_confirmed(a)'. Property-based testing finds a retry path that resends without confirmation, which is fixed before launch.
sources: Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 5 — State, Transition & the Logic of Interaction
Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
Gödel Escher Bach (Hofstadter)
reference: Dix, A. J. (1991). Formal Methods for Interactive Systems. Academic Press.

name: Predict Stage (Forward-Thinking Loop)
aka: Stage 1: Predict with CPM-GOMS and Mental Models
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Stage 1 of the forward-thinking loop: pair CPM-GOMS time predictions with mental-model interviews to produce falsifiable hypotheses and decision bars before any testing.
description: Prediction front-loads insight: before recruiting participants, the researcher models task structure and estimates where bottlenecks will occur. The quant lens is CPM-GOMS with operator estimates (cognitive about 1.2s, perceptual about 0.4s, motor 0.2–0.3s) summed along the task to predict ideal completion time and the cost of misroutes. The qual lens is 4–8 quick contextual interviews asking where users would look first and why, sketched as an 'expected IA' and compared with the actual IA. Combined, they produce a hypothesis such as 'users will misroute to Notifications when creating Alerts, leading to 2–3× longer task time than predicted'. Rigour comes from setting a decision bar up front and logging qual with the first two Miles & Huberman steps (compiling, disassembling) plus a recursive evidence log of expected loop points. The stage is explicitly hypothesis generation, not proof.
steps: Decompose the target task into CPM-GOMS operators: cognitive ≈ 1.2s, perceptual ≈ 0.4s, motor ≈ 0.2–0.3s (e.g. 5 characters × 0.2s = 1s of typing).
Sum the operators to predict ideal completion time (≈ 5.5–6.0s for the price-alert example) and estimate added time per misroute (two wrong tabs add 6–10s).
Set a decision bar up front, e.g. predicted ideal 6s; an observed median above 15s is classified as a significant breakdown.
Run 4–8 contextual interviews asking 'If you wanted to set a price alert, where would you look first? Why?' and sketch each participant's expected IA.
Compile verbatims and sketches into one worksheet (participant, exact quote, expected-IA notes, initial hunch) and code each utterance with short low-granularity labels.
Keep a recursive evidence log: capture the described order (e.g. Settings → Back → Markets), mark expected loop points and flag them as risk loops.
Triangulate: compare CPM-GOMS time if the expected location is correct against added misroute time, and write a falsifiable hypothesis for Stage 2.
outputs: Predicted task time benchmark, expected-versus-actual IA comparison (e.g. 5/8 expect Alerts under Markets), risk-loop list, falsifiable hypothesis and decision bar.
useWhen: Before usability testing of routine, well-defined flows, to sharpen hypotheses and give benchmarks for observed data.
avoidWhen: For creative or ill-structured tasks where GOMS does not apply; avoid vague hypotheses such as 'users might struggle'.
whyLost: Original stage design by Vivek Gopinath; predictive modelling largely vanished from UX practice in favour of observe-first testing.
whereToUse: Fintech navigation, settings and alert flows, enterprise forms, any routine high-frequency task.
example: Before testing a trading app, the researcher predicts a 6s ideal for creating a price alert while 5 of 8 interviewees expect alerts under Markets rather than Notifications, yielding the hypothesis of a 2–3× longer task time.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Bonnie E. John & Wayne D. Gray (1995), CPM-GOMS: An Analysis Method for Tasks with Parallel Activities, CHI '95 Conference Companion
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Stage 1.

name: Predictive Human Error Analysis (PHEA)
origin: David Embrey, Human Reliability Associates, early 1990s
summary: A taxonomy-driven walkthrough of a task analysis that predicts planning, action, checking, retrieval, communication and selection errors with their consequences and recovery.
description: PHEA is a close relative of SHERPA used heavily in chemical process safety. It uses a broader error taxonomy covering planning errors as well as execution, and emphasises performance-influencing factors such as time pressure, feedback quality and procedure clarity. Each task step is examined with the taxonomy, and analysts record error description, consequences, recovery points and error-reduction measures. Its strength is the explicit link between context (performance-influencing factors) and error likelihood, which helps teams see that the same interface can be safe in a calm setting and dangerous under interruption. In UX it can be run as a structured workshop with engineers and support staff, producing a shared error forecast.
steps: Produce or reuse an HTA and agree the scenario conditions (time pressure, interruptions, user expertise).
Walk each step with the PHEA taxonomy: planning, action, checking, retrieval, transmission and selection errors.
List performance-influencing factors present for each step, such as poor feedback, similar options or fatigue.
Record consequences and recovery opportunities, noting whether the interface makes recovery visible and easy.
Rate likelihood qualitatively and prioritise steps with high consequence and low recovery.
Specify error-reduction measures and assign owners; revisit after the next design iteration.
outputs: PHEA worksheet, a list of performance-influencing factors per step, prioritised error-reduction measures.
useWhen: Procedural tasks performed under variable context (shift work, interruptions, alarms) where the team wants a structured error forecast.
avoidWhen: Exploratory discovery phases or tasks with little procedure; use field observation instead.
whyLost: It sits in process-industry consulting and HSE literature, not HCI venues. UX rarely models context factors explicitly as error drivers.
whereToUse: Operations consoles, warehouse and logistics apps, clinical documentation, customer support tools.
example: A logistics firm runs PHEA on its handheld picking app and identifies that interruptions during scanning drive retrieval errors. A persistent 'where you were' banner reduces mis-picks in pilot by a measurable margin.
sources: Embrey, Quantitative and qualitative prediction of human error in safety assessments (1992)
Kirwan, A Guide to Practical Human Reliability Assessment (1994)
reference: Kirwan, B. (1994). A Guide to Practical Human Reliability Assessment. Taylor & Francis.

name: Predictive Model Validation
origin: Stone, 1974; Kuhn & Johnson, 2013
summary: Tests whether models predicting UX outcomes such as churn, conversion or satisfaction generalise to new data, using cross-validation, holdout sets and calibration checks.
description: Predictive model validation asks whether a model's performance will hold for data it has not seen. Following Kuhn and Johnson, the analyst splits data into training and test sets, or uses k-fold or time-based cross-validation, tunes models only within training folds, and evaluates on held-out data with metrics appropriate to the task: AUC, precision and recall for imbalanced outcomes, RMSE for continuous ones, and calibration for probability estimates. Performance is compared with simple baselines such as the base rate or a logistic model. Leakage checks ensure that predictors do not contain information from after the outcome. Rigour comes from pre-specifying the validation scheme, reporting uncertainty in performance estimates, and monitoring for drift after deployment.
steps: Validation protocol for UX predictive models:
Split data: 70% training, 30% held-out test.
(2) Within training: cross-validation (10-fold CV) for model selection and hyperparameter tuning.
(3) Evaluate on held-out test set only once.
(4) Report: both training CV accuracy AND held-out test accuracy. Large gap (> 5pp) = overfitting.
(5) Temporal validation: for time-series data, use time-based split (train on months 1–9, test on months 10–12).
(6) Subgroup analysis: validate performance separately for key user segments.
outputs: Cross-validated performance metrics, calibration plots, comparison against baselines, overfitting diagnostics and a documented validation report.
useWhen: Whenever a model will inform decisions: churn prediction, propensity scores, satisfaction drivers, lead scoring or segmentation models used in production.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating validation as optional for explanatory models presented as predictive; for purely descriptive analysis, focus on effect sizes and uncertainty instead.
whyLost: UX analytics often fits models on all available data and reports in-sample fit; validation discipline sits with ML engineering, not research.
whereToUse: Churn prediction, feature adoption modeling, user segmentation validation, NPS driver analysis.
example: A subscription service's churn model reports 92% accuracy in-sample; five-fold time-split cross-validation drops it to 71%, barely above the 68% base rate, so a planned intervention is put on hold.
sources: Applied Predictive Modeling — Kuhn & Johnson
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
reference: Kuhn M & Johnson K (2013) Applied Predictive Modeling. Springer

name: Prescribe Stage (Forward-Thinking Loop)
aka: Stage 5: Prescribe, from evidence to design action
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Stage 5 of the forward-thinking loop: translate hazard ratios, SHAP drivers and quotes into mechanism-linked fixes placed on an effort × impact grid, each with a decision bar.
description: Prescribing turns statistical drivers and qualitative mechanisms into actionable fixes. The researcher reviews top quant drivers (SNR, mistake rate, retries), cross-checks them with qual evidence, drafts prescriptions in a 'because → therefore' structure, places each on an effort × impact grid and attaches decision bars. An evidence ⇒ prescription table records problem area, quant driver, qual mechanism, design prescription, effort and impact. QCA sufficiency results are used to bundle fixes: if Low SNR * High Mistakes is sufficient for failure, labelling and SNR uplift ship together. Mechanism memos and one quote per fix keep the mechanism salient in design review. Rigour comes from refusing insights without fixes, quantifying effort, and binding each fix to a threshold such as tree success ≥ 85%, OTP success ≥ 80% within 3 attempts, TLX frustration ≤ 40/100 and end-to-end completion ≥ 60%.
steps: Review the top quantitative drivers from Prove and Forecast (e.g. HR per mistake = 1.31, first-click 74% vs 49%, OTP 65% → 80% predicts +5 points).
Cross-check each driver with qualitative evidence to name its mechanism (e.g. 'I looked under Notifications, not Markets').
Draft prescriptions in 'because → therefore' form and record them in an evidence ⇒ prescription table with effort and impact ratings.
Place fixes on an effort × impact grid: low effort/high impact now, high effort/high impact on the roadmap, low/low opportunistic, high effort/low impact deferred.
Bundle fixes that QCA shows are jointly sufficient (do not ship labelling without SNR uplift if Low SNR * High Mistakes drives failure).
Attach a decision bar to each prescription, e.g. first-click ≥ 75%, tree direct ≥ 85%, HR ≤ 0.80, OTP success ≥ 80%, TLX frustration ≤ 40/100.
Attach one representative quote per fix for design review.
outputs: An evidence ⇒ prescription table, an effort × impact grid, mechanism memos and per-fix decision bars.
useWhen: After evidence exists and a team needs a prioritised, defensible set of changes.
avoidWhen: When evidence is thin or mechanisms are unknown; return to Diagnose rather than prescribing from opinion.
whyLost: Original stage design by Vivek Gopinath; most research reports stop at insights without bound fixes or thresholds.
whereToUse: Design reviews, roadmap planning, research readouts for product leadership.
example: The trading app team moves Alerts to top nav (low effort, high impact), renames to 'Price Alerts', adds a rule wizard with examples (medium effort, high impact) and extends the OTP window with reassurance copy (low effort, medium impact).
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Stage 5.

name: Prior elicitation from qualitative research
origin: Structured expert elicitation (O'Hagan et al., Uncertain Judgements, 2006; SHELF framework by Oakley and O'Hagan); applied to linking qualitative UX evidence to quantitative priors in The Inquiry Series
summary: Converts evidence and expert judgement from qualitative research into explicit probability distributions that serve as priors for subsequent quantitative tests.
description: Qualitative research often produces strong beliefs about effects, for example that a trust badge will matter for first-time users, but these beliefs are lost when the A/B test starts from zero. Structured prior elicitation captures them as explicit distributions. Following frameworks such as SHELF, experts who know the qualitative evidence give quantiles (for example median, 25th and 75th percentiles) for the quantity of interest, individually and then through facilitated discussion, avoiding anchoring and overconfidence. A distribution, such as a Beta for a rate or a Normal for a log-odds effect, is fitted to the agreed quantiles. Rigour comes from documenting the evidence base, training elicitors in calibration, using the roulette or quantile method, and running sensitivity analyses so that the prior informs but does not dominate.
steps: Define the quantity precisely, such as the conversion rate of the control or the relative uplift from the trust badge among first-time users.
Compile an evidence dossier from qualitative studies, past experiments and benchmarks, and share it with 3 to 6 elicitors.
Brief elicitors on biases (anchoring, overconfidence) with a short calibration exercise on known quantities.
Elicit individual judgements privately using quantiles (lower plausible, 25th, median, 75th, upper plausible) or the roulette method.
Hold a facilitated discussion to reach a consensus distribution, or pool individual distributions mathematically, and fit a parametric distribution to the result.
Translate into prior strength (for example a Beta prior equivalent to 50 observations), pre-register it, and plan a sensitivity analysis with a weaker prior.
outputs: An evidence dossier, individual and consensus elicited distributions, a fitted prior with stated effective sample size, and a sensitivity plan.
useWhen: Low-traffic experiments where prior knowledge is substantial; linking qualitative and quantitative research programmes; decisions requiring explicit expert judgement.
avoidWhen: Little relevant prior evidence exists, stakeholders would distrust informative priors, or the experiment has enough data that priors will not matter; use weakly informative priors instead.
whyLost: Structured elicitation is established in decision analysis, health economics and risk assessment, but UX treats qualitative and quantitative research as separate tracks and rarely formalises beliefs.
whereToUse: Fintech and health experiments with limited traffic, B2B products, feature bets in early markets, AI feature evaluations.
example: Before testing a trust badge on a fintech sign-up page, researchers who had run 20 interviews elicited a median uplift of 4% (50% interval 1% to 8%). Encoded as a prior, it allowed a decision after 3,000 sign-ups instead of 9,000, with a sensitivity check showing the conclusion held under a weak prior.
sources: Statistical Rethinking (McElreath)
Bayesian Methods for Interaction & Design
Behavioral Drift Playbook (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 40 — Bayesian Thinking & Sequential Study Design
reference: O'Hagan, A., Buck, C. E., Daneshkhah, A., Eiser, J. R., Garthwaite, P. H., Jenkinson, D. J., Oakley, J. E., & Rakow, T. (2006). Uncertain Judgements: Eliciting Experts' Probabilities. Wiley.

name: Probability inflation ratio
donor: Judgement and decision-making research (calibration and overconfidence)
origin: Calibration research by Lichtenstein, Fischhoff and Phillips (1982) and the planning fallacy (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979); applied to feature adoption forecasts in The Inquiry Series
summary: Quantifies how much stakeholders or users overestimate the probability of a behaviour by dividing predicted probability by observed frequency.
description: Teams routinely overestimate how often users will adopt features, complete flows or use advanced functions, through availability, representativeness and optimism biases. The probability inflation ratio makes the bias measurable: collect explicit probability forecasts before data exists, then divide the forecast by the observed rate. A ratio of 1.0 is perfectly calibrated; 3.0 means the event was predicted three times as often as it happened. Tracked across forecasts and forecasters, it shows systematic bias by person, feature type or user segment, and can be used to discount future estimates. Rigour comes from recording forecasts in writing in advance, defining the behaviour and denominator precisely, and pairing the ratio with a proper scoring rule such as the Brier score.
steps: Define the behaviours to forecast with an exact numerator, denominator and time window, for example 'share of active health workers who use the referral feature at least once in 30 days'.
Before launch or before data is visible, collect written probability forecasts from each stakeholder or participant, ideally a central estimate plus an 80% interval.
After the window closes, compute the observed rate from logs and the inflation ratio as forecast divided by observed for each forecaster and behaviour.
Aggregate ratios using the geometric mean (ratios are multiplicative) and compute Brier scores to separate calibration from discrimination.
Break results down by forecaster role and behaviour type (basic versus advanced features, new versus habitual behaviours) to find systematic inflation patterns.
Feed back results to forecasters and apply the historical ratio as a correction factor in roadmap business cases, re-estimating every 2 to 4 forecasting cycles.
outputs: Inflation ratios and Brier scores per forecaster and behaviour type, a calibration chart, and a correction factor for future adoption forecasts.
useWhen: Roadmaps rely on adoption assumptions; stakeholders consistently expect higher use of advanced features; you want to show the gap between belief and behaviour with a single defensible number.
avoidWhen: Behaviours cannot be measured reliably in logs, or the number of forecasts is too small to distinguish bias from noise (fewer than about 10 forecast-outcome pairs); use a qualitative prediction gap discussion instead.
whyLost: Calibration scoring is routine in forecasting research and intelligence analysis but product teams rarely record forecasts in advance, so there is nothing to score.
whereToUse: Feature prioritisation, business cases, AI feature adoption planning, public-sector digital rollouts, health programme design.
example: District managers forecast that 60% of community health workers would use an advanced symptom checker monthly; observed use was 12%, an inflation ratio of 5.0. Across 14 features, advanced features averaged 3.8 and basic features 1.3, which led the programme to discount advanced-feature business cases.
sources: Heuristics & Biases (Kahneman ed.)
Judgment Under Uncertainty
Choices Values & Frames (Kahneman/Tversky)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 21 — Heuristics, Biases & the Architecture of Judgment
reference: Lichtenstein, S., Fischhoff, B., & Phillips, L. D. (1982). Calibration of probabilities: The state of the art to 1980. In Kahneman, Slovic & Tversky (Eds.), Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Cambridge University Press.

name: Probability Sampling
origin: Standard survey-sampling practice; presented by Gratton and Jones (2010) as the four main quantitative sampling techniques: random, stratified random, cluster and systematic.
summary: Choosing survey or study participants by a chance process from a defined population so that results can be generalised with a known margin of error.
description: Probability sampling gives every member of a defined population a known, non-zero chance of selection. Gratton and Jones set out four variants. Simple random sampling gives everyone an equal chance, using a draw, a random number table or software. Stratified random sampling divides the population into subgroups (for example by age or sex) and draws randomly within each, so that each subgroup is properly represented. Cluster sampling randomly selects whole groups (such as teams or sites) and studies everyone in them. Systematic sampling takes every kth case from a list or a stream of people, which works only when the list order is not itself patterned. The book stresses that the first step is defining the population, that sample size, not the percentage of the population, drives precision, and that every subgroup to be compared needs enough cases. For UX researchers, most participant pools are convenience or panel samples, so claims such as '40% of users want X' are often stated with no basis for generalisation. Drawing an intercept or email sample at random from the real user base, stratified by plan or platform, is cheap with product data and makes survey percentages defensible.
steps: Define the population precisely (for example all accounts active in the last 90 days) and obtain a sampling frame such as a user list.
Decide which subgroups must be compared and whether to stratify on them (plan tier, platform, region).
Choose the variant: simple random, stratified random, cluster (random selection of teams, sites or organisations) or systematic every kth case.
Set the target achieved sample size from the precision you need overall and within each subgroup, allowing for expected non-response.
Draw the sample with software or a random number generator and log the seed and frame date.
Field the study, then compare the achieved sample against the frame to check representativeness before generalising.
outputs: A documented, randomly drawn sample list, stratum allocations and the margins of error that apply to the results.
useWhen: You want to report proportions or averages for a user population (attitudinal surveys, satisfaction tracking, feature-demand estimates) and you have a list or stream of users to draw from.
avoidWhen: The aim is qualitative depth rather than generalisation, or no sampling frame exists; purposive or theoretical selection then fits better.
whyLost: UX research leans on small qualitative samples, recruitment panels and in-product prompts shown to whoever passes by, so formal sampling design is rarely taught in UX courses and is left to market research or data science teams.
whereToUse: Customer satisfaction and NPS surveys, feature-prioritisation surveys, B2B studies sampling organisations as clusters, intercept surveys on high-traffic pages.
example: A SaaS team wants to know how many admins would use a new audit-log feature. Rather than surveying the most engaged forum users, they export all 12,000 admin accounts, stratify by plan tier, randomly draw 400 per tier and email the survey, so the tier estimates come with known margins of error.
sources: Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Gratton, C. and Jones, I. (2010) Research Methods for Sports Studies, 2nd edn. London and New York: Routledge.

name: Problem Discovery Sample Size Model (1 − (1 − p)^n)
origin: Virzi (1992), Nielsen & Landauer (1993); small-sample p adjustment by Lewis (2001)
summary: Plans how many users a formative test needs to find problems of a given frequency, and checks how many remain unseen.
description: The famous "five users find 85% of problems" claim is a special case of the cumulative binomial model: the chance of seeing a problem at least once in n users is 1 − (1 − p)^n, where p is how often that problem affects users. Five users find 85% of problems only if the average p is about 0.31. Lewis showed that p estimated from a small test is inflated and corrected it by averaging a Good-Turing adjustment with a normalisation step. Used properly, the model turns sample size into a deliberate choice: "we want a 90% chance of seeing any problem that affects at least 15% of users", which needs 15 people. It also estimates how many problems the study probably missed.
steps: Decide the smallest problem frequency p you care about and the discovery probability you want (for example p = 0.15 at 90%).
Solve n = ln(1 − goal) / ln(1 − p) and round up.
Run the test and record a participant-by-problem 0/1 matrix.
Estimate p from the matrix and apply Lewis's adjustment (average of Good-Turing and normalisation) to deflate it.
Compute the expected proportion of problems found and the likely number still undiscovered; decide whether to run more sessions.
outputs: A justified formative sample size and an estimate of undiscovered problems.
useWhen: Planning iterative formative tests and defending the number of sessions to stakeholders.
avoidWhen: Summative measurement, where sample size depends on precision and power instead.
whyLost: The "five users" slogan survived while the model behind it, and its conditions, was forgotten. Teams either test five by habit or dismiss small tests altogether.
whereToUse: Agile research sprints, safety-critical formative evaluation, budgeting research.
example: A medical device team wants a 95% chance of seeing any use problem affecting at least 10% of users, which requires 29 participants rather than five.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
reference: Lewis, J. R. (2001). Evaluation of procedures for adjusting problem-discovery rates estimated from small samples. IJHCI 13(4).

name: PROCESS macro (Hayes) for moderation and mediation
origin: Andrew F. Hayes, 2012 (PROCESS); v4 released 2022; building on Baron and Kenny (1986) and Preacher and Hayes (2004, 2008)
summary: Using Hayes's PROCESS models to test whether a UX effect operates through a mechanism (mediation) or depends on user characteristics (moderation), with bootstrapped inference.
description: PROCESS is a regression-based macro for SPSS, SAS and R that implements over 90 numbered templates for mediation, moderation and their combinations (conditional process analysis). Model 4 tests simple mediation (X to M to Y), Model 1 simple moderation (X by W predicting Y), and Models 7 and 14 moderated mediation. It estimates indirect effects with percentile bootstrap confidence intervals, probes interactions with simple slopes and Johnson-Neyman regions, and reports an index of moderated mediation. Rigour comes from specifying the model from theory before analysis, mean-centring where appropriate, using at least 5,000 bootstrap samples, and recognising that cross-sectional mediation cannot establish temporal or causal ordering; the X to M to Y order must be justified by design.
steps: Specify the conceptual model (which variable is X, M, W, Y and covariates) and choose the matching PROCESS model number.
Install PROCESS v4 and run it from syntax, e.g. process y=sat/x=design/m=ease/model=4/boot=5000/seed=2026.
For moderation, request simple slopes at the 16th, 50th and 84th percentiles of W and the Johnson-Neyman region.
Interpret indirect effects as significant only if the 95% bootstrap CI excludes zero; for moderated mediation check the index of moderated mediation CI.
Check standard regression assumptions and use heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors (hc3) where needed.
Report path coefficients, the indirect effect with CI and a diagram, and state the causal assumptions.
outputs: Path coefficients, indirect and conditional effects with bootstrap CIs, Johnson-Neyman regions and a model diagram.
useWhen: Testing mechanism hypotheses from qualitative work (e.g. a redesign improves satisfaction via perceived control) and whether effects differ by segment, especially in experiments where X is randomised.
avoidWhen: Avoid with latent variables and multiple indicators (use SEM), with clustered or longitudinal data (use multilevel or longitudinal models), and for causal mediation claims from purely cross-sectional observational data.
whyLost: PROCESS is ubiquitous in academic psychology and communication research but rarely used in UX practice, where mechanism testing is uncommon.
whereToUse: Experiments on fintech trust, health app adherence mechanisms, AI explanation effects and onboarding redesigns.
example: An AI product randomises users to explanations or no explanations. PROCESS Model 7 shows explanations increase reliance via perceived understanding, but only for novice users (index of moderated mediation CI excludes zero).
sources: SPSS REGRESSION
PLUM
LOGISTIC REGRESSION procedures; Hayes PROCESS macro v4
Hayes, A. F. (2022) Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis, 3rd ed.
Baron, R. M. & Kenny, D. A. (1986) The moderator-mediator variable distinction. JPSP
Preacher, K. J. & Hayes, A. F. (2008) Asymptotic and resampling strategies for assessing and comparing indirect effects. Behavior Research Methods
The Inquiry Series, C8 — SPSS for Regression, Moderation & Mediation
reference: Hayes, A. F. (2022) Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis, 3rd ed.

name: Process Mining
donor: Business process management and computer science
origin: Wil van der Aalst, Eindhoven, late 1990s-2011 (Process Mining, 2011/2016)
summary: Discovers the actual process model from event logs, checks conformance to the intended flow, and shows bottlenecks and deviations.
description: Process mining requires event logs with a case identifier, activity name and timestamp. Discovery algorithms (alpha, heuristic miner, inductive miner) build process models such as Petri nets or BPMN from the logs. Conformance checking replays logs against an intended model to quantify fitness and locate deviations. Enhancement overlays performance: waiting times, rework loops, bottlenecks. For UX, this formalises the comparison between the designed flow and what users actually do, at scale, with quantitative fitness metrics. It is particularly suited to multi-step, multi-actor processes such as claims, onboarding with verification or B2B approval flows.
steps: Extract an event log with case ID, activity, timestamp and optional resource and attributes.
Clean and abstract activities to a meaningful level; filter infrequent noise variants.
Discover process models with the inductive miner (guaranteeing sound models) and inspect variants.
Run conformance checking against the intended design flow and compute fitness and precision.
Analyse performance: throughput times, waits, loops and handovers between actors.
Investigate deviations with qualitative research, then redesign and re-mine to measure change.
outputs: Discovered process models, variant frequencies, conformance metrics, bottleneck and rework analyses.
useWhen: Multi-step processes with good event logs where you need to see the real flow and its deviations.
avoidWhen: Unstructured exploratory behaviour without clear cases, or poor event logging.
whyLost: It belongs to BPM and enterprise analytics, rarely taught in UX; product analytics tools offer only path diagrams.
whereToUse: Insurance claims, KYC onboarding, procurement and approval tools, healthcare pathways, support ticket lifecycles.
example: A lender mines 80,000 loan applications and finds only 41% follow the designed path; 23% loop through document re-upload three or more times, adding a median 4 days. Redesigning document guidance halves the loops.
sources: van der Aalst, Process Mining: Data Science in Action (2nd ed., 2016)
IEEE Task Force on Process Mining, Process Mining Manifesto (2011)
reference: van der Aalst, W. M. P. (2016). Process Mining: Data Science in Action. Springer.

name: Process Tracing
donor: Political science and comparative historical analysis
origin: Alexander George (1979); Stephen Van Evera (1997); George and Bennett (2005); Beach and Pedersen (2013)
summary: Tests causal explanations within a single case by examining whether the predicted sequence of intermediate steps and evidence is present, using formal evidential tests.
description: Process tracing examines the causal chain linking a cause to an outcome within a case, asking what observable implications each step of a hypothesised mechanism would leave. Van Evera classified evidential tests by necessity and sufficiency: straw-in-the-wind (weak), hoop (necessary: failing eliminates the hypothesis), smoking gun (sufficient: passing strongly confirms) and doubly decisive. Bayesian process tracing formalises updating. In UX, single cases are common: one enterprise customer's failed rollout, one user's journey to churn, one incident. Process tracing turns case narratives into disciplined causal inference, with rival hypotheses tested against specific evidence.
steps: Define the outcome and candidate causal explanations, including rivals.
For each explanation, specify the mechanism as a sequence of steps and the evidence each step should leave.
Classify predicted evidence as hoop, smoking-gun, straw-in-the-wind or doubly decisive tests.
Collect evidence: logs, documents, emails, interviews, timelines, with attention to source reliability.
Evaluate each hypothesis against the tests, eliminating those that fail hoop tests.
Write a causal narrative with the evidence chain, and state remaining uncertainty.
outputs: Mechanism diagrams, evidence-test tables, eliminated and supported hypotheses and a defensible causal account.
useWhen: Explaining a single important case (an account churn, a failed launch, an adoption success) where comparison or experiments are unavailable.
avoidWhen: Questions about population-level effect sizes; use quantitative causal methods.
whyLost: Case-based causal inference is taught in political science; UX case studies are usually descriptive narratives.
whereToUse: Enterprise account reviews, incident investigations, launch retrospectives, policy change effects.
example: Why did a hospital abandon a scheduling tool? A hoop test (clinicians used it in the first month) passes for the 'workflow mismatch' hypothesis, while a smoking gun (emails showing a leadership change cancelled funding) confirms an organisational explanation instead.
sources: George & Bennett, Case Studies and Theory Development in the Social Sciences (2005)
Van Evera, Guide to Methods for Students of Political Science (1997)
Beach & Pedersen, Process-Tracing Methods: Foundations and Guidelines (2013)
Collier, Understanding process tracing (2011), PS: Political Science & Politics
reference: Collier, D. (2011). Understanding process tracing. PS: Political Science & Politics, 44(4), 823-830.

name: Progress communication audit
origin: Goal-gradient hypothesis (Hull, 1932; Kivetz, Urminsky and Zheng, 2006), endowed progress effect (Nunes and Drèze, 2006) and progress bar perception research (Myers, 1985; Harrison et al., 2007)
summary: Audits how a product communicates progress and completion against users' reference points, identifying where feedback creates felt loss, stalls motivation or undermines satisfaction.
description: Users judge progress relative to reference points: where they expected to be, what the previous system offered, and how far there is to go. The goal-gradient effect shows effort accelerates near a goal; the endowed progress effect shows a loyalty card with 2 of 10 stamps pre-filled was completed by 34% of customers versus 19% for a blank 8-stamp card. Progress bars with accelerating rather than decelerating motion are perceived as faster. A progress communication audit inspects every progress and completion signal (steps, bars, counters, confirmations, success screens) for these effects, and checks whether the completion moment delivers a felt gain relative to the previous practice. Rigour comes from mapping reference points empirically and testing alternatives with completion and satisfaction measures.
steps: Inventory all progress and completion signals across key flows: step indicators, bars, percentages, counters, waits, confirmations and success screens.
Elicit users' reference points for each flow through 6 to 10 interviews: how long they expect it to take, what 'done' looked like in their previous method, and what proof of completion they value.
Evaluate each signal against principles: show early endowed progress, avoid decelerating bars and late surprise steps, give accurate remaining effort, and provide tangible proof of completion.
Identify reference-point losses where the new system offers less than the previous practice, such as no stamp, receipt or visible artefact compared with a paper form.
Prototype improved signals and test them with 5 to 8 users for perceived duration and satisfaction, or A/B test in production on completion rate and post-task satisfaction.
Report changes with measured effects and add progress-signal standards to the design system.
outputs: An inventory of progress signals with issues against reference points, prototype alternatives, and measured effects on completion and satisfaction.
useWhen: Long or multi-step flows have mid-flow abandonment; digital processes replace tangible paper rituals; completion screens fail to generate satisfaction.
avoidWhen: Flows are short single-step actions; focus on response time and feedback latency instead.
whyLost: Progress bars are designed as visual components, and the behavioural research on reference points and perceived progress has not been turned into a standard audit in UX practice.
whereToUse: Onboarding and KYC flows, insurance claims, loan applications, learning products, health data entry, long AI generation tasks.
example: Health workers felt less satisfied submitting a digital form than a paper one, because paper ended with a stamped carbon copy. The audit found the success screen offered only a small tick; adding a reference number, a day's tally and a shareable receipt increased post-task satisfaction scores.
sources: Prospect Theory works (Kahneman/Tversky)
Nash Equilibrium in UX (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 23 — Reference Points, Prospect Theory & the Mechanics of Satisfaction
reference: Nunes, J. C., & Drèze, X. (2006). The endowed progress effect: How artificial advancement increases effort. Journal of Consumer Research, 32(4), 504–512; Kivetz, R., Urminsky, O., & Zheng, Y. (2006). The goal-gradient hypothesis resurrected. Journal of Marketing Research, 43(1), 39–58.

name: Project structure for reproducible research
origin: Noble (2009) on organising computational biology projects; Cookiecutter Data Science template (DrivenData, 2016)
summary: A standard, templated folder layout that separates raw data, processed data, code, notebooks and outputs so any UX study can be rerun and audited.
description: A reproducible project structure encodes good practice in the file system. Raw data is immutable and read-only; every processed file is regenerated by code; notebooks, source code, figures and reports each have a fixed home; and a README states how to rebuild results end to end. Templating the layout (for example with cookiecutter) means every study in a research organisation looks the same, so colleagues can audit, reuse and hand over work. The rigour comes from the directional flow (raw to interim to processed to outputs), from relative paths via pathlib rather than hard-coded personal paths, and from a single entry point (a Makefile or pipeline script) that reproduces every figure.
steps: Generate each new study from a shared cookiecutter template rather than an empty folder.
Place original exports (survey files, transcripts, logs) in data/raw and make them read-only; never edit them by hand.
Write all transformations as code that reads from data/raw and writes to data/interim or data/processed.
Keep notebooks in notebooks/, reusable functions in src/, and generated figures and tables in reports/.
Use pathlib with paths relative to the project root, never absolute personal paths.
Provide one command (e.g. make all) that rebuilds every reported output from raw data, and test it before delivery.
Document data sources, consent constraints and the rebuild command in the README.
outputs: A consistent project skeleton, immutable raw data, a rebuild command and a README that lets anyone regenerate the findings.
useWhen: Any multi-week quantitative or computational qualitative study, research repositories shared across a team, and studies that will be reused or audited.
avoidWhen: Overkill for a single afternoon's ad hoc chart; a dated, documented notebook is enough there.
whyLost: UX research organisations invested in insight repositories for findings but not in reproducible structures for the analyses that produce them.
whereToUse: Research operations, tracking studies, survey programmes, log analysis and AI-assisted qualitative pipelines.
example: A fintech research team adopts a template for all studies. When an auditor asks how a reported 12-point SUS improvement was computed, the team reruns make all from the raw export and reproduces the figure exactly.
sources: Python (pandas, numpy, pathlib)
Jupyter Lab
Git
conda/venv
cookiecutter project templates
Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology
Noble, W. S. (2009) A quick guide to organizing computational biology projects. PLOS Computational Biology
The Inquiry Series, C1 — The Python Research Environment — Setup, Philosophy & Reproducibility
reference: Noble, W. S. (2009) A quick guide to organizing computational biology projects. PLOS Computational Biology 5(7)

name: Prompt UX Research
origin: Grew from conversational UI research (2016 onwards) and generative AI product practice from 2022
summary: Research on prompt-driven interfaces that tests how people discover capabilities, form mental models of the AI, phrase requests and recover from poor outputs.
description: Prompt UX research addresses the 'blank box' problem of generative and conversational interfaces: users must guess what the system can do and how to ask. It studies capability discoverability, the mental models people form about the model's knowledge and limits, prompt formulation strategies, iteration and repair after unsatisfactory outputs, and trust calibration. Typical designs combine task-based sessions with think-aloud, analysis of logged prompt sequences (reformulation rate, turns to success, abandonment), and mental-model elicitation before and after use. Rigour comes from realistic open tasks rather than scripted prompts, coding prompt logs against an intent and repair taxonomy, and distinguishing failures of the model from failures of the interface such as missing suggestions, poor affordances or unclear scope.
steps: Define the core user intents and the capability boundaries you want users to discover.
Elicit prior mental models: ask 6-12 participants what they expect the assistant can and cannot do before first use.
Run open-ended task sessions with think-aloud, letting participants phrase requests in their own words.
Log every prompt, response and reformulation, and code them for intent, strategy, repair type and outcome.
Compute behavioural indicators from logs at scale: reformulation rate, turns to success, abandonment after first response, use of suggested prompts.
Re-elicit mental models after use, compare with actual capabilities, and identify interface changes such as starter prompts, scoping cues or examples.
outputs: Intent and repair taxonomy, prompt-log metrics, mental-model gaps, and interface recommendations for discoverability and recovery.
useWhen: Designing or improving chat assistants, copilots, AI search and any interface where the main input is free-form natural language.
avoidWhen: When the issue is output quality rather than interaction (use LLM evaluation), or when the feature is not yet built (use Wizard of Oz prototyping).
whyLost: Still in use: New discipline emerging rapidly with LLM adoption.
whereToUse: Chatbots; AI copilots; prompt-based tools; AI search interfaces.
example: A spreadsheet copilot's logs show 38% of first prompts are abandoned after one reply. Sessions reveal users think the assistant cannot see their data; adding a visible 'Using: Sheet1, rows 1-500' scope chip halves first-turn abandonment.
sources: AI for Humans
Chatbot Research and Design
Designing Voice User Interfaces (Cathy Pearl)
Amershi et al., Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (CHI 2019)
reference: Amershi S et al. (2019) Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. CHI 2019

name: Propensity Score Matching
origin: Paul Rosenbaum and Donald Rubin, 1983
summary: Balances treated and untreated users on observed covariates via their estimated probability of treatment, approximating a randomised comparison from observational data.
description: Listed in the treatise's causal inference curriculum and its borrowing matrix, propensity score methods estimate each unit's probability of receiving treatment given observed covariates, then match, stratify or weight so that treated and comparison groups are balanced. Rosenbaum and Rubin showed that conditioning on the propensity score suffices to remove bias from observed confounders. Its limit is fundamental: it cannot correct for unobserved confounders, so sensitivity analysis (for example Rosenbaum bounds or E-values) is essential, and covariates must be chosen with a causal model, avoiding post-treatment variables. In UX it suits comparisons between users who did and did not adopt a feature when an experiment was not run.
steps: Define treatment, outcome and pre-treatment covariates using a DAG.
Estimate propensity scores with logistic regression or a flexible model.
Match, stratify or weight, and check covariate balance (standardised differences below 0.1).
Trim units outside common support.
Estimate the effect on the balanced sample.
Run sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding and report it.
outputs: Balance diagnostics, effect estimate, sensitivity analysis.
useWhen: Observational comparisons of adopters versus non-adopters with rich pre-treatment data.
avoidWhen: When key confounders (motivation, intent) are unmeasured and no sensitivity analysis is possible.
whyLost: Common in tech data science teams and health research, but rarely in UX research, which leaves causal claims to experimentation teams.
whereToUse: Feature adoption impact, accessibility settings outcomes, programme evaluations of onboarding calls.
example: Users who joined a webinar retained 25% better; after matching on prior activity and plan, the gap shrinks to 6%, with an E-value showing modest robustness.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)

name: Prospect Theory Application
origin: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, 1979
summary: Applies prospect theory's reference dependence, loss aversion and probability weighting to design and test how options, prices and risks are presented.
description: Prospect theory describes choice under risk with three core features: outcomes are evaluated as gains or losses relative to a reference point; losses weigh roughly twice as much as equivalent gains; and small probabilities are overweighted while moderate-to-high ones are underweighted. In UX it becomes a method for systematically analysing and testing the presentation of choices. Analysts identify the reference point users bring to a decision, the framing of each option as gain or loss, and how probabilities are communicated, then design alternative framings and test their effects on choice and comprehension. Rigour lies in predicting direction of effect from the theory before testing, using between-subjects designs to avoid contrast effects, and measuring both choice and understanding so that persuasive framings do not reduce informed decision-making.
steps: Identify the decision, the options and the reference point users are likely to hold.
Classify current presentation of each option as gain or loss framed, and note how probabilities are shown.
Write predictions from prospect theory for alternative framings (e.g. loss framing increases uptake of protective options).
Build between-subjects variants differing only in framing.
Test with an online sample or live A/B test large enough to detect a 5-point difference (typically several hundred per arm).
Measure choice and comprehension, and reject framings that raise uptake but lower understanding.
outputs: Framing analysis of current design, theory-derived predictions, experimental choice and comprehension results.
useWhen: Pricing pages, insurance and protection add-ons, subscription cancellation, health risk communication and financial products.
avoidWhen: Low-stakes choices without uncertainty or clear reference points; and where framing would be used to push choices against user interest.
whyLost: Latent: Theory widely cited; systematic UX application remains rare.
whereToUse: Pricing UI; risk communication; insurance/financial products; subscription cancellation design.
example: An insurer tested 'Protect your £600 phone' against 'Avoid losing £600 if your phone breaks'. The loss frame lifted add-on uptake by 4 points but comprehension of the excess fell, so the team combined loss framing with an explicit excess statement.
sources: Choices Values and Frames
Judgement under Uncertainty
Thinking, Fast and Slow (Daniel Kahneman)
reference: Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect theory: An analysis of decision under risk. Econometrica, 47(2), 263-291.

name: Prospective memory audit
origin: Prospective memory research by Einstein and McDaniel, 1990; applied to aviation and medicine by Dismukes (2012)
summary: Identifies every point where users must remember to perform an action later and evaluates whether the design provides cues to prevent forgotten intentions.
description: Prospective memory is remembering to carry out an intended action in the future: event-based (when X happens, do Y) or time-based (at 3 pm, do Y). Failures are a major source of errors in aviation and medicine, often triggered by interruptions, task switching and the absence of salient cues at the moment of action. A prospective memory audit lists each deferred intention a workflow creates (for example 'resume the infusion after the scan', 'save before closing', 'complete the second signature'), classifies its type, measures the delay and interruptions between intention and action, and checks whether a cue is present at the right moment. Dismukes' work shows that distinctive, well-timed cues and forcing functions dramatically reduce these errors.
steps: Map workflows to identify every deferred intention, including those created by interruptions.
Classify each as event-based or time-based and estimate the delay and likelihood of interruptions in between.
Check for a cue at the moment of action: is there a reminder, a visible pending state, or a forcing function?
Mine incident reports, support logs or observation notes for forgotten actions and match them to intentions.
Rate risk using delay length, interruption likelihood, cue absence and consequence severity.
Design cues (pending-state indicators, reminders, checklists, forcing functions) and test with 6-10 users including an interruption manipulation.
outputs: An inventory of deferred intentions with risk ratings, incident linkage, and cue or forcing-function designs.
useWhen: In workflows with interruptions, handovers or deferred steps; in safety-critical or compliance-heavy processes.
avoidWhen: For single-session tasks completed without delay; use working memory audits or standard usability testing.
whyLost: Prospective memory is a well-developed research area in aviation and medicine but UX rarely thinks in these terms, framing such failures as user forgetfulness.
whereToUse: Clinical workflows, surgical robot setup, banking (scheduled transfers), project management tools, and AI agents that hand tasks back to users.
example: An audit of a robotic surgery workflow finds the intention 'recalibrate camera after port change' has no cue; it is missed in 1 in 9 cases. A pending-task badge on the camera view eliminates misses in simulation.
