name: Protocol-Aided Document Evaluation (Schriver)
origin: Karen Schriver, 1991-1997 (Carnegie Mellon Document Design Center)
summary: Captures readers' real-time processing of a document through think-aloud protocols to locate comprehension failures and predict revisions that improve understanding.
description: Document design research studied how the visual organisation of text and graphics affects comprehension and usability, and by the 1980s had rigorous methods for testing comprehension, navigation and recall. The treatise singles out Karen Schriver's Dynamics in Document Design (1997) and its protocol-based evaluation methods, in which readers' processing of a document is captured in real time, as far more sophisticated than anything routinely used in content UX. In protocol-aided revision, representative readers think aloud while reading a draft; analysts code points of confusion, misreading and inference, then revise. Schriver showed that writers trained with reader protocols became markedly better at predicting readers' problems. The treatise notes content decisions today are driven by brand guidelines and intuition rather than empirical understanding of how audiences process content.
steps: Select representative readers, including low-literacy and non-native readers where relevant.
Have each read the document or content flow while thinking aloud, with comprehension questions after.
Transcribe and code protocols for misreadings, inference gaps, skipped sections and navigation problems.
Locate each problem in the text and categorise by cause (wording, structure, visual hierarchy, graphics).
Revise and re-test with new readers.
Measure comprehension and task accuracy before and after.
outputs: Coded reader protocols, located comprehension problems, revised content, comprehension metrics.
useWhen: Consent forms, instructions, policy content, financial disclosures, medical information, onboarding copy.
avoidWhen: Microcopy where A/B testing with behavioural outcomes is cheaper and sufficient.
whyLost: Document design was absorbed into technical communication and never integrated with UX content practice.
whereToUse: Terms and consent UX, insurance policy documents, medication leaflets, AI output explanations, regulatory disclosures.
example: Reader protocols on a pension transfer warning show readers interpret 'guaranteed benefits' as guaranteed growth; revision and retest raise correct comprehension from 41% to 83%.

name: Prototype / Wizard-of-Oz A/B Test
origin: Wizard-of-Oz technique: J. F. Kelley, 1984
summary: A randomised comparison of design variants using prototypes or human-simulated systems, measuring the same task and metrics as a live A/B test when shipping code is impossible.
description: The randomised A/B test is the gold standard for proving a design change caused improvement, but it needs shipped code and traffic. When shipping is impossible, Vivek Gopinath's playbook runs the comparison on low-fidelity prototypes or Wizard-of-Oz simulations with the same task and metrics. In the worked example, 600 participants are randomised to the old or new IA for 'Create a price alert for stock ABC', logging time to completion or abandonment, error type and clicks; completion rises from 62% to 81%, median completion time falls from 214s to 182s and median abandonment time rises from 46s to 71s. Decision bars and guardrails are set upfront and results feed a Cox survival model.
steps: Set decision bars and guardrails before the test (e.g. completion ≥ 80%, HR ≤ 0.80, no error increase elsewhere).
Build control and variant prototypes (or a Wizard-of-Oz simulation) that differ only in the change under test.
Randomise participants to arms with adequate sample size (the example uses N = 600).
Run the identical task and log completion or abandonment time, error types and clicks.
Compare completion, median completion time and median abandonment time, and fit a survival model.
Issue a verdict against the bars and plan a confirmatory live test.
outputs: Arm-level outcome comparison, survival inputs and a decision bar verdict.
useWhen: When a change must be tested causally before engineering investment, or live traffic is too low or risky.
avoidWhen: When prototype fidelity would distort behaviour (e.g. real money or real latency matters); confirm with a live test.
whyLost: A/B testing survives because it is the clearest causal tool; prototype variants are less used but well known.
whereToUse: IA changes, onboarding concepts, AI assistant concepts simulated by humans, fintech flows.
example: A trading app tests a new alerts IA on prototypes with 600 randomised participants and sees completion rise from 62% to 81% before writing any production code.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Kelley, J. F. (1984). An iterative design methodology for user-friendly natural language office information applications. ACM Transactions on Information Systems, 2(1), 26–41.

name: Prototype Testing
origin: Paper prototyping in HCI, 1980s to 1990s; Snyder (2003)
summary: Evaluates low to high fidelity prototypes with users to test concepts, flows and interactions before committing to full implementation.
description: Prototype testing puts representations of a design, from paper sketches and clickable wireframes to high-fidelity interactive prototypes, in front of users to learn whether the concept and interaction work before building. The fidelity should match the question: low-fidelity prototypes invite feedback on concepts and structure, while high-fidelity prototypes test details such as visual hierarchy and microcopy. Its value lies in cheap, fast learning that reduces costly rework. Rigour comes from defining what the prototype must answer, making sure the critical paths work, using realistic content and data, framing sessions as tests of the design not the participant, and avoiding treating enthusiasm for a concept as evidence of future use.
steps: Define the questions the prototype must answer and choose a fidelity that fits them.
Build the prototype covering the critical paths with realistic content.
Write task scenarios and questions focused on those paths.
Test with 5 to 8 participants per round, moderated or unmoderated.
Record where the concept or interaction breaks down and why.
Iterate the prototype and test again, ideally in rapid cycles.
outputs: Evidence about concept comprehension and interaction problems, iterated designs and reduced implementation risk.
useWhen: Any design project, especially early before significant development investment, and when comparing alternative concepts.
avoidWhen: Avoid using prototype reactions to forecast adoption or demand; use experiments or market tests. Avoid when the experience depends on real data or performance the prototype cannot mimic.
whyLost: Still in use: Core design validation method; enables fast learning before expensive development.
whereToUse: Any design project; most valuable early in the process before costly commits.
example: An AI note-taking startup tests a clickable prototype of meeting summaries with seven managers. Most distrust summaries without links to transcript moments, so source links become a core feature before engineering begins.

name: Prove Stage (Forward-Thinking Loop)
aka: Stage 3: Prove with Experiments and Causal Models
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Stage 3 of the forward-thinking loop: show a design change caused improvement using A/B tests, Cox survival models, QCA and counterfactual probing, with fallbacks when randomisation is impossible.
description: Proving answers 'Did our change cause improvement, or was it coincidence?' by showing that changing X changes Y and ruling out chance, seasonality and user mix. The playbook gives a selection rule: randomised A/B as gold standard; prototype or Wizard-of-Oz A/B when shipping code is impossible; Cox proportional hazards when the question is when users abandon, not just whether; Rubin's potential outcomes with matched cohorts when randomisation is impossible; Bradford Hill criteria as a principled checklist for observational data. Small-N moderated data are analysed with crisp-set QCA for sufficient condition combinations, and counterfactual probing in interviews explains the mechanism behind the hazard ratio. Decision bars are set upfront (completion ≥ 80%, HR ≤ 0.80, no error increase elsewhere). Rigour includes testing the proportional hazards assumption with Schoenfeld residuals and always checking guardrails.
steps: Set decision bars before the test, e.g. completion ≥ 80% (up from 62%), hazard ratio of abandonment ≤ 0.80, and no increase in error rates elsewhere.
Randomise participants to control and variant (the worked example uses N = 600) on the same task, logging time to completion or abandonment, error type and clicks.
Compare completion, median completion time and median abandonment time between arms (62% vs 81%; 214s vs 182s; 46s vs 71s).
Fit a Cox model h(t|X) = h0(t)·exp(β1·Variant + β2·SNR + β3·Mistake rate), report HRs with 95% CIs, and test proportional hazards with Schoenfeld residuals.
For small moderated samples, run crisp-set QCA on calibrated conditions (e.g. Low SNR, High Mistakes, High TLX, Timed OTP) to find sufficient paths to abandonment.
Use counterfactual probing in interviews to explain the mechanism, and write mechanism memos linking the QCA path, quotes and HRs.
If randomisation is impossible, match cohorts under the Rubin model to estimate ATE and use Bradford Hill criteria (temporality, strength, consistency, plausibility) as a narrative check.
Deliver the A/B table, Cox table, mechanism quotes, guardrail checks and a decision bar verdict.
outputs: A/B results, Cox hazard ratio table with CIs, QCA solution, mechanism quotes and a pass/fail verdict against pre-set bars.
useWhen: When a fix must be shown to cause improvement before rollout, and when timing of abandonment matters.
avoidWhen: When traffic or prototypes are unavailable and no comparison cohort exists; then use Bradford Hill as a confidence checklist rather than claiming proof.
whyLost: Original stage design by Vivek Gopinath; causal and survival methods are standard in medicine but rarely joined to qual mechanism work in UX.
whereToUse: Onboarding, checkout and KYC funnels, alert creation, any flow where abandonment timing matters.
example: A new IA for price alerts lifts completion from 62% to 81%; the Cox model gives HR 0.68 [0.59, 0.77] for the variant, HR 0.92 per +0.10 SNR and HR 1.28 per extra mistake per minute, and QCA shows Low SNR * High Mistakes is sufficient for abandonment.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Stage 3.

name: Proxemic Analysis
origin: Edward T. Hall, 1963-1966 (The Hidden Dimension); proxemic interaction in HCI by Saul Greenberg et al. (2011)
summary: Analyses how distance, orientation, movement and identity between people and devices shape interaction, using Hall's intimate, personal, social and public zones.
description: Hall described culturally variable distance zones: intimate (0-45 cm), personal (45-120 cm), social (1.2-3.6 m) and public (beyond 3.6 m), and how people use space to regulate interaction. Greenberg and colleagues extended proxemics to ubiquitous computing with five dimensions: distance, orientation, movement, identity and location. Rigorous proxemic analysis records spatial configurations through video, floor plans or tracking, codes them, and relates them to interaction behaviours such as privacy management, turn-taking and engagement. It is essential for shared screens, kiosks, voice assistants in homes, AR/VR social spaces, retail and in-car experiences.
steps: Define the setting and the interactions of interest (e.g. sharing a screen, approaching a kiosk).
Record spatial data with overhead video, floor plan notation or sensors, with consent.
Code distance zones, body orientation, movement and identity of actors over time.
Relate spatial configurations to interaction events (initiating use, privacy shielding, disengaging).
Compare across cultures or contexts where zones may differ.
Design proxemic-aware behaviours (e.g. content shifting as people approach) and test them in situ.
outputs: Coded spatial-interaction data, proxemic patterns and design requirements for spatially aware interfaces.
useWhen: Designing for shared, public, ambient or embodied interactions where physical arrangement matters.
avoidWhen: Private single-user screen interactions without spatial variation.
whyLost: Screen-based UX ignored bodies in space; proxemic interaction remained an academic ubicomp topic.
whereToUse: Retail kiosks, ATMs (shoulder surfing), smart displays, AR/VR social apps, hospital bedside devices, cars.
example: At pharmacy kiosks, proxemic coding shows users angle their bodies to shield screens when others enter personal distance; the kiosk adds privacy filters and hides medication names when a second person is detected nearby.
sources: Hall, The Hidden Dimension (1966)
Greenberg et al., Proxemic interactions: The new ubicomp? (2011), ACM Interactions
Marquardt & Greenberg, Proxemic Interactions: From Theory to Practice (2015)
reference: Greenberg, S., et al. (2011). Proxemic interactions: The new ubicomp? ACM Interactions, 18(1), 42-50.

name: Proxemics Applied to Interface Design
origin: Edward T. Hall, 1966; proxemic interaction (Greenberg et al. 2011)
summary: Uses Hall's intimate, personal, social and public zones as a principled model for how intrusive interface elements may be, given the user-system relationship.
description: Hall showed that human interaction is regulated by four spatial zones (intimate 0-45 cm, personal 45 cm-1.2 m, social 1.2-3.6 m, public 3.6 m+), with culturally varying norms, and that violations produce discomfort, distrust and withdrawal. The treatise maps these to interfaces: full-screen takeovers and modals violate the intimate zone and are appropriate only when trust is established; notifications and banners operate in the personal zone, where too many too soon feel like a stranger standing too close. The metaphor makes 'intrusive design' visceral and gives a basis for deciding when and how to intrude. In XR and ubiquitous computing, proxemics applies literally to distances between people, devices and virtual content.
steps: Inventory interface interruptions and content by their zone (modal, overlay, notification, ambient).
Characterise the relationship stage with the user (new, established, trusted) for each touchpoint.
Flag zone violations: intimate-zone intrusions early in the relationship or unrequested.
Research comfort through interviews or experiments varying intrusiveness and timing.
Define a proxemic policy for escalation from public to intimate zones.
In XR, measure physical distances and comfort directly.
outputs: Zone map of interruptions, violation list, proxemic interruption policy.
useWhen: Notification strategy, modal and overlay design, onboarding prompts, AR/VR spatial UI.
avoidWhen: When intrusion is safety-critical and must override comfort (alarms).
whyLost: Anthropological theory never formalised as a UX method; intrusiveness judged by intuition and metrics.
whereToUse: Push notification strategy, mobile density, AR/VR layouts, in-car displays, AI proactive suggestions.
example: A new banking user receives a full-screen upsell on second login; the proxemic policy restricts intimate-zone takeovers until after 30 days or a user-initiated action, reducing early uninstalls.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Hall ET (1966) The Hidden Dimension
Greenberg S et al. (2011) Proxemic interactions: the new ubicomp? interactions 18(1)
Müller J et al. (2010) digital proxemics work presented at NordiCHI
reference: Hall ET (1966) The Hidden Dimension. Doubleday.

name: PSSUQ / CSUQ (Post-Study and Computer System Usability Questionnaires)
origin: James R. Lewis at IBM (1992, 1995; version 3 in 2002)
summary: A 16-item IBM questionnaire with subscales for system usefulness, information quality and interface quality.
description: Developed at IBM by Jim Lewis, the PSSUQ is administered after a lab study and the near-identical CSUQ is worded for field surveys. Sixteen seven-point items load on three factors: system usefulness, information quality (error messages, documentation, feedback) and interface quality. Unlike SUS, which gives one score, the PSSUQ's subscales point at where the problem lies, and it has published norms from IBM studies. Lower scores are better, a source of confusion. It has excellent reliability and was among the first usability questionnaires validated with factor analysis.
steps: Administer the 16 items at the end of the session (PSSUQ) or in a survey of users (CSUQ).
Allow N/A responses and average available items.
Compute the overall score and three subscale scores (items 1-6, 7-12, 13-15).
Compare with the published normative means and confidence intervals.
Use subscale differences to direct improvement work.
outputs: An overall usability score plus diagnostic subscales.
useWhen: Enterprise and business software where information quality (messages, help) matters as much as the interface.
avoidWhen: You need a very short instrument or modern web norms (use UMUX-Lite or SUPR-Q).
whyLost: SUS won on brevity and free use; the PSSUQ's IBM origins and reversed scoring made it feel dated.
whereToUse: B2B software, admin consoles, documentation-heavy products.
example: A CRM scores well on interface quality but poorly on information quality, which leads the team to rewrite error messages rather than redesign screens.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
reference: Lewis, J. R. (2002). Psychometric evaluation of the PSSUQ using data from five years of usability studies. IJHCI 14.

name: Psychoacoustic Principles in Audio UX Design
origin: Auditory scene analysis by Albert Bregman (1990); earcons by Blattner, Sumikawa and Greenberg (1989)
summary: Designs and evaluates interface sounds using psychoacoustic principles, auditory streaming, masking, urgency mapping and entrainment, testing identification, discrimination and annoyance.
description: Interface sounds are usually chosen by taste, yet psychoacoustics predicts how they will be perceived. Auditory streaming determines whether sounds group or separate based on frequency proximity and timing, which matters when alerts overlap. Masking means sounds in the same frequency band as background noise go unheard. Perceived urgency follows measurable parameters such as pitch, speed and repetition (Edworthy's work on alarm design). Entrainment to rhythm affects pacing and arousal. Earcons (abstract musical motifs) and auditory icons (everyday sounds) differ in learnability. The method specifies sound parameters from these principles, then tests them with listeners for detection in realistic noise, identification accuracy, discriminability within the sound set, urgency ranking and annoyance over repeated exposure. Medical alarm standards show how rigorous this can be.
steps: Apply psychoacoustic principles to audio interface design:
Notification sound design — use auditory streaming principles to ensure notification sounds are perceptually segregated from background audio.
(2) Feedback sound timing — design sounds to arrive within 100ms of the triggering action for psychoacoustic integration.
(3) Alert hierarchy — use increasing harmonic dissonance to signal increasing urgency levels. Measure: can users identify alert priority from sound alone with > 80% accuracy?
outputs: Sound specifications with acoustic parameters, detection and identification accuracy, confusion matrices, urgency rankings and annoyance ratings over exposure.
useWhen: Notification and alert design, voice and audio interfaces, medical devices, automotive, wearables, games and accessibility audio cues.
avoidWhen: When sound is purely decorative and carries no information; standard preference testing suffices.
whyLost: Psychoacoustics stayed in audio engineering, music psychology and alarm standards, while UX teams treated sound as branding handled by sound designers.
whereToUse: Voice assistant audio design, notification sound design, accessibility (visual impairment), spatial audio UX, AR audio design.
example: An infusion pump maker tests eight alarm sounds in recorded ward noise. Two high-priority sounds are confused 30% of the time, and a low-priority chime is rated more urgent than a high-priority alert, so the set is redesigned by urgency parameters.
sources: The Science and Psychology of Music — William Forde Thompson
Bregman, Auditory Scene Analysis (1990)
Edworthy, Loxley & Dennis, Improving auditory warning design (Human Factors, 1991)
reference: Thompson WF (2009) Music, Thought, and Feeling: Understanding the Psychology of Music. Oxford University Press

name: Psychometric Network Analysis
origin: Developed over the past fifteen years by the Psychosystems group in Amsterdam and others; summarised in Isvoranu et al. (2022), Network Psychometrics with R.
summary: Estimating a network in which questionnaire items are nodes and edges are partial correlations, to see how individual beliefs, feelings and behaviours reinforce each other instead of assuming they reflect one latent factor.
description: Survey analysis in UX usually assumes that items reflect a common latent cause, such as satisfaction or trust, and sums them. Network psychometrics treats the items themselves as interacting components. A Gaussian graphical model (or an Ising model for binary items, or a mixed graphical model for mixed data) estimates conditional associations between every pair of items after controlling for all others, usually with regularisation to remove spurious edges. The network is visualised, central items are identified with measures such as strength, betweenness or bridge centrality, communities of items are detected, and networks from different groups are compared with permutation tests or bootstrapping. The book stresses the limits: cross-sectional networks are descriptive, not causal; missing nodes distort results; self-report dominates; and replicability needs stability checks. For UX researchers the method shows which perceptions are hubs (for example whether 'feels in control' links usability and trust items), how attitude structures differ between segments, and which components might be worth targeting.
steps: Select items that each measure a distinct belief, feeling or behaviour and avoid near-duplicate wording that creates trivial edges.
Collect a large sample and choose the estimator matching the data type (Gaussian graphical model, Ising model or mixed graphical model).
Estimate a regularised network and visualise it.
Compute centrality and detect communities of items.
Check edge and centrality stability with bootstrapping before interpreting.
Compare networks across segments or time with a network comparison test and report the findings as associations, not causes.
outputs: A network diagram of survey items with edge weights, centrality indices, item communities, stability estimates and between-group comparisons.
useWhen: You have multi-item attitude, trust or experience survey data and want to understand how components relate, or suspect that a single summed score hides structure.
avoidWhen: The sample is small relative to the number of items, items are redundant, or the question requires causal claims from cross-sectional data.
whyLost: UX survey practice relies on summed scales and factor analysis; network methods spread mainly through clinical psychology and need R tooling and care to avoid over-interpreting unstable edges.
whereToUse: Trust and attitude surveys, technology acceptance studies, satisfaction and loyalty drivers, wellbeing and digital-stress questionnaires.
example: A banking app collects 18 items on security, convenience, control and anxiety from 2,500 users. The network shows 'I understand what the app does with my money' as a hub bridging the convenience and anxiety clusters, and the network for older users has much stronger anxiety links, which shapes the research agenda for explanatory messaging.
sources: van der Maas, H., Complex Systems Research in Psychology (2024)
reference: van der Maas, H. L. J. (2024). Complex Systems Research in Psychology. Santa Fe, NM: SFI Press.

name: Psychophysical Threshold Methods (JND)
origin: Gustav Fechner (1860); Ernst Weber (1834); adaptive staircases (Levitt 1971)
summary: Measures detection and discrimination thresholds for interface parameters (contrast, size, latency, haptics) using controlled stimulus variation.
description: The treatise's quantitative curriculum includes psychophysics methods. Classical procedures (method of limits, adjustment, constant stimuli) and adaptive staircases estimate the absolute threshold for detecting a stimulus and the just-noticeable difference between two stimuli. Weber's law states the JND is roughly a constant proportion of the baseline. In UX these answer questions designers usually settle by opinion: how much latency users notice, how large a contrast difference is perceptible, what haptic intensity is felt, how much a progress bar must move to look like progress. Results give defensible parameter thresholds for design systems and performance budgets.
steps: Choose the parameter and a stimulus range spanning undetectable to clearly detectable.
Select a procedure: constant stimuli for precision, adaptive staircase for efficiency.
Run a forced-choice task (for example two-interval: which was faster?) with 15-30 participants.
Fit a psychometric function per participant and estimate threshold (for example 75% correct).
Aggregate thresholds and examine variation by device or population.
Set design or performance budgets below the detection threshold where invisibility is desired.
outputs: Psychometric functions, thresholds and JNDs, parameter guidance.
useWhen: Latency budgets, animation timing, contrast and colour, haptics, audio cues, compression quality.
avoidWhen: Questions about meaning or preference rather than perception.
whyLost: UX dropped experimental perception research in favour of guidelines and A/B tests.
whereToUse: Performance engineering, design tokens, XR rendering, wearables haptics, video streaming quality.
example: A staircase study finds users detect added input latency at about 70 ms on touch scrolling, setting the platform's performance budget.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Fechner GT (1860) Elemente der Psychophysik
Gescheider GA (1997) Psychophysics: The Fundamentals. 3rd ed
Levitt H (1971) Transformed up-down methods in psychoacoustics. JASA
reference: Gescheider GA (1997) Psychophysics: The Fundamentals. 3rd ed. Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Purposive Sampling (Maximum Variation and Criterion)
origin: Michael Quinn Patton, 1980/1990 (Qualitative Evaluation and Research Methods)
summary: Deliberately selecting information-rich participants by criteria derived from the research question, either spanning variation or meeting a defined threshold.
description: Purposive sampling selects participants because they can best inform the research question, not to estimate population parameters. Patton catalogued many strategies; two dominate applied work. Maximum variation sampling chooses participants spanning the widest range on three or four dimensions thought to matter, so that shared patterns are robust and differences are documented. Criterion sampling includes only cases meeting a defined threshold, such as users who abandoned onboarding within seven days. Rigour comes from deriving criteria from research questions, documenting them and borderline decisions, and reporting the rationale so readers can judge transferability. In practice UX screeners often default to demographics and convenience rather than information-rich criteria.
steps: Define characteristics that make a participant information-rich for your specific question. Criteria must flow from research questions, not convenience.
Maximum variation sampling: Identify 3–4 key variation dimensions. Deliberately recruit participants representing the full range on each.
Criterion sampling: All participants meet a specific threshold criterion. State explicitly. Document borderline cases and rationale.
Document your sampling rationale — why these participants and not others is a methodological decision requiring reporting.
outputs: A sampling frame with explicit criteria and variation dimensions, screeners derived from them, and a documented sampling rationale.
useWhen: Nearly all qualitative UX studies, especially when segments differ meaningfully or when a specific behaviour defines who can inform the question.
avoidWhen: When you need statistical generalisation or prevalence estimates; use probability sampling.
whyLost: Recruitment is outsourced to panels with demographic screeners, so criteria rarely flow from research questions and rationale is seldom documented.
whereToUse: Screener design, research ops recruitment, multi-segment discovery, and B2B studies with role and company-size variation.
example: Studying invoice approval software, the team samples for maximum variation on company size, approval chain length and ERP type, rather than on age and gender, uncovering three distinct approval patterns.
sources: Sampling and Choosing Cases in Qualitative Research
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods (Patton)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Patton, M. Q. (2015). Qualitative Research and Evaluation Methods (4th ed.). Sage.

name: Q Methodology
origin: William Stephenson, 1935; developed for political science by Steven R. Brown, 1980
summary: Participants rank-sort 40 to 80 statements into a forced distribution; by-person factor analysis reveals a small number of shared viewpoints and what distinguishes them.
description: Q methodology, devised by William Stephenson in 1935, studies subjectivity systematically. A concourse of everything said about a topic is reduced to a balanced Q-set of 40 to 80 statements. Each participant sorts all statements into a forced, quasi-normal grid from most disagree to most agree, so every placement is relative to every other. Sorts are then correlated person by person and factor analysed, typically with centroid or principal components extraction and varimax or judgemental rotation; each factor is a shared viewpoint, expressed as an idealised sort. A post-sort interview explains placements at the extremes. Because the people, not the statements, are the variables, Q needs modest samples and reveals the structure of opinion rather than its distribution. Rigour comes from a well-balanced Q-set, the forced distribution and transparent factor decisions.
steps: Develop the Q-set (40–80 statements): Represent the full range of perspectives on the topic. Sources: interviews, literature, media. Include minority views, not just majority positions.
Design the sorting grid: Forced quasi-normal distribution (e.g., −5 to +5, fewer slots at extremes). Forces discriminating choices.
Sorting session: Participant sorts all statements into the grid. Then conduct a post-sort interview: 'Tell me about the statements you placed at the extremes — why?'
Factor analysis: Correlate Q-sorts across participants. Extract factors (clusters of similar Q-sorts). Rotate to simple structure.
Interpret factors: Each factor represents a shared viewpoint. The factor array (the ideal Q-sort for that factor) shows what someone holding this viewpoint values and rejects.
outputs: A Q-set, completed sorts, a factor solution with loadings, idealised factor arrays, distinguishing and consensus statements, and narrative descriptions of each viewpoint.
useWhen: You want to identify the distinct perspectives that exist on a contested or subjective topic, such as attitudes to data sharing, AI, money or health, with a modest sample of 20 to 60 participants.
avoidWhen: You need to know how prevalent each viewpoint is in a population; Q does not estimate prevalence. Follow up with a survey built on the factors, or use cluster or latent class analysis on survey data.
whyLost: It requires specialised software and factor-analytic judgement, and its inverted logic (correlating people rather than variables) is unfamiliar, so UX teams default to card sorts or attitudinal surveys.
whereToUse: Segmenting attitudes to privacy, AI and automation, financial behaviour, clinical decision-making, stakeholder alignment workshops, and value-based persona development.
example: A health-data platform runs 40 Q-sorts on statements about sharing records. Three viewpoints emerge: 'altruistic sharers', 'control-first pragmatists' and 'institutional sceptics'. Consent design is then tailored so each group sees the controls it cares about.

Brown (1980) Political Subjectivity
Watts, S. & Stenner, P. (2012) Doing Q Methodological Research

name: Qual-to-Quant Bridge (Theme-to-Construct Operationalisation)
origin: Exploratory sequential mixed-methods design (Creswell & Plano Clark); scale development practice (DeVellis)
summary: Converting qualitative themes into defined constructs and survey items in participants' language, then pretesting and validating them with factor analysis.
description: This bridge turns qualitative insight into something measurable at scale. For each major theme, the researcher defines the underlying construct and its observable indicators, drafts candidate items using participants' own language (which improves face validity), and pretests the items with cognitive interviews. The items are then fielded to a sample large enough for exploratory factor analysis (typically 200 or more), checked for expected structure and reliability, and confirmed on a fresh sample with confirmatory factor analysis. The result is a validated scale grounded in user experience rather than borrowed from another context. Reporting what the quantitative construct captures and what it misses keeps the link to the qualitative origin honest.
steps: From each major qualitative theme, derive: what is the underlying construct? What observable behaviours or self-report items would indicate its presence?
Write candidate items using participants' own language from the qualitative phase — in-vivo language produces more face-valid items.
Cognitive interview candidate items with 5–8 members of the target population.
Run Exploratory Factor Analysis to determine whether items group as expected.
Validate with CFA. Report both what the quantitative construct captures and what it misses.
outputs: Construct definitions, an item pool in user language, cognitive pretest results, EFA and CFA results, reliability statistics, and a validated scale.
useWhen: When qualitative research uncovers a concept (trust, anxiety, control) that needs measuring across a population or over time.
avoidWhen: When a validated scale for the construct already exists and fits your population; adopt it instead. Avoid without sample sizes for factor analysis.
whyLost: UX rarely has psychometric expertise in-house, so themes are turned into ad hoc survey questions without validation.
whereToUse: Trust in AI products, financial anxiety measures, clinical app experience scales, and custom UX metrics for product dashboards.
example: Interviews about an AI writing assistant reveal 'authorship anxiety'. Twelve items drafted from participants' words are pretested, fielded to 400 users, and reduced to a reliable six-item scale tracked quarterly.
sources: Quantitative User Experience Research (Chapman)
Oxford Handbook of Multimethod & Mixed Methods Research
Scale Development: Theory and Applications (DeVellis)
Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (Creswell & Plano Clark)
reference: DeVellis, R. F. (2017). Scale Development: Theory and Applications (4th ed.). Sage.

name: Qualitative Comparative Analysis
origin: Charles Ragin, 1987 (crisp-set); 2000 (fuzzy-set)
summary: A case-based method using Boolean logic and set theory to identify combinations of conditions that are necessary or sufficient for an outcome across small to medium numbers of cases.
description: Qualitative Comparative Analysis, developed by Charles Ragin, bridges case-oriented and variable-oriented research. Each case, such as a customer account, team or product deployment, is described by a set of conditions and an outcome, coded as crisp (0 or 1) or fuzzy (degrees of membership) sets. A truth table lists all observed combinations of conditions, and Boolean minimisation identifies which configurations are consistently linked to the outcome. QCA embraces conjunctural causation (conditions matter in combination), equifinality (different paths lead to the same outcome) and asymmetry. It suits 10 to 50 cases, where statistics are weak but cases are too many to compare by eye. Rigour comes from theory-based condition selection, transparent calibration, consistency and coverage thresholds, and returning to cases to interpret solutions.
steps: Define the outcome and select 10 to 50 cases with variation in the outcome.
Choose 3 to 6 conditions based on theory and case knowledge.
Calibrate conditions and outcome into crisp or fuzzy set membership with documented thresholds.
Build a truth table of configurations and assess consistency (typically 0.8 or higher).
Run Boolean minimisation to derive solution pathways and report consistency and coverage.
Test for necessary conditions separately.
Return to cases to interpret pathways and check robustness to calibration choices.
outputs: Truth tables, solution pathways (combinations of conditions sufficient for the outcome), consistency and coverage metrics, and case interpretations.
useWhen: When comparing a modest number of cases (for example enterprise deployments, sites or teams) to find which combinations of conditions lead to success or failure.
avoidWhen: Avoid with very few cases (under about 10) or large samples suited to regression; use case studies or regression. Not suitable when conditions cannot be meaningfully calibrated.
whyLost: Latent: Powerful for small-n comparative studies; largely unknown in UX; imported from political science.
whereToUse: Cross-cultural UX; comparative product studies; policy design research.
example: An enterprise SaaS vendor analyses 28 customer rollouts. QCA shows successful adoption follows either executive sponsorship with training or an internal champion with simple data migration, two distinct pathways that shape onboarding playbooks.
sources: The Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis
The Comparative Method (Ragin)
Redesigning Social Inquiry (Ragin)
reference: Ragin, C. C. (1987). The Comparative Method. University of California Press; Ragin, C. C. (2008). Redesigning Social Inquiry: Fuzzy Sets and Beyond. University of Chicago Press.

name: Qualitative Meta-Synthesis
origin: George Noblit & Dwight Hare, 1988 (Meta-Ethnography); Sandelowski & Barroso, 2007
summary: Systematically synthesising findings from completed qualitative studies into higher-order interpretations that no single study could produce.
description: Meta-synthesis treats the findings of existing qualitative studies as data. Unlike meta-analysis, which pools effect sizes, it integrates concepts, themes and theoretical propositions. Noblit and Hare's meta-ethnography translates concepts from one study into another, identifies refutations, and builds a 'line of argument' synthesis. The process involves a defined question, systematic search and selection (often reported with PRISMA or ENTREQ), quality appraisal, and a three-order construct analysis: participants' views, original authors' interpretations, and the synthesist's new interpretation. Findings robust across studies are distinguished from context-specific ones. In organisations it can also synthesise an internal research archive, turning past studies into cumulative knowledge.
steps: Systematic search and selection: Define inclusion criteria. Use PRISMA reporting standards for the search process.
Quality appraisal: Apply a trustworthiness appraisal framework. Studies failing basic credibility or confirmability criteria are excluded.
Three-order construct analysis: First-order = what participants said. Second-order = what original researchers concluded. Third-order = what you conclude from comparing across studies.
Report: Distinguish between findings robust across studies and findings appearing in only one or two specific contexts.
outputs: A documented search and selection record, quality appraisal, translation tables of concepts across studies, and a synthesised line-of-argument model with robustness ratings.
useWhen: When many studies exist on a topic (internal or published) and you need cumulative, evidence-weighted understanding before commissioning new research.
avoidWhen: When few or poor-quality studies exist, or when a quick literature scan suffices; use a rapid review or new primary research.
whyLost: It is standard in health evidence synthesis, but UX rarely treats its own archives or published studies as data for formal synthesis.
whereToUse: Research repository synthesis, health product evidence reviews, accessibility research, and strategy work drawing on academic literature.
example: A digital health company synthesises 14 internal and 9 published studies on medication adherence apps. The line-of-argument model shows that 'feeling monitored' undermines adherence across contexts, guiding notification design.
sources: Oxford Handbook of Multimethod & Mixed Methods Research
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Meta-Ethnography: Synthesizing Qualitative Studies (Noblit & Hare)
Handbook for Synthesizing Qualitative Research (Sandelowski & Barroso)
reference: Noblit, G. W. & Hare, R. D. (1988). Meta-Ethnography: Synthesizing Qualitative Studies. Sage.

name: Qualitative Research Protocol as Mental Framework
donor: Case study and qualitative field research
origin: Robert K. Yin, Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2011; 2nd ed. 2016), building on his case study protocol
summary: A set of topics and questions addressed to the researcher, each paired with likely sources of evidence, that is carried in the head to guide conversational fieldwork instead of a scripted interview guide.
description: Yin separates a protocol from an instrument. An instrument scripts the spoken questions or tasks a participant receives; a protocol states the topics and questions the researcher must answer through the whole line of inquiry. Protocol questions are written to the fieldworker (for example 'Ask about how long R has lived here, and why'), and each is accompanied by the sources of evidence that might answer it: interviews, documents, observation. In the field the researcher does not read from it. The protocol is internalised as a mental framework, like a doctor's clinical line of questioning or a detective's working hypotheses, and spoken questions are composed on the spot in natural conversation. Yin gives three benefits: it keeps the original questions in view, it points to chances to seek contrary as well as supporting evidence, and it helps evidence converge across sources. When something unexpected turns up, the protocol is paused and revised. In multi-site work the same protocol supports parallel data collection, with the fieldworker composing a written answer to each question per site. For UX, it is an alternative to the scripted discussion guide when studying workplaces, services or organisations through mixed sources.
steps: Group the study's research questions into topics covering the full line of inquiry
Write each protocol question in the voice of the researcher, not as words to be spoken to a participant
Next to each question, list the anticipated sources of evidence: who to talk to, which documents, what to observe
Add operational definitions for key terms and distinguish observed events from reported ones
Study the protocol until it can be carried in the head; do not read from it during fieldwork
In the field, compose spoken questions on the spot and seek contrary as well as supporting evidence
After each site or session, write an answer to each protocol question citing the evidence, and revise the protocol if discoveries require it
outputs: A topic-by-question protocol with evidence sources, and per-site or per-study written answers to each protocol question that support cross-site comparison.
useWhen: Field studies, customer site visits or service research that draw on interviews, documents and observation together, especially across several sites or fieldworkers.
avoidWhen: You need identical wording across participants for comparison, as in a survey, a standardised usability task script or a quantitative interview.
whyLost: UX practice standardised on the printed discussion guide, which blends researcher questions with participant wording; the idea of a private protocol answered from multiple evidence sources stayed within case study methodology.
whereToUse: B2B and enterprise discovery, service design research, multi-site contextual studies, research ops templates.
example: Before visiting six hospital pharmacies, a team writes protocol questions such as 'How are urgent orders escalated, and who decides?' with sources listed as the pharmacist interview, the escalation log and observation of the morning rush. At each site they converse freely, then fill in an answer per question, making the six sites directly comparable.
sources: Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2016). Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.

name: Qualitative Trajectory Arrays (Sentiment Drift Forecasting)
donor: Qualitative data display (Miles & Huberman) applied to longitudinal diaries
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Convert diary or ESM entries into per-participant trajectories of clarity, trust and frustration, cluster them into patterns such as 'fragile success', and use them to qualify quantitative forecasts.
description: Monte Carlo and SHAP extrapolate numbers; diaries and experience sampling extrapolate feelings over time. The playbook argues that even if completion rises short-term, negative sentiment drift predicts future drop-off ('Even when I succeeded, I felt drained'; 'After three tries, I stopped trusting the feature'). Diary entries are arrayed with columns for session index, perceived clarity (−2..+2), trust (1..5), frustration (0..100), success (Y/N) and a key quote, then sorted by outcome and clustered into patterns such as 'fast trust gain', 'fragile success' and 'churn risk'. Clusters are triangulated with top SHAP drivers (e.g. high mistake rate clusters with fragile success) and turned into what-if notes. The deliverable is a panel of two or three curated trajectories shown beside forecast curves to argue for emotional sustainability.
steps: Run a diary or ESM study across multiple sessions with structured prompts for clarity, trust and frustration plus an open quote.
Array entries per participant: session index, clarity (−2..+2), trust (1..5), frustration (0..100), success (Y/N), key quote.
Sort trajectories by outcome and cluster them into patterns (e.g. fast trust gain, fragile success, churn risk).
Link clusters to the top quantitative drivers from SHAP or survival models.
Write what-if notes, e.g. 'If SNR uplift holds and the rules wizard ships, expect the fragile cluster to shrink.'
Present two or three curated trajectories alongside Monte Carlo curves and re-check them at 1, 3 and 6 months after launch.
outputs: Trajectory clusters, curated example trajectories and what-if statements qualifying forecasts.
useWhen: When forecasting adoption or retention and emotional sustainability may diverge from short-term completion.
avoidWhen: When only a single-session snapshot is possible; use post-task questionnaires instead.
whyLost: Original technique by Vivek Gopinath building on qualitative data display.
whereToUse: Onboarding, trading and investing apps, health behaviour apps, AI assistants.
example: Diaries from a trading app show a cluster of users who complete price alerts but report rising frustration and falling trust; the team flags them as 'fragile success' and prioritises the rule wizard.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Section 5.3 and 'Qualitative Trajectories to Complement Forecasts'.

name: Quality gates at each pipeline stage
donor: Software engineering; manufacturing quality control; data engineering
origin: Stage-gate and statistical quality control traditions (Shewhart, 1931); data validation in pipelines (e.g. Great Expectations, 2017)
summary: Defining measurable acceptance criteria between stages of a research pipeline so poor-quality transcripts, parses or codes are caught before they contaminate findings.
description: In a multi-stage pipeline errors compound: a hallucinated transcript passage becomes a coded segment, then a theme. Quality gates set explicit, measurable thresholds at each hand-off, for example transcription WER and confidence, diarisation sanity checks, NLP component F1, LLM schema validity and quote-verification rates, and human-AI coding agreement. Failing items are halted, flagged or routed to review rather than passed silently. Rigour comes from setting thresholds before running, automating checks, recording pass and fail rates in run reports, and periodically auditing items that passed to make sure gates are not too lenient.
steps: List each stage's outputs and the failure modes that matter for findings.
Set thresholds before running, e.g. sampled WER of 10% or below, at least 98% schema-valid outputs, 100% verbatim quote match, kappa of 0.70 or above against human coders.
Automate checks in the pipeline and halt or quarantine failing items.
Route quarantined items to human review with the reason for failure.
Audit a random sample of passed items each run (e.g. 5%) to estimate leakage.
Report gate statistics with every set of findings.
outputs: Gate definitions, automated checks, quarantine queues and a quality report per run.
useWhen: Any automated or AI-assisted research pipeline, especially at scale or where findings inform major decisions.
avoidWhen: Excessive for manual small studies, where the researcher's own reading serves as the check.
whyLost: Researchers rarely treat their analysis as a production process, so manufacturing-style quality control never migrated.
whereToUse: AI-assisted qualitative analysis, transcription programmes, feedback analytics and research repositories.
example: A pipeline's quote-verification gate quarantines 3% of coded segments whose quotes do not appear in transcripts. Investigation reveals a prompt change had caused paraphrasing, which is fixed before the report is produced.
sources: Whisper.cpp
spaCy
Claude API (multi-turn agent)
asyncio
pandas
Prefect/Airflow for pipeline orchestration
Shewhart, W. A. (1931) Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product
Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology
The Inquiry Series, C13 — The Full Agentic Research Pipeline — Whisper → spaCy → AI Coder → Synthesis
reference: Shewhart, W. A. (1931) Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product

name: Quantum Probability Models of Judgement
aka: QQ equality test for question-order effects
origin: Busemeyer and Bruza (2012); question-order test by Wang, Solloway, Shiffrin and Busemeyer (2014)
summary: Models judgements with quantum probability, where asking one question changes the answer to the next, to explain and test order and framing effects in surveys and choices.
description: Classical probability assumes that a person holds fixed opinions and a question simply reads them out, so the order of questions should not matter. In practice it does: asking about trust before satisfaction gives different answers from the reverse order. Quantum cognition treats a mental state as a set of possibilities that a question resolves, in the way a measurement changes a physical system. That framing makes specific, testable predictions. The best known is the QQ equality: for two yes/no questions asked in both orders to split samples, a particular combination of the order effects should be zero if the quantum account holds. For UX research this offers more than a curiosity. It gives a principled way to decide whether an order effect in a survey is noise, a carry-over bias you should counterbalance away, or a real feature of how people build judgements on the spot, which matters for in-product micro-surveys, onboarding questions and preference elicitation.
steps: Pick pairs of judgement questions where order could matter, such as trust and satisfaction, or price fairness and value.
Randomly assign respondents to answer each pair in one order or the other (A then B, or B then A).
For yes/no or binarised answers, tabulate the four joint outcomes for each order.
Compute the order effects and the QQ equality statistic; check whether it is close to zero.
If order effects exist and satisfy the QQ equality, treat answers as constructed in context: fix a deliberate order that matches the real product moment rather than averaging orders away.
If order effects break the equality, look for ordinary carry-over or fatigue and counterbalance.
outputs: A diagnosis of each order effect in a questionnaire, and a decision on question order grounded in a model rather than habit.
useWhen: Designing short in-product surveys, preference or consent flows, or any study where the same two judgements are asked together.
avoidWhen: Long validated scales with fixed item orders, or small samples that cannot be split by order.
whyLost: Quantum cognition grew in mathematical psychology and is written in Hilbert-space notation, so it rarely reaches survey practice even though its core test needs only split samples and a few proportions.
whereToUse: NPS and CSAT micro-surveys, pricing pages, consent dialogues, onboarding questionnaires.
example: An app asks 'Do you trust us with your data?' and 'Are you satisfied?' in random order. Satisfaction drops 9 points when trust comes first, and the QQ equality holds, so the team keeps the trust question after satisfaction to mirror when users actually think about privacy, and reports the order with the result.
sources: Cognitive Modeling: Nine Paradigms (slide deck)
Busemeyer, J. & Bruza, P., Quantum Models of Cognition and Decision (2012)
reference: Busemeyer, J. R., & Bruza, P. D. (2012). Quantum Models of Cognition and Decision. Cambridge University Press. Wang, Z., Solloway, T., Shiffrin, R. M., & Busemeyer, J. R. (2014). Context effects produced by question orders reveal quantum nature of human judgments. PNAS, 111(26), 9431-9436.

name: Questionnaire Pilot Testing
origin: Standard survey practice; Gratton and Jones (2010) list its functions and recommend repeated piloting until the design is settled.
summary: Running a small-scale version of a survey under real conditions before launch to check wording, order, timing, administration and analysis.
description: A pilot survey is a small administration of the full questionnaire before the main survey. Gratton and Jones give it five jobs: checking that wording is clear and unambiguous to the intended respondents; checking that the sequence is logical; estimating completion time; testing the whole administration process from distribution to receipt of responses; and doing a dry run of the analysis by entering the pilot data and trying to answer the research question with it. The last is the step most often skipped, and it is where researchers discover that a question cannot support the comparison they need. The pilot should run in conditions as close to the main survey as possible and with a similar group (if the main sample includes children, so must the pilot). After changes, the questionnaire is piloted again until no further changes are needed. It differs from cognitive interviewing, which probes how individuals understand items one by one; a pilot tests the instrument and the fielding pipeline end to end. For UX teams launching in-product or email surveys, a pilot to a small random slice catches broken logic, unclear items and unusable data before the whole user base is surveyed once and cannot be asked again.
steps: Prepare the questionnaire, invitation and delivery mechanism exactly as they will be used.
Field it to a small group similar to the target sample, in conditions as close as possible to the main survey (for example a small random slice of users).
Record completion times, drop-off points and any questions respondents skip, query or misread; optionally ask pilot respondents to comment on the design.
Enter or export the pilot data and run the planned analysis to confirm the data can answer the research question.
Revise wording, order, response options, routing and administration based on what you find.
Repilot after changes and repeat until no further changes are needed, then launch.
outputs: A revised questionnaire, estimated completion time, a tested delivery and data pipeline, and a draft analysis template.
useWhen: Before any survey that will go to a large or hard-to-reach sample, uses routing logic, or feeds a decision.
avoidWhen: It is a quick throwaway poll with no consequence, or the instrument is a validated standard scale used unchanged (though the delivery still benefits from a pilot).
whyLost: Survey tools make launching so fast that teams skip the pilot or reduce it to a colleague clicking through; the analysis dry run in particular has largely disappeared from UX practice.
whereToUse: In-app and email surveys, onboarding questionnaires, diary-study entry forms, benchmark surveys, recruitment screeners.
example: Before emailing a feature-satisfaction survey to 50,000 users, a researcher sends it to a random 200. Completion averages twice the estimate, a matrix question has high drop-off on mobile and the dry-run analysis shows that the usage-frequency categories overlap. All three are fixed and a second pilot of 200 confirms the changes before full launch.
sources: Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
reference: Gratton, C. and Jones, I. (2010) Research Methods for Sports Studies, 2nd edn. London and New York: Routledge.

name: Queueing Theory and Little's Law
origin: Agner Krarup Erlang (1909, telephone traffic); John Little (1961, L = lambda W); Kendall's notation (1953)
summary: Models arrivals, service times and capacity to predict waiting times and backlog, using Little's law (items in system = arrival rate x time in system).
description: Wherever users wait, for support agents, approvals, deliveries, moderation or AI responses, queueing theory predicts how waits behave. Little's law holds for any stable system: the average number in the system equals arrival rate times average time in system. Models like M/M/c (Poisson arrivals, exponential service, c servers) give waiting time distributions; Kingman's formula shows waits explode as utilisation approaches 100% and grow with variability. These insights correct common intuitions (e.g. that adding small capacity barely matters) and allow designers to reason about perceived waiting, prioritisation, triage and self-service deflection quantitatively.
steps: Map the waiting system: arrivals, queues, servers (people, machines, models), priorities and abandonment.
Measure arrival rates, service time distributions and current waits from logs.
Check Little's law against observed data to validate measurement.
Fit an appropriate model (M/M/c, M/G/1, Erlang C with abandonment) or simulate.
Explore scenarios: staffing, deflection, priority rules, variability reduction.
Combine with perceived-wait research to design communication (position in queue, estimates).
outputs: Queue models, predicted waits under scenarios, utilisation targets and design implications for waiting experiences.
useWhen: Any service with waiting: support, onboarding approvals, claims, deliveries, AI rate limits, content review.
avoidWhen: Experiences without capacity constraints or waiting.
whyLost: Operations research is owned by ops and engineering; UX focuses on wait screens rather than wait dynamics.
whereToUse: Customer support, telehealth, KYC review queues, food delivery, AI inference capacity planning.
example: A telehealth service runs at 92% clinician utilisation with waits of 40 minutes. Kingman's formula shows that cutting service time variability via structured intake would reduce waits more than hiring one extra clinician.
sources: Little, A proof for the queuing formula L = lambda W (1961), Operations Research
Kleinrock, Queueing Systems, Volume 1: Theory (1975)
Hopp & Spearman, Factory Physics (3rd ed., 2008)
reference: Little, J. D. C. (1961). Operations Research, 9(3), 383-387.

name: QUIS (Questionnaire for User Interaction Satisfaction)
origin: Chin, Diehl & Norman (1988), Human-Computer Interaction Lab, University of Maryland
summary: The first published standardised usability questionnaire, rating specific interface factors such as screen, terminology, learning and system capabilities on 9-point bipolar scales.
description: Created by Shneiderman's Human-Computer Interaction Lab at Maryland, the QUIS measures satisfaction with specific parts of an interface rather than giving a single score. Version 7 has a demographic section, overall reactions on six scales, and hierarchically organised sections for nine interface factors: screen, terminology and system feedback, learning, system capabilities, technical manuals, online tutorials, multimedia, teleconferencing and software installation. Items use 9-point bipolar scales (for example, messages on screen: confusing to clear) with an N/A option. A short form has 41 items and a long form 122; most teams use only the sections that apply. Chin and colleagues reported an overall reliability of 0.94 for the 27-item short form and showed it separated liked and disliked systems. It requires a paid licence.
steps: License the QUIS (student, academic or commercial fee) and pick the sections relevant to your product.
Administer it after participants have used the system enough to judge each factor.
Score each item 1 to 9, allowing N/A, and average items within each section.
Compare section means across versions or products to find the weakest interface factors.
Pair with task data so low-scoring factors can be traced to observed problems.
outputs: Satisfaction scores for overall reaction and each interface factor.
useWhen: You need diagnostic, factor-by-factor satisfaction data on desktop or enterprise software and can license the instrument.
avoidWhen: You need a short, free instrument or comparison to modern norms (use SUS or UMUX-Lite).
whyLost: SUS was free and ten items long, so it displaced the licensed, much longer QUIS; its factor list also reflects 1980s software (manuals, teleconferencing).
whereToUse: Legacy enterprise systems, government software procurement, academic HCI replications.
example: A hospital records system scores well on screen layout but poorly on terminology and system feedback, so the team rewrites messages and labels before redesigning screens.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Measuring the User Experience (Tullis & Albert)
reference: Chin, J. P., Diehl, V. A. & Norman, K. L. (1988). Development of an instrument measuring user satisfaction of the human-computer interface. CHI 88.

name: Quota Sampling
origin: Market research and polling practice; described by Veal and Darcy mainly for street surveys
summary: Interviewers fill pre-set quotas of people in each category, such as age and sex, in the proportions known to exist in the population.
description: Quota sampling gives interviewers a predetermined number of different types of people to interview, for example by age, sex or occupation, so that the final sample matches the population on those characteristics. Veal and Darcy present it as the usual answer to the problems of street surveys, where the people passing a given spot at a given time are not representative of the wider population. The proportions in each category must be known in advance, for example from the census or, for some sport tourism activities, from booking data. If the completed sample is still out of line on key characteristics, weighting can correct it further. Where nothing is known about the population, quota sampling cannot be used. Selection within each quota cell is left to the interviewer, so it is not a probability sample, and bias can enter on characteristics that are not controlled. In UX, quotas are the normal way recruiters balance study participants by segment, platform or experience level; the book's emphasis on using known population figures for the quotas, rather than arbitrary equal splits, is the part UX often misses.
steps: Decide which characteristics most affect the answers and are known for the population.
Obtain population proportions for those characteristics from census, analytics or booking data.
Set quota targets for each category, or combinations of categories, in proportion to the population.
Brief interviewers or recruiters to fill each quota and stop when it is full.
Monitor fill rates during fieldwork and adjust effort to hard-to-reach cells.
Compare the final sample with the population on other characteristics and weight if needed.
Report the method as non-probability and avoid presenting margins of error as exact.
outputs: A sample that matches the population on the controlled characteristics, with records of quota fill and any weighting applied.
useWhen: No sampling frame exists or probability sampling is too costly, but key population proportions are known.
avoidWhen: Population proportions are unknown, or precise, defensible population estimates with confidence intervals are required.
whyLost: It survived: UX recruiting screeners routinely use quotas, though often set as equal splits rather than population proportions.
whereToUse: Street and intercept research, panel surveys, participant recruitment for usability and concept testing, market sizing surveys.
example: For a survey of potential users of a city bike-share app, recruiters fill quotas of age group and gender matching the city's census profile, then weight slightly by car ownership, which was over-represented among people stopped near car parks.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge.

name: RAMP Model for Intrinsic Gamification
origin: Andrzej Marczewski, 2013; drawing on Deci & Ryan's self-determination theory
summary: Designs and audits engagement features against four intrinsic motivators (relatedness, autonomy, mastery, purpose) instead of relying on points and badges.
description: RAMP organises gamification around four intrinsic motivators derived from self-determination theory and Pink's synthesis: relatedness (social connection), autonomy (meaningful choice), mastery (growing competence) and purpose (contribution to something meaningful). Rather than adding extrinsic mechanics such as points, the designer audits a product for each motivator, identifies which are absent for each user type, and designs features that satisfy them, with extrinsic rewards used sparingly and informationally. The approach guards against the overjustification effect, where external rewards reduce intrinsic interest. It becomes rigorous when paired with user-type analysis, validated motivation measures (e.g. intrinsic motivation inventories) and experiments that test whether engagement changes are sustained beyond novelty.
steps: Audit every reward/engagement mechanic in the product against RAMP: Relatedness (does this mechanic connect users to others, or is it purely individual?), Autonomy (does this mechanic constrain or enable choice?), Mastery (does this mechanic provide feedback on growing competence?), Purpose (does this mechanic connect to a meaningful goal?).
Mechanics scoring 0 on all four dimensions are likely extrinsic-only — predict motivation crowding out over time.
outputs: A RAMP audit of current features, motivator gaps per user type, intrinsic-motivation design concepts, and measures to test their effect.
useWhen: Enterprise software, learning, health or habit products where sustained voluntary engagement matters and extrinsic rewards risk crowding out motivation.
avoidWhen: Avoid when engagement is not a legitimate goal (manipulative contexts), or when tasks are mandatory and should simply be made efficient; avoid untested claims, so pair with experiments.
whyLost: Gamification became synonymous with points, badges and leaderboards; motivation-theory-based design was lost in the hype and backlash.
whereToUse: Enterprise software engagement design, health behavior change apps, learning product design, community platform design.
example: A compliance-training platform audits its badges with RAMP and finds no autonomy or purpose; adding choice of learning path and stories about prevented incidents increases voluntary completion.
sources: Gamification at Work — Janaki Kumar
reference: Kumar J & Herger M (2013) Gamification at Work: Designing Engaging Business Software. Interaction Design Foundation

name: Random Forest Key Driver Analysis
origin: Leo Breiman (2001); conditional variable importance by Carolin Strobl et al. (2007-2008)
summary: Uses random forests to estimate which experience attributes most strongly predict an outcome like satisfaction or churn, with careful importance measures.
description: Key driver analysis asks which attributes (speed, support, reliability, ease) matter most for an overall outcome. Multiple regression struggles with correlated attributes and nonlinearity. Random forests capture interactions and nonlinear effects, and provide variable importance. However, default impurity-based importance is biased toward variables with many categories, and permutation importance is biased under correlation; conditional permutation importance or SHAP values with care, plus partial dependence plots, are needed. Drivers are predictive, not causal, and should be presented as such. Many dashboards show 'drivers' from naive correlations or default importances, the vestigial form.
steps: Collect outcome measures and candidate attributes (survey ratings, behavioural metrics) for a large sample (e.g. 500+).
Fit a random forest with tuned parameters and evaluate out-of-sample predictive accuracy.
Compute conditional permutation importance or SHAP-based importance, and compare with a relative weights or dominance analysis.
Examine partial dependence and accumulated local effects plots to see shape (thresholds, saturation).
Check stability with bootstrapped importance rankings.
Present drivers as predictive associations, then test top drivers causally where possible.
outputs: Stable importance rankings, response-shape plots and predictive accuracy metrics.
useWhen: Prioritising experience attributes from survey and behavioural data with many correlated predictors.
avoidWhen: Small samples, or when causal effects are required; use experiments or causal methods.
whyLost: Dashboards adopted 'key drivers' as a feature, often with biased importance measures and causal language.
whereToUse: NPS and CSAT programmes, churn analysis, app store review analysis, B2B relationship surveys.
example: A telco's driver analysis shows network reliability dominates satisfaction only below a threshold of 2 outages a month; above that, billing clarity matters most, so investment is targeted by segment.
sources: Breiman, Random forests (2001), Machine Learning
Strobl et al., Conditional variable importance for random forests (2008), BMC Bioinformatics
Molnar, Interpretable Machine Learning (2nd ed., 2022)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
reference: Breiman, L. (2001). Random forests. Machine Learning, 45(1), 5-32.

name: Randomised Response Technique
origin: Stanley Warner, 1965
summary: Uses a private randomising device to let respondents answer sensitive questions truthfully, recovering population prevalence while protecting individuals.
description: When asked directly about sensitive behaviour, people under-report. In randomised response, each respondent privately uses a randomiser (e.g. a die) that decides whether they answer the sensitive question truthfully or give a forced answer. The researcher never knows which applied, but because the probabilities are known, the prevalence can be estimated. Variants include Warner's original, forced response and unrelated question designs. Meta-analyses show RRT yields more valid prevalence estimates than direct questions in many contexts, though comprehension matters. For UX, it measures sensitive behaviours like password sharing, account sharing, policy violations, cheating or risky use.
steps: Choose the sensitive question and the RRT variant (forced response is easiest to explain).
Set randomisation probabilities (e.g. 75% answer truthfully, 25% forced 'yes' or 'no').
Implement an online randomiser that respondents trust (e.g. a birthday-based rule or visible die) and explain protection clearly.
Include comprehension checks; consider a direct-question control group for comparison.
Estimate prevalence and its standard error using the design formulas, accounting for the larger variance.
Size the sample accordingly (RRT needs several times the sample of direct questioning).
outputs: Privacy-protected prevalence estimates with confidence intervals and comparison to direct questions.
useWhen: Estimating prevalence of sensitive, stigmatised or rule-breaking behaviours relevant to design.
avoidWhen: Individual-level analysis is needed, or samples are small.
whyLost: It needs larger samples and careful explanation; UX surveys rarely handle sensitive behaviours with special designs.
whereToUse: Account sharing, security practices, misuse of AI tools at work, health behaviours, financial distress.
example: A streaming service estimates password sharing. Direct questions yield 18%, a forced response design yields 34%, giving a more accurate basis for policy and UX design.
sources: Warner, Randomized response: A survey technique for eliminating evasive answer bias (1965), JASA
Lensvelt-Mulders et al., Meta-analysis of randomized response research (2005), Sociological Methods & Research
Blair, Imai & Zhou, Design and analysis of the randomized response technique (2015), JASA

name: Rapid Affinity Building (2-Day Sprint Version)
origin: Karen Holtzblatt, Jessamyn Burns Wendell and Shelley Wood (Rapid Contextual Design, 2005)
summary: A compressed but disciplined team affinity process: individual interpretation notes from field sessions are built bottom-up into a two-level hierarchy within a few hours.
description: The affinity diagram in Contextual Design is a bottom-up, team synthesis of interpretation notes from contextual interviews, grouped by similarity of meaning rather than predefined categories, and labelled in the user's voice. The full version uses four levels and hundreds of notes. Holtzblatt's rapid version preserves the core discipline for time-boxed projects: each researcher conducts one or two contextual inquiry sessions, writes 50-100 interpretation notes per session in a team interpretation meeting, and the team builds the affinity in about four hours with a two-level hierarchy. Rules still apply: no pre-set categories, groups of no more than about four to six notes, labels written as first-person user statements, and walking the wall to generate design ideas. Popular sticky-note clustering keeps the look but loses these rules.
steps: Preparation: Each researcher conducts 1–2 contextual inquiry sessions. From each session, create 50–100 data notes — one idea, observation, or quote per note. Physical sticky notes or digital equivalents.

Day 1, Hours 1–4 — Individual sorting: Each researcher silently sorts their notes into groups, labelling each group with a description that captures the shared meaning. No discussion during this phase.
Day 1, Hours 4–6 — Team merge: Teams combine overlapping groups. Negotiate on group labels. Every note must belong to exactly one group.
Day 1, Hours 6–8 — Second-level labels: Create higher-level labels over grouped sets. These are your themes.
Day 2, Hours 1–4 — Design insights: For each theme, generate design insights: what does this theme tell us about what users need? Convert insights to design opportunities.
outputs: Interpretation notes, a two-level affinity wall with user-voice labels, walked-wall design ideas and prioritised insights.
useWhen: Time-boxed discovery sprints with field data, small teams needing shared understanding quickly, and synthesising 6-12 sessions.
avoidWhen: When large volumes of transcripts need systematic coding and audit trails (use framework analysis or thematic analysis), or when there is no field data, only opinions.
whyLost: Affinity mapping became generic sticky-note grouping, often with top-down categories and no interpretation sessions, so Holtzblatt's rules were lost even as the name spread.
whereToUse: Agile UX programs, design sprints, any context where full Beyer-Holtzblatt affinity is not feasible.
example: After eight contextual interviews with pharmacists, four researchers write 520 notes and build a two-level affinity in an afternoon. A cluster labelled 'I don't trust the stock count, so I check the shelf' redirects the inventory feature.
sources: Rapid Contextual Design — Morgan Kaufmann (Holtzblatt et al.)
Universal Methods of Design (Martin)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Error Taxonomy Playbook (Gopinath)
Contextual Design (Karen Holtzblatt & Hugh Beyer)
Rapid Contextual Design (Morgan Kaufmann / Holtzblatt)
Rapid Contextual Design (Morgan Kaufmann)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 34 — Framework Analysis & Systematic Qualitative Synthesis
reference: Holtzblatt K, Wendell JB & Wood S (2005) Rapid Contextual Design: A How-To Guide to Key Techniques for User-Centered Design. Morgan Kaufmann

name: RAS-based alert design
origin: Reticular activating system described by Moruzzi and Magoun, 1949; arousal-performance relation by Yerkes and Dodson, 1908; applied to alarm design in human factors
summary: Designs alerts around the brain's arousal system, using onset, novelty and modality to raise arousal enough to capture attention without tipping users into startle or overload.
description: The reticular activating system in the brainstem regulates arousal and wakefulness, and responds strongly to abrupt onsets, novelty and changes in stimulation; it habituates to repeated, predictable stimuli. Alert design informed by this works on two levels.
