First, it uses features that reliably drive arousal: abrupt onset, change from background, auditory or haptic channels during visual work, and novelty. Second, it manages habituation and the inverted-U arousal-performance curve: too frequent or too intense alerts lead to tuning out or startle, which degrades performance. The approach is mostly a design rationale rather than a measured protocol, but it can be made rigorous by testing response latencies, habituation curves across repeated exposures and physiological arousal markers such as skin conductance.
steps: Classify alerts by urgency (for example three levels) and estimate how often each fires per hour in real use.
Assign arousal features by urgency: abrupt onset and cross-modal cues for high urgency, gentle onset and single-channel cues for low urgency.
Limit high-urgency alert frequency; habituation becomes significant when a stimulus repeats frequently without consequence, so review any high-urgency alert firing more than a few times per hour.
Avoid startle: keep auditory onset rise times above roughly 20-30 ms and levels within about 15-25 dB above ambient.
Test with 10-15 participants across repeated exposures, measuring response latency per exposure to detect habituation, and optionally skin conductance responses.
Adjust alert variation, frequency or escalation to sustain response without startle.
outputs: An urgency-to-arousal feature mapping, habituation curves, response latency data and a revised alert scheme.
useWhen: When alerts are ignored over time (habituation), when alerts must interrupt deep focus, or when startle responses cause errors.
avoidWhen: When the issue is false-alarm rates or threshold setting; use ROC analysis. For simple notification copy, use content testing.
whyLost: The neuroscience is well known but rarely translated into concrete UX alert guidance, and 'RAS' is often cited loosely in pop psychology, which deters rigorous use.
whereToUse: Clinical alarms, driver drowsiness alerts, aviation warnings, security operations, and wearable notifications.
example: Nurses respond to a pump occlusion alarm in 4 s on first exposure but 19 s by the tenth in a shift. Varying the sound pattern by escalation stage and adding a haptic pulse to the nurse's badge holds response near 6 s across exposures.
sources: Bear, M., Connors, B. & Paradiso, M., Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain
Garrett, B., Brain & Behavior: An Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Neuroscience (Bear et al.)
Brain & Behaviour (Garrett)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 9 — Attention — The Gatekeeper
reference: Moruzzi, G. & Magoun, H. W. (1949). Brain stem reticular formation and activation of the EEG. Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology, 1, 455-473.

name: RCT design for UX
origin: Ronald Fisher, 1925-1935; first modern clinical RCT (streptomycin) by the MRC, 1948
summary: Randomly assigns users or participants to design conditions so differences in outcomes can be attributed to the design, with power, metrics and analysis set in advance.
description: An RCT is the reference design for causal claims: randomisation balances known and unknown confounders in expectation, so outcome differences estimate the effect of the intervention. A/B testing is its online form, but UX practice often strips out the discipline that makes it rigorous: pre-specified primary metric, sample size from a power calculation, a fixed stopping rule, checks for sample ratio mismatch, guardrail metrics and a pre-registered analysis plan. Fisher's principles of randomisation, replication and blocking still apply, along with clinical-trial ideas such as intention-to-treat analysis and CONSORT-style reporting. Lab RCTs comparing prototypes, with counterbalancing and within-subject designs, are the small-sample sibling of online tests.
steps: Write a hypothesis, one primary metric, guardrail metrics and the minimum detectable effect that would change the decision.
Compute sample size for alpha 0.05 and power 0.8 (or 0.9 for high stakes), accounting for variance and the unit of randomisation.
Choose the randomisation unit (user, account, session, region) to avoid interference and contamination between arms.
Pre-register the analysis plan, including stopping rule, segments and handling of outliers.
Run an A/A test or check sample ratio mismatch (chi-squared p below 0.001 signals a fault) before reading results.
Run for the full planned duration and at least one full weekly cycle; avoid peeking unless using a sequential method.
Analyse by intention-to-treat, report effect size with confidence intervals and guardrail results, and document the decision.
outputs: An unbiased effect estimate with confidence interval on a pre-specified metric, guardrail checks, and a documented ship or no-ship decision.
useWhen: When a design change can be randomised and you need to know whether it causes a meaningful change in behaviour or outcomes.
avoidWhen: Avoid when traffic is too low for the minimum detectable effect, when randomisation is unethical or illegal, or when strong network effects cause interference; use quasi-experiments or switchback designs instead.
whyLost: A/B testing is ubiquitous but often reduced to dashboard-watching, peeking and multiple metric fishing, so the trial discipline that gives it causal force has eroded.
whereToUse: Product experimentation in e-commerce, SaaS, fintech and health apps; lab comparisons of prototypes; pricing and onboarding tests.
example: A banking app pre-registers a test of a simplified transfer flow with completion rate as the primary metric and error rate as a guardrail. With 40,000 users per arm it detects a 1.5-point lift and confirms errors did not rise.
sources: Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (Scott Maxwell & Harold Delaney)
Methods Atlas (Vivek Gopinath)
Forward-Thinking Playbook (Vivek Gopinath)
Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang & Ya Xu)
The Design of Experiments (Ronald Fisher)
Designing Experiments & Analyzing Data (Maxwell/Delaney)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
Forward-Thinking Playbook (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 47 — Experimental Design — From A/B to Quasi-Experiments
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Kohavi, R., Tang, D. & Xu, Y. (2020) Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press.

name: Reaction time distribution analysis
origin: Luce, Response Times, 1986; ex-Gaussian modelling, Ratcliff, 1979
summary: Analyses the full shape of response-time distributions, not just means, to reveal slow tails, lapses and distinct processes that averages conceal.
description: Response times are positively skewed: most responses cluster near a mode with a long right tail. Means are pulled by the tail and medians ignore it, yet the tail often carries the safety-relevant information, such as occasional very slow responses to alerts. RT distribution analysis fits models such as the ex-Gaussian (a Gaussian component mu, sigma plus an exponential tail tau) or log-normal, or examines quantiles and cumulative distribution functions across conditions. A design change that shifts mu speeds routine responses, whereas one that reduces tau eliminates lapses. Rigour comes from enough trials per participant (ideally 100+ for ex-Gaussian fits), proper outlier handling decided in advance, and comparing quantiles rather than only means.
steps: Collect trial-level response times, ideally 50-100+ trials per participant per condition, with timestamps accurate to about 10 ms.
Pre-register outlier rules (for example exclude anticipations under 150 ms) instead of trimming by standard deviations after the fact.
Plot histograms, quantile (vincentised) plots and cumulative distributions per condition.
Fit ex-Gaussian or log-normal models per participant and condition, reporting mu, sigma and tau or log-scale parameters.
Compare conditions at 10th, 50th, 90th and 99th percentiles, and compare tau to detect differences in lapses.
Translate findings into design implications: tail problems suggest attention or alerting issues, central shifts suggest perceptual or motor issues.
outputs: RT distribution plots, fitted parameters per condition, percentile comparisons, and an interpretation separating routine speed from lapses.
useWhen: When response timing matters, especially for alerts and safety tasks, or when means show no difference but users report occasional failures.
avoidWhen: When you have only a few trials per participant or only aggregate timings; use median task times with confidence intervals (Sauro and Lewis) instead.
whyLost: Standard in cognitive psychology, but UX reports mean task time; the distributional tools sit in R packages unfamiliar to practitioners.
whereToUse: Alert response, emergency stops, gaming, assistive technology, and performance benchmarks of AI agents with humans in the loop.
example: Two alert designs produce near-identical mean response times of 1.4 s, but the ex-Gaussian tau is 900 ms in the old design versus 300 ms in the new one: the new design removes the rare 4-6 s lapses that matter most in surgery.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
Card, S., Moran, T. & Newell, A., The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (1983) and GOMS/KLM literature
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
Cognitive Psychology (Goldstein)
GOMS/KLM literature
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 4 — Time, Rhythm & the Three Timescales of Experience
reference: Luce, R. D. (1986). Response Times: Their Role in Inferring Elementary Mental Organization. Oxford University Press.

name: Readability Analysis
origin: Rudolf Flesch (1948); Robert Gunning (1952); Kincaid et al. for the US Navy (1975)
summary: Desk measurement of text complexity using formulas such as Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning Fog, combined with plain-language checks, to flag content too hard for its audience.
description: Readability analysis estimates how hard a text is to read from surface features: sentence length, word length, syllable counts and proportion of complex words. Formulas such as Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Gunning Fog, SMOG and Coleman-Liau convert these into scores or reading grade levels. In UX it is a fast triage tool for large content estates, legal and health information, and AI-generated text. Used rigorously, it is a screening measure, not a verdict: formulas ignore vocabulary familiarity, layout, structure and the reader's domain knowledge, and can be gamed by chopping sentences. Good practice sets a target grade for the audience (often age 9-11 reading level for public services), applies a consistent formula across the corpus, and pairs scores with plain-language heuristics and readability testing with real users.
steps: Define the target audience and a target reading level (for example UK reading age 9 or US grade 8 for general public content).
Extract the content to plain text, removing navigation and boilerplate so scores reflect the actual body copy.
Compute at least two formulas consistently (for example Flesch-Kincaid Grade and SMOG) for every page or string set.
Flag pages more than two grades above target and inspect them against plain-language checks: jargon, passive voice, nominalisations, sentence length over 25 words.
Rewrite flagged content and re-score, without simply fragmenting sentences to game the formula.
Validate the highest-risk rewritten content with readability testing on target users.
outputs: Readability scores per page, a ranked list of content above target, and plain-language rewrite guidance.
useWhen: Auditing large volumes of content, health, legal, financial or government information, and checking AI-generated responses at scale.
avoidWhen: When you need to know whether specific users actually understand content (use readability testing or cloze tests), or for very short UI strings where formulas are unreliable.
whyLost: Still in use: Essential for health, government, and any product serving general populations.
whereToUse: Health products; government services; financial products; any public-facing content.
example: An insurer scores 400 policy explanation pages and finds the median at US grade 14. Rewriting the 30 most-visited pages to grade 8 and testing with customers halves calls asking what 'excess' means.
sources: Strategic Content Design
Flesch, A new readability yardstick (Journal of Applied Psychology, 1948)
Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov)
reference: Flesch R (1948) A new readability yardstick. Journal of Applied Psychology 32(3):221-233

name: Readability Testing
origin: Cloze procedure by Wilson Taylor (1953); user-testing of medicine leaflets by Sless and Wiseman (1994), mandated in EU from 2005
summary: Testing whether real readers can find and understand content, using cloze tests, comprehension questions and think-aloud reading, with pass thresholds rather than formula scores.
description: Readability testing measures comprehension directly with target readers, in contrast to readability formulas that only estimate difficulty. Techniques include the cloze test (every fifth or sixth word deleted, readers fill gaps, 60% or more correct indicates adequate comprehension), comprehension questions requiring readers to locate and explain key points, paraphrase tasks, and think-aloud reading. European medicines regulation formalised a rigorous version: 20 participants in rounds of ten, with a criterion that 90% must find each key piece of information and 90% of those must understand it. In UX the method is vestigial: it survives as informal 'does this make sense?' checks, losing the explicit thresholds, the find-versus-understand distinction and the iterative rounds that made it reliable.
steps: Identify 10-15 key points the content must convey (actions, risks, eligibility, deadlines).
Write neutral questions for each point that require locating and explaining it, not just recognising wording.
Test with target readers in rounds of about 10, recording whether each point was found and whether it was understood correctly.
Optionally run a cloze test on key passages, deleting every fifth word and scoring exact or acceptable answers, with 60% as the comprehension threshold.
Apply a criterion such as 90% of participants finding and 90% of those understanding each key point; revise content that falls short.
Retest revised content with a fresh round until all key points meet the criterion.
outputs: Find and understand rates per key point, cloze scores, identified misreadings and revised content that meets the threshold.
useWhen: High-stakes content where misunderstanding causes harm or cost: medicine information, consent forms, financial terms, benefits guidance, AI disclosures.
avoidWhen: When you only need a rapid triage of a large corpus (use readability analysis) or when the content is short interface microcopy (use comprehension testing within UX writing research).
whyLost: Vestigial: Rarely done rigorously; replaced by expert-led readability analysis in most contexts.
whereToUse: Health literacy; legal/financial documents; safety instructions.
example: A pension provider tests its retirement options letter with 20 savers. Only 55% understand that taking a lump sum is irreversible, so the letter is restructured with a decision box and passes 90/90 in round two.
sources: Strategic Content Design
Taylor, Cloze procedure (Journalism Quarterly, 1953)
Sless & Wiseman, Writing About Medicines for People (1994)
Taylor, 'Cloze procedure': A new tool for measuring readability (1953), Journalism Quarterly
Bormuth, Cloze test readability: Criterion reference scores (1968), Journal of Educational Measurement
reference: Taylor WL (1953) Cloze procedure: A new tool for measuring readability. Journalism Quarterly 30(4):415-433

name: Recognition-Primed Decision Model Analysis
origin: Gary Klein, 1985-1989 (fireground commanders study); Sources of Power (1998)
summary: Analyses expert decisions as pattern recognition and mental simulation of a single option, rather than comparison of alternatives, to design tools that support recognition.
description: Klein found that experienced fireground commanders rarely compared options. Instead they recognised a situation as typical, which brought with it expectancies, relevant cues, plausible goals and a typical action, then mentally simulated the action to check it would work, modifying or discarding it if not. The RPD model has three variants: simple match, diagnose the situation, and evaluate a course of action. Analysing users through RPD shifts design from decision matrices and option comparisons to supporting situation recognition, expectancy violations and mental simulation. It is especially relevant for AI recommendation tools, which often present ranked alternatives to people who actually decide by recognition.
steps: Collect decision incidents through CDM interviews or observation of experts in natural settings.
For each decision, code whether options were compared or whether one option was recognised and simulated.
Identify the patterns experts recognise, the cues that trigger them, expectancies and typical actions.
Note expectancy violations that triggered diagnosis or re-evaluation.
Derive design requirements: surface critical cues, flag anomalies against expected patterns, support quick 'what would happen if' simulation.
Evaluate designs with scenario-based tests including anomalies, measuring detection and decision quality.
outputs: Pattern and cue inventories, RPD variant frequencies, design requirements for recognition and simulation support.
useWhen: Users are experienced professionals making time-pressured decisions; you are designing alerts, triage or AI recommendations.
avoidWhen: Novices or deliberative decisions with ample time, where multi-attribute decision support is appropriate.
whyLost: UX imported rational-choice framing from product management, and NDM research sits in military and safety contexts.
whereToUse: Clinical decision support, emergency dispatch, cybersecurity triage, trading, AI copilots for experts.
example: An ICU early-warning tool shows a ranked list of differential diagnoses, which nurses ignore. RPD analysis shows nurses recognise deterioration patterns; the redesign highlights deviations from each patient's expected trajectory and adoption rises.
sources: Klein, Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions (1998)
Klein, A recognition-primed decision (RPD) model of rapid decision making (1993), in Klein et al. (eds.), Decision Making in Action
reference: Klein, G. (1998). Sources of Power. MIT Press.

name: Recurrence Quantification Analysis
origin: Jean-Pierre Eckmann, Sylvie Oliffson Kamphorst and David Ruelle (1987, recurrence plots); Joseph Zbilut and Charles Webber (1992, RQA)
summary: Quantifies how often and in what structure a behavioural time series revisits similar states, measuring determinism, stability and coordination.
description: A recurrence plot marks every pair of time points at which a system's state is similar. RQA quantifies the plot: recurrence rate, determinism (proportion of recurrent points forming diagonal lines, indicating repeated sequences), laminarity (vertical lines, indicating stuck states), entropy of line lengths and trapping time. Cross-recurrence quantification compares two time series, such as two collaborators or a user and an agent, to measure coordination and leading/following. RQA works on short, nonstationary, noisy data where classical methods fail, and has been applied in psychology to movement, eye gaze and conversation. For UX it offers measures of routine, rigidity and coordination in interaction streams.
steps: Choose the behavioural time series (e.g. action categories, cursor positions, gaze, speech features).
For continuous data, choose embedding dimension and delay (false nearest neighbours, mutual information); for categorical data use direct matching.
Set the radius threshold to achieve a target recurrence rate (e.g. 2-5%).
Compute RQA measures: recurrence rate, determinism, laminarity, trapping time, entropy.
Compare measures across conditions, users or time, with surrogate data tests to check against randomness.
Use cross-recurrence for dyads (e.g. human-AI turn-taking) to measure coordination and lag.
outputs: Recurrence plots and RQA metrics describing routine, rigidity and coordination, with surrogate comparisons.
useWhen: Analysing dynamics of interaction (habits, getting stuck, coordination) in rich time series.
avoidWhen: When simple frequency or funnel metrics answer the question, or with very sparse data.
whyLost: It is a physics and cognitive science technique with little exposure outside nonlinear dynamics.
whereToUse: Collaborative tools, conversational AI dialogue rhythm, games, habit formation in apps, VR movement.
example: Cross-recurrence of typing activity between pair programmers using an AI assistant shows lower coordination than human-only pairs, prompting design of shared AI suggestion views.
sources: Marwan et al., Recurrence plots for the analysis of complex systems (2007), Physics Reports
Webber & Zbilut, Recurrence quantification analysis of nonlinear dynamical systems (2005), in Riley & Van Orden (eds.), Tutorials in Contemporary Nonlinear Methods for the Behavioral Sciences
reference: Marwan, N., Romano, M. C., Thiel, M., & Kurths, J. (2007). Physics Reports, 438(5-6), 237-329.

name: Recursive Evidence Arrays and Loop Test
aka: Did we break the recursive loop?
donor: Qualitative data display and process tracing
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Participant × episode arrays exposing failure cascades (Mistake → extra clicks → frustration → lapse), re-run after a fix to confirm the mechanism itself changed.
description: Across the forward-thinking loop, qualitative rigour is kept auditable with 'triangulation hooks'. In Stage 1, a recursive evidence log captures the order a participant describes (e.g. Settings → Back → Markets) and flags expected loop points as risk loops. In Stage 2, an evidence array has rows as participants and columns for first click, path nodes, error code, quote, time to first click and SNR snapshot, sorted by first misroute node then error type so clusters emerge (e.g. a Mistake cluster at Notifications). A compact relationship sketch shows cascades such as an early mistake leading to extra clicks, a frustration spike and a later lapse at a timed OTP step. In Stage 6 the loop test re-runs the small array on a fresh sample and confirms the typical loop is absent or vastly reduced, alongside a QCA truth-table re-check. This verifies mechanism repair, not merely metric movement.
steps: During early interviews, record the sequence each participant describes and mark expected backtrack or loop points as risk loops.
During diagnosis, build an evidence array: rows participants; columns first click, path nodes, Slip/Lapse/Mistake code, quote, time to first click, SNR snapshot.
Sort by first misroute node, then by error type, and note clusters.
Sketch recursive relationships between episodes (e.g. Mistake → extra clicks → frustration → lapse risk).
After the fix, re-run the array on a fresh sample and check whether the loop is absent or vastly reduced.
Rebuild the QCA truth table to confirm the previous sufficient path no longer holds, and write a concluding note on mechanism fixed or not fixed.
outputs: Evidence arrays, recursive loop sketches, and a before/after mechanism verdict.
useWhen: In mixed-methods studies where failures cascade across steps and you must verify that a fix broke the cascade.
avoidWhen: For single-step defects with no cascade; a simple before/after metric suffices.
whyLost: Original technique by Vivek Gopinath building on qualitative data display traditions.
whereToUse: Multi-step fintech flows, onboarding with verification steps, enterprise wizards.
example: Arrays show early misroutes to Notifications are followed by OTP timeouts in the same sessions; after relabelling, the re-run array shows almost no Mistake-to-Lapse cascades.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook, Qual Triangulation Hooks and Stage 6.

name: Recursive navigation trap detection
donor: Formal methods in HCI and accessibility engineering
origin: Thimbleby's device graph analyses (1990s-2000s); keyboard trap criterion in WCAG 2.0 SC 2.1.2 (2008)
summary: Detects states or nested structures that users can enter but cannot leave in a reasonable way, including recursive modals, focus traps and nested wizards.
description: A navigation trap is a strongly connected set of states with no exit edge, or one whose exits are hidden, ambiguous or unavailable to some input methods. Traps are often recursive: a modal opens another modal, a nested wizard re-enters itself, or a component re-embeds its parent. Detection combines graph analysis (finding sink components), input-method checks (can a keyboard, switch or screen-reader user exit?), and depth analysis (how many levels deep can recursion go, and how many steps to return?). WCAG formalises one case: keyboard focus must be movable away from any component using standard keys. Rigour comes from testing every input modality and every recursion depth, not only the designed path.
steps: List all containers that can nest or capture input: modals, drawers, wizards, embedded frames, full-screen modes and kiosk modes.
Model them as a graph with nesting depth and identify sink components with no exit edge for each input modality.
Test each container with keyboard only, screen reader, switch access and touch, confirming exit via Escape, back, or a visible close control.
Probe recursion by triggering nested opens and record maximum depth and steps to return to the root; flag depths above 2 or returns needing more than 3 steps.
Cross-check logs for force-quits, app restarts or session timeouts immediately after entering flagged containers.
Fix traps and add automated checks (for example focus-trap tests) to CI.
outputs: A trap inventory by container and modality, recursion depth findings, log evidence, and fixed exit paths with tests.
useWhen: When interfaces use nested modals or modes, in accessibility audits, kiosk or locked-down devices, and when logs show force-quits.
avoidWhen: When the issue is general findability rather than inescapability; use tree testing or IA graph analysis.
whyLost: Keyboard traps are checked in accessibility audits, but recursive and mode traps in general UX are rarely analysed structurally.
whereToUse: Surgical and medical consoles, kiosks, accessibility compliance, single-page applications, and in-car systems.
example: A surgical console's calibration wizard can open its own settings, which can relaunch calibration; after two nests the 'Exit' control disappears. Surgeons have been locked out mid-procedure; detection and a global exit restore control in one action.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Gödel Escher Bach (Hofstadter)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 6 — Strange Loops, Recursive Failures & Navigation Traps
reference: W3C (2008). Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.0, Success Criterion 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap.

name: Red Teaming
origin: Military war-gaming (red forces) dating to the 19th-century Kriegsspiel; formalised in the UK MOD Red Teaming Guide (2010, 2nd ed. 2013) and US Army UFMCS
summary: An independent team deliberately challenges a plan, design or conclusion from an adversarial or alternative perspective to expose weaknesses before reality does.
description: Red teaming institutionalises challenge. A red team, independent from the planners, adopts the perspective of adversaries, competitors, misusers or sceptical stakeholders, and attacks assumptions, logic and execution using structured techniques: alternative analysis, pre-mortems, adversary emulation, devil's advocacy, and stress-testing. It requires organisational backing, clear scope, and rules that protect challengers. In UX it applies to research conclusions (is the synthesis sound?), to abuse and misuse of features (how could this be weaponised?), and to AI products, where red teaming already exists for model safety but rarely for user experience harms.
steps: Secure sponsorship and define scope: the plan, design or conclusion to challenge, and the perspectives to adopt.
Form an independent team with diverse expertise, including domain experts and potential adversary perspectives.
Brief the red team with full materials, then let them work separately with structured techniques.
Generate attack scenarios: misuse cases, competitor responses, failure modes, alternative interpretations.
Present findings to decision-makers in a protected format; prioritise by likelihood and impact.
Track responses to each finding and repeat at key milestones.
outputs: Red team report with challenges, misuse scenarios, alternative interpretations and tracked responses.
useWhen: High-stakes launches, features open to abuse, strategic plans and contested research conclusions.
avoidWhen: Organisations unwilling to act on challenge; red teaming then becomes theatre.
whyLost: UX critique focuses on improving designs collaboratively; adversarial review is seen as hostile and belongs to security.
whereToUse: Generative AI features, social platforms, location sharing, payments, content moderation policies.
example: Before launching a 'share live location' feature, a red team of trust and safety staff and domestic abuse advocates identifies stalking scenarios; the launch adds periodic reminders and hard-to-hide sharing indicators.
sources: UK Ministry of Defence DCDC, Red Teaming Guide (2nd ed., 2013)
Zenko, Red Team: How to Succeed by Thinking Like the Enemy (2015)
reference: UK Ministry of Defence (2013). Red Teaming Guide (2nd ed.). Development, Concepts and Doctrine Centre.

name: Redundancy analysis
origin: Claude Shannon, 1948; redundancy in display design formalised in human factors by Garner (1962)
summary: Measures how much of an interface's signal is repeated or predictable, separating protective redundancy that resists error from wasteful redundancy that adds load.
description: In information theory, redundancy R = 1 - H/Hmax is the fraction of a message that is predictable and could in principle be removed. Redundancy is not waste by default: Shannon showed it is what allows a receiver to correct errors over a noisy channel. Redundancy analysis applies this to interfaces by cataloguing every way a critical piece of state is encoded (colour, position, label, icon, sound, haptic) and every place it is repeated, then classifying each repetition as error-protective (independent channels encoding the same critical fact) or load-adding (repeated low-value information competing for attention). Rigour comes from computing redundancy on observed or specified message sets and from distinguishing correlated encodings, which fail together, from independent encodings that survive one channel failing, such as colour-blindness or a noisy room.
steps: Select the critical state variables the interface must communicate (for example mode, armed/disarmed, patient identity, unsaved changes).
For each variable, list every encoding channel used (hue, shape, position, text, sound, vibration) and every screen location where it appears.
Classify encodings as independent or correlated, checking failure scenarios such as colour-vision deficiency, glare, gloves, and auditory masking above 85 dB.
Compute message redundancy 1 - H/Hmax for repeated content blocks and notification streams using observed frequencies.
Mark critical variables with fewer than two independent encodings as under-protected and non-critical content with redundancy above 0.6 as candidates for removal.
Propose a rebalanced encoding scheme and verify with a quick detection test (for example 10 participants, single-channel-degraded conditions).
outputs: An encoding matrix (state variable by channel), a redundancy score per content stream, and a list of under-protected critical states and removable repetitions.
useWhen: When designing for safety-critical state awareness, accessibility robustness, or alarm and notification streams that feel noisy; when deciding whether duplicated information is a safeguard or clutter.
avoidWhen: When the problem is comprehension of meaning rather than detection of state; use cognitive walkthroughs or comprehension testing. Avoid on early concept work where encodings are not yet fixed.
whyLost: Redundancy was a core concept in 1960s display research but UX absorbed only the slogan 'don't repeat yourself' and minimalism, losing the idea that redundancy is the mechanism of error correction.
whereToUse: Medical device displays, automotive HMIs, accessibility audits, trading and monitoring dashboards, and AI assistants that must signal uncertainty or mode clearly.
example: A banking app shows 'pending' payments only with a grey colour. Redundancy analysis shows a single correlated encoding that fails for users with low vision; adding a clock icon and the word 'Pending' gives three independent channels while the duplicated balance shown in three places is cut to one.

Shannon, C. E., A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Kolmogorov via MIT Press

name: Reference Point Manipulation
origin: Kahneman & Tversky, 1979
summary: Designs and tests how the reference points users compare against (prior state, expectations, anchors, defaults) shape perceived gains, losses and satisfaction.
description: Prospect theory holds that people evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, not in absolute terms, and that losses weigh roughly twice as heavily as equivalent gains. Reference point manipulation applies this to UX by first auditing what users compare against: their previous experience (including paper or competitor processes), stated expectations, anchors such as displayed original prices, defaults and progress indicators. The team then designs framings that set accurate, fair reference points and tests their effect on satisfaction, choice and perceived value. Rigour comes from measuring users' actual reference points through interviews or surveys, pre-registering experimental comparisons, and an ethics check that distinguishes honest framing from manipulative anchoring.
steps: Reference point audit: for every outcome a user experiences, identify:
What reference point does the current design establish?
(2) Does the outcome appear as a gain or loss relative to that reference point?

(3) What reference point would make the same outcome appear as a gain? Redesign to establish the reference point that makes good outcomes feel like gains. Example: change 'Your account charged $29' to 'You saved $10 with your subscription'.
outputs: An audit of reference points users bring and those the interface sets, framing alternatives, experimental results on satisfaction and choice.
useWhen: Pricing pages, success and confirmation screens, progress displays, subscription changes, savings and investment outcomes, and any experience judged relative to expectation.
avoidWhen: Avoid when used to manipulate users against their interests (dark patterns); avoid relying on framing when the underlying value is poor, and fix the product instead.
whyLost: Prospect theory is cited constantly in UX writing but rarely operationalised as an audit and testing method; anchoring is used tactically by marketing.
whereToUse: Pricing UX, progress and achievement communication, error message design, subscription value communication.
example: A government benefits portal's success screen shows 'Application submitted' while paper forms gave a stamped receipt; users judge the digital outcome as a loss against that reference, so adding a reference number and timeline raises satisfaction.
sources: Choices, Values, and Frames — Kahneman & Tversky (eds.)
Prospect Theory works (Kahneman/Tversky)
Nash Equilibrium in UX (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 23 — Reference Points, Prospect Theory & the Mechanics of Satisfaction
reference: Kahneman D & Tversky A (1979) Prospect theory: An analysis of decision under risk. Econometrica 47(2):263-291

name: Regression Analysis
origin: Francis Galton, 1886; Karl Pearson; least squares by Legendre and Gauss, early 1800s
summary: Models how an outcome varies with predictors, estimating effect sizes and enabling prediction of satisfaction, retention or conversion from user and product variables.
description: Regression analysis models an outcome variable as a function of one or more predictors. Linear regression handles continuous outcomes such as satisfaction scores, logistic regression handles binary outcomes such as conversion or churn, and mixed-effects models handle repeated measures and nested data such as tasks within participants. In UX it is used to estimate which factors are associated with outcomes, control for confounders, and predict outcomes. Rigour comes from specifying models in advance, checking assumptions such as linearity, independence, homoscedasticity and multicollinearity, using appropriate models for data structure, reporting effect sizes with confidence intervals rather than only p-values, validating predictions on held-out data, and recognising that observational regression shows association, not causation.
steps: Define the outcome, predictors and covariates based on the research question.
Prepare data, handle missing values and code categorical variables.
Choose the model type for the outcome and data structure (linear, logistic, count or mixed-effects).
Fit the model and check assumptions with residual plots and diagnostics such as variance inflation factors.
Interpret coefficients as effect sizes with confidence intervals.
Validate predictive performance on held-out data where prediction is the goal.
Report results with clear statements about causal limitations.
outputs: Coefficient estimates with confidence intervals, model fit and diagnostics, predicted values and identification of influential factors.
useWhen: For estimating which factors relate to UX outcomes, controlling for confounders, predicting satisfaction or conversion, and analysing benchmark or survey data.
avoidWhen: Avoid causal claims from observational data; use A/B tests or quasi-experimental designs. For time-to-event outcomes use survival analysis.
whyLost: It survived because product analytics and growth teams need churn and conversion models, and it is built into every analytics stack. Usability practice still often reports raw success percentages instead.
whereToUse: Satisfaction prediction; feature impact modeling; conversion rate analysis.
example: A SaaS company regresses account renewal on feature usage, support tickets and company size. Logistic regression shows that adopting the reporting feature is associated with 2.1 times higher odds of renewal, prompting an onboarding experiment.

name: Regression diagnostics
origin: Cook, 1977; Belsley, Kuh & Welsch, 1980
summary: A systematic check of a fitted regression for violated assumptions, influential points and collinearity so its coefficients and predictions can be trusted.
description: Regression diagnostics test whether a model is fit for the claims made from it. They examine residuals for non-linearity and unequal variance, check normality of residuals for small-sample inference, find influential observations through leverage and Cook's distance, and measure multicollinearity through variance inflation factors. In UX data, common culprits are skewed task times, ceiling effects on satisfaction scales, a few expert participants dominating the fit and repeated measures treated as independent. Rigour means running diagnostics routinely, documenting remedies (log-transforming time, robust standard errors, mixed models) and reporting whether conclusions change after them, rather than silently deleting awkward points.
steps: Plot residuals against fitted values to check linearity and constant variance; a funnel shape signals heteroscedasticity.
Inspect a Q-Q plot of residuals and, for task time, consider log transformation before modelling.
Compute leverage and Cook's distance and investigate any point above 4/n or with a Cook's D above 1.
Compute VIFs and treat values above 5 as a warning and above 10 as serious collinearity.
Check independence: if participants contribute multiple observations, refit with clustered errors or a mixed model.
Refit with remedies (transformations, robust or HC3 standard errors, removing justified outliers) and report whether conclusions change.
outputs: A diagnostic report with residual and influence plots, VIF table, documented remedies and a sensitivity statement on the main findings.
useWhen: Every time a regression result will inform a decision, especially with skewed UX metrics, small samples or repeated measures.
avoidWhen: Not a substitute for design: diagnostics cannot fix confounding or bad measurement. For purely predictive black-box models rely on cross-validation instead.
whyLost: Point-and-click tools output coefficients without prompting diagnostics, so many UX regressions are reported unchecked. The practice survives mostly in statistics-trained quantitative teams.
whereToUse: Quality assurance for driver analyses, benchmark models, survey regressions and any model feeding a roadmap or board deck.
example: A SaaS team's driver model claims support-ticket volume drives churn. Cook's distance flags three enterprise accounts with extreme ticket counts; refitting without them halves the coefficient, so the team reports the finding as fragile.
sources: Applied Predictive Modeling (Max Kuhn & Kjell Johnson)
R for Marketing Research and Analytics (Chris Chapman & Elea McDonnell Feit)
Regression Diagnostics (Belsley, Kuh & Welsch)
Applied Predictive Modeling (Kuhn & Johnson)
R for Marketing Research (Chapman & Feit)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 43 — Regression, Moderation & Mediation for UX Researchers
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)

name: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
origin: Donald Thistlethwaite and Donald Campbell, 1960
summary: Estimates a causal effect by comparing users just above and just below a sharp eligibility threshold that determines treatment.
description: When treatment is assigned by a known cutoff on a running variable (score, session count, date), units just either side of the cutoff should be comparable on everything but treatment. Fitting local regressions on each side and measuring the jump at the threshold gives a local average treatment effect for users near the cutoff. The treatise's examples: users with more than X sessions get a new onboarding, users scoring above Y are promoted to a premium tier, users who joined before date Z kept the old interface. Validity requires that users cannot precisely manipulate the running variable (checked with a McCrary density test) and that covariates are balanced at the cutoff. Fuzzy RDD handles imperfect compliance.
steps: Identify a rule assigning treatment at a known threshold of a running variable.
Plot outcomes against the running variable and inspect for a discontinuity.
Test for manipulation with a density test and check covariate balance at the cutoff.
Estimate the jump with local linear regression using a data-driven bandwidth.
Check robustness to bandwidth, polynomial order and placebo cutoffs.
Report the local effect and its limited generalisability away from the cutoff.
outputs: RD plot, local treatment effect with CI, validity diagnostics.
useWhen: Features, tiers, notifications or prices allocated by thresholds; legacy cohort cutoffs.
avoidWhen: When users can game the threshold, data near the cutoff are sparse, or effects far from the cutoff matter.
whyLost: Unknown outside econometrics and education research; product teams rarely notice their own threshold rules as natural experiments.
whereToUse: Freemium limits, loyalty tiers, credit limit UX, notification thresholds, eligibility screens.
example: Users reaching 10 saved items receive an upgrade prompt. RDD around 10 items shows the prompt lifts upgrades by 1.4 points but increases 7-day churn by 0.8 points.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)

name: Regression to the Mean and Selection Bias Checks
origin: Francis Galton (1886); selection bias literature in epidemiology
summary: Guards against "improvements" that are really just extreme scores drifting back to normal, or samples that were chosen in a biased way.
description: If you study the worst-performing tasks or the angriest customers, they will usually look better next time even if nothing changed, because extreme scores contain extra noise that does not repeat. This is regression to the mean, and it makes many redesigns look successful. Selection bias arises when the people or data you analyse were chosen by a process related to the outcome, such as only surveying active users or only reviewing sessions that triggered a feedback widget. Bruce and Bruce show how to recognise both; the cure is control groups, random sampling and pre-registration of what will be compared.
steps: Ask how the sample or items were selected, and whether selection depended on the outcome.
When following up extreme cases, include a comparison group that received no change.
Re-measure baseline twice where possible to estimate natural fluctuation.
Prefer random samples of users or sessions over self-selected ones.
State likely biases explicitly in the report.
outputs: Claims of improvement that survive scrutiny.
useWhen: Evaluating fixes to "worst" tasks or segments, and analysing self-selected feedback.
avoidWhen: Not applicable; it is a check rather than a method to choose.
whyLost: UX rarely uses control groups for redesigns, so regression to the mean goes unnoticed.
whereToUse: Before/after studies, NPS follow-ups, top-complaint fix programmes.
example: The ten lowest-rated help articles are rewritten and ratings rise 18%, but ten untouched low-rated articles also rose 12%, so the real effect is far smaller.
sources: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
reference: Bruce & Bruce (2017), chapter 2.

name: Regression with assumption checks
origin: Least squares, Legendre and Gauss (c. 1805); regression diagnostics, Belsley, Kuh and Welsch (1980) and Cook (1977)
summary: Fitting multiple linear regression to UX outcomes while formally checking linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality of residuals, multicollinearity and influential cases.
description: Multiple regression estimates how predictors such as task success, perceived ease and tenure relate to an outcome such as satisfaction, holding others constant. Its estimates and p-values are only trustworthy if assumptions hold: linear relationships, independent errors, constant error variance, approximately normal residuals (for small-sample inference) and no excessive multicollinearity, with no single cases driving results. SPSS REGRESSION provides residual plots, Durbin-Watson, VIF and tolerance, Cook's distance and leverage. Rigour comes from a pre-specified model, inspecting diagnostics rather than just R squared, using robust standard errors or transformations where needed, and not interpreting regression coefficients causally without a causal design.
steps: Specify the model from theory, including a sample-size check (common heuristic: at least 10-20 cases per predictor).
Run REGRESSION from syntax with /STATISTICS COEFF CI R ANOVA COLLIN TOL and /RESIDUALS DURBIN, saving ZRESID, ZPRED, COOK and LEVER.
Plot standardised residuals against predicted values to check linearity and homoscedasticity, and a Q-Q or histogram of residuals.
Check VIF (investigate above about 5, act above 10) and Durbin-Watson (roughly 1.5 to 2.5).
Inspect cases with Cook's distance above 1 or above 4/n, and standardised residuals beyond plus or minus 3, re-running with and without them.
Use HC3 robust standard errors or transformations if heteroscedasticity is present, and report standardised and unstandardised coefficients with CIs.
outputs: Coefficient table with CIs, model fit, diagnostic plots and statistics, and a sensitivity check for influential cases.
useWhen: Explaining variation in UX outcomes from several predictors, building driver models for satisfaction or NPS, and adjusting comparisons for covariates.
avoidWhen: Avoid for binary outcomes (use logistic regression), ordinal single items (use ordinal regression), clustered data (use multilevel models) or causal claims without a causal design.
whyLost: Regression is ubiquitous, but key-driver analyses in UX and CX tools hide diagnostics, so the checking discipline has largely gone.
whereToUse: Satisfaction and NPS driver analysis, SaaS health scores and survey-based product strategy.
example: A SaaS team's driver model suggests 'reporting speed' is the top satisfaction driver. Diagnostics reveal VIF of 12 with 'performance' and two influential enterprise accounts; after combining the collinear items and checking influence, 'data accuracy' emerges as the stronger driver.

PLUM
LOGISTIC REGRESSION procedures; Hayes PROCESS macro v4

name: Reinforcement Learning Models of User Behaviour
aka: Computational reinforcement learning analysis of choices
origin: Sutton and Barto's reinforcement learning framework (1998), applied to human choice data in computational psychiatry and neuroscience
summary: Fit a simple learning-from-reward model to people's sequences of choices to estimate how fast they learn from outcomes and how much they explore.
description: Reinforcement learning describes an agent that tries actions, receives rewards or penalties and gradually prefers what pays off. In psychology the same equations are fitted to people's trial-by-trial choices, producing interpretable parameters: a learning rate (how much one outcome shifts behaviour), an exploration or temperature parameter (how often people try something other than the best-known option) and sometimes separate rates for gains and losses. In UX this turns logs of repeated decisions into measures of learning rather than just conversion. You can ask whether a new feedback design makes people learn faster, whether some segments stop exploring early and miss features, or whether a recommendation system is teaching users to stop trying alternatives. It needs repeated choices with observable outcomes, which many products already log.
steps: Find a repeated choice with a visible outcome: which recommendation to open, which tool to use, which route to take.
Extract per-user sequences of choices and outcomes from logs or a task study.
Specify a simple model, such as Q-learning with a softmax choice rule, with a learning rate and an exploration parameter.
Fit the parameters per user or per group by maximum likelihood or hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
Check the model by simulating choices from the fitted parameters and comparing them with real behaviour.
Compare parameters between designs or segments, and relate them to outcomes such as retention.
outputs: Learning-rate and exploration estimates per user or group, and a validated model that can simulate how behaviour would change under a new design.
useWhen: Products built on repeated choices with feedback: recommendations, games, learning apps, marketplaces, tools with several ways to do a task.
avoidWhen: One-off decisions, or outcomes users cannot see.
whyLost: The method lives in computational neuroscience and machine learning papers. UX analytics measures outcomes and funnels, not the learning process that produces them.
whereToUse: Recommender interfaces, learning and habit apps, games, feature discovery analysis.
example: Fitted to playlist choices, users in a new design show a higher learning rate but a much lower exploration parameter: they quickly settle on the top suggestion and stop trying others, which explains a fall in catalogue reach.
sources: Cognitive Modeling: Nine Paradigms (slide deck)
Sutton, R. & Barto, A., Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2018)
reference: Sutton, R. S., & Barto, A. G. (2018). Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.). MIT Press.

name: Reliability analysis (Cronbach's alpha, split-half, omega)
origin: Spearman and Brown, 1910 (split-half); Lee Cronbach, 1951 (alpha); McDonald, 1999 (omega)
summary: Estimating how consistently the items of a UX scale measure the same construct, to judge whether composite scores are trustworthy enough for decisions.
description: Internal consistency reliability estimates the proportion of score variance that is true-score variance. Split-half reliability correlates two halves of a scale and corrects with the Spearman-Brown formula; Cronbach's alpha is the average of all possible split-halves under strict assumptions. Alpha assumes tau-equivalence (equal loadings) and unidimensionality; when these fail it underestimates reliability or masks multidimensionality, so McDonald's omega from a factor model is now recommended. Thresholds commonly used are 0.70 for research and 0.90 or above for high-stakes individual decisions. Alpha also rises with item count, so very high values (above 0.95) can indicate redundant items. In UX, alpha is often quoted without checking dimensionality, which makes the practice vestigial.
steps: Confirm unidimensionality of the item set (via EFA or CFA) before computing reliability.
Reverse-code negative items and run RELIABILITY in SPSS (/MODEL=ALPHA and /MODEL=SPLIT) or pingouin.cronbach_alpha in Python.
Compute McDonald's omega from a one-factor model where possible and report alongside alpha with confidence intervals.
Review corrected item-total correlations, flagging items below about 0.30, and 'alpha if item deleted' values.
Interpret against purpose: about 0.70 for group comparisons, 0.80 for applied research, 0.90 or higher for individual decisions; treat above 0.95 as possible redundancy.
Report reliability for each sample and segment, since it is a property of scores in a population, not of the instrument.
outputs: Alpha, omega and split-half estimates with CIs, item-total statistics and decisions about item retention.
useWhen: Any use of multi-item UX scales, including adapted standard instruments and custom scales in new populations.
avoidWhen: Avoid for formative indices, single items, or speeded tests; use test-retest reliability for stability over time and inter-rater reliability for coding.
whyLost: Alpha is the one reliability statistic everyone knows, so it is reported reflexively while its assumptions and alternatives are ignored.
whereToUse: Usability and satisfaction instruments, trust and AI acceptance scales, and cross-cultural adaptation.
example: A health app's 6-item 'perceived support' scale yields alpha 0.68. Item-total statistics show one item correlates 0.12 with the rest; removing it yields omega 0.81 and a cleaner single factor.

name: Repertory Grid Technique
origin: George Kelly, 1955
summary: A structured interview that elicits the bipolar constructs people use to compare products or concepts, then rates every element on each construct for analysis.
description: The repertory grid technique, from George Kelly's Personal Construct Psychology, elicits the bipolar dimensions (constructs) through which a person makes sense of a domain. Participants compare elements, such as products, features or scenarios, typically in triads, and say how two are alike and different from the third, which yields a construct such as 'feels trustworthy versus feels gimmicky' in their own words. They then rate every element on every construct, producing a grid of numbers. The method combines the openness of qualitative interviewing with quantitative analysis: principal components analysis and cluster analysis reveal how constructs and elements relate. Its rigour comes from minimising researcher-imposed vocabulary, systematic elicitation and structured statistical analysis of each participant's grid.
steps: Define elements: 6–12 specific examples of the topic — products, features, task scenarios. Must be representative of the domain.

Triadic elicitation: Present elements three at a time. Ask: 'In what important way are two of these similar to each other and different from the third?' Similarity = emergent pole. Contrast = implicit pole. Together = one bipolar construct.
Elicit 8–12 constructs per participant. Continue until constructs repeat or the participant cannot generate more.
Rating phase: Participant rates all elements on each construct on a 1–7 scale.
Analysis: Qualitative (interpret the construct system) or quantitative (PCA of the rating matrix reveals underlying structure; similarity matrix shows element clusters).
Laddering extension: After each construct, probe upward ('Why is that important to you?') to reach values, and downward ('What would that look like?') to reach behavioural criteria.
outputs: Individual grids of elements by constructs with ratings, construct lists in participants' own words, PCA or cluster plots, and aggregated construct categories across participants.
useWhen: When you need to understand the implicit criteria people use to evaluate products, brands, concepts or expert judgements without imposing your vocabulary.
avoidWhen: Avoid with participants who struggle with abstract comparison or when time is very short; use semi-structured interviews. For large-sample measurement, build a survey from elicited constructs instead.
whyLost: Extinct in UX: it demands expertise in elicitation and in analysis such as principal components, and it is largely unknown outside specialist and academic practitioners, so teams default to unstructured preference interviews.
whereToUse: Brand/product comparison research; implicit attitude elicitation; competitive perception studies. Implicit attitude elicitation; brand comparison; expert knowledge capture.
example: A banking team presents nine competitor apps as triads to 15 customers. Elicited constructs such as 'shows me where money goes versus hides it' load heavily on a trust component, shaping the redesign brief.

name: Repertory Grid-Derived Rating Scales
origin: Cunningham, Weinel and Picking (Chapter 5), building on Kelly (1955) and focus analysis (Shaw 1980)
summary: Using repertory grid interviews to elicit users' own bipolar descriptions of a domain, then consolidating them into a short set of rating scales for later testing.
description: Imposed rating scales can use words that users do not understand or would not choose. This method builds scales from users' own language. A small group takes part in repertory grid interviews using a shared set of elements, in the chapter eight game audio clips from altered-state and normal gameplay. Using the triad technique (which two of three are alike and how the third differs) or simple differentiation, each participant produces bipolar constructs and rates every element on each construct from 1 to 5. The grids are concatenated and analysed, for example with focus analysis or clustering, to find constructs used interchangeably. Similar constructs are then grouped into categories, each represented by one bipolar scale; the chapter derived seven for game audio: valence (nonviolent to violent), attention (atmospheric to urgent), distance, fear (nice to eerie), noise, speed and distortion. Ratings can be compared across element groups with modal analysis, plotted on a radar chart. The result is a quick, domain-specific instrument grounded in user vocabulary, which still needs further validation.
steps: Choose a domain and a common set of representative elements (clips, screens, products).
Run one-to-one repertory grid interviews, using triads or differentiation to elicit bipolar constructs, with a practice construct first.
Have participants rate every element on each of their constructs on a 1 to 5 scale.
Combine grids and use focus analysis or clustering to find related constructs.
Group related constructs into categories and choose one bipolar label per category as a scale.
Test the draft scales by checking they separate element groups that should differ, then refine and validate.
outputs: A short set of bipolar rating scales in users' own vocabulary, plus combined grids and construct groupings.
useWhen: No suitable instrument exists for a sensory or aesthetic domain (sound, haptics, visual style) and you want scales users understand.
avoidWhen: Validated scales already exist, or you cannot run enough interviews for a range of constructs.
whyLost: Repertory grids are time-consuming and few UX teams take the extra step of turning elicited constructs into reusable instruments.
whereToUse: Game audio, product sound design, haptics, brand and visual style evaluation.
example: Six players rate eight soundscape clips through repertory grid interviews, producing 36 constructs; grouped into seven scales such as nice to eerie and slow to fast, these show clear differences between intoxication-effect audio and ordinary game audio.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Cunningham, S., Weinel, J. and Picking, R. (2016). In-game intoxication: demonstrating the evaluation of the audio experience of games with a focus on altered states of consciousness. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 5. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Reporting AI-assisted analysis in publications
aka: Transparent reporting of AI in qualitative research
origin: Publisher and ICMJE/COPE guidance on AI use (2023 onwards); qualitative reporting standards COREQ (Tong et al., 2007) and SRQR (O'Brien et al., 2014)
summary: Disclosing exactly how AI tools were used in analysis, including model, version, prompts, tasks, validation and human oversight, so readers can judge the credibility of findings.
description: Journals and conferences now require disclosure of AI use, but disclosures are often vague ('ChatGPT was used to assist analysis'). A rigorous report states the tools and versions, the tasks delegated (transcription, coding, summarisation), prompts or prompt templates, settings, data handling and privacy measures, validation procedures and results (e.g. inter-rater agreement between AI and humans), human checkpoints, and limitations. This extends established reporting standards for qualitative research such as COREQ and SRQR. Rigour comes from making AI's role replicable in principle and from not listing AI as an author, consistent with COPE guidance, while taking human responsibility for findings.
steps: Record AI usage throughout the project: tools, model versions, dates, settings and prompts.
Describe each delegated task and its place in the analytic process.
Report validation: sample sizes, agreement statistics (e.g. kappa per code) and how disagreements were resolved.
Describe data protection measures (local versus cloud processing, anonymisation, provider terms).
State human oversight checkpoints and who was accountable for interpretation.
Provide prompts and schemas in supplementary materials and discuss limitations and possible biases.
outputs: A methods section and supplement describing AI use, validation results and limitations.
useWhen: Any publication, internal research report or regulatory submission where AI contributed to analysis.
avoidWhen: Not applicable where AI was used only for editing prose, though many venues still require a brief statement.
whyLost: Reporting norms are new and fragmented, and practitioners fear that disclosure will undermine credibility.
whereToUse: Academic HCI and UX publications, research reports to leadership, health and policy research.
example: A CHI submission reports that Claude (model version and date given) applied a 24-code codebook to 6,400 segments, that two researchers coded 15% independently with kappa 0.81, that data were anonymised before API calls, and that themes were developed by the authors.

publication disclosure norms

name: Representational Consistency Analysis (Language of Thought)
origin: Jerry Fodor, 1975
summary: Audits whether interface language and symbols compose systematically, so that users can combine known terms and structures to understand new commands and states.
description: Fodor's language of thought hypothesis proposes that thinking occurs in a compositional mental representational system, where meanings of complex thoughts are built from the meanings of their parts and structure, giving thought systematicity: anyone who can think 'A acts on B' can think 'B acts on A'. Applied to interface design, representational consistency analysis asks whether the product's language, icons and syntax are similarly compositional, so users can generalise from known constructions to novel ones. The analyst inventories terms, symbols and constructions, checks that each maps consistently to one concept, and tests whether combinations behave predictably. Rigour comes from a systematic inventory, explicit grammar rules, and verification with users attempting novel combinations.
steps: Compositionality audit for interface language: for each multi-word label or complex instruction, test:
Meaning of the whole = function of meaning of parts?
(2) Ask users to predict what 'X Y' means, given they know what 'X' means and what 'Y' means separately.
(3) Compute prediction accuracy. < 70% accuracy on a label's composed meaning = the composition is non-transparent. Redesign: either break the composition or make components more predictable.
outputs: An inventory of interface terms and constructions, a compositionality audit, inconsistencies that break systematic inference, and a revised controlled vocabulary.
useWhen: Command languages, query builders, rules and automation editors, developer tools and complex settings where users must combine concepts productively.
avoidWhen: Avoid as a purely theoretical exercise; for most products a terminology audit plus usability testing is sufficient and the philosophical framework is unnecessary.
whyLost: Language-of-thought theory influenced early cognitive HCI but fell from favour as cognitive science moved towards embodied and connectionist accounts.
whereToUse: Feature naming, error message design, onboarding language, design system naming conventions.
example: An automation builder uses 'when', 'if' and 'trigger' inconsistently; an audit enforces a compositional grammar ('When [event], if [condition], then [action]') and rule creation errors fall in testing.
sources: Language of Thought — Jerry Fodor
reference: Fodor JA (1975) The Language of Thought. Harvard University Press

name: Representational State Transition Analysis
aka: Handover analysis across artifacts and people
origin: Edwin Hutchins (1995); Zhang and Norman (1994) on representational effects
summary: Traces how a piece of information is transformed as it moves across media and people, identifying each representational state and the transitions where errors and delays enter.
description: Within distributed cognition, Hutchins analysed computation as the propagation of representational states across media: for example, an air traffic instruction moves from speech to a handwritten strip, to a position on a board, to a pilot's action. Each transition re-represents the information and can add, lose or distort it. Zhang and Norman showed that how information is represented, internally or externally, changes task difficulty. The method follows a specific information item end to end, recording every state (medium, format, location, who holds it) and every transformation (who performs it, with what tool, what can go wrong). The resulting diagram exposes error-prone transcriptions, redundant states and missing feedback, and helps decide which transitions a new system should eliminate, automate or preserve.
steps: For any information flow in a system: document the sequence of representational states the information passes through.
For each transition: what transformation is performed?
By whom or what?
What could go wrong?
What information is lost or added in the transformation?
Build the representational state transition diagram.
Identify the transitions with lowest redundancy and highest consequence — these are the design priorities.
outputs: Representational state transition diagram for key information items, inventory of transformations with error risks, and redesign options that remove or support transitions.
useWhen: Clinical handovers, order entry, logistics, finance operations and any workflow where information is re-keyed, re-written or verbally relayed across people and systems.
avoidWhen: For individual, single-medium tasks with no handoffs; use GOMS or usability testing.
whyLost: It was embedded in Hutchins' theoretical work rather than packaged as a method, and lighter process maps replaced it in practice.
whereToUse: Medical record UX, legal document workflow design, any multi-step information processing system, financial transaction UX.
example: A surgical team's implant information travels from surgeon's speech to a console, a nurse's tablet and a billing system. Mapping seven representational states reveals two manual transcriptions with error risk, which barcode scanning removes.

name: Representativeness Heuristic Audit
origin: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, 1972-1974; UX application via prediction-before-interaction testing
summary: Asks users to predict what interface elements will do before using them, measuring where judgements based on resemblance to familiar patterns produce mistaken expectations.
description: The representativeness heuristic describes how people judge likelihood by similarity to a prototype rather than by base rates or underlying logic. Applied to interfaces, users judge what a control does, or whether a feature will work, by how much it resembles patterns they already know. When an element looks like a familiar pattern but behaves differently, users form confident but wrong expectations, producing mistake-type errors (wrong intention) rather than slips. The audit makes this measurable: participants predict an element's behaviour before interacting, and the gap between prediction and actual behaviour is coded. Elements with high prediction-gap rates are flagged as misleading prototypes. Rigour comes from collecting predictions before any exposure, using a coding scheme for gap size, and setting explicit flag thresholds such as more than 30% of participants with a substantial gap.
steps: Present users with interface elements, ask them to predict behavior before interaction.
Code gap between prediction and actual behavior.
Flag elements where > 30% of participants show prediction gap > 50%.
outputs: Prediction-gap rates per interface element, list of misleading prototype matches, and redesign or relabelling recommendations.
useWhen: Testing icons, novel controls, look-alike components, and features borrowed from other products where users may import wrong expectations.
avoidWhen: When elements are entirely novel with no plausible prototype, or when you need to observe real usage over time (use usability testing or analytics).
whyLost: It sits in judgement and decision-making research and reached UX only as a general bias name; the operational protocol of eliciting predictions before interaction and scoring the gap was never standardised in UX toolkits.
whereToUse: Icon design audits, affordance testing, affordance labeling research.
example: A trading app uses a toggle that resembles an on/off switch to choose between market and limit orders. In a prediction audit, 46% of participants expect it to enable or disable trading, so it is replaced by a labelled segmented control.
sources: Heuristics and Biases — Kahneman (ed.)
Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Science, 1974)

name: Requirements Traceability Matrix for UX
origin: Requirements engineering practice, 1970s-1990s; Gotel and Finkelstein (1994)
summary: Links each research finding to requirements, design decisions, implementation items and verification tests so user insights are not lost between research and development.
description: The treatise describes a once-productive exchange between UX and requirements engineering: UX contributed ethnographic methods, requirements engineers contributed formal specification, traceability matrices and verification procedures. That intersection dissolved, and UX now produces user stories, JTBD statements and journey maps rarely integrated with formal requirements, creating a gap where insights are lost in translation. A UX traceability matrix restores the link: each requirement traces backwards to evidence (study, participant, observation) and forwards to design artefacts, tickets and acceptance tests, including usability acceptance criteria. Bidirectional traceability makes it possible to see which insights were never implemented and which features lack evidence.
steps: Assign identifiers to research findings and store them in a repository.
Write requirements, including measurable usability requirements, each citing finding IDs.
Link requirements to design artefacts and backlog items.
Define verification for each requirement (usability test criterion, analytics metric).
Maintain the matrix through releases, flagging orphan findings and unsupported features.
Review coverage at release gates.
outputs: Bidirectional traceability matrix, coverage reports, list of orphan insights and unsupported features.
useWhen: Regulated or large programmes where research must demonstrably shape delivery; audit or compliance contexts.
avoidWhen: Small exploratory projects where overhead outweighs value.
whyLost: Agile replaced formal requirements with user stories, and UX and requirements engineering communities drifted apart.
whereToUse: Medical device software (IEC 62366 files), government services, fintech compliance, large enterprise programmes.
example: A medical app's matrix shows that 9 of 31 high-severity findings from formative studies have no linked requirement; three are added before the summative validation.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)

name: Research Ethics Protocol
origin: Belmont Report, 1979; Marsh, 2018
summary: A systematic pre-study ethics review across seven checkpoints: consent, data minimisation, participant wellbeing, vulnerability, power, data storage and researcher wellbeing.
description: The research ethics protocol is a systematic review completed before a study begins, organised around seven checkpoints. Informed consent must be specific about recording, use, access and withdrawal, and treated as ongoing. Data minimisation requires justifying every data type collected. Participant wellbeing anticipates emotional, reputational or financial distress and prepares a response and signposting. Vulnerable populations (minors, people with cognitive impairment, marginalised groups) trigger enhanced safeguards. Power asymmetry examines whether relationships with the researcher or sponsor compromise voluntary participation. Data storage and anonymisation define location, access, deletion and residual re-identification risk. Researcher wellbeing plans debriefs and support for distressing fieldwork. Rigour comes from written answers to each checkpoint and review by a second person for higher-risk studies.
steps: Describe the study's purpose, participants, topics and data types in a one-page brief that the review can refer to.
Draft consent materials that state what will be recorded, how data will be used, who will access it and how to withdraw, and plan to reconfirm consent during sessions.
Justify each data type against the research question and remove anything not strictly needed (for example, video when audio suffices).
Assess risks of distress and identify vulnerable or power-dependent participants, adding enhanced consent, signposting resources and a stop rule for sessions.
Define storage location, access rights, retention period (for example, delete raw recordings after 90 days) and anonymisation approach, including residual re-identification risks.
Plan researcher wellbeing support, such as debriefs after sensitive sessions and access to supervision.
Have a second person review high-risk studies, record decisions and mitigations, and revisit the protocol if the study design changes.
outputs: A completed seven-checkpoint review, consent materials, distress and escalation protocols, a data management plan, and researcher support arrangements.
useWhen: Before any study, and necessarily before research with vulnerable participants, sensitive topics, employees or customers in dependent relationships, or retained recordings.
avoidWhen: Not a replacement for formal ethics committee approval where required (academic, clinical); a lighter checklist suits low-risk anonymous studies.
whyLost: Commercial research lacks review boards; ethics is reduced to a consent form, and researcher wellbeing is rarely considered at all.
whereToUse: Health, finance, children's and social services products; research involving employees, patients or customers dependent on the sponsor; studies using recordings or AI transcription; any organisation building a research operations function.
example: Before interviewing families about a child's hospital stay, a team applies the seven checkpoints: it adds a counsellor contact, removes video recording, excludes current inpatients, and books debriefs for researchers after each session.
sources: User Research (Stephanie Marsh)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Research Ethics
Research Design (Leavy)
User Research — Stephanie Marsh

Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
