extra.Seven Ethics Checkpoints: Informed consent: Do participants know what will be recorded, how data will be used, who will have access, and how to withdraw at any time without consequence? Consent must be ongoing — not a one-time signature. Data minimisation: Are you collecting only what you genuinely need for your research question? Every additional data point is an additional privacy risk. Document the justification for each data type collected. Participant wellbeing: Could the study cause distress — emotional, reputational, or financial? What is your protocol if distress occurs during a session? Have signposting resources ready. Vulnerable populations: Any participant under 18, with cognitive impairment, in a power-asymmetric relationship with the researcher (e.g., employee of researcher's client), or from a marginalised group requires enhanced consent procedures and additional safeguards. Power asymmetry: Is the participant in any relationship with the researcher or sponsor that could compromise genuine voluntary consent (employee, student, customer)? Document and mitigate. Data storage and anonymisation: Where will data live? Who can access it? When will it be deleted? How will you anonymise — and what re-identification risks remain even after anonymisation? Researcher wellbeing: Fieldwork on distressing topics affects researchers. Plan for debriefs, supervision, and mental health support.

name: Research Learning Spiral (Travis)
origin: David Travis and Philip Hodgson, 2019
summary: A staged planning cycle linking objectives, research questions, method selection, fieldwork, analysis and communication, with checks at each stage that the chain still holds.
description: The research learning spiral is a planning discipline for UX studies. It moves from objectives (what decision the research must inform), to specific research questions, to choosing a method for each question, then to conducting the research, analysing data and communicating findings, after which the next turn of the spiral begins with what is now known and unknown. Its value lies in traceability: each method choice should map to a question, each question to an objective, and each finding back to a decision. Travis emphasises checking at every stage whether the previous one still holds, so studies do not drift into collecting interesting but unusable data. As a cycle it also supports cumulative learning across studies rather than one-off projects. In practice most teams skip the explicit question-to-method mapping, which is where the rigour lies.
steps: For any upcoming study: write objectives (business/design goals).
Derive research questions from objectives (what would you need to know to achieve the objective?).
Map each question to a method (not the reverse).
For each method, verify: is this the minimal-cost method that validly answers the question?
Document the objective→question→method chain before data collection begins.
outputs: Research plan with traced objectives, questions and methods, a question-by-method matrix, findings mapped to decisions, and inputs for the next research cycle.
useWhen: Planning any non-trivial study, especially multi-method programmes, and teaching teams to justify method choices.
avoidWhen: For very small, well-defined evaluative tests where the question and method are obvious; a lightweight test plan suffices.
whyLost: Planning frameworks are seen as overhead under time pressure, so teams jump from a stakeholder request to a favourite method and the traceability step is lost.
whereToUse: Research planning, study design review, stakeholder alignment. Makes research decisions traceable from objectives to findings.
example: A SaaS research lead maps the objective 'reduce trial churn' to four research questions and chooses interviews for two, funnel analysis for one and a survey for one. The matrix exposes that the planned usability test answered none of them, saving two weeks.
sources: Think Like a UX Researcher — David Travis
Just Enough Research (Erika Hall)
reference: Travis D & Hodgson P (2019) Think Like a UX Researcher. CRC Press

name: Research Operations and Method Repository
origin: ResearchOps community, 2018 onward
summary: An organisational function maintaining method standards, research repositories, training and planning advice so methods and findings survive turnover.
description: The treatise presents research operations as critical for method-resilient organisations. A strong ResearchOps function maintains a methodological standards library (canonical protocols for complex methods), manages research repositories preserving institutional knowledge, provides training and coaching in complex methods, and advocates for methodological appropriateness in research planning. It addresses the institutional memory problem: high turnover, valuing tool proficiency over experience, and lack of knowledge management cause organisations to lose accumulated knowledge when people leave. The method library is the organisational counterpart of the treatise's proposed field-level canon.
steps: Audit current methods, artefacts and knowledge loss points.
Create canonical method protocols with quality criteria, starting with high-priority methods.
Stand up a searchable repository linking findings to evidence and studies.
Run training, coaching and peer review for complex methods.
Add method-appropriateness review to research planning.
Measure reuse, quality and onboarding time.
outputs: Method standards library, research repository, training programme, planning review process.
useWhen: Teams beyond a few researchers, high turnover, regulated environments.
avoidWhen: Very small teams, where lightweight shared documents suffice.
whyLost: Not lost: an emerging function, though often focused on recruitment logistics rather than method stewardship.
whereToUse: In-house research teams, agencies, research-heavy product organisations.
example: A ResearchOps team publishes canonical protocols for diary studies and UFMEA, and onboarding time for new researchers to run them independently falls from months to weeks.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Dixon E (2020) ResearchOps community framework
Sharon T (2016) Validating Product Ideas Through Lean User Research
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 34 (The Research Operations Function).

name: Research Question Prioritisation Matrix
origin: Erika Hall, 2013; David Travis, 2019
summary: Ranks research questions by criticality, reversibility of the resulting decision and current uncertainty, multiplying 1-5 scores to research consequential questions first.
description: This matrix ranks candidate research questions by the decisions they inform rather than by curiosity. Criticality (1-5) asks how bad the consequence of a wrong answer would be, from cosmetic mistake to product failure or harm. Reversibility (1-5) asks how hard it would be to undo a wrong decision, from a sprint-level change to something baked into architecture or regulatory compliance. Uncertainty (1-5) asks how little is currently known, from well-evidenced to pure speculation. Priority is the product of the three. Low-reversibility questions deserve disproportionate attention even at moderate uncertainty, because errors cannot be recovered. Rigour comes from scoring collaboratively with written rationales, checking 'known' claims against evidence, and rescoring as research reports.
steps: List every candidate research question from stakeholders, the backlog and assumption mapping, phrased as questions that would change a decision.
Score each question for criticality on a 1-5 scale, from cosmetic mistake (1) to product failure or user harm (5).
Score reversibility on a 1-5 scale, from easily changed within a sprint (1) to baked into architecture or regulatory compliance (5).
Score uncertainty on a 1-5 scale, from well-evidenced (1) to pure speculation (5), citing evidence for any low score.
Multiply the three scores to obtain a priority score (maximum 125) and rank the questions.
Give extra weight to questions with reversibility of 4 or 5, even where uncertainty is moderate, and agree a cut-off for what will be researched this cycle.
Select methods only for the top-ranked questions, record why lower-ranked questions are deferred, and rescore as new evidence arrives.
outputs: A scored and ranked research backlog, rationales per score, explicitly deprioritised questions, and a research plan linked to decisions.
useWhen: When research capacity is limited, when stakeholders compete for research time, and at the start of planning cycles, before selecting any method.
avoidWhen: Avoid when one urgent question already dominates or the space is so new that questions cannot yet be formulated; start with exploratory research instead.
whyLost: Teams research what is interesting or what a stakeholder asks for; the explicit scoring step feels bureaucratic and is skipped.
whereToUse: Quarterly research planning, research operations and backlog management, product strategy reviews, and regulated domains (health, finance, government) where irreversible decisions carry high cost.
example: A health platform scores 'will clinicians accept AI triage suggestions?' at 5 (criticality) × 5 (reversibility, since it is embedded in regulatory approval) × 4 (uncertainty) = 100, ahead of a colour-scheme question at 1×1×3, so research capacity goes to the triage question.
sources: Just Enough Research (Erika Hall)
Think Like a UX Researcher (David Travis)
Just Enough Research — Erika Hall
Continuous Discovery Habits (Torres)
Practical Empathy (Young)
Just Enough Research (Hall)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 35 — Continuous Discovery & Opportunity Solution Trees
reference: Hall E (2013) Just Enough Research. A Book Apart

extra.The Three-Axis Matrix: Criticality (1–5): If this question were answered incorrectly, how bad would the consequence be? 1 = cosmetic mistake; 5 = product failure or harm to users. Reversibility (1–5): If the decision based on this answer turns out to be wrong, how hard is it to undo? 1 = easily changed in a sprint; 5 = baked into architecture or regulatory compliance. Uncertainty (1–5): How little do you currently know? 1 = well-evidenced; 5 = pure speculation.
extra.Priority Score: Priority = Criticality × Reversibility × Uncertainty. Research the highest-scoring questions first. Questions with low reversibility deserve disproportionate attention even if uncertainty seems moderate — you cannot afford to be wrong and unable to recover. This matrix prevents the most common research failure: researching what is interesting rather than what is consequential.

name: Research through Design
origin: Zimmerman, Forlizzi and Evenson (2007); applied by Xu and MacIntyre in Chapter 9
summary: Treating the design and study of a working artefact as the means of producing knowledge, rather than only as an application of existing knowledge.
description: Research through design recognises interaction design as a form of inquiry. Instead of first establishing facts and then designing, the team designs an artefact that embodies a hypothesis or set of ideas, often drawing on several disciplines, and then studies how people use it. The artefact becomes both a contribution and a research instrument. Chapter 9 uses the approach to build NerdHerder, a colocated augmented-reality game: guidelines derived from sociological theory and from earlier AR work were embodied in design choices, and a user study with eight groups of four, recorded from multiple cameras and synchronised with game logs, showed which player behaviours the design actually triggered. The authors argue RtD suits creative design problems where problem setting and problem solving interact, as in games, because it is hard to talk about the link between interfaces and experience without having made a product that embodies it. For UX teams, RtD is a way to explore new interaction territory where users cannot describe needs in advance.
steps: Frame the inquiry: the question or theory the design will explore.
Gather knowledge from relevant disciplines and earlier work, and turn it into design intentions or guidelines.
Design and iterate a working artefact that embodies those intentions, playtesting along the way.
Study people using the artefact with rich data such as video, logs, questionnaires and interviews.
Analyse how specific design features relate to observed behaviour and experience.
Report both the artefact and the transferable insights or guidelines it produced.
outputs: A working artefact, evidence of how its design features shape behaviour, and refined design guidelines or theory.
useWhen: Exploring novel technologies or experiences where there is no existing product to study and users cannot articulate needs.
avoidWhen: The goal is to evaluate or optimise an existing product against defined requirements.
whyLost: Common in academic HCI, but product teams often see it as too open-ended and slow for delivery timelines.
whereToUse: New interaction paradigms, AR and VR, social and colocated games, speculative products, research labs.
example: A lab designs a multiplayer AR game around theory-based guidelines on shared attention and then video-records groups playing it, finding that shared physical objects became hot spots for social interaction.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Xu, Y. and MacIntyre, B. (2016). NerdHerder: designing colocated physical-digital games with sociological theories. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 9. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Researcher positionality audit
donor: Qualitative social science, feminist methodology and anthropology
origin: Reflexive turn in anthropology and feminist research (for example Haraway, 1988; Harding, 1991); formalised in qualitative methods texts by Finlay (2002) and others
summary: A structured examination of how the researcher's identity, assumptions and relationship to participants shape access, data and interpretation, documented and revisited throughout a study.
description: Interpretivist research treats the researcher as an instrument: what they notice, ask and conclude is shaped by their social position, disciplinary training, employer and relationship to participants. A researcher positionality audit makes this explicit before, during and after fieldwork. It covers identity dimensions (class, gender, caste, ethnicity, language, urban or rural background), insider or outsider status, power relative to participants, organisational interests, and prior beliefs about the outcome. Rigour comes not from a one-off statement but from linking positionality to concrete methodological decisions: who interviews whom, which language is used, which interpretations are checked with participants, and how disconfirming evidence is sought. It supports confirmability and credibility in Lincoln and Guba's terms.
steps: Before fieldwork, write a 1 to 2 page positionality memo covering identity dimensions, relationship to participants, organisational stake in the findings and your prior expectations about the answer.
For each dimension, note specific risks to access, rapport, data and interpretation, for example participants telling a company-affiliated researcher what the company wants to hear.
Translate risks into design decisions: pairing with a local co-researcher, choosing interview language, neutral introductions, and planning member checks for the interpretations most exposed to bias.
During fieldwork, add short reflexive entries after each session noting moments where your position visibly shaped the interaction.
During analysis, have a colleague with a different position review at least 3 coded transcripts and your emerging themes, and record disagreements.
Report a concise positionality statement with the mitigation steps in the final report, and note findings that should be read with particular caution.
outputs: A positionality memo, a log of reflexive entries, documented mitigation decisions, peer review notes and a concise positionality statement in the report.
useWhen: Research crosses social distance (class, culture, language, power); the researcher is employed by the product owner; findings will inform high-stakes or equity-sensitive decisions.
avoidWhen: Purely quantitative behavioural measurement where the researcher does not interact with participants; even then, consider bias in metric choice. Avoid a formulaic statement with no methodological consequences.
whyLost: It is standard in academic qualitative research but rare in industry UX, where research is framed as neutral fact-finding and reports rarely discuss who the researcher is.
whereToUse: Global and emerging-market research, healthcare and social services, research with marginalised groups, internal research with employees, AI fairness studies.
example: An urban, English-speaking researcher from the platform company studied rural health workers. The audit predicted deference and over-reporting of tablet use, so a local co-researcher conducted interviews in Kannada and the team triangulated self-reports with logs, which revealed far lower actual use.
sources: Practice of Qualitative Research
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Research Design (Leavy)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 25 — The Philosophy of Seeing — Epistemological Foundations of Qualitative Inquiry
reference: Finlay, L. (2002). Negotiating the swamp: The opportunity and challenge of reflexivity in research practice. Qualitative Research, 2(2), 209–230.

name: Residual Burst Analysis (Noise as Emotion)
donor: Signal processing reinterpreted for affective research
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Treat deviations from a user's expected rhythm as candidate emotional or cognitive events: compute residuals, flag large bursts, and validate them qualitatively instead of filtering them out.
description: In astrophysics noise is meaningless randomness; in UX, 'noise' often represents hesitation, frustration or novelty, precisely the behaviour that reveals cognition. Standard denoising therefore deletes insight. The Behavioral Spectral Framework reframes noise contextually: compute residuals between observed behaviour and the expected rhythm, flag large residual bursts as potential emotional spikes, and validate them with video, transcripts or sentiment notes. Residual energy is read as psychological arousal, and residual energy variance as emotional arousal or confusion. The practical rule is 'never filter without first interpreting'. Because the same burst can signal stress or excitement (one case user showed high-frequency bursts with positive tone), interpretation must come from narrative context, not amplitude alone.
steps: Fit the expected rhythm for each user or session (e.g. dominant Fourier bands or a smoothed baseline).
Compute residuals between observed behaviour and the expected rhythm.
Flag residual bursts that exceed a chosen threshold as candidate affective or decision-hesitation events.
Retain flagged segments rather than filtering them, and export timestamps for review.
Validate each flagged burst with qualitative artefacts (video, transcript, sentiment note) and code it.
Report residual energy variance per session alongside the qualitative codes, noting divergent cases.
outputs: A list of validated emotional or hesitation events with timestamps and residual energy statistics.
useWhen: When micro-frustration, hesitation or surprise matters and dense interaction or biometric streams exist.
avoidWhen: When qualitative validation is impossible; unvalidated residuals invite over-interpretation.
whyLost: Original technique by Vivek Gopinath.
whereToUse: Form-heavy flows, KYC and OTP steps, game and media engagement, AI conversation pacing.
example: During checkout telemetry review, residual bursts appear at the address step; video shows repeated field corrections and a sigh, coded as frustration, leading to inline validation.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). From Stars to Signals, Sections 3.3, 4.3 and B.3.

name: Resource conflict analysis
origin: Wickens's computational multiple resource model with conflict matrix, 2002; workload models such as W/INDEX (North and Riley, 1989)
summary: Predicts interference between concurrent tasks by scoring their combined demand and their overlap on shared resources, before any user testing.
description: Resource conflict analysis turns multiple resource theory into a quantitative prediction. Each task receives a demand score, and each pair of tasks receives a conflict score based on how many resource dimensions they share (modality, code, stage, visual channel). Total interference is the sum of demand scores plus weighted conflict scores. Wickens's model and W/INDEX use a conflict matrix with values from 0 (no shared resources) to 1 (all shared). The analysis compares candidate designs, for instance whether an alert should be visual text, an icon, a tone or speech. It is analytical, so it can be done early, but results should be validated with dual-task or simulator studies. Rigour comes from transparent coding and sensitivity analysis on uncertain weights.
steps: Decompose the scenario into concurrent task pairs or time segments.
Assign each task a demand score (for example 0 for automatic, 1 for easy, 2 for difficult).
Code each task's resource profile and compute a conflict value for each pair from a conflict matrix (0 to 1, higher with more shared dimensions).
Compute total interference for each design alternative and rank them.
Run sensitivity analysis by varying uncertain demand and conflict weights by plus or minus 25%.
Validate the top-ranked design with a dual-task test or simulator study.
outputs: Conflict matrices, interference scores per design, sensitivity analysis, and a recommended allocation of information to channels.
useWhen: Early design decisions about modality allocation in multitasking environments; when user testing is expensive or unsafe.
avoidWhen: When task interactions are poorly understood or tasks are highly strategic; use observation and simulation first.
whyLost: Used in defence and aviation workload modelling tools but unknown in most UX teams, who lack both training and tooling.
whereToUse: Surgical robotics, automotive HMIs, aviation, control rooms and military interfaces.
example: Comparing alert options for a robotic surgery console, visual text scores interference 2.8 against instrument control while a spoken alert scores 1.6. A simulator study confirms faster responses to spoken alerts without reduced precision.
sources: Salvendy, G. (ed.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Handbook of Human Factors & Ergonomics (Salvendy)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 12 — Multiple Resource Theory — The Bandwidth of the Human
reference: Wickens, C. D. (2002). Multiple resources and performance prediction. Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science, 3(2), 159-177.

name: Resource pool mapping (visual-verbal/visual-spatial/auditory-verbal/auditory-spatial)
origin: Christopher Wickens's multiple resource theory, 1984 and 2002
summary: Maps every concurrent task demand onto Wickens's resource dimensions, modality, code and stage, to identify where tasks compete for the same mental resources.
description: Multiple resource theory holds that time-sharing performance depends on whether tasks draw on the same or different resources along dimensions: perceptual modality (visual versus auditory), processing code (spatial versus verbal), processing stage (perception and cognition versus response) and visual channel (focal versus ambient). Tasks using different resources interfere less. Resource pool mapping lists each concurrent task demand and assigns it to cells such as visual-spatial, visual-verbal, auditory-verbal and auditory-spatial, plus response channels (manual versus vocal). Overloaded cells predict interference and suggest reallocation, such as moving verbal alerts from visual text to speech when the primary task is visual-spatial. Related tools like VACP rating scales add demand levels to each channel.
steps: List the concurrent tasks and information sources a user handles in a scenario.
Assign each demand to modality (visual/auditory/tactile), code (spatial/verbal), stage (perceptual-cognitive/response) and response type (manual/vocal).
Rate demand per channel on a 0-7 scale (as in VACP) for each time segment of the scenario.
Sum demands by channel over time; flag segments where any channel exceeds about 7 or two tasks share the same modality-code cell at high load.
Propose reallocations to less-loaded channels (for example auditory-verbal alerts during visual-spatial manual work).
Validate with a dual-task or simulator study.
outputs: A channel-by-time resource demand map, flagged conflicts, and reallocation proposals.
useWhen: When users multitask in high-tempo environments; when deciding which modality to use for alerts or information.
avoidWhen: For single-task, low-tempo interfaces; resource conflicts are unlikely to matter.
whyLost: Standard in aviation and defence human factors but rarely used outside, where multitasking is treated generically.
whereToUse: Surgical robotics, driving and in-vehicle systems, aviation, emergency dispatch, and AR head-mounted displays.
example: Mapping a robotic procedure shows surgeons' visual-spatial channel saturated by instrument control while alerts arrive as on-screen text (visual-verbal). Routing alerts to brief spoken messages moves them to an unused auditory-verbal channel.
sources: Salvendy, G. (ed.), Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Handbook of Human Factors & Ergonomics (Salvendy)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 12 — Multiple Resource Theory — The Bandwidth of the Human
reference: Wickens, C. D. (2002). Multiple resources and performance prediction. Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science, 3(2), 159-177.

name: Response Surface Methodology
origin: George Box and K. B. Wilson, 1951
summary: Fits a quadratic model of an outcome over continuous design parameters to locate optimal settings, moving sequentially toward the optimum.
description: Many UX parameters are continuous: font size, animation duration, recommendation count, delay before a prompt, price. RSM treats the outcome as a surface over these parameters. It starts with first-order designs and steepest ascent to move toward improvement, then uses second-order designs such as central composite or Box-Behnken to fit curvature and find the optimum or a ridge of near-optimal settings. It also reveals trade-offs among multiple outcomes via desirability functions. This beats guessing a few discrete A/B levels and is efficient in the number of conditions.
steps: Choose 2-4 continuous factors and plausible ranges, and the outcome(s) to optimise.
Run a first-order design (e.g. 2^k factorial with centre points) and fit a linear model.
If far from optimum, move along the path of steepest ascent with a few runs.
Near the optimum, run a central composite or Box-Behnken design and fit a quadratic model.
Locate the stationary point, check if it is a maximum, minimum or saddle, and examine contour plots.
Use desirability functions for multiple outcomes and confirm the chosen setting in a validation test.
outputs: Fitted response surfaces, contour plots, optimal parameter settings and validation results.
useWhen: Tuning continuous parameters such as timing, size, density, quantity or thresholds.
avoidWhen: Categorical design choices or when interactions with context are poorly understood.
whyLost: UX thinks in discrete design variants, and engineering DoE was never taught alongside design.
whereToUse: Notification timing, autoplay delay, recommendation list length, typography for reading apps, haptic intensity.
example: A reading app tunes line height and font size with a central composite design measuring reading speed and comfort, finding an optimum at 18 px with 1.55 line height for long-form text.
sources: Box & Wilson, On the experimental attainment of optimum conditions (1951), JRSS B
Myers, Montgomery & Anderson-Cook, Response Surface Methodology (4th ed., 2016)
reference: Box, G. E. P., & Wilson, K. B. (1951). JRSS Series B, 13(1), 1-45.

name: Retrospective (Survey-Based) UX Benchmark
origin: Sauro, Benchmarking the User Experience (2018), chapter 1
summary: Benchmarks a product by surveying existing users about their past experience, without having them do tasks.
description: Sauro distinguishes two kinds of benchmark. Task-based benchmarks watch people attempt tasks. Retrospective benchmarks ask current users to recall and rate their experience with standard instruments such as SUPR-Q, SUS, UMUX-Lite and NPS, plus top-task ratings and open comments. Retrospective studies are cheap, fast, can reach hundreds of real customers and include competitors' customers, but they capture attitudes and memory rather than behaviour and cannot pinpoint task-level problems. Many programmes run a retrospective benchmark every quarter and a task-based one annually.
steps: Define the population of current users (and competitor users if comparing).
Select standardised measures and a short list of top tasks to rate.
Screen respondents for recent, real use of the product.
Field the survey and clean the data for speeders and straight-liners.
Report scores with intervals against previous waves and competitors, plus themes from verbatims.
outputs: Attitudinal UX scores over time and against competitors.
useWhen: Tracking UX quality frequently and cheaply, or when task access is impossible (logged-in products, competitors).
avoidWhen: You need to know why tasks fail; pair with a task-based study.
whyLost: Not lost, but often confused with marketing satisfaction surveys and run without standardised instruments.
whereToUse: SaaS products, consumer apps, multi-brand competitive programmes.
example: A streaming service surveys 400 subscribers each quarter; UMUX-Lite drops 6 points after a navigation change, triggering a task-based follow-up.
sources: Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
reference: Sauro, J. (2018). Benchmarking the User Experience, chapters 1 and 5.

name: Rhetorical Analysis of Interface Communication
origin: Aristotle's Rhetoric, applied to digital interfaces in technical communication studies
summary: Applies classical rhetoric (ethos, pathos, logos, kairos and implied audience) to analyse how an interface persuades and instructs, and where that persuasion fails or excludes.
description: Every interface argues: it asks users to trust it, to act, to believe a claim about safety or value. Rhetorical analysis makes that argument explicit using classical categories. Ethos covers how credibility is established; pathos how emotion is invoked; logos what reasons and evidence are offered; kairos whether persuasive moves occur at the right moment. Implied-audience analysis reconstructs the user the text assumes, with their knowledge and values, and counter-audience analysis asks who that rhetoric excludes. Each finding is tied to a specific screen or message and translated into a design change. The method is rigorous when applied systematically across a defined corpus with a consistent framework, rather than as an impressionistic copy critique.
steps: Three appeals (Aristotle): Ethos (how does the interface establish credibility?), Pathos (what emotional appeals?), Logos (what rational arguments or evidence?).
Implied audience analysis: What user does this rhetoric assume? What knowledge, values, and desires does it presuppose? Is this assumption accurate for your actual user population?
Kairos — timing: Does the interface make its persuasive moves at the right moment? An appeal compelling at one moment is intrusive at another.
Counter-audience analysis: Who does this rhetoric exclude or alienate? Rhetorical analysis reveals not just who is being addressed but who is implicitly told they are not the intended audience.
Design recommendations: Each rhetorical finding should translate directly to a specific copy, flow, or design change.
outputs: A rhetorical audit of key screens and messages, an implied-audience profile, an exclusion analysis, and specific copy and sequencing recommendations.
useWhen: Persuasive moments matter: onboarding, pricing, upgrade prompts, consent, safety warnings, AI explanations, or when trust is low and you need to understand how the product argues for itself.
avoidWhen: You need evidence of actual user response; rhetorical analysis is expert desk work, so pair it with comprehension testing or A/B tests. For power and ideology questions use Critical Discourse Analysis.
whyLost: Rhetoric lives in humanities departments and its vocabulary sounds old-fashioned to product teams, who rebranded parts of it as persuasive design or UX writing without the analytical framework.
whereToUse: Pricing and paywall pages, onboarding, consent and privacy notices, health and safety messaging, fundraising, and AI assistant tone guidelines.
example: A pension app's contribution prompt relies on fear (pathos) at the moment of login (poor kairos). Rhetorical analysis suggests moving the prompt to after a balance review and adding a concrete projection (logos); the variant improves opt-ins in testing.
sources: Conversational Design (Erika Hall)
Strategic Content Design (Jorgensen)
reference: Aristotle. Rhetoric (trans. W. Rhys Roberts). Also: Hall, E. (2018). Conversational Design. A Book Apart.

name: Rich Pictures (Soft Systems Methodology)
origin: Peter Checkland, 1970s to 1981 (Systems Thinking, Systems Practice)
summary: Participants draw holistic pictures of a complex situation, showing actors, structures, processes, relationships, conflicts and concerns, to externalise multiple perspectives at once.
description: Rich pictures (Checkland, Soft Systems Methodology) are hand-drawn representations of a complex situation that capture: people, structures, processes, relationships, conflicts, and atmosphere in a single visual. Unlike structured diagrams (which impose a notation), rich pictures use free-form drawing, symbols, and caricature — the goal is to capture the complexity and messiness of a real-world situation before trying to impose order on it. Applied to UX research: rich pictures make visible the systemic complexity of a product's context of use — the competing interests, power dynamics, and interdependencies that questionnaires and interviews capture only partially.
steps: Brief participants: 'Draw a picture of [the situation you want to explore]. Include the people involved, what they do, how they relate to each other, and what feels problematic or in tension. Use any symbols, stick figures, or representations that feel right. There is no wrong way to draw this.'
Non-evaluative environment: Explicitly state that drawing ability is irrelevant. The purpose is to externalise thinking, not produce artwork.

Drawing discussion: After participants complete their picture, ask them to walk you through it. 'Tell me what's happening here.' 'What does this symbol represent?' 'What's the relationship between these elements?'
Analyst interpretation: Identify recurring elements across participants' rich pictures. What structures appear in all pictures? What conflicts are depicted? What is notably absent?

Cross-participant comparison: Compare pictures from different stakeholder groups. Where do their pictures differ — what does one group see that another doesn't? These differences reveal perspective-specific constructions of the situation.
outputs: Individual or group rich pictures, participant explanations, recurring elements and conflicts across pictures, and comparisons between stakeholder groups.
useWhen: The situation is messy and ill-defined, with multiple stakeholders and conflicting views, and you need to understand the problem before defining it, as in services, organisations or ecosystems.
avoidWhen: The problem is well defined and task-level; use task analysis or usability testing. Avoid if participants are uncomfortable drawing without careful framing.
whyLost: Soft Systems Methodology remained in systems and management science, while UX developed stakeholder maps and ecosystem maps that lack SSM's emphasis on worldviews and conflict.
whereToUse: Service design and public services, internal platform strategy, healthcare pathways, multi-stakeholder B2B products, and organisational change.
example: Before redesigning a university's student support portal, staff from five departments each draw a rich picture. Comparison shows each department believes another owns 'at-risk students', explaining duplicated outreach and gaps.
sources: Soft Systems Methodology in Action (Checkland)
When Words Fail Us — Elicitation Techniques (PMC 2024)
reference: Checkland, P. & Scholes, J. (1990). Soft Systems Methodology in Action. Wiley.

name: Right-skew detection
origin: Classical descriptive statistics (Pearson's skewness measures, 1895); normality testing by Shapiro and Wilk (1965)
summary: Diagnoses whether a UX metric is positively skewed before summarising or testing it, so the right summary statistic, transformation or test is chosen.
description: Many UX metrics are right-skewed: task times, number of errors, sessions per user, revenue per user, support contacts. Applying means and parametric tests without checking shape produces misleading summaries and inflated error rates. Right-skew detection combines visual and numerical diagnostics: histograms, box plots, Q-Q plots, sample skewness and the comparison of mean and median. With small samples, formal normality tests such as Shapiro-Wilk have low power and with large samples they flag trivial departures, so visual checks and sample skewness are emphasised. The output is a decision about analysis, such as log transform, non-parametric test, bootstrap or modelling a mixture, not a test result in itself.
steps: Plot a histogram (with sensible bin widths) and a box plot of the metric, and a Q-Q plot against a normal distribution.
Compute the mean, median, sample skewness and the ratio of mean to median; skewness above about 1, or a mean noticeably above the median, indicates substantial right skew.
Inspect the right tail for outliers and check whether they are genuine (slow users) or errors (abandoned sessions, logging issues).
Check for multiple peaks that suggest mixed populations rather than simple skew.
Choose the analysis: log transform for approximately log-normal data, rank-based tests, bootstrap confidence intervals, or generalised linear models (for example gamma or negative binomial).
Document the diagnostics and the chosen approach in the analysis plan or report.
outputs: Distribution plots, skewness statistics, an outlier review and a documented choice of summary statistic and test.
useWhen: Before summarising or testing any continuous or count UX metric, especially times, counts and money.
avoidWhen: Data are already known to be bounded and symmetric, such as well-behaved composite scale scores; it remains good practice but adds little.
whyLost: Dashboard tooling summarises with averages by default, and few UX researchers routinely look at distributions before reporting.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarks, product analytics dashboards, A/B test metric design, performance and latency reporting.
example: An investment platform's 'time to first trade' had a mean of 9.2 days and median of 2.1 days, with skewness of 4.3. The histogram also showed a second hump at about 20 days, triggering a bimodality check before any average was reported.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Statistics for HCI (Dix)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 39 — The Distribution of Human Performance — Why Averages Lie
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
reference: Sauro, J., & Lewis, J. R. (2016). Quantifying the User Experience: Practical Statistics for User Research (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Risk and Time Preference Elicitation (Holt-Laury and Discounting Tasks)
origin: Charles Holt and Susan Laury (2002); delay discounting from Ainslie (1975) and Kirby and Maraković (1996); review by Frederick, Loewenstein and O'Donoghue (2002)
summary: Incentivised choice lists that measure individual risk aversion and impatience, used to segment users and predict responses to risky or delayed rewards.
description: Holt-Laury presents ten paired lotteries with increasing probability of the high payoff; the switching point between safe and risky options indexes risk aversion under expected utility. Delay discounting tasks offer choices between smaller-sooner and larger-later amounts, estimating discount rates and present bias (beta-delta models). Using real incentives for a randomly selected choice keeps answers honest. These measures predict behaviour in savings, insurance, health and subscription contexts. For UX, they explain why some users respond to annual plan discounts, loss framing or delayed rewards and others do not, and they offer validated covariates for heterogeneous treatment effects.
steps: Choose the instruments (Holt-Laury list, a delay discounting list such as Kirby's 27-item questionnaire) and incentive scheme.
Administer with clear instructions and pay one randomly chosen decision for real.
Identify switching points; flag inconsistent multiple switching for exclusion or special handling.
Estimate risk aversion (e.g. CRRA coefficient) and discount parameters (k or beta-delta) per participant.
Relate parameters to product behaviours (plan choice, savings, adherence) or use them as moderators in experiments.
Design framing or reward timing variations for segments with different preferences.
outputs: Individual risk and time preference parameters, segment distributions and links to product behaviour.
useWhen: Products involving uncertainty or delayed rewards: insurance, investing, savings, subscriptions, health adherence, loyalty programmes.
avoidWhen: When choices in the product are not plausibly shaped by risk or time preferences.
whyLost: Behavioural economics entered UX as a list of biases and nudges, not as measurement of individual preference parameters.
whereToUse: Robo-advisors, BNPL, health behaviour apps, loyalty and rewards, annual versus monthly pricing.
example: A savings app measures present bias in 1,500 users; highly present-biased users respond strongly to a commitment-device feature while others do not, so the feature is offered selectively.
sources: Holt & Laury, Risk aversion and incentive effects (2002), American Economic Review
Frederick, Loewenstein & O'Donoghue, Time discounting and time preference: A critical review (2002), Journal of Economic Literature
Kirby & Maraković, Delay-discounting probabilistic rewards (1996), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review
reference: Holt, C. A., & Laury, S. K. (2002). American Economic Review, 92(5), 1644-1655.

name: RITE Method
origin: Michael Medlock, Dennis Wixon and colleagues, Microsoft, 2002
summary: A usability testing approach where the team fixes the prototype as soon as a problem is clearly identified, often after one participant, then tests the fix with the next.
description: RITE was developed at Microsoft Games Studios to speed up iteration in usability testing. Instead of running all sessions on a fixed prototype and reporting at the end, the product team observes each session together, agrees on problems and fixes those with clear causes and solutions immediately, sometimes after a single participant. The next participants test the revised version, which shows whether the fix works and whether it introduced new problems. Rigour comes from having decision-makers present, explicit criteria for when to change (obvious cause, clear fix, low cost) versus wait for more data, and logging every change and its outcome across sessions. The method trades statistical comparison for learning speed and works best with prototypes that can be changed quickly.
steps: Agree a test plan, task set and decision criteria for when a problem is fixed immediately versus after more sessions.
Ensure decision-makers (designers, developers, product owner) observe every session.
Run a session, then debrief immediately to list problems and decide which to fix now.
Update the prototype before the next session for problems with clear causes and solutions.
Continue with the next participant, checking whether fixes work and new problems appear; typical studies run 6-15 participants.
Log every change, its rationale and subsequent results, and report the problem and fix trajectory.
outputs: Iterated prototype, problem and fix log across sessions, record of fixes verified by subsequent participants.
useWhen: Early prototype iteration, onboarding and tutorial flows, games, and agile sprints with tightly integrated teams.
avoidWhen: When you need benchmark metrics or statistical comparison between designs; use summative usability testing or A/B testing.
whyLost: Renamed/consolidated: Concept absorbed into lean UX and agile UX practices; rarely named distinctly.
whereToUse: Rapid prototype iteration; lean UX contexts; agile sprint cycles.
example: A tax-filing app team ran RITE on onboarding with 10 participants over two days. A misunderstood income question was reworded after participant 2 and verified by participants 3 to 6, and completion rose from 4 of 6 to 10 of 10 by the final version.
sources: Moderated Usability Tests
Using the RITE method to improve products (Medlock et al.)
reference: Medlock, M. C., Wixon, D., Terrano, M., Romero, R., & Fulton, B. (2002). Using the RITE method to improve products: A definition and a case study. Usability Professionals' Association conference.

name: ROC curve analysis for UI alerts
donor: Signal detection theory, radar engineering and clinical diagnostics
origin: Radar engineering in WWII; Peterson, Birdsall and Fox, 1954; Swets, 1988 for diagnostics
summary: Plots hit rate against false-alarm rate across alert thresholds or user confidence levels to choose the threshold that best balances misses against alarm fatigue.
description: An ROC curve shows the trade-off between true-positive and false-positive rates as a decision threshold varies. For UI alerts it can be applied at two levels: the system level (what detector threshold triggers an alert) and the human level (how users respond, using confidence ratings to trace their curve). The area under the curve (AUC) summarises discriminability independent of threshold; the optimal operating point depends on base rates and the costs of misses versus false alarms, via the slope beta = [P(noise)/P(signal)] x [(cost FA)/(value hit)]. The method makes explicit that every alert threshold is a value judgement and that high false-alarm rates degrade human trust and response, a key cause of alarm fatigue. Rigour comes from labelled ground truth and explicit cost weighting.
steps: Assemble a labelled dataset of events (true conditions versus benign) with the detector score for each, ideally at least 100 positives and 100 negatives.
Sweep thresholds and compute true- and false-positive rates at each to plot the system ROC and AUC.
Elicit stakeholder costs for misses and false alarms and the base rate, and compute the optimal operating slope.
Run a user study where participants respond to alerts and give confidence ratings on a 6-point scale; construct the human ROC from cumulative rating thresholds.

Compare the joint human-plus-system performance at candidate thresholds, noting positive predictive value; alerts with PPV below about 10-20% are associated with override rates above 90% in clinical settings.
Select the threshold, document the trade-off, and set monitoring to recompute ROC after launch as base rates drift.
outputs: System and human ROC curves, AUC values, a cost-weighted recommended threshold, PPV at that threshold, and a monitoring plan.
useWhen: When tuning alert, notification, anomaly or AI-confidence thresholds; when alarm fatigue or override rates are high; when stakeholders disagree about sensitivity.
avoidWhen: When no ground truth labels exist or events are not binary; start with log analysis of override behaviour or qualitative alarm reviews.
whyLost: ROC analysis is routine in radiology and machine learning but UX teams rarely own alert thresholds, which are left to engineers, so the human side of the curve is seldom measured.
whereToUse: Clinical decision support, security and fraud alerts, observability tools, AI confidence indicators, and push-notification strategy.
example: A fraud team sees agents override 96% of alerts. ROC analysis shows the detector runs at a threshold giving PPV of 4%; moving to a stricter point halves volume while losing 6% of true frauds, and agent override rates fall to 70% with higher hit rates on remaining alerts.

name: Root Cause Analysis and the 5 Whys
origin: Sakichi Toyoda; formalised by Taiichi Ohno in the Toyota Production System (1978)
summary: Iteratively asks why a problem occurred to move from symptoms to systemic causes, ideally with evidence at each step and multiple branches.
description: The 5 Whys asks 'why' repeatedly until reaching a cause that, if fixed, prevents recurrence. In disciplined form, each answer must be verified with evidence, branches are allowed when there are several causes, and the analysis stops at a cause within the organisation's control, usually a process or design decision rather than a person. Formal RCA (as in healthcare, per The Joint Commission) adds timeline reconstruction, cause-and-effect charting and action hierarchies that favour design changes over retraining. The method is vestigial in UX: teams ask 'why' five times in a meeting with no evidence, follow a single linear chain and stop at 'user didn't read'. Restoring the evidence and branching rules makes it rigorous.
steps: State the problem precisely with measurable symptoms, scope and time window.
Reconstruct a factual timeline from logs, recordings and interviews before any causal discussion.
Ask why the problem occurred and record each candidate cause, requiring evidence (data, observation, reproduction) for every link.
Allow branching where several causes contribute, and continue each branch until reaching a controllable process or design cause, typically 3-7 levels.
Reject causes that blame individuals; reframe as 'why was this error possible and not caught'.
Select corrective actions using an action hierarchy (forcing functions and automation stronger than warnings and training) and set a verification metric.
outputs: An evidence-backed causal tree, root cause statements and corrective actions with verification metrics.
useWhen: Investigating a specific recurring problem, incident or metric drop where evidence is available.
avoidWhen: Complex sociotechnical incidents with emergent causes; use STAMP/CAST or FRAM, as linear whys oversimplify.
whyLost: The name survived as a workshop ritual while its evidence requirements and action hierarchy were dropped. Linear 'why' chains are easy to run in a meeting and feel conclusive.
whereToUse: Post-incident reviews, conversion drops, support ticket spikes, onboarding failures.
example: A SaaS signup completion drops 8%. A branched 5 Whys traced through logs finds two roots: a password rule change without inline feedback and a slow email verification service; both are fixed and completion recovers.
sources: Ohno, Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production (1988 English ed.)

The Joint Commission, Framework for Root Cause Analysis and Corrective Actions

name: Rubin Causal Model (Potential Outcomes)
origin: Donald B. Rubin, 1974 (building on Jerzy Neyman, 1923)
summary: Defines a causal effect as the difference between potential outcomes under treatment and control, estimated from matched cohorts when randomisation is impossible.
description: Each unit has a potential outcome under treatment and under control, only one of which is observed; the average treatment effect (ATE) is the mean difference across units. Without randomisation, unbiased estimation requires that assignment be independent of potential outcomes given measured covariates (unconfoundedness), which motivates matching or weighting on those covariates. Vivek Gopinath's playbook prescribes it for UX when an A/B test cannot be run: match cohorts by user type (novice versus advanced traders), device and session time, then estimate ATE, documenting the unconfoundedness assumption. It is paired with Bradford Hill criteria as a narrative check on the resulting evidence.
steps: State the treatment (e.g. new IA exposure), the outcome and the unit of analysis.
List confounders that drive both exposure and outcome (user type, device, session time, tenure).
Match or weight treated and untreated users on those confounders and check balance.
Estimate the ATE as the mean outcome difference across matched cohorts with an interval.
Document the unconfoundedness assumption and run sensitivity checks with additional plausible confounders.
Corroborate with Bradford Hill criteria and qualitative mechanism evidence.
outputs: An ATE estimate with balance diagnostics and stated assumptions.
useWhen: When a change shipped to some users without randomisation, or ethics or engineering prevent an A/B test.
avoidWhen: When key confounders are unmeasured; prefer a randomised or quasi-experimental design such as difference-in-differences.
whyLost: Core to statistics and econometrics, but UX teams either randomise or fall back to naive before/after comparisons.
whereToUse: Staged rollouts, opt-in features, regulatory changes, enterprise deployments.
example: A new alerts IA was rolled out to Android first; the researcher matches Android and iOS users by trader experience and session time to estimate the ATE on completion.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation

name: Safety-II and Work-as-Done Analysis
origin: Erik Hollnagel, David Woods and others, 2006-2014 (Safety-I and Safety-II, 2014)
summary: Studies why everyday work usually succeeds despite variability, contrasting work-as-imagined by designers with work-as-done by users to find adaptive strategies.
description: Safety-I defines safety as the absence of failures and studies incidents. Safety-II defines it as the ability to succeed under varying conditions and studies normal work. The core analytic move is comparing work-as-imagined (procedures, specifications, designers' flows) with work-as-done (observed practice), and also work-as-prescribed, work-as-disclosed and work-as-normal. Gaps are not treated as violations but as evidence of adaptations users make to cope with the system's shortcomings. Researchers then identify which adaptations are protective and should be supported, and which create latent risk. For UX this reframes workarounds as data about design debt and shows where rigid automation would remove the very flexibility that keeps work going.
steps: Document work-as-imagined: specs, flows, help content, training material and stakeholder descriptions of the task.
Observe work-as-done in context across normal, busy and unusual days, focusing on successful outcomes.
Catalogue adaptations and workarounds, with their triggers (time pressure, missing data, edge cases) and effects.
Interview practitioners about trade-offs they make, such as efficiency versus thoroughness, using Hollnagel's ETTO framing.
Classify adaptations as protective, neutral or risky, and map each to the design gap that prompts it.
Design to support protective adaptations and make risky ones unnecessary; share findings with the people observed.
outputs: A work-as-imagined versus work-as-done gap map, an adaptation catalogue, and design recommendations that preserve resilience.
useWhen: Redesigning or automating complex professional workflows where users have built workarounds, or after incidents where blame is tempting.
avoidWhen: Simple, highly standardised tasks; usability testing of the designed flow suffices.
whyLost: UX research looks for pain points and failures, which is a Safety-I mindset. Studying success is counter-intuitive and not supported by typical research templates.
whereToUse: Clinical and EHR workflows, operations and logistics tools, customer support platforms, automation and AI copilots.
example: Before automating invoice matching, a fintech studies accountants' successful month-ends and finds they routinely override supplier names using a private spreadsheet. The automation is designed to learn from those overrides rather than block them.
sources: Hollnagel, Safety-I and Safety-II: The Past and Future of Safety Management (2014)
Hollnagel, The ETTO Principle: Efficiency-Thoroughness Trade-Off (2009)
Hollnagel, Woods & Leveson, Resilience Engineering (2006)
reference: Hollnagel, E. (2014). Safety-I and Safety-II. Ashgate.

name: Saliency Map Analysis for Interface Attention Prediction
origin: Laurent Itti, Christof Koch and Ernst Niebur (1998); later GBVS and deep models such as DeepGaze
summary: Uses computational saliency models to predict which regions of a screen will attract early visual attention, checking designs before eye tracking or live testing.
description: Saliency models compute where bottom-up visual features such as colour contrast, intensity, orientation and, in deep models, learned features like faces and text, will draw early attention. Itti, Koch and Niebur's model combines feature maps into a saliency map; deep models such as DeepGaze predict human fixations much more accurately on natural images, and models trained on webpages and UIs perform better still for interfaces. In UX, saliency maps provide quick checks: does the primary call to action stand out, are warnings competing with decoration, is visual hierarchy consistent with task priority? Rigour requires understanding the limits: models predict early, stimulus-driven attention, not task-driven search or comprehension, so predictions should be validated against eye tracking or click data and used comparatively between variants rather than as absolute truth.
steps: Apply a saliency model (open-source: MIT Saliency Benchmark; Python: pySaliency) to interface screenshots. Compute predicted fixation density map. Compare to:
designer's intended attention hierarchy (what should users look at first?),
actual eye-tracking data (if available). Overlap coefficient between predicted and intended: < 0.60 = visual hierarchy redesign needed. Use as a rapid pre-testing filter.
outputs: Predicted saliency maps per design, saliency scores for regions of interest, comparisons between variants, and validation against eye-tracking or click data where available.
useWhen: Early design checks of visual hierarchy, landing pages, ads, packaging, dashboards and warnings, especially when eye tracking is unavailable.
avoidWhen: For task-driven search, reading or decision behaviour, which saliency models do not capture; use eye tracking or usability testing.
whyLost: Saliency research advanced in computer vision but UX either relied on eye tracking or used commercial tools uncritically, without understanding what the models predict.
whereToUse: Interface visual hierarchy validation, A/B test variant screening, dashboard design optimization, landing page visual hierarchy.
example: A pharmacy app's dosage warning has lower predicted saliency than a promotional banner on the same screen. The team reduces the banner's contrast and confirms with a 20-person eye-tracking check that the warning is now fixated earlier.
sources: Computer Vision: A Modern Approach — David A. Forsyth
Itti, Koch & Niebur, A model of saliency-based visual attention for rapid scene analysis (IEEE PAMI, 1998)
Kümmerer et al., DeepGaze II (2016)
reference: Itti L, Koch C & Niebur E (1998) A model of saliency-based visual attention for rapid scene analysis. IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 20(11):1254-1259

name: Saliency model application
origin: Itti, Koch and Niebur, 1998; deep saliency models such as DeepGaze (Kümmerer et al., 2014 onwards)
summary: Applies computational models of bottom-up visual saliency to screens to predict where attention will be drawn first, before any eye-tracking study is run.
description: Saliency models compute, for each point in an image, how much it stands out in colour, intensity, orientation and other features relative to its surroundings, combining them into a saliency map. Itti and Koch's model was biologically inspired; modern deep models trained on eye-tracking data predict fixations considerably better. Applied to interfaces, they indicate whether critical elements are salient and whether decoration competes with them. Commercial 'predictive eye-tracking' tools are mostly renamed saliency models, often presented without their limitations: they capture bottom-up salience but not task-driven, top-down attention, which dominates in expert work. Rigour comes from using models validated on UI images (for example models trained on webpage datasets), comparing salience ranks with intended priority, and validating with real eye tracking where stakes are high.
steps: Capture screenshots of key screens in realistic states, including alerts and busy conditions.
Run at least one validated saliency model, preferably one trained on UI or webpage data, to produce saliency maps.
Define areas of interest for critical elements and compute their mean saliency rank relative to other elements.
Flag critical elements outside the top 3 most salient regions and decorative elements that rank in the top 3.
Adjust the design and re-run the model to compare versions.
For safety-critical screens, validate with a short eye-tracking study (10-15 participants) measuring time to first fixation on critical areas.
outputs: Saliency maps, salience ranks for critical elements, before/after comparisons, and optional eye-tracking validation.
useWhen: Early in visual design to check visual hierarchy, when comparing layout variants cheaply, and when eye tracking is impractical.
avoidWhen: When users are experts searching with clear goals, because top-down attention dominates; use task-based eye tracking or inattentional blindness testing instead.
whyLost: It survives as 'AI attention heat maps' in commercial tools, but the scientific origin and limits are forgotten.
whereToUse: Dashboards, landing pages, packaging, advertising, medical device screens and alert placement.
example: A saliency model shows that on a surgical console the decorative 3D robot render is the most salient region, while the bleeding-risk alert ranks fifth. Muting the render and enlarging the alert moves the alert to first, confirmed by eye tracking.
sources: Bear, M., Connors, B. & Paradiso, M., Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain
Garrett, B., Brain & Behavior: An Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Neuroscience (Bear et al.)
Brain & Behaviour (Garrett)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 9 — Attention — The Gatekeeper
reference: Itti, L., Koch, C. & Niebur, E. (1998). A model of saliency-based visual attention for rapid scene analysis. IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 20(11), 1254-1259.

name: Sample size planning (G*Power)
origin: G*Power software by Erdfelder, Faul and Buchner (1996; G*Power 3, Faul et al., 2007), implementing Cohen's power framework
summary: Uses G*Power or equivalent tools to calculate the sample needed for a specific test, effect size, alpha and power before running a quantitative UX study.
description: G*Power is a free tool that computes required sample sizes, achievable power and detectable effects for t-tests, F-tests (ANOVA, regression), chi-square tests, z-tests and exact tests. It is the standard tool in psychology and behavioural science for a priori power analysis. Applied to UX it forces precise decisions about design (between or within subjects), the test family, the expected correlation among repeated measures, and the effect size of interest. Within-subjects designs, common in usability comparisons, can require far fewer participants when measures are correlated, and G*Power makes this explicit. Rigour comes from justifying each input, entering the effect size in the metric the tool expects (for example f for ANOVA, not d), and documenting the screenshot or parameters in the study plan.
steps: Select the test family and statistical test matching the analysis plan (for example t-tests, means: difference between two dependent means for a within-subjects comparison).
Choose 'A priori: compute required sample size' and enter the tail(s), alpha (for example 0.05) and power (for example 0.80).
Enter the effect size in the required metric (d, f, w or f²), derived from pilot data, prior studies or the smallest effect of interest, using G*Power's effect size calculator if needed.
For repeated measures, enter a realistic correlation among measures (often 0.5 to 0.7 for task ratings), and a non-sphericity correction if relevant.
Record the output sample size, inflate for expected exclusions or attrition (for example 10% to 20%), and round up to balance conditions.
Save the protocol output and include it in the pre-registration or research plan.
outputs: A documented sample size with inputs and justification, and a power curve showing sensitivity to effect size.
useWhen: Planning lab or unmoderated quantitative UX studies, survey experiments, and within-subjects design comparisons.
avoidWhen: Online A/B tests with proportions and large traffic, where platform calculators or specialised sequential designs fit better; qualitative or formative studies.
whyLost: G*Power is ubiquitous in academic psychology but little known in industry UX, where sample sizes are set by budget or convention such as 5 users or 100 respondents.
whereToUse: Comparative usability studies, survey experiments on messaging, preference and perception tests, academic-industry collaborations.
example: Planning a within-subjects comparison of two dashboard layouts on SEQ ratings, a researcher assumed d = 0.4 and a correlation of 0.6 between conditions. G*Power returned 52 participants for 80% power, which grew to 60 after allowing 15% exclusion.

Designing Experiments & Analyzing Data (Maxwell & Delaney)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 41 — Frequentist Inference Done Right

name: Sample Size Planning for Summative UX Studies
origin: Classical estimation and power formulae; UX tables in Sauro & Lewis ch. 6 and Benchmarking the User Experience ch. 6
summary: Works out how many participants a benchmark or comparison needs to hit a target precision or detect a meaningful difference.
description: Summative studies measure rather than discover, so sample size follows from statistics, not the five-user rule. There are three situations. For a stand-alone benchmark, n depends on the margin of error you can accept around a completion rate or mean. For comparisons, n depends on the smallest difference worth detecting, the variability, the confidence level and the power, and within-subjects designs need far fewer people than between-subjects ones. For comparisons against an industry benchmark, n depends on how close to the benchmark you expect to be. Sauro and Lewis give iterative t-based formulas that work for small samples, and practical tables, such as roughly 93 people for a ±10 point margin on a completion rate.
steps: Classify the study: stand-alone estimate, comparison (within or between), or test against a benchmark.
Choose confidence level and, for comparisons, power (80% is typical).
Get a variability estimate from past studies (SUS SD is about 17.7; for proportions use 0.5 if unknown).
Apply the formula or table, iterating the t value until n stabilises.
Inflate for expected drop-outs and data cleaning losses (often 10 to 20% unmoderated).
outputs: A justified participant count and the precision it buys.
useWhen: Planning benchmarks, competitive studies and A/B tests where numbers will be compared over time.
avoidWhen: Formative studies aimed at finding problems (use the problem discovery model).
whyLost: UX teams set sample sizes by budget or habit and then over-interpret results. The formulas exist but sit in statistics texts few designers read.
whereToUse: Annual UX benchmarks, competitive evaluations, survey programmes.
example: To detect a 10-point SUS difference between two designs at 90% confidence and 80% power, a within-subjects study needs about 21 people; a between-subjects one needs about 40 per group.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)

name: Saturation detection
donor: Sociology (grounded theory) and health research methodology
origin: Theoretical saturation in Glaser and Strauss (1967); operationalised by Guest, Bunce and Johnson (2006) and Guest, Namey and Chen (2020)
summary: Determines empirically when additional qualitative data stop yielding new codes or category properties, justifying sample size with evidence instead of convention.
description: Glaser and Strauss defined theoretical saturation as the point where new data add no new properties to categories. In practice 'we reached saturation' is often asserted without evidence. Guest, Bunce and Johnson found that in a relatively homogeneous sample about 92% of codes emerged within the first 12 interviews; Guest, Namey and Chen (2020) proposed a transparent method using a base size (for example 4 interviews), a run length (for example 2 further interviews) and a new-information threshold (for example 5% or less) to declare saturation. Hennink and colleagues distinguished code saturation, hearing it all, from meaning saturation, understanding it all, which takes longer. Saturation detection tracks new codes per interview, applies these thresholds and reports them, separating code from meaning saturation.
steps: Define the saturation type you need: code saturation for descriptive inventories, or meaning or theoretical saturation for explanatory work.
Code interviews in the order they were conducted and record, for each interview, the number of new codes added to the codebook.

Set parameters in advance: a base size (for example the first 4 interviews), a run length (for example 2 or 3 interviews) and a new-information threshold (for example 5% or less of the base codebook).
After each run, compute the ratio of new codes in the run to the base codebook size; declare code saturation when the ratio falls at or below the threshold.
For meaning saturation, track whether each important code's properties and dimensions are still changing, and continue sampling until the main codes are fully understood.
Check saturation within each important subgroup separately (for example each region), since saturation across a pooled heterogeneous sample can hide gaps.
Report the saturation curve, parameters and subgroup results in the methods section.
outputs: A saturation curve of new codes per interview, a documented stopping decision with parameters, and subgroup saturation checks.
useWhen: Planning or justifying qualitative sample size; deciding when to stop fieldwork; reporting rigour to sceptical stakeholders.
avoidWhen: The study is evaluative usability testing with defined tasks (use problem-discovery models such as 1-(1-p)^n), or the sample is fixed by access constraints; then report information power instead.
whyLost: Saturation became a ritual phrase used to justify convenient samples, and the quantified procedures from health research methodology are rarely applied in UX.
whereToUse: Discovery interview programmes, multi-region studies, continuous discovery cadences, research operations sample planning.
example: Across 20 interviews in 3 regions, pooled new codes fell below 5% after interview 11, but region-level tracking showed the northern region still added codes at interview 6 of 6; two further northern interviews were added before the theory was finalised.
sources: Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 26 — Grounded Theory — Generating Theory from Data
reference: Guest, G., Namey, E., & Chen, M. (2020). A simple method to assess and report thematic saturation in qualitative research. PLoS ONE, 15(5), e0232076; Guest, G., Bunce, A., & Johnson, L. (2006). How many interviews are enough? Field Methods, 18(1), 59–82.

name: Saturation Monitoring
origin: Builds on Glaser & Strauss (1967); operationalised by Guest, Bunce & Johnson, 2006, and Hennink et al., 2017
summary: Tracking new codes per interview in a table and curve so the decision to stop sampling is based on evidence rather than intuition.
description: Saturation is routinely claimed but rarely demonstrated. Saturation monitoring operationalises it: after each interview the analyst records new codes, revised codes and new themes, then plots new codes per interview. Guest, Bunce and Johnson found most codes in a homogeneous sample emerged within about twelve interviews, while Hennink and colleagues distinguished code saturation (hearing it all) from meaning saturation (understanding it all), which takes longer. Saturation is judged per category: two or three consecutive sessions adding no new codes on core categories, after theoretical sampling toward expected variation. The decision and its evidence are documented, giving stakeholders a defensible answer to 'why this many participants?'.
steps: After each interview: update a tracking table. Columns: interview number, new codes generated, codes revised, new themes identified.
Plot the curve of new codes per interview. Saturation = the rate of new code generation approaches zero.
Saturation is indicated when: (a) 2–3 consecutive interviews produce zero new codes on core categories AND (b) you have used theoretical sampling toward expected variation.
Category-specific saturation: Track saturation per major category. Continue theoretical sampling until all major categories are saturated.
Document the saturation decision with specific evidence: how many sessions produced no new codes, what theoretical sampling was done.
outputs: A saturation tracking table, new-codes-per-interview curve, category-level saturation status, and a written stopping justification.
useWhen: Iterative interview studies with flexible sample size, when sample size will be questioned, or in research ops standards for qualitative work.
avoidWhen: Fixed-sample fieldwork without concurrent analysis, or interpretive designs like IPA where saturation is not the goal.
whyLost: Concurrent coding during fieldwork is rare in industry, so there is nothing to track and saturation is asserted rather than shown.
whereToUse: Discovery studies, academic-industry research, regulated research, and sample size justification in research proposals.
example: During interviews on telehealth booking, the team logs new codes after each session. Sessions 9 to 11 add none on core categories, but 'caregiver booking' is still growing, so two caregivers are recruited before stopping.
sources: Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Sampling and Choosing Cases in Qualitative Research
How Many Interviews Are Enough? (Guest, Bunce & Johnson)
Code Saturation Versus Meaning Saturation (Hennink, Kaiser & Marconi)
reference: Guest, G., Bunce, A. & Johnson, L. (2006). How many interviews are enough? An experiment with data saturation and variability. Field Methods, 18(1), 59-82.

name: Scale construction and validation
origin: Lee Cronbach & Paul Meehl's construct validity, 1955; Gilbert Churchill's paradigm, 1979; DeVellis's guidelines, 1991
summary: A staged process for building a multi-item measure of a UX construct that is reliable, valid and fit for comparison, from item generation to confirmatory testing.
description: Scale construction turns a construct such as trust in an AI assistant into a defensible measurement instrument. The process defines the construct, generates items from qualitative research and literature, tests content validity with experts, pilots items with cognitive interviews, runs EFA on one sample to refine the structure, confirms it with CFA on another, and then establishes reliability, convergent, discriminant and criterion validity, plus measurement invariance across groups. Established UX instruments such as SUS, UMUX and SUPR-Q followed parts of this path. Rigour lies in each stage being explicit and reported; most homegrown UX surveys skip all of it.
steps: Define the construct and its boundaries, distinguishing it from neighbouring constructs.
Generate an item pool of roughly twice the intended final length from interviews and literature.
Assess content validity with 5-10 experts (e.g. content validity ratio) and run cognitive interviews with 5-15 target users.
Administer to a development sample (200 or more) and refine items with EFA and item analysis.
Confirm the structure with CFA on an independent sample and test invariance across key groups.
Establish reliability (omega or alpha above 0.7, ideally 0.8) and validity against related measures and behavioural criteria.
Publish a scoring guide with norms or benchmarks for interpretation.
outputs: A validated scale with documented reliability, structure, validity evidence, invariance, scoring rules and benchmarks.
useWhen: When a key construct will be tracked over time, compared across segments or used as an outcome in experiments, and no adequate validated instrument exists.
avoidWhen: Avoid for one-off pulse checks, when an established validated scale fits (use it), or when the construct is better measured behaviourally.
whyLost: Teams write ad hoc questions under time pressure; the multi-sample validation process is seen as academic, so the label 'validated' is applied loosely.
whereToUse: Trust and AI reliance measures, product-specific satisfaction trackers, accessibility experience measures, B2B relationship health indices.
example: An AI assistant team builds a 9-item calibrated reliance scale through two survey waves of 400 users each. The final scale predicts override behaviour in logs (r = 0.42) and is now the outcome metric for explainability experiments.
