name: Scale scoring
origin: Rensis Likert, 1932; standardised UX scoring rules such as SUS (Brooke, 1996)
summary: Converting multi-item questionnaire responses into reliable composite scores by applying documented reverse-coding, aggregation and missing-item rules.
description: Scale scoring turns item responses into the construct score used in analysis. Correct scoring requires reverse-coding negatively worded items, applying the published algorithm (for example SUS: odd items minus 1, 5 minus even items, sum multiplied by 2.5 to give 0-100), deciding how many missing items are tolerable (a common rule is the person-mean of available items when at least 80% are answered), and choosing between sum, mean or factor scores. Rigour comes from scoring in code, checking reliability before using the composite, verifying scores fall within the theoretical range, and only summing items that a factor analysis supports as unidimensional. UX teams frequently mis-score standard instruments or average items across distinct factors, which is why the practice is vestigial.
steps: Document each scale's items, response range, reversed items and published scoring algorithm.
Reverse-code negatively worded items in code (e.g. new = (max + min) minus old).
Apply a missing-item rule, such as person-mean imputation when at least 80% of a scale's items are present, otherwise set the score to missing.
Compute the composite (sum, mean or published transformation such as SUS x 2.5) and check that all scores fall within the theoretical range.
Check internal consistency (e.g. omega or alpha of 0.70 or above) and unidimensionality before using the composite.
Where norms exist, convert to percentiles or grades (e.g. SUS 68 is roughly the 50th percentile).
outputs: Composite scale scores per respondent, reliability estimates, range checks and normative comparisons.
useWhen: Any analysis of standard UX instruments (SUS, UMUX-Lite, SUPR-Q, NASA-TLX) or custom multi-item attitude scales.
avoidWhen: Avoid summing items that do not form one factor; use factor scores or separate subscales. For single-item measures, analyse the item directly.
whyLost: Survey platforms auto-calculate averages without reverse-coding or reliability checks, so scoring became an invisible, unchecked step.
whereToUse: Usability benchmarking, satisfaction tracking, trust and perceived-risk measurement in fintech and health, and AI product attitude scales.
example: A health app's SUS appeared to fall from 72 to 58. Auditing the scoring code showed even items had not been reverse-coded in the new survey export; correct scoring gave 71.

name: SCARF Model for Design Critique Facilitation
origin: David Rock, 2008; applied to design by Tom Greever, 2015
summary: Uses five social threat and reward domains to plan and run design critiques and stakeholder reviews so feedback does not trigger defensiveness.
description: David Rock's SCARF model proposes that people respond to social situations through five domains of perceived threat or reward: Status, Certainty, Autonomy, Relatedness and Fairness. Tom Greever's work on articulating design decisions shows how stakeholder resistance often stems from these social threats rather than from the design itself. Applied to critique facilitation, the facilitator plans how each domain might be threatened (a stakeholder losing face, unclear next steps, decisions imposed without input, in-group versus out-group dynamics, unequal treatment) and designs the session to reduce threat: clear agendas, criteria-based feedback, explicit decision rights and acknowledgement of contributions. The neuroscientific claims are heuristic; rigour lies in consistent preparation, criteria agreed in advance, and documenting decisions.
steps: SCARF-safe critique protocol:
Status — begin by acknowledging what works ('this navigation structure is really clear').
(2) Certainty — explain the basis for feedback ('this pattern conflicts with users' expectations based on [research]').
(3) Autonomy — offer options, not mandates ('we could address this by either X or Y').
(4) Relatedness — frame feedback as shared problem-solving, not evaluation.
(5) Fairness — apply the same criteria to all design decisions.
outputs: A critique plan addressing each SCARF domain, facilitation scripts, ground rules, and more productive, decision-oriented feedback.
useWhen: Design reviews, research readouts with contentious findings, cross-team critiques and stakeholder presentations where status and autonomy tensions run high.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating it as validated neuroscience or a manipulation tool; it is a heuristic. For formal decision disputes, use structured decision analysis.
whyLost: It sits in leadership coaching literature; designers learn critique through studio culture, not explicit facilitation frameworks.
whereToUse: Design critique facilitation, stakeholder review sessions, cross-functional design collaboration.
example: Before presenting research that contradicts a VP's roadmap, a researcher frames findings as options (autonomy), states clearly what is and is not known (certainty), and credits the VP's earlier hypothesis (status); the review ends with an agreed test.
sources: Articulating Design Decisions — Tom Greever
reference: Rock D (2008) SCARF: A brain-based model for collaborating with and influencing others. NeuroLeadership Journal 1

name: Scenario generation under uncertainty
origin: Herman Kahn's scenario method (RAND, 1950s); Shell scenario planning (Pierre Wack, 1970s); diffusion modelling (Frank Bass, 1969)
summary: Constructs a set of plausible futures for a product decision by varying uncertain drivers systematically and simulating outcomes such as adoption under each scenario.
description: Scenario generation combines foresight and simulation. Key uncertain drivers (market conditions, user trust, competitor moves, regulation, the size of a redesign effect) are identified, given ranges or distributions, and combined into coherent scenarios. Outcomes are then simulated under each, for example with a Bass diffusion model of adoption, producing comparative forecasts and robustness insights: which design option performs acceptably across all scenarios rather than best in one. The method guards against planning for a single assumed future. Rigour comes from grounding drivers in research, checking internal consistency of scenarios, representing uncertainty quantitatively, and stress-testing decisions against extreme but plausible cases.
steps: Define the decision and the outcome metrics to forecast (e.g. 12-month adoption of a redesigned feature).
Identify 4-8 key uncertain drivers from research and expert input, and rank them by impact and uncertainty.
Build 3-5 internally consistent scenarios from the most critical drivers (e.g. a 2x2 of market volatility and trust), plus a baseline.
Assign quantitative ranges or distributions to drivers within each scenario.
Simulate outcomes for each design option under each scenario (e.g. Bass diffusion with Monte Carlo, 10,000 runs).
Compare options on robustness, such as worst-case performance and regret, and identify signposts that indicate which scenario is unfolding.
outputs: A set of documented scenarios, simulated outcomes per option and scenario, robustness comparisons and signposts to monitor.
useWhen: Strategic product decisions with high uncertainty, such as redesign options, market entry or AI feature launches.
avoidWhen: Avoid for small reversible decisions or when uncertainty is low and a single forecast suffices.
whyLost: Scenario planning lives in strategy and foresight units, and simulation in operations research; UX rarely joins them to forecast experience outcomes.
whereToUse: Fintech feature launches, health product rollouts, AI assistant adoption planning, platform migration decisions.
example: A trading app compares three redesign options across scenarios of calm, volatile and bear markets. Simulation shows option B wins in calm markets but option C maintains adoption across all three, so the team picks C and monitors volatility as a signpost.

name: Scenario-Based Design
origin: John M. Carroll, 1995; Rosson and Carroll, 2002
summary: Uses concrete narrative scenarios of use as the central design representation from analysis through evaluation, paired with claims analysis.
description: Scenario-based design treats stories of people using a system as the primary design artefact. It moves through problem scenarios (current practice), activity scenarios, information and interaction scenarios, and finally usability-test scenarios, each paired with claims about consequences. The treatise presents claims analysis as born within this approach. Scenarios keep design grounded in specific activity, are accessible to non-specialists and expose assumptions. Contemporary practice retains user stories and scenarios as fragments, but rarely uses them as a systematic, staged method linked to claims, which is why the method is vestigial.
steps: Write problem scenarios describing current practice from field data.
Extract claims about current practice and its tradeoffs.
Write activity scenarios describing new ways of working.
Elaborate into information and interaction scenarios for the proposed design.
Derive usability specifications and test scenarios from them.
Iterate scenarios and claims as evaluation results come in.
outputs: Staged scenario sets, claims tables, usability specifications.
useWhen: Early-to-mid design of new products or major features where shared understanding of use is needed.
avoidWhen: Fine-grained optimisation of existing flows; use analytics or A/B testing.
whyLost: Reduced to user stories in agile backlogs, which keep the narrative shape but drop the staging and claims.
whereToUse: New product definition, AI assistant behaviour design, service design, cross-functional alignment.
example: A telehealth team writes problem scenarios from clinic visits, then activity scenarios for asynchronous consults; claims about patient anxiety while waiting drive a status-update feature.

name: Schema activation analysis
origin: Bartlett's schema theory, 1932; Schank and Abelson's scripts, 1977; Rumelhart, 1980
summary: Identifies which prior knowledge structures, schemas and scripts, a design triggers in users, and whether those activated expectations match how the system actually behaves.
description: Schemas are organised knowledge structures that let people interpret new situations quickly by filling gaps with expectations; scripts are schemas for event sequences, such as a restaurant visit. Interfaces activate schemas through visual cues, labels and flow structure: a shopping cart icon triggers an e-commerce checkout script. When the activated schema matches system behaviour, interaction feels intuitive; when it does not, users make confident, systematic errors. Schema activation analysis elicits users' expectations at key points (via prediction probes, think-aloud or 'what happens next' questions) and compares them with actual behaviour, identifying which cues triggered which schema. Rigour comes from eliciting expectations before the outcome is shown and coding mismatches systematically.
steps: Select key moments where users must anticipate system behaviour (first screens, mode changes, confirmations).
Before each moment, ask participants (6-10) to predict what will happen and what they will do, without showing the outcome.
Ask what cues led to their prediction, to identify the activated schema (for example 'it looks like a printer queue').
Code predictions as matching or mismatching the actual system behaviour, and group mismatches by schema.
Map each mismatched schema to the cues that triggered it and decide whether to change the cues or align behaviour with the schema.
Re-test with new participants to confirm prediction accuracy improves (for example above 80%).
outputs: A map of activated schemas, prediction accuracy per moment, mismatch causes, and recommended cue or behaviour changes.
useWhen: When introducing novel products or interaction models, migrating users between systems, or seeing confident but wrong user behaviour.
avoidWhen: When users have no relevant prior experience at all; use learnability testing. For terminology issues, use a compositionality or vocabulary audit.
whyLost: Schema theory underlies mental model research in UX, but schema elicitation as a structured protocol has largely been replaced by loose 'mental model' talk.
whereToUse: New AI interfaces, medical device migrations, fintech products reinventing banking patterns, and smart home controls.
example: Surgeons switching to a new robotic system press 'Pause' expecting it to freeze instruments in place, as on their old system, but it retracts them. Prediction probes show 9 of 10 hold the old schema, so the action is relabelled 'Retract' and a separate 'Hold' is added.

name: Scree plot vs. parallel analysis
aka: Cattell's scree test vs. Horn's parallel analysis
origin: Raymond Cattell, 1966 (scree test); John Horn, 1965 (parallel analysis)
summary: Comparing the subjective scree elbow with the objective parallel analysis criterion to decide how many factors a UX questionnaire really measures.
description: Retaining too many or too few factors is the most consequential error in EFA. Cattell's scree plot charts eigenvalues in descending order and retains factors above the 'elbow', which is subjective and can be ambiguous. The Kaiser rule (eigenvalues above 1) over-extracts. Parallel analysis compares observed eigenvalues against those from many random datasets of the same size, retaining factors whose eigenvalues exceed the random 95th percentile; simulation studies (Zwick and Velicer, 1986) found it among the most accurate rules. Velicer's MAP test is a further check. Rigour comes from using parallel analysis as the primary criterion, the scree and MAP as corroboration, and examining interpretability of adjacent solutions (k minus 1 and k plus 1).
steps: Compute eigenvalues from the correlation matrix (reduced matrix for common factor analysis where possible).
Draw the scree plot and note the elbow position independently before running parallel analysis.
Run parallel analysis with at least 1,000 random datasets, retaining factors whose eigenvalues exceed the 95th percentile.
Optionally run Velicer's MAP test as a further check.
If criteria disagree, fit the k minus 1, k and k plus 1 solutions and choose based on interpretability and item loadings.
Report all criteria and the rationale for the final choice.
outputs: Overlaid scree and parallel analysis plot, agreed factor count, and documented rationale.
useWhen: Every exploratory factor analysis of UX attitude or experience items.
avoidWhen: Not needed when confirming a known structure (use CFA fit and model comparison instead).
whyLost: SPSS and many textbooks default to the Kaiser rule and scree plot; parallel analysis needs extra syntax or code, so it stayed in psychometric specialist practice.
whereToUse: Scale development for new UX constructs and checking borrowed scales in new markets.
example: For a 30-item fintech onboarding questionnaire, the scree elbow is ambiguous between 3 and 5 factors and Kaiser suggests 7. Parallel analysis retains 4, and the 4-factor solution is the most interpretable.

name: Secondary Analysis of Qualitative Data
origin: Janet Heaton, 2004 (Reworking Qualitative Data); UK Data Archive Qualidata, 1994
summary: Re-analyses existing qualitative datasets for new questions, with explicit checks for fitness for purpose, lost context, consent coverage and transparent reporting.
description: Secondary analysis of qualitative data (Heaton) involves re-using data collected for one purpose to address a different research question. Unlike secondary analysis of quantitative data (which is technically straightforward), secondary analysis of qualitative data raises specific methodological challenges: the original data was collected with different questions in mind, the relational and contextual knowledge the original researcher had is not transferred with the data, and consent for re-use may not have been obtained.
steps: Assess fitness for purpose: Is the original dataset adequate for the new research question? Consider: was data collected from appropriate participants? Were the appropriate topics covered? Was the data collected with sufficient depth?

Account for context loss: The original researcher had knowledge — of the participants, the settings, the research relationship — that is not transferred with the data. Be transparent about this gap in your analysis.

Ethical clearance for re-use: Check whether the original consent covers secondary analysis. If not, what anonymisation procedures are in place? Can re-use harm participants whose data will now be used for a different purpose?

Supplementary data collection: In many cases, secondary analysis is strengthened by collecting supplementary data (additional interviews or observations) specifically to address gaps in the original dataset.

Transparency in reporting: Report fully: the original study's purpose, the secondary analysis purpose, the time gap between collection and re-analysis, and the limitations of working with data collected by someone else.
outputs: A fitness-for-purpose assessment, consent and ethics review, re-analysis findings, identified gaps for supplementary data collection, and a transparent methods account.
useWhen: You have a research repository or past studies relevant to a new question, recruiting is costly or burdensome for participants, or you want to compare across previous studies.
avoidWhen: Original data lack context, quality or consent for re-use, or the new question needs data the original prompts never covered; run primary research instead.
whyLost: Research repositories promised re-use, but most re-use is skimming tagged highlights, without assessing context loss, consent or fitness for the new question.
whereToUse: Research repositories and research operations, meta-synthesis across studies, sensitive populations where repeat interviewing is burdensome, and quick-turnaround strategy questions.
example: A team asked about older users' attitudes to AI re-analyses 30 interviews from an earlier accessibility study. They find consent covers re-use, note the original prompts never mentioned AI, and run 5 supplementary interviews to fill the gap.

name: Segment Typing Tool (Discriminant Classification of New Users)
origin: Fisher's linear discriminant (1936) applied to market segment typing
summary: Uses a few survey questions to assign any new person to an existing persona or segment.
description: Once segments or personas exist, teams need to recognise members in new studies and recruitment screeners. A typing tool uses discriminant analysis (or logistic regression) on the original segmentation data to find the smallest set of "golden questions" that predicts segment membership accurately. The resulting equations are added to screeners and surveys so every future participant can be tagged with their persona. Sauro and Lewis demonstrate it as the practical payoff of factor and cluster analysis, keeping personas alive and measurable rather than posters on the wall.
steps: Start from a segmentation study with known segment membership for each respondent.
Run stepwise discriminant analysis to find questions that best separate segments.
Check classification accuracy with holdout data or cross-validation (aim for 80% or more).
Reduce to the fewest items that keep accuracy acceptable.
Embed the items and scoring in screeners, surveys and analytics.
outputs: A short scoring tool that types new participants into personas.
useWhen: Personas or segments need to be used in recruitment, surveys and analytics.
avoidWhen: Segments were built qualitatively without data to train a classifier.
whyLost: Persona work in UX usually ends at the deliverable; the market research practice of typing tools never came across.
whereToUse: Research recruiting, product surveys, CRM tagging.
example: Six golden questions classify new respondents into five insurance personas with 84% accuracy, so every benchmark can now be reported by persona.
sources: Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)

name: Selective Coding and Core Category Identification
origin: Glaser & Strauss, 1967; formalised by Strauss & Corbin, 1990
summary: The final grounded theory stage: choosing one core category that integrates all others into a bounded, testable theoretical proposition.
description: Selective coding is the final stage of Grounded Theory. You identify a single core category — the central phenomenon — and relate all other categories to it. The core category must: appear frequently in the data, be connected to all other major categories, be analytic rather than descriptive, and be able to absorb variation. When you find the core category, all the categories you identified in axial coding should make sense in relation to it.
steps: Review all your categories and axial coding memos. Ask: What is the central phenomenon that everything else relates to? What is the story of this data?
Write a storyline: a descriptive narrative of the central phenomenon and its relationship to all other categories. This is typically 2–3 paragraphs.
Test the core category: does every major category connect to it? If a major category does not connect, either the core category is wrong, or that category needs more investigation.
Write the theoretical proposition: a statement of the theory generated from the data. This should be generalisable beyond your specific sample while remaining grounded in the data.
Identify what the theory does NOT explain — these are the boundaries of your theory and honest reporting requires you to state them.
outputs: A core category, a written storyline, a theoretical proposition with stated scope and boundaries, and an integrated category diagram.
useWhen: When a programme of research must yield a single explanatory model that the organisation can reuse, test and design against.
avoidWhen: When stakeholders need a list of issues or opportunities rather than a theory; when data are insufficient or not theoretically sampled. Use thematic synthesis or an affinity diagram.
whyLost: Industry timelines reward actionable findings over theory, and few UX researchers are trained to write and bound a theoretical proposition, so studies stop at themes.
whereToUse: Strategic foundational research, research-led product strategy, and academic-industry collaborations where a reusable model of user behaviour is the deliverable.
example: After axial coding of interviews about a telehealth app, the team identifies 'maintaining clinical legitimacy' as the core category linking privacy concerns, video reluctance and note-taking workarounds. The proposition guides a roadmap and a follow-up survey.
sources: Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick ed.)

name: Semantic Differential
origin: Charles Osgood, George Suci and Percy Tannenbaum, 1957
summary: Rates a concept on bipolar adjective pairs to map its connotative meaning along evaluation, potency and activity dimensions.
description: Osgood's semantic differential asks people to rate a concept on seven-point scales anchored by opposite adjectives, such as good-bad, strong-weak, active-passive. Factor analyses across many concepts and cultures showed ratings consistently load on three dimensions: evaluation, potency and activity (EPA), which together form a 'semantic space'. The rigorous method selects adjective pairs relevant to the concept and representative of each dimension, randomises pole direction to avoid response sets, and uses factor analysis or the established EPA structure to score concepts and compute distances between them. In UX it is the ancestor of AttrakDiff and UEQ, but the original technique remains useful for custom brand and emotion research where no standard instrument fits, such as comparing how users perceive an AI persona against intended brand attributes.
steps: Define the concepts to rate (e.g. product versions, brand, competitor, ideal product).
Select 12-20 relevant adjective pairs covering evaluation, potency and activity, plus domain-specific pairs, and pilot them for relevance.
Randomise the left-right position of positive poles across items.
Collect ratings from 30+ participants per concept.
Run factor analysis or score by established dimensions and compute concept profiles.
Compare profiles and distances between concepts, such as actual versus ideal product.
outputs: Concept profiles on adjective pairs, dimension scores, semantic space plots and distances between concepts.
useWhen: Brand perception, persona and tone-of-voice research, emotional response comparison and cross-cultural meaning studies.
avoidWhen: When a validated UX instrument (UEQ, AttrakDiff) already covers the constructs; use that for benchmarkable results.
whyLost: Vestigial: Original technique less used than derivative instruments (AttrakDiff, UEQ); still valid for brand/emotion research.
whereToUse: Brand perception; emotional response measurement; cross-cultural comparison.
example: A bank tested how customers perceived its new AI assistant persona. Semantic differential profiles showed it rated as friendly but weak and passive, far from the intended 'competent' brand, prompting a revised tone of voice.

name: Semantic leaps analysis
origin: Seana Coulson, Semantic Leaps, 2001; Fauconnier and Turner's conceptual blending, 2002
summary: Identifies points where users must reinterpret a word, icon or metaphor by shifting frames or blending concepts, and measures whether they make the leap correctly.
description: Coulson showed that comprehension often requires frame-shifting: reanalysing meaning when new information conflicts with an initial interpretation, as in jokes and garden-path sentences. Conceptual blending describes how people combine elements of different domains into new meanings, which is how interface metaphors such as 'desktop', 'trash' or 'cloud' work. Semantic leaps analysis catalogues the frames and blends an interface relies on, identifies places where users must shift frames mid-task, and tests whether they do so correctly and at what cost. Failure points include metaphors whose source domain implies wrong behaviours and messages that require reinterpretation. Rigour comes from explicit frame mapping and from measuring reinterpretation through prediction and reading-time tasks.
steps: Inventory metaphors, icons and key terms and identify the source frame each relies on.
Map which source-domain properties are carried into the interface blend and which are not.
Identify frame-shift points, where users must abandon an initial interpretation (for example 'archive' that deletes after 30 days).
Test with 8-12 users using prediction tasks and think-aloud, noting misinterpretations and hesitation.
Optionally measure reading or decision time at shift points versus control points.
Redesign misleading metaphors or add cues that trigger the correct frame earlier, and re-test.
outputs: A frame and blend inventory, frame-shift points with failure rates, and revised metaphors or cues.
useWhen: When designing novel metaphors, naming new features, or when users misread messages that are literally accurate.
avoidWhen: For literal, conventional interfaces with established terms; compositionality or content audits suffice.
whyLost: Cognitive linguistics has rich theory but little applied tradition in UX, where metaphor choice is treated as branding.
whereToUse: AI assistants and agents, financial product naming, health apps, and novel interaction models.
example: A surgical system labels a mode 'Autopilot'. Users carry over the aviation frame, expecting the robot to hold position safely, but it only stabilises the camera. Prediction tests show 7 of 10 surgeons misread it, so the mode is renamed 'Camera steady'.

name: Semiotic Analysis
origin: Charles Sanders Peirce and Ferdinand de Saussure, late 19th/early 20th century; semiotic engineering by Clarisse de Souza, 2005
summary: Analyses icons, labels and visual language as signs, classifying how they signify (icon, index, symbol) and testing whether intended meanings reach users.
description: Semiotics studies how signs carry meaning. Peirce classified signs by their relation to what they stand for: icons resemble it, indexes are causally or physically connected to it, and symbols depend on learned convention. Saussure separated the signifier from the signified and showed meaning arises from difference within a system. Semiotic engineering (de Souza) treats the whole interface as a message from designer to user. As a method, analysts inventory signs, classify each, document intended meaning and cultural dependencies, and then test interpretation with users through comprehension and matching tasks. Rigour comes from explicit classification, considering the sign system as a whole (are distinctions consistent?), and empirical checking across cultural groups, since symbolic signs carry least transferable meaning.
steps: Inventory the signs in scope: icons, labels, colours, sounds and metaphors.
Classify each as icon, index or symbol and record its intended meaning.
Analyse the sign system for consistency and contrast, flagging signs whose meaning depends on unlearned conventions.
Run comprehension tests with 15-30 users per audience segment, asking them to name the meaning of signs out of context and in context.
Score comprehension (ISO 9186 suggests 66-85% correct as acceptance thresholds for public symbols).
Redesign signs that fail, preferring iconic or indexical forms or adding labels, and re-test.
outputs: Sign inventory with classifications, system consistency analysis, comprehension scores by audience, redesign recommendations.
useWhen: Icon sets, visual languages, international and cross-cultural products, and accessibility reviews of non-text cues.
avoidWhen: When labels are textual and the issue is information architecture; use card sorting or tree testing.
whyLost: Siloed: Academic foundation; icon and visual language work applies semiotic principles but rarely names them.
whereToUse: Icon design; visual language systems; cross-cultural UX; accessibility.
example: A global health app used a floppy-disk icon for saving records. Comprehension testing in Kenya and India found under 40% recognition among younger health workers; replacing it with a labelled checkmark raised recognition above 90%.
sources: Louder Than Words
Semantic Leaps
The Semiotic Engineering of Human-Computer Interaction (Clarisse de Souza)
ISO 9186 Graphical symbols: Test methods
reference: de Souza, C. S. (2005). The Semiotic Engineering of Human-Computer Interaction. MIT Press.

name: Semiotic Analysis of Interfaces
origin: Charles S. Peirce (1867-1914); Ferdinand de Saussure (1916); Roland Barthes (1957-1972)
summary: Diagnoses icon, label and visual-language failures as breakdowns at iconic, indexical, symbolic, connotative or mythic levels of signification.
description: Peirce's trichotomy distinguishes icons (resemble their referent), indexes (causally connected to it) and symbols (conventional). Saussure contributes the signifier/signified dyad; Barthes adds denotation, connotation and myth (naturalised ideology). The treatise argues every UI element is a sign: the floppy disk icon is now a symbol, functioning through convention rather than resemblance. Analysing icon failures semiotically asks whether the failure is iconic (does not look like its referent), indexical (no causal link to the function) or symbolic (convention not established in this user population), and the diagnosis changes the design response. Connotative analysis reveals cultural meanings that differ across markets. In HCI it was developed further as semiotic engineering by de Souza.
steps: Inventory signs in scope: icons, labels, colours, layout conventions, sounds.
For each, record intended referent and classify the sign relation (icon, index, symbol).
Test comprehension with target users (for example open-ended icon naming) across cultures.
Classify failures by semiotic level and analyse connotations and myths.
Redesign signs according to the failing level (resemblance, causal cue, or convention-building).
Re-test comprehension and document the visual language rules.
outputs: Sign inventory with semiotic classification, comprehension results, redesign rationale, visual-language guidelines.
useWhen: Icon and visual language design, cross-cultural products, error and status communication.
avoidWhen: Problems driven by flow or performance rather than meaning.
whyLost: Semiotics remained an academic and media-studies discipline, and de Souza's semiotic engineering stayed within HCI research; practitioners treated icon choice as visual design rather than sign analysis.
whereToUse: Design systems, global apps, AI status indicators, automotive symbols, medical device labelling.
example: A 'sparkle' icon for AI features is recognised by 80% of US users but 30% of users in another market; analysis shows it functions purely symbolically, so a text label is added until the convention establishes.

name: Sensemaking Research
origin: Karl Weick, 1995; Brenda Dervin, 1983 (Sense-Making Methodology)
summary: Investigates how people construct meaning from ambiguous, incomplete cues, revealing the gaps, questions and bridges users build when information environments fall short.
description: Sensemaking describes how people make meaning when cues are ambiguous. Weick emphasised that sensemaking is retrospective, social and driven by plausibility rather than accuracy. Dervin's Sense-Making Methodology operationalised the idea as an interviewing approach: a situation-gap-bridge metaphor in which people encounter gaps in understanding and construct bridges using questions, information and ideas. Micro-moment timeline interviews walk participants through a specific episode step by step, asking at each moment what questions arose, what helped, what hindered and what they concluded. Pirolli and Card's sensemaking loop added a model of analysts foraging for and structuring information. Rigour comes from anchoring interviews in real episodes, systematically probing each moment with the same neutral question set, and coding gaps and bridges across participants.
steps: Recruit 8-15 participants who recently faced an ambiguous situation the product should support.
Have each participant reconstruct the episode as a timeline of discrete moments.
For each moment ask a fixed set of neutral questions: what was unclear, what questions arose, what helped, what hindered, what conclusion followed.
Code responses into situations, gaps, bridges and outcomes.
Compare across participants to identify recurring gaps and the bridges people improvise.
Translate recurring gaps into information and tool requirements.
outputs: Micro-moment timelines, gap and bridge taxonomy, requirements for information support.
useWhen: Data analysis tools, enterprise knowledge systems, crisis or incident tools, health information and any domain where users must interpret ambiguous information.
avoidWhen: Well-structured, routine tasks; contextual inquiry or task analysis is more efficient.
whyLost: Siloed: Organizational theory; applied in enterprise UX and knowledge management; rarely in consumer products.
whereToUse: Enterprise knowledge tools; crisis communication; complex dashboards; data analysis tools.
example: A security operations product interviewed analysts about recent ambiguous alerts. Timelines showed a recurring gap: whether the asset involved was business-critical. Analysts bridged it by messaging colleagues, so asset criticality was surfaced in the alert view.
sources: Mapping Experiences

name: Sensitivity analysis with the E-value
origin: Tyler VanderWeele and Peng Ding, 2017
summary: Quantifying how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away an observed causal estimate from non-randomised UX data.
description: Every observational causal estimate rests on the assumption of no unmeasured confounding. The E-value is the minimum strength of association, on the risk ratio scale, that an unmeasured confounder would need with both the treatment and the outcome, conditional on measured covariates, to fully explain away the observed association. For a risk ratio RR above 1, E = RR + sqrt(RR x (RR minus 1)). An E-value is also computed for the confidence limit closest to the null. Large E-values (e.g. above 3) indicate robustness; values near 1 mean modest confounding could nullify the result. Rigour comes from reporting both E-values, benchmarking against the strength of measured confounders, and interpreting them in context rather than as a pass or fail threshold.
steps: Estimate the adjusted effect as a risk ratio, or convert odds ratios, hazard ratios or standardised differences using published approximations.
Compute the E-value for the point estimate and for the confidence limit nearest the null (e.g. with dowhy, the EValue package or the formula).
Benchmark: compare with the associations of the strongest measured confounders with treatment and outcome.
Name plausible unmeasured confounders from qualitative work and judge whether any could reach the E-value.
Report the E-values and benchmarks alongside the estimate, stating the conclusion's robustness in plain language.
outputs: Point and confidence-limit E-values, benchmark comparisons and a robustness statement for decision-makers.
useWhen: Any observational causal claim from product data, such as feature impact, programme evaluation or health outcomes, especially when presented to leadership or regulators.
avoidWhen: Not needed for randomised experiments with good compliance. For bias from selection or measurement error, use other bias analysis methods.
whyLost: The E-value is recent (2017) and epidemiological; UX causal work rarely reaches the stage of formal bias analysis.
whereToUse: Health and wellbeing apps, fintech financial outcomes, retrospective feature evaluations and board-level causal claims.
example: A fintech team finds that users of a spending insights feature are 1.5 times as likely to stay within budget. The E-value of 2.36 (CI limit 1.9) means an unmeasured confounder like conscientiousness would need a risk ratio of about 2.4 with both variables, stronger than any measured confounder, so the claim is reported as moderately robust.

name: Sensory Ethnography
origin: Sarah Pink, 2009 (Doing Sensory Ethnography)
summary: Ethnographic fieldwork that attends to sound, smell, touch, temperature and movement as well as sight, to understand the embodied texture of practices and environments.
description: Sensory ethnography (Sarah Pink) challenges the visualist bias of most ethnographic fieldwork — the assumption that what matters is what can be seen and documented photographically. Pink argues that smell, sound, touch, taste, and kinaesthetic sense are equally important in understanding how people experience and navigate their environments. For UX research: sensory ethnography is appropriate for any research context where the full sensory environment shapes how people interact with digital products — hospitals, kitchens, vehicles, outdoor environments, manufacturing floors.
steps: Sensory audit of the fieldwork site: Before formal data collection, systematically attend to all senses. What sounds are prominent? What smells? What textures do people handle? What kinaesthetic patterns (postures, movements) characterise the environment?
Sensory diaries: Ask participants to keep sensory diaries — recording not just what they did but what they smelled, heard, touched, and felt during their interactions with products and environments.
Sensory walks: Conduct walking interviews with explicit sensory focus: 'As we walk through, tell me what you can smell / hear / feel underfoot.' Sensory attention reshapes what gets noticed.

Video and audio recording as sensory data: Video is not only a document of visual events — it captures sound, movement, and spatial arrangement. Analyse video for what senses are engaged, not just what is visible.

Researcher sensory reflexivity: Document your own sensory experience of the field. How did the environment smell, sound, feel? Your sensory experience is data — it documents the sensory texture of the field.
outputs: Sensory audits, participant sensory diaries, multisensory recordings, reflexive researcher accounts, and insights on how sensory context shapes product use.
useWhen: Products are used in physically rich or demanding environments, such as kitchens, hospitals, factories, cars or homes, or the product itself is sensory (devices, food, retail spaces).
avoidWhen: The research concerns abstract digital tasks where environment is not a factor; use remote usability testing or interviews. Avoid if you cannot spend time in the field.
whyLost: UX ethnography became visually documented (photos, screen recordings), and sensory methods remained in anthropology and design academia.
whereToUse: Smart home and appliances, healthcare environments, automotive, retail and hospitality, wearables, and accessibility research with people with sensory impairments.
example: Studying a smart thermostat, researchers conduct sensory walks through homes and find people judge warmth by drafts and floor temperature rather than numbers, leading to room-feel presets instead of target temperatures.
sources: Doing Sensory Ethnography (Sarah Pink)
Ethnographic Thinking (Hasbrouck)
Handbook of Ethnography

name: Sentiment Analysis
donor: Computational linguistics and natural language processing
origin: Pang, Lee and Vaithyanathan, 2002; Turney, 2002
summary: Automatically classifies the emotional valence of text such as reviews, tickets and open-ended responses, scaling qualitative signal across thousands of documents.
description: Sentiment analysis classifies text as positive, negative or neutral, or scores it on a continuous scale, using lexicons, supervised machine learning or transformer-based models and large language models. Aspect-based sentiment goes further by attaching sentiment to specific features or topics, which is far more useful for product decisions. In UX research pipelines, tools such as spaCy with transformer models handle tokenisation and entity extraction before classification. Rigour comes from validating the model on a hand-labelled sample from your own domain (general models misread sarcasm, domain jargon and negation), reporting accuracy or F1, monitoring drift over time, and combining sentiment with topic or aspect extraction so results point to causes. Aggregated scores should be treated as indicators prompting deeper reading, not as findings in themselves.
steps: Collect and clean the text corpus (reviews, tickets, survey comments), removing duplicates and personal data.
Choose an approach: lexicon, pretrained transformer or LLM-based classification, ideally aspect-based.
Hand-label a validation sample of 200-500 items from your domain with two coders.
Evaluate model accuracy or F1 against the labels and adjust or fine-tune until performance is acceptable (e.g. F1 above 0.8).
Run the model across the corpus, combining sentiment with topic or aspect extraction.
Read representative examples behind key trends and monitor scores over time for drift.
outputs: Sentiment scores by document and aspect, validation metrics, trend dashboards, representative quotes.
useWhen: Large volumes of unstructured feedback: app reviews, support tickets, social media, open-ended survey responses.
avoidWhen: Small qualitative datasets where manual thematic analysis is feasible and more nuanced, or highly sarcastic or specialised language without validation data.
whyLost: Still in use: Scalable qualitative signal from unstructured text; growing with AI tools.
whereToUse: Voice of customer; product review analysis; support ticket triage; social listening.
example: A telecom app analysed 60,000 app reviews with aspect-based sentiment. Negative sentiment about 'login' tripled after a release; reading samples showed biometric login failures on one OS version, which engineering fixed within a week.

name: Sentiment analysis pipeline
origin: Pang, Lee & Vaithyanathan, 2002; Bo Pang & Lillian Lee, 2008; Bing Liu, 2012
summary: An automated pipeline that classifies the polarity, emotion or aspect-level opinion of user text at scale, validated against human coding.
description: Sentiment analysis assigns positive, negative or neutral polarity, emotional categories or aspect-level opinions (sentiment about fees versus sentiment about speed) to text. A rigorous pipeline cleans and segments text, chooses a model suited to the domain (lexicon, fine-tuned classifier or LLM), validates against human-coded samples, and reports accuracy by class and segment. In practice sentiment is often a dashboard number from a generic model that misreads domain language (e.g. 'the market is killing it' or sarcasm), so the method has become vestigial. Aspect-based sentiment is far more actionable than document-level polarity, and accuracy must be checked per language and channel.
steps: Define the unit (sentence, comment, ticket) and the labels needed (polarity, emotion, aspects).
Create a human-coded validation set of 300-1,000 items with inter-rater reliability of 0.7 or above.
Choose a model: fine-tuned transformer, domain lexicon or LLM prompt, and run it on the validation set.
Report precision, recall and F1 per class and per language or channel; set a minimum (e.g. macro F1 of 0.75) before use.
Apply aspect extraction to attribute sentiment to product features.
Monitor sentiment trends with confidence intervals and recheck accuracy quarterly for drift.
outputs: Validated sentiment and aspect labels at scale, trend lines with uncertainty, and per-class accuracy documentation.
useWhen: Monitoring opinion over time across large volumes of reviews, tickets or comments, and identifying which product aspects drive negative sentiment.
avoidWhen: Avoid for nuanced understanding of why people feel something (use qualitative analysis), for small samples, or without validation in the domain's language.
whyLost: Off-the-shelf dashboards made sentiment a vanity metric, stripping the validation and aspect-level analysis that make it meaningful.
whereToUse: App store reviews, NPS verbatims, support tickets, social listening, AI assistant conversation logs.
example: A fintech team validates an aspect-based model on 600 coded reviews (macro F1 0.81). It shows that negative sentiment after an update is driven by the new fee display rather than app speed, as the dashboard had implied.
sources: A Practical Guide to Sentiment Analysis (Erik Cambria et al.)

name: Sentinel UX Surveillance
origin: Sentinel surveillance systems; adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Intensively monitors a few carefully chosen high-harm domains or sites with standardised usability protocols to give a high-resolution signal of UX health.
description: Sentinel surveillance collects detailed, high-quality data from a small number of selected sites. The treatise proposes sentinel UX surveillance in high-harm contexts, financial services, healthcare, government services and employment platforms, where failures have serious consequences. Sentinel sites run regular detailed usability assessments of products in their domain using standardised protocols that allow cross-product comparison and trend tracking. The trade-off is representativeness for depth: sentinel data are not population prevalence estimates, but they detect emerging problems early and characterise them richly, complementing passive and active systems.
steps: Select sentinel domains and products based on harm potential and reach.
Develop standardised assessment protocols (tasks, metrics, severity, accessibility checks).
Train assessors and calibrate inter-rater reliability.
Run assessments at regular intervals (for example quarterly) and after major releases.
Compare products and track trends; flag emerging problems.
Share findings with providers and regulators.
outputs: Standardised domain scorecards, trend data, early warnings, cross-product comparisons.
useWhen: High-stakes sectors needing early detection and rich characterisation of UX harms.
avoidWhen: When population prevalence is needed; use active surveillance.
whyLost: No institutional owner; UX evaluations are proprietary and non-standardised.
whereToUse: Banking, health portals, benefits systems, job platforms, telecoms.
example: A consumer body assesses the ten largest banks' apps quarterly on standard fraud-reporting tasks; one bank's completion rate drops from 90% to 55% after a redesign, prompting rapid engagement.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
WHO (2006) Communicable disease surveillance and response systems: guide to monitoring and evaluating
Teutsch SM & Churchill RE (2000) Principles and Practice of Public Health Surveillance
reference: Teutsch SM & Churchill RE (Eds) (2000) Principles and Practice of Public Health Surveillance. 2nd ed. Oxford University Press.

name: Sequence Alignment of Behavioural Paths
origin: Needleman and Wunsch (1970); Abbott (1990s) optimal matching in sociology
summary: Measures similarity between users' action sequences by edit cost, then clusters paths to reveal typical routes and deviant trajectories.
description: Listed in the treatise's borrowing matrix, sequence alignment comes from bioinformatics (aligning DNA sequences) and was adapted to social science by Abbott as optimal matching. The distance between two sequences is the minimum cost of insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn one into the other. Pairwise distances are then clustered to produce typologies of trajectories. In UX it compares whole navigation paths rather than single transitions: which routes do users take to complete onboarding, and how do failing paths differ from successful ones? Cost settings must be justified, and results visualised with sequence index plots.
steps: Encode sessions or journeys as sequences of states or actions.
Define substitution and indel costs (data-driven or theory-based).
Compute pairwise distances with optimal matching or alternatives (for example LCS).
Cluster sequences and select a typology using quality indices.
Visualise with sequence index and state distribution plots.
Relate typology to outcomes and investigate deviant paths qualitatively.
outputs: Path typologies, representative sequences, path-outcome associations.
useWhen: Comparing whole journeys (onboarding, checkout, multi-session adoption) across users.
avoidWhen: When only immediate transitions matter (use lag sequential analysis) or sequences are extremely long and noisy.
whyLost: Unknown outside bioinformatics and life-course sociology; analytics tools focus on fixed funnels.
whereToUse: Onboarding journeys, multi-week adoption, learning paths, patient portal journeys.
example: Optimal matching on first-week sequences of a language app finds four path types; 'explorers' who sample many lesson types retain best, so recommendations encourage variety early.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)

Gabadinho A et al. (2011) Analyzing and visualizing state sequences in R with TraMineR. J Stat Software

name: Sequential Explanatory Design
origin: John Creswell and colleagues, 2003
summary: Runs a quantitative phase first, then a qualitative phase designed to explain its results, using quantitative findings to select participants and focus questions.
description: In an explanatory sequential design, the quantitative strand comes first and has priority; the qualitative strand follows to explain surprising, significant or ambiguous results. Integration happens at two points: quantitative results determine who is sampled for the qualitative phase (for example extreme cases, outliers or specific segments) and what the interviews probe. The final interpretation explains how qualitative findings account for quantitative patterns. Rigour comes from defining in advance which results will trigger follow-up, selecting participants purposefully from the quantitative sample using clear criteria, designing interview guides around the specific results, and reporting how the explanation connects back. In UX it formalises the common pattern of following analytics or surveys with interviews, adding discipline to participant selection that is often missing.
steps: Design and run the quantitative phase (survey, analytics or experiment) with clear hypotheses.
Analyse results and identify findings needing explanation: surprises, outliers, segment differences.
Select qualitative participants purposefully from the quantitative sample using explicit criteria (e.g. 6-10 per contrasting segment).
Develop interview or observation guides targeting the specific quantitative results.
Conduct and analyse the qualitative phase.
Integrate by explaining each quantitative finding with qualitative evidence, noting where explanation is partial.
outputs: Quantitative results, purposeful follow-up sample, qualitative explanations, integrated report linking the two.
useWhen: Explaining survey or analytics results, understanding why segments differ, and following up A/B test outcomes.
avoidWhen: When the domain is unknown and measures cannot yet be defined; use an exploratory sequential design instead.
whyLost: Teams often interview a convenience sample after a metric change, skipping profile-based sampling and formal integration, so the design survives in name only.
whereToUse: Large-scale product research; survey follow-up interviews; analytics-driven qualitative.
example: A survey of 3,000 e-commerce customers showed loyalty members rated delivery lower than non-members. Follow-up interviews with 10 low-scoring members revealed they expected priority delivery that the programme did not offer.
sources: Research Design
Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (Creswell & Plano Clark)
Oxford Handbook of Multimethod & Mixed Methods Research
Research Design (Leavy)

name: Sequential Pattern Mining
origin: Rakesh Agrawal and Ramakrishnan Srikant (1995-1996); PrefixSpan by Jian Pei et al. (2001)
summary: Finds frequent ordered subsequences of actions across many sessions, optionally with gaps, to reveal common behavioural paths and those that discriminate outcomes.
description: Sequential pattern mining finds subsequences (not necessarily contiguous) that occur in at least a minimum proportion of sequences. Algorithms such as GSP, SPADE and PrefixSpan scale to millions of sessions. Constraints on gaps, window length and pattern length keep results meaningful. Contrast or discriminative pattern mining compares support between groups (e.g. converters vs abandoners) to find sequences characteristic of each. Compared with path diagrams, which show only contiguous next steps, this finds patterns like 'viewed pricing ... opened docs ... invited teammate' wherever they occur, giving hypotheses for qualitative follow-up.
steps: Encode sessions or user histories as sequences of abstracted events.
Set minimum support (e.g. 2-5%) and constraints on maximum gap and pattern length.
Run PrefixSpan or SPADE to extract frequent patterns.
For outcome comparison, compute support in each group and rank patterns by lift or statistical tests, correcting for multiple testing.
Filter redundant patterns (closed or maximal patterns) and review top patterns with session replays.
Turn discriminative patterns into hypotheses and test them experimentally.
outputs: Frequent and discriminative sequential patterns with support, lift and significance.
useWhen: Large logs where you want to discover characteristic action sequences or 'aha' paths.
avoidWhen: Small samples; or when timing and duration matter more than order (use sequence analysis or survival models).
whyLost: It stayed in data mining venues, and product teams rely on predefined funnels.
whereToUse: Activation analysis, feature discovery paths, learning platforms, game progression.
example: In a collaboration tool, the pattern 'create doc ... share link ... receive comment' within 7 days has support of 31% among retained users versus 6% among churned, guiding an onboarding nudge.
sources: Srikant & Agrawal, Mining sequential patterns: Generalizations and performance improvements (1996), EDBT
Pei et al., PrefixSpan (2001), ICDE
Fournier-Viger et al., A survey of sequential pattern mining (2017), Data Science and Pattern Recognition
reference: Pei, J., et al. (2001). PrefixSpan: Mining sequential patterns efficiently by prefix-projected pattern growth. ICDE 2001.

name: Sequential Testing (SPRT and Group Sequential Designs)
origin: Abraham Wald, 1945 (SPRT); Pocock (1977) and O'Brien and Fleming (1979) group sequential boundaries; Lan-DeMets alpha spending (1983); mSPRT for online tests (Johari et al., 2017)
summary: Lets experimenters monitor results repeatedly and stop early for benefit, harm or futility while controlling the false positive rate.
description: Peeking at a fixed-horizon A/B test and stopping when p < 0.05 inflates false positives dramatically, to 20-30% with frequent looks. Sequential methods fix this. Wald's SPRT compares the likelihood ratio of two hypotheses after each observation against boundaries set by desired error rates, typically requiring far fewer observations on average. Clinical trials use group sequential designs with a few planned interim analyses and alpha-spending functions (O'Brien-Fleming boundaries are conservative early). Mixture SPRT gives always-valid p-values for continuous monitoring. These methods let teams stop harmful tests early and avoid wasted traffic, legitimately.
steps: Pre-specify hypotheses, minimum detectable effect, alpha, power and the monitoring plan (continuous or K interim looks).
Choose a method: SPRT or mSPRT for continuous monitoring; O'Brien-Fleming or Pocock boundaries via alpha spending for planned looks.
Compute boundaries and expected sample size; register the plan.
Monitor at planned points, stopping when a boundary is crossed for efficacy, harm or futility.
Report the stopping time, adjusted estimates (correcting for bias from early stopping) and confidence intervals.
Never switch to naive tests mid-experiment.
outputs: A pre-registered monitoring plan, stopping decisions with controlled error rates and adjusted effect estimates.
useWhen: Experiments where early stopping matters (risky changes, scarce traffic) or stakeholders will inevitably peek.
avoidWhen: Very short tests with one planned analysis; a fixed-horizon test is simpler.
whyLost: Most UX teams use fixed-horizon calculators and peek anyway; clinical-trial statistics did not travel to product design.
whereToUse: Pricing tests, checkout changes, guardrail monitoring, risky AI feature rollouts.
example: A fintech tests a new onboarding flow with an O'Brien-Fleming design and four looks. At the second look, account-funding rate is significantly lower, so the test stops early, saving two weeks of exposure to a worse flow.

name: Sequential vs. Random Access Learning in Onboarding
origin: Susan Weinschenk, 2011; drawing on instructional design research
summary: Decides whether onboarding should present content in a fixed sequence or allow self-directed access, based on task dependencies, learner expertise and goals.
description: People learn some material best in a fixed sequence, where later concepts depend on earlier ones, and other material best through self-directed, random access driven by immediate needs. Instructional research also shows that learner control helps experienced users but can overwhelm novices (the expertise reversal effect). This method applies those findings to onboarding: the team maps dependencies among concepts and tasks, segments users by prior expertise, and designs a sequenced core for prerequisites with random-access resources for everything else. Variants are tested by measuring time to first value, error rates, completion and later retention. Rigour comes from evidence-based dependency mapping, expertise-segmented analysis and measuring learning outcomes rather than tutorial completion alone.
steps: Identify which learning type dominates your user population: track navigation paths in onboarding.
Sequential users follow prescribed paths; random access users skip, revisit, and explore.
Compute: what % of users complete onboarding in the intended sequence?
If < 50%, the onboarding is designed for sequential users but a majority are random access.
Design: offer both a guided track (sequential) and an exploration mode (random access) with the same content.
outputs: A dependency map of what must be learned in order, a mixed onboarding design (sequenced core plus on-demand extras), and test results on learning and activation.
useWhen: Designing onboarding, tutorials and help for complex products, especially where users vary widely in prior expertise.
avoidWhen: Avoid elaborate onboarding for simple products that should be self-explanatory; fix the product instead.
whyLost: Onboarding is driven by growth metrics and pattern libraries (carousels, checklists) rather than learning theory about sequence and learner control.
whereToUse: Onboarding design, tutorial design, help documentation architecture, learning product design.
example: An accounting SaaS finds novices fail when allowed to skip bank setup, while accountants resent forced tours; a sequenced core for prerequisites plus a random-access library raises activation for both groups.
sources: 100 Things Every Designer Should Know About People — Susan Weinschenk
reference: Weinschenk S (2011) 100 Things Every Designer Should Know About People. New Riders

name: Service Design Research
origin: G. Lynn Shostack, 1984 (service blueprint); Birgit Mager and others, 1990s
summary: Researches and designs a service across all touchpoints, channels, staff and backstage processes, using blueprints and journey maps grounded in field research.
description: Service design treats a service as a system of interactions between customers, staff, technology and processes over time and across channels. Research combines field methods (shadowing, interviews with customers and frontline staff, diary studies) with mapping. The central artefact, Shostack's service blueprint, aligns customer actions with frontstage staff actions, backstage activities and support processes, separated by lines of interaction, visibility and internal interaction. Journey maps and ecosystem maps complement it. Rigour comes from grounding maps in observed evidence rather than workshop assumptions, including staff and back-office perspectives, quantifying pain points where possible (wait times, failure rates) and prototyping changes to the service as a whole, not only its digital touchpoints. It is particularly suited to hybrid digital-physical services where failure often originates backstage.
steps: Define the service scope and the customer and staff groups involved.
Conduct field research: shadow frontline staff, interview 8-15 customers and staff, and collect operational data.
Build a current-state service blueprint with customer actions, frontstage, backstage and support processes, citing evidence for each step.
Mark failure points, wait points and handoffs, quantifying them where data exists.
Co-design future-state blueprints with staff and customers.
Prototype and pilot service changes end to end, measuring outcomes across channels.
outputs: Evidence-based service blueprints (current and future), journey and ecosystem maps, prioritised failure points, pilot results.
useWhen: Multichannel services spanning digital and physical touchpoints, such as healthcare, banking, government, retail and logistics.
avoidWhen: Isolated feature work with no backstage or cross-channel dependencies; use usability testing or journey mapping alone.
whyLost: Still in use: Grew rapidly; especially relevant for hybrid digital-physical services.
whereToUse: Healthcare; banking; retail; government services; any multichannel experience.
example: A hospital outpatient booking app had good usability scores but high no-show rates. Blueprinting showed letters and SMS reminders came from separate systems with conflicting times, so the fix was backstage data integration rather than app redesign.

name: SERVQUAL
origin: Parasuraman, Zeithaml and Berry (1985); presented by Veal and Darcy as the conceptual framework for a customer service quality study in sport and leisure
summary: Measures service quality as the gap between what customers expected and what they say they actually received, attribute by attribute.
description: SERVQUAL is a survey approach to service quality based on disconfirmation: quality is judged by comparing customers' expectations of a service with their assessment of how it actually performed. Veal and Darcy set it out as a conceptual framework for a customer service quality study. Service quality attributes are first identified from the literature, focus groups or an earlier survey. Customers then score each attribute twice, once for expectation and once for perceived performance, and the researcher computes the difference between the two for every attribute. Negative gaps, where performance falls short of expectation, point managers to the aspects of service needing action. The original instrument groups items into a small number of service quality dimensions, but the procedure can be applied to a locally developed attribute list. The authors note that the approach is similar to importance-performance analysis. For UX and service designers it gives a structured way to measure the service layer of a digital product, such as support, onboarding or fulfilment, against what users expected, and it suits products where human service and software are tightly combined.
steps: Define the service and the customer group to be studied.
Identify service quality attributes from the literature, focus groups or exploratory interviews, and phrase them as survey items.
Collect expectation scores for each attribute, ideally before or independently of the service encounter.
Collect perceived performance scores for the same attributes after the encounter.
Compute the gap (performance minus expectation) for each attribute and summarise by dimension and by customer segment.
Rank the largest negative gaps and investigate their causes with follow-up interviews or service blueprints.
Repeat the measurement after changes to see whether gaps have closed.
outputs: Expectation and performance scores and gap scores for each attribute and dimension, with a ranked list of service shortfalls.
useWhen: A product includes a significant human or operational service component and you want to know where delivery falls short of what customers expect.
avoidWhen: Users cannot form meaningful expectations in advance, the survey would become too long with doubled items, or only the software interface is in scope.
whyLost: UX research grew from interface usability rather than services marketing, and the doubled expectation-performance format is long and has been criticised psychometrically, so UX teams rarely use it directly even when doing service design.
whereToUse: Service design, customer support and help centres, onboarding and account management, fitness and leisure memberships, banking and public services with digital channels.
example: A gym chain with a booking app measures members' expectations and experiences of class booking, waitlists, staff help and refunds. The largest negative gap is on refunds after cancelled classes, so the team redesigns the refund flow and staff script together.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge. Parasuraman, A., Zeithaml, V. A. and Berry, L. L. (1985) A conceptual model of service quality and implications for future research. Journal of Marketing, 49(4), 41-50.

name: Session feature engineering
origin: Web usage mining (Cooley, Mobasher and Srivastava, 1997); session timeout conventions from web analytics
summary: Turning raw clickstream events into theoretically meaningful per-session and per-user features, such as depth, dwell, backtracking and error recovery, for modelling behaviour.
description: Behavioural logs record events, but models and personas need features. Session feature engineering first groups events into sessions (commonly with a 30-minute inactivity timeout), then derives variables such as session length, number of distinct features used, depth into funnels, revisits, backtracking (returns to earlier steps), search-then-browse ratios, error events and time between sessions. Rigour comes from grounding each feature in a construct identified in qualitative work (for example 'hesitation' operationalised as dwell longer than the 90th percentile before a commit action), documenting definitions in a feature dictionary, handling bots and internal traffic, and checking feature distributions and correlations before clustering or modelling. Poorly chosen features determine poorly grounded segments.
steps: Define the analytical unit (session, user-week, user) and the session timeout (30 minutes is conventional; validate against the inter-event time distribution).
List target constructs from qualitative research and specify an operational feature for each in a feature dictionary.
Remove bots, internal users and test accounts, and document the filters.
Compute features with pandas group-by operations, log-transforming skewed counts and durations.
Check distributions, missingness and pairwise correlations, dropping or combining features with correlations above about 0.85.
Standardise features and validate a sample of feature values against session replays or raw event sequences.
outputs: A documented feature dictionary and a clean per-session or per-user feature matrix ready for clustering, survival or classification models.
useWhen: Building behavioural segments, predicting churn or conversion, detecting friction patterns at scale, and linking qualitative constructs to logged behaviour.
avoidWhen: Avoid when the question is why users behave a certain way (use interviews or contextual inquiry), or when instrumentation is incomplete or inconsistent.
whyLost: Feature engineering lives in data science teams; UX researchers rarely have log access or the skills, so behavioural features are designed without user-research grounding.
whereToUse: SaaS product analytics, e-commerce journey analysis, fintech engagement monitoring and AI product usage studies.
example: A SaaS team operationalises 'struggle' from interviews as repeated undo actions plus help-page visits within a session. The feature identifies 8% of sessions, which are three times more likely to precede churn in the following month.
sources: lifelines (survival)
scikit-learn (GMM, LDA, UMAP)
pandas (log parsing)
matplotlib
plotly

Zheng, A. & Casari, A. (2018) Feature Engineering for Machine Learning

name: Session Replay Analysis
origin: Commercial session replay tools, mid-2000s (e.g. ClickTale, 2006)
summary: Reviews reconstructed recordings of real user sessions to see clicks, scrolls, hesitations and errors behind analytics metrics, at scale and without moderation.
description: Session replay tools capture DOM changes and user input events, then reconstruct sessions as videos showing how individual users moved through a product. They bridge quantitative analytics and qualitative observation: an analyst can filter for sessions that dropped from a funnel step, triggered an error or showed rage clicks, and watch what happened. Rigour comes from sampling deliberately (filtering by the behaviour of interest and reviewing a defined number, such as 20-50 sessions), coding observations with a consistent scheme rather than noting anecdotes, counting how often each issue appears, and validating hypotheses quantitatively. Privacy is integral: sensitive fields must be masked, consent and legal requirements respected, and retention limited. Replays show what users did but not their intentions, so pairing with interviews or tests remains important.
steps: Define the question and filter criteria (e.g. sessions abandoning at checkout step 3 on mobile).
Confirm masking of sensitive fields and compliance with consent and data retention rules.
Sample a defined number of sessions, typically 20-50, randomly within the filter.
Code each session with a consistent scheme: issues, hesitations, errors and workarounds.
Count issue frequencies and confirm patterns with quantitative signals such as rage-click or error events.
Prioritise fixes and validate them with A/B tests or follow-up usability testing.
outputs: Coded session observations, issue frequency counts, illustrative clips, prioritised fix list.
useWhen: Explaining analytics anomalies, conversion optimisation, bug triage and finding usability issues in live products.
avoidWhen: When privacy risks are high (health, finance without strong masking) or you need user intentions; use moderated testing or interviews.
whyLost: Still in use: Popular for bug hunting and UX issue identification; privacy concerns growing.
whereToUse: Conversion optimization; bug investigation; UX issue triage.
example: An e-commerce team filtered 40 mobile sessions that abandoned at payment. Coding showed 17 users tapping a non-responsive 'apply voucher' button hidden behind the keyboard, which a layout fix resolved.
sources: UX Research
reference: Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M., & Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Session-as-feature-vector representation
origin: Web usage mining (Cooley, Mobasher & Srivastava, 1999); sequence embeddings such as prod2vec (Grbovic et al., 2015)
summary: Encodes each user session as a fixed-length numeric vector of counts, durations, sequences or learned embeddings, so sessions can be compared, clustered and modelled.
description: Sessions are variable-length sequences of events, but most analytical and generative models require fixed-length input. Representations range from hand-crafted aggregates (event counts, durations, depth, error counts), through n-gram and transition-matrix features capturing order, to learned embeddings from sequence models such as word2vec-style event embeddings, recurrent networks or transformers. The choice determines what similarity means: two sessions with the same events in different order are identical under counts but different under sequence representations. Rigour requires defining session boundaries consistently (e.g. 30 minutes inactivity), choosing representations that retain the behaviours of interest, checking that similar vectors correspond to qualitatively similar sessions, and documenting the encoding.
steps: Define session boundaries consistently, commonly a 30-minute inactivity timeout or app foreground/background events.
Select a representation: aggregates, bag of events, n-grams or transition probabilities, or learned embeddings.
Compute vectors and normalise (e.g. TF-IDF weighting for event counts, standardisation for numeric features).
Sanity-check by retrieving nearest-neighbour sessions for samples and reviewing them as replays.
Evaluate representation quality on a downstream task (e.g. predicting task success) and compare alternatives.
Document the encoding and version it alongside event schema changes.
outputs: A session-level vector dataset with documented encoding, validated similarity behaviour and readiness for clustering, classification or generative modelling.
useWhen: When analysing large numbers of sessions computationally, for clustering, classification of frustration, anomaly detection or synthetic generation.
avoidWhen: Avoid when questions concern individual sessions in depth (use replay review) or when event logging is too sparse to characterise sessions.
whyLost: The representation step is usually left to engineers, while UX researchers analyse replays one by one; the bridge is rarely framed as a research method.
whereToUse: Frustration detection in fintech and e-commerce, session clustering in SaaS, inputs to AI-driven synthetic testing.
example: An investment app encodes sessions with event-transition probabilities and dwell times. Nearest-neighbour review confirms that vectors near a known frustrated session also show repeated back-navigation, validating the representation for classification.
sources: Deep Generative Modeling (Jakub Tomczak, Springer)
Deep Learning (Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio & Aaron Courville)
