name: Seven Causes of Method Death
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Diagnoses why a method declined: complexity, technological displacement, paradigm shift, lost training infrastructure, faster competitors, failed validity, or fashion.
description: The treatise's systematic analysis of why methods die names seven causes. Complexity exceeds organisational patience (contextual inquiry demanded too much). Technological displacement (desktop methods not transferring to mobile, often producing death where adaptation would do). Paradigm shift (the 1990s move from cognitive to social perspectives; agile marginalising sequential methods). Loss of training infrastructure (curricula, consultancies and textbooks disappear; GOMS is in every history but almost no programme teaches it). Competitive displacement by faster methods (richer outputs are hard to demonstrate, cost differences obvious). Failed replication and validity concerns (legitimate, but often confused with implementation failure). Fashion and novelty preference. Diagnosing the cause tells you whether a method should stay dead or how to revive it.
steps: Select a method in decline or already lost.
Trace its lifecycle: development, early adoption, mainstream simplification and decline.
Gather evidence on each of the seven causes (literature, practitioner interviews, curricula).
Distinguish legitimate validity failure from implementation failure.
Identify the dominant causes and their reversibility.
Design a recovery strategy targeted at those causes, or archive the method.
outputs: Cause-of-death diagnosis, reversibility assessment, recovery or archive decision.
useWhen: Deciding whether and how to revive a method; designing training and ResearchOps investments.
avoidWhen: Methods in healthy use with no decline.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: Research leadership, curriculum committees, professional associations, ResearchOps.
example: Analysing why the team stopped using diary studies shows the cause was tooling cost (complexity), not validity; a lightweight instrument template revives them.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Rogers EM (2003) Diffusion of Innovations
Kuhn TS (1962) The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 31 (Why Methods Die).

name: Severity Rating Scale (Nielsen)
origin: Jakob Nielsen, 1993-1995
summary: Rates each usability problem 0-4 based on frequency, impact and persistence, by independent raters, so findings can be prioritised defensibly.
description: The treatise identifies the severity rating scale as a lost part of Nielsen's framework. Severity combines three factors: frequency (how many users encounter it), impact (how hard it is to overcome) and persistence (one-time or recurring), plus market impact. Ratings run from 0 (not a problem) to 4 (usability catastrophe, imperative to fix before release). Nielsen showed single-rater severity judgements are unreliable and recommended averaging ratings from at least three independent evaluators, collected after aggregation of the problem list. Without severity classification, organisations cannot prioritise findings, and reports become flat lists that are easy to ignore.
steps: Compile an aggregated, deduplicated problem list with descriptions and evidence.
Send the list to at least three evaluators who rate independently.
Rate each problem on frequency, impact and persistence, then assign 0-4 overall.
Average ratings and check agreement; discuss large disagreements.
Sort problems by severity and map to the release plan.
Track severity distributions across releases.
outputs: Prioritised problem list with mean severity and agreement, severity trend metrics.
useWhen: After any evaluation study to prioritise fixes and communicate risk.
avoidWhen: When no problem list exists yet; severity is an add-on, not a discovery method.
whyLost: Single researchers now assign ad hoc high/medium/low labels without independent raters or defined criteria.
whereToUse: Release gating, design QA, accessibility audits, research reporting to executives.
example: Three researchers independently rate 30 issues in a payroll app; mean severity 3.7 for 'cannot undo submitted run' moves it into the current sprint.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Nielsen J (1993) Usability Engineering
Nielsen J (1994) Severity ratings for usability problems (NN/g)
reference: Nielsen J (1993) Usability Engineering. Academic Press.

name: Severity Rating with Impact x Frequency x Persistence
origin: Jakob Nielsen (1994), severity components of frequency, impact and persistence; extended in Dumas and Redish's handbook
summary: Rates each usability problem separately on impact, frequency and persistence, then combines them into a severity score, giving a defensible and reproducible prioritisation.
description: Nielsen defined usability problem severity as a combination of frequency (how many users meet it), impact (how hard it is to overcome) and persistence (whether users keep encountering it once learned), plus market impact. In practice teams assign a single gut-feel 0-4 rating, which correlates poorly between evaluators and favours dramatic over pervasive problems. The multidimensional approach rates each component on its own anchored scale, using observed data where possible (for example frequency as the proportion of participants affected), combines them with an explicit rule (multiplicative or a lookup table), and has at least two raters score independently before reconciling. This prevents high-frequency, low-impact problems from being dismissed and makes prioritisation transparent to stakeholders and comparable across studies.
steps: Rate each usability problem on three dimensions (1–5 each): impact (1=cosmetic, 5=task failure), frequency (1=rare, 5=universal), persistence (1=one screen, 5=systemic).
Priority score = impact × frequency × persistence.
This moves problems from anecdote ('this confused 3 users') to a quantified severity that can drive engineering prioritization decisions.
outputs: Per-problem ratings on impact, frequency and persistence, combined severity scores, inter-rater agreement and a ranked problem list.
useWhen: Prioritising findings from usability tests and heuristic evaluations, building comparable issue backlogs across studies, and justifying fixes to stakeholders.
avoidWhen: When there are only a handful of obvious problems that need no ranking, or when business impact dominates priority; then add a business-value dimension or use a cost-benefit matrix.
whyLost: Single holistic severity scales were quicker and became the norm, so the separate dimensions Nielsen described were collapsed and their inter-rater checks forgotten.
whereToUse: Heuristic evaluation reporting, usability study findings prioritization, design system defect triage.
example: After testing a checkout with 8 users, a team rates 22 problems on three anchored scales. A minor label confusion affecting 7 of 8 users and recurring each visit outranks a dramatic but rare crash, changing the sprint's priorities.
sources: Handbook of Usability Testing
Usability Engineering (Jakob Nielsen)
Sauro, Rating the severity of usability problems (MeasuringU)
reference: Nielsen J (1994) Usability Engineering. Morgan Kaufmann

name: Shannon Entropy Audit
origin: Claude Shannon, 1948
summary: Quantifies the uncertainty a user faces at each decision point or in an information space using Shannon entropy, giving a principled complexity measure for IA and navigation.
description: Shannon entropy, H = -Σ p log2 p, measures the average uncertainty in a probability distribution in bits. Applied to interfaces, it quantifies how unpredictable a user's next choice is at a decision point, how evenly traffic spreads across navigation items, or how much information a notification stream carries. An entropy audit computes these values from usage logs or from structural models, then compares them with what users need. High entropy at a point where most users want the same thing indicates poor prioritisation; very low entropy across a whole menu indicates items nobody uses. Rigour comes from defining the random variable precisely, using sufficient log data for stable probability estimates, and pairing entropy with outcome measures such as success rate so that lower entropy is not mistaken for better design in itself.
steps: Define the decision points or distributions to measure (e.g. first click on the home page, menu selections, notification types).
Extract choice frequencies from logs over a representative period, ideally thousands of events per point.
Compute entropy and normalised entropy (H / log2 n) for each point.
Compare entropy with task success and time to identify points where uncertainty is high and outcomes poor.
Model redesigns by estimating new distributions and the resulting entropy reduction.
Validate changes with A/B tests or tree tests and re-measure entropy post-launch.
outputs: Entropy and normalised entropy per decision point, complexity hotspot map, predicted entropy reduction for redesigns.
useWhen: Large IA and navigation systems, search result pages and notification systems with rich log data.
avoidWhen: New products with no usage data, or when qualitative reasons for choices matter more; use tree testing or interviews.
whyLost: Shannon entropy entered HCI through the Hick-Hyman law in the 1950s-80s but UX practice dropped the information-theoretic framing in favour of qualitative 'cognitive load' talk. The maths and log access needed felt out of reach for most research teams.
whereToUse: IA complexity evaluation; search system design; notification prioritization.
example: A government services portal had 14 home-page tiles. First-click entropy was 3.6 bits, close to the maximum, yet three services accounted for most completed tasks; promoting them cut entropy to 2.4 bits and first-click success rose 12 points.
sources: Information Theory Inference and Learning Algorithms
A Mathematical Theory of Communication (Claude Shannon)
MacKay, D. J. C., Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003)
Kolmogorov complexity literature (MIT Press)
Shannon, C. E., A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)
MacKay (Information Theory)
Kolmogorov via MIT Press
Shannon's works
The Inquiry Series, Ch 1 — Entropy, Complexity & the Information Architecture of Interaction

name: SHAP Driver Analysis
donor: Machine learning interpretability and cooperative game theory
origin: Scott Lundberg & Su-In Lee, 2017 (from Shapley values, Lloyd Shapley, 1953)
summary: Train a predictive model on task-level features and decompose its predictions with SHAP values to rank which UX factors most drive success or drop-off.
description: SHAP attributes each prediction to features using Shapley values from cooperative game theory, giving additive contributions that sum to the prediction. Vivek Gopinath's playbook trains a gradient boosting model on a 70/30 split using task time per step, error counts (slips, lapses, mistakes), SNR, TLX scores and retries, evaluates it on holdout data, checks calibration with reliability plots, and ranks features by mean absolute SHAP value. In the example, mistake rate (0.33) and SNR (0.27) dominate, followed by OTP time (0.18), frustration (0.13) and retries (0.09), guiding fix priority. Pitfalls are leakage from post-outcome features, overfitting (use holdout or cross-validation) and treating importance as causal; SHAP must be paired with experiments and with qualitative quotes explaining each top driver. In the Behavioral Spectral Framework, SHAP or Integrated Gradients explain which frequencies contributed to change.
steps: Assemble task-level features measured before the outcome (task time, error counts, SNR, TLX, retries).
Train a gradient boosting model on a 70/30 split and evaluate on the holdout set.
Check calibration with reliability plots and guard against leakage.
Compute SHAP values and rank features by mean absolute SHAP.
Attach qualitative quotes explaining the mechanism of each top driver.
Prioritise fixes by driver rank and validate with experiments.
outputs: A SHAP bar chart of top drivers, model validation metrics and a prioritised fix list.
useWhen: When many candidate factors exist and teams need to know which matter most for prediction.
avoidWhen: When data are small or causal claims are needed; SHAP explains a model, not the world.
whyLost: Standard in data science but rarely used by UX researchers, who tend to rely on correlation tables.
whereToUse: Onboarding success, churn prediction, AI feature adoption, support deflection.
example: SHAP on a trading app's onboarding model shows OTP retries (0.31) and task time (0.27) drive drop-off, so the team fixes retries first.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
reference: Lundberg, S. M., & Lee, S.-I. (2017). A unified approach to interpreting model predictions. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30.

name: SHAP Explanations for Behavioural Models
origin: Scott Lundberg and Su-In Lee, 2017 (Shapley values, 1953)
summary: Attributes a predictive model's outputs (for example churn risk) to input features using Shapley values, showing which experiences drive predictions.
description: Cited in the treatise's bibliography, SHAP computes each feature's contribution to an individual prediction based on Shapley values from cooperative game theory, satisfying properties such as local accuracy and consistency. Applied to UX, teams fit predictive models of churn, conversion or satisfaction from behavioural and experience features, then use SHAP to see which experiences push predictions up or down overall and for individual users. The crucial caveat is that attributions are predictive, not causal: they explain the model, not the world, and correlated features share credit unpredictably. SHAP findings should generate hypotheses for causal methods or experiments, not substitute for them.
steps: Define the outcome and assemble behavioural and experience features measured before it.
Train and validate a predictive model with held-out data.
Compute SHAP values globally (summary plots) and locally for representative users.
Examine dependence plots for non-linear effects and interactions.
Flag correlated features and avoid causal language.
Turn top drivers into hypotheses for experiments or qualitative study.
outputs: Global and local feature attributions, dependence plots, hypotheses list.
useWhen: Prioritising which experience factors to investigate from large behavioural datasets.
avoidWhen: When causal effects are needed for decisions; use experiments or quasi-experimental designs.
whyLost: Recent and ML-native; UX rarely collaborates closely with modelling teams.
whereToUse: Churn modelling, support escalation prediction, satisfaction driver analysis, AI feature adoption.
example: A churn model's SHAP plot shows failed bank-link attempts in week one are the strongest driver; an experiment then confirms that a better linking flow reduces churn.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Lundberg SM & Lee S-I (2017) A unified approach to interpreting model predictions. NeurIPS
Molnar C (2022) Interpretable Machine Learning
reference: Lundberg SM & Lee S-I (2017) A unified approach to interpreting model predictions. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30.

name: SHAP values for feature attribution
origin: Lloyd Shapley, 1953; Scott Lundberg & Su-In Lee, 2017
summary: Attributes a model's prediction to its input features using Shapley values from game theory, explaining both individual decisions and global model behaviour.
description: SHAP assigns each feature a contribution to a prediction, relative to a baseline, such that contributions sum to the prediction and satisfy fairness axioms from cooperative game theory. Aggregated across cases, SHAP values show global importance and the direction of effects; for single cases, they explain why a user received a particular recommendation or risk score. In a UX audit of an AI system, SHAP reveals whether models rely on features users would find inappropriate or opaque, and supplies raw material for user-facing explanations. Rigour requires understanding that SHAP explains the model, not reality; correlated features distort attributions; and the choice of background data affects results.
steps: Obtain access to the model and representative data, and define the prediction to explain.
Choose an explainer (TreeSHAP for tree models, KernelSHAP or DeepSHAP otherwise) and a background dataset of 100-1,000 representative cases.
Compute SHAP values for a sample of predictions and plot global summaries (beeswarm, mean absolute SHAP).
Review individual explanations for key user cases, especially edge cases and complaints.
Flag features that are sensitive, proxies for protected attributes, or misaligned with user expectations.
Translate findings into design and governance actions, and test candidate user-facing explanations with users.
outputs: Global and local feature attributions, flagged problematic features and inputs for explanation design and governance.
useWhen: Auditing AI recommendations, risk scores or personalisation for explainability, fairness and alignment with user mental models.
avoidWhen: Avoid presenting raw SHAP plots to end users, relying on it with strongly correlated features without caution, or treating attributions as causal effects.
whyLost: SHAP is standard in ML engineering and responsible AI teams, but UX researchers rarely have model access or the skills to use it.
whereToUse: Investment and credit recommendations, health risk models, AI assistants, content ranking systems.
example: A SHAP audit of an investment recommender shows the top driver of high-risk suggestions is recent app engagement rather than stated risk tolerance. The finding triggers redesign of both the model inputs and the explanation shown to users.
sources: The Alignment Problem (Brian Christian)
Artificial Intelligence for Humans (Jeff Heaton)
Methods Atlas (Vivek Gopinath)
Lundberg & Lee (2017) A unified approach to interpreting model predictions
Interpretable Machine Learning (Christoph Molnar)
The Alignment Problem (Christian)
AI for Humans (Heaton)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 58 — AI Explainability & Value Alignment Audit
reference: Lundberg, S. M. & Lee, S.-I. (2017) A unified approach to interpreting model predictions. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30.

name: SHERPA (Systematic Human Error Reduction and Prediction Approach)
origin: David Embrey, 1986
summary: Predicts which errors users are likely to make at each bottom-level task step using a fixed error-mode taxonomy, then rates consequence, recovery and probability.
description: SHERPA takes the bottom-level operations of a hierarchical task analysis and classifies each as an action, retrieval, checking, selection or information communication behaviour. Each behaviour type has a defined list of error modes (for example A4 'operation too little/much', C1 'check omitted', R2 'wrong information obtained'). The analyst applies the taxonomy to every step, describing each credible error, its consequence, recovery opportunity, ordinal probability and criticality, and proposes remedies. Validation studies by Stanton and colleagues found SHERPA among the most accurate and reliable error-prediction methods, with sensitivity comparable to empirical testing at a fraction of the cost. It is structured, repeatable and teachable, which is exactly what ad hoc 'error state' design lacks.
steps: Complete an HTA of the task to the level of individual operations.
Classify each bottom-level step into one of the five SHERPA behaviour types.
Apply the corresponding error modes to each step and record every credible error with a description.
For each error, note the consequence, whether and how it can be recovered, probability (low, medium, high) and criticality (critical or not).
Propose remedial strategies under equipment, training, procedures and organisational headings.
Where possible, validate predictions against observed errors in testing and calculate hit rate and false-alarm rate.
outputs: A SHERPA table of predicted errors with consequences, recovery, probability, criticality and remedies; optional validation statistics.
useWhen: You need to predict user errors before building or testing, for a well-defined procedural task such as configuration, checkout, dosing or setup.
avoidWhen: Highly creative or open-ended tasks without a stable procedure; use contextual inquiry or critical incident technique.
whyLost: SHERPA is taught in ergonomics degrees and used in aviation, rail and nuclear, but UX programmes rarely teach HTA-based predictive analysis. Product teams default to finding errors empirically.
whereToUse: Device setup flows, B2B configuration wizards, kiosk and point-of-sale, medical and in-car interfaces.
example: Before launching a smart thermostat app, a researcher runs SHERPA on schedule setup and predicts a high-probability 'wrong value selected' error on the AM/PM toggle; testing confirms it and the toggle becomes a 24-hour picker with preview.
sources: Embrey, SHERPA: A systematic human error reduction and prediction approach (1986)
Stanton et al., Human Factors Methods: A Practical Guide for Engineering and Design (2013)
Stanton & Stevenage, Learning to predict human error (1998), Ergonomics
reference: Embrey, D. E. (1986). SHERPA: A systematic human error reduction and prediction approach. International Meeting on Advances in Nuclear Power Systems.

name: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules (Empirical Application)
origin: Ben Shneiderman, Designing the User Interface (1986)
summary: Inspects an interface against Shneiderman's eight golden rules using their empirical rationale and measurable criteria, rather than as a superficial checklist.
description: Shneiderman's eight golden rules (strive for consistency, enable shortcuts for frequent users, offer informative feedback, design dialogues to yield closure, prevent errors, permit easy reversal of actions, keep users in control, reduce short-term memory load) were derived from experimental HCI work and are well known. In practice they survive as a poster-level checklist, with little attention to how compliance should be judged or what evidence each rule rests on. The empirical application reinstates that rigour: each rule is turned into observable criteria (for example, undo available for every destructive action, feedback within 1 second for frequent actions, no more than about four items to hold in memory across screens), evaluators inspect independently, and violations are linked to observed or predicted user costs. Findings are rated for severity and, where possible, verified through usability testing.
steps: Apply each rule as an evaluable hypothesis, not a heuristic: for Rule 6 (easy reversal), measure: what % of participant error-recovery attempts succeed on first try?
For Rule 8 (memory load), measure active recall requirements per screen.
Build a measurement instrument (1–5 per rule with evidence citation) rather than a yes/no checklist.
outputs: Rule-by-rule compliance assessment with operational criteria, violation list with severity and evidence, and targeted test hypotheses.
useWhen: Expert reviews of desktop and enterprise software, design system governance, and early checks before usability testing.
avoidWhen: As a substitute for testing with users, or for domains where the rules conflict with specialised needs (for example safety-critical confirmations); use domain-specific heuristics there.
whyLost: The rules became so familiar that teams cite them without operationalising them, and Nielsen's heuristics became the default inspection set, so the empirical grounding behind each rule was forgotten.
whereToUse: Evidence-based heuristic evaluation, design system specification, accessibility and compliance auditing. Connects Nielsen's heuristics back to their empirical origins.
example: Reviewing a hospital EHR's order-entry screen against the eight rules, three evaluators find no undo for cancelled orders and a requirement to remember a patient ID across four screens. Both are confirmed in sessions with nurses and prioritised for fixing.
sources: Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines — Ben Shneiderman
Designing the User Interface (Ben Shneiderman & Catherine Plaisant)
reference: Shneiderman B & Plaisant C (2010) Designing the User Interface: Strategies for Effective Human-Computer Interaction. 5th ed. Addison-Wesley

name: Shortest path mapping
origin: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm, 1959; applied to hypertext navigation in 1990s structural analysis
summary: Computes the minimum number of steps from entry points to each key destination and compares it with the paths users actually take, revealing structural distance and detours.
description: Shortest path mapping applies Dijkstra's or breadth-first search algorithms to a navigation graph to compute the minimal step count between any two nodes, particularly from common entry points to priority tasks. Weighted versions use estimated interaction cost per edge (for example KLM time) rather than raw clicks. Comparing structural shortest paths with observed paths from logs gives a 'lostness' or path efficiency ratio: Smith's lostness measure combines total nodes visited, unique nodes visited and the minimum required. The method separates structural problems (destinations genuinely far away) from wayfinding problems (short paths exist but users do not find them). It is rigorous when the graph is complete and the cost model is explicit.
steps: Build the navigation graph and define entry points and priority destinations from task analysis.
Compute shortest path lengths (or weighted costs) from each entry point to each destination.
Extract observed paths from logs or tests for the same tasks.
Compute path efficiency (optimal/observed) and Smith's lostness L = sqrt((N/S - 1)^2 + (R/N - 1)^2); treat L above about 0.4 as lost.
Classify each problem as structural (long optimal path) or wayfinding (short optimal path, inefficient observed path).
Fix structural problems with new links or shortcuts and wayfinding problems with labels, scent or signposting; re-measure.
outputs: A matrix of optimal path lengths, observed path efficiency and lostness per task, and a classification of structural versus wayfinding issues.
useWhen: When users take long routes to important tasks; when prioritising shortcuts; when evaluating navigation redesigns.
avoidWhen: When tasks are search-led or exploratory without defined destinations; use search log analysis or diary studies.
whyLost: Click-count rules ('three-click rule') replaced measured path analysis in practice, and lostness metrics stayed in academic papers.
whereToUse: Surgical and industrial menus, enterprise apps, government services, help centres, and mobile apps with deep navigation.
example: In a hospital scheduling tool the optimal path to 'reschedule' is 3 steps, but observed paths average 9 with lostness of 0.55. The problem is wayfinding, so the team relabels and surfaces the action rather than restructuring.
sources: Rosenfeld, L., Morville, P. & Arango, J., Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond (O'Reilly, 4th ed., 2015)
Martin, L. M., Everyday Information Architecture (2019)
Covert, A., How to Make Sense of Any Mess (2014)

The Inquiry Series, Ch 7 — Graph Theory & the Architecture of Information

name: Signal Detection Theory
origin: Peterson, Birdsall & Fox, 1954; Tanner & Swets, 1954; Green & Swets, 1966
summary: Separates a person's ability to discriminate signal from noise (sensitivity, d') from their tendency to respond 'yes' (criterion), clarifying whether failures are perceptual or strategic.
description: Signal detection theory models decisions under uncertainty where a person must distinguish signals from noise, such as a real alert among false alarms, a phishing email among legitimate ones or an anomaly in a chart. Every response falls into one of four outcomes: hit, miss, false alarm or correct rejection. From hit and false alarm rates, SDT estimates sensitivity (d'), the ability to discriminate, independently of the response criterion, which reflects bias toward saying yes or no. This shows whether a design improves perception or merely shifts caution, and supports ROC analysis. In UX, it suits alert design, security warnings, content moderation and AI-assisted decision tasks. Rigour comes from designed trial sets with known ground truth, enough trials per condition (often 50 or more), and reporting both d' and criterion.
steps: Define the detection task, the signal and the noise, with known ground truth for each trial.
Build a trial set with a realistic or controlled base rate of signals, with 50 or more trials per condition.
Run participants through trials, recording yes or no responses and optionally confidence ratings.
Compute hit and false alarm rates per participant and condition, applying corrections for extreme rates.
Calculate d' and criterion (c or beta), and ROC curves if confidence ratings were collected.
Compare designs on sensitivity and bias, and consider the costs of misses versus false alarms.
Translate results into alert thresholds, interface design or training.
outputs: Hit and false alarm rates, sensitivity (d') and criterion estimates, ROC curves and recommendations on thresholds and design.
useWhen: For alert and notification design, phishing and security warnings, anomaly detection in dashboards, content moderation and human-AI decision tasks.
avoidWhen: Avoid when there is no ground truth for signal and noise, or for open-ended tasks; use usability testing or observation.
whyLost: Latent: SDT is foundational in perception psychology and widely used in radiology, aviation and security research, but UX teams rarely use it to separate sensitivity from bias in detection tasks, relying instead on simple accuracy.
whereToUse: Alert/notification design; error detection research; accessibility studies.
example: A hospital tests two sepsis alert designs with 30 nurses on 80 patient cases. The new design increases d' from 1.1 to 1.8 without shifting criterion, showing better discrimination rather than more cautious clicking.
sources: Sensation and Perception

Van Drongelen (Signal Processing for Neuroscientists)

The Inquiry Series, Ch 2 — Signal, Noise & the Detection of Intent

name: Signalling Game Analysis
origin: Michael Spence (1973, job market signalling); Amotz Zahavi (1975, handicap principle); Crawford and Sobel (1982, cheap talk)
summary: Analyses whether signals in a product (badges, reviews, verification, credentials) can credibly separate high-quality from low-quality senders, given their costs.
description: In a signalling game, a sender with private information (e.g. seller quality) chooses a signal, and a receiver infers type and acts. A separating equilibrium exists only if the signal is costlier for low types than high types; otherwise low types mimic and the signal becomes uninformative (pooling). Cheap talk, costless signals, is credible only when interests align. This explains why 'verified' badges, review counts or certifications succeed or fail, and why designs that make signals cheap destroy their value. Rigorous analysis models types, costs and incentives, then tests predictions with behavioural data or experiments.
steps: Identify the information asymmetry: who knows what about quality, honesty or intent.
List available signals and estimate their cost to high and low types (money, effort, risk, time).
Determine whether the single-crossing condition holds and whether separating, pooling or semi-separating outcomes are expected.
Check empirical data: do signals predict outcomes (ecological validity) and do receivers rely on them?
Redesign signals to restore differential cost (e.g. verification tied to accountability, history-based badges).
Test with field experiments or lab games, monitoring for gaming over time.
outputs: A signalling model of the product's trust system, predicted equilibria, signal validity evidence and redesign proposals.
useWhen: Designing trust, reputation, credentials, verification or quality signals in marketplaces and social platforms.
avoidWhen: Contexts without meaningful information asymmetry.
whyLost: Game-theoretic modelling is unfamiliar in UX, which designs badges by convention rather than incentive analysis.
whereToUse: Marketplaces, dating apps, freelance platforms, social verification, AI-generated content labels.
example: A freelance platform's 'Top Rated' badge pools as inflated ratings make it cheap to obtain. Tying it to repeat-client rate, costlier for low-quality freelancers to fake, restores its predictive value for client satisfaction.
sources: Spence, Job market signaling (1973), Quarterly Journal of Economics
Connelly et al., Signaling theory: A review and assessment (2011), Journal of Management
Crawford & Sobel, Strategic information transmission (1982), Econometrica
reference: Spence, M. (1973). Quarterly Journal of Economics, 87(3), 355-374.

name: Silhouette scores and gap statistic validation
origin: Peter Rousseeuw's silhouette, 1987; Tibshirani, Walther & Hastie's gap statistic, 2001
summary: Quantitative checks of whether clusters are compact and well separated, and whether the data has more cluster structure than random noise.
description: Clustering algorithms always return clusters, even in structureless data, so internal validation is essential. The silhouette compares each point's mean distance to its own cluster with the nearest other cluster, ranging from -1 to 1; averages above 0.5 indicate reasonable structure, above 0.7 strong, and below 0.25 essentially none. The gap statistic compares within-cluster dispersion against that expected under a null reference distribution, choosing the smallest K where the gap is within one standard error of the next. Together with stability checks via bootstrapping, these indices guard against segmenting noise. Rigour requires computing them on the same standardised features used for clustering and reporting them honestly when structure is weak.
steps: Compute average silhouette width for each candidate K and plot silhouette profiles per cluster.
Interpret silhouette: above 0.7 strong, 0.5-0.7 reasonable, 0.25-0.5 weak, below 0.25 no substantial structure.
Compute the gap statistic with at least 100 reference datasets and select the smallest K with Gap(K) at or above Gap(K+1) minus its standard error.
Assess stability by bootstrapping and computing Jaccard similarity per cluster (above 0.75 stable, below 0.5 dissolved).
Report all indices together; if structure is weak, describe a continuum rather than discrete segments.
outputs: Validity indices per K, silhouette plots, gap curves, cluster stability scores and an honest statement on how real the segments are.
useWhen: After any clustering of user behaviour or attitudes, before segments are named, presented or used for targeting.
avoidWhen: Silhouette is misleading for non-convex or density-based clusters (use density-based validation such as DBCV), and these indices do not test meaningfulness.
whyLost: Segmentation outputs are often presented without any validity evidence, and UX researchers rarely see the clustering code.
whereToUse: Persona validation, behavioural segmentation, survey-based attitudinal segmentation and customer tiering.
example: A SaaS team's five behavioural segments have an average silhouette of 0.21 and low bootstrap stability. They abandon discrete personas and instead describe two continuous dimensions of usage.

name: Simulation Heuristic for Task Difficulty Prediction
origin: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, 1982
summary: Measures how easily users can mentally simulate completing a task before attempting it, using that perceived simulation ease to predict reluctance, abandonment and perceived usability.
description: The simulation heuristic holds that people judge how likely or hard something is by how easily they can construct a mental simulation of it. In UX terms, before acting, users imagine the steps a task will require; if the simulation is hard to run because steps are unclear, numerous or unfamiliar, they judge the task difficult and may avoid it, regardless of actual difficulty. The method collects pre-task ratings of expected difficulty and asks users to narrate the steps they expect, then compares these with post-task ratings and actual performance. Large gaps show where interfaces fail to support simulation (hidden steps, no progress cues) or where they look harder than they are. It complements single ease questions by separating expectation from experience.
steps: Ask users to mentally simulate the task and rate simulation ease (1–7).
Correlate with actual completion rates (target r > 0.65).
Low-simulation-ease screens are redesign candidates.
outputs: Pre-task expected difficulty ratings, narrated expected step sequences, expectation-versus-experience gaps, and design cues to improve task previewability.
useWhen: Flows with high abandonment before starting (applications, set-up, migrations), onboarding, and features users avoid because they appear complex.
avoidWhen: When users already know the task well, since simulation differences vanish with expertise; use performance measures instead.
whyLost: It remained a theoretical heuristic in decision research; UX adopted post-task ease questions but not the pre-task simulation measure that explains avoidance.
whereToUse: Pre-test difficulty prediction, cognitive walkthrough grounding.
example: A tax-filing service asks users to describe the steps they expect before starting a self-employment return; most imagine 20 or more steps and rate it 2 out of 7. Adding a 'what you'll need, about 15 minutes, 4 sections' preview raises starts by 22%.
sources: Heuristics and Biases — Kahneman (ed.)
Kahneman & Tversky, The simulation heuristic (in Judgment Under Uncertainty, 1982)
reference: Kahneman D & Tversky A (1982) The simulation heuristic. In Kahneman D, Slovic P & Tversky A (Eds.) Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Cambridge University Press

name: Single Ease Question (SEQ) Benchmarking
origin: Sauro & Dumas, 2009
summary: A single seven-point post-task question on difficulty, benchmarked against published norms to compare tasks, designs and releases quickly.
description: The Single Ease Question asks, immediately after each task, 'Overall, how difficult or easy was this task to complete?' on a seven-point scale from very difficult to very easy. Sauro and Dumas found it performed as well as or better than more complex post-task instruments while taking seconds to administer. Its real value emerges when scores are interpreted against norms (the historical average is roughly 5.5) and reported with confidence intervals, enabling meaningful comparison between tasks, designs and releases. Low scores flag tasks for diagnostic follow-up, and pairing SEQ with completion and time data reveals mismatches between perceived and actual difficulty. Rigour lies in consistent wording, administration timing and sample sizes adequate for the precision required.
steps: Administer SEQ immediately after each task (before the next task begins — memory decay is rapid).
Score: 1=Very Difficult, 7=Very Easy.
Compute: mean SEQ per task, % scoring 5–7 (top box).
Benchmarks (from Sauro's database): > 5.5 mean = good; < 4.5 = poor.
Correlate SEQ with task completion: expect r ≈ 0.5–0.7 between success and SEQ.
Discrepancies (high success + low SEQ) reveal effortful completion.
outputs: Mean SEQ per task with confidence intervals, comparison against the normative average (about 5.5), task difficulty rankings and trends across releases.
useWhen: Moderated or unmoderated usability tests needing a lightweight, validated, comparable measure of perceived task difficulty.
avoidWhen: Avoid as the only measure (pair with success and time), when tasks are too short or trivial to rate, or when you need diagnostic detail; use follow-up probes or interviews for the why.
whyLost: The SEQ itself survived because it is cheap; what was lost is benchmarking against norms and confidence intervals, so scores are often reported raw and uninterpreted.
whereToUse: Usability testing task evaluation, iterative design comparison, longitudinal benchmarking.
example: A SaaS team runs SEQ after six tasks; 'export a report' averages 3.9 (95% CI 3.3 to 4.5), well below the 5.5 norm, so it is prioritised even though its completion rate looked acceptable.
sources: Measuring the User Experience — Tullis & Albert
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
