name: Single Usability Metric (SUM)
origin: Sauro & Kindlund (2005), CHI
summary: Combines completion, time, errors and satisfaction for a task into one standardised usability score.
description: Stakeholders want one number; usability has several. SUM standardises each task metric against a specification limit and averages them. Completion is already a proportion. Task time is converted to the probability of finishing under a target time (using a z-score of log times). Errors become the proportion of error opportunities avoided. Post-task satisfaction is converted to the probability of exceeding a target rating. The result is a percentage between 0 and 100 per task, with a confidence interval, that can be rolled up across tasks. Principal components work by Sauro and Kindlund showed the four metrics share enough variance to justify combining them, while still being worth inspecting separately.
steps: Collect completion, time, errors (with error opportunities) and a post-task rating for each task.
Set specification limits: a target time (for example from expert times or goals) and a target satisfaction score.
Convert each metric to a percentage: success rate; proportion under target time; proportion of opportunities error-free; proportion above satisfaction target.
Average the percentages per task, compute an interval, and average across tasks for a product-level SUM.
Report SUM with the component metrics so a low score can be diagnosed.
outputs: A 0 to 100% usability score per task and per product, with drill-down to components.
useWhen: Executive dashboards, benchmarks over releases, competitive comparisons.
avoidWhen: Formative work where diagnosis matters more than a score, or when error data was not collected.
whyLost: It requires collecting four metrics consistently and setting spec limits, which most teams skip in favour of SUS alone.
whereToUse: Benchmark programmes, procurement comparisons, enterprise software scorecards.
example: A travel site's "change booking" task scores SUM 54% against a competitor's 78%, driven mostly by time, which focuses the redesign on the number of steps.
sources: How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Sauro, J. & Kindlund, E. (2005). A method to standardize usability metrics into a single score. CHI 2005.

name: Single-Subject Experimental Design
origin: B.F. Skinner tradition; Barlow & Hersen, 1984
summary: Establishes causal effects within individual users by repeatedly measuring behaviour across baseline and intervention phases (e.g. ABAB, multiple baseline).
description: Single-subject experimental designs establish causality at the level of the individual by repeatedly measuring a behaviour and systematically introducing and withdrawing an intervention. In an ABAB reversal design, baseline (A) and intervention (B) phases alternate; in a multiple-baseline design, the intervention is introduced at staggered times across participants, behaviours or settings. If behaviour changes reliably each time the intervention is applied, alternative explanations become implausible. In UX this suits accessibility work, highly individual users and behaviour-change features. Rigour comes from stable baselines (at least three to five data points per phase), visual analysis of level, trend and variability, non-overlap effect sizes, randomisation of phase starts where possible, and replication across participants.
steps: AB design for UX behavior change:
Baseline phase (A): measure the target behavior (e.g., task completion time, error rate) across multiple sessions without the design change.
(2) Treatment phase (B): introduce the design change. Continue measuring.
(3) Analysis: plot the data. Visual inspection: is there a change in level (immediate shift), trend (gradual change), and/or variability at the phase change point?
(4) ABAB extension: withdraw the treatment (return to A) and reintroduce (B). Reversal of the behavior confirms the causal effect of the design change.
outputs: Phase-by-phase time series per participant, visual analysis of level, trend and variability, effect sizes such as Tau-U, and replication across participants.
useWhen: Accessibility and assistive technology studies, rare or highly individual users, and behaviour change features where group averages hide individual responses.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need population-level estimates or when effects cannot be reversed or staggered; use randomised experiments instead.
whyLost: UX experimentation is equated with A/B tests on large samples; within-person experimental logic stayed in behaviour analysis and clinical research.
whereToUse: Accessibility UX testing for individual users, assistive technology evaluation, personalized interface adaptation research.
example: An assistive app for a user with motor impairments alternates switch-scanning and predictive layout modes over four phases; entry speed rises each time predictive mode returns, confirming a causal effect for her.
sources: Research Methods in Applied Behavior Analysis — (various)
reference: Cooper JO, Heron TE & Heward WL (2020) Applied Behavior Analysis. 3rd ed. Pearson

name: SIR Transmission Models for Dark Pattern Spread
origin: Kermack and McKendrick (1927); adapted to UX by the treatise
summary: Models products as susceptible, infected (adopted a pattern) or recovered (abandoned it) to describe and project the spread of dark patterns across an industry.
description: Compartmental models track population flows between states governed by transmission and recovery rates. The treatise adapts SIR to design ecosystems: 'susceptible' products have not adopted a pattern, 'infected' have adopted it, and 'recovered/resistant' adopted then abandoned it under regulatory or reputational pressure. Transmission depends on how easily a pattern can be identified and copied and on competitive pressures incentivising adoption. Fitting the model to adoption timelines estimates parameters, projects spread and simulates interventions (raising recovery via regulation, lowering transmission via standards). Extensions include SIS (re-adoption) and network-based models. Rigour requires careful adoption data, e.g. from web crawls and archives.
steps: Define the pattern and population of products (for example top 1,000 subscription apps).
Build an adoption timeline from crawls, archives and audits.
Fit SIR (or SIS/SEIR) parameters for transmission and recovery rates.
Estimate R0 and check fit against observed curves.
Simulate interventions such as regulation increasing recovery rate.
Report projections with uncertainty and update as data arrive.
outputs: Fitted transmission and recovery rates, R0, adoption projections, intervention simulations.
useWhen: Industry-level analysis of pattern spread, regulatory planning, standards strategy.
avoidWhen: Single-product analysis or when adoption data are unavailable.
whyLost: Epidemic modelling never applied to design; UX lacked cross-product adoption data.
whereToUse: Regulators, consumer advocacy, research on dark patterns, design-system ecosystems.
example: Fitting SIR to 'confirmshaming' adoption across 800 retail sites gives R0 of about 2.3; simulations show a disclosure rule halving transmission would cap prevalence near 15%.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kermack WO & McKendrick AG (1927) A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proc R Soc A 115
Anderson RM & May RM (1991) Infectious Diseases of Humans
Mathur A et al. (2019) Dark patterns at scale. CSCW
reference: Kermack WO & McKendrick AG (1927) A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proceedings of the Royal Society A 115:700-721.

name: Site Visit Fieldwork
origin: Long-standing practice in evaluation research (e.g. Herriott and Firestone, 1983); described as a formal fieldwork procedure by Robert K. Yin, Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2011; 2nd ed. 2016)
summary: Short, scheduled visits of a few days, often by a small team, to many comparable settings so that cross-site patterns can be found, at the cost of the depth of participant observation.
description: Yin presents site visits as the form fieldwork usually takes in policy, organisational and evaluation studies, and as a procedure in its own right rather than a weak form of ethnography. A typical visit lasts only a few days and may use two or more fieldworkers who split interviews and events. Each setting is studied more shallowly than in participant observation, but a dozen or more settings can be covered, so the method suits studies whose main questions concern cross-site patterns; repeat visits add a time perspective. Because time is short, visits follow a pre-arranged schedule and agenda. Yin is explicit about the costs: hosts help set the schedule and may stage it, interviews in a booked meeting room lose the serendipity of seeing people's own workplaces, and a host who accompanies the visitor may alter what others say. Visitors should agree in advance when they will go unaccompanied. Team visits need common training, a shared protocol and rules for joint interviewing, and they allow cross-checking between fieldworkers. For UX, this is the disciplined version of the B2B customer visit programme.
steps: Define the cross-site questions and choose a set of comparable sites, with repeat visits if change over time matters
Prepare a shared protocol and train all team members so fieldwork is consistent
Negotiate a schedule and agenda with each site, noting which parts the host arranged
Agree in advance when the team will interview or observe without the host present
During the visit, split events and interviews between team members and seek informal observation beyond the agenda
Debrief nightly as a team, cross-check what each person saw and heard, and note staged or idealised elements
Write a site report against the protocol, then compare sites to identify patterns
outputs: Per-site reports structured by the protocol, team cross-check notes, and a cross-site comparison of patterns.
useWhen: Many organisational customers or locations must be compared within limited time, such as B2B, healthcare, retail or field-service products.
avoidWhen: The question needs deep understanding of everyday practice in one setting over time; use participant observation or longer ethnography.
whyLost: UX inherited contextual inquiry and ethnography as its models of fieldwork, while customer visits were left to sales and account teams without method; the evaluation-research literature on site visits rarely reached design.
whereToUse: Enterprise software, clinical and lab systems, retail and logistics operations, franchise or branch networks.
example: A two-person team visits eight warehouses over a month, two days each, to understand why a picking app is adopted unevenly. They note that at three sites the manager scheduled only top performers for interviews, ask to spend time on the floor unaccompanied, and find a cross-site pattern linked to shift handover practice.
sources: Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
reference: Yin, R. K. (2016). Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.

name: Situated Action Analysis
origin: Lucy Suchman, 1987
summary: Studies how people improvise action moment by moment in response to circumstances, rather than following plans, to expose where systems assume scripted behaviour.
description: Lucy Suchman's study of users struggling with a Xerox copier's expert help system showed that plans are resources for action, not programmes that determine it. People act in response to the unfolding situation, repairing misunderstandings as they go. Situated action analysis applies this through close video-based interaction analysis of real use: researchers record people using a system, transcribe talk and action in fine detail, and examine how users interpret the system's responses and how the system fails to grasp the user's situation. Rigour comes from detailed sequential transcripts, attention to repair and breakdown episodes, and collaborative data sessions where interpretations are challenged against the record. The method is a corrective to task models and flowcharts and is especially pertinent to conversational and agentic AI systems that infer user intent.
steps: Select real or realistic use situations where the system must interpret user intent.
Video-record 6-12 sessions capturing screen, speech and body, ideally in the actual setting.
Transcribe selected episodes sequentially, aligning user actions, talk and system responses.
Identify breakdowns and repairs where user and system understanding diverge.
Hold group data sessions to interpret episodes and test alternative readings against the recording.
Derive design implications for feedback, repair mechanisms and flexibility versus scripted flows.
outputs: Annotated interaction transcripts, catalogue of breakdown and repair patterns, design implications for system responsiveness.
useWhen: Conversational UI, AI assistants, help systems and workflow tools that assume users follow predefined plans.
avoidWhen: When you need quantitative performance data or quick evaluative findings; use usability testing or analytics.
whyLost: Siloed: Theoretical foundation for contextual and field research methods; rarely referenced directly in practice.
whereToUse: Research design philosophy; conversational UI; adaptive/responsive system design.
example: An AI coding assistant assumed users wanted complete solutions. Situated analysis of recorded sessions showed developers repeatedly interrupted to redirect partial outputs, leading the team to design for incremental, interruptible suggestions.
sources: Being There
Plans and Situated Actions (Lucy Suchman)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Suchman L (1987) Plans and Situated Actions: The Problem of Human-Machine Communication
Suchman L (2007) Human-Machine Reconfigurations
reference: Suchman, L. A. (1987). Plans and Situated Actions: The Problem of Human-Machine Communication. Cambridge University Press.

name: Situated Knowledge and Positionality in Cross-Cultural Research
origin: Donna Haraway, 1988; Nicholas Dirks, 2001
summary: Examines how the researcher's culture, power and categories shape what is observed in cross-cultural research, so findings are not imported assumptions dressed as data.
description: Drawing on Haraway's notion of situated knowledges and on historical work such as Dirks's account of how colonial administration produced the categories it claimed to observe, this method asks researchers to treat their own categories as artefacts of position and power. Before and during cross-cultural research, the team documents where its concepts come from (bank forms, Western personas, prior markets), examines how its identity and sponsorship shape what participants say, and invites local partners to challenge interpretations. Findings are then labelled as emic (participants' own framings) or etic (researcher frameworks). Rigour comes from making these steps explicit and auditable, so that apparent 'user needs' are not simply the team's assumptions reflected back by participants eager to please a powerful outsider.
steps: Positionality audit for any product with global or cross-cultural reach:
Who designed the categories? What cultural context do they come from?
(2) What categories are mandatory vs. optional? Mandatory categories impose the designer's framework on users.
(3) What is missing — what social realities cannot be expressed in the current category system?
(4) Conduct research with users from the non-dominant cultural context to identify category impositions.
outputs: A positionality statement, an inventory of imported categories, local-partner critique notes and revised findings that distinguish emic from etic interpretations.
useWhen: Research in cultures, regions or communities different from the team's own, especially in the Global South, with marginalised groups, or where categories such as caste, kinship or gender organise life.
avoidWhen: Not needed as a heavyweight exercise for studies within the team's own context and with low cultural distance; a lightweight reflexivity journal is enough there.
whyLost: It belongs to anthropology's internal critique of colonial knowledge production; UX imported ethnography's techniques for speed but not its epistemological self-scrutiny.
whereToUse: International product design, gender/identity category design, government digital services, any product serving culturally diverse populations.
example: A payments team from Bengaluru designing for rural Bihar audits its personas and finds that 'household head' was imported from bank forms; local co-researchers show that purchase decisions are distributed across women's self-help groups.
sources: Castes of Mind — Nicholas B. Dirks
reference: Haraway D (1988) Situated knowledges: The science question in feminism and the privilege of partial perspective. Feminist Studies 14(3):575-599

name: Situation Awareness Measurement (SAGAT)
origin: Mica Endsley, 1988; theory in Endsley (1995)
summary: Freezes a simulation at random points, blanks the display and asks users queries about what is happening, objectively measuring perception, comprehension and projection.
description: Endsley defined situation awareness at three levels: perception of elements (Level 1), comprehension of their meaning (Level 2) and projection of future status (Level 3). SAGAT measures it objectively by pausing a realistic simulation at unpredictable moments, hiding all displays and administering queries derived from a goal-directed task analysis of SA requirements. Answers are scored against ground truth from the simulation. Because the freezes are random and queries numerous, users cannot anticipate them, and the scores reflect what they genuinely hold in mind. SAGAT reveals whether a dashboard actually supports understanding and anticipation, which preference ratings and task completion cannot.
steps: Conduct a goal-directed task analysis to list SA requirements at levels 1, 2 and 3 for the user's goals.
Build a realistic, scripted simulation or high-fidelity prototype with ground truth for every queried element.
Plan 3-6 freezes per session at random times, avoiding the first 3-5 minutes, each lasting up to about 2 minutes.
At each freeze, blank the display and administer a random subset of queries; record answers.
Score answers against ground truth per level and per requirement; compare designs with within-subject designs where possible.
Identify requirements with low accuracy and redesign displays to support them; retest.
outputs: SA accuracy scores by level and requirement, comparisons between design alternatives, and a list of poorly supported SA requirements.
useWhen: Dashboards, monitoring tools and operational interfaces where users must understand and anticipate changing situations.
avoidWhen: Static or transactional interfaces; use comprehension testing or usability testing. Avoid where a realistic simulation cannot be built.
whyLost: It needs simulation infrastructure and ground truth, which product teams rarely build. UX substitutes subjective dashboard satisfaction ratings.
whereToUse: Observability dashboards, trading terminals, fleet management, clinical monitoring, autonomous vehicle takeover interfaces.
example: A fleet operations dashboard is compared in a replayed day of data. With SAGAT, dispatchers using the new map view answer projection queries ('which vehicle will be late next?') correctly 71% of the time versus 44% on the list view.
sources: Endsley, Toward a theory of situation awareness in dynamic systems (1995), Human Factors
Endsley, Measurement of situation awareness in dynamic systems (1995), Human Factors
Endsley & Jones, Designing for Situation Awareness (2nd ed., 2011)
reference: Endsley, M. R. (1995). Measurement of situation awareness in dynamic systems. Human Factors, 37(1), 65-84.

name: Situational Analysis
aka: Grounded theory after the postmodern turn
origin: Adele E. Clarke, 2005 (Situational Analysis: Grounded Theory After the Postmodern Turn)
summary: Extends grounded theory by mapping a whole situation, including human and nonhuman elements, social worlds, arenas and discursive positions, through situational, social-worlds and positional maps.
description: Situational Analysis (Adele Clarke, 2005) extends Grounded Theory by mapping the full situation — including nonhuman elements, discourses, and structural conditions — rather than focusing only on human actors and their meanings. It produces three types of maps: situational maps (all elements), social worlds/arenas maps (collective actors and their negotiations), and positional maps (discursive positions on key debates). Applied to UX: it reveals all the stakeholders, artefacts, and competing discourses shaping the product situation, not just the individual user's experience.
steps: Messy situational map: Brainstorm every element in the situation — human actors, nonhuman elements (artefacts, technologies, infrastructure), implicitly implied elements, symbolic elements, discursive constructs, political/economic factors. Put every element on the map regardless of apparent importance.
Ordered situational map: Organise the messy map into categories: individual human, collective human, discursive, nonhuman, political/economic, temporal/historical, spatial/geographic.
Social worlds/arenas map: Identify the collective actors (social worlds — those sharing a particular commitment or practice) and the arenas (sites of ongoing negotiation between those worlds).

Positional map: For each major controversy or debate in the situation: map out the positions that are taken. Each position occupies a location on axes defined by the key dimensions of the debate. This reveals which positions are represented, which are absent, and which might be silenced.
outputs: Messy and ordered situational maps, a social worlds and arenas map, positional maps of contested issues including unoccupied positions, and analytic memos.
useWhen: The problem space is complex and contested, involving many stakeholders, institutions, technologies, regulations and discourses, as in health systems, platforms or public services.
avoidWhen: You need to understand a single user group's task experience or have little time; use contextual inquiry or thematic analysis. For a lighter systems view, use Rich Pictures.
whyLost: It is a sophisticated sociological extension of grounded theory that UX rarely encounters, and its maps resemble stakeholder maps enough that its analytic depth is overlooked.
whereToUse: Healthcare and public service ecosystems, platform governance, AI policy and adoption, multi-sided marketplaces, and strategy research in regulated domains.
example: Exploring adoption of AI triage in GP surgeries, a team builds situational maps including regulators, clinical guidelines, liability discourse and legacy systems. The positional map reveals no actor voicing patient choice, an unoccupied position that shapes the service design.
sources: Situational Analysis (Adele Clarke)
Grounded Theory in Practice (Strauss & Corbin)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
reference: Clarke, A. E. (2005). Situational Analysis: Grounded Theory After the Postmodern Turn. Sage.

name: Skill Acquisition Curve Design
origin: Kathy Sierra, 2015; drawing on Ericsson's deliberate practice
summary: Designs products around the user's progression to competence, mapping where users get stuck on the skill curve and reducing cognitive load to move them through it.
description: Kathy Sierra argues that users do not want better products so much as to be better at what the product enables. Skill acquisition curve design maps the progression from novice to competent user, identifying the 'suck zone' where effort is high and capability low and where most users abandon. Design interventions reduce cognitive resource drain, provide high-quality examples that train perception, structure deliberate practice with small chunks and immediate feedback, and show users progress in the skill rather than in the product. The method becomes rigorous when progression is operationalised with behavioural markers of competence, time-to-competence is measured across cohorts, and interviews explain why users stall at specific points.
steps: Map the target skill: what does 'expert user' look like? What do they know/do/feel that novices don't? Build a skill progression map: novice → competent → proficient → expert. For each stage, identify:
the beliefs that distinguish this stage,
the knowledge required,
the ability (can do it under real conditions). Design each product feature to move users up this map, not to make the product itself easier.
outputs: A skill progression map, identified 'suck zones' and drop-off points, perceptual and practice exercises, and metrics of time-to-competence.
useWhen: Complex tools (creative software, analytics, developer tools) where retention depends on users becoming capable, and onboarding beyond first-run tutorials.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple, single-use products where competence is immediate; then optimise for efficiency instead.
whyLost: Teams optimise for feature adoption and engagement metrics rather than user competence; Sierra's framing remained popular reading, not a practised method.
whereToUse: Professional tool design, learning product design, any product where user competence is the value proposition.
example: A data-visualisation SaaS maps how users progress from importing data to building dashboards, finds a plateau at calculated fields, and adds worked examples that halve time-to-first-dashboard.
sources: Badass: Making Users Awesome — Kathy Sierra
reference: Sierra K (2015) Badass: Making Users Awesome. O'Reilly Media

name: Skill-Rule-Knowledge Analysis
origin: Jens Rasmussen, 1983
summary: Classifies the cognitive control level a task demands (skill, rule or knowledge based) to predict error types and design displays that support each level.
description: Rasmussen's SRK framework distinguishes three levels of cognitive control. Skill-based behaviour is automatic and driven by perceptual signals; rule-based behaviour applies stored if-then rules triggered by recognised signs; knowledge-based behaviour is effortful reasoning about symbols and models in novel situations. Each level has characteristic errors and needs different interface support: skill-based tasks need direct manipulation and consistent spatial mappings; rule-based tasks need clear cues that match rules; knowledge-based tasks need representations of the system's functional structure. As a method, researchers analyse tasks and incidents to determine which level is in use at each step, often through observation and cognitive interviews, and then check that the interface supports that level. It underpins ecological interface design and Reason's GEMS error model.
steps: Decompose the task into steps using observation and interviews with experienced and novice users.
Classify each step as skill, rule or knowledge based by the cues used and the degree of deliberation.
Map known or observed errors to SRK levels (e.g. slips at skill level, misapplied rules, knowledge-based mistakes).
Assess whether the interface provides signals, signs or symbols appropriate to each level.
Redesign to support the right level, for example functional displays for knowledge-based fault diagnosis.
Test performance under both routine and novel scenarios to confirm support at each level.
outputs: SRK-classified task model, error-level mapping, interface support gaps and design recommendations.
useWhen: Expert and safety-critical tools where users shift between routine operation and novel problem solving, such as control rooms and clinical systems.
avoidWhen: Simple consumer tasks performed infrequently; standard task analysis or usability testing suffice.
whyLost: Extinct in UX: Academic cognitive engineering framework; rarely applied in practice.
whereToUse: Expert system design; safety-critical task design; error-prediction for cognitive states.
example: A network operations centre tool supported routine alarms well but outages required knowledge-based diagnosis. SRK analysis showed no view of service dependencies; adding a functional topology view reduced time to diagnose novel faults.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
Information Processing and Human-Machine Interaction (Jens Rasmussen)
reference: Rasmussen, J. (1983). Skills, rules, and knowledge; signals, signs, and symbols, and other distinctions in human performance models. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, SMC-13(3), 257-266.

name: Small Multiples
origin: Edward Tufte, 1983/1990; Cleveland's trellis displays, 1990s
summary: Shows the same chart repeated across segments, conditions or time periods on a shared scale, so differences can be compared at a glance.
description: Small multiples, popularised by Edward Tufte, are series of small charts using identical design, axes and scales, each showing a different slice of the data: a segment, condition, location or time period. Because the design is constant, the eye reads the structure once and then attends only to differences, enabling rapid comparison across many groups without the tangle of overlaid lines. In UX research they suit comparing metrics across variants, markets, platforms or cohorts, and revealing which segment departs from the pattern. Rigour comes from a shared scale (or explicitly flagged exceptions), meaningful ordering of panels (by magnitude or logic rather than alphabet), minimal non-data ink, and clear labelling so each panel can be identified instantly.
steps: Identify any UX analysis with multiple conditions (users × tasks, designs × demographic groups, time points).
Convert: replace a single multi-series chart with N small charts, one per condition, at the same scale.
Arrange in a logical grid (e.g., 3 designs × 4 user segments = 12 small charts).
The visual structure makes differences and similarities immediately apparent.
Data-ink ratio: maximize by removing all repeated axes.
outputs: A grid of comparable charts with shared axes, visible segment differences and outliers, and a compact comparative view for reports and dashboards.
useWhen: Comparing a metric across many segments, variants, platforms, markets or periods, such as funnel shapes by country or task times by design variant.
avoidWhen: Avoid when there are only two series (overlay them), when panels need different scales to be readable, or when the audience needs a single headline; then highlight one comparison.
whyLost: Default dashboard tools favour single overloaded charts with many coloured lines; faceting requires deliberate design and is rarely taught to researchers.
whereToUse: Usability study findings visualization, longitudinal data presentation, A/B test result communication, segmentation analysis.
example: An e-commerce team plots checkout funnel drop-off for twelve markets as small multiples on a common scale; Brazil's panel alone shows a cliff at the address step, traced to postcode validation.
sources: Envisioning Information — Edward Tufte
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
reference: Tufte ER (1990) Envisioning Information. Graphics Press

name: SMEQ (Subjective Mental Effort Question)
origin: Zijlstra & van Doorn (1985), Delft University of Technology; online slider version by Sauro & Dumas (2009)
summary: A single post-task rating of mental effort on a 0 to 150 scale with calibrated verbal anchors, one of the most sensitive post-task measures.
description: The SMEQ is a vertical scale from 0 to 150 with nine verbal labels from "not at all hard to do" just above 0 to "tremendously hard to do" just above 110. The labels were placed by psychometric calibration rather than at equal intervals. On paper, participants draw a line across the 150 mm scale; online, they use a slider. Sauro and Dumas (2009) found it correlated 0.94 with the SEQ and strongly with completion time, completion rate and errors, and in their comparison it was at least as sensitive as the SEQ with small samples. It is free and works well when you want a finer-grained measure of task difficulty than a 7-point item.
steps: Present the SMEQ scale immediately after each task.
Ask participants to mark or slide to the level of mental effort the task required.
Record the value from 0 to 150.
Compare task means with confidence intervals, as for any continuous measure.
Look at tasks with high effort but successful completion: they are hidden friction.
outputs: A fine-grained mental-effort score per task.
useWhen: Comparing tasks or designs where small differences in difficulty matter.
avoidWhen: Survey contexts where a slider or drawn line is awkward; the SEQ is simpler.
whyLost: The SEQ is easier to explain and administer, and the SMEQ's Dutch work-psychology roots are little known in UX.
whereToUse: Lab and unmoderated task-based studies, cognitive load comparisons.
example: Two checkout designs have identical completion rates, but SMEQ effort falls from 62 to 35, showing the new design is easier even though both work.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Sauro, J. & Dumas, J. (2009). Comparison of three one-question, post-task usability questionnaires. CHI 2009.

name: Snowball and Respondent-Driven Sampling
origin: Snowball sampling from Leo Goodman, 1961; respondent-driven sampling by Douglas Heckathorn, 1997
summary: Recruiting hard-to-reach participants through referrals from existing participants, with RDS adding coupons and chain tracking to correct network bias.
description: Snowball sampling uses participants' social networks to reach populations with no sampling frame: specialists, stigmatised groups, informal workers or small professional communities. Each participant refers one or two others who meet criteria. Its weakness is homophily: chains reproduce the characteristics of the seeds, producing homogeneous samples. Heckathorn's respondent-driven sampling formalises the process for HIV research among hidden populations, issuing a limited number of coupons per participant, tracking recruitment chains, recording network size, and using these to weight estimates so that, with long enough chains, results become less dependent on seeds. In qualitative UX the main safeguard is monitoring diversity after early interviews and introducing new seeds from other parts of the network.
steps: Recruit an initial seed participant who meets criteria and is known to others in the target population.
After each interview, ask for 1–2 referrals. Get permission to use their name.
RDS extension: Give each participant 2–3 formal recruitment coupons. Track chains. RDS attempts to correct network bias mathematically.
Monitor for homophily: After 5–7 interviews, check whether the sample is inadvertently homogeneous. If so, introduce new seeds from different network parts.
outputs: A recruited sample of hard-to-reach participants, referral chain maps, homophily checks, and, for RDS, network-size data for weighting.
useWhen: Populations without accessible lists or panels: niche professionals, informal economy workers, rare conditions, or communities wary of outsiders.
avoidWhen: When panels or customer lists can reach the population directly, or when independence of cases matters for statistical claims; use direct or probability sampling.
whyLost: Snowball referral is used informally, but RDS chain tracking and bias correction remain in public health research.
whereToUse: Gig and informal worker tools, rare disease patient apps, specialised B2B roles, security researchers, and emerging-market financial services.
example: Recruiting mobile money agents in rural Uganda, researchers start with three seeds in different districts and give each participant two coupons. After seven interviews they notice all agents share one distributor and add new seeds elsewhere.
sources: Sampling and Choosing Cases in Qualitative Research
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Snowball Sampling (Goodman)
Respondent-Driven Sampling: A New Approach to the Study of Hidden Populations (Heckathorn)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Heckathorn, D. D. (1997). Respondent-driven sampling: A new approach to the study of hidden populations. Social Problems, 44(2), 174-199.

name: SNR Interface Evaluation Framework
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Measures interface clarity as the share of essential elements on screen (element SNR) and the share of attention they receive (behavioural SNR), with thresholds linked to errors and success.
description: The framework defines signal as elements that directly support task completion (primary label, key button, required field) and noise as elements that distract, mislead or are irrelevant. Element SNR = signal elements / total visible actionable or reading elements; behavioural SNR = dwell on signal / total dwell, from eye-tracking, click heatmaps or cursor dwell. Low SNR correlates with misroutes and mistakes and often elevates slips and lapses, so auditing SNR before and after a redesign predicts whether clutter reduction will lower errors. Target bars are element SNR ≥ 0.60 and behavioural SNR ≥ 0.70. SNR also appears as a covariate in Cox models (HR 0.92 per +0.10) and as a multiplier in the Deviation Utility model, where a new form's utility is scaled by how legibly it presents its value. Rigour depends on a consistent signal inventory and counting rules across variants.
steps: Define a signal inventory: the essential elements for the focal task.
Count signal versus total visible actionable or reading elements per key screen, using the same counting rules for every variant (e.g. Alerts before: 9/20 = 0.45).
Collect attention data (eye-tracking or cursor dwell) and compute behavioural SNR (e.g. 35.1s / 60.3s = 0.58).
Compare against bars of element SNR ≥ 0.60 and behavioural SNR ≥ 0.70.
Pair SNR with error taxonomy and task outcomes in a side-by-side table (success, misroutes, coded errors).
Redesign to remove non-essential links and promote primary labels, then re-compute both SNRs (after: 12/18 = 0.67; 36.4s / 47.9s = 0.76).
Report SNR deltas alongside success, misroutes and coded errors.
outputs: Element and behavioural SNR baselines and deltas per screen, linked to success and error rates.
useWhen: When clutter, competing links or low salience of primary actions is suspected, and as a quick clarity metric stakeholders understand.
avoidWhen: When the problem is conceptual (wrong labels or mental model mismatch) rather than salience; use tree testing and mental-model interviews.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath (the 'SNR Interface Evaluation Framework'); signal-to-noise thinking exists in information design but is rarely quantified in UX.
whereToUse: Dashboards, fintech home screens, settings pages, enterprise consoles, AI product surfaces with many controls.
example: A redesign of a trading app's alerts screen raises element SNR from 0.45 to 0.67 and behavioural SNR from 0.58 to 0.76, while Mistake-coded errors on the navigation step fall from 39 to 18 per 100 sessions.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
Studio Aghora

Information Theory

The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (Edward Tufte)

name: SNR measurement
origin: Communications engineering, early 20th century; formalised in Shannon's channel capacity theorem, 1948
summary: Quantifies the ratio of task-relevant signal to irrelevant noise in a display, alert stream or notification channel, to show where meaning is being drowned.
description: In engineering, SNR is signal power divided by noise power, often in decibels (10 log10 S/N). Applied to interfaces it takes two forms. Physical SNR measures, for example, alarm loudness above ambient noise or luminance contrast of a target against its background. Informational SNR measures the proportion of actionable to non-actionable items in a stream: actionable alerts over total alerts, task-relevant pixels over total pixels, or relevant results over results shown. Both connect to Shannon's capacity theorem, which shows the information a channel can carry rises with log(1 + S/N). The method is rigorous when signal and noise are defined operationally before counting, and when measurements are taken in realistic conditions rather than in a quiet lab.
steps: Define what counts as signal (actionable, task-relevant) and noise (irrelevant, redundant, non-actionable) for the channel in scope.
For physical channels, measure levels in situ: alarm SPL versus ambient noise (aim for at least 10 dB above ambient), or luminance contrast (WCAG minimum 4.5:1 for text).
For informational channels, sample at least one representative week of alerts, notifications or results and code each item as signal or noise using two coders; target Cohen's kappa of 0.7 or higher.
Compute SNR per channel and per user role, and in decibels where useful.
Identify the largest noise contributors (Pareto: often 20% of alert types produce 80% of noise).
Remove, batch or demote noise sources and recompute SNR after the change.
outputs: SNR values per channel and role, a Pareto list of noise sources, and a before/after comparison.
useWhen: When users complain of overload or alarm fatigue; when dashboards or feeds feel cluttered; when evaluating notification strategy or search result quality.
avoidWhen: When the issue is discriminability between two similar signals rather than signal versus noise; use d' or ROC analysis instead.
whyLost: UX uses 'signal to noise' as a metaphor but rarely measures it; operationalising signal and noise requires explicit coding that teams skip.
whereToUse: Clinical alarms, observability and DevOps alerting, enterprise notifications, news feeds, AI assistant verbosity, and search results.
example: A surgical console shows 42 status messages per hour of which coders judge 5 actionable, an informational SNR of 0.13. Suppressing routine confirmations and batching device chatter raises it to 0.6, and surgeons' response time to genuine warnings falls by a third.
sources: Van Drongelen, W., Signal Processing for Neuroscientists
MacKay, D. J. C., Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003)
Gopinath, V., Forward-Thinking Playbook
Van Drongelen (Signal Processing for Neuroscientists)
MacKay
Forward-Thinking Playbook (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 2 — Signal, Noise & the Detection of Intent
reference: Shannon, C. E. (1949). Communication in the presence of noise. Proceedings of the IRE, 37(1), 10-21.

name: Social Media and Digital Trace Data Analysis
donor: Internet research and computational social science
origin: Internet research tradition from the late 1990s; formalised in social media research methods in the 2010s
summary: Systematically samples and codes naturally occurring online communication such as reviews, forums, social posts and tickets, as unprompted evidence of user experience.
description: Users constantly describe their experience without being asked: in app store reviews, Reddit threads, community forums, social posts and support tickets. This data avoids researcher reactivity but brings its own biases, since vocal, extreme and platform-specific users dominate. Rigorous analysis starts with an ethical assessment (public versus semi-public spaces, identifiability, platform terms), then defines a sampling strategy, such as purposive sampling of extreme cases or stratified random sampling across time and rating. Posts are coded in their conversational context, because a reply means little without the thread. Findings are treated as hypotheses about the experience and triangulated with primary research, never as population estimates.
steps: Ethical framework first: Is this data public or semi-public? Are users identifiable? Apply the Public Benefit / No Harm test.
Sampling strategy: For large corpora: purposive sampling (extreme negative reviews, specific terms). For small corpora: total population analysis.
Qualitative coding: Apply thematic analysis or content analysis. Code for: expressed needs, frustrations, workarounds, emotional valence, social context.
Context preservation: Always code text in its conversational context — a sentence means something different in a heated complaint thread than in a first review.
Triangulate with primary research: Social media data reveals unprompted opinions but lacks context. Always triangulate with interviews or observations.
outputs: A documented corpus and sampling frame, coded themes in context, representative excerpts (anonymised), trend patterns over time, and hypotheses for primary research.
useWhen: You need fast, low-cost insight into real complaints and language, want to track reaction to a release, or are researching a domain where recruiting is hard but online discussion is rich.
avoidWhen: You need representative prevalence estimates or insight into silent or non-online users; use surveys or field research. Avoid when data involves vulnerable communities without careful ethical review.
whyLost: It survived and grew because data is abundant and cheap and social listening tools industrialised it, though the sampling and context discipline is often skipped.
whereToUse: App store and marketplace products, release monitoring, competitor research, community-driven products, and health or finance topics with active online communities.
example: After a banking app redesign, a researcher samples 400 one- and two-star reviews stratified by week and codes them in context. Complaints about 'missing' features turn out to be about relocated navigation, which follow-up usability tests confirm.
sources: Social Media Research Methods
Research Methods for Everyday Life
reference: Sloan, L. & Quan-Haase, A. (eds.) (2017). The SAGE Handbook of Social Media Research Methods. Sage.

name: Social Network Analysis (SNA) for Collaborative Tool UX
origin: Jacob Moreno (1934, sociometry); Wasserman and Faust (1994)
summary: Maps who interacts with whom through a product to find bottlenecks, structural holes and how features diffuse across an organisation.
description: SNA models actors as nodes and interactions as edges, computing measures such as degree centrality, betweenness centrality (how often a node lies on paths between others), clustering coefficients and structural holes (gaps a node bridges). The treatise's transfer: map how information and decisions flow through a team using a collaborative tool. Which users are structural bottlenecks? Where are structural holes the design fails to bridge? Which features are adopted in clusters but not diffused? Network analysis reveals organisational topology to which individual-level UX research is blind. Data can come from product logs (mentions, shares, comments) or surveys, and ethics and privacy require care.
steps: Define actors and the relation of interest (messages, shares, approvals, mentions).
Extract edges from logs or collect via survey with consent and privacy safeguards.
Build the network and compute centrality, clustering and community structure.
Identify bottlenecks, isolates, bridges and feature adoption clusters.
Interview selected nodes (bridges, isolates) to interpret structure.
Design interventions (routing, visibility, shared spaces) and re-measure the network.
outputs: Network maps, centrality metrics, community and diffusion analysis, design interventions.
useWhen: Collaboration, communication and enterprise tools; design system or feature adoption across teams.
avoidWhen: Single-user products, or when interaction data cannot be collected ethically.
whyLost: Network science sits in sociology and data science; UX research focuses on individuals.
whereToUse: Slack-like tools, document collaboration, enterprise approvals, design system adoption studies.
example: SNA of approval flows in a procurement tool shows one finance manager on 64% of paths; adding delegation rules cuts median approval time from 4 days to 1.5.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Wasserman S & Faust K (1994) Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications
Borgatti SP et al. (2009) Network analysis in the social sciences. Science 323:892-895
Burt RS (1992) Structural Holes
reference: Wasserman S & Faust K (1994) Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications. Cambridge University Press.

name: Solomon Four-Group Design
origin: Richard Solomon, 1949
summary: Combines pretest-posttest and posttest-only groups to estimate an intervention's effect and whether the pretest itself changed responses.
description: Pretests can sensitise participants: answering questions about privacy before using a feature may make them notice privacy cues. Solomon's design uses four groups: pretest-treatment-posttest, pretest-control-posttest, treatment-posttest only and control-posttest only. A 2x2 analysis of posttest scores (treatment by pretested) estimates the treatment effect, the pretest effect and their interaction. It is the classic way to detect testing effects and remains relevant whenever UX research measures attitudes or knowledge before and after an intervention, such as onboarding, education or trust-building features.
steps: Define the intervention, the pretest and posttest measures.
Randomly assign participants to the four groups, balancing group sizes.
Administer pretests to groups 1 and 2 only; deliver the intervention to groups 1 and 3.
Administer posttests to all groups under identical conditions.
Analyse posttest scores with a 2x2 ANOVA (treatment x pretest) and check the interaction for sensitisation.
Use pretest data from groups 1 and 2 for gain analysis only if no sensitisation is found.
outputs: Estimates of treatment effect, pretest effect and pretest-by-treatment interaction.
useWhen: Evaluating interventions on attitudes, awareness or knowledge where pretesting may prime participants.
avoidWhen: Behavioural outcomes unaffected by measurement, or when sample size cannot support four groups.
whyLost: It doubles sample requirements, and UX rarely considers testing effects of its own questionnaires.
whereToUse: Security awareness features, privacy dashboards, financial literacy tools, AI explanation evaluations.
example: Evaluating a privacy dashboard, the team finds that pretested participants reported much higher awareness gains than posttest-only participants: the pretest itself explained half of the apparent effect.
sources: Solomon, An extension of control group design (1949), Psychological Bulletin
Campbell & Stanley, Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Research (1966)
reference: Solomon, R. L. (1949). An extension of control group design. Psychological Bulletin, 46(2), 137-150.

name: spaCy NLP Pipeline for Qualitative Research
origin: spaCy library by Matthew Honnibal & Ines Montani (Explosion), 2015 onward
summary: Using spaCy pipelines for entity recognition, dependency patterns and sentiment to extract and aggregate linguistic evidence across large transcript corpora.
description: Natural language processing can surface patterns across hundreds of transcripts that human readers would miss or take weeks to find. A spaCy pipeline loads a transformer-based model for conversational text, adds custom named entity recognition for domain terms (products, competitors, features), and uses dependency-parse patterns to extract structured statements such as first-person habitual claims ('I always...', 'I never...'), which are direct evidence of behaviour and mental models. Sentence-level sentiment can be aggregated by participant and topic, and custom components can flag segments matching codebook criteria by keyword and syntactic context. Outputs guide human analysis by locating relevant passages; interpretation remains human.
steps: Model selection: en_core_web_trf (transformer-based) for maximum accuracy on conversational text.
Named entity recognition: Identify product names, competitors, specific features. Build custom NER for domain-specific entities.
Dependency parsing: Extract first-person behavioural statements ('I always…', 'I never…') using dependency parse patterns — most direct evidence for mental model data.
Sentiment aggregation: Sentence-level sentiment classification aggregated by participant and topic to build emotional response profiles.
Custom research code component: Build a spaCy component that flags sentences matching qualitative codes based on keyword + syntactic context patterns.
outputs: Entity frequency tables, extracted habitual and attitudinal statements, sentiment profiles by participant and topic, and flagged segments for coding.
useWhen: Large text corpora (transcripts, reviews, tickets) where you need systematic extraction of mentions, statements or patterns to guide analysis.
avoidWhen: Small studies, or when no one can validate NLP output; sentiment models can misread sarcasm and domain language. Use manual coding.
whyLost: It requires programming skills uncommon on UX teams, and LLM tools now compete for the same role, so rule-based linguistic pipelines are rarely built.
whereToUse: Customer feedback mining, competitive mention tracking, large interview programmes, and app store review analysis.
example: Processing 300 interviews about project management tools, dependency patterns extract 1,200 'I always' statements. Clustering shows 'I always export to Excel before meetings', guiding a reporting feature.
sources: spaCy (en_core_web_trf)

displacy
spaCy documentation (Explosion)
reference: Honnibal, M., Montani, I., Van Landeghem, S. & Boyd, A. (2020). spaCy: Industrial-strength Natural Language Processing in Python. Zenodo.

name: Spatial Cognition Analysis for Information Architecture
origin: Barbara Tversky, 2019; Kevin Lynch, 1960
summary: Applies research on how people think spatially (landmarks, routes, survey knowledge, gestures and diagrams) to design and evaluate navigation and information structures.
description: Barbara Tversky's work shows that spatial thinking is the foundation of abstract thought: people use space, gesture and diagrams to organise ideas, and spatial knowledge develops from landmarks to routes to survey (map-like) understanding. Kevin Lynch's study of city images adds elements such as paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks. Applied to information architecture, this method examines whether a product offers stable landmarks, coherent districts and visible overviews that let users build survey knowledge, or forces route-only navigation. Techniques include asking users to sketch the product's structure, analysing navigation paths and orientation errors, and mapping the IA's spatial metaphors. Rigour comes from combining sketch-map analysis with tree testing and navigation metrics.
steps: Spatial IA audit:
Does the IA have a coherent spatial metaphor? (hierarchical = tree, linear = path, faceted = multi-dimensional space).
(2) Do users develop a consistent spatial mental map? Test: ask users to draw the IA from memory. Compare to actual structure.
(3) Are spatial landmarks present? (elements that serve as navigation anchors).
(4) Are spatial invariants preserved? (if an item is 'deep', it should always be deep — inconsistency destroys the spatial map).
outputs: Analysis of spatial metaphors and landmarks in the IA, users' sketch maps of the product, route versus survey knowledge findings, and navigation redesigns.
useWhen: Large information spaces (intranets, documentation, enterprise apps, e-commerce catalogues) where users get lost or fail to form a mental map.
avoidWhen: Avoid for small, flat products where navigation is trivial; for labelling issues, use card sorting and tree testing instead.
whyLost: Spatial cognition research is rich but rarely translated; IA practice focuses on labels and hierarchy rather than how people form spatial representations.
whereToUse: IA design, navigation design, large-scale information environment design, VR/AR navigation design.
example: Users of a hospital intranet draw sketch maps showing no sense of 'where' policies live; adding stable landmarks (persistent hubs) and a visible overview map improves findability in tree tests.
sources: Mind in Motion — Barbara Tversky
reference: Tversky B (2019) Mind in Motion: How Action Shapes Thought. Basic Books

name: Speaker diarisation (pyannote)
origin: Diarisation research from NIST evaluations (late 1990s-2000s); pyannote.audio, Hervé Bredin et al., 2020
summary: Automatically segmenting an interview recording by speaker, so transcripts distinguish participant from moderator and analysis uses only participant speech.
description: Speaker diarisation answers 'who spoke when'. pyannote.audio uses neural voice activity detection, speaker change detection and speaker embeddings clustered into speakers, producing time-stamped speaker turns that can be aligned with Whisper's word timestamps. In UX research this separates moderator prompts from participant answers, supports focus groups and co-interviews, and prevents moderator language from contaminating coding and NLP. Rigour comes from specifying the expected number of speakers when known, measuring diarisation error rate on a reference sample, and handling overlapping speech, which remains the main error source. Speaker labels are anonymous (SPEAKER_00); mapping them to roles must be checked.
steps: Prepare 16 kHz mono WAV files and accept the model licence terms; run locally for sensitive data.
Run the pyannote speaker-diarisation pipeline, passing num_speakers when known (e.g. 2 for one-to-one interviews).
Align speaker turns with Whisper word timestamps to produce speaker-attributed transcripts.
Map anonymous speaker labels to roles (moderator, participant) using a rule such as who speaks first, and verify on every file.
Measure diarisation error rate on 5-10 hand-labelled files and investigate files with heavy overlap.
Exclude or flag moderator turns before coding and NLP analysis.
outputs: Speaker-attributed, time-stamped transcripts, role mappings and diarisation error estimates.
useWhen: Interviews, focus groups, usability sessions and call recordings where analysis must separate speakers.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on it for highly overlapping group conversations or very short recordings; use manual turn labelling or separate microphones per speaker.
whyLost: Diarisation matured in speech research and became accessible to researchers only with open pre-trained pipelines around 2020.
whereToUse: Interview programmes at scale, focus groups, contact-centre research and co-design session recordings.
example: A SaaS research team diarises 80 customer interviews and removes moderator speech before topic modelling. Previously, the moderator's repeated phrase 'walk me through' had dominated a spurious topic.
sources: whisper.cpp (local, privacy-preserving)
openai-whisper (cloud)
pyannote.audio (diarisation)
ffmpeg
pydub
Bredin, H. et al. (2020) pyannote.audio: neural building blocks for speaker diarization. ICASSP
Radford, A. et al. (2023) Robust speech recognition via large-scale weak supervision. ICML
The Inquiry Series, C9 — Whisper — Batch Transcription at Scale

name: Species Accumulation and Good-Turing Coverage for Saturation
origin: I. J. Good and Alan Turing (1953, Good-Turing frequency estimation); species accumulation in ecology (Gotelli and Colwell, 2001); Chao and Jost coverage (2012)
summary: Estimates how complete a set of discovered themes, codes or problems is from the frequency of items seen only once, giving a quantitative basis for saturation.
description: Good and Turing, while breaking Enigma codes, showed that the probability of encountering a new type next is estimated by the proportion of observations that are singletons (types seen once). Ecologists use accumulation and rarefaction curves to estimate species richness and sample coverage. Applied to qualitative research, codes or themes are the 'species' and interviews are samples. Coverage estimates (1 minus singletons/total) and extrapolated accumulation curves (e.g. with the iNEXT method) show the expected number of new codes per extra interview. This gives an auditable complement to the vague notion of saturation. Lewis (2001) applied Good-Turing adjustments to usability problem discovery rates.
steps: Code data incrementally and record which codes appear in each interview or session.
Plot the accumulation of unique codes against sample size, randomising order to get a smooth curve.
Count singletons and doubletons; compute Good-Turing coverage and Chao1 richness estimates.
Extrapolate with rarefaction/extrapolation methods (e.g. iNEXT) to predict new codes from additional sessions.
Set stopping criteria (e.g. coverage above 0.9 for themes of interest) before fieldwork.
Report coverage alongside qualitative judgements of meaning saturation.
outputs: Accumulation curves, coverage estimates, estimated total codes and expected yield of further sampling.
useWhen: Justifying sample sizes in qualitative or problem-discovery studies, or deciding whether to continue fieldwork.
avoidWhen: Highly interpretive studies where codes are not countable units, or when theoretical sampling deliberately shifts the population.
whyLost: Qualitative researchers resist counting, and quantitative ecologists never met UX researchers; Lewis's work stayed niche.
whereToUse: Interview programmes, usability problem discovery, review and ticket coding, diary studies.
example: After 14 interviews, 9 of 61 codes are singletons; coverage is 0.85 and extrapolation predicts about 6 new codes from 6 more interviews, so the team runs 6 more targeted at under-sampled segments.
sources: Good, The population frequencies of species and the estimation of population parameters (1953), Biometrika
Chao & Jost, Coverage-based rarefaction and extrapolation (2012), Ecology
Lewis, Evaluation of procedures for adjusting problem-discovery rates estimated from small samples (2001), International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction

name: Spectral Annotation Matrix
donor: Signal processing combined with ethnographic coding
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A table aligning each spectral peak or burst (time, frequency band) with the UX event, user quote, qualitative code and interpretation, bridging mathematics and ethnography.
description: The Spectral Annotation Matrix is the core artefact of Stage 3 (Contextual Annotation) of the Behavioral Spectral Framework. Each row records the time, the frequency band of a detected peak or burst, the UX event at that moment, the qualitative code from open coding and an interpretation. Examples: 03:15, 0.8–1.2 Hz, interface pause, Confusion, micro-frustration; 05:40, 0.1–0.3 Hz, slow repetition, Confidence, skill consolidation. In the fintech case, rows include 02:13 at 0.95 Hz on a KYC page loop ('I kept re-entering the OTP', Frustration), 04:32 at 0.40 Hz on tooltip use (Relief) and 07:45 at 0.18 Hz on portfolio preview (Satisfaction). Frustration-labelled moments coincided with transient high-frequency spikes and relief followed a low-frequency rebound. Its rigour depends on multiple observers agreeing on codes and repetition across participants exceeding random expectation.
steps: Export timestamps of spectral peaks, wavelet bursts and drift points from the decomposition stage.
Pull aligned qualitative material for each timestamp: screen recording, transcript or think-aloud quote, and the UX event.
Open-code each event (e.g. frustration, curiosity, learning, boredom, relief, satisfaction).
Record rows as Time | Frequency band | UX event | Quote | Qualitative code | Interpretation.
Look for regularities across rows and participants (e.g. Frustration ↔ high-frequency spikes) and note divergences such as excitement with high-frequency bursts.
Have multiple coders review the matrix and retrain models with the grounded labels.
outputs: An annotated event matrix linking frequency features to coded experiences, plus labelled data for retraining.
useWhen: Whenever spectral or time-series analysis of behaviour needs qualitative meaning before it is reported.
avoidWhen: When no qualitative record aligned in time exists; then spectral features remain uninterpreted.
whyLost: Original technique by Vivek Gopinath.
whereToUse: Onboarding studies, AI chat interaction analysis, biometric UX studies, emotional journey mapping.
example: Reviewing a KYC session, the researcher logs a 0.95 Hz burst at 02:13 with the quote 'I kept re-entering the OTP' coded as Frustration, which later supports a real-time validation prescription.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). From Stars to Signals, Section 5.4 and 6.4.

name: Spectral Drift Metrics (Centroid Shift and Drift Rate)
donor: Signal processing (audio and astronomy) applied to longitudinal UX
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: Longitudinal metrics reading change in a user's frequency signature as learning or fatigue: spectral centroid shift per session, relative drift rate ḟ/f, and phase offset to system signals.
description: In astronomy drift complicates classification; in behaviour, the playbook argues, drift is the story. Three metrics quantify it: spectral centroid shift (Δfc) per session, tracking the movement of the energy-weighted mean frequency; drift rate ḟ/f as a learning-speed or design-fatigue indicator, where negative drift means stabilisation; and phase offset between user and system signals as a synchrony measure. Relative energy drift ΔP/P serves as a proxy for stability or novelty. In the fintech case the spectral centroid shifted toward lower frequencies by the end of session three, indicating reduced reactivity, and reductions in drift rate correlated with improved SUS scores. Drift timelines (centroid shift versus time) are the recommended report visual.
steps: Compute a spectrum per session per user from the chosen behavioural signal.
Calculate the spectral centroid for each session and the shift Δfc between sessions.
Compute drift rate ḟ/f across sessions and relative energy drift ΔP/P.
Where user and system signals both exist, compute their phase offset as a synchrony measure.
Plot a drift timeline and correlate drift metrics with established measures such as SUS.
Interpret drift with qualitative evidence: stabilisation as learning, rising high-frequency energy as overload or fatigue.
outputs: Per-user drift trajectories, drift timelines and correlations with UX outcomes.
useWhen: Longitudinal studies of learning curves, habit formation, fatigue or design sustainability.
avoidWhen: Single-session studies, or data too sparse to compute stable spectra.
whyLost: Original operationalisation by Vivek Gopinath; spectral centroid is common in audio analysis but absent from UX.
whereToUse: Onboarding learning curves, retention interventions, AI assistant adoption, wearable and biometric studies.
example: Across three onboarding sessions the centroid of a new investor's interaction rhythm shifts lower and ḟ/f turns negative, matching higher SUS and interview statements of growing confidence.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). From Stars to Signals, Sections 4.7 and B.8.

name: Spectral Entropy
origin: Inouye et al., 1991 (EEG spectral entropy), from Shannon entropy
summary: Shannon entropy of a normalised power spectrum, quantifying whether behaviour is dominated by a few rhythms (routine) or spread across many (exploration or overload).
description: Spectral entropy normalises the power spectrum into a probability distribution and computes its Shannon entropy. Low values mean energy concentrated in a few frequencies; high values mean energy spread broadly. The Behavioral Spectral Framework uses it to quantify exploration versus routine: stable low-frequency dominance indicates habit formation, while rising entropy indicates curiosity or cognitive overload, which only context can separate. In the fintech onboarding case, spectral entropy decreased from 0.89 to 0.62 across three sessions, signalling an emergent routine, and served with wavelet burst counts and mean frequency as predictors in a Random Forest that classified sessions as stable or volatile with 82% accuracy. Entropy drift plots are a recommended visual.
steps: Compute the power spectrum for each session or user.
Normalise spectral power to sum to 1.
Compute Shannon entropy of the normalised spectrum, scaled to 0–1 if comparing different resolutions.
Track entropy across sessions and plot entropy drift.
Use entropy as a feature in interpretable models alongside burst counts and mean frequency.
Disambiguate high entropy (curiosity versus confusion) with qualitative evidence.
outputs: Entropy values per session, entropy drift plots and model features.
useWhen: When distinguishing routinisation from exploration or overload in dense behavioural or biometric signals.
avoidWhen: When spectra cannot be computed reliably; use interaction entropy over action categories instead.
whyLost: Used in anaesthesia monitoring and EEG research, unknown in UX.
whereToUse: Onboarding learning curves, habit products, cognitive load studies.
example: Onboarding sessions of new investors show spectral entropy falling from 0.89 to 0.62 by the third session, matching interview reports of growing confidence.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
reference: Inouye, T., Shinosaki, K., Sakamoto, H., Toi, S., Ukai, S., Iyama, A., Katsuda, Y., & Hirano, M. (1991). Quantification of EEG irregularity by use of the entropy of the power spectrum. Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology, 79(3), 204–210.

name: Speculative and Design Fiction Research
origin: Anthony Dunne and Fiona Raby, 1990s to 2013 (Speculative Everything); Julian Bleecker, 2009 (Design Fiction)
summary: Uses plausible fictional products, interfaces or scenarios as research probes to elicit participants' values, concerns and assumptions about technology futures.
description: Speculative design research (Dunne & Raby; Bleecker) uses designed artefacts that do not yet exist — products, interfaces, scenarios for possible futures — as research stimuli. By asking participants to respond to plausible-but-fictional designs, researchers access values, concerns, and assumptions about technology that participants cannot easily articulate in relation to existing products. Design fiction is particularly powerful for: exploring long-term implications of current design trajectories, surfacing values that only become visible when confronted with design choices, and including participants in discussions about technology futures.
steps: Design the speculative artefact: Create a designed object, interface, or scenario for a plausible-but-not-yet-existing product. Diegetically: produce it as if it exists — packaging, marketing materials, instruction manual — to increase the sense of reality.
Brief participants without framing its status: Present the speculative design as you would a real product: 'We're working on something new. Here's an early version. What do you think?'
Elicit responses: Observe what participants attend to, what they accept without question, and what they question or resist. Each question or acceptance reveals an assumption.

Defamiliarisation elicitation: After initial reactions, reveal that the design is speculative. Then: 'What does this design imply about how [organisation / technology / society] should work?' The juxtaposition of real and fictional elicits values.

Analysis: Analyse: what futures did participants accept as inevitable? What futures did they resist? What values did their responses reveal? These are your findings about participants' implicit assumptions about technology and society.
outputs: Speculative artefacts, recorded participant reactions, accepted versus contested assumptions, value tensions, and implications for product principles and policy.
useWhen: Exploring emerging technologies (AI agents, biometrics, autonomous systems) or long-horizon strategy, where users cannot evaluate what does not yet exist through standard methods.
avoidWhen: You need evaluation of a concrete near-term design; use prototyping and usability testing. Be cautious with deception when not revealing an artefact's fictional status.
whyLost: It is valued in design academia and galleries but seen as provocative art rather than research in product companies, which want near-term, validated findings.
whereToUse: AI and automation strategy, health data futures, smart city and mobility, financial futures, ethics and responsible innovation reviews.
example: A bank shows participants a fictional ad for an AI that negotiates bills automatically. Reactions show acceptance of automation but strong objection to the AI 'speaking as me', defining a principle of disclosure in agent design.
sources: Speculative Everything (Dunne & Raby)
Design Fiction (Bleecker)
Research Design (Leavy)
reference: Dunne, A. & Raby, F. (2013). Speculative Everything: Design, Fiction, and Social Dreaming. MIT Press.

name: Speculative Design
origin: Anthony Dunne and Fiona Raby, 1990s-2013
summary: Creates provocative artefacts from possible futures to surface values, consequences and alternatives, using them as research instruments to provoke discussion.
description: Speculative design uses design not to solve problems but to ask questions. Dunne and Raby proposed making artefacts from plausible or preferable futures, such as objects, interfaces or scenarios, that provoke people to reflect on values and consequences of technology. Design fiction (Sterling, Bleecker) is a close relative. As a research method, speculative artefacts become probes: researchers show them to participants and stakeholders and analyse reactions, debates and value conflicts. Rigour comes from grounding speculations in real signals and trends, deliberately varying futures along defined axes (for example using the futures cone of probable, plausible and possible), and analysing responses systematically rather than treating the artefact itself as the output. It is valuable for surfacing ethical concerns and latent assumptions before they become product decisions.
steps: Scan for signals of change relevant to the domain (technology, regulation, social trends).
Define two or three future scenarios along explicit axes such as probable, plausible and preferable.
Design concrete artefacts from each future (e.g. fake product pages, objects, interface mock-ups).
Present artefacts to 8-20 participants or stakeholders in interviews or workshops and probe reactions and values.
Analyse responses for value conflicts, fears, desires and assumptions.
Translate insights into ethical principles, strategic risks or research questions for the product.
outputs: Future scenarios, speculative artefacts, analysis of value conflicts and reactions, strategic and ethical implications.
useWhen: Long-range strategy, emerging technology (AI, biometrics, neurotech), ethics reviews and when teams need to question assumptions.
avoidWhen: Short-term feature decisions or usability questions; use evaluative research instead.
whyLost: Latent: Academic; growing in design education and ethics; occasionally used in corporate futures research.
whereToUse: Long-range futures research; design ethics work; organizational strategy.
example: An insurer created a speculative app that adjusted premiums daily based on wearable data. Showing it to 15 customers surfaced strong reactions about surveillance and fairness, leading the board to rule out continuous behavioural pricing.
sources: Universal Methods of Design
Speculative Everything (Dunne & Raby)
reference: Dunne, A., & Raby, F. (2013). Speculative Everything: Design, Fiction, and Social Dreaming. MIT Press.

name: Speech act analysis
origin: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words, 1962; John Searle's taxonomy, 1969 and 1976; Winograd and Flores applied it to computing, 1986
summary: Classifies what each system and user utterance does, such as requesting, committing, declaring or informing, to check that interface language performs the intended acts.
description: Austin and Searle showed that utterances perform actions. Searle's five classes are assertives (stating), directives (requesting), commissives (committing), expressives (expressing attitude) and declarations (changing reality by saying, such as 'You are now signed in'). Interface language performs these acts: a button labelled 'I agree' is a commissive; 'Order placed' is a declaration. Speech act analysis classifies messages and actions by their illocutionary force and checks felicity conditions (is the speaker entitled, are conditions met, is the act sincere?). Winograd and Flores built the Coordinator system on speech acts in the 1980s; the approach faded but is directly relevant to conversational AI. Rigour comes from explicit classification and checking each act's conditions and consequences.
steps: Collect system messages, button labels and conversational turns in a flow.
Classify each by Searle's five classes and note the intended act.
Check felicity conditions: does the system have authority, are preconditions met, is the commitment real and fulfilled?
Identify mismatches, such as a message that reads as a declaration ('Payment sent') when the act is only a request.
Validate high-risk mismatches with 5-10 users asking what they believe has happened or been committed to.
Rewrite to align surface language with the real act and its status.
outputs: A speech act classification of the flow, felicity condition checks, mismatch list, and rewritten language.
useWhen: For conversational interfaces, transactions, consent and agreements, and workflows where language creates commitments.
avoidWhen: For purely informational content; use readability or content audits.
whyLost: Speech act theory influenced 1980s CSCW (the Coordinator), which was criticised as too rigid, and the approach largely disappeared from HCI.
whereToUse: AI agents acting on users' behalf, payments, legal consent, clinical orders and team coordination tools.
example: A surgical robot says 'Instrument locked' when it has only sent a lock request. Speech act analysis flags a false declaration; the message becomes 'Locking instrument' followed by 'Instrument locked' only when confirmed.
sources: Gleason, J. B., The Development of Language
Hall, E., Conversational Design (2018)
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas (Gricean audit)
Development of Language (Gleason)
Conversational Design (Hall)
Methods Atlas — Gricean audit (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 18 — Pragmatics — What Language Actually Does
reference: Searle, J. R. (1969). Speech Acts: An Essay in the Philosophy of Language. Cambridge University Press.

name: Spot Count Visitor Estimation
donor: Recreation planning and sport facility management
