origin: Recreation and park management practice; set out by Veal and Darcy (building on Veal's leisure research methods texts) as 'counting heads'
summary: Estimates how many different people used a place from periodic counts of people present, multiplied into visitor-hours and divided by average length of stay.
description: Where there are no ticket sales, such as parks, beaches or free facilities, managers still need to know how many visits a site gets. Veal and Darcy call this 'counting heads' and show that it usually combines sources: administrative data such as bookings or parking tickets, automatic counters, surveys and observation. The core observational procedure is the spot count. At set intervals an observer records how many people are present, often by zone and activity. Averaging the counts over the opening hours and multiplying by the hours open gives visitor-hours, which is a valid measure of use in its own right. To convert visitor-hours into the number of visits, divide by the average length of stay, which usually comes from a user survey. Spot counts can be done by one person touring the site, whereas continuous counts at every entrance are costly. The counts also weight survey samples. In UX the logic applies to concurrent-user and session data: peak concurrency and session length together give total use, and the same reasoning sizes kiosk, venue or service capacity.
steps: Decide what counts as a visit and which activities or user types are to be distinguished.
Choose count times across the opening period, sampling densely at first to capture peaks and troughs.
At each count time, tour the site or view it from fixed points and record the number of people present by zone and activity.
Average the counts per period and multiply by the hours open to obtain visitor-hours per day.
Obtain average length of stay for each activity from a short user survey or observation of a sample of groups.
Divide visitor-hours by average length of stay to estimate the number of visits, and scale up across days and seasons.
Cross-check against any administrative data such as bookings, parking or counter figures.
outputs: Visitor-hours and estimated visit numbers by activity, time of day and period, plus usage profiles that can be used to weight survey results.
useWhen: You must estimate total use of a free or unticketed place or service, or convert snapshot occupancy data into numbers of users.
avoidWhen: Accurate entry records or analytics already exist, or length of stay cannot be estimated with any confidence.
whyLost: Digital products log every session, so UX rarely needs to infer totals from snapshots; the method survives in park, recreation and tourism management.
whereToUse: Physical venues and public spaces, retail floors, libraries and co-working spaces, kiosks, events, and concurrency-based estimates for real-time services.
example: A council testing a booking app for free outdoor courts runs hourly spot counts for two weeks: an average of 41 people present over 12 hours gives 493 visitor-hours, and with an average stay of about 1.6 hours from a short survey this suggests roughly 300 visits a day, sizing the expected booking load.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge.

name: Spradley's Developmental Research Sequence (Domain, Taxonomic and Componential Analysis)
origin: James Spradley, 1979-1980 (The Ethnographic Interview; Participant Observation); componential analysis from Goodenough and Lounsbury (1956)
summary: A step-by-step ethnographic method that builds cultural domains from semantic relationships, organises them into taxonomies, and identifies the contrasting attributes that define terms.
description: Spradley's twelve-step sequence alternates interviewing and analysis. Domain analysis finds cultural categories using universal semantic relationships (X is a kind of Y; X is a way to do Y; X is a reason for Y). Structural questions elicit members of domains. Taxonomic analysis organises domains into hierarchies; contrast questions and componential analysis identify the dimensions of contrast (attributes) that distinguish terms. Finally, themes are discovered across domains. This produces an emic map of how users categorise their world, extraordinarily useful for information architecture, terminology and mental model work, and far more systematic than open-ended 'tell me about' interviews.
steps: Conduct descriptive interviews and collect native terms used by participants.
Perform domain analysis using Spradley's semantic relationships to identify cover terms and included terms.
Ask structural questions to complete domains (e.g. 'what are all the kinds of X?').
Build taxonomies showing hierarchical relations among terms; verify with participants.
Ask contrast questions and build a componential paradigm of attributes distinguishing terms.
Discover cultural themes across domains and relate them to design.
outputs: Domain lists, folk taxonomies, componential paradigms of attributes and cultural themes.
useWhen: Learning users' own categories and vocabulary in unfamiliar domains, especially for IA, content and conversational design.
avoidWhen: Quick evaluative studies or domains with well-established shared terminology.
whyLost: Cognitive anthropology fell out of fashion, and UX adopted card sorting as a quick proxy for folk taxonomies.
whereToUse: Specialist B2B domains, healthcare terminology, financial products for underserved groups, chatbot intent design.
example: Researching small-scale farmers for an agritech app, a team uses domain and componential analysis to find farmers classify pests by damage pattern and season, not species; navigation is designed around those attributes.
sources: Spradley, The Ethnographic Interview (1979)
Spradley, Participant Observation (1980)
Goodenough, Componential analysis and the study of meaning (1956), Language
reference: Spradley, J. P. (1979). The Ethnographic Interview. Holt, Rinehart and Winston.

name: SPSS FACTOR procedure for exploratory factor analysis
origin: SPSS FACTOR procedure; factor analytic tradition from Spearman (1904) and Thurstone (1947)
summary: Running exploratory factor analysis in SPSS with deliberate choices of extraction, retention and rotation rather than the misleading menu defaults.
description: SPSS FACTOR defaults to principal components extraction, the Kaiser eigenvalue-above-1 rule and Varimax rotation, a combination methodologists have long criticised (Costello and Osborne, 2005). Done properly, FACTOR is run from syntax with principal axis factoring or maximum likelihood, a fixed number of factors chosen by parallel analysis (run via a macro such as O'Connor's or the Python plugin), and an oblique rotation (Oblimin or Promax) when constructs are expected to correlate. Output includes KMO, Bartlett's test, communalities, pattern and structure matrices and the factor correlation matrix. Rigour comes from overriding defaults with justification and interpreting the pattern matrix after oblique rotation.
steps: Screen the data and confirm a sample of at least about 200 with adequate item variance.
Run FACTOR with /PRINT KMO and check KMO of 0.60 or above and a significant Bartlett's test.
Determine the number of factors with parallel analysis (O'Connor's SPSS syntax or the Python plugin) rather than the eigenvalue-above-1 default.
Specify /EXTRACTION PAF or ML and /CRITERIA FACTORS(k), with /ROTATION OBLIMIN or PROMAX unless factors are theoretically orthogonal.
Interpret the pattern matrix, flagging loadings below about 0.40 and cross-loadings above about 0.30, and check communalities.
Save the syntax and iterate item removal one item at a time, then confirm in a new sample.
outputs: A justified EFA solution with KMO, communalities, pattern and structure matrices, factor correlations and saved syntax.
useWhen: Teams using SPSS to develop or check UX attitude scales or to reduce a long questionnaire to dimensions.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on defaults; avoid FACTOR entirely when confirming a known structure (use CFA in AMOS or semopy) or with fewer than about 100 cases.
whyLost: SPSS made factor analysis easy to run but its defaults encode outdated practice, so most applied use outside psychometrics inherits weak choices.
whereToUse: Market and UX research teams in SPSS environments, academic UX projects and scale adaptation for new markets.
example: An insurance UX team factor-analyses 18 claim-experience items. Defaults give five components; parallel analysis and PAF with Oblimin give three correlated factors (clarity, speed, fairness) that match the team's qualitative findings.
sources: SPSS FACTOR
RELIABILITY procedures; syntax automation; parallel analysis via Python plugin
Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
Costello, A. B. & Osborne, J. W. (2005) Best practices in exploratory factor analysis. Practical Assessment, Research & Evaluation
O'Connor, B. P. (2000) SPSS and SAS programs for determining the number of components using parallel analysis. Behavior Research Methods
The Inquiry Series, C7 — SPSS for Survey Analysis — EFA, Reliability & Scale Validation
reference: Costello, A. B. & Osborne, J. W. (2005) Best practices in exploratory factor analysis. Practical Assessment, Research & Evaluation 10(7)

name: SPSS syntax over menus
origin: SPSS command syntax since SPSS's origins (Nie, Bent and Hull, 1968); reproducibility argument from social science methods teaching
summary: Running every SPSS analysis through saved, commented syntax files rather than point-and-click menus, so analyses are documented, repeatable and reviewable.
description: SPSS menus generate command syntax behind the scenes; the 'Paste' button exposes it. Working from syntax turns a sequence of unrepeatable clicks into a script that records every recode, filter, weight and test option. This makes analyses repeatable when data are updated, reviewable by colleagues, and auditable, and it prevents classic errors such as a forgotten active filter or split file. Rigour comes from one master syntax file per study, header comments, defined order (get file, recode, compute, analyse), never altering raw .sav files, and saving output alongside syntax. Researchers often use SPSS menus only and keep no record, which is why the practice is vestigial.
steps: Create a study syntax file with a header stating project, author, date, input file and purpose.
Use the menus if helpful but always click Paste rather than OK, then run from the syntax window.
Order the file: GET FILE, data cleaning and RECODE/COMPUTE, variable labels, then analyses.
Comment every recode and exclusion with its rationale, and SAVE OUTFILE to a new processed file, never overwriting raw data.
Reset FILTER, SPLIT FILE and WEIGHT explicitly after each use.
Rerun the entire syntax from the raw file before reporting, and archive syntax, output (.spv) and data together under version control.
outputs: A commented master syntax file, processed data files and reproducible output.
useWhen: Any SPSS-based UX analysis, especially tracking surveys rerun each wave, shared team analyses and work that will be audited.
avoidWhen: If the team is moving to Python or R, script there instead; the principle is the same.
whyLost: Point-and-click convenience is SPSS's selling point, so many users never learn syntax, and UX teams adopted SPSS mostly for one-off survey analyses.
whereToUse: Market and UX research teams using SPSS, academic collaborations, regulated survey reporting and multi-wave tracking studies.
example: A bank's UX team runs a quarterly customer effort survey. Moving to a single syntax file means each wave is analysed by rerunning the file on new data, and a reviewer spots that a FILTER left active had excluded all mobile respondents from one wave's means.
sources: SPSS Syntax Editor
Python integration (SPSS Python plugin)
pyreadstat for Python ↔ SPSS bridge
Field, A. (2024) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics, 6th ed.
IBM (2023) IBM SPSS Statistics Command Syntax Reference
The Inquiry Series, C6 — SPSS for UX Researchers — The Right Way
reference: IBM SPSS Statistics Command Syntax Reference

name: Stakeholder Interview Protocol (Organisational Research)
origin: Erika Hall, 2013
summary: Structured interviews with internal stakeholders to surface goals, constraints, politics, assumptions and success criteria that will shape a product and its research.
description: Organisational research applies interview rigour to the people inside the organisation who will build, fund, sell, support or regulate a product. A protocol covers each stakeholder's role, goals, definition of success, constraints (technical, legal, budgetary), assumptions about users, past attempts, and fears. Interviews are conducted one-to-one so that political dynamics do not suppress dissent, and they are synthesised like user research: themes, conflicts and assumptions are documented and shared back. The method reveals the real decision environment the work sits in, prevents late surprises, and builds stakeholders' ownership of later findings. Rigour comes from a consistent guide, sampling across functions and levels, and separating stakeholder beliefs about users from evidence.
steps: Stakeholder interview protocol (30 min):
'What does success look like in 6 months?'
'What would make this project fail?'
'What assumptions are you making about users that haven't been validated?'
'What constraints — technical, business, political — will shape what we can build?'
'Who else should I talk to?' Synthesize: identify assumption conflicts between stakeholders before user research begins.
outputs: Stakeholder map, documented goals and constraints, assumption list, conflicting definitions of success, and a shared problem statement.
useWhen: Project kick-off, entering a new organisation or domain, when stakeholders disagree, or before user research to understand what decisions the research must serve.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating stakeholder views as evidence about users; validate with user research. Avoid when the project scope is tiny and stakeholders are already aligned.
whyLost: Stakeholder interviews are done informally as kick-off chats, without protocol, synthesis or documentation, so organisational constraints surface late as surprises.
whereToUse: Project kickoff, design brief construction, cross-functional alignment, product discovery.
example: Before redesigning a hospital's referral portal, the researcher interviews eight stakeholders and discovers that legal requires a signature step the product owner planned to remove, reshaping the brief.
sources: Just Enough Research — Erika Hall
reference: Hall E (2013) Just Enough Research. A Book Apart

name: Stakeholder Mapping
origin: Edward Freeman, stakeholder theory (1984); power-interest grid by Mendelow (1981)
summary: Identifying everyone who affects or is affected by a product or study and mapping their interests, influence and relationships to plan research, engagement and design.
description: Stakeholder mapping makes the social system around a product explicit. It identifies internal stakeholders (sponsors, teams, decision-makers) and external ones (users, customers, regulators, partners, indirect stakeholders), then characterises each by interest, influence, attitude and relationships. Common representations include the power-interest grid, onion diagrams placing stakeholders in rings around the product, and relationship maps showing flows of value, information and conflict. A systems-thinking variant maps each stakeholder's perspective on the same problem, revealing why the problem looks different from each position. Rigour comes from grounding the map in interviews rather than assumptions, including indirect and dissenting stakeholders, documenting each placement's rationale, and revisiting the map as the project changes. It informs who to recruit, who must be involved in decisions and where research findings will meet resistance.
steps: Brainstorm all individuals and groups who affect or are affected by the product, including indirect stakeholders and regulators.
Interview or survey a selection of stakeholders to learn their goals, concerns, decision rights and view of the problem.
Place each stakeholder on a power-interest grid or onion diagram, noting the evidence for each placement.
Draw relationships between stakeholders: flows of money, information, authority and conflict.
Capture each key stakeholder's perspective on the problem and where perspectives diverge.
Derive an engagement plan (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor) and a research recruitment plan, and revisit the map at each project phase.
outputs: Stakeholder inventory, power-interest grid or onion map, relationship diagram, perspective comparison and engagement plan.
useWhen: Starting a project in a complex organisation or ecosystem, planning research recruitment and communication, and designing services with many parties.
avoidWhen: When the product context is simple and stakeholders are already well known; avoid treating the map as a substitute for user research.
whyLost: Still in use: Essential project planning tool; helps manage political dynamics of design.
whereToUse: Service design; complex enterprise products; public sector; any multi-stakeholder context.
example: A hospital theatre-scheduling project maps surgeons, anaesthetists, nurses, porters, bed managers and patients. Perspective mapping shows each defines 'delay' differently, so research is planned to capture a shared timeline from all six viewpoints.
sources: Mapping Experiences
Methods Atlas — DSRP protocol (Gopinath)
PACT analysis (Dix)
Freeman, Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach (1984)
This Is Service Design Doing (Stickdorn et al.)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 13 — DSRP Systems Thinking & Wicked Problems
reference: Freeman RE (1984) Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach. Pitman

name: STAMP / STPA (Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis)
origin: Nancy Leveson, 2004 (STAMP); 2011-2018 (STPA handbook)
summary: Models the system as control loops and identifies unsafe control actions, including normally correct user actions that become hazardous in particular system states.
description: STAMP treats safety as a control problem rather than a chain of component failures. STPA identifies losses and hazards, models the control structure (controllers, control actions, feedback), then finds unsafe control actions: actions provided when hazardous, not provided when needed, provided too early or late, or stopped too soon. It traces causal scenarios, including flawed process models in controllers' minds. Crucially, hazards can arise from normal operation in unexpected contexts, without failures. The treatise's transfer: a UX-level STPA identifies situations where a normally correct user action becomes hazardous (submit is safe when validation passes, unsafe when validation has silently failed), producing requirements task analysis misses. Rated MEDIUM priority (feasibility two stars, impact five).
steps: Define losses and system-level hazards with stakeholders.
Model the control structure, including the human operator, interface, automation and feedback.
For each control action, identify the four types of unsafe control action in relevant system states.
Identify causal scenarios, especially mismatches between the user's mental model and system state.
Derive interface and feedback requirements that prevent or mitigate scenarios.
Verify requirements in simulation or usability testing with hazard-oriented scenarios.
outputs: Control structure diagram, unsafe control action table, causal scenarios, safety-driven UX requirements.
useWhen: Safety-critical or high-stakes interfaces with automation, and AI agents taking real-world actions.
avoidWhen: Low-consequence consumer features where the analysis overhead is unjustified.
whyLost: It originated in aerospace and system safety engineering and is taught in engineering schools, not design programmes. Its diagrams look like engineering artefacts, so UX researchers rarely encounter it.
whereToUse: Medical device UX, autonomous driving handovers, industrial control, AI agents executing payments or code.
example: STPA on an AI agent that can send payments finds an unsafe control action: the user approves a batch while the agent's payee list has silently changed. The design adds a diff of changed payees before approval.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Leveson NG (2004) A new accident model for engineering safer systems. Safety Science 42(4):237-270
Leveson NG (2011) Engineering a Safer World
Leveson NG & Thomas JP (2018) STPA Handbook
Leveson, Engineering a Safer World: Systems Thinking Applied to Safety (2011)
Leveson & Thomas, STPA Handbook (2018)
reference: Leveson NG (2011) Engineering a Safer World: Systems Thinking Applied to Safety. MIT Press.

name: Standard Gamble and Time Trade-Off Utility Elicitation
origin: von Neumann-Morgenstern utility theory (1944); time trade-off by George Torrance, Warren Thomas and David Sackett (1972); review by Torrance (1986)
summary: Measures how much people value a state (e.g. living with a product limitation) by the risk or time they would trade to avoid it, yielding cardinal utilities.
description: Health economists needed utilities for health states to compute QALYs. In the standard gamble, people choose between a certain state and a gamble with probability p of the best outcome and 1 - p of the worst; the indifference p is the state's utility. In the time trade-off, people choose between t years in the state and fewer years in full health; the ratio gives the utility. These methods produce cardinal, interpersonally comparable values, with known biases (loss aversion in SG, time preference in TTO). Adapted to UX, they quantify the burden of persistent problems such as accessibility barriers, chronic friction or unreliable service, beyond satisfaction ratings.
steps: Describe the states clearly with vignettes, including the best and worst anchors.
Use a structured iterative procedure (e.g. ping-pong or titration) to find indifference points.
Train respondents with practice items and include consistency checks.
Compute utilities per respondent and aggregate with confidence intervals.
Compare utilities across states or segments and convert into burden metrics (e.g. utility loss times prevalence).
Validate against behavioural data such as switching or abandonment.
outputs: Cardinal utilities for states, burden estimates and segment comparisons.
useWhen: Quantifying the burden of persistent conditions or service states to prioritise investment, especially accessibility and reliability.
avoidWhen: Transient micro-frictions where trade-offs would be meaningless to participants.
whyLost: It belongs to health economics; UX measures satisfaction rather than utilities.
whereToUse: Digital health, accessibility, assistive technology, reliability of essential services, public sector services.
example: Screen-reader users complete TTO tasks about living with an inaccessible banking app; the mean utility of 0.82 versus 0.97 for the accessible version quantifies burden for a business case.
sources: Torrance, Measurement of health state utilities for economic appraisal (1986), Journal of Health Economics
Drummond et al., Methods for the Economic Evaluation of Health Care Programmes (4th ed., 2015)
reference: Torrance, G. W. (1986). Journal of Health Economics, 5(1), 1-30.

name: Standing recruitment pipeline
origin: Teresa Torres, Continuous Discovery Habits (2021); research operations practice and in-house participant panels from the 2010s
summary: Sets up an always-running system that recruits, screens and schedules participants weekly, so continuous discovery interviews happen without bespoke recruiting each time.
description: Continuous discovery depends on talking to customers every week, which fails if each round needs a new recruiting effort taking 2 to 3 weeks. A standing recruitment pipeline automates the path: in-product or email intercepts invite users, a short screener captures attributes, qualified participants self-schedule into reserved slots, and incentives are paid automatically. Torres recommends at least one customer interview per week per product trio. A good pipeline also manages the panel: tracking participation to avoid over-using the same people, balancing segments, and handling consent and data retention. Rigour comes from monitoring sample composition against the user base, so convenience does not slowly skew the voices teams hear towards the most engaged users.
steps: Define the segments and attributes you need to hear from regularly, and set quotas so that no single segment exceeds an agreed share of interviews, for example 40%.
Implement a recruiting trigger, such as an in-product intercept to a sampled share of users, an email to a random sample or a support follow-up, with a 3 to 6 question screener.
Connect the screener to self-scheduling for reserved weekly slots and automated reminders and incentive payment.
Maintain a panel database recording consent, attributes, participation dates and a cool-off rule (for example no more than one study per participant every 3 months).
Review composition monthly against the active user base, and adjust sampling to correct skew towards highly engaged or vocal users.
Track pipeline health: show rate (aim for 70% or more), time from invite to interview and weekly interviews completed per team.
outputs: A running recruitment system, a consented panel with attributes and participation history, weekly interview slots filled, and composition and health metrics.
useWhen: Teams practise continuous discovery or frequent evaluative testing; recruitment delays are blocking research; you need steady access to specific segments.
avoidWhen: Research needs hard-to-reach non-users or highly specific populations that intercepts cannot reach (use specialist recruiters or field recruitment), or regulatory constraints forbid contacting users this way.
whyLost: It survived because continuous discovery and research operations became mainstream; the vulnerability is sample bias, since pipelines over-represent engaged, digitally confident users.
whereToUse: SaaS and fintech products, marketplaces, consumer apps, internal platforms, any team practising weekly customer interviews.
example: A fintech team building a Savings feature added an in-app intercept to 2% of weekly active users, screening for savings habits and income type. They held three interviews a week, fed their opportunity solution tree, and adjusted sampling when informal-income users fell below their 25% quota.
sources: Continuous Discovery Habits (Torres)
Practical Empathy (Young)
Just Enough Research (Hall)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 35 — Continuous Discovery & Opportunity Solution Trees
reference: Torres, T. (2021). Continuous Discovery Habits: Discover Products that Create Customer Value and Business Value. Product Talk LLC.

name: Standing Youth Tester Panel
origin: NMSU Learning Games Lab (Chamberlin and colleagues, 2012 to 2016), described in Chapter 3
summary: An ongoing programme that keeps a trained group of target users on site so that developers can run short formative tests at any point in development.
description: The Learning Games Lab solved the hardest part of frequent testing, getting access to target users, by running year-round 'think tanks' for young people. Youth consultants spend their days on engaging activities such as coding, animation and game design, and are pulled into 1 to 2 hour test sessions whenever a developer needs them. They are trained to review games, building a shared vocabulary for genre, challenge and flow so that feedback goes beyond 'it was boring'. Several methods run side by side: one-on-one interactions for early prototypes where a reviewer can explain missing parts, one-on-two observations where one reviewer silently watches two players, short focus groups to prime topics, a video closet, and written blogging. Developers act as testers so they see problems first-hand, while a testing manager observes the testers themselves to note leading questions and bias. Straight after each session the testers compare notes, agree what they saw, and the manager records a testers' consensus and recommendations in a testing journal for that project. The model trades some independence for speed, empathy and continuous access.
steps: Recruit a cohort of target users for a recurring programme, with consent covering ongoing testing and recording.
Run a daily programme of worthwhile activities and train participants in a shared vocabulary for reviewing products.
Before each test, agree specific questions and methods with the developers and note them in the testing journal.
Run the session with a mix of methods, for example one-on-two observation plus a short group discussion and individual reflections.
Have a testing manager observe the testers and note their questions and biases.
Immediately afterwards, hold a debrief where testers reconcile observations and agree recommendations.
Record the version tested, objectives, findings and testers' consensus in the journal and track changes across versions.
outputs: A testing journal per project with findings, consensus recommendations and version history, plus a pool of trained users available on demand.
useWhen: A studio or product team builds many products for a specific audience and needs frequent formative feedback throughout development.
avoidWhen: You need independent, unbiased summative evidence, or cannot sustain the space, staff and programme costs.
whyLost: It needs dedicated space, a teacher or coordinator and institutional support; most teams instead recruit fresh participants per study or use online panels.
whereToUse: Educational games, children's media, studios serving a narrow audience, in-house research labs.
example: A studio making maths games keeps a summer think tank of middle-school students; when a ratio game build is ready, two developers each watch two students play while a testing manager notes the developers' prompts, and within an hour the consensus that the fail condition is unclear is in the journal.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Chamberlin, B., Trespalacios, J. H., Muise, A. S. and Garza, M. C. (2016). User testing in the Learning Games Lab: getting valuable feedback through frequent formative evaluation. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 3. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: State transition diagrams
origin: Finite automata from the 1950s; state transition networks for dialogue design by Parnas (1969) and Wasserman; statecharts by David Harel, 1987
summary: Models an interface as states and the user or system events that move between them, making modes, dead ends and missing transitions visible and checkable.
description: A state transition diagram represents each distinct interface state as a node and each event (tap, timeout, error, sensor input) as a labelled edge. Harel's statecharts extend this with hierarchy, concurrency and history, making large systems tractable. The rigorous version is complete: every state has a defined response to every event, including error and timeout events. Analysis then reveals hidden modes, states with no exit, events with no handler and inconsistent responses to the same event in different states. Modern UX uses flow diagrams that look similar but usually show happy paths only, which is why the method is vestigial. The tabular form, a state-event matrix, is the best completeness check.
steps: Enumerate states, including transient and error states, from the design, code or observation.
Enumerate events: user actions, system responses, timeouts, errors and external inputs.
Build a state-event matrix and fill every cell with the resulting state or an explicit 'ignored'; empty cells are specification gaps.
Draw the diagram, using statechart hierarchy for nested modes and concurrent regions for parallel subsystems.
Check for states without exits, unreachable states, mode ambiguity (same display, different states) and inconsistent responses to the same event.
Review with engineers and domain experts and convert into test cases for every transition.
outputs: A complete state-event matrix, a statechart, a list of gaps and mode hazards, and transition-level test cases.
useWhen: When designing complex modes, multi-step workflows, device interfaces, or conversational flows; when bugs cluster around unexpected states.
avoidWhen: For content-heavy, largely stateless experiences; use content audits or IA methods instead.
whyLost: Statecharts remain common in engineering (XState, embedded systems), but UX replaced them with happy-path flow diagrams, keeping the look and losing completeness.
whereToUse: Medical devices, checkout and payment flows, onboarding, IoT devices, voice and chat assistants, and AI agent tool loops.
example: A state-event matrix for a payments flow reveals 17 empty cells, including what happens when the bank times out after 3D Secure succeeds. Defining that transition prevents duplicate charges that were generating support tickets.
sources: Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 5 — State, Transition & the Logic of Interaction
Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
Gödel Escher Bach (Hofstadter)
reference: Harel, D. (1987). Statecharts: A visual formalism for complex systems. Science of Computer Programming, 8(3), 231-274.

name: Statistical power analysis
origin: Neyman and Pearson (1933); popularised in behavioural science by Jacob Cohen, Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (1962; 1988)
summary: Determines the probability that a study will detect an effect of a given size, used to plan sample sizes or to judge what a completed study could have found.
description: Power is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when a specified true effect exists, equal to 1 minus the Type II error rate. It depends on effect size, sample size, alpha, variability and design. Cohen found that psychology studies in the 1960s had a median power of only about 0.46 for medium effects, and underpowered research remains common, producing both missed effects and exaggerated estimates among significant results (the winner's curse). A priori power analysis sets sample size before data collection, typically targeting 80% or 90% power for the smallest effect of interest. Sensitivity analysis asks what effect a fixed sample could detect. Post-hoc 'observed power' is uninformative and should not be used. Rigour comes from basing the effect size on decision relevance or credible prior evidence rather than optimism.
steps: Define the primary outcome, test and design (for example two-proportion test, two independent groups).
Set the smallest effect size of interest from business relevance or prior evidence, such as a 2 percentage point uplift from a 10% baseline.
Choose alpha (usually 0.05, two-sided) and target power (usually 0.80, or 0.90 for important decisions).
Compute the required sample with appropriate software, adjusting for expected attrition, clustering or multiple comparisons.
If the available sample is fixed, run a sensitivity analysis to state the minimum detectable effect and decide whether the study is worth running.
Document the calculation in the pre-registration or analysis plan, and do not compute observed power after the fact.
outputs: Required sample sizes or minimum detectable effects, documented assumptions, and a go or no-go decision on study feasibility.
useWhen: Planning any confirmatory quantitative study, A/B test or survey comparison, and assessing whether completed null results are informative.
avoidWhen: Exploratory or qualitative studies where hypothesis testing is not the goal; use saturation or problem-discovery models for sample planning instead.
whyLost: Experimentation platforms embed sample size calculators, but UX researchers often run studies with convenient samples and skip power, or compute meaningless post-hoc power.
whereToUse: A/B tests, quantitative usability benchmarks, survey segment comparisons, unmoderated studies, pricing tests.
example: Before testing a Trust Badge, a team set the smallest meaningful uplift at 1.5 points on a 12% sign-up rate. At alpha 0.05 and 80% power, the two-proportion calculation required about 7,700 users per arm, so the test was scheduled for 3 weeks instead of the planned 5 days.
sources: Statistics for Dummies series (Rumsey)
Designing Experiments & Analyzing Data (Maxwell & Delaney)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 41 — Frequentist Inference Done Right
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum.

name: Statistical Process Control (Control Charts)
origin: Walter Shewhart, Bell Labs, 1924-1931; Western Electric rules (1956); promoted by W. Edwards Deming
summary: Plots a metric with statistically derived control limits to separate routine (common-cause) variation from signals of special causes that warrant investigation.
description: Shewhart's insight was that every process varies, and reacting to every fluctuation (tampering) makes things worse. Control charts set limits at about three sigma from the centre line, estimated from the process's own short-term variation (e.g. moving ranges in XmR charts). Points outside the limits, or patterns such as eight consecutive points on one side (Western Electric or Nelson rules), signal special causes. Healthcare quality improvement adopted SPC widely. For UX metrics programmes, SPC stops teams from narrating random week-to-week variation and directs attention to genuine signals, and run charts show whether improvements produced real process change.
steps: Choose a metric measured regularly (e.g. weekly task success, daily error rate) and the right chart type (XmR, p-chart, u-chart).
Establish a baseline period of at least 20-25 points to compute centre line and control limits.
Plot ongoing data and apply detection rules (beyond limits, runs, trends).
Investigate signals for special causes; do not react to points within limits.
After a deliberate process change, recalculate limits for the new phase.
Report charts instead of week-over-week percentage changes.
outputs: Control charts with limits, identified special-cause signals and documented process phases.
useWhen: Ongoing UX or service metrics reviewed regularly, especially where teams overreact to fluctuations.
avoidWhen: One-off comparisons or experiments; use appropriate experimental statistics.
whyLost: Manufacturing quality methods never entered digital product culture, which prefers dashboards and percentage changes.
whereToUse: Experience metric reviews, support quality, content quality, AI output quality monitoring, accessibility regressions.
example: A weekly CSAT dip prompts a war room. An XmR chart shows the dip is within control limits; two weeks later a genuine signal (8 points below centre) leads to a real cause, a shipping partner change.
sources: Shewhart, Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product (1931)
Wheeler, Understanding Variation: The Key to Managing Chaos (2nd ed., 2000)
Provost & Murray, The Health Care Data Guide (2011)
reference: Wheeler, D. J. (2000). Understanding Variation. SPC Press.

name: Steering Law
origin: Johnny Accot and Shumin Zhai, 1997, extending Rashevsky (1959) and Drury (1971)
summary: Predicts the time to move a pointer or finger through a constrained path from the path's length and width, for designing cascading menus, sliders and gesture tunnels.
description: The steering law generalises Fitts' law from point targets to paths. For a straight tunnel of length A and width W, movement time T = a + b(A/W); for a curved path it is the integral of ds/W(s) along the path. Movement time thus grows linearly with the path's index of difficulty, not logarithmically as in Fitts' law, so narrow tunnels are disproportionately costly. It applies to hierarchical cascading menus, drag-to-reorder, sliders, scroll scrubbing, drawing tools and gesture paths. Rigour comes from empirically fitting a and b for the device and population, since constants differ greatly between mouse, touch, stylus and gloved hands, and from checking model fit (R squared above 0.9 is typical in well-controlled studies).
steps: Identify interactions where the user must keep a pointer within a bounded path (cascading menus, sliders, drag lanes, gesture corridors).
Measure path length A and width W (or W as a function of position for curved or variable paths) in physical units on the target device.
Calculate index of difficulty ID = A/W, or the integral form for curved paths.
Fit constants a and b from a calibration study: 10-16 participants, at least 5 ID levels, 10+ trials each, logging movement time and path exits.
Predict movement time and exit-error likelihood for candidate designs and compare variants.
Redesign high-ID paths (for example widen tunnels, add hover delay or diagonal tolerance to cascading menus) and verify with a follow-up timing test.
outputs: Fitted steering constants for the device, predicted movement times per design, error rates per ID level, and design recommendations for tunnel widths.
useWhen: When designing cascading or mega menus, sliders, drag-and-drop lanes, swipe gestures, drawing tools or any constrained-path interaction, especially with gloves or on small screens.
avoidWhen: When targets are discrete points (use Fitts' law) or when cognitive choice time dominates motor time (use Hick-Hyman or KLM).
whyLost: HCI researchers know it well but practitioners cite only Fitts' law; the steering law needs calibration studies and its insights are usually rediscovered ad hoc through menu tolerance hacks.
whereToUse: Surgical and industrial touch consoles, mega menus in e-commerce, mobile sliders, VR ray-cast menus, and sketching tools.
example: A surgical console's cascading menu requires dragging through a 6 mm-wide submenu corridor with sterile gloves. Steering-law calibration predicts 1.8 s and 22% path exits; widening the corridor to 14 mm and adding a 300 ms intent delay cuts both by more than half.
sources: Clark, J., Designing for Touch (2015)
Shneiderman, B. & Plaisant, C., Designing the User Interface
Touch IT
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Designing for Touch (Josh Clark)
Shneiderman & Plaisant
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 3 — The Ballistics of the Human Body — Fitts' Law & Motor Control
reference: Accot, J. & Zhai, S. (1997). Beyond Fitts' law: models for trajectory-based HCI tasks. Proceedings of CHI '97, 295-302.

name: Stevens' scales (nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio)
origin: S. S. Stevens, 'On the Theory of Scales of Measurement', 1946
summary: Classifies every measure by its scale type, nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio, to determine which transformations, summaries and statistical tests are legitimate.
description: Stevens defined four levels of measurement by the transformations that preserve their meaning: nominal (categories; any one-to-one relabelling), ordinal (order; any monotonic transformation), interval (equal differences; linear transformations) and ratio (true zero; multiplication by a constant). Each level permits different statistics: mode for nominal, median and percentiles for ordinal, mean and standard deviation for interval, and ratios and geometric means for ratio. UX regularly breaks these rules, for instance averaging single Likert items as if interval, or claiming that task time 'doubled' satisfaction. The debate about treating multi-item rating scales as interval is legitimate and well studied, but it should be a reasoned choice. Applying Stevens' scales is the first step of any measurement plan.
steps: List every variable in the study, from task success to satisfaction ratings to time.
Classify each by scale type and record the justification (for example task time is ratio; a single 5-point item is ordinal; a validated multi-item scale such as SUS is commonly treated as interval).
Specify permissible summaries and tests per variable before collecting data (for example median and Mann-Whitney for ordinal items).
Check transformations and composite scores for legitimacy, for example not summing nominal codes.
Where you treat ordinal data as interval, state the assumption and run a sensitivity analysis with an ordinal method.
Review the reporting plan so claims match scale properties (no ratios on interval data).
outputs: A variable-by-scale table with permissible statistics and claims, and an analysis plan consistent with measurement levels.
useWhen: At the start of any quantitative study, when designing surveys or metrics, and when reviewing dashboards or research reports for statistical errors.
avoidWhen: It is never wrong to classify, but avoid rigid application that forbids defensible practices such as treating summed multi-item scales as interval; consult measurement models such as Rasch for stronger claims.
whyLost: Taught in introductory statistics but rarely applied in UX practice, where tooling defaults to means for every number.
whereToUse: Survey programmes, UX metrics and dashboards, A/B test reporting, and benchmarking studies.
example: A product team reports 'satisfaction rose 25%' from a mean single-item rating of 3.2 to 4.0. Classifying the item as ordinal, the researcher re-reports the change as a shift in the proportion rating 4 or 5 from 38% to 71%, with a valid test.
sources: Dix, A., Statistics for HCI: Making Sense of Quantitative Data (2020)
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
Leavy, P., Research Design: Quantitative, Qualitative, Mixed Methods, Arts-Based, and Community-Based Participatory Research Approaches (2017)
Statistics for HCI (Alan Dix)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Research Design (Leavy)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 8 — Measurement Theory — Before You Measure Anything
reference: Stevens, S. S. (1946). On the theory of scales of measurement. Science, 103(2684), 677-680.

name: Stimulated Recall Interview
origin: Benjamin Bloom, 1953 (stimulated recall of classroom thinking)
summary: Replaying recordings of a participant's own session to cue detailed retrospective accounts of what they were thinking at specific moments.
description: Stimulated recall separates doing from explaining. The participant first works naturally, unburdened by concurrent think-aloud, while screen, audio and optionally eye-tracking are recorded. Soon afterwards, ideally within 24 hours, the researcher plays back the recording and pauses at pre-selected moments such as hesitations, errors or unusual actions, asking what the participant was thinking, trying to do and expecting. Because the recording shows behaviour, probing targets cognition: decisions, expectations and interpretations of feedback. Analysis maps cognitive events onto behavioural events, and mismatches between what participants believed they were doing and what the recording shows are the richest data. It avoids reactivity of concurrent verbalisation, at the cost of some reconstruction risk that increases with delay.
steps: Recording phase: Record the participant's work session (screen + audio + optionally eye-tracking). This recording is the stimulus material — not data to be analysed independently.

Interview phase (immediately after or within 24 hours): Play back the recording. Pause at pre-selected moments (moments of hesitation, errors, unusual behavior). Ask: "What were you thinking here?" "What were you trying to do at this point?" "What did you expect to happen?"

Probing for thought, not behavior: The recording shows behavior. The retrospective interview accesses the cognitive process behind behavior. Target: thoughts about decisions, expectations, and interpretations — not descriptions of what they did (the recording shows that).

Analysis: Code for cognitive processes: error detection, goal clarification, interpretation of feedback, decision points. Map cognitive events to behavioral events in the recording. Mismatches between what the participant thought they were doing and what the recording shows are the richest data.
outputs: Time-aligned behaviour and cognition records, coded decision points, and documented mismatches between intent and action.
useWhen: Fast, high-workload or expert tasks where think-aloud would disrupt performance (trading, clinical work, gaming, driving), or when eye-tracking data need explanation.
avoidWhen: When recall delay will be long or the task trivial; use concurrent think-aloud or a simple post-task interview.
whyLost: Retrospective think-aloud is known in usability, but the structured cueing and cognitive coding from education research are rarely applied.
whereToUse: Expert tools, safety-critical interfaces, eye-tracking studies, games, and AI-assisted decision tools where users evaluate model outputs quickly.
example: Radiologists review scans with an AI triage overlay while recorded. Replaying moments where they ignored the AI flag reveals that they distrust its confidence colour scale, not the model itself.
sources: Observing the User Experience (Goodman)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar)
Thought Processes in Lectures and Discussions (Bloom)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Bloom, B. S. (1953). Thought processes in lectures and discussions. Journal of General Education, 7(3), 160-169.

name: Strange Loop Analysis of Recursive Interactions
origin: Douglas Hofstadter, 1979
summary: Identifies recursive and self-referential patterns in interactions, where system outputs become inputs to user behaviour and back, producing emergent or paradoxical effects.
description: Hofstadter described strange loops as hierarchies in which moving through levels eventually returns to the starting point, producing self-reference and emergent phenomena such as the self. In interaction design, analogous loops arise when system outputs shape user behaviour, which in turn reshapes the system: personalisation that narrows what users see and therefore what they choose, interfaces that configure themselves, or AI assistants trained on user responses to their own outputs. Strange loop analysis traces these recursive structures across levels (individual action, model state, interface presentation), looks for runaway amplification, self-fulfilling predictions and paradoxes, and designs interventions such as exploration, transparency or level separation. Rigour comes from tracing loops with log evidence rather than metaphor.
steps: Strange loop audit for complex interfaces:
List all elements whose function is to change other elements.
(2) For each: trace the chain — if the user follows this element's effect, do they end up back at the starting point unexpectedly?
(3) Identify all recursive paths in the navigation graph (using graph theory: cycles in the navigation directed graph).
(4) For each cycle: is the recursion intentional (breadcrumb navigation) or accidental (confusing settings interdependence)?
outputs: Maps of recursive loops between user behaviour and system response, identified runaway or paradoxical loops, and design interventions to stabilise or exploit them.
useWhen: Recommender systems, personalisation, social feeds, AI assistants that learn from users, and settings screens that configure the interface itself.
avoidWhen: Avoid for linear, stateless tasks where no feedback exists; for operational loop modelling use system dynamics or causal loop diagrams.
whyLost: Hofstadter's ideas inspired 1980s cognitive science and AI but were never turned into an HCI method; systems thinking tools took over loop analysis.
whereToUse: Complex settings and preferences UX, navigation audit, information architecture quality review, developer tool UX.
example: A music app finds users' 'skip' behaviour trains the recommender to narrow choices, which increases skipping; the loop analysis leads to a deliberate exploration slot that breaks the spiral.
sources: Gödel, Escher, Bach — Douglas Hofstadter
reference: Hofstadter DR (1979) Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books

name: Strange loop audit
origin: Concept of the strange loop from Douglas Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach, 1979; operationalised for navigation by combining with graph cycle detection
summary: Finds paths where navigation or system logic loops back on itself, so that users moving 'forward' or 'up' end where they started, often without realising it.
description: Hofstadter's strange loop is a hierarchy that, by moving consistently in one direction, returns to its starting level. In interfaces this appears as settings that link to help that links back to settings, 'back' that re-opens the dialog it closed, error recovery that leads to the step that caused the error, or authentication flows that bounce between login and verification. Such loops are invisible locally, because each step is sensible, but trap users globally. The audit models the navigation and recovery structure as a directed graph, detects cycles with algorithms such as Tarjan's strongly connected components, then classifies each cycle as intentional (hub-and-spoke returns) or pathological (no exit towards the goal). Rigour comes from including error, timeout and back-stack behaviour in the graph.
steps: Map navigation and recovery behaviour as a directed graph, including back, cancel, errors, timeouts and deep links.
Run cycle detection (Tarjan's or Johnson's algorithm) to list strongly connected components and elementary cycles.
For each cycle, check whether at least one exit edge leads closer to the user's goal or a safe state; flag cycles with none as pathological.
Validate flagged loops against session logs, looking for repeated sequences (for example the same 3-screen sequence occurring 3 or more times in a session).
Observe 5-8 users on flagged tasks to confirm whether they recognise the loop and how they escape.
Redesign to break the loop with an explicit exit, state preservation or escalation path, and re-run cycle detection.
outputs: A list of detected cycles with classification, log evidence of loop frequency, user observations, and loop-breaking design changes.
useWhen: When users report going round in circles; in recovery, authentication, settings and support flows; in complex modal systems where back-stack behaviour is unclear.
avoidWhen: For simple linear flows with no back-links; a cognitive walkthrough suffices. For general IA findability, use IA graph analysis.
whyLost: Hofstadter's idea is well known as philosophy but was never turned into a practical audit; loops are found anecdotally in testing rather than systematically.
whereToUse: Account recovery and authentication, customer support and chatbot flows, surgical and industrial menus, and multi-step government services.
example: Session logs show 6% of users of a banking app cycling through 'Verify identity', 'Help' and 'Contact us', which links back to verification. The audit confirms no exit edge; adding a callback request breaks the loop and cuts abandoned recoveries by 40%.
sources: Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Gödel Escher Bach (Hofstadter)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 6 — Strange Loops, Recursive Failures & Navigation Traps
reference: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books.

name: Structural Equation Modeling
origin: Karl Jöreskog, 1970s (LISREL); building on Sewall Wright's path analysis, 1921
summary: Jointly estimates a measurement model of latent constructs and a structural model of paths between them, giving direct, indirect and total effects with fit indices.
description: SEM combines confirmatory factor analysis (latent constructs measured by indicators) with path models among constructs. In Vivek Gopinath's payments case (n = 520, robust ML), constructs are Trust, Fraud Risk, Slowness and Support with 3 Likert items each, plus observed Double-Checking and Adoption. Loadings range from 0.70 to 0.82 with CR 0.81–0.87 and AVE 0.57–0.69. Structural paths follow the DAG: FR → TR −0.45, SR → TR +0.31, TR → DC −0.50, DC → SL +0.42, SL → AD −0.28 and TR → AD +0.26, with indirect TR → AD ≈ +0.059 and total ≈ +0.32. Fit is reported with CFI 0.962, TLI 0.951, RMSEA 0.041 (90% CI .032–.050) and SRMR 0.037 against thresholds CFI/TLI ≥ 0.95, RMSEA ≤ 0.06, SRMR ≤ 0.08. Interpretation rules: |β| ≈ 0.10 small, 0.30 medium, 0.50 large; never interpret paths without qual context. The Nash protocol uses SEM in its Prove stage.
steps: Specify the measurement model (each latent construct with its indicators).
Screen missingness (< 10% per item, FIML), check α ≥ 0.70, and run CFA, dropping loadings < 0.60 unless theory demands.
Add structural paths exactly as the DAG specifies.
Estimate with robust ML (MLR) and report CFI, TLI, RMSEA and SRMR.
Decompose direct, indirect and total effects.
Test multi-group invariance, sensitivity to added confounders and out-of-sample stability.
Report with the template: measurement reliabilities and fit, structural effects with significance, and prescriptions.
outputs: A path diagram with standardised coefficients, fit indices, effect decomposition and reliability statistics.
useWhen: When latent constructs and mediators matter and samples are in the hundreds.
avoidWhen: With small samples, poorly understood constructs or no theory to specify paths; use EFA or qualitative work first.
whyLost: Standard in marketing science and psychology, but UX researchers seldom have training in it and default to correlations.
whereToUse: Trust and adoption in fintech, technology acceptance studies, satisfaction drivers, design adoption (ΔU) validation.
example: SEM on 520 bank customers shows trust raises tap-to-pay adoption directly (+0.26) and indirectly by reducing double-checking and perceived slowness, for a total effect of about +0.32.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), DAGs, SEM & Mixed Methods in UX: Turning Insight into Evidence in Banking & Payments
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Equilibrium and the Design Object: How Nash Equilibrium Illuminates Why Designs Stabilise, Plateau, and Change
Principles and Practice of SEM
Statistical Analysis in JASP
Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (Kline)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Kline, R. B. (2016). Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (4th ed.). Guilford Press.

name: Structural Topic Modelling
donor: Computational social science and political science
origin: Margaret Roberts, Brandon Stewart, Dustin Tingley and colleagues, 2013-2014
summary: A topic model in which document metadata (segment, date, rating) shapes topic prevalence and wording, allowing statistical comparison of themes across groups.
description: LDA discovers topics but treats documents as exchangeable. STM incorporates covariates: topic prevalence can depend on metadata (e.g. how much churned versus retained users discuss pricing) and topic content can vary by covariate (how different segments talk about the same topic). Estimates come with uncertainty, enabling regression-style inference about themes. Tools for model selection (semantic coherence and exclusivity), stability across initialisations and representative document retrieval support validation. For UX, STM links open-ended survey responses, reviews or tickets to user attributes and time, making qualitative-scale text quantitatively comparable.
steps: Assemble a corpus (survey comments, reviews, tickets) with document-level metadata.
Preprocess text carefully (stop words, lemmatisation) and document decisions.
Fit STMs for a range of K, choosing by semantic coherence, exclusivity and held-out likelihood.
Label topics by reading representative documents, ideally with two researchers independently.
Estimate covariate effects on topic prevalence with uncertainty (estimateEffect) and examine content covariate differences.
Validate key topics against human-coded samples and follow up qualitatively.
outputs: Labelled topics, covariate effects on topic prevalence, content differences and validation results.
useWhen: Large open-text datasets where you need to compare themes across segments, versions or time.
avoidWhen: Small corpora (under a few hundred documents) or when nuanced interpretation is needed; use qualitative coding.
whyLost: It is known in political science text analysis, but UX text analytics relies on sentiment and keyword tools.
whereToUse: NPS verbatims, app reviews, support tickets, community forums, open-ended survey questions.
example: An STM on 60,000 app reviews shows the 'battery drain' topic prevalence tripled after version 5.2 among Android users only, pinpointing a platform-specific regression.
sources: Roberts et al., Structural topic models for open-ended survey responses (2014), American Journal of Political Science
Roberts, Stewart & Tingley, stm: An R package for structural topic models (2019), Journal of Statistical Software
reference: Roberts, M. E., et al. (2014). American Journal of Political Science, 58(4), 1064-1082.

name: Structured Diary Study
origin: Time-use and diary research in sociology from the 1920s; diary methods in psychology (Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli, 2003)
summary: Participants record experiences, behaviours and thoughts at set intervals or triggering events over days to weeks, capturing real-context use over time.
description: A diary study asks participants to record their experiences with a product or behaviour at regular intervals over an extended period (typically 1 day to 6 weeks). Unlike in-person observation, diary studies capture naturally occurring experiences in their real context — including moments that would never occur in a lab (middle-of-the-night usage, failure under stress, integration with other life activities). The fundamental tradeoff: ecological validity (high) vs. data quality control (low — you cannot verify what participants report).
steps: Onboarding session: Train participants on diary completion. Show example entries. Clarify what counts as a recordable event. Emphasise completeness over literacy.
Pilot the diary: Run a 2–3 day pilot with 2–3 participants before full deployment. Identify questions that participants cannot answer, skip, or misinterpret.
Mid-study check-ins: Contact participants every 3–4 days to maintain engagement, answer questions, and identify compliance issues early.
Exit interview: After diary completion, conduct a retrospective interview using key diary entries as stimuli. Ask participants to elaborate on entries that raise questions.
outputs: Time-stamped diary entries, coded episodes and patterns over time, exit interview data, and compliance metrics.
useWhen: Behaviours that unfold over days or weeks, occur in private or mobile contexts, or are hard to observe directly, such as habits, onboarding or intermittent tasks.
avoidWhen: When you need precise interaction detail (use usability testing or analytics), or when participants cannot sustain the burden; consider experience sampling for momentary states.
whyLost: It remains active in UX, supported by dedicated tools, though pilots, check-ins and exit interviews are often trimmed.
whereToUse: Onboarding and habit formation in health, fitness and finance apps; household technology; cross-device journeys; and B2B tools used intermittently.
example: Twenty new users of a budgeting app keep a two-week diary of every money decision. Entries show they check balances before social plans, prompting a 'can I afford this?' quick view.
sources: Diary Methods (Flick ed.)
User Research (Stephanie Marsh)
Observing the User Experience (Goodman)
Diary Methods: Capturing Life as It Is Lived (Bolger, Davis & Rafaeli)
reference: Bolger, N., Davis, A. & Rafaeli, E. (2003). Diary methods: Capturing life as it is lived. Annual Review of Psychology, 54, 579-616.

extra.Design Decisions: Diary format: Structured (specific questions after each episode) vs. semi-structured (open narrative + fixed fields) vs. unstructured (free description). Structure increases comparability; openness increases richness. For most UX research: semi-structured is optimal. Trigger timing: Event-contingent (participants record after each occurrence of the target behaviour) vs. time-contingent (participants record at fixed intervals regardless of whether the target behaviour occurred) vs. signal-contingent (random signals prompt recording — see ESM, Method 50). Entry method: App-based diaries allow multimedia (photos, audio), time-stamping, and reminders. Paper diaries allow participants with limited digital access. Choose based on population and what the medium adds to data quality. Duration: Long enough to capture the full range of the phenomenon (including infrequent critical incidents) but short enough to maintain participant compliance. Most diary studies see compliance degrade significantly after 2 weeks.

name: Structured Observation
donor: Social science and sport performance research
origin: Long-established observational method; Gratton and Jones (2010) set out planning stages and recording with a predefined checklist, illustrated by a basketball tactics coding sheet.
summary: Observing people in a real setting and recording predefined behaviours on a checklist, with sampled times and checks on observer reliability.
description: Structured observation records specific, predefined behaviours rather than everything that happens. Gratton and Jones describe four planning stages: define the variables to be observed and link them to the research objectives; decide the sample, including a sample of times and locations, not just of people; decide how the variables will be recorded (pre-printed data sheet, video or dictation); and pilot the observation before the real event. Recording usually uses a simple checklist where each action by a sampled individual is ticked against categories, as in their example of coding each basketball play as 'dribbled then shot', 'immediate pass', 'lost possession' and so on. Because it is hard to record more than one variable at a time, observers should keep the variable list short, alternate between variables in set periods, use video or use several observers, in which case inter-observer reliability must be trained and checked. Typical mistakes are trying to record too much, ignoring the observer's effect on behaviour, not sampling times or locations and relying on memory. In UX it suits counting behaviours in physical or shared settings (kiosks, retail, hospital wards, control rooms) or coding session videos, giving frequencies that complement interviews and analytics.
steps: Define the behaviours or events to record and write clear category definitions tied to your research questions.
Choose who to observe and sample times and locations (for example peak and off-peak sessions on different days).
Build a checklist or coding sheet, or a video coding scheme, keeping the number of variables manageable.
Pilot the sheet in the real setting and refine categories that are ambiguous or never used.
Train observers and, where more than one observer is used, double-code a sample to check inter-observer agreement.
Collect the data, noting context and any signs that observers are affecting behaviour.
Tally frequencies and compare across times, locations or groups, and triangulate with other data.
outputs: Frequency counts and rates of defined behaviours by time, location and group, with reliability figures and supporting field notes.
useWhen: You need to know how often behaviours actually occur in a real setting rather than what people say they do, and the behaviours can be defined in advance.
avoidWhen: You do not yet know what matters (use open field observation first) or the behaviour is private, rare or invisible.
whyLost: Digital analytics now counts on-screen behaviour automatically, so hand-coded observation survives mainly in human factors and service design work in physical settings.
whereToUse: Self-service kiosks, retail and hospitality, healthcare and control rooms, classrooms, coding of usability-session videos, physical-digital service journeys.
example: A transport operator wants to know why ticket machines cause queues. Researchers observe six stations at morning peak and midday over two weeks, ticking each customer's actions (language switch, card retry, abandons, asks staff). A second observer double-codes 20% of sessions. Card retries turn out to account for most of the delay, which interviews had not revealed.
sources: Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Gratton, C. and Jones, I. (2010) Research Methods for Sports Studies, 2nd edn. London and New York: Routledge.

name: Structured output schemas for first-order codes
origin: JSON Schema specification (from 2009); first-order and second-order concepts from Gioia, Corley and Hamilton, 2013; LLM structured outputs from 2023
summary: Defining a strict machine-readable schema for each code an AI or human coder produces, so first-order codes always carry evidence, location, rationale and confidence and can be audited.
description: First-order codes, in the Gioia tradition, stay close to participants' own language before being abstracted into second-order themes. When an LLM produces them, free-text output is hard to verify and aggregate. A structured schema forces each code record to contain fields such as segment ID, participant ID, code label in participant terms, verbatim quote span with character offsets, rationale, confidence and whether the code is new or from the codebook. The schema is validated programmatically; invalid outputs are rejected and retried. Rigour comes from schema design that encodes methodological commitments (no code without evidence), validation of quote spans against source text, and version control of the schema itself.
steps: Decide the analytic commitments the schema must enforce (e.g. every code needs a verbatim quote; codes stay in participant language).
Write a JSON Schema with required fields: segment_id, participant_id, code_label, quote, quote_start, quote_end, rationale, confidence (0-1), is_new_code.
Pass the schema to the model's structured output or tool-use feature and validate every response.
Reject and retry outputs that fail validation, up to a fixed limit (e.g. 3), then route to human review.
Verify programmatically that each quote matches the source text at the given offsets.
Version the schema and store outputs in a table ready for second-order synthesis.
outputs: A versioned schema and a validated table of first-order codes with evidence and provenance.
useWhen: Any AI-assisted or multi-coder qualitative analysis at scale where codes must be auditable and aggregated.
avoidWhen: Unnecessary for small manual analyses in a CAQDAS tool, which already links codes to text.
whyLost: Structured outputs are an engineering feature, and qualitative researchers have rarely translated their methodological rules into data contracts.
whereToUse: AI-assisted analysis pipelines, research repositories and multi-team coding programmes.
example: A health research pipeline rejects 4% of LLM coding outputs whose quotes do not match the transcript, catching paraphrased 'quotes' that would otherwise have appeared in a report as participants' words.
sources: Anthropic Claude API (claude-sonnet-4-20250514)
structured outputs (JSON schema)
asyncio
Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G. & Hamilton, A. L. (2013) Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research. Organizational Research Methods
JSON Schema specification (json-schema.org)
The Inquiry Series, C12 — AI Agents for Structured Qualitative Analysis at Scale
reference: Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G. & Hamilton, A. L. (2013) Seeking qualitative rigor in inductive research: Notes on the Gioia methodology. Organizational Research Methods 16(1)

name: SUMI (Software Usability Measurement Inventory)
origin: Jurek Kirakowski, Human Factors Research Group, University College Cork (1993-1996); successor to the CUSI (1988)
summary: A 50-item questionnaire with a global usability score and five subscales (efficiency, affect, helpfulness, control, learnability), scored against a normative database.
description: The SUMI was built with unusually thorough psychometrics: 150 candidate items were cut to 75 by expert review, then to 50 by factor analysis of 139 users, and the five-factor structure was confirmed on an independent sample. Items use a three-point scale (agree, undecided, disagree) and mix positive and negative statements. A Global scale uses the 25 items that load most strongly on general usability. Its distinctive strength is standardisation: scores are converted against a reference database so 50 is average and the standard deviation is 10, making comparisons with other software meaningful. It was widely used in European ISO 9241 work and is available in 12 languages under licence (free for students).
steps: License the SUMI from the Human Factors Research Group and choose the language version.
Have at least 10 to 12 representative users complete it after real use of the software.
Submit responses for scoring against the reference database.
Read the Global score and the five subscale scores (mean 50, SD 10) with their confidence intervals.
Use item consensual analysis to find specific items where your users differ most from the norm.
outputs: Standardised global and subscale usability scores relative to a reference database.
useWhen: Comparing software against an external norm, especially in European or ISO-driven evaluations.
avoidWhen: Websites (use WAMMI or SUPR-Q) or when licensing is not possible.
whyLost: Licensing and its European academic home kept it out of the free-tool culture of North American UX practice.
whereToUse: Enterprise software procurement, public-sector systems, ISO 9241-11 conformance studies.
example: A payroll package scores 58 on Efficiency but 41 on Helpfulness, eight points below the database mean, directing effort to in-product help.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Measuring the User Experience (Tullis & Albert)
reference: Kirakowski, J. (1996). The Software Usability Measurement Inventory: Background and usage. In Usability Evaluation in Industry.

name: SUPR-Q (Standardized User Experience Percentile Rank Questionnaire)
origin: Sauro (2015); mobile app version SUPR-Qm by Sauro & Zarolia (2017)
summary: An 8-item website questionnaire measuring usability, trust, appearance and loyalty, scored as percentile ranks against hundreds of sites.
description: SUS measures perceived usability alone; websites also live or die on credibility, looks and loyalty. The SUPR-Q has eight items: two each for usability, trust (or credibility for non-commerce sites), appearance and loyalty, the last including the likelihood-to-recommend item. It was built through factor analysis and has strong reliability with only eight questions. Its distinctive feature is normative scoring: raw scores are converted to percentile ranks against a regularly updated database of websites, so a score of 75 means the site beats 75% of the benchmark. The SUPR-Qm is a 16-item Rasch-scaled version for mobile apps. Sauro recommends it over SUS for website benchmarks because it covers more of the experience in fewer items.
steps: Administer the eight items at the end of a study (or as a stand-alone survey of recent users).
Compute subscale means and the overall mean, treating the 11-point recommend item as half-weighted.
Convert to percentile ranks using the current normative database (licensed from MeasuringU).
Compare against competitors and industry averages in the same database.
Track over releases alongside task-level metrics.
outputs: Overall and subscale percentile ranks for a website or app.
useWhen: Website or app benchmarks where trust and appearance matter, and competitive comparisons.
avoidWhen: Internal tools where trust and loyalty are not meaningful, or when you cannot license the norms.
whyLost: Norms are commercial, so academic UX teaching favours free instruments like SUS and UMUX-Lite.
whereToUse: E-commerce, banking, insurance, travel and media sites; app store competitive reviews.
example: An insurer's site scores at the 82nd percentile for usability but the 31st for trust, redirecting effort toward reassurance content rather than navigation.
sources: Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Sauro, J. (2015). SUPR-Q: A comprehensive measure of the quality of the website user experience. Journal of Usability Studies 10(2).

name: Survey data cleaning
origin: Meade and Craig (2012) on careless responding; Curran (2016) on detection methods
summary: Systematically screening raw survey responses for careless, fraudulent, duplicate and out-of-range data using pre-stated rules before any analysis.
description: Survey cleaning is the first and most consequential analytic step: careless responses typically make up 10-15% of online samples and can create spurious factors, inflate or deflate correlations and distort means. Rigorous cleaning uses multiple indicators: attention or instructed-response items, response time (speeders), long-string analysis (straight-lining), even-odd consistency, Mahalanobis distance for multivariate outliers, duplicate and bot detection, and open-text checks. Rules and thresholds are written before looking at results, applied in code rather than by hand, and every exclusion is counted in a flow table. In UX practice this is often reduced to deleting obviously blank rows, which is why it is vestigial.
steps: Write exclusion rules and thresholds in the analysis plan before inspecting outcomes.
Import the raw export programmatically (e.g. pyreadstat for .sav files) and keep it unchanged.
Flag speeders, commonly those completing in under one third or under half of the median duration.
Flag failed attention checks, long strings exceeding about half the items in a scale block, and multivariate outliers at Mahalanobis distance p below 0.001.
Detect duplicates and bots via IP, device fingerprint, identical open text and impossible response patterns.
Recode out-of-range values to missing, reverse-score items as specified, and document every recode.
Exclude respondents meeting pre-stated combinations of flags and report counts at each step in a flow table; run a sensitivity analysis with and without exclusions.
outputs: A cleaned dataset, a flag table per respondent, an exclusion flow table and a sensitivity check on key results.
useWhen: Every survey analysis, especially online panels, incentive-driven samples, long instruments and psychometric work such as EFA or SEM.
