avoidWhen: Never skipped, but avoid aggressive post-hoc exclusions chosen after seeing results; that is a forking path. For very small qualitative screeners, a manual review suffices.
whyLost: Survey tools offer one-click exports and dashboards that hide the raw data, and UX teams rarely received training in response-quality screening.
whereToUse: Product satisfaction surveys, scale validation, segmentation studies, panel research and in-product intercepts.
example: A SaaS team running a 1,500-person panel survey flags 11% as speeders or attention-check failures. Removing them changes the leading pain point from 'pricing' to 'integration', because careless respondents had straight-lined the pricing block.

semopy
pyreadstat (SPSS import)
scikit-learn (MICE)
pingouin (reliability)
pandas

Curran, P. G. (2016) Methods for the detection of carelessly invalid responses in survey data. JESP
The Inquiry Series, C3 — Survey Pipeline in Python — From Raw Responses to Structural Equation Model
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)

name: Survey scale quality audit
origin: Classical test theory and reliability (Cronbach, 1951), construct validity (Cronbach and Meehl, 1955), survey error framework (Groves et al., Survey Methodology, 2004/2009) and cognitive interviewing (Willis, 2005)
summary: Systematically checks a survey's items and scales for wording problems, reliability, validity, response patterns and data quality before or after fielding.
description: Many UX surveys use home-made scales with untested wording, unvalidated item groupings and unknown reliability. A scale quality audit evaluates surveys through several lenses. Item wording is checked for double-barrelled, leading, ambiguous or jargon-laden items and for balanced, labelled response options. Cognitive interviews test whether respondents understand items as intended. Psychometric checks on fielded data examine internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha or, better, McDonald's omega, with about 0.70 as a common minimum), item-total correlations, factor structure, and floor and ceiling effects. Data quality checks look for straightlining, speeding and inattentive responding. Groves' total survey error framework connects these to coverage, sampling, non-response and measurement error. Rigour comes from combining qualitative pre-testing with quantitative psychometric evidence.
steps: Review each item against a checklist: one idea per item, neutral wording, no jargon, clear time frame, balanced and fully labelled response options, and consistent scale direction.
Run cognitive interviews with 5 to 15 respondents using think-aloud and verbal probes ('What does "reliable" mean to you here?') and revise problem items.
After fielding, compute item distributions and flag floor or ceiling effects, for example more than 15% of responses at either extreme.
Calculate reliability (omega or alpha, targeting 0.70 or above, and investigating values above about 0.95 for redundancy) and corrected item-total correlations (flag below 0.30).
Check structure with exploratory or confirmatory factor analysis where samples allow (often 200 or more), and test validity against related measures or behaviour.
Screen data quality: straightlining across grids, completion times below a plausible minimum (for example under one-third of the median), and failed attention checks.
Replace weak home-made scales with validated instruments where possible (for example SUS, UMUX-Lite, SUPR-Q) and document changes.
outputs: An item-level issues log, cognitive interview findings, reliability and validity statistics, data quality flags, and a revised instrument.
useWhen: Before launching a recurring or high-stakes survey, when inheriting an existing tracker, or when survey results conflict with behaviour.
avoidWhen: Using an established validated instrument unchanged with a comparable population, where a light data-quality check suffices.
whyLost: Survey tools make questionnaires easy to build, and UX teams rarely include psychometricians, so home-made scales go unvalidated for years.
whereToUse: Satisfaction and NPS trackers, relationship surveys, onboarding surveys, employee experience surveys, AI trust questionnaires.
example: A satisfaction tracker run for 6 months had a 4-item 'ease' scale with omega of 0.58 and one double-barrelled item ('fast and reliable'). Cognitive interviews showed rural respondents read 'reliable' as 'honest company'; splitting and rewording the items raised omega to 0.81.
sources: Statistics for Behavioral Sciences
Discovering Statistics via SPSS (Field)
Survey Methodology (Groves)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 42 — Ordinal Logic — Treating Likert & Survey Data Correctly
reference: Groves, R. M., Fowler, F. J., Couper, M. P., Lepkowski, J. M., Singer, E., & Tourangeau, R. (2009). Survey Methodology (2nd ed.). Wiley; Willis, G. B. (2005). Cognitive Interviewing: A Tool for Improving Questionnaire Design. Sage.

name: Survey Weighting
origin: Standard survey statistics practice; Veal and Darcy show it with site survey and count data and in SPSS's Weight Cases procedure
summary: Gives each respondent a weight so the sample's make-up on known characteristics matches the real user population before results are reported.
description: Survey weighting corrects a sample that is known to be unbalanced. Veal and Darcy's example is a site survey where interviews were spread evenly through the day, while counts showed that more than half of users came around midday; because midday users may differ, they are under-represented. For each group, such as a time-period, the weighting factor is the number in the population divided by the number in the sample, so each interview 'grosses up' to the users it represents. The weighted sample then matches the population. They note that the true sample size has not changed, so for significance tests the factors should be rescaled so the weighted total equals the actual number of interviews. Any characteristic known for the population can be used, such as age from the census, membership records or observed gender balance. They also suggest weighting to correct for different response rates in mail surveys. For UX surveys, which often over-represent engaged or recent users, weighting against analytics data on plan, tenure, platform or activity is a cheap way to make results more representative.
steps: Identify a characteristic that matters for the results and is known for the whole user population (for example time of use, plan, platform, age group).
Tabulate the sample and the population across the categories of that characteristic.
Compute a weighting factor for each category as population number divided by sample number.
Rescale the factors so the weighted total equals the actual sample size if significance tests will be run.
Attach the weights as a variable and apply them in the analysis software.
Compare weighted and unweighted results and report both the weighting basis and any large differences.
Avoid weighting on characteristics with very small sample cells, or combine categories first.
outputs: A weight variable for each respondent and weighted estimates that better reflect the user population, with a note of the weighting basis.
useWhen: A survey sample's make-up on a known characteristic clearly differs from the population and that characteristic plausibly relates to the answers.
avoidWhen: Population figures are unreliable, sample cells are tiny so weights become extreme, or the bias lies on unmeasured characteristics that weighting cannot fix.
whyLost: UX surveys are usually treated as convenience samples and reported raw, and few UX researchers are trained in survey statistics, though analytics now make population benchmarks easy to obtain.
whereToUse: In-product surveys, NPS and satisfaction programmes, panel surveys, site and event surveys, any survey that will be generalised to a user base.
example: An app's satisfaction survey gets 70 per cent of its responses from daily users, who make up 30 per cent of the active base. Weighting by usage frequency from analytics lowers reported satisfaction from 4.3 to 3.9 and shows that occasional users drive most complaints.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge.

name: Surveys
origin: Survey research tradition, 1930s onward (e.g. Gallup, Likert 1932)
summary: Structured self-report instruments administered to samples to measure attitudes, behaviours and characteristics at scale, from satisfaction tracking to validated scales.
description: Surveys collect structured self-reported data from a sample to estimate characteristics of a population, compare groups or track change over time. In UX they range from short satisfaction and loyalty measures, such as CSAT and NPS, to validated instruments like SUS and UMUX-Lite, and bespoke attitudinal questionnaires. Their power comes from scale; their weakness comes from the many sources of error described in the total survey error framework: coverage, sampling, non-response and measurement. Rigour comes from clearly defined constructs, well-worded and pretested questions, validated scales where possible, appropriate sampling and response-rate management, attention checks, and analysis that reports uncertainty and avoids over-interpreting small differences.
steps: Define research questions, target population and the decisions the survey will inform.
Specify the constructs to measure and reuse validated items or scales where possible.
Write clear, single-barrelled, neutral questions with balanced response options.
Pretest with 5 to 10 cognitive interviews and a small pilot.
Define the sampling frame and calculate sample size for the precision needed (for example about 385 for plus or minus 5 percent at 95 percent confidence in a large population).
Field the survey with reminders, monitoring response rates and data quality.
Clean data, weight if needed, analyse with confidence intervals and report limitations.
outputs: Descriptive statistics, segment comparisons, validated scale scores, trend data and open-ended response themes.
useWhen: For measuring attitudes, satisfaction or self-reported behaviour across large populations, segment comparisons and tracking over time.
avoidWhen: Avoid for understanding why or for discovering unknown issues; use interviews. Avoid self-report for precise behaviour when logs exist; use analytics.
whyLost: Still in use: Scalable data collection; but validity requires careful design and interpretation.
whereToUse: Satisfaction tracking; large-population attitudes; longitudinal benchmarking.
example: A SaaS company surveys 2,000 admins quarterly with UMUX-Lite and three bespoke items. A drop among admins of large accounts prompts follow-up interviews about permissions management.
sources: Survey Methodology
Questionnaire Design
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Groves, R. M. et al. (2009). Survey Methodology (2nd ed.). Wiley.

name: SWAT (Subjective Workload Assessment Technique)
origin: Gary Reid and Thomas Nygren, US Air Force Armstrong Laboratory, 1988
summary: Measures workload on time load, mental effort and psychological stress, scaled with each user's own conjoint-measured weighting of the three dimensions.
description: SWAT asks users to rate workload on three dimensions, each with three levels: time load, mental effort load and psychological stress load. What makes it rigorous is the scale development phase: before the task, each participant sorts 27 cards representing all combinations of levels by perceived workload, and conjoint measurement converts the sort into an interval scale from 0 to 100 unique to that person or group. Event ratings are then mapped onto this scale. SWAT thus respects individual differences in what feels demanding. It is more laborious than NASA-TLX, which displaced it, but its conjoint foundation makes it an instructive example of psychometric rigour in workload measurement.
steps: Explain the three dimensions and their three levels to participants with standard descriptors.
Run the card sort: each participant ranks all 27 combinations from lowest to highest workload.
Apply conjoint scaling to derive interval workload values; check Kendall's coefficient of concordance to decide between group and individual scales (group scale if W >= 0.75).
After each task or event, collect quick 1-2-3 ratings on the three dimensions.
Convert ratings to scaled workload scores and compare conditions or task segments.
Triangulate with performance and physiological measures.
outputs: Interval-scaled workload scores per task, with dimension contributions and individual weighting profiles.
useWhen: Comparing workload across designs when you need individually calibrated scaling or quick in-task ratings.
avoidWhen: Most product contexts; NASA-TLX or a single-item rating is quicker. The card sort is tedious for participants.
whyLost: NASA-TLX offered similar information with less setup, and the conjoint software became obsolete. It survives mainly in older military literature.
whereToUse: Comparative evaluation of control-room displays, vehicle HMIs, complex enterprise workflows.
example: A rail operator compares two dispatch screens. SWAT shows similar total workload, but stress load dominates in one design during disruptions, pointing to alarm handling as the issue.
sources: Reid & Nygren, The subjective workload assessment technique (1988), in Hancock & Meshkati (eds.), Human Mental Workload
reference: Reid, G. B., & Nygren, T. E. (1988). The subjective workload assessment technique. In Hancock & Meshkati (Eds.), Human Mental Workload. North-Holland.

name: Swiss Cheese Model Analysis
donor: Safety science and healthcare risk management
origin: James Reason, 1990
summary: Traces incidents through layered defences to show how latent conditions and active failures align, so design fixes target system weaknesses rather than blaming users.
description: Reason's model represents a system's safeguards as slices of Swiss cheese, each with holes caused by active failures (unsafe acts by people at the sharp end) and latent conditions (design decisions, staffing, procedures). Harm occurs when holes in successive layers align. As a research method it structures incident analysis: for each incident or near miss, analysts reconstruct the sequence, identify every defence that should have stopped it, and classify why each failed. The resulting picture usually shows that interface design, alerts and confirmations are some of the layers, and that user error is an outcome rather than a root cause. Rigour comes from systematic reconstruction with evidence, analysing near misses as well as harms, and aggregating across incidents to find recurring holes. Frameworks such as HFACS formalise the classification.
steps: Collect incidents and near misses with supporting evidence such as logs, screenshots and interviews.
Reconstruct each event timeline from initiating action to outcome.
List every defence layer that could have intercepted it: interface constraints, confirmations, alerts, procedures, reviews.
Classify each layer's failure as an active failure or latent condition, using a scheme such as HFACS.
Aggregate across incidents to find layers that fail repeatedly.
Design fixes that strengthen recurrent weak layers or add independent ones, and monitor near-miss rates.
outputs: Incident reconstructions, defence-layer failure maps, aggregated weak-layer analysis, systemic design recommendations.
useWhen: Healthcare, aviation, fintech operations, infrastructure tools and any product where errors cause serious harm.
avoidWhen: Low-consequence consumer flows with no incident history; standard error analysis or usability testing is lighter.
whyLost: Siloed: Lives in safety engineering and healthcare; rarely applied in consumer UX.
whereToUse: Healthcare UI; aviation; financial risk systems; any safety-critical interface.
example: A trading platform analysed a fat-finger order that lost £2m. The model showed four layers failed: no unit display, a dismissible warning, a disabled limit check and no second review. Fixes targeted the latent conditions, not just the trader.
sources: Handbook of Human Factors and Ergonomics
Human Error (James Reason)
Managing the Risks of Organizational Accidents (James Reason)
reference: Reason, J. (2000). Human error: Models and management. BMJ, 320(7237), 768-770.

name: Switchback and Cluster-Randomised Experiments
donor: Agricultural and clinical trial design; operations research
origin: Cluster randomised trials in public health (Donner and Klar, 2000; Hayes and Moulton, 2009); switchback designs formalised by Bojinov, Simchi-Levi and Zhao (2023)
summary: Randomises at the level of time periods, regions or groups instead of users when users interfere with each other, avoiding biased estimates in networks and marketplaces.
description: User-level A/B tests assume no interference (SUTVA). In marketplaces, social networks and shared resources, treating some users changes the experience of others: discounted riders consume drivers' supply, or a feature changes group chats. Cluster randomisation assigns whole groups (cities, teams, communities) to arms; switchback designs alternate treatment and control over time windows within a region. Analysis must account for clustering (intra-cluster correlation drives the design effect) and, for switchbacks, carryover between windows. Rigorous design balances window length against carryover and the number of clusters against power.
steps: Map interference: who affects whom (shared supply, social ties, team accounts).
Choose the randomisation unit: cluster (region, team, network component) or time window (switchback).
Estimate the intra-cluster correlation and compute the design effect (1 + (m - 1) x ICC) for sample size.
For switchbacks, choose window length longer than carryover time and randomise sequences; consider burn-in periods.
Analyse with cluster-robust or mixed-effects models, or design-based estimators for switchbacks.
Compare with user-level estimates to quantify interference bias.
outputs: Unbiased treatment effect estimates under interference, design-effect calculations and interference bias estimates.
useWhen: Marketplaces, social features, collaborative tools, shared-resource systems, pricing or dispatch algorithms.
avoidWhen: Independent users with no interaction; standard user-level A/B tests are more powerful.
whyLost: Platforms default to user-level randomisation, and UX researchers rarely consider interference.
whereToUse: Ride-hailing, delivery, team collaboration tools, social apps, multiplayer games.
example: A team-chat app tests a new notification digest. Randomising by workspace instead of user shows a smaller effect, because user-level tests had treated users replying to untreated colleagues.
sources: Hayes & Moulton, Cluster Randomised Trials (2009)
Bojinov, Simchi-Levi & Zhao, Design and analysis of switchback experiments (2023), Management Science
Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (2020)
reference: Bojinov, I., Simchi-Levi, D., & Zhao, J. (2023). Management Science, 69(7), 3759-3777.

name: Syndromic Surveillance of User Complaints
origin: Syndromic surveillance systems after 2001 (Henning, 2004); Farrington algorithm (1996); CDC EARS algorithms
summary: Continuously monitors grouped 'syndromes' from free-text complaints and signals, using statistical aberration detection to catch emerging problems early.
description: Public health agencies monitor emergency department chief complaints, pharmacy sales and absenteeism, grouped into syndromes (e.g. respiratory, gastrointestinal), and flag unusual increases before diagnoses are confirmed. Aberration detection algorithms (Farrington, EARS C1-C3, CUSUM) compare current counts with expected baselines accounting for seasonality and day-of-week effects, controlling false alarms. For products, user complaints, support tickets, reviews and in-app feedback can be classified into syndromes (e.g. 'login trouble', 'billing confusion') with NLP, and monitored the same way. It provides early warning of emergent UX problems with explicit sensitivity and false-alarm trade-offs.
steps: Define syndromes as groups of related complaints and build a classifier (rules or ML) with validated precision.
Assemble daily or hourly counts per syndrome, with denominators (active users).
Choose an aberration detection algorithm suited to the data (Farrington for seasonal counts, EARS for short baselines).
Calibrate thresholds to an acceptable false alarm rate using historical data.
Set up alert triage: who investigates, with what playbook (e.g. outbreak investigation).
Evaluate system sensitivity and timeliness against past incidents and refine syndromes.
outputs: Syndrome definitions, monitoring dashboards, alerts with statistical basis, and system performance evaluation.
useWhen: Products with large volumes of user feedback where emerging problems must be detected quickly.
avoidWhen: Low feedback volumes where counts are too sparse for statistical detection.
whyLost: Voice-of-customer tools show sentiment dashboards without aberration statistics; public health methods are unfamiliar.
whereToUse: Support operations, app review monitoring, AI assistant feedback, marketplace disputes, health app adverse events.
example: Classifying in-app feedback into 15 syndromes, a ride app's Farrington-based system flags a 'driver can't find pickup' rise in one city two days before ticket volume becomes visible, traced to a map data update.
sources: Henning, What is syndromic surveillance? (2004), MMWR Supplement
Farrington et al., A statistical algorithm for the early detection of outbreaks of infectious disease (1996), JRSS A
Hutwagner et al., The bioterrorism preparedness and response Early Aberration Reporting System (EARS) (2003), Journal of Urban Health
reference: Farrington, C. P., et al. (1996). JRSS Series A, 159(3), 547-563.

name: Synthetic Control Method
origin: Alberto Abadie and Javier Gardeazabal (2003); Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010)
summary: Builds a weighted combination of untreated units that tracks a treated unit before a change, and uses its post-change path as the counterfactual.
description: When one market, city or customer segment receives a change, synthetic control finds weights on a donor pool of untreated units so that the weighted combination matches the treated unit's pre-period outcomes and predictors. The post-period gap between treated and synthetic unit estimates the effect. Inference uses placebo tests, reapplying the method to each donor and comparing the treated unit's post/pre RMSPE ratio with the placebo distribution. It is transparent (weights are inspectable) and suited to the few-treated-unit situations common in product launches by country.
steps: Define the treated unit (e.g. a country), donor pool of untreated units, outcome and launch date.
Exclude donors exposed to similar changes or spillovers.
Choose predictors and fit weights minimising pre-period discrepancy (using e.g. the Synth or augsynth packages).
Check pre-period fit; poor fit invalidates the analysis.
Estimate post-period gaps and run in-space placebo tests on each donor, and in-time placebos on fake dates.
Report effect paths, weights and the placebo-based p-value.
outputs: Synthetic counterfactual series, effect estimates over time, donor weights and placebo inference.
useWhen: A launch affects one or a few markets, regions or enterprise customers, with comparable untreated units and long pre-periods.
avoidWhen: Many treated units with staggered adoption (use modern DiD estimators) or when the treated unit lies outside the donors' range.
whyLost: It is relatively recent and sits in econometrics; product analytics teams default to naive country comparisons.
whereToUse: Market-level launches, regional pricing, regulatory changes by country, offline marketing campaigns.
example: A food-delivery app launches a new checkout in Portugal only. A synthetic Portugal built from Spain, Italy and Greece regions shows a 3.1% order uplift, larger than any placebo gap.
sources: Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller, Synthetic control methods for comparative case studies (2010), JASA
Abadie, Using synthetic controls: Feasibility, data requirements, and methodological aspects (2021), Journal of Economic Literature
reference: Abadie, A., Diamond, A., & Hainmueller, J. (2010). JASA, 105(490), 493-505.

name: Synthetic session generation at cluster boundaries
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Methods Atlas; building on generative modelling and boundary-value testing in software engineering
summary: Uses a generative model to create synthetic user sessions in the ambiguous regions between behavioural clusters, stress-testing systems on the users they are most likely to misclassify.
description: AI systems such as recommenders, risk models and adaptive interfaces tend to fail on users who sit between typical patterns. This method trains a generative model (often a VAE) on real sessions, identifies cluster boundaries in latent space (where membership probabilities are near equal), and samples or interpolates synthetic sessions there. These sessions are fed to the target system to observe outputs, measure inconsistency, and find failure modes before real users encounter them. It borrows from boundary-value analysis in software testing. Rigour requires validating that synthetic sessions are realistic, labelling them as synthetic throughout, and confirming discovered failures with real users or real logs. Synthetic sessions test systems; they do not replace user research.
steps: Train a generative model on real sessions and fit clusters in its latent space.
Identify boundary regions where the top two cluster probabilities differ by less than 0.2.
Sample or interpolate thousands of latent points in those regions and decode them into synthetic sessions (e.g. 10,000).
Validate realism by comparing synthetic sessions with real boundary users on key distributions and expert review of 30-50 samples.
Run synthetic sessions through the target system and measure outputs: recommendation stability, risk score variance, inappropriate suggestions.
Confirm high-severity failures with real user data or targeted research before acting.
outputs: A synthetic test set at behavioural boundaries, a catalogue of system failure modes and prioritised issues for confirmation.
useWhen: Before launching or updating AI recommendation, classification or personalisation systems, especially in high-stakes domains.
avoidWhen: Avoid using synthetic sessions as evidence of user needs or attitudes, or when the generative model is poorly validated; use real-user testing instead.
whyLost: It is a new combination of ML and testing practice, and most UX teams lack access to generative models of their users' behaviour.
whereToUse: Investment recommendation AI, credit and fraud models, adaptive learning platforms, health triage systems.
example: An investment platform generates 10,000 synthetic sessions between 'cautious saver' and 'active trader' archetypes. The recommendation AI suggests leveraged products to 14% of them, a failure confirmed in real logs and fixed before scale-up.
sources: Deep Generative Modeling (Jakub Tomczak, Springer)
Deep Learning (Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio & Aaron Courville)
Methods Atlas (Vivek Gopinath)
Kingma & Welling (2013) Auto-encoding variational Bayes
Deep Generative Modelling (Springer)
Deep Learning (Goodfellow)
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 53 — Generative Models & Synthetic User Testing
reference: Kingma, D. P. & Welling, M. (2019) An introduction to variational autoencoders. Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning, 12(4), 307-392.

name: System Dynamics Stock-and-Flow Modelling
origin: Jay Forrester, MIT, 1956-1961 (Industrial Dynamics); John Sterman (Business Dynamics, 2000)
summary: Builds quantitative simulations of stocks (users, trust, backlog) and flows with feedback and delays to explore long-term dynamics of products and services.
description: Causal loop diagrams show feedback qualitatively; stock-and-flow models make it quantitative. Stocks accumulate (active users, content, support backlog, trust); flows change them (sign-ups, churn, resolution); auxiliary variables and delays connect them. Simulating the model reveals non-intuitive behaviour: overshoot and collapse, tipping points, worse-before-better dynamics after interventions. Sterman's work shows that people systematically misjudge stock-flow dynamics. Rigorous practice involves calibrating to historical data, testing extreme conditions, and sensitivity analysis. For UX strategy, it shows how growth tactics, support capacity and user trust interact over months and years.
steps: Define the problem behaviour over time (reference mode), such as growth then stagnation.
Elicit a causal loop diagram with stakeholders and data, then convert to stocks, flows and delays.
Quantify relationships from data, research and expert estimates; build the model (Vensim, Stella, PySD).
Validate: reproduce historical behaviour, test extreme conditions and dimensional consistency.
Run policy experiments and sensitivity analysis on uncertain parameters.
Communicate insights with simulation runs and use them to frame research questions.
outputs: A calibrated simulation model, policy scenario results, sensitivity analysis and dynamic hypotheses.
useWhen: Strategic questions about growth, trust, quality and capacity dynamics over long horizons.
avoidWhen: Short-term tactical design questions or where data cannot support even rough calibration.
whyLost: System dynamics is taught in management schools and policy, not design; 'systems thinking' in UX usually stops at diagrams.
whereToUse: Marketplace growth, community moderation capacity, trust and safety strategy, freemium conversion, technical debt and UX debt.
example: A social platform models how moderation backlog affects user trust and posting. Simulation shows that aggressive growth campaigns produce a delayed trust collapse after 9 months unless moderation capacity scales ahead of growth.
sources: Sterman, Business Dynamics: Systems Thinking and Modeling for a Complex World (2000)
Forrester, Industrial Dynamics (1961)
Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008)
reference: Sterman, J. D. (2000). Business Dynamics. McGraw-Hill.

name: System Usability Scale (SUS)
origin: John Brooke, 1986 (published 1996)
summary: A 10-item questionnaire producing a 0-100 perceived usability score that can be benchmarked against thousands of published studies.
description: SUS consists of ten statements rated on a five-point agreement scale, alternating positive and negative wording. Odd items contribute (score minus 1), even items (5 minus score), and the sum is multiplied by 2.5 to give 0-100. It is not a percentage: Sauro and Lewis's normative data put the average around 68, with roughly 80 or above in the top decile. SUS is reliable (alpha typically above 0.9) with small samples and is technology-agnostic. Rigour comes from administering it unchanged immediately after realistic tasks, reporting confidence intervals, converting to percentile ranks using normative data, and not treating it as diagnostic: it tells you how usable a product is perceived to be, not why. Small wording substitutions, such as 'website' for 'system', are acceptable.
steps: Administer SUS after participants complete representative tasks, before any discussion.
Use the standard ten items unchanged apart from replacing 'system' with the product name if needed.
Score each response: odd items minus 1, 5 minus even items, sum and multiply by 2.5.
Compute the mean and 95% confidence interval; aim for at least 12-20 participants for usable precision.
Convert to a percentile rank or grade using published norms (mean about 68).
Compare with previous releases or competitors and pair with task metrics to explain scores.
outputs: SUS score per participant, mean with confidence interval, percentile rank and grade, comparisons over time or across products.
useWhen: Usability benchmarking, comparing releases or competitors, and summative evaluations needing a standard perceived usability metric.
avoidWhen: When you need diagnostic detail about problems; use usability testing observations. For in-product micro-surveys, UMUX-Lite is less burdensome.
whyLost: Still in use: Free, validated, quick; enables benchmarking and comparison across products.
whereToUse: Usability testing; benchmarking; longitudinal usability tracking.
example: A SaaS analytics product measured SUS with 20 users each quarter. The score rose from 61 (about 30th percentile) to 74 (about 70th percentile) after a navigation redesign, giving leadership a clear benchmarked improvement.
sources: Measuring the User Experience
Quantifying the User Experience
SUS: A quick and dirty usability scale (John Brooke)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
reference: Brooke, J. (1996). SUS: A 'quick and dirty' usability scale. In P. W. Jordan et al. (Eds.), Usability Evaluation in Industry (pp. 189-194). Taylor & Francis.

name: Systematic Probe Schedule
origin: Joseph Dumas & Janice Redish, 1993 (A Practical Guide to Usability Testing)
summary: Pre-defining behavioural triggers and matching probe questions for usability sessions, and coding probed responses separately from spontaneous think-aloud.
description: Think-aloud sessions often drift between unstructured observation and ad hoc questioning that varies across moderators and participants. A systematic probe schedule pre-defines, for each critical task step, a behavioural trigger (a pause over three seconds, backtracking, a verbal sign of confusion) and a standard probe question. When a trigger fires, the moderator delivers the probe, and analysis keeps probed responses separate from spontaneous verbalisation. This makes moderation consistent across sessions and moderators, reduces leading, and lets the analyst compare what participants think unprompted with what they say when asked. The discipline also exposes moderator effects that otherwise contaminate usability findings.
steps: Pre-session preparation: For each critical task step in the usability test, define a behavioral trigger (e.g., "participant pauses > 3 seconds," "participant backtracks," "participant expresses confusion verbally") and a probe question ("I noticed you paused — what's going through your mind?").

During the session: When a trigger fires, deliver the associated probe. Code probes separately from spontaneous verbalizations — this separates researcher-elicited from user-generated cognition in your analysis.

Post-session analysis: Analyse spontaneous verbalizations and probe responses separately. Probe responses reveal what participants thought when asked; spontaneous verbalizations reveal what participants thought without prompting. The gap between them is informative.
outputs: A trigger-probe schedule per task, coded probe and spontaneous responses, and comparisons between the two.
useWhen: Moderated usability tests with several moderators, comparative tests where consistency matters, or high-stakes evaluations requiring defensible moderation.
avoidWhen: Exploratory or generative sessions where rigid probing would constrain discovery; use open contextual interviewing.
whyLost: Moderation is taught as an intuitive skill and discussion guides rarely specify triggers, so the systematic schedule from the early usability engineering literature faded.
whereToUse: Benchmark usability studies, medical device formative and summative testing, multi-moderator programmes, and regulated product evaluations.
example: In a multi-site test of a banking app, three moderators use the same trigger list. Probe responses show that hesitation at the transfer limit screen stems from fear of fees, consistently across sites.
sources: Handbook of Usability Testing (Dumas & Redish)
Research Methods in HCI (Lazar)
A Practical Guide to Usability Testing (Dumas & Redish)
reference: Dumas, J. S. & Redish, J. C. (1999). A Practical Guide to Usability Testing (rev. ed.). Intellect.

name: Systems Thinking
origin: Jay Forrester, 1950s-1960s; Peter Senge, 1990; Donella Meadows, 2008
summary: Maps feedback loops, delays and interdependencies in the system around a product to explain emergent behaviour and find leverage points rather than local fixes.
description: Systems thinking studies how the structure of a system, its stocks, flows, feedback loops and delays, produces behaviour over time. Forrester founded system dynamics at MIT; Senge popularised systems thinking for organisations; Meadows described leverage points where small changes produce large effects. In UX it treats a product as embedded in a system of users, organisations, incentives and other products. The method builds causal loop diagrams from research evidence, identifies reinforcing and balancing loops and delays, and, at higher rigour, builds stock-and-flow simulation models. Rigour comes from grounding each causal link in evidence, naming loop polarity explicitly, validating diagrams with stakeholders and data, and testing interventions against the model to anticipate unintended consequences such as growth loops undermining trust.
steps: Define the problem behaviour over time (e.g. engagement rising then collapsing).
Identify key variables from research and data and draw causal links with polarities.
Identify reinforcing and balancing loops and important delays.
Validate the diagram with stakeholders and with available quantitative data.
Identify leverage points and test interventions, optionally with a stock-and-flow simulation.
Monitor indicators for each loop after intervention.
outputs: Behaviour-over-time graphs, causal loop diagrams, identified leverage points, optional simulation model.
useWhen: Platforms, marketplaces, ecosystems, services with many stakeholders, and recurring problems that resist local fixes.
avoidWhen: Contained usability problems with clear local causes; use usability testing.
whyLost: Latent: Growing in design thinking extensions; rarely applied rigorously in product UX.
whereToUse: Platform product design; ecosystem mapping; service design; organizational design.
example: A social app's growth team mapped a reinforcing loop where notifications drove opens but also unsubscribes with a delay. The causal model showed a balancing loop eroding the user base, leading to capped notification frequency.
sources: Mapping Experiences
The Fifth Discipline (Peter Senge)
Thinking in Systems (Donella Meadows)
Industrial Dynamics (Jay Forrester)
reference: Meadows, D. H. (2008). Thinking in Systems: A Primer. Chelsea Green.

name: Systems Thinking Loops in UX Analysis (DSRP)
origin: Derek Cabrera, 2006 (DSRP theory); Cabrera and Colosi (2008)
summary: Applies Cabrera's four patterns, distinctions, systems, relationships and perspectives, to map the system around a user problem so it is not reduced to a single screen or task.
description: DSRP proposes that systems thinking consists of four universal cognitive patterns, each with two elements: making Distinctions (identity and other), organising Systems (part and whole), recognising Relationships (action and reaction) and taking Perspectives (point and view). Applied to UX, a DSRP map makes explicit what is inside and outside the problem boundary, how the product is part of larger wholes (workflows, organisations, ecosystems), the causal and feedback relationships among actors and artefacts, and how the situation appears from each stakeholder's viewpoint. This counters the habit of framing problems as isolated screen issues, especially in wicked problems such as healthcare or public services. Rigour comes from deriving elements from research data, mapping relationships including feedback loops, and checking each perspective with the people who hold it.
steps: For any UX problem:
Distinctions — what is in scope (user, interface, context, organization) vs. out of scope?
(2) Systems — what are the parts and how do they nest?
(3) Relationships — what causal relationships connect parts?
(4) Perspectives — how does the problem look from each stakeholder's position? Map all four before solution generation.
outputs: DSRP map with explicit boundaries, part-whole structures, relationship and feedback loops, and perspective comparisons; reframed problem statements.
useWhen: Complex sociotechnical problems, service design, healthcare and public sector projects, and situations where fixing one screen keeps failing.
avoidWhen: For well-bounded interface problems where systemic factors are minimal; use task analysis or usability testing.
whyLost: DSRP stayed within systems education and evaluation research; UX adopted journey maps and ecosystem maps, which capture some relationships but not boundaries or perspectives systematically.
whereToUse: Wicked problem UX analysis, organizational UX research, systems design for complex products, enterprise UX.
example: A surgical scheduling tool keeps failing adoption despite usability fixes. A DSRP map shows the operating list is part of a bed-management system whose perspective was ignored, so the project shifts to integrating with bed availability.
sources: Modular Design Frameworks — James Cabrera
Systems Thinking Made Simple (Derek & Laura Cabrera)
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas (DSRP protocol)
PACT analysis (Dix; Benyon, Designing Interactive Systems)
Methods Atlas — DSRP protocol (Gopinath)
PACT analysis (Dix)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 13 — DSRP Systems Thinking & Wicked Problems
reference: Cabrera D, Colosi L & Lobdell C (2008) Systems thinking. Evaluation and Program Planning 31(3):299-310

name: T-SNE
origin: Laurens van der Maaten & Geoffrey Hinton, 2008
summary: A non-linear method that maps high-dimensional user data to two dimensions while preserving local neighbourhoods, for visual exploration of behavioural groupings.
description: t-SNE converts pairwise distances into probabilities of being neighbours in high-dimensional space and finds a 2D layout whose neighbour probabilities match, using a heavy-tailed t-distribution to avoid crowding. It reveals local cluster structure that PCA can flatten. But its maps are easily misread: distances between clusters, cluster sizes and densities carry little meaning, results vary with the perplexity parameter and random seed, and it can produce apparent clusters from noise. Rigour means using it for exploration only, running several perplexities (e.g. 5, 30, 50) and seeds, initialising with PCA, and confirming any visual grouping with clustering and validation on the original features.
steps: Standardise features and reduce to around 30-50 dimensions with PCA to remove noise and speed computation.
Run t-SNE with perplexity values of 5, 30 and 50, PCA initialisation and at least 1,000 iterations.
Repeat with several random seeds and compare whether the same groupings recur.
Colour maps by known variables (outcomes, segments, platforms) to interpret regions.
Do not interpret inter-cluster distances or cluster sizes; confirm any apparent groups with clustering and validation on original data.
outputs: Exploratory 2D maps of the user space showing local neighbourhoods and candidate groupings for further analysis.
useWhen: Exploring high-dimensional behavioural, embedding or survey data visually to spot potential groupings or anomalies.
avoidWhen: Avoid for quantitative conclusions, for preserving global structure (use PCA or UMAP), or for very large datasets without optimised implementations.
whyLost: It is widely used in data science and ML research; within UX it appears in analytics collaborations, often misinterpreted.
whereToUse: Exploration of session embeddings, support ticket embeddings, behavioural logs in fintech and media.
example: A team maps 50,000 sessions with t-SNE and sees an isolated island of sessions. Colouring by app version shows they all come from a buggy release, prompting an error investigation rather than a new persona.
sources: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Space and Time (Marc Leordeanu)
van der Maaten & Hinton (2008) Visualizing data using t-SNE
Wattenberg, Viégas & Johnson (2016) How to use t-SNE effectively
Pattern Recognition & ML (Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Time & Space
The Inquiry Series, Ch 52 — Dimensionality Reduction — The Geometry of Behavioral Space
reference: van der Maaten, L. & Hinton, G. (2008) Visualizing data using t-SNE. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 9, 2579-2605.

name: t-Tests for Comparing Designs (Paired and Two-Sample)
origin: W. S. Gosset ("Student", 1908); Welch (1947)
summary: Tests whether average ratings or task times differ between two designs, for the same or different participants.
description: The t-test is the workhorse for comparing two means: SUS scores, SEQ ratings, log task times. The paired version works on each participant's difference score in within-subjects designs and gains power by removing between-person variation. The two-sample version, preferably the Welch form that does not assume equal variances, compares independent groups. Sauro and Lewis show the t-test is robust for rating scales and works at small sample sizes, which settles a long debate about whether ordinal scale data can be analysed this way. Reporting the confidence interval around the difference matters more than the p-value.
steps: Decide whether the design is within-subjects (paired) or between-subjects (two-sample).
Log-transform task times first; leave rating scales as they are.
For paired data, compute each person's difference and run a one-sample t-test on the differences against zero.
For independent groups, run Welch's t-test using each group's own variance and adjusted degrees of freedom.
Report the mean difference, its confidence interval, t, df and p.
outputs: An estimate of how much two designs differ on a continuous measure, with significance.
useWhen: Two designs or versions, one continuous outcome.
avoidWhen: More than two conditions (use ANOVA), binary outcomes (use proportion tests), or heavy outliers with tiny n (consider a permutation test).
whyLost: Not lost, but often misapplied: paired data analysed as independent, task times left raw, or Student's equal-variance form used by default.
whereToUse: Prototype comparisons, redesign evaluations, competitive benchmarks.
example: Twelve people rate two onboarding flows with the SEQ. The paired t-test shows a mean improvement of 0.9 points (95% CI 0.3 to 1.5, p = 0.008).
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Practical Statistics for Data Scientists (Bruce & Bruce)
Myatt, G., Making Sense of Data: A Practical Guide to Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Mining (2007)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Sauro & Lewis (2016), Quantifying the User Experience, chapter 5.

name: Taguchi Robust Design
origin: Genichi Taguchi, 1950s-1980s (Introduction to Quality Engineering, 1986)
summary: Chooses design settings that perform well across uncontrollable noise conditions, optimising signal-to-noise ratios rather than average performance.
description: Taguchi distinguished control factors (designer chooses) from noise factors (users, environments, devices the designer cannot control). Using crossed or combined arrays, experiments vary both, and robustness is measured with signal-to-noise ratios or variance models. The quality loss function quantifies that any deviation from target imposes cost, not just out-of-specification results. For UX, noise factors are everywhere: screen size, lighting, connectivity, literacy, age, assistive tech. Robust design finds layouts and parameters whose performance is stable across them, rather than optimal for the average user and poor for many.
steps: List control factors (design options) and noise factors (device, bandwidth, ambient light, user skill).
Choose an orthogonal array for control factors and a noise array or deliberate noise sampling.
Run each control combination across noise conditions and record performance.
Compute S/N ratios (e.g. larger-the-better or nominal-the-best) or model mean and variance separately.
Select settings that maximise robustness, then adjust a scaling factor to hit the target mean.
Confirm with a validation run under fresh noise conditions.
outputs: Robust control settings, S/N or variance analysis, and confirmation results.
useWhen: Products used across highly variable conditions, where consistency of experience matters as much as average.
avoidWhen: Homogeneous user populations and controlled settings; standard experiments suffice.
whyLost: Taguchi methods lived in manufacturing quality and were criticised by statisticians on analysis details; UX never adopted the robustness mindset.
whereToUse: Emerging-market apps, accessibility, outdoor and in-vehicle UIs, IoT devices, video calls under variable bandwidth.
example: A ticketing app tests QR code size and contrast across lighting and phone age conditions. The robust choice has a slightly lower best-case scan rate but halves failures in sunlight and old devices.
sources: Taguchi, Introduction to Quality Engineering (1986)
Phadke, Quality Engineering Using Robust Design (1989)
Nair (ed.), Taguchi's parameter design: A panel discussion (1992), Technometrics
reference: Phadke, M. S. (1989). Quality Engineering Using Robust Design. Prentice Hall.

name: Tailored Design Method
origin: Don Dillman and colleagues (Dillman, Smyth and Christian, 2009); the follow-up sequence is reproduced by Veal and Darcy for mail surveys
summary: A planned sequence of contacts, reminders and replacement questionnaires, plus attention to letter, design and incentives, to raise self-completion survey response rates.
description: Response to self-completion surveys depends on the topic, the questionnaire's length and presentation, the covering letter, the ease of reply, rewards and, above all, reminders. Veal and Darcy call well-planned follow-ups perhaps the most important tool available, and reproduce Dillman's sequence: the initial mailing with the questionnaire; a postcard reminder after about a week; a reminder letter with a second copy of the questionnaire, 'in case the original has been mislaid', after about two weeks, possibly offering a telephone interview; and a final reminder after about three weeks. Email or phone can replace post. In their example of a residents' survey, returns would have stopped at about 40 per cent, but surges after each reminder lifted the final rate to 75 per cent. Reminders require responses to be identifiable, which raises confidentiality concerns that can be eased by numbering the reply envelope rather than the questionnaire. Identification also lets researchers check representativeness and weight. For UX email and in-product surveys, which commonly send one invitation and accept a few per cent response, a planned follow-up schedule is a direct way to reduce non-response bias.
steps: Write a covering message that explains who is asking, why it matters and how answers will be used.
Design the questionnaire to look easy to complete, with clear layout and a simple way to return it.
Send the initial invitation and track who has responded with an identifier kept apart from the answers.
Send a short reminder to non-respondents after about a week.
After about two weeks send a fuller reminder with a fresh copy or link, and offer an alternative mode such as a short call.
Send a final reminder after about three weeks, then close fieldwork.
Plot daily returns, report the response rate and compare respondents with the population to judge non-response bias.
outputs: A higher and documented response rate, a returns curve showing the effect of each contact, and data for checking non-response bias.
useWhen: You run self-completion surveys by email, post or in-product messages and need results that represent the invited group.
avoidWhen: Repeated contact would breach consent, marketing rules or goodwill, or the survey is an anonymous open link where non-respondents cannot be identified.
whyLost: UX surveys are often run as quick one-shot links with tools that make sending cheap, so the craft of contact sequencing from survey methodology was rarely carried over.
whereToUse: Email surveys of customers or members, B2B account surveys, research panels, longitudinal surveys, post-service follow-ups.
example: A sports federation's member survey drew 22 per cent after the first email. Following the reminder schedule, a short reminder at day 8, a fresh link at day 15 and a final note at day 22 took the response to 51 per cent and brought in more casual members, who rated the app lower.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge. Dillman, D. A., Smyth, J. D. and Christian, L. M. (2009) Internet, Mail, and Mixed-Mode Surveys: The Tailored Design Method, Third edn. New York: Wiley.

name: Task Success Coding and Error-Opportunity Rates
donor: Human reliability analysis and Six Sigma
origin: Defects-per-opportunity from Six Sigma; applied to usability by Sauro (2004 onward)
summary: Rules for scoring each task attempt as a success or failure and counting errors against the number of chances to make them.
description: Completion rates and error counts are only comparable when they are coded consistently. Sauro's guidance defines success in advance (a correct end state, ideally checkable by URL or answer), treats assisted completions as failures, and codes partial success only with explicit criteria. For errors, raw counts are misleading because a twelve-field form offers more chances to slip than a two-click task. Dividing errors by error opportunities, the places a user could reasonably go wrong, gives an error rate that can be compared across tasks and products, and the proportion of error-free attempts feeds into SUM. Published data put the average completion rate around 78% and suggest about 0.7 errors per task is typical.
steps: Write a success criterion for each task before testing, including what counts as assistance.
Code each attempt as 1 (success) or 0 (failure), never as a percentage of steps.
Define error opportunities by walking the ideal path and listing each point where a slip or mistake is possible.
Log each error with its type and step during sessions or from recordings.
Compute errors per task, error rate per opportunity and the proportion of error-free attempts.
outputs: Comparable completion and error metrics per task.
useWhen: Any summative or benchmark test where tasks or products will be compared.
avoidWhen: Purely exploratory sessions with open-ended tasks.
whyLost: Error logging is laborious and moderators rarely agree on what counts, so many reports drop errors entirely.
whereToUse: Form-heavy flows, data entry systems, medical and financial software.
example: Two checkout designs have similar raw error counts, but per opportunity the new one is 40% lower because it has twice as many fields.
sources: How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2016). Quantifying the User Experience, chapter 2; Sauro, How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test.

name: Task-Action Grammar
origin: Stephen Payne and Thomas Green, 1986
summary: Describes an interface's command language as a feature-based grammar so that the number of rule schemas measures consistency and predicts learnability.
description: TAG represents tasks as sets of semantic features (direction, unit, object) and writes rewrite rules mapping tasks to action sequences. A consistent language lets one rule schema with feature variables cover many tasks, for example 'move [direction] by [unit]' mapped to a key pattern. Inconsistencies show up as extra rules. The number of schemas therefore indexes how much users must learn, and family resemblance between rules predicts transfer. TAG also captures world knowledge used in mapping, such as the conventional association of 'up' with 'previous'. It is a precise way to audit consistency in command sets, keyboard shortcuts, gesture vocabularies and voice command grammars.
steps: List the simple tasks the interface supports and identify their semantic features and values.
Write task-action rules for each task, generalising into schemas with feature variables wherever mappings are systematic.
Count rule schemas and note exceptions that require special rules.
Identify mappings that rely on world knowledge or conventions and check they are culturally valid for users.
Propose a revised command set that minimises schemas, then compare learning or error rates with a small study.
Document the grammar as a design-system rule for future additions.
outputs: A TAG description, schema counts, inconsistency list and a proposed consistent command grammar.
useWhen: Designing or auditing shortcut sets, gesture vocabularies, voice command grammars, CLI syntax or API naming.
avoidWhen: GUI flows dominated by visual recognition rather than recalled commands.
whyLost: Direct manipulation reduced interest in command languages, and formal grammar notations felt academic. Voice and CLI tools have revived the need without the method.
whereToUse: Voice assistants, developer CLIs, keyboard-first productivity apps, gesture systems in VR.
example: A note-taking app has 48 shortcuts. A TAG analysis finds 19 schemas, with heading levels mapped inconsistently; a revision covering the same functions with 9 schemas cuts recall errors in testing.
sources: Payne & Green, Task-action grammars: A model of the mental representation of task languages (1986), Human-Computer Interaction
Dix, Finlay, Abowd & Beale, Human-Computer Interaction (3rd ed., 2004)
reference: Payne, S. J., & Green, T. R. G. (1986). Task-action grammars. Human-Computer Interaction, 2(2), 93-133.

name: Taxonomy of Loss
origin: Vivek Gopinath, Lost Methods in UX (treatise)
summary: Classifies how research methods disappear (extinct, vestigial, siloed, renamed, latent) and, with cause of loss, locates priority targets for recovery.
description: The treatise defines a lost method as one that (a) was once practised with regularity and rigour, (b) has largely disappeared from practice, education or discourse, and (c) retains significant value if recovered. Its taxonomy has five types: Extinct (no current practitioners; knowledge only in literature; the methodological community has dissolved), Vestigial (practised in reduced or distorted form; original intent and theory lost, leaving a surface procedure), Siloed (active in academic or specialist contexts but absent from industry), Renamed (rebranded without credit or theoretical connection to origins) and Latent (known but rarely used; infrastructure for revival exists). The extended edition adds unmigrated methods, rigorous in donor disciplines but never adopted. Appendix A crosses survival degree with cause of loss (legitimate validity failure versus illegitimate organisational pressure); high-value, low-survival methods are recovery priorities.
steps: Inventory methods used in or relevant to the organisation or field.
Check each against the three lost-method criteria.
Assign a loss type: extinct, vestigial, siloed, renamed, latent or unmigrated.
Assess the cause of loss, distinguishing validity failure from organisational pressure.
Plot methods by potential value and current survival.
Select high-value, low-survival methods for recovery.
outputs: Classified method inventory, value-by-survival map, recovery shortlist.
useWhen: Auditing a research team's toolkit, curriculum design, building method libraries.
avoidWhen: Choosing a method for a single study; use method selection guidance instead.
whyLost: Original framework of the treatise.
whereToUse: ResearchOps, UX education, professional associations, research leadership strategy.
example: A research team classifies its 40 listed methods and finds 12 vestigial (including 'thematic analysis' and 'contextual inquiry'), prompting training in the full protocols.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kuhn TS (1962) The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
reference: Gopinath V. Lost Methods in UX: A Complete Treatise, Chapter 1 and Appendix A.

name: Teach-Back Mental Model Elicitation
donor: Clinical health literacy practice; cybernetics (Pask's conversation theory)
origin: Gordon Pask's teachback in conversation theory (1970s); clinical teach-back popularised by Dean Schillinger et al. (2003)
summary: Asks users to explain or teach how a system works in their own words, then scores the explanation against a reference model to expose mental model gaps.
description: In medicine, teach-back confirms patient understanding: the clinician asks the patient to explain the instructions back, corrects misunderstandings and repeats until correct. Pask used 'teachback' to externalise a learner's conceptual structure. As a UX method, participants explain to a confederate novice how a feature works (e.g. how their data is shared, how the AI decides), sometimes with drawing. Explanations are coded against a reference conceptual model for correct, missing and incorrect propositions, giving a quantitative mental model accuracy score. It is far more diagnostic than asking 'did that make sense?', and directly tests whether interface explanations transfer understanding.
steps: Write a reference conceptual model of the system as a list of key propositions (e.g. 10-20).
After users interact with the product or explanation, ask them to teach a novice (or the researcher playing one) how it works.
Allow drawing and probing with neutral prompts ('and then what happens?').
Code transcripts for correct, missing and incorrect propositions; compute accuracy and misconception frequency with two coders.
Identify common misconceptions and the interface elements that produce them.
Revise explanations and repeat teach-back until a target (e.g. 80% of key propositions correct) is met.
outputs: Mental model accuracy scores, a misconception inventory and links to interface causes.
useWhen: Users must understand how a system works to use it safely: privacy settings, AI behaviour, financial products, health instructions.
avoidWhen: Simple tasks where procedural success is sufficient evidence.
whyLost: UX relies on 'did that make sense' questions and task success; clinical communication methods rarely cross into design research.
whereToUse: AI assistants, privacy and data sharing, insurance and lending, medical devices, security features.
example: Users of a budgeting app teach back how 'round-ups' work; 60% wrongly believe the money leaves their account immediately. A redesigned explainer raises correct propositions from 55% to 84%.
sources: Schillinger et al., Closing the loop: physician communication with diabetic patients who have low health literacy (2003), Archives of Internal Medicine
Pask, Conversation, Cognition and Learning (1975)
reference: Schillinger, D., et al. (2003). Archives of Internal Medicine, 163(1), 83-90.

name: Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) Questionnaires
aka: Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use scales
origin: Fred Davis (1989), MIS Quarterly
summary: Two six-item scales for perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, which together predict whether people intend to adopt a technology.
description: The TAM proposes that intention to use a technology depends on perceived usefulness (the belief it will improve performance) and perceived ease of use (the belief it will be effortless), and that intention drives actual use. Davis built two six-item scales with 7-point likely to unlikely responses. A notable finding: his original mixed-tone items produced a muddled factor structure because reversed items correlated with the wrong construct, so he removed negative items, an early warning about alternating item tone that Sauro and Lewis echo for SUS. Coefficient alpha was 0.98 for usefulness and 0.94 for ease of use. TAM is one of the most cited models in information systems research.
steps: Administer the six perceived usefulness and six perceived ease-of-use items, adapted to your product.
Optionally add items on intention to use.
Average each scale.
Model intention or actual use as a function of the two scales (regression or SEM).
Act on whichever belief is weaker as the main adoption barrier.
outputs: Scores for perceived usefulness and ease of use, and their power to predict adoption.
useWhen: Predicting or explaining adoption of new tools, especially in workplaces.
avoidWhen: You need detailed usability diagnosis rather than adoption prediction.
whyLost: It lives in information systems journals, and UX teams rarely model adoption intention.
whereToUse: Enterprise tool rollouts, AI assistants at work, health technology adoption.
example: Nurses rate a new charting tool high on ease of use but low on usefulness, explaining low adoption better than any usability finding.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Davis, F. D. (1989). Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and user acceptance of information technology. MIS Quarterly 13(3).

name: Template Analysis
origin: Nigel King, 1998 onwards
summary: Develops a hierarchical coding template from a priori and data-driven codes, applies and revises it iteratively, and suits larger datasets where some themes are already anticipated.
description: Template Analysis (Nigel King) is a method of thematic analysis in which a hierarchical coding template is developed, applied to data, and iteratively revised. It is more structured than Braun & Clarke's reflexive TA (because it involves an explicit a priori template) but less constrained than framework analysis (because the template is substantially modified during analysis). It is particularly appropriate when you have some prior knowledge of the topic that should inform the template, but do not want to impose a full a priori framework on the data.
steps: Develop a priori codes: Before reading the full dataset, develop a provisional list of codes based on: your research questions, relevant existing literature, and any preliminary data. This is the initial template.

Apply the template to a subset of data: Code several transcripts using the initial template. Note: where do codes fit comfortably? Where are they inadequate, overlapping, or missing? Where does data resist being coded?
Modify the template: Revise the template based on the initial coding. Add new codes, merge overlapping ones, redefine inadequate ones, and build hierarchy (organise codes into themes and sub-themes).
Apply the revised template to the full dataset: Code all data using the revised template. Continue modifying as needed, but document all changes.
Final analysis: Use the completed template to write a thematic analysis of the full dataset. The template structure should be visible in the presentation of findings.
outputs: An initial and final hierarchical template, coded transcripts, documented template revisions, and a thematic account structured by the template.
useWhen: You have a medium to large dataset (around 15 to 60 interviews), some prior expectations or research questions to structure the analysis, and several analysts who need a shared framework.
avoidWhen: You want fully inductive theory building (use Constructivist Grounded Theory) or highly interpretive themes from a small sample (use Reflexive Thematic Analysis).
whyLost: It is well known in organisational and health psychology but rarely taught in UX, which tends to oscillate between unstructured affinity mapping and rigid tagging taxonomies.
whereToUse: Multi-researcher studies, evaluation programmes, research repositories with evolving taxonomies, and longitudinal tracking studies.
example: Three researchers analysing 40 interviews about a telehealth service start with a priori codes for access, trust and technology, test them on 6 transcripts, add a 'family as proxy user' branch, and code the remainder consistently.
sources: The Use of Template Analysis in Qualitative Psychology (King)
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
reference: King, N. & Brooks, J. M. (2017). Template Analysis for Business and Management Students. Sage.

name: Temporal cognition mapping
origin: Allen Newell's bands of cognition, 1990; Card, Moran and Newell's response-time thresholds, 1983; Miller, 1968
summary: Maps each interaction to the cognitive timescale it lives on, perceptual, cognitive or task-level, and checks system latencies against each band's thresholds.
description: Human cognition operates in distinct time bands: perceptual fusion around 100 ms, unit cognitive operations and immediate responses around 1 s, and unit tasks around 10 s, with rational and social bands beyond. Interactions feel instantaneous, responsive or interrupting depending on which band their latency falls into, as reflected in the familiar 0.1 s, 1 s and 10 s thresholds. Temporal cognition mapping assigns each interaction to its band, measures actual system latency and user operation times, and identifies band violations: a perceptual-band action (dragging, scrolling, robotic hand-eye coordination) with 200 ms lag breaks the sense of direct causation. Rigour comes from measured, not assumed, latencies, including the 95th percentile, not just means.
steps: List the interactions in scope and assign each to its intended band: perceptual (under about 100 ms), cognitive (around 1 s), or task (around 10 s).
Measure end-to-end latency for each interaction on target hardware and network, capturing median and 95th percentile across at least 100 instances.

Flag violations: perceptual-band latency above 100 ms (and above 50 ms for direct manipulation or tracking), cognitive-band above 1 s without feedback, task-band above 10 s without progress indication.
Observe users (5-8) on flagged interactions to note behavioural signs such as repeated input, overshoot or disengagement.
Prioritise fixes by band severity and frequency, and specify feedback strategies (immediate acknowledgement, progress indicators) where latency cannot be reduced.
Re-measure after changes, reporting percentile shifts.
outputs: A timescale map of interactions, latency distributions per interaction, a list of band violations, and latency budgets per band.
useWhen: When performance or responsiveness is part of the experience problem; when setting latency budgets for engineering; for teleoperation, real-time control or streaming products.
avoidWhen: When the problem is content or comprehension rather than timing; use standard usability testing. For precise task time prediction, use KLM or GOMS.
whyLost: The 0.1/1/10 s thresholds survive as folklore, but the underlying band theory and systematic mapping were lost when performance moved to engineering teams.
whereToUse: Surgical robotics, remote control and drones, gaming, collaborative editing, voice assistants and AI streaming responses.
example: A surgical robot's instrument tracking runs at 200 ms 95th-percentile latency, inside the perceptual band. Mapping shows surgeons compensate with slower, overshooting movements; engineering sets a 60 ms budget for tracking while allowing 1 s for menu actions.
sources: Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
Card, S., Moran, T. & Newell, A., The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (1983) and GOMS/KLM literature
Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R., Quantifying the User Experience (2nd ed., 2016)
Cognitive Psychology (Goldstein)
GOMS/KLM literature
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 4 — Time, Rhythm & the Three Timescales of Experience
reference: Newell, A. (1990). Unified Theories of Cognition. Harvard University Press.

name: Temporal Sentiment Modeling (TSM)
donor: Affective computing and longitudinal UX research
origin: Vivek Gopinath
summary: A framework for mapping shifts in users' emotional state across a journey over time, used to inform redesign decisions in OTT products.
description: Temporal Sentiment Modeling is listed among Vivek Gopinath's selected contributions as a framework to map emotional state shifts in OTT journeys that informed redesign decisions. The source gives only this one-line definition, so the protocol below is a reconstruction consistent with the sentiment-drift and trajectory methods he documents elsewhere rather than a published specification. The underlying idea is that sentiment is a time series: the order and timing of emotional shifts across sessions and journey stages matter as much as average satisfaction, and declining sentiment can precede behavioural drop-off even while usage looks healthy. Rigour would come from repeated structured sentiment measures, alignment to journey stages, and triangulation with behavioural telemetry and quotes.
steps: Define the journey stages and time steps over which emotion will be tracked (e.g. browse, select, play, post-play across weeks).
Collect repeated sentiment measures at each step via in-product prompts, diaries or coded transcripts.
Array sentiment per user over time and identify shifts and inflection points by stage.
Cluster trajectories into patterns and align them with behavioural telemetry for the same users.
Attach quotes explaining each inflection and prioritise redesigns at stages with consistent negative shifts.
Re-measure after redesign to confirm the trajectory changed.
outputs: Sentiment trajectories by journey stage, inflection points and redesign priorities.
useWhen: When emotional experience across a journey drives retention, as in OTT and media products.
avoidWhen: When only one-off satisfaction scores are available; use a standard survey instead.
whyLost: Original framework by Vivek Gopinath; documented in the sources only as a selected contribution.
whereToUse: OTT streaming, media, subscription products, AI companions.
example: An OTT service maps sentiment across browse, select and play stages and finds a negative shift at title selection after the second week, which informs a redesign of recommendations.
sources: Vivek Gopinath, professional research profile (Selected Contributions)
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation

name: Testing Against a Benchmark (One-Sample Tests)
origin: Acceptance testing logic from industrial quality control; adapted for UX targets in Sauro & Lewis, Quantifying the User Experience ch. 4
summary: Decides whether a product beats a specific target, such as 80% completion or a SUS of 68, rather than just reporting a score.
description: Teams often set goals like "at least 75% of users complete the task" or "SUS above 68" and then eyeball whether the sample result clears the bar. A one-sample test makes the decision explicit. For completion rates with small samples, the exact (mid-p) binomial test gives the probability of seeing this many successes if the true rate were only at the benchmark. For larger samples a normal approximation works. For continuous measures such as SUS, SEQ or log task times, a one-sample t-test compares the mean to the target. Because the claim is directional (better than the goal), one-tailed tests are appropriate, and the same logic can be read off a confidence interval: the goal is met if it lies below the lower bound.
steps: State the benchmark and direction before collecting data (for example, completion > 70%).
For proportions with n under about 30, run an exact or mid-p binomial test of x successes in n trials against the benchmark p.
For larger samples, use the z test with the normal approximation.
For rating scales and log-transformed times, run a one-sample t-test of the mean against the benchmark value.
Report the one-tailed p-value alongside the confidence interval and state plainly whether the goal was met.
outputs: A yes/no decision on whether a target was met, with the confidence behind it.
useWhen: Release gates, regulated summative validation, and benchmark programmes with agreed targets.
avoidWhen: No meaningful target exists, or the goal was set after seeing the data.
whyLost: UX rarely writes targets down in advance, so there is nothing to test against, and benchmark comparisons get reduced to traffic-light colours.
whereToUse: Medical-device summative tests, enterprise procurement acceptance, OKRs that name UX metrics.
example: A banking app targets 80% success on adding a payee. Twenty-two of 25 succeed (88%); the mid-p binomial test gives p = 0.13, so the team cannot yet claim the target is beaten and extends the sample.
