name: Thematic Analysis
donor: Psychology and social science qualitative research
origin: Virginia Braun & Victoria Clarke, 2006 (six-phase method); reflexive TA, 2019
summary: A systematic six-phase method for identifying, developing and reporting patterns of shared meaning (themes) across qualitative data.
description: Thematic analysis identifies, analyses and reports patterns of meaning across a qualitative dataset. Braun and Clarke's six phases are familiarisation, generating initial codes, constructing candidate themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming themes, and producing the report. It can be inductive or deductive, semantic or latent, and in its reflexive form treats the researcher's interpretation as a resource rather than bias. A theme is a pattern of shared meaning organised around a central concept, not a topic summary or a frequently mentioned word. Rigour comes from coding the whole dataset systematically, reviewing themes against both coded extracts and the full dataset, writing analytic narrative that does interpretive work beyond quotes, and documenting decisions transparently.
steps: Familiarise yourself with the data by reading transcripts in full and writing a familiarisation memo, without coding yet.
Code the entire dataset systematically, capturing everything potentially relevant, inductively or from theory.
Collate codes into candidate themes organised around a central concept and draw a thematic map.
Review themes against coded extracts and then against the whole dataset, revising until both fit.
Define and name each theme with a short analytic description of its essence and boundaries.
Write the report, weaving analytic narrative with illustrative extracts so the narrative carries the analysis.
outputs: Coded dataset, thematic map, defined and named themes with analytic narratives and supporting extracts.
useWhen: For analysing interview, diary, open-ended survey or field data when you need a flexible, defensible way to report patterns of meaning.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need to build an explanatory theory of a process; use grounded theory. For counting frequencies across large text corpora, use content analysis.
whyLost: Still in use, but often only in name: Braun and Clarke's method is the dominant qualitative approach, yet in industry it is frequently reduced to sorting quotes into topic buckets, without systematic coding, theme review or analytic narrative.
whereToUse: Interview and diary data analysis; any qualitative UX research synthesis.
example: A mental health app analyses 20 interviews with lapsed users. Instead of a topic theme like 'notifications', the team develops 'the app as another obligation', which reframes reminders as permission to rest.

extra.The Six Phases: Familiarisation: Read and re-read the data. Note initial ideas. Write a familiarisation memo. Do not code yet. Generating initial codes: Code the data systematically across the entire dataset. Capture everything that might be relevant. Codes are data-driven (bottom-up) in inductive TA; theory-driven (top-down) in deductive TA. Searching for themes: Collate codes into potential themes. Create a thematic map. A theme is a pattern of shared meaning, not merely a topic or a frequent code. Reviewing themes: Two levels — (a) do the coded data extracts form a coherent pattern? (b) does the thematic map accurately represent the dataset as a whole? Revise until both are satisfied. Defining and naming themes: Write a full analysis of each theme: what is its essence? What does it tell us beyond the surface content? Generate a clear, analytic name that captures the theme's meaning, not its topic. Producing the report: Weave together analytic narrative and data extracts. The narrative — not the extracts — should do the analytical work. Extracts illustrate the analysis; they do not constitute it.

name: Theoretical Sampling
origin: Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss, 1967 (The Discovery of Grounded Theory)
summary: Chooses each next participant, site or data source to develop, test or saturate emerging concepts, rather than to represent demographics, until theoretical saturation is reached.
description: In grounded theory, sampling and analysis proceed together. After initial purposive sampling, the analyst decides whom or what to study next based on the concepts emerging from analysis: to explore a category's properties, to find variation along a dimension, or to test where a concept breaks down. Sampling is of concepts and conditions, not people as demographic representatives. It continues until theoretical saturation, when new data no longer add properties or dimensions to categories. This makes samples adaptive and efficient, focusing effort where understanding is weakest. Rigour comes from documenting each sampling decision and its analytic rationale, and from defining saturation in terms of categories rather than simply repetition of themes.
steps: Start with an initial purposive sample of about 4 to 8 participants relevant to the phenomenon.
Analyse early data immediately using open coding and memos to identify emerging categories and gaps.
Decide the next sampling targets by asking which people, situations or events would elaborate, vary or challenge each category, and record the rationale.
Recruit and collect data from those targets, adapting interview questions to probe the categories in focus.
Repeat the cycle, using constant comparison, until new data add no new properties or dimensions to the core categories.
Report the sampling sequence, rationale for each round and the evidence for saturation.
outputs: A sampling log with analytic rationales, an evolving set of categories with properties and dimensions, and documented saturation evidence.
useWhen: Building explanatory understanding of a process or behaviour iteratively, with flexibility to recruit across rounds, for instance in discovery for a new product area.
avoidWhen: You need representative estimates or a fixed protocol sample, such as a benchmark study or survey; use probability or quota sampling. Avoid if recruitment cannot be adapted mid-study.
whyLost: Not taught; researchers use convenience sampling throughout
whereToUse: Discovery research, grounded theory studies, churn and adoption research, emerging AI usage, and multi-round research programmes.
example: Interviewing 6 users about distrust of a health app, researchers notice distrust linked to prior data breaches. They next recruit users with and without breach experiences and then clinicians, refining a theory of 'inherited distrust' over 20 interviews.

name: Theoretical Sampling and Saturation
origin: Glaser & Strauss, 1967
summary: Choosing each next participant according to what the emerging theory needs, and stopping only when categories are saturated with documented evidence.
description: Theoretical sampling is the process of sampling additional participants, sites, or time periods based on what the emerging theory requires for its development, not based on demographic or statistical representation. In practice: after your first 5 interviews, your emerging codes tell you what kind of participant would most challenge, confirm, or extend the emerging theory. That participant is who you recruit next. This is fundamentally different from purposive sampling (selecting participants based on prior criteria) — theoretical sampling criteria evolve as the theory evolves.
steps: After each new interview, update your code frequency table. Add: "new codes generated this session" count.
Track the rate of new code generation across sessions. Plot this as a curve.
Saturation is indicated when: (a) no new codes emerge across 2–3 consecutive sessions AND (b) you have theoretically sampled toward the areas where you expected the most variation.
Critically: saturation is category-specific. A category may be saturated while another still requires investigation. Theoretical sampling continues until all major categories are saturated.
Document your saturation decision in writing, including: how many sessions produced no new codes, what theoretical sampling you did, and which categories you consider saturated.
outputs: A sampling log showing why each participant was recruited, a new-codes-per-session curve, category-level saturation judgements and a written stopping rationale.
useWhen: Iterative qualitative studies where analysis runs alongside recruitment and you need a defensible answer to 'how many participants is enough'.
avoidWhen: When recruitment must be fixed in advance (agency fieldwork, single field trip) or when you need population estimates; use purposive quotas or probability sampling instead.
whyLost: 'Saturation' became a vague justification for stopping at five to eight interviews, with no iterative sampling or evidence, leaving only the vocabulary.
whereToUse: Discovery programmes with flexible recruitment panels, continuous discovery pipelines, and research-led strategy work in new markets.
example: After six interviews about a budgeting app, codes on 'shared household money' are thin, so the researcher deliberately recruits couples with joint accounts. Three more sessions add no new codes in that category, which is documented as saturated.
sources: Rocking Qualitative Social Science
Sampling and Choosing Cases in Qualitative Research
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
The Discovery of Grounded Theory (Glaser & Strauss)
reference: Glaser, B. G. & Strauss, A. L. (1967). The Discovery of Grounded Theory. Aldine.

name: Theory of Constraints Bottleneck Analysis
origin: Eliyahu Goldratt, 1984 (The Goal)
summary: Identifies the single constraint limiting a system's throughput and improves it first, recognising that improvements elsewhere do not raise overall output.
description: Goldratt argued every system has at least one constraint that determines throughput. The five focusing steps are: identify the constraint, exploit it (get maximum from it), subordinate everything else to it, elevate it (add capacity), and repeat as the constraint moves. TOC's thinking processes (current reality trees, evaporating clouds) extend the logic to policy constraints. In UX and service design, constraints may be a verification step, a scarce expert, an approval policy or a user's limited attention. Teams often optimise non-constraints, such as polishing early funnel steps when the bottleneck is a manual review, achieving nothing.
steps: Define the system's goal and throughput measure (e.g. completed onboardings per week).
Map the flow and measure capacity and queues at each step to find where work accumulates.
Confirm the constraint (the step with highest utilisation or growing backlog).
Exploit it: remove waste at the constraint (e.g. pre-check documents before human review).
Subordinate other steps: pace intake to the constraint, avoid flooding it.
Elevate if needed, then re-measure to find the next constraint.
outputs: Identified constraint, exploitation and subordination actions, throughput improvement and next-constraint analysis.
useWhen: Throughput-limited services and flows: onboarding with manual steps, support, fulfilment, research operations.
avoidWhen: Pure self-service digital flows without capacity constraints; use funnel and usability analysis.
whyLost: Operations management books did not enter UX curricula, and design work focuses on interfaces rather than flow capacity.
whereToUse: B2B onboarding, KYC, marketplace seller verification, clinical workflows, research recruitment pipelines.
example: A B2B SaaS improves sign-up conversion but contracts stall at legal review, the constraint. A pre-approved terms option exploits the constraint, raising signed deals 30% with no front-end changes.
sources: Goldratt & Cox, The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement (1984)
Goldratt, What Is This Thing Called Theory of Constraints (1990)
reference: Goldratt, E. M., & Cox, J. (1984). The Goal. North River Press.

name: Therblig Micro-Motion Analysis
origin: Frank and Lillian Gilbreth, 1910s
summary: Breaks recorded human movement into 17-18 elementary motion units (therbligs) to find wasted motions and redesign tools and layouts around them.
description: The Gilbreths extended Taylor's time study into motion study. They defined therbligs, basic units of human motion such as search, select, grasp, transport loaded, hold and position, from which any manual task can be composed. Using high-speed film (micromotion study) and light traces of moving hands (cyclegraphs), they analysed movement in ways the naked eye could not perceive. The treatise identifies this as one of the earliest forms of behavioural research in design. Its rigour comes from a fixed, exhaustive coding vocabulary applied frame by frame, which makes inefficient or 'ineffective' therbligs (search, hold, delay) explicitly visible. The digital equivalent is frame-level analysis of screen and body recordings for mobile, kiosk, AR and physical-digital tasks, where 'search' and 'hold' therbligs map onto visual search and waiting.
steps: Record the task on video at sufficient frame rate (60 fps or more for hand movements), ideally from two angles.
Code each segment against the therblig vocabulary, marking start and end frames for every motion unit.
Build a simultaneous motion (SIMO) chart for left hand, right hand and eyes or screen interaction.
Classify therbligs as effective (grasp, use, assemble) or ineffective (search, select, hold, delay, plan).
Redesign layout, controls or flow to eliminate or shorten ineffective therbligs and re-record to compare.
Report motion counts and durations before and after redesign.
outputs: Coded motion timeline, SIMO chart, list of ineffective motions with durations, redesign rationale.
useWhen: Physical-digital interaction such as handheld scanners, kiosks, surgical or lab devices, AR tasks and one-handed mobile use where motion economy matters.
avoidWhen: Purely cognitive or decision-heavy tasks where motion is not the bottleneck; use CPM-GOMS or verbal protocol analysis instead.
whyLost: Tainted by association with Taylorism and made to look obsolete by the shift to screen-based, cognitive work. Few UX curricula ever taught frame-level motion coding.
whereToUse: Warehouse and retail handhelds, medical devices, automotive controls, XR interaction design, accessibility for motor impairments.
example: A pharmacy dispensing app is filmed in use and coded into therbligs; 22% of time is 'search' and 'hold' while pharmacists hold a bottle and hunt for the scan button. Moving the trigger to a hardware key removes most of the hold therbligs.

Barnes RM (1980) Motion and Time Study

name: THERP (Technique for Human Error Rate Prediction)
origin: Alan Swain and Henry Guttmann, Sandia National Laboratories, 1983 (NUREG/CR-1278)
summary: Decomposes a task into an event tree of human actions, assigns tabled error probabilities with performance shaping factors and dependence, and computes overall task failure probability.
description: THERP is the original full-scale human reliability analysis. Each task is broken into steps represented as binary success/failure branches in an HRA event tree. Basic human error probabilities come from data tables in the Swain and Guttmann handbook, adjusted for performance shaping factors such as stress, experience and interface quality. Crucially, THERP models dependence between steps (zero, low, moderate, high, complete), recognising that a person who misreads one display is likely to misread the next. Recovery factors such as independent checks are included. The method yields an overall failure probability and, through sensitivity analysis, shows where a design change buys the most reliability. It is laborious but uniquely explicit about dependence and recovery.
steps: Conduct a task analysis and identify the human actions relevant to the failure of interest.
Build an HRA event tree with success and failure branches for each action, in sequence.
Assign nominal error probabilities from THERP tables or empirical data, with uncertainty bounds.
Adjust for performance shaping factors and apply the dependence model between successive actions.
Add recovery branches (self-check, second-person check, system alerts) and compute the end-state failure probability.
Run sensitivity analysis to identify which steps and factors dominate risk, and redesign accordingly.
outputs: HRA event tree, overall task failure probability with uncertainty bounds, sensitivity ranking of steps.
useWhen: Very high-consequence procedural interactions where regulators or leadership need an explicit probabilistic argument.
avoidWhen: Most consumer UX; HEART or SHERPA give most of the insight for far less effort.
whyLost: Its tables were built for 1970s nuclear control rooms and the method demands specialist training. HCI moved toward empirical testing and never adopted probabilistic risk thinking.
whereToUse: Clinical infusion and dosing software, financial settlement operations, safety-critical industrial HMIs, two-person approval workflows.
example: A bank models its manual high-value payment release. THERP shows the second-approver check has high dependence on the first because both see the same summary view; giving the approver an independent view of beneficiary details substantially lowers failure probability.
sources: Swain & Guttmann, Handbook of Human Reliability Analysis with Emphasis on Nuclear Power Plant Applications (NUREG/CR-1278, 1983)
Kirwan, A Guide to Practical Human Reliability Assessment (1994)
reference: Swain, A. D., & Guttmann, H. E. (1983). NUREG/CR-1278. US Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

name: Thesaurus and Controlled Vocabulary Construction (ISO 25964)
origin: Standards ISO 2788 (1974/1986) and ANSI/NISO Z39.19; superseded by ISO 25964-1 (2011)
summary: Builds preferred terms with equivalence, hierarchical and associative relationships following standard rules, so search and tagging match how users actually speak.
description: A thesaurus defines preferred terms, non-preferred synonyms (USE/UF), broader and narrower terms (BT/NT, distinguishing generic, partitive and instance relations) and related terms (RT), with scope notes. The standards provide rules on term form, singular versus plural, compound terms and polyhierarchy. Term candidates come from literary warrant (content) and user warrant (search logs, interviews). Rigour lies in consistent relationship types and documented decisions. For digital products, this underpins search synonyms, tagging, chatbot intents and filter labels, and avoids the familiar problem of users searching for terms the product never uses.
steps: Gather candidate terms from content (literary warrant) and from search logs, support tickets and interviews (user warrant).
Group synonyms and variants into equivalence sets, choosing preferred terms by user frequency and clarity.
Build hierarchical relations, distinguishing generic, whole-part and instance relations, and add associative relations sparingly.
Write scope notes for ambiguous terms and apply ISO 25964 rules on term form.
Test with users: search success for synonym queries, and indexer consistency when tagging.
Set up governance for adding terms, with change logs and periodic review of zero-result queries.
outputs: A documented thesaurus with relationships and scope notes, synonym rules for search, and governance process.
useWhen: Search quality problems, inconsistent tagging, multi-team content, chatbot intent design, or multilingual products.
avoidWhen: Very small content sets where a simple label audit suffices.
whyLost: Librarianship was sidelined by full-text search and machine learning; product teams rarely employ taxonomists.
whereToUse: E-commerce search, enterprise knowledge bases, healthcare portals (lay vs clinical terms), support centres.
example: A pharmacy site finds 22% of searches use lay terms ('water tablets') not present in clinical product names. A thesaurus maps lay to preferred terms, cutting zero-result searches by half.
sources: ISO 25964-1:2011 Thesauri and interoperability with other vocabularies
ANSI/NISO Z39.19-2005 Guidelines for the Construction, Format, and Management of Monolingual Controlled Vocabularies
Aitchison, Gilchrist & Bawden, Thesaurus Construction and Use (4th ed., 2000)

name: Thick Description and Dual-Pass Field Notes
origin: Gilbert Ryle, 1949; Clifford Geertz, 1973
summary: Writes field notes that record not just behaviour but the context, intentions and meanings that make it intelligible, enabling interpretation others can audit.
description: Thick description, a term from Gilbert Ryle popularised by Clifford Geertz, distinguishes describing what people do (a contraction of the eyelid) from describing what it means in context (a wink, a parody of a wink, a rehearsal). Thick field notes record the behaviour, the surrounding situation, the participants' apparent intentions, and the cultural codes that make it intelligible, while keeping these layers distinguishable. In UX field research this means writing up visits promptly, separating literal observation from inference, capturing sequence, setting, artefacts and social relations, and recording questions for follow-up. Rigour comes from the auditability of the chain from observation to interpretation, so that other researchers can follow and challenge how meaning was attributed.
steps: Field note protocol: immediately after each observation session, write notes in two passes.
Pass 1 (within 30 minutes): factual description — exactly what you observed, in sequence, without interpretation.
Include direct quotes where possible.
Pass 2 (within 2 hours): interpretive layer — what might this mean?
What is unclear?
What surprised you?
Keep the two passes separate.
Review: can someone who wasn't there reconstruct what happened from your Pass 1 notes?
outputs: Layered field notes separating observation, context and interpretation; analytic memos; vignettes usable in synthesis and stakeholder communication.
useWhen: Contextual inquiry, ethnography and field visits where meaning depends on context, such as workarounds, rituals, social norms and informal practices.
avoidWhen: Avoid for narrow evaluative studies where structured observation sheets are more efficient; avoid when you cannot spend time writing up immediately after fieldwork.
whyLost: UX field notes shrank to quotes on sticky notes and photos; the interpretive layer that distinguishes a wink from a twitch is lost.
whereToUse: Field research, diary study analysis, observational UX research, contextual inquiry documentation.
example: In a pharmacy, a researcher notes that staff tap the screen twice, not as an error but to 'wake' a lagging terminal they distrust, and writes up the trust history behind the gesture, which reshapes the performance brief.

name: Think-Aloud Protocol
origin: Karl Duncker, 1945; formalised by Ericsson & Simon, 1980; adopted in HCI by Clayton Lewis, 1982
summary: Participants verbalise their thoughts while (or after) performing a task, giving direct evidence of expectations, interpretations and confusions behind their behaviour.
description: The think-aloud protocol asks participants to say what they are thinking as they work through a task. In concurrent think-aloud they verbalise during the task, which gives access to working-memory contents with minimal reconstruction. In retrospective think-aloud they verbalise afterwards, usually while watching a recording, which avoids interfering with task performance but relies on memory. Ericsson and Simon's theory distinguishes pure verbalisation of attended information from explanations, which can alter cognition. Rigour comes from a short practice task, neutral prompts such as 'keep talking' rather than 'why did you do that?', avoiding interruptions during critical steps, and analysing verbalisations alongside behaviour rather than treating comments as opinions.
steps: Explain the procedure and run a short practice task, such as counting windows in one's home, to train verbalisation.
Choose concurrent or retrospective think-aloud according to whether task timing matters.
During tasks, use only neutral reminders such as 'please keep talking' after about 15 seconds of silence.
Avoid asking for explanations mid-task; save probes for after the task.
Record audio, screen and, where useful, face video.
Transcribe or annotate verbalisations against task steps and code expectations, confusions and decisions.
outputs: Recordings and transcripts linked to behaviour, coded evidence of expectations and misunderstandings, and explanations for observed problems.
useWhen: In usability tests and prototype evaluations when you need to understand why users act as they do and what they expect.
avoidWhen: Avoid concurrent think-aloud when measuring task time or in high-workload tasks; use retrospective think-aloud or eye tracking. Not suitable with participants who struggle to verbalise, such as young children.
whyLost: Still in use: Direct window into user cognition; requires no special equipment; widely taught and practiced.
whereToUse: Usability testing sessions; prototype evaluations; any task-based research.
example: In testing a new insurance claim form, a participant says 'I assume excess means extra money they'll pay me', revealing a terminology misunderstanding that observation alone would have missed.
sources: Think Like a UX Researcher
Observing the User Experience
Protocol Analysis (Ericsson & Simon)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Ericsson, K. A. & Simon, H. A. (1993). Protocol Analysis: Verbal Reports as Data (rev. ed.). MIT Press.

name: Think-Aloud Protocol with Systematic Probe Schedules
donor: Cognitive psychology (protocol analysis) and usability engineering
origin: Ericsson and Simon (protocol analysis, 1984/1993); probing practices in Dumas and Redish (1993); Boren and Ramey (2000)
summary: Think-aloud sessions in which moderator probes are pre-planned and triggered by defined behavioural events, keeping elicitation consistent across participants and limiting reactivity.
description: Think-aloud is the core usability method, but moderation is usually improvised: moderators interrupt at different moments with different questions, introducing reactivity and making sessions incomparable. A systematic probe schedule fixes this. Before sessions, the researcher defines trigger events (for example hesitation over 3 seconds, backtracking, silence over 15 seconds, an error, or reaching a key decision point) and writes a standard, neutral probe for each, such as 'keep talking' for silence, or 'what are you looking for?' after backtracking. Probes are delivered only when triggers occur, and retrospective probes are reserved for the end. This draws on Ericsson and Simon's distinction between concurrent verbalisation, which preserves cognitive processes, and explanation, which alters them, and Boren and Ramey's speech-communication guidance.
steps: Before the session: for each critical task step, define:
the behavioral trigger (e.g., 'user pauses > 3s'),

the probe question ('I noticed you paused — what's going through your mind?'). During session: when trigger fires, deliver the probe. After session: code probes separately from spontaneous verbalizations. This separates researcher-elicited from user-generated cognition.
outputs: Probe schedule with triggers and scripted probes, consistent session transcripts, probe logs per event, and findings comparable across participants.
useWhen: Moderated usability tests where several moderators run sessions, comparative tests between designs, and studies requiring credible, reproducible qualitative data.
avoidWhen: Where measuring time on task is essential (probing distorts timing; use unprompted or retrospective think-aloud), or highly exploratory sessions where flexibility matters more than consistency.
whyLost: Speed and informal practice turned think-aloud into conversational sessions; the protocol-analysis grounding and planned probes were dropped as academic.
whereToUse: Usability test moderation training, protocol analysis, any study distinguishing spontaneous from elicited verbalization.
example: Three researchers test a mortgage application across 15 sessions using a schedule with five triggers. Comparable transcripts show that 11 of 15 participants hesitated at the 'deposit source' field, a finding unmistakable because every hesitation received the same probe.
sources: Handbook of Usability Testing
Ericsson & Simon, Protocol Analysis: Verbal Reports as Data (1993)
Boren & Ramey, Thinking aloud: Reconciling theory and practice (IEEE TPC, 2000)
reference: Dumas JS & Redish JC (1999) A Practical Guide to Usability Testing. Revised ed. Intellect

name: Think-Aloud Usability Testing (Contemporary Practice)
origin: Lewis (1982) at IBM; popularised by Nielsen (1993)
summary: Participants verbalise while attempting tasks on a design so observers can detect usability problems; valid for issue detection, over-interpreted for mental models.
description: The ubiquitous moderated think-aloud test descends from verbal protocol analysis, but the treatise argues it now bears only superficial resemblance. Moderators often probe with 'why' questions mid-task, ask for preferences and treat retrospective rationalisations as evidence of mental models. Used with the right claims, it is an excellent problem-detection method: observation of behaviour plus verbalisation reveals where and often why people struggle. The rigorous version separates concurrent from retrospective commentary, uses neutral prompts, records task success and time, rates problem severity and reports what the data can and cannot show. This entry documents the contemporary method with the treatise's warning about over-interpretation.
steps: Define tasks and success criteria tied to research questions.
Recruit 5-8 participants per user segment.
Give neutral think-aloud instructions and a practice task; keep prompts minimal during tasks.
Record success, time, errors and verbalisations; save probing for after each task.
Rate problem severity and frequency across participants.
Report findings with explicit limits on claims about users' mental models.
outputs: Problem list with severity, task metrics, annotated clips.
useWhen: Formative evaluation of prototypes and live products to find usability problems.
avoidWhen: Claims about cognition or preferences at population scale; use verbal protocol analysis or surveys.
whyLost: Not lost: survived because it is cheap and persuasive, but its theoretical grounding was stripped away.
whereToUse: Any interface evaluation, especially early prototypes and critical flows.
example: A travel booking team runs six think-aloud sessions on a new filter panel; four users fail to find the price slider. The team reports the observed failure but avoids claiming users 'don't think in price ranges'.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Nielsen J (1993) Usability Engineering
Dumas JS & Redish JC (1999) A Practical Guide to Usability Testing
Ericsson KA & Simon HA (1993) Protocol Analysis
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Dumas JS & Redish JC (1999) A Practical Guide to Usability Testing. Rev. ed. Intellect.

name: Think-Aloud with Emotional Annotation
origin: Extension of think-aloud usability testing (Lewis, 1982; Dumas & Redish, 1993) with affective coding
summary: Adds a systematic emotional annotation layer to standard think-aloud sessions, capturing affective reactions alongside cognitive process and aligning both to interface events.
description: Standard think-aloud captures what users are thinking but systematically under-represents what they feel: participants narrate goals and actions, not frustration or relief. This method adds a second researcher who annotates the session record for affective markers (sighs, laughter, prosody changes, hedges, self-blame, expletives) using a defined code set, timestamped and aligned with screen events. After tasks, participants rate their emotional state at key moments, giving a self-report anchor to compare with observed markers. Rigour comes from a predefined emotion codebook, independent annotation by someone other than the moderator, and explicit comparison between observed and self-reported affect, which often diverge. It is a low-cost bridge between conventional usability testing and instrumented affective measurement.
steps: Standard think-aloud protocol: Participant narrates thinking while completing tasks.

Emotional annotation layer: A second researcher annotates the think-aloud recording for: (a) affective word choice, (b) prosodic cues (raised pitch/rapid speech = frustration; slow speech/long pauses = confusion), (c) affective exclamations.
Map to interface events: Align emotional annotations with screen recording timestamps. Affective hotspots are the data.
Post-session emotional interview: After the session, ask the participant to rate emotional intensity of 3–4 moments you identified. Validate observational coding with self-report.
outputs: Session timelines with cognitive and affective annotations, an emotional hotspot map per task, observed versus self-reported affect comparisons, and prioritised issues weighted by emotional severity.
useWhen: Usability testing of flows where emotional reactions affect completion or trust, such as payments, health forms or error recovery, and you lack biometric equipment.
avoidWhen: You need precise, continuous affect measurement or the emotional signal is mostly physiological; use Multi-Channel Affective Measurement. For pure efficiency benchmarking use timed task metrics without think-aloud.
whyLost: Usability testing became efficiency-focused and moderators annotate on the fly, so affect is noted anecdotally rather than coded systematically by a second observer.
whereToUse: Moderated usability tests of checkout, insurance claims, patient portals, AI assistants whose responses may frustrate, and error-state design reviews.
example: An insurer tests its claims flow with 8 participants. The annotator codes self-blame utterances clustering on the document-upload step, while post-task ratings show anxiety peaking there; clearer file requirements become the top fix.
sources: Handbook of Usability Testing (Dumas & Redish)
Affective Computing (Picard)
reference: Dumas, J. S. & Redish, J. C. (1999). A Practical Guide to Usability Testing (rev. ed.). Intellect.

name: Thinking-Style Sensitive Interviewing
origin: Indi Young, 2015
summary: An interviewing practice that follows the participant's inner reasoning, emotional reactions and guiding principles rather than the researcher's agenda or product questions.
description: Thinking-style sensitive interviewing, from Indi Young's practical empathy work, aims to understand how a person reasons through a purpose: their inner thinking, emotional reactions and guiding principles. The interviewer opens with a broad question about a past experience and then follows the participant, asking for more depth on what went through their mind rather than steering to the researcher's topics. Opinions, preferences and generalisations are gently redirected towards specific occasions. Across participants, recurring patterns of reasoning are clustered into thinking styles, which segment users by how they think rather than by demographics. Rigour depends on non-directive discipline, recording and transcribing, and analysis that preserves the participant's own words.
steps: Identify participant thinking style in first 5 minutes: sequential (describes experiences as a linear sequence), simultaneous (jumps between connected topics), reactive (responds with feelings before facts).
Adjust: for sequential thinkers, follow their sequence without redirecting.
For simultaneous thinkers, map the connections between topics they generate.
For reactive thinkers, probe the underlying thought: 'You mentioned feeling frustrated — what was happening right before that feeling?'
outputs: Transcripts rich in inner thinking, reactions and guiding principles; thinking-style patterns; inputs for mental model diagrams and behavioural audience segments.
useWhen: Discovery research where you need to understand how people reason about a purpose, and team empathy building beyond demographic personas.
avoidWhen: Avoid when you need to evaluate a specific design or gather feature feedback; use usability testing or structured interviews.
whyLost: It requires unlearning habits of leading and product-focused questioning, and sessions feel unstructured to stakeholders who want direct answers.
whereToUse: Qualitative interview training, research participant diversity, cross-cultural UX research.
example: A pension provider runs non-directed sessions asking 'what went through your mind when you thought about retiring?', revealing a 'protector' thinking style organised around family duty rather than returns.
sources: Practical Empathy — Indi Young
reference: Young I (2015) Practical Empathy: For Collaboration and Creativity in Your Work. Rosenfeld Media

name: Thinking-Style Sensitivity
origin: Framed in Indi Young's listening practice (Practical Empathy, 2015)
summary: Identifying early in an interview whether a participant thinks sequentially, simultaneously or reactively, then adapting probes and stimuli to fit.
description: Participants do not all access and report experience the same way. Sequential thinkers narrate chronologically and resist 'why' questions before context is set; simultaneous thinkers jump across linked threads and generate rich but tangled material; reactive thinkers struggle with abstract recall but respond in detail to a concrete stimulus. In the first few minutes the interviewer asks about a recent concrete experience and observes which pattern appears, then adjusts: following chronology and asking 'what happened next' for sequential thinkers, tracking and later reconstructing threads for simultaneous thinkers, and introducing screenshots, prototypes or artefacts for reactive thinkers. The aim is to reduce the mismatch between interviewer style and participant cognition that produces thin data.
steps: In the first 3–5 minutes: ask an open question about a recent, concrete experience related to your research topic. Observe: does the participant describe events in sequence (sequential), jump between related ideas (simultaneous), or wait for you to offer a specific stimulus (reactive)?
Adjust your probing style for the rest of the session based on the observed thinking style.
outputs: Session notes tagged with observed thinking style, adapted probing records, and more complete accounts from participants who would otherwise give thin answers.
useWhen: Semi-structured and generative interviews with varied participants, especially when previous sessions produced uneven depth.
avoidWhen: Highly standardised interviews where every participant must receive the same stimulus and order for comparability (cognitive pretests, structured surveys).
whyLost: It is an experiential craft heuristic rather than a published protocol, so it travels only through mentoring and is rarely written into guides.
whereToUse: Discovery interviews, stakeholder interviews, research with older adults or low-literacy users, and interviewer coaching.
example: Interviewing nurses about shift handovers, a researcher notices one participant gives one-line answers. Switching to show a printed handover sheet unlocks a ten-minute account of how she annotates it.
sources: Practical Empathy (Indi Young)
Mental Models (Indi Young)
Listening (Blee)
Practical Empathy (Young)
Mental Models (Young)
Qualitative Interviewing
The Inquiry Series, Ch 32 — Advanced Elicitation — The Archaeology of the Interview
reference: Young, I. (2015). Practical Empathy. Rosenfeld Media.

extra.The Three Thinking Styles: Sequential thinkers process in ordered steps. They describe things chronologically. They are uncomfortable with "why" questions asked before they have established context. For sequential thinkers: follow their natural chronology. Do not interrupt to redirect. Ask "what happened next?" rather than "why did you do that?" Let the story arrive at the moment you want to probe, then probe. Simultaneous thinkers process multiple threads at once. They jump between topics. They are the most generative interviewees but the hardest to follow. For simultaneous thinkers: take comprehensive notes during the session. Do not try to redirect them back to your original question — follow each thread and note where each one ends. After the session, you can reconstruct the narrative structure. Reactive thinkers need a stimulus to think. They cannot easily access their experience in the abstract but respond in detail when shown something concrete. For reactive thinkers: use artifacts (screenshots, prototypes, example documents) as elicitation stimuli. "When you look at this screen, what comes to mind?" is more productive than "how do you typically complete this task?"

name: Thompson Sampling Bandits
origin: William R. Thompson, 1933
summary: An adaptive experiment that allocates interventions in proportion to the probability each is best, balancing exploration of new options with exploitation of the best-known one.
description: Thompson Sampling maintains a posterior distribution over each arm's reward, samples from each posterior, and chooses the arm with the highest sample, so traffic shifts toward better arms while uncertain arms still get explored. In Vivek Gopinath's drift playbook it selects adaptive UX interventions per user (personalised re-onboarding, dynamic UI scaling, context-aware nudging), with the objective of reducing DriftScore, increasing entropy and diversity, and improving CTR. In the e-commerce case it chooses between 'explore collections' and 'deal of the day' per user. Bandit results are then confirmed with A/B tests on DriftScore reduction and entropy lift and with longitudinal interviews on regained delight.
steps: Define the candidate interventions (arms) and the reward (e.g. DriftScore reduction, entropy lift, CTR).
Set priors for each arm's reward (e.g. Beta priors for binary outcomes).
For each eligible user, sample from each arm's posterior and serve the arm with the highest sample.
Observe the reward and update the chosen arm's posterior.
Monitor allocation and guard against spamming users with nudges.
Confirm the winning policy with an A/B test and qualitative follow-up.
outputs: An adaptive allocation policy, per-arm reward estimates and a validated intervention.
useWhen: When several interventions compete and you want to minimise exposure to poor options while learning.
avoidWhen: When you need clean causal estimates for each arm or rewards are long-delayed; use a fixed A/B test.
whyLost: Common in ad tech and growth engineering but rarely designed or interpreted by UX researchers.
whereToUse: Personalised nudges, re-onboarding, recommendation modules, notification strategy.
example: An e-commerce app uses Thompson Sampling to choose per user between an 'explore collections' card and a 'deal of the day', shifting traffic to whichever lifts entropy.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Detecting Behavioral Drift: A Mixed Methods Playbook and E-commerce Case Study
reference: Thompson, W. R. (1933). On the likelihood that one unknown probability exceeds another in view of the evidence of two samples. Biometrika, 25(3/4), 285–294.

name: Threats-to-Validity Audit (Shadish, Cook and Campbell)
origin: Donald Campbell (1957); Campbell and Stanley (1966); Cook and Campbell (1979); Shadish, Cook and Campbell (2002)
summary: Systematically checks a study against named threats to statistical conclusion, internal, construct and external validity, and designs them out before data collection.
description: Campbell's tradition catalogues specific threats: for internal validity, history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression to the mean, selection, attrition and their interactions; for construct validity, mono-operation bias, hypothesis guessing, experimenter expectancies, novelty effects; for statistical conclusion validity, low power, fishing, unreliable measures; for external validity, interactions of treatment with units, settings and outcomes. The audit names each threat, assesses its plausibility and specifies design features that rule it out (e.g. a comparison group, multiple pretests, a non-equivalent dependent variable). This structured scepticism is rarely applied to UX studies, where novelty effects and regression to the mean routinely masquerade as findings.
steps: Describe the study design in Campbell notation (O and X sequences, R for randomisation, dashed lines for non-equivalent groups).
Go through each named threat for the four validity types and rate plausibility given the context.
For plausible threats, add design elements: control groups, extra pretests, holdouts, blinded assessment, multiple measures.
Plan analyses that test specific threats (e.g. checking regression to the mean when sampling on extreme scores).
Document residual threats explicitly in the report with their likely direction of bias.
Have a colleague red-team the audit before data collection.
outputs: A validity threat register, design modifications and an explicit limitations statement.
useWhen: Planning any evaluative or causal study, especially quasi-experiments, pilots and before-after comparisons.
avoidWhen: Purely generative exploratory research where validity criteria of trustworthiness apply instead.
whyLost: UX inherited the experiments but not the methodological scepticism of social science, and limitation sections are often boilerplate.
whereToUse: Feature pilots, beta programmes, onboarding evaluations, benchmark studies, research review processes.
example: A pilot shows support tickets dropped after a new help widget. The audit flags regression to the mean (the pilot was triggered by a ticket spike) and history (a bug fix released the same week); a staggered rollout is added.
sources: Shadish, Cook & Campbell, Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference (2002)
Campbell & Stanley, Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Research (1966)
reference: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference. Houghton Mifflin.

name: Three Horizons Framework
origin: Developed by Bill Sharpe, Anthony Hodgson and Andrew Curry (Curry and Hodgson, 2008; Sharpe, 2013); distinct from McKinsey's growth horizons
summary: Maps the current dominant system (H1), emerging transformative practices (H3) and the contested transition space (H2) to plan change over time.
description: In the futures version of Three Horizons, the first horizon is the current way of doing things, which declines as it loses fitness; the third is an emerging, transformative pattern visible today in pockets of innovation; the second is the turbulent transition zone where innovations either get captured by H1 (H2-) or help build H3 (H2+). Participants map evidence of each horizon, discuss values and tensions, and identify actions. It makes strategic conversations about transformation concrete and acknowledges the role of current systems. For UX and product, it helps teams locate their work in industry transitions such as AI-native workflows or open banking.
steps: Choose the domain and time frame (e.g. how people manage money over 10-15 years).
Map Horizon 1: current dominant practices, structures, and signs of declining fitness.
Map Horizon 3: visions and pockets of the future already present (seeds of change).
Map Horizon 2: innovations in transition, distinguishing those that sustain H1 from those that build H3.
Discuss values, tensions and stakeholders across horizons.
Identify actions and research to nurture H3 and steer H2 innovations.
outputs: A three horizons map, identified seeds of change, H2 innovation classification and strategic actions.
useWhen: Strategic conversations about transformation and how current products relate to emerging futures.
avoidWhen: Short-term feature decisions.
whyLost: Futures practice and product strategy rarely mix; the name is also confused with McKinsey's three horizons of growth.
whereToUse: Financial services transformation, healthcare digitalisation, energy, education, AI workplace adoption.
example: A bank maps H1 (branch and app banking), H3 (embedded finance managed by AI agents) and H2 (open banking aggregators). It reclassifies its aggregator feature as H2- and invests in agent-ready APIs instead.
sources: Sharpe, Three Horizons: The Patterning of Hope (2013)
Curry & Hodgson, Seeing in multiple horizons: Connecting futures to strategy (2008), Journal of Futures Studies
Sharpe, Hodgson, Leicester, Lyon & Fazey, Three horizons: a pathways practice for transformation (2016), Ecology and Society
reference: Sharpe, B., et al. (2016). Three horizons: A pathways practice for transformation. Ecology and Society, 21(2), 47.

name: Thurstone Scaling (Law of Comparative Judgement)
origin: L. L. Thurstone, 1927
summary: Converts paired-comparison preferences into an interval scale of perceived quality or preference, with explicit model assumptions.
description: Listed in the treatise's borrowing matrix under psychophysics, Thurstone's law of comparative judgement models each stimulus as producing a normally distributed internal response; the proportion of times A is preferred to B maps to the distance between their means. Case V assumes equal variances and zero correlations. The output is an interval scale, so differences between items are meaningful, which ratings and rankings do not guarantee. Bradley-Terry models are a logistic analogue. In UX, paired comparisons are easier and more reliable for participants than absolute ratings, making Thurstone scaling well suited to visual design variants, voices, tones or AI response quality.
steps: Select 5-15 stimuli (designs, voices, responses).
Present all or a balanced subset of pairs, randomising order and position.
Collect preference judgements from 20-100 participants.
Compute choice proportions and convert to z-scores (Case V) or fit a Bradley-Terry model.
Check model fit (circular triads, goodness-of-fit).
Report the interval scale with confidence intervals and segment differences.
outputs: Interval-scale values for stimuli, fit diagnostics, segment comparisons.
useWhen: Comparing many subjective variants where absolute ratings are unreliable; AI output evaluation.
avoidWhen: When behavioural outcomes, not perceptions, are the target; use experiments.
whyLost: Psychometric scaling dropped out of design research, replaced by Likert ratings and preference votes.
whereToUse: Visual design exploration, brand voice, TTS voices, LLM response quality evaluation, icon sets.
example: Eight candidate onboarding illustrations are compared in pairs by 60 users; scaling shows two cluster at the top with negligible difference, so the team picks the cheaper one.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Thurstone LL (1927) A law of comparative judgment. Psychological Review 34:273-286
Bradley RA & Terry ME (1952) Rank analysis of incomplete block designs. Biometrika
Thurstone, A law of comparative judgment (1927), Psychological Review
Thurstone & Chave, The Measurement of Attitude (1929)
Torgerson, Theory and Methods of Scaling (1958)
Feature Prioritization Methods (slide deck)
reference: Thurstone LL (1927) A law of comparative judgment. Psychological Review 34(4):273-286.

name: Time Study and Task Decomposition (Scientific Management)
origin: Frederick Winslow Taylor, 1880s-1911
summary: Decomposes work into timed elemental steps through direct observation, giving an empirical baseline of where effort and delay accumulate in a task.
description: Taylor's scientific management introduced the systematic observation of work as a discipline: a task is broken into constituent elements, each element is timed repeatedly with a stopwatch across skilled workers, and allowances are added for fatigue and delay. The treatise argues that, stripped of its ideological baggage of labour exploitation, the method contributes three principles UX still needs: careful decomposition of tasks, systematic timing of performance, and empirical observation rather than intuition as the basis for design recommendations. Its rigour lies in repeated measurement, explicit element boundaries and the separation of observed time from normalised time. In digital contexts it becomes an evidence base for high-frequency operational workflows such as data entry, claims handling or warehouse scanning, where seconds per transaction compound across thousands of repetitions.
steps: Select a stable, repeated task performed by experienced users and define its start and end points precisely.
Decompose the task into elements with observable break points (for example locate record, read field, key value, confirm).
Time each element across at least 10-20 cycles per participant and several participants, recording anomalies separately.
Compute mean and variance per element and identify elements with high time share or high variability.
Redesign or remove the dominant elements and re-time the new workflow to verify the saving.
Report time per transaction and projected annual hours saved, alongside qualitative notes on strain and errors.
outputs: Element-level time table, task time baseline, ranked list of time sinks, projected savings model.
useWhen: Repetitive, high-volume operational tasks (back-office, call centre, logistics, clinical documentation) where efficiency gains multiply across many repetitions.
avoidWhen: Exploratory, creative or infrequent tasks where time is not the right quality measure; use contextual inquiry or diary studies instead.
whyLost: Taylorism became associated with labour exploitation and dehumanising work, and UX defined itself in opposition to mechanistic views of people. The measurement discipline was discarded along with the ideology.
whereToUse: Enterprise and internal tools, point-of-sale and warehouse apps, EHR documentation burden studies, agent desktops in customer service.
example: A claims-processing team times 15 agents through 20 claims each and finds that 31% of handling time is spent re-keying policy numbers between two screens. Auto-populating the field cuts mean handling time by 48 seconds per claim.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Taylor FW (1911) The Principles of Scientific Management
Barnes RM (1980) Motion and Time Study: Design and Measurement of Work
reference: Taylor FW (1911) The Principles of Scientific Management. Harper & Brothers.

name: Time-Use Survey
donor: Sociology, official statistics and leisure studies
origin: Multinational Comparative Time-Budget Research Project in the 1960s (Szalai, 1972); earlier BBC listening studies in Britain in the 1930s; national time-use surveys described by Veal and Darcy
summary: Respondents keep a detailed diary of everything they do over one or two days, so researchers can see how time is shared between all activities.
description: A time-use or time-budget survey collects information on how people allocate their time across all activities. It is usually run as the main or a subsidiary part of a household survey: as well as answering a questionnaire, respondents complete a diary covering one or two days. They record their waking activities with starting and stopping times, where each activity took place, with whom, and sometimes whether they saw it as paid work, domestic work or leisure. Secondary activities, such as listening to music while exercising, are also recorded. Because the diary covers the whole day rather than asking about one activity, it captures activities done briefly and often, and avoids the over-reporting that direct questions can produce, though the short reference period means rarer activities are missed. Veal and Darcy note that coding and analysis are demanding, since hundreds of activities must be coded across many quarter-hour periods. For UX the method shows where a product sits within the whole of a person's day, what it competes with for time, and what people are doing at the same moment, which a product-specific diary study does not reveal.
steps: Define the population, the diary days to sample (weekdays and weekends) and the time slots, for example quarter-hours.
Design the diary with columns for main activity, secondary activity, location, who else was present and any device used.
Recruit a representative sample, usually alongside a short background questionnaire.
Ask respondents to complete the diary on the assigned days, recording as they go rather than at the end.
Code free-text activities into an activity classification, including categories relevant to your product.
Aggregate minutes per activity, participation rates and timing profiles across the day, by segment.
Interpret where the product's use fits, what it displaces or accompanies, and which time windows matter.
outputs: Coded diary data giving minutes per activity, the share of people doing each activity, time-of-day profiles and co-occurrence of main and secondary activities.
useWhen: You need to understand the whole daily context of use, competition for time or media multitasking, rather than behaviour within your product alone.
avoidWhen: The behaviour of interest is rare or irregular, the sample cannot sustain the diary burden, or you only need in-product usage, which logs provide more cheaply.
whyLost: UX diary studies focus on one product and are qualitative, and product analytics measure in-app time directly, so the whole-day, statistically coded time-budget diary remained the domain of national statistics offices and leisure researchers.
whereToUse: Media and streaming, fitness and health apps, smart home, mobile and wearable products, attention-economy research, public sector digital services.
example: A fitness app team analyses two-day time-use diaries from 400 adults and finds that the evening slot they target is dominated by television watching with a phone as a secondary activity, while short morning commutes have unused time, prompting a test of five-minute commute workouts.
sources: Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Veal, A. J. and Darcy, S. (2014) Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management: A Practical Guide. London: Routledge. Szalai, A. (ed.) (1972) The Use of Time: Daily Activities of Urban and Suburban Populations in Twelve Countries. The Hague: Mouton.

name: Timeline Method (River of Life)
origin: Participatory rural appraisal and narrative psychology traditions; timeline interviewing (Adriansen, 2012)
summary: Participants draw a timeline of their experience, marking events, turning points and emotional highs and lows, making the temporal structure of their relationship with a product or condition visible.
description: The timeline method and its variants (river of life, experience timeline, journey timeline) ask participants to construct a visual representation of their experience over time — marking significant events, turning points, high and low periods, and their emotional quality. Unlike verbal retrospective accounts (which tend to flatten temporal complexity and highlight only the most salient moments), timeline methods make the temporal structure of experience visible and discussable.
steps: Materials: Large paper, markers, stickers, printed icons, or a digital template. The format should feel generative, not constraining.
Calibration anchor: Define the time period: 'Draw your experience from when you first started using [product] to today.' Or: 'Map a typical week of [activity].'
Dual-axis variant: Horizontal axis = time. Vertical axis = intensity, satisfaction, or emotional quality. This produces a graph-like timeline that makes both sequence and experience quality visible.
Event marking: Ask participants to mark the significant events, changes, and turning points in the timeline. Each marked event becomes a prompt for narrative probing.
Group timelines: Comparing timelines across participants reveals: shared critical periods, divergent trajectories, and the relationship between life events and product experience.
outputs: Participant-drawn timelines, interview narratives, critical incidents and turning points, emotional curves, and cross-participant patterns of shared moments.
useWhen: The relationship with a product or condition unfolds over months or years, such as adoption, churn, chronic illness or financial change, and you need retrospective structure quickly.
avoidWhen: You need accurate recall of fine detail or real-time data; use a diary study or Descriptive Experience Sampling. Avoid treating drawn curves as quantitative measurements.
whyLost: It largely survives as journey mapping, but journey maps are usually built by teams for users rather than drawn by participants, losing the participant-led temporal account.
whereToUse: Subscription and retention research, onboarding to mastery journeys, chronic health management, financial life events, and B2B customer lifecycle.
example: Eleven former subscribers of a meal-kit service draw rivers of their subscription. Most show a dip at week 3 tied to repetitive recipes, not price, which shifts retention efforts to recipe variety.
sources: Universal Methods of Design (Martin)
Diary Methods (Flick)
Mapping Experiences (Kalbach)
reference: Adriansen, H. K. (2012). Timeline interviews: A tool for conducting life history research. Qualitative Studies, 3(1), 40-55.

name: Tool adoption zone mapping
origin: Lev Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, 1930s (published in English 1978); scaffolding by Wood, Bruner and Ross, 1976
summary: Maps which product capabilities users can master alone, which they can master with support, and which are beyond reach, to design scaffolding and staged adoption.
description: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do unaided and what they can do with guidance. Applied to tool adoption, it distinguishes three zones for each capability: independent use, use with scaffolding (help, coaching, templates, a colleague) and out of reach for now. Mapping these zones by user group shows where onboarding and support should focus and which advanced features need staged exposure. Wood, Bruner and Ross's scaffolding functions, such as reducing degrees of freedom and highlighting critical features, translate into design patterns. Rigour comes from observing actual performance at each level of support rather than relying on self-report, and from re-mapping over time as zones shift.
steps: List the product capabilities relevant to adoption, ordered by complexity.
Recruit users across experience levels (for example 3-5 per level) and observe them attempting tasks unaided.
Introduce graded prompts (hint, demonstration, step-by-step guidance) and record the least support at which each user succeeds.
Assign each capability-user pair to a zone: independent, scaffolded or out of reach.
Design scaffolding for scaffolded-zone capabilities and defer out-of-reach capabilities to later stages.
Re-map after weeks of use to track zone movement and fade scaffolding where independence is reached.
outputs: A capability-by-user zone map, the support level needed per capability, scaffolding designs, and an adoption roadmap.
useWhen: When introducing complex tools to professionals, designing onboarding and training, or planning progressive disclosure.
avoidWhen: When products are simple enough for immediate independent use; standard onboarding tests suffice.
whyLost: ZPD is central in education but rarely operationalised in UX, where onboarding is designed without measured support levels.
whereToUse: Surgical robotics training, enterprise software rollout, developer tools, AI assistants, and educational products.
example: Junior surgeons can dock the robot independently but need step prompts for instrument exchange and cannot yet use dual-console mode. The team adds guided exchange and hides dual-console mode until 20 cases.
sources: Newell, A., Unified Theories of Cognition (1990)
Hollnagel, E. (ed.), Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (2003)
Unified Theories of Cognition (Newell)
Handbook of Cognitive Task Design (Hollnagel)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 15 — Activity Theory, Contradictions & the Zone of Proximal Development
reference: Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in Society: The Development of Higher Psychological Processes. Harvard University Press.

name: Top Task Analysis
origin: Gerry McGovern (2010, The Stranger's Long Neck); used for benchmark task selection by Sauro
summary: Asks many users to pick their few most important tasks from a long list, revealing the small set that matters most.
description: Most products have a "long neck": a handful of tasks account for most of what users care about, followed by a long tail of trivial ones. Top task analysis compiles an exhaustive list of 50 to 100 candidate tasks from analytics, search logs, support and stakeholders, then asks a large sample to vote for their top five. Because people must choose quickly from a long randomised list, votes reflect genuine priority. The top 5 to 10 tasks typically receive about a quarter to half of all votes. Sauro uses it to choose which tasks to benchmark; McGovern uses it to focus whole organisations.
steps: Gather every candidate task from analytics, search, support tickets, competitors and stakeholders.
Consolidate into 50 to 100 clearly worded, non-overlapping tasks in users' language.
Survey a large representative sample (several hundred) asking each person to choose up to five tasks from the randomised list.
Rank tasks by vote share and plot the long-neck curve.
Use the top tasks to focus design, navigation and benchmarking, and the tail to decide what to de-emphasise.
outputs: A ranked list of the tasks that matter most, and a clear tail of those that do not.
useWhen: Large sites or products with sprawling content, before a redesign or benchmark.
avoidWhen: Small products with only a few tasks, or when you cannot reach a large sample.
whyLost: Not lost, but often replaced with stakeholder opinion or analytics page views, which measure what people do now rather than what they need.
whereToUse: Government sites, intranets, university and enterprise portals, SaaS feature prioritisation.
example: A council website surveys 1,800 residents; "pay council tax" and "report a missed bin" take 31% of votes, while 40 news and events tasks share 3%.
sources: Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Factor and Discriminant Analysis (Sauro & Lewis, MeasuringU training)
reference: McGovern, G. (2010). The Stranger's Long Neck. A&C Black.

name: Top-Box Analysis of Rating Scales
origin: Market research dashboard practice; analysis guidance in Sauro & Lewis (2012) chapter 4
summary: Converts rating responses to the share choosing the top one or two options, then analyses that share as a proportion.
description: Dashboards often report "percent who agree" (top-two-box on a 5-point scale) rather than means. To test a claim such as "at least 75% agree", convert 4s and 5s to 1 and everything else to 0, then use the binomial methods for completion rates: a mid-p test against the benchmark and an adjusted-Wald interval. Sauro and Lewis show the trade-off clearly: converting discards intensity, so the same data that gives a 72.5% chance of meeting the goal as top-box gives 81.4% when analysed as a mean with a t-test. Top-box is easy to communicate but needs larger samples to detect changes, so analyse raw means where you can and report top-box where dashboards require it.
steps: Decide the top-box rule before analysis (for example 4 or 5 on a 5-point scale).
Convert each response to 1 or 0.
Compute the proportion with an adjusted-Wald interval.
Test against any benchmark with the mid-p binomial test for small samples.
Also report the mean and its interval so intensity is not lost.
outputs: The share of respondents in the top box(es) with an interval, and a benchmark test.
useWhen: Stakeholders or dashboards define targets as percentages of agreement.
avoidWhen: You want to detect small improvements with small samples; use means.
whyLost: Not lost, but usually reported without intervals and without acknowledging the lost information.
whereToUse: Customer satisfaction dashboards, NPS-style reporting, survey summaries.
example: Ten of twelve participants agree they feel confident buying on a site (83%), but the 80% interval of 65% to 93% includes the 75% goal, so the claim is not yet supported.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2012). Quantifying the User Experience, chapter 4.

name: Topic labelling
origin: Topic interpretation practices in computational social science (e.g. DiMaggio, Nag and Blei, 2013); automated labelling by Lau et al., 2011
summary: Giving each machine-derived topic a meaningful, defensible name by reading its top words and representative documents, ideally with multiple analysts and documented rationale.
description: Topic models output word lists and document weights, not meanings. Labelling is the interpretive step that turns them into research findings, and it is where most errors enter: labels based on top words alone can misrepresent what documents actually say. A rigorous protocol has at least two analysts read top words, distinctive words (e.g. FREX or c-TF-IDF) and 10-20 representative documents per topic, independently propose labels and short definitions, reconcile disagreements and mark topics that are incoherent or artefactual. Large language models can propose candidate labels, but analysts should verify them against documents. Labels should be descriptive rather than prematurely evaluative.
steps: For each topic, extract top words, distinctive words and the 10-20 highest-weighted documents.
Have two analysts independently write a label (2-6 words) and a one-sentence definition from the documents, not only the words.
Compare labels, discuss disagreements and record the agreed label with rationale.
Mark topics as coherent, mixed or junk (e.g. greetings, transcription artefacts) and exclude junk from reporting.
Optionally use an LLM to propose labels from the same evidence, and accept them only after analyst verification.
Publish a topic codebook with labels, definitions, example quotes and prevalence.
outputs: A topic codebook with labels, definitions, quality ratings and example quotes.
useWhen: After any topic model or clustering of UX text, before results are shared with stakeholders.
avoidWhen: Not needed if topics are only used as machine features. Avoid presenting labels as themes without interpretive analysis of their content.
whyLost: Labelling is often done hastily by one person from top words, so the interpretive rigour of qualitative coding was never carried over to computational outputs.
whereToUse: Feedback analysis programmes, research repositories and AI-assisted synthesis.
example: A topic with top words 'card, wait, week, arrive' is first labelled 'shipping delays'. Reading documents shows it concerns physical debit card delivery during onboarding, so it is relabelled 'debit card arrival wait' and routed to the onboarding team.

BERTopic

hdbscan
