name: Topological Analysis of Information Spaces
origin: Henri Poincaré, 1890s; topological data analysis by Carlsson, Edelsbrunner and others, 2000s
summary: Examines properties of an information or navigation space that survive deformation, such as connectedness, loops and holes, to reveal structural gaps and dead ends.
description: Topology studies properties preserved under continuous deformation: whether a space is connected, how many loops or holes it has, which regions are reachable from which. Applied to information spaces, it abstracts away from exact layout and asks about the shape of navigation: are there isolated regions, cycles that trap users, or holes where expected connections are missing? Topological data analysis extends this to high-dimensional usage data, for example finding the shape of user journeys or content similarity spaces using persistent homology or Mapper. The method is rigorous when the space is formally defined (as a graph or point cloud), topological features are computed rather than eyeballed, and features are checked for persistence across scales so that noise is not mistaken for structure.
steps: Define the space formally: a navigation graph, a content similarity space or a point cloud of user journey features.
Compute basic topological properties such as connected components and cycles.
For high-dimensional data, apply topological data analysis (e.g. Mapper or persistent homology) across scales.
Retain features that persist across a wide range of scales and discard short-lived ones as noise.
Interpret features as UX structures: isolated sections, loops, missing bridges between content clusters.
Validate interpretations with path analysis or tree testing and propose structural fixes.
outputs: Topological summary of the information space, persistence diagrams or Mapper graphs, list of disconnected regions and structural gaps.
useWhen: Large content estates, knowledge bases, VR or spatial environments, and exploratory analysis of complex journey data.
avoidWhen: Small sites or apps where a sitemap review suffices; use graph analysis or tree testing for routine IA questions.
whyLost: Latent: Academic; potential in graph-based navigation analysis and spatial computing.
whereToUse: Navigation graph analysis; VR environment design; abstract information space mapping.
example: A clinical knowledge base with 40,000 articles was analysed with Mapper on article similarity and link data. It found a cluster of paediatric dosing content with no links into the main graph, explaining why clinicians rarely reached it.
sources: Where Mathematics Comes From
Topology and Data (Gunnar Carlsson)
reference: Carlsson, G. (2009). Topology and data. Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, 46(2), 255-308.

name: Total Survey Error Framework
origin: Groves, 1989; Groves et al., 2009
summary: Audits a survey for every source of error (coverage, sampling, nonresponse, measurement, processing) rather than sampling error alone, to design and interpret UX surveys defensibly.
description: The total survey error (TSE) framework, associated with Robert Groves, decomposes the difference between a survey estimate and the true population value into distinct sources. On the representation side are coverage error (the frame misses parts of the population), sampling error, and nonresponse error; on the measurement side are validity problems, measurement error from question wording, mode and respondents, and processing error in coding and editing. Applied to UX surveys, TSE shifts attention from margin of error, which reflects only sampling, to the often larger biases from who is invited and who responds and how questions are understood. Rigour comes from auditing each source at design time, collecting paradata, and testing for bias with follow-up samples.
steps: TSE audit for any UX survey:
Coverage error — who is excluded from the sampling frame? Users who never complete tasks? Low-literacy users?
(2) Sampling error — is the sample representative of the population? Compute design effect if cluster sampling.
(3) Nonresponse error — who declines to respond? Is there a pattern?
(4) Measurement error — do items measure what they intend? (cognitive interview pre-testing).
(5) Processing error — coding/data entry errors. Estimate the magnitude of each error type and prioritize the largest.
outputs: An error-source audit, design changes to reduce the largest errors, nonresponse and coverage analyses, and honest statements of what results can support.
useWhen: Designing or interpreting any consequential UX survey: satisfaction tracking, NPS programmes, market sizing, or surveys with low response rates or convenience samples.
avoidWhen: Overkill for quick internal pulse checks with no inferential claims. Not a replacement for qualitative work when constructs are still unclear.
whyLost: UX surveys are run as quick tools; survey methodology as a discipline remains in social statistics and official statistics agencies.
whereToUse: UX survey design and analysis, benchmarking study methodology, longitudinal survey programs, NPS validity assessment.
example: A SaaS company's in-app satisfaction survey shows 82% satisfied; a TSE audit reveals coverage error (only active users see it) and nonresponse bias, and an email sample of churned users reduces the estimate to 64%.
sources: Survey Methodology — Groves et al.
reference: Groves RM, Fowler FJ, Couper MP, Lepkowski JM, Singer E & Tourangeau R (2009) Survey Methodology. 2nd ed. Wiley

name: Touch Target Fitts' Law Calibration for Mobile
origin: Paul Fitts (1954); touch extensions such as Bi, Li and Zhai's FFitts law (2013); design guidance by Josh Clark (2015)
summary: Calibrates Fitts' law for touch by measuring effective target size, finger imprecision and posture on real devices, producing evidence-based minimum target sizes and spacing.
description: Fitts' law predicts movement time from the distance to a target and its width (MT = a + b log2(D/W + 1)). On touchscreens the standard form breaks down because finger contact is imprecise and occludes the target, so effective width depends on finger pad size, posture (one thumb versus two hands), device size, grip and feedback. Bi, Li and Zhai's FFitts law adds an absolute imprecision term to the target width. Calibration studies have participants tap targets of varied size and distance on the actual device and posture, measuring time and the spread of touch points to estimate effective width and error rates. The results set minimum target sizes and spacing for a given acceptable error rate and reveal thumb-reach zones, replacing generic platform guidelines with evidence for the product's own users.
steps: Measure empirical error rates for touch targets at sizes from 5mm to 15mm in your specific product context.
Fit a logistic regression: P(error) = f(target_size, user_group).
Identify the target size at which P(error) < 0.05 for your target user group.
Compare to: Apple HIG (44pt = 7.7mm), Google Material (48dp = 9mm), WCAG 2.5.5 (24×24px minimum).
Your empirically derived minimum may differ from all guidelines.
outputs: Fitted Fitts' parameters for the device and posture, touch-point dispersion, error rate by target size, minimum size and spacing recommendations, and thumb-reach maps.
useWhen: Mobile apps with dense controls, one-handed use, older users or users with tremor, kiosks, in-car touchscreens and wearables.
avoidWhen: When platform minimums (44 pt or 48 dp) are already met with generous spacing and errors are low; standard usability testing suffices.
whyLost: Platform guidelines replaced measurement, so teams apply fixed minimum sizes without calibrating for their users, devices or postures.
whereToUse: Mobile UX design, touchscreen accessibility, wearable UX, kiosk design for diverse user populations.
example: A ride-hailing app's driver interface is used one-handed in a dashboard mount. A calibration study with 16 drivers shows a 7 mm target yields 9% errors at the top of the screen, so critical buttons are enlarged to 11 mm and moved into the thumb zone.
sources: Designing for Touch — Josh Clark
Bi, Li & Zhai, FFitts law: Modeling finger touch with Fitts' law (CHI 2013)
Parhi, Karlson & Bederson, Target size study for one-handed thumb use on small touchscreen devices (MobileHCI 2006)
reference: Fitts PM (1954) The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement. Journal of Experimental Psychology 47(6):381-391

name: Toulmin Argument Analysis
origin: Stephen Toulmin, 1958 (The Uses of Argument)
summary: Breaks arguments into claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal, used to audit research findings and to analyse how users or AI systems justify conclusions.
description: Toulmin modelled practical arguments on legal reasoning: a Claim is supported by Grounds (data), connected by a Warrant (the inferential rule), supported by Backing, limited by a Qualifier ('probably') and open to Rebuttals (exceptions). Making each part explicit exposes hidden warrants and overclaiming. Applied to UX research reports, it audits whether insights are justified: is the warrant connecting five interviews to 'users want X' sound? Applied to product content, it evaluates how AI explanations, recommendations or persuasive content argue, and whether users can evaluate them. It is a lightweight but rigorous critique tool.
steps: Select the arguments to analyse (research insights, recommendations, AI explanations, persuasive copy).
For each, identify the claim and the grounds offered.
Make the warrant explicit: what rule licenses the move from grounds to claim?
Identify backing for the warrant, the qualifier strength and potential rebuttals.
Assess weaknesses: missing grounds, unstated or weak warrants, missing qualifiers, unaddressed rebuttals.
Revise arguments (or design explanation templates) to include explicit grounds, qualifiers and rebuttals.
outputs: Toulmin diagrams of key arguments, identified weaknesses and revised, better-qualified claims.
useWhen: Reviewing research reports and decision memos, designing AI explanations or evaluating persuasive content.
avoidWhen: Exploratory note-taking where arguments are not yet formed.
whyLost: Argumentation theory is taught in rhetoric and law; UX research critique relies on intuition about rigour.
whereToUse: Research review processes, AI explanation design, health information, financial advice interfaces.
example: A research insight claims 'Gen Z distrusts banks' from 8 interviews. Toulmin analysis reveals the warrant (these 8 represent Gen Z) lacks backing; the claim is qualified to 'participants in urban, renting households expressed...'.
sources: Toulmin, The Uses of Argument (1958; updated ed. 2003)
Walton, Reed & Macagno, Argumentation Schemes (2008)
reference: Toulmin, S. E. (2003). The Uses of Argument (updated ed.). Cambridge University Press.

name: Transcript quality audit
donor: Speech recognition evaluation; qualitative research quality
origin: Word error rate metric from speech recognition evaluation (NIST); transcription quality concerns in qualitative methods (Poland, 1995)
summary: Systematically checking a sample of automated transcripts against human reference transcripts to quantify errors and decide whether they are fit for analysis.
description: Automated transcripts are data, and their errors propagate into coding and quotes. A transcript quality audit selects a stratified sample of recordings (covering accents, audio quality and languages), produces careful human reference transcripts for segments, and computes word error rate (WER = substitutions + deletions + insertions divided by reference words). It also checks qualitative error types that WER under-weights: hallucinated sentences during silence, mis-heard domain terms, negations dropped ('can' versus 'can't'), and mis-attributed speakers. Poland (1995) showed that even human transcription has systematic errors. Rigour comes from pre-set acceptance thresholds, stratified sampling, reporting the audit, and correcting or flagging transcripts that fail.
steps: Define acceptance criteria before auditing, e.g. WER of 10% or less and zero meaning-changing errors in quoted passages.
Draw a stratified sample of about 10% of recordings (at least 5), covering speakers, accents, languages and audio conditions.
Create human reference transcripts for 3-5 minute segments from each sampled file.
Compute WER with a tool such as jiwer after normalising case and punctuation.
Review for meaning-changing errors: negations, numbers, product and drug names, hallucinated passages and speaker swaps.
Correct failing transcripts, build a glossary or prompt for recurrent terms and re-run, and verify every quote used in reporting against audio.
outputs: A WER table by stratum, a catalogue of error types, a pass or fail decision per file and a verified quote list.
useWhen: Whenever automated transcription feeds qualitative analysis, especially for accented speech, technical domains, multiple languages or published research.
avoidWhen: Less necessary for informal internal note-taking where recordings are consulted directly; never skip it for quotes in reports.
whyLost: Teams treat transcripts from modern ASR as ground truth because they read fluently, so error rates are rarely measured.
whereToUse: Health research with medical terminology, multilingual UX research, accessibility research with atypical speech and AI-assisted analysis pipelines.
example: A fintech team's audit finds 7% WER overall but 19% for participants with strong regional accents, and two instances where 'I wouldn't trust it' was transcribed as 'I would trust it'. Those files are hand-corrected before coding.

openai-whisper (cloud)
pyannote.audio (diarisation)
ffmpeg
pydub

Jurafsky, D. & Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing, 3rd ed. draft
The Inquiry Series, C9 — Whisper — Batch Transcription at Scale

name: Transcription confidence scoring
origin: Confidence measures in ASR (Jiang, 2005, review); Whisper token log-probabilities and no-speech probabilities
summary: Using the speech model's own token probabilities and compression signals to flag low-confidence transcript segments for targeted human review.
description: Whisper exposes per-token and per-segment signals: average log-probability, no-speech probability and compression ratio (very repetitive output signals hallucination). Combining these yields a confidence score per segment so reviewers can focus effort where errors are most likely rather than auditing randomly. Rigour comes from calibrating thresholds against audited segments (checking that low-confidence segments really have higher WER), recognising that models can be confidently wrong, especially on domain terms, and marking flagged segments in the transcript so analysts treat quotes from them cautiously.
steps: Enable word or segment-level probabilities and timestamps in the transcription output.
Compute per-segment signals: average log-probability, no-speech probability and compression ratio.
Set initial flags using Whisper's own defaults (avg_logprob below -1.0, compression ratio above 2.4, no_speech_prob above 0.6).
Calibrate by auditing flagged and unflagged samples and adjusting thresholds so flagged segments have markedly higher error rates.
Mark flagged segments in transcripts and route them to human review, prioritising those in quoted or coded passages.
Report the proportion of flagged content per file as a quality indicator.
outputs: Per-segment confidence scores, flagged segments for review, calibrated thresholds and a file-level quality indicator.
useWhen: Large transcription batches where full auditing is impractical, and AI-assisted analysis pipelines that need quality gates.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating high confidence as correctness for proper nouns, numbers and negations; still verify all quotes against audio.
whyLost: Confidence signals exist in every model but are hidden by default outputs, and few UX teams know how to read them.
whereToUse: Large interview programmes, voice-of-customer call audio, multilingual research and regulated domains.
example: In a batch of 250 support call recordings, confidence scoring flags 6% of segments. Audit shows flagged segments have 31% WER versus 5% elsewhere, so review time is focused on that 6%.

openai-whisper (cloud)

ffmpeg
pydub

name: Transferability through Thick Description
origin: Lincoln & Guba, 1985, drawing on Geertz's thick description (1973)
summary: Providing rich setting, participant and analytic context so readers can judge whether qualitative findings apply to their own situation.
description: Transferability replaces the claim of statistical generalisation with a shared responsibility. The researcher provides thick description of the setting, participants, data collection conditions and analytic stance; the reader judges fittingness, whether their context is similar enough for findings to apply. The quality of a study is therefore partly measured by how well it enables that judgement. In practice this means describing physical and organisational context, the pressures participants face, sampling rationale, when and how each piece of data was gathered, and the analyst's framework and positionality. It counters the common failure where UX findings from one segment or market are silently assumed to apply everywhere.
steps: Describe the research setting in depth: Physical environment, organizational context, historical conditions, social relationships, time period. Not just "a rural health clinic in Kerala" but what that clinic looks like, how it operates, who works there, what pressures they face.
Describe the participants in depth: Demographic information relevant to the research question, their relationship to the phenomenon, their range of experience, and the sampling rationale.

Describe the context of data collection: When, where, with whom, under what conditions each piece of data was collected. A transcript from a one-hour interview in a private office is different data from a ten-minute conversation during a busy clinic shift.
Describe the analytical context: What theoretical and methodological framework was applied, by whom, with what background and positionality.
outputs: A context section in reports describing setting, participants, data collection conditions and analytic positionality, plus explicit statements of where findings may and may not transfer.
useWhen: When findings from one market, segment or site will be reused elsewhere, when building a research repository, or when reporting to teams in other contexts.
avoidWhen: When you need a statistical estimate of how widespread a finding is; use a survey or analytics follow-up instead.
whyLost: Short slide-based reporting strips context, and repositories store atomised insights without the conditions under which they were observed.
whereToUse: Global product research, research repositories and insight libraries, multi-country health and fintech studies, and enterprise research reused across accounts.
example: A ride-hailing team's Lagos study of cash payments includes detailed description of driver economics and connectivity. A team in Nairobi uses this context to decide which findings transfer and which need local validation.
sources: Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba)
Ethnographic Thinking (Hasbrouck)
The Interpretation of Cultures (Geertz)
Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba) via Sage Handbook
Qualitative Research Ethics (Sage)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 27 — Lincoln & Guba — Trustworthiness in Qualitative Research
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)

name: Transition Design
donor: Design studies, sustainability transitions and futures
origin: Terry Irwin, Gideon Kossoff and Cameron Tonkinwise, Carnegie Mellon University, 2015
summary: A framework for designing toward long-term societal transitions by mapping wicked problems, stakeholder relations and visions, then seeding interventions at multiple scales.
description: Transition design, developed at Carnegie Mellon, addresses wicked problems such as climate, food systems and mobility that cannot be solved by single products. It combines systems thinking, futures, social practice theory and stakeholder research. The method maps the problem as a system across scales and time, maps stakeholders' concerns, fears and hopes and the relations between them, co-creates long-term visions, and then 'backcasts' to identify interventions at different scales and horizons. Rigour comes from mapping the problem's history and interconnections with evidence, including diverse stakeholders and their conflicts, and treating interventions as experiments monitored for systemic effects. For product teams it provides a way to situate features within larger transitions, for example energy behaviour or circular commerce.
steps: Map the wicked problem across scales (household to global) and over time, including its historical roots.
Identify stakeholders and map their concerns, fears, hopes and relationships, including conflicts.
Co-create a long-term future vision with stakeholders, typically 20-50 years out.
Backcast from the vision to identify milestones and intervention points at different scales.
Design and launch small, linked interventions as experiments.
Monitor systemic effects and adapt interventions over time.
outputs: Problem map, stakeholder relations map, future vision, backcasting roadmap, portfolio of interventions.
useWhen: Sustainability initiatives, public policy, energy, food and mobility products, and organisations repositioning around societal change.
avoidWhen: Contained product problems with short horizons; use service design or design thinking.
whyLost: Latent: Academic/activist context; emerging in sustainability-focused design practices.
whereToUse: Sustainability design; systems change initiatives; policy design.
example: An energy supplier used transition design to frame home electrification. Stakeholder mapping across tenants, landlords and installers led to an intervention portfolio including landlord incentives and an installer marketplace rather than just a usage app.
sources: Universal Methods of Design
Transition Design: Provocation (Irwin, Kossoff & Tonkinwise)
reference: Irwin, T. (2015). Transition design: A proposal for a new area of design practice, study, and research. Design and Culture, 7(2), 229-246.

name: Tree + Taxonomy Diagnostic Loop
aka: Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy framework
Two-phase tree test and taxonomy design
donor: Information architecture research and human error analysis
origin: Vivek Gopinath, 2025
summary: A two-phase protocol pairing an unmoderated tree test (where findability fails) with moderated micro-sessions coded as Slip, Lapse or Mistake (why), joined in a joint display and re-tested.
description: The framework turns 'navigation was confusing' into decision-ready action. Phase A is an unmoderated tree test (N = 80–150) on a text-only IA of 2–3 levels with 8–12 randomised tasks, yielding direct and indirect success, failure, first-click accuracy, extra clicks, time to first click and misroute hotspots. Phase B is 10–15 moderated 30–40 minute think-aloud micro-sessions on the same tree and tasks, with each breakdown coded by a one-page codebook and two coders on 30–40% of sessions (κ ≥ 0.70). The glue analysis joins phases in a joint display mapping quant signal → taxonomy read → prescribed fix → effort and impact. Decision bars are set before changes (direct ≥ 85%, misroute ≤ 10%, extra clicks ≤ 1.0, first-click ≥ 80%) and the tree test is re-run with the same tasks and similar N, plus 5–8 verification think-alouds.
steps: Detect: export the IA as plain text (depth ≤ 3), write 8–12 tasks without label leakage, and run an unmoderated tree test with 80–150 participants, logging first click, final node, path, time and backtracks.
Compute direct success, indirect success, failure (1 − direct − indirect), misroute share per node, first-click accuracy, extra clicks and time to first click.
Diagnose: run 10–15 moderated 30–40 minute think-alouds on the same tree, using prompts such as 'What do you expect to find under this label?'
Code each breakdown as Slip, Lapse or Mistake; double-code 30–40% and compute Cohen's κ, refining the codebook until κ ≥ 0.70.

Prescribe: build a joint display mapping quant signal → mechanism → fix with effort and impact ratings, using the insight pattern 'Because [quant evidence] and think-aloud revealed [mechanism], we recommend [fix] with decision bar [thresholds]'.
Decide: confirm bars set upfront (direct ≥ 85%, misroute ≤ 10%, extra clicks ≤ 1.0, first-click ≥ 80%).
Re-test: re-run the tree test with the same tasks and similar N and 5–8 verification think-alouds to confirm the mechanism is resolved.
outputs: Tree-test dashboard, taxonomy table by step with quotes and κ, joint display with effort and impact, decision bars, and before/after comparison.
useWhen: IA redesigns, label changes and any situation where you need both where users go wrong and why.
avoidWhen: When the issue lies in visual layout or interaction mechanics rather than labels and hierarchy; use usability testing on the full UI.
whyLost: Original pairing by Vivek Gopinath; tree testing is common but rarely paired with a reliability-checked cognitive error taxonomy.
whereToUse: Fintech navigation, enterprise menus, content-heavy sites, app settings, IA migrations.
example: Creating a price alert yields 59% direct success with 31% misrouting to Notifications; think-alouds code the cause as Mistake ('Notifications sounded like app updates'); after promoting Price Alerts to top nav, direct success reaches 89% and misroutes fall to 7%.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
reference: Gopinath, V. (2025). Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers.

name: Tree Testing
origin: Donna Spencer's paper-based 'card-based classification evaluation', early 2000s; popularised by online tools from 2008
summary: Participants find destinations in a text-only hierarchy, isolating whether labels and structure work, measured by direct and indirect success, first-click accuracy, extra clicks and misroutes.
description: Tree testing removes visual chrome (colours, icons, layout) and tests whether labels and hierarchy alone let people find things. Vivek Gopinath's protocol specifies trees of 2–3 levels from the current and a proposed IA, 6–12 realistic randomised tasks without label leakage, and N = 80–150 per audience segment, run unmoderated. Metrics for N attempts: direct success (correct node with no detours / N), indirect success (correct node with detours / N), failure (1 − direct − indirect), first-click accuracy, extra clicks (total minus minimum path), time to first click, and misroute share per node. Pitfalls include leaking the target label in the task, using 4+ levels, and ignoring first-click accuracy, which strongly predicts success. Decision bars: direct success ≥ 85%, top misroute ≤ 10%, first-click ≥ 75–80%, extra clicks ≤ 1.0.
steps: Export current and proposed IAs as plain text, keeping depth to 2–3 levels and using real labels.
Write 6–12 realistic tasks that avoid the target label (e.g. 'Set a price alert for ABC', not 'Go to Price Alerts').
Recruit 80–150 representative participants per segment and run unmoderated, randomising task order.
Log first click, final node, full path, time and backtracks per attempt.
Compute direct and indirect success, failure, first-click accuracy, extra clicks, time to first click and misroute share per node.
Compare against decision bars (direct ≥ 85%, misroute ≤ 10%, first-click ≥ 75%) and build a misroute heatmap.
Re-run with the same tasks and similar N after changes.
outputs: A tree-test dashboard: success rates, first-click accuracy, extra clicks, misroute heatmap and before/after comparison.
useWhen: Comparing competing IAs or label sets before visual design, or whenever findability is suspected.
avoidWhen: When problems stem from visual layout, search or content quality; use usability testing or first-click testing on real UI.
whyLost: Survived because tools made it cheap and its metrics are clear; rigour suffers when tasks leak labels or why is never explored.
whereToUse: App navigation, fintech menus, e-commerce category structures, intranets, documentation sites.
example: A trading app's current IA gives 59% direct success, 49% first-click accuracy and 31% misroutes to Notifications; the proposed IA reaches 89% direct, 74% first-click and 6% top misroute.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), Tree Testing and Error Taxonomy: A Complete Chapter for UX Researchers
Vivek Gopinath (2025), Forward-Thinking UX Research Playbook: A Mixed-Methods, Decision-Ready Approach from Prediction to Validation
Information Architecture
Observing the User Experience
reference: O'Brien, D. (2009). Tree Testing. Boxes and Arrows.

name: Tree Testing and Navigation Error Taxonomy
aka: Reverse card sort with error coding
donor: Information architecture and human error research
origin: Tree testing from Donna Spencer's paper-based 'card-based classification evaluation' (2003) and Dave O'Brien's Treejack; error taxonomy layer by Vivek Gopinath
summary: Testing a text-only navigation tree with task scenarios and coding each failure as wrong branch, backtrack failure, label failure or false confidence to target fixes.
description: Tree testing isolates information architecture from visual design: participants navigate a text-only hierarchy to find where they would complete a task scenario. Standard analysis reports success, directness and time per task. Gopinath's framework adds a navigation error taxonomy so that failures point to specific remedies. Each failed task is coded as wrong branch (the top-level taxonomy misled), backtrack failure (participants could not recover), label failure (right area, but item labels did not discriminate) or false confidence (a wrong answer accepted without doubt). Full click paths and first clicks are analysed because the first click strongly predicts eventual success. The taxonomy converts success rates into a diagnosis: restructure, relabel or add recovery cues.
steps: Build the tree: Text-only representation of your IA — no visual design, no colours, no icons. This isolates IA findability from visual design quality.

Task scenarios: Write 8–12 task scenarios. Each should be answerable by finding a specific item in the tree. Scenarios must be written in participant language — not using the exact label names in the tree (this defeats the test).
Record full navigation paths: Track every node click, not just the final answer. The path is the data — correct destination via incorrect path is as informative as an incorrect destination.

Error taxonomy coding: Code each failed task by type: (a) wrong branch (participant went to entirely wrong area), (b) backtrack failure (couldn't find the way back after going wrong), (c) label failure (correct branch but couldn't identify specific item from labels), (d) false confident (reached wrong destination and didn't try again).

First-click analysis: What was the first node each participant clicked? First-click accuracy predicts overall task success with ~87% accuracy — and first-click errors reveal where the IA's top-level taxonomy fails to match users' mental model.
outputs: Task success, directness and first-click rates; coded error type distributions per task; path diagrams; and targeted IA remedies.
useWhen: Validating a new or revised navigation structure, comparing candidate trees, or diagnosing why users cannot find content.
avoidWhen: Generating categories from scratch (use open card sorting first) or evaluating visual navigation, search or page layout (use usability testing).
whyLost: Tree testing is active, but its analysis usually stops at success rates; error-type coding that links failures to fixes is this framework's contribution.
whereToUse: E-commerce navigation, help centres, banking app menus, intranets and government information sites.
example: A bank's new menu tree scores 58% success on 'dispute a card payment'. Error coding shows mostly label failures inside the correct 'Cards' branch, so items are relabelled rather than restructured, raising success to 84% in a retest.
sources: Tree Testing Playbook (Gopinath)
Information Architecture (O'Reilly)
How to Make Sense of Any Mess (Covert)

name: Triangulation
origin: Eugene Webb et al., 1966; Norman Denzin, 1970
summary: Corroborates findings by comparing multiple data sources, methods, researchers or theories, strengthening credibility and exposing where evidence diverges.
description: Triangulation uses more than one vantage point to study the same phenomenon. Denzin distinguished four types: data triangulation (different sources, times or places), investigator triangulation (multiple researchers), theory triangulation (multiple interpretive frameworks) and methodological triangulation (different methods). The logic is that each source and method has different biases, so convergent findings are more credible, while divergence is informative and calls for explanation. In UX, it commonly combines analytics, interviews, usability tests and support data. Rigour comes from planning triangulation in advance, documenting a convergence matrix that shows which sources support, contradict or are silent on each finding, and treating contradictions as data rather than discarding inconvenient sources. It is a credibility strategy, not a guarantee of truth, because sources can share biases.
steps: List the key findings or research questions to be corroborated.
Identify independent sources, methods, researchers or theories with different biases for each.
Collect or retrieve data from each source.
Build a convergence matrix marking each finding as supported, contradicted or silent per source.
Investigate contradictions to explain them (e.g. differing populations or measurement).
Report findings with their level of corroboration and any unresolved divergence.
outputs: Convergence matrix, findings rated by corroboration strength, explanations for divergence.
useWhen: High-stakes decisions, synthesis across multiple studies, and when stakeholders question the credibility of a single study.
avoidWhen: Low-stakes, quick evaluations where a single well-chosen method suffices.
whyLost: 'We triangulated' is commonly asserted after running two methods, without a planned protocol or analysis of divergence.
whereToUse: Research synthesis; multi-study programs; mixed-method interpretation.
example: Interviews suggested users abandoned a fintech app due to fees, but analytics showed abandonment peaked before fees were shown. Triangulating with support tickets revealed confusion about identity checks, reframing the finding.
sources: Research Design
Mixed Methods
Unobtrusive Measures (Webb et al.)
The Research Act (Norman Denzin)
Naturalistic Inquiry (Lincoln & Guba)
Oxford Handbook of Multimethod & Mixed Methods Research
The Research Act (Denzin)
Convergent and Discriminant Validation by the Multitrait-Multimethod Matrix (Campbell & Fiske)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Denzin, N. K. (1978). The Research Act: A Theoretical Introduction to Sociological Methods (2nd ed.). McGraw-Hill.

name: TRIZ (Theory of Inventive Problem Solving)
origin: Genrich Altshuller, USSR, 1946-1985, from analysis of hundreds of thousands of patents
summary: Resolves design contradictions (improving one parameter worsens another) using inventive principles derived from patent analysis, instead of compromising.
description: Altshuller found that inventive solutions across fields resolve recurring contradictions using a limited set of principles. Technical contradictions (e.g. more security worsens ease of use) map via the contradiction matrix to suggested principles among 40 (segmentation, taking out, local quality, asymmetry, prior action, dynamics, and so on). Physical contradictions (a parameter must be both high and low) are resolved by separation in time, space, condition or scale. Further tools include ideal final result, resources analysis and trends of evolution. For UX, contradictions are everywhere (simple yet powerful, secure yet frictionless) and TRIZ offers structured ways to transcend trade-offs.
steps: State the problem and the ideal final result (the function achieved with no cost or harm).
Formulate the core contradictions explicitly: what improves and what worsens.
Translate them into TRIZ parameters or physical contradictions.
Use the contradiction matrix or separation principles to identify candidate inventive principles.
Generate concrete concepts applying each principle to the UX context.
Evaluate concepts and test the most promising with users.
outputs: Explicit contradiction statements, candidate principles, generated concepts and evaluated solutions.
useWhen: Design problems framed as trade-offs between desirable qualities.
avoidWhen: Problems that are not contradictions but simply unknown needs; do discovery research first.
whyLost: TRIZ is popular in engineering and manufacturing innovation but its matrix is mechanical-engineering flavoured and unfamiliar to designers.
whereToUse: Security versus convenience, personalisation versus privacy, feature richness versus simplicity, speed versus accuracy in AI.
example: Faced with 'stronger authentication worsens login ease', TRIZ separation in condition (principle: local quality) leads to risk-based authentication: strong checks only when signals are unusual, frictionless otherwise.
sources: Altshuller, Creativity as an Exact Science (1984)
Altshuller, 40 Principles: TRIZ Keys to Technical Innovation (1997)
Savransky, Engineering of Creativity: Introduction to TRIZ Methodology (2000)
reference: Altshuller, G. S. (1984). Creativity as an Exact Science. Gordon and Breach.

name: Trust in Automation Scale (Jian et al.)
aka: Checklist for Trust between People and Automation
origin: Jiun-Yin Jian, Ann Bisantz and Colin Drury, 2000; trust calibration theory from Lee and See, 2004
summary: A 12-item empirically derived scale measuring trust and distrust in automated systems, used with reliability data to assess whether trust is calibrated.
description: Jian, Bisantz and Drury derived their scale empirically from word-elicitation and cluster studies, yielding 12 items on a 7-point scale covering deception, suspicion, harmful outcomes, confidence, integrity, dependability and familiarity. Lee and See's theory adds that trust should be calibrated: matched to the actual reliability of the automation. Rigorous use therefore pairs the scale with objective measures of system reliability and of reliance behaviour (acceptance of correct and incorrect recommendations). Over-trust appears as accepting wrong advice; under-trust as rejecting correct advice. This turns 'do users trust our AI?' into 'is their trust appropriate?', which is the question that matters.
steps: Define the automation's actual reliability on the task set, including a planned proportion of errors (e.g. 10-30%).
Administer the 12-item scale before and after exposure, and at intervals in longitudinal studies.
Log reliance behaviour: agreement with correct suggestions, agreement with incorrect suggestions, verification actions.
Compute calibration: compare trust scores and reliance rates with actual reliability; plot trust trajectories after errors.
Test design interventions such as confidence displays or explanations for their effect on calibration, not just trust level.
Report over-reliance and under-reliance rates alongside the scale score.
outputs: Trust and distrust scores, reliance rates on correct and incorrect advice, calibration plots and the effect of design changes.
useWhen: Evaluating AI recommendations, copilots, autopilot-like features or any system whose output users must accept or reject.
avoidWhen: Systems without automated recommendations; use general satisfaction or credibility measures instead.
whyLost: AI product teams measure trust as a single satisfaction-like rating to maximise, ignoring calibration. The human factors literature on reliance is rarely cited in product research.
whereToUse: LLM assistants, medical AI, fraud scoring, navigation, autonomous vehicles.
example: A radiology AI shows a confidence bar. Trust scores rise with the bar, but acceptance of incorrect AI findings also rises from 18% to 31%; the team redesigns to show uncertainty regions instead, improving calibration.
sources: Jian, Bisantz & Drury, Foundations for an empirically determined scale of trust in automated systems (2000), International Journal of Cognitive Ergonomics
Lee & See, Trust in automation: Designing for appropriate reliance (2004), Human Factors
reference: Jian, J.-Y., Bisantz, A. M., & Drury, C. G. (2000). International Journal of Cognitive Ergonomics, 4(1), 53-71.

name: TURF Analysis
origin: Media audience research (1950s-60s); product line application by Miaoulis, Free and Parsons (1990)
summary: Finds the combination of items (features, plans, content) that reaches the largest number of users at least once, rather than the individually most popular items.
description: Ranking items by popularity often picks items liked by the same people. TURF asks which portfolio of k items maximises unduplicated reach: the proportion of respondents for whom at least one item is appealing, with frequency as a secondary measure. Computation is combinatorial (exhaustive for small sets, greedy or optimisation for larger). Inputs can be survey acceptability, MaxDiff utilities with thresholds or behavioural usage. It is useful for deciding bundles, menu items, plan features or which content to commission, especially where breadth of appeal matters more than average preference.
steps: Collect per-respondent acceptability for each candidate item (binary or thresholded from MaxDiff utilities).
Define the portfolio size k or a cost constraint.
Compute reach and frequency for all combinations (or use greedy/optimised search for large sets).
Examine the incremental reach curve to see diminishing returns as k grows.
Check robustness with bootstrap resamples and segment-level reach.
Choose the portfolio balancing reach, frequency, cost and strategic fit.
outputs: Optimal portfolios with reach and frequency, incremental reach curves and segment reach.
useWhen: Selecting bundles, plan features, default content, templates or onboarding paths to maximise breadth of appeal.
avoidWhen: When intensity of preference or revenue matters more than reach; use conjoint simulations.
whyLost: It is a marketing media tool unfamiliar in product research; roadmaps prioritise by average score.
whereToUse: Template galleries, starter plans, content commissioning, notification types, food or retail assortments.
example: A presentation app chooses 8 starter templates from 40. The top 8 by popularity reach 64% of users; the TURF-optimal set reaches 86% by including two niche templates for educators and sales.
sources: Miaoulis, Free & Parsons, TURF: A new planning approach for product line extensions (1990), Marketing Research
Orme, Getting Started with Conjoint Analysis (4th ed., 2019)
Feature Prioritization Methods (slide deck)
reference: Miaoulis, G., Free, V., & Parsons, H. (1990). TURF: A new planning approach for product line extensions. Marketing Research, 2(1), 28-40.

name: Tversky Contrast Model (Asymmetric Similarity)
origin: Amos Tversky, 1977
summary: Measures similarity judgements in both directions to reveal which interface or concept users treat as the prototype, using Tversky's feature-matching model of common and distinctive features.
description: Tversky's contrast model treats similarity as a weighted function of common features minus each object's distinctive features, rather than a symmetric distance in a geometric space. Because the weights differ, similarity is often asymmetric: people say a variant resembles the prototype more than the prototype resembles the variant. The direction of the asymmetry reveals which item functions as the reference. Applied to UX, asking 'how similar is our app to X?' and 'how similar is X to our app?' separately reveals whether users treat a competitor, a legacy system or a familiar convention as the standard against which new designs are judged. Feature listing then identifies which shared and distinctive features drive judgements. The method was briefly used in early HCI similarity research and has largely disappeared.
steps: Present pairs of interface elements.
Ask 'does A resemble B?' then 'does B resemble A?' Measure asymmetry.
Large asymmetry reveals the prototype.
Redesign unfamiliar elements toward the prototype direction.
outputs: Directional similarity ratings, asymmetry indices, identification of the reference prototype, and weighted common and distinctive feature lists.
useWhen: Positioning a redesign against a legacy system or competitor, deciding which conventions to keep, and understanding brand or interface prototypes.
avoidWhen: When you need fine-grained usability findings or when the products are unfamiliar to participants; use card sorting or preference testing instead.
whyLost: Multidimensional scaling and later preference testing displaced feature-based similarity research in HCI, and the asymmetric-question protocol was never packaged as a UX method.
whereToUse: Mental model research, migration UX, icon family design.
example: A bank redesigning its legacy desktop banking asks customers both directions; the new design is rated as resembling the old more than the reverse. Feature listing shows the account summary table is the anchor, so it is preserved while navigation changes.
sources: Preference, Belief, and Similarity — Amos Tversky
Tversky, Features of similarity (Psychological Review, 1977)
reference: Tversky A (1977) Features of similarity. Psychological Review 84(4):327-352

name: UEQ (User Experience Questionnaire)
origin: Bettina Laugwitz, Theo Held and Martin Schrepp, SAP, 2008
summary: A 26-item semantic differential measuring six UX dimensions (attractiveness, perspicuity, efficiency, dependability, stimulation, novelty) with a public benchmark dataset.
description: The UEQ was developed at SAP through a data-driven process: a large pool of word pairs was reduced by factor analysis to 26 seven-point items forming six scales. Attractiveness is an overall valence; perspicuity, efficiency and dependability capture pragmatic quality; stimulation and novelty capture hedonic quality. A free analysis spreadsheet computes scale means, reliability and comparison with a benchmark of several hundred products, classifying results from 'bad' to 'excellent'. An 8-item short form (UEQ-S) suits in-product use, and UEQ+ allows modular scales. Rigour comes from using official translations, checking item consistency to detect careless responses, reporting confidence intervals, and using the benchmark to interpret values rather than arbitrary thresholds.
steps: Choose UEQ (26 items), UEQ-S (8 items) or a UEQ+ configuration based on respondent burden and dimensions of interest.
Administer after use, using an official translation for non-English audiences.
Collect at least 20-30 responses per product or version for stable scale estimates.
Use the official analysis tool to compute scale means, confidence intervals and Cronbach's alpha, and flag inconsistent respondents.
Compare with the UEQ benchmark to classify each scale.
Track scales across releases and pair low scales with qualitative research to explain them.
outputs: Six scale scores with confidence intervals, benchmark classification, release-to-release comparisons.
useWhen: Holistic UX evaluation, comparing design alternatives or releases, and international studies needing validated translations.
avoidWhen: When only perceived usability matters and benchmark comparability with SUS is needed; or for very short in-product surveys use UMUX-Lite or UEQ-S.
whyLost: Siloed: More comprehensive than SUS; academic origin; growing adoption in Europe.
whereToUse: Holistic UX evaluation; comparing design alternatives; longitudinal UX tracking.
example: An HR software vendor ran UEQ with 60 customers before and after a redesign. Efficiency moved from 'below average' to 'good' against the benchmark, but novelty stayed low, which the team accepted for a work tool.
sources: Measuring the User Experience
Construction and Evaluation of a User Experience Questionnaire (Laugwitz, Held & Schrepp)
reference: Laugwitz, B., Held, T., & Schrepp, M. (2008). Construction and evaluation of a user experience questionnaire. In USAB 2008, LNCS 5298 (pp. 63-76). Springer.

name: UMAP
origin: Leland McInnes, John Healy and James Melville, 2018
summary: Projects high-dimensional behavioural or text embeddings into two dimensions to visualise structure, clusters and outliers in user populations.
description: UMAP, listed in the treatise's borrowing matrix for machine learning, is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method that preserves local neighbourhood structure and more global structure than t-SNE. Applied to user feature vectors, session embeddings or embedded open-text responses, it produces maps where similar users or comments sit together, revealing clusters, continua and rare groups. For UX it is an exploratory instrument: it suggests segments and edge cases to investigate qualitatively. Rigour requires caution: distances between clusters and cluster sizes are not reliably meaningful, results depend on hyperparameters (n_neighbors, min_dist), and clusters should be confirmed with a separate method (for example HDBSCAN plus stability checks).
steps: Build feature vectors per user or session, or embed text with a language model.
Scale features and choose hyperparameters; run several settings.
Project to 2D and colour by known attributes (plan, tenure, outcome).
Cluster in the embedding or original space and test stability across seeds.
Sample users from clusters and outliers for qualitative follow-up.
Document caveats about interpreting distances.
outputs: 2D behavioural maps, candidate clusters and outliers, sampling frames for qualitative work.
useWhen: Exploratory analysis of large behavioural or feedback datasets to find unexpected groups.
avoidWhen: As evidence of segment size or distance; use confirmatory clustering or modelling.
whyLost: New and ML-native; UX teams lack the data science pairing the treatise recommends.
whereToUse: Feature usage exploration, LLM conversation log exploration, survey verbatim mapping.
example: Embedding 50,000 AI assistant prompts and mapping them with UMAP reveals a dense island of spreadsheet formula requests, a use case the team had not designed for.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
McInnes L, Healy J & Melville J (2018) UMAP: Uniform manifold approximation and projection for dimension reduction. arXiv:1802.03426
Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Space and Time (Marc Leordeanu)
McInnes, Healy & Melville (2018) UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for dimension reduction
Pattern Recognition & ML (Bishop)
Unsupervised Learning in Time & Space
The Inquiry Series, Ch 52 — Dimensionality Reduction — The Geometry of Behavioral Space
reference: McInnes L, Healy J & Melville J (2018) UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction. arXiv:1802.03426.

name: UMAP visualisation
origin: Leland McInnes, John Healy and James Melville, 2018
summary: Projecting high-dimensional behavioural or text-embedding features into two dimensions to see clusters and gradients among users, sessions or responses.
description: UMAP builds a weighted nearest-neighbour graph in the original feature space and finds a low-dimensional layout preserving its structure. It is faster than t-SNE and preserves more global structure, making it useful for visually inspecting behavioural segments or semantic clusters of open-text responses. Its key parameters are n_neighbors (local versus global emphasis, typically 15-50) and min_dist (how tightly points pack). Rigour comes from treating UMAP as exploratory: distances and cluster sizes in the plot are not directly interpretable, apparent clusters can be artefacts of parameters, and results vary with the random seed. Clusters should be confirmed with a model fitted in the original space and checked across several parameter settings.
steps: Prepare a standardised feature matrix or sentence embeddings and remove near-duplicate rows.
Run UMAP with default parameters (n_neighbors 15, min_dist 0.1) and a fixed random seed.
Repeat with n_neighbors of 5, 30 and 50 and at least three seeds, keeping only structure that persists.
Colour points by known variables (plan type, tenure, GMM segment, sentiment) to interpret regions.
Confirm apparent clusters with a model fitted in the original space (GMM, HDBSCAN) and report its fit statistics, not the picture.
Annotate plots with caveats that axes and distances are not meaningful.
outputs: Two-dimensional maps of users, sessions or texts, stability checks across parameters, and hypotheses about clusters to test formally.
useWhen: Exploring large behavioural or text-embedding datasets, communicating segment structure, and checking whether a clustering solution looks plausible.
avoidWhen: Avoid as evidence of cluster existence or for measuring distances between groups; use clustering with fit indices or LDA instead. For small datasets under a few hundred points, PCA is usually clearer.
whyLost: UMAP is recent and lives in bioinformatics and machine learning; UX teams rarely work with high-dimensional feature matrices directly.
whereToUse: Behavioural persona discovery, open-ended feedback mapping, AI product prompt clustering and support-ticket analysis.
example: An AI writing assistant team embeds 40,000 user prompts and projects them with UMAP. A stable region of 'formal email rewrite' prompts emerges across parameter settings and is confirmed by HDBSCAN, guiding a new template feature.
sources: lifelines (survival)
scikit-learn (GMM, LDA, UMAP)
pandas (log parsing)
matplotlib
plotly
McInnes, L., Healy, J. & Melville, J. (2018) UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction. arXiv:1802.03426
The Inquiry Series, C4 — Behavioural Log Analysis — From Clickstreams to Personas
reference: McInnes, L., Healy, J. & Melville, J. (2018) UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction. arXiv:1802.03426

name: UMUX (Usability Metric for User Experience)
origin: Kraig Finstad (2010), Intel
summary: A four-item questionnaire aligned with the ISO definition of usability that tracks SUS closely with less than half the items.
description: Finstad designed the UMUX to give a SUS-like score with fewer items that map to the ISO 9241-11 definition (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction). Its four 7-point items are: this system's capabilities meet my requirements; using this system is a frustrating experience; this system is easy to use; I have to spend too much time correcting things with this system. Items alternate tone. Each is recoded to 0 to 6, summed, divided by 24 and multiplied by 100. In validation with 558 users of two systems, reliability was 0.94 and correlation with SUS was 0.96. The two positive items later became the UMUX-Lite.
steps: Administer the four items on 7-point agreement scales.
Recode positive items as response minus 1 and negative items as 7 minus response.
Sum the four, divide by 24 and multiply by 100.
Compare with SUS norms, which the UMUX closely tracks.
Report means with confidence intervals.
outputs: A 0 to 100 perceived usability score comparable to SUS.
useWhen: You need a SUS-comparable score in very little survey space.
avoidWhen: You can only ask two items (use UMUX-Lite) or need diagnostic subscales.
whyLost: Not lost; it has largely been superseded by its own two-item UMUX-Lite.
whereToUse: In-product surveys, large-scale tracking, enterprise IT satisfaction.
example: An internal IT portal scores 58 on UMUX, close to its SUS of 60, letting the team switch to the shorter instrument without losing comparability.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Finstad, K. (2010). The usability metric for user experience. Interacting with Computers 22(5).

name: UMUX-Lite
origin: James Lewis, Brian Utesch and Deborah Maher, 2013
summary: A two-item usability questionnaire (capabilities meet requirements; easy to use) that correlates strongly with SUS and suits in-product micro-surveys.
description: UMUX-Lite derives from Finstad's four-item UMUX, keeping two positively worded items: 'This system's capabilities meet my requirements' and 'This system is easy to use', rated on seven-point scales. The two items map to the usefulness and ease-of-use constructs of the Technology Acceptance Model. Lewis and colleagues showed scores correlate highly with SUS and provided a regression adjustment to place UMUX-Lite on the SUS scale, enabling comparison with SUS norms. Its brevity makes it practical for continuous in-product measurement where a full questionnaire would suppress response rates. Rigour comes from using exact wording and scale points, applying the published conversion consistently, collecting enough responses (typically hundreds in-product) and accounting for sampling bias in who responds to intercept surveys.
steps: Use the exact two items on seven-point agreement scales.
Trigger the survey at a meaningful moment, such as after task completion, and sample users randomly to reduce bias.
Compute the raw score ((sum of items minus 2) / 12 × 100).
Apply the published regression adjustment to estimate a SUS-equivalent score if comparison with SUS norms is needed.
Report means with confidence intervals and segment by user type or feature.
Track scores over time and investigate drops with qualitative follow-up.
outputs: UMUX-Lite scores (raw and SUS-equivalent), trends over time, segment comparisons.
useWhen: Continuous in-product usability measurement, high-volume intercept surveys and dashboards tracking perceived usability over time.
avoidWhen: Lab studies where SUS is just as easy to administer and gives more stable estimates with small samples, or when you need diagnostic detail.
whyLost: Still in use: Minimal friction; good for in-product surveys at scale.
whereToUse: In-product NPS/usability measurement; continuous UX monitoring.
example: A project management SaaS added UMUX-Lite after report creation, collecting 1,800 responses a month. A drop from 78 to 69 SUS-equivalent after a release pointed to the new filter panel, confirmed in follow-up interviews.
sources: Measuring the User Experience
UMUX-LITE: When there's no time for the SUS (Lewis, Utesch & Maher)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
Companion Book to Quantifying the User Experience (Lewis & Sauro)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: Lewis, J. R., Utesch, B. S., & Maher, D. E. (2013). UMUX-LITE: When there's no time for the SUS. Proceedings of CHI 2013, 2099-2102.

name: Unmoderated Remote Testing
origin: Remote usability testing research, late 1990s; commercial platforms such as UserTesting (2007)
summary: Participants complete tasks on their own devices without a facilitator, recording screens and think-aloud, allowing fast, larger and geographically diverse samples.
description: Unmoderated remote testing uses an online platform to deliver tasks and questions to participants who complete them on their own, in their own environment and time. Sessions may record screen, audio and face, along with task success, time and post-task ratings. Because no facilitator is needed, tests can run in hours with dozens of participants across regions. The trade-off is the loss of real-time probing and clarification, so study design must anticipate misunderstandings. Rigour comes from unambiguous task wording, clear success criteria and validation questions, screening for attentive and representative participants, piloting, and combining behavioural metrics with recordings rather than relying on self-reported success.
steps: Define tasks, success criteria and post-task questions such as the Single Ease Question.
Write self-explanatory task instructions and include validation questions to confirm success.
Set screening criteria and recruit from a panel or your own users.
Pilot with 2 to 3 participants and fix confusing instructions.
Launch with 10 to 20 participants for qualitative insight, or 30 or more for metrics.
Review recordings and exclude low-quality sessions with documented criteria.
Analyse success, time, ratings and clips, and report findings.
outputs: Task success, time and ease ratings, recordings and highlight clips, and a list of observed problems.
useWhen: For iterative validation, quick comparisons, geographically diverse users and when you need moderate samples quickly.
avoidWhen: Avoid for complex or sensitive tasks, early concepts that need explanation, or specialist users who are hard to recruit on panels; use moderated testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Speed and scale advantage; widely adopted during/after COVID-19 shift to remote.
whereToUse: Iterative design; quick validation; when geographic diversity is needed.
example: A travel booking site tests a new date picker with 30 panel participants in two days. Recordings show 40 percent select the wrong return date on mobile, prompting a fix before release.
sources: UX Research
Rocket Surgery Made Easy
Beyond the Usability Lab (Albert, Tullis & Tedesco)
Benchmarking the User Experience (Sauro)
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
reference: Albert, W., Tullis, T. & Tedesco, D. (2010). Beyond the Usability Lab: Conducting Large-Scale Online User Experience Studies. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Unobtrusive Measures (Physical Traces and Archives)
origin: Eugene Webb, Donald Campbell, Richard Schwartz and Lee Sechrest, 1966 (Unobtrusive Measures)
summary: Infers behaviour from traces people leave without being studied (wear, accumulations, archives, workarounds), avoiding reactivity of interviews and observation.
description: Webb and colleagues catalogued nonreactive measures: erosion (wear on floor tiles in front of exhibits indicating popularity), accretion (fingerprints on glass, notes stuck to monitors), running records (archives, logs) and episodic records. Their argument for multiple operationalism held that every method has biases, and nonreactive traces triangulate reactive self-reports. In digital UX, logs are the obvious descendant, but physical and informal traces (sticky notes with passwords, laminated cheat sheets, printouts, home-made labels on devices, worn keys) are rich, unreactive evidence of design failures and workarounds, routinely overlooked.
steps: Identify the behaviours of interest and brainstorm traces they would leave (physical, digital, documentary).
Seek access to settings and archives ethically, including consent where traces are personal.
Systematically document traces with photographs, counts and location, using a coding scheme.
Assess biases of each trace (selective survival, deposit bias) as Webb et al. recommend.
Triangulate traces with interviews and logs.
Interpret traces as evidence of needs, workarounds and design failures.
outputs: A documented trace inventory, coded counts, and triangulated interpretations of behaviour and workarounds.
useWhen: Studying real practice where self-report may be biased, or where observation would change behaviour.
avoidWhen: When traces cannot be ethically accessed or interpreted without context.
whyLost: Digital analytics absorbed the 'running records' idea, while physical trace research disappeared from UX practice.
whereToUse: Workplace software rollouts, clinical settings, kiosks and public devices, home technology, shared devices.
example: A hospital audit photographs workstations and finds 63% have handwritten notes with EHR shortcuts or login workarounds. These traces drive a redesign of the most-annotated workflows.
sources: Webb, Campbell, Schwartz & Sechrest, Unobtrusive Measures: Nonreactive Research in the Social Sciences (1966)
Lee, Unobtrusive Methods in Social Research (2000)
Yin, R., Qualitative Research from Start to Finish, 2nd ed. (2016)
Gratton, C. & Jones, I., Research Methods for Sports Studies (2010)
Veal, A. J. & Darcy, S., Research Methods in Sport Studies and Sport Management (2014)
reference: Webb, E. J., Campbell, D. T., Schwartz, R. D., & Sechrest, L. (1966). Unobtrusive Measures. Rand McNally.

name: Unreachable state detection
origin: Reachability analysis in model checking, Clarke, Emerson and Sifakis, 1980s; applied to interactive systems by Thimbleby and Harrison
summary: Systematically explores an interface's state space to find states that cannot be reached and, conversely, critical actions that cannot be reached from some states.
description: Reachability asks two questions of a state model: can every intended state be reached from the start state, and can every critical state (home, stop, cancel, save) be reached from every other state within an acceptable number of steps? Unreachable intended states signal dead features or specification errors; states from which a critical state is unreachable are traps. Analysis uses breadth-first search on a state graph or a model checker for large or concurrent systems, and reports shortest path lengths so designers can see not just whether but how quickly safety actions can be reached. Thimbleby's work on device graphs showed many real devices fail these checks. Rigour comes from a complete model, including timeouts and errors, and from automated, not visual, checking.
steps: Build or extract a state model of the interface (from specification, code or systematic exploration).
Define the start state(s) and critical target states (stop, home, undo, save, help).
Run breadth-first search or a model checker to compute reachability from start to all states and from all states to each critical state.
Report unreachable states and states lacking a path to each critical state, plus shortest-path lengths; flag any critical action needing more than 2 steps in safety contexts.
Review findings with designers and engineers to classify each as dead design, model error or real hazard.
Fix hazards and add automated reachability checks to the build or test pipeline.
outputs: Reachability matrix, list of unreachable and trap states, path-length distribution to critical actions, and regression checks.
useWhen: When the interface has many modes or states and safety or recoverability matters; when users report getting 'stuck'.
avoidWhen: When no reasonably complete state model can be built; use exploratory usability testing and dead-end identification on observed paths.
whyLost: Reachability is a staple of formal verification but UX teams rarely have state models to run it on, so the analysis remains in engineering and academic HCI.
whereToUse: Medical devices, surgical robots, automotive infotainment, kiosks, set-up wizards, and conversational agents.
example: Breadth-first search over a 340-state infusion pump model shows Emergency Stop needs 4 presses from the drug-library edit state. Adding a global stop key reduces it to 1 from every state.
sources: Weyers, B., Bowen, J., Dix, A. & Palanque, P. (eds), The Handbook of Formal Methods in Human-Computer Interaction (2017)
Handbook of Formal Methods in HCI
The Inquiry Series, Ch 5 — State, Transition & the Logic of Interaction
Hofstadter, D., Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid (1979)
Gödel Escher Bach (Hofstadter)
reference: Thimbleby, H. (2007). Press On: Principles of Interaction Programming. MIT Press.

name: Uplift Modelling
origin: Nicholas Radcliffe and Patrick Surry (1999); Victor Lo, 'The true lift model' (2002)
summary: Predicts the individual-level causal effect of an intervention from randomised data, to target users who will respond because of it, not regardless of it.
description: Response models predict who will convert; uplift models predict who will convert because they were treated. Users fall into four groups: persuadables, sure things, lost causes and 'sleeping dogs' who react negatively to treatment. Using randomised treatment and control data, uplift models (two-model approach, class transformation, uplift trees, meta-learners such as T-, S- and X-learners) estimate conditional treatment effects. Evaluation uses Qini or uplift curves on held-out data, not accuracy. In UX, uplift modelling identifies who should receive nudges, onboarding help or retention offers, and who would be harmed or annoyed by them.
steps: Run a randomised experiment of the intervention with a sufficiently large control group.
Prepare pre-treatment features for each user, avoiding any post-treatment variables.
Fit uplift models (e.g. two-model baseline, X-learner, uplift random forest) with cross-validation.
Evaluate with Qini coefficient and uplift curves on holdout data, comparing to random targeting.
Identify segments with negative uplift (sleeping dogs) and examine them qualitatively.
Deploy targeting with a persistent randomised holdout to confirm incremental impact.
outputs: Individual uplift scores, Qini curves, segment profiles including negatively affected users, targeting policy.
useWhen: Deciding whom to show prompts, offers, tutorials or interventions, given randomised data.
avoidWhen: Without randomised data, or with small samples; heterogeneous effect estimates are noisy.
whyLost: It stayed in marketing analytics, and UX experimentation focuses on average effects.
whereToUse: Retention offers, onboarding nudges, notification targeting, upsell prompts, health behaviour interventions.
example: A streaming service finds its 'come back' email has positive average effect, but uplift modelling shows 18% of recipients are sleeping dogs more likely to cancel when emailed; excluding them improves net retention.
sources: Radcliffe & Surry, Real-world uplift modelling with significance-based uplift trees (2011), Stochastic Solutions white paper
Lo, The true lift model (2002), ACM SIGKDD Explorations
Künzel et al., Metalearners for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects (2019), PNAS
reference: Lo, V. S. Y. (2002). The true lift model. ACM SIGKDD Explorations, 4(2), 78-86.

name: Usability Engineering Lifecycle (Mayhew)
origin: Deborah Mayhew, 1999
summary: Phase-gated process model integrating requirements analysis, conceptual and detailed design, evaluation and installation, with defined usability goals and deliverables.
description: Mayhew's lifecycle gave UX an engineering-level process model: a defined sequence of activities, deliverables and decision points that could integrate with software development at the rigour appropriate to safety-critical systems. Its phases cover requirements analysis (user profiles, contextual task analysis, platform constraints, general design principles, usability goals), design/testing/development across three levels (conceptual model, screen design standards, detailed UI) with iterative evaluation at each, and installation with user feedback. The treatise argues that what was lost when agile displaced it was the insistence that usability is a system requirement to be managed with the rigour of performance or reliability, especially the setting of measurable usability goals.
steps: Produce user profiles, contextual task analysis and platform capability analysis.
Set measurable qualitative and quantitative usability goals.
Design and evaluate a conceptual model through iterative testing.
Define and test screen design standards.
Develop detailed UI design and evaluate iteratively against goals.
Install, collect user feedback and feed it into the next cycle.
outputs: Usability goals, conceptual model, screen standards, evaluation reports, installation feedback.
useWhen: Large or safety-critical programmes needing explicit usability gates and goals.
avoidWhen: Fast-moving consumer products with continuous delivery, unless adapted to sprints.
whyLost: Its sequential, phase-gated structure clashed with agile, so the whole model was abandoned instead of adapted.
whereToUse: Medical device programmes, defence, public-sector digital transformation, enterprise ERP rollouts.
example: A national tax agency adapts Mayhew's usability goals into each programme increment, requiring 90% first-time completion on core filing tasks before release.
sources: Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Mayhew DJ (1999) The Usability Engineering Lifecycle: A Practitioner's Handbook for User Interface Design
reference: Mayhew DJ (1999) The Usability Engineering Lifecycle. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Usability Magnitude Estimation (UME)
origin: Cordes (1984); McGee (2003, 2004); from Stevens' magnitude estimation in psychophysics
summary: Asks participants to rate each task's difficulty as a ratio of a baseline task, aiming for ratio-scale usability measurement.
description: Magnitude estimation comes from psychophysics, where people judge stimulus intensity relative to a reference (twice as bright, half as loud). Applied to usability, participants first complete an easy baseline task assigned a value (for example 10), then rate each later task relative to it, so a task rated 40 is judged four times as difficult. The goal is a ratio scale, where differences and ratios are meaningful. Participants usually need training with simple stimuli such as line lengths, and analysis uses log transformation and geometric means. Sauro and Dumas (2009) found UME was harder for participants to use and less sensitive than the SEQ or SMEQ, which is why it has largely disappeared from practice.
steps: Train participants on magnitude estimation with simple stimuli such as line lengths.
Have them complete a very easy baseline task and assign it a fixed value.
After each target task, ask for a number expressing its difficulty relative to the baseline.
Log-transform each participant's ratings to remove individual scale use.
Compare tasks using geometric means.
outputs: Ratio-scale difficulty estimates per task.
useWhen: Research contexts where ratio-level perception of difficulty is the question.
avoidWhen: Routine usability testing; the SEQ is easier and more sensitive.
whyLost: Training burden and participant confusion, and comparative studies showing simpler single items work better.
whereToUse: Academic measurement research, psychophysics-inspired UX studies.
example: With a baseline icon-selection task set at 10, participants rate "export a report" at 55 on average, more than five times as difficult.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
reference: McGee, M. (2003). Usability magnitude estimation. Proceedings of HFES 47.

name: Usability Testing
origin: Human factors labs, 1970s to 1980s; formalised by Dumas & Redish (1993) and Rubin (1994)
summary: Representative users attempt realistic tasks while researchers observe, revealing where and why the design causes difficulty and how severe each problem is.
description: Usability testing asks representative participants to attempt realistic tasks with a product or prototype while researchers observe behaviour, record difficulties and often collect think-aloud commentary. It can be formative, finding problems to fix during design, or summative, measuring task success, time and errors against targets. The underlying idea is that observed behaviour on real tasks is more trustworthy than opinion or expert prediction. Rigour comes from realistic task scenarios with defined success criteria, recruitment that matches the target users, a neutral and consistent moderation protocol, and severity ratings that combine frequency, impact and persistence. Small formative rounds of about five users per segment find most frequent problems, while summative benchmarks need larger samples and confidence intervals.
steps: Define research questions, target user segments and success criteria for each task.
Write 5 to 8 realistic task scenarios that avoid interface vocabulary and leading cues.
Recruit participants who match the target users, typically 5 to 8 per segment for formative rounds or 20 or more for summative measurement.
Pilot the protocol with one participant and fix ambiguous tasks.
Run sessions with a consistent script, observing behaviour and recording success, time, errors and comments.
Log each problem with evidence and rate severity by frequency, impact and persistence.
Report prioritised problems with recommendations and retest after redesign.
outputs: A prioritised list of usability problems with severity ratings and evidence clips, plus task success, time-on-task and error metrics.
useWhen: When you need to know whether real users can complete key tasks and where they struggle, from early prototypes to pre-launch builds.
avoidWhen: Avoid for questions about needs, motivations or market demand; use interviews or field studies. For measuring causal impact at scale, use A/B testing.
whyLost: Still in use: Gold standard for usability validation; supported by decades of evidence and widely understood by stakeholders.
whereToUse: Pre-launch validation; iterative design cycles; redesign projects.
example: Before launching a new loan application flow, a fintech team tests it with six first-time borrowers. Four fail to find how to upload proof of income, a severity-one problem fixed and verified in a second round.
sources: Handbook of Usability Testing
Rocket Surgery Made Easy
How to Conduct a Quantitative Usability Test (Sauro)
Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Rubin, J. & Chisnell, D. (2008). Handbook of Usability Testing (2nd ed.). Wiley.

name: Use Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (UFMEA)
aka: Usability Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (UFMEA)
origin: FMEA from US military reliability engineering (1949); adapted for usability by Desurvire (1992) per the treatise
summary: Enumerates every way a user could fail at each task step, rating severity, occurrence and detectability to produce a ranked, falsifiable usability risk register.
description: FMEA identifies potential failure points before they occur. UFMEA applies this to use: for each task step, analysts list possible use errors, their causes and effects, and rate severity, occurrence and detection (typically 1-10 each) to compute a risk priority number. The treatise highlights that UFMEA is one of the few UX methods producing a falsifiable risk register: predictions about where failures will occur that can be validated against later testing and field data. It is especially valuable in medical, aviation and financial products where failures matter beyond inconvenience, and it aligns with use-related risk analysis required by IEC 62366 for medical devices. Rated HIGH recovery priority.
steps: Build a task analysis (for example HTA) of the critical user workflows.
For each step, brainstorm failure modes using error taxonomies (slips, lapses, mistakes).
Record cause, effect and existing controls for every failure mode.
Rate severity, occurrence and detectability, and compute a risk priority number or use a risk matrix.
Design mitigations for the highest-risk modes and re-rate residual risk.
