name: Video Confessional Booth
donor: Reality television testimonials, adapted by a learning-games studio
origin: NMSU Learning Games Lab (Chamberlin and colleagues), described in Chapter 3
summary: A small private room with a self-operated camera where participants record their answers to a written question, alone and in their own time.
description: The video closet was inspired by the testimonials in reality television shows. A small closet holds a mounted camera and a whiteboard with one specific question written on it. The participant enters alone, thinks about the question, and starts and stops the recording with a remote control when ready. Because no researcher is present, it reduces the social pressure that shapes answers in interviews and group discussions, and it gives quieter or introverted participants a way to say things they would not say in front of peers. The Learning Games Lab found it works best in combination with other methods: participants gave richer answers after a group discussion or after writing their thoughts in a blog, because they had already organised their ideas. Videos are rarely transcribed. Instead they are used to clarify observers' notes and, above all, as vivid evidence for developers and clients, shared through an internal site. Regular use, even when nothing is being tested, helps participants become comfortable on camera. For UX teams it is a cheap way to collect candid, quotable reflections in a lab or event setting.
steps: Set up a small, quiet space with a fixed camera, a microphone and a remote or button the participant controls.
Write one clear, specific question on a board in view of the camera.
Prime participants first with another activity, such as play, a group discussion or a short written reflection.
Let each participant enter alone, think, and record their answer when ready, as many takes as they like.
Collect the clips, tag them by question, product version and participant code, and restrict access to the research and development team.
Review clips to clarify observations and select excerpts to show developers or clients.
outputs: Short, candid video answers to targeted questions, used as qualitative evidence and as clips for stakeholder communication.
useWhen: Participants may be shy in groups, you want unmoderated reflection after hands-on sessions, or you need compelling clips for stakeholders.
avoidWhen: Participants are uncomfortable being filmed, consent for video cannot be obtained, or you need probing follow-up questions.
whyLost: Most UX teams rely on moderated interviews or remote video tools and seldom build a dedicated private recording space.
whereToUse: Games and edtech labs, youth panels, on-site research events, conference or retail intercept research.
example: After a group discussion about a new maths game, each 12-year-old tester goes into the closet and answers 'What would make you want to keep playing this game?'; the developers watch several clips that all mention the confusing fail condition.
sources: Garcia-Ruiz, M. (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach (2016)
reference: Chamberlin, B., Trespalacios, J. H., Muise, A. S. and Garza, M. C. (2016). User testing in the Learning Games Lab: getting valuable feedback through frequent formative evaluation. In M. A. Garcia-Ruiz (ed.), Games User Research: A Case Study Approach, Chapter 3. Boca Raton, FL: A K Peters / CRC Press.

name: Video-Reflexive Ethnography
origin: Rick Iedema, Katherine Carroll and colleagues, 2000s (Visualising Health Care Practice Improvement, 2013)
summary: Records participants' real practice on video and plays selected clips back to them, individually or in groups, to surface tacit knowledge and collectively reflect on how practice could change.
description: Video-reflexive ethnography (Iedema, Carroll, Collier) involves collecting video recordings of participants in their natural practice, then showing those recordings back to participants or groups to stimulate discussion and collaborative analysis. It is particularly powerful for: accessing tacit, embodied, and procedural knowledge that participants cannot easily describe verbally; stimulating collective reflection and learning in workplace settings; and revealing what is 'seen but unnoticed' in practice.
steps: Video collection phase: Record participants in their natural practice with their knowledge and consent. Focus camera on the work activity rather than faces where possible — this shifts focus from person to practice.

Clip selection: From the recordings, select 3–6 clips of 1–3 minutes each. Select clips that illustrate: (a) typical practices, (b) moments of complexity or adaptation, (c) moments you want participants to reflect on.

Reflexive session: Play clips to participants (individually or in groups). Your role: facilitate observation, not evaluation. Opening prompt: 'What do you notice when you watch this?' Not: 'What did you do well or badly?'
Capture participant observations: What do participants see in the video that they weren't aware of during the activity? These moments of 'I didn't realise I was doing that' are your primary data.
Group reflexive sessions: Playing clips to groups generates collective reflection — participants compare practices, debate why things happened as they did, and negotiate shared understandings.
outputs: Practice video, selected clips with rationale, recorded reflexive discussions, participant-identified insights and improvement ideas, and documentation of tacit routines.
useWhen: Studying skilled or collaborative practice where people cannot describe what they do, and when you want practitioners to own the insights and change, as in clinical teams or operations.
avoidWhen: Consent to filming is not feasible or the setting is highly sensitive; use observation with field notes. For individual consumer tasks, a usability test with retrospective review is lighter.
whyLost: It developed in hospital quality improvement, and its participatory, change-oriented framing and filming logistics made it rare in commercial UX.
whereToUse: Clinical and care workflows, operations centres, retail and hospitality service, manufacturing, and teams adopting new tools or AI assistance.
example: A hospital pharmacy team watches clips of its own medication rounds. Nurses notice they repeatedly rescan wristbands because the scanner beep is inaudible, a problem none had raised in interviews, and the device team changes the feedback.
sources: When Words Fail Us (PMC 2024)
Video-Reflexive Ethnography — Carroll et al.
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
reference: Iedema, R., Mesman, J. & Carroll, K. (2013). Visualising Health Care Practice Improvement: Innovation from Within. Radcliffe.

name: Vignette Method and Factorial Survey
origin: Peter H. Rossi, 1970s (factorial survey approach)
summary: Presents systematically varied short scenarios and asks for judgements, revealing which factors drive decisions and attributions without asking people to explain their own reasoning.
description: People are poor at reporting which factors drive their judgements, but they judge concrete scenarios easily. The factorial survey exploits this: the researcher defines the judgement of interest and a set of dimensions (for example price, social proof, data requested, brand), generates vignettes by crossing their levels, and has each participant rate a random subset of 10 to 20. Because dimensions vary independently, multilevel regression estimates the causal weight of each factor on the judgement, controlling for respondent effects. Fractional designs keep the vignette universe manageable while preserving key effects. A short qualitative follow-up explores reasoning. Rigour comes from orthogonal design, randomisation of vignettes and order, plausible combinations, and analysis that respects the nested data structure.
steps: Define the target judgment: What decision, evaluation, or attribution are you investigating?
Identify experimental dimensions: What scenario characteristics do you want to vary? Each dimension should have 2–4 levels.
Generate vignettes by factorial combination. Use fractional factorial design for large parameter spaces.
Randomised presentation: Each participant sees 10–20 vignettes randomly selected. Rate or respond to each.
Analysis: Multilevel regression with rating as outcome and vignette characteristics as predictors. Coefficients reveal which characteristics significantly influence judgments.
Qualitative follow-up: After the rating task, interview participants about their reasoning on selected vignettes.
outputs: A vignette universe and design matrix, ratings data, multilevel model estimates of each factor's effect, interaction effects, and qualitative accounts of reasoning.
useWhen: You want to know how users weigh factors in a judgement such as trust, fairness, willingness to share data or acceptability of an AI decision, especially where direct questions would produce socially desirable answers.
avoidWhen: You can observe real behaviour with a live A/B test, or the decision depends heavily on context a short vignette cannot convey. For product attribute trade-offs with prices, conjoint analysis may be a better fit.
whyLost: It sits between survey methodology and experimental design, needs design and multilevel modelling skills, and UX borrowed conjoint from market research instead.
whereToUse: AI fairness and explainability perception, trust and safety policy, privacy and consent decisions, pricing fairness, and content moderation judgements.
example: A lender varies AI loan-denial explanations across four dimensions (reason specificity, appeal option, human review mention, tone). Across 400 respondents, offering an appeal route raises perceived fairness more than specificity does, shaping the explanation design.
sources: Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods
Research Methods for Everyday Life
Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Collection (Flick)
Auspurg, K. & Hinz, T. (2015) Factorial Survey Experiments
reference: Rossi, P. H. & Nock, S. L. (eds.) (1982). Measuring Social Judgments: The Factorial Survey Approach. Sage.

name: Virtual environments
origin: Python virtualenv (Ian Bicking, 2007); venv in the standard library (PEP 405, 2011); conda (Anaconda, 2012)
summary: Isolating each research project's interpreter and libraries so that analyses run with known package versions and do not break when other projects update.
description: A virtual environment is a self-contained interpreter plus library set scoped to one project. Without it, upgrading pandas or scikit-learn for one study can silently change results in another, for example by altering default parameters in factor analysis or clustering. The rigour comes from one environment per project, created from a declared specification file, and from never installing packages ad hoc into the base interpreter. conda additionally manages non-Python binaries such as ffmpeg or CUDA libraries, which matters for transcription and transformer models. Combined with a lockfile, an environment lets a colleague or reviewer recreate the exact computational instrument used for an analysis months later.
steps: Create one environment per project (python -m venv .venv or conda create -n project python=3.11) at project start.
Record every dependency in a specification file (requirements.txt, pyproject.toml or environment.yml) rather than installing ad hoc.
Pin exact versions for anything that affects results (pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, statsmodels, factor_analyzer) once analysis begins.
Never install into the base or system interpreter; activate the project environment before every session.
Rebuild the environment from the specification file on a clean machine or container at least once before reporting results.
Register the environment as a named Jupyter kernel so notebooks cannot accidentally run under a different interpreter.
outputs: A per-project environment, a committed environment specification and a named kernel for notebooks.
useWhen: Every Python-based UX analysis, especially those using statistical or machine learning libraries whose defaults change between versions.
avoidWhen: Unnecessary for no-code analysis in SPSS or spreadsheets; there, document the software version and syntax instead.
whyLost: UX researchers rarely came from software backgrounds and analysis tools were GUI-based, so environment isolation never became part of UX training.
whereToUse: Quant UX teams, research operations, transcription and NLP pipelines with heavy binary dependencies, and long-running tracking studies.
example: A health app team reruns a 2024 SUS benchmark in 2026 and gets different factor loadings. Rebuilding the original pinned environment shows the difference came from a library default change, not from users.
sources: Python (pandas, numpy, pathlib)
Jupyter Lab
Git
conda/venv
cookiecutter project templates
Wilson, G. et al. (2017) Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLOS Computational Biology
The Inquiry Series, C1 — The Python Research Environment — Setup, Philosophy & Reproducibility
reference: Python Software Foundation (2011) PEP 405: Python Virtual Environments

name: Visual Search Paradigm Testing
origin: Anne Treisman and Garry Gelade, 1980 (feature integration theory); Jeremy Wolfe's Guided Search (1994)
summary: Measures response time to find a target as a function of the number of distractors, revealing whether a design element pops out or requires serial search.
description: In a visual search experiment, participants find a target among distractors while set size varies. If response time does not increase with set size (slope near 0 ms per item), the target pops out through parallel feature processing; slopes of 20-40 ms per item on target-present trials suggest serial, effortful search. Target-absent trials show how long users take to give up. Applied to UX, these slopes quantify the findability of icons, badges, alerts and status markers under realistic clutter, and test whether a design element truly guides attention as intended. It is more diagnostic than eye-tracking heatmaps because it isolates the attentional mechanism.
steps: Define the target element and distractors from the real interface (e.g. an error badge among other badges).
Create displays at several set sizes (e.g. 4, 8, 16, 32 items), with target present on half the trials.
Run participants on many trials (e.g. 200+) with randomised positions, recording response time and accuracy.
Fit linear regressions of RT on set size for present and absent trials; compute slopes and intercepts.
Compare design variants: a good salient design shows near-flat slopes and low error rates.
Confirm in the full interface context with a smaller task-based test.
outputs: Search slopes and intercepts, error rates and a classification of elements as pop-out or serial-search.
useWhen: Designing alerts, status indicators, icons and badges that must be found quickly in cluttered displays.
avoidWhen: Questions of meaning, preference or navigation strategy; use semantic or usability methods.
whyLost: Experimental psychology paradigms are rarely adapted to product questions, and teams rely on saliency heuristics or heatmaps.
whereToUse: Dashboards, monitoring displays, map pins, notification badges, inventory grids.
example: A monitoring dashboard tests three error indicators. A red outline yields a 28 ms/item slope while a red fill plus motion yields 3 ms/item, so the latter is adopted for critical alerts.
sources: Treisman & Gelade, A feature-integration theory of attention (1980), Cognitive Psychology
Wolfe, Guided Search 2.0 (1994), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review
Wolfe & Horowitz, Five factors that guide attention in visual search (2017), Nature Human Behaviour
reference: Treisman, A. M., & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.

name: Voice and Tone Framework with Decision Matrix
origin: Mailchimp's Voice and Tone guide (Kate Kiefer Lee, 2011); research-based treatment by Erica Jorgensen (2023)
summary: Defines a constant brand voice and maps user emotional state and task type to tone settings, then tests tone choices with users rather than relying on brand intuition.
description: Voice is who the product is and stays constant; tone adapts to the situation. A decision matrix makes this operational: rows are situations defined by user emotional state (anxious, frustrated, neutral, celebrating) and task type (error, payment, onboarding, success), and cells specify tone settings along dimensions such as formal to casual, direct to empathetic, and brief to detailed, with example strings. Jorgensen emphasises testing tone with users: comprehension and perceived appropriateness surveys, A/B tests on key messages, and analysis of support contacts, because what a brand team finds charming may feel flippant to someone whose payment failed. The matrix becomes a shared decision tool for writers, designers and AI-generated content prompts.
steps: Build a tone decision matrix: rows = user emotional states (anxious, excited, frustrated, neutral, confused), columns = task types (onboarding, error recovery, success, routine action, high-stakes decision). For each cell, specify:
vocabulary register,
sentence length,
active/passive voice ratio,
use of first/second person. Validate: show content examples to users in each context and measure: does the tone match the moment?
outputs: Voice attributes, a situation-by-tone decision matrix with example strings, user test results on tone appropriateness, and guidance for writers and AI prompts.
useWhen: Products with emotionally varied moments (finance, health, insurance), content teams scaling across writers, and configuring the tone of AI assistants.
avoidWhen: For products with very narrow, uniform contexts where tone rarely varies, or before core comprehension issues are solved (fix clarity first).
whyLost: Voice and tone guides became brand documents with adjectives and examples; the situational matrix and user testing of tone were rarely carried through.
whereToUse: Microcopy design, chatbot dialogue design, error message writing, onboarding content, customer communication design.
example: An insurer's claim rejection message uses the brand's playful voice. Testing shows customers rate it as disrespectful; the matrix assigns 'anxious, bad news' situations a direct, empathetic and detailed tone, and complaint rates fall.
sources: Strategic Content Design — Erica Jorgensen
Mailchimp Content Style Guide (Mailchimp)
Nicely Said (Nicole Fenton & Kate Kiefer Lee)
reference: Jorgensen E (2023) Strategic Content Design: Tools and Research Techniques for Better UX Writing. Rosenfeld Media

name: Walking Interview (Go-Along)
origin: Margarethe Kusenbach, 2003; Evans and Jones, 2011
summary: Interviews conducted while accompanying participants through their own environment, accessing place-specific knowledge, embodied routines and tacit spatial reasoning that a static interview misses.
description: The walking interview or go-along method (Kusenbach, 2003; Evans & Jones, 2011) involves the researcher accompanying participants as they move through their natural environment — a commute, a shopping trip, a hospital visit — while simultaneously conducting an interview. Moving through space with participants accesses knowledge that cannot be accessed in a static interview setting: how people navigate, how their environment triggers memories and associations, how place shapes experience. Applied to UX: walking interviews are particularly powerful for studies of wayfinding, mobile app use in context, digital service touchpoints across physical journeys, and the relationship between physical and digital environments.
steps: Route selection: Either participant-led (participant chooses the route) or researcher-specified (participant does a specific journey relevant to the research question). Participant-led routes reveal habitual paths and navigation strategies; researcher-specified routes enable comparison.

Interview style during movement: Questions are opportunistically timed — ask about specific elements as participants encounter them in the environment. 'What do you usually do at this point?' 'How does being here affect how you use [app]?'
Researcher participation: Walk alongside, not behind. Co-presence in the environment affects what is noticed and discussed — sharing the sensory experience changes the conversation.
Recording: Audio recording + periodic photography or video. GPS track of the route. Note timestamps at key spatial moments.

Analysis: Map the spatial trajectory alongside the interview content. Identify where conversation changed, deepened, or stalled in relation to spatial location. What places triggered what kinds of talk?
outputs: Route-linked audio and photographs, GPS traces, place-anchored themes, and maps of where experiences, frictions and decisions occur.
useWhen: Experience is tied to place and movement: commuting, shopping, wayfinding, deliveries, hospital visits, field work, or any mobile and location-based product.
avoidWhen: The experience is desk-bound or private, safety or noise makes conversation impractical, or you need comparable structured data; use contextual inquiry or a diary study.
whyLost: UX adopted the 'ride-along' informally but without the method's attention to place, route choice and spatial analysis, which stayed in geography and urban sociology.
whereToUse: Mobility and transport apps, retail and omnichannel, logistics and field-service tools, wayfinding in hospitals and airports, and location-based services.
example: Researchers go along with 8 delivery couriers on shifts. Route-linked notes show most app frustration occurs at building entrances where GPS fails, leading to courier-contributed access notes per address.
sources: Kusenbach (2003) Street Phenomenology
When Words Fail Us — Integrative Review of Elicitation Techniques (PMC 2024)
Ethnographic Thinking (Hasbrouck)
Evans, J. & Jones, P. (2011) The walking interview, Applied Geography
reference: Kusenbach, M. (2003). Street phenomenology: The go-along as ethnographic research tool. Ethnography, 4(3), 455-485.

name: WAMMI (Website Analysis and Measurement Inventory)
origin: Kirakowski & Cierlik (1998), Human Factors Research Group with Nomos Management AB
summary: A 20-item website questionnaire covering attractiveness, controllability, efficiency, helpfulness and learnability, compared with a database of hundreds of site surveys.
description: WAMMI was one of the first instruments designed specifically for websites. Its items came from opinions collected from designers, users and webmasters about good and bad web experiences, and factor analysis produced the same five-factor structure as SUMI. The original had 60 items; the current version has 20 five-point items plus a global measure. Like SUMI, global scores are standardised to a mean of 50 and SD of 10 against a reference database of more than 300 surveys, which is its main value. Sauro and Lewis note the shorter version's subscale reliabilities (around 0.63 to 0.70) are lower than ideal, so the global score is the most dependable number.
steps: Arrange permission or a commercial licence and embed the 20 items in a site intercept or post-test survey.
Collect responses from genuine visitors after they have used the site.
Score against the WAMMI reference database.
Report the global score with its interval, treating subscales as indicative.
Compare with previous waves or competitor surveys in the database.
outputs: A standardised website satisfaction score and five indicative subscales.
useWhen: You want website satisfaction scores benchmarked against an external database, especially in European projects.
avoidWhen: You need highly reliable subscales or free norms (consider SUPR-Q or UMUX-Lite).
whyLost: Commercial licensing and the rise of free, shorter instruments.
whereToUse: Public-sector and corporate websites, intranets.
example: A university site scores 46 globally, with Controllability lowest, consistent with tree test failures in its navigation.
sources: Quantifying the User Experience (Sauro & Lewis)
Measuring the User Experience (Tullis & Albert)
reference: Kirakowski, J. & Cierlik, B. (1998). Measuring the usability of web sites. Proceedings of HFES 42.

name: Wardley Mapping
donor: Business strategy (with roots in military strategy)
origin: Simon Wardley, 2005 onward (Wardley Maps, 2016 online book)
summary: Maps the components needed to meet user needs along a value chain (visibility) and an evolution axis (genesis to commodity) to inform strategic choices.
description: A Wardley map starts with a user and their need at the top, then lists the components required to meet it, arranged vertically by visibility to the user and horizontally by evolution stage: genesis, custom-built, product (and rental), commodity (and utility). Components evolve over time under supply and demand competition, and each stage calls for different methods (exploration versus efficiency) and attitudes (pioneers, settlers, town planners). Maps reveal where to build, buy or use utilities, inertia, and opportunities for gameplay. For UX research, the map anchors strategy in user needs and shows which needs are commoditising, where differentiation lies, and where research should focus.
steps: Define the user and their need, grounded in research.
List the components required to meet the need and their dependencies (value chain).
Place components on the evolution axis using characteristics of each stage (ubiquity, certainty, market maturity).
Draw the map, then discuss movement: which components are evolving, where inertia exists.
Identify strategic options: build versus buy, where to differentiate, which gameplays apply.
Revisit and update maps as markets and research evidence change.
outputs: A Wardley map of user needs and components with evolution positions, movement and strategic options.
useWhen: Strategy discussions about where to invest, build or buy, and how technology evolution affects user experience.
avoidWhen: Interface-level design questions.
whyLost: It comes from IT strategy and is popular in tech strategy circles but rarely linked to UX research.
whereToUse: AI product strategy, platform strategy, public sector digital services, developer tools.
example: A legal-tech firm maps its contract review service. Text extraction has become a commodity (LLM APIs), while clients' need for defensible risk explanations is at genesis, so the firm reallocates design research toward explanation and audit trails.
sources: Wardley, Wardley Maps (2016), online book (medium.com/wardleymaps)
Wardley, Bits or pieces? (blog, 2007-2015)
reference: Wardley, S. (2016). Wardley Maps. Online book, published on Medium.

name: Wargaming (Matrix Games)
origin: Prussian Kriegsspiel (von Reisswitz, 1824); matrix games by Chris Engle (1988); Peter Perla, The Art of Wargaming (1990)
summary: Players representing actors (users, competitors, regulators, platform) make moves in turns, argue outcomes and adjudicate them, to explore dynamic responses to a strategy.
description: Wargames simulate a conflict or competitive situation with players taking roles and making decisions over turns under uncertainty. Matrix games are a lightweight form: each player proposes an action with reasons for and against; others counter-argue; an umpire or dice adjudicate success; the narrative evolves. This surfaces second-order effects and interactions that static analysis misses. Business wargaming adopted the format for strategy. For UX and product, wargames explore how users, competitors, bad actors, regulators and partners might react to a launch or policy, generating research questions and design requirements.
steps: Define the objective, scenario, time horizon and key actors (e.g. users segments, competitor, regulator, scammers).
Assign players to roles with briefs describing their goals, resources and constraints.
Run turns: each actor proposes an action with arguments; others counter-argue; adjudicate by umpire judgement or dice weighted by argument strength.
Record the evolving narrative, decisions and surprises.
Debrief: identify insights, vulnerabilities, and assumptions to research.
Translate insights into design changes, research questions and indicators.
outputs: Game narrative, identified second-order effects, vulnerabilities and follow-up research questions.
useWhen: Strategic launches with multiple interacting actors, policy changes, marketplaces and platforms with adversaries.
avoidWhen: Single-user usability questions or when actors have no strategic agency.
whyLost: Wargaming stayed in defence and strategy consulting; UX research seldom models multiple actors' dynamic responses.
whereToUse: Marketplace policy changes, platform API changes, content moderation, AI launches, fintech regulation responses.
example: A ride-hailing company wargames a new surge transparency policy with players as drivers, riders, a competitor and a city regulator; drivers' coordinated log-offs emerge, prompting research on driver earnings perceptions.
sources: Perla, The Art of Wargaming (1990)
Engle, Matrix games (1988), self-published rules; Curry & Price, Matrix Games for Modern Wargaming (2014)
UK MOD DCDC, Wargaming Handbook (2017)
reference: Perla, P. P. (1990). The Art of Wargaming. Naval Institute Press.

name: Wavelet and Cross-Spectral Coherence
origin: Coherence analysis from classical spectral theory; wavelet coherence by Torrence & Webster, 1999 and Grinsted et al., 2004
summary: Measures frequency-specific synchrony between two signals, such as user actions and system feedback or interaction density and sentiment, as an index of flow or misalignment.
description: Coherence is a frequency-resolved correlation between two time series (0 = unrelated, 1 = perfectly linearly related at that frequency); wavelet coherence localises it in time. In the Behavioral Spectral Framework, high cross-spectral coherence between click rhythm and feedback rhythm indicates flow, while low coherence implies latency, confusion or interface mismatch; phase difference measures lag. In the fintech case, coherence between interaction density and sentiment reached 0.78 during flow states and dropped to 0.35 during breakdowns. Proposed uses include synchrony between human prompts and AI agent responses, cross-modal coherence of gesture, gaze and emotion, and spectral alignment as a metric for AI-human coherence. Coherence maps are a recommended visual.
steps: Choose two aligned signals (e.g. user input rhythm and system feedback, or interaction density and sentiment).
Normalise each signal's frequency range and sampling.
Compute cross-spectral or wavelet coherence and phase difference.
Identify periods and bands of high and low coherence.
Align low-coherence periods with qualitative evidence of breakdowns.
Report coherence maps and summary values per state.
outputs: Coherence maps, phase offsets and coherence values by state.
useWhen: When studying alignment between user and system, between people, or between modalities over time.
avoidWhen: When signals are not time-aligned or are too short; coherence estimates become unstable.
whyLost: Standard in neuroscience, climatology and engineering, unexplored in UX.
whereToUse: Conversational and agentic AI, collaborative tools, multimodal biometric studies, gaming.
example: In an AI chat study, coherence between user message rhythm and assistant response timing drops during misunderstandings, prompting adaptive response timing.
sources: Vivek Gopinath (2025), From Stars to Signals: Translating Matteo Paz's Fourier-Wavelet Model into Behavioral and UX Research Methodology
reference: Grinsted, A., Moore, J. C., & Jevrejeva, S. (2004). Application of the cross wavelet transform and wavelet coherence to geophysical time series. Nonlinear Processes in Geophysics, 11, 561–566.

name: Wayfinding
donor: Architecture, urban planning and environmental psychology
origin: Kevin Lynch, 1960 (The Image of the City); Romedi Passini, 1984 (Wayfinding in Architecture)
summary: Designs orientation and navigation cues that help people know where they are, where they have been, where they can go and how to get there in complex spaces.
description: Wayfinding originated in architecture and urban design. Kevin Lynch identified the elements people use to form mental maps of cities (paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks), and Passini framed wayfinding as spatial problem solving involving decision-making, decision execution and information processing. Applied to digital products, wayfinding concerns how users orient themselves in large information spaces and multi-step processes: identity cues, landmarks, consistent paths, breadcrumbs, progress indicators and signage at decision points. It complements information architecture by focusing on the moment-to-moment experience of moving through a structure. Rigour comes from mapping decision points, assessing each for orientation cues, testing with tasks that involve getting lost and recovering, and measuring backtracking, disorientation and path efficiency.
steps: Map the information space or process, identifying key decision points and routes.
Audit each decision point for orientation cues: location identity, landmarks, signage and progress.
Analyse behavioural data for backtracking, loops and dead ends.
Test with tasks requiring navigation across distant areas, asking participants where they are and how to return.
Design cues using Lynch's elements such as landmarks, distinct districts and consistent paths.
Retest and measure path efficiency, backtracking and self-reported disorientation.
outputs: Decision point maps, cue audits, disorientation and backtracking metrics, and wayfinding design recommendations.
useWhen: For large information spaces, complex enterprise applications, multi-step processes, documentation sites and spatial or mixed-reality interfaces.
avoidWhen: Avoid for small, shallow products where orientation is trivial; use heuristic evaluation. For the underlying structure itself, use card sorting and tree testing.
whyLost: Latent: Concept widely understood informally; systematic wayfinding design rarely applied rigorously in digital UX.
whereToUse: Complex information spaces; multi-step processes; large-scale applications.
example: A cloud console analyses logs and finds users frequently loop between services while configuring networking. Adding persistent context headers and a 'recent locations' landmark reduces backtracking by a third in testing.
sources: Information Architecture
The Image of the City (Lynch)
Wayfinding in Architecture (Passini)
reference: Lynch, K. (1960). The Image of the City. MIT Press; Passini, R. (1984). Wayfinding in Architecture. Van Nostrand Reinhold.

name: Week-in-the-Life Study
origin: Practitioner hybrid of observation, diary and interview methods common in applied research
summary: An intensive week combining baseline observation, event-contingent diaries, mid-week check-in and closing interview to map weekly patterns of product use.
description: A week-in-the-life study combines several methods into a tight seven-day protocol. Day one pairs a baseline interview with an observation session in the participant's environment to catalogue artefacts and routines. Days two to five use an event-contingent diary capturing each meaningful product interaction: time, place, device, goal, outcome, emotion and workarounds. A short mid-week call maintains engagement and catches problems. A closing interview uses diary entries as stimuli to explore typical and atypical days and patterns participants notice themselves. Analysis codes entries for occasion, outcome and workarounds and builds temporal usage maps across participants, giving more depth than a diary alone and more temporal coverage than one visit.
steps: Day 1 — Onboarding + Observation: Baseline interview (15 min) + 90-min observation session in participant's natural environment. Establish baseline usage patterns and artifact catalog.

Days 2–5 — Diary: Event-contingent diary entries for every product interaction over 30 seconds. Entry fields: time, location, device, what they were trying to do, what happened, how they felt, any workarounds used.
Day 3 — Mid-week check-in: 15-minute call. Any problems with the diary? Any notable events they want to flag? This maintains engagement and surfaces early dropout risk.

Day 7 — Closing interview: 45-minute retrospective interview using the week's diary entries as stimuli. Ask about: the most typical day, the most atypical day, any patterns they notice in their own diary, anything they expected to find but didn't.

Analysis: Code diary entries for: usage occasion (context, trigger, goal), success/failure, workaround use. Map temporal patterns: is usage concentrated at particular times of day/week? Do certain tasks correlate with certain times? Build a temporal usage map across participants.
outputs: Temporal usage maps, coded diary entries, typical and atypical day profiles, and observational baselines per participant.
useWhen: Products used across a week with rhythms (workdays, weekends, routines), and when a single session would miss variation.
avoidWhen: Very infrequent behaviours (monthly bills) or tight budgets; use a longer, lighter diary or retrospective interviews.
whyLost: It survives in agencies and service design under various names, as a pragmatic bundle rather than a codified method.
whereToUse: Meal planning and grocery apps, family scheduling tools, commuting and mobility services, and productivity software.
example: Eight households take part in a week-in-the-life study of a grocery app. Temporal maps show Sunday evening planning and weekday top-ups, leading to separate 'plan' and 'quick add' modes.
sources: User Research (Marsh)
Handbook of Longitudinal Research
Observing the User Experience (Goodman)
reference: Goodman, E., Kuniavsky, M. & Moed, A. (2012). Observing the User Experience (2nd ed.). Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Weekly Customer Interview Cadence
origin: Teresa Torres, 2021
summary: Establishes a sustainable rhythm in which the product trio talks to at least one customer every week, supported by automated recruiting and story-based interviews.
description: Teresa Torres's continuous discovery practice asks the product trio (product manager, designer, engineer) to interview at least one customer every week. The cadence is made sustainable by automating recruitment, for example through in-product intercepts, scheduling links and standing panels, so that interviews happen without heroic effort. Interviews collect specific stories about past behaviour rather than opinions or feature requests, and each is summarised as an interview snapshot capturing opportunities, insights and memorable quotes, which feed an opportunity solution tree. The value is cumulative: small, frequent exposures keep decisions grounded and let teams notice change. Rigour depends on story-based questioning, deliberate sampling across segments, and synthesis across snapshots rather than reacting to the latest interview.
steps: Continuous interview infrastructure:
Set up a standing recruitment pipeline (not per-study recruitment).
(2) 30-minute sessions, same day each week.
(3) Interview protocol: open with 'walk me through your last week using [product]'.
(4) Focus: collect specific stories, not opinions.
(5) After each interview: add new opportunities to the tree, update evidence for existing ones.
(6) Monthly: review the tree with the product team — what opportunities have the most evidence?
outputs: A running interview cadence, interview snapshots, an evolving opportunity solution tree, and a continuously refreshed evidence base.
useWhen: Product teams practising continuous discovery who need a steady flow of customer contact rather than periodic large studies.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on it alone for rigorous, sampled answers to high-stakes questions; run dedicated studies. Avoid if interviews will be leading or sales-like rather than story-based.
whyLost: The cadence is admired but rarely sustained; recruiting friction and delivery pressure cause weekly interviews to lapse into occasional calls.
whereToUse: Product teams with continuous discovery mandates, lean UX programs, startup product development, agile UX research.
example: A fintech savings team embeds an intercept in its app that books one interview a week; each interview produces a snapshot added to the opportunity tree, which shifts priorities towards irregular-income savers.
sources: Continuous Discovery Habits — Teresa Torres
Practical Empathy (Young)
Just Enough Research (Hall)
Continuous Discovery Habits (Torres)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 35 — Continuous Discovery & Opportunity Solution Trees
reference: Torres T (2021) Continuous Discovery Habits: Discover Products that Create Customer Value and Business Value. Product Talk LLC

name: Wicked problem framing
origin: Horst Rittel and Melvin Webber, 'Dilemmas in a General Theory of Planning', 1973
summary: Frames a design challenge using Rittel and Webber's ten characteristics of wicked problems, to decide how to approach it rather than prematurely solving it.
description: Rittel and Webber described wicked problems as having no definitive formulation, no stopping rule, solutions that are better or worse rather than true or false, no immediate test of a solution, every attempt counting, no enumerable set of solutions, uniqueness, being symptoms of other problems, multiple explanations, and planners having no right to be wrong. Wicked problem framing assesses a challenge against these characteristics and selects appropriate approaches: iterative and participatory processes, multiple framings, and argumentation-based methods such as Rittel's Issue-Based Information System (IBIS). In UX, the term is widely cited as a label for 'hard problems' but rarely applied as an analysis that changes method choice, which is why it is vestigial.
steps: Write the problem statement as stakeholders currently express it.
Assess it against the ten wickedness characteristics, scoring each as absent, partial or present with evidence.
Collect alternative framings from at least 4-6 stakeholder groups, noting conflicting causal explanations.
Map issues, positions and arguments using IBIS or dialogue mapping.
Choose an approach suited to the degree of wickedness: iterative small experiments, participatory processes and explicit trade-off documentation.
Define provisional success criteria and review points rather than a single solution test.
outputs: A wickedness assessment, alternative framings, an issue map, and an approach plan with provisional success criteria.
useWhen: For complex sociotechnical challenges with conflicting stakeholders, such as healthcare systems, policy and platform governance.
avoidWhen: For tame problems with clear criteria and solutions; standard design and testing processes are more efficient.
whyLost: The label became fashionable in design thinking, but the analytical characteristics and IBIS tooling were mostly forgotten.
whereToUse: Healthcare delivery, climate and sustainability products, AI governance, public services, and organisational change.
example: Framing 'reduce OR turnaround time' reveals conflicting explanations from surgeons, nurses and managers and no clear stopping rule. The team switches from a single redesign to iterative experiments and dialogue mapping of trade-offs.
sources: Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas (DSRP protocol)
PACT analysis (Dix; Benyon, Designing Interactive Systems)
Methods Atlas — DSRP protocol (Gopinath)
PACT analysis (Dix)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 13 — DSRP Systems Thinking & Wicked Problems
reference: Rittel, H. W. J. & Webber, M. M. (1973). Dilemmas in a general theory of planning. Policy Sciences, 4(2), 155-169.

name: Wigmore Evidence Charting
origin: John Henry Wigmore, 1913 (The Principles of Judicial Proof); revived by Terence Anderson, David Schum and William Twining (Analysis of Evidence, 2005)
summary: Charts the full chain of inferences from each piece of evidence to the ultimate conclusion, including corroborating and contradicting evidence and the credibility of sources.
description: Wigmore devised a graphical notation for analysing masses of mixed evidence in legal cases: each proposition is a node, with symbols for testimonial and circumstantial evidence, explanatory and corroborative relations, and the analyst's belief in each. The key protocol is Anderson, Schum and Twining's seven-step method: clarify standpoint, formulate ultimate probanda (what must be proved), penultimate probanda, theories of the case, list evidence (key list), construct the chart, and refine. Schum extended it to probabilistic inference networks. For research synthesis across many studies, interviews and data sources, Wigmore charts make inferential chains auditable and reveal where conclusions rest on single, weak sources.
steps: Clarify standpoint and the question the synthesis must answer.
Formulate the ultimate proposition (e.g. 'small businesses will adopt automated bookkeeping if X') and the penultimate propositions it depends on.
Compile a key list of all evidence items, noting source and credibility.
Build the chart linking evidence through intermediate inferences to propositions, marking corroboration and contradiction.
Assess the strength of each link and identify weak or single-source chains.
Refine the conclusion and target new research at the weakest links.
outputs: A Wigmore chart and key list, explicit inferential chains, strength assessments and targeted research gaps.
useWhen: High-stakes syntheses drawing on many heterogeneous sources, or where conclusions will be challenged.
avoidWhen: Simple studies with a single data source and narrow conclusions.
whyLost: Even in law the notation was considered laborious; it was never introduced to design research.
whereToUse: Strategic research synthesis, regulatory submissions (e.g. medical device usability), investigations, contested product decisions.
example: A synthesis claiming clinicians will accept AI triage is charted. The chart shows the key inference rests on a single pilot site's survey, while three interview sources contradict it; the conclusion is downgraded and a multi-site study commissioned.
sources: Anderson, Schum & Twining, Analysis of Evidence (2nd ed., 2005)
Wigmore, The Principles of Judicial Proof (1913)
Schum, The Evidential Foundations of Probabilistic Reasoning (1994)
reference: Anderson, T., Schum, D., & Twining, W. (2005). Analysis of Evidence (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

name: Within-case and cross-case analysis
donor: Education research, comparative sociology and case study methodology
origin: Miles and Huberman (1994); case study methodology by Robert Yin (1984 onwards); comparative logic from Ragin (1987)
summary: First builds an understanding of each case as a whole, then compares cases systematically to find patterns, configurations and explanations that hold across them.
description: Variable-oriented synthesis pools quotes across participants and loses the configuration of conditions within each case. Within-case analysis first constructs a coherent account of each case (a person, a clinic, an account), often as a case summary and display. Cross-case analysis then compares cases using strategies such as stacking comparable displays, partitioning cases by outcome, building meta-matrices, and identifying configurations of conditions associated with outcomes. Yin's replication logic treats each case like an experiment: literal replication predicts similar results, theoretical replication predicts contrasting results for predictable reasons. Rigour comes from standardising within-case write-ups so they can be compared, from case selection that supports replication logic, and from explaining every case, including deviant ones.
steps: Define the case unit (a user, household, clinic or organisation) and select cases to allow literal and theoretical replication, typically 6 to 20 cases.
For each case, write a standardised within-case summary of 2 to 4 pages and build a within-case display, such as a time-ordered matrix or causal network.
Choose cross-case dimensions from the research questions and build a meta-matrix with cases as rows and dimensions as columns.
Partition and sort cases by outcome (for example adopters versus non-adopters) and look for conditions that consistently differ between groups.
Identify configurations of conditions that co-occur with outcomes, and check each deviant case to explain or bound the pattern.
State cross-case propositions with the number of supporting and contradicting cases, and link back to within-case evidence.
outputs: Standardised case summaries and displays, a cross-case meta-matrix, outcome-partitioned comparisons and cross-case propositions with support counts.
useWhen: Studying organisations, sites or households where context matters; explaining differing outcomes such as why some clinics adopted and others did not.
avoidWhen: Cases are not meaningful units or the interest is in individual opinions across a large sample; use thematic analysis or a survey.
whyLost: It is standard in case study research and evaluation but UX synthesis usually pools participant data, losing case configurations.
whereToUse: B2B and enterprise research, multi-site health and education deployments, household fintech research, organisational AI adoption.
example: A 20-participant cross-cultural study treated each clinic as a case. Cross-case analysis showed adoption occurred only where reliable power and supervisor acceptance of digital records coincided; neither condition alone was sufficient, a configuration lost in pooled themes.
sources: Qualitative Data Analysis (Miles & Huberman) via Sage Handbook
Cambridge Handbook of Research Methods
The Inquiry Series, Ch 29 — Miles & Huberman — Systematic Qualitative Data Analysis
reference: Miles, M. B., & Huberman, A. M. (1994). Qualitative Data Analysis: An Expanded Sourcebook (2nd ed.). Sage; Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M., & Saldaña, J. (2014). Qualitative Data Analysis: A Methods Sourcebook (3rd ed.). Sage. Yin, R. K. (2018). Case Study Research and Applications (6th ed.). Sage.

name: Wizard of Oz Prototyping
donor: Human-computer interaction and speech technology research
origin: J. F. Kelley, 1983 (coined term, IBM natural-language studies); Gould, Conti and Hovanyecz listening typewriter study (1983)
summary: A hidden human operator simulates system intelligence such as speech, AI or recommendation logic, letting you test interaction concepts before the technology exists.
description: In a Wizard of Oz study the participant interacts with what appears to be a working system while a hidden 'wizard' produces the system's responses in real time. It lets teams study how people speak to, trust and recover from errors with intelligent systems before investing in models or infrastructure. Rigour depends on wizard consistency: a written response protocol, constrained response libraries, deliberate simulated error rates, and timing that mirrors realistic latency. Without these, the wizard behaves like an idealised human, inflating satisfaction and hiding the failure modes real systems produce. Ethical practice requires debriefing participants about the deception. The method is widely used for conversational, voice and generative AI concepts, and for exploring how much automation people want.
steps: Define the system capabilities to simulate and the questions to answer (vocabulary, turn-taking, trust, error recovery).
Write a wizard protocol with response rules, a library of permitted replies, target latency and a planned error rate (for example 10-20% misrecognitions).
Build a front end that routes participant input to the wizard and wizard output back to the participant without revealing a human.
Pilot with 2-3 people to train the wizard and check the illusion holds and responses stay consistent.
Run 6-12 sessions, logging all inputs, wizard responses, timings and participant reactions, with a separate observer.
Debrief participants about the simulation, then analyse utterance patterns, failure recovery and expectations to specify the real system.
outputs: Corpus of real user utterances, interaction patterns, error-recovery behaviours, capability requirements and validated conversation design.
useWhen: Early testing of conversational agents, voice interfaces, AI assistants, adaptive recommendations or any system whose intelligence is expensive to build.
avoidWhen: When the real model already exists (test it directly, since wizards hide true error profiles) or when the deception would be ethically inappropriate for the population.
whyLost: Still in use: Essential for AI product research; enables testing of intelligent behavior without engineering.
whereToUse: Conversational AI; voice UI; recommendation systems; any AI feature early research.
example: A telehealth company tests an AI symptom checker by having a nurse act as the wizard behind a chat interface, constrained to a scripted library with deliberate misunderstandings. Sessions reveal patients abandon after the second clarifying question, shaping the eventual model's dialogue policy.
sources: Universal Methods of Design
Chatbot Research and Design
Kelley, An iterative design methodology for user-friendly natural language office information applications (ACM TOIS, 1984)
Lost Methods in UX — A Complete Treatise (Gopinath)
Kelley JF (1984) An iterative design methodology for user-friendly natural language office information applications. ACM TOIS 2(1)
Dahlbäck N, Jönsson A & Ahrenberg L (1993) Wizard of Oz studies: why and how. IUI

name: Wood's friction theory
donor: Social psychology (habit science and Lewinian field theory)
origin: Wendy Wood, Good Habits, Bad Habits (2019), building on Kurt Lewin's driving and restraining forces (1951)
summary: Analyses the small situational frictions, such as distance, steps and delay, that make desired behaviours harder and undesired ones easier, then redesigns friction deliberately.
description: Wood argues that behaviour is shaped more by context than by willpower, and that friction, the time, distance and effort a behaviour requires, is one of the strongest contextual forces. Lewin described behaviour as a balance of driving and restraining forces and argued that removing restraints is often more effective than adding drivers. In Wood's habit research, small changes in proximity, ease or delay produce large shifts in repeated behaviour. Friction analysis inventories frictions on the desired path and the competing path, measures them in concrete units (taps, seconds, metres, waiting time, permissions), and redesigns to lower friction for desired behaviours and raise it for undesired ones. Rigour comes from quantifying friction rather than labelling it, and from comparing both paths rather than optimising one in isolation.
steps: Define the desired behaviour and the competing behaviour users currently choose (for example digital entry versus paper register).
Walk both paths in context and list every friction point: physical distance, steps, taps, typing, waits, logins, connectivity checks, approvals and social awkwardness.
Quantify each friction in concrete units, such as time in seconds, taps, metres or failure probability, using timing from at least 5 to 10 observed repetitions.
Build a force-field table that compares total friction on each path, highlighting the restraining forces on the desired path that exceed the competing path's equivalents.
Redesign to remove the largest restraining forces on the desired path and, where ethical, add small friction to the competing path, such as removing blank paper forms from the desk.
Measure behaviour share for the desired path before and after over at least 4 weeks, since friction changes act through repetition.
outputs: A quantified friction inventory for desired and competing paths, a force-field comparison, and measured behaviour change after friction redesign.
useWhen: Users know the desired behaviour and intend it but do not do it consistently; a competing legacy behaviour is easier in context.
avoidWhen: Users lack motivation or understanding rather than ease, or friction serves safety (confirmation for irreversible actions); in those cases use motivation research or keep protective friction.
whyLost: UX uses 'friction' as loose jargon for anything annoying, detached from Wood's habit science and Lewin's force-field analysis, so friction is seldom quantified on both competing paths.
whereToUse: Digital replacement of paper processes, health adherence, savings automation, security behaviours such as MFA, sustainable choices in commerce.
example: Digital entry required unlocking a tablet, a 30-second login and a sync wait, about 70 seconds before the first field, while the paper register was open on the desk. Keeping the app session alive for the shift and caching offline cut start friction to 8 seconds and halved paper duplication.
sources: Persuasive Technology (Fogg)
Behavioral Drift Playbook (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 24 — Behavior Models, Habits & the Anatomy of Non-Adoption
reference: Wood, W. (2019). Good Habits, Bad Habits: The Science of Making Positive Changes That Stick. Farrar, Straus and Giroux; Lewin, K. (1951). Field Theory in Social Science. Harper.

name: Word embeddings and semantic similarity
origin: Distributional hypothesis (Firth, 1957; Harris, 1954); word2vec by Mikolov et al., 2013; sentence embeddings (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019)
summary: Represents words, sentences or documents as dense vectors where semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness, enabling clustering, search and comparison of user text.
description: Embeddings encode meaning learned from large corpora, so 'can't find my money' and 'funds missing' sit close together even without shared words. Sentence and document embeddings let researchers cluster open-ended feedback, deduplicate tickets, find all comments similar to a key quote, map feedback onto existing codebooks and measure how semantically close user language is to product terminology. Rigour involves choosing a model suited to the domain and language, checking that similarity matches human judgement on a sample, being aware of biases embedded from training corpora, and avoiding treating cosine similarity thresholds as universal. Clustering embeddings should be validated by reading samples, as with any computational qualitative method.
steps: Choose an embedding model suited to the text type and languages (e.g. a multilingual sentence-transformer).
Clean the text and compute embeddings for each document or sentence.
Calibrate similarity: have researchers rate 50-100 pairs and pick thresholds that match human judgement.
Apply to the task: semantic search for quotes, clustering (e.g. UMAP plus HDBSCAN), or matching feedback to codebook definitions.
Review samples from each cluster or match set to verify meaning, and refine thresholds.
Document model version, thresholds and known biases.
outputs: Embedding vectors, calibrated similarity thresholds, semantic clusters or search results and documentation of model choices.
useWhen: Large volumes of open text where you need to find, group or map meaning beyond keyword matching.
avoidWhen: Avoid when exact terminology matters (legal or medical coding needs controlled vocabularies), with tiny corpora, or when embedding bias could distort sensitive analyses without audit.
whyLost: It survived and spread because embedding APIs became cheap and are built into research repositories and feedback tools.
whereToUse: Feedback repositories, support ticket triage, terminology research for IA, mapping AI chat logs, research repository search.
example: A research team embeds 12,000 survey comments and searches with a quote about 'fear of pressing the wrong button'. It retrieves 340 semantically similar comments, quantifying a theme from six interviews.
sources: A Practical Guide to Sentiment Analysis (Erik Cambria et al.)
Artificial Intelligence for Humans (Jeff Heaton)
Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Christopher Bishop)
Mikolov et al. (2013) Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space
Reimers & Gurevych (2019) Sentence-BERT
Practical Guide to Sentiment Analysis
AI for Humans (Heaton)
Pattern Recognition (Bishop)

name: Words of Estimative Probability
origin: Sherman Kent, CIA, 1964; codified in ICD 203 Analytic Standards (US ODNI, 2007/2015) and the UK PHIA probability yardstick
summary: Standardises the probability phrases used in reports (e.g. 'likely' = 55-80%) so readers interpret confidence consistently.
description: Kent found that analysts and policymakers interpreted words like 'probable' and 'serious possibility' with wildly different probabilities. He proposed a fixed mapping of phrases to probability ranges. Modern intelligence standards (ICD 203, the UK Professional Head of Intelligence Assessment yardstick) require estimative language and separate statements of analytic confidence based on evidence quality. UX research reports are full of 'most users', 'many participants' and 'likely', which stakeholders interpret inconsistently. Adopting a probability yardstick and separate confidence ratings makes research claims calibrated, comparable and auditable.
steps: Adopt a yardstick, such as remote (<5%), highly unlikely (10-20%), unlikely (25-35%), realistic possibility (40-50%), likely (55-75%), highly likely (80-90%), almost certain (>95%).
Train researchers and stakeholders on the mapping with examples.
For each key finding, state an estimative judgement and a separate confidence level (low, moderate, high) based on evidence quality.
Avoid ambiguous quantifiers ('many', 'some') unless tied to counts or ranges.
Track outcomes of estimative judgements over time and assess calibration.
Include the yardstick in report templates and repositories.
outputs: Reports with standardised probability language, confidence ratings and calibration tracking.
useWhen: Communicating research findings and forecasts to decision-makers, especially in synthesis and strategy work.
avoidWhen: Purely descriptive qualitative accounts where probabilistic claims are not being made.
whyLost: UX reporting evolved from journalism and storytelling conventions, not intelligence analysis.
whereToUse: Research reports, insight repositories, launch risk assessments, competitive intelligence.
example: A research team replaces 'users will probably adopt the feature' with 'likely (55-75%) that a majority of admins enable it within 30 days; moderate confidence, based on 14 interviews and beta data'. Leadership questions become more precise.
sources: Kent, Words of estimative probability (1964), Studies in Intelligence
ODNI, Intelligence Community Directive 203: Analytic Standards (2015)
Friedman, War and Chance: Assessing Uncertainty in International Politics (2019)
reference: Kent, S. (1964). Words of estimative probability. Studies in Intelligence, 8(4), 49-65.

name: Work Modeling (5-Model Framework)
origin: Hugh Beyer & Karen Holtzblatt, 1998
summary: Five complementary models of work practice, flow, sequence, artefact, cultural and physical, built from contextual inquiry to capture the whole context of work.
description: Contextual Design's five work models represent work practice from complementary perspectives. The flow model shows roles, responsibilities and communication between people. The sequence model shows the ordered steps, triggers, intents and breakdowns of a task. The artefact model shows the things people create and use and how they are structured. The cultural model shows the influences, values and constraints that shape behaviour. The physical model shows the environment and how its layout supports or hinders work. Models are built for each contextual inquiry participant, then consolidated across participants to reveal common structure and variation. Rigour comes from grounding every element in observed data, marking breakdowns explicitly and consolidating systematically rather than drawing idealised processes.
steps: Conduct contextual inquiries with 6 to 12 participants across relevant roles.
In interpretation sessions, build each relevant model for each participant from observed data.
Mark breakdowns (problems and workarounds) on the models with lightning bolts or equivalent markers.
Consolidate each model type across participants, identifying common patterns and variants.
Walk the consolidated models with stakeholders to identify design opportunities.
Use the models to drive visioning and storyboarding of new work practice.
outputs: Individual and consolidated flow, sequence, artefact, cultural and physical models, with breakdowns and design opportunities.
useWhen: For enterprise software, healthcare IT and complex workplace tools where work involves multiple roles, artefacts and environments.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple consumer flows or when no contextual inquiry data exists; use journey mapping or task analysis. The full set takes considerable time.
whyLost: Siloed: Lives primarily in Contextual Design practice; rarely applied in full outside specialized teams.
whereToUse: Enterprise software; healthcare IT; any complex workplace tool design.
example: A logistics firm's flow model shows dispatchers acting as an informal hub between drivers and customers, and the cultural model shows drivers distrusting central planning. The new routing tool adds driver-proposed changes.
sources: Rapid Contextual Design
Lost Methods in UX
Contextual Design (Beyer & Holtzblatt)
reference: Beyer, H. & Holtzblatt, K. (1998). Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered Systems. Morgan Kaufmann.

name: Working memory load audit
origin: Miller, 1956; Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model, 1974; Cowan's capacity estimate of about 4 chunks, 2001
summary: Counts how many items a user must hold in mind at each step of a task and flags steps exceeding working memory limits of around four chunks.
description: Working memory holds a small amount of information for active use. Miller's '7 plus or minus 2' is widely quoted, but Cowan's review places capacity nearer 4 chunks when rehearsal and grouping are prevented, and capacity falls further under stress, fatigue and interruption. A working memory load audit walks through a task step by step, listing every item the user must remember from previous screens or external sources (codes, values, goals, pending steps) and noting when each can be released. Steps where load exceeds about 3-4 items, or where items must be retained across interruptions, are flagged. Remedies include keeping information visible, carrying values forward, and checklists. The method is vestigial because '7 plus or minus 2' is cited as a rule without any actual counting.
steps: Select critical tasks and write each as a sequence of steps.
For each step, list items the user must hold in memory (not visible on screen) and mark when each enters and leaves memory.
Plot the load curve and flag steps exceeding 3-4 items, or any step requiring retention across an interruption or screen change of more than about 15-20 seconds.
Adjust capacity assumptions for context: reduce by one or more for high stress, fatigue or concurrent tasks.
Validate flagged steps with users (5-8) using think-aloud or a secondary probe task, and note memory-related errors.
Redesign to externalise information (persistent display, auto-fill, recognition over recall) and re-audit.
outputs: A step-by-step memory load curve per task, flagged overload points, observed memory errors, and externalisation recommendations.
useWhen: For multi-step workflows, crisis procedures, configuration tasks, and flows that require copying information between screens.
avoidWhen: When tasks are short or fully visible; use heuristic evaluation. For overall workload, use NASA-TLX or dual-task methods.
whyLost: Miller's number became a slogan; the actual counting procedure and newer capacity estimates were lost in practice.
whereToUse: Emergency procedures, two-factor authentication, banking transfers, surgical device setup, and AI prompt workflows.
example: A crisis procedure on a surgical robot requires remembering an error code, two instrument positions and a reset sequence across three screens, peaking at 6 items. Displaying the code and positions persistently drops peak load to 2.
sources: Sternberg, R. J., Cognitive Psychology
Goldstein, E. B., Cognitive Psychology: Connecting Mind, Research and Everyday Experience
MIT Psychology course materials
Gopinath, V., Methods Atlas
Cognitive Psychology (Sternberg, Goldstein)
MIT Psychology
Methods Atlas (Gopinath)
The Inquiry Series, Ch 10 — Memory — The Architecture of Knowledge
reference: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory: a reconsideration of mental storage capacity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87-114.

name: Writing Qualitative Findings (Evidence Standards)
origin: Qualitative reporting traditions; codified in standards such as COREQ (Tong, Sainsbury & Craig, 2007) and SRQR (O'Brien et al., 2014)
summary: Standards for writing qualitative findings: lead with analytic claims, select representative verbatim quotes, state frequency honestly, report negative cases and declare the scope of claims.
description: Qualitative findings are only as credible as their write-up. These standards require each finding to lead with an analytical claim rather than a list of participant statements, with evidence beneath it. Quotes must be verbatim, representative of the pattern rather than merely vivid, and attributed with consistent pseudonyms or IDs. Frequency language is explicit and consistent ('all 12', 'most (10 of 12)', 'several (4 of 12)') rather than vague. Each major finding states its exceptions and what explains them. Every report includes a scope statement defining the population, context and time to which claims apply, and notes methodological limits. Reporting checklists such as COREQ and SRQR formalise these expectations in academic publishing. The rigour comes from making the evidential basis of every claim inspectable.
steps: Lead with the analytical claim, not the data: Never write 'Participant 3 said X.' Write: 'Users experienced the confirmation step as accusatory [theme], illustrated by Participant 3: [short quote].' Analysis leads; data supports.
Quote selection: Each quote must be (a) verbatim, (b) representative of the pattern — not the most dramatic exception, and (c) necessary.
Explicit frequency language: 'All 12 participants' vs. 'most (10/12)' vs. 'several (4/12)' vs. 'one participant.' Use numbers, not vague qualifiers.
Negative cases in the report: Every major finding should include: what the exceptions are, how many participants showed them, and what conditions seem to predict them.
Scope statement: Every report should state explicitly for what population, context, and time period the findings apply.
outputs: Findings written as evidence-backed claims, a quote selection log, consistent frequency language, negative case notes, a scope and limitations statement, and an optional reporting checklist.
useWhen: Writing any qualitative research report, especially when findings will inform significant decisions, be challenged by sceptical stakeholders, or be reused in a repository.
avoidWhen: Never skip it entirely; for quick informal shares, a lightweight version (claim, evidence, scope) still applies. Use the Decision Memo Format on top when the audience needs only the decision.
whyLost: Speed-driven reporting favours quote collages and 'users said' bullets, and most UX researchers are not trained in qualitative reporting standards from the social sciences.
whereToUse: Research reports, repository insights, executive readouts, regulated product research, and any synthesis that will be quoted out of context.
example: A researcher rewrites 'Users hate the new dashboard' as 'Most (9 of 12) operations managers could not locate overdue items, because the status filter was hidden; the 3 who succeeded had used the legacy filter.' Stakeholder debate shifts from opinion to the fix.
sources: Sage Handbook of Qualitative Data Analysis (Flick)
Qualitative Research from Start to Finish (Yin)
Tong, Sainsbury & Craig (2007) COREQ, International Journal for Quality in Health Care
reference: O'Brien, B. C. et al. (2014). Standards for reporting qualitative research: a synthesis of recommendations. Academic Medicine, 89(9), 1245-1251.

name: Z Notation for Interface State Specification
aka: Z schema specification of interactive systems
Z notation for formal interface specification
origin: Jean-Raymond Abrial, late 1970s; Spivey, 1989
summary: Specifies interface states and operations in set-theoretic, mathematical notation, so properties such as predictability and safety can be checked before implementation.
description: Z is a formal specification language based on set theory and first-order predicate logic, using schemas to describe system states, invariants and operations. In HCI, researchers such as Harrison and Thimbleby used Z and related notations to specify interactive systems precisely and reason about usability properties: whether every state is visible to the user, whether operations can be undone, whether modes are distinguishable, and whether the same input always produces predictable results. Writing the specification exposes ambiguities in requirements early. Rigour comes from complete state schemas, explicit invariants, and either proof or tool-supported checking of interaction properties, with results traced back to interface design decisions.
steps: Z specification process for critical UI flows:
Define the state space: all variables that constitute the interface state, their types, and their invariants.
(2) Define each operation: pre-condition (state must satisfy X before the operation), post-condition (state satisfies Y after the operation).

(3) Check for: operations that have no valid pre-condition (dead operations), states that no operation can reach (inaccessible states), state transitions that violate invariants (inconsistency). Formal verification catches entire classes of bugs before implementation.
outputs: A formal specification of states, invariants and operations, proofs or checks of interaction properties (e.g. undo, mode visibility), and a list of ambiguities resolved.
useWhen: Safety-critical interactive systems (medical devices, avionics, rail control) where mode errors and unpredictable states must be ruled out.
avoidWhen: Avoid for consumer products with fast iteration and low risk; use state diagrams, prototypes and usability testing instead.
whyLost: Formal methods in HCI flourished in the late 1980s and 1990s but required mathematical expertise and slowed iteration, so they retreated to safety-critical engineering.
whereToUse: Safety-critical interface specification, medical device UI design, financial transaction flow specification.
example: A team specifying an infusion pump's dose entry in Z discovers that two operations can leave the system in an undisplayed mode; the interface is changed to show mode at all times before any code is written.

name: Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique (ZMET)
origin: Gerald Zaltman, Harvard Business School, early 1990s (Zaltman and Coulter, 1995; Zaltman, 1997)
summary: Participants collect images representing their thoughts and feelings about a topic, then a structured interview elicits deep metaphors and builds a consensus map.
description: ZMET assumes most thought is unconscious and image-based. A week before the interview, participants gather 8-10 images expressing their feelings about a topic. A two-hour interview uses structured steps: storytelling about each image, missed images, sorting, construct elicitation using a Kelly repertory grid triad technique, the most representative image, opposite images, sensory images, a mental map and a summary collage, often with laddering. Analysis codes constructs and connections across 20-25 interviews into a consensus map and identifies 'deep metaphors' (e.g. balance, journey, container, connection). It reveals emotional and symbolic meanings that direct questions miss.
steps: Recruit participants and instruct them to collect 8-10 images representing their thoughts and feelings about the topic.
Conduct a one-on-one interview of about two hours following the ZMET steps, including image stories and triad sorts.
Use laddering to connect attributes to consequences and values.
Have participants create a summary collage or mental map of key constructs.
Code constructs and links across interviews; build a consensus map of constructs shared by at least a third of participants.
Identify deep metaphors and translate them into design, content and brand implications.
outputs: Construct maps, consensus maps, deep metaphors and participant collages.
useWhen: Understanding emotional and symbolic meanings of a category, brand or experience for strategy and design direction.
avoidWhen: Usability questions or when quick tactical answers are needed.
whyLost: ZMET is a proprietary, trademarked process used by consultancies in marketing research, rarely taught to UX researchers.
whereToUse: Financial wellbeing, health conditions, home and family technologies, luxury and lifestyle products, AI companions.
example: A ZMET study on retirement saving reveals a dominant 'container' metaphor (protecting a fragile nest) rather than 'journey'; the app's growth-chart framing is replaced by protection and safety imagery.
sources: Zaltman, Rethinking market research: Putting people back in (1997), Journal of Marketing Research
Zaltman & Coulter, Seeing the voice of the customer: Metaphor-based advertising research (1995), Journal of Advertising Research
Zaltman & Zaltman, Marketing Metaphoria (2008)
reference: Zaltman, G. (1997). Rethinking market research. Journal of Marketing Research, 34(4), 424-437.
